Oñate declared the Acoma children under twelve innocent. He still ordered them taken from their parents and handed to the friars. On Oñate's order, about seventy girls under twelve were sent south along the road to Mexico, to convents there. Neither the National Park Service's account nor the Pueblo council's statement names the men who took them. A convent is a house where nuns live, women who have promised their lives to the Catholic church. The National Park Service's account states that almost certainly none of the girls ever came home. The Pueblo council's 2023 statement gives sixty children taken to Mexico, and it also states that none returned. According to PBS, some scholars believe the children were later sold as slaves.

Oñate's sentence is in the written record. Whether anyone carried out the cutting of feet is disputed. Acoma people have passed down their own account since 1599: Oñate had the right feet of 24 captive men cut off. The New York Times reported that account in 1998. Two historians who worked for years in these records doubt that the feet were cut off. Marc Simmons first wrote that they were, and he later came to doubt it. John Kessell notes that no record describes a one-footed Acoma man.

Spanish officials charged Oñate with thirty crimes. Accounts date the charges to 1612 or 1613 and the judges' decision to 1614. The judges found him guilty of twelve, among them using too much force against Acoma. They banished him from New Mexico for life, which means they ordered him never to return. They also barred him from Mexico City for four years and fined him 6,000 ducats, a Spanish gold coin. PBS gives the Mexico City term as five years. Oñate had rebuilt a fortune in his family's mines at Zacatecas. Rebecca Carlson, who wrote about his trial in a 2008 university paper, calls the fine unimportant to him. He spent years working to have that decision undone. Accounts differ on whether he was ever pardoned, which means officially forgiven by the king. Carlson writes that he was pardoned in 1623. Other accounts say the proof of a pardon is unclear.

### The 1600s

Native nations still held nearly the whole continent through the 1600s. Along the eastern coast, the European settlements were a thin strip. Those settlers needed food and trade from the nations around them, and they stayed only as long as those nations let them. In New Mexico, Spanish colonists had ruled the Pueblo nations by force since 1598. Native leaders chose which newcomers to deal with: the Dutch, the French, the English or the Spanish. They played those newcomers against one another, which means they used each group's rivalry with the others to bargain.

Haudenosaunee leaders made alliances with the newcomers and recorded them on wampum belts. In New England, English colonists fought two wars against coastal nations, the Pequot War of 1636 to 1638 and Metacom's war of 1675 and 1676. In the Southwest in 1680, the people of the Pueblo nations rose together and drove the Spanish off their land. They kept the Spanish out for twelve years.

#### Tsenacommacah

In eastern Virginia, Wahunsenacawh inherited rule over six tribes. He built them into a group of more than thirty tribes that paid him tribute. His country was called Tsenacommacah. The English called him "the Powhatan." His own title was mamanatowick, or paramount chief. A paramount chief is a chief whom other chiefs answer to. About 15,000 people lived in his country, spread across some 10,000 square miles between the James River and the Potomac. A tribe here means a people with its own leader. Each tribe's leader was called a weroance, and each weroance paid tribute to Wahunsenacawh.

English colonists founded Jamestown inside Tsenacommacah in 1607, on land that Wahunsenacawh ruled.

#### Wampum diplomacy and the Covenant Chain

Haudenosaunee diplomats, the people who spoke for their nations with other nations, recorded agreements on wampum belts. Speakers kept the words of each agreement in memory, and the pattern of the belt recorded its terms.

The Two Row Wampum, Guswenta, records the Haudenosaunee account of their first agreement with the Dutch. It has two purple rows of beads on a white background. The rows stand for two boats traveling the same river side by side, with neither one steering the other. Haudenosaunee tradition dates the agreement to 1613. A paper document with the same date also exists, and accounts differ about whether it is genuine.

The Haudenosaunee alliance with the English colonies was called the Covenant Chain. A covenant is a serious promise. The oldest surviving record of the Silver Covenant Chain dates from 1677. That year Haudenosaunee leaders and the New York governor, Edmund Andros, made the alliance official at Albany. Silver tarnishes, which means it turns dark over time, so a silver chain has to be polished to stay bright. Haudenosaunee and English leaders "polished" the Covenant Chain again and again. That meant they renewed the alliance at councils, with speeches and wampum.

#### The coastal wars

In Connecticut, English colonists and their Mohegan and Narragansett allies fought the Pequot from 1636 to 1638. Before dawn on May 26, 1637, an English-led force set fire to the Pequot town at Mystic, which was protected by walls. In under an hour they killed hundreds of people, most of them elders, women and children.

A treaty is a formal written agreement between nations. In the Treaty of Hartford of 1638, the English colonists and their Mohegan and Narragansett allies declared that the Pequot nation no longer existed. They made it illegal to use the name Pequot. Under the treaty, the winners took Pequot survivors for themselves or sold them into slavery. Colonists had already begun selling captives during the war. In July 1637 Captain William Peirce sailed the ship *Desire* out of Boston with seventeen Pequot captives, fifteen of them children. Governor John Winthrop of Massachusetts wrote, "We sent fifteen of the boys and two of the women to Bermuda, by Mr. Pierce." Peirce sold them in the Caribbean. The Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation is in Connecticut today.

In 1675, nearly forty years after the Pequot War, Metacom led a coalition of nations against the New England colonies. A coalition is a group that agrees to act together. Metacom was the Wampanoag sachem, and a sachem is the leader of a nation. His coalition fought the colonists from 1675 to 1676. Colonial soldiers and their Native allies killed Native people, and the coalition's fighters killed colonists. About 9,000 people died in all, and estimates put Native deaths at roughly half of all the Native people in New England. For the size of the population, writers for Britannica and other histories call it the bloodiest war in American history.

On October 13, 1675, the men who governed the Massachusetts colony ordered that Native people from the praying towns be taken to Deer Island in Boston Harbor and kept there. The praying towns were villages of Native people who had become Christians. The colonists feared these people would turn against the English and join Metacom. Colonists took the people of Natick to the island first. The National Park Service puts the number held there at about 500 to 1,100, most of them women and children. They had too little food and shelter through a freezing winter. The two accounts of the deaths differ. The National Park Service says that very few of them survived. The Partnership of Historic Bostons, a Boston history group, says that more than half of them died over the winter. Colonists released the survivors in May 1676. An unknown number had been smuggled off the island and sold as slaves in the West Indies or in Tangier, in North Africa. No surviving record names the men who voted for the island prison, and the National Park Service's account does not name the men who sold the captives. Every year, descendants of the nations in the war hold a gathering on Deer Island to remember them.

Inland, from the middle to the late 1600s, Haudenosaunee warriors fought the Beaver Wars against nations to the west and north. They fought for control of the fur trade, the trade in animal furs with Europeans.

<a id="story-metacom-native-nations"></a>

#### Metacom (King Philip)

> **Who:** Wampanoag sachem, son of Massasoit, who led the coalition war of 1675 and 1676 against the New England colonies. The English called him King Philip.
>
> **When and where:** Southern New England. Killed at Mount Hope, August 12, 1676.

Metacom was the son of Massasoit, the Wampanoag leader who had made an arrangement with the Plymouth colonists in 1621. In 1675 Metacom led a coalition of nations to war against the New England colonies.

In early August 1676 the company of the Plymouth captain Benjamin Church captured Metacom's wife and his nine-year-old son.

On August 12, 1676, at Mount Hope, a Native man named Alderman, who was serving with Church's company, shot Metacom dead. Church wrote his own account of what came next. He ordered that "not one of his bones should be buried," because Metacom had left English dead unburied. Church told a Native man he called his "old Indian Executioner" to cut off Metacom's head and to quarter his body, which means to cut it into four pieces. Church gave the head and one of Metacom's hands to Alderman. Alderman showed the hand to colonists who paid him to see it. Plymouth's leaders paid Church's men thirty shillings, a sum in English money, for each enemy they had killed or captured, and they paid the same for Metacom's head. At Plymouth the head was set on a pole. Church's book does not say who put it there. By the account of a later editor of Church's book, it stayed there for more than 24 years.

The leaders of Plymouth Colony asked ministers what to do with Metacom's son. On September 7, 1676, two ministers, Samuel Arnold and John Cotton, wrote that the children of such enemies could be put to death. In March 1677 Cotton wrote in a letter, "Philip's boy goes now to be sold." The boy and his mother were sold into slavery. Cotton's letter does not say who sold them. Most accounts say the two were sent to Bermuda. Others say they were sent to the West Indies.

Colonial leaders sold hundreds of other captives into slavery to pay what the war had cost the colonies. On August 4, 1675, Plymouth's council of war ruled that 112 Native men, women and children held at Plymouth were "to be sold." The council named the colony's treasurer to sell them. Church wrote that these people had surrendered because of promises made to them, and that about 160 of them were "sold, and transported out of the Country."

#### The Pueblo Revolt

The Pueblo nations along the Rio Grande had lived under Spanish rule since Juan de Oñate founded the New Mexico colony in 1598. In 1675 the Spanish governor, Juan Francisco Treviño, ordered 47 Pueblo religious leaders arrested. The Spanish called their religious practice sorcery, which means using magic to do harm. Spanish officials sentenced four of the leaders to be hanged. Three were hanged, and the fourth killed himself. Spanish officials whipped the others in public and put them in prison. Pueblo people went to Santa Fe and demanded that the prisoners be freed, and the Spanish let them go. One of the freed leaders was Po'pay.

On August 10, 1680, the people of many separate towns rose against the Spanish on the same day. They spoke Tewa, Tiwa, Towa, Tano, Keres and other languages, and the Zuni and the Hopi also promised to help. Pueblo fighters besieged Santa Fe, which means they surrounded the town and cut it off. They took the town and drove the Spanish out of New Mexico. In the rising they killed 401 settlers and 21 Franciscan friars. The Pueblo fighters let most of the Spanish leave, and the Spanish went south.

The Pueblos governed themselves for the next twelve years. In those years they lived through drought, raids and famine, which is a long shortage of food. Diego de Vargas led Spanish forces back into New Mexico in 1692 to retake it, and Pueblo fighters kept up armed resistance for years after that. Writers of the EBSCO Research Starters history guide call the Pueblo Revolt the most successful uprising by Native people against European rule in North America.

<a id="story-pope"></a>

#### Po'pay (Popé)

> **Who:** A Tewa religious leader from Ohkay Owingeh who organized the 1680 rising across dozens of towns and several languages.
>
> **When and where:** New Mexico, August 1680.

Po'pay had to get the people of dozens of towns to rise on a single day. The people of those towns did not all speak the same language.

Pueblo accounts say that runners carried knotted cords from town to town. The knots on each cord marked the days left until the rising. Po'pay set the rising for August 11, by one account, or August 13, by another.

On August 9 the Spanish captured two of the runners, Pedro Omtua and Nicolás Catua of Tesuque Pueblo. Spanish officials tortured them to make them explain the knotted cords. Torture means hurting a person on purpose to force them to talk. The Smithsonian's account of the runners does not say how they were hurt. Later the Spanish hanged them. No surviving record names the men who did it. When Po'pay learned that the runners had been caught, he ordered the rising to begin early. It began on August 10, 1680.

A statue of Po'pay stands in the United States Capitol. It is one of New Mexico's two statues in the Capitol's Statuary Hall collection, which holds statues of two people from each state's history.

When the Spanish left New Mexico in 1680, they left their horses behind. An estimated 1,500 or more horses passed into Native hands at once. Writers for the Smithsonian's National Museum of the American Indian call it the largest single transfer of horses. According to the traditional account, Native people then traded horses west and north along Native trade routes. The horses reached the Ute, the Navajo, the Apache, the Comanche, the Kiowa, the Shoshone and the nations of the northern Plains.

In 2023 a team led by William Taylor published a study in the journal *Science*. Its findings do not fit this account. Lakota, Comanche and Pawnee people were among the study's writers, and other Native partners worked on it too. The team used radiocarbon dating on the remains of horses from Wyoming, Kansas and New Mexico. Radiocarbon dating measures a form of carbon that breaks down at a steady rate. The amount left shows how old a bone is. The horses had been ridden and had eaten corn that people fed them. They had also worn bridles, which are straps around a horse's head used to steer it. They were there by the early 1600s, decades before the revolt. Native oral histories, which are accounts passed down by telling, had said the same thing. The timing is not settled.

By either account, Plains nations had horses by the 1700s.

### 1700 to 1750

French and British officials both wanted Native allies in the first half of the 1700s. Haudenosaunee leaders bargained with both sides. Native nations also went on making their own agreements with one another.

In these years the Haudenosaunee accepted the Tuscarora as a member nation. South Carolina forces had defeated the Tuscarora, and colonists had taken their land in North Carolina. On the southern Plains, the Comanche built the strongest power in the region on horses and trade.

The printed speeches of the Onondaga speaker Canasatego, from these years, are among the best records of Native diplomacy from that century. Diplomacy means dealing with other nations through talks and agreements.

#### Neutrality as strategy

On August 4, 1701, about 1,300 delegates from more than thirty nations met at Montreal. Delegates are people sent to speak for a group. There they made peace with the leaders of New France, the French colony in what is now Canada. As part of the same peace, the Haudenosaunee promised to stay neutral. That meant they would fight for neither France nor Britain.

For half a century, Haudenosaunee leaders used their neutrality to bargain with both sides.

#### The Tuscarora move north

In 1710 more than 400 Swiss and German settlers, led by Baron Christoph von Graffenried, founded the town of New Bern, North Carolina, on Tuscarora land. They pushed the people of the Native town of Chattoka off the spot where the Neuse and Trent rivers meet. Slave raiders were also capturing Tuscarora people to sell them as slaves. The State Library of North Carolina's history of the war does not name the raiders. On September 22, 1711, Tuscarora fighters struck back in attacks they had planned together. The war lasted until 1713. South Carolina colonial forces, with Native allies of their own, defeated the Tuscarora. By that library's count, 1,400 Tuscarora were dead and 1,000 had been captured and enslaved.

About 1,500 Tuscarora survivors then moved north, roughly 500 miles. They asked the Five Nations of the Haudenosaunee to sponsor them, which meant to speak for them and accept them. The Oneida took them in. In 1722 the whole Tuscarora nation became the sixth nation of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. Since then the Confederacy has had six member nations, and it is also known as the Six Nations.

#### Comanche power

The Comanche moved onto the southern Plains in the early 1700s and became the most powerful nation there. Comanchería, the country they controlled, later covered about 240,000 square miles.

The Comanche built their power on horses. They bred, trained and traded horses, and they controlled the horse trade from the southern Plains to the northern Plains. In the 1740s they traded bison robes and horses to French traders for guns. The French guns were better than the weapons the Comanche could get from the Spanish. Comanche fighters also raided other peoples. A raid is a quick attack to seize goods, horses or people. Comanche leaders made agreements with other nations as well as fighting them.

#### Treaty councils

A treaty council was a meeting where Native leaders and colonial officials bargained and made agreements. At these councils, speakers on both sides made speeches and exchanged wampum.

At Lancaster, Pennsylvania, in June and July of 1744, colonial officials paid the Haudenosaunee to give up their claims to the Shenandoah Valley.

<a id="story-canasatego"></a>

#### Canasatego

> **Who:** Onondaga leader and the Haudenosaunee's speaker at treaty councils, whose 1744 speech on union Benjamin Franklin printed.
>
> **When and where:** Lancaster, Pennsylvania, June and July 1744. He gave the union speech on July 4, 1744.

Canasatego spoke for the Haudenosaunee Confederacy at treaty councils with colonial officials.

On July 4, 1744, he closed the council at Lancaster by advising the colonies to unite, as his own nations had done centuries earlier: "We heartily recommend Union and a good Agreement between you our Brethren... you, as well as we, will become the stronger."

Benjamin Franklin printed the minutes of the council, the written record of what was said there, including the speech.

### 1750 to 1800

After 1750, French and British forces fought their wars on Native land. Then the leaders, soldiers and settlers of a new country, the United States, moved onto that land and fought the nations for it.

British forces beat the French in 1763. An empire is a country that rules other lands and peoples. After 1763, Native nations had no second empire to bargain with against Britain. Then the colonists went to war with Britain in the American Revolution. The Haudenosaunee nations took different sides in that war, and their Confederacy split for the first time in centuries. During the war, in 1778, United States officials signed their first treaty with a Native nation. In 1791 fighters from a confederacy of nations in the Ohio Country destroyed a United States army.

#### Pontiac and the Line

French and British commanders both needed Native allies in the French and Indian War, which lasted from 1754 to 1763.

In 1763 a loose confederacy of nations from the Great Lakes, the Illinois Country and the Ohio Country rose against the British. Under the Odawa leader Pontiac, their fighters took or besieged British forts across the west. Pontiac lifted his siege of Detroit in October 1763, but the fighting went on until 1766.

At Fort Pitt in 1763, British officers tried to give smallpox to the Native fighters around them. Smallpox is a disease that spreads from person to person and can kill. Delaware, Shawnee and Mingo fighters had besieged the fort, where Pittsburgh stands today, and smallpox had broken out among the British soldiers inside. On June 24, 1763, the fort's commander, Captain Simeon Ecuyer, and the trader William Trent gave two Delaware men, Turtle's Heart and Mamaltee, two blankets and a handkerchief from the fort's smallpox hospital. Trent wrote in his journal, "I hope it will have the desired effect." In July the British commander in North America, General Jeffery Amherst, asked Colonel Henry Bouquet in a letter whether smallpox could be sent among the nations at war. Bouquet answered that he would try to spread it with blankets. A month after the June meeting, Trent saw the two Delaware men again, and they showed no sign of smallpox. A man named Gershom Hicks later said that about 100 Native people died of smallpox between the spring of 1763 and April 1764. The historian Elizabeth Fenn writes that no one can know whether the attempt to spread smallpox worked.

British officials answered the war by drawing a line. They issued the Royal Proclamation on October 7, 1763. A proclamation is an official public announcement of an order. In it they forbade colonists to settle west of the Appalachian Mountains, and they set aside the land beyond for the Native nations. Colonists were angry about the line and crossed it anyway. Writers for Encyclopedia Virginia call the Proclamation a foundation of later treaty law, the set of rules for agreements between governments.

In December 1763 armed settlers from Paxton Township, Pennsylvania, killed the twenty Conestoga people who lived in a small town near Lancaster. The Conestoga were unarmed. On December 14, fifty-seven men came at daybreak and found three men, two women and a boy at home. They shot them, stabbed them and killed them with hatchets. One of the dead was Shehaes, a very old man who had helped make a treaty with William Penn in 1701. They killed him in his bed. The attackers scalped all six, which means they cut away the skin and hair from the top of each head, and burned the huts. Lancaster's officials put the other fourteen Conestoga in the town workhouse to keep them safe. A workhouse was a building where poor people were made to work, and Franklin called this one "a strong Building." On December 27 about fifty men broke down the workhouse door and killed all fourteen with guns and hatchets, children a year old among them. The Paxton men claimed the Conestoga had hidden enemy spies. The historian Michael Goode writes that the charge was made up. British soldiers stationed nearby did nothing to stop the killings, and no one was ever put on trial for them. Benjamin Franklin wrote down the names of the dead in 1764.

#### The Revolution splits the Haudenosaunee

Under the Great Law, the Five Nations, and then the Six, had stayed united for centuries. In the American Revolution they split. The Oneida and the Tuscarora sided with the Americans. The Mohawk, the Seneca, the Cayuga and the Onondaga fought with the British. Many of them fought under the Mohawk leader Joseph Brant, whose own name was Thayendanegea. At the Battle of Oriskany, on August 6, 1777, Haudenosaunee men fought on both sides.

In 1779 George Washington ordered an expedition into Seneca and Cayuga country. In his written orders, Washington directed "the total destruction and devastation of their settlements." From July 31 to October 15, General John Sullivan's soldiers burned more than forty Seneca and Cayuga towns and the crops in their fields. Thousands of people fled to the British at Fort Niagara. That winter many of them starved or froze to death there.

In 1790 Seneca chiefs spoke to Washington directly. "When your army entered the country of the Six Nations, we called you the Town-destroyer," they said, "and to this day, when that name is heard, our women look behind them and turn pale." The name was older than the burning of their towns. Washington had been given the name Conotocaurius, Town Destroyer, in 1753, and his great-grandfather had been given it before him.

#### The treaty system begins

On September 17, 1778, at Fort Pitt, United States officials signed their country's first treaty with a Native nation. The Lenape leaders White Eyes, John Kill Buck Jr. and Pipe signed for their nation. The treaty identifies the Lenape as the Delaware. In the treaty, the American officials recognized Lenape sovereignty, which means the right of a nation to govern itself. They also asked the Lenape to let American troops cross their land safely. The negotiators raised the idea of a Native fourteenth state, which would join the thirteen and send its own representatives to Congress. No one in Congress ever acted on that idea.

In all, United States officials and Native leaders made 374 treaties that were formally approved, or ratified. The last of them date from the 1860s. The National Archives holds all 374, and its archivists, the people who keep its records, have put every one online. Each of the 374 is an agreement between the United States and a Native nation.

#### The Northwest Confederacy

North of the Ohio River, the nations built a confederacy to defend their country. Its leaders included Little Turtle of the Miami, Blue Jacket of the Shawnee and Buckongahelas of the Lenape.

On November 4, 1791, about a thousand confederacy fighters fought the army of General Arthur St. Clair. About 930 of his soldiers began the fight. The confederacy's fighters destroyed his army. Counts of the soldiers they killed run from more than 630 to more than 650. Counts of the wounded run from 264 to more than 270. The casualty rate, which counts the killed and the wounded together, was about 97 percent of the soldiers who fought. No battle in the history of the U.S. Army has had a higher rate. Native casualties were roughly 100. St. Clair's defeat is still the largest defeat Native forces have ever given a United States army, larger than the Battle of the Little Bighorn, fought 85 years later. After the defeat, members of Congress held the first investigation by Congress in the country's history.

In 1794 Anthony Wayne led a legion, an army unit of 3,300 men, against the confederacy. On August 20, 1794, at Fallen Timbers, near where Toledo, Ohio, stands today, Wayne's legion defeated the confederacy. At Greenville, on August 3, 1795, after that defeat, the confederacy's leaders signed a treaty with Wayne, who signed for the United States. They had lost the war, and in the treaty they signed away most of Ohio and part of Indiana to the United States.

<a id="story-little-turtle"></a>

#### Little Turtle (Mishikinaakwa)

> **Who:** Miami war leader who co-led the confederacy that destroyed St. Clair's army in 1791, then decided the war could not be won and argued for peace.
>
> **When and where:** The Wabash and Maumee country, in present-day Indiana and Ohio, in the 1780s and 1790s.

Little Turtle was one of the leaders of the confederacy that beat St. Clair on November 4, 1791.

Three years later the same confederacy lost at Fallen Timbers. Little Turtle decided that the war could not be won. On August 3, 1795, he signed the Treaty of Greenville, in which the defeated confederacy's leaders signed away most of Ohio to the United States. He spent his last years arguing against more war with the United States.

### 1800 to 1850

In the first half of the 1800s, Native leaders east of the Mississippi River tried several ways to keep their nations' land. North of the Ohio River, people from many nations joined a confederacy, a union of nations that agree to act together, and fought American armies. In the Southeast, Cherokee leaders wrote a constitution, a written plan for their government and its basic laws, and took their fight to court. In Florida, Seminole fighters went to war against removal.

Two Shawnee brothers, Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa, built the northern confederacy around one idea. Tecumseh said that the land belonged to all the nations together, so no single nation could sell any part of it. In 1811 soldiers under the American commander William Henry Harrison burned the confederacy's center. American soldiers killed Tecumseh in battle in 1813.

The Cherokee changed their nation fast in the eleven years from 1821 to 1832. In 1821 Sequoyah showed a way to write the Cherokee language. In 1827 Cherokee leaders approved their constitution, with three branches of government, and in 1828 they began printing a newspaper. In 1832 Chief Justice John Marshall, the head of the Supreme Court of the United States, wrote the court's ruling in the Cherokee Nation's favor.

In 1830 members of Congress passed the Indian Removal Act. Under it, United States soldiers forced the nations of the Southeast out of their homes and moved them west. In the Cherokee removal alone, soldiers held about 16,000 people in stockades, pens fenced with upright logs, and more than 4,000 of them died of cold, hunger and disease. In the West, the people of those nations built their governments again.

#### Tecumseh and Tenskwatawa

Around 1805 a Shawnee man named Tenskwatawa began preaching that Native people should return to Native ways of living. His brother Tecumseh took the movement to other nations and asked them to join it. In 1808 the brothers built a town on the Wabash River as the center of a confederacy of many nations. The town was called Prophetstown. Tenskwatawa was known as the Prophet.

William Henry Harrison, an American governor, was buying Native land through treaties. A treaty is a written agreement between nations. In 1809 Native leaders signed the Treaty of Fort Wayne with him and sold him land. Tecumseh said those leaders had no right to sell land that all the nations held together. In August 1810 Tecumseh met Harrison at Vincennes and told him that the land belonged to all the nations in common, meaning together. "No part has a right to sell, even to each other, much less to strangers," Tecumseh said. He called the latest sale "bad," because "it was made by a part only." By that argument, every sale made by one nation alone counted for nothing.

On November 7, 1811, while Tecumseh was away asking more nations to join the confederacy, Harrison marched about a thousand men to Prophetstown and fought the people there. The fight became known as the Battle of Tippecanoe. On the next day, November 8, Harrison burned the town.

Fighters from the confederacy fought on beside the British in the War of 1812. On October 5, 1813, they fought the Battle of the Thames at Moraviantown, in the British colony of Upper Canada. Their British ally, Major General Henry Procter, left the battlefield in the middle of the fight. British army officers later put Procter on trial for his failures in that campaign. American soldiers killed Tecumseh in the battle. After his death the confederacy broke apart.

<a id="story-tecumseh"></a>

#### Tecumseh

> **Who:** Shawnee leader who went from nation to nation arguing that Native land belonged to all the nations together, so no single nation could sell it.
>
> **When and where:** the Wabash River country and the South, 1805 to 1813. Killed in battle at the Thames, October 5, 1813.
>
> **Movie:** *We Shall Remain: Tecumseh's Vision* (PBS, 2009), a documentary about him and his brother.

Tecumseh traveled to other nations to ask them to join the confederacy. In October 1811 he arrived at the yearly great council of the Creek Nation at Tuckabatchee, where more than 5,000 Creek people had gathered. The Creek leader Big Warrior refused to join him, because he was afraid of losing the support of the United States.

Tecumseh's argument was that no single nation could sell land that belonged to all of them. In 1810 he told William Henry Harrison that the land "never was divided, but belongs to all for the use of each." He added, "Any sale not made by all is not valid." Not valid means it does not count.

Enough nations joined him to make Prophetstown the center of a confederacy. In 1811 Harrison burned the town while Tecumseh was away. Two years later American soldiers killed Tecumseh in Upper Canada, where he was fighting beside the British, and his confederacy broke apart.

#### The Cherokee renaissance

In 1821 a Cherokee man named Sequoyah showed a syllabary he had made. A syllabary is a set of written characters in which each character stands for a whole syllable, not a single sound. Sequoyah's had 86 characters. Within a few years most Cherokee people could read and write it. Writers at the website History.com state that by the 1830s a larger share of Cherokee people could read than of the white settlers around them.

Cherokee leaders set up a capital at New Echota in 1825. In 1827 they approved a written constitution. They modeled it on the United States Constitution, with three branches of government. Officials of the state of Georgia answered by declaring the Cherokee government abolished, which means ended by law.

In 1828 the Cherokee began printing the *Cherokee Phoenix*, the first Native American newspaper. They printed it in Cherokee and in English.

<a id="story-sequoyah-native-nations"></a>

#### Sequoyah

> **Who:** Cherokee silversmith who could not read or write any language, and made a way to write his own. He is the only person in recorded history known to have created a writing system alone, without first being able to read and write another language.
>
> **When and where:** born in Taskigi, Tennessee, about 1770. First showed his syllabary in 1821. Died 1843 in Mexico.

Sequoyah could not read or write English or any other language. He worked on the problem for about twelve years.

By 1821 he had made 86 characters, one for each syllable in spoken Cherokee. Within a few years most of the Cherokee Nation was reading and writing them.

Sequoyah's birth year is not certain. The years given for it run from 1770 to 1778. The Library of Congress lists it as 1770 with a question mark, which means the year is not certain. He died in 1843, in Mexico.

#### Removal

President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act into law on May 28, 1830. Under it, the president could give Native nations land west of the Mississippi River in exchange for their land in the East.

Cherokee leaders took their fight with Georgia to the courts. Georgia's lawmakers had made it a crime for a white person to live in the Cherokee Nation after March 1, 1831, without a license from the state. Samuel Worcester was a minister from Vermont who translated parts of the Bible into Cherokee. He and another missionary, Elizur Butler, decided to challenge the law, and they would not leave. Missionaries are people sent to spread their religion. On July 7, 1831, Georgia guards arrested Worcester, Butler and nine other missionaries. In September 1831 they were tried in Georgia and found guilty. Each was sentenced to four years in prison at hard labor, which means forced hard work. The New Georgia Encyclopedia's account of the case does not name the judge.

In *Worcester v. Georgia*, decided in 1832, Chief Justice John Marshall, the head of the Supreme Court, ruled that the laws of Georgia had no force inside the Cherokee Nation. He held that the Nation was under the protection of the United States. That ruling is still one of the foundations of tribal sovereignty law, the law about a Native nation's right to govern itself. Georgia's officials ignored the ruling, and United States officials went ahead with removal anyway.

Worcester stayed in the Georgia prison at Milledgeville until January 1833. He came out after he accepted a pardon, an order forgiving the crime, from Georgia's governor, Wilson Lumpkin.

In May 1838 President Martin Van Buren sent General Winfield Scott with about 7,000 soldiers to round up the Cherokee people who had not moved west. Georgia's militia, its citizen soldiers, joined them. In 1838 and 1839, soldiers came to Cherokee houses in the Southeast and took families out at gunpoint, often with no time to pack. They held about 16,000 Cherokee people in stockades in Tennessee and Alabama. Then the soldiers forced them to go to Indian Territory, in what is now Oklahoma. More than 4,000 of them died of cold, hunger and disease. That figure is the traditional estimate. The National Park Service counts more than a thousand deaths on the trip itself, and perhaps several thousand more from what the removal did to people afterward. In 1984 Russell Thornton, a scholar at the University of Minnesota, wrote that the number of deaths "may have been twice" that figure. The Cherokee named the removal *Nunna daul Tsuny*, the Trail Where We Cried. In English it is called the Trail of Tears.

United States officials and soldiers forced all five of the large southeastern nations to move to Indian Territory: the Cherokee, the Muscogee (Creek), the Choctaw, the Chickasaw and the Seminole. From 1831 to 1833 they removed more than 14,000 Choctaw people, and hundreds died. In 1836 and 1837 they removed more than 14,500 Creek people. Several hundred died on the way, and about 3,200 died after they arrived, of disease, hunger and cold. In Indian Territory, the people of those nations rebuilt their governments, their courts, their newspapers and their schools.

<a id="story-rebecca-neugin-native-nations"></a>

#### Rebecca Neugin

> **Who:** a Cherokee woman who was about three years old when soldiers took her family out of their home in Georgia in 1838.
>
> **When and where:** Georgia to Indian Territory, 1838 and 1839. Interviewed in 1932.

In 1838 soldiers took Rebecca Neugin's family out of their home in Georgia. Rebecca was about three years old. The soldiers held the family in a camp in Tennessee, and in September 1838 the family set out west. Rebecca and the smaller children rode in a wagon, while her mother, her father and her older brother Dick walked the whole way.

In 1932 the historian Grant Foreman interviewed her, and she told him what she remembered of the journey. She was about 97 years old. The interview came 94 years after the removal, and she was one of the last people still alive who had been on it. She died on July 15, 1932.

#### The Seminole resistance

In Florida many Seminole people refused to leave, and United States soldiers fought them in the Second Seminole War, from 1835 to 1842. It was the longest war between United States forces and a Native nation east of the Mississippi, and the one that cost the most. National Park Service writers give its cost in a count. For every four Seminole people the army forced out of Florida, soldiers killed one Seminole. Three soldiers died for each four forced out, and the army spent $32,000.

On October 21, 1837, General Thomas Jesup lured the Seminole war leader Osceola to a talk under a white flag of truce. Under a flag of truce, both sides promise not to attack or seize anyone while they talk. Osceola came in under the flag, and Jesup had him seized. Many people in the United States protested the trick in public at the time. Osceola died a prisoner at Fort Moultrie, South Carolina, on January 30, 1838.

Most of the fighting stopped in 1842. A few hundred Seminole people never surrendered and stayed in the Everglades. Their descendants belong to two tribes today. Federal officials, meaning officials of the national government, recognized the Seminole Tribe of Florida in 1957 and the Miccosukee Tribe in 1962. That means they accepted each tribe as a nation with its own government. Leaders of both tribes point out that the Seminole were never conquered.

<a id="story-osceola-native-nations"></a>

#### Osceola

> **Who:** Seminole war leader in the fight against removal from Florida.
>
> **When and where:** Florida. Seized by General Thomas Jesup under a flag of truce, October 21, 1837. Died a prisoner at Fort Moultrie, South Carolina, January 30, 1838.

Osceola was born in 1804 in the Creek town of Talisi, in what is now Alabama, and he was named Billy Powell at birth. He grew up to be a Seminole war leader in the fight against removal from Florida. On October 21, 1837, General Thomas Jesup lured him to a talk under a white flag of truce. When Osceola arrived, Jesup had him seized.

Many people in the United States said in public at the time that the trick was wrong.

Osceola died three months later, on January 30, 1838, a prisoner at Fort Moultrie. After he died, the army doctor Frederick Weedon cut off his head before the burial and put it on display in his drug store. The Seminole kept fighting until 1842.

### 1850 to 1900

United States officials and soldiers forced Native nations onto reservations in the second half of the 1800s. A reservation is an area of land that United States officials set aside for a nation, in a treaty or by an order. Soldiers and officials forced the nation's people onto it and held them there. Officials and settlers then took the rest of the nation's country.

In these years United States soldiers killed hundreds of Native people at a time. In 1862 army officers hanged 38 Dakota men at one time at Mankato, Minnesota. At Bear River in 1863 soldiers killed an estimated 250 to 500 Shoshone people, and at Sand Creek in 1864 about 230 Cheyenne and Arapaho people, most of them women, children and elders. Cavalry, soldiers on horseback, killed about 177 Piikani people on the Marias River in 1870, by the best estimate. Soldiers at Wounded Knee in 1890 killed between 250 and 300 Lakota people.

In 1868 Navajo leaders signed a treaty in which United States officials agreed to let their people go home. Hunters killed off the bison herds that fed the Plains nations, and army officers encouraged the killing. In 1871 members of Congress stopped making treaties with Native nations. Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho fighters beat George Custer's soldiers at the Little Bighorn in 1876. The next year the Nez Perce fled toward Canada with the army behind them.

In 1879 an Army officer named Richard Henry Pratt opened the first federal boarding school for Native children built far from the reservations. Federal means run by the national government of the United States. Federal officials used Pratt's school as the model for many more. Pratt stated his aim in his own words: "Kill the Indian in him, and save the man." Federal investigators later counted at least 973 children who died at the federal boarding schools.

In 1887 members of Congress passed a law under which federal officials cut nations' shared land into private pieces. The officials opened what was left over to white settlers.

#### The wars, from the nations' side

In Minnesota in 1862, United States officials failed to deliver the food and the payments that they had promised the Dakota in treaties. Dakota fighters went to war, and the war lasted six weeks. Afterward, army officers sitting as military commissions tried 392 Dakota men. A military commission is a court run by the army. Some of the trials took less than five minutes. The men had no defense lawyers and no interpreters, the people who translate between two languages. The army officers on the commissions sentenced 303 of the men to death by hanging.

President Abraham Lincoln and his lawyers read the trial records. Lincoln looked first for men found guilty of rape, which means forcing a person into sex, and found two. Then he added men found to have taken part in killing people who were not soldiers. He cut the list of men to be executed down to 39. One of the 39 was reprieved, which means his execution was called off. On December 26, 1862, at Mankato, army officers hanged 38 Dakota men together while about 4,000 people watched. The hanging at Mankato is the largest mass execution, the most people put to death at one time, in United States history. Captain William Duley cut the rope. Several members of his family had been killed in a Dakota attack on the Lake Shetek settlement. The bodies were put in a shallow grave on a sandbar. The Minnesota Historical Society's account does not say who buried them. Before morning, doctors had dug up most of the bodies to use for medical study.

Two of the men had been hanged by mistake. By the Minnesota Historical Society's account, Wicaŋȟpi Wastedaŋpi, who went by the name Caske, stepped forward when the name "Caske" was called. The name called was another man's, and he was hanged in that man's place. The other, Wasicuŋ, was a young white man whom the Dakota had adopted as a child, and the commission had found him not guilty at his trial.

On January 29, 1863, Colonel Patrick Edward Connor led soldiers against a winter camp of Northwestern Shoshone people on the Bear River, near what is now Preston, Idaho. Connor had announced that he would take no prisoners. His soldiers killed an estimated 250 to 500 Shoshone people. Afterward army leaders promoted Connor to brigadier general, a higher rank.

In 1863 and 1864, United States soldiers marched about 8,500 Navajo people more than 300 miles to Bosque Redondo and held them there. This forced march is known as the Long Walk. Thousands of the Navajo died while soldiers held them at Bosque Redondo. In 1868 Navajo leaders negotiated a treaty in which United States officials agreed to let the survivors go home. The Navajo were one of the very few removed nations who got their homeland back.

Colonel John Chivington led about 675 volunteer soldiers against Black Kettle's Cheyenne and Arapaho camp at Sand Creek in Colorado on November 29, 1864. The camp was flying a United States flag and a white flag. Earlier that month Major Scott Anthony, the commander at nearby Fort Lyon, had told Black Kettle's people to camp at Sand Creek. In his report of November 16 he wrote that he told them "no war would be waged against them." That promise was to hold until his own commander decided what to do. When Chivington arrived, Anthony agreed to the attack. The attack lasted eight hours. The soldiers killed about 230 people, most of them women, children and elders. A massacre is the killing of many people who cannot defend themselves.

Captain Silas Soule, one of the officers there, refused to let his men fire. He wrote to his mother that he saw "a Massacre of three hundred Indians mostly women and children." In another letter he wrote that it was "hard to see little children on their knees have their brains beat out." Soldiers cut scalps and other body parts from the dead.

Members of a committee of Congress later wrote that Chivington "deliberately planned and executed a foul and dastardly massacre." Dastardly means cowardly and cruel. Chivington left the army and was never put on trial, and no officer or soldier was punished. In April 1865, about two months after Soule spoke against Chivington before investigators, a man shot Soule dead on a Denver street. No one was ever punished for killing him. National Park Service staff look after the place of the massacre today as the Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site.

Lakota fighters fought the army over the Bozeman Trail in a war named for the Lakota leader Red Cloud, Red Cloud's War. After it, United States officials and Lakota leaders signed the Treaty of Fort Laramie in 1868. In it, the officials agreed to close the Bozeman Trail. They also set up the Great Sioux Reservation "for the absolute and undisturbed use" of the Lakota. It covered all of what is now South Dakota west of the Missouri River, including the Black Hills.

On January 23, 1870, Major Eugene Baker's cavalry came to a camp of Piikani (Piegan Blackfeet) people on the Marias River in Montana. His scout, Joe Kipp, told him it was the camp of Heavy Runner's band, which was at peace with the United States. By one account, Baker answered, "That makes no difference, one band or another of them, they are all Piegans and we will attack them." By the best estimate, his soldiers killed 37 men, 90 women and 50 children. The army's own count was 173 dead. Neither Baker nor any of his men was ever punished.

In 1874 members of an expedition led by George Custer announced that there was gold in the Black Hills. Federal officials ignored their own 1868 treaty. In December 1875 they ordered the winter camps that were off the reservation to come onto it by January 31, 1876. When the camps did not come in, the officials sent the army.

George Custer led part of the 7th Cavalry, an army unit of soldiers on horseback, on June 25, 1876. He attacked a camp where Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho people had gathered as allies, meaning they had agreed to fight on the same side. The camp stood by the Little Bighorn River, also called the Greasy Grass. Fighters from the camp killed Custer and about 200 of the soldiers with him in about an hour. Those soldiers made up five companies, smaller units of the 7th Cavalry.

Crazy Horse, one of the battle leaders at the Little Bighorn, surrendered on May 6, 1877, less than a year after the battle. On September 5, 1877, at Fort Robinson, soldiers were arresting him. A Lakota man named Little Big Man jumped on his back and held him, and a soldier on guard stabbed him with a bayonet. A bayonet is a blade fixed to the end of a rifle. Crazy Horse died of the wound. Most accounts say a soldier on guard stabbed him. The name most often given is Private William Gentles, but only one witness named him, so who the soldier was is disputed. Little Big Man later told a different story, in which Crazy Horse was cut by his own knife.

Geronimo, of the Chiricahua Apache, surrendered on September 4, 1886. He was the last Native leader to formally surrender to the United States. United States officials then held the Chiricahua people as prisoners of war for 27 years. Prisoners of war are people an army holds after capturing them in a war.

<a id="story-sitting-bull-native-nations"></a>

#### Sitting Bull

> **Who:** Hunkpapa Lakota leader and holy man. The camp that fought at the Greasy Grass gathered around him.
>
> **When and where:** the northern Plains. Canada from 1877 to 1881. Killed by Indian police at Standing Rock, December 15, 1890.
>
> **Movie:** *Sitting Bull: A Stone in My Heart* (2006), a documentary built from his own recorded words.

The camp on the Greasy Grass in June 1876 formed around Sitting Bull, and Crazy Horse was one of its battle leaders.

In 1877 Sitting Bull took his people north into Canada. Hunters were killing off the bison, and by 1881 there were not enough left to feed his people. He surrendered at Fort Buford in July of that year.

On June 6, 1885, at the Standing Rock Agency, he signed a contract with Buffalo Bill's Wild West, a traveling show. The show paid him fifty dollars a week for a four-month season, and only he could sell his own photographs and autographs.

On December 15, 1890, at Standing Rock, Indian police came to arrest him. Indian agents, the federal officials who ran the reservations, were alarmed by the Ghost Dance, a new religious dance spreading across the reservations. Indian police were Native men who worked as police for the agency, the government office that ran the reservation. The policemen killed Sitting Bull.

<a id="story-chief-joseph"></a>

#### Chief Joseph

> **Who:** Nez Perce leader in the flight of 1877. About 750 people, only some 200 of them fighters, fled with the United States Army behind them.
>
> **When and where:** the Wallowa Valley of Oregon to the Bear Paw Mountains of Montana, 1877. Surrendered October 5, 1877, forty miles from Canada.
>
> **Movie:** *I Will Fight No More Forever* (1975, television film).

Joseph's band of the Nez Perce lived in the Wallowa Valley of northeastern Oregon. In 1877 General Oliver O. Howard told the Nez Perce chiefs that their people had 30 days to move onto the reservation in Idaho, or the army would move them by force. That year about 750 Nez Perce people fled with the army behind them, and only about 200 of them were fighters. The rest were families.

They traveled about 1,170 miles. That is the National Park Service's figure for the trail. Some accounts state a longer distance, up to about 1,700 miles.

They surrendered on October 5, 1877, at the foot of the Bear Paw Mountains in Montana, forty miles short of the Canadian border. Lieutenant C. E. S. Wood recorded Joseph's words at the surrender: "From where the sun now stands I will fight no more forever."

Colonel Nelson Miles had promised Joseph that his people would be taken back to the reservation in Idaho. General William Tecumseh Sherman, the commanding general of the army, overruled the promise, which means he cancelled it. He wanted the Nez Perce punished as an example to other nations and never allowed to go home. "I believed General Miles, or I never would have surrendered," Joseph said afterward. United States officials sent his people to Kansas, then to Indian Territory. There, many of them were sick and short of supplies, and their number fell from 410 to 391.

In May 1885, 268 Nez Perce people left Indian Territory for the Northwest. Officials sent Joseph to the Colville reservation in Washington, and he died there, at Nespelem, in 1904. Officials never allowed him back to the Wallowa Valley.

#### The bison, and the end of treaties

There were roughly 30 million bison on the Plains in the early 1800s. One count in 1884 found 325. By 1900 there were fewer than a thousand.

Railroads carried hunters into the herds' country. Hunters made hide hunting into a large business, killing bison for their skins. Disease and drought killed others. Army officers encouraged the killing, because the herds were the Plains nations' food and the base of how they made a living, and the bison were part of their religion.

In 1871 members of Congress stopped making treaties with Native nations. They did it with a rider, a short passage attached to a spending bill called the Indian Appropriations Act. Treaties already made stayed in force. After 1871, United States officials dealt with Native nations through acts of Congress and orders from the president instead of treaties.

#### Allotment

Allotment means cutting land that a whole nation owned together into private pieces.

The Dawes Act, also called the General Allotment Act, became law in 1887. Under it, federal officials divided nations' land into separate parcels, or pieces. The head of a family got 160 acres, a single man got 80 acres, and each child got 40 acres. Officials called everything left over "surplus," meaning extra, and opened it to white settlers.

Between 1887 and 1934, under the allotment that federal officials carried out, Native nations lost about 90 million acres. The land they held fell from about 138 million acres to 48 million. The lost land was about two-thirds of all the land Native nations still had in 1887. The Meriam Report, a federal study published in 1928, states the figures as 137 million and 47 million acres. The loss is about the same by either count.

In 1934 members of Congress passed the Indian Reorganization Act. In it they ended allotment, and they allowed up to $2,000,000 a year to be spent buying land for Native people.

#### The boarding schools

The Carlisle Indian Industrial School opened on November 1, 1879, at Carlisle, Pennsylvania. Its founder was an Army officer named Richard Henry Pratt. It was the first federal boarding school for Native children built far from the reservations. Federal officials used Carlisle as the model for the schools that followed.

Pratt stated the purpose himself. In 1892 he spoke to a national conference of charities in Denver. He said that "all the Indian there is in the race should be dead. Kill the Indian in him, and save the man." People often quote the line in a shorter form, "kill the Indian, save the man." Pratt's recorded words are the longer ones, printed in the conference's official report.

Members of Congress passed two laws to get the children into the schools. In 1891 they gave the Commissioner of Indian Affairs the power to make and enforce rules forcing Native children to attend school. The Commissioner was the federal official in charge of Native affairs. In 1893 they let federal officials hold back rations, clothing and annuity payments from parents who would not send their children. Rations, clothing and annuities were the food, goods and yearly payments that United States officials had promised a nation in its treaties.

Some Indian agents sent reservation police to seize children. An Indian agent was the federal official in charge of a reservation. Some families sent their children willingly, hoping the schooling would help them. Many families had no real choice.

When a child arrived, staff at school after school cut the child's hair and replaced the child's clothes with a uniform. They gave the child an English name and forbade the child to speak the language of home. Staff punished children for speaking their own languages. The federal investigation of the schools and survivors' own accounts document the punishments: beatings, solitary confinement, withholding food, and washing children's mouths out with soap. Solitary confinement means locking a child away alone.

Children spent half of each school day doing unpaid work that kept the school running. Pratt also ran what he called the outing system. Under it, he sent students to live and work with white families, in the summers and during school terms.

Investigators at the United States Department of the Interior studied the schools. They published their findings in 2022 and again on July 30, 2024. They counted 417 federal Indian boarding schools in 37 states and territories, open between 1819 and 1969. Their first report, in 2022, listed 408. They also found more than a thousand other places that had similar aims. At least 973 children died at the federal schools. The investigators found at least 74 marked and unmarked burial sites at 65 of the schools. The report states that its count of the dead is low.

Children kept their languages by speaking them where the staff could not hear. At these schools, children made friends with children from other nations. Those friendships were one of the starting points of the Native organizing of the next century. Some students, Zitkala-Ša among them, used the reading and writing they learned at the schools to argue against the schools.

<a id="story-sarah-winnemucca-native-nations"></a>

#### Sarah Winnemucca

> **Who:** Northern Paiute writer, interpreter, and lecturer who argued her people's case in front of audiences across the East.
>
> **When and where:** Nevada, and the lecture halls of the East, in the 1870s and 1880s.

Sarah Winnemucca worked as an interpreter, a person who puts spoken words from one language into another.

Just before Christmas 1878, Winnemucca learned that President Rutherford B. Hayes had ordered her people taken to the Yakama reservation under an army guard. "My people were only given one week to get ready in," she wrote. Officials were punishing the whole group because a few Paiute men had fought in the Bannock War of 1878.

In 1879 United States officials forced about 550 Northern Paiute men, women and children to move 350 miles north, from the Malheur reservation in Oregon to the Yakama reservation. The march took nearly a month through snow and over two mountain ranges. The officials in charge made some of the men walk in leg irons, chains locked around the ankles. Five children, one woman and an old man died on the road. Their bodies were left beside it because the ground was too cold to dig graves. The Oregon Historical Society's account of the march does not say who decided to leave them. The historian Sally Zanjani estimated that more than one fifth of the group died far from home after they were sent away, mostly of hunger and disease.

Winnemucca went east and gave lectures about what officials had done to her people. In 1880 she met with Secretary of the Interior Carl Schurz in Washington. He gave her a written promise that the Paiute could go back to Malheur, and then he broke it. Her people never returned there. In 1882 and 1883 President Chester Arthur ended the Malheur reservation, and white settlers could then claim its land. In 1883 she published *Life Among the Piutes: Their Wrongs and Claims*. It is the first known autobiography written by a Native American woman. An autobiography is a book a person writes about their own life. In 1884 she asked Congress to give her people back their reservation. She was also the first Native woman known to hold a United States copyright, the legal right to control who copies and sells a piece of writing.

In the mid-1880s she opened a school of her own for Paiute children near Lovelock, Nevada. The school opened in 1884 or 1885, and accounts of her life give both years. Staff at the government boarding schools forbade children to speak their own languages. At her school, Winnemucca taught in both Paiute and English.

The school ran out of money and closed within a few years.

<a id="story-zitkala-sa-native-nations"></a>

#### Zitkala-Ša

> **Who:** Yankton Dakota writer, musician, and organizer, taken as a child to a boarding school in Indiana.
>
> **When and where:** the Yankton reservation, South Dakota, and Washington, D.C. Born February 22, 1876. Died January 26, 1938.

Zitkala-Ša wrote about how she left home in her essay "The Big Red Apples." She was in her eighth year, in March, when two white missionaries came to her village on the Yankton reservation. Her mother told her they had come "to take away Indian boys and girls to the East." A young white interpreter told the girl she could pick all the red apples she wanted and ride on "the iron horse," a train. "I had never seen a train, and he knew it," she wrote. She begged to go. Her mother warned her, "Their words are sweet, but, my child, their deeds are bitter." Then her mother agreed. The missionaries took the girl to White's Indiana Manual Labor Institute. The essay does not name them.

In 1900 the editors of the *Atlantic Monthly*, a magazine, published a set of her essays about her own life. One of them was "The School Days of an Indian Girl." In the essays she described her time at the school and criticized it. She was working at Carlisle when she published them. In 1921 they appeared again in her book *American Indian Stories*.

In 1926 she helped start the National Council of American Indians, and she led it until she died in 1938.

#### The Ghost Dance and Wounded Knee

On January 1, 1889, a Northern Paiute man named Wovoka, from the Walker Lake country of Nevada, had a vision. It came during a solar eclipse, when the moon blocked the sun. He taught that if people lived rightly and danced a round dance, a dance in which people move in a circle, the dead would return and the world would be made whole.

On reservations where people were hungry, they took up the dance, which became known as the Ghost Dance. Indian agents who were frightened by it called it the start of an uprising, meaning an armed revolt. Newspaper writers printed frightening stories that said the same.

Indian police killed Sitting Bull at Standing Rock on December 15, 1890, while they were trying to arrest him.

On December 29, 1890, soldiers of the 7th Cavalry under Colonel James W. Forsyth were disarming Spotted Elk's band, also called Big Foot's band, at Wounded Knee Creek. Disarming means taking away people's weapons. A band is a group of families who live and travel together. During the disarming, a rifle belonging to Black Coyote, a deaf man, went off. By some accounts he fired first, and by others a soldier tried to grab his gun and it went off. The soldiers opened fire.

They fired carbines, which are short rifles, and four Hotchkiss guns, which are small cannon, set on a hill above the camp. The soldiers killed between 250 and 300 Lakota people. In early January 1891 a burial party put 146 of the dead in one grave at the site. They were 84 men and boys, 44 women and 18 children. Others died later of their wounds, and some bodies were never found, so no count gives the women and children among all the dead. The killing is known as the Wounded Knee Massacre. Twenty-five soldiers also died. Writers for Britannica and History.com say that most of those soldiers were hit by their own side's fire. Twenty soldiers of the 7th Cavalry received the Medal of Honor for what they did that day. The Medal of Honor is the top award the United States military gives for bravery in battle. Some of the medal statements praise soldiers for driving out "Sioux Indians" who were hiding in a ravine, a narrow, steep valley.

In 1900 census takers counted about 250,000 Native people in the United States. That is the lowest number on record for the Native population.

### 1900 to 1950

In 1900 the United States census, the official count of everyone in the country, counted about 250,000 Native people. No United States census has recorded a lower number.

Between 1900 and 1950, Native people founded national organizations that they ran themselves, starting with the Society of American Indians in 1911. Oil was found under Osage land in Oklahoma, and Osage people became rich from it. In 1921 members of Congress passed a law that put many Osage adults' money under white guardians, people given legal control of someone else's money, whom judges in local courts appointed. Guardians and husbands stole the money. In the early 1920s, Osage people who held headrights, equal shares of the nation's oil money, were murdered or died in ways that looked like murder. Counts of the dead run from about 24 to more than sixty. Federal agents proved that a cattle rancher named William Hale had ordered several of the killings. In 1929 he was sentenced to life in prison.

In 1924 members of Congress made every Native person born in the country a citizen. Ten years later they ended allotment, the cutting of nations' shared land into private pieces, which federal officials had carried out since 1887.

Native men fought for the United States in both world wars. In 1918 Choctaw soldiers passed orders in Choctaw, and German soldiers tapping the telephone lines could not read them. From 1942 Navajo Marines sent messages in a code built from Navajo, and no enemy ever broke it.

Through all fifty years, federal boarding schools stayed open, and federal officials still took tens of thousands of children from their homes to them every year.

#### Organizing

On October 12, 1911, a group of Native doctors, lawyers and writers met in Columbus, Ohio, and founded the Society of American Indians. It was the first national Native rights organization that Native people built and ran themselves. Its leaders included Dr. Charles Eastman, who was Santee Dakota, and Dr. Carlos Montezuma, who was Yavapai-Apache. Zitkala-Ša edited its journal.

Many of the members had gone through the boarding schools, and some of them used that schooling to argue against federal Indian policy. The Society lasted from 1911 to 1923.

In 1912 twelve men and one woman founded the Alaska Native Brotherhood at Sitka. They wanted citizenship for Alaska Natives. The Alaska Native Sisterhood began in 1915. For the next fifty years, these two groups were the only civil rights organizations Alaska Natives had. Civil rights are the rights every citizen has to equal treatment under the law.

On November 16, 1944, eighty delegates from more than fifty tribes and associations met in Denver. Delegates are people chosen to speak for a group. At that meeting they founded the National Congress of American Indians. Native nations still use it as one of their main ways to act together.

#### High steel

Mohawk men from Kahnawake had worked on structural iron since the 1880s. Structural iron is the metal frame that holds up a bridge or a tall building. In 1930 and 1931, Kahnawake crews worked on the riveting gangs that put up the Empire State Building in New York. A riveting gang joined the steel beams together with hot metal pins called rivets.

Kahnawake ironworkers kept building towers in Manhattan for generations. One of them, Harold McComber, is the subject of *High Steel*. Don Owen directed that documentary film for the National Film Board of Canada in 1965.

#### The Osage and the Reign of Terror

In the 1920s Osage people in Oklahoma earned so much from oil that they were among the wealthiest people in the world, counted per person. White guardians and some of the men who married Osage women stole that money, and killers murdered Osage people to get it.

In 1906 Osage leaders, led by Chief James Bigheart, won their own terms in the Osage Allotment Act, which members of Congress passed that year. Federal officials had forced other nations to take 160 acres a person and sell the rest of their land. The Osage divided all of their reservation among their own people instead, 657 acres each for 2,229 people. They kept the minerals under the ground as shared property. Oil companies paid royalties, which are payments for the oil they took out. Each Osage member got an equal share of that money. The share was called a headright.

In 1921 members of Congress passed a guardianship law. Under it, judges in local courts appointed white guardians over the money of many Osage adults. A guardian is a person given legal control over someone else's money. Under the law, the guardian, not the Osage owner, controlled the money. Guardians stole from the people whose money they controlled. Some of the men who married Osage women stole from their wives.

Between about 1920 and 1925, Osage headright holders died in murders and in suspicious deaths, deaths that might have been murders. Counts of the dead disagree. Osage Nation officials count more than sixty. Writers at the Oklahoma Historical Society count about 24, and FBI writers say at least two dozen.

In 1923 the Osage Tribal Council asked the federal government to send detectives. Agents of the new Bureau of Investigation, which later became the FBI, took the case. They proved that William Hale, a cattle rancher whom people called "the King of the Osage Hills," had ordered the murders of Anna Brown and members of her family so that he could inherit their oil rights. To inherit is to receive what a person owned after that person dies. Hale's nephew, Ernest Burkhart, was married to Anna's sister Mollie.

On Hale's orders, Anna Brown was shot in May 1921. Her mother, Lizzie Q. Kyle, died in July 1921, and poison was suspected. In March 1923 a bomb blew up the house of Anna's sister Rita Smith, killing Rita, her husband Bill and their servant, Nettie Brookshire. The agents also proved that Hale had Anna's cousin Henry Roan killed for insurance money.

Burkhart pleaded guilty in 1926 and was sentenced to life in prison. Another man, Kelsie Morrison, was also sentenced to life in 1926. In 1929 Hale was found guilty and sent to prison for life, and so was a man named John Ramsey. Hale, Ramsey and Burkhart were all later let out on parole, which means freed early under watch. These years are known as the Reign of Terror.

#### Citizenship and the Indian New Deal

The Indian Citizenship Act became law on June 2, 1924. Under it, every Native person born in the United States became a citizen. In some states they still could not vote, because each state's lawmakers wrote that state's voting rules. The Library of Congress records that officials in some states kept Native people from voting until 1957.

In 1928 a federal survey called the Meriam Report came out. Its full title was *The Problem of Indian Administration*. It records that under allotment, tribal land had fallen from 137 million acres to 47 million. It also records the poverty and disease Native people lived with after that loss.

The Meriam Report's writers condemned the boarding schools in detail, which means they judged the schools to be wrong and showed why. One of the things they condemned was the half-day system. Under that system, school staff made children spend half of every school day on unpaid work. That work kept the schools running.

The Indian Reorganization Act became law on June 18, 1934. It was written while John Collier was Commissioner of Indian Affairs, the federal official in charge of dealings with Native nations. Collier held that job from 1933 to 1945. In the act, members of Congress ended allotment and extended the protections on land held in trust. Land held in trust is land the United States holds on behalf of a Native nation or person.

Members of Congress also allowed up to $2,000,000 a year in the act for buying land for Native people. Nations could now write constitutions, which are written sets of a government's basic laws, and set up their own governments. After 1934 federal officials began to recognize the governments that nations set up under the act. For the forty-seven years before, since 1887, federal officials had used allotment to break nations up into single landowners.

#### The schools continue

Federal boarding schools kept running after 1900. The federal investigators counted the schools that ran between 1819 and 1969. Some kept going after that. Enrollment, the number of children in the schools, kept climbing for decades and reached its peak of about 60,000 children in 1973.

In the 1930s Collier and the officials under him moved toward day schools, where children went home at night. They allowed some teaching in Native languages, and they closed some boarding schools. Federal officials still took tens of thousands of children from their homes to the schools every year.

Chester Nez, a Navajo boy, was one of those children. Staff at the Fort Defiance boarding school washed his mouth out with soap for speaking Navajo. In 1942 Marine Corps recruiters signed him up to help build a military code in Navajo.

#### The code talkers

Code talkers were Native soldiers who sent military messages in their own languages, so that the enemy could not understand them. The first code talkers were Choctaw.

In the autumn of 1918, American soldiers were fighting in the Meuse-Argonne campaign, a long series of battles in France. German soldiers were tapping American telephone lines. They were also capturing about one in four runners, the soldiers who carried messages on foot. Choctaw soldiers of the 36th Division began passing orders in Choctaw. They sent the first secure messages, ones the Germans could not read, on October 26, 1918. When Choctaw had no word for a piece of equipment, the men made one up. A machine gun became "little gun shoot fast."

In the Second World War, Marine Corps officers had Navajo speakers do the same work. Twenty-nine Navajo recruits arrived in San Diego on May 5, 1942, and built the code. Between 350 and 420 Navajo served as code talkers, in all six Marine divisions in the Pacific. At Iwo Jima, Major Howard Connor was the 5th Division's signal officer, in charge of its messages. He said: "Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima."

No enemy ever broke the code. It stayed classified, meaning officially secret, until 1968. On July 26, 2001, the original twenty-nine received the Congressional Gold Medal, a medal that members of Congress vote to give, and the code talkers who came after them received silver medals.

<a id="story-jim-thorpe-native-nations"></a>

#### Jim Thorpe

> **Who:** Sac and Fox athlete and Carlisle student, the first Native American to win an Olympic gold medal.
>
> **When and where:** Stockholm, July 1912. Olympic officials took his medals in 1913 and named him the sole champion again in 2022.
>
> **Movie:** *Jim Thorpe – All-American* (1951)

Jim Thorpe was a citizen of the Sac and Fox Nation. He was a student at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, a federal boarding school in Pennsylvania. There he was twice named a football All-American, one of the best college football players in the country.

At the Stockholm Olympics in 1912, he won the pentathlon on July 7 and the decathlon on July 15. The pentathlon is a contest of five track and field events, and the decathlon is a contest of ten. His decathlon score stood as the world record until 1927.

In 1913 Olympic officials took both medals back. In 1909 and 1910 Thorpe had played minor-league baseball for a reported two dollars a game, up to $35 a week. The Olympic rules of the time allowed only amateurs, athletes who are not paid to play. In October 1982 officials of the International Olympic Committee named him co-champion, sharing the titles with Hugo Wieslander in the decathlon and Ferdinand Bie in the pentathlon. On July 15, 2022, 110 years to the day after his decathlon win, they named him the sole champion of both events.

<a id="story-ira-hayes"></a>

#### Ira Hayes

> **Who:** Akimel O'odham (Pima) Marine from the Gila River community in Arizona, one of the six men who raised the second flag on Mount Suribachi.
>
> **When and where:** Iwo Jima, February 23, 1945. He died in Arizona on January 24, 1955.
>
> **Movie:** *The Outsider* (1961). Adam Beach also plays him in *Flags of Our Fathers* (2006).

Ira Hayes was a Marine paratrooper, a soldier trained to jump from planes by parachute. He came from the Gila River Indian Community in Arizona. On February 23, 1945, on Iwo Jima, he was one of the six men who raised the second American flag on Mount Suribachi. Americans celebrated the photograph of that flag-raising.

Hayes came home to a fame he had not asked for. On May 9, 1945, he and two other men from the photograph raised a flag at a ceremony in Washington. The ceremony started a tour to sell war bonds, which were loans people made to the government to pay for the war. Later that month the Marines ordered Hayes back to his unit. Americans celebrated the photograph, but Hayes got little help after the war. Police arrested him 52 times for being drunk in public. Years later President Dwight Eisenhower met him and called him a hero.

On the morning of January 24, 1955, Ira Hayes was found dead near an empty mud-brick hut close to his home at Sacaton, in the Gila River community. He had been drinking the night before. The coroner, the official who decides how a person died, gave the cause as exposure and alcohol poisoning. Dying of exposure means dying from being left out in the cold or in other harsh weather without shelter. He was 32.

<a id="story-chester-nez-native-nations"></a>

#### Chester Nez

> **Who:** Navajo Marine, one of the twenty-nine who built the code. As a boarding-school student, he was punished for speaking the language the code was made from.
>
> **When and where:** the Fort Defiance boarding school, Arizona, then the Pacific, 1942 to 1945. He died June 4, 2014.

When Chester Nez spoke Navajo at the Fort Defiance boarding school, staff washed his mouth out with soap.

In 1942 Marine Corps recruiters signed Nez up. He was one of the twenty-nine who went to San Diego and built the code out of the language.

He wrote about what happened to him in *Code Talker*, a memoir published in 2011 with Judith Schiess Avila. A memoir is a book about the writer's own life. It is the only memoir by one of the original twenty-nine. Nez outlived the other twenty-eight and died on June 4, 2014.

### 1950 to 2000
