Members of Congress declared in 1953 that the United States should end its recognition of Native nations. Recognition means that United States officials deal with a nation as a government. Twenty-two years later, in 1975, President Ford signed a law under which Native nations could take control of their own schools, clinics and police.

The Menominee, whose nation members of Congress had terminated, meaning they had ended its recognition, organized until members of Congress restored it. Fishermen in the Northwest kept fishing until a federal judge ruled on their 1850s treaties, the written agreements their nations had made with the United States. A group called Indians of All Tribes took Alcatraz Island and held it for nineteen months. In 1980, in the Sioux Nation's Black Hills case, the justices of the Supreme Court ruled that United States officials had broken the 1868 treaty when they took the hills.

#### Termination and relocation

On August 1, 1953, members of Congress passed House Concurrent Resolution 108. A resolution is a formal statement of policy that members of Congress vote on. In this one they declared that the United States should end its recognition of Native nations, along with the federal services that came with it. The policy's name was termination. Termination meant that members of Congress and federal officials stopped treating a tribe as a nation with its own government, and the tribe lost its federal services.

Between 1953 and 1970, members of Congress ran about sixty termination proceedings, the formal legal steps that ended a nation's recognition. Those proceedings covered more than a hundred tribes and bands. More than 3 million acres of land stopped being held in trust, which meant the United States no longer held that land on the nations' behalf.

The Menominee of Wisconsin ran a profitable timber business. Members of Congress passed the Menominee termination act in 1954. It took effect in 1961, and the Menominee, who had done well before, became poor. Menominee people organized a movement called DRUMS, with Ada Deer among its leaders. They kept pushing until members of Congress reversed the termination. The Menominee Restoration Act became law on December 22, 1973.

In the same years, officials of the Bureau of Indian Affairs moved Native people off reservations and into cities. The Bureau of Indian Affairs is the federal agency in charge of Indian affairs. Its officials began this relocation program between about 1948 and 1952. Members of Congress backed it with the Indian Relocation Act of 1956. People who signed up got a one-way ticket and short-term help. About 30,000 people moved in the 1950s, and more than 100,000 had moved by the time the program ended in the 1970s.

Many of them lived in poverty in the cities. They also built lasting Native communities in Minneapolis, Chicago, Oakland and San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Denver. The next Native movement started in those cities.

#### Red Power

In July 1968, in Minneapolis, George Mitchell, Dennis Banks, Clyde Bellecourt and about 200 other people founded the American Indian Movement, known as AIM. Its members began with street patrols against police abuse. Many Native people had moved to Minneapolis under relocation.

On November 20, 1969, a group calling itself Indians of All Tribes landed on Alcatraz Island in San Francisco Bay. They occupied the island's federal prison, which had been closed since 1963. Occupied means they moved in and held it. Richard Oakes, who was Mohawk, was among the leaders. In their proclamation, a public statement, they offered to buy the island for "$24 in glass beads and red cloth." They held it for nineteen months, until June 11, 1971.

After the occupation began, President Nixon ended termination as federal policy. On December 15, 1970, he signed a law that members of Congress had passed, H.R. 471, which gave Blue Lake and 48,000 acres of sacred land back to Taos Pueblo.

On December 18, 1971, the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act became law. Under it, Alaska Native land claims were settled for 44 million acres and $962.5 million. To settle a claim is to end it by agreement. The land and money went to twelve regional corporations, later thirteen, and to more than 200 village corporations. A corporation is a business, and the people who own it are called its shareholders. Alaska Natives became the shareholders.

In 1973 about 200 Oglala Lakota and AIM members occupied the village of Wounded Knee, on the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota. They chose it because soldiers of the 7th Cavalry, an army unit of soldiers on horseback, had killed between 250 and 300 Lakota people there in 1890. Of the 146 dead whom a burial party put in one grave there, 62 were women and children. The occupiers held the village for seventy-one days, from February 27 to May 8, against federal marshals and FBI agents, who surrounded it with armored vehicles. Federal marshals are officers who carry out the orders of the national courts. The FBI is the national police force that looks into federal crimes. The occupiers were protesting against the tribal chairman at Pine Ridge and against the treaties that United States officials had broken.

Both sides fired shots during the siege, the seventy-one days in which federal forces surrounded the village. Early in the siege, someone shot US Marshal Lloyd Grimm, and afterward he could not move his legs. Accounts of the siege do not say who shot him. On April 17 Frank Clearwater, an Eastern Cherokee man, was shot in the head while he rested in a church during a gunfight with federal forces. He died on April 25. In 2000 the FBI released a report on deaths on the Pine Ridge Reservation. It found that Clearwater was killed by gunfire from federal officers, who were firing back after people shot at them. On April 26 a federal agent firing as a sniper, a hidden marksman, shot and killed Lawrence "Buddy" Lamont, an Oglala man, with a bullet through the heart. In 1974 Judge Fred Nichol threw out the charges against the AIM leaders Dennis Banks and Russell Means. He wrote that "the misconduct by the government in this case is so aggravated that a dismissal must be entered in the interests of justice." Misconduct means breaking the rules.

#### The fish-ins and the Boldt decision

In the 1850s leaders of the Northwest nations signed treaties with Isaac Stevens, the governor of Washington Territory. In them they gave up land and kept the right to fish. The Treaty of Medicine Creek, signed by the Nisqually, the Puyallup and other nations on December 26, 1854, says that "the right of taking fish, at all usual and accustomed grounds and stations, is further secured to said Indians." That means the treaty protected their right to keep fishing at all the places where they had always fished. A century later, Washington State officers were arresting their people for fishing.

Through the 1960s and into the 1970s, the Nisqually, the Puyallup and other nations held fish-ins. At a fish-in, people fished in the open, in front of the state's officers, and let themselves be arrested. They did it to force the treaties into a courtroom. Frank's Landing on the Nisqually River was the center of the fish-ins.

Judge George Boldt heard the treaty case, *United States v. Washington*, in federal court. On February 12, 1974, he ruled that the treaty rights still stood. Under them, the tribes had a right to half the harvestable salmon, the salmon that could be caught each year. He also ruled that the tribes were co-managers of the fishery, the salmon catch and the waters it comes from. That means tribal governments and the state run it together. The justices of the Supreme Court upheld the ruling in 1979, which means they let it stand.

#### The Black Hills

In the Fort Laramie treaty of 1868, United States officials guaranteed the Black Hills of South Dakota to the Lakota. In 1874 members of an Army expedition led by George Custer announced that they had found gold there. United States officials ignored the treaty and took the hills.

The Lakota call one mountain in the Black Hills Tunkasila Sakpe, the Six Grandfathers. It is the mountain known in English as Mount Rushmore.

In 1980, in *United States v. Sioux Nation*, the justices of the Supreme Court held that United States officials had broken the treaty when they took the hills. They awarded the Lakota compensation, which is money paid to make up for a loss.

The Lakota have refused the money. With the interest it has earned, it is now more than a billion dollars. Lakota leaders say that the Black Hills were never for sale.

#### Nations run their own programs

President Ford signed the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act in January 1975. Self-determination means a nation deciding its own affairs. Under the act, a nation could sign a contract with the federal government and run federal programs itself, such as its own schools, clinics and police. The word Education is in the act's name because schools were at the center of it.

For decades before 1978, workers at agencies took Native children from their families. Writers at the National Indian Child Welfare Association state that 25 to 35 percent of Native children were taken. They also state that 85 percent of them were placed outside their families, even when relatives or members of their tribe could care for them. In 1978 members of Congress passed the Indian Child Welfare Act. In it they set federal standards for those cases, meant to keep Native children with Native families. They also gave tribal courts the power to decide the cases.

In the same years, doctors at Indian Health Service hospitals sterilized thousands of Native women. The Indian Health Service is the federal agency that runs hospitals and clinics for Native people. Sterilization is an operation after which a woman can never become pregnant. The doctors at these hospitals did two kinds of operation. In a tubal ligation, a surgeon cuts or ties the two tubes that carry eggs to the womb. In a hysterectomy, the surgeon cuts out the womb.

Investigators from the General Accounting Office, a federal office, studied 4 of the agency's 12 areas. In 1976 they reported 3,406 sterilizations of Native women there from 1973 to 1976. Writers at the National Library of Medicine state that the women had not given their permission. The investigators' report does not name the doctors. No surviving record says how many of the women had each kind of operation.

Thirty-six of the women were under 21, although a court had ordered a stop to sterilizing women that young. Two years before the report, Dr. Connie Pinkerton-Uri, a Choctaw and Cherokee doctor, had found that one in four Native women had been sterilized without agreeing to it.

The Indian Gaming Regulatory Act became law on October 17, 1988. Gaming means gambling businesses, such as casinos. The act sorts tribal gaming into three classes of games. It lets a nation and a state make a compact, a formal agreement about the games. It also set up the National Indian Gaming Commission to watch over tribal gaming. For some nations gaming became a large source of income. The amount varies a great deal from nation to nation.

The Native American Graves Protection and Repatriation Act, known as NAGPRA, became law on November 16, 1990, when President George H. W. Bush signed it. Under it, Native human remains and sacred objects held in museums and federal collections belong to the nations and families they came from. The act requires the people holding them to send them back. Repatriation means sending them home.

#### Nations take the schools back

Navajo leaders founded a college of their own at Tsaile, Arizona, in 1968. It was called Navajo Community College, and today it is Diné College. It was the first college in the country controlled by a Native nation. Native nations have founded dozens of tribal colleges since.

In November 1969 the senators on a Senate subcommittee on Indian education published their report. A subcommittee is a small group of senators assigned to one subject. The report's title is *Indian Education: A National Tragedy, A National Challenge*. It is known as the Kennedy Report, because Senator Robert F. Kennedy led the work at first and Senator Edward Kennedy finished it.

The report states that federal policy had been "coercive assimilation" with "disastrous effects." Coercive assimilation means forcing a group of people to give up their own language and ways of life. Its authors called for Native people to run Native schools.

Boarding-school enrollment peaked at about 60,000 children in 1973. After that it fell, as the leaders of Native nations took over schools under the 1975 law and other schools closed. A few boarding schools are still open. Tribes or the federal Bureau of Indian Education, the federal office in charge of Indian schools, run them. People who had been children at the schools began publishing accounts of what had happened to them there.

<a id="story-wilma-mankiller"></a>

#### Wilma Mankiller

> **Who:** the first woman elected Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation.
>
> **When and where:** Cherokee Nation, Oklahoma. She was chief from December 14, 1985 to August 14, 1995.
>
> **Movie:** *Mankiller* (2017)

Wilma Mankiller was a child when her family moved to San Francisco under the relocation program. In 1969 Indians of All Tribes took Alcatraz, and she joined the movement during the occupation.

She went back to Oklahoma. There she worked on projects in which Cherokee communities built their own water lines and health clinics, with the people who lived there doing the work.

On December 14, 1985, when Ross Swimmer left the office, she became Principal Chief of the Cherokee Nation. The principal chief is the head of the Cherokee Nation's government. Cherokee voters elected her in her own right in 1987 and re-elected her in 1991 with 83 percent of the vote. Until August 14, 1995, she led a nation of about 140,000 citizens. In 1998 she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, an award given by the president of the United States. Mankiller died on April 6, 2010.

<a id="story-billy-frank-jr-native-nations"></a>

#### Billy Frank Jr.

> **Who:** Nisqually fisherman. Washington State officers arrested him more than fifty times for fishing under his nation's treaty.
>
> **When and where:** Frank's Landing on the Nisqually River, Washington. He was first arrested at fourteen.

Billy Frank Jr. was fourteen the first time officers arrested him for fishing the Nisqually River. In all, he was arrested more than fifty times.

In the Treaty of Medicine Creek of 1854, the Nisqually kept "the right of taking fish" at all the places where they had always fished. Washington State officers arrested him anyway. He kept fishing, and in the 1960s and 1970s he and others staged fish-ins at Frank's Landing and were arrested again and again.

The fish-ins ended in the Boldt decision of 1974. Later Frank chaired the Northwest Indian Fisheries Commission.

He died in May 2014, and in 2015 he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom after his death. As of 2026, Washington State officials planned to place his statue in the National Statuary Hall in the United States Capitol.

<a id="story-adam-fortunate-eagle"></a>

#### Adam Fortunate Eagle

> **Who:** Ojibwe writer. He was a Pipestone boarding-school student who became a lead organizer of the Alcatraz occupation.
>
> **When and where:** Pipestone Indian Boarding School, Minnesota, 1935 to 1945. San Francisco Bay, 1969 to 1971.

Adam Fortunate Eagle spent ten years at the Pipestone Indian Boarding School in Minnesota, from 1935 to 1945. In those years John Collier was Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and federal officials were changing some of the schools. Three decades later, Fortunate Eagle was one of the lead organizers of the occupation of Alcatraz.

In 2010 he published his account of the school, *Pipestone: My Life in an Indian Boarding School*. In it he calls his school days there "a little bit of heaven." In the same book he writes about the harm the boarding-school system did.

Other people who were children at the schools told it differently. Staff at the Fort Defiance school washed Chester Nez's mouth out with soap for speaking Navajo. In 1900 Zitkala-Ša published essays about her own school that criticized it.

### 2000 to Today

There are 574 federally recognized Native nations in the United States. Federally recognized means that United States officials deal with the nation as a government. Each of these nations has its own government.

There are also nations recognized by their states, and nations still working to win federal recognition. More than 200 Alaska Native villages have their own corporations. Native Hawaiians have no federally recognized government of their own.

In the 2020 census, 9.7 million people identified as American Indian or Alaska Native, alone or together with another group. That was 2.9 percent of the people in the country. In 1900 the census had counted about 250,000.

The Navajo Nation's land covers more than 27,000 square miles across Arizona, New Mexico and Utah. It is the largest reservation in the country. The number of Cherokee Nation citizens passed 450,000 in 2023, counting enrolled citizens, people officially listed as members. Some counts in 2024 and 2025 put it above 475,000.

On September 21, 2004, the National Museum of the American Indian opened on the National Mall in Washington. About 25,000 Native people from across North and South America walked in the opening procession.

#### Sovereignty in court and in office

Sovereignty is the right of a nation to govern itself. When United States officials forced the Muscogee (Creek) Nation to move to Oklahoma, they promised it a reservation there. On July 9, 2020, the justices of the Supreme Court decided *McGirt v. Oklahoma*, a case about whether that reservation still existed. Five of the nine justices held that members of Congress had never ended it. Four justices disagreed.

Under the ruling, about 3.25 million acres of eastern Oklahoma, including much of Tulsa, are still reservation land. That matters for federal criminal law, the national laws about crimes. Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote the opinion, the written decision of the court. Its first sentence is: "On the far end of the Trail of Tears was a promise." The Trail of Tears was the forced removal of the Cherokee and the other Southeastern nations to Indian Territory, in what is now Oklahoma, in the 1830s. In later rulings, judges applied the same reasoning to the reservations of the other nations that United States officials had forced out of the Southeast.

On June 15, 2023, in *Haaland v. Brackeen*, seven of the nine justices upheld the Indian Child Welfare Act, which means they kept it in force. The people challenging the act had claimed that it broke the Constitution. Two justices disagreed with the ruling.

In 2018 Deb Haaland of Laguna Pueblo and Sharice Davids, who is Ho-Chunk, became the first Native American women elected to Congress. On March 15, 2021, members of the Senate voted to approve Haaland as Secretary of the Interior. The Secretary of the Interior heads the federal department in charge of the government's dealings with Native nations. She was the first Native American to hold a cabinet office, the job of heading one of the main federal departments.

#### Standing Rock and land back

In 2016 leaders of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe opposed the Dakota Access Pipeline, a long pipe built to carry oil. Its route ran under Lake Oahe, upstream of the reservation. The lake is the reservation's water supply.

From April 2016, people set up camps, among them one called Oceti Sakowin. Young people carried the tribe's message on foot. They ran a 500-mile relay to the office of the Army Corps of Engineers in Omaha, and then a 2,000-mile run to Washington, D.C. The Army Corps of Engineers is the part of the army whose permission the pipeline needed. Thousands of people came to the camps. News reports at the time called the camps the largest gathering of Native nations in more than a century.

North Dakota's governor, Jack Dalrymple, declared an emergency in August 2016 and put the Morton County Sheriff's Office and other police forces under one command. On November 20, 2016, at the Backwater Bridge, officers fired tear gas, rubber bullets and bags filled with lead into a crowd of protesters. They also sprayed the protesters with a fire hose.

A protester named Sophia Wilansky was hit that night. In 2026 the judges of a federal appeals court set out her account, which they accepted as true for her appeal. Officers Dvorak, Arndt and Hanson fired rounds at her as she ducked behind a metal sheet, and one hit her arm. She ran. About 30 yards away, Officer Jonathan Moll fired a round called an aerial warning munition, which the judges described as an exploding flash-bang inside a bullet made to hurt rather than kill. "It tore the flesh off her arm, and she fell to the ground," the judges wrote. "Her left hand and forearm are permanently and severely injured." Federal judges threw out her lawsuits and those of the other injured protesters, and no officer was held responsible.

On December 4, 2016, an Army official, the Assistant Secretary for Civil Works, turned down the easement. An easement is the legal permission the pipeline needed to cross under the lake. That same week, more than 2,000 United States military veterans arrived to stand with the camps. On January 24, 2017, President Donald Trump ordered the Army to approve the pipeline quickly. Army officials granted the easement on February 8, 2017, and oil has moved through the pipeline since June 2017. In 2020 a federal judge cancelled the easement, but the oil kept flowing for about five years without one. In 2026 Army officials granted the easement again, and in June 2026 the tribe's leaders asked the court to end their own appeal.

Some land has gone back to Native nations. In 1908 federal officials took 18,800 acres out of the Flathead Reservation in Montana for the National Bison Range, a federal wildlife refuge. A wildlife refuge is land set aside to protect wild animals. In December 2020 members of Congress passed a law that gave the range back to the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes, and the tribes took over running it in 2022.

#### The boarding-school investigation

In June 2021 Secretary Haaland started an investigation of the boarding schools. Earlier officials of her own department had run them.

The first volume of the investigators' report came out in May 2022. It identifies 408 federal schools, and marked and unmarked burial sites at 53 of them. The final volume came out on July 30, 2024. It lists 417 federal Indian boarding schools in 37 states or places that were then territories, open from 1819 to 1969. It also lists 1,025 more places with similar aims that fell outside the four rules the investigators used to count federal schools.

The report records what school staff did to the children. Staff cut the children's hair, replaced their clothes with uniforms, and gave them English names. They forbade the children to speak the languages they had grown up speaking. The punishments the report records for speaking those languages include beatings, solitary confinement, holding back food, and washing children's mouths out with soap. Solitary confinement means being locked up alone.

At least 973 children died at the schools. The investigators found at least 74 burial sites at 65 schools. The report states that the real number of deaths is higher than the number the investigators could count.

On October 25, 2024, President Biden apologized on behalf of the United States for the boarding-school system. He spoke at the Gila River Indian Community in Arizona, which was Ira Hayes's home community. It was the first formal presidential apology for the system. He called the system "a sin on our soul."

Children who died at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School are buried in a cemetery at the Carlisle Barracks, an Army post. Army officials have been digging up the children's remains and returning them to their nations. In 2017 they returned two children, Little Chief and Horse, to the Northern Arapaho. When they opened the grave of a third child, Little Plume, they found two other children in it. They found Little Plume and returned him the next year. In July 2021 nine Rosebud Sioux children went home to South Dakota, and Rosebud young people escorted them.

#### Languages come home

Boarding-school staff punished children for speaking Native languages. In the two world wars, soldiers used two of those languages, Choctaw and Navajo, to send messages the enemy could not read. Today Native nations run schools that teach children in their own languages.

In Hawaii, lawmakers banned teaching in Hawaiian in a law dating from 1896. In 1984 the first Pūnana Leo immersion preschool opened at Kekaha on Kaua'i. In an immersion school, teachers give every lesson in the language itself, so children learn arithmetic and reading in Hawaiian instead of learning Hawaiian as one subject. The Pūnana Leo schools were the first Indigenous-language immersion preschools in the United States. Indigenous means belonging to the people who lived in a place first.

The ban on teaching in Hawaiian was lifted in 1986, and the first public immersion classes opened in 1987. According to ʻAha Pūnana Leo, the group that started the Pūnana Leo schools, students can now be taught in Hawaiian from preschool through graduate school, the university study that comes after a first degree.

Wôpanâak, the Wampanoag language of Massachusetts, had no living speakers after the middle of the 1800s. In 1993 Jessie Little Doe Baird helped found the Wôpanâak Language Reclamation Project, and she began rebuilding the language from documents written in it. Reclamation means taking something back. Wôpanâak is the first American language with no living speakers to come back into living use. In September 2016 the project opened Mukayuhsak Weekuw, the Children's House, a school in Mashpee where Wampanoag children are taught mostly in Wôpanâak.

Cherokee, Lakota, Diné and many other nations run immersion schools of their own.

<a id="story-deb-haaland-native-nations"></a>

#### Deb Haaland

> **Who:** Laguna Pueblo. She was one of the first two Native American women elected to Congress, and the first Native American cabinet secretary.
>
> **When and where:** New Mexico and Washington, D.C., from 2018.

Deb Haaland is a citizen of Laguna Pueblo. She describes herself as a 35th-generation New Mexican. In 2018 she and Sharice Davids became the first Native American women elected to Congress.

On March 15, 2021, members of the Senate voted to approve her as Secretary of the Interior. She was the first Native American to run a cabinet department. Earlier officials of that department had run the federal boarding schools.

By her own account, her grandparents were taken to boarding school as children. Her account does not name who took them. In June 2021 she ordered officials of her department to investigate the department's own record and count what its officials had done. They published the final count on July 30, 2024, while she was still the secretary.

<a id="story-jessie-little-doe-baird"></a>

#### Jessie Little Doe Baird

> **Who:** Mashpee Wampanoag social worker who became a linguist and brought back a language that no one had spoken since the middle of the 1800s.
>
> **When and where:** Mashpee, Massachusetts, from 1993.
>
> **Movie:** *We Still Live Here: Âs Nutayuneân* (2011)

By her own account, the work began with a dream about the language.

The language had no living speakers after the middle of the 1800s. Written records of it survived. Among them was the Eliot Bible, a Bible printed in Wôpanâak in 1663. Baird used that Bible and the other documents to rebuild the language.

She helped found the Wôpanâak Language Reclamation Project in 1993. She went to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and earned a degree in linguistics, the study of how languages work. She raised her daughter speaking Wôpanâak. In 2010 she received a MacArthur Fellowship, a prize that the MacArthur Foundation gives to people for their work.

Since September 2016, Wampanoag children have been taught mostly in Wôpanâak at Mukayuhsak Weekuw, a school run by the project she helped found.

<a id="ch-land-environment"></a>

## Chapter 3: Land and Environment

### Before 1500

Before 1500, the Native nations of North America managed the land they lived on. In the eastern forests, people set fires on purpose to keep the woods open and to grow food for the animals they hunted. Farmers planted crops together in ways that kept the soil in good condition. In southwest Florida, the Calusa built pens in the water to hold live fish.

Beavers dammed streams across the continent. Bison grazed the Plains. Nobody knows how many bison lived there before 1500. The figure usually given is for a much later time: about 30 million in the early 1800s, before hunters killed off the herds.

#### Fire as a tool

For thousands of years, Native people in what is now the eastern United States burned their forests on purpose. They set low fires in the understory, the layer of brush and small plants under the tall trees. They burned the same ground again and again. The repeated fires kept the woods open and helped oaks and other trees that can live through fire. Food plants grew back after each burn, and the burns produced food for the game animals that people hunted. Game means wild animals hunted for food.

In 2019, researchers at Penn State, a university in Pennsylvania, published a study in the journal *Annals of Forest Science*. They found that which trees grew in the eastern forests depended more on Native burning than on the climate. Climate is the usual weather of a place over many years. Even small groups of people burned large areas, over and over. European colonists treated this burning as unimportant.

In the 1900s, officials of the US Forest Service tried to put out every forest fire. The Penn State researchers call the total stopping of fires after about 1940 "an ecologically transformative event in all forests." Ecology is the study of how living things depend on each other and on the land, and transformative means causing a big change.

#### Three crops in one field

Native farmers grew corn, beans and squash together in the same field. The three crops are known as the Three Sisters. The beans put nitrogen into the soil. Nitrogen is a natural substance that plants take up from the soil to grow. The wide squash leaves shaded the ground and held the soil in place. The tall corn stalks gave the bean vines something to climb.

Growing the three crops together kept the soil in good condition. A field planted with only one crop, year after year, wears out.

#### Beavers, bison and fish pens

Beavers changed whole watersheds. A watershed is all the land that drains into one stream or river. Beaver dams held back water in ponds. The ponds slowed floods, and the wet ground around them became wet meadows. Estimates of how many beavers lived in North America before the fur trade run from 60 million to 400 million. These numbers are estimates, because nobody counted the beavers. The fur trade was the buying and selling of animal skins between European traders and Native trappers.

Bison lived on the Plains, the wide grasslands in the middle of the continent. About 30 million bison lived there in the early 1800s. Estimates for the years before Europeans came are less certain.

In what is now southwest Florida, the Calusa people built watercourts between 1300 and 1400. Watercourts were pens in the water that held live fish until people needed them for food.

### The 1500s

Ships from Europe brought pigs, horses, cattle and earthworms to the Americas. Pigs that escaped from the Spanish explorer Hernando de Soto and his men went wild in the Southeast. European earthworms moved into northern forests that had no worms before.

After 1492, most of the Native people of the Americas died. Most died of diseases carried by European settlers and by enslaved Africans. European soldiers and settlers killed others in wars to take Native lands, and many starved. Enslaved people were held as property and forced to work without pay. Forest grew back over the farmland of the people who died.

#### Pigs, horses and cattle

Pigs that escaped from Hernando de Soto's herd became the ancestors of the feral hogs of the Southeast. Feral hogs are pigs from farm stock that live in the wild.

De Soto landed near Tampa Bay, in what is now Florida, in May 1539. He brought about 600 men and a herd of pigs. An expedition is a journey made by a group for a purpose. Chronicles, the written histories of de Soto's expedition, list the first herd as 13 pigs. By the time de Soto died in 1542, the herd had grown to about 700. That count leaves out the pigs the men ate or gave away and the pigs that escaped.

Horses and cattle came with the Spanish. Columbus brought horses on his second voyage, in 1493. Spanish colonists brought horses and cattle to their colony in New Mexico in 1598.

#### Earthworms

Before Europeans came, the forests of northern North America had no earthworms. Glaciers, thick sheets of ice that once covered the north, had scraped the ground bare of them. For roughly the last 12,000 years, the forests that grew back after the ice stood on a thick, soft layer of fallen leaves called duff. Native wildflowers and young trees grew in the duff.

European earthworms crossed the ocean hidden in ballast soil. Ballast is heavy material carried low in a ship to keep it steady. Worms also came in the soil around the roots of plants brought from Europe. Later they spread west with wagons, horses and farms. Where European worms move into a northern forest, they eat the duff that the wildflowers and young trees need.

#### Forest over lost farms

After 1492, most of the Native people of the Americas died from epidemics and famine or were killed in war. An epidemic is a disease that spreads quickly to many people. A famine is a lack of food so great that people starve. European settlers brought the diseases, and so did enslaved Africans whom Europeans had carried across the ocean. The diseases included smallpox, measles and influenza, and Native people had never been exposed to any of them before. European soldiers and settlers made war on Native nations to take their land, and they enslaved Native people. Famine followed when too few people were well enough to farm.

In 2019, a team of researchers at University College London, in England, published an estimate of what those deaths did to the land. They estimated that the Native population of the Americas fell from about 60 million to about 6 million within roughly a hundred years. Other estimates of the starting number differ. For North America north of Mexico alone, estimates run from 1 million to 18 million.

The team estimated that about 55.8 million hectares of farmland grew back into forest after its farmers died. A hectare is a square of land 100 meters long on each side. The new trees took carbon dioxide, a gas that traps heat, out of the air. The team estimated that the regrowth lowered the carbon dioxide in the air by 7 to 10 parts in every million parts of air, and cooled the whole planet by about 0.15 degrees Celsius. That is about a quarter of a degree on the Fahrenheit scale used in American weather reports. All of these figures are the estimates of this one team.

### The 1600s

English colonists of the 1600s treated land as property that one owner held forever, marked off with fences and recorded in deeds. A deed is a paper that says who owns a piece of land. The Native nations of New England used their land by season. They had planting grounds, fishing places and hunting grounds, and they did not treat land as something one person owned forever. The historian William Cronon describes how English colonists and Native nations in New England used land in these different ways in his 1983 book *Changes in the Land*.

The colonists brought cattle and hogs and let them roam free. The animals got into Native planting fields, and colonists and Native people quarreled over this again and again. In 1642 the Narragansett leader Miantonomi described what the English were doing to the land. In the same century, the number of beavers began a long fall as trappers caught them for the fur trade.

#### The beaver trade

Hat makers in Europe wanted beaver fur to make felt, a thick cloth made by pressing fur together. Native trappers caught the beavers, and European traders paid for the furs with goods made in Europe. In the 1600s the number of beavers began to fall in the Northeast.

The fall went on until about 1900. By then about 100,000 beavers were left in North America, most of them in Canada. Today there are roughly 15 million. Both of these numbers are estimates.

#### The first limits on cutting trees

Under a Plymouth Colony rule of 1626, no one could cut timber on the colony's land, or sell it, without official permission. Timber is wood cut for building. It was among the earliest conservation rules in the colonies. Conservation means protecting land, water, plants and animals so that people do not use them up.

In 1681 William Penn wrote rules for settlers in Pennsylvania. For every five acres a settler cleared of trees, Penn's rules required the settler to leave one acre of trees standing. An acre is a piece of land a little smaller than a football field. The rules named oaks and mulberry trees, which were useful for silk and for ships. Settlers widely ignored this rule.

<a id="story-miantonomi"></a>

#### Miantonomi

> **Who:** A sachem, or leader, of the Narragansett nation. He put into words what English settlers were doing to the land, about one generation after they began to settle there.
>
> **When and where:** A speech to the Montaukett people on Long Island in 1642, written down by the English soldier Lion Gardener. Miantonomi lived from about 1600 to 1643.

In 1642 Miantonomi told the Montaukett people on Long Island what the English were doing to the land. English settlement in New England was then about one generation old. Miantonomi was a sachem, a leader, of the Narragansett nation.

His words were written down by Lion Gardener, an English soldier. Gardener wrote them in his *Relation*, an account he set down in 1660, years after the speech. By Gardener's record, Miantonomi said that "our fathers had plenty of deer and skins and our plains were full of game and turkeys." He said that the English "with scythes cut down the grass, and with axes fell the trees." A scythe is a tool with a long curved blade for cutting grass. To fell a tree means to cut it down. He went on: "their cows and horses eat the grass, and their hogs spoil our clam banks, and we shall all be starved."

The exact wording is Gardener's, set down by an Englishman years later. The complaints themselves match what colonists were doing at the time: cutting the forests and letting their cattle and hogs roam into Native fields.

In 1643 Uncas, the sachem of the Mohegan nation, captured Miantonomi and took him to Hartford. That September, the commissioners of the United Colonies of New England met in Boston. They were English officials from the Massachusetts Bay, Plymouth, Connecticut and New Haven colonies. They passed the case to a group of ministers, who were church leaders. Then the commissioners sentenced Miantonomi to death and handed him back to Uncas to carry out the sentence. Governor John Winthrop of Massachusetts Bay wrote in his journal that "they all agreed that he ought to be put to death." He gave their reason: "Uncas could not be safe while Miantonomo lived." Miantonomo is another spelling of Miantonomi. Mohegan men took him to the place near present-day Norwich, Connecticut, where he had been captured. There one of Uncas's men, walking behind Miantonomi, killed him with a hatchet blow to the head. Mohegan tradition and later histories name that man as Wawequa, the brother of Uncas. By the account of the historian Neal Salisbury, several Englishmen went along to make sure the killing was carried out.

### 1700 to 1750

Tobacco planters in colonial Virginia wore out the soil of a field in three or four years. Planters were people who owned large farms called plantations. When a field wore out, they cleared new ground farther up the rivers and moved on. In New England, cutting the largest white pines was against the law. The king's officials kept them for the masts of the Royal Navy, Britain's navy. By the middle of the 1700s, whalers from the island of Nantucket were sailing far out into the ocean to hunt sperm whales.

#### The king's pines

The king's officials kept the largest white pines in New England for the masts of the Royal Navy's ships. A mast is the tall pole that holds up a ship's sails. A charter is a written grant from the king or queen that sets up a colony's government. In the Massachusetts Bay charter of 1691, the rule covered every white pine 24 inches across or more.

Under the White Pine Act of 1722, cutting any white pine more than 12 inches across without a license was against the law in New Hampshire and nearby colonies. A license is written permission. The king's trees carried a mark called the Broad Arrow, which was three slashes cut with a hatchet. Royal officials enforced these laws loosely until the 1760s.

#### Worn-out tobacco fields

A tobacco field in colonial Virginia gave good crops for only three or four years. After that, planters cleared new ground and let the old field grow over with scrub, which is brush and small trees. The land around Jamestown wore out early. Planters moved up the rivers and reached the Rappahannock and the Potomac by about 1650. They kept moving up the rivers all through the 1700s. Because new land was cheap, planters kept wearing out one field after another.

The new land along the Rappahannock River was the homeland of the Rappahannock Tribe. The tribe's own history states that English settlement there began illegally in the 1640s. By that history, Rappahannock leaders sold their first land to the English in 1651. They spent more than ten years in county courts trying to get paid for that sale and others. They never received full payment. The tribe's history goes on to say that by the late 1660s, settlers and bands of settlers who acted as their own law had forced the Rappahannock to move. The tribe moved first inland on the north side of the Rappahannock River, and later to its old hunting grounds on the south side. In 1683, the history states, officials of the Virginia colony forced the tribe out of their homes and moved them to a place called Portobago Indian Town.

Indentured servants and enslaved Africans did the work in the tobacco fields. An indentured servant worked for a master for a set number of years, often four to seven, to pay for the trip to America. Planters held enslaved Africans as property and forced them to work without pay for life. Under a Virginia law of 1662, a child born to an enslaved mother was enslaved for life too. Growing tobacco took a great deal of hand work, and planters wanted more and more workers to do it.

#### Whaling from Nantucket

By the middle of the 1700s, whalers from Nantucket, an island off Massachusetts, were hunting sperm whales far out in the ocean. Before that, New Englanders hunted right whales, a kind of whale, from the beaches. On Nantucket, people tell a story that deep-sea whaling began there in 1712. In the story, wind blew Christopher Hussey's boat out to sea, and the men aboard killed a sperm whale. Obed Macy first wrote the story down in his history of Nantucket in 1835, more than 120 years later. It may be a legend. Historians at the Nantucket Historical Association call 1712 the traditional date.

### 1750 to 1800

In 1785 members of Congress ordered the land north and west of the Ohio River measured into a grid of squares. Then US officials could sell it. The Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, Miami, Ottawa, Chippewa, Potawatomi and other nations lived on that land. In January 1785, US commissioners claimed most of Ohio through a treaty signed under threat. Commissioners are officials sent to do a certain job, and a treaty is a written agreement between nations.

Surveyors measured the land under army guard. From 1790 to 1794, US generals led armies against the nations, who had joined together to stop settlement. After General Anthony Wayne's army defeated them in 1794, leaders of eleven nations signed a treaty in 1795 that handed most of Ohio to the United States.

Before independence, the king's officials had claimed New England's biggest white pines. In 1772, men in Weare, New Hampshire, beat a sheriff who came to arrest a mill owner fined for cutting them. After independence, settlers crossed the Appalachian Mountains and cleared the forest for farms.

<a id="story-ebenezer-mudgett"></a>

#### Ebenezer Mudgett

> **Who:** A sawmill owner in Weare, New Hampshire, fined for cutting the king's white pines, who led the Pine Tree Riot.
>
> **When and where:** South Weare, New Hampshire, April 13 and 14, 1772.

Ebenezer Mudgett owned a sawmill in Weare, New Hampshire. He had been fined for cutting the king's white pines, the trees kept by law for the masts of the Royal Navy.

On April 13, 1772, Sheriff Benjamin Whiting rode into South Weare with a warrant to arrest Mudgett. A warrant is a paper from a court that allows an arrest. Mudgett told him he would pay in the morning. At dawn on April 14, Mudgett came back with 20 to 30 men who had blackened their faces with soot, the black powder that smoke leaves behind. They beat the sheriff and his deputy with rods and drove them out of town. The fight became known as the Pine Tree Riot.

In September 1772, eight men stood trial in the Superior Court at Amherst, New Hampshire, for rioting and for beating Whiting. They pleaded guilty. The four judges fined each man only 20 shillings and made them pay the cost of the hearing. A shilling was a British coin. After the riot, officials mostly stopped enforcing the law that kept the pines for the navy. Some accounts count the riot as a forerunner of the Boston Tea Party, a protest in December 1773. A forerunner is an earlier event of the same kind. No one has proved that the riot led to the Tea Party.

#### The grid, 1785

On May 20, 1785, members of the Confederation Congress passed the Land Ordinance. The Confederation Congress was the national government of the United States before the Constitution. An ordinance is a law. This one specified how the public land would be sold. Public land was land that US officials claimed for the nation, and Native nations lived on much of it. Under the ordinance, surveyors had to survey that land before anyone could buy it. To survey land means to measure it and map it.

The surveyors divided the land into townships, which were squares six miles long on each side. They cut each township into 36 sections. A section was one square mile, which is 640 acres. The sections were numbered, and members of Congress set aside section 16 in every township to support public schools.

After changes to the system in 1796, surveyors carried the grid across the continent to the Pacific Ocean. People in airplanes over the Midwest can still see its checkerboard pattern on the ground.

#### Whose land the grid covered

In 1785 the land north and west of the Ohio River was the home of the Shawnee, Delaware, Wyandot, Miami, Ottawa, Chippewa, Potawatomi and other nations. George W. Knepper wrote a history of these lands, *The Official Ohio Lands Book*, for Ohio's Auditor of State, an official of the state government. He writes that, as members of Congress saw it, "Indian claims to that land had to be cleared." Here, cleared means ended, so that no Native nation still had a right to the land.

A commissioner is an official sent to do a certain job. A treaty is a written agreement between nations. In January 1785, four months before the Land Ordinance passed, US commissioners met representatives of several nations at Fort McIntosh. The commissioners made a treaty there. In it, they said that most of the Native people of Ohio had to stay inside a reserve between the Cuyahoga and Maumee rivers. A reserve is an area set aside for a nation to live on. Knepper writes that under the treaty, "Most Ohio lands would now be open for settlement."

Knepper writes that the Shawnee in particular "refused to abide by" the treaty. To abide by means to obey. He says the treaty was "negotiated under duress by minor tribal chiefs who lacked authority to speak for their people." Under duress means under threat or force.

On September 30, 1785, Thomas Hutchins began the first survey of this land for the national government. His title was Geographer of the United States. A geographer is a person who studies and maps the land. He and his crew worked in eastern Ohio, in an area called the Seven Ranges. On October 8 the crew heard news of an attack by Native people on the Tuscarawas River. Hutchins and his men stopped after only a few miles of their first line and went back to Pittsburgh.

Hutchins asked for soldiers to protect his crew. In 1786 Lieutenant Colonel Josiah Harmar, the commander of the US army, ordered Major John Francis Hamtramck and soldiers of the First American Regiment to guard the surveyors. A regiment is a large unit of soldiers. Under that guard, the crew ran a line 42 miles west from Pennsylvania, called the Geographer's Line. Then they cut the land into ranges, which are long strips, and into townships and sections. They measured the land for sale while the nations who lived on it still rejected the treaty.

In 1786, Knepper writes, US commissioners "coerced" the Shawnee into another treaty at Fort Finney. Coerced means forced.

#### The war for Ohio and the Treaty of Greenville

The nations of the region joined in a confederacy, which is a union of nations, to stop American settlement. In 1790 Josiah Harmar led a US army against them. He was the same officer who had sent soldiers to guard the surveyors, and since 1787 he had held the title of brigadier general. Warriors led by Little Turtle, a Miami war chief also known as Meshekinoquah, defeated Harmar's army.

In 1791 Major General Arthur St. Clair led another army against the confederacy. St. Clair was the governor of the Northwest Territory, the US name for the land north and west of the Ohio River. On November 4, 1791, the confederacy's warriors defeated his army at the place later called Fort Recovery. A US Army history of the campaign counts more than 900 soldiers, and women and children traveling with the army, killed or wounded. Knepper calls it "the worst defeat ever inflicted upon the U.S. Army by Indian warriors."

In 1794 Major General Anthony Wayne led an army that defeated the confederacy at the Battle of Fallen Timbers. On August 3, 1795, leaders of eleven northwestern nations signed the Treaty of Greenville. In it, a year after their defeat, they handed 16,930,417 acres to the United States. Under the treaty, the nations kept only the northwest quarter of Ohio and the lands beyond it, behind a boundary called the Greenville Treaty Line.

#### Clearing after independence

After independence, the British king no longer had any right to the white pines in the United States. Settlers crossed the Appalachian Mountains, some of them into the Northwest Territory, and cut down the forest to make farms.

### 1800 to 1850

In the first half of the 1800s, dams across the rivers of New England stopped the salmon from swimming upstream to lay their eggs. By 1850 farmers had cut down most of New England's forest, and a boom in sheep raising was one cause.

In 1832 the painter George Catlin wrote about keeping a huge park for the bison and the Plains nations, which he called "a nation's park." He meant a park that would hold both the bison and the Native nations who lived there. In these same years John James Audubon painted the birds of North America. Henry David Thoreau lived for two years in a cabin he built at Walden Pond, in Massachusetts.

#### Dams stop the fish

Atlantic salmon live in the ocean but swim up rivers to spawn, which means to lay their eggs. A dam across a river blocks them on the way. The first dam across the Connecticut River went up at Turners Falls, Massachusetts, in 1798. It cut the salmon off from the water where they spawned. By the War of 1812, no salmon came into the Connecticut River at all.

Workers for the Essex Company, a company formed to use the river's water to power mills, built the Great Stone Dam across the Merrimack River at Lawrence, Massachusetts. They finished it in 1848. It stood 30 miles from the sea, and salmon could not get past it. By 1865 the salmon runs were gone from the rivers of southern New England. A run is the yearly trip of fish up a river. The runs of shad, another fish, collapsed as well.

In 1857 the writers of a report in New Hampshire named the causes. They blamed the dams, fishing with no limits, and mill machinery that killed young fish.

#### The bare East

By 1850 New Englanders had cut down most of their forest. Estimates of how much was cleared run from about 60 percent to 80 percent of the land, and some places were cleared even more. One estimate puts the forest left in 1850 as low as a quarter of New England.

A boom in Merino sheep, a kind of sheep raised for its wool, was one cause of the clearing. By 1840 New England farmers kept about 4 million sheep, more sheep than there were people. Farmers cleared still more forest to feed them.

Across the eastern United States, the forest reached its smallest size around 1872. By then it covered roughly half the land it had covered in 1620. After that, many eastern farmers left their farms and moved west. Trees grew back on the fields they left behind.

#### A park for people and bison

In 1832 the painter George Catlin traveled far up the Missouri River, into the West. He feared that the bison and the Plains nations would be destroyed together. He wrote of "a magnificent park," which he called "a nation's park, containing man and beast, in all the wild and freshness of their nature's beauty." In Catlin's plan, the people who lived on the land would stay on it with the animals.

Forty years later, in 1872, President Ulysses S. Grant signed a law, and under it Yellowstone became the first national park. In 1879 Philetus W. Norris, Yellowstone's superintendent, the official in charge of the park, had the Tukudika people who lived there forced out and taken to a reservation. A reservation is land set aside for a Native nation to live on.

<a id="story-john-james-audubon"></a>

#### John James Audubon

> **Who:** A painter and naturalist, a person who studies animals and plants in the wild. He painted *The Birds of America*, 435 life-size pictures of birds.
>
> **When and where:** He lived from 1785 to 1851. His book came out from 1827 to 1838. In 1813, on the way to Louisville, Kentucky, he saw a flock of passenger pigeons that he figured at more than 1 billion birds.
>
> **Movie:** *John James Audubon: Drawn from Nature* (PBS American Masters, 2007)

John James Audubon painted the birds of North America at their real size. His book *The Birds of America* contains 435 of these paintings. It came out from 1827 to 1838. Audubon worked on it for about 18 years.

In 1813 Audubon was riding to Louisville, Kentucky, when a flock of passenger pigeons flew over him. Passenger pigeons were wild pigeons that flew in huge flocks. In Audubon's own account, one flock darkened the sky for three days. He did the arithmetic himself and put that single flock at more than 1 billion birds.

<a id="story-henry-david-thoreau"></a>

#### Henry David Thoreau

> **Who:** A writer who also worked as a land surveyor, measuring woodlots for a living.
>
> **When and where:** He lived from 1817 to 1862. He lived in a cabin at Walden Pond, near Concord, Massachusetts, from July 4, 1845, to September 6, 1847.

Henry David Thoreau wrote about wild nature, and he earned his money measuring land. He worked as a land surveyor, a person who measures land and maps it. Thoreau measured woodlots, pieces of land kept for growing trees.

On July 4, 1845, Thoreau moved into a cabin he had built himself at Walden Pond, near Concord, Massachusetts. He lived there until September 6, 1847, which comes to two years, two months and two days. His book about those years, *Walden*, came out in 1854.

On April 23, 1851, Thoreau gave a talk called "Walking" in Concord. It came out as an essay in June 1862, just after he died. In it he wrote: "in Wildness is the preservation of the world." Preservation means keeping something safe.

### 1850 to 1900

In 1862 members of Congress passed laws for giving away land taken from Native nations. Under those laws, officials gave the land to railroad companies, to settlers called homesteaders and to the states for colleges. By one historian's count, US officials took more than 1.5 billion acres from the nations between 1776 and 1887.

On the Plains, hide hunters killed most of the bison for their skins, which are called hides. About 30 million bison lived there in the early 1800s, and fewer than 1,000 were left by 1900. The Plains nations lived on the bison. Army generals wrote in favor of the killing, to take away the nations' food and force them onto reservations. Columbus Delano, the Secretary of the Interior and one of the president's top officials, wrote that he would not seriously regret the bison's disappearance. Without the bison, he wrote, Native people would have to live by farming. Professional hunters also killed passenger pigeons at their nesting grounds, a reported 50,000 birds a day for months at one Michigan nesting in 1878.

In 1851 volunteer soldiers drove the Ahwahneechee people out of Yosemite Valley. President Abraham Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant in 1864. In 1872 President Ulysses S. Grant signed a law, and under it Yellowstone became the first national park. In 1879 Philetus W. Norris, the park's superintendent, had the Tukudika people forced out and taken to a reservation. In 1892 John Muir helped found the Sierra Club, a club formed in part to protect the forests and mountains of California's Sierra Nevada.

#### Land taken from Native nations, in acres

From 1776 to 1887, US officials took more than 1.5 billion acres from Native nations. They took it by treaty and by executive order. A treaty is a written agreement between nations, and an executive order is a command from the president. Historian Claudio Saunt, of the University of Georgia, made this count. He built it on maps that Charles C. Royce published in 1899. Royce mapped every piece of land that US officials took from the nations by treaty or order from 1784 to 1894.

Once officials had taken the land, it counted as public land, meaning land that US officials claimed for the nation. Members of Congress then passed it on to railroads, settlers and colleges.

On July 1, 1862, President Abraham Lincoln signed the Pacific Railway Act. Under it, railroad companies received "every alternate section of public land, designated by odd numbers." They got five of these sections for each mile of track on each side of the line. Alternate means every other one. A section is one square mile, or 640 acres. The act also states: "The United States shall extinguish as rapidly as may be the Indian titles to all lands falling under the operation of this act." To extinguish a title means to end someone's legal ownership of land. The lawmakers were telling officials to end the nations' ownership of the land along the railroads as fast as they could.

From 1850 to 1871, members of Congress granted railroad companies about 129 million to 131 million acres. The counts differ, and some reach 175 million acres by including grants the companies later lost. State lawmakers granted the railroads about 51 million acres more. The Northern Pacific railroad alone got about 44 million acres.

Lincoln signed the Homestead Act on May 20, 1862. Under it, a person could claim up to 160 acres of public land. A person who lived on the land or farmed it for five years got to keep it. Over the life of the law, US officials handed 270 million acres to private owners this way, which is 10 percent of the area of the United States. A National Park Service page states that much of this land "was seized from the Native Americans who previously inhabited it." Seized means taken by force.

On July 2, 1862, Lincoln signed the Morrill Act. Under it, each state received 30,000 acres of public land for each of its senators and representatives in Congress. State officials sold the land to pay for colleges of "agriculture and the mechanic arts," which means farming and the use of machines. A page about the act from the National Archives, the office that keeps the government's records, states that the act "resulted in the expropriation of over 10 million acres from Native American tribal lands." Expropriation means taking property away from its owners.

In 2020 the reporters Robert Lee and Tristan Ahtone, writing for the magazine *High Country News*, traced 10.7 million acres of this land. It came from nearly 250 tribes, bands and communities. US officials got it through more than 160 takings of land that the reporters call "violence-backed," meaning that violence or the threat of it forced the nations to give it up. US officials paid less than $400,000 in all to end the nations' ownership of it. By the early 1900s, sales of the land had raised $17.7 million for 52 universities. In 2020 the universities still held more than 500,000 acres of it.

One example comes from Minnesota. In the summer of 1851, four bands of Dakota people signed treaties at Mendota and Traverse des Sioux. The reporters describe the conditions as "withholding of rations, the threat of violence, enforced starvation." Rations are supplies of food. The Dakota received "less than 2.4¢ per acre." The University of Minnesota's share of the money from the land came to "nearly $580,000."

Members of Congress passed the Dawes Act in 1887. A reservation is land set aside for a Native nation to live on. Under the Dawes Act, US officials cut reservations into separate plots, 160 acres for a family farm or 320 acres for grazing animals. This is called allotment. Officials then sold the land left over, which they called "surplus." By the National Park Service's count, reservation land fell from 138 million acres in 1887 to 48 million acres in 1934, a loss of 65 percent. The Meriam Report, a 1928 study of Native life made for Secretary of the Interior Hubert Work, records 137 million and 47 million. Either way, the nations lost about 90 million acres.

#### Fire made a crime, 1850

On April 22, 1850, California's state lawmakers passed a law called the *Act for the Government and Protection of Indians*. Under Section 10 of the law, it was a crime to set the prairie on fire, or to refuse to help put out a prairie fire. Section 10 states that such people "shall be subject to fine or punishment, as a Court may adjudge proper." That means a judge would choose the punishment.

Section 10 speaks of "any person or persons." The whole law was about Native people, though, and burning the land on purpose was a Native practice. Reporters at the news outlet ICT write that under California law, cultural fire was "explicitly banned" for more than 150 years. Cultural fire means burning done by Native people to care for the land.

Under other sections of the same law, white people could take custody of Native children until the children were grown. Custody means control over a child and where the child lives. Officials could also arrest Native people they called "vagrants," meaning people with no home or work. Within 24 hours, officials could hire those people out "to the best bidder" for up to four months. This was forced labor: the arrested person had to work for whoever won the bidding.

#### Yosemite and the Ahwahneechee

The Ahwahneechee people lived in Yosemite Valley, in California's Sierra Nevada mountains. Their headman, or leader, was Tenaya. In 1851 volunteer soldiers burned their villages and their food and drove them out of the valley.

James D. Savage was a trader who had moved onto Ahwahneechee land to mine gold and to trade. In December 1850, Ahwahneechee fighters attacked his trading post on the Fresno River. One account says Chowchilla fighters joined them. They took his supplies and killed two of his men.

Early in 1851, California's governor, John McDougal, called for volunteers after attacks on miners and traders. About 200 men on horseback formed the Mariposa Battalion on January 24, 1851. A battalion is a unit of soldiers. Their commander was Major James D. Savage. State officials supplied their camp gear and supplies. Federal money paid for the battalion, through federal officials called US Indian commissioners.

The battalion's men first entered Yosemite Valley on March 27, 1851, by the Park Service's date. A National Park Service page states that they "systematically burned villages and food supplies and forced men, women, and children away from their homes."

Lafayette H. Bunnell rode with the battalion and wrote an account of it in 1880. He writes that in Captain John Boling's company, men on foot had orders "to burn any caches they might find." A cache is a hidden store of food. Acorns were the people's main food for the winter.

On the upper San Joaquin River, next to Yosemite, Bunnell says the huts and "adjacent supplies of acorns, were at once given to the flames." He estimated the acorns burned there at 800 to 1,000 bushels, and pine nuts too. A bushel is a measure of dry goods that fills a large basket. In Yosemite Valley, Bunnell found that "nearly all the acorns had been burnt." The battalion's men marched Tenaya and his people to a reservation on the Fresno River.

Battalion men held Tenaya's youngest son and another young man as hostages, tied to a tree. A hostage is a person held prisoner to force others to do something. Bunnell writes that the guards let the two untie themselves "in order to fire upon them, expecting to kill them both." One guard shot Tenaya's son in the back and killed him. The other young man escaped.

Bunnell describes the shooter only as "a young man" urged on by "an old Texan," and he names neither of them. Captain Boling told the guards "that they had committed murder." Bunnell writes that "no punishment was ever inflicted upon the perpetrators," meaning the men who did it. Tenaya was killed in 1853 in a fight with Mono Lake Paiutes. Accounts of why the fight happened differ.

On June 30, 1864, President Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant. With it, US lawmakers set aside Yosemite. It was the first land that the nation's lawmakers set aside to protect and to keep for public use. California's state officials took charge of it under the grant. Yosemite became a national park on October 1, 1890. The National Parks Conservation Association is a group that campaigns for the parks. An article by the group states that the 1890 park came "with authorization to remove anyone making homes without permission." Authorization means official permission. Ahwahneechee families came back and lived in the valley anyway, and they worked for the hotels and the park.

A Park Service page states that by 1910, more than 90 percent of the Ahwahneechee who had lived in the valley were dead or missing. The page does not say how each of them died or went missing. To Tu Ya, also called Maria Lebrado Ydrte, saw the 1851 raid as a child. She saw the battalion's men destroy her home in Yosemite Valley, and during the raid she saw her uncle murdered. To Tu Ya was Tenaya's granddaughter, so her uncles were Tenaya's sons. The Park Service page does not state which uncle was killed or who killed him. It describes her as the last survivor of the raid. In the late 1920s she came back to Yosemite and told her story.

#### Hide hunters and the railroads

Hide hunters, who sold the skins for money, killed most of the Plains bison. About 30 million bison lived on the Plains in the early 1800s. By 1900 fewer than 1,000 were left, and one count in 1884 found only 325. The hunters called themselves "buffalo runners," because bison are also called buffalo.

The first railroad across the country, finished in 1869, carried hunters out to the herds. In 1871 leather makers at a tannery in Pennsylvania found a way to turn bison hides into leather for harnesses and machine belts. A tannery is a place where animal skins are made into leather. Each hide sold for $1 to $3. The Kansas Pacific and the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe railroads carried the hides east.

Lieutenant Colonel Richard Irving Dodge, an army officer, made an estimate of the hides shipped. By his figures, three railroads carried 1,378,389 hides from the southern Plains in 1872, 1873 and 1874. He counted 459,463 hides on the Santa Fe line and guessed that each of the other two lines carried as many. Dodge also figured that before 1874, hunters wasted so many hides that for every hide shipped, about three bison had been killed. His totals were 3,158,730 bison killed by white hunters and about 1,215,000 killed by Native hunters. William T. Hornaday of the Smithsonian Institution reported these totals in 1889. They are Dodge's estimates, not counts.

Dodge described Kansas in the fall of 1873: "Where there were myriads of buffalo the year before, there were now myriads of carcasses. The air was foul with a sickening stench." Myriads means huge numbers. Carcasses are the dead bodies of animals.

#### Officers who wanted the bison gone

Army officers encouraged the hide hunters. Several officers also wrote that killing the bison would force the Plains nations onto reservations.

Historians disagree about whether the army had an official plan to wipe out the bison. Historian David D. Smits argues that the army followed a plan that was mostly never written down. Historians Robert M. Utley and Robert Wooster write that the army had no such official policy. Smits reports that no one has found a written order to kill off the bison. Utley writes that officials "applauded the slaughter," because they saw that it would "force the Indian onto the reservation." Historian William A. Dobak questions how much of the killing the army caused.

In 1867 an Englishman named W. F. Butler told Dodge he was sorry for killing more than 30 bulls, which are grown male bison. Butler wrote in 1911, decades later, that Dodge answered: "Kill every buffalo you can! Every buffalo dead is an Indian gone."

On May 10, 1868, General William T. Sherman wrote to General Philip H. Sheridan: "as long as Buffalo are up on the Republican the Indians will go there." The Republican is a river on the Plains. Sherman went on: "I think it would be wise to invite all the sportsmen of England and America there this fall for a Grand Buffalo hunt, and make one grand sweep of them all." In 1869 Sherman became the commanding general of the whole army.

Sheridan answered in a letter of October 15, 1868: "The best way for the government is to now make them poor by the destruction of their stock, and then settle them on the lands allotted to them." By "stock," Sheridan meant the nations' bison and horses. A month earlier, Lieutenant Colonel Luther P. Bradley had written in his journal that his orders were "to kill all the buffalo we find, and drive the Arapahoes and Cheyennes south, and the Sioux north."

At least one officer disagreed. On January 20, 1872, Colonel William B. Hazen wrote: "The theory that the buffalo should be killed to deprive the Indians of food is a fallacy." A fallacy is a false idea. He called the killing "wicked and wanton waste." Wanton means done for no good reason.

Officers at army posts, among them Forts Griffin, Dodge, Concho and Richardson, gave the hunters protection and supplies and helped them ship hides. In 1873 hide hunters asked Dodge, then in command at Fort Dodge, what he would do if they hunted south into Texas. The 1867 Medicine Lodge Treaty had reserved that hunting ground for the Kiowa, Comanche, Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho. The hunter J. Wright Mooar recalled Dodge's answer in 1930: "Boys, if I were a buffalo hunter I would hunt buffalo where buffalo are."

In December 1874, during the Red River War of 1874 and 1875, Colonel Nelson A. Miles wrote out his plan: "I would leave as few Indians or Buffalo behind, and as little for them to subsist on as possible." To subsist means to stay alive. In a book about his own life, published in 1896, Miles wrote that "the buffalo, like the Indian, stood in the way of civilization and in the path of progress, and the decree had gone forth that they must both give way." A decree is an order.

#### Officials in Washington

Leaders of the Plains nations asked officials to stop the hunters, and the officials did not stop them. In 1871 a Sioux delegation asked Columbus Delano to keep white hunters out of Sioux country. A delegation is a group sent to speak for its people. Delano was the Secretary of the Interior, one of the president's top officials. He refused.

In 1872 Colonel Edward Wynkoop reported words that Little Robe, a Cheyenne chief, had said to him. Wynkoop had been the government's agent to the Cheyenne. An Indian agent was the US official in charge of a reservation. Little Robe said: "What do you think my people ought to do when they see their cattle, the buffaloes, killed by your race when they are not hungry?" Only Wynkoop's report records these words.

Delano's yearly report for 1873 records that he "would not seriously regret the total disappearance of the buffalo from our western prairies, in its effect on the Indians." He saw the loss of the bison as "a means of hastening their sense of dependence upon the products of the soil and their own labors." He meant that without the bison, Native people would have to live by farming.

Members of both houses of Congress passed a bill to protect the bison in 1874. Under it, no one but a Native person could kill a female bison, or more males than needed for food. The fine would be $100 for each animal. President Grant did not sign the bill. Members of Congress ended their meeting before he signed it, so the bill never became law. This is called a pocket veto.

Grant had promised a Southern Cheyenne and Arapaho delegation that hunters would be kept out of their country. On September 30, 1874, their agent, John D. Miles, wrote that "they looked in vain." In vain means without success: they watched for the hunters to be kept out, and the hunters kept coming.

Texas lawmakers brought in their own bill to protect the bison in 1875. The *Handbook of Texas*, published by the Texas State Historical Association, states that Sheridan protested it, "contending that peace with the Indians could be maintained only if their food supply was eliminated." The lawmakers did not pass the bill.

A speech that Sheridan is said to have given against the bill comes from one source only. The former hide hunter John R. Cook wrote about it in 1907, about 32 years later. Cook wrote that Sheridan told the lawmakers to give each hunter "a medal of bronze, with a dead buffalo on one side and a discouraged Indian on the other." In Cook's account, Sheridan also said: "let them kill, skin, and sell until the buffaloes are exterminated." Exterminated means killed off completely. Smits reports that no official record of Sheridan speaking to the lawmakers has turned up, but he judges Cook believable. Writing in *Harper's* magazine in 2008, Christopher Ketcham called the speech "believed to be apocryphal," which means probably made up.

<a id="story-frank-mayer"></a>

#### Frank Mayer

> **Who:** A buffalo runner, one of the hunters who killed bison for their hides, from 1872 to 1878.
>
> **When and where:** The Plains in the 1870s. He died in Fairplay, Colorado, in February 1954, at a reported age of 104.

Frank H. Mayer killed bison for their hides from 1872 to 1878. At about age 100 he told his story to a writer, Charles B. Roth. It came out in 1958 as a book, *The Buffalo Harvest*, four years after Mayer died. The book describes the business: the rifle, the wagons, the skinners who cut the hides off the dead animals, and hides that sold for a dollar or two each.

Mayer said that "army officers in charge of plains operations encouraged the slaughter of buffalo in every possible way." They gave hunters "free ammunition, all you could use." "All you had to do to get it was apply at any frontier army post," he said. "I received thousands of rounds in this way." Mayer also quoted an officer he did not name: "if we kill the buffalo we conquer the Indian." The last part of the book records Mayer's regret for what the runners did.

Mayer told this story when he was very old. The numbers in it are his own, and some people have questioned even his age.

#### The pigeon nestings

Professional hunters killed passenger pigeons where the birds gathered to nest, and by the mid-1890s the wild flocks were almost gone. At their peak, an estimated 3 to 5 billion passenger pigeons lived in North America. They may have made up four of every ten birds on the continent.

In 1871 an estimated 136 million pigeons nested across about 850 square miles of Wisconsin. In 1878 professional netters, who caught the birds in nets, and shooters worked one of the last great nesting grounds, near Petoskey, Michigan. They killed a reported 50,000 birds a day for months. Railroads carried the dead birds to city markets. Hunters learned where each big nesting ground was from telegraph messages, which were sent over wires.

#### Yellowstone and the Tukudika

On March 1, 1872, President Grant signed a law, and under it Yellowstone became the first national park. In the law, members of Congress set the park apart "for the benefit and enjoyment of the people." The Tukudika, a band of Mountain Shoshone also called the Sheep Eaters, already lived there. A Park Service page states that they had lived in that area "for thousands of years." The Shoshone, Bannock, Crow, Blackfeet and other nations also have ties to the park's land.

Philetus W. Norris was Yellowstone's superintendent, the official in charge, from 1877 to 1882. In the fall of 1879 he found a Tukudika camp near Bunsen Peak that its people had just left. Norris asked the Indian agent at Fort Washakie for help. An Indian agent was the US official in charge of a reservation. The writer John Clayton, in a 2024 article in *Mountain Journal*, names that agent as James Patten. The agent sent a party of Shoshone, who found the Tukudika and brought them to the Wind River Reservation.

In the words of a Park Service page, the Tukudika "were forcibly removed to reservations." Forcibly means by force. The letters between Norris and Patten have not survived. The records do not say how many Tukudika were taken or what force the Shoshone party used.

In the spring of 1880, Norris met in Washington with a Crow delegation. Officials were asking the Crow to give up 1.6 million acres. That spring Norris also got a "solemn promise" from people at the Lemhi agency, the office of another Indian agent, and at the Wind River Reservation to stay out of the park.
