Under a British law of 1718, the Transportation Act, merchants shipped about 50,000 convicts, people found guilty of crimes, from Britain to the American colonies. Some counts put the number as high as 60,000, and more than 20,000 went to Virginia. Officials of the British treasury, the office that handled the government's money, paid the merchants for each convict. The first merchant to get this contract was Jonathan Forward. In the colonies the merchants sold the convicts as bound laborers, workers who had to work for a buyer for a set number of years. Most had to work seven years, and some had to work fourteen. Buyers included merchants, tradesmen, shipbuilders and ironworks owners, because a convict cost less than an indentured servant or an enslaved African. The shipping went on until 1775.

Convicts made up roughly a quarter of the people who emigrated from Britain in the 1700s. To emigrate means to leave one's own country to live in another. Indentured servants also kept coming alongside the convicts.

#### Forced arrival through Charleston

In these years the number of enslaved Africans that slave traders brought to the mainland colonies rose sharply. Rice planters in the South Carolina Lowcountry, the low coastal land, bought large numbers of West and Central Africans. Some planters chose Africans who already knew how to grow rice. Charleston, South Carolina, was the main mainland port where enslaved Africans arrived. Many were held first at a quarantine station on Sullivan's Island, at the mouth of Charleston's harbor. Quarantine means keeping new arrivals apart so that any disease they carry does not spread. They were kept in buildings called pest houses, where people who might carry disease were held apart, and checked for disease there. The histories of the island do not name the people who kept them. Then slave traders took them to Charleston and sold them at public auction.

In 1974 the historian Peter Wood wrote that Sullivan's Island "might well be described as the Ellis Island of black Americans." Ellis Island was the New York station where millions of European immigrants later arrived. Published estimates put at least 200,000 Africans through Charleston harbor, and that about 40 percent of African Americans today have an ancestor who came that way. Nic Butler, a historian at the Charleston County Public Library, argues that the share credited to Sullivan's Island is too high.

Across the whole slave trade, slave traders forced about 12.5 million Africans onto ships. About 10.7 million lived through the crossing. About 1.8 million died on the slave traders' ships on the way. Fewer than 4 percent of the people who lived through the crossing were brought to mainland North America. About 305,000 came straight from Africa, and close to 388,000 came in all, counting those brought by way of the Caribbean.

### 1750 to 1800

Fewer people crossed the Atlantic to settle during the American Revolution, from 1775 to 1783, than before it. After the war, members of Congress passed the national government's first law on who could become a citizen, a full legal member of the country. They limited it to free white people. In the 1790s thousands of refugees arrived from a revolution in the Caribbean.

<a id="story-alexander-hamilton-immigration"></a>

#### Alexander Hamilton

> **Who:** An orphaned clerk from the Caribbean whose writing about a hurricane led men on St. Croix to pay for his schooling in North America. He came as a teenager and stayed.
>
> **When and where:** Born on Nevis. Sailed from St. Croix in late 1772 or early 1773. King's College, New York.
>
> **Movie:** *Hamilton* (2020), the filmed Broadway stage musical with its original cast, released on Disney+ on July 3, 2020. It is a dramatization, not a documentary.

Alexander Hamilton came to North America from the Caribbean as a teenager, to go to school. Men on the island of St. Croix paid for it.

He was born on the Caribbean island of Nevis on January 11. The year is disputed. Accounts of his life give either 1755 or 1757. He was an orphan, which means both of his parents had died. He worked on St. Croix as a clerk, a worker who keeps written records for a business.

On August 31, 1772, a hurricane struck St. Croix. Hamilton wrote a letter describing the storm, dated September 6, 1772. It was printed in a newspaper called the *Royal Danish American Gazette* on October 3. After reading it, men on the island raised money to send him to school in North America.

He sailed in late 1772 or early 1773. Accounts differ on the date. He studied at King's College in New York, and he stayed. Later he worked for the new national government at the Treasury, the department that handles the government's money.

#### The Revolution and the Loyalists

The Revolutionary War lasted from 1775 to 1783. During those years fewer immigrants crossed the Atlantic than in the years before. The shipping of British convicts to the colonies ended in 1775. During and after the war, tens of thousands of Loyalists left the country, many of them for Canada. Loyalists were colonists who sided with the British king against the Revolution.

Under the peace of 1783, the western border of the United States was the Mississippi River. Spanish and French officials claimed the land beyond the river. Most of the land away from the Atlantic coast was still Native land.

#### The Naturalization Act of 1790

In 1790 members of Congress passed the Naturalization Act. Naturalization is the legal process by which a person born in another country becomes a citizen. The act was the national government's first law on who could become a citizen. It allowed naturalization only for "a free white person" of "good character." To qualify, a person had to live in the United States for two years, including at least one year in the state where they applied, and swear loyalty to the Constitution. Children born abroad to citizens were included as citizens.

Under this law, an immigrant who was enslaved or was not white could not become a citizen. Members of Congress did not fully remove the limit to white people until 1952, 162 years later.

The men who wrote the Constitution in 1787 also set a date for arrivals by force. In Article I, Section 9, they barred Congress from stopping the bringing in of enslaved people before 1808. So for about twenty more years, slave traders could legally bring captives into the country.

<a id="story-pierre-toussaint"></a>

#### Pierre Toussaint

> **Who:** A man born enslaved in Saint-Domingue and brought to New York by the family that enslaved him. He became a leading hairdresser and was freed in 1807.
>
> **When and where:** Brought to New York in 1787. Freed July 2, 1807. Died in New York, June 30, 1853.

In 1787 the Bérard family took Pierre Toussaint, whom they enslaved, from Saint-Domingue to New York. Saint-Domingue was a French colony in the Caribbean. Toussaint was born enslaved there in about 1766, though some recent accounts give 1781. The Bérards were fleeing fighting and disorder in the colony. They came four years before the revolution in Saint-Domingue began.

In New York he trained under a hairdresser and became one of the city's leading hairdressers. The husband of Marie Elisabeth Bérard, of the family that enslaved him, died, and Toussaint supported her. He was still enslaved at the time.

Marie Elisabeth Bérard had married again, to a Mr. Nicolas, and she died in 1807. On her deathbed she made her second husband promise to free Toussaint. Mr. Nicolas kept the promise, and Toussaint was free on July 2, 1807. If Toussaint was born in about 1766, he was about 41 when he was freed. One account says he was 45. He took the surname Toussaint to honor Toussaint Louverture, a leader of the revolution in Saint-Domingue.

Toussaint used his money to care for orphans and to fund early Catholic charities in New York, groups that helped the poor. During a yellow fever outbreak in New York in 1798, he nursed sick people who were kept apart from others. Yellow fever is a deadly disease spread by mosquitoes. In 1811 he married Juliette Noel, an enslaved woman, after he paid for her freedom.

He died on June 30, 1853. In 1990 Cardinal John O'Connor, the head of the Catholic Church in New York, had his remains moved to the crypt of St. Patrick's Cathedral in New York, a burial room beneath the church. In 1996 Pope John Paul II declared him Venerable, a title the pope gives to a person whom church leaders are studying as a possible saint.

#### Refugees from Saint-Domingue

On August 21, 1791, enslaved Africans in Saint-Domingue rose up against the French planters who enslaved them and against French rule. Saint-Domingue was a French sugar colony. The fighting went on until January 1, 1804, when Saint-Domingue became the independent country of Haiti. Refugees fled to cities in the United States. They included white planters and free people of color, meaning people of African or mixed descent who were not enslaved. They also included enslaved people, whom their owners brought with them.

That first year a ship called the *Charming Sally* carried 15 refugees to Philadelphia. By 1794 more than 3,000 refugees had come to that city. Nearly 20,000 refugees from Saint-Domingue came to the United States across the 1790s and the 1800s.

### 1800 to 1850

In the first half of the 1800s, the first large wave of people who chose to come here arrived, mostly from Germany and Ireland. Germans were the largest group of newcomers from about 1840. Between 1845 and 1855, during and after a famine in Ireland, a time when food ran so short that many people died of hunger, more than 1.5 million Irish people reached American ports. New York was the main port where they landed. Large numbers also came ashore at Boston and at New Orleans. Protestant mobs attacked Catholics near Boston in 1834 and burned Irish Catholic homes in Philadelphia in 1844. Protestants are Christians whose churches split away from the Catholic Church, the church led by the pope in Rome.

Early in these years, on January 1, 1808, a national ban on bringing enslaved people into the country from abroad began.

#### The end of legal arrival from Africa

On March 2, 1807, President Thomas Jefferson signed a law that banned bringing enslaved people into the United States from other countries. It is called the Act Prohibiting Importation of Slaves. Importation means bringing people or goods in from abroad. The ban began on January 1, 1808, the earliest date the Constitution allowed.

After 1808 no one could legally bring an enslaved African across the ocean. Smugglers kept bringing in captives against the law. From then on, the number of enslaved people in the country grew mainly through children born to enslaved mothers. Enslavers held those children as property from birth.

#### Germans and the Forty-Eighters

From about 1840 to 1890, more immigrants came from Germany than from any other country. Many Germans left home because their crops had failed. They came for farmland, most of all in the Midwest. Roughly three out of every five German immigrants settled there to farm. About 6 million Germans came to the United States between 1820 and World War I.

In 1848 and 1849, revolutions broke out in Germany. The people who fought in them wanted democratic government, in which the people choose their leaders. Soldiers from Prussia, a kingdom in what is now Germany, crushed the revolutions, and some of the revolutionaries fled abroad. The ones who came to the United States are called the Forty-Eighters, after the year 1848. There were only about 4,000 to 10,000 of them. Many were journalists or professionals, meaning people trained for skilled work such as law or medicine. Some of them later became leaders in their new country.

<a id="story-jette-bruns"></a>

#### Jette Bruns

> **Who:** A German woman who settled in Missouri with her doctor husband and wrote letters home to her brother for more than fifty years.
>
> **When and where:** Born 1813 in Oelde, Westphalia. Arrived at the Westphalia Settlement, central Missouri, in 1836. Died 1899.

Jette Bruns came from Germany to a settlement in Missouri in 1836. For more than fifty years afterward she wrote letters home to her brother Heinrich. Her full name was Henriette Geisberg Bruns.

She was born in 1813 in Oelde, a town in Westphalia, a region of Germany. She arrived at the Westphalia Settlement in central Missouri with her husband, the doctor Bernhard Bruns. Their baby son came too, along with her two brothers and a maid.

Her husband Bernhard became mayor of Jefferson City, the capital of Missouri. He died in office during the Civil War. After he died, Jette had almost no money. She ran a boardinghouse, a house where people paid to sleep and eat, across from the Missouri state capitol. The capitol is the building where the state's lawmakers meet. She died in 1899.

Her letters survive. In 1988 the University of Missouri Press printed them, along with a short account of her life that she wrote after the Civil War. Adolf E. Schroeder edited them and translated them into English. The book is called *Hold Dear, As Always: Jette, a German Immigrant Life in Letters*.

#### Mobs against Catholics, 1834 and 1844

Some Protestant Americans turned against the Irish newcomers and against Catholics. Before the Irish famine, Protestant mobs attacked Catholics in two cities and burned their buildings.

On the night of August 11, 1834, a mob of mostly Protestant workmen burned a Catholic convent school in Charlestown, near Boston. A convent is a home for nuns, women who give their lives to the church. The nuns and 47 girl students were inside, and only six of the girls were Catholic. One Boston newspaper put the mob at 50 to 60 men, and another put it at 150 to 200. About 2,000 people gathered to watch. The mob broke down the doors and windows, set fire to the buildings and burned them to the ground. The men also broke open the tomb where several dead nuns were buried. The records of the attack list no deaths.

Police arrested 13 men. At trial, juries found 12 of them not guilty, including their leader, John R. Buzzell. He later wrote that the evidence against him was enough "to have convicted twenty men, but somehow I proved an alibi." Convicted means found guilty. An alibi is proof that a person was somewhere else when a crime happened. The one man found guilty was 16 years old. Governor John Davis pardoned him, which means the governor forgave the crime and ended the punishment. Massachusetts lawmakers at first voted down a request from Catholic church leaders to be paid for the loss. In 1846 they voted the church $10,000. Church leaders put the loss at about $100,000 and refused the money.

In Philadelphia in 1844, the fighting began over schools. Teachers in the public schools made Catholic children read the Protestant version of the Bible. Francis Patrick Kenrick, the Catholic bishop of Philadelphia, the leader of the city's Catholic churches, objected. Nativists, people who wanted power kept for native-born Protestants, then claimed that Catholics were trying to throw the Bible out of the schools. On May 6, 1844, nativists held a rally in Kensington, a mostly Irish Catholic neighborhood. Shooting and fighting broke out between the nativists and the Irish Catholics. An 18-year-old nativist named George Shiffler was shot dead. The records do not say who fired the shot.

On May 7 and 8, nativist crowds burned Irish Catholic homes, a fire station and a market. They also burned two Catholic churches, St. Michael's and St. Augustine's, and the school of St. Augustine's. They burned a seminary of the Sisters of Charity too. The Sisters of Charity are a group of Catholic nuns, and a seminary is a school that trains people for church work. One count gives about 30 homes burned and about 200 people driven from their homes. In July, nativist crowds learned that the brother of the priest at a third church, St. Philip de Neri, had stored guns in it to defend it. They gathered there and brought a cannon. Soldiers of the state militia under General George Cadwalader fired on the crowd. A militia is a force of citizens called up to serve as soldiers. The crowd attacked the soldiers with bricks, stones, bottles and guns.

Accounts give different counts of the dead. For the May riots, the counts run from at least 14 dead to 20 dead. One of the Catholics killed was Joseph Rice. The Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia lists four soldiers and "probably a dozen rioters" dead in July. EBSCO's reference articles give figures that add up to about 34 dead and at least 126 wounded in both riots together. There is no agreed total.

A grand jury charged 19 of the rioters. A grand jury is a group of citizens who decide whether there is enough evidence to put a person on trial. Juries found only a handful of the 19 guilty. In June 1844 a grand jury blamed the Catholics who had been attacked. It said the May riots came from efforts "to exclude the Bible from the public schools." Catholics answered that the jury had called no Catholic to testify. That October, Philadelphia voters elected Lewis Levin to Congress. Levin was a newspaper editor who had founded the nativist group that held the Kensington rally.

#### The Irish famine

From 1845 to 1852, a plant disease called potato blight rotted Ireland's potatoes. The blight is a water mold, a tiny living thing that grows on the plant and makes it rot. At least two out of every three people in Ireland lived mainly on potatoes. People starved, and about 1 million people in Ireland died. This is called the Great Famine.

Since 1801 Ireland had been part of the United Kingdom, ruled by the government and the lawmakers in London. Ships kept carrying food from Ireland to Britain while people starved. The historian Christine Kinealy counted almost 4,000 ships that carried butter, grain and farm animals from Ireland to British ports in 1847. Soldiers guarded some of those shipments. About 400,000 people in Ireland died that year. Accounts still differ about how much of the need that food could have met. In an earlier food shortage, in the 1780s, British officials had banned grain from leaving Ireland, and the ban had worked. In 1846 and 1847, Prime Minister Lord John Russell and his ministers refused to ban grain from leaving Ireland again. A prime minister is the head of the British government, and the ministers were the officials who ran its departments. They also made Irish taxpayers pay for famine relief, the food and work given to people who were starving.

Charles Trevelyan was the senior official at the Treasury, the government's money department, who ran famine relief. In December 1846, writing to Lord Monteagle about Ireland, he said that the real problem was not the famine. He said it was "the selfish, perverse and turbulent character of the people," meaning the Irish. Perverse means stubbornly wrong, and turbulent means unruly. In 1847 members of the British Parliament, the lawmakers in London, added a rule to the law on help for the poor. The rule was named for one of them, William H. Gregory. Under it, a family holding more than a quarter of an acre of land could get no relief. To get food, a family had to give up its land.

Tenants are families who rent the land they farm. Landlords forced tenant families off their land and often pulled their houses down. This is called eviction. Police records list almost 250,000 people evicted from 1849 to 1854. The historian James S. Donnelly Jr. judged that count too low. He also counted families forced to give up their land in other ways from 1846 to 1854. He wrote that the total "would almost certainly exceed half a million persons." Lord Palmerston, a minister in the British government, cleared about 2,000 tenants from his land in County Sligo and paid their fares overseas. Major Denis Mahon evicted thousands of tenants in County Roscommon.

Most of the people who died in the famine died of disease, which people then called fever. Officials in Ireland did not record deaths then, so the numbers are estimates. They run from about 1 million to 1.5 million dead.

At least 2.1 million people left Ireland from 1845 to 1855, and most of them went to the United States. People called the crowded ships of those years "coffin ships." In 1847 the *Virginius* sailed to Canada with 496 passengers. A report in the Toronto *Globe* said that 158 of them had died, "nearly one third." More than 1.5 million Irish people arrived at American ports between 1845 and 1855. Most of them were poor when they landed. They settled in cities of the Northeast, such as New York and Boston, and in other cities in Pennsylvania, Massachusetts and beyond.

<a id="story-patrick-kennedy-bridget-murphy"></a>

#### Patrick Kennedy and Bridget Murphy

> **Who:** Two people from County Wexford, Ireland, who married in Boston during the famine years. Patrick was the great-grandfather of President John F. Kennedy.
>
> **When and where:** Patrick left Ireland in 1848 or 1849. They married in September 1849. East Boston, Massachusetts.

Patrick Kennedy left Ireland during the Great Famine and made a new home in East Boston, Massachusetts. He was born in 1823 at Dunganstown, in County Wexford. Accounts differ on whether he left Ireland in 1848 or in 1849. In East Boston he worked as a cooper, a person who makes barrels.

In September 1849 he married Bridget Murphy. She also came from County Wexford, from a place called Owenduff. The couple had five children.

Patrick died of cholera on November 22, 1858, at the age of 35. Cholera is a disease people catch from dirty water or food. It causes heavy diarrhea, and a sick person can lose so much water from the body that they die within days.

Patrick's son Patrick Joseph Kennedy, known as P.J., had a son named Joseph P. Kennedy. Joseph's son was John F. Kennedy, who later became president of the United States.

### 1850 to 1900

Between 1855 and 1890, about 11 million immigrants arrived through the port of New York alone. Germans still came in the largest numbers in the 1850s. Chinese immigrants began arriving on the West Coast in 1849. Toward the end of the century, Italians, Poles, Hungarians, Greeks and Jews from the Russian Empire came in growing numbers.

From 1871 to 1887, mobs in the West killed Chinese immigrants and drove whole Chinese communities out of their towns. In these years lawmakers also began to shut some immigrants out. The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 was the first law in the United States to bar a group of people because of their nationality, meaning the country they came from.

#### Germans and the Know-Nothings

More than 950,000 Germans came to the United States in the 1850s. About 220,000 of them arrived in 1854 alone.

In the 1850s, members of secret societies that opposed immigrants and Catholics formed a political party. Its official name was the American Party. Members who were asked about the group answered, "I know nothing," and the party came to be called the Know-Nothings. The Know-Nothings feared that Catholics were a danger to the Protestant faith and to democracy. In the 1854 elections in Massachusetts, Know-Nothing candidates won all but 3 of the 400 seats in the state's lawmaking body.

On Monday, August 6, 1855, Know-Nothing mobs attacked immigrants in Louisville, Kentucky. It was election day, and people call it Bloody Monday. Irish and German immigrants made up about a third of the city. In the weeks before the vote, George D. Prentice, editor of the *Louisville Journal*, wrote newspaper articles against immigrants.

On election day, Know-Nothing gangs stopped immigrants from voting. Mobs led by party members attacked the German neighborhoods east of downtown and the Irish neighborhoods to the west. They set fires and robbed homes and businesses, and they damaged more than 100 homes and businesses. Accounts written later say the mob burned Quinn's Row, a row of houses owned by an Irishman named Quinn, and shot people as they ran from the flames. A study published in the 2020s in the Kentucky Historical Society's journal uses court statements from the 1850s to challenge many of the stories told about the riot.

The Kentucky Historical Society lists at least 22 dead. Other counts give 19 to 22, and Catholic leaders at the time put the number at well over 100. Most of the dead were Irish and German. A grand jury charged five people, and none was found guilty. No one paid the victims for their losses. The Catholic bishop, Martin John Spalding, asked Catholics to stay calm and not to take revenge.

Then the party's members split over slavery. By 1860 the party had broken apart, and many of its members had joined the new Republican Party.

<a id="story-carl-schurz"></a>

#### Carl Schurz

> **Who:** A German revolutionary who fled after the revolutions of 1848 and 1849 failed. In the United States he became a Union general, a senator and Secretary of the Interior.
>
> **When and where:** Born March 2, 1829, in the Rhine Province of Prussia, near Cologne. Settled in Watertown, Wisconsin, in 1852. Died May 14, 1906.

Carl Schurz was one of the Forty-Eighters. He came to the United States in 1852 as a refugee, a person who flees danger at home, after the German revolutions failed.

He was born on March 2, 1829, near the city of Cologne, in the Rhine Province of Prussia. Prussia was a kingdom in what is now Germany. Schurz joined the revolutions of 1848 and 1849. When Prussian forces crushed them, he fled to France and then to London. In 1852 he crossed the Atlantic and settled in Watertown, Wisconsin.

In the Civil War he served as a general in the Union army, the army of the United States government, which fought the Southern states that had broken away. From 1869 to 1875 he represented Missouri in the United States Senate, as the first senator born in Germany. President Hayes then chose him as Secretary of the Interior, one of the heads of government departments who advise the president. He held that job from 1877 to 1881, and he died in 1906.

#### The last known slave ship

Around July 8, 1860, a sailing ship called the *Clotilda* carried about 110 African captives to Mobile, Alabama. Bringing captives into the country had been against the law for 52 years. The businessman Timothy Meaher paid for the voyage, reportedly to win a bet that he could smuggle captives in. The *Clotilda* is the last documented slave ship to reach the United States.

One of the captives was Oluale Kossola, born in about 1841 in what is now Benin, in West Africa. Accounts say soldiers of the kingdom of Dahomey captured him in a raid and took him to the coast. In Alabama, Meaher, his brothers and some friends enslaved the captives for the next five years, until slavery ended in 1865. The ship's captain, William Foster, set the *Clotilda* on fire near Twelve-Mile Island. After the end of slavery the survivors could not pay for the trip home. They built their own town near Mobile and called it Africatown. In 1927 the writer Zora Neale Hurston interviewed Kossola, and her book about him, *Barracoon*, came out in 2018. The wreck of the *Clotilda* was found in the Mobile River and confirmed in 2019.

#### Chinese immigrants in the West

Chinese immigration to the United States began with the California Gold Rush, when crowds of people went to California to look for gold. About 325 Chinese people came in 1849. Three years later, in 1852, some 20,000 came. Between 1851 and 1860 about 40,400 arrived in all. Most came from Guangdong province, also called Canton, in southern China. By 1880 about 105,465 Chinese people lived in the United States.

Between 1865 and 1869, managers of the Central Pacific Railroad had about 10,000 to 12,000 Chinese workers on the job at any one time. These workers built the western part of the first railroad to cross the country. About nine out of every ten of the railroad's workers were Chinese. Chinese workers earned about $35 a month and paid for their own food and housing. White workers got about $42 a month plus housing.

In June 1867 thousands of Chinese workers went on strike, which means they stopped work together to press for better terms. They asked for $40 a month, a 10-hour workday instead of 11 hours, and shorter shifts in the tunnels. Charles Crocker was the railroad director in charge of building. He cut off all food and supplies to their camps and brought in the sheriff and his deputies. After about eight days the workers went back to work.

The railroad's managers kept no record of how many workers died. A figure of about 1,200 dead comes from one newspaper report in 1870. A reporter for the *Sacramento Reporter* wrote that a train had brought in "the accumulated bones of perhaps 1,200" Chinese men from along the line. Chinese aid societies paid to send such bones home to China. On the same day, the *Sacramento Union* reported about 50 dead. Researchers at a railroad history museum think about 100 to 150 Chinese workers died building the railroad. Other estimates run from hundreds to thousands. No one knows the real count.

Snow, explosions and disease killed Chinese railroad workers. In the winter of 1866 and 1867, 44 storms hit the Sierra Nevada mountains. An avalanche is a mass of snow sliding down a mountainside. One avalanche at Strong's Canyon carried away the camp of two work crews of Chinese workers who were building tunnels there. One worker's body was not found until spring. Workers blasted through solid granite rock with black powder, an early kind of gunpowder. From 1867 they also used nitroglycerin, a liquid explosive that can go off from a jolt. Smallpox broke out in 1868 and 1869. Smallpox is a disease that passes from person to person and covers the body in sores.

#### The Page Act and the Chinese Exclusion Act

In 1875 members of Congress passed the Page Act, the national government's first law to limit immigration. Under it, contract laborers from China and other Asian countries could not come in. A contract laborer was a worker brought over already bound by a contract to work for someone. The law called these workers by an insulting name used then for Asian laborers. Immigration officers at the ports decided which women to turn away, and in practice they kept out most Chinese women under the Page Act. The stated reason for keeping them out was to stop prostitution, which means selling sex for money. That reason was a pretext, meaning a false excuse.

On May 6, 1882, President Chester A. Arthur signed the Chinese Exclusion Act. Exclusion means shutting people out. Under the act, Chinese laborers could not immigrate for 10 years. It was the first law in the United States to bar a group of people because of their nationality or their ethnicity. Ethnicity means the group of people, with its own language and ways, that someone belongs to. Members of Congress later renewed the law and made it wider. They did not cancel it until 1943, 61 years after Arthur signed it.

#### Attacks on Chinese immigrants, 1871 to 1887

Before and after the Exclusion Act, mobs in the West attacked Chinese immigrants. In the cases below, juries and judges punished almost none of the attackers.

In Los Angeles on October 24, 1871, a gunfight broke out between two groups of Chinese residents. A local rancher, Robert Thompson, fired into a Chinese store. He was hit by return fire and died about an hour later. A mob of about 500 non-Chinese men then spent about two hours pulling Chinese people out of the Chinese part of town. They shot, beat and hanged them, and they robbed Chinese homes and stores.

They killed 18 Chinese men and boys, about one in ten of the city's Chinese people. Only one of the dead is thought to have taken part in the first gunfight. The mob hanged seven men from the wooden crossbar of a porch and three more from the side of a wagon. The dead included Chee Long Tong, a doctor who healed people with herbs, and a teenager, Ah Loo. Dr. Tong offered the mob money and the diamond ring on his finger if they would spare his life. The geographer Reece Jones writes that a man in the crowd shot him in the mouth and cut off his finger to take the ring. The mob also hanged him. A grand jury charged 25 men. By one account eight were found guilty of manslaughter, and by another account nine. Manslaughter is the crime of killing someone without planning to. A judge sentenced them to two to six years in San Quentin prison. About a year later the judges of the California Supreme Court threw out the guilty verdicts because of a mistake in how the charges were written. None of the men was tried again.

On September 2, 1885, 100 to 150 armed white miners and railroad workers attacked the Chinese miners they worked beside in Rock Springs, Wyoming Territory. A territory was land the national government ran before it became a state. Managers of the Union Pacific Railroad had hired the Chinese miners at lower pay. Most of the attackers were immigrants themselves, from Britain, Ireland, Wales and Scandinavia. The attackers shot Chinese miners, struck them with picks, hatchets and clubs, and burned all 79 houses in the Chinese part of town. Some Chinese people burned to death in their cellars. About 600 Chinese people fled.

The Wyoming State Historical Society lists 28 Chinese killed and 15 wounded. Other counts put the dead at 40 to 50, because some who fled were never found. President Grover Cleveland sent army troops, and the railroad's managers brought the Chinese miners back to work under army guard. Officials arrested 16 men, or 22 by some accounts. A grand jury charged none of them. It said that no one had been able to testify to "a single criminal act committed by any known white person that day."

Other mobs drove Chinese people out of their towns. In Eureka, California, in February 1885, a stray bullet from a gunfight between two Chinese groups killed a city councilman, David Kendall. That night more than 600 white residents gathered and put up a gallows, a frame for hanging people. City leaders ordered every Chinese resident to leave within 24 hours. A committee of white residents put about 480 Chinese people, nearly all of the town's Chinese residents, on two steamships to San Francisco. No one was killed. The Chinese families left behind their furniture, goods, shrimp boats and vegetable farms. Chinatown was torn down, and the accounts do not name who did it. In 1886 a Chinese aid group, the Six Companies, sued the city, and the case was dropped. Rules keeping Chinese people out stayed in Eureka's city charter, its basic set of laws, until 1959.

In Tacoma, Washington Territory, Mayor Jacob Weisbach led a year-long campaign to drive the Chinese out. He called them "a curse." Tacoma's leaders ordered all Chinese residents to leave by November 3, 1885, and about 150 left before that date. On November 3, a mob forced about 200 more Chinese residents out of their homes in the rain and onto trains out of town. The mob then burned their houses. Officials charged 27 Tacoma men, Weisbach among them, and later dropped every charge. In February 1886 mobs in Seattle forced more than 300 Chinese residents to the docks, and ships carried about 300 of them away. Of 13 men tried for the Seattle riot, none was found guilty.

In May 1887, a gang of white horse thieves shot and killed as many as 34 Chinese gold miners. The miners were camped in Hells Canyon, on the Snake River in Oregon. They took the miners' gold dust. One of the gang, Frank Vaughan, confessed that they had agreed nearly a year earlier to murder the miners. Vaughan testified for the state and was not tried. Three of the accused men fled before trial. A jury found the three who stood trial not guilty. A stone marker placed at the site in 2012 states, "No one was held accountable." Its words are in English, in Chinese and in Nez Perce, a Native American language.

#### Jews from the Russian Empire, and others from southern and eastern Europe

Italians, Poles, Hungarians and Greeks came in growing numbers late in the century. So did Jews from the Russian Empire.

In March 1881 revolutionaries murdered the ruler of the Russian Empire, Tsar Alexander II. Six weeks later, on April 15, 1881, a crowd attacked Jews in the town of Elisavetgrad, in what is now Ukraine. It was the first of about 250 pogroms, violent riots in which a crowd attacks Jewish people and their homes, shops and synagogues, the buildings where Jews worship. The pogroms went on until 1884, in Kiev, Warsaw and many other places. Another count gives 259 pogroms from 1881 to 1883.

The historian John Klier describes many of the attackers as laborers who drifted from place to place looking for work. Railroad workers, factory workers and local business rivals of Jews also took part. Peasants, poor farm workers, joined in mostly to steal. The attackers robbed and wrecked Jewish homes and shops. They beat, raped and killed Jews. Rape means forcing a person into sex. Counts of the dead differ. One count says at least 40 Jews were killed from April to December 1881. Klier counts about 50 deaths in the whole wave. About half of those dead were Jews, and about half were rioters killed while the tsar's officials put down the riots.

For many years, accounts said that officials of the tsar's government had planned the attacks. Later, Hans Rogger, I. Michael Aronson and John Klier looked for evidence of that and found none. Some local officials helped stir the attacks up. Klier writes that more than a thousand rioters were punished in some way. Another account says the tsar pardoned most of the rioters who were brought to trial. The two accounts do not agree.

In May 1882 Nikolai Ignatiev, the tsar's minister in charge of the police and of other matters inside the country, proposed rules called the May Laws. Tsar Alexander III approved them. Ignatiev blamed the pogroms on the Jews themselves. The rules were for Jews in the Pale of Settlement, the region of the Russian Empire where Jews were allowed to live. Under the May Laws, Jews could not move to new homes outside towns. They could not buy or rent land in the countryside, and they could not trade on Sunday mornings or on Christian holidays.

More than 2 million Jews from the Russian Empire came to the United States between 1881 and 1914. Many of them were escaping the pogroms and the May Laws. Over 1.5 million of them had arrived by 1910, most of them from Russia.

#### The Statue of Liberty and Emma Lazarus

The Statue of Liberty, a gift from France, was opened with a ceremony in New York Harbor on October 28, 1886.

Three years earlier, in 1883, the poet Emma Lazarus wrote a poem called "The New Colossus." She wrote it to help raise money for the statue's pedestal, the stone base it stands on. The poem includes the lines "Give me your tired, your poor, / Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free." Nobody read the poem at the opening ceremony in 1886, and people mostly forgot it.

Lazarus was born in New York in 1849, into a Sephardic Jewish family, whose ancestors were Jews of Spain and Portugal. She had worked with Jewish refugees from Russia who arrived in the 1880s. She died in 1887. Later her friend Georgina Schuyler had the poem cast on a bronze plaque, and in 1903 the plaque was mounted inside the pedestal. After that, people began to link the statue with the idea of America as a refuge, a safe place, for immigrants.

#### Castle Garden and Ellis Island

From August 1855 to April 1890, most immigrants who landed at New York passed through Castle Garden. It stood at Castle Clinton, in Battery Park, at the southern tip of Manhattan. It was the country's first official depot for immigrants, a building where officials received newcomers, checked them and recorded them. New York State and New York City officials ran it together. About 11 million immigrants arrived through New York in those years, and about 8 million of them passed through Castle Garden.

People had complained that officials at Castle Garden were dishonest. When it closed in 1890, officials of the national government took charge of immigration. On January 1, 1892, they opened Ellis Island, the national government's immigration station on an island in New York Harbor, in its place.

<a id="story-annie-moore"></a>

#### Annie Moore

> **Who:** A 17-year-old from County Cork, Ireland, the first immigrant processed at Ellis Island. For about a century, another woman's life was told as hers.
>
> **When and where:** Arrived January 1, 1892, on the steamship *Nevada*. Lived on the Lower East Side of New York. Died in 1924.

Annie Moore was the first immigrant processed at Ellis Island, on the day it opened, January 1, 1892. She was 17 and came from County Cork, Ireland. She arrived on the steamship *Nevada* with her two younger brothers, Anthony, who was about 15, and Philip, who was about 12. She received a $10 gold piece, a gold coin worth ten dollars.

For about a century, writers described the wrong woman as Annie Moore. That woman went west and died in Texas, and she had been born in Illinois. In 2006 the genealogist Megan Smolenyak offered $1,000 to anyone who could find the real Annie. A genealogist is a person who traces family histories through old records. Researchers who took up the challenge found her.

The real Annie Moore never left New York. She lived in a tenement, a crowded apartment building, on Monroe Street on the Lower East Side. She married a clerk at a fish market. She died in 1924, at the age of 50. A headstone was placed on her grave in 2008. Statues of her stand at Ellis Island and at Cobh, in Ireland.

<a id="story-irving-berlin"></a>

#### Irving Berlin

> **Who:** A Jewish boy from the Russian Empire who arrived at Ellis Island at five and grew up to write "White Christmas" and "God Bless America."
>
> **When and where:** Born in 1888 in the Russian Empire (the place is uncertain). Arrived at Ellis Island September 14, 1893. Died September 22, 1989, at 101.

At the age of five, Irving Berlin arrived at Ellis Island. He later wrote the songs "White Christmas," "Easter Parade" and "God Bless America."

He was born Israel Beilin in 1888 in the Russian Empire. The place of his birth is uncertain. Recent research points to Tyumen, in Siberia, and older accounts give the region around Mogilev. His family used May 11 as his birthday, but one account gives May 23.

His memory of Russia was of his family's house burning during violence against Jews. No record says who set the fire. The family arrived at Ellis Island on September 14, 1893. In America their surname became Baline.

He wrote his songs under the name Irving Berlin. He wrote a first version of "God Bless America" in 1918. The singer Kate Smith first performed it for the public in 1938. Berlin died on September 22, 1989, at the age of 101.

<a id="story-wong-kim-ark"></a>

#### Wong Kim Ark

> **Who:** A cook born in San Francisco to Chinese immigrant parents. Officials refused to let him back into the country, and his case went to the Supreme Court.
>
> **When and where:** Born 1873, San Francisco. Refused landing August 1895. Supreme Court decision March 28, 1898.

In 1895 John H. Wise, the official in charge of collecting taxes on goods coming into the port of San Francisco, refused to let Wong Kim Ark back into the United States, the country where he was born. Wise acted under the Chinese exclusion laws. His case reached the Supreme Court, and he won. The justices, the judges of the Supreme Court, ruled that anyone born in the United States is a citizen.

He was born in San Francisco in 1873. His parents were Chinese immigrants, and he worked as a cook. In August 1895 he was coming home from a visit to China on the steamship *Coptic*. Wise said Wong was not a citizen, because his parents had not become citizens, and he held Wong on the ship.

On October 2, 1895, a writ of habeas corpus was issued for him in the national government's court in San Francisco. A writ of habeas corpus is a court order. It requires the people holding someone to bring that person before a judge and give a lawful reason for holding them. Judge William Morrow ruled that Wong was a citizen and ordered him freed. Henry Foote, the national government's lawyer in San Francisco, had brought the case against Wong. Lawyers for the national government took it higher. The case, *United States v. Wong Kim Ark*, went on to the Supreme Court. On March 28, 1898, the justices decided it 6 to 2. They ruled that under the Fourteenth Amendment, an addition to the Constitution, everyone born in the United States is a citizen.

### 1900 to 1950

The great wave of newcomers to the United States peaked in the early 1900s. In 1907 alone, officials at Ellis Island admitted 1,004,756 people. Then members of Congress passed quota laws in 1921 and 1924. A quota is a fixed number of people allowed in. Under the 1924 law, no more than about 165,000 immigrants could come each year, and almost no one from Asia could come at all. On the West Coast, officials at Angel Island held Chinese arrivals anywhere from a few days to many months.

From 1929 to 1936, officials pushed somewhere between 500,000 and 2 million people of Mexican descent out of the country. By the two larger counts, about 6 in 10 of them were US citizens. In 1939 officials in Cuba, the United States and Canada refused to let a ship full of Jewish refugees land.

#### Ellis Island's busiest years and the melting pot

Ellis Island's busiest year was 1907. Officials there admitted 1,004,756 immigrants that year. On the busiest single day, April 17, 1907, 11,747 people came through. From 1892 to 1954, about 12 million immigrants passed through Ellis Island. Older claims of about 17 million are too high.

On October 5, 1908, a play by Israel Zangwill called *The Melting Pot* opened in Washington, D.C. Theodore Roosevelt watched the first night from his box and praised it. After that, the phrase "melting pot" spread. A melting pot is a pot in which different metals melt together into one. People used the phrase to mean that newcomers from many lands would blend together into one nation.

<a id="story-frank-capra"></a>

#### Frank Capra

> **Who:** A boy from Sicily who crossed to America in the cheapest part of a ship in 1903. He grew up to win three Academy Awards for directing films.
>
> **When and where:** Born May 18, 1897, in Bisacquino, Sicily. Came through Ellis Island in 1903, then went on to Los Angeles.
>
> **Movie:** *Frank Capra's American Dream* (1997), a documentary made for television. Kenneth Bowser directed it, and Ron Howard hosted it.

Frank Capra came to the United States from Sicily in 1903 as a young boy. As a grown man he directed films, and in the 1930s he won three Academy Awards as best director.

He was born Francesco Rosario Capra on May 18, 1897, in the town of Bisacquino. Sicily is an island that belongs to Italy. His family crossed the Atlantic on the ship *Germania*. They traveled in steerage, the cheapest space on a ship, below the decks. They passed through Ellis Island and then rode a train across the whole country to Los Angeles.

In 1946 he made the film *It's a Wonderful Life*.

<a id="story-doukenie-bacos"></a>

#### Doukenie Bacos

> **Who:** A Greek girl who reached Ellis Island at 16. She was traveling underage and was afraid officials would send her back.
>
> **When and where:** Born December 18, 1904, to a Greek family in Thrace. Sailed from Piraeus, Greece. Reached Ellis Island January 5, 1921.

Doukenie Bacos reached Ellis Island at the age of 16. She was traveling underage, which means she was younger than an adult. She was afraid the officials would send her home.

Her full name was Doukenie Babayanie Bacos. She was born on December 18, 1904, to a Greek family in Thrace, a region of southeastern Europe now divided among Greece, Turkey and Bulgaria. She sailed on the ship *King Alexander* from Piraeus, the port city of Athens. She left on December 22, 1920, and reached Ellis Island on January 5, 1921. Some records give 1919 as the year she left, and National Park Service staff marked that year as a mistake.

Officials at Ellis Island held her for three days. Her uncle was a bachelor, a man who had never married. The officials would not hand a girl her age to a bachelor alone, so he had to find a family for her to live with. She was afraid they would send her back, and she later said she had thought of jumping into the water rather than be sent home. On the third day the officials let her go. That night her uncle came with a woman he called her "aunt," and Doukenie went to live with that family. In 1991 she told her story to the Ellis Island Oral History Project, which records interviews with people who came through the island. Her interview is number 49 in its EI series.

#### Angel Island

Angel Island Immigration Station opened in 1910 on an island in San Francisco Bay. The officials who worked there mainly enforced the Chinese Exclusion Act, an 1882 law that barred Chinese workers from coming in, and other laws against Asian immigrants. They held many Asian arrivals for days or months. The National Park Service states that some stays lasted several years, while the longest stay in other records is 22 months. Officials refused entry to about 18 out of every 100 people who arrived at Angel Island. At Ellis Island the figure was 1 to 3 out of every 100.

Station officials kept the detainees, the people being held, locked in crowded dormitories. A dormitory is a large room full of beds. No detainee could leave it without a guard. Officers read every letter the detainees sent or received. No one could visit a detainee until the officials had decided the case.

Doctors from the Public Health Service examined the arrivals. They turned people's eyelids inside out to look for trachoma, an eye infection that can cause blindness. They took samples of blood, spit, urine or stool, which means bowel movements. They tested Asian arrivals for worms that live inside the body, such as hookworm. When officials doubted a person's age, doctors made the person strip naked. The doctors then examined the person's hair, skin, teeth, voice and genitals, the private parts of the body.

Under the exclusion laws, most Chinese people could get in only by showing a family tie to a US citizen. Some claimed a tie that was false. They were called "paper sons" and "paper daughters," because the family tie existed only on paper. To catch them, a group of officials called a Board of Special Inquiry questioned each Chinese applicant about home villages and relatives. The board was made up of two inspectors, a translator and a stenographer, a clerk who wrote down every word. One inspector said in 1934 that "well over ninety percent" of his time went to questioning arriving Chinese people.

Some detainees killed themselves. The historian Judy Yung said in 2026 that a few were driven to it, most of them by hanging themselves in the bathrooms. She gave no names and no count.

Detainees carved poems into the wooden walls of the barracks where they were held. The poems were almost lost before a park ranger, Alexander Weiss, found them in 1970, and then they were saved.

Counts of the Chinese people who passed through the station differ. One count is about 175,000 between 1910 and 1940, and the National Park Service states 250,000.

On August 12, 1940, a fire burned the station's main office building, and the station closed soon after.

<a id="story-lee-puey-you"></a>

#### Lee Puey You

> **Who:** A Chinese woman who came as a "paper daughter" in 1939. Officials held her on Angel Island for about 20 months and then sent her back to China.
>
> **When and where:** Arrived at Angel Island in 1939. Deported to China in November 1940. Came back in 1947 and settled in San Francisco.

Officials held Lee Puey You on Angel Island for about 20 months, one of the longest stays known for a Chinese detainee. Then they refused to let her in and deported her, which means they forced her to leave the country.

She arrived in 1939 as a "paper daughter." Inspectors asked her about 170 questions. In November 1940 officials sent her back to China. She later said she "cried a bowlful of tears."

In 1943 members of Congress canceled the Chinese Exclusion Act. In 1947 Lee Puey You came back to the United States as a war bride, meaning a woman engaged or married to a man who served in the war. She married and settled in San Francisco. Judy Yung later wrote about her in an article called "A Bowlful of Tears Revisited."

#### The quota laws of 1921 and 1924

In 1921 members of Congress passed the Emergency Quota Act, the first law to put number limits on immigration. The yearly quota for each nationality was 3 percent of the people born in that country who lived in the United States in 1910. That count came from the census, the official count of everyone living in the country.

In 1924 members of Congress passed the Immigration Act of 1924, which set much lower limits. It is also called the Johnson-Reed Act, after the two lawmakers behind it. Representative Albert Johnson of Washington State was chairman of the House committee on immigration. David Reed was a senator from Pennsylvania. President Calvin Coolidge signed the law on May 26, 1924.

Under the 1924 law, each country's quota was 2 percent of the people born there who lived in the United States in 1890. Lawmakers picked 1890 because it came before the large wave from southern and eastern Europe. Italy's yearly quota fell from more than 42,000 to fewer than 6,000. Lawmakers also shut out anyone "ineligible for citizenship," meaning anyone who could not become a citizen under US law. At that time the law let only white people and people of African birth or descent become citizens. In 1922 and 1923 the justices, the judges of the Supreme Court, ruled that immigrants from Japan and from India could not count as white. Under that rule, almost no one from Asia could come in.

Lawmakers capped the total at about 165,000 people a year. Under the 1921 law it had been about 355,000. About 86 of every 100 quota places went to northern and western Europe. About 9 went to southern and eastern Europe. Under those limits, the great rush of newcomers from Europe came to an end.

In December 1923, in his first message to Congress, Coolidge had said, "America must be kept American. For this purpose, it is necessary to continue a policy of restricted immigration." The State Department's Office of the Historian states: "The most basic purpose of the 1924 Immigration Act was to preserve the ideal of U.S. homogeneity." Homogeneity means sameness.

#### Eugenics and the men behind the 1924 law

The men who shaped the 1924 law argued for it with eugenics. Eugenics was a false belief that a nation could improve its people by controlling who had children and who came into the country. Its believers ranked groups of people as "better" or "worse" by birth.

Harry H. Laughlin ran the Eugenics Record Office at Cold Spring Harbor, New York. He testified, meaning he spoke under oath at a hearing, to Johnson's committee three times between 1920 and 1924. He claimed that immigrants from southern and eastern Europe had higher rates of "feeblemindedness, insanity, criminality, and dependency." He meant mainly Italians and Jews. Those were old words for low intelligence, mental illness, crime and needing public charity. He said that too many of the people in mental hospitals came from southern and eastern Europe. His own figures showed high rates for German and Irish immigrants as well. Johnson named Laughlin the committee's "expert eugenics agent."

In 1922 Laughlin also wrote a model law for forced sterilization. A model law is a sample law for lawmakers to copy. Sterilization is an operation after which a person can never have a baby. For a woman, a doctor cut or tied the two tubes that carry eggs from the ovaries to the womb, or cut out a piece of each tube, so that no egg could reach the womb again. For a man, a doctor cut the tubes that carry sperm. The operation could not be undone.

In part because of Laughlin's work, lawmakers in dozens of states passed laws that let officials force people to be sterilized against their will. By the 1960s doctors in the United States had sterilized more than 62,000 people this way, about 60 out of every 100 of them women. On May 2, 1927, in the case Buck v. Bell, the justices of the Supreme Court ruled 8 to 1 that Virginia could sterilize Carrie Buck, a Virginia woman, against her will. On October 19, 1927, Dr. John H. Bell cut out a piece of each of her tubes. In 1933 the Nazis, the party of Adolf Hitler that then ruled Germany, passed a forced sterilization law based in part on the American practice. Under it, special courts of a judge and two doctors decided each case, and an approved doctor did the operation. About 400,000 people in Nazi Germany were sterilized this way. In 1936 leaders of the University of Heidelberg, in Germany, gave Laughlin an honorary degree, a degree given as an honor instead of for study.

Madison Grant was a New York lawyer. In 1916 he wrote a book called *The Passing of the Great Race*. In it he claimed that a "Nordic race" from northwestern Europe was better than all other people. Grant helped Johnson write the 1924 law. Hitler wrote to Grant and called the book his "Bible."

#### Mexican arrivals and the Mexican Repatriation

The Mexican Revolution was a war in Mexico that lasted from 1910 to 1920. During those years about 350,000 people fled north across the border into the United States. More kept coming in the 1920s.

From 1929 to 1936, officials pushed people of Mexican descent out of the United States. This is called the Mexican Repatriation. Repatriation means sending people back to their own country. By the larger counts, most of the people sent to Mexico had been born in the United States, so they were being sent out of their own country. It happened during the Great Depression, the years when many people in the United States had no work.

Secretary of Labor William N. Doak, who served under President Herbert Hoover, led a national campaign to remove Mexicans. He claimed they were taking jobs from other workers. In Los Angeles, Charles P. Visel, head of the city's unemployment relief committee, planned a publicity campaign. Relief was public money for people without work.

Officials raided Mexican American neighborhoods and public places. County welfare officers, the officials who handed out relief money, told families that their relief money would stop unless they took free train tickets to Mexico. Officials of the Los Angeles County welfare office ran the trains, and the first one left on March 23, 1931. Hospital staff carried patients on stretchers to trucks bound for the border. Families lost their property. In a 2005 California law, state lawmakers wrote that this property "often was sold by local authorities" as "payment" for the cost of removing the families.

On February 26, 1931, immigration agents blocked the exits of La Placita, a park in Los Angeles, while about 400 people were inside. Accounts of what happened next differ. According to the California Migration Museum, the agents arrested about a dozen people and deported a few. According to a History.com article, they rounded up more than 400 people and deported them.

Counts of the people removed run from about 500,000 to about 2 million. The California Migration Museum states about 1 million, following the historians Francisco Balderrama and Raymond Rodríguez. By that count, about 60 of every 100 were citizens born in the United States. The 2005 California law states about 2 million, and about 1.2 million of them had been born in the United States. Officials pushed about 35,000 people out of Los Angeles, about a third of the Mexican people living there.

California lawmakers apologized for the removals in that 2005 law. In February 2012 the members of the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors, who run the county, apologized and put up a plaque, a metal sign with words on it, at LA Plaza. No apology from the federal government, the national government in Washington, is on record.

In August 1942, US and Mexican officials started the Bracero Program. Under it, Mexican farmworkers came to the United States on contracts to work for a set time and then go home. Bracero is a Spanish word for a man who works with his arms, from *brazo*, the word for arm.

#### The St. Louis and the first refugee law

On May 13, 1939, the German ship *St. Louis* left Hamburg for Havana, Cuba, with 937 passengers. Almost all of them were Jewish refugees, people fleeing their country to escape danger. Cuba's president, Federico Laredo Brú, canceled their papers to land, and Cuban officials let only 28 passengers off at Havana. The passengers asked President Franklin D. Roosevelt for help, and he never answered them. State Department officials told them they must "await their turns on the waiting list." Canadian officials refused them too.

The passengers were fleeing attacks on Jews that had grown worse in 1938. The Nazi government of Germany had taken over Austria in March 1938. On the night of November 9 and 10, 1938, Nazi leaders set off attacks on Jews across Germany. Nazis burned more than 1,400 synagogues, the buildings where Jews worship, wrecked thousands of Jewish-owned shops and broke into Jewish homes. German police locked about 26,000 Jewish men in concentration camps, prison camps for people the Nazis targeted, just because they were Jewish. That night is called Kristallnacht, the Night of Broken Glass. Afterward Nazi officials seized property that Jews owned.

On June 6 the ship turned back to Europe. The passengers went to four countries: 288 to Britain, 224 to France, 214 to Belgium and 181 to the Netherlands. Of the 620 who went back to the European mainland, 87 moved on to other countries before the German army invaded in 1940. Of the rest, 254 were killed in the Holocaust, and 278 survived. The Holocaust was the murder of Jews and other people by the Nazis, the party that ruled Germany, during World War II.

In 1948 members of Congress passed the Displaced Persons Act. It was the first refugee law in the United States. Displaced persons were Europeans who had lost their homes in the war. Under the law, 200,000 people could come at first. They were counted against the yearly quotas. In 1950 lawmakers raised the total. Between 1948 and 1952 about 350,000 to 400,000 European refugees settled in the United States. One count gives 393,542.

### 1950 to 2000

In 1954 federal officers rounded up Mexicans and Mexican Americans and sent them to Mexico. Many of the people they sent were US citizens. In 1965 members of Congress ended the quota system that had favored northern and western Europe since the 1920s. After that, the main sources of immigration shifted to Asia, Latin America, Africa and the Caribbean.

Refugees came from Cuba after 1959 and from Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia after 1975. Counts credited to the United Nations refugee agency give at least 200,000 Vietnamese who died at sea while escaping by boat, from storms, hunger, disease and attacks by pirates. About 2.7 million people who had lived in the country for years without legal permission got legal status under a 1986 law.

#### The braceros and the 1954 deportations

The Bracero Program lasted until 1964. Over those years, Mexican farmworkers signed about 4.5 million short-term contracts to work in the United States. The workers came for the length of a contract and were expected to go home afterward.

In 1954 federal officers carried out a mass deportation of Mexicans. It was a federal operation whose official name used an insult for Mexican people. The insult was aimed at Mexicans who crossed the border without papers, and it suggested that they had swum across the Rio Grande, the river along the border between Texas and Mexico.

Attorney General Herbert Brownell Jr., the head of the US Justice Department, pushed for the operation. He served under President Dwight D. Eisenhower. General Joseph M. Swing ran it. He was the commissioner, or head, of the Immigration and Naturalization Service (INS), the federal office in charge of immigration. Swing announced the operation on June 9, 1954. INS officials planned it with officials of the Mexican government. Officers started in California and Arizona and moved into Texas in the middle of July.

Border Patrol officers, the federal agents who guard the border, ran the roundups in a military style. Newspapers covered them heavily. Officials meant the coverage to scare people into leaving on their own. On the first day in Texas, July 15, 1954, officers caught 4,800 people. Officers sent people south by truck, bus, train and plane. From Port Isabel, Texas, they also put people on two ships, the *Emancipation* and the *Mercurio*, bound for Veracruz, Mexico. About a quarter of the people removed from Texas went by ship. A History.com article states that the ships were later compared to slave ships.

Seven deportees jumped from the *Mercurio*. The *Handbook of Texas* says a mutiny followed, meaning the people on board rose up against the crew. Other accounts say the seven drowned. After protests in Mexico, officials stopped sending people by ship.

The historian Mae M. Ngai reports that in July 1955 officers rounded up workers in 112-degree heat, and 88 braceros, Mexican farm workers hired under contract, died of sunstroke as a result. Sunstroke is an illness in which the body gets so hot that it can no longer cool itself. A labor official told Ngai that more would have died without help from the Red Cross.

Ngai also quotes a Mexican labor leader. He reported that deportees were carried into Mexico on trucks "like cows" and unloaded in the desert, fifteen miles down the highway from the border. US immigration officials also left deportees in Mexicali, a Mexican border city where the summer heat averages 108 degrees. No record says whether the 88 were left in the desert, and no record names the officers who ran that roundup. Other deportees died of disease and other causes while officers held them. No full count of the dead is on record, and no record shows that any official was charged for the deaths.

INS officials claimed that as many as 1,300,000 people had left. That count included people who, officials said, had fled out of fear. An INS report gave nearly 1.1 million people caught. Katrina Burgess, a professor at Tufts University, wrote in 2024 that the 1.1 million figure covered a whole government year, which ended in June 1954. The operation was announced on June 9, 1954, so most of those people had been caught before it began. Burgess also wrote that many of the arrests were the same people caught again, sometimes on the same day. The real number of arrests was far lower. In the San Antonio district, officers caught slightly more than 80,000 people. In Texas in July 1954, officers held 42,000 people, and more than 63,000 left on their own. The historian Kelly Lytle Hernández puts the true number deported at "likely closer to 300,000." Many of the people deported were US citizens of Mexican descent. No one knows how many.

<a id="story-antonio-garcia-bracero"></a>

#### Antonio García

> **Who:** A Mexican farmworker who joined the Bracero Program at seventeen, after having his military ID card changed to say he was eighteen.
>
> **When and where:** Born June 13, 1937, in Tepehuanes, Durango, Mexico. Worked on contracts in Texas, California, Colorado and New Mexico into the early 1960s. Told his story in Chicago in 2003.

To get into the Bracero Program at seventeen, Antonio García had his military ID card changed to say he was eighteen. He then worked in the United States on and off for years as a contract farmworker.

He was born on June 13, 1937, in Tepehuanes, in the Mexican state of Durango. He grew up in Nuevo Ideal and left school after fourth grade. He signed up at the contracting centers in Chihuahua and in Empalme, Sonora, where Mexican workers signed contracts to work in the United States. His first contract was for work in the cotton fields of Texas. Within a week he was seriously ill. He kept working on contracts into the early 1960s, in California, Colorado, New Mexico and Texas.

On March 12, 2003, Claudia Morales Haro recorded his life story in Chicago. The recording is item 162 in the Bracero History Archive, which contains more than 700 such interviews. His record does not say whether he settled in the United States for good.

#### The 1965 law

In 1965 members of Congress passed the Immigration and Nationality Act, also called the Hart-Celler Act. With it, lawmakers ended the national-origins quotas, the rules that had limited immigration country by country since the 1920s. Under the new law, people got in mainly through family ties to people already here or through their job skills. Lawmakers also ended the bars against Asians and against southern and eastern Europeans.

For the first time, lawmakers also set a limit on the number of immigrants from the Western Hemisphere, the half of the world that includes North and South America. That limit included Mexico. Over the following decades, the main sources of immigration shifted away from Europe, toward Asia, Latin America, Africa and the Caribbean.

#### Cubans and the Mariel boatlift

In 1959 Fidel Castro led a revolution in Cuba. Through the 1960s, many Cubans came to the United States, especially to Florida.

In 1980 Castro briefly let people leave. From April to October 1980, about 125,000 Cubans crossed by boat from the port of Mariel to Florida. This was the Mariel boatlift.

About a month before the boatlift began, members of Congress passed the Refugee Act of 1980. With it, lawmakers created a permanent system for admitting refugees. They defined a refugee the same way the United Nations does: a person outside their own country who cannot go back because of a real fear of being harmed for their race, religion, nationality, group or political beliefs.

<a id="story-reinaldo-arenas"></a>

#### Reinaldo Arenas

> **Who:** A Cuban novelist whom Cuban government officials persecuted and jailed for his writing and for being gay. He left Cuba in the Mariel boatlift.
>
> **When and where:** Born July 16, 1943, near Holguín, Cuba. Left through the port of Mariel in May 1980. Lived in New York. Died December 7, 1990.
>
> **Movie:** *Before Night Falls* (2000), a drama based on his life story. Julian Schnabel directed it. Javier Bardem played Arenas, a role that earned an Oscar nomination.

Reinaldo Arenas was a novelist whom Cuban government officials put in prison for his writing and for being gay. Gay means loving people of the same sex. In May 1980 he left Cuba through the port of Mariel. He was one of about 125,000 Cubans in the boatlift.

He was born on July 16, 1943, near Holguín, in Cuba. Cuban officials persecuted him, which means they punished him again and again for who he was and what he wrote. In 1973, according to records at Princeton University Library, officials charged him with "ideological deviation." That means holding ideas that Cuba's rulers banned. The second charge was publishing his books in other countries without permission. Other accounts differ. One says the court found him guilty of being "extravagant," which here means living too freely, and "immoral." The Mexican writer Rafael Lemus writes that officials accused him in 1973 of abusing children. Lemus says Arenas hid for four months and was held from January 1974.

Arenas escaped from prison and tried to leave Cuba by floating away on a tire inner tube. Cuban officers caught him and locked him in El Morro, an old fort in Havana used as a prison. Officers of State Security, the political police of Fidel Castro's government, moved him to their headquarters, called Villa Marista. Lemus writes that at Villa Marista officers sent steam into the prisoners' closed cell until it became a steam room. There officers forced Arenas to sign a paper saying he was sorry for being gay and for his books. He was released in 1976, after he signed a promise not to write again. No record names any of the officers who held him.

In the United States he lived and wrote in New York. He wrote the story of his own life, called *Before Night Falls*. It was published in 1992, and in English in 1993.

He became sick with AIDS, a disease caused by a virus that destroys the body's defenses against other illnesses. On December 7, 1990, at the age of 47, he killed himself.

#### Refugees from Southeast Asia and the boat people

In 1975 North Vietnamese soldiers took Saigon, the capital of South Vietnam, at the end of the Vietnam War. After that, refugees fled Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia. They included the Hmong, an ethnic group from the mountains of Laos. Many Vietnamese escaped in small boats, and they became known as the boat people.

Storms, hunger, disease and pirates killed many of them at sea. Counts credited to the United Nations refugee agency run from 200,000 to 400,000 dead. The journalist Barry Wain estimated 30,000 dead by 1981. No one knows the exact number.

According to a UN refugee official in 1986 and a later study, the pirates were Thai fishermen in the Gulf of Thailand. Robert C. McCabe, a researcher at Maynooth University in Ireland, writes that some fishermen turned to piracy after big commercial fishing boats had cut the catch in their villages. No record names a single pirate.

Pirates robbed and raped refugees, murdered some and set others adrift. Rape means forcing a person into sex. In 1981 alone, the UN refugee agency counted 452 boats that reached Thailand with 15,479 refugees. Pirates had attacked 349 of those boats, on average three times each. They kidnapped 228 women, and 881 people were dead or missing.

In June 1982 officials of the UN refugee agency and of the Thai government started a program against the pirates. The governments of twelve countries paid for it, and the US government gave $1.2 million of the $3.67 million. By October 1987, 96 suspects had been arrested. No record names the officers who arrested them. Judges gave sentences of two to fifty years in prison, and one pirate was sentenced to death in December 1986.

From 1975 to 1997, US officials accepted 402,382 Vietnamese refugees from camps in Southeast Asia and Hong Kong, more than any other country. A different count gives nearly 281,000 Vietnamese refugees settled in the United States from 1981 to 1990 alone. About 500,000 more Vietnamese came to the United States by 1994 through the Orderly Departure Program, a legal way to leave Vietnam without the boat trip.

<a id="story-tung-trinh"></a>

#### Tung Trinh

> **Who:** One of 52 survivors of a refugee boat from Vietnam that drifted at sea for 37 days in 1988.
>
> **When and where:** Left Vietnam by boat in 1988. Brought ashore at Bolinao, in the Philippines. Later settled in Orange County, California.
>
> **Movie:** *Bolinao 52* (2008), a documentary directed by Duc Nguyen. It won two regional Emmy awards in 2009.

In 1988 Tung Trinh was one of 110 people on a small boat that left Vietnam. The boat's engine stopped working, and the boat drifted at sea for 37 days.

More than 20 ships passed the boat during those days. On June 10, 1988, one of them, the USS Dubuque, a ship of the United States Navy, stopped. The ship's commanding officer ordered food, water and sea charts given to the people on the boat. The sailors guessed 50 to 70 people were on the boat, not 110. Then the Dubuque left, and the boat stayed adrift.

As many as 58 of the 110 people on board died. An estimated 20 had died before the Dubuque came, and the others died after it left. During the drift, some of the people on the boat ate human flesh to stay alive. Eating human flesh is called cannibalism.

On August 11, 1988, Navy leaders removed the Dubuque's commanding officer from his command. At his own request, he was tried by a military court, and its officers found him guilty of breaking orders to help people in danger at sea, and he received a letter of reprimand, a written scolding.

Filipino fishermen found the boat and brought the 52 survivors to Bolinao, in the Philippines. Tung Trinh later came to the United States and settled in Orange County, California.

<a id="story-sergey-brin"></a>

#### Sergey Brin

> **Who:** A Jewish boy from Moscow whose family left the Soviet Union in 1979. In 1998 he started Google with Larry Page.
>
> **When and where:** Born 1973 in Moscow. Arrived in the United States October 25, 1979, at six.

Sergey Brin came to the United States from the Soviet Union on October 25, 1979, when he was six. In 1998 he and Larry Page started the company Google.

He was born in Moscow in 1973. The Soviet Union was a communist country, where the government owned the businesses and only one party was allowed, and Moscow was its capital. His family was Jewish. In the Soviet Union his parents were held back in their careers and harassed because they were Jews. The accounts of his life do not name the people who did it.

In 1979 the family got permission to leave. About 51,000 Soviet Jews left that year, the most in any single year. In the United States his father, Michael, taught mathematics at the University of Maryland. His mother, Eugenia, became a researcher at NASA, the US space agency.

#### The 1986 law

On November 6, 1986, President Ronald Reagan signed the Immigration Reform and Control Act, called IRCA. About 2.7 million people who had lived in the country for years without legal permission got legal status under it. To qualify, they had to show they had lived in the country without a break since before 1982. Certain farmworkers could also qualify.

The same law, for the first time, let the government punish employers who knowingly hired workers without legal permission. These punishments are called employer sanctions. After 1986 the number of people living in the country without legal permission grew again.

### 2000 to Today

About 47.8 million people living in the United States in 2023 had been born in another country, by the Census Bureau's count. That was 14.3 percent of the population, the highest share since 1910. More of them came from Mexico than from any other country.

The US Border Patrol counted 895 migrant deaths along the border with Mexico in the year ending September 2022, the most on record. In April 2018 Attorney General Jeff Sessions announced a "zero tolerance" policy: every adult who crossed the border illegally was to be charged with a crime. Border Patrol agents then took thousands of children from their parents. In January 2026 immigration officers held more than 71,000 people in detention, the most ever, according to a report by two human rights groups.

#### Who comes now

In 2023 the Census Bureau's American Community Survey counted about 47.8 million foreign-born people in the United States. Foreign-born means born in another country. They made up 14.3 percent of everyone living here. That was the highest share since 1910, when it was 14.7 percent. The highest share ever recorded was 14.8 percent, in 1890. The lowest was 4.7 percent, in 1970.

The Pew Research Center counted where the immigrants living here in 2023 were born. About 11 million came from Mexico, 22 of every 100 immigrants. India came next with 3.2 million, then China with 3 million, the Philippines with 2.1 million and Cuba with 1.7 million.
