About 52 of every 100 immigrants were born in Latin America, and 27 of every 100 in Asia. The Pew researchers found that immigration from Mexico has slowed since about 2007.

The number of immigrants from Africa south of the Sahara Desert roughly tripled from 2000 to about 2.5 million in 2024, the Migration Policy Institute found. Communities of people born in Jamaica, Haiti, the Dominican Republic and other Caribbean countries also grew.

Pew and the Department of Homeland Security both publish estimates of how many people live in the country without legal permission. Their estimates reached about 12 million in 2007, then fell to about 11 million, and rose again in the 2020s. The estimates are uncertain.

#### Homeland Security and DACA

On September 11, 2001, hijackers from the group al-Qaeda flew planes into the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon near Washington, and a fourth plane crashed in Pennsylvania. They killed 2,977 people. After those attacks, members of Congress passed the Homeland Security Act of 2002. With it, lawmakers created the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which began work in 2003. Lawmakers ended the old INS and gave its immigration work to three new DHS agencies: US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP). ICE officers arrest and hold immigrants inside the country. CBP officers, including the Border Patrol, work at the borders.

On June 15, 2012, DHS officials started DACA, short for Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals. Under DACA, some people who were brought to the country as children can apply to have their removal from the country deferred, or put off, and to work legally. DACA has faced challenges in court again and again. In September 2017 Sessions advised ending it, and Elaine Duke, the acting Secretary of Homeland Security, ended it. On June 18, 2020, the justices of the Supreme Court ruled that the way officials had ended DACA broke federal law, so DACA stayed. On January 17, 2025, a federal appeals court ruled that its work permits were unlawful and limited that ruling to Texas. About 455,000 people held DACA status on March 31, 2026, according to the National Immigration Forum, an immigrant rights group, using USCIS figures.

#### Deaths at the border

Every year hundreds of migrants die trying to cross from Mexico into the United States. Border Patrol officials count these deaths by the federal budget year, which runs from October to September. Their count was 281 in 2018, 300 in 2019, 254 in 2020, 568 in 2021 and 895 in 2022. The 2022 count is the highest on record. For 2023, a report of April 2025 from the Government Accountability Office, which checks federal agencies for Congress, gives 704 deaths and more than 5,800 rescues.

In 2022 the government's own auditors found that the Border Patrol's counts were too low. Border Patrol officials had not collected complete records of migrant deaths. They had left out deaths found by sheriffs, by medical examiners, the doctors who find out why a person died, and by other agencies. The auditors later reported that Border Patrol officials had made the changes they asked for.

People die of heat and thirst in the desert, drown in the Rio Grande, or die during or after chases by Border Patrol agents. Some die in custody, meaning while officers are holding them. Investigators inside CBP counted 171 deaths in the 2022 budget year in which CBP officers were involved "in some way." Of those people, 52 died in CBP custody.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM), a United Nations agency, keeps a second count. Its staff recorded 686 deaths and disappearances on the US-Mexico border in 2022, and they called it "the world's deadliest migration land route." Of those people, 307 died crossing the Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts, most of them from heat. IOM staff call their figures minimums. Texas county coroners, the officials who look into deaths, and Mexican search teams do not report every death to the IOM, so the real numbers are higher.

For 2025, the IOM counted 409 migrant deaths in all of North and South America, the lowest count since 2014. Its staff linked the drop to fewer people trying to cross the US-Mexico border and the Darién, a jungle between Colombia and Panama. In February 2026 they said the 2025 figures would not be final until the middle of 2026.

#### Children taken from their parents, 2018

On April 6, 2018, Attorney General Jeff Sessions announced a "zero tolerance" policy. The Attorney General is the head of the Justice Department. Sessions told federal prosecutors along the southwest border to charge with a crime every adult whom DHS officers sent to them for crossing the border illegally. That included parents who came with their children. Officers sent the parents to jail to face criminal charges, and Border Patrol agents took their children away from them.

Inside DHS, three agency heads proposed charging those parents in a memo dated April 23, 2018. They were Kevin K. McAleenan, the head of CBP, Thomas Homan, the acting head of ICE, and L. Francis Cissna, the head of USCIS. They recommended sending every adult who crossed illegally to be charged, "including those initially arriving or apprehended with minors." Apprehended means caught, and minors are children. Sessions urged Kirstjen Nielsen, the Secretary of Homeland Security, to approve the memo's plan. She was the head of DHS, and she approved it on May 4, 2018.

Border Patrol leaders told their commanders along the Mexican border to begin on May 5. McAleenan left out parents with children under five who were crossing illegally for the first time. Agents asked a federal refugee office to take each child, and ICE officers held the parents. In a later court case, government lawyers wrote that there was "no prescribed specific course of action for reunification." That means no one had set a plan for putting the families back together.

On May 7, 2018, Sessions said in a speech, "If you are smuggling a child, then we will prosecute you and that child will be separated from you as required by law." In 2017, under a trial program in El Paso, Texas, officials had already separated about 280 families.

Michael Horowitz, the Justice Department's inspector general, later investigated. An inspector general is an official who checks the work of a government department. In January 2021 Horowitz reported that Sessions and a small number of other Justice Department officials knew, when the policy was issued in April 2018, that DHS "would change its long-standing practice" and separate families. He found that the Attorney General's office "was a driving force" in that change. He also wrote that the department's "single-minded focus on increasing immigration prosecutions came at the expense of careful and appropriate consideration of the impact of child separations."

Officials deported hundreds of parents without their children before a court ordered the families put back together in June 2018. Counts of the children differ, because each measures something different. Staff of a federal group, the Family Reunification Task Force, counted 3,924 children taken from their parents between January 20, 2017, and January 20, 2021. In February 2023 task force staff said that more than 600 had been reunited by then. They said that 998 were still separated and that the true number still apart was "likely greater than 1,000."

On December 11, 2023, a federal judge approved a settlement in a lawsuit brought by the American Civil Liberties Union, called *Ms. L. v. ICE*. A settlement is an agreement that ends a lawsuit. It covers an estimated 4,500 to 5,000 children and their parents. By March 20, 2024, task force staff had confirmed 1,120 separated children as part of that group. No final count of children returned to their parents is on record. As of September 2026, no record shows that any official had been charged for the separations.

#### Arrests, detention and deportation, 2025 and 2026

Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. swore in Donald Trump as president on January 20, 2025, in the Rotunda, the round central hall of the US Capitol. A year later, in January 2026, ICE officers held more than 71,000 people in detention, a record. Detention means holding people in custody while officials decide whether to deport them. Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights gave that figure in a report of June 25, 2026. ABC News reported on July 21, 2026, that ICE officers held 65,765 people, citing figures ICE had posted.

The same report counted 52 people who died in ICE custody from January 20, 2025, to June 4, 2026. Thirty-nine of them died in the first year. Of those 39, seven were apparent suicides, meaning they appeared to have killed themselves, and five died of injuries. The others died of strokes, heart failure, long-term illness and failure to breathe. The death rate reached about 8.4 for every 10,000 people held, which the report describes as "nearly four times" the rate under the previous president.

Removal is the government's word for deportation. ABC News reported that ICE had posted 356,389 removals in the 2026 budget year through about July 21, 2026. For the 2025 budget year, the immigration researcher Austin Kocher counted about 329,018 ICE removals. On January 20, 2026, DHS officials claimed "more than 675,000 deportations" and "an estimated 2.2 million self-deportations" in the year since January 20, 2025. Self-deportation means leaving the country on one's own, without being deported by officers. Kocher notes that DHS officials have not published how they count these numbers. He found that ICE's own removals made up only about 54 percent of an earlier DHS claim of 605,000. In the year after January 20, 2025, DHS officials counted 90,084 people caught along the southwest border.

Federal immigration officers shot and killed at least four people from January 2025 to late January 2026, PBS NewsHour reported. One was Silverio Villegas González, a citizen of Mexico. On September 12, 2025, ICE officers stopped his car in Franklin Park, a suburb of Chicago. He had just dropped his children at school. One officer shot him in the neck, and he died. ICE officer Jonathan Ross shot Renée Nicole Good, a US citizen, in Minneapolis on January 7, 2026. CBP officers shot Alex Pretti in Minneapolis on January 24, 2026. As of that report, no officer had been charged.

DHS officials said that Villegas González drove his car at officers and dragged one of them, and that the officer fired "fearing for his own life." In body-camera video, an agent described his own injuries as "nothing major." Federal officials have not released the name of the officer who shot him, and federal prosecutors declined to charge that officer. In spring 2026, at the request of the Franklin Park police, investigators of the Illinois State Police opened their own case. It was still open in September 2026, the Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ reported.

<a id="story-giannis-antetokounmpo"></a>

#### Giannis Antetokounmpo

> **Who:** A basketball player born in Greece to Nigerian parents. He grew up a citizen of no country and came to the United States when a National Basketball Association (NBA) team picked him in 2013.
>
> **When and where:** Born December 6, 1994, in Athens, Greece. Came to the United States in 2013, at 18, to play for the Milwaukee Bucks.
>
> **Movie:** *Rise* (2022), a Disney+ drama about the Antetokounmpo family, made with the family. It is a dramatization, not a documentary.

Giannis Antetokounmpo grew up stateless, meaning no country counted him as its citizen. In 2013, at the age of 18, he came to the United States to play basketball for the Milwaukee Bucks.

He was born in Athens on December 6, 1994. His parents, Charles and Veronica Antetokounmpo, were immigrants from Nigeria with no legal status in Greece. Under Greek law, a child does not become a citizen just by being born in Greece. As boys, Giannis and his brothers sold goods on the street.

Greek officials made him a citizen in 2013. A few weeks later, in June 2013, the Bucks' managers picked him 15th in the NBA draft, the yearly event in which teams choose new players. He was named the league's Most Valuable Player in 2019 and in 2020. In 2021 he won the NBA championship with the Bucks and was named the most valuable player of the finals. His parents and brothers joined him in the United States.

<a id="story-lost-boys-of-sudan"></a>

#### Peter Dut and Santino Chuor, Lost Boys of Sudan

> **Who:** Two Dinka teenagers whose parents were killed when government forces attacked their villages in Sudan's civil war. They lived for years in a refugee camp in Kenya. They were among the "Lost Boys" resettled in the United States.
>
> **When and where:** From Sudan. Kakuma refugee camp, Kenya. Houston, Texas, in their first year in the United States, during the resettlement that began in 2001.
>
> **Movie:** *Lost Boys of Sudan* (2003), a documentary that records the lives of these two young men. Megan Mylan and Jon Shenk made it. It was nominated for an Emmy and won the Truer Than Fiction Award at the Independent Spirit Awards.

Peter Nyarol Dut and Santino Majok Chuor were two of about 4,000 young refugees from Sudan who were resettled in the United States starting in 2001. They were called the "Lost Boys of Sudan."

They were Dinka, an ethnic group of southern Sudan. Sudan's civil war was a war inside one country, between the government in the north and rebels in the south. Military forces of the central government attacked the boys' villages, destroyed them and killed their families, according to the notes for the PBS film about them. Those notes do not state which soldiers or fighters killed each boy's parents. Researchers at Human Rights Watch report that in these years Sudan's rulers gave modern weapons to militias, armed groups outside the regular army, called the muraheleen. The militia fighters burned Dinka villages, stole cattle and food, and carried off women and children as slaves. Human Rights Watch does not say that these militias attacked the two boys' own villages. The rebel army of the south, the Sudan People's Liberation Army, also took many of the older Lost Boys as soldiers. The two boys survived a long walk out of Sudan and then spent years in Kakuma, a refugee camp in Kenya.

The documentary records their first year in the United States, which began in Houston. After a time, Peter left Houston for Kansas to go to high school.

<a id="ch-migration"></a>

## Chapter 5: Migration Across America

### Before 1500

People were moving across this land for thousands of years before any European saw it. The first people came on foot from Asia during the ice age. Their descendants kept moving after that. Some built towns and later left them, and whole peoples traveled south over a long time. Many families moved with the seasons to hunt, fish and gather food.

Hundreds of Native nations lived here. There were no horses and no wagons. Trails and trade paths crossed the continent, and later newcomers followed many of them.

#### Cahokia and Chaco Canyon: towns people built and left

Cahokia was the largest town north of Mexico. It stood on the Mississippi River, near where the city of St. Louis is today, on the Illinois side. People lived there from about the year 700 to about 1400. Around 1100, between 10,000 and 20,000 people lived in the city. Some estimates put as many as 50,000 people in the area around it. That made Cahokia about as big as London was at the time.

By about 1350 most of the people of Cahokia had moved away, and by the 1400s the town was nearly empty. Nobody knows for sure why they left. The main explanations are drought, floods, and a shortage of wood and food. A drought is a long time with little or no rain. No single cause has been settled.

Chaco Canyon, in what is now New Mexico, was a center of the Ancestral Puebloan people, the ancestors of today's Pueblo peoples. Around 1140, after a run of bad droughts, people started to leave the canyon. By the end of the 1100s most of them had gone. They moved out and joined the Pueblo communities of the Southwest.

#### The Navajo and Apache move south

The ancestors of the Navajo and the Apache came from the far north. They lived in what is now western Canada and eastern Alaska. The Navajo call themselves the Diné. Their long move south is called the Athabascan migration.

Over a long time, groups of them moved south. They traveled along the edge of the Rocky Mountains and the Great Plains toward the Southwest. Accounts differ about when they arrived. Many place their arrival between the 1400s and about 1525. Others argue that they came earlier, in the 1200s.

#### Seasonal rounds and trade paths

Many peoples moved in a pattern called a seasonal round. A seasonal round is a yearly circuit from one camp to the next. Over a year, a family moved between its fishing places, its hunting grounds and the spots where wild plants ripened.

Trade goods also moved across the land. Traders passed turquoise, seashells, copper and obsidian from nation to nation along trade paths. Obsidian is a natural black glass made by volcanoes. Some of these goods ended up hundreds of miles from where they were found.

### The 1500s

In the 1500s the whole land from coast to coast was still Native land. Europeans reached its edges, but no crowds of settlers moved across the interior. Two things changed in this century. Spanish colonists brought horses back to North America. Then, in 1598, Juan de Oñate led Spanish colonists north into what is now New Mexico. They came with their families, wagons and herds, and they meant to stay.

#### The horse comes back

Horses lived in North America during the ice age. They died out here thousands of years ago. Spanish sailors and colonists brought them back.

Christopher Columbus carried horses on his second voyage across the Atlantic, in 1493. Spanish expeditions, groups of men sent out to explore, then brought horses onto the mainland. Francisco Vázquez de Coronado's expedition had them from 1540 to 1542, and Juan de Oñate's colonists brought them to New Mexico in 1598. Horses changed how people lived on the Great Plains in the next century, the 1600s.

#### Oñate's colony on the Camino Real, 1598

Juan de Oñate and his colonists left Santa Bárbara, a town in northern New Spain, in January 1598. New Spain was the Spanish colony that included Mexico. Earlier Spanish expeditions had followed the Conchos River north. Oñate's column, the long line of people, wagons and animals, cut straight across the Chihuahuan Desert instead.

In late April the column reached the Rio Grande at El Paso del Norte, near where El Paso, Texas, and Ciudad Juárez, Mexico, stand today. On April 30, 1598, Oñate claimed New Mexico for Spain in a ceremony called La Toma, which means "the taking." In July he set up the colony's headquarters at San Juan Pueblo, which its people call Ohkay Owingeh.

The colonists moved onto land that was the homeland of the Pueblo peoples. Families from Chaco Canyon had joined the Pueblo communities after the droughts of the 1100s, about 400 years earlier. The road the colonists traveled was later called El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the royal road of the interior. It ran from Mexico City to northern New Mexico. With his march, Oñate made that road more than 600 miles longer. Its stretch inside the United States is a National Historic Trail today.

Before Oñate, two groups of Spanish colonists had come to what is now the United States by sea. In 1559 Tristán de Luna y Arellano brought about 1,500 people in 11 ships to Pensacola Bay, in what is now Florida. They were soldiers, colonists, enslaved people and Aztec allies. A hurricane a month later sank many of the ships, and in 1561 Spanish ships took the survivors back to Mexico. In 1565 Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine, also in Florida, with about 600 settlers.

<a id="story-juan-de-onate"></a>

#### Juan de Oñate

> **Who:** The Spanish leader of the first known colonists to travel over land, with families, wagons and herds, into what is now the United States.
>
> **When and where:** From Santa Bárbara in northern New Spain to San Juan Pueblo (Ohkay Owingeh), New Mexico, January to July 1598.

Juan de Oñate led a colony north in 1598, and its people meant to stay. His column had about 400 men, about 130 of them with their families, and 83 wagons and carts. The colonists also drove more than 7,000 head of livestock, which means farm animals. Horses were among them.

The colony included soldiers, Franciscan friars, farmers, workers and servants. A friar is a man who belongs to a Catholic religious order, and the Franciscans were one of those orders. Enslaved people also walked in the column. The surviving records do not say how many.

In December 1598 Oñate's nephew, Juan de Zaldívar, went to Acoma Pueblo with about thirty soldiers to demand food. In the Acoma people's own account, the soldiers also raped an Acoma woman. Rape means forcing a person into sex. The Acoma killed Zaldívar and between eleven and fourteen of his men.

In January 1599 Oñate sent Zaldívar's brother, Vicente de Zaldívar, with about seventy soldiers. Acoma stands on top of a mesa, a steep hill with a flat top. The soldiers climbed it, killed Acoma men, women and children, and burned much of the town.

Nobody counted the Acoma dead at the time. Estimates run from about 300 to about 1,500. About 800 is the number given most often. Pueblo leaders gave that number in a 2023 statement from the All Pueblo Council of Governors. Its members are the 20 Pueblo nations of New Mexico and Texas, and each of those nations is led by a governor.

The soldiers captured about 500 people. In February 1599 Oñate sentenced the men over 25 to have a foot cut off. He also sentenced them to be forced to work as slaves for twenty years. Reporters for AP and NPR, and Pueblo leaders, say it was the right foot. News reports and the Acoma's own account, passed down since 1599, give the number of men whose feet were cut off as 24. Two historians, Marc Simmons and John Kessell, doubt that the feet were ever cut off. Simmons had once written that they were.

Oñate sentenced boys and men from 12 to 25, and girls and women over 12, to twenty years of forced work as slaves as well. He ordered the children under 12 taken from their families and given to the friars. A National Park Service page on the Camino Real states that about 70 Acoma girls were sent down the road to convents in Mexico. A convent is a home for nuns, women who have given their lives to the church. The same page states that probably none of the girls ever came home. Pueblo leaders count 60 children taken to Mexico, and they say none came home.

### The 1600s

In the 1600s the biggest change in how people moved came from the horse. Horses spread among the Native nations of the Plains and the Rocky Mountains. People on horseback could travel farther and faster than on foot, and they could follow the buffalo herds.

English, Dutch and other colonists settled along the Atlantic coast in this century. Jamestown was founded in 1607 and Plymouth in 1620. Almost none of them went far inland. The Appalachian Mountains were hard to cross, and many Native nations lived on the far side of them. The few colonists who moved inland went short distances. Thomas Hooker's group walked from Massachusetts to the Connecticut River in about two weeks.

#### The horse spreads to Native nations

There are two accounts of how horses spread. The timing is still not settled.

The older account starts with the Pueblo Revolt of 1680. In 1675 the Spanish governor, Juan Francisco Treviño, had ordered the arrest of 47 Pueblo medicine men, who were religious leaders, on a charge of sorcery, or witchcraft. Spanish officials sentenced four of them to be hanged. They hanged three, and the fourth killed himself. Treviño's men whipped the others in public and put them in prison. Pueblo people went to Santa Fe and demanded that the prisoners be let go, and the Spanish freed them. One of the freed men was Popé, a religious leader of the Tewa, one of the Pueblo peoples. In 1680 Popé led the Pueblo peoples of what is now New Mexico in a rising against Spanish rule. They killed about 400 Spaniards and drove the rest out of New Mexico for more than a decade. The Spanish left behind large numbers of horses, perhaps more than 1,500. It was the largest number of horses to pass into Native hands at one time.

In that account, the horses then moved north and east through trade. The Ute, Navajo and Apache got them first, and then the Comanche, Kiowa and Shoshone. Over the next few decades horses reached the nations of the northern Plains, among them the Lakota, Crow, Cheyenne, Blackfoot and Nez Perce.

The newer account comes from a study published in 2023 in the journal *Science*. The archaeologist William Taylor led it, working with Lakota, Comanche, Pawnee and other Native partners. An archaeologist studies the past through the things people left behind. The team tested horse bones from Kansas, New Mexico and Wyoming to find their age. Some dated from the 1500s and 1600s.

Marks on the teeth and bones showed that people had put bridles on these horses and fed them corn. So people were keeping and caring for them. The team found that many nations across the Plains and the Rocky Mountains had horses by the early 1600s. That is decades before the Pueblo Revolt. The finding matches what Native people have long said in their nations' own histories, passed down by word of mouth.

Over the next century, horses changed how the Comanche, Lakota, Cheyenne and the other Plains nations hunted and traveled.

#### The first colonial moves inland

In 1636 two English ministers moved out of the colony of Massachusetts Bay and started new towns in what are now Connecticut and Rhode Island. Thomas Hooker chose to go. He led about 100 members of his church west to the Connecticut River.

The other minister, Roger Williams, did not choose. The leaders of Massachusetts ordered him out of the colony for what he preached. He taught that the government should not force religious beliefs on people. He fled in the winter rather than be sent back to England. Wampanoag people helped him survive. Then, with help from Wampanoag and Narragansett people, he traveled by canoe to a freshwater spring at a place called Moshassuck. He settled there with the permission of the Narragansett and named the place Providence. In 1638 two Narragansett sachems, or leaders, named Miantonomi and Canonicus signed a deed for the settlement. A deed is a signed paper that says who owns a piece of land.

<a id="story-thomas-hooker"></a>

#### Thomas Hooker

> **Who:** A minister who led about 100 members of his church from Massachusetts to the Connecticut River, where they settled Hartford.
>
> **When and where:** From Newtown (now Cambridge), Massachusetts, to Hartford, Connecticut, May and June 1636.

Thomas Hooker was the pastor of the church at Newtown, a town that is now Cambridge, Massachusetts. A pastor is the minister who leads a church. In May and June of 1636 he led about 100 members of his church west to the Connecticut River. The walk took about two weeks.

They drove 160 cattle with them and lived partly on the cows' milk. They followed Native trails. Later people called the route the Old Connecticut Path. John Winthrop, a leader of Massachusetts Bay, wrote about the departure in his journal on May 31, 1636: "Mr. Hooker, pastor of the church of Newtown, and most of his congregation, went to Connecticut." A congregation is the people who belong to a church. Winthrop also noted that Hooker's wife rode on a horse litter, a stretcher carried by horses.

The place where they settled was Suckiaug, which means "black earth." It was the main village of the River Indians, and their sachem, or leader, was Sequassen. In 1636 Sequassen and his people signed the land over by deed to Samuel Stone and William Goodwin, two men in Hooker's group. The land ran along the river between the towns of Wethersfield and Windsor, and six miles west of the river.

Nobody wrote the deed into the official land records at the time. The settlers and the Native owners argued over its terms for generations. The histories of the deed do not say what Sequassen's people received for the land. Dutch traders had also built a fort there, the House of Hope, before Hooker's group came. The town the settlers built there is Hartford. In 1639 the people of Hartford and the towns near it adopted a plan of government called the Fundamental Orders of Connecticut.

### 1700 to 1750

Settler families began moving inland from the Atlantic coast in the first half of the 1700s. Land near the coast had filled up, and it had grown expensive. Families moved into the valleys and hills behind the older settlements, an area colonists called the backcountry. The main route inland was the Great Wagon Road.

Native nations were moving too. After a war with colonists in North Carolina, the Tuscarora walked north to New York. On the southern Plains, the Comanche moved in on horseback and took control, and many Apache there fled south. The country beyond the Appalachian Mountains was still Native land.

#### The Great Wagon Road and the backcountry

The Great Wagon Road ran about 730 miles. It started in Philadelphia and went southwest through the Shenandoah Valley of Virginia. Then it ran down through the hill country of the Carolinas, called the Piedmont, toward Augusta, Georgia. Heavy traffic began in the 1720s.

Many of the families on the road were German or Scots-Irish. The Scots-Irish were Protestants, Christians whose churches had split from the Catholic Church. Their families had moved from Scotland to the north of Ireland in the 1600s and then on to America. Both groups had come to Pennsylvania and found land there too costly. The Germans were called the "Pennsylvania Dutch." The word Dutch came from *Deutsch*, the German word for German. Moravians, members of a Protestant Christian church from central Europe, came along the road as well.

The road followed an older Native path. Colonists called it the "Indian Road." When settlers began arriving in the Shenandoah Valley in about 1729, Shawnee people were the main residents near the present-day town of Winchester, Virginia. Iroquois, Delaware and Conoy people also used the valley. The Iroquois were the Haudenosaunee, a league of six nations, also called the Six Nations. The valley's north-south trail was a war path between the Seneca and Delaware nations to the north and the Catawba nation to the south.

In 1744 officials sent by Virginia's governor, William Gooch, met Six Nations leaders at Lancaster, Pennsylvania. A treaty is a written agreement between nations, and the one they signed there is the Treaty of Lancaster. In it, Gooch's officials bought the Six Nations' claim to the valley, meaning their right to the land. Under the treaty, colonists also got the right to use the Indian Road. Accounts of how much the officials paid do not agree. After 1744, even more settlers traveled the road.

#### The Tuscarora walk north, 1713 to 1722

The Tuscarora nation moved about 500 miles north, from North Carolina toward Pennsylvania and New York, after colonists defeated them in war. The move took from 1713 to 1722, and they traveled in stages.

The war ended at Neoheroka, a Tuscarora fort on Contentnea Creek in what is now Greene County, North Carolina. Colonel James Moore of South Carolina led the attack. He commanded militia from both Carolinas and Native warriors who fought on the colonists' side. Militia were colonists called up to fight as soldiers. The siege began on March 1, 1713. In a siege, an army surrounds a fort or town and attacks it until the people inside give up or are beaten. Moore's men dug under an outer wall and set the fort on fire. It fell on March 23.

History pages from North Carolina's state government list 950 Native people killed or captured at Neoheroka. They list about 1,000 Tuscarora sold into slavery during the whole war. The colonists and allies who won the war sold these captives. Those state pages do not name who bought them. The colonists' side also forced more than 3,000 other Native people from their homes. About 200 colonists and about 1,000 Native people died in the war.

About 1,500 Tuscarora survivors made the walk north. The Oneida nation sponsored them in the Haudenosaunee league, which means the Oneida backed their joining. In 1722 the Tuscarora became its sixth nation.

#### The Comanche move onto the southern Plains

By the early 1700s the Comanche had moved onto the southern Plains. They became the strongest power there. The land they held became known as Comanchería, which means Comanche country.

Apache groups were already living on the southern Plains. The Handbook of Texas, a history reference, states that by 1700 the Comanche, Wichita and Tejas Indians were "better armed through trade with the French." Those nations took control of the southern Plains, and the Apache began moving southwest. Many Apache, most of all the Lipan and the Mescalero, "fled southward into Central Texas as well as into northern Mexico."

### 1750 to 1800

In 1755 British officers began forcing French-speaking Acadians out of Nova Scotia, north of the British colonies. They removed about 10,000 to 11,500 people, and about 2,600 to 3,000 of them later made their way to Louisiana.

Large crowds of settlers crossed the Appalachian Mountains for the first time after 1775. From that year, as many as 300,000 of them went through the Cumberland Gap into Kentucky and beyond by about 1810. After the Revolutionary War ended in 1783, more settlers moved into the Ohio Valley. The land they moved onto belonged to Native nations. In 1785 and 1787 the members of Congress passed two laws that set out how western land would be measured, sold and governed.

#### The Acadians forced from Nova Scotia, 1755

The Acadians were French-speaking Catholic farm families in Nova Scotia and the land around it, in what is now eastern Canada. Between 14,000 and 18,000 Acadians lived there in 1755. Nova Scotia was a British colony. Charles Lawrence was the colony's lieutenant governor, one of the top British officials there. On July 28, 1755, Lawrence and his council of advisers in Halifax decided to remove the Acadians from the colony. Admiral Boscawen, a navy commander, and Chief Justice Belcher, the colony's top judge, sat on the council that day. Some council members had recently come from New England and wanted the Acadians' farmland.

Lawrence had first asked Acadian delegates, men chosen to speak for their villages, to swear loyalty to Britain with no conditions. When they refused, Lawrence and his council had them jailed. Lieutenant Colonel John Winslow commanded New England troops. On September 5, 1755, he ordered every Acadian male aged 10 and older at Grand-Pré to gather in the church there at 3 p.m. He held them there. The order read to them said that their land, houses, cattle and other livestock now belonged to the Crown, meaning the British king. They could keep their money and household goods, and they would be removed from the colony. Winslow wrote that the order was "very disagreeable to my nature," but that his job was "to obey such orders as I receive." Colonel Robert Monckton and Major John Handfield led arrests and removals in other districts.

Charles Morris, a New Englander, drew up the plan. Soldiers would surround the churches on a Sunday morning and capture as many men as they could. Then they would break the earth walls that kept the sea off the Acadians' fields, and burn their houses and crops. In 1755 New England and British soldiers did burn many Acadian houses, barns and churches. Around the Minas Basin, where Grand-Pré stands, they set fire to about 700 houses, barns and other buildings. When the men refused to go, the soldiers threatened their families with bayonets. A bayonet is a blade fixed to the end of a gun. By the fall of 1755, soldiers had put about 1,100 Acadians on ships bound for South Carolina, Georgia and Pennsylvania.

British officers and soldiers kept removing Acadians until 1764. One count gives about 10,000 Acadians forced out between 1755 and 1763. Another gives about 11,500 between 1755 and 1764. British ships carried them to the thirteen colonies, to England and to France. Many Acadians escaped into the forests, and British soldiers hunted them for the next five years. In French the forced removal is called *Le Grand Dérangement*, the great upheaval.

Counts of how many Acadians died differ. One count says close to 5,000 died of disease, shipwreck or violence. Other counts put the dead at as many as half of those forced out. In one group of about 3,100 Acadians removed in 1758, about 1,649 died by drowning or disease.

#### The road to Louisiana and the Cajuns

Between 1764 and 1785, about 2,600 to 3,000 Acadians made their way to Louisiana. Louisiana was then a Spanish colony. The largest group came in 1785. That year, Spanish officials paid for seven ships that carried 1,596 Acadians from Nantes, in France, to Louisiana. The first of them reached New Orleans on July 29, 1785.

The Acadians settled along the bayous and prairies west of New Orleans. A bayou is a slow-moving stream through low, wet land. Their descendants are the Cajuns. The word Cajun comes from the word Acadian.

<a id="story-joseph-broussard"></a>

#### Joseph Broussard (Beausoleil)

> **Who:** An Acadian who fought the British removal of his people, then led one of the first Acadian groups to Louisiana.
>
> **When and where:** Acadia (Nova Scotia and New Brunswick), 1755 to 1762. New Orleans and the Attakapas district of Louisiana, 1765. Born about 1702, died 1765.

Joseph Broussard led about 200 Acadians to Louisiana in 1765. He was one of the first Acadians to settle there. People called him Beausoleil. He was born in about 1702.

When British officers began forcing the Acadians out in 1755, Broussard organized armed resistance. He and his men raided British troops. British soldiers captured him and held him at Halifax until 1763. That year Britain and France signed the Treaty of Paris, a peace agreement that ended their war.

In late 1764 Broussard and about 600 Acadians hired a ship to carry them to Saint-Domingue, the island colony that is now Haiti. In February 1765 he and about 193 to 200 of them sailed on to Louisiana. They reached New Orleans in late February. On April 8, 1765, colonial officials named him a militia captain, an officer over citizen soldiers. They also made him the commander of the "Acadians of the Attakapas." The Attakapas district was the area around the present-day town of St. Martinville.

A sickness spread through the new settlement that year. Most accounts say it was yellow fever. Broussard died of it in October 1765. Officials at Parks Canada, the Canadian government office that runs historic sites, have named him a National Historic Person. Canadian officials give that title to people who were important in Canada's history.

#### The Wilderness Road and the Cumberland Gap

The Cumberland Gap is a low notch through the mountains near the place where Kentucky, Virginia and Tennessee meet. In 1775 Daniel Boone and about 30 axmen cut a road through it called the Wilderness Road. As many as 300,000 settlers traveled that road into Kentucky and beyond between 1775 and about 1810. Kentucky filled with settlers and became a state in 1792.

Boone cut the road for Richard Henderson's Transylvania Company, a business formed to buy up wild land and open it to settlers. From March 14 to 17, 1775, at Sycamore Shoals on the Watauga River, Henderson got a deed from Cherokee leaders. Attakullakulla, Oconostota and Old Tassel were among them. The deed covered about 20 million acres between the Cumberland and Ohio rivers. That was most of Kentucky and part of Tennessee. In return the Cherokee received trade goods. One estimate values the goods at about 10,000 British pounds.

Dragging Canoe, Attakullakulla's son, spoke against selling land that the Cherokee nation held in common, and he rejected the sale. Other nations had claims to the land too. The Shawnee had once lived on part of it. The Tennessee Encyclopedia describes the Cherokee claim as the strongest of these. By buying the land, Henderson broke a British rule of 1763, the Royal Proclamation, which banned private buyers from buying Native land. Officials in Virginia and North Carolina and members of the Continental Congress, the meeting of leaders from the colonies, all refused to accept Henderson's colony as lawful.

#### Into the Ohio Valley, and a grid laid over the land

The Revolutionary War ended in 1783. Settlers then moved in large numbers into the Ohio Valley and the Northwest Territory. The Northwest Territory was the land north of the Ohio River that later became the states of Ohio, Indiana, Illinois, Michigan and Wisconsin. It was the land of the Shawnee, Miami, Delaware and other nations. In the 1790s those nations and the settlers fought each other.

On May 20, 1785, the members of Congress adopted the Land Ordinance. An ordinance is a law. Under it, surveyors measured the western land into squares called townships, each six miles on a side. Each township was divided into 36 sections of 640 acres. In the law, the members of Congress set aside one section in every township to pay for public schools. Because of that grid, much of the American countryside is laid out in squares today.

On July 13, 1787, the members of Congress passed the Northwest Ordinance. In it they wrote the rules for governing the territory, set out how parts of it could become new states equal to the original thirteen, and banned slavery north of the Ohio River. Five states later came from the territory.

### 1800 to 1850

In 1803 the United States about doubled in size, and by 1850 its land reached the Pacific Ocean. Hundreds of thousands of people moved west. Families drove wagons over the Oregon, California and Mormon trails, and from 1848 to 1855 about 300,000 people rushed to California for gold.

Other journeys were forced. United States soldiers drove the Cherokee, Choctaw, Muscogee, Chickasaw and Seminole nations from their homelands in the Southeast. Slave traders and enslavers forced more than a million enslaved Black people to move from the Upper South to the Deep South, in chains or in ships.

#### The Louisiana Purchase, 1803

In 1803 American officials bought about 827,000 square miles of land west of the Mississippi River from France. The price was 15 million dollars. After the purchase, the country was about twice as big as before. All or part of 15 later states came from this land.

Thousands of Native people, in dozens of nations, already lived on this land. None of them had a part in the sale. After the purchase, American settlers began moving onto it, into the interior of the West.

#### The domestic slave trade: a forced march south

Between about 1790 and 1860, slave traders and enslavers forced more than one million enslaved people to move. They took them from the Upper South to the Deep South. The Upper South meant Virginia, Maryland, the Carolinas, and later Kentucky and Tennessee. The Deep South meant the cotton lands from Georgia west to Texas.

From 1820 to 1860, traders and enslavers moved about 200,000 people this way every ten years. This trade inside the country was later called the "Second Middle Passage." The first Middle Passage was the voyage of captured Africans across the Atlantic Ocean.

Traders moved people south in two ways. They marched some on foot in coffles. A coffle is a line of enslaved people chained together and marched over land. They shipped others down the coast to New Orleans, which had the largest slave market in the country.

The largest slave-trading company in the country was Franklin and Armfield, founded in February 1828 in Alexandria, Virginia. John Armfield bought people in Alexandria. Isaac Franklin sold them in Natchez, Mississippi, and after 1829 in New Orleans. Rice Ballard joined them in the early 1830s and ran their office in Richmond. Franklin, Armfield and Ballard bought, moved and sold more than 8,500 people. In their busiest years, the mid-1830s, the partners moved 1,000 to 1,500 people a year.

Near the end of each summer, the partners sent coffles "in chains over the mountains." Each coffle held from several dozen to several hundred people. The partners timed each coffle to reach the Deep South for the fall selling season. The partners also owned three ships fitted to carry enslaved people, named the *Tribune*, the *Uncas* and the *Isaac Franklin*. The voyage from Virginia to Louisiana took about three weeks. At the busiest time, one of these ships left every two weeks. The last shipload left in November 1836.

Historians disagree about how many of these people were sold to traders and how many were forced to move when the enslavers who held them moved to new land and took them along as slaves. Their estimates of the traders' share run from about 16 percent (the historians Fogel and Engerman) to about half (Jonathan Pritchett). Walter Johnson counts about two-thirds sold and one-third taken along by their enslavers. Michael Tadman puts the traders' share at 60 to 70 percent of moves from one state to another after 1808.

<a id="story-charles-ball-migration"></a>

#### Charles Ball

> **Who:** An enslaved man who was chained into a coffle and marched from Maryland to South Carolina. He later escaped and told his life story.
>
> **When and where:** Sold in Maryland about 1805. Marched to Columbia, South Carolina. His story was printed in Philadelphia in 1837.

In about 1805, in Maryland, the man who held Charles Ball in slavery sold him away from his wife and children. The man who bought him was a slave trader from Georgia. The trader chained Ball into a coffle of 52 people and marched them south.

The trader locked a strong iron collar around each person's neck. A padlock on each collar closed on a link of one chain about 100 feet long. He also handcuffed the men in pairs. The coffle walked for more than a month, from Maryland to Columbia, South Carolina. Ball was then sold again, into Georgia.

Years later Ball escaped. He walked north back to Maryland, hiding by day and moving at night. He was captured again and held as a slave, and he escaped a second time. He settled near Philadelphia.

Ball told his story to Isaac Fisher, a white abolitionist. An abolitionist was a person who worked to end slavery. Fisher wrote it down, and it came out in 1837 as *Slavery in the United States: A Narrative of the Life and Adventures of Charles Ball*. Because Fisher did the writing, the book records Ball's story in Fisher's words. Many of the dates in Ball's life are known only roughly. He was born in about 1780 in Calvert County, Maryland.

#### Indian removal and the Trail of Tears

In 1830 President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act. Jackson then directed the removal of the Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole nations from their homelands in the Southeast. Federal troops forced them to Indian Territory, which is now Oklahoma.

Federal troops removed the Choctaw from 1831 to 1833. The troops forced the first groups out in snow and river ice. Andrew K. Frank, writing for the Oklahoma Historical Society, counts more than 14,000 Choctaw removed and says hundreds died. Other counts give about 15,000 removed and about 2,500 dead.

In August and September of 1836, after a war with the Creek, United States troops marched the remaining Creek people west in five large groups. Soldiers put chains on Creek men taken prisoner in the war and marched them to Montgomery, Alabama. Their families followed in wagons. More than 14,500 Creek were removed. Several hundred died on the way. About 3,200 more died after they arrived, from disease, hunger and exposure. Exposure means harm to the body from cold and bad weather.

In October 1837 the steamboat *Monmouth*, carrying about 600 Creek people, was in a collision. About half of the Creek on board died.

More than 500 Chickasaw died of smallpox during their removal.

The Cherokee removal of 1838 and 1839 is called the Trail of Tears. In May 1838, United States Army troops under General Winfield Scott began rounding up Cherokee people who had not moved west. President Martin Van Buren had sent Scott with about 7,000 soldiers, and state militia, including Georgia's, joined them. Militia are part-time soldiers called up by a state. Soldiers took families from their homes and farms, often with no time to pack.

The soldiers held about 16,000 Cherokee in stockades in Tennessee and Alabama. A stockade is a pen with walls of tall logs. Soldiers sent three groups west by river in June 1838. After that, Scott agreed to let John Ross organize the rest. Ross was the Cherokee's Principal Chief, their top leader. Ross organized fourteen groups, which left between August and December 1838. The walk over land was about 800 miles. People died on the way from cold, hunger and disease.

The number of Cherokee dead is not settled. The National Park Service's history of the trail states that more than 1,000 people died on the journey itself, and "perhaps several thousand" more died later because they had been forced from their homes. The count most often given is about 4,000. An article on the History.com website states a figure above 5,000. In 1984 Russell Thornton, a scholar who studies population, estimated that about 8,000 or more Cherokee died because of the removal, twice the usual figure. Andrew K. Frank, writing for the Oklahoma Historical Society, says as many as one in four Cherokee died.

<a id="story-rebecca-neugin-migration"></a>

#### Rebecca Neugin

> **Who:** A Cherokee woman who, at about three years old, was forced west on the Trail of Tears. She told what she remembered when she was 97 or 98.
>
> **When and where:** Soldiers took her from Georgia in 1838. Interviewed in 1932 in what is now Oklahoma.

Rebecca Neugin was about three years old in 1838 when soldiers rounded up her family in Georgia. Her father was Tickaneesky, and her mother was Sallie Ketcher. The soldiers held the family in a camp in Tennessee.

In September 1838 the family started west with the group led by Mose Daniel and George Still. Rebecca and the smaller children rode in a wagon. Her mother, her father and her older brother Dick walked the whole way.

In 1932 the historian Grant Foreman interviewed her. She was 97 or 98 years old and one of the last living people who had made the journey. Her memory of it is one of the few first-hand accounts by a survivor. She died on July 15, 1932.

#### The overland trails

Most of the western trails started from towns on the Missouri River, mainly Independence and St. Joseph, in Missouri.

The Santa Fe Trail opened in 1821. That fall, William Becknell led the first trading trip from Missouri to Santa Fe, which then belonged to Mexico. The Santa Fe Trail was mainly a road for traders hauling freight.

The Oregon Trail ran about 2,000 to 2,170 miles, from Independence, Missouri, to the Willamette Valley in Oregon. The trip took four to six months. On May 22, 1843, about 1,000 people set out with about 120 wagons and thousands of oxen and cattle. They reached Oregon that fall. This trip was called the "Great Migration" of 1843. After it, other families knew that wagon trains could make the whole journey. Hundreds of thousands followed over the next twenty years. From the 1840s on, tens of thousands of them came to the Willamette Valley, where at least twenty Native nations lived, among them the Kalapuya, Molala and Chinook peoples.

The California Trail split off from the Oregon Trail and turned southwest toward California. Traffic on it grew fast after gold was found in 1848.

#### Life and death on the wagon trails

About one in ten people who set out on the wagon trails died on the way. That was between 20,000 and 30,000 people. Most of the dead had cholera or typhoid. Cholera is a disease that causes severe diarrhea and vomiting. Typhoid is a disease that causes a high fever. Both spread through dirty water at crowded camps. Other emigrants died in accidents, or drowned while crossing rivers. An emigrant is a person who leaves one home to settle in another. Later stories often showed Native people attacking wagon trains. Most of the emigrants who died on the trails died of disease, not in attacks.

Families traveled in groups for safety, in covered wagons pulled by oxen.

#### The Latter-day Saints move west

Members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, also called Mormons, moved west after armed men attacked them in Missouri and in Illinois. On October 27, 1838, Missouri's governor, Lilburn Boggs, ordered that the Latter-day Saints be driven out of Missouri. If necessary, in the order's own word, they were to be "exterminated." To exterminate people means to kill them all. Three days later, on October 30, about 200 armed Missourians led by Colonel Thomas Jennings attacked the Mormon settlement at Haun's Mill. They killed seventeen or eighteen men and boys. One of the boys, Sardius Smith, was ten years old. No record shows that anyone was ever tried for the killings.

That year both sides in Missouri used force. The Missouri State Archives records that mobs of older Missouri settlers and armed Mormon groups roamed the countryside. In mid-October 1838, armed Mormon groups raided the towns of Gallatin and Millport and burned property there. Over the next year, about 8,000 church members left Missouri for Illinois, many of them ragged and stripped of their property. They settled at Nauvoo.

On June 27, 1844, about 100 men from Illinois militia units broke into the jail at Carthage, Illinois. They killed the church's founder, Joseph Smith, and his brother Hyrum. Five men were tried for the killings, and all five were found not guilty. Vigilantes then attacked Mormon farms around Nauvoo. A vigilante is a person who uses force to punish others without any legal right to do so.

Brigham Young, a leader of the church, planned to move about 15,000 people west. On February 4, 1846, the first wagons crossed the Mississippi River into Iowa. By March 1 about 500 wagons were on the move. By 1869 more than 70,000 Latter-day Saints had traveled the Mormon Trail. Some of the poorer groups pulled handcarts instead of driving wagons. A handcart is a small two-wheeled cart that people pull by hand.

The Salt Lake Valley lay between the lands of the Ute, to the south, and the Shoshone, to the north. A few Native people crossed the valley itself, but none had camps there. The Ute, Goshute, Shoshone, Paiute and Navajo peoples lived in what is now Utah, and their homelands had been there for thousands of years.

<a id="story-brigham-young"></a>

#### Brigham Young

> **Who:** The Latter-day Saint leader who led the first company of Mormon emigrants to the Salt Lake Valley.
>
> **When and where:** From Winter Quarters, in what is now Nebraska, to the Salt Lake Valley, in what is now Utah. Arrived July 1847.

Brigham Young led the first company of Latter-day Saints to the Salt Lake Valley in 1847. Before that, after Illinois militiamen killed Joseph Smith in 1844, Young had planned the move of about 15,000 people out of Nauvoo, Illinois, which began in February 1846.

The Saints called the 1847 group the vanguard company, which means the group that goes ahead of the rest. About 148 people traveled in it.

Counts of who was in the company differ. One count lists 143 men, 3 women and 2 children. Three of the men were enslaved Black men: Hark Lay, Green Flake and Oscar Crosby. William Lay and his wife, Sytha, held Hark Lay in slavery and took him along. The National Park Service's page on Hark Lay does not name the people who held Green Flake and Oscar Crosby. The three men hunted for the travelers, guarded the animals, and went into the Salt Lake Valley on July 22, 1847, ahead of most of the company.

The company started from Winter Quarters, a camp in what is now Nebraska, and traveled about 1,300 miles. Its members reached the valley in July 1847. Young himself arrived on July 24.

#### New land from Mexico, and the Gold Rush

In 1845 a journalist named John O'Sullivan wrote the phrase "Manifest Destiny" in the *Democratic Review*. It named an idea that many Americans held. They believed the United States was meant to spread across the continent to the Pacific Ocean. People used the idea to argue for moving west and for going to war with Mexico.

The Mexican-American War lasted from 1846 to 1848. It ended with the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo in 1848. A treaty is a written agreement between nations. In this one, Mexican officials, after losing the war, gave up California, Nevada and Utah, most of Arizona and New Mexico, and parts of Colorado and Wyoming. This land is called the Mexican Cession. Texas had already been annexed in 1845, which means it was made part of the United States. In 1846 officials of the United States and Britain agreed on the border of Oregon.

In early 1848, gold was found at Sutter's Mill in California. The rush came in 1849. About 80,000 people, called forty-niners, arrived that year. From 1848 to 1855 about 300,000 people came to California. About half came by sea, and about half came over land on the California Trail.

California's population, not counting Native people, grew from about 14,000 in 1848 to about 250,000 in 1852. San Francisco grew from about 200 people in 1846 to about 36,000 in 1852.

The forty-niners arrived on the land of California's Native nations. About 150,000 Native people lived in California in 1848. By 1870 only about 30,000 were left, about 120,000 fewer. The historian Benjamin Madley documents the causes: killings, kidnapping, forced labor, disease, hunger, and newcomers driving Native people off their land. Between December 1849 and May 1850, vigilantes and United States Army soldiers killed 1,000 or more Native people. On the last day of 1854, 116 volunteer militiamen attacked the Tolowa people and killed hundreds of them. One militiaman died. Madley documents that state and federal officials took part in the killings, and that taxpayers paid for militia campaigns.

### 1850 to 1900

In the second half of the 1800s, settlers moved onto the Great Plains and the far West, where Native nations lived. Under a law of 1862 they could claim free farmland, and settlers filed about 4 million claims under it. After 1869 a railroad could carry them across the country in about a week. Tens of thousands of Black Southerners also moved west, to Kansas, to get away from violence and cheating in the South.

As the settlers came, United States soldiers forced Native nations onto reservations. A reservation is an area of land that federal officials set aside for a Native nation, often far from its homeland. In 1864 soldiers marched about 8,500 Navajo people more than 300 miles to one of them. By 1890 the officials who counted the country's population no longer found a clear line between settled land and thinly settled land in the West.

<a id="story-amelia-stewart-knight"></a>

#### Amelia Stewart Knight

> **Who:** A wife and mother who kept a diary, day by day, of her family's wagon journey on the Oregon Trail.
>
> **When and where:** From Monroe County, Iowa, to the Willamette Valley near Milwaukie, Oregon Territory, April to September 1853.

Amelia Stewart Knight crossed the Oregon Trail in 1853 while she was pregnant, and she kept a diary of the trip. She traveled with her husband and their seven children. They left Monroe County, Iowa, in April.

Her diary records rain and mud, dust, sick children and hard river crossings. It also records the daily work of handling the wagons and the cattle.

The family reached Oregon on September 17, 1853. The next day, September 18, she gave birth to her eighth child, a son named Adam. Her diary does not mention that she was pregnant until the day the baby was born.

#### The handcart companies, 1856

In 1856 more than 1,000 Latter-day Saint emigrants set out late in the season to walk to Salt Lake City pulling handcarts. A handcart is a small two-wheeled cart that people pull by hand. Many of them were trapped by snow in what is now Wyoming. Counts of the dead run from about 170 to about 250.

The emigrants traveled in two companies. The Willie company, about 500 people, left Florence, in Nebraska Territory, on August 17. A territory was land the United States governed that was not yet a state. The Martin company left on August 27.

An early blizzard struck on October 19, 1856. The Martin company had just waded across the North Platte River, near where Casper, Wyoming, is today. More than 300 rescuers came from Salt Lake with wagons. They brought the survivors in through November.

Counts of the dead differ. Modern counts give about 67 to 77 dead in the Willie company and about 103 to 150 in the Martin company. Older accounts say about 200 to 250 people died in the stranded companies and the wagon trains traveling with them.

<a id="story-levi-savage"></a>

#### Levi Savage

> **Who:** A leader in the Willie handcart company who warned the emigrants not to leave so late, then stayed with them through the blizzards. His journal records what happened.
>
> **When and where:** From Florence, Nebraska Territory, to Salt Lake City, August to November 1856. Born 1820 in Ohio.
>
> **Movie:** *17 Miracles* (2011), a film directed by T. C. Christensen about the Willie handcart company. It draws on Savage's journal.

Levi Savage warned the Willie handcart company that leaving so late would bring snow and deaths. He was 36 and one of the company's sub-captains, the leaders under the captain.

At a camp meeting at Florence on August 13, 1856, Savage spoke to the roughly 500 emigrants. They still had more than 1,000 miles to go. He urged them to wait until spring. In his journal, Savage wrote that most of the emigrants still meant to go on if the church's leaders said go. At later meetings, church leaders urged them to go forward whatever happened. On September 12, out on the trail, the church leader Franklin D. Richards scolded Savage "very severely in open meeting for his lack of faith in God."

Savage went with the company anyway. When the blizzards came, he worked through them to keep people alive. His journal survives, and most modern accounts of the Willie company rely on it.

#### The Weeping Time, 1859

The domestic slave trade went on through the 1850s. The largest single sale took place on March 2 and 3, 1859, at the Ten Broeck Race Course near Savannah, Georgia. Pierce Mease Butler sold between 429 and 436 enslaved men, women and children to pay his gambling debts. The sale brought him $303,850. It rained hard on both days of the sale.

A broker is a person who arranges sales for others. The broker who ran this sale was Joseph Bryan, the largest slave dealer in Savannah. For weeks he advertised it in newspapers across the South, from Richmond to New Orleans. Bryan sold people in family groups as far as the terms of the sale allowed. Those same terms sometimes kept husbands and wives from being bought together. The surviving accounts do not say where the buyers took the people they bought.

Mortimer Thomson, a reporter for the *New York Tribune*, came to the sale dressed as a buyer and wrote a long account of it. Black Georgians remembered the sale as "the weeping time."

#### Free land and the railroad

President Abraham Lincoln signed the Homestead Act on May 20, 1862. Under it, an adult who headed a household could claim up to 160 acres of public land for free. Federal officials had taken much of that land from the Native nations who lived on it. After living on the land and farming it for five years, the settler owned it. Women could claim land. After the Civil War, freed people could claim land too, and so could immigrants who planned to become citizens.

Over the years the law was in force, settlers filed about 4 million claims. Settlers and other private owners got about 270 million acres this way. That was about 10 percent of all the land in the United States. Many settlers moved onto the Great Plains to claim land under the law.

The first railroad across the country was finished at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869. By wagon, a trip from coast to coast took four months or more. By train it took about a week. Under the Pacific Railroad Act, which Lincoln signed in 1862, each railroad company got 6,400 acres of federal land for every mile of track it built. They sold that land to settlers and carried settlers and immigrants west by the trainload.

#### The Long Walk of the Navajo, 1864

From 1863 to 1866, United States soldiers forced more than 10,000 Navajo people from their homeland in what is now Arizona and New Mexico. General James Henry Carleton ordered Colonel Christopher "Kit" Carson to make the Navajo surrender. From August 1863, Carson's troops, guided by Ute scouts and warriors, burned Navajo fields, took their animals and destroyed their food. The troops took more than 5,000 sheep, goats and mules and destroyed more than 75,000 pounds of wheat and the Navajo peach orchards.

By March 1864, 6,000 Navajo had gathered at Fort Canby and Fort Wingate, starving. Soldiers then marched about 8,500 people more than 300 miles to the Bosque Redondo reservation at Fort Sumner, New Mexico. The walk took from 18 to 40 days. The soldiers gave them food planned to last 8 days. This march is known as the Long Walk.

About 200 people died on the march, in winter. Navajo accounts passed down in families say soldiers shot people who could not keep up, among them old people, sick people and pregnant women. Soldiers held more than 8,000 Navajo and Mescalero Apache people at Bosque Redondo. Thousands more died there. On June 1, 1868, Navajo leaders signed a treaty with the United States, and under it the Navajo could go home. Through the 1870s and 1880s, soldiers forced many other nations onto reservations.

<a id="story-laura-ingalls-wilder"></a>

#### Laura Ingalls Wilder

> **Who:** The author of the Little House books. As a child she moved with her family by covered wagon again and again.
>
> **When and where:** Born February 7, 1867, near Pepin, Wisconsin. Family moves from 1869 to 1879. Her own last move, to Mansfield, Missouri, in 1894.
>
> **Movie:** *Little House on the Prairie* (NBC series, 1974 to 1983). It ran for nine seasons and 205 episodes, with Michael Landon as Charles Ingalls. It is loosely based on the books.

Laura Ingalls Wilder's family moved six times between 1869 and 1879. She was born near Pepin, Wisconsin, on February 7, 1867.

In 1869 the family moved to Montgomery County, Kansas, near the town of Independence. Their cabin stood on the Osage Diminished Reserve, land that still belonged to the Osage Nation. The family had no right to be there. They left in 1871 and went back to Pepin.

The family moved to Walnut Grove, Minnesota, in 1874, and swarms of grasshoppers ate their wheat crops there in 1875 and 1876. Then they moved to Burr Oak, Iowa, where they helped run a hotel from 1876, then Walnut Grove again in 1877. In 1879 they settled at De Smet, in Dakota Territory. There Laura's father, Charles Ingalls, took a job at a railroad camp and then claimed a homestead.

Laura married Almanzo Wilder in 1885. In 1894, a year of drought, Laura, Almanzo and their daughter Rose drove a covered hack, a light wagon with a cover, about 650 miles from De Smet to Mansfield, Missouri. She kept a diary of the trip. It was published in 1962 as *On the Way Home*. In Mansfield she later wrote the Little House books.

The books came out from 1932 to 1943. In them, Wilder changed the real story. In *Little House on the Prairie*, Laura is several years older than she really was in Kansas, where she was 2 to 4 years old. The books leave out the Burr Oak years completely. They also do not say that the family was living on Osage land.

#### The cattle drives

After the Civil War, cowboys drove herds of longhorn cattle north from Texas to Kansas. They took the cattle to railheads, the towns at the end of a railroad line, where the cattle were loaded onto trains. Abilene was one of these towns. The railroad reached Abilene in 1867, and after that the Chisholm Trail from Texas was used heavily.

About 5 million cattle or more were driven north from Texas between 1866 and 1884. Some estimates put the total for the whole era at about 6 million. In 1871 alone, about 700,000 cattle reached the railheads in Kansas.

The long drives ended in the mid-1880s for several reasons. Barbed wire fences went up across the open range. Railroads reached deeper into Texas, so the cattle no longer had to walk to Kansas. In 1885 and 1886 Kansas lawmakers passed a quarantine law to keep Texas cattle out of the state. A quarantine keeps animals or people apart to stop the spread of disease. Then the cold of the winter of 1886 and 1887 killed much of the cattle herd.

#### The Exodusters, 1879

In 1879 thousands of Black Southerners left their homes and moved to Kansas. People called them Exodusters. The name comes from the Exodus, the story in the Bible of the Israelites' escape from slavery in Egypt. Many came from Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas and Tennessee. As many as 40,000 moved to Kansas, Oklahoma and Colorado between about 1879 and 1881. About 6,000 reached Kansas in the spring of 1879 alone.

They left because former Confederates took away their votes, white landowners cheated them, and armed white men attacked them. The Confederates were the Southerners who had fought against the United States in the Civil War to keep slavery. After the presidential election of 1876, former Confederates took back control of the Southern states, and they took away Black Southerners' right to vote. The historian Damani Davis calls what Black Southerners faced "relentless terror."

Many Black Southerners were sharecroppers. A sharecropper farms someone else's land and pays with a share of the crop. Benjamin Singleton, who led many of the migrants to Kansas, was angry that white landowners cheated the Black sharecroppers who farmed their land.

In Louisiana, the Black organizer Henry Adams collected the names of nearly 700 Black people who had been attacked. For each one he listed where it happened and what was done. Most of them had been whipped, beaten, shot or killed by white men, often by armed groups. Some entries name the man. One entry says that a white man, Dr. Moore, killed a Black man named Calvin in 1871, after Calvin was accused of cursing a white woman.

Many Exodusters traveled up the Mississippi River by steamboat. Crowds of them waited on the docks at St. Louis. In 1880 members of a United States Senate committee looked into why they had left. The members who disagreed with the majority wrote their own report. It said the migrants had fled because they could no longer bear the hardship, unfair treatment and suffering that "a class of Democrats in the South" had brought on them. The migrants saw Kansas as a safe place. John Brown, who fought to end slavery, had lived there. Before the Civil War, many Kansans had wanted it to be a free state, a state without slavery.

<a id="story-benjamin-pap-singleton"></a>

#### Benjamin "Pap" Singleton

> **Who:** A man born into slavery who organized Black Southerners to move to Kansas. He called himself the "Father of the Exodus."
>
> **When and where:** Born enslaved in Nashville, Tennessee, about 1809. Led the move to Kansas in the late 1870s. Died 1900.

Benjamin Singleton helped thousands of Black Southerners move to Kansas in the 1870s. He called himself the "Father of the Exodus."

He was born into slavery in Nashville, Tennessee, in about 1809. He ran away several times. In the end he escaped to the North and to Canada. In about 1871, after the Civil War, he came back to Tennessee. He worked there as a carpenter, a cabinetmaker and an undertaker, a person who prepares the dead for burial.

Singleton was angry that white landowners cheated the Black sharecroppers who worked their land. He believed Black Southerners would never get a fair chance at land in the South. He printed handbills, short printed notices, to draw Black settlers to Kansas. He formed a group called the Edgefield Real Estate and Homestead Association to move people there.

Singleton said under oath, at a hearing, that his work helped more than 7,400 people move. Between 1877 and 1879, his group steered more than 20,000 people toward Kansas. He died in 1900.

#### The Oklahoma Land Run, 1889

At noon on April 22, 1889, about 50,000 people raced into central Oklahoma to claim land. The land they entered was called the Unassigned Lands. It covered about 1.9 million acres in the middle of Indian Territory. Nearly 2 million acres were claimed in a single day.

Indian Territory was the land in present-day Oklahoma where federal officials had moved many Native nations. The Unassigned Lands were the last part of it that federal officials had not given to any of those nations. Federal officials had taken land in Indian Territory from the nations there.

After the Civil War, federal officials pressed the Creek and Seminole nations to give up land. Dennis N. Cooley, the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, was the federal official in charge of dealings with Native nations. In 1865 he told the nations' leaders that they had lost their rights under the old treaties by joining the Confederacy. In treaties of 1866 the Creek had to sign over the western half of their land for $975,168. The Seminole had to sign over all of theirs for fifteen cents an acre. The Five Tribes were the Cherokee, Choctaw, Muscogee (Creek), Chickasaw and Seminole nations. With these treaties, they lost the western half of present-day Oklahoma.

From 1879 to 1888, groups of settlers called boomers, led by David L. Payne and William Couch, entered the Unassigned Lands against the law. Cavalry soldiers, soldiers who fought on horseback, arrested them and took them out again and again. In 1889 Representative William Springer of Illinois changed a bill in Congress so that President Benjamin Harrison could open the land. Harrison announced the opening on March 23, 1889.

Each settler could claim 160 acres under the Homestead Act. People who sneaked in before the start to grab land were called "Sooners." By the end of that day, Guthrie and Oklahoma City were towns of about 10,000 to 15,000 people each.

#### The frontier line disappears from the census, 1890

In 1890 the officials who ran the United States census reported that the country no longer had a clear "frontier line." The census is the official count of the population, taken every ten years. The frontier line had been the edge of thinly settled land in the West, where two to six people lived on each square mile.

In 1893 the historian Frederick Jackson Turner wrote an essay about that census finding. It was called "The Significance of the Frontier in American History." Many people later treated 1890 as the end of the years when settlers could still find open land in the West, land that had belonged to Native nations.

### 1900 to 1950

From about 1910 to 1970, roughly 6 million Black Americans left the South for cities in the North, the Midwest and the West. Most of the early travelers went by train. In the late 1930s more than 250,000 people moved from the dried-out farms of the southern Plains to California.

In 1942 United States Army officers ordered Japanese Americans out of their homes on the West Coast. Soldiers and officials forced them into camps.

#### The Great Migration, the first wave

The movement of Black Americans out of the rural South from about 1910 to 1970 is called the Great Migration. The first wave, from about 1910 to 1940, went mostly to cities in the North and the Midwest. Most people rode the trains north. Later travelers also went by car and by bus.

Between 1910 and 1920 the Black population of Chicago grew by about 148 percent. Detroit's grew by about 611 percent, and Philadelphia's by about 500 percent. In New York City it about doubled, from about 152,000 people to 328,000. In 1900 about 90 percent of Black Americans lived in the South. By 1970 fewer than 55 percent did.

Black Georgians had several reasons to leave. In 1915 and 1916 the boll weevil, a beetle that eats cotton plants, and floods ruined the cotton crop. Between 1880 and 1930, lynch mobs in Georgia killed more than 450 people, most of them Black. A lynch mob is a crowd that kills a person without any trial. Jim Crow laws were Southern laws that required Black people and white people to be kept apart. Under them, nearly all Black Georgians could not vote. About 74,000 Black Georgians left between 1910 and 1920, and about 260,000 more left in the 1920s.

Some people in the North urged Black Southerners to come. In 1905 Robert S. Abbott started a Black newspaper, the *Chicago Defender*. In its pages, job listings and train schedules ran beside editorials, articles that give a newspaper's opinion. The editorials urged Black Southerners to come north. The *Defender* listed May 15, 1917, as the date for a "Great Northern Drive." Some Northern employers paid migrants' train fares and then took the money back out of their wages.

White officials in the South worked to keep Black workers from leaving. A labor recruiter is a person hired to find workers. Officials in Macon, Georgia, charged Northern labor recruiters a license fee of $25,000, a payment for permission to work there.

Black people in the North also met violence. On July 27, 1919, Eugene Williams, who was 17, and four friends drifted on a homemade raft in Lake Michigan in Chicago. They crossed an unmarked line into the water off a beach at 29th Street where only white people were allowed. George Stauber, a 24-year-old white man, threw rocks at them until Williams drowned. A white police officer, Daniel Callahan, refused to arrest Stauber and stopped a Black officer from arresting him.

Five days of attacks followed, through August 3. The white attackers included youth gangs and groups that called themselves athletic clubs. Thirty-eight people were killed, 23 Black and 15 white. The histories of the riot do not say who killed each of them. About 537 people were injured, and two-thirds of them were Black. Hundreds of homes were burned or damaged. Of the 138 people charged with crimes afterward, two-thirds were Black.

<a id="story-ida-mae-brandon-gladney"></a>

#### Ida Mae Brandon Gladney

> **Who:** A sharecropper's wife who left Mississippi with her family after white men nearly beat a cousin to death.
>
> **When and where:** From Chickasaw County, Mississippi, by train, late October 1937. Settled in Chicago.

Ida Mae Brandon Gladney and her family left Mississippi in 1937 after a group of white men beat a cousin of theirs nearly to death. The cousin, Joe Lee, had been falsely accused of stealing turkeys. The men beat him with heavy chains. The turkeys turned up the next day, and no one apologized to him. The accounts of the beating do not name the men.

Ida Mae and her husband, George Gladney, were sharecroppers in Chickasaw County. A sharecropper farms someone else's land and pays the owner with part of the crop.
