They grew cotton on the plantation of Edd Pearson, whom they called Mr. Edd. After the beating, George came home and told her, "This is the last crop that we're making."

In late October 1937 the cotton was picked, and George settled with Mr. Edd over what the year's work was worth. None of the family had ever been on a train or out of Mississippi. A brother-in-law drove Ida Mae and the two children, James and Velma, in his truck to the train station at Okolona. There they met George and rode north through the night.

The family settled in Chicago. One account says they stopped first in Milwaukee, where Ida Mae's sister Irene lived. In Chicago, George hauled ice up four and five flights of stairs. Ida Mae did housework for other people and then found work as a hospital aide. In time the family bought a house. Ida Mae died in 2002. The writer Isabel Wilkerson told Ida Mae's life, from interviews with her, in the 2010 book *The Warmth of Other Suns*.

#### The Dust Bowl move

In the 1930s, drought and windstorms tore the topsoil off farms across the southern Great Plains. A drought is a long stretch of time with too little rain. The Dust Bowl was the name for those parts of Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado and New Mexico.

From about 1935 to 1940, more than 250,000 people left the Dust Bowl states for California. Another count covers only Oklahoma but every destination. That count is everyone who left Oklahoma for any place, minus the people who moved in. By that count Oklahoma may have lost as many as 440,000 people. Many of the travelers went west on U.S. Route 66. In California the newcomers were called "Okies."

In February 1936 the Los Angeles police chief, James E. Davis, sent his officers to the state line to turn back poor migrants. People called it the "bum blockade." From February 3, 136 Los Angeles officers stood at 16 crossing points. Those points were on California's roughly 700-mile border with Arizona, Nevada and Oregon, far outside the city. Davis pointed to a 1933 state law against bringing poor people into California. His officers stopped trains, cars and people hitchhiking. They took people's fingerprints and turned back anyone they judged unable to support themselves.

On February 8 alone, the officers arrested 122 people for vagrancy, the crime of having no home or means of support. A week into the blockade, Davis announced that he would force the people arrested into unpaid labor, quarrying rock, sand and gravel for public projects. Forced labor is work people are made to do against their will. Many of the people arrested were locked up in prisons far from the state line. Quarrying means cutting and breaking stone out of the ground.

Railroad executives and some county sheriffs backed the blockade. So did the people who ran the *Los Angeles Times* and the Los Angeles Chamber of Commerce, a group of the city's business owners. California's attorney general, the state's top lawyer, Ulysses S. Webb, said Davis had "no jurisdiction beyond the city's territorial limits." That meant he had no power outside Los Angeles. Arizona's governor, Benjamin Moeur, called the blockade illegal and unconstitutional, which means against the Constitution. Davis called his officers home in early April 1936. He claimed they had turned back about 11,000 people. Writing in *Smithsonian* magazine in 2025, Olatunji Osho-Williams reports that the real number was probably much lower.

<a id="story-florence-owens-thompson"></a>

#### Florence Owens Thompson

> **Who:** A farmworker born in what is now Oklahoma, whose parents said their families were Cherokee, who moved from crop to crop in California. She is the woman in Dorothea Lange's 1936 photograph "Migrant Mother."
>
> **When and where:** Born in Indian Territory in 1903. Moved to California in the 1920s. Photographed at a pea-pickers' camp in Nipomo, California, in March 1936.

Florence Owens Thompson moved to California in the 1920s, years before the Dust Bowl, and worked in its fields as a farm laborer. She was born Florence Leona Christie on September 1, 1903, in Indian Territory, which is now Oklahoma. Both of her parents said their families were Cherokee.

In 1921 she married Cleo Owens. During the 1920s they moved west with several of his relatives to Oroville, California. Cleo died in 1931. In about 1933 she and her parents moved to Shafter, California. She followed the crops from one harvest to the next.

On March 6, 1936, the timing chain in the family's car snapped. The timing chain is an engine part, and the car could not run without it. The family stopped at a camp of pea pickers near Nipomo. Freezing rain had destroyed the pea crop there. The photographer Dorothea Lange took seven pictures of Thompson in about ten minutes. One of them became known as "Migrant Mother," and it became one of the most reproduced pictures of the 1930s.

Thompson's name was not made public until 1978. That year Emmett Corrigan, a reporter for the *Modesto Bee*, found her. She died on September 16, 1983.

#### The forced removal of Japanese Americans, 1942

In 1942 United States Army officers forced more than 110,000 Japanese Americans out of their homes on the West Coast. On February 19, 1942, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066. An executive order is a rule issued by a president. Under this one, military commanders could keep "any or all persons" out of areas they named. General John L. DeWitt commanded the Army on the West Coast. In March and April 1942 he issued orders aimed at "all persons of Japanese ancestry," meaning everyone whose family came from Japan. United States citizens and people who were not citizens were ordered out alike.

On March 11, DeWitt set up an Army office to carry out the removal. Karl Bendetsen, an Army officer, commanded it. The next day, at 34, he was made a colonel. Bendetsen's staff divided the coast into 108 areas of about 1,000 Japanese Americans each. They issued a separate order for each area. Under each order, the people in that area had to report on a set day, about a week later. They could bring only what they could carry. Under the first order, issued on March 24, the 55 Japanese American families on Bainbridge Island, near Seattle, had six days to leave their homes. Army officers carried out the 108 orders and forced out 110,442 people.

Army engineers built 15 temporary camps, many of them at fairgrounds and racetracks. When people arrived, soldiers searched their bags. At the Tanforan camp in California, half of the people lived in horse stables, three to six people in a stall built for one horse. After about three months, on average, officials moved them again. This time they went to 10 larger camps run by officials of a federal office called the War Relocation Authority. The National Archives counts about 120,000 people removed in all, a larger total than the count for the 108 orders alone.

<a id="story-george-swanson-starling"></a>

#### George Swanson Starling

> **Who:** A Florida fruit picker who organized the other pickers to ask for better pay, then fled north when he learned that the grove owners were plotting to hang him.
>
> **When and where:** From Wildwood, Florida, to Harlem in New York City, by train, April 14, 1945.

George Swanson Starling fled Florida on April 14, 1945, because the owners of the citrus groves where he worked were plotting to kill him.

Starling grew up in Eustis, in Lake County, Florida. He finished first in his high school class and went to Florida Agricultural and Mechanical State College in Tallahassee. In the middle of his second year, his father told him he had had enough schooling and must go to work. Starling went to work picking citrus fruit. The pickers climbed trees as tall as 40 feet. Some fell and broke arms or legs.

Starling organized the pickers to ask for about 10 cents more a box. In one dispute the price at the packing house, where the fruit was packed for sale, was ten cents a box for picking tangerines, and the pickers asked for twenty. In 1944 tangerines sold at auction for an average of $4.40 a box.

The grove owners were angry. Someone overheard them planning to take Starling and two other pickers out to the cypress swamps at Blackwater Creek and hang them. Starling left within days. A man named Roscoe Colton drove him in his truck to the train station in Wildwood. There Starling boarded the Silver Meteor, a train to New York. He rode in the Jim Crow car, the car set aside for Black passengers, where the railroad also stored luggage. The ride took 23 hours. His wife, Inez, stayed behind until he could send for her.

Starling settled in Harlem, where an aunt and many of his friends lived. He later got a steady job working on the same train that had carried him north. Isabel Wilkerson's book *The Warmth of Other Suns* also describes his life. The accounts of Starling's life do not name the grove owners who planned to kill him.

### 1950 to 2000

Large numbers of Americans moved from the North to the South and the West between 1950 and 2000. Between 1970 and 1990 the population of the South grew by about 36 percent, and the population of the West by about 51 percent. In the second wave of the Great Migration, many Black Southerners moved to cities on the West Coast. Federal officials paid for Native people to move from reservations to cities. Reservations are lands set aside for Native nations.

By the late 1990s more Black Americans were moving to the South than were leaving it.

#### The second wave of the Great Migration

The second wave of the Great Migration lasted from about 1940 to 1970, and it was larger than the first. More of its travelers went west, to Los Angeles, Oakland, Seattle and Portland. They went for factory jobs, first during World War II and then after it. These travelers are counted in the same total of about 6 million people who left the South between 1910 and 1970.

<a id="story-robert-joseph-pershing-foster"></a>

#### Robert Joseph Pershing Foster

> **Who:** A Black surgeon who could not work in the hospital of his own home town in Louisiana. He drove alone to California and opened his own medical practice in Los Angeles.
>
> **When and where:** From Monroe, Louisiana, to Los Angeles, California, by car, April 1953.

Robert Joseph Pershing Foster drove from Louisiana to California in 1953 because he could not work as a surgeon at home. He had served as a surgeon in the Army. When he came back to Monroe, Louisiana, he found that he could not work in the hospital in his own home town. The people who ran St. Francis Hospital there would not let Black doctors do even a simple operation to take out a patient's tonsils. Isabel Wilkerson traced his trip in *The Warmth of Other Suns*.

Foster set out alone on Easter Monday, April 6, 1953, in his 1949 Buick Roadmaster, a dark red car with white-walled tires. He planned to send for his family once he was settled. Once he was long past Texas, he thought he was a safe distance from the South. In Arizona, motel clerks turned him away, a Black man traveling alone, even under "vacancy" signs, which tell drivers that rooms are free. One clerk told him they had forgotten to turn off the sign. Others said the rooms had just been rented. He could not find a place to stay the night, and he drove on until he reached California. Alone in the dark desert, he asked himself what he was doing. If he turned back, Wilkerson writes, "the I-knew-its would ring in his ear." The "I-knew-its" were the people who would say they had known he would fail.

In Los Angeles, Foster opened his own medical practice. Many of his patients were migrants from the South, as he was. One of them was the musician Ray Charles.

#### The move to the Sun Belt

After World War II, many Americans moved from the older factory states of the North to the South and the West. People later nicknamed the Northern factory states the "Rust Belt" and the South and the West the "Sun Belt." People moved for jobs, for warmer weather and for cheaper land. Air conditioning made hot places comfortable all year, and that helped the Sun Belt grow.

Between 1970 and 1990 the South grew by about 36 percent and the West by about 51 percent. By counts from the Census Bureau, the federal office that counts the population, the whole country grew by about 22 percent in those years, from about 203 million people to about 249 million. In 1962 California passed New York as the state with the most people. It had about 17 million people then, roughly three times as many as before World War II.

In 1956 members of Congress passed the Federal-Aid Highway Act. Under it, work began on the Interstate Highway System, a network of big highways across the country. The interstates made long moves by car easier. They also made it easier to live in a suburb, a town at the edge of a city.

#### Federal officials move Native families to cities

From about 1950 into the 1970s, officials of the Bureau of Indian Affairs paid for Native people to move from reservations to cities. The Bureau of Indian Affairs is the federal office in charge of the government's dealings with Native nations. Its officials started the program, called Relocation, between about 1948 and 1952. In 1956 members of Congress backed it with the Indian Relocation Act.

The officials gave people one-way tickets to a city and help for a short time after they arrived. About 30,000 Native people moved to cities in the 1950s. By the time the program ended in the 1970s, more than 100,000 had moved. They went to Minneapolis, Chicago, Oakland and San Francisco, Los Angeles, Denver and other cities. Many of them lived in poverty there. They also built new Native communities in those cities.

#### The Great Migration turns around

In the 1970s a small number of Black Americans began moving back to the South. The number grew through the 1990s. By the late 1990s the South gained more Black migrants than it lost to each of the other three regions of the country, the Northeast, the Midwest and the West. For 35 years before that, more Black Americans had left the South than moved to it. William H. Frey, a researcher at the Brookings Institution, a research group, calls this return the New Great Migration.

### 2000 to Today

Hurricane Katrina drove more than 1 million people out of the New Orleans area and the Gulf Coast in 2005. It was the largest sudden move of people in these years. After Hurricane María hit Puerto Rico in 2017, about 130,000 people left the island for the mainland within a year.

The steadier flow toward the South went on through these years. The Census Bureau is the federal office that counts the population. By its estimates, from 2020 to 2024 the South gained about 2.7 million more people from other states than it lost to them.

#### The pull of the South

Census Bureau staff count moves between states as net domestic migration. That is the number of people who move into a state from other states, minus the number who move out to other states. By this measure the South gained about 2.7 million people from 2020 to 2024.

Many of the people who moved between states left coastal states where homes cost a lot. From April 2020 to July 2022, California lost about 343,000 people to other states, and New York lost about 300,000, by Census Bureau counts. A metro area is a city together with its suburbs. The metro areas that lost the most people included New York, Los Angeles, San Francisco and Chicago. After 2020 some people could work from home. The Pew Research Center is a group that studies how Americans live and what they think. Its researchers reported that working from home let some people choose where to live by the cost of a home and the space it offered, not by where their job was.

Florida's gains from other states shrank after 2022. By Census Bureau counts, Florida had a net gain of about 311,000 people from other states in 2022 and about 184,000 in 2023. In the year from July 2024 to June 2025, Florida gained about 23,000. The Census Bureau released the 2025 figures in January 2026. In that same year North Carolina gained the most people from other states, about 84,000. Texas and South Carolina each gained about 67,000.

The National Association of Realtors, a group for people who sell houses, ranked the states from the same Census figures. In that ranking, nine of the fifteen states with the biggest gains in 2024 to 2025 were in the South. The Midwest also gained about 16,000 people from other states that year, its first such gain this decade.

The New Great Migration of Black Americans to the South went on. William Frey of the Brookings Institution found that the Black population of metro Atlanta grew about five times over from 1970 to 2020. By 2010 it had passed Chicago's to rank second in the country. From 2000 to 2018, Atlanta was the most common destination of young Black adults aged 16 to 26 who moved. Seven of their ten most common destinations were in the South.

#### Leaving New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina, 2005

In late August 2005, Hurricane Katrina struck the Gulf Coast, and the levees around New Orleans broke. A levee is a wall of earth or concrete built to hold back water. The storm and the broken levees forced more than 1 million people from their homes in the New Orleans area and along the Gulf Coast. A month later, the people of up to 600,000 homes were still away. These counts come from The Data Center, a research group in New Orleans, and from the federal housing department.

Many people never came back. New Orleans had 484,674 people at the 2000 census. By July 2006 an estimated 230,172 people lived there, fewer than half as many, The Data Center reported. In 2024 the city had about 363,000 people, by an estimate reported by the news site The Center Square in 2025. That was about 120,000 fewer than in 2000. In July 2025 the seven parishes of the New Orleans metro area had 970,849 people, 3.6 percent fewer than in April 2020, The Data Center found. In Louisiana a parish is what other states call a county.

Some of the people who tried to walk out of the flooded city were stopped by police. On September 1, 2005, officers from three police forces blocked the Crescent City Connection bridge over the Mississippi River. They were the Gretna police, the bridge police and the Jefferson Parish sheriff's office. They turned back people on foot at gunpoint. Two paramedics, medical workers who ride ambulances, were in the crowd. They came from San Francisco, and they reported that police "fired their weapons above their heads."

Gretna Police Chief Arthur Lawson made the decision together with officials of the sheriff's office and the bridge police. Gretna's mayor, Ronnie Harris, defended it. He said the town was not a shelter or an evacuation route and had no running water, no electricity and no food. Members of the Gretna City Council voted to support the blockade. It lasted until Labor Day, September 5, 2005. No count survives of how many people the officers turned back.

Evacuees are people who leave a place to escape danger. By Houston officials' own estimates, reported by the *Texas Tribune* in 2010, about 250,000 evacuees came there at the peak, and about 150,000 were still there a year later. By 2010 Houston's mayor, Annise Parker, said city officials no longer counted them apart from other residents: "They are Houstonians."

<a id="story-kimberly-rivers-roberts"></a>

#### Kimberly Rivers Roberts

> **Movie:** *Trouble the Water* (2008), a documentary about Kimberly and Scott Roberts, directed by Tia Lessin and Carl Deal and built largely on her own video. It won the Grand Jury Prize for documentary at the 2008 Sundance Film Festival and was nominated for an Academy Award.
>
> **Who:** A woman of 24 from the Lower Ninth Ward of New Orleans who wanted to be a rap singer. With her husband, Scott Roberts, she filmed the Katrina flood from inside it.
>
> **When and where:** New Orleans, August 2005. Then Alexandria and northern Louisiana, then Memphis, Tennessee, then home to New Orleans.

Kimberly Rivers Roberts and her husband, Scott Roberts, were still in their New Orleans neighborhood when Katrina's flood came, because someone had recently stolen their car. "If I had wheels I'd be gone too," she told a neighbor. On August 28, 2005, she began filming with a camcorder she had bought for $20.

As the water rose, the couple and their neighbors climbed into an attic. They called 911 and heard that police would not come until conditions got better. A neighbor floated people to safety on a punching bag.

Afterward the group tried to take shelter at a Navy base that stood nearly empty. The couple's film shows men at the gate turning them away at gunpoint. A voice says, "Get off our property, or we're going to start shooting." Navy officials deny that this happened. The accounts of the film do not name the men at the gate.

Kimberly's grandmother died in a hospital that was not emptied of its patients. Her uncle was later found dead in his home. The accounts do not say who decided to leave the hospital's patients there, and they do not state the cause of either death.

The couple went to a Red Cross shelter in Alexandria, Louisiana, then to her uncle's trailer in northern Louisiana. Next they moved to Memphis, Tennessee, to stay with one of Kimberly's cousins and try to start over. They were waiting for a promised check from FEMA, the federal office for disaster help. It did not arrive, and they had a hard time settling in a new city.

Kimberly and Scott went back to their home in the Ninth Ward and set out to rebuild it. Scott got a job with a builder repairing houses that the flood had ruined. Kimberly started her own record label, Born Hustler Records.

#### Leaving Puerto Rico after Hurricane María, 2017

Hurricane María hit Puerto Rico in September 2017, and within a year about 130,000 people had left the island for the mainland. That was almost 4 percent of the people of Puerto Rico. The count is the Census Bureau's estimate for July 2017 to July 2018. Researchers writing in the science journal PNAS in 2020 described other counts, made from air travel records, phone records and social media data. Those estimates run from about 160,000 to 470,000, depending on which data they used.

Puerto Rico is a territory of the United States, land that belongs to the country but is not a state. Puerto Ricans are United States citizens, so a move from the island to the mainland is a move within the country. By Census Bureau figures, about a third of the people who moved from Puerto Rico to the mainland in 2018 went to Florida.

<a id="ch-city-building"></a>

## Chapter 6: City Building

### Before 1500

People built planned cities on this land between about 900 and about 1350, hundreds of years before any European came here. In a planned city, people decide ahead of time where each open square, wall and mound will go, and then they build it that way. The largest of these cities stood beside the Mississippi River. In the Southwest, people cut and stacked stone to build towns. Their descendants still live in towns along the Rio Grande.

The people who built these places kept no written records. No builder's, planner's or ruler's name survives. Archaeologists, the scientists who dig up and study what people left behind long ago, know them only from the mounds, walls, rooms and roads they left.

#### Cahokia, a city laid out on purpose

In what is now Illinois, across the Mississippi River from where St. Louis, Missouri, stands today, people built up the city of Cahokia quickly from about 1050. It was the largest town north of Mexico before Europeans came. At its peak, around 1100, roughly 10,000 to 20,000 people lived in the center. London had about as many people at the same date. Some estimates put as many as 50,000 people in the wider settlement around the center. Those larger figures are estimates, and they do not agree.

The people of Cahokia planned where the big pieces of their city would go. At its center they raised Monks Mound, the largest prehistoric structure made of earth in the Americas. Prehistoric means built before anyone living here kept written records. The mound holds about 814,000 cubic yards of earth. Workers carried every basketload of it by hand, and they raised the mound in stages.

It has four terraces, or wide steps, and its top stands about 100 feet high. Its base covers roughly 14 acres. UNESCO is the United Nations body that keeps the World Heritage list of historic sites. Its listing for Cahokia records fourteen separate building stages in the mound.

The Grand Plaza, about 50 acres of open ground, lay at the foot of the mound. Its builders leveled the ground and filled in the low spots by hand so that it was flat. They made it flat for ceremonies and for the game of chunkey. In chunkey, one player rolled a stone disk across the ground, and the players threw spears to see whose spear landed closest to the spot where the stone stopped.

West of Monks Mound the builders set up a circle of red cedar posts. They built five of these circles, one after another, and each new circle took the place of the last. The posts line up with the points on the horizon where the sun rises at the solstices and the equinoxes. The solstices are the longest day and the shortest day of the year. The equinoxes are the two days between them when day and night are equal in length. So the posts worked as a calendar, and the builders set them into the plan of the city.

A palisade, a wall of upright logs about two miles long, ran around the central part of the city. People began it around 1100 and rebuilt it three times over about two hundred years. Each rebuilding took between 15,000 and 20,000 logs of oak and hickory, each roughly a foot thick and twenty feet tall.

By about 1350 the people of Cahokia had scattered and left the city.

#### Stone towns of the Southwest

In what is now northwestern New Mexico, Chaco Canyon was the center of the Ancestral Puebloan world. Ancestral Puebloan people are the ancestors of the people who live in the pueblos of the Southwest today. Pueblo is the Spanish word for a town, and Spanish colonists used it for the stone and adobe towns they found there. Adobe is brick made of mud and dried in the sun. At Chaco they built great houses, which are large buildings of shaped stone. They went on building and using the great houses for roughly 280 years, from about 900 to about 1180. One of them, Pueblo Bonito, had more than 650 rooms.

The people of Chaco also built roads, and they built them to a plan. The roads run straight for miles across the Four Corners country, where Colorado, Utah, Arizona and New Mexico meet. They average about 30 feet wide, and they connected farther-off villages to the canyon.

In southwestern Colorado, at Mesa Verde, people built rooms of sandstone blocks and mud into the hollows under overhanging cliffs. Cliff Palace is the largest of those cliff dwellings. It has 150 rooms and 23 kivas, and people built it between 1190 and 1280. A kiva is a round room, usually sunk into the ground, used for ceremonies and for meetings. More than 100 people lived at Cliff Palace.

People began leaving Chaco in the 1140s. That date marks the start of the leaving, and the years 900 to 1180 mark the whole time the great houses were built and used. The last building and the last living in the canyon came to an end by about 1180 to 1200. People had left Mesa Verde by the 1280s. The people who left both places gathered again in the pueblo towns along the Rio Grande, and their descendants still live in those pueblos today.

### The 1500s

In 1565 the Spaniard Pedro Menendez de Aviles founded St. Augustine on the Florida coast, in a Timucua town. The Spanish settlers moved their town twice in its first seven years, but people have lived in St. Augustine without a break since 1565. Eight years after the founding, the king of Spain issued written orders that stated how Spanish officials must lay out every new town.

#### St. Augustine and the Laws of the Indies

In September 1565 Pedro Menendez de Aviles founded St. Augustine on the coast of Florida. He placed it in Seloy's town, a town of the Timucua people whose chief was named Seloy. Menendez landed there on September 8 with about 800 colonists, among them 26 women and an unknown number of enslaved Africans. The colonists moved into Seloy's town, and they used the chief's council house as their first fort. Timucua council houses were round, roofed with thatch, which is dried straw or reeds, and big enough to hold up to a thousand people.

The Timucua did not want the Spaniards living in their town. They attacked them again and again to drive them away. In 1566, according to the Florida Museum of Natural History, the Timucua shot flaming arrows at the fort. The fort was the Timucua's own council house, and the museum's account says that is why the attack did so much harm. On April 1, 1566, half of the fort burned, and the Spaniards lost all their supplies. In May 1566, about nine months after landing, Menendez moved the settlement across the bay to Anastasia Island, where the Spaniards felt safer from attack. They lived on the island for about six years. By about 1572 they had moved back to the mainland, to the site of today's St. Augustine.

The town stood in three places in its first seven years. Through both moves, people went on living in it, and people have lived in St. Augustine without a break since 1565. Of all the cities Europeans founded on the mainland of the United States, it is the oldest one that people have lived in the whole time.

In 1573 King Philip II of Spain issued a set of ordinances called the Laws of the Indies. The Indies was the Spanish name for Spain's lands in the Americas. An ordinance is a written order that people must obey as law. These ordinances stated exactly how the men who founded Spanish towns had to lay them out.

Each town began with a central plaza, which is a public square of open ground with the town built around it. The plaza's sides had to face north, south, east and west, and it had to be one and a half times as long as it was wide. The streets ran out from it in a grid. A grid is a pattern of straight streets that cross each other at right angles. The founders had to set aside certain lots, or pieces of land, for the church and for the government buildings. These ordinances were among the first written rules anywhere in the world that set the same town plan for every new town, wherever Spanish officials founded one.

St. Augustine's Plaza de la Constitucion was laid out under those 1573 ordinances, after the town already existed. Government buildings and the church faced onto it, and traders began holding a market there in 1598. It is the oldest public square in the country. Across what is now the Southwest, Spanish town-builders went on laying out towns in the same plaza-and-grid pattern.

### The 1600s

Each of the colonial towns in this era went up in the homeland of a Native nation. English colonists began Jamestown in 1607 as a fort. Boston, founded in 1630, had no plan at all, and its streets formed around the houses and the hills. Spanish officials laid out Santa Fe around a plaza. In 1682 William Penn had his surveyor, the man who measured the land and marked out the streets, draw the whole of Philadelphia on paper before a single street existed on the ground. The founders of many early American towns later followed Penn's example.

#### Fort towns, walls, and watchmen

On April 26, 1607, three English ships sailed into the Chesapeake Bay with 144 English men and boys. They settled on Jamestown Island, on the James River in Virginia. The island lay inside the land of the Paspahegh people, who hunted there and had a town about four miles away. The Paspahegh were one of 28 to 32 nations, each with its own chief, that paid tribute to one ruler, Powhatan. Tribute is a payment of goods to a ruler. On May 26 the Paspahegh attacked the newcomers. By June 15 the colonists had finished James Fort, a three-sided fort. Its wall was a stockade, a fence of upright oak and poplar logs about 14 feet high. In the 1620s the surveyor William Claiborne laid out a settlement east of the fort called New Towne. Archaeologists have dug up the foundations of rows of houses there.

Governor Pedro de Peralta founded Santa Fe about 1610 and planned it around a central plaza, in the Spanish pattern. He and his men laid it out at the foot of the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, on the ruins of an older Pueblo town. The Tewa people call that place O'Ga P'Ogeh, which means "white shell water place." The Palace of the Governors stands on Santa Fe's plaza. People have used it as a public building without a break for longer than any other building in the United States.

English colonists founded Boston in 1630 without any plan, on a peninsula that the Massachusett people called Shawmut. A peninsula is land with water on almost every side. The colonists put their houses up near the waterfront, and the streets formed around the hills, brooks and marshes that were already on the ground. The biggest hill was the Trimountain, a steep hill with three tops, which is now called Beacon Hill. According to a well-known story, Boston's crooked streets follow old cow paths. The story is a legend. A writer for Boston Magazine checked it in 2018 and traced it to a line that the American writer Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote in 1860.

Boston's first houses had chimneys made of wood and roofs made of thatch, which is dried straw or reeds. Several of them burned in the colony's first months. In March 1631 Thomas Dudley wrote in a letter to the Countess of Lincoln that he and the colony's other leaders had ordered "that noe man shall build his chimney with wood nor cover his house with thatch." The fires, he wrote, always began "in the wooden chimneys." That same year the people of Boston set up a night watch. The watchmen walked the streets at night to guard the town against criminals, wild animals and fire. The Boston Police Department's own history lists that watch as the start of the city's police.

Wall Street in New York City runs along the line of a wall that is long gone. The wall ran across the northern edge of New Amsterdam, the Dutch town on the southern tip of Manhattan. Manhattan was part of the homeland of the Lenape people. The wall stretched from the East River to the North River, which is now called the Hudson. In 1653 a gang of Black men dug the trench for it. The Dutch West India Company owned them, though some of them had gained what the Dutch called half-freedom. A half-free man could hold land of his own, but he still owed the Company work and a yearly payment, and his children stayed the Company's property. The Company was a Dutch trading company, and its officials ran the colony. According to a Columbia University history project, the men dug as long as daylight allowed. Their trench was three feet deep and ran all the way across the island. They stood logs 12 feet long and 18 inches around up in it and packed dirt and stones around each one. The finished wall was made of planks and stood about five or six feet high, from river to river.

Petrus Stuyvesant and the men who ran the town, called burgomasters and schepens, ordered the wall on March 13, 1653. Stuyvesant was the director general, the man who governed the Dutch colony of New Netherland for the Company. He and the town's officials had heard that the English in New England were preparing to attack. Under their order, the soldiers, the other servants of the Company and the half-free Black men, "no one excepted," had to build up the fort. The townsmen, also "without exception," had to dig the ditch from river to river. The officials put the cost at 3,166 guilders, the Dutch money of the time. Townsmen paid that money in, and the minutes of the officials' meetings, their written record, name the men who paid. Officials reported the wall finished on July 28, 1653.

The Columbia project, called MAAP, names three of the men who dug the trench: Paulo d'Angola, Simon Congo and Anthony Portuguese. All three had what the Dutch called half-freedom. They were among eleven enslaved men who had worked for the Company for eighteen or nineteen years. The eleven asked the colony's council to free them, saying the Company had promised them their freedom. On February 25, 1644, the Company's director, Willem Kieft, and his council granted half-freedom to the eleven men and their wives, on conditions. Under half-freedom the eleven could hold land, and Kieft and his council gave them plots north of the town. But their children, "at present born or yet to be born," stayed the property of the Dutch West India Company. Each of the eleven also owed the Company a yearly payment that Dutch colonists did not owe. It was 30 skepels of grain or beans, plus one hog. A skepel was a Dutch measure for dry goods such as grain. Each also had to come back and work for the Company whenever its officials called.

On August 12, 1658, a rattle watch began walking the streets of New Amsterdam. Its members were paid night patrolmen. They carried wooden rattles, noisemakers that clack loudly when spun. The rattle watch was among the first paid public police forces in America.

#### Penn's plan

In 1682 William Penn made Thomas Holme his surveyor-general, the chief surveyor of his colony of Pennsylvania. The land along the Delaware River was the homeland of the Lenape people. When Penn's colonists arrived, about 2,500 Lenape and about 3,000 Europeans lived on the two sides of the river. The Europeans were Dutch, Swedish and Finnish settlers, and English settlers in West New Jersey. From 1682 to 1684 Penn bought land in southeastern Pennsylvania from the Lenape, paying at least £1,200, which is 1,200 English pounds, in goods. Penn himself landed on October 28, 1682. Holme laid out the grid of Philadelphia in December 1682. His map, "A Portraiture of the City of Philadelphia," was printed in 1683. Penn used the map to guide the work. He also used it to advertise the town and draw settlers to it.

<a id="story-william-penn"></a>

#### William Penn

> **Who:** The founder of Pennsylvania, a Quaker, who had Philadelphia planned on paper before it existed on the ground. Quakers, also called the Religious Society of Friends, are a Christian group that began in England in the 1600s.
>
> **When and where:** The grid laid out by his surveyor-general Thomas Holme in December 1682, and Holme's map published in 1683.
>
> **Movie:** *Penn of Pennsylvania* (1941), released in the United States as *The Courageous Mr. Penn* (1942). The film tells Penn's life in general, not the making of the city plan.

Penn wrote down the kind of town he wanted: "a greene Country Towne which will never be burnt, and always be wholesome." He wrote those words in his instructions for laying out the town. Wholesome meant healthy to live in.

Holme drew a straight grid on the land between the Delaware and the Schuylkill rivers. Two wide main streets crossed it, Broad Street and High Street. High Street is now called Market Street. Holme drew the streets wide, partly because of the fire that burned London in 1666. Where the two main streets crossed, Holme placed a large central square, with one smaller public square in each of the four quarters of the town.

All five squares are still there. The four quarter squares are called Logan, Franklin, Washington and Rittenhouse squares, and Philadelphia's City Hall stands on the center square.

### 1700 to 1750

By about 1750, four colonial ports each held between 8,000 and 13,000 people. In towns that size, people organized to fight fire.

Around 1750 about 13,000 people lived in Philadelphia, about 12,000 in Boston, about 11,000 in New York, and about 8,000 in Charleston. Some of the counts for Charleston come from 1760 rather than 1750. These four were the biggest towns in the colonies. London at the same date had over 700,000 people.

Boston was the busiest port until about 1750. After that, New York and Philadelphia passed it.

#### Fire in wooden towns

On October 2 and 3, 1711, a fire burned through Boston. It destroyed some of the town's main buildings and left many families without homes. A few months later, twelve men became Boston's first Board of Fire Wards, a group of town officers for fires. The Boston Public Library's guide to the city's great fires does not say who chose them or list their duties. Charleston had "firemasters," officers chosen by a vote. At a fire, everyone had to obey a firemaster's orders as if they were the law.

People in Boston also formed mutual fire societies. Mutual means that the members help one another. The members of each society agreed to protect one another's houses, and they had no duty to fight a fire at the house of anyone outside the society.

In 1736 men in Philadelphia formed a company of volunteers who agreed to fight a fire at any house in the town.

<a id="story-benjamin-franklin-fire-company-city-building"></a>

#### Benjamin Franklin

> **Who:** A Philadelphia printer. He helped start the first volunteer fire company in the colonies that protected a whole town rather than only its own members.
>
> **When and where:** Philadelphia, December 7, 1736.

Franklin printed a newspaper, the *Pennsylvania Gazette*. On February 4, 1735, he printed an unsigned letter in it, "On Protection of Towns from Fire," which he had written himself. In the letter he warned people about carrying live coals from room to room. His advice began with the line "an Ounce of Prevention is worth a Pound of Cure." The next year he and other men in the city set up a fire company themselves.

On December 7, 1736, about twenty-five men, Franklin among them, signed the Articles of the Union Fire Company, the written rules of the group. Each member had to bring six leather buckets and two strong linen bags to every fire. Members carried water in the buckets. They used the bags to pack up people's belongings and carry them out of a burning house. Every member had to come out at every fire alarm, to any house in the town, whether its owner was a member or not.

Other Philadelphians soon set up more fire companies, among them the Heart-in-Hand, the Britannia and the Fellowship, and Franklin encouraged them. Volunteer companies fought the fires in American towns until April 1, 1853. On that day firefighters in Cincinnati, Ohio, began work as the first fire department in the United States whose firefighters were all paid. Miles Greenwood was their first chief.

### 1750 to 1800

In 1790 the members of Congress passed a law that put the capital city of the new country on the Potomac River, and in 1791 President George Washington chose the exact ground. Pierre L'Enfant drew the whole city on paper in 1791, before anyone built it. Three Native towns had once stood on that ground. By the spring of 1791 the chosen square held two towns that shipped tobacco, and enslaved people worked the farmland around them.

In 1793 yellow fever killed about one person in every ten in Philadelphia. After the fever came back in 1798, workers in Philadelphia built the first public waterworks in the country driven by steam.

#### The ground the capital was built on

On July 16, 1790, President George Washington signed the Residence Act, a law the members of Congress had passed. In it they placed the capital somewhere on the Potomac River, inside a square no bigger than ten miles on each side. They left it to Washington to say exactly where, and to appoint three commissioners and a surveyor for the work. The commissioners were officials put in charge of building the capital. He rode out and looked at the country himself and chose the ground at and beside Georgetown. He told Congress his choice on January 24, 1791.

Three Native towns had stood inside that square of land. The largest was Nacotchtank, on the southeast side of the Anacostia River, and the river's name comes from the town's name. A second town, Nameroughquena, stood on the west bank of the Potomac, across from today's Theodore Roosevelt Island. The third stood on a bluff, a high, steep bank, in the northwest part of today's city, and the record does not give its name.

In 1608 Captain John Smith reached that stretch of the Potomac. A National Park Service history of the Native peoples of Washington states what followed. Within forty years of that first contact, only about a quarter as many Native people lived in the region as before 1608. Many had died of diseases that Europeans brought, and others had been killed in wars. Others joined nations to the north, south and west. The Histories of the National Mall project at George Mason University puts it this way: the Native communities on that land "had been driven away by war and disease."

Two towns stood inside the square by the spring of 1791, and both are still there. In 1749 Virginia's colonial lawmakers voted to create the town of Alexandria. The county surveyor, John West, laid out its first sixty acres around Hugh West's tobacco warehouse. In 1751 Maryland's colonial lawmakers approved the town of Georgetown. They bought sixty acres for it from George Gordon and George Beall for £280, which is 280 English pounds. The site already had a tobacco inspection house, a building where tobacco was checked before it was shipped. Georgetown grew into a tobacco port. Washington chose ground at and next to Georgetown. On March 3, 1791, the members of Congress changed the law so that the district, the land set aside for the capital, could reach south and take in Alexandria too. Jones Point, where the survey of the district's boundary began, is at Alexandria.

The rest of the land was farms, and the main crop was tobacco. Five men owned the ground where the National Mall is now: Daniel Carroll of Duddington, David Burnes, Notley Young, Benjamin Oden and Samuel Davidson. The Histories of the National Mall project reports that the men who owned this land enslaved people, and the enslaved men and women raised tobacco, corn, wheat and cattle on it.

Notley Young's tobacco plantation, a big farm worked by enslaved people, covered 800 acres. The Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture stands on part of that plantation. The museum gives the number of people enslaved there as 245, from the census of 1790. A census is a count of the people. The Histories of the National Mall project gives 260. Federal officials bought Young's land in 1791.

In all, nineteen men owned the land for the new city. Washington met them at a dinner in Georgetown, and they signed an agreement on March 30, 1791. The owners put about 6,000 acres together. They got nothing for the land that became streets. For land taken for public buildings and squares, the agreement gave them £25 an acre. The rest of the land was split into 20,272 building lots, and half of the lots went back to the owners. These men were later called the Original Proprietors, which means the owners of the land when the city was laid out.

Before anyone could build the city, a crew had to survey the boundary of the district. To survey is to measure the ground and mark exactly where its corners and edges lie. Someone also had to draw the plan of the city that would go inside it. Andrew Ellicott ran the boundary survey. Benjamin Banneker, a free Black farmer from Baltimore County, Maryland, did the astronomy for it, working under Ellicott. Astronomy is the science of the stars and planets. Pierre L'Enfant, an engineer born in France, drew the city plan in 1791, and Washington dismissed him the next year.

<a id="story-pierre-lenfant"></a>

#### Pierre L'Enfant

> **Who:** The French-born engineer who designed the plan of Washington, D.C., and was dismissed before it was built.
>
> **When and where:** The federal district, 1791 to February 1792.

In 1791 Pierre Charles L'Enfant drew the plan of the capital. He laid down a street grid and then drew diagonal avenues across it that meet at circles and squares.

Under the Residence Act, Washington appointed three commissioners, officials in charge of building the capital. The commissioners asked for his original drawing so that an engraver could cut it into a printing plate and print copies. L'Enfant refused to hand it over, and he clashed with the commissioners. In February 1792 George Washington dismissed him for insubordination, which means refusing to obey the people in charge of you.

Andrew Ellicott, with help from his brother Benjamin, rebuilt the plan and changed parts of it. He straightened Massachusetts Avenue and took out some of the squares. The engravers Thackara and Vallance made an engraving of Ellicott's version in March 1792. Copies of their engraving were the first plan of the city that many people saw. The city was built from that engraving, which was L'Enfant's plan as Ellicott had changed it.

L'Enfant died poor in 1825. He was buried on a farm in Prince George's County, Maryland, that belonged to his friend William Dudley Digges. In 1908 the members of Congress set aside $1,000 for a new grave. On April 28, 1909, his coffin lay at the U.S. Capitol for three hours, so that people could pay their respects. He was the first person from another country to be given that honor. That afternoon he was buried again at Arlington National Cemetery, on a hillside above the city he had planned.

<a id="story-benjamin-banneker"></a>

#### Benjamin Banneker

> **Who:** A free Black tobacco farmer and self-taught astronomer who made the observations that fixed the starting corner of the federal district.
>
> **When and where:** The survey's base camp at Jones Point, Virginia, February to April 1791.

George Ellicott recommended Banneker, and Major Andrew Ellicott hired him as scientific assistant on the survey of the ten-mile square. Banneker was nearly sixty. He farmed tobacco, and he had taught himself astronomy, the science of the stars and planets.

Banneker worked at night. To find a position on the earth by astronomy, an observer watches particular stars cross a particular point in the sky and records the exact moment. The observer then calculates the position from those times. Banneker made those observations and did those calculations. He also kept the survey's regulator clock, a very exact clock, running true. Banneker used his observations and calculations to fix the district's south corner at Jones Point. He was paid $2 a day, an ordinary day's pay for an assistant. Andrew Ellicott was paid $5.

Banneker left the survey in the spring of 1791, before the crew had run the full forty miles of the boundary. He was in poor health. His first almanac was the one for the year 1792. An almanac is a book printed once a year with a calendar and tables of the sun, moon and stars.

According to a popular story, Banneker redrew the whole plan of Washington from memory after L'Enfant was dismissed. The story is a legend. Banneker had left the project about ten months before L'Enfant was dismissed, and Andrew Ellicott rebuilt the plan. The historian Silvio Bedini and writers for the National Park Service and the Library of Congress have worked through the records. They credit Banneker with the astronomy for the boundary survey.

#### Water after the fevers

Yellow fever is a disease caused by a virus, a germ far too small to see. People catch it from the bite of a mosquito that carries the virus. Most people who fall sick with it have fever, chills, headache and vomiting, and they get better within a week.

In about one case in seven, the fever eases and then comes back worse. In that stage the virus destroys cells in the liver. As the liver fails, the skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow, and that color gives the disease its name. The person bleeds from the mouth, the nose and the eyes, and into the stomach. In the stomach the blood mixes with stomach acid, and the person vomits it up black. People at the time called it the black vomit. The kidneys fail as well. Of the people who reach that stage, between 30 and 60 percent die.

Yellow fever killed about 5,000 people in Philadelphia between August 1 and November 9, 1793. About 50,000 people lived in the city, so the fever killed roughly one of every ten of them. About 20,000 other people fled the city, among them the officials of the new federal government.

In 1797 a group of Philadelphians asked the city's councils to take charge of the water supply, and the council members formed a Watering Committee. The fever came back in 1798. The city's leaders then hired Benjamin Henry Latrobe, an English-born architect and engineer, to design a waterworks, and in 1799 the members of the Watering Committee accepted his design. Workers began building the Centre Square Water Works that year. Nicholas J. Roosevelt built its engines and pumps under a contract worth $33,000. The steam engine went up from February 1800.

On January 21, 1801, the steam pumps started supplying the city. The engines pumped water from the Schuylkill River through a tunnel along Chestnut Street to the pump house, a white marble building on Centre Square. From there the water ran through the streets in pipes made of hollowed-out logs. Philadelphia was the first American city with a public water supply driven by steam.

The engines broke down often and cost a great deal to keep running. Centre Square ran for only fourteen years. In 1815 the Fairmount Water Works took its place.

### 1800 to 1850

Rochester, New York, grew from about 1,500 people in 1820 to about 12,630 in 1834, after the Erie Canal reached it. Chicago went from about 350 people in 1833 to 4,170 in 1837. San Francisco went from about 200 people in 1846 to about 36,000 in 1852. Each of these towns grew up beside water that boats could reach, on land that had belonged to Native nations.

In New York, people drew their water from wells, springs and rain barrels, and there was no clean piped water. In 1832 cholera, a disease people catch from water with human waste in it, killed about 3,500 New Yorkers. In December 1835 a fire burned about seventeen blocks while the firefighters ran short of water. After those two disasters, New York's city leaders had workers bring water into the city through a channel forty-one miles long from the Croton River. The water arrived in 1842.

In 1811 three men finished a plan of straight streets for Manhattan, from Houston Street north. New York's state lawmakers had appointed them. Much of that ground was rocky hills or swamp, with farms, houses and barns on it. For about sixty years afterward, workers dug away hills and filled in low ground to make the island fit the plan.

#### Boomtowns

A boomtown is a town whose number of people grows very fast, in a few years. Rochester, Chicago and San Francisco all grew that way between 1800 and 1850.

The City of Rochester's own history and the Monroe County Library's Rochester Voices project both describe Rochester as America's first boomtown. The land there was Seneca land. In 1788 Seneca leaders signed a treaty that handed about 2,600,000 acres east of the Genesee River to two land dealers, Oliver Phelps and Nathaniel Gorham. A treaty is a written agreement between nations or governments. The Seneca leaders also granted land west of the river for a mill, on the condition that a mill be built for the Seneca to use. In 1789 Ebenezer Allen built a sawmill and a mill for grinding grain on that tract.

The Erie Canal ran through Rochester from 1825, and workers finished the whole canal across New York that October. The falls of the Genesee River turned the mills' wheels. Grain from the Genesee Valley came to the mills, and canal boats carried the flour away. Before the canal, shipping a ton of flour from Rochester cost $100. By canal it cost $7. By 1838 the mills at Rochester ground more flour than the mills of any other American city, and Rochester got the nickname the Flour City.

About 1,500 people lived in Rochester in 1820. Census takers, who count the country's people every ten years, counted 9,269 there in 1830. By 1834, the year Rochester became a city, about 12,630 people lived there. That was more than eight times as many people as in 1820.

Chicago grew where the Chicago River runs into Lake Michigan, beside Fort Dearborn, an army fort built at the river's mouth in 1803. It became a town in 1833, when about 350 people lived there. That September, in the Treaty of Chicago, Potawatomi leaders signed over their last lands in Illinois and Wisconsin and their last reservations in Michigan, about 5,000,000 acres. A reservation is an area of land kept for a Native nation. The Potawatomi leaders agreed to move west of the Mississippi River. Chicago became a city on March 4, 1837, when 4,170 people lived there.

Chicago's ground was low and flat, and its clay soil soaked up little water. Nothing drained off it, and for most of the year the streets were mud and standing water. Starting in 1855, crews raised Chicago's streets so that sewers, underground pipes that carry waste water away, could drain the city. In January 1858 crews began raising its brick and stone buildings to match.

San Francisco grew on the homeland of the Yelamu, an Ohlone people. About 200 people lived in the town in 1846. By 1852 about 36,000 people lived there. They had come in the California Gold Rush, a race to California to dig for gold. The town was put together in a hurry. People lived in tents and in hulks, which are the hulls of old ships that no longer sailed. Between December 1849 and June 1851, six great fires burned the town. The fire of May 3 and 4, 1851, destroyed as much as three-quarters of it. People rebuilt after each one.

#### The 1811 grid

On April 3, 1807, New York's state lawmakers appointed three commissioners, men given the job of laying out the streets of Manhattan. They were Gouverneur Morris, John Rutherfurd and Simeon De Witt. They filed their plan in March 1811.

The commissioners laid the streets out as a grid. Their plan covered Manhattan from Houston Street north to 155th Street. It had twelve avenues and 155 numbered cross streets, which cut the land into rectangles. The commissioners drew the lines straight over the island's hills without bending them. Manhattan was Lenape land, and by 1811 much of this part of it was rocky hills, swamps and marshes, with farms, houses and barns scattered across it.

John Randel Jr. was the chief surveyor, a person who measures land and marks where lines fall on it. He was hired for the job at twenty. In 1808 he mapped the island's hills, rocks, swamps, streams and ponds, and its houses, barns, fences and fields. Then his crews set 1,549 marble markers and 98 iron bolts into the ground to fix the grid in place.

Workers then had to make the island match the drawing. To build each street, they dug away hills or filled in hollows, leveled the strip of ground and paved it. The new streets ran through the spots where about 721 of the 1,825 buildings north of Houston Street stood in 1811, so those buildings had to be moved out of the way. The work took about sixty years to reach 155th Street.

The commissioners set aside very little land for parks, and Central Park was not in their plan. State lawmakers added it in 1853, in a separate law. People already lived on part of that ground, in Seneca Village, a community of about 225 people, roughly two-thirds of them Black. New York City officials took their land, and by October 1857 they had evicted the last of them, which means they forced them out of their homes under the law.

#### Cholera, fire, and the Croton

Cholera is a disease people catch by swallowing water that has human waste in it. It causes watery diarrhea so heavy that the body loses its water very fast. A person with a bad case who does not get water back into the body fast enough can die of it within hours. In 1832 cholera killed about 3,500 out of about 250,000 New Yorkers. That is about one person in every seventy.

New York had no clean piped water then. People drew water from wells, ponds and springs inside the city. Workers for a private firm, the Manhattan Company, sank wells and laid wooden pipes to send the water out. Carters drove barrels of country spring water around town and sold it for a penny a gallon, and that water was often dirty too. Others caught rain in tanks called cisterns. By the 1830s the water from the downtown wells was dirty. More and more privies stood near the wells, and liquid from old graves soaked into the ground as well. A privy is an outdoor toilet built over a pit in the ground. When people sick with cholera used the privies, the waste overflowed into nearby wells and cellars.

On the evening of December 16, 1835, a fire started in a five-story warehouse on Merchant Street, near Wall Street, in lower Manhattan. A strong wind blew it toward the East River. It burned about seventeen blocks and destroyed between 600 and 700 buildings, and the damage came to about $20 million. Two people died in it. The firefighters could not get enough water onto the fire. There was little water to be had. What there was froze in the wells, in the hoses and in the hydrants, the street pipes that firefighters draw water from.

The Croton Aqueduct, a channel built to carry water a long way, became the first large city water supply in the United States that ran without a break. New York's city leaders had decided by the late 1820s that they needed a cleaner and bigger supply of water. After the cholera and the fire, they had the aqueduct built. Workers began building it in 1837, with John B. Jervis as chief engineer.

The workers dammed the Croton River in Westchester County, north of the city. Then they built a covered tunnel of brick on a stone base, forty-one miles long, to carry the water down to Manhattan. Inside, the tunnel was eight and a half feet high and seven and a half feet wide. It dropped about 13 inches in every mile, so gravity carried the water along it. Water entered the city on June 22, 1842. On July 4 the distributing reservoir at 42nd Street and Fifth Avenue began filling. It was a large basin that held the water and fed it out to the city's pipes.

On October 14, 1842, New Yorkers held a celebration across the whole city. A parade seven miles long marched through the streets, and the new fountain in City Hall Park threw water fifty feet into the air. The celebration included what people called Croton cocktails.

<a id="story-george-templeton-strong"></a>

#### George Templeton Strong

> **Who:** A young New York lawyer whose diary records how much he enjoyed bathing at home once Croton water reached his house.
>
> **When and where:** New York City, 1842.

George Templeton Strong was born in 1820 and was twenty-two when the Croton water arrived. He kept a diary from 1835 until his death in 1875, and it runs to about 2,250 pages. It is a first-hand record of New York in the 1800s. Two editors, Nevins and Thomas, published it in 1952.

In 1842, while the water was still on its way, Strong wrote that "Croton Water is slowly flowing towards the city, which at last will stand a chance of being cleaned." The sentence goes on: "if water can clean it." He thought the city was so dirty that even water might not get it clean.

Once Croton water reached his house, Strong could take a bath at home, and his diary records how much he enjoyed it.

### 1850 to 1900

Between 1850 and 1900, builders made American cities taller, dug sewers under them, and spread them outward along streetcar lines.

Once elevators had a safety catch, people were willing to ride them to upper floors. Builders also began to hold up tall buildings with frames of iron and steel, so the outside walls no longer had to carry the weight.

Chicago's ground was so flat and wet that a sewer could not run downhill through it. Crews there laid new sewer pipes along the streets, raised the streets over them, and lifted the downtown buildings up to the new street level. In the census of 1890, Chicago had 1,099,850 people. It was the second-largest city in the country.

The first large electric streetcar line began regular service in Richmond, Virginia, on February 2, 1888. A ten-minute ride on one covered the distance of a thirty-minute walk, and builders put up houses along the tracks.

In New York in the same years, poor families crowded into tenements, apartment buildings put up to hold as many people as a plot of land would hold.

#### Raising Chicago's streets and buildings

Chicago's ground was low and almost level, and its clay soil took in little water. Rain and waste had nowhere to drain, so pools of dirty water stood in the streets, and for most of the year the streets were mud. Diseases spread from that standing water, among them typhoid fever and dysentery. In 1854 cholera killed six of every hundred people in the city.

In December 1855 the members of the Board of Sewerage Commissioners, the officials in charge of Chicago's sewers, hired Ellis S. Chesbrough. He had been the water engineer in Boston. His plan of 1856 was the first plan for a complete sewer system covering a whole American city. Workers laid the sewer pipes along the existing streets and then buried them under several feet of new fill, which is earth dumped on top. That raised the level of the street, by an average of four to five feet, and by as much as eight feet in places. A building left at the old level now sat below its own street, and its ground floor became a basement.

Next the buildings had to come up to the new street level. The tool for lifting them was the jackscrew, a screw inside a case that a man turned by hand with a lever. Crews set many jackscrews under a building, and the men turned them together.

The first masonry building, one built of brick or stone, went up this way in January 1858. It was a four-story brick block at Randolph and Dearborn streets that weighed about 750 tons. It rose 6 feet 2 inches on 200 jackscrews. Reporters of the time wrote that it rose "without the slightest injury" to the building. More than fifty buildings like it were raised that same year. Every figure for these raisings comes from those newspaper reports.

In 1860 a group of engineers that included George Pullman raised half a city block. It was the row of brick and stone buildings on Lake Street between Clark and LaSalle streets, 320 feet long. With its sidewalks, the row weighed about 35,000 tons. About 600 men worked about 6,000 jackscrews, and the block went up 4 feet 8 inches in five days. The shops in it stayed open the whole time, and people came and went, shopped and worked in them while the buildings rose.

#### Up: the elevator and the steel frame

Builders could not make tall buildings without two inventions: an elevator people trusted, and a frame that could hold the building up.

The danger in an elevator was that the rope could break and drop the platform. Elisha Graves Otis made a brake from a steel wagon spring that locked into a ratchet, a bar with teeth, and held the platform if the rope broke. In 1854 he showed it at the Crystal Palace exposition in New York, a large public show of new machines and goods. He rode a platform up an open-sided shaft, and halfway up he had the rope cut with an axe. The brake caught, and the platform held.

On March 23, 1857, workers put the first commercial passenger elevator in the country into the E. V. Haughwout Building at 488 Broadway in New York. A commercial elevator is one sold for everyday use in a building. A steam engine drove it. It cost $300 and rose about two-thirds of a foot per second. Before elevators, the higher a room was, the lower its rent, because people had to climb the stairs to reach it. Once elevators ran, floors above the fourth or fifth could rent for as much as the floors below, or more.

In a wall-bearing building, the outside walls hold up everything. The taller the building, the thicker the walls at the bottom have to be. The Monadnock Building in Chicago, finished in 1891, is 16 stories tall, the tallest building ever held up by brick walls. Its walls are six feet thick at the bottom. In a framed building, a skeleton of iron or steel columns and beams carries the weight. The walls hang on that frame as a covering.

The Home Insurance Building in Chicago is the building most often called the first skyscraper, which means a very tall building held up by a metal frame. William Le Baron Jenney designed it, and it was finished in 1885. It stood ten stories and 138 feet tall, and builders added two more floors in 1890. Its frame of iron and steel carried loads that walls had carried in older buildings. Workers tore it down in 1931 to make room for the Field Building.

That title is in dispute. The Home Insurance Building was not built all of steel, and it was not the first building with a metal frame. Jenney's own account of the building, written in 1885, describes mostly its foundations, not a new way of holding up a building. Jason Barr, in his book *Building the Skyline* and in his Skynomics writing, traces the labels "first skyscraper" and "father of the skyscraper" partly to a later publicity campaign. People close to Jenney ran it, along with Chicago boosters, people who promoted their city to bring in money and business. Barr calls the story the "Jenney Myth."

Other buildings of the time also have a claim to be the first. New York's Equitable Life Building of 1870 was the first office building with an elevator. The Produce Exchange of 1884 had an inner skeleton designed by George B. Post. Chicago's Tacoma Building of 1889 is named as well. Builders used the frame and the elevator to roughly triple the height of buildings within one generation.

In 1893 the World's Columbian Exposition, a world's fair, opened in Chicago. Daniel Burnham directed the building work, and Frederick Law Olmsted drew the site plan, which is the layout of the grounds. Workers put up a matched set of white buildings in the style of ancient Greek and Roman buildings, with rows of columns. Electric lights lit them, and the fair got the name the White City.

The buildings were temporary, built to stand only while the fair ran. Under their fronts they were steel-framed sheds. The fronts were made of staff, a mix of plaster, cement and plant fiber that workers poured into molds, and then painted white. More than 27 million people visited the fair in its six months. Planners in the City Beautiful movement of the 1890s and 1900s took the White City as their model. They worked to bring grand public buildings, wide avenues and parks into American cities.

Ironworkers from two Mohawk communities, Kahnawake and Akwesasne, helped build bridges and tall buildings across the Northeast from 1886 on. That year, at a bridge job at Kahnawake, a Mohawk town near Montreal, Mohawk men started working high steel. Working high steel means joining the steel frames of bridges and buildings high above the ground. From Kahnawake and Akwesasne, the men traveled to bridge and skyscraper jobs wherever the steel work was, and they called that "booming out." An exhibition at the Smithsonian's National Museum of the American Indian, *Booming Out: Mohawk Ironworkers Build New York*, documents their work. It records their work in the next century on the Empire State Building, the Chrysler Building, the George Washington Bridge and the World Trade Center.

#### The tenement

A tenement is an apartment building put up cheaply to hold as many poor families as its plot of land will take. On May 14, 1867, New York's state lawmakers passed a tenement law, the first broad housing law in the country. Under it, cellar apartments were banned unless the ceiling stood at least a foot above the street, and every building needed fire escapes and one toilet for every twenty people. Officials did little to make builders obey it. To meet its rule about windows, builders cut windows in the walls between inside rooms, so the windows let in no outside air.

The Tenement House Act of 1879, later known as the Old Law, was the lawmakers' answer to that failure. Under it, every room a person lived in had to have a window that opened to outside air. Builders met that rule with the dumbbell tenement.

Builders pinched each building in at its middle, which left room for a narrow air shaft. Rooms in the middle of the building got their required window onto that shaft. Seen from above, the building was wide at both ends and thin in the middle. A dumbbell, an exercise weight with a ball at each end of a short bar, has the same shape.

The shaft was too narrow and too deep to bring daylight or moving air down below the top floors, so most of the rooms it was built for stayed dark and stale. The shafts filled up with garbage. The shaft also worked as a flue, a channel that draws hot air and smoke upward, as a chimney does. A fire in the shaft could climb it to the floors above.

In 1901 New York's state lawmakers passed a new Tenement House Act, later known as the New Law. In it they banned the dumbbell design and required windows facing outward in every room, along with courtyards, indoor toilets and protection against fire. The rules covered old buildings as well, so owners had to change those too.

<a id="story-jacob-riis"></a>

#### Jacob Riis

> **Who:** A Danish immigrant and police reporter who took up flash photography early and used it to show how the poor of a city lived.
>
> **When and where:** New York's tenement districts. *How the Other Half Lives* came out in 1890.

Jacob Riis used flash photographs as evidence in an argument about how poor families in New York lived. He was born on May 3, 1849, in Ribe, Denmark, and moved to the United States in 1870. He worked as a police reporter for the *New York Tribune* and then the *Evening Sun*. As a reporter he covered the city's poorest streets, among them Mulberry Street. The police there also ran shelters for homeless people, called police lodging houses, and Riis saw inside them and wrote about them.

Around 1887 he began using magnesium flash. Magnesium powder burns for an instant with a light bright enough to record a picture on a photographic plate, a glass sheet coated with chemicals that change where light hits them. With the flash he photographed tenements, saloons and slums at night.

In 1889 Riis published an eighteen-page article in *Scribner's* magazine. In 1890 he published the book *How the Other Half Lives*, with seventeen photographs and a number of engravings, pictures printed from lines cut into metal or wood. The *Dictionary of American History* credits Riis's work, along with the work of other reformers, with pushing New York's lawmakers toward the tenement law of 1901, which banned the dumbbell design. Theodore Roosevelt, as New York City's police commissioner, became Riis's ally. Riis died in 1914.

<a id="story-bridget-joseph-moore"></a>

#### Bridget and Joseph Moore

> **Who:** An Irish immigrant waiter and his wife, one tenement family the records document, whose apartment the Tenement Museum has recreated.
>
> **When and where:** 97 Orchard Street, on New York's Lower East Side, 1869.

Bridget Moore married at seventeen, in 1865. Joseph Moore worked as a waiter, and some of the Tenement Museum's accounts record him as a bartender. In 1869 the couple moved with their daughters into 97 Orchard Street, a tenement built in 1863. They were one of the few Irish families in a building where most people were German. They lived there about a year.

On April 21, 1869, their daughter Agnes Mary died at five months old. The cause given in the records was marasmus. Marasmus is severe malnutrition, a form of starvation. The body gets too little food of every kind, so it uses up its own fat and then its own muscle, and the child wastes away.

The Tenement Museum's account ties two things to the deaths of babies at that time. One was swill milk. Swill milk came from cows kept in stables beside distilleries, where liquor was made. The cows ate the leftover grain mush from making the liquor. Their milk was thin and dirty, and in the 1850s New Yorkers blamed it for the deaths of many babies. The museum says Agnes Mary's marasmus came from tainted milk. The other was the building itself. The water at 97 Orchard Street came from a pump in the back yard, beside the privies.

Of the eight children Bridget and Joseph Moore had, four lived to be adults.

The building still stands, and museum staff have recreated the Moores' apartment as it was in 1869. Between 1863 and 1935, when the floors where people lived were sealed shut, an estimated 7,000 people from more than twenty countries lived at 97 Orchard Street. The Moores are one of the families among them whose names appear in the records.

#### Central Park and Seneca Village

The commissioners who drew the 1811 plan had left almost no land for public parks. In 1853 New York's state lawmakers set aside more than 700 acres in the middle of Manhattan for a park. Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux won the design contest in 1858 with a plan they called Greensward, and building began that year.

People already lived on part of that land, in Seneca Village. In 1825 John and Elizabeth Whitehead had divided their farmland there into about 200 lots, or pieces of land for sale. On September 27 of that year, Andrew Williams, a twenty-five-year-old Black shoeshiner, bought the first three lots for $125. Epiphany Davis bought twelve lots for $578, and the AME Zion Church bought lots as well. By 1855 about 225 people lived in Seneca Village. Roughly two-thirds of them were African American, and Irish and German families lived there too. They had built three churches and a school.

Under New York law at the time, a Black man could vote only if he owned at least $250 worth of property. In 1845 about 100 Black men in the whole city met that rule, and 10 of them lived in Seneca Village.

New York City officials took the whole park site by eminent domain. Eminent domain is the power of a government to take private property for public use, paying the owner whether the owner wants to sell or not. Officials set a price for each piece of land, and the owners in Seneca Village were paid. Many of them said the price of their land was too low, and they objected in court. Researchers at the Central Park Conservancy, the group that looks after the park, have studied the records and found that, with few exceptions, the owners got about what their land would have sold for. In February 1856 the New York State Supreme Court, the state's main trial court, approved the prices, and the land became the city's property. The officials took the land from its owners, including Black men whose right to vote depended on owning it. The Central Park Conservancy's histories of the village do not name the commissioners who set the prices.

Many people left in 1856. Others stayed on as renters of the city. In the summer of 1856, Mayor Fernando Wood sent the people of Seneca Village a final notice to leave. In October 1857, once the money to build the park was in place, city officials evicted the last of them. In all, city officials forced about 1,600 people off the whole park site by the end of 1857.

Accounts differ on how the last people were made to leave. A New York Public Library research guide says the people of Seneca Village fought the police sent to put them out, and that in August 1857 the last Black landowners were "forcibly and violently scattered throughout the city." The historians Roy Rosenzweig and Elizabeth Blackmar studied the records from the time for their 1992 history of the park. They found that the people left "quietly and without violence."
