<a id="ch-home-family"></a>

## Chapter 7: Home and Family Life

### Before 1500

Before 1500, the households of Native nations were built around kin. Kin are a person's relatives by birth or by marriage. Each nation built a kind of house that suited its climate and the way its families got their food. In many nations, several related families lived under one roof. Children learned to work by working beside adults, and old people lived in the same household as the young.

#### The longhouse

The Haudenosaunee are several Native nations joined together in one union. In a Haudenosaunee longhouse, every family traced itself back through the mothers' side. The longhouse was a long building with a frame of wooden posts, covered with bark. One longhouse held many related families. Two families lived in each section of the house, one on each side of an aisle, and they shared one fire in the middle. By different counts, one house held 30 to 60 people, or 20 families or more.

Each longhouse family began with one woman who lived long ago, and everyone in the house came down from her. The head of the house was the clan mother, the eldest or most respected woman of the clan. A clan is a large group of families who come down from the same ancestor. Women ran the longhouse and owned its everyday goods.

A woman's daughters and granddaughters lived in their longhouse all their lives. When they married, their husbands came to live with them. A son moved out when he married, into his wife's longhouse. He still belonged to his mother's longhouse.

#### The earth lodge

Among the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara nations on the upper Missouri River, women built the houses and owned them. Their house was the earth lodge, a dome made of timber and packed over with earth. An older woman directed the building, and women kept the lodge in repair.

One earth lodge held about 10 to 20 people, most often sisters and their families. Some lodges held as many as 30. A lodge lasted about ten years, and then the women built it again. The large villages had more than 100 lodges each.

#### Pueblos, wigwams and tipis

A pueblo is a Native town of many homes joined together and stacked on top of one another. Taos Pueblo is the northernmost of the nineteen Pueblos of what is now New Mexico. Its people built their homes of adobe, which is earth mixed with water and straw. They poured the adobe into molds or shaped it into bricks and dried them in the sun. The two main buildings, the North House and the South House, rise five stories high. By the Pueblo's own estimate, people built them between about 1000 and 1450. Families have lived in them ever since. People have lived at Taos Pueblo without a break for more than 1,000 years.

In the Eastern Woodlands, the forests of the eastern part of the continent, many families lived in wigwams. A wigwam had a frame of saplings, which are thin young trees, covered with bark or with woven mats. On the Plains, the grasslands in the middle of the continent, families lived in tipis covered with animal hides. A family could take a tipi down and pack it up, so the household could move with the hunt.

### The 1500s

Few European families lived on this land in the 1500s. Most of the Europeans who came were soldiers, priests and sailors. Native households went on living in their own towns. The European newcomers carried diseases that Native people had never had before. Those diseases made Native people sick and killed many of them. About 200,000 Timucua people lived in what is now northern Florida and southern Georgia before the Spanish came. After one outbreak of disease after another, only about 2,000 were left by the 1650s. No record counts how many died in the 1500s alone. At St. Augustine in Florida, marriages between Spanish soldiers and Native women were common.

#### St. Augustine, built in Seloy's town

In September 1565, the Spanish sea commander Pedro Menéndez de Avilés and about 800 colonists came ashore at Seloy, a town of the Timucua people. Its chief was also named Seloy. The colonists included 26 women and an unknown number of enslaved Africans. Enslaved people were owned by other people as property and forced to work without pay. Menéndez and his colonists made their first settlement inside Seloy's town. Seloy offered Menéndez his council house, the building where the town held its meetings, and the Spanish used it as their first fort. Seloy's town covered more than 12 acres. Its remains lie under what is now the Fountain of Youth Park in St. Augustine.

The settlement Menéndez started became St. Augustine. People have lived there ever since. It is the oldest European settlement on the US mainland where people have lived without a break.

The Timucua traced their families and their inheritance through the mother's line. Fewer than half of the Spanish men in St. Augustine were married, and fewer than half of the married men had a Spanish wife. From 1565 on, many Spanish soldiers married Native women.

Church officials in the town wrote down the names of the church's members. A parish is the group of people who belong to one church, and these are called the Cathedral Parish records. They begin on January 24, 1594. They are the oldest church records that survive in the United States. The first marriage in them is dated February 2, 1594, and the first baptism June 25. A baptism is a church ceremony that welcomes a person, often a baby, into the church.

<a id="story-teresa-camacho-household"></a>

#### Teresa and Francisco Camacho

> **Who:** A Spanish soldier, his Native wife, her sister and her sister's son, living as one household.
>
> **When and where:** St. Augustine, Florida, 1580.

In 1580 one household in St. Augustine held four people. They were Francisco Camacho, his wife Teresa, Teresa's sister Catalina and Catalina's son Juan. Teresa was a Native woman. The account of this household does not name Teresa's nation.

Francisco came to Florida in the 1560s from San Lúcar de Barrameda, a town near Cádiz in Spain. He was a soldier in a regiment, a unit of the army. He also worked as a fisherman.

### The 1600s

In 1600s Massachusetts, the usual English colonial house had one room. The household cooked and worked in that room, around the hearth, the open fireplace. The fire in the hearth gave the room its heat and light. Many boys left home for good at about 14 to learn a trade in another household.

#### Plymouth, built at Patuxet

The English who founded Plymouth Colony in 1620 built their houses at Patuxet, a Wampanoag village on Plymouth harbor. The Wampanoag are a Native nation of the coast of what is now Massachusetts. Between 1616 and 1619, before they came, a disease killed most of the Native people living on the southeast coast of what is now Massachusetts. Estimates of the deaths run from one-third of the people to as many as 90 percent. Nobody knows for certain what the disease was. Researchers have proposed several deadly diseases, among them plague, yellow fever and smallpox.

In 1614 an English sea captain named Thomas Hunt kidnapped 20 Native people from Patuxet and 7 from Nauset, another Native community. He took them to Spain to sell them as slaves. One of the Patuxet men was Tisquantum, also known as Squanto. He made his way home to Patuxet in 1619. He found the houses empty and the cornfields grown over. When the English arrived the next year, he was one of the last of the Patuxet people.

#### One room, then two

The basic English house in Massachusetts had a single room, called the hall. Next to the hall stood the chimney bay, the part of the house that held the chimney, the front door and the stairs. The hearth in the hall was where the family cooked, kept warm, had light and did its work.

The next step up was a house with a second room, called the parlor. This plan is called the hall-and-parlor house. The hall was still for cooking and work. The parlor was the best room, and it usually held a bed. Colonists went on building one-room houses well into the 1700s.

#### Births, deaths, servants and apprentices

A New England mother had about 8 babies, on average, and about 6 of them lived to grow up. People in New England lived long lives for the time. In the Chesapeake, the colonies around Chesapeake Bay, far more children died. About 1 baby in 4 died as an infant. About another 1 in 4 died before the age of 20. Most children in the Chesapeake lost a mother, a father or both before they reached their teens.

A household also held people who were not family. Indentured servants lived and worked in the house as members of the household. An indentured servant had signed a contract to work for a master for a set number of years. During the 1600s, colonists also owned more and more enslaved people, whom they forced to work in their households without pay.

At about 14, and sometimes younger, a boy could leave home for good. His parents and a master signed a written contract, called an indenture. Under the indenture, the boy had to live with the master and work for him. The boy served the master until the age of 21, for as long as 7 years, and learned the master's trade.

The master took the place of a parent. In the indenture, he promised to feed the boy, give him a place to sleep, train him in the trade and give him some schooling. About two-thirds of these contracts required the master to teach the boy reading or writing. At the end, the young man got freedom dues, a payment of clothes, tools or money.

<a id="story-mary-ring"></a>

#### Mary Ring

> **Who:** A widow in Plymouth Colony whose will and list of belongings survive.
>
> **When and where:** Plymouth Colony. She came in 1629 or 1630 and died in July 1631.

After Mary Ring died, her belongings were written down one by one. A list like this is called an inventory. Her inventory survives, and it records what one Plymouth household owned.

Mary Ring's husband, William Ring, died in the city of Leiden, in the Netherlands, sometime between 1620 and 1629. In 1620 the couple had planned to sail to America. They were among 20 people who could not go when their ship, the Speedwell, turned back. In 1629 or 1630 Mary Ring came to Plymouth as a widow with her three children, Elizabeth, Susanna and Andrew. She died in July 1631.

She wrote her own will and signed her name to it. A will is a paper that says who gets a person's belongings after death. Her will was proved in court on October 28, 1633. That means the colony's court officials agreed the will was real, so it could be carried out.

Her inventory lists her books. They were a Bible, a psalm book, and books called *A Plea for Infants* and *Garland of Virtuous Dames*. A psalm book contains the songs from the Bible's Book of Psalms. Her clothes came in violet, red, blue, grey, white and black, and in a mixed color. Her will lists green cloth "to make a coat."

The inventory also lists money owed to her. Governor William Bradford owed her 2 pounds in English money, and Edward Winslow owed her beaver fur. All three of her children married in the colony.

### 1700 to 1750

Wealthy colonists of the early 1700s built houses in which each room had its own use. Most families still lived in houses of one or two rooms. Women and children made much of what a household used, from cloth to candles, and much of that work went on at the hearth.

#### The Georgian house

Wealthy colonists built a style of house now called Georgian. A Georgian house was built to match on both sides. Its builders based its balanced look on ancient Greek and Roman buildings. A central hall ran through the middle of the house, with rooms opening off it. The formal rooms, the parlors and the dining room, were at the front. The rooms for work were farther back. Some Georgian houses had four chimneys, one to heat each of the four main rooms.

In a house with separate rooms, the people in a family could be apart from one another. Being apart like this is called privacy. Houses like this belonged to wealthy families.

#### The hearth as a workplace

Cooks worked over the open fire in the hearth. Around that fire, a household made much of what it used. Its members spun and wove cloth, and they made candles, soap, butter and cheese. They also preserved food so it would keep. Women and children did most of this work. The historian Laurel Thatcher Ulrich described this work in northern New England in her 1982 book *Good Wives*.

<a id="story-sarah-kemble-knight"></a>

#### Sarah Kemble Knight

> **Who:** A Boston businesswoman who rode from Boston toward New Haven and New York and kept a journal of the households where she stayed.
>
> **When and where:** October 1704 to early 1705, on the road from Boston to New Haven and New York and back. She lived from 1666 to 1727.

Sarah Kemble Knight kept a journal, a written record of each day, on a trip she made on horseback in 1704. In it she wrote about the road, the inns and the households where she stayed the night. An inn was a house where travelers paid for a bed and a meal. Few pieces of writing by American women survive from that time, and her journal is one of them.

Knight lived in Boston, where she ran a business and also taught. In October 1704 she set out from Boston for New Haven and New York on legal business. The journal records what she saw inside the houses where she stopped along the way.

She stayed in New York for about two weeks. On December 21 she started home. Near Eastchester, New York, her party got lost in a great storm of wind and snow. One woman would hardly let them through her door. The woman's son invited them in. He showed Knight a bed "as hard as it was high," and he warmed it with a hot stone at her feet. The family had nothing in the house but milk. They boiled it and sweetened it with molasses for her.

Her journal stayed unprinted for about 120 years, until Theodore Dwight printed it in 1825.

### 1750 to 1800

Families on the frontier lived in log cabins in the late 1700s, and families in older settlements lived in farmhouses. The frontier was the edge of the colonists' settlements, on land where Native nations lived. Households of both kinds made most of what they used. Spinning, weaving, making candles and soap, and preserving food were the work of women and children. When men left home during the Revolutionary War, women ran the households.

#### Where the log cabin came from

Settlers from Sweden and Finland brought the log cabin with notched corners to America. In a cabin like this, the builders cut notches near the ends of the logs so that the logs locked together at the corners. These settlers came to the colony of New Sweden on the Delaware River from 1638. Among them were the Forest Finns, who were skilled at building with logs. The Nothnagle Log House in Greenwich Township, New Jersey, was built in about 1638 to 1643, and it still stands.

New Sweden was built on Lenape land. In the spring of 1638, Peter Minuit's Swedish and Dutch crew sailed up the Delaware River. They made agreements with several sachems, or leaders, of the Lenape and Susquehannock nations. With the sachems' permission, the crew built Fort Christina. Several thousand Lenape lived in separate communities along the river, and people at the time counted them as the owners of the land beside it. The Lenape welcomed the colony because its people brought goods to trade. New Sweden lasted 17 years before the Dutch took control of it.

A common story says the first English colonists lived in log cabins. The English at Plymouth and at Jamestown did not build them. By the second half of the 1700s, the log cabin was the usual first house of a family on the frontier.

<a id="story-abigail-adams-home-family"></a>

#### Abigail Adams

> **Who:** Ran her family's farm, its money and her children's education through the Revolutionary War while her husband, John Adams, was away.
>
> **When and where:** Braintree, Massachusetts, in the part that is now the city of Quincy, 1774 to 1784.
>
> **Movie:** *John Adams* (2008), a miniseries made for HBO. It is about John Adams and his family, and Abigail Adams is one of its main characters.

From 1774, Abigail Adams ran the family farm at Braintree, Massachusetts, and managed its money. Her husband, John Adams, was away for years at a time. First he served in the Continental Congress, the meeting of leaders from the colonies. Then he worked in Europe as a diplomat, a person who represents a country to other governments. Abigail taught the children herself. She and John wrote each other more than 1,100 letters. In 1784 she and their daughter Nabby sailed to Europe to join him.

In July 1776 she took her four children to Boston to be inoculated against smallpox. To inoculate a person meant giving a healthy person smallpox on purpose, so that the person got a milder case. Caught the natural way, smallpox killed about 30 of every 100 people who got it. A doctor cut the skin with a small blade called a lancet. Then he put in a thread soaked in pus from a smallpox sore. Pus is the thick yellowish liquid inside a sore. About 2 or 3 of every 100 people inoculated died. People who lived through smallpox usually did not catch it again, so inoculation gave them that protection at far less risk.

On July 13, 1776, Abigail wrote to John from Boston: "I yesterday arrived and was with all 4 of our Little ones innoculated for the small pox." Their doctor was Dr. Bulfinch. She wrote that the children "stood the opperation Manfully," which meant they were brave about it. Nabby, who was 10, broke out in many painful sores, while 9-year-old Johnny had a light case. Charles was 6, and he had to be inoculated three times before he caught the smallpox. Thomas, the fourth child, showed no sickness at first and had to be inoculated again.

<a id="story-martha-ballard"></a>

#### Martha Ballard

> **Who:** A midwife in Maine whose daily diary, kept for 27 years, records the work of an ordinary American household.
>
> **When and where:** Hallowell, Maine. The diary runs from January 1785 to 1812.
>
> **Movie:** *A Midwife's Tale* (1997), a documentary made for the PBS series *American Experience*. It is about Martha Ballard.

Martha Ballard wrote in her diary nearly every day for 27 years, from January 1785 to 1812. It contains about 10,000 entries over 9,965 days. She was a midwife in Hallowell, Maine. A midwife is a woman who helps other women give birth. The diary records 816 births that Ballard helped with, each one with a name and a number.

Around those births, the diary records the daily work of her own household. It describes her garden, spinning, weaving, quilting and brewing, along with the work her daughters did, the visitors who came and the weather each day.

In 1990 the historian Laurel Thatcher Ulrich published a book about the diary, *A Midwife's Tale*. Ulrich received the Pulitzer Prize, a yearly American prize for writing, for the book. The whole diary can be read online at DoHistory.org.

### 1800 to 1850

Middle-class families in towns and cities began, in the early 1800s, to treat the home as a place set apart from paid work. Middle-class families were the families in between the rich and the poor. In the 1830s cooks began to trade the open hearth, the open fireplace where food cooked over the fire, for the iron stove. On farms, children's chores came first and school fitted around them. In the South, enslavers could sell any member of an enslaved family at any time. Lawmakers and courts in the slave states did not count enslaved people's marriages as legal marriages.

#### The parlor and the home apart from work

In the early 1800s, many middle-class families lived in towns and cities. They came to see the home as a place apart, and paid work happened somewhere else. In this view the home was the mother's to run. The parlor, the front room where the family received visitors, became the room for showing off the family's best things. Domestic means having to do with the home. These ideas are called the cult of domesticity. Here a cult means a set of beliefs that many people held strongly.

Catharine Beecher's 1841 book, *A Treatise on Domestic Economy*, described how to run a home of this kind. A treatise is a long book that explains one subject, and domestic economy meant running a home. Readers used the book as a guide for running a home in this way.

#### The stove takes the place of the fire

Iron cookstoves spread through American kitchens from the 1830s. Foundries, the workshops where iron was melted and poured into molds, made stoves of many designs. By 1850 most middle-class kitchens in the cities had a stove in place of the open hearth. Poorer families and families far from towns changed over later.

For the woman who did the cooking, a stove meant less bending and lifting. It gave off less smoke, and no ash fell into the food. But a stove took hard work to clean. Stoves were also drafty and hard to control. In 1846 the writer Henry David Thoreau complained that the stove "concealed the fire." He wrote that cooking had become "merely a chemic process," by which he meant a kind of chemistry.

#### A child's day, and where school fit in

On a farm, a child's chores came first. Country schools, called district schools, usually held two terms a year. The summer term ran from about May to August, for the younger children, and women usually taught it. The winter term ran from about November to April. Older boys could go then, because they were not needed for work on the farm. Men were often hired to teach the winter term. Children missed school when the weather was bad or when there was work to do at home.

The teacher often lived with the students' families, staying with one family and then the next. People called this boarding around.

At home, parents expected children to obey. Many parents hit their children with a rod, a stick or switch used for punishment. They pointed to a verse in the Bible's book of Proverbs: "He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes." It means that a father who does not use the rod hates his son. A father who loves his son punishes him early. In the 1800s some writers of advice books for parents began to tell parents to punish children calmly and firmly instead. One of them told parents never to punish a child in anger.

#### Home under slavery

Enslavers could break up an enslaved family on any day. They sold enslaved people, and slave traders bought them and moved them. Between about 1790 and 1860, traders forced more than 1 million enslaved people to move from the Upper South to the Deep South. The Upper South was the more northern of the Southern states, and the Deep South was the states farther south. From 1820 they moved about 200,000 people every ten years. Traders marched them overland in chained lines called coffles, or shipped them by sea to New Orleans. New Orleans had the largest slave market in the country.

The Equal Justice Initiative is an American organization. By its count, the traders separated nearly half of the people they moved from a husband, a wife or a parent. Lawmakers and courts in the slave states did not count the marriages of enslaved people as legal marriages. Enslavers sold husbands and wives apart.

<a id="story-catharine-beecher-home-family"></a>

#### Catharine Beecher

> **Who:** Wrote a book of instructions for running an American home, and argued that keeping house was a skill to be studied and taught in schools.
>
> **When and where:** Born September 6, 1800, in East Hampton, New York. Her *Treatise on Domestic Economy* came out in 1841. She died on May 12, 1878, in Elmira, New York.

Catharine Beecher wrote *A Treatise on Domestic Economy*, published in 1841. It was the first American book to describe every part of running a home. Economy here means managing a household. Printers issued it in about 15 editions and put out new copies nearly every year for years.

Beecher argued that housekeeping was a profession. By that she meant a skilled job that people should study and that schools should teach. In 1823 she founded the Hartford Female Seminary, a school for girls and young women, in Connecticut. Later she wrote another book about the home with her sister Harriet Beecher Stowe. It was called *The American Woman's Home*, and it came out in 1869.

<a id="story-buffalo-bird-woman-home-family"></a>

#### Buffalo Bird Woman (Waheenee)

> **Who:** A Hidatsa woman who grew up in her mothers' earth lodge and later told the story of her life to the anthropologist Gilbert Wilson.
>
> **When and where:** About 1839 to 1932. Born by the Knife River and raised at Like-a-Fishhook village on the Missouri River, in what is now North Dakota.

Buffalo Bird Woman grew up in an earth lodge in the 1840s. An earth lodge was a large round house with a frame of timber, covered over with packed earth. Her household held her father, his four wives, her grandmother and her great-grandmother. Late in her life she told the story of that household to Gilbert Wilson, an anthropologist, a scientist who studies how groups of people live. He interviewed her every summer from 1906 or 1907 to 1918. The National Park Service gives 1906 as the first year. She spoke Hidatsa and never learned English. Wilson published her story in 1921 as *Waheenee: An Indian Girl's Story*. Her son, Edward Goodbird, drew the pictures for Wilson's books.

She was born in an earth lodge near where the Knife River meets the Missouri. The National Park Service gives her birth year as about 1839. She said she was born "three years after the smallpox winter," and Wilson dated that winter to 1837 and 1838, which would make it about 1840 or 1841.

Smallpox is a deadly disease that spreads from person to person. In June 1837 the steamboat *St. Peters*, owned by the American Fur Company, carried passengers sick with smallpox up the Missouri River. Francis A. Chardon ran Fort Clark, a trading post near the Mandan and Hidatsa villages. At a trading post, traders swapped goods for furs. Chardon met the boat 30 miles downstream and heard that people on it were sick. The boat landed at Fort Clark on June 18, by the State Historical Society of North Dakota's account, or June 19, by others. In less than a day, workers from the boat and the fort unloaded goods and loaded furs, and villagers came and went from the boat.

About 2,000 Mandan people were alive in the spring of 1837. By October, smallpox had killed all but 138 of them. Buffalo Bird Woman's great-grandmother told her: "More than half of my tribe died in the smallpox winter. Of the Mandans only a few families were left alive. All the old people and little children died."

When she was ten days old, an old man named Nothing-but-Water gave her the name Good Way. Later her father gave her the name Waheenee-wea, Buffalo Bird Woman, because she was a sickly child. People believed a new name could move the gods to help her. Her father, Small Ankle, was a Hidatsa chief. He had four wives, and they were sisters. Her mother, Weahtee, was one of them. The others were Red Blossom, Stalk-of-Corn and Strikes-Many Woman. "I was taught to call all these my mothers," she said. "Such was our Indian custom." Her great-grandmother White Corn and her grandmother Turtle lived with the family too.

When she was four, the Mandan and Hidatsa chiefs moved their people together to one new village, at Like-a-Fishhook Point on the Missouri. The village stood by 1845. The chiefs made the move to protect their people from attacks by the Dakota and the Yanktonai. Women and dogs carried the family goods there. Some loads went on their backs, and dogs dragged others on travois. A travois is a frame of two poles that a dog dragged along the ground. The people built about seventy summer earth lodges at the new village, most of them in the second summer. For the winter, families built small huts in the woods, and the June flood often swept them away.

In the first hard winter, the family camped at Many-Frogs Brook, three miles from the village. Smallpox broke out with the first snow. "My brother, my mother Weahtee, and her sister Stalk-of-Corn, died," she said. Her grandmother Turtle made her a doll of deerskin with eyes of bone beads.

The women of a household owned its earth lodge. Her mothers' lodge had a floor more than forty feet across. The fire burned in the center. A screen of upright split logs stood between the fire and the door and kept out drafts and dogs. Her father's bed, of cottonwood planks and buffalo robes, stood in front of the fire. The oldest person in the family usually slept there, because it was the warmest place. The rest of the family slept in covered beds against the back wall. The buffalo-skin bedding could not be washed, so her mothers aired it on the raised platform, called a stage, where they dried their corn. The family believed that "an earth lodge was alive and had a spirit."

Her first husband was Magpie. Her son, Edward Goodbird, was born in 1869. A reservation is land set aside for a Native nation to live on. In the late 1880s, federal officials, the officials of the national government, carried out a law of 1887 called the Dawes Act. They divided reservation land into allotments. An allotment was a plot of reservation land that federal officials assigned to one family. Federal officials sold the land left over after the allotments. Native nations held about 138 million acres in 1887 and about 48 million in 1934. By the late 1880s, as the allotments began, the people of Like-a-Fishhook village had left it. In 1921 she said: "We no longer live in an earth lodge, but in a house with chimneys." She added that "my son's wife cooks by a stove." She still got up at daybreak to hoe her corn and sing to it. She died in 1932.

### 1850 to 1900

Between 1850 and 1900, American families lived in many kinds of homes. In New York, a family might live in a tenement flat of small rooms, with shared toilets out in the yard. A middle-class family might have a house with a parlor for guests, a dining room for meals, and a paid servant to help run it. On the plains, where few trees grew, settler families cut their houses out of the ground. State lawmakers began to require children to go to school, and federal officials took Native children away from their homes to distant schools.

#### The tenement flat

A tenement was a building of small apartments, called flats, rented to working families. Builders put up the tenement at 97 Orchard Street in New York in 1863. Over the years, about 7,000 people from more than 20 countries lived there. Families lived in small rooms, and some took in boarders, people who paid to sleep in the family's rooms. They carried water into the flat by hand and shared privies, outdoor toilets, in the yard.

Lawmakers in New York began to change what a tenement had to include. Under the Tenement House Act of 1879, builders added air shafts, narrow gaps between buildings meant to let in air and light. In 1900 Governor Theodore Roosevelt appointed a group of people, called a commission, to study the housing laws. Lawrence Veiller, the commission's secretary, did most of the investigating and helped write a new law. New York's state lawmakers passed it on April 12, 1901. It required a window in every room and a toilet in every new apartment. Owners of old tenements had to give them better light and add one toilet for every two families.

#### Bigger houses and paid help

Families who could pay for them built houses with a parlor for guests and a separate dining room. City homes got running water inside the house first, and farm families waited decades longer. In 1890, 24 of every 100 American households had running water, and 8 of every 100 had electricity.

Some middle-class homes also had paid help. The census is the count of the country's people taken every ten years. The census of 1870 was the first to record the jobs of working women in full, by a set method. The census takers counted 867,354 women in domestic service, which means paid work in another family's home. That was about 47 of every 100 women who worked for pay. It was by far the most common paid job for women.

#### Sod houses and dugouts

The plains had few trees, so settler families there could not build with logs. They built with sod instead. Sod is the top layer of prairie soil, held together by the roots of the grass. Settlers used a plow to cut about an acre of ground into strips 12 inches wide and 4 inches thick. They cut the strips into pieces about three feet long. Builders laid these sod bricks grass side down, turning each layer lengthwise and then crosswise, to make walls two feet thick. Most early sod houses had dirt floors. Women who lived in them complained about the dirt, the bugs, the snakes, the leaking roofs and the poor light.

Some families dug their home into the side of a hill or a creek bank. A house like this is called a dugout, and it took less work to build than other kinds of house. In May 1874 Charles and Caroline Ingalls settled in a dugout on Plum Creek, near Walnut Grove, Minnesota. Their crops failed three years in a row, and in 1876 they left. The hollow in the creek bank where the dugout stood is still there, on what was once the Gordon farm.

Walnut Grove lies on land the Dakota signed away under treaties in 1851. A treaty is a written agreement between nations. At Traverse des Sioux on July 23, 1851, three men bargained with the Sisseton and Wahpeton Dakota for about 24 million acres. They were Luke Lea, the official who spoke for the US government, Alexander Ramsey, the governor of Minnesota Territory, and Henry Sibley. A territory was land the United States held that was not yet a state. The three men agreed to pay about 7.5 cents an acre. The Dakota believed US officials would take the land by force if they refused. After the treaty was signed, the fur trader Joseph R. Brown had Dakota leaders sign another paper. No one read it aloud to them or translated it. That paper let traders take the annuity money, the yearly payments promised to the Dakota, for debts the traders claimed the Dakota owed them. Within ten years, more than 100,000 white settlers moved onto the land.

#### School laws and the boarding schools

In 1852 Massachusetts lawmakers passed a law that required children to go to school. The law applied to children aged 8 to 14, for twelve weeks a year. By 1900, 32 states had such a law, and by 1918 every state had one. Mississippi was the last. Under these laws, families had to send their children to school for part of the year.

Federal officials took Native children from their families to boarding schools far away. On November 1, 1879, Richard Henry Pratt, an Army officer, opened the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, a boarding school for Native children. In 1891 members of Congress gave the Commissioner of Indian Affairs the power to make and enforce rules forcing Native children to attend school. He was the federal official in charge of Native affairs. In 1893 members of Congress allowed officials to hold back food rations, clothing and payments owed to parents who refused to send their children.

At the schools, staff cut the children's hair, took away their clothes and gave them English names. Staff beat children who spoke their own language, locked them up alone, held back their food or washed their mouths out with soap. Survivors and a federal investigation later reported these punishments.

In 2022 and 2024, officials of the US Department of the Interior reported on these schools. They counted 417 federal boarding schools for Native children in 37 states or territories, open between 1819 and 1969, and at least 973 children who died at those schools. Their report states that this count is low.

<a id="story-nathalie-gumpertz"></a>

#### Nathalie Gumpertz

> **Who:** A tenement mother of four who became a dressmaker after her husband disappeared.
>
> **When and where:** 97 Orchard Street, New York. Her husband Julius disappeared in 1874. A judge declared him dead in 1883.

Nathalie Gumpertz supported her four children by sewing dresses in her tenement flat. One morning in 1874, her husband Julius left for work and never came back.

Nathalie and Julius Gumpertz were immigrants from East Prussia who lived at 97 Orchard Street. They were living there during the Panic of 1873, a money crash in which many people lost their jobs. When Julius left, Nathalie had four young children.

She became a dressmaker and worked in the front room of the flat, the parlor. She made about three dresses a week and earned 8 to 9 dollars. In 1883 a judge declared Julius legally dead, which meant that under the law he counted as dead. Because of that, Nathalie could claim 600 dollars that he was due from his father's estate, the money and property his father left when he died. She then moved the family to upper Manhattan.

Later, genealogists working for the Tenement Museum in New York found that Julius had gone to Cincinnati. Genealogists are people who trace family histories.

<a id="story-rachel-calof"></a>

#### Rachel Calof

> **Who:** A young woman from Russia who came to North Dakota for an arranged marriage and later wrote down what keeping a homestead house was like.
>
> **When and where:** Near Devils Lake, North Dakota, 1894 to 1904. She wrote her memoir in 1936, and it was published in 1995.

In 1894, at the age of 18, Rachel Calof traveled from Russia to marry Abraham Calof. It was an arranged marriage, planned by other people rather than by the couple. Abraham was a homesteader, a settler who claimed land from the US government to live on and farm.

The couple lived in a shanty, a small, roughly built house, 12 feet by 14 feet with a dirt floor. In the winters, Abraham's parents and brothers, and the chickens, shared the one room with the couple to save fuel. Of all the hardships, she wrote, "the lack of privacy was the hardest to bear."

In 1936 she wrote a memoir, a book about her own life, in Yiddish, a language spoken by many Jews in Eastern Europe. It records her years on the homestead from 1894 to 1904. Indiana University Press published it in English in 1995 as *Rachel Calof's Story*.

The land around Devils Lake was Dakota land. Under a treaty of 1867, the land south of the lake became a reservation for the Sisseton and Wahpeton Dakota and the Cut Head band of Yanktonai Dakota. The Dakota name for the lake is Mni Wakan, Spirit Water. Settlers who were not Native illegally claimed 64,000 acres of the reservation. The Dakota bargained with the US government and accepted 345,000 dollars for that land. In 1904 federal officials opened 100,000 more acres of the reservation to settlers, at about 4 dollars and 50 cents an acre. By 1934 the Dakota owned a little more than 50,000 acres of the reservation. The State Historical Society of North Dakota's history of the reservation does not say whether the Calofs' own claim lay on land taken from it.

### 1900 to 1950

Running water and electric power reached most American homes between 1900 and 1950. City homes got them first, and many farm homes got them decades later. In the Great Depression, the hard times of the 1930s, families who could not pay their home loans lost their houses. Federal officials, the officials of the national government, then changed home loans so that a family could pay for a house month by month over many years. Federal officials also rated the neighborhoods where Black people lived as the worst risk, and they usually refused to back loans there. In 1947 the first families moved into Levittown on Long Island, New York. It was a new suburb, a town of houses built at the edge of a city.

#### Water, wires and washday

Without running water or electric power, washing a family's clothes by hand took more than one day. The person doing the wash first sorted the clothes and treated the stains. The clothes then soaked in warm soapy water for one or two days. Next the washer scrubbed them on a washboard, a ridged board set in a tub of warm water and soap. Then the washer boiled the clothes in a pot with soap and soda to kill lice, stirring them with a wooden stick called a dolly. After rinsing the clothes, the washer hung them out to dry, with the whites in the sun to bleach them. Last came the ironing, with flatirons, solid metal irons heated over the coals and held with a rag around the handle.

Some homes got water pipes and electric wires long before others. By 1940, 74 of every 100 American homes had running water and 83 had electric lights. By 1950, 83 of every 100 households had running water and 94 had electricity. The Census Bureau is the federal office that counts the country's people and homes. Its officials counted a home as having complete plumbing only if it had three things. These were hot and cold running water, a bathtub or shower, and a flush toilet. In 1940 nearly half of American homes lacked complete plumbing, and more than one home in three had no flush toilet. In about ten states, the share without complete plumbing was near 70 percent or higher. Most of the homes without running water were in the country. In 1940 more than half of American homes were heated with coal, and another quarter with wood.

Farms got electric power later than city homes. In 1935 fewer than 11 of every 100 farms had it. About half had it by 1945, and about 9 in 10 by 1950.

Families also changed how they kept food cold. In 1930, 14 of every 100 households had a modern refrigerator. The number rose to 44 in 1940 and to 80 in 1950. Households without one used an icebox, a cabinet cooled by a block of ice. They also relied on milk delivered each day, on canned food and on stores that sold fresh food.

The historian Ruth Schwartz Cowan studied what the new machines did to a housewife's work. In her 1983 book *More Work for Mother*, she argued that the machines mostly replaced work that servants, children and men had done before. At the same time, families expected clothes washed more often, houses kept cleaner and more cooking done. So, in Cowan's argument, the housewife's own hours of work did not fall. Another scholar, Joel Mokyr, took up her argument in a paper called "Why Was There More Work for Mother?" Census counts record one part of the change. The number of domestic servants fell by 32 percent between 1940 and 1950.

#### The bungalow and the mail-order house

The small family house of this era was the bungalow. A bungalow was a small house of one main floor, with a low roof and a front porch, and sometimes rooms tucked under the roof. In Chicago, more than 80,000 brick bungalows built between 1910 and the mid-1930s still stand today. From 1908 to 1940, Sears, Roebuck and Company sold whole houses by catalog. A buyer chose a design from the catalog. The house came by railroad in boxcars, as a kit. The average kit held about 25 tons of materials and more than 30,000 parts. Many buyers put the house together themselves with relatives, friends and neighbors. Others hired local carpenters. The first Sears house catalog, in 1908, offered 44 designs priced from 360 dollars to 2,890 dollars. Nobody kept an official count of how many kit houses Sears sold. The usual estimate is 70,000 to 75,000, and some estimates run as high as 100,000.

#### Sickness in a tenement flat

When Abraham Rogarshevsky died of tuberculosis in 1918, his widow kept the family in its tenement home by working for the building and renting out space. The Rogarshevskys were a Jewish family from Lithuania who lived at 97 Orchard Street in New York from about 1908. The building was a tenement, a building of small apartments rented to working families. Abraham died on July 17, 1918. Tuberculosis is a disease caused by a germ. It usually infects the lungs, and it spreads through the air when a sick person coughs or talks. Tuberculosis was then known as "the tailor's disease." After Abraham died, his widow, Fanny, became the building's janitor, the worker who cleaned the building and kept it in repair. She also took in boarders, people who paid to live in the family's rooms.

#### The mortgage remade

Before the 1930s, a home loan was hard to pay off. A mortgage is a loan to buy a house. If the borrower does not repay it, the lender can take the house. The usual mortgage ran for 5 to 10 years. Each month the borrower paid only the interest, the fee for borrowing the money. At the end, the borrower owed the whole amount at once. Buyers usually had to pay about half the price up front, as a down payment. In the Great Depression many borrowers could not pay. Lenders then foreclosed, which means they took the houses back.

In June 1933 members of Congress passed the Home Owners' Loan Act. Under it, federal officials set up the Home Owners' Loan Corporation, or HOLC. HOLC officials replaced families' old loans with new loans that ran for 15 years at a fixed rate, which means the interest charge never changed. The family paid the same amount every month, and each payment paid off part of the loan itself. In 1934 members of Congress set up the Federal Housing Administration, or FHA. FHA officials insured home loans, which means they promised to repay the lender if the family could not. Those loans ran 20 to 25 years and needed only a small down payment. After the Second World War the 30-year loan became the usual kind.

Between 1935 and 1940, HOLC staff graded neighborhoods in many American cities. They worked with local bank loan officers, city officials, real estate agents and appraisers. An appraiser is a person whose job is to judge what a property is worth. Each neighborhood got a letter and a color. A was green, for "Best." B was blue, for "Still Desirable." C was yellow, for "Definitely Declining." D was red, for "Hazardous." FHA officials used maps of their own. They rated neighborhoods where Black people lived "D" and usually refused to insure loans there. Drawing a red line around a neighborhood to cut it off from loans is called redlining.

Researchers at the National Community Reinvestment Coalition studied 115 of the HOLC maps. Of the neighborhoods graded "Hazardous," they found that 74 of every 100 are low or moderate income today. Nearly 64 of every 100 are neighborhoods where most people belong to racial or ethnic minority groups.

#### Depression households

During the Great Depression, families changed who lived together under one roof. Couples waited to marry. In 1929 there were 10.1 marriages each year for every 1,000 Americans. By 1932 there were 7.9. For the first time in US history, parents had too few babies to replace their own generation. Families doubled up in one home. Young married couples moved back in with their parents, and old parents moved in with their grown children. By 1940, 1.5 million married women lived apart from their husbands.

In Chicago, Black families who had moved north from the South settled in a South Side neighborhood called Bronzeville. On many blocks in the rest of the city, white owners signed restrictive covenants. These were written agreements that the owners would not sell or rent to Black people. Black Chicagoans were limited mostly to the Black Belt, an area between 12th and 79th streets on the South Side that took in Bronzeville. Landlords there split apartments into one-room units called kitchenettes and charged very high rents for them. Bronzeville held more than 80,000 of them. A whole family lived in one room and shared a bathroom down the hall with everyone else on the floor. Some buildings had no proper heat. Families lit kerosene lamps, and the stoves they rigged up often overheated and started fires. In one year, about 751 fires broke out in the Black Belt. The writer Richard Wright recorded this life in his 1941 book *12 Million Black Voices*.

#### Spanking and the new advice

In the 1920s and 1930s, many parents began to take advice from experts on child development and psychology. Psychology is the study of the mind and of how people behave. In 1928 John B. Watson published *Psychological Care of Infant and Child*, and it sold 100,000 copies within months. Watson told parents: "Never hug and kiss them. Never let them sit in your lap." He went on: "If you must, kiss them once on the forehead when they say goodnight." He advised them to "shake hands with them in the morning."

Between 1924 and 1939, parents wrote to Angelo Patri, a popular expert on raising children, to ask for advice. In 2004 three researchers published a study of 147 of these letters that mentioned corporal punishment, which means hitting a child as a punishment. Most came from middle-class parents, families in between the rich and the poor. The parents wrote more about how useful hitting was than about a child's right to be kept safe from harm. The reasons they gave most often were that the child had disobeyed or been rude. One letter in four described an argument about hitting with another adult close to the family.

#### The teenager, and the war at home

A new stage of life got its own name in these years. More children stayed in high school instead of going to work, and that is part of why people began to see the teenage years as a stage of their own. Writers had printed "teen ager," as two words, as early as 1913. A 1941 article in *Popular Science* printed "teen-agers," and this is usually named as the first use in print as a single word. The word spread in the late 1940s, when advertisers used it to sell goods to young people.

During the Second World War, individuals and families moved to cities with war factories to take well-paid jobs. More Americans moved from one part of the country to another in these years than in any earlier period. Richmond, California, grew from fewer than 24,000 people to more than 100,000 during the war. Six million women worked in war-industry jobs that women had not held before. At home, federal officials limited how much of twenty kinds of goods each family could buy, and families shopped with ration books.

<a id="story-baldizzi-family"></a>

#### The Baldizzi family

> **Who:** A Sicilian immigrant family who lived through the Great Depression in a tenement flat. Museum staff later rebuilt their apartment from the daughter's memories.
>
> **When and where:** 97 Orchard Street, New York, 1928 to 1935.

Adolfo and Rosaria Baldizzi raised their children, Josephine and Johnny, in a flat at 97 Orchard Street from 1928 until 1935. Adolfo came to the United States from Palermo, in Sicily, in 1923. He was a trained woodworker who made fine furniture. During the Depression he could find only odd jobs. Rosaria sewed the linings into coats in a garment factory. In the evenings the family sat at the kitchen table to play cards and listen to the radio. Adolfo built a corner cabinet himself.

In 1934 and 1935, New York City officials required owners of old tenements to make costly repairs, such as fireproofing. The owner of 97 Orchard Street chose to empty the apartments rather than pay for the work. The owner evicted the families who still lived there, which means the owner forced them to leave. Next the owner boarded up the upper windows and sealed off the floors where people had lived. The Baldizzis had to move.

After the Tenement Museum was founded in 1988, Josephine Baldizzi came back to 97 Orchard Street and recorded hours of memories of her childhood there. Museum staff rebuilt the family's apartment from what she remembered.

<a id="story-levittown-family"></a>

#### Theodore and Patricia Bladykas

> **Who:** The first family to move into Levittown, with their 14-month-old twin daughters, Patricia Ann and Betty Ann.
>
> **When and where:** October 1, 1947, 67 Bellmore Road, Levittown, Long Island, New York.

Theodore and Patricia Bladykas were the first family to move into a house in Levittown. They moved in on October 1, 1947, with their twin daughters, Patricia Ann and Betty Ann, who were 14 months old. A photographer from the newspaper *Newsday* took their picture that day. The first 300 families moved into Levittown that day.

The builder was the company Levitt and Sons, run by William Levitt. The first houses rented for 60 dollars a month, and a renter could buy the house for 7,500 dollars after a year. A ranch house, a long, low house of one story, sold for 7,990 dollars in 1949. By 1951 Levitt and Sons had built 17,447 houses there. Many of the fathers who moved in were veterans just back from the Second World War.

William Levitt and his company rented and sold these houses to white families only. A lease is the paper that sets the rules for renting a home. Clause 25 of the Levittown lease stated that no "person other than members of the Caucasian race" could live in the house. Caucasian here means white. The only exception was for servants, who also had to be white. In 1948, in the case *Shelley v. Kraemer*, the justices of the US Supreme Court ruled that courts could not enforce rules like this. William Levitt dropped the written clause and kept refusing to sell to Black families. His sales contracts forbade buyers to resell their houses to African Americans. He said that if a Black family bought a house in Levittown, white families would stop buying there. In 1954 he told the *Saturday Evening Post*: "We can solve a housing problem, or we can solve a racial problem. But we cannot combine the two."

### 1950 to 2000

After 1950 the house in the suburbs became the common picture of American family life. Home ownership rose from 43.6 of every 100 households in 1940 to 61.9 in 1960. Lenders and sellers kept Black families out of many of the new suburbs. In Levittown, Pennsylvania, a mob attacked the house of the first Black family to move in. Inside their homes, families planned their evenings around the new television set. Later in the century, more mothers took paid jobs and the divorce rate more than doubled. Some parents began to teach their children at home.

#### Suburbia as the norm

Between 1946 and 1964, 76 million babies were born in the United States. People call these years the baby boom. Builders put up more towns like Levittown, including a second Levittown in Pennsylvania from 1952. From 1949 Levitt and Sons also sold ranch houses there.

After the 1948 Supreme Court ruling, builders, sellers and lenders kept up redlining and whites-only sales for many years. Activists campaigned against these practices. In 1968 members of Congress passed the Fair Housing Act, which made it against the law to refuse to sell or rent a home to someone because of race.

#### The TV in the living room

Most American families bought their first television set in the 1950s. About 9 of every 100 households had a set in 1950. By 1955 the figure was 64.5, and by 1960 it was 87. Families began to plan their evenings around the programs.

#### The household changes shape

The divorce rate more than doubled between 1960 and 1980. In 1960 there were 9.2 divorces each year for every 1,000 married women. By 1980 there were 22.6. The rate reached its peak in 1981 and then began to fall.

More mothers took paid jobs. In 1948 about 17 of every 100 married mothers were in the labor force, which means they worked for pay or were looking for paid work. By 1985 the figure was 61, and by 1995 it was about 70. Counting all mothers with children under 18, the share rose from 47 percent in 1975 to a peak of 73 percent in 2000, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the federal office that keeps numbers on workers. With both parents at work, more families paid for day care.

Some children went home after school to an empty house. People called them latchkey children, because they carried their own key to the house. The people who counted them came up with very different numbers. A 1987 study by Census Bureau researchers found about 2.1 million children aged 5 to 13 regularly home alone. Advocacy groups, which campaign for a cause, estimated 6 to 7 million. In the fall of 1995 Census Bureau workers counted 6.9 million children aged 5 to 14, or 18 of every 100, who regularly looked after themselves. On average they spent six hours a week that way.

#### School comes home

In the 1970s and 1980s some parents began to teach their children at home instead of sending them to school. This is called homeschooling. Homeschooling had two separate starting points. John Holt wanted to change how schools taught, and in August 1977 he started a newsletter called *Growing Without Schooling*. On the religious side, Raymond Moore argued for keeping young children at home, in his 1981 book *Home Grown Kids*. In many states, homeschooling was against the law, or nearly impossible to do legally, into the 1980s. In the 1970s most state laws did not say whether it was allowed, and many families taught their children in secret. In 1978 a judge in a Massachusetts court ruled that homeschooling was legal under three conditions. The parents had to be able to teach, they had to cover the required subjects, and they had to show that the children were learning. Over the next fifteen years, judges in other states ruled that homeschooling was legal, each state with its own rules.

In most homeschooling families the mother did the teaching, and many mothers stayed home to do it. Families also met in homeschool groups.

<a id="story-daisy-william-myers"></a>

#### Daisy and William Myers

> **Who:** The first Black family in Levittown, Pennsylvania: a war veteran, a teacher and their three small children, who stayed in their house while crowds attacked it.
>
> **When and where:** 43 Deepgreen Lane, Levittown, Pennsylvania, from August 13, 1957, to 1961.
>
> **Movie:** Crisis in Levittown (1957), a documentary by Lee Bobker and Lester Becker, filmed while the events were happening.

On August 13, 1957, William and Daisy Myers and their three small children moved into 43 Deepgreen Lane in Levittown, Pennsylvania. They were the first Black family to live in Levittown. William had served in the Army in the Second World War. Daisy was a teacher. Lewis Wechsler, a white Jewish friend, helped them arrange to buy the house.

Crowds of 200 to 1,000 people gathered on Deepgreen Lane for more than a week. People in the crowds threw rocks through the windows of the house and threw Molotov cocktails, bottles filled with fuel and set on fire. They burned crosses, one of them at the Wechsler house. For decades, members of the Ku Klux Klan, a group whose members bombed and attacked Black Americans, had burned crosses as a threat. In 2003 the justices of the US Supreme Court wrote that a burning cross is often meant to make its targets fear they will be attacked. Callers threatened the family by telephone. Milk, bread and oil stopped coming to the house. The Baltimore Sun's 1997 account does not say who stopped the deliveries. The family's fire insurance was canceled, and that account does not name the insurance company. On the seventh night more than 500 people gathered before state troopers, the state police, broke up the crowd.

Members of the Levittown Betterment Committee passed around a petition against letting Black families live in Levittown. A petition is a paper that many people sign to ask for something. The committee's members also organized the harassment of the family, the steady stream of acts meant to frighten them. A judge ordered the Betterment group to stop. Pennsylvania Governor George Leader sent the state police, and after about six weeks the troopers had ended the open violence. A court found two people guilty of burning the cross on the Wechsler lawn. The Baltimore Sun's account does not name them.

Neighbors, Quaker families and church members brought the Myers family food and flowers. Quakers are members of a Christian church, the Society of Friends. The family stayed in the house until 1961, when they moved to York, Pennsylvania. Daisy Myers told the story in her memoir, *Sticks 'n Stones*, published in 2005. A memoir is a book a person writes about their own life.

<a id="story-clyde-ross-home-family"></a>

#### Clyde Ross

> **Who:** A Second World War veteran and soup-factory worker who could not get a mortgage and bought his Chicago house on contract.
>
> **When and where:** North Lawndale, on Chicago's West Side, from 1961.

Clyde Ross bought a house in Chicago in 1961 on terms that let the seller take back everything if he missed a single payment. He was born in 1923 near Clarksdale, Mississippi. In the Second World War he was drafted, which means draft officials ordered him into the armed forces, and he served on Guam. In 1947 he moved to Chicago and took a job as a taster at Campbell's Soup.

Ross tried to get an ordinary mortgage for a house in another neighborhood. A loan officer told him there was no money to lend. The records do not name the officer or the bank. FHA officials rated neighborhoods where Black people lived "D," colored them red on their maps, and usually refused to back loans there.

In 1961 Ross bought a house in North Lawndale for 27,500 dollars. The seller was a speculator, a person who buys property to sell it again at a profit, and had paid 12,000 dollars for the house. Ross bought on contract. Under the contract the seller kept the deed, the paper that shows who owns a house, until Ross made the last payment. If Ross missed a single payment, he would lose his 1,000-dollar down payment, every monthly payment he had made, and the house. A 2014 account on BillMoyers.com gives the year as 1958 and the price as 27,000 dollars. The journalist Ta-Nehisi Coates cited one estimate that 85 of every 100 Black families who bought homes in Chicago bought them on contract.

In 1968 Ross joined the Contract Buyers League, a group of Black homeowners on Chicago's South and West Sides, and became its vice president. About 500 families in the league stopped making their payments together, as a strike against the contracts. By July 1971, the league and the sellers had worked out new terms for 155 contracts, saving each family an average of 14,000 dollars. About 70 league families lost their homes to eviction. The Chicago Reporter's account does not name who had each family put out. The league also took its fight to court and lost. Coates wrote that the league lost a jury trial in 1976. The Chicago Reporter says its last appeal, its last request for a higher court to change the ruling, was turned down in 1983. In 2014 Coates told Ross's story in *The Atlantic* magazine. Ross was 91, and he still lived in the house and owned it.

<a id="story-colfax-family-homeschool"></a>

#### David and Micki Colfax and their sons

> **Who:** Parents who built their own house on a ranch in California and taught their four sons at home.
>
> **When and where:** Near Boonville, Mendocino County, California, from 1973.

David and Micki Colfax taught their four sons at home on a ranch in California, where the family built its own house. Their eldest son, Grant, started public school in St. Louis. After six weeks his parents took him out, because they found the lessons "very rote and uncreative." Rote learning means learning by repeating things over and over.

In 1973 the family moved to land near Boonville, in Mendocino County, California. The land had no house, no electricity and no running water. The Harvard Crimson gives the land as 40 acres, and the Anderson Valley Advertiser gives 50. Everyone, the young sons included, helped build the house, the barns and the sheds. The family raised goats, sheep, chickens and pigs and sold them to restaurants in San Francisco.

Lessons fit around the work of the ranch. "Some days we did a lot of homework, some days we had none," Reed Colfax said later. "It depended on the weather and what had to be done on the ranch." The boys studied four or five days a week, summers included. Grant, Drew and Reed went on to Harvard University and graduated in 1987, 1990 and 1992. The youngest son, Garth, was still being taught at home in 1989. That year about 500,000 American children were taught at home by their parents, according to a count reported in *The Harvard Crimson*. David and Micki Colfax wrote a book about their method, *Homeschooling for Excellence*.

### 2000 to Today

New American houses kept growing larger until 2015, while households kept growing smaller. In the crash that began in 2007, lenders took back millions of homes from families who could not pay their loans. In 2020, during the pandemic, a worldwide outbreak of disease, many homes became an office and a school at the same time.

#### More house, fewer people

The median house is the one in the middle when all are ranked by size. By Census Bureau figures, the median new house built for one family grew from 983 square feet in 1950 to a peak of 2,467 square feet in 2015. Households shrank over many of the same years. By the Census Bureau's count, the average household held 3.67 people in 1940 and 2.50 people in 2025.

The kinds of households changed too, by the Census Bureau's count. In 2025, 29 of every 100 households were one person living alone, up from 20 in 1975, and married couples made up 47, down from 66. That year 58 of every 100 young adults aged 18 to 24 lived in their parents' home.

By the Census Bureau's count, 65 of every 100 households owned their home in the second quarter of 2026, the months of April, May and June.

#### 2008 at the kitchen table

Between 2007 and 2010, lenders foreclosed on about 3.8 million homes. Estimates for the whole crisis run from about 7.7 million to 10 million homes lost, because researchers counted in different ways. Federal Reserve History, a website of the Federal Reserve, the country's central bank, and the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago list these figures.

In the years before the crash, lenders made many subprime loans. A subprime loan is a loan made at a higher cost to a borrower with weaker credit, a weaker record of paying back debts. In 2009 reporters at the Center for Public Integrity, a news organization, ranked Countrywide Financial the largest subprime lender of 2005 to 2007. They found that Countrywide made at least 97.2 billion dollars in high-interest loans in those years. Angelo Mozilo founded the company and ran it for 39 years.

A foreclosure filing is the paper a lender files to start taking back a home. Foreclosure filings reached their peak in 2010, at nearly 2.9 million homes. In 2025 there were 367,460, according to ATTOM, a private company that collects property records.

More Americans came to live in households of several generations, such as grandparents, parents and children together. Researchers at the Pew Research Center, which studies American life, counted them. In 1971, 7 of every 100 Americans lived in such a household. By 2021 the share was 18 of every 100, or 59.7 million people. The number grew faster during the years of the crash than in the years before.

#### Homelessness, counted

Each January, local volunteers count the people who are homeless on a single night. Officials of the US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), the federal housing department, report the count. In January 2024 volunteers counted 771,480 people, the highest number on record and 18 percent more than a year before. The number of homeless people in families with children rose 39 percent in that year.

In January 2025 the count was 745,652 people. HUD officials called the change a drop of 3 percent. The National Low Income Housing Coalition gave the drop as 3.4 percent. People in families with children fell 11 percent, to 230,366. The number of people counted as chronically homeless, homeless for a long time, reached 155,750, the highest on record.

#### 2020: office and school at once

In 2020 many homes became a workplace and a classroom at once. The share of workers who worked mainly from home tripled, from 5.7 percent in 2019 to 17.9 percent in 2021, according to the Census Bureau's American Community Survey. In 2025 nearly 22 percent of workers worked from home at least part of the time, according to Census data reported by the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis.

Homeschooling rose too. Here homeschooling means that the family taught the children, not that teachers at a school taught them online. In the spring of 2020, 5.4 percent of households with school-age children were homeschooling. By the fall of 2020 the figure was 11.1 percent, according to the Census Bureau's Household Pulse Survey. Among Black households it rose from 3.3 to 16.1 percent.

Many children did their schoolwork online, and some homes had no fast internet connection. Broadband is the fast home internet used for online classes. Pew researchers reported that 35 percent of households with children aged 6 to 17 and incomes under 30,000 dollars a year had no broadband. Among households with incomes over 75,000 dollars, 6 percent had none.

In a survey by the National Center for Education Statistics, parents reported that 5.2 percent of children aged 5 to 17 learned at home in the 2022-23 school year. That count includes children in full-time online school. In 2018-19 the figure had been 3.7 percent. The 2020 survey and this survey asked different questions, so the exact trend cannot be measured. The share learning at home in 2022-23 was higher than before the pandemic and much lower than in the fall of 2020.

<a id="story-solon-familia-foreclosure"></a>

#### Pierre Solon and Katty Familia

> **Who:** Immigrant parents, from Haiti and the Dominican Republic, who lost their Boston house to foreclosure.
>
> **When and where:** Hyde Park, Boston, Massachusetts, about 2006 to 2010.

Pierre Solon and Katty Familia lost their house in Boston in 2009. Solon came from Haiti and Familia from the Dominican Republic. In about 2006 they bought a green wooden house in Boston's Hyde Park neighborhood for 584,000 dollars. They borrowed the whole price. The loans came from Fremont Investment and Loan, a subprime lender. Their lawyer was Nadine Cohen of Greater Boston Legal Services. She said the two mortgage payments came to almost 5,000 dollars a month more than the couple's whole income.

Each parent worked two jobs. Then each lost one. "Sometimes we don't even have food," Katty Familia said. The couple fell more than 150,000 dollars behind. Staff at Wells Fargo, the bank that collected their payments, offered lower monthly payments on a debt that would have grown to more than 600,000 dollars. The couple turned the offer down. Wells Fargo's staff then foreclosed, and late in 2009 the family moved out with their children.

In November 2010 Wells Fargo sold the house at auction, a sale where the highest bidder wins, to an investor, a buyer who hopes to sell later for more, for 115,000 dollars. Two weeks later that investor sold it to another investor for 270,000 dollars. The Massachusetts Attorney General, the state's top lawyer, sued Fremont for deceptive lending, which means lending by misleading borrowers. Fremont sold its loans to investors, then went bankrupt, which means it could not pay its debts, and closed. In 2010 the couple ran a day care center in Boston. "I worked 20 years in this country for this," Katty Familia said. The reporter Anthony Brooks told their story on the radio program *Morning Edition*, on NPR, in December 2010.

<a id="story-munoz-family-2020"></a>

#### The Munoz family

> **Who:** A Las Vegas family whose four school-age children did school online at the dining room table while both parents went out to work.
>
> **When and where:** Las Vegas, Nevada, August 2020.

In August 2020, four of the five Munoz children in Las Vegas, Nevada, started the school year on laptops at the dining room table. Both parents worked in the food industry, away from home. While they were at work, the family's 10th-grade son helped the younger children. He worked with a fourth-grader with reading and a new middle-schooler with writing. When he had trouble, he emailed the teachers.

The father, Johnathan Munoz, recorded the family's first week as an audio diary for NPR's radio program *Weekend Edition Sunday*. On the second day he said, "it was a challenge because we couldn't log in." The middle-schooler said that one teacher kept marking her absent. Another teacher did not allow a brother or sister to be seen in the background.

<a id="part-3"></a>

# Part 3: Making and Building

<a id="ch-technology"></a>

## Chapter 8: Technology

### Before 1500

Before 1500, people in North America made their tools from wood, stone, bone, clay, animal skin and, near Lake Superior, copper. Without any metal machines, they built traps that caught fish with the tide, fields that grew three crops together, and boats made of birch bark. The names of the people who first worked out these methods are not recorded. Some of the methods are still practiced today.

#### Weapons and food machines

Before the bow and arrow, hunters in western North America threw spears with an atlatl. An atlatl is a spear-thrower, a stick that holds the back end of the spear while the hunter throws it.

About 1,400 years ago, around the years A.D. 600 to 700, hunters across the West began using the bow and arrow. A study published in 2026 in the *Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory* states that date. South of an east-west line called the 55th parallel, archaeologists stop finding atlatls soon after the bow appears. Archaeologists are scientists who dig up and study objects people left behind. North of that line, hunters used both weapons side by side for more than 1,000 years.

People also built fixed traps to catch fish. A fish weir is a fence of wooden stakes set across the water, with bundles of brush woven between the stakes. Fish swim in over the mud flats with the rising tide, and the fence traps them when the water goes out. People then scooped them up with baskets and nets, or caught them by hand. Lines of wooden stakes from fish weirs lie under Boylston Street in Boston. People built these weirs in channels that filled and emptied with the tide, between about 4,700 and 3,700 years ago. They used them for more than a thousand years, until mud filled the bay around 1550 B.C., about 3,500 years ago.

Native farmers planted corn, beans and squash together in the same field. These three crops are called the Three Sisters. People also set controlled fires, which means fires they started on purpose and kept in bounds, to shape the land.

#### Built crafts and a calendar in wood

People made pottery from clay and wove baskets. They tanned animal hides, which means they treated the skins so they would not rot and would stay soft, and they made canoes from the bark of birch trees.

At Cahokia, in what is now Illinois, people built the largest city north of Mexico before 1500. Between about A.D. 900 and 1100, builders there raised five circles of upright wooden posts, one after another. Each circle had between 24 and 72 posts and measured about 240 to 475 feet (73 to 145 meters) across. The posts marked the places on the horizon where the sun rose at different times of the year, so the circles worked as a calendar.

Near Lake Superior, people worked copper for thousands of years. They worked the copper cold, which means they shaped it without melting it.

<a id="story-wayne-valliere"></a>

#### Wayne Valliere

> **Who:** An Ojibwe builder of birchbark canoes and a teacher of the Ojibwe language. A National Heritage Fellow of the National Endowment for the Arts in 2020.
>
> **When and where:** Lac du Flambeau, Wisconsin, in the present day.

Birchbark canoes were among the boats people built before 1500, and Wayne Valliere builds them today. He is a member of the Lac du Flambeau Band of Lake Superior Ojibwe, in Wisconsin. The National Endowment for the Arts is a US government agency that gives money and honors to artists. Its profile of Valliere describes the Ojibwe way of building canoes as handed down over many generations.

According to the profile, Valliere began learning at 16. He learned from elders, among them Joe Chosa, Marvin DeFoe and Ojaanimigiizhig. He also studied old objects kept in museums, along with writings and photographs.

Valliere builds each canoe from birchbark, cedar, spruce roots and pitch. The hull, the body of the boat, is thick birchbark. Ribs of straight-grained cedar hold the hull in shape, and spruce roots serve as thread to sew the pieces of bark together. Pitch, a sticky tree sap, is mixed with oak ash and deer tallow, which is fat from a deer, to seal the seams against water. The builder gathers each material in a different season of the year.

Valliere has taught more than 100 students. At least one of them now builds canoes without his help. A second is learning as an apprentice, a beginner who learns a craft by working beside a master. Valliere also teaches the Ojibwe language at Lac du Flambeau Public School. In 2020 he received a National Heritage Fellowship from the National Endowment for the Arts. It is the highest honor in the United States for folk and traditional arts, the crafts and music that families and communities hand down.

### The 1500s

European metal reached Native towns on the East Coast in the 1500s, before most Europeans did. Native smiths, people who shape metal into tools, cut European copper and brass into tools of their own design. Brass is a yellow metal made by melting copper and zinc together.

#### Kettle metal, new tools

Copper and brass from Europe reached the East Coast through trade with Europeans along the shore. Both metals had been made in European furnaces from rock dug out of the ground. Native traders passed the metal from one group to the next, so it spread along the East Coast ahead of most Europeans. In 1524 Verrazzano, a European sailing along the Northeast coast, wrote that the Native people there had sheets of worked copper.

Some of the metal came as kettles, large cooking pots. Native smiths cut the kettles apart and hammered the pieces into arrow points, knives, pipe stems, bells and ornaments. They took the new metal and made it into the tools and goods they already used.

Spanish expeditions, groups of men sent out to explore, also crossed parts of what is now the United States in the 1500s, through lands where Native nations lived. The men on these expeditions carried iron weapons and tools. No lasting trade in tools followed their visits.

### The 1600s

English colonists built water-powered mills and ironworks here in the 1600s. An ironworks is a place where workers make iron from rock dug out of the ground. Colonists dammed streams to turn waterwheels. The wheels drove grist mills, which ground grain into flour, and sawmills, which cut logs into boards. At the ironworks they worked the bellows and hammers. The first ironworks begun in the English colonies stood on Powhatan land in Virginia. The first one that ran for years stood on Pawtucket land in Massachusetts. Its workers were skilled English ironworkers, nearby farmers, at least two Native woodcutters, and Scottish prisoners of war who were forced to work there for seven years.

#### Falling Creek, 1619 to 1622

At Falling Creek, Virginia, colonists began the first ironworks in the English colonies. They began building it on Powhatan land at the falls of the James River, where the river drops over rocks, near present-day Richmond. The Virginia Company was the English company that ran the colony. Its officers hired Captain Benjamin Bluett in 1619 to run the ironworks. Chesterfield County's history of the site states that he sailed with 80 men. A county tourism page gives the number as 150.

Bluett died on the voyage or soon after he arrived. Others of his men died too, of what colonists called seasoning.
