Seasoning was the sickness that killed between 50 and 90 percent of early newcomers, according to the county's history. The men who lived could not finish the furnace, the tall oven where iron is melted out of rock. In 1621 company officers hired John Berkeley to take over. He sailed with his son Maurice and 25 other men, according to the county. He promised iron by June 9, 1622.

Opechancanough, a Powhatan leader, planned an attack on English settlements across the colony. From 1618 to 1620, English tobacco planters, owners of large farms called plantations, had taken Powhatan land without paying for it. Virginia Company officials had also pressed to take Powhatan children for English schooling.

On March 22, 1622, Powhatan warriors attacked the ironworks. They killed 27 English people there, John Berkeley among them. Two children at Falling Creek survived. The warriors left the works in ruins. Across the colony that day, Powhatan warriors killed about 350 English colonists. Maurice Berkeley was away from the works and lived. He tried to start the ironworks again and failed. Sir John Zouch tried again from 1634 to 1636 and also failed.

The records disagree about whether Falling Creek ever made iron. Virginia's official list of historic places states that workers produced iron there in 1620. The county's history states that Bluett's men could not finish the furnace, and in 1621 Berkeley was still promising iron for the next year.

#### Iron from water power at Saugus

The first ironworks in the English colonies that ran for years stood on the Saugus River in Massachusetts. By 1643 John Winthrop Jr. had gathered about two dozen investors for it, people who put in money hoping for a profit. They formed the Company of Undertakers of the Iron Works in New England. Undertakers here meant people who take on a big job. The works ran from 1646 to about 1670.

Seven waterwheels drove three kinds of machine. The first was a blast furnace, a tall furnace for melting iron out of rock. Air blown into its fire made the fire hot enough to do it. Bellows, giant bags that squeeze air into a fire, pumped the air. They were 18 feet long, and the fire reached about 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit. Next came a forge, where 10 to 12 men hammered the iron. The last was a rolling and slitting mill, which pressed iron into flat sheets and cut it into thin rods.

The ironworks burned more than 3,600 cords of wood a year. A cord is a stack of wood 8 feet long, 4 feet wide and 4 feet high. Workers cut the wood with axes and saws made at the works.

The Saugus works closed because of debt, high costs and competition from iron brought in from overseas. The men who had lent money sued. Some of the ironworkers, such as James Leonard, went on to run forges in other places. The works have been rebuilt on the old site, which is now the Saugus Iron Works National Historic Site.

#### Who did the work at Saugus

The Saugus works stood on the land of the Pawtucket, the Native people who lived there when the English arrived. Saugus had been a Native settlement. The English first called it Lynn. About 100 people worked at the ironworks. They lived in a village the company owned, called Hammersmith after the English town that many of the ironworkers came from.

The company's managers brought skilled ironworkers over from the iron-making parts of England. Colonists from nearby farms did the unskilled work. Company records show that at least two Native people cut wood for the same wages as the other workers. The records do not give their names.

Some of the workers were prisoners of war. In September 1650, Oliver Cromwell's English soldiers defeated a Scottish army at Dunbar, in Scotland, and captured Scottish soldiers. Members of England's Council of State, the group of leaders that ran England's government at the time, ordered 150 of the prisoners handed over. Sir Arthur Haselrig gave them to agents of John Becx and Joshua Foote, two of the company's investors. The agents shipped the prisoners across the ocean on the ship *Unity*, which left Gravesend, England, on November 11, 1650. How many died on the voyage is not known.

The company's agents kept 62 of the Scots. About 36 of them reached Saugus in December 1650, and the agents put them to work there. A National Park Service history states the number as about 35, arriving in 1651. The company's agents held the Scots to seven years of forced labor. The papers that bound them were called indentures. An indenture is a written contract that requires a person to work for a master for a set number of years. The Scots cut wood, worked as colliers, who make charcoal, and did other labor. They received clothing, food and tobacco.

Some of the Scots are known by name. A list of 35 Scots at the works in 1653 includes James Adams, John Clark, Alexander Innes, Peter Grant, John Stewart and Thomas Tower. A November 1653 list of the property of the works includes Alexander Innes, with a value of 10 pounds. The Scottish Prisoners of War Society prints these lists from the company's record books.

At the forge, flying sparks and pieces of hot metal were a constant danger to the men. The forge hammer weighed 500 pounds. Many workers lost their hearing from its noise. The surviving records of the works do not give a count of deaths.

#### The Cambridge printing press

The first printing press in the English colonies arrived in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1638. A printing press is a machine that presses paper down hard onto metal letters covered in ink. The Reverend Jose Glover, a minister, bought the press and hired a locksmith named Stephen Daye to run it. Glover died on the voyage across the ocean. His widow, Elizabeth Glover, owned the press, and Daye ran it.

In 1640 Daye printed the *Bay Psalm Book* on the press. It was a book of psalms, the religious songs of the Bible, and it was the first book printed in what is now the United States.

<a id="story-joseph-jenks"></a>

#### Joseph Jenks

> **Who:** A sword maker from London who had worked at a water-powered sword mill at Hounslow, England, and then ran the blacksmith shop at the Saugus ironworks. US Patent Office officials credit him with the first patent for a machine in what is now the United States.
>
> **When and where:** Saugus, then part of Lynn, Massachusetts. At the works from 1646. Died in 1683.

US Patent Office officials credit Joseph Jenks with the first patent for a machine in what is now the United States. A National Park Service page about his shop states this. A patent is a government grant that gives an inventor the only right to make and sell an invention for a set number of years. Massachusetts leaders granted Jenks his patent in 1646.

Jenks was born in about August 1599 and baptized in a church in London. His father was a cutler, a maker of knives. In the 1630s Jenks worked for a sword maker named Benjamin Stone, who ran a sword mill powered by water at Hounslow, England. A sword marked with Jenks's name as its maker survives in a museum in Wales. He next appears in court records in the Kittery area of Maine.

In May 1646 Jenks asked the Massachusetts General Court for the only right, for 14 years, to build water-driven mills. The General Court was the group of leaders who made the colony's laws. The mills would make scythes, long curved blades for cutting grass. He also asked to build "a new Invented Saw Mill" and other machines for making tools with edges. He explained why he wanted protection. Without it, he wrote, "Another when he seeth it makes the like." He went on, "and soe I loose the benefit." He meant that another man would see his machine and copy it, and Jenks would lose the profit. The court's magistrates, the leaders who sat as its judges, granted his request. His petition, the written request, survives in the Massachusetts Archives. The copy there is dated May 10, 1646.

On January 20, 1647, Richard Leader, the agent in charge of the ironworks, let Jenks build a water-driven hammer at the tail of the blast furnace. It ran on the water that had already turned the furnace wheel. The company owned the shop, and Jenks paid rent. There he made saw blades, felling saws for cutting down trees, and steelyards, which are weighing scales. He also drew iron into fine wire, which means he pulled it through small holes to make it thin. In 1652 he sent two saw blades for a water-powered sawmill that John Winthrop Jr. ran in Connecticut.

The ironworks company went bankrupt, which means it could not pay its debts. In September 1656 Jenks bought a share of his shop, and in October the rolling and slitting mill, with a loan from Simon Bradstreet.

By October 1667 he was "very weak in estate," which meant he had little money. He asked the court for 50 pounds to start making iron wire. He died in March 1683. His son, Joseph Jenks Jr., began working at Saugus at 16 in 1649 and built his own forge in the town of Pawtucket, Rhode Island, in 1672. That town is a different place from the land of the Pawtucket people at Saugus.

In 1952 the archaeologist Roland Robbins dug up the site of Jenks's shop. He found waterwheels, the supports of a water-driven hammer, an anvil base and a stone forge. A marker put up in 1898 states that Jenks made the dies, the stamps, for the first silver coins made in New England in 1652. No document from the time shows that he did.

### 1700 to 1750

At the Baltimore Iron Works in Maryland, which opened in 1731, 42 of the first 89 workers were enslaved. It was one of many iron furnaces and forges that colonists built in Pennsylvania, Maryland and Virginia between 1700 and 1750. Waterwheels still drove the machines, and the furnaces still burned charcoal. In Philadelphia, the printer Benjamin Franklin designed a new kind of stove in 1741 or 1742 and refused to patent it.

#### The Franklin stove

Benjamin Franklin designed a stove that sent more of a fire's heat into the room and less of it up the chimney. He made it in 1741 or 1742. The Franklin Institute, a science museum in Philadelphia, states 1742 in its history of his inventions.

Franklin's stove was a fireplace lined with metal. It stood a few inches out from the chimney. At the back was a hollow iron wall, called a baffle. Air from the room flowed into the baffle, picked up the fire's heat and came back out into the room. Behind the baffle was a U-shaped passage called an inverted siphon. The smoke had to go up over the baffle, down behind it and only then up the chimney. On that longer path, the iron took in more of the smoke's heat. The stove also made less smoke than an ordinary fireplace.

Franklin refused to patent the stove. He gave his reason later in his autobiography, the story of his life that he wrote himself. He wrote: "That as we enjoy great Advantages from the Inventions of others, we should be glad of an Opportunity to serve others by any Invention of ours." He went on: "and this we should do freely and generously." He meant that everyone gains from other people's inventions, so people should share their own inventions for free. He never patented any of his inventions.

#### Who worked the iron furnaces

Many of the workers at the Maryland ironworks were enslaved people or convicts. In 1719, investors in Britain set up the Principio Company in Cecil County, Maryland. In 1731 five Maryland planters founded the Baltimore Iron Works on the Patapsco River. They were Dr. Charles Carroll, another man named Charles Carroll, Daniel Carroll, Daniel Dulaney and Benjamin Tasker. Dr. Carroll put in 2,200 acres of land and served as the first manager. The five partners supplied the money and the enslaved workers.

The Patapsco valley lay in a region where the Susquehannock and the Piscataway lived. In 1652 five Susquehannock war chiefs had signed a treaty, a written agreement between nations, with Maryland colonial officials. In it they gave up their claim to the western shore of the Chesapeake Bay from the Patuxent River north to Palmer's Island. That stretch of shore includes the Patapsco. Emma Bilski, a history graduate student at Johns Hopkins University, points out that the land was not really the Susquehannock's to give away. Other nations, such as the Piscataway, lived in the region too.

The Baltimore Iron Works opened with 89 workers. Forty-two of them were enslaved. Over the years, many other workers there were convicts. They were people found guilty of crimes in Britain. Under a British law of 1718, English judges sentenced many such people to be shipped to the colonies. Merchants who held contracts with the British government carried them across the ocean and sold their labor to colonists, most often for seven years. Iron makers were among the buyers. The managers of the Baltimore Iron Works preferred enslaved workers to convicts. Many of the enslaved ironworkers were Igbo people from West Africa, who brought their own skill at working metal. By 1785 an advertisement for the works listed a workforce of "more than 200 Negroes." Negro was a word used then for a Black person.

The workers hauled charcoal, oyster shells and iron ore to the top of the furnace. They worked 12-hour shifts, day and night, six or seven days a week. The owners lived away from the works and often quarreled, and they refused to send the food and workers they had promised. In 1775 the manager, Clement Brooke, wrote to the partners: "I cannot do my job unless you send more slaves and more corn." The Mount Clare Museum's history of the works states that the workers and the animals were starving.

Each of the five owners took one fifth of the iron. In good years the partners earned 55 percent on their money each year. The works closed in 1799. In 1810 the 30 heirs of the original owners, the people who had inherited their shares, had the land that was left sold at auction. It came to more than 30,000 acres. The heirs had 200 enslaved people sold at the same auction.

Some workers ran away. In August 1754 the *Maryland Gazette* newspaper printed a notice for the capture of people who had escaped. Others worked slowly. In the spring of 1771, an enslaved blacksmith named Anthony and an indentured servant named Thomas Livy were jailed for robbing a store. They were caught with the stolen goods, most likely food. The Mount Clare Museum's account of the case does not say who caught them or who jailed them. The overseer, the man in charge of the workers, was William Hammond. He wrote about Anthony: "We shall feel the loss of Anthony's time very much, I cannot tell how we can carry on the Forge business without him."

<a id="story-benjamin-franklin-technology"></a>

#### Benjamin Franklin

> **Who:** A Philadelphia printer who designed the Franklin stove and later the lightning rod. He refused to patent any of his inventions.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Boston in 1706. Worked in Philadelphia. Died there in 1790.
>
> **Movie:** *Benjamin Franklin* (2022), a two-part documentary by Ken Burns, shown on PBS. It is about Franklin's life.

The printer Benjamin Franklin also designed devices for homes and buildings. He was born in Boston on January 17, 1706. Under the calendar used in the colonies at the time, the date was January 6. He made his living in Philadelphia, where he printed a newspaper and a yearly almanac, a book of calendars, weather guesses and sayings.

In 1741 or 1742 he designed the Franklin stove, a metal fireplace that put more of a fire's heat into the room. In the 1750s he designed the lightning rod, an iron rod that protects a building from lightning. He also ran experiments with electricity.

Franklin took out no patent on any of these inventions. In his autobiography he wrote that people gain from the inventions of others, so they should share their own inventions "freely and generously."

Franklin died in Philadelphia on April 17, 1790.

### 1750 to 1800

Benjamin Franklin's lightning rods went up on Philadelphia roofs in the 1750s. By 1755 the first steam engine in America was pumping water from a New Jersey mine. In 1790 Samuel Slater's cotton-spinning mill began work at Pawtucket, Rhode Island. It was the start of the factory cloth industry in the United States, and Slater hired children to run its machines. In 1793 Eli Whitney built the cotton gin. One small gin could clean about 50 pounds of cotton a day, work that took several hundred hours by hand. Planters then grew far more cotton, from fewer than 9,000 bales a year around 1790 to more than 200,000 by 1800. A bale is a large bundle of cotton pressed tight and tied. Planters also held far more people in slavery to grow it. About 700,000 people were enslaved in the United States in 1790. By 1860 the number was nearly 4 million.

#### The lightning rod

In a letter of 1750 to Peter Collinson, Franklin described a way to protect buildings from what he called "electrical fire." In 1752 there were lightning tests in France and then Franklin's own kite test. After those tests, the first lightning rods went up on buildings in Philadelphia.

Franklin printed instructions for making one in *Poor Richard's Almanack* for 1753. He told readers to take a small iron rod. One end went three or four feet into moist ground. The other end stood six or eight feet above the top of the building. A foot of brass wire, sharpened to a fine point, went on the top end. Small staples held the rod to the house. When lightning struck, it would hit the point and pass through the metal into the ground, "without hurting any Thing," Franklin wrote. The Franklin Institute's history of his inventions states that pointed rods soon stood on buildings throughout the colonies.

#### The first steam engine in America

The first steam engine in America pumped water out of a mine. It was ordered from England in 1748 for Colonel John Schuyler's copper mine, in what is now North Arlington, New Jersey. The parts arrived in 1753. An engine builder named Josiah Hornblower put it together, and it was pumping by 1755.

It was a Newcomen engine, named for Thomas Newcomen, who built the first one in England in 1712. A boiler filled a large tube, called a cylinder, with steam. Then a spray of cold water turned the steam back into water, which left the cylinder nearly empty. The weight of the air outside pushed a piston, a tight-fitting plug, down into the cylinder. The piston pulled one end of a big rocking beam, and the other end of the beam worked the pump in the mine.

#### The cotton gin and what it did

Upland cotton has sticky seeds caught in its fiber. Before 1793, enslaved people pulled the seeds out by hand. One worker needed many hours to clean a single pound of cotton. Planters could grow only as much cotton as their workers could clean.

Eli Whitney's cotton gin did the cleaning by machine. It used two cylinders that combed the cotton through small holes. The seeds could not pass through the holes and stayed behind. A history of the gin by the Eli Whitney Museum states that one small gin could clean 50 pounds of cotton a day. By hand, that much cotton took several hundred hours of work.

Planters used the gin to grow far more cotton. Across the United States they grew fewer than 9,000 bales of cotton a year around 1790, more than 200,000 bales by 1800 and about 4 million by 1860. A bale is a large bundle of cotton pressed tight and tied.

With the gin cleaning cotton so fast, planters wanted far more enslaved people to grow and pick it. The 1790 census, the government's count of everyone in the country, counted 697,897 enslaved people in the United States. By 1860 there were nearly 4 million, and about 2.5 million of them lived in the cotton-growing regions from eastern Maryland to Texas. Slaveholders spread slavery west across the South.

Enslaved people picked the cotton by hand in the summer sun, about 200 pounds each a day. Solomon Northup was a free Black man from New York. Kidnappers seized him in Washington, D.C., in 1841 and forced him into slavery. Slaveholders held him for twelve years. He picked cotton on Edwin Epps's plantation in Louisiana until he was rescued in 1853.

In his book *Twelve Years a Slave*, published that year, Northup described the rule: "An ordinary day's work is two hundred pounds. A slave who is accustomed to picking, is punished, if he or she brings in a less quantity than that." Each night the cotton was weighed at the gin-house, the building where the gin stood. "After weighing, follow the whippings," Northup wrote.

The punishment was the lash. A lash is one stroke of a whip on a person's bare body. Northup wrote that twenty-five lashes were "deemed a mere brush," which means they were thought of as a small punishment. Fifty was "the ordinary penalty," and one hundred was "called severe." Northup described Epps himself seizing the whip and lashing the people he enslaved. Epps once forced Northup to whip an enslaved woman named Patsey, and then took the whip himself. Northup wrote that her back was "covered with long welts," raised and swollen stripes. He wrote that "the lash was wet with blood," meaning the whip itself. Epps then had her washed with salt and water.

Enslaved people also ran the gins and the cotton presses, the machines that squeezed cotton into bales. The machines had many moving parts that could catch and injure a worker. The tiny cotton fibers the gins threw into the air damaged the workers' lungs.

The profit went to the people who owned the plantations. With the gin, Southern plantation owners gained money and political power. Their cotton supplied cloth mills in the Northern states and in Britain. By 1830, cloth and other finished cotton goods were the largest group of factory-made goods the country sold to other countries.

Planters also wanted new land for cotton. The Eli Whitney Museum's history of the gin states that this demand was "a major factor" in the removal of five Native nations from their homelands in the Southeast. They were the Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee (Creek) and Seminole. On May 28, 1830, President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act. Under it, the president could trade land west of the Mississippi River for the lands of Native nations inside the states. US officials then forced the five nations west to Indian Territory. That land is now part of the state of Oklahoma. At least 60,000 people were forced to make the journey, and more than 8,000 of them died on the way.

In 1838 US Army soldiers under General Winfield Scott began forcing the Cherokee out of their homeland. Scott was sent to another post soon after the removal began. In the fall and winter of 1838 and 1839, about 4,000 Cherokee died on the march west that the soldiers forced them to make. The soldiers first held them in crowded, dirty camps, where many died. On the march they faced heavy rain, rivers blocked by ice and too little food. Many died of illness, and some died of disease after drinking dirty standing water. White landowners took the land the five nations had been forced to leave.

<a id="story-eli-whitney"></a>

#### Eli Whitney

> **Who:** The builder of the cotton gin, patented in 1794. He also promoted the idea of machine-made, interchangeable gun parts, which the workers at his own factory never managed to make.
>
> **When and where:** Georgia and New Haven, Connecticut. Born 1765, died 1825.

The patent on the cotton gin belonged to Eli Whitney. He was born in Westborough, Massachusetts, on December 8, 1765. He graduated from Yale College in 1792 and traveled south to work as a tutor, a private teacher.

On the way, Catherine Littlefield Greene invited him to her plantation, Mulberry Grove, north of Savannah, Georgia. She was the widow of General Nathanael Greene, who had died in 1786 and left her dozens of enslaved people. Enslaved workers on the plantation grew mostly rice and some cotton. There, in 1793, Whitney built the machine that pulled cotton fiber away from its seeds. He applied for a patent in 1794, and the patent was granted on March 14, 1794.

Whitney held the patent. In 1870 the women's rights activist Matilda Joslyn Gage wrote that Catherine Greene invented the cotton gin. The Eli Whitney Museum states that it "has been suggested that Catherine Greene also contributed ideas to the design." The record does not settle how much of the design was hers.

In 1798 Whitney signed a contract to make muskets for the federal government. He promoted the idea of making gun parts by machine, so that any part would fit any gun of the same model. Parts like these are called interchangeable parts. According to a famous story, Whitney showed government officials such parts in 1801.

In 1960 the historian Robert S. Woodbury showed that Whitney did not start the idea of interchangeable parts. The credit people gave Whitney for it rests on a myth. Gunmakers at French armories, factories that made weapons, had worked on the idea before Whitney. Workers at Whitney's own factory never made parts that truly fit any gun. The best-documented first American use of interchangeable parts in a factory came at John H. Hall's rifle works at the Harpers Ferry armory. Hall's workers were putting rifles together from interchangeable parts by 1819.

Whitney died in New Haven, Connecticut, on January 8, 1825.

<a id="story-samuel-slater"></a>

#### Samuel Slater

> **Who:** An English mill worker who rebuilt English spinning machines from memory at Pawtucket, the start of the American factory cloth industry. He hired children to run the machines.
>
> **When and where:** Trained in Derbyshire, England. The mill ran at Pawtucket, Rhode Island, from December 1790.

Samuel Slater rebuilt English cotton-spinning machines from memory in the United States. In England, Richard Arkwright had patented a spinning machine in 1769. It was called the water frame because a waterwheel drove it. Arkwright and his partners built a mill several floors high at Cromford, in Derbyshire, with waterwheels to drive the machines. He moved cotton spinning out of homes and into powered mills with hundreds of workers. Other mill owners copied his system.

Slater trained in a mill in Derbyshire that used Arkwright's machines. British law did not allow machines for making cloth to leave the country. It also did not allow skilled cloth-mill workers to move abroad. In 1789 Slater left England without telling officials that he was a trained mill worker.

In December 1789 Moses Brown hired him. Brown's family firm, Almy & Brown, put up the money and the building. With local mechanics, people who build and repair machines, among them the Wilkinson family, Slater rebuilt the carding and spinning machines from memory. A carding machine combs raw cotton so the fibers lie straight. A spinning machine twists the fibers into thread, called yarn. The machines at Pawtucket spun their first yarn in December 1790.

Slater had worked in a factory for part of his own childhood. At Pawtucket he hired children to run the machines. The machines were built for children to run. Most of the children at Slater's mill were about 10 years old. Some were as young as six. They were paid by the hour, and they earned much less than adults. In 1801 a Boston politician described mills that employed "children from four to Ten years old." In the mill villages that grew up later, the child workers were 8 to 14 years old. The names of the first children who worked for Slater are not recorded.

### 1800 to 1850

Between 1831 and 1846, inventors in the United States built machines to cut grain, plow prairie soil and sew cloth. Charles Goodyear found a way to treat rubber with sulfur so that heat did not melt it. In 1839 people in Philadelphia made a new French way of taking photographs work within weeks of hearing about it. On May 24, 1844, Samuel Morse sent a message by electric telegraph from Washington to Baltimore, 40 miles away. Morse, Goodyear, the sewing machine maker Elias Howe and the reaper maker Cyrus McCormick each held a patent. A patent is a government grant that gives an inventor the only right to make and sell an invention for a set number of years. The men whose names went on the patents had help. Morse's partner Alfred Vail built the telegraph instruments. Jo Anderson, a man enslaved by the McCormick family, worked on the first McCormick reaper.

#### The telegraph, 1844

The electric telegraph sent messages as pulses of electricity through a wire. At the receiving end, each pulse worked an electromagnet, a magnet that works only while electricity flows through it. The magnet moved an arm with a pen-like point, called a stylus. A clockwork motor, which ran on gears like the inside of a wind-up clock, pulled a strip of paper tape past the stylus. For each pulse, the stylus pressed a small dent into the tape, a short one for a dot or a longer one for a dash. Every letter and number had its own pattern of dots and dashes, and that pattern is called Morse code.

In 1843 Morse asked Congress for $30,000 to build a telegraph line from Washington to Baltimore. Members of the House and then senators voted for the money, and President John Tyler signed the bill. Ezra Cornell's job was to lay the wire underground. When Cornell ran into bad wire, he suggested stringing the wires overhead on trees and poles instead. A signal in a long wire grows weaker as it goes. Leonard Gale showed Morse how to boost it at points along the line with a device called a relay.

On May 24, 1844, Morse sent the first public message over the line from the US Capitol in Washington. Alfred Vail received it in Baltimore. The words were "What hath God wrought," from the Bible, in the book of Numbers, chapter 23, verse 23. They mean "What has God done." Annie G. Ellsworth chose them. She was the daughter of the commissioner of the Patent Office, the head of the government office that grants patents. The paper tape with the message still exists. The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History holds it.

<a id="story-samuel-morse"></a>

#### Samuel Morse

> **Who:** The inventor who held the patents on the electric telegraph and sent the first public message over the Washington to Baltimore line.
>
> **When and where:** The story is that the idea came to him in 1832. The first public message went from Washington to Baltimore on May 24, 1844.

Samuel Morse held the patents on the American electric telegraph and got the fame for it. The story told in a Library of Congress history is that the idea of sending messages over a distance by electricity came to Morse in 1832. He was on a ship coming home from Europe, during a conversation on board.

Other men helped Morse build the telegraph. Leonard Gale showed him how to boost a weakening signal with a relay. Alfred Vail built and improved the instruments in the shop at the Speedwell Ironworks. The same Library of Congress history identifies hiring Vail as one of the keys to Morse's success. Vail received the first public message in Baltimore on May 24, 1844.

Who worked out the dot and dash code is still argued. Morse held the patents, and people call the code Morse code. Starting in 1887, Vail's son Stephen Vail sent letter after letter to newspaper editors claiming the credit for his father. In 1911 another son, J. Cummings Vail, had Alfred's gravestone changed to read "INVENTOR OF THE TELEGRAPHIC DOT AND DASH ALPHABET." In a 2020 article in *American History* magazine, the writer Joseph Connor credits Vail with the practical version, which gives the shortest codes to the letters people use most. According to Connor, Vail learned which letters were most common from printers, who kept the metal type for those letters closest at hand.

#### Sewing machines, rubber and the camera

Elias Howe patented a sewing machine on September 10, 1846. It sewed a lockstitch, in which two threads lock together through the cloth. Isaac Singer made a more practical machine, and it sold better than Howe's. Howe sued the makers who used his invention. In 1854 judges ruled that Howe's patent was good, and the makers had to pay him royalties, which are fees for using a patent. At the peak, the fees paid to Howe reached as much as $4,000 a month.

In 1856 Howe and the biggest makers, Singer, Wheeler & Wilson, and Grover & Baker, pooled their patents. That meant each member could use the others' patented inventions. Their group was called the Sewing Machine Combination. Its members controlled the sewing machine trade until 1877.

In 1839, in Woburn, Massachusetts, a piece of Charles Goodyear's mix of rubber and sulfur landed on a hot stove. The rubber charred like leather instead of melting. The stories of how it reached the stove differ. Mass Moments, a Massachusetts history site, states that he either dropped it or placed it there. A speech in his honor printed in 1860 says that the piece was in his hand and was thrown into the stove "by a violent gesture." The encyclopedia Britannica's account says it flew from his hand while he was trying to sell his rubber. It took Goodyear five more years to learn to make the change happen every time. He patented the process in 1844. Rubber treated this way is called vulcanized rubber.

In late August and September of 1839, news of the daguerreotype reached the United States. It was an early way of making photographs, invented by Louis Daguerre, a French artist. François Arago announced it at a meeting of the French Academy of Sciences in Paris on August 19, 1839. Within weeks, people in Philadelphia had made the process work for themselves. In October or November of 1839, Robert Cornelius of Philadelphia made a photograph of himself. It is the oldest surviving portrait photograph made in America. The Library of Congress holds it.

<a id="story-mccormick-deere"></a>

#### Cyrus McCormick and John Deere

> **Who:** Two makers of farm machines. McCormick's reaper cut grain, and Deere's steel plow cut through prairie soil.
>
> **When and where:** The reaper at Walnut Grove and Steele's Tavern, Virginia, 1831. The plow at Grand Detour, Illinois, 1837.

A reaper is a machine that cuts ripe grain. Cyrus McCormick held the patent on the McCormick reaper and built the business that sold it. Other people also worked on the first one.

His father, Robert McCormick, tried for several years to build a reaper at Walnut Grove, the family farm in Rockbridge County, Virginia. In 1831 he gave up. Within six weeks, Cyrus showed a working reaper by cutting oats at nearby Steele's Tavern. A blacksmith named John McCown worked on the machine. So did Jo Anderson, a man the McCormicks enslaved.

Anderson was born on Robert McCormick's plantation in about 1807. In 1885 a white interviewer, William J. Hanna, wrote down Anderson's words in dialect spelling, which tries to show how a person's speech sounded. "I was his slave," Anderson said of Robert McCormick, "but when a baby was given to Massa Cyrus." Massa meant master. Robert McCormick held him in slavery from birth. Hanna recorded Anderson as 78 years old and unable to walk. Anderson said he carried grain to the blacksmith shop to test the machine: "I fotched loose grain to the shop so he could see how it cut it." He also worked as "blower and striker for the blacksmith." That is the helper who pumps the bellows and swings the heavy hammer. The bellows is a big bag that blows air onto the fire. Anderson gave Cyrus the credit for the reaper and said Robert "tried it and gave it up." He said Cyrus freed him before the Civil War.

In December 1833 another inventor, Obed Hussey, patented a reaper. McCormick patented his own in 1834 and printed a warning against Hussey's machine in *Mechanics' Magazine*. McCormick made his first sales in 1840 and moved to Chicago in 1847. In 1859 he and his brothers made and sold more than 5,000 reapers.

John Deere made plows at Grand Detour, Illinois. The sticky prairie soil there clogged iron plows. In 1837 Deere built a plow with a polished steel moldboard, the curved blade that turns the soil over. The sticky soil slid off the smooth steel, so the plow scoured, or cleaned, itself as it moved. By 1846 Deere was selling nearly 1,000 plows a year.

Ho-Chunk people, long called the Winnebago in English, had lived in a village at the bend of the Rock River where Grand Detour stands. Settlers who came later said they could still see signs of that village. In 1832, at Fort Armstrong in Illinois, Ho-Chunk leaders signed a treaty with two men sent to make it for the United States. A treaty is a written agreement between nations. The two men were General Winfield Scott and John Reynolds, the governor of Illinois. In the treaty the Ho-Chunk signed over their lands south and east of the Wisconsin River and the Fox River of Green Bay. The boundary ran up the Rock River to its source. Under the treaty, US officials paid the Ho-Chunk $10,000 a year for 27 years. The records do not make clear which treaty covered the exact spot where Grand Detour stands.

### 1850 to 1900

After 1850, some inventors worked with patent lawyers and with teams of workers. On February 14, 1876, Alexander Graham Bell's lawyer filed an application for a telephone patent. A few hours later, papers from a rival, Elisha Gray, arrived. Thomas Edison's team at Menlo Park, New Jersey, made a long-lasting electric lamp in 1879, building on 40 years of work by other inventors. Not everyone could own an invention. In 1858 the US attorney general, the government's chief lawyer, ruled that an invention by an enslaved person could not be patented. According to the law scholar Kara Swanson, after that ruling free Black inventors could not get patents either.

#### Who could own an invention

By August 1857 an enslaved blacksmith named Ned, near Holmesville in Pike County, Mississippi, had invented a new farm tool. It was a "double Cotton Scraper, and two plows" that could "Scrape both Sides of the Cotton ridge at the same time, and plough out the middles." A cotton ridge is a raised row of soil where the cotton grows, and the middles are the low strips between the rows. Everything known about Ned comes from the letters of Oscar J. E. Stuart, a white planter and lawyer who claimed to own him. Ned's second name, if he had one, is not recorded. How his life ended is not known.

On November 15, 1857, Stuart applied for a patent on Ned's invention. He swore that he owned Ned and that Ned was the inventor. Stuart also threatened Ned. If Ned wrote to the Patent Office himself, Stuart said, he would "correct" Ned "according to our Southern usage." To correct meant to punish. Stuart made the threat in a letter he later sent to the secretary of the interior, one of the president's top officials. He did not write in it what the punishment would be.

The patent commissioner, Joseph Holt, sent the application back. The law required the inventor to swear an oath, a solemn promise before the law, that he had made the invention. Holt decided that an enslaved man could not take the oath. Stuart complained to Jacob Thompson, the secretary of the interior. Thompson sent the question to the attorney general, Jeremiah S. Black, the government's chief lawyer.

In 1858 Jeremiah Black ruled that "a machine invented by a slave, though it be new and useful, cannot, in the present state of the law, be patented." He based his ruling on the *Dred Scott* decision of 1857. In that case, the judges of the Supreme Court, called justices, ruled that African Americans were not citizens. Without citizenship, Jeremiah Black reasoned, an enslaved inventor could not swear the oath. The owner could not get the patent either, because only the "original and first inventor" could. Free Black inventors had received patents before this. The law scholar Kara Swanson writes that Jeremiah Black's opinion "created a formal racial barrier" to the patent system. After it, free Black inventors could not get patents either.

Stuart asked Congress twice for a patent and failed both times. In 1859 Senator Albert Gallatin Brown of Mississippi backed a bill that would let enslavers patent the inventions of the people they enslaved. Senators never moved the bill forward. Stuart sold the "Stuart Double Plough and Scraper" anyway, without a patent. In February 1861, delegates from seven Southern states that had broken away from the United States met in Montgomery, Alabama. There they set up their own government, the Confederate States of America, also called the Confederacy. Under a Confederate patent law of May 21, 1861, enslavers could patent the inventions of enslaved people.

Benjamin Montgomery was enslaved in Mississippi by Joseph Davis. Montgomery invented a better propeller for boats. Joseph Davis tried to patent it through his brother, Senator Jefferson Davis, and failed. Once he was free, Montgomery tried to patent the propeller in his own name, and that failed too, according to his son Isaiah Montgomery. In 1865, at the end of the Civil War, members of Congress and lawmakers in the states added the 13th Amendment to the Constitution. An amendment is a change to the Constitution. With it they ended slavery everywhere in the country, except as a punishment for a crime. Under the 13th Amendment and the amendments that followed it, Black inventors could get patents again. In 1913 Henry E. Baker, a Black patent examiner who checked patent applications for the government, published *The Colored Inventor*. "Colored" was a word used then for Black Americans. He wrote it to mark 50 years since emancipation, the freeing of enslaved people. It appeared in *The Crisis*, the magazine of the NAACP, a group that works for the rights of Black Americans.

#### The telephone, 1876

A telephone turns the sound of a voice into electric current and back into sound. In Bell's own description from 1876, the voice makes a thin sheet, called a membrane, shake in time with the sound. The shaking makes the electric current in the wire grow stronger and weaker in the same pattern. At the other end, the changing current makes a second sheet shake, and the listener hears the voice.

On the morning of February 14, 1876, Bell's lawyer filed an application for a patent called "Improvement in Telegraphy." It was the fifth filing at the Patent Office that day. A few hours later, papers from Elisha Gray arrived as the 39th filing. Gray filed a caveat, a notice that he was working on an invention and planned to apply for a patent. Both papers described a liquid transmitter, a sending part that used a liquid. On the advice of his lawyers, Gray withdrew.

Patent Office officials issued patent number 174,465 to Bell on March 7, 1876. On March 10 Bell spoke the first sentence ever sent by telephone. He spoke to his assistant, Thomas A. Watson, who was in the next room of Bell's laboratory in Boston. Bell's notebook records the words "Mr. Watson," then "come here," then "I want to see you."

Bell filed first and held the patent. People have argued ever since about whether Bell or Gray deserved the credit. In November 2020 Benjamin Lathrop Brown published a new study of the case in an engineering journal, the *Proceedings of the IEEE*. He titled it "The Bell Versus Gray Telephone Dispute: Resolving a 144-Year-Old Controversy."

<a id="story-alexander-graham-bell"></a>

#### Alexander Graham Bell

> **Who:** An inventor in Boston whose lawyer filed for the telephone patent a few hours before a rival's papers arrived. He received the patent.
>
> **When and where:** Boston, 1876.

The first telephone patent, number 174,465, went to Alexander Graham Bell on March 7, 1876. His lawyer had filed the application on February 14, a few hours before Elisha Gray's papers for a similar instrument reached the Patent Office.

Gray withdrew on the advice of his lawyers, and the patent stayed with Bell. People have argued ever since about who deserved the credit.

Lewis Latimer, a draftsman at a patent law firm, made the drawings for Bell's patent application. A draftsman makes exact drawings of machines and buildings. Latimer later worked on the electric lamp.

<a id="story-emma-nutt"></a>

#### Emma Nutt

> **Who:** The first woman telephone operator.
>
> **When and where:** Boston, hired September 1, 1878.

On September 1, 1878, Emma Nutt left a job at a telegraph office to work for the telephone dispatch company in Boston. She became the first woman to work as a telephone operator. An operator connected each caller to the person being called. Her pay was $10 a month for a 54-hour week. Her sister, Stella, started work as an operator the same day.

The first operators had been teenage boys, who were rude to callers and played pranks on them. The telephone companies' managers replaced the boys with women. By the late 1880s, almost every telephone operator was a woman. It was one of the first big jobs in a new technology open to women.

Emma Nutt worked as an operator for more than 30 years. The New England Historical Society, *Boston Magazine* and *Time* give the exact length as anything from about 33 to about 37 years.

#### Edison's invention factory

An electric lamp makes light when an electric current heats a thin thread inside it, called a filament, until the filament glows. Inventors had worked on electric lamps for 40 years before Edison's team made its lamp in 1879. British inventors showed arc lamps, which make light from a spark between two rods, starting in 1835. Joseph Swan in England patented a lamp design before Edison did, and so did William Sawyer and Albon Man.

Edison ran a laboratory at Menlo Park, New Jersey, with a team of workers. Among them were Charles Batchelor, John Kruesi and Francis Upton. In October 1879 the team made a lamp with a filament of cotton thread that had been baked into carbon. It burned for about 14.5 hours. Edison showed the lamps to the public at Menlo Park on New Year's Eve, 1879. The team kept testing filaments and settled on one made of bamboo. It let Edison's lamps burn for up to 1,200 hours.

Edison's team also built the other parts needed to light a whole district. These included the dynamo, a machine that makes electricity when it is turned, along with the wiring and a meter to measure how much electricity each customer used. On September 4, 1882, the Pearl Street station at 257 Pearl Street in Manhattan began supplying electricity. It lit the first district of paying customers.

The Menlo Park team built other machines too. Two years before the lamp, in early December 1877, John Kruesi built a phonograph to Edison's design. A phonograph records sound and plays it back. The first one recorded on a sheet of tinfoil. On December 6, 1877, Edison recorded himself saying "Mary had a little lamb."

<a id="story-thomas-edison-technology"></a>

#### Thomas Edison

> **Who:** An inventor who ran a laboratory with a team of workers. His team made a long-lasting electric lamp, the phonograph and the system that brought electric light to paying customers.
>
> **When and where:** Menlo Park and West Orange, New Jersey. Born 1847, died 1931.
>
> **Movie:** *Edison* (2015), a documentary in the PBS series *American Experience*. It is about Edison's life and work.

In 1879 Thomas Edison's team made an electric lamp that burned for about 14.5 hours, and later lamps burned for up to 1,200 hours. Other inventors had built electric lamps for 40 years before that. Edison was born in Milan, Ohio, on February 11, 1847.

Edison and his team at Menlo Park found a filament that lasted. They also built the dynamos that made the electricity, the wires that carried it to customers and the meters that measured how much each customer used. In 1882 Edison's company began selling electricity from the Pearl Street station in Manhattan to the first district of paying customers.

Edison worked with a team. John Kruesi built the phonograph that Edison designed. Charles Batchelor and Francis Upton worked with him on the lamp. Lewis Latimer made patent drawings and gave expert testimony for Edison's company from 1884.

In November 1887 Edison opened a new laboratory in West Orange, New Jersey. He died at his home in West Orange on October 18, 1931.

<a id="story-lewis-latimer"></a>

#### Lewis Latimer

> **Who:** A self-taught draftsman who later oversaw the building of electric lighting systems. He patented a better way to make the carbon filaments inside electric lamps.
>
> **When and where:** Boston and New York. Born 1848, died 1928.

A patent of 1882 gave Lewis Latimer the rights to a better way of making the carbon filaments that glow inside electric lamps. The patent, number 252,386, was issued on January 17, 1882, for a "Process of Manufacturing Carbons." His method made filaments that were more even and lasted longer.

Latimer was born in Chelsea, Massachusetts, on September 4, 1848. His parents had freed themselves from slavery in Virginia by escaping. He taught himself to be a draftsman. While he worked at a patent law firm, he made the patent drawings for Bell's 1876 telephone application.

He received his filament patent while working at the U.S. Electric Lighting Company of Hiram Maxim. In 1884 he went to work for Edison's company. He made patent drawings and testified in court as an expert on patents. He also oversaw lamp factories and the setting up of electric lighting in New York, Philadelphia, Montreal and London.

On January 24, 1918, Latimer became one of the 28 first members of the Edison Pioneers, a group of people who had worked closely with Edison before 1885. He was its only Black member. From 1903 he lived in a house in East Flushing, in Queens, New York. He died in Flushing on December 11, 1928, at the age of 80. The house is now the Lewis Latimer House Museum.

<a id="story-granville-t-woods"></a>

#### Granville T. Woods

> **Who:** A Black inventor who patented a way to send messages between moving trains and railroad stations.
>
> **When and where:** Cincinnati, Ohio. Patent issued November 29, 1887.

Granville T. Woods invented a way for moving trains and stations to send messages to each other. He patented it as the Synchronous Multiplex Railway Telegraph on November 29, 1887, while working in Cincinnati. With it, the people who directed train traffic, called dispatchers, could know where the trains were.

Woods's telegraph worked by induction. In induction, a changing electric current in one wire makes a current flow in another wire nearby, without the two touching. Woods used it to carry messages between moving trains and stations.

Twice, people on Edison's side claimed that inventions Woods had patented were theirs. Each time Patent Office officials held a hearing, called an interference proceeding, to decide who had invented first. Woods won both times. Edison offered him a job, and Woods turned it down. Over his career Woods received dozens of patents for electrical and railroad inventions.

<a id="story-nikola-tesla-technology"></a>

#### Nikola Tesla

> **Who:** A Serbian immigrant inventor whose induction motor used alternating current to make a shaft turn.
>
> **When and where:** New York. Patent issued May 1, 1888.

Alternating current, or AC, is electric current that switches direction back and forth many times each second. Nikola Tesla patented a motor that used AC to turn a shaft. His motor used induction, in which a changing current in one coil of wire makes a current flow in a part nearby without the two touching. The motor worked without brushes, the sliding electrical contacts that other motors used to carry current to their turning part.

Tesla was a Serbian immigrant who came to the United States in 1884. He filed for the motor patent in October 1887. The patent, number 381,968, was issued on May 1, 1888.

In July 1888 the Westinghouse company bought a license to Tesla's polyphase patents. A license is the right to use someone else's patent. Polyphase means his motors ran on two or more alternating currents at once. Tesla received $60,000 in cash and stock, which are shares in owning the company. Under the deal he was also to get $2.50 for each horsepower of the motors the company sold. Horsepower is a measure of how much work a motor can do.

#### The office and the fence line

Christopher Latham Sholes, Carlos Glidden and Samuel Soule patented a typewriter on June 23, 1868. E. Remington & Sons began making it on March 1, 1873. The Sholes & Glidden Type-Writer went on sale in 1874 for $125. Its keyboard began with the letters Q, W, E, R, T and Y across the top row of letters. That arrangement, called QWERTY, is still used on keyboards today.

On November 24, 1874, Joseph Glidden, a farmer from De Kalb, Illinois, received patent number 157,124 for barbed wire. He was a different man from the Carlos Glidden of the typewriter. Joseph Glidden's barb was a short piece of wire that locked onto a wire of two strands. He also built machines to make the wire in large amounts. Nine wire-fence designs were patented, and Glidden's was the one that sold well.

With barbed wire, farmers and ranchers could fence land where there was little wood to build fences. In the West, ranchers and homesteaders, families who had claimed farms, fenced off land and water that had been open to all. By fencing it, they ended the open range, the unfenced land where cattle had grazed freely. In Texas, New Mexico, Colorado and Wyoming, cattlemen found their old grazing land fenced off. They first asked officials for the right to use it. Then they fought what the National Archives calls "fierce range wars" against the farmers who owned the fenced land. The fences also blocked Native peoples who moved with the seasons from more of the lands they had always used, according to the National Archives. Those Native peoples called barbed wire "the Devil's rope."

### 1900 to 1950

Wilbur and Orville Wright flew a powered airplane in North Carolina on December 17, 1903. Ten years later, on October 7, 1913, workers at Henry Ford's car plant in Michigan started a moving assembly line. A motor and a rope pulled each car frame past 140 workers, who added parts as it moved. Over the next few decades, electric refrigerators and radios went into American homes. Chemists made new materials too, starting in 1907 with Leo Baekeland's Bakelite, the first plastic made entirely from chemicals. In February 1946 engineers at the University of Pennsylvania showed ENIAC, the first general-purpose electronic computer, one that could be set up to solve many kinds of problems. In December 1947 scientists at Bell Labs made the first transistor work. A transistor is a small part that controls the flow of electricity and can make a weak signal stronger. Transistors later replaced the glass vacuum tubes that machines like ENIAC used.

<a id="story-wright-brothers-technology"></a>

#### The Wright brothers

> **Who:** Wilbur and Orville Wright, bicycle builders from Dayton, Ohio. They invented an airplane with an engine that a pilot could steer and control.
>
> **When and where:** Near Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, December 17, 1903.
>
> **Movie:** *Wright Brothers' Flying Machine* (2003), a documentary in the PBS series *NOVA*, first shown on November 11, 2003. It is about the brothers' flying machine.

On December 17, 1903, near Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, the Wright brothers made four flights in an airplane with an engine. Orville flew first. He stayed in the air for 12 seconds and covered 120 feet. On the fourth flight of the day, Wilbur flew 852 feet in 59 seconds. Five people watched. One of them, John T. Daniels of the Life-Saving Station at Kill Devil Hills, squeezed the camera's shutter bulb and took the photograph of the first flight. It was the first photograph he had ever taken.

The brothers worked out how to steer an airplane on gliders, which have no engine, in 1901 and 1902. Besides going forward, an airplane can roll, with its wing tips moving up and down, pitch, with its nose moving up and down, and yaw, with its nose swinging from side to side. The Wrights used cables that twisted the tips of the wings up or down to control roll. In 1901 they added a movable part at the front, called an elevator, to control pitch. In 1902 they added a movable upright part at the back, called a rudder, to control yaw.

To test the shapes of wings, the brothers built their own wind tunnel, in which a fan blows a steady stream of air past a model. They also built a light gasoline engine in the workshop of their bicycle shop in Dayton.

On September 17, 1908, Army officers were testing the Wright airplane at Fort Myer, Virginia. Orville flew it with Lieutenant Thomas E. Selfridge of the Army Signal Corps as his passenger. The Signal Corps was the Army's communications branch, and it was then in charge of the Army's first aircraft. One of the propellers split and hit a wire, and the plane dived into the ground. Selfridge's skull was broken. He never woke up, and he died that evening. He was the first person killed in an airplane crash. Orville broke a leg and several ribs and spent seven weeks in the Army hospital.

<a id="story-henry-ford-technology"></a>

#### Henry Ford

> **Who:** The carmaker whose workers at Highland Park, Michigan, built the Model T on a moving assembly line.
>
> **When and where:** Highland Park, Michigan. The moving chassis line started on October 7, 1913.
>
> **Movie:** *Henry Ford* (2013), a documentary in the PBS series *American Experience*, directed by Sarah Colt. It is about Ford's life and his company.

At Henry Ford's plant in Highland Park, Michigan, the time it took to build the frame of a car fell from more than 12 hours to about 93 minutes. The workers got that speed by building on a moving assembly line. On a moving line, a motor pulls the car or part past the workers, and each worker adds parts or does one task as it goes by.

Ford's workers tried the line first on one part. In the spring of 1913 they put together the flywheel magneto, an engine part that makes electricity, on a line. The job was split into 29 steps done by 29 men along a moving belt. On October 7, 1913, the chassis line started. The chassis is the frame of the car, with its wheels. A motor and a rope pulled each chassis along a line 150 feet long, past 140 workers. At first the time to build one fell to under 3 hours, and later to about 93 minutes.

In January 1914 Ford announced a pay of $5 for an eight-hour day. Before that, workers had earned about $2.34 for nine hours. Part of his reason was to keep workers who hated the pace of the line.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics is a federal office whose staff gather facts about work. Its count for 1913 recorded about 23,000 deaths of workers in industry, among 38 million workers. That was 61 deaths for every 100,000 workers. The count covers all kinds of industrial work, not only work at machines.

#### The wired home

In 1906 Lee de Forest invented the Audion, a part that made weak radio signals stronger. The Audion was a vacuum tube, a glass tube with the air taken out, like a light bulb. Inside it were a thin wire called a filament, a metal plate, and a bent wire between them called the grid. A small electric current on the grid controlled a bigger current between the other two parts. The Audion could also pick up radio signals. Tubes like it made radios for the home practical.

On September 7, 1927, Philo Farnsworth, age 21, sent the first all-electronic television picture from his lab on Green Street in San Francisco. The picture was a straight line. He made it with his own camera tube, called the image dissector.

The same year, the General Electric company began selling the Monitor Top, an electric refrigerator for the home. It cost about $300. By the middle of 1929, buyers had bought more than a quarter of a million of them. It was the first home electric refrigerator sold in large numbers. The researcher Emanuela Cardia studied what American households owned, using the census, the government's count of everyone in the country, taken every ten years. In 1930, 14 percent of households had a mechanical refrigerator, one that kept itself cold with a motor instead of a block of ice. By 1940 the share was 44 percent, and by 1950 it was 80 percent.

A plastic is a material that can be shaped while it is soft and then sets hard. In 1907 Leo Baekeland, a chemist born in Belgium who lived in the United States, made Bakelite from two chemicals, phenol and formaldehyde. It was the first fully synthetic plastic, which means it was made entirely from chemicals rather than from anything that grew. He filed for a patent in July 1907 and received it on December 7, 1909. A patent is a government grant that gives an inventor the only right to make and sell an invention for a set number of years. Nylon, a strong thread-like material made from chemicals, came from Wallace Carothers's work at the DuPont chemical company, which he joined in 1928. On February 28, 1935, Gerard Berchet made the first half ounce of nylon. DuPont officials announced it to the public on October 27, 1938.

#### Tractors replace horses

In 1920 census takers counted 246,000 tractors on American farms, and about 26 million horses and mules. The Fordson tractor of 1917 was cheap and made in large numbers. About three out of every four American tractors built in the 1920s were Fordsons.

In 1924 the International Harvester company began selling the Farmall. It could do the jobs other tractors did. It could also cultivate, which means breaking up the soil and clearing weeds between rows of growing crops. Cultivating was the last farm job that horses still did. The Census of Agriculture of 1954 was the first to record more tractors than horses and mules on American farms. It recorded about 4.6 million tractors and about 4 million horses and mules.

#### The first computers and the transistor

ENIAC, the first general-purpose electronic computer, was shown to the public at the University of Pennsylvania in February 1946. General-purpose means it could be set up to solve many kinds of problems, not only one. John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert designed it at the university's Moore School, and the US Army paid to build it. It was built to work out artillery firing tables, charts that told soldiers how to aim their big guns. ENIAC had 17,468 vacuum tubes, weighed more than 27 tons, and filled 1,800 square feet. It could not store a program. For each new set of calculations, its programmers moved its switches and plugged its cables into new places by hand.

At Bell Labs, a group of scientists led by William Shockley looked for a replacement for vacuum tubes, which often failed. On December 16, 1947, John Bardeen and Walter Brattain placed two gold contacts, very close together, on a small slab of germanium, a chemical element. The electric push, or voltage, on one contact controlled the flow of electricity, or current, through the other. The device made a signal up to 100 times stronger. It was the first transistor. Workers at Bell Labs chose the name "transistor" in a vote, and the company's officials announced it to the public on June 30, 1948. Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1956.

<a id="story-eniac-programmers"></a>

#### The six ENIAC programmers

> **Who:** Jean Jennings Bartik, Betty Snyder Holberton, Kathleen McNulty Mauchly Antonelli, Marlyn Wescoff Meltzer, Frances Bilas Spence and Ruth Lichterman Teitelbaum. They were the six women who programmed ENIAC, the first general-purpose electronic computer.
>
> **When and where:** University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, 1945 and 1946.
>
> **Movie:** *The Computers* (2014), a short documentary first shown at the Seattle International Film Festival in 2014. The six programmers are its subject.

Six women programmed ENIAC, but no one invited them to the dinner held for the machine's public showing in 1946. The records do not say who made the guest list. Their names were Jean Jennings Bartik, Betty Snyder Holberton, Kathleen McNulty Mauchly Antonelli, Marlyn Wescoff Meltzer, Frances Bilas Spence and Ruth Lichterman Teitelbaum.

ENIAC had no way to store a program. At first the six had only drawings of the machine's wiring to learn from. To give ENIAC a new problem, they moved its switches and plugged its cables into new places by hand. They were hired to work out the paths of artillery shells for the Army, and later they also ran calculations for the scientists at Los Alamos, the laboratory in New Mexico where the atomic bomb was built.

Their story stayed untold for decades. Kathy Kleiman learned about the six while she was researching her college thesis, a long paper written at the end of college. She started the ENIAC Programmers Project to record their story. In 1997 the group Women in Technology International named all six to its Hall of Fame. Four of them were there to accept. Ruth Teitelbaum had died, and her husband, Adolph, accepted for her.

<a id="story-ernest-lawrence-technology"></a>

#### Ernest Lawrence

> **Who:** A scientist who built the cyclotron, a machine that whirls particles in a spiral and uses them to smash atoms.
>
> **When and where:** Berkeley, California, from 1930 and 1931.

Ernest O. Lawrence's first cyclotron was small enough to hold in one hand. He built it at Berkeley, California, in 1930 and 1931, out of glass, sealing wax and bronze. It sped up hydrogen ions, which are hydrogen atoms with an electric charge, to an energy of 80,000 electron volts. An electron volt is a very small unit of energy used for particles.

Each machine Lawrence built after that was bigger. The first model was followed by machines 11 inches, 27 inches and 37 inches across. The 60-inch cyclotron of 1939 had a magnet that weighed 220 tons. Inside each machine, particles whirled in a spiral and then struck atoms and broke them apart.

Scientists used cyclotrons to make elements that do not occur in nature. They also made radioactive materials for use in medicine. A radioactive material is one whose atoms break down and give off energy and tiny particles. Lawrence won the Nobel Prize in 1939. One later machine at Berkeley, the 88-Inch Cyclotron, still runs today.

### 1950 to 2000

Jack Kilby of Texas Instruments built the first integrated circuit in 1958. It put a whole electronic circuit on one small chip. On October 29, 1969, a student at the University of California, Los Angeles, or UCLA, sent the first message between two computers on ARPANET, a network that linked computers at universities. Martin Cooper of Motorola made the first call on a handheld cell phone four years later. The magazine *Popular Electronics* announced the Altair 8800, a computer sold as a kit of parts, in January 1975, and IBM began selling the IBM PC in 1981. The IBM PC became the standard office computer. All 24 satellites of the Global Positioning System, or GPS, were working by 1995.

<a id="story-grace-hopper"></a>

#### Grace Hopper

> **Who:** A mathematician and Navy officer who built the A-0 compiler, a program that lets people write instructions for a computer in words closer to English.
>
> **When and where:** Harvard University from 1944, then Remington Rand, the company that made the UNIVAC computer. Born in New York in 1906, died in 1992.
>
> **Movie:** *The Queen of Code* (2015), a short documentary directed by Gillian Jacobs, part of the FiveThirtyEight series *Signals*. It is about Hopper's life and work.

Grace Hopper built the A-0 compiler in 1951 and 1952. A compiler is a program that takes instructions written closer to human language and translates them into instructions the computer can carry out.

Hopper was born in New York on December 9, 1906, and trained as a mathematician. During World War II she served as a lieutenant in the WAVES, the women's branch of the Navy. In July 1944 she was assigned to the Harvard Mark I computer, and she became one of its first programmers. In 1946 she wrote the first long manual on how to program a computer.

She built the A-0 compiler while working on the UNIVAC computer at the Remington Rand company. From 1955 to 1959 she worked on FLOW-MATIC, a programming language for business that used English words. A programming language is a set of words and rules for writing instructions a computer can follow. Later, the designers of COBOL, another business programming language, drew on FLOW-MATIC.

Hopper retired from the Navy in 1986 as a rear admiral, one of the Navy's highest ranks. She was 79, and at that time she was the oldest officer still serving in the Navy. She died on January 1, 1992.

#### The chip and its two inventors

An integrated circuit, or chip, is a whole electronic circuit built on one small piece of material. A circuit is a path that electricity flows through, with parts along the way that do jobs such as switching it on and off. Two engineers working at two different companies each made a chip. The encyclopedia Britannica and the German Patent and Trade Mark Office both name the two men as its inventors.

Jack Kilby of Texas Instruments showed the first integrated circuit on September 12, 1958. He made it from germanium, and he connected its parts with wires by hand. In 1959 Robert Noyce of Fairchild Semiconductor designed a chip made of silicon, another chemical element. On Noyce's chip the wiring lay flat and was printed onto the surface. That meant factories could make chips in large numbers. Every later chip was built in Noyce's flat form. Silicon Valley, the area south of San Francisco where many computer companies started, takes its name from this element.

Kilby received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2000. Noyce had died in 1990. Kilby said in public that Noyce deserved to share the prize.

<a id="story-marty-cooper"></a>

#### Martin Cooper

> **Who:** A Motorola engineer who made the first call on a handheld cell phone.
>
> **When and where:** A street in Manhattan, New York City, April 3, 1973.

The first call on a handheld cell phone was made on a street in Manhattan on April 3, 1973. Martin Cooper, an engineer for the Motorola company, made it while walking. He used the phone to call Joel Engel, his rival at Bell Labs.

The phone Motorola sold to the public came 10 years later. The DynaTAC 8000X went on sale in 1983. It cost $3,995 and weighed 28 ounces, almost 2 pounds. One charge of its battery gave about 30 minutes of talking.

#### The personal computer

In January 1975 the Altair 8800, a computer sold as a kit, was announced in the magazine *Popular Electronics*. A kit is a box of parts that the buyer puts together. On March 5, 1975, about 30 people came through a rainstorm to Gordon French's garage in Menlo Park, California, to see an Altair. That meeting was the first of the Homebrew Computer Club, a group of people who built their own computers.

Apple Computer was founded on April 1, 1976. Its founders were Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak and, for a short time, Ron Wayne. The Apple II came out in June 1977. It was a finished computer that people could plug in at home. On August 12, 1981, IBM brought out the IBM PC, and its design became the standard for computers in offices.

<a id="story-lee-felsenstein"></a>

#### Lee Felsenstein

> **Who:** An engineer who ran the meetings of the Homebrew Computer Club and designed two early small computers, the Sol-20 and the Osborne 1.
>
> **When and where:** Berkeley and the San Francisco Bay Area, California, from 1973. Born in Philadelphia in 1945.

In 1973, Lee Felsenstein and four other people set up a computer terminal that anyone could use, in a record store in Berkeley, California. A terminal is a keyboard and a printer or screen connected to a computer somewhere else. His partners were Efrem Lipkin, Ken Colstad, Jude Milhon and Mark Szpakowski. They called the project Community Memory. They put the terminal at Leopold's Records, next to the store's paper bulletin board. People typed notes about music, politics, housing, services, women's groups and technology, and other people read them. The Computer History Museum's profile of Felsenstein describes it as one of the earliest online communities. The last version of the project closed in 1992.

Community Memory ran on a large computer called an SDS-940, which was donated for the project. It was a time-sharing computer, which means many people could use it at once from different terminals. The project worked with Resource One. Three students who had dropped out of computer science at Berkeley started it as a nonprofit, a group run for a cause rather than for profit.

Felsenstein was born in Philadelphia in 1945. In 1964, as a student at the University of California, Berkeley, he took part in the Free Speech Movement, a protest by Berkeley students for the right to speak and organize about politics on campus. He was at the Sproul Hall sit-in, a protest in which students sat inside a campus building and refused to leave. On December 3, 1964, hundreds of police officers went into the building and arrested nearly 800 students, Felsenstein among them. He earned a degree in electrical engineering and computer science at Berkeley in 1972.

He was one of the first members of the Homebrew Computer Club. He ran its open meetings, keeping order with a blackboard pointer. With Gordon French and Bob Marsh, at a company called Processor Technology, he designed the Sol-20. It was one of the first small computers sold with its own case and keyboard. More than 10,000 were sold from 1977 to 1979. He then designed the Osborne 1 for Adam Osborne's company. It was a portable computer with a 5-inch screen. It cost $1,795, and more than 125,000 were sold in 1982.

His motto, as the Computer History Museum records it, is "To change the rules, change the tools." In 2016 the museum's leaders gave him their Fellow Award, an honor, for his influence on early personal computing.

<a id="story-jobs-wozniak"></a>

#### Steve Jobs and Steve Wozniak

> **Who:** The two founders of Apple Computer. Wozniak designed the Apple I and the Apple II. Jobs made the first sale.
>
> **When and where:** Jobs's garage in California, from 1976.
>
> **Movie:** *Steve Jobs* (2015), directed by Danny Boyle and written by Aaron Sorkin. It is a drama, not a documentary. Actors play the real people, and it is based on Walter Isaacson's biography of Jobs. *Steve Jobs: The Man in the Machine* (2015), directed by Alex Gibney, is a documentary about Jobs.

Steve Wozniak designed Apple's first two computers, and Steve Jobs found the first buyer. The two met while they were both working at the Hewlett-Packard company. In 1975 Wozniak began developing the Apple I. He later said that the Homebrew Computer Club was where the Apple I got its start.

To pay for the first working model, Jobs sold his Volkswagen and Wozniak sold his scientific calculator, for $1,300 in all. On April 1, 1976, they founded Apple Computer. Ron Wayne was a partner for a short time. Jobs and Wozniak built the first Apple I computers in Jobs's garage. On Jobs's first sales call, a store called the Byte Shop ordered 50 of them at $500 each. The Apple I came without a case, a keyboard, a screen or a power supply. Buyers added their own.

Wozniak designed the Apple II in 1977. It came in one case, with the electronics, the keyboard and the power supply inside. It could show color pictures. It also came with the programming language BASIC stored in its permanent memory, a part that keeps what is stored in it even when the power is off. In 1978 a floppy disk drive for storing files became available for it. In 1979 VisiCalc came out, a spreadsheet program for working with tables of numbers. With those two, the Apple II sold in large numbers. Apple's sales grew from $7.8 million in 1978 to $117 million in 1980.

#### The network

ARPANET was a computer network paid for by the Department of Defense to link computers at universities. On October 29, 1969, Charley Kline, a student programmer in Leonard Kleinrock's lab at UCLA, tried to log in to a computer at Stanford Research Institute. He typed "L" and "O," the first two letters of LOGIN, and then the system crashed. So the first message ever sent on the network was "LO." About an hour later the full login worked. On January 1, 1983, the computers on ARPANET began using TCP/IP, the internet's shared set of rules for moving data between computers. ARPANET was the network from which the internet began.

Many people use "the web" and "the internet" to mean the same thing. They are two different things. The internet is the network of linked computers. The World Wide Web is a system of pages linked to one another, which people read over the internet. A British computer scientist, Tim Berners-Lee, invented it at CERN, a European physics laboratory in Switzerland. He proposed it in 1989 and opened it to the public on August 6, 1991. Americans built the program that let ordinary people use the web easily. On April 22, 1993, Marc Andreessen, Eric Bina and others at the University of Illinois released Mosaic. It was the first widely used graphical browser, a program that shows web pages with pictures.

GPS, the Global Positioning System, is a set of satellites owned by the United States. Each satellite sends out a signal that gives its position and the time. A GPS receiver picks up these signals and uses them to work out where it is. The first GPS satellite went up on February 22, 1978. The full set of 24 satellites was working in 1995. Until 2000, under a policy called Selective Availability, US government officials made the GPS signals for the public less exact on purpose, for national security. In May 2000 President Bill Clinton ordered the policy ended. After that, ordinary GPS receivers could find their place to within about 10 to 20 meters or better, close enough to give driving directions turn by turn.

#### The smoke detector

The ionization smoke detector, a cheap alarm made in large numbers for homes, holds about a third of a millionth of a gram of americium-241. Americium is a radioactive element, one whose atoms break down and give off energy and tiny particles. Scientists discovered it in 1944 and 1945. It gives off tiny particles called alpha particles. The particles knock bits of electric charge loose from the air in a small chamber inside the detector, so a very small electric current can flow through the air. When smoke enters the chamber, it disturbs the current, and the alarm goes off.

### 2000 to Today

A survey by the Pew Research Center found that 91 percent of American adults owned a smartphone in 2025. A smartphone is a pocket-sized computer that is also a phone. Apple began selling the iPhone in 2007. In 2022 the company OpenAI released ChatGPT, a program that writes answers to typed requests. By February 2026, 44 percent of American adults told Pew they had used it. ChatGPT is an artificial intelligence, or AI, program, and AI programs also make mistakes. In 2020 Detroit police arrested the wrong man after a face-recognition search, a computer comparison of a photo of a face with a collection of photos, returned a false match.

#### The smartphone

Steve Jobs of Apple announced the iPhone on January 9, 2007. It went on sale on June 29, 2007, for $499 or $599, with a phone contract, a promise to pay a phone company for service every month. On September 10, 2007, Apple announced that it had sold its one millionth iPhone the day before, 74 days after the phone went on sale. A smartphone puts a computer, a camera, a phone, a GPS receiver and a music player into one machine that fits in a pocket. Social media apps, programs for posting and sharing with other people, run on these phones.

The Pew Research Center is a research group that runs large surveys. Its researchers have asked Americans whether they own a smartphone since 2011.
