In their first count, in 2011, 35 percent of adults owned a smartphone. In a survey of 5,022 adults from February to June 2025, 91 percent did, and 98 percent owned some kind of cell phone. Older people were less likely to own one. Among adults aged 18 to 29, 97 percent had a smartphone, against 78 percent of those 65 and older.

For some Americans, the phone is the only way to get online. In the same 2025 survey, 78 percent of adults had broadband at home, a fast internet connection that is always on. Among adults in households earning less than $30,000 a year, 34 percent reached the internet only through a smartphone. Among those earning $100,000 or more, 4 percent did.

#### Batteries, printers and gene tools

The battery in an electric car is a lithium-ion battery, a kind that can be recharged many times. Scientists in three countries worked on it, starting in the 1970s. M. Stanley Whittingham began work on rechargeable lithium batteries then, working for the company Exxon in New Jersey. John Goodenough, an American chemist then working at Oxford in England, found the material for the battery's cathode, its positive end, in 1980. The material was lithium cobalt oxide. Akira Yoshino in Japan built a safe early model with a carbon anode, the negative end, in 1985. In 1991 the Sony company in Japan began selling the first lithium-ion batteries. Whittingham, Goodenough and Yoshino shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2019.

A 3D printer builds a solid object out of many thin layers, one on top of another. Chuck Hull invented stereolithography, a method of 3D printing in which the machine hardens each thin layer in turn, in 1983 and 1984. He applied for a patent on August 8, 1984, and received it on March 11, 1986. In the 2010s, 3D printers spread to factories and to hobbyists' desks.

On June 28, 2012, the scientists Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier published a paper on CRISPR, a tool for changing the genes of living things. Genes are the instructions inside living cells that shape how a living thing grows and works. The two shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2020.

<a id="story-limor-fried"></a>

#### Limor Fried

> **Who:** An engineer trained at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, or MIT, who founded Adafruit Industries, a company that makes electronics kits and teaches people to build with them.
>
> **When and where:** MIT in Cambridge, Massachusetts, then New York City, from 2005.

Adafruit Industries began in 2005 in Limor Fried's dorm room at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, or MIT, a university in Cambridge, Massachusetts. She had earned a bachelor's degree from MIT in 2003, and she finished a master's degree in engineering there in 2005. Adafruit sells electronics kits along with lessons on how to build them. Its designs are open source, which means anyone may copy them and change them.

According to the company's website, Fried was the first woman engineer on the cover of *Wired* magazine, and women own all of the company. Adafruit's workers make its products in the company's factory in New York City. In 2024 Adafruit moved to Industry City in Brooklyn. The company's website states that it has more than 100 employees.

#### AI, plainly

AI, short for artificial intelligence, is a name for computer programs that do tasks such as recognizing a face or writing a paragraph. A neural network is one kind of AI program. A computer adjusts the network's settings by running the network on a huge number of examples, so no person writes out its rules step by step. People call this tuning learning.

In 2012 a neural network called AlexNet won ImageNet, a contest in which computer programs try to name what is in photographs. Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton built it at the University of Toronto. AlexNet's top five guesses missed the right answer for 15.3 percent of the pictures. The second-place program missed for 26.2 percent. After AlexNet's win, neural networks came into wide use, a time called the deep-learning era.

On November 30, 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT. Five days later, OpenAI's chief executive, Sam Altman, posted online that it had "crossed 1 million users." Analysts at the bank UBS estimated that by the end of January 2023, about 100 million people a month were using it. ChatGPT and programs like it produce text, pictures and computer code from requests typed in plain language.

In July 2024 staff at the National Institute of Standards and Technology, a federal agency, published a report. It describes how large language models, programs that write text, work and why they make mistakes. A program of this kind predicts the next word in a sentence, over and over. That kind of guessing can produce true statements, and it can also produce false ones. The report states that the programs give false answers in a confident way, and that people who believe them can be misled.

In 2023, in a federal court case in New York, lawyers filed court decisions that ChatGPT had made up. Roberto Mata had sued the airline Avianca, saying a metal serving cart struck his knee on a flight. On March 1, 2023, his lawyers Steven A. Schwartz and Peter LoDuca filed a court paper that pointed to earlier court decisions to support Mata's side. Those decisions did not exist. ChatGPT had produced them, with fake quotes.

Schwartz later said that he asked ChatGPT whether one case was real, and it answered that the case "does indeed exist." In written orders, the judge then asked whether the cases existed, and the lawyers kept standing by them. On June 22, 2023, Judge P. Kevin Castel found that the lawyers had acted in bad faith, which means dishonestly. He ordered the two lawyers and their law firm to pay a penalty of $5,000.

<a id="story-karla-ortiz"></a>

#### Karla Ortiz

> **Who:** A concept artist and illustrator in San Francisco whose designs went into Marvel films. She told the US Senate how AI image programs affected artists.
>
> **When and where:** San Francisco and Washington, D.C., from 2022.

On July 12, 2023, Karla Ortiz gave written testimony to a subcommittee of the US Senate Judiciary Committee about AI programs that make pictures. Testimony is a statement given to a court or to lawmakers. Ortiz is a concept artist, an artist who draws the first designs for characters and scenes. Her designs went into Marvel films, including *Doctor Strange*, *Black Panther* and *Avengers: Infinity War*. She also worked on the video game *Final Fantasy 16* and the card game *Magic: the Gathering*.

Ortiz first saw an AI image program in April 2022. A website showed pictures made by a machine that copied the styles of named artists, her friends among them. No one had asked them. By August and September of 2022, the programs Midjourney, Stable Diffusion and DALL-E were in wide use.

In her testimony, Ortiz explained how the popular image programs were built. Their makers trained them on a collection of 5.8 billion pictures with captions, "taken indiscriminately from the web." That means the pictures were taken without anyone choosing which ones. A nonprofit group called LAION, which the company Stability AI funded, built the collection. Ortiz wrote that the collection "includes almost all of my fine art work."

She described what she had seen in her own work. "I have personally been a part of three productions where Generative AI has been utilized at different levels," she wrote. Utilized means used. Generative AI is AI that makes new pictures, text or sound. "Some of my peers have lost jobs, some have had their duties lessened (and of course, their proposed pay)." She also wrote, "I am no longer certain of my future as an artist." She worked with researchers at the University of Chicago on Glaze, a program meant to protect artists' pictures from having their style copied.

On January 12, 2023, Ortiz, Sarah Andersen, Kelly McKernan and other artists sued Stability AI, Midjourney and DeviantArt in federal court. They said the companies had broken copyright law, the law that protects an artist's right to decide who copies their work. On August 12, 2024, US District Judge William Orrick ruled that their main copyright claims could go forward toward a trial. As of October 2, 2026, the case had not gone to trial. On September 28, 2026, Judge Orrick changed the schedule so that the next major motions in the case are to be heard by September 29, 2027.

#### A wrongful arrest and face recognition

Face-recognition software compares a picture of a face with a collection of photos and names possible matches. In January 2020, Detroit police officers arrested Robert Williams, a Black man, at his home in Farmington Hills, Michigan. They arrested him in front of his wife and two young daughters and in view of his neighbors. A face-recognition search had matched a blurry picture from a store's security video to his expired driver's license photo. The video showed a theft of watches from a Shinola store in Detroit in 2018. Williams was not the man in the video.

Police used the match to build a photo lineup, a set of photos shown to someone who might pick out the thief. They showed it to a contractor hired to prevent theft at the store, who had not seen the theft and knew it only from the video. Detroit police held Williams for 30 hours. The ACLU, the civil rights group whose lawyers represented him, called the place he was held "an overcrowded, dirty cell." Wayne County prosecutors dropped the charges, but they kept the right to bring them again. The county's prosecutor, Kym Worthy, apologized. "This case should not have been issued based on the DPD investigation, and for that we apologize," she said. DPD is the Detroit Police Department. His was the first publicly reported case in which police wrongly arrested someone after a false face-recognition match.

At least three Detroit arrests of this kind are publicly known, according to reporting by Michigan Public in 2024. In 2023 Detroit police wrongly arrested Porcha Woodruff for a carjacking, which is stealing a car from its driver. She was pregnant. On June 28, 2024, Williams and lawyers for the City of Detroit settled his lawsuit. Under the settlement, Detroit police may not arrest anyone based on a face-recognition result without other evidence. They may not build a photo lineup from a face-recognition match alone. They must train officers, including on the higher rate of wrong matches for people of color, and they must review cases back to 2017.

#### AI at work, by the numbers

In a survey of 5,119 American adults in February 2026, researchers at the Pew Research Center found that 44 percent had used ChatGPT. The share was 18 percent in 2023 and 34 percent in 2025. About half of adults in the 2026 survey used some AI chatbot, a program that answers typed questions in sentences. Among adults with jobs, 38 percent used chatbots for tasks at work. Forty percent of adults expected AI to have a bad effect on society over the next 20 years.

Some employers say AI is the reason they are cutting jobs. Challenger, Gray & Christmas is an outplacement firm, a company that helps laid-off workers find new jobs. Its staff count the job cuts that American employers announce, and the reasons the employers give. From January through August 2026, employers named AI as the reason for 116,175 announced job cuts. That was about 22 percent of all the cuts they announced, more than for any other reason. These numbers are employers' own statements. They are not a government count of jobs lost to AI.

<a id="ch-science"></a>

## Chapter 9: Science

### Before 1500

Long before 1500, the people of Native nations here held careful, tested knowledge about the world. They watched the sky over many generations and learned where the sun rose at each time of year. They studied plants, fire, the weather and the tides. Each generation taught what it knew to the next.

People marked what they knew about the sky with posts and with carvings in rock. At Cahokia, people set up circles of wooden posts that marked where the sun rose. At Chaco Canyon, sunlight falls on two carved spirals in set places at certain times of year.

#### Woodhenge at Cahokia

The place where the sun comes up moves along the horizon over the course of a year. The people of Cahokia, in what is now Illinois, tracked that movement with circles of upright wooden posts. The circles are known today as Woodhenge. Nations such as the Chickasaw and the Osage descend from the people who lived at Cahokia.

They built five of these circles, one after another, between about the years 900 and 1100. Each circle had between 24 and 72 posts. The largest was about 145 meters across, which is about 475 feet. The posts marked the points where the sun rose at different times of the year.

Among them were the sunrise points on the solstices and the equinoxes. The solstices are the longest day of the year and the shortest day. The equinoxes are the two days each year when day and night are about the same length.

#### The Sun Dagger at Chaco Canyon

Chaco Canyon, in what is now New Mexico, was a center for the ancestral Pueblo people from 850 to 1250. Ancestral means they were the long-ago family of people living today. Their descendants include the Hopi, the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico and the Navajo Nation. In the canyon, three slabs of sandstone lean against a cliff near the top of Fajada Butte. A butte is a steep hill with a flat top. Two spirals are carved into the rock there. A carving in rock like this is called a petroglyph.

Sunlight passes the edges of the slabs and falls on the spirals as thin blades of light, called daggers. The daggers land on the spirals in set places at the solstices and the equinoxes. Researchers in a group called the Solstice Project argue that the spirals also mark a cycle of the moon. Over 18.6 years, the points where the moon rises and sets swing out to their widest and back again. Other researchers who study ancient astronomy still debate that claim.

The daggers no longer form the way they did in 1977. That year, at the summer solstice, Anna Sofaer recorded them. She was a volunteer making a record of rock art. By the summer solstice of 1989, two of the three slabs had shifted. Visitors walking on the butte had made the ground wear away faster, even though park officials limited visits there.

#### Knowledge of living things

Scientists today have a name for the knowledge that Native nations built up about plants, fire, weather and the land. They call it Traditional Ecological Knowledge, or TEK for short. Part of it is knowledge of how fire changes the land and the living things on it.

Ecology is the study of how living things depend on each other and on the land around them. TEK is knowledge of those ties that people gained by watching closely over many generations. The Ecological Society of America, a group of scientists who study ecology, has a section for TEK. A botanist named Robin Wall Kimmerer helped to found that section. A botanist is a scientist who studies plants.

<a id="story-robin-wall-kimmerer"></a>

#### Robin Wall Kimmerer

> **Who:** A botanist of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation who uses Native knowledge and laboratory science together in her work.
>
> **When and where:** The present day. The State University of New York's College of Environmental Science and Forestry.

Robin Wall Kimmerer is a scientist of the present day. She is a member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation. In her work she uses two ways of knowing about plants together. One is the knowledge that Native nations have built up and taught. The other is the science of the laboratory.

She earned a PhD in botany, the highest degree a university gives, at the University of Wisconsin. Today she teaches at the College of Environmental Science and Forestry, part of the State University of New York. She holds the title Distinguished Teaching Professor. It is the top rank the State University of New York gives for teaching. At that college she founded the Center for Native Peoples and the Environment. Outside it, she helped found the TEK section of the Ecological Society of America.

Her book *Braiding Sweetgrass* came out in 2013. It has been a New York Times bestseller since February 2020. In 2022 she was named a MacArthur Fellow, an award from the MacArthur Foundation.

### The 1500s

Europeans who crossed the ocean in the 1500s studied this land only on short visits. They collected what they found here and described it in writing. Then they published their descriptions in Europe.

#### Thomas Hariot's report

Thomas Hariot was an English mathematician. In 1585 and 1586 he went with the English expedition that Walter Raleigh sent to Roanoke Island, among the islands and shallow waters of the Outer Banks, in what is now North Carolina. He spent a year there and recorded the plants, the animals and the foods he found. He also wrote about the Native nations who lived there, such as the Secotan. They spoke Algonquian languages, a group of languages related to each other.

In 1588 Hariot published *A Briefe and True Report of the New Found Land of Virginia*. It was the first book in English about North America written by someone who had been there. In 1590 a publisher named Theodor de Bry printed the book again, with pictures made from drawings by John White.

### The 1600s

English colonists in New England founded Harvard, the first college in their colonies, in 1636. Three years later they printed their first almanac. A few colonists wrote careful records of what they saw in the sky and in the weather. One of them, Increase Mather, measured comets and also wrote that they were warnings from God.

#### A college, an almanac and a telescope

In 1636 members of the Massachusetts Bay General Court, the lawmaking body of the colony, voted to found a college. It was the first college in the English colonies. John Harvard died in 1638 and left the college his books and half of everything else he owned. On March 13, 1639, members of the same court voted to name the college Harvard, after him.

That same year a mariner named William Pierce worked out *An Almanack for New England for the Year 1639*. A mariner is a sailor. An almanac is a yearly booklet with a calendar and tables of the sun and moon. Stephen Daye printed it at Cambridge, in Massachusetts. It was one of the first two things printed on the first printing press in the colonies. For the next two hundred years, ordinary families learned about astronomy from almanacs. Astronomy is the study of the sun, the moon, the planets and the stars.

John Winthrop Jr. was a governor of Connecticut. He visited London from 1661 to 1663. While he was there, members of the Royal Society, a group of scientists in London, elected him a fellow, which is a full member. He was one of the first colonists to join. In about 1672 he gave Harvard his telescope, which was 3.5 feet long. It was the college's first scientific instrument.

#### The comet of 1680

A comet appeared in the sky in November and December of 1680. It is called the Great Comet of 1680. Thomas Brattle, who had finished his studies at Harvard in 1676, followed it with a telescope from Boston. He worked out that the comet seen in November and the comet seen in December were one comet. It had swung around the sun between the two sightings.

In 1683 Increase Mather wrote a book about comets called *Kometographia*. In it he listed comets as warnings sent by God. He also measured comets with a method called parallax. Parallax works by looking at an object from two different places. A near object seems to shift against the stars far more than a distant one. His measurements showed that comets were distant bodies rather than vapors, a kind of gas.

That same year Mather founded the Boston Philosophical Society, a group modeled on the Royal Society in London. In those days the study of nature was called natural philosophy, so a philosophical society was a group for studying nature. Mather's group met for about three years.

In 1687 the English scientist Isaac Newton published his book the *Principia*. In it Newton set out his laws of motion and of gravity. He also wrote about Brattle's New England observations of the comet of 1680.

<a id="story-john-campanius-holm"></a>

#### Rev. John Campanius Holm

> **Who:** A chaplain in the colony of New Sweden who kept the first known weather record in what is now the United States.
>
> **When and where:** Near what is now Wilmington, Delaware, 1644 and 1645.

John Campanius Holm kept the first known record of the weather in what is now the United States. He wrote down the weather twice a day through 1644 and 1645. He did it with no instruments.

Holm was a chaplain, a minister who serves a group of people away from home. He served New Sweden, a Swedish colony on the Delaware River, near what is now Wilmington, Delaware. His record was systematic, which means he made it the same way on a fixed plan, day after day.

Today, officials of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the US government's weather and ocean agency, give the John Campanius Holm Award. It goes to volunteers who take weather readings. Up to 25 people receive it each year.

### 1700 to 1750

From 1730 the farmer John Bartram traveled through the colonies to collect and study American plants. In 1743 Benjamin Franklin organized a society in Philadelphia where colonists could share such work. From 1747 he ran experiments with electricity and mailed the results to London. Scientists in Britain read those letters, and Franklin became the first American scientist known outside the colonies.

#### The American Philosophical Society, 1743

In 1743 Benjamin Franklin organized the American Philosophical Society in Philadelphia. It is the oldest learned society in the United States. A learned society is a group of people who meet to share and discuss what they have found out.

The botanist John Bartram first suggested the idea in 1739. Franklin started the society with a pamphlet, a short printed booklet. The pamphlet was titled *A Proposal for Promoting Useful Knowledge among the British Plantations in America*. In that title, the word plantations means colonies.

The society grew out of the Junto, a club Franklin had started in 1727 with about twelve friends, most of them tradesmen. Its members met on Friday nights to argue about right and wrong, about government and about nature. Franklin meant the new society to be an American answer to the Royal Society in London.

<a id="story-benjamin-franklin-science"></a>

#### Benjamin Franklin

> **Who:** A Philadelphia man whose experiments with electricity made him the first American scientist known in other countries.
>
> **When and where:** Philadelphia, experiments from 1747 to 1751.
>
> **Movie:** *Benjamin Franklin* (2022), a two-part documentary by Ken Burns, shown on PBS. It is about Franklin's life.

Benjamin Franklin was the first American to be known in other countries as a scientist. From 1747 to 1751 he ran experiments with electricity in Philadelphia. He reported his results in letters to Peter Collinson, a member of the Royal Society in London.

Franklin thought of electricity as a single fluid. He called an object positive when it held more of this fluid than normal, and negative when it held less. Scientists still use his words positive and negative. He also argued that electric charge is never made or destroyed. It only moves from one object to another. Scientists call this idea the conservation of charge. Franklin also proposed that lightning is electricity.

In April 1751 his letters were published in London as a book, *Experiments and Observations on Electricity*. In 1753 members of the Royal Society gave him the Copley Medal, their highest honor. He was the first person from outside Britain to receive it.

<a id="story-john-bartram"></a>

#### John Bartram

> **Who:** A Quaker farmer who studied plants, built the oldest surviving botanic garden in America, and first suggested the American Philosophical Society.
>
> **When and where:** Kingsessing, on the Schuylkill River. Lived 1699 to 1777.

John Bartram and his sons introduced more than 200 American plants to science. That means scientists first learned of those plants through the Bartrams.

Bartram was a farmer and a Quaker, a member of a Christian group also called the Society of Friends. In 1728 he bought a farm of 102 acres on the Schuylkill River, at a place called Kingsessing. There he built a botanic garden, a garden where plants are grown so they can be studied. It is the oldest botanic garden in America that survives today.

From 1730 to 1765 he traveled to collect plants, from New York as far south as Florida. In 1739 he suggested the idea that became the American Philosophical Society. In 1765 King George III named him the King's Botanist for North America.

The Swedish botanist Carl Linnaeus made the system scientists use to name living things. Other people reported that Linnaeus called Bartram "the greatest natural botanist in the world."

### 1750 to 1800

In 1752 a test that Benjamin Franklin designed showed that lightning is electricity. Men in France ran it first, and Franklin followed with his kite. In 1769 four men at Norriton timed the planet Venus as it crossed the sun, and members of the Royal Society in London reprinted their results.

In his book *Notes on the State of Virginia*, Thomas Jefferson used evidence to argue with a scientist in France about the size of American animals. In that same book, Jefferson wrote that Black people were inferior to white people, meaning less able, in body and mind. He called this claim "a suspicion only." Benjamin Banneker, a free Black farmer who taught himself astronomy, sent Jefferson an almanac he had calculated as proof against that claim.

#### The lightning test

Franklin published a plan for a test that would show whether lightning is electricity. The first people to carry it out were in France. On May 10, 1752, at Marly-la-Ville, Thomas-François Dalibard arranged the test with a tall iron rod. He followed Franklin's printed plan. On May 13 Dalibard reported the test to the French Academy, a society of scholars.

The test at Marly-la-Ville showed that lightning is electricity. Franklin ran his own test in Philadelphia with a kite. Nobody recorded the exact day or the exact spot. Franklin first described the kite in print on October 19, 1752, in the *Pennsylvania Gazette*, a newspaper. The date most often given, June 1752, comes from an account that Joseph Priestley wrote in 1767. In a 2004 book called *Bolt of Fate*, the writer Tom Tucker argued that Franklin never flew the kite at all.

#### Timing Venus, 1769

On June 3, 1769, the planet Venus passed across the face of the sun, as seen from Earth. This event is called a transit of Venus. Members of the American Philosophical Society chose teams of observers to time it. Astronomers in many parts of the world timed the same transit. They planned to use the times to work out the distance from Earth to the sun. This work by society members was the first large, organized science project in the colonies.

Society members planned to watch from three places. One was Norriton, the home of David Rittenhouse, in what is now Montgomery County, Pennsylvania. Rittenhouse built most of the instruments used there. At Norriton, Rittenhouse, William Smith, John Lukens and John Sellers timed Venus as it crossed the sun. Their results filled the first volume of the society's *Transactions*, its printed record of research, which came out in 1771. Members of the Royal Society in London reprinted the results.

<a id="story-david-rittenhouse"></a>

#### David Rittenhouse

> **Who:** A Pennsylvania instrument maker and astronomer who taught himself both trades. One of the four men who timed Venus at Norriton in 1769.
>
> **When and where:** Pennsylvania. Born 1732, died 1796.

David Rittenhouse taught himself to make scientific instruments and to study the stars. He was one of the four men who timed the transit of Venus at Norriton on June 3, 1769.

Rittenhouse built orreries. An orrery is a machine that shows the planets moving around the sun. When its gears turn, small models of the planets move along their paths.

In 1791 he followed Franklin as president of the American Philosophical Society. Later he became the first director of the United States Mint, where the country's coins are made.

#### Jefferson, Buffon and the moose

A scientist in France named Buffon taught that animals and people grew "degenerate" in the Americas. By that he meant smaller and weaker. Thomas Jefferson argued against this with evidence in his book *Notes on the State of Virginia*.

Jefferson wrote the book to answer a list of questions that a French official had sent. He called each chapter a Query, an old word for a question. In the chapter called Query XIV, Jefferson made a claim about Black people. He wrote: "I advance it therefore as a suspicion only, that the blacks, whether originally a distinct race, or made distinct by time and circumstances, are inferior to the whites in the endowments both of body and mind." Inferior means lower or less able. Endowments here means natural abilities. He wrote that in reason Black people were "much inferior, as I think one could scarcely be found capable of tracing and comprehending the investigations of Euclid." Euclid was an ancient Greek mathematician. Jefferson himself enslaved more than 600 people during his life.

Jefferson also used a moose as evidence against Buffon. Jefferson was the United States minister in Paris, the country's official representative to the French government. On January 7, 1786, he wrote to John Sullivan of New Hampshire, a former general and governor. He asked for "the skin, the skeleton, and the horns of the Moose."

Sullivan's party of men killed a moose in Vermont. Its body reached Sullivan on April 3, 1787, badly rotted. The skull and antlers could not be saved, so Sullivan sent the antlers of another animal. He wrote that they were "not the horns of this moose but may be fixed on at pleasure." That meant Jefferson could attach them however he liked.

The shipment reached France in about late September 1787. Around October 1, 1787, Jefferson gave Buffon the moose's bones and skin, along with the antlers from the other animal. Jefferson wrote that the moose "convinced Mr. Buffon. He promised in his next volume to set these things right." Buffon died in April 1788 without printing a correction.

<a id="story-benjamin-banneker-science"></a>

#### Benjamin Banneker

> **Who:** A free Black tobacco farmer who taught himself mathematics and astronomy and calculated almanacs for the years 1792 through 1797.
>
> **When and where:** Baltimore County, Maryland. Born November 9, 1731. Died 1806.

Benjamin Banneker calculated the astronomy for six years of printed almanacs, for 1792 through 1797. He worked out where the sun, the moon and the planets would be on each day. Tables like these are called ephemerides. Banneker was a free Black tobacco farmer in Baltimore County, Maryland. He taught himself mathematics and astronomy from books and instruments that he borrowed.

He correctly predicted the solar eclipse of April 14, 1789, though better-known almanac makers had calculated it differently. In a solar eclipse, the moon passes between the earth and the sun and blocks some or all of the sun's light.

On August 19, 1791, Banneker sent Jefferson his almanac in manuscript, which means written by hand. He sent it as proof against Jefferson's claim about Black people. With it he sent a letter that challenged Jefferson about slavery. He wrote that "however variable we may be in society or religion, however diversified in situation or colour, we are all of the same family."

Jefferson wrote back on August 30, 1791: "no body wishes more than I do to see such proofs as you exhibit, that nature has given to our black brethren, talents equal to those of the other colours of men." Exhibit means show, and brethren means brothers. Jefferson sent the almanac on to a man named Condorcet in Paris.

Banneker's first almanac, for the year 1792, went on sale in December 1791. Goddard & Angell of Baltimore printed it, and it sold in Baltimore, Philadelphia and Alexandria. Joseph and George Ellicott, Banneker's Quaker neighbors, had already interested other Quakers in his work. They had also interested the abolition societies of Baltimore and Philadelphia in him. An abolition society was a group that worked to end slavery. Members of the abolition societies of Pennsylvania and Maryland promoted Banneker's almanacs. Several printers published them, and they sold in the United States and in England.

The 1792 almanac opened with words of support from James McHenry, a Maryland politician. He wrote: "I consider this Negro as fresh proof that the powers of the mind are disconnected with the colour of the skin." Negro was a word used then for a Black person.

Banneker died in 1806. Three years later, on October 8, 1809, Jefferson wrote about him in a letter to Joel Barlow: "we know he had spherical trigonometry enough to make almanacs, but not without the suspicion of aid from Ellicot, who was his neighbor & friend, & never missed an opportunity of puffing him." Spherical trigonometry is the mathematics of angles and distances on a sphere, such as the sky. Puffing meant praising someone too much. Jefferson was hinting that Banneker's neighbor Ellicott had helped him with the mathematics. Jefferson himself called this a suspicion.

#### Jefferson's fossil, 1797

On March 10, 1797, Jefferson presented a paper to the American Philosophical Society about a fossil animal named Megalonyx. The name means "giant claw." A fossil is the remains of a living thing kept in rock. Jefferson's paper was printed in 1799. Megalonyx was the first genus of fossil animal from the United States to receive a name. A genus is a group of closely related kinds of animals or plants.

Caspar Wistar wrote a second paper to go with Jefferson's. With it, Wistar began the study of paleontology in the United States. Paleontology is the study of ancient life through fossils.

### 1800 to 1850

Between 1800 and 1850, Americans founded the country's first lasting science journal, a magazine where scientists publish their research. They also founded a national center for science. Benjamin Silliman became Yale's professor of chemistry in 1802 and founded the journal in 1818. In 1846 President James K. Polk signed a law to set up the Smithsonian Institution in Washington. An Englishman who never visited the country had left the money for it. Its first head, Joseph Henry, set up a network of volunteers who reported the weather.

In Philadelphia in the same years, a doctor named Samuel George Morton collected hundreds of human skulls. Some of the men who supplied him robbed graves to get them. Morton measured the skulls and used the numbers to rank the races of people. The idea that skull size shows the intelligence or worth of a group of people is false.

#### A professor, a fallen stone and a journal

Benjamin Silliman became Yale's professor of chemistry and natural history in 1802. Chemistry is the study of what things are made of and how substances change. Natural history is the study of plants, animals and rocks. Silliman gave his first lectures in 1804.

On December 14, 1807, a meteorite fell at Weston, Connecticut. A meteorite is a rock from space that falls to the ground. Silliman and James Kingsley wrote down what was known about the fall. They also ran chemical tests to learn what the meteorite was made of. It was the first meteorite fall in the Americas that scientists recorded and studied in this way.

In 1818 Silliman founded the *American Journal of Science*. A scientific journal is a magazine in which scientists publish their research. His was the first one in the country that lasted. For decades people called it "Silliman's Journal."

#### Joseph Henry, magnets and credit

Joseph Henry discovered self-induction and published it in July 1832, in Silliman's journal. When the electric current in a coil of wire changes, the coil makes its own push of electricity against that change. That effect is self-induction.

Henry was a teacher at the Albany Academy, a school in Albany, New York. His best years of research there ran from 1826 to 1832. He built the strongest electromagnets of his day. An electromagnet is a magnet made by sending electricity through a coil of wire.

Henry also saw a related effect, called electromagnetic induction. It is the making of an electric current with a magnet. Michael Faraday in London published his discovery of it first, in 1831. Henry had found it on his own but published later. Faraday keeps the credit for that discovery, and Henry has the credit for self-induction. Scientists measure the strength of self-induction in a coil with a unit called the henry, named after him.

#### Samuel Morton's skulls

Samuel George Morton was a Philadelphia doctor who collected human skulls and used them to rank the races of people. He lived from 1799 to 1851. He was a member of the Academy of Natural Sciences of Philadelphia, a society of scientists. In 1830 he prepared a lecture on how skulls differ. In the early 1830s he began to collect them. When he died in 1851, he owned 867 human skulls.

He got the skulls through 138 contacts: scientists, traders, military men and missionaries, people sent by churches to spread their religion. Army surgeons at far-off posts were his most useful suppliers. Some of his collectors robbed graves. About a dozen skulls came from a potter's field in Philadelphia, a burial ground for poor people. Poor Black Philadelphians were buried there.

Morton worked as a doctor at the city's almshouse, a public home for poor people. In those same years he himself got the remains of at least 14 Philadelphians, Black and white. Remains are what is left of a dead body, such as the bones. A 2021 report on these remains by Paul Wolff Mitchell, a researcher for a University of Pennsylvania project, does not name who dug up their bodies. In 2021 reporters at WHYY, a Philadelphia news station, wrote that the Philadelphia skulls were likely bought from grave robbers.

In 1840 a doctor in Havana, José Rodríguez Cisneros, dug up the graves of enslaved Africans in Cuba and shipped their skulls to Morton. He wrote that he had got 50 skulls. Other records count 51 or 55. More skulls came from battlefields and from gallows, the frames on which people were hanged. Many of the skulls were those of Native Americans.

Morton filled each skull with peppercorns, and later with lead shot, which means tiny balls of lead. Then he poured them out and measured how much the skull had held. He believed that a bigger skull meant a more intelligent person. He ranked the races by the average size of their skulls, with white Europeans at the top.

His book *Crania Americana*, Latin for "American skulls," came out in 1839. It made him famous in other countries. The Penn Museum's own account states that Morton is sometimes called the "father of scientific racism." Scientific racism means using the look of science to claim that some races are better than others.

Two of Morton's followers, the doctor Josiah Nott and George Gliddon, used his work to defend slavery. In 1854 they published a book in Morton's honor called *Types of Mankind*. Nott argued in it that Black people were a separate species, a separate kind of living thing, naturally and forever below white people. His aim was to show that freeing enslaved people would be a disaster for both races. Nott wrote to protect his clients, who were slaveholders.

Scholars still argue about how carefully Morton measured. In 1978, and again in a 1981 book, Stephen Jay Gould of Harvard wrote that Morton's numbers were biased. That means his mistakes leaned toward the answer he wanted. In 2011 six scholars led by Jason E. Lewis measured 308 of the 670 skulls Morton had published. They found his errors small and random. A 2016 paper argued against parts of their work. The argument is only about whether Morton measured carelessly. His main idea, that skull size ranks the intelligence or worth of groups of people, is false.

Today the Penn Museum, at the University of Pennsylvania, holds Morton's skulls. Museum staff took them off a classroom display in 2020. On April 12, 2021, the museum's director, Christopher Woods, apologized for "the unethical possession of human remains in the Morton Collection." Unethical means wrong. He announced a plan to return the remains. In January 2024, on the order of a Philadelphia court, museum staff buried the skulls of 19 Black Philadelphians from the collection at Eden Cemetery in Collingdale, Pennsylvania. It is one of the oldest Black burial grounds near Philadelphia. A group called the Black Philadelphians Descendant Community Group objected. Its members said that the Black community, not the museum, should decide what happened to the remains.

<a id="story-james-smithson"></a>

#### James Smithson

> **Who:** An English chemist who left his fortune to the United States to found the Smithsonian Institution. He never set foot in the country.
>
> **When and where:** Died in Genoa, Italy, on June 27, 1829. The Smithsonian was founded in Washington on August 10, 1846.

James Smithson paid for the Smithsonian Institution, even though he never set foot in the United States. He was an English chemist. He died in Genoa, Italy, on June 27, 1829.

His will left his money to his nephew. It also stated a condition. If the nephew died without heirs, meaning children or other family to inherit the money, it was to go to the United States. The will said the money was "to found at Washington, under the name of the Smithsonian Institution, an establishment for the increase & diffusion of knowledge." An establishment here means a place set up for a purpose, and diffusion means spreading. Smithson never explained why he left his fortune to a country he had never seen, and nobody knows the reason.

The nephew died without heirs in 1835. In September 1838, more than 100,000 gold coins called sovereigns reached the mint in Philadelphia, where the country's coins are made. Workers there turned them into American coins worth more than $500,000. Members of Congress then argued for eight years about what to do with the money. On August 10, 1846, President James K. Polk signed a law to set up the Smithsonian.

<a id="story-joseph-henry"></a>

#### Joseph Henry

> **Who:** A teacher at the Albany Academy who discovered self-induction and became the first Secretary, or head, of the Smithsonian Institution.
>
> **When and where:** Albany, New York, for his research of 1826 to 1832. Princeton from 1832. Washington from 1846.

Joseph Henry was the first Secretary, or head, of the Smithsonian Institution. On December 3, 1846, he won seven of the twelve votes cast by the Smithsonian's Board of Regents, the group that runs it. He held the job for 32 years, until he died in 1878.

Before that he had taught at the Albany Academy, where he discovered self-induction. In 1832 he became a professor at Princeton.

At the Smithsonian, from 1849, Henry ran the Smithsonian Meteorological Project. Meteorology is the science of weather. About 150 volunteers wrote down the weather where they lived. They sent their reports by mail, and by telegraph at no charge. A telegraph sent messages along a wire as bursts of electricity. Henry used the reports to build the first weather maps of the whole country.

A decade later, about 600 observers were sending reports. The project ran from 1849 to 1870. This project led to the National Weather Service, the weather agency of the United States government today.

#### Charting the winds at sea

Matthew Fontaine Maury made charts of the winds and currents at sea from thousands of old ships' logs. A log is the daily record a ship's crew keeps of its position, the wind and the sea. A current is a stream of moving water inside the ocean. A chart is a map for sailors.

From 1842 Maury ran the Navy's Depot of Charts and Instruments, where old logs were stored. He went through thousands of them for facts about winds and currents. In 1847 he issued the first Wind and Current Chart of the North Atlantic. He then collected logs from ship captains around the world, all kept in the same format. Captains who used his charts cut their sailing times.

In April 1861 Virginia's leaders took the state out of the United States. Maury then resigned from the US Navy and joined the Confederacy. The Confederacy was the group of Southern states that broke away from the United States and fought against it in the Civil War. Before the war, Maury had wanted slavery to spread into the American West and also into Cuba and Brazil.

<a id="story-maria-mitchell"></a>

#### Maria Mitchell

> **Who:** A librarian and astronomer on Nantucket who found a comet in 1847. She was the first American and the first woman to win the King of Denmark's gold medal for finding a comet.
>
> **When and where:** Nantucket, Massachusetts. She found the comet on October 1, 1847.

On October 1, 1847, Maria Mitchell found a comet that no chart of the sky showed. A comet is a frozen body that travels around the sun. She was on the roof of the Pacific National Bank building on Nantucket, an island off Massachusetts. Her father worked at the bank. She was sweeping the sky with a small telescope, moving it slowly across the stars. The comet is known as "Miss Mitchell's Comet."

The King of Denmark offered a gold medal for each new comet found with a telescope. Mitchell won it. She was the first American and the first woman to receive it. An Italian astronomer named de Vico saw the same comet two days after she did.

In 1836 she had become the first librarian of the Nantucket Atheneum, a library on the island. For the 20 years she held that job, Mitchell read in the library by day. At night she and her father watched the sky from the roof of the bank, where he was in charge.

In 1848 Mitchell became the first woman elected to the American Academy of Arts and Sciences, a society of scholars.

### 1850 to 1900

Louis Agassiz, the most famous scientist in America, used his fame to argue that the races of people were created separately. In 1850 he had seven enslaved people in South Carolina photographed, with their clothes taken off, as "evidence" for that claim. From 1868, officials of an Army museum in Washington asked Army doctors to send them the skulls of Native Americans. Scientists there measured the skulls to rank the races. Agassiz also attacked Charles Darwin's book *On the Origin of Species*, and Asa Gray, a botanist, or plant scientist, defended it.

In 1879 Albert Michelson measured the speed of light to within about 0.05 percent of the value used today. Josiah Willard Gibbs of Yale founded the science of energy in chemical changes with a paper published in 1876 and 1878. Williamina Fleming, first hired as a maid, sorted more than 10,000 stars at Harvard's observatory.

#### The argument over Darwin's book

Charles Darwin's book *On the Origin of Species* came out in London in November 1859. In it, Darwin argued that species were not each created separately. A species is one kind of living thing. He wrote that species change over time. He called the way they change natural selection. A trait is a feature of a living thing, such as its color or size. Some living things have a trait that helps them survive and have young where they live. They have more young, and the young are likely to have the trait too. In time, the trait spreads through the group. Copies of the book reached Harvard quickly, and two American scientists there took opposite sides.

Asa Gray, a botanist, defended Darwin's theory. Gray had arranged for Darwin's book to be published in America. Louis Agassiz was a zoologist, a scientist who studies animals, and the most famous scientist in America. He attacked the book. He insisted that every species had been created separately.

The two men argued it out at the American Academy of Arts and Sciences in early 1860. Agassiz opened his attack there on January 10, 1860. Gray also defended Darwin in essays in the *Atlantic Monthly*, a magazine. In 1876 he collected them in a book called *Darwiniana*. In it he argued that a person could accept science and keep a religious faith at the same time.

#### Agassiz and the fifteen photographs

Louis Agassiz used his standing as America's most famous scientist to push a racist idea called polygenism. Polygenism is the false claim that the races of people were created separately. In the winter of 1850, Agassiz hired a photographer named Joseph T. Zealy to photograph enslaved people in South Carolina as "evidence" for it.

On a tour of plantations, Agassiz looked among the enslaved people for ones who had been born in Africa. A plantation is a large farm. Agassiz thought that people born in Africa were racially "pure."

Zealy made 15 daguerreotypes. A daguerreotype is an early kind of photograph made on a polished metal plate. The pictures show seven people: Renty Taylor, his daughter Delia, Alfred, Drana, Fassena, Jack and Jem. Agassiz had examined them himself. He left instructions with Robert W. Gibbes, a doctor in Columbia, South Carolina, to collect photographs as evidence. Gibbes arranged for Zealy to photograph the people Agassiz had examined.

In 1976 Elinor Reichlin found the daguerreotypes again at Harvard's Peabody Museum. They are the earliest known photographs of enslaved people in America. In 1977 Reichlin wrote that each person had been posed naked. News reports in 2025 said that Renty and Delia were posed with no shirts on and photographed from several angles. Reichlin's account does not make clear whether Gibbes or Zealy did the posing.

B. F. Taylor enslaved Renty on his plantation, called Edgehill. Delia was Renty's daughter, born in America to parents from Africa. Jack worked in Taylor's fields as a driver, an enslaved man put in charge of other enslaved workers. F. W. Green of Columbia enslaved Jem. Reichlin's account does not name who enslaved Alfred, Drana and Fassena.

Tamara Lanier sued Harvard over the pictures in 2019. She identifies Renty as her great-great-great-grandfather. In 2022 the judges of the Supreme Judicial Court of Massachusetts, the state's highest court, let her claim for emotional distress go forward. Emotional distress means harm to a person's mind and feelings. On May 28, 2025, Lanier and Harvard's lawyers settled the case, and Harvard's leaders agreed to give up the images. In December 2025 Harvard's leaders handed the pictures over from the Peabody Museum to the International African American Museum in Charleston, South Carolina. Museum staff there unveiled them to the public on March 11, 2026.

#### Skulls for the Army Medical Museum

From the 1860s, Army doctors and other collectors sent the skulls of Native Americans to the US Army Medical Museum in Washington. Collectors took many of them from graves and battlefields. Scientists at the museum measured the skulls to rank the races.

The museum got the remains of a Dakota man killed in May 1864. Near an Army post in rural Minnesota, militiamen shot him twice. Militiamen are part-time citizen soldiers, and these were fighting against the Native people there. One bullet shattered his skull. The other went through his mouth or neck. Soldiers dragged his body to a nearby fort, where settlers beat it. Someone cut off his scalp, the skin and hair of the top of the head, and carried it away to keep. Someone buried the body in a shallow grave. A few months later, his skeleton was dug up again. The historian Samuel Redman, who told this man's story in 2016, does not name the militiamen, the settlers or the person who dug him up. He was about 25 to 35 years old. Nobody recorded his name. Alfred Muller, an Army doctor with the title of acting assistant surgeon, examined the man's remains and sent them to the Army Medical Museum. They ended up at the Smithsonian.

In 1867 officials in the Army's Surgeon General's Office, which ran the Army's doctors, sent out a letter called Circular No. 2. In it they asked Army medical officers to collect skulls, along with Native weapons, clothing, tools, food and medicine. From 1868, officials at the Army Medical Museum asked Army doctors in "Indian country," the lands where Native nations lived, to send them Native American skulls.

The museum's scientists did craniometry, which means measuring skulls. Craniometry was part of a false "racial science." People who did it used the measurements to sort humans into races. Then they ranked the races by how intelligent they believed each one was. George A. Otis, the museum's curator, collected and measured hundreds of the skulls. A curator is the person in charge of a museum's collection.

Redman's history of these collections tells how the collectors got the skulls. They dug some out of graves, sometimes months after the burial, and emptied whole cemeteries. Others came from battlefields, from people who had just been killed there. Redman's account does not say who did the killing. Some skulls arrived at the museum without anyone asking for them.

One of the collectors was B. E. Fryer, the Army surgeon at Fort Harker in Kansas. In late January 1869, US soldiers and Kansas settlers attacked a party of Pawnee men at a farm near Mulberry Creek, in Kansas. James Riding In, a Pawnee historian, calls it a massacre. The Pawnee said the soldiers fired first, and Army officers said the Pawnee did. Two soldiers were wounded. The soldiers and settlers killed eight or nine Pawnee men. Settlers captured one of the Pawnee men and killed him, and the reason given was that he was "trying to escape." Five men escaped and hid their dead friends' bodies from the soldiers. Three of those five later died of exposure, which means from cold out in the open. So as many as twelve Pawnee men may have died because of the attack.

On January 30, Fryer sent a civilian to cut off the dead men's heads. Over the next weeks, Fryer or men he sent searched for the hidden bodies. On March 11, 1869, Fryer shipped 26 Native skulls to Washington, and six of them were Pawnee. He wrote to Otis that two of the skulls were damaged because soldiers "shot into the bodies and heads several times after the fight." From 1868 to 1872 Fryer sent Otis the remains of at least 42 people. They were Cheyenne, Wichita, Caddo, Osage, Kansa and people of other nations. Riding In told what Fryer did in a 1992 article, quoting Fryer's letter to Otis.

By about 1900 the museum's collection held about 3,000 skulls. In 1898 and again in 1904, Army officials moved the Native remains to the Smithsonian's national museum. The only ones kept back were those of interest for the study of surgery. One record counts 2,000 skulls in the transfer.

#### Colleges and farm research in every state

The Morrill Act became law on July 2, 1862. Under it, members of Congress gave each state 30,000 acres of public land for each of its senators and representatives. The states sold the land and used the money to start colleges that taught farming and the skills of machines and building. These are called land-grant colleges. The land had been taken from Native nations. The reporters Robert Lee and Tristan Ahtone counted about 10.7 million acres of this land. US officials had taken it from nearly 250 Native nations, bands and communities, in more than 160 land deals backed by violence. For all of it the United States paid less than $400,000. Through them, students in every state could study science.

Under the Hatch Act of 1887, members of Congress set aside federal money for an agricultural experiment station in every state. An agricultural experiment station is a place where scientists run tests to improve farming. Scientists at the stations did research for the public in every state, including places far from the old college towns.

#### Maria Mitchell's eclipse trip, 1878

In 1878 Maria Mitchell led a team of women about 2,000 miles by train to Denver to watch a total solar eclipse. In a total solar eclipse, the moon blocks all of the sun's light for a short time. The eclipse took place on July 29, 1878. Her team was made up of students and graduates of Vassar College, a college for women. The women ran the trip themselves, and reporters for newspapers across the country followed it.

Mitchell had become a professor at Vassar in 1865. She was the first American woman to be a professor of astronomy.

<a id="story-josiah-willard-gibbs"></a>

#### Josiah Willard Gibbs

> **Who:** A Yale physicist whose long paper of 1876 and 1878 founded chemical thermodynamics, the science of energy in chemical changes.
>
> **When and where:** Yale, in New Haven, Connecticut. Professor from 1871.

Josiah Willard Gibbs founded chemical thermodynamics. Thermodynamics is the science of heat and energy. Chemical thermodynamics uses its rules to explain what happens to energy when substances change.

He published this work in two parts, in 1876 and 1878. It was called *On the Equilibrium of Heterogeneous Substances*. Equilibrium means a steady balance. Heterogeneous substances are mixtures of different materials. The work came out in the *Transactions of the Connecticut Academy*, a journal that was little known. It was also very hard to follow.

Scientists in Europe took notice of Gibbs's work before scientists in America did. In 1873 Gibbs had published shorter papers that described a curved surface in mathematics. In 1874 the Scottish physicist James Clerk Maxwell, a scientist who studied matter and energy, built a model of that surface with his own hands. He shaped it in clay, made copies in plaster and mailed one to Gibbs in New Haven.

Gibbs had earned the first American doctorate in engineering, at Yale in 1863. A doctorate is the highest degree a university gives. From 1871 he was Yale's professor of mathematical physics. For his first nine years in that job he received no pay, and he lived on money he had inherited. In 1880 leaders of Johns Hopkins University offered him a job. Yale's leaders then began to pay him so that he would stay.

In 1901 he received the Copley Medal, at that time the top science honor in the world.

<a id="story-albert-michelson"></a>

#### Albert Michelson

> **Who:** An immigrant from Prussia, raised in mining towns in the West, who measured the speed of light to within about 0.05 percent of today's value.
>
> **When and where:** Annapolis, Maryland, in 1879. Cleveland, Ohio, in 1887.

In 1879, at Annapolis in Maryland, Albert Michelson measured the speed of light. His result came within about 0.05 percent of the value scientists use today. That is an error of about 1 part in 2,000. He measured 299,864 kilometers per second, in air. Some books print his figure as 299,910.

Michelson was born on December 19, 1852, in Strelno, a town in Prussia. Prussia was a German kingdom, and the town is now Strzelno, in Poland. His parents brought him to the United States in 1855, when he was 2. He grew up in mining towns in California and Nevada. He graduated from the US Naval Academy at Annapolis.

From April to July 1887, in Cleveland, Ohio, Michelson and the chemist Edward Morley ran the test now called the Michelson-Morley experiment. Scientists then thought that light traveled as waves through an unseen substance they called the ether. Michelson and Morley found no trace of the ether. A result like this, where the test finds nothing, is called a null result. Their null result was an early clue for the theory of relativity. Albert Einstein put forward that theory, a new account of space, time and light, in 1905.

In 1907 Michelson became the first American to win a Nobel Prize in science.

<a id="story-williamina-fleming"></a>

#### Williamina Fleming

> **Who:** An immigrant from Scotland, hired as a maid in the house of the Harvard College Observatory's director, who went on to classify more than 10,000 stars.
>
> **When and where:** Harvard College Observatory, from about 1879.

Williamina Fleming sorted more than 10,000 stars by type for the Draper Catalogue, a list of stars published in 1890. She was an immigrant from Scotland. In about 1879 she took a job as a maid in the house of Edward Pickering, the director of the Harvard College Observatory. An observatory is a building for studying the sky. In 1881 she moved onto the observatory's staff.

She was one of the observatory's "computers." At that time a computer was a person whose job was to do calculations and measurements. Fleming studied photographic plates, which are glass sheets that hold photographs of the night sky. On a plate from 1888 she spotted the Horsehead Nebula. A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in space.

Fleming discovered 59 nebulae, more than 310 variable stars and 10 novae. A variable star is a star whose brightness changes. A nova is a star that suddenly grows much brighter for a time. In 1899 she became Curator of Astronomical Photographs, the person in charge of the observatory's photographs of the sky.

Harvard's time capsule of 1900, called the Chest of 1900, holds an entry by Fleming. A time capsule is a box of papers sealed to be opened in the future. Her entry records that she earned $1,500 a year, while men in similar jobs earned $2,500. She wrote: "Does he ever think that I have a home to keep and a family to take care of as well as the men?"

### 1900 to 1950

Between 1900 and 1950, American scientists measured distances across the universe and ran the first controlled nuclear chain reaction. Edwin Hubble showed in 1929 that the galaxies are moving apart. On December 2, 1942, Enrico Fermi's team in Chicago ran the chain reaction. Albert Einstein, Fermi and Emilio Segrè all came to American labs from Europe in the 1930s. Fermi and Segrè made their homes in America after Italy's ruler, Benito Mussolini, put laws against Jews into force in 1938.

In the same years, some American scientists used people as research material without asking them. From 1910 to 1939, the staff of the Eugenics Record Office in New York collected family records to claim that poverty and behavior are inherited. At the Smithsonian, Aleš Hrdlička collected human brains and bones to rank the races. From 1945 to 1947, doctors working for the Manhattan Project, the secret program that built the atomic bomb, injected 18 hospital patients with plutonium to learn where it goes in the human body.

#### The charge of an electron and the place of a gene

Robert Millikan measured the electric charge of a single electron in experiments with drops of oil, from 1909 to 1913. An electron is one of the tiny particles inside every atom, and it carries electricity. Millikan showed that electric charge comes in exact, equal pieces. He won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1923. The Nobel Prizes are awards first given in 1901 under the will of Alfred Nobel, a Swedish inventor. Each year they go to people for work in physics, chemistry, medicine, writing and peace, and later also economics.

In 1910 Thomas Hunt Morgan found a fruit fly with white eyes in his lab at Columbia University in New York. People called the lab the "fly room." After that fly, Morgan and his team spent 17 years working in the fly room. Morgan and his team proved that genes sit in a line along the chromosomes. A gene is a piece of the instructions, passed from parents to children, that shapes a living thing. A chromosome is a thread inside a cell that carries genes.

Morgan won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1933. Physiology is the study of how living bodies work. It was the first Nobel Prize for genetics, the study of how living things pass on their traits.

<a id="story-frank-chapman-bird-count"></a>

#### Frank Chapman and the first Christmas Bird Count

> **Who:** An ornithologist, a scientist who studies birds, at the American Museum of Natural History. He proposed counting birds at Christmas instead of shooting them.
>
> **When and where:** Across North America, from Toronto to Pacific Grove, California, on December 25, 1900.

On Christmas Day in 1900, Frank M. Chapman replaced a Christmas hunt with a count of birds. Hunters had a Christmas custom called the "side hunt." In a side hunt, they shot at every bird and animal they could reach.

Chapman worked at the American Museum of Natural History in New York. He had founded a bird magazine called *Bird-Lore* and was its editor. He proposed that people count the birds instead of shooting them.

On December 25, 1900, 27 bird-watchers ran 25 separate counts. The counts stretched from Toronto in Canada to Pacific Grove in California. Together the volunteers counted about 18,500 birds of 90 species. A species is one kind of living thing.

The count has run every winter since 1900. It is one of the longest-running citizen-science records in the world. Citizen science is research done by ordinary volunteers.

<a id="story-robert-goddard"></a>

#### Robert Goddard

> **Who:** A physics teacher at Clark University who built and flew the first rocket that burned liquid fuel. The New York Times mocked his rocket science in an editorial in 1920 and printed a correction in 1969.
>
> **When and where:** Worcester and Auburn, Massachusetts. The first flight was on March 16, 1926.

On March 16, 1926, at Auburn, Massachusetts, Robert Goddard launched the first rocket that ran on liquid fuel. It rose 41 feet, flew for 2.5 seconds and came down in a farm field 184 feet away.

Goddard grew up in Worcester, Massachusetts. In 1914 he began teaching physics at Clark University in Worcester. He later ran its physics department, and he became a full professor in 1934. In all he spent 29 years in Clark's physics department.

His paper *A Method of Reaching Extreme Altitudes* came out from the Smithsonian Institution in January 1920. Extreme altitudes are very great heights. On January 13, 1920, the editors of the New York Times answered it with an editorial, an article giving the newspaper's own opinion. Its title was "A Severe Strain on Credulity." Credulity means a willingness to believe things.

In the editorial, the editors mocked Goddard for thinking that a rocket could push itself forward in a vacuum. A vacuum is a space with no air in it, like outer space. They wrote that he lacked "the knowledge ladled out daily in high schools."

On July 17, 1969, the three Apollo 11 astronauts were on their way to the Moon. That day the Times editors printed a correction. It read: "...it is now definitely established that a rocket can function in a vacuum as well as in an atmosphere. The Times regrets the error."

#### Henrietta Leavitt's rule for measuring space

Henrietta Swan Leavitt found a way to measure how far away stars are. She was a computer, a person hired to do calculations and measurements, at the Harvard College Observatory. An observatory is a building for studying the sky. Leavitt was one of more than 100 women hired as computers at the observatory to study photographs of the stars. She was paid 30 cents an hour, five cents more than most of the others. She had been deaf since an illness in her twenties.

Leavitt studied a kind of variable star called a Cepheid. A Cepheid grows brighter and dimmer over and over, in a steady rhythm. In 1912 she published a paper on 25 Cepheids in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a patch of stars in the southern sky. She showed that the time a Cepheid takes for one blink tells how bright it truly is.

Astronomers compare that true brightness with how bright the star looks from Earth. The dimmer it looks compared with its true brightness, the farther away it is. With Leavitt's rule, Cepheids became markers for measuring distance across the universe. Her rule is called the period-luminosity law. The period is the time of one blink, and luminosity means true brightness.

Leavitt died on December 12, 1921. In 1925 a Swedish mathematician who did not know she had died wrote to begin nominating her for a Nobel Prize.

<a id="story-edwin-hubble"></a>

#### Edwin Hubble

> **Who:** An astronomer who showed that there are galaxies far outside our own and that the universe is expanding.
>
> **When and where:** Mount Wilson Observatory, California, from 1923 to 1929.

Edwin Hubble showed that the universe is expanding. In 1929 he published his finding that the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it is moving away from us. A galaxy is a huge group of billions of stars. Our own galaxy is the Milky Way.

Hubble worked with the Hooker telescope at Mount Wilson, which has a main mirror 100 inches across. On the night of October 4 to 5, 1923, he found a Cepheid star on a photograph of the Andromeda "nebula," a faint cloudy patch in the sky. The photograph was on a photographic plate, a glass sheet that holds a photograph of the sky. Hubble marked the plate "VAR!" for variable star.

Using Leavitt's law, Hubble worked out how far away the star was. His answer was about 900,000 light-years. A light-year is the distance light travels in one year. At that distance, Andromeda lay far outside the Milky Way, so it had to be a separate galaxy. He announced the result at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society on January 1, 1925.

For his 1929 paper, published in March, Hubble used measurements of the galaxies' light made by Milton Humason. Georges Lemaître, a Belgian scientist, had already worked out and published the expansion of the universe in 1927. His paper appeared in a journal that few people read. In 2018 the members of the International Astronomical Union, the world society of astronomers, renamed Hubble's law the Hubble-Lemaître law.

#### Aleš Hrdlička's brain collection

Aleš Hrdlička collected human brains and bones for the Smithsonian to try to prove that the races differ in their bodies. From 1903 into the early 1940s he ran the physical anthropology division of the Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History in Washington. Physical anthropology is the study of human bodies and bones. Hrdlička believed that white people were superior to other races. Scientists have since shown his theories about the races' bodies to be false.

In 1903 Hrdlička began what he himself called the "racial brain collection." Reporters at the Washington Post, a newspaper, looked into his collecting and published what they found in August 2023. They reported that the museum held at least 255 brains, and that Hrdlička or people working at his direction collected most of them.

Collectors took most of the remains without the consent of the dead people or their families. Consent means agreeing to something after being told what it is. Many of these people had died in hospitals, were poor, or had no relatives nearby to claim and bury them. Collectors also dug up burial grounds. Hrdlička and a small team dug up the remains of about 1,000 people in Alaska and shipped them to the Smithsonian. In the 1930s they dug them from the Uyak site on Kodiak Island. The people of Larsen Bay are Alutiiq. They asked the Smithsonian for their dead in 1987. In September 1991 museum staff sent the remains back to Larsen Bay. It was one of the first returns of Native American remains in the country.

The Post's reporters also found that in 2023 the museum held more than 30,700 human remains. More than 19,000 of them, about 62 percent, were collected while Hrdlička led the division.

#### The Eugenics Record Office

From 1910 to 1939, the staff of the Eugenics Record Office at Cold Spring Harbor, New York, collected family records. They used the records to argue that some people should not have children. Eugenics was the claim that a country should decide which of its people may have children, and stop the rest. The men who ran the office presented it as the science of heredity. Heredity is the passing of traits from parents to children.

The biologist Charles B. Davenport directed a research station at Cold Spring Harbor. The station belonged to the Carnegie Institution of Washington, a private group that paid for scientific research. In 1910 Davenport persuaded Mary Harriman, the widow of a railroad owner, to give $10,000. She bought an 80-acre farm next to the station and built an office on it. The Eugenics Record Office opened there in 1910, with Harry H. Laughlin in charge.

Staff at the office ran summer courses that trained field workers. Photographs of the courses survive from 1913 to 1922. The field workers went door to door and filled out forms of questions about families. By 1924 the office's files held 750,000 index cards, along with family trees and reports. Davenport, Laughlin and their workers traced traits through families, such as blindness and musical ability. They also traced what they called "feeblemindedness," their label for people they judged to be of low intelligence. They treated poverty and behavior as traits that parents pass to their children.

Laughlin used the office's records to push for laws to keep immigrants out and to sterilize people labeled "defective." To sterilize a person is to operate on the body so that the person can never have a child. In a woman, for example, a doctor cut out a piece of each of the two tubes that carry eggs to the womb. It cannot be undone.

Scientists who studied heredity, among them Thomas Hunt Morgan, Raymond Pearl and Herbert Jennings, pointed out flaws in eugenics research. They showed that the eugenicists' experiments were badly designed and that the eugenicists used the new science of genes too simply. They also showed that the eugenicists' work was racist and unfair to poor people. In 1935 leaders of the Carnegie Institution gathered a panel of scientists to judge the office's work. The panel found that almost none of it had any scientific worth.

In the 1930s Americans also learned what Nazi Germany's leaders were doing with eugenics. Under a German law of July 14, 1933, judges and doctors sat on special courts, each made up of a judge and two doctors. By 1945 the judges and doctors on these courts had forced about 400,000 people to be sterilized. Doctors usually cut the tubes that carry sperm in men, and tied or cut the tubes that carry eggs to the womb in women. The forced operations killed hundreds of people, most of them women. In 1939 Vannevar Bush, the president of the Carnegie Institution, cut off the office's money, and it closed in December 1939. Its records went to the University of Minnesota in 1948. Staff at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory now publish this history on the laboratory's archive website, under the heading "Good genes, bad science."

<a id="story-albert-einstein-science"></a>

#### Albert Einstein

> **Who:** A physicist who moved to America in 1933, the year the Nazis took control of Germany. He became a US citizen in 1940.
>
> **When and where:** Princeton, New Jersey, from October 1933.

Albert Einstein arrived in the United States on October 17, 1933. Earlier that year the Nazis had taken control of Germany. He joined the new Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, as one of its first professors.

Einstein had done his most famous physics, the theory of relativity, in Europe between 1905 and 1915. Relativity explains how space, time and gravity are tied together.

On August 2, 1939, Einstein signed a letter to President Franklin Roosevelt. The physicist Leo Szilard wrote it, with Edward Teller and Eugene Wigner. The letter stated that Germany might build atomic bombs. Historians at the Atomic Heritage Foundation, a group that records the history of the bomb, trace the start of the Manhattan Project back to this letter. The Manhattan Project was the secret American program to build an atomic bomb during World War II.

On October 1, 1940, Einstein became a citizen of the United States. He also kept his Swiss citizenship.

In May 1946 the leaders of Lincoln University, a Black university in Pennsylvania, gave Einstein an honorary degree. An honorary degree is a degree a college gives to honor a person's life and work. At Lincoln he called racism "a disease of white people." He said, "I do not intend to be quiet about it."

<a id="story-emilio-segre-science"></a>

#### Emilio Segrè

> **Who:** An Italian physicist who lost his job at home in 1938 under Mussolini's laws against Jews, stayed at Berkeley, and won a Nobel Prize.
>
> **When and where:** Berkeley, California, from the summer of 1938.

In the summer of 1938, Emilio Segrè was visiting Ernest Lawrence's Radiation Laboratory at the University of California, Berkeley. That year Benito Mussolini, who ruled Italy, put antisemitic racial laws into force. Antisemitic means hostile to Jews. Italian officials used those laws to take away his job as a professor in Palermo, Italy.

Segrè stayed in America. Lawrence gave him a job as a research assistant, at low pay.

Segrè later helped discover the elements technetium and astatine, and plutonium-239, one form of plutonium. With Owen Chamberlain he discovered the antiproton. A proton is a tiny particle with a positive electric charge, found in the center of every atom. An antiproton matches a proton but has a negative charge. Segrè and Chamberlain shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1959.

#### Splitting the atom, and the big laboratories

In December 1938 two chemists in Berlin, Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann, discovered nuclear fission. Fission is the splitting of the center of an atom, called the nucleus, into two pieces. The split gives off energy. In January 1939 Lise Meitner and her nephew Otto Frisch explained what the chemists' results meant. Meitner was a Jewish refugee living in Sweden. A refugee is a person who flees their home country to be safe. In 1944 the Nobel judges gave the prize for the discovery to Hahn alone and left Meitner out.

News of fission reached America in January 1939. On December 2, 1942, Enrico Fermi's team of 49 people ran the first controlled nuclear chain reaction. In a chain reaction, each atom that splits sets off more atoms splitting. The team's reactor, a machine built to run a chain reaction, was called Chicago Pile-1. It stood under the west stands of Stagg Field, an unused football field at the University of Chicago. The reaction kept itself going for 28 minutes and made about half a watt of power. Controlled means the team could keep it steady and stop it.

Fermi was an Italian physicist. He won the Nobel Prize in 1938. He sailed straight from the ceremony in Stockholm to New York. His wife, Laura, was Jewish, and Mussolini had just put his new laws against Jews into force.

Chicago Pile-1 belonged to the Manhattan Project. The project's leaders set up three large laboratories: the Metallurgical Laboratory in Chicago, Clinton Laboratories at Oak Ridge in Tennessee, and Los Alamos in New Mexico. They were the start of the national laboratories, the government's big science labs. In August 1945 American bomber crews dropped the project's two atomic bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The Radiation Effects Research Foundation is a research group that Japan and the United States run together. Its researchers estimate that within two to four months the bombs killed 90,000 to 166,000 people in Hiroshima and 60,000 to 80,000 in Nagasaki. The exact numbers are not known, and a US study in 1946 gave lower counts.

An older lab came before these, the Radiation Laboratory at the University of California, Berkeley. Ernest Lawrence built it around his cyclotrons.
