In 1848, when he was 16, James Garfield ran away to work on a canal boat called the *Evening Star*. The boat carried freight, which means goods being shipped, on the Ohio and Erie Canal. For about six weeks he helped haul coal, copper ore and wood.

Garfield could not swim. One night he fell overboard. He later caught malaria and went home. Writers of biographies for his campaign for president claimed he fell into the canal fourteen times. That number comes from those later stories and not from the record of his time on the boat.

<a id="story-moses-grandy"></a>

#### Moses Grandy

> **Who:** An enslaved man who ran boats through the Dismal Swamp canals, bought his own freedom three times, and described the men who dug the canals.
>
> **When and where:** Camden County, North Carolina, and the canals to Norfolk, Virginia, from the early 1800s. His narrative was published in London in 1843.

Moses Grandy was born into slavery in Camden County, North Carolina, around 1786. His owners hired him out each year to other men. He worked canal boats that carried shingles, boards and other freight through the Dismal Swamp canals to Norfolk.

Grandy paid for his own freedom three times. First he paid $600 to his owner, James Grandy. James Grandy kept the money and sold him to a man named Trewitt. Over two and a half years, Moses Grandy earned $600 more and paid it to Trewitt. Then Trewitt's business failed, and a man named Mews claimed Grandy to cover Trewitt's debt. Grandy's next owner, a Mr. Sawyer, put him to work in the fields. A captain from Deep Creek, Edward Minner, lent Grandy the third price, $650, and Sawyer set him free. Grandy paid Minner back over three years.

While Grandy worked on the canal, his wife's owner sold her. A group of enslaved people passed along the road beside the canal, and she called out to him. The man who had bought her, Mr. Rogerson, pulled out a pistol. He said he would shoot Grandy if he came near the wagon. Grandy wrote: "I have never seen or heard of her from that day to this."

Grandy also described the enslaved men who dug the canals. They worked "up to the middle or much deeper in mud and water, cutting away roots and baling out mud." Baling out means scooping out. They slept in open huts, still covered in mud, with no bedding. Once a month their owners came to collect the men's pay.

An overseer named Wiley M'Pherson gave every man the same amount of digging each day. An overseer was the man in charge of the workers. When men had not finished the day before, M'Pherson tied them up and flogged them. Flogging means whipping a person's bare back until the skin splits. Then he had "pork or beef brine," the salt water used to keep meat, put "on their bleeding backs, to increase the pain." He left men tied all day with their feet barely touching the ground, while flies and mosquitoes settled on the cuts.

Grandy wrote: "I have seen him flog slaves with his own hands, till their entrails were visible." Entrails are the organs inside the body. Grandy went on: "I have seen the sufferers dead when they were taken down. He never was called to account in any way for it."

Grandy later married again. He lived in Boston, sawed wood, worked in coal yards, loaded and unloaded ships, and went on more voyages. He saved enough to buy his second wife out of slavery in Virginia, and she joined him in Boston. He raised $450 to buy his son's freedom. His daughters in New Orleans paid for their own freedom, $1,200 for each of them. His book was sold to raise money for his relatives who were still enslaved.

#### The first railroads

The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad was the first railroad in the United States to carry both passengers and freight on a schedule for anyone who paid. Its builders laid the first stone on July 4, 1828. Its first 13 miles of track, from Baltimore to Ellicott's Mills, opened in 1830.

In a well-known story, Peter Cooper's steam engine, the *Tom Thumb*, raced a horse pulling a railroad car on August 28, 1830. In the story, the engine lost when a belt on it slipped. The story comes from a talk that John H. B. Latrobe gave in 1868, 38 years later. No record from 1830 shows that the race took place. The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad Museum's page on the *Tom Thumb* describes the race as a legend.

On August 9, 1831, a locomotive named the *DeWitt Clinton* pulled the first steam passenger train in New York State. A locomotive is the engine that pulls a train. The train ran 16 miles from Albany to Schenectady in about an hour, on the Mohawk and Hudson line.

City transit began in these years too. From 1827, Abraham Brower ran a horse-drawn coach called an omnibus on the streets of New York City. On November 14, 1832, the *John Mason*, a horse-drawn car that rolled on rails, began carrying passengers in lower Manhattan for the New York and Harlem Railroad. It was the first street railway in the country.

In the South, enslaved people built most of the railroads. As early as 1841, the men running Southern railroad companies bought hundreds of enslaved men between the ages of 16 and 35. In the 1850s they bought or rented enslaved workers in groups of hundreds. The historian Theodore Kornweibel Jr. found enslaved workers on 85 of the 113 railroads in the Confederate states. These were the Southern states that later fought the United States in the Civil War. In 1860 Southern railroad companies owned about 15,000 enslaved people, and women and children were among them. In 1855 the president of the Mississippi Central Railroad told the people who owned shares in the company that "the slave is preferable to free labor, and far better adapted to the construction of railways in the south." Free labor meant workers who were not enslaved.

### 1850 to 1900

Railroad track spread across the United States in the second half of the 1800s. In 1850 the country had about 9,000 miles of railroad track. By 1900 it had more than 190,000 miles. Counts for 1900 run from about 193,000 to 215,000, depending on whether side tracks are counted.

In 1869 the first railroad across the country cut the trip from one coast to the other from about four months to about a week. Central Pacific managers hired about 10,000 to 12,000 Chinese workers to build the western part of the line. The tracks of the two companies that built it crossed the lands of the Cheyenne, Lakota, Arapaho, Shoshone and Paiute nations. Streetcars were passenger cars that ran on rails laid in city streets. By the end of the century, the companies that ran them were switching from horse-drawn cars to electric ones, and many Americans, women among them, were riding bicycles.

#### The railroad across the continent

Two companies built the first railroad across the country. Union Pacific crews built west from Omaha, Nebraska, while Central Pacific crews built east from Sacramento, California. The two lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869. A golden spike marked the place where they joined.

Members of Congress voted to give the two companies land and loans. On July 1, 1862, President Abraham Lincoln signed the Pacific Railroad Act. Under it, each company got 6,400 acres of public land for every mile of track it built. Each company also got up to $48,000 in government bonds for every mile. A bond is a kind of loan. The top rate of $48,000 was for miles built through mountains.

The act also said: "The United States shall extinguish as rapidly as may be the Indian titles to all lands falling under the operation of this act." To extinguish a title means to end someone's ownership of land. With those words, the lawmakers directed federal officials to end Native nations' ownership of the land along the railroad as fast as they could. From 1850 to 1871, members of Congress voted to give railroads about 130 million acres of federal land. Some counts run as high as 175 million acres. State lawmakers gave railroads about 51 million acres more.

#### Whose land the railroad crossed

While the two lines were built, the companies' builders and US officials took land from many Native nations and drove people from their homes. Among those nations were the Cheyenne, Lakota (also called Sioux), Arapaho, Shoshone and Paiute. Historians at the Utah Division of State History count 15 Native homelands that the track crossed.

The Lakota, Arapaho and Cheyenne hunted bison, also called buffalo, for food, shelter and trade. As the railroad moved west, soldiers, railroad workers and travelers hunted the bison too. National Park Service writers state that the bison fell from tens of millions in the early 1800s until they had almost died out.

Some Paiute people worked for the Central Pacific. Union Pacific managers and US officials hired hundreds of Pawnee, who guarded the work crews alongside the US Army. On January 13, 1865, four army units of Pawnee soldiers, called companies, joined the Army under Major Frank J. North.

On November 29, 1864, at Sand Creek in Colorado, US soldiers on horseback led by Colonel John Chivington attacked a camp of Cheyenne and Arapaho people. The camp flew a US flag and a white flag. The soldiers killed between about 150 and about 230 people, most of them women and children. The people killed were not armed. PBS writers give the count of 150. Britannica and the National Park Service give about 230.

Cheyenne, Arapaho and Lakota fighters struck back for Sand Creek. On January 7, 1865, they burned the town of Julesburg, Colorado. They also cut the telegraph line, the wire that carried messages by electric signals. Two and a half years later, on August 27, 1867, at Plum Creek, Nebraska, Cheyenne men pulled up railroad track, wrecked a work train and killed its crew. One man survived.

#### The Chinese workers

Central Pacific managers hired about 10,000 to 12,000 Chinese workers from 1865 to 1869. Most came from Guangdong, a province in southern China. The Chinese workers were paid about $35 a month, and they had to buy their own food and housing. White workers got about $42 a month, plus housing.

The Central Pacific's managers kept no record of the Chinese workers who died, so no one knows how many there were. Avalanches, masses of snow sliding down the mountains, killed workers in the winter of 1866 to 1867. There were 44 storms that winter. In one, snow carried away the camp at Strong's Canyon. Blasts of black powder and nitroglycerin, both explosives used to cut through rock, killed others. Smallpox, a disease that spreads from person to person, killed more in 1868 and 1869.

On June 30, 1870, writers at two Sacramento newspapers printed guesses of the dead. The writer at the *Sacramento Union* reported "about fifty." The writer at the *Sacramento Reporter* told of "the accumulated bones of perhaps 1,200," about 20,000 pounds of bones being shipped home to China. Researchers on the online forum of the Central Pacific Railroad Photographic History Museum estimate 100 to 150 dead. Other estimates run to hundreds or thousands.

On June 25, 1867, Chinese workers in the Sierra Nevada mountains went on strike, which means they stopped work to demand better terms. Estimates of how many struck run from 2,000 to 5,000. They asked for $40 a month instead of $35, for workdays of no more than ten hours, and for shorter shifts in the cramped tunnels. The construction boss, Charles Crocker, and his foreman, the man who ran the work crews, James Harvey Strobridge, cut off food and supplies to the Chinese camps. After a week with little food, Crocker told the strikers that men who went back at once would only be fined. Men who stayed out would lose all their pay for June. Most men, weak from lack of food, went back. The men who refused faced a group of armed white men, and work started again. Crocker gave the strikers no raise, though pay for experienced men later rose a little, according to the Library of Congress. It was the largest strike by workers in the country up to that time.

On April 28, 1869, crews laid 10 miles and 56 feet of track in one day. Eight Irish workers carried the rails, and several thousand Chinese workers did the rest of the work. Twelve days later, at Promontory Summit, eight Chinese workers laid the last track joining the two lines. Three of them, Ging Cui, Wong Fook and Lee Shao, rode on a float at the celebration of the railroad's 50th anniversary on May 10, 1919.

<a id="story-hung-wah"></a>

#### Hung Wah

> **Who:** The leading Chinese headman on the Central Pacific.
>
> **When and where:** The Central Pacific Railroad, from January 1864.

Hung Wah is one of the few Chinese railroad workers whose names appear in the records. The company's payroll, its list of the people it paid, usually named only headmen, the men who led the Chinese work gangs. So the names of most of the thousands of Chinese laborers are not in the records.

Hung Wah first appears on the Central Pacific's payroll in January 1864. With another headman, Ah Toy, he supervised the railroad's first Chinese crew, about 23 men. He became the leading Chinese headman on the line, over hundreds of Chinese workers and at times thousands. He handled the workers' pay and their living arrangements, and he dealt with the company for them.

<a id="story-cornelius-vanderbilt-transportation"></a>

#### Cornelius Vanderbilt

> **Who:** A ferryman who moved his money from steamboats into railroads and left the largest American fortune of his time.
>
> **When and where:** New York, 1810 to 1877.

Cornelius Vanderbilt began as a ferryman and died in 1877 with about $100 million, the largest American fortune of his time. In 1810, at 16, he began carrying freight and passengers between Staten Island and Manhattan. His boat was a periauger, a shallow sailboat with two masts. Accounts of how he got the boat differ. One says he borrowed $100 from his mother and named the boat *Swiftsure*. The first account of his life, printed in 1853, says the boat was his father's and he kept half the profit. The website Biography.com describes the story of the young ferryman as a legend. Other boat captains called him "the Commodore," at first as a joke. A commodore is a navy officer who commands a group of ships.

Vanderbilt owned steamboats and moved his money into railroads in the early 1860s. In 1867 he took control of the New York Central Railroad. On November 1, 1869, he joined it with his Hudson River Railroad. In 1871 he opened Grand Central Depot, a train station in Manhattan.

<a id="story-mark-twain-transportation"></a>

#### Mark Twain, steamboat pilot

> **Who:** Samuel Clemens, who steered steamboats on the Mississippi River before he wrote books as Mark Twain.
>
> **When and where:** The Mississippi River. He got his pilot's license on April 9, 1859.
>
> **Movie:** *Mark Twain* (2001), a documentary by Ken Burns about his whole life. PBS showed it in January 2002.

Samuel Clemens was a licensed steamboat pilot on the Mississippi River. A pilot is the person who steers a boat. He got his license on April 9, 1859, when he was 23. He piloted boats until 1861, when the Civil War began and traffic on the river stopped.

He took his pen name from a call used on the river. A leadsman was the crew member who measured the depth of the water and called it out to the pilot. "Mark twain" meant two fathoms. A fathom is six feet, so two fathoms is twelve feet of water. In 1883 he published *Life on the Mississippi*, a book about his years as a pilot.

#### Clocks, sleeping cars and danger on the railroads

On November 18, 1883, railroad managers in the United States and Canada began using standard time zones. A time zone is a region where all clocks show the same time. Before then, each railroad company ran its trains by its own clocks. William F. Allen, the editor of the *Traveler's Official Railway Guide*, a book of train schedules, drew up the plan. On the day of the switch, railroad workers reset every railroad clock to the new time, even clocks that had already passed noon. In those places noon came twice, so people called it "the day of two noons." Members of Congress did not vote time zones into law until the Standard Time Act of March 19, 1918.

In 1865 George Pullman built the *Pioneer*, his first sleeping car built for luxury. It had upper beds that folded away and seats that pulled out. His company, the Pullman Palace Car Company, began in 1867.

Railroad work was dangerous. In 1889, about 8.5 of every 1,000 American trainmen, the workers who ran the trains, were killed on the job. That was twice the rate for trainmen in Britain. That year 1.73 of every 1,000 trainmen were killed while coupling, the job of joining railroad cars together. With the old link-and-pin coupler, a brakeman, the crew member who set the brakes and joined the cars, had to stand between two moving cars to join them. Mangled hands were known as "the badge of the experienced worker."

Safer equipment existed for years before lawmakers required railroad owners to use it. In 1873 Eli Janney got a patent, the legal right to be the only one to make and sell an invention, for an automatic coupler. It joined cars without a worker standing between them. George Westinghouse's air brake existed from 1869. In it, a pump on the locomotive pushed air through hoses to every car. When the engineer opened a valve, the air set the brakes on all the cars at once. In 1893 members of Congress passed the Safety Appliance Act. It required automatic couplers and air brakes on trains that crossed state lines, starting in 1900. Accidents while coupling cars fell from about 11,000 in 1892 to about 2,000 in 1902, while the number of railroad workers grew.

#### Separate cars by race

Train crews and lawmakers decided where Black passengers could sit. In 1884 Ida B. Wells had a first-class ticket on a train in Tennessee. The train crew ordered her into the car for Black passengers. She refused, and they forced her off the train. She sued the railroad and won $500 in a Tennessee court. In 1887 the judges of the Tennessee Supreme Court threw out that decision.

On June 10, 1890, Louisiana lawmakers passed the Separate Car Act. It required railroads to provide "equal but separate" cars for Black and white passengers. A passenger who broke it could be fined $25 or jailed for 20 days. Homer Plessy, a shoemaker in New Orleans, offered to test the law. To test it, he would break it on purpose so that judges would have to decide whether the law was allowed. On June 7, 1892, he bought a ticket on the East Louisiana Railroad and sat in the car for white passengers. The railroad's officials agreed to the test, because separate cars cost the company money. A private detective hired by the group planning the test, the Citizens' Committee, arrested him. Judge John H. Ferguson ruled against Plessy. On May 18, 1896, the justices of the US Supreme Court ruled against him too, 7 to 1, in *Plessy v. Ferguson*. With that ruling, the justices allowed states to keep separating Black and white passengers by law. Nearly sixty years later, in 1954, the justices of the Supreme Court threw out that ruling's reasoning in *Brown v. Board of Education*.

#### Electric streetcars and bicycles

Electric streetcars replaced horse-drawn ones in American cities between 1888 and 1902. Electric streetcars ran earlier in East Cleveland in 1884, in Baltimore in 1885 and in Montgomery, Alabama, in 1886. The Dictionary of American History describes the system that Frank Sprague built in Richmond, Virginia, in 1888 as the first successful one. By 1891, about 200 streetcar systems had switched to electricity or planned to. Street railway track grew from about 8,000 miles in 1890 to 22,500 miles in 1902. In those same years, the share of streetcar service pulled by animals fell from 75 percent to 1 percent. The last horse-drawn streetcar in paid service in New York City ran on July 26, 1917.

In the 1890s cycling became a craze, something that very many people took up at the same time. Riders used the safety bicycle, which had two wheels of the same size, a chain drive and air-filled tires. Women rode as well as men. On February 2, 1896, Susan B. Anthony told the reporter Nellie Bly in the *New York World* that bicycling "has done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world." To emancipate means to set free. She said: "I stand and rejoice every time I see a woman ride by on a wheel."

<a id="story-frank-sprague"></a>

#### Frank Sprague

> **Who:** The engineer whose streetcar system in Richmond showed that electric streetcars could work in a city.
>
> **When and where:** Richmond, Virginia. Regular service began February 2, 1888.

Frank Sprague built the Richmond Union Passenger Railway, which began regular electric streetcar service on February 2, 1888. It started with 10 cars. By May 1888 it had about 12 miles of track and 23 cars. Other electric streetcars had run before, in East Cleveland, Baltimore and Montgomery. Richmond's was the first large system that worked well. Within about two years, about 110 electric railways had been built or ordered using Sprague's equipment. Members of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, a society of engineers, have named his Richmond railway a milestone in the history of engineering.

### 1900 to 1950

By 1927 Ford's workers had built 15 million Model T cars, and airplanes were carrying mail and paying passengers on schedules. The Model T first went on sale in 1908 for $825. The first airline to fly on a schedule began in 1914, across Tampa Bay in Florida.

Trains moved about 43.7 million members of the armed forces in World War II, from 1941 to 1945. In Virginia, bus drivers had the power of police officers to make Black passengers sit apart from white passengers, and to arrest riders who refused.

#### The Model T and the new roads

The Ford Model T went on sale on October 1, 1908, at $825. Its price fell to $260 by 1925. On May 26, 1927, the 15 millionth Model T left the factory, and that was the last day Ford made the car.

In 1913 a group of private backers, among them Carl Fisher and Henry Joy, laid out the Lincoln Highway. It was the first named road for cars across the whole country, from Times Square in New York City to San Francisco. After 1926 highway officials made parts of it into sections of numbered routes.

On November 11, 1926, state and federal highway officials gave the main highways of the United States numbers. Route 66 got its number that day. It ran 2,448 miles, from Chicago to Santa Monica, California. People called it the "Main Street of America." It was fully paved only by the late 1930s.

In 1913 car crashes killed about 4,100 to 4,200 people in the United States. In 1937 they killed about 37,800 to 39,600, which was about 30 of every 100,000 Americans. The counts differ because the National Safety Council, a private safety group, and the federal officials who kept the national tables counted deaths in different ways.

<a id="story-wright-brothers-transportation"></a>

#### The Wright brothers

> **Who:** Orville and Wilbur Wright, the brothers who flew their powered airplane four times in one day.
>
> **When and where:** Near Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina, December 17, 1903.

On December 17, 1903, Orville and Wilbur Wright made four flights in a powered airplane near Kill Devil Hills, North Carolina. Orville flew first. He stayed in the air for 12 seconds and went 120 feet. Wilbur made the fourth and last flight of the day, 852 feet in 59 seconds. Five people watched. One of them, John T. Daniels, took the photograph. He belonged to a lifesaving station, a crew that rescued people from wrecked ships.

About ten years after those flights, an airplane in Florida was carrying paying passengers on a schedule.

#### Airplanes start carrying mail and passengers

The St. Petersburg-Tampa Airboat Line in Florida was the first airline in the world to fly on a schedule. Its first flight left on January 1, 1914. The pilot, Tony Jannus, flew a Benoist flying boat, a plane that takes off from and lands on water. The trip across Tampa Bay took about 23 minutes, low over the water. Abram C. Pheil, a former mayor of St. Petersburg, paid $400 at an auction for the first round-trip ticket. The airline ran for about four months.

Airplanes began carrying mail on a regular route on May 15, 1918. The route ran 218 miles, from Washington to Philadelphia to New York. Army pilots flew it first, and Post Office pilots took over in August 1918. In 1925 members of Congress passed the Kelly Act. Under it, private companies flew the airmail on contract. The airline companies grew out of those mail contracts.

On May 20 and 21, 1927, Charles Lindbergh, an airmail pilot, flew the *Spirit of St. Louis* alone and without stopping from New York to Paris. He covered about 3,600 miles in 33 hours and 30 minutes. Airline passengers in the United States rose from 5,782 in 1926 to 173,405 in 1928. Applications for pilot licenses tripled in 1927.

The Douglas DC-3 airliner first flew passengers in 1936. An airliner is a large plane built to carry passengers. It carried 21 or more passengers at up to 207 miles an hour. Van der Linden is a curator at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum. In van der Linden's words, the DC-3 is "widely considered to be the first airliner capable of making money just by carrying passengers." By 1939 DC-3s carried about 90 percent of the world's airline travel.

<a id="story-jack-knight"></a>

#### Jack Knight

> **Who:** An airmail pilot who flew through the night and a snowstorm to finish a test that kept the airmail going.
>
> **When and where:** North Platte, Nebraska, to Chicago, the night of February 22 to 23, 1921.

In February 1921 Post Office officials ran a test to show that airplanes could carry mail across the country faster than trains. Pilots flew the mail in a relay, day and night, each pilot handing it to the next. Jack Knight flew his part, from North Platte, Nebraska, to Omaha.

At Omaha the next pilot refused to take off in the storm. Knight flew on to Chicago himself, at night, through snow and fog, over ground he had never flown before. The mail crossed the country, 2,629 miles, in 33 hours and 20 minutes. After the test, members of Congress voted money to keep the airmail flying.

#### The sleeping-car porters

Pullman Company managers hired Black men as the porters who served passengers in the company's sleeping cars. After the Civil War, George Pullman looked for men who had been enslaved to hire as his porters. By the early 1900s the Pullman Company was the largest single employer of Black men in the United States.

Porters often had to work at least 400 hours a month to earn a full month's pay. A porter who worked every day of a 30-day month would still need more than 13 hours a day to reach 400. Their pay was among the lowest of all the workers on the train. Company managers built tips from passengers into the porters' pay, which saved the company money. To earn those tips, porters had to do whatever passengers asked.

Passengers called porters "George," whatever their real names were, after George Pullman. Calling an enslaved person by the owner's name was a practice from slavery. Some passengers called the porters "boy." The porters formed a union, a group of workers who bargain together with their employer. In 1937 the union's leaders won a contract that limited the porters' work to 240 hours a month.

<a id="story-miles-of-smiles-porters"></a>

#### The porters of Miles of Smiles

> **Who:** C. L. Dellums, E. D. Nixon and six other retired Pullman porters, with Rosina Tucker, a porter's wife, who described the porters' work in their own words.
>
> **When and where:** Pullman sleeping cars across the country, from the 1910s to the 1940s. Filmed in 1982.
>
> **Movie:** *Miles of Smiles, Years of Struggle* (1982), a documentary by Jack Santino and Paul Wagner, made from the porters' own accounts.

In 1982 eight retired Pullman porters told the filmmakers Jack Santino and Paul Wagner what their job had been like. Rosina Tucker, a porter's wife who worked to build the porters' union, tells the story in the film. The porters describe the smile the company required them to wear for passengers. They talk about living on tips, working through the night without sleep, and being called "George" instead of their own names.

Two of the men in the film are C. L. Dellums and E. D. Nixon. Pullman managers fired Dellums in October 1927 for organizing porters into a union. Nixon later called the meeting for the bus boycott in Montgomery, Alabama.

#### Trains and Jeeps in World War II

From December 1941 to August 1945, trains carried about 43.7 million members of the armed forces. That was more than 97 percent of all the troops moved in organized groups. About 100,000 members of the armed forces rode troop trains on an average day. Half of all Pullman sleeping cars were in use carrying troops.

The Jeep was a small army car. About 640,000 were built in the war. About 363,000 of them were the Willys MB, and about 280,000 were the Ford GPW.

#### Separate seats on the buses

In Virginia, the law required buses to seat Black and white passengers apart. The same law made bus drivers "special policemen." A driver could decide a passenger's race, order the passenger to another seat, throw the passenger off the bus and make an arrest. Refusing a driver was a crime with a fine of $5 to $25. Greyhound's own rules stated that the company had "full control and discretion as to the seating of passengers." Discretion means the power to decide.

In August 1932, Bessie Nelson and Mamie Kinchlow were thrown off a Greyhound bus in Alexandria, Virginia, and jailed for more than a week. On January 16, 1943, Mildred Turpin and Caroline Johnson, clerks for the Navy Department, were jailed at Clarendon, Virginia. On February 19, 1945, in Johnson City, Tennessee, Tonito Holmes was beaten, removed from a Greyhound bus and fined $14.25. The Encyclopedia Virginia account of these cases does not name the drivers and officers who threw the riders off, jailed them or beat them.

<a id="story-irene-morgan"></a>

#### Irene Morgan

> **Who:** A Baltimore war worker who refused to give up her bus seat in Virginia and won her case in the US Supreme Court.
>
> **When and where:** A Greyhound bus near Saluda, Virginia, July 16, 1944. The Supreme Court decided her case on June 3, 1946.

Irene Morgan, of Baltimore, was 27 and built B-26 bombers in a wartime factory. On July 16, 1944, she had been visiting her mother in Gloucester County, Virginia, and took a Greyhound bus home. She was going back to her husband and to see a doctor. Near Saluda, two white passengers got on the crowded bus. The driver told Morgan and the woman next to her, a Black woman holding a baby, to move to the back seat.

"I refused to move," Morgan said years later. The driver drove the bus to the jail in Saluda. The sheriff showed her a warrant, a paper that allows an arrest. She "just took it and tore it up and just threw it out the window." "So then he put his hands on me," she said, and she kicked him. The sheriff and a deputy forced her off the bus. Her mother paid $500 to get her out of jail.

On October 18, 1944, Morgan paid a $100 fine for resisting arrest. She would not admit breaking the seating law. She was found guilty of it anyway, and she refused to pay the $10 fine. The Encyclopedia Virginia account of her case does not name the judge. Her lawyer was Spottswood W. Robinson III. The lawyers Thurgood Marshall and William H. Hastie of the NAACP, a civil rights group, joined him. The judges of the Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals ruled against her on June 6, 1945.

On June 3, 1946, the justices of the US Supreme Court ruled for her. Justice Stanley Reed wrote that Virginia's law made travel between states harder, so it could not apply to buses crossing state lines. The ruling covered only trips between states. Reporters at the *Afro-American* newspaper wrote that bus companies' seating rules did not change right away.

### 1950 to 2000

After 1950, Americans moved people and goods over long distances on three new systems: shipping containers, jet airliners and Interstate highways, the big highways that join the states. In 1956 President Dwight Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act, the law for the Interstate highways. That year a ship called the *Ideal X* carried 58 shipping containers from New Jersey to Texas. The writer Marc Levinson worked out that in 1956 loading a ton of cargo in containers cost about 16 cents. Loading it by hand cost about $5.86. In 1958 Pan Am began flying jet airliners across the Atlantic Ocean, about twice as fast as the older planes.

Highway officials forced the people of more than 475,000 households, more than a million people, out of their homes to make room for federal roads. A household is the people who live in one home, and federal roads are roads paid for by the national government. That number is the US Department of Transportation's estimate, a figure worked out rather than an exact count. Private railroads were losing money on passenger trains, and in 1971 a new company, Amtrak, took over most of them.

#### The Interstate highways

On June 29, 1956, President Eisenhower signed the Federal-Aid Highway Act. The law allowed for 41,000 miles of new highways, called the Interstate Highway System. It was the largest public works program in the history of the United States up to then. Public works are projects that the government pays for and the public uses, such as roads and bridges. The system is about 48,900 miles long today. In 1990 members of Congress added Eisenhower's name to it.

Interstate highways went around Route 66. Officials of AASHTO, the association of state highway officials, took Route 66 off the list of numbered U.S. highways on June 27, 1985.

<a id="story-dwight-eisenhower-transportation"></a>

#### Dwight Eisenhower

> **Who:** The president who signed the Interstate highway law, 37 years after he crossed the country in an Army motor convoy.
>
> **When and where:** The 1919 convoy from Washington, D.C., to San Francisco. The highway law, June 29, 1956.

In 1919 the Army's first convoy of motor vehicles crossed the country. A convoy is a group of vehicles traveling together. It had 81 vehicles and went 3,251 miles, from Washington, D.C., to San Francisco. The trip took 62 days. Its vehicles sank in mud and broke down, and bridges failed under them.

Dwight Eisenhower was a young Army officer, a lieutenant colonel, and he volunteered to go. He wrote a report on the trip. In 1945, at the end of World War II, he saw the autobahns, Germany's highways. After those two experiences, he argued for a system of highways across the United States. As president he signed the law for it on June 29, 1956.

#### The homes the highways took

The people who planned the Interstates ran many of them through city neighborhoods, and they took the homes that stood in the way. By the US Department of Transportation's estimate, highway officials took the homes of more than 475,000 households, more than a million people, for federal roads. The planning scholar Alan Altshuler made an estimate in those years. He said the new system would push out up to a million people, "a disproportionate number of them Black." Disproportionate means more than their share. The law professor Deborah N. Archer says the neighborhoods chosen "were largely Black and poor."

In Montgomery, Alabama, Interstate 85 ran south of the city in the plans drawn up in 1955. Sam Engelhardt became head of the Alabama State Highway Department in 1959. His business cards read "I Stand for White Supremacy and Segregation." Under Engelhardt, state highway officials chose a final route through Montgomery's only middle-class Black neighborhood. Ralph Abernathy, a minister and civil rights leader, lived there, and Alabama State University stood next to it. An engineering firm had suggested a route through Oak Park. City officials had closed that park rather than let Black people use it.

Highway officials took about 356 homes in the Centennial Hill, Bel Air and Bottoms neighborhoods. They paid owners an average of $3,300 a house. In 1961 Abernathy sent a telegram, a short message sent over electric wires, to President John F. Kennedy. He wrote that the route "will destroy one of the best negro neighborhoods in the south." "Negro" was the common word for Black people in his time. Rebecca Retzlaff, a researcher at Auburn University, told this history in a 2019 study.

In St. Paul, Minnesota, highway officials built Interstate 94 through the Black neighborhood of Rondo from 1956 to 1968. Counts of what was lost differ. One puts it at about 600 families. Another puts it at about 700 homes and 300 businesses.

#### Jets in the sky

Two airliners left Los Angeles three minutes apart on June 30, 1956. One was TWA Flight 2, and the other was United Air Lines Flight 718. Over the Grand Canyon in Arizona, they flew into each other. The crash killed all 128 people on the two planes. It was the deadliest airplane crash in the world up to that time. The crash was a major reason the Federal Aviation Agency was set up in 1958.

Pan Am flew a Boeing 707 jet from New York to Paris with 111 passengers and 12 crew members on October 26, 1958. It was the first jet service across the Atlantic by an American airline, and the trip took about 8 hours. The older airliners were propeller planes. The 707 flew about twice as fast and carried about twice as many people.

Before 1978 the members of a federal board, the Civil Aeronautics Board, decided which airlines could start or stop flying and what they could charge. President Jimmy Carter signed the Airline Deregulation Act on October 24, 1978. Under that law, the board lost its control of fares and routes. Under the CAB Sunset Act, a part of that law, lawmakers set dates for the board to lose its powers one by one. The board shut down on December 31, 1984. Two economists, Morrison and Winston, studied the change for the Brookings Institution, a research group. Economists study money, prices and trade. Morrison and Winston worked out that fares ended up about 22 percent lower than they would have been under the old rules. Counted in dollars adjusted for rising prices, average fares fell about 40 to 45 percent in the decades after 1978, by government and industry figures.

<a id="story-barbara-dusty-roads"></a>

#### Barbara "Dusty" Roads

> **Who:** An American Airlines stewardess who fought the airline's rule that fired women at age 32 or when they married.
>
> **When and where:** American Airlines, from 1950. She lived from 1928 to 2023.
>
> **Movie:** *Fly With Me* (2024), a PBS *American Experience* documentary about flight attendants, directed by Sarah Colt and Helen Dobrowski. Roads appears in it.

Barbara Roads, called Dusty, joined American Airlines as a stewardess in 1950. A stewardess was a woman who served passengers on an airplane. Today the job is called flight attendant. In 1953, American's managers put a rule into a contract that any stewardess hired after November 1953 would be fired at age 32. A stewardess who married was fired too. In a radio interview, Roads gave her view of the reason: "It was cheaper to have someone that'll never get married, never have babies, never get pensions, never get the highest rate of pay."

Roads lobbied members of Congress on her own flights to Washington, D.C. To lobby is to try to talk lawmakers into doing something. In 1963 she held a news conference that made the papers. At news conferences she also asked reporters to pick the 32-year-old stewardesses out of a lineup. Representative Martha Griffiths helped her. In August 1968 the stewardesses came close to a strike, a refusal to work until their demands were met. By Roads's account, American's managers dropped the age rule the day after someone asked Griffiths to press the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. That is the federal office that handles complaints of unfair treatment at work.

In 1977 Roads helped start the Association of Professional Flight Attendants, a union. She worked for American Airlines for 44 years.

#### The Freedom Rides

In May 1961 Black and white riders traveled together by bus into the South. They were called Freedom Riders. They were testing a court order that banned separating Black and white travelers in bus stations used for trips between states. On May 4, two groups, John Lewis among them, left Washington, D.C., on a Greyhound bus and a Trailways bus, headed for New Orleans.

On May 14, at Anniston, Alabama, a white mob with clubs and bats attacked the Greyhound. They broke its windows and slashed its tires, then chased the bus until the flat tires stopped it several miles out of town. One of the attackers threw a firebomb, a bomb that starts a fire, through a window. The riders and other passengers barely got out of the flames. E. L. Cowling, a state officer riding the bus in plain clothes, held the attackers back with his gun. The mob beat the riders while the bus burned, until police arrived. Later that day white men got on the Trailways bus at Anniston and beat the riders on it. Their beating left one rider, Walter Bergman, a white man, with permanent brain damage.

The same day, a crowd met the Trailways bus in Birmingham with pipes, chains and baseball bats. Many in the crowd belonged to the Ku Klux Klan, a group that used violence against Black people and their supporters. Eugene "Bull" Connor, the city official in charge of the police, had told Klan leaders that the police would hold back from the bus station for 15 minutes. He encouraged the Klan to attack the riders. With no police there, Klansmen beat the riders in the waiting room and in a dark hallway. They beat James Peck, a white rider, until he was unconscious, and he needed more than 50 stitches. Walter Bergman was beaten for the second time that day.

On May 20, a white crowd in Montgomery attacked a new group of riders arriving by Greyhound. They beat John Seigenthaler, a Justice Department official, until he was unconscious. Alabama's public safety director, Floyd Mann, had arranged protection for the buses up to Montgomery. Montgomery police did not take over the protection, and Mann went into the fighting himself. Governor John Patterson blamed the riders for the violence.

Justice Department officials asked the Interstate Commerce Commission to act. Its members were federal officials in charge of trade and travel between states. They banned keeping Black and white passengers apart in bus and train stations. The ban was issued on September 22, 1961, and took effect on November 1, 1961. People in many Southern towns kept ignoring it.

#### Amtrak takes over the passenger trains

Private railroad companies were losing money on their passenger trains. In 1970 members of Congress passed the Rail Passenger Service Act and created a new company called Amtrak. On May 1, 1971, Amtrak began running most of the passenger trains between American cities, which the private railroads gave up.

#### The shipping container

Before containers, dockworkers loaded cargo onto ships by hand. On April 26, 1956, a ship called the *Ideal X* left Port Newark, New Jersey, carrying 58 metal boxes. Each box was 35 feet long, the size of a truck trailer. These boxes are called shipping containers. The ship reached Houston, Texas, five days later.

Marc Levinson worked out what the change saved in his book *The Box*. In 1956 loading cargo by hand cost about $5.86 a ton. Loading it in containers cost about 16 cents a ton. In the late 1960s, an international standards group set standard sizes for containers, and the same boxes came into use around the world.

<a id="story-malcom-mclean"></a>

#### Malcom McLean

> **Who:** A North Carolina trucking owner who sold his trucking company to start shipping truck-sized boxes by sea.
>
> **When and where:** Port Newark, New Jersey, April 26, 1956.

Malcom McLean sent the *Ideal X* to sea with its 58 containers on April 26, 1956. He had started in 1934 in North Carolina with one used truck and built it into a trucking company. Then he sold the trucking company and put the money into shipping containers by sea.

#### Deaths in car crashes

Car crashes killed 54,589 people in the United States in 1972. That is the most in any single year, before or since. By 1975 the yearly count had fallen to 44,525.

#### The minivan

Workers in Windsor, Ontario, in Canada, built the first Dodge Caravan and Plymouth Voyager minivans on November 2, 1983. A minivan is a tall, boxy car with room for a family and its bags. They went on sale as 1984 models.

### 2000 to Today

Since 2000, Americans have used phones to find their way and to hire rides, and some of them drive electric cars. In 2024 about 8 of every 100 new cars sold were electric, according to Kelley Blue Book. In 2025 about 7 of every 100 bridges in the country were rated in poor condition in federal records, by the count of a road builders' group.

Federal safety officials counted 43,230 deaths in car crashes in 2021. Their early estimate for 2025, published in April 2026, is about 36,640. In 2024 a container ship that had lost power hit a bridge in Baltimore. The bridge fell, and the fall killed six road workers. In 2025 an Army helicopter and a passenger jet collided near Washington, D.C., and the crash killed all 67 people aboard.

#### Maps and rides on a phone

GPS, the Global Positioning System, uses signals from satellites to show a GPS device where it is. Until 2000 a setting called Selective Availability made GPS less exact for ordinary users. Federal officials switched the setting off a few minutes after midnight at the end of May 1, 2000. According to the government's GPS website, the error of an ordinary GPS device shrank from about 100 meters to about 20 meters.

People also began hiring rides through apps on their phones. According to Britannica and news reports, Uber began in March 2009 as a company called UberCab. It started its app service in San Francisco on July 5, 2010. In October 2010, after receiving an official order to stop, the company's owners changed its name to Uber. Lyft started its service in June 2012.

In a ride-hailing app, a rider asks for a ride, and a driver using a personal car takes the job. The companies' managers called their drivers independent contractors, meaning people in business for themselves rather than employees. In 2015 a California state hearing officer ruled that one driver, Barbara Ann Berwick, was Uber's employee and that Uber owed her money for the costs of her car.

<a id="story-barbara-berwick"></a>

#### Barbara Ann Berwick

> **Who:** A San Francisco Uber driver who asked the state of California to decide whether she was Uber's employee, and won.
>
> **When and where:** San Francisco, July to September 2014. The decision came on June 3, 2015.

Barbara Ann Berwick drove for Uber in San Francisco, in her own car, for about eight weeks in the summer of 2014. She quit on September 18, 2014. Uber's managers called her an independent contractor, and the company did not pay her back for the costs of her car. She took a claim to the California Labor Commissioner, the state office that handles pay disputes. On March 10, 2015, she argued her case herself at a hearing, a meeting where each side tells its story to an official who decides. Uber sent two lawyers and a product manager, Brian Tolkin.

The hearing officer, Stephanie Barrett, listed the rules Uber's managers set for its drivers. The car could be no more than 10 years old, counted by its model year, and the company had to approve it. Drivers needed $1,000,000 in insurance. They had to keep a rating from riders of 4.6 stars or higher, or the company turned off their app. The agreement said riders did not tip. Barrett wrote that Uber was "involved in every aspect of the operation."

On June 3, 2015, Barrett ruled that Berwick was Uber's employee. She ordered Uber to pay Berwick $4,152.20. That was 56 cents a mile for 6,468 miles, plus $256 in bridge tolls and $274.12 in interest, extra money owed for the time she had waited to be paid. Barrett turned down Berwick's claim for unpaid wages, because Berwick agreed that Uber had paid her.

Uber's lawyers asked a court in San Francisco to undo the decision. In a statement, Uber's spokespeople said the ruling applied to Berwick alone. Uber's managers kept treating the company's other drivers as contractors.

#### The fight over drivers' pay

In November 2020, California voters decided the question for app drivers in their state. They passed Proposition 22, a law put to the voters directly, 58.6 percent to 41.4 percent. The law kept app drivers as contractors. It also set a minimum for their pay: 120 percent of the minimum wage for the time drivers spent working on a ride request, plus 30 cents a mile. Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, Instacart and Postmates paid for the campaign for it, which raised $205.7 million. Ballotpedia tracks state ballot questions from official vote counts and money reports. It lists that as the most money raised for any California ballot question up to then.

On January 12, 2021, four drivers and a union went to court to overturn the law. The drivers were Hector Castellanos, Joseph Delgado, Saori Okawa and Michael Robinson. The union was the Service Employees International Union, a group of workers who bargain together with their employers. On July 25, 2024, the justices of the California Supreme Court ruled that the law could stand.

In Massachusetts, the state's top lawyer, Attorney General Maura Healey, sued Uber and Lyft in 2020. On June 27, 2024, the next attorney general, Andrea Campbell, ended the case with a deal, as WBUR, a Boston public radio station, reported. Leaders of Uber and Lyft agreed that the two companies would pay $175 million. They also agreed that the companies would pay drivers in the state at least $32.50 an hour for time spent driving to a rider or carrying one. The drivers stayed contractors.

#### Bigger vehicles and electric ones

In 2001, Americans bought more light trucks than cars for the first time. Light trucks are pickups, sport utility vehicles (SUVs) and minivans. They made up 50.8 percent of new vehicle sales that year, against 49.2 percent for cars, according to trade magazines that follow the business. The gap grew wider in the years after.

Tesla delivered its first Model S electric cars to buyers on June 22, 2012, in Fremont, California, according to the company and news reports. The company is named after the inventor Nikola Tesla, who died in 1943. He had no connection to the company.

Americans bought about 1.3 million electric cars in 2024 and almost as many in 2025. Kelley Blue Book and Cox Automotive, car-market research companies, published those counts in January 2026. Electric cars made up 8.1 percent of new car sales in 2024 and 7.8 percent in 2025. Tesla sold nearly half of all the electric cars bought in 2025. A tax credit is money taken off what a buyer owes in taxes. In July 2025 members of Congress passed a budget law, and President Donald Trump signed it on July 4. Under it, the federal tax credits for buying electric cars ended for cars bought after September 30, 2025. In the last three months of 2025, Americans bought 234,000 electric cars, 46 percent fewer than in the three months before.

In September 2017, a company called Bird put electric scooters for rent on the streets of Santa Monica, California. In 2018 another company, Lime, followed, and city officials began trial programs for scooters.

#### Ports, trains and bridges

In 2021 ships carrying containers backed up outside American ports. On January 9, 2022, staff at the Marine Exchange of Southern California counted a record 109 container ships waiting off the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. By October 2022 the line was down to about 4 ships.

In November 2008 California voters approved $9.95 billion in bonds, a kind of loan, for high-speed trains from San Francisco to Anaheim. The state's high-speed rail officials then put the cost of the whole system at $33.6 billion. Workers broke ground in Fresno on January 6, 2015. The first section planned is 171 miles, from Merced to Bakersfield.

In July 2025, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy canceled about $4 billion in federal grants, money the national government had promised, for the California line. He said the state's rail agency had "no viable plan," meaning no plan that could work. California officials sued, then dropped the case in December 2025. The project now gets $1 billion a year through 2045 from cap-and-trade, a state program that makes polluters pay for permits to pollute. Associated Press reporters wrote in December 2025 that cost estimates are now above $100 billion. No passenger had ridden a California high-speed train as of 2026.

Researchers at ARTBA, a trade group for companies that build roads, counted the federal bridge records for 2025. The United States had 624,167 bridges, and 41,677 of them were rated in poor condition, about 7 of every 100. Drivers crossed those poor bridges 163 million times a day.

#### Deaths on the roads and in the air

Car crashes killed 43,230 people in the United States in 2021, the most in recent years. The count then fell four years in a row. In April 2026 officials at the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration published an early estimate of 36,640 deaths in 2025. That is 1.10 deaths for every 100 million miles driven. The only lower rate on record was 1.08, in 2014.

At about 1:30 in the morning on March 26, 2024, the container ship *Dali* was leaving Baltimore for Sri Lanka. It lost power and steering and hit a support of the Francis Scott Key Bridge. The bridge fell into the Patapsco River. The fall killed six men who were filling potholes on the bridge on an overnight shift. They were Dorlian Ronial Castillo Cabrera, Carlos Daniel Hernandez Estrella, Alejandro Hernandez Fuentes, Miguel Angel Luna Gonzalez, Jose Mynor Lopez and Maynor Yassir Suazo Sandoval. They were immigrants from Mexico and Central America. Maryland Governor Wes Moore named them in a statement.

In November 2025, members of the National Transportation Safety Board, the federal board that investigates crashes, reported the cause. A label band had been put on a wire the wrong way. The band kept the wire from going all the way into its connector, so the connection came loose. The loose connection cut the ship's power. The board's press release does not say who put the band on or when. The board's members sent safety advice to several groups, among them the ship's builder, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries of South Korea. On May 12, 2026, federal prosecutors, the government lawyers who bring criminal cases, charged the two Synergy Marine companies that ran the ship with crimes. They also charged the *Dali*'s technical superintendent, the manager in charge of the ship's machinery and upkeep, Radhakrishnan Karthik Nair. The charges include causing the deaths of the six workers. A charge is an accusation, not proof. The law treats the companies and Nair as innocent unless a judge or jury finds them guilty. The same day, Attorney General Anthony Brown, Maryland's top lawyer, announced a $2.25 billion settlement with the ship's owner, Grace Ocean, and with Synergy. A settlement is a deal that ends a legal claim.

On January 29, 2025, an Army Black Hawk helicopter collided with an American Eagle passenger jet that was landing at Reagan National Airport near Washington, D.C. The crash killed all 67 people on the two aircraft, 64 on the jet and three soldiers on the helicopter. It was the deadliest crash of an American passenger airline in more than 20 years. On January 27, 2026, the head of the National Transportation Safety Board, Jennifer Homendy, said: "This was preventable. This was 100% preventable." CNN reported that the board's members blamed Federal Aviation Administration officials for helicopter routes that ran close to the path planes took down to the runway. The board's members also blamed those officials for failing to act on years of reports of near misses.

<a id="ch-landmarks"></a>

## Chapter 12: Landmarks

### Before 1500

The oldest landmarks in the United States were built by Native people, hundreds and even thousands of years before any European arrived. They piled up mounds of earth, and one of them covers more ground than the Great Pyramid in Egypt. In the Southwest they built stone houses with hundreds of rooms and set whole villages under cliffs.

No one wrote down the names of the people who built these places. In the Southwest, the builders' descendants, among them the Pueblo peoples, still live in the same region.

#### Monks Mound and the mound builders

The largest structure made of earth in North and South America is Monks Mound, at Cahokia in what is now Illinois. A mound is a hill that people build by piling up earth. People built Monks Mound in stages, mostly between about the years 1050 and 1200. It stands about 100 feet tall, and its base covers about 14 acres. The base of the Great Pyramid of Giza, in Egypt, covers about 13 acres. The pyramid is far taller, so the mound beats it only in the ground it covers.

Poverty Point, in Louisiana, is much older. People built it between about 1700 BC and 1100 BC. BC means "before Christ," and it counts years backward from the year 1 of the calendar used today. The builders lived by hunting, fishing and gathering wild food. They raised five mounds and six curved ridges of earth, set one inside another around a wide open space in the middle. It is the largest earthwork of its age north of Mexico. An earthwork is anything people build by moving earth.

UNESCO is an agency of the United Nations, and its World Heritage List names places chosen for their importance to all people. On June 22, 2014, members of UNESCO's World Heritage Committee, meeting in Doha, Qatar, added Poverty Point to that list. It was the 1,001st place on the list and the 22nd in the United States.

Serpent Mound, in Ohio, is a snake shaped out of earth, about a quarter of a mile long. It is the largest snake-shaped mound in the world. Nothing found inside it shows who built it. Archaeologists, scientists who study the past from the things people left behind, have tested it with radiocarbon dating. That method measures the age of material that was once alive. Tests done in 1991 gave a date of about the year 1070, which matches a people archaeologists call the Fort Ancient culture. Tests done in 2014 gave a date of about 300 BC, which matches a people they call the Adena culture. Archaeologists' later work has found evidence for both dates. They now think it possible that people built the mound in one period and rebuilt it in another.

#### Stone buildings of the Southwest

In Chaco Canyon, in what is now New Mexico, people built large stone buildings called great houses between about 850 and 1150. The largest, Pueblo Bonito, rose four stories high. It held about 600 to 650 rooms, or more. The counts differ because some of them include a guess at how many rooms the upper floors held, and some do not.

At Mesa Verde, in what is now Colorado, people built Cliff Palace between about 1190 and 1280. They set it under an overhang, a place where the rock of the cliff sticks out above like a roof. Cliff Palace has about 150 rooms and 23 kivas. A kiva is a room used for religious ceremonies. It is the largest cliff dwelling in North America.

The builders' descendants are the Pueblo peoples of the Southwest. The National Park Service lists 26 tribes with a special tie to Mesa Verde. Among them are the Hopi Tribe, the 19 Pueblos of New Mexico, including Zuni, Taos and Acoma, and the Navajo Nation. The Ute Mountain Ute, the Southern Ute, the Northern Ute and the Jicarilla Apache are also on the list.

#### The Hopewell earthworks of Ohio

About 2,000 years ago, Native people in southern Ohio built long walls of earth in the shapes of circles and eight-sided figures. Archaeologists call these people the Hopewell culture. Hopewell is a name archaeologists gave them, and it is not the name of any nation. Written accounts differ on when the building went on. A National Park Service article states that the work took about 400 years, and an article in the Smithsonian's *American Indian* magazine dates it from about the year 1 to about the year 400. A report on WVXU, a public radio station in Cincinnati, states a longer span, from 200 BC to the year 500.

The Octagon Earthworks, in Newark, Ohio, is a large circle of earth joined to an eight-sided wall. An octagon is a shape with eight sides. Together the two walls surround nearly 70 acres. The walls line up with the points where the moon rises, in a pattern that repeats every 18.6 years.

In 1910 the Moundbuilders Country Club began leasing the Octagon and used it as a golf course. To lease land is to rent it. The Ohio Historical Society has owned the land since 1933. It is a group set up under state law, and it is not run to make money. It is now called the Ohio History Connection, and for decades its leaders kept leasing the site to the club.

On September 19, 2023, the members of UNESCO's World Heritage Committee voted to add eight Hopewell earthwork sites to the World Heritage List. The Octagon was one of them.

<a id="story-glenna-wallace"></a>

#### Glenna Wallace

> **Who:** Chief of the Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma from 2006 to 2026, the first woman to be the tribe's chief.
>
> **When and where:** The Octagon Earthworks, Newark, Ohio, from the late 2000s to 2025.

Glenna Wallace worked for years to get a golf course off the Octagon Earthworks. She was born in about 1939 in Ottawa County, Oklahoma. She taught and worked at Crowder College in Neosho, Missouri, for 38 years. In 2006 the Eastern Shawnee elected her chief. She was the first woman to hold that job.

Her people once lived in western Ohio, near a place called Lewistown, on land they shared with a band of Seneca. On July 20, 1831, the band signed a treaty with James B. Gardiner, a commissioner, or special official, sent by the United States. A treaty is a written agreement between nations. In it the band gave up about 48 square miles of land near Lewistown, plus 8,960 acres of a reservation dating from 1818. A reservation is land set aside for a Native nation. In return Gardiner promised, for the United States, 60,000 acres west of the Mississippi River. Under the treaty, US officials had to move the band there.

In 1832 US officials forced the people out of Ohio. A profile of Wallace by the Ohio History Connection states that they walked about 800 miles. More than 15 percent of them died on the way. No record of the march names the officials who led it. In December 1832 the band received the 60,000 acres Gardiner had promised, as a reservation in what is now Ottawa County, Oklahoma.

Wallace first visited the Octagon Earthworks in the late 2000s. An article in the Smithsonian's *American Indian* magazine gives the year as 2007, and other accounts give 2009. While she was there, a golfer shouted at her, "Out of the way! You don't belong here!" She decided to get the golf course off the earthworks and to win World Heritage status for them.

Leaders of the Ohio History Connection went to court to end the club's lease. They used eminent domain, a legal power to take property for public use as long as the owner is paid. On December 7, 2022, the judges of the Ohio Supreme Court ruled 5 to 1 that they could do it.

In 2023 the members of the World Heritage Committee met in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and voted to add the Hopewell earthworks to the list. Wallace gave the main speech at that meeting. In August 2024 leaders of the club and of the Ohio History Connection agreed to end the court case. They did not make the terms of their deal public. Wallace said, "At last. So many people have worked so long for this to become reality." The club ran the golf course until the end of 2024. The Octagon opened to the public on January 1, 2025. Wallace retired as chief in 2026, after 20 years.

### The 1500s

Nothing that Europeans built here in the 1500s still stands. The Spanish built their first forts in Florida of wood and earth. Those forts burned many times, and the Spanish rebuilt them again and again. A mission was a settlement run by Catholic priests, where Native people lived and were taught the Catholic religion. Spanish mission buildings of this century, in Florida and in the Southwest, survive only as remains in the ground that archaeologists dig up. Native mounds and stone buildings of earlier centuries, such as Monks Mound and Cliff Palace, were still standing, and they still stand today.

#### St. Augustine's founding site

St. Augustine, Florida, began in a Native town. On September 8, 1565, Pedro Menéndez de Avilés landed at Seloy, a town of the Timucua people. The Spanish made their first settlement in Seloy's village. People have lived in St. Augustine without a break ever since. Of all the cities that Europeans founded on the mainland of the United States, it is the oldest that people never left.

In 1586 Francis Drake and his men burned the town. The only landmark left from this century is the place where the Spanish settled. Nothing they built there in the 1500s survives above ground. The stone fort that still stands in St. Augustine, about a mile south of Seloy, was begun in 1672.

### The 1600s

Three buildings from the 1600s are among the oldest buildings put up by Europeans that still stand in the United States. One is a Spanish stone fort in Florida. Another is a chapel in Santa Fe, New Mexico, made of adobe, or sun-dried mud brick. The third is a wooden church building in Massachusetts, called a meetinghouse. Spanish officials forced Native men from their towns to work on the fort in Florida, cutting its stone.

#### A fort built of shell stone

Spanish officials ordered a stone fort built at St. Augustine after pirates attacked the town. On the night of May 28, 1668, about a hundred English pirates came ashore at midnight and looted St. Augustine. They killed more than 50 Spaniards. The pirates said they would come back and take the town's fort. Queen Mariana of Spain then named Manuel de Cendoya governor of Florida. She sent him to the viceroy of New Spain, the king's highest official in Mexico. There he was to collect 12,000 pesos, which were Spanish coins, to begin a fort of stone.

Workers broke ground on October 2, 1672. Cendoya laid the first foundation stone on November 9. The main work was finished in about 1687, under Governor Juan Cabrera. Governor Laureano de Torres had the last stones set on the fort's water defenses in 1695 or 1696. Two histories written for the National Park Service give different years. Albert Manucy, who wrote the first one in 1942, gives 1696, and a 1993 park handbook gives August 1695. By 1696 the fort had cost close to 100,000 pesos. It is called the Castillo de San Marcos, and it is the oldest masonry fort in the continental United States. Masonry means built of stone or brick.

The fort is made of coquina, a soft stone made of packed seashells. Workers cut the coquina from quarries on Anastasia Island, across the bay from the town. A quarry is a pit where stone is cut out of the ground. The workers cut grooves in the rock with picks and axes, then broke the blocks loose with bars and wedges. The largest blocks were 2 feet thick and 4 feet long. Manucy wrote that six strong men "could hardly lift" one of them. Oxen dragged the blocks to a dock, and rafts carried them across the bay.

The stones are held together with mortar, a paste that hardens. Workers made lime, a white powder, for the mortar by burning oyster shells in kilns, or very hot ovens. By the spring of 1672 they had stored about 7,000 bushels of lime. A bushel is a measure of about 8 gallons. The walls they built are 14 feet thick at the base and about 9 feet thick at the top.

English soldiers attacked the fort twice and failed both times. In November 1702, Governor James Moore of Carolina came with an army, and Colonel Robert Daniel was at his side. Almost 1,500 people crowded into the fort for safety. The siege lasted about two months. A siege is an attack in which an army surrounds a place and tries to force the people inside to give up. The English cannonballs did not shatter the walls. The shell stone crushed inward where each ball hit, so the balls sank into the wall or bounced off.

When a Spanish force arrived to help, the English set fire to their own ships and retreated. As they left, Daniel's troops and their Native allies burned the rest of St. Augustine to the ground. The fort and the people inside it survived. In 1740 General James Oglethorpe of Georgia besieged the fort for 27 days, and he failed too. The fort is now the Castillo de San Marcos National Monument.

#### Who cut the stone

Spanish officials forced Native men to work on the Castillo. At times up to 300 Native people were working for the Spanish king in St. Augustine, on the fort and in the corn fields. The men came from three nations: the Guale of what is now Georgia, the Timucua of eastern Florida and the Apalache of western Florida. Officials drafted them for labor in their home towns. A draft is an order that forces people to serve. Some of the men had to walk about 200 miles to reach St. Augustine. Manucy wrote that "many of them served unwillingly."

A drafted man had two choices. He could bring his family with him, or he could leave his wife and children in the village to feed themselves. Officials drafted even some chiefs. They kept men working past the end of their terms. One chief was forced to work on the fort for more than three years without once going home. Some governors used Native men as their own servants. Spanish officials had sentenced the Apalache, years before, to work on the forts as a punishment for rebelling.

The Native laborers were paid 1 real a day, plus a daily share of corn. A real was a Spanish silver coin. Manucy counted it as worth 12 and a half cents, and the 1993 park handbook puts it at about 20 cents. Spanish master masons on the same job earned 20 reales a day.

The work needed about 150 laborers, and officials found it hard to get even 100. In the first winter, a sickness the Spanish called El Contagio, "the contagion," spread among the Native laborers. The crew shrank to almost no one. Manucy's history does not count how many men died. The payrolls, the lists of workers and their pay, counted the Guale, Timucua and Apalache men who cut the stone. Manucy's history and the 1993 park handbook were both written from those payrolls. They give the men's nations and numbers, but not their names.

Spanish officials also put convicts to work on the fort. These were men sentenced to work there for a set number of years. One Spaniard caught smuggling English goods got 6 years of labor on the fort. His term would double if he ran away. Enslaved Black people owned by the Spanish king worked there too. In 1687 Spanish officials added eighteen of the king's slaves to the work crew.

That same year, eleven people escaped slavery in Carolina and reached St. Augustine. They were eight men, two women and a nursing baby. Governor Diego de Quiroga y Losada gave them shelter. He had them baptized in the Catholic Church, a ceremony with water that makes a person a member of the church. He hired the men as paid workers, and six of them worked on the Castillo. In 1693 King Charles II of Spain ordered that enslaved people who escaped from the English colonies and became Catholic would be free.

<a id="story-john-collins-castillo"></a>

#### John Collins

> **Who:** An English prisoner who burned lime and ran the stone quarry for the Castillo de San Marcos.
>
> **When and where:** St. Augustine, Florida, from 1670 for 19 years or more.

John Collins was an English mason, a builder in stone, whom the Spanish held as a prisoner and put to work on the Castillo. In 1670 a ship was sailing for the new English colony at Charleston, in Carolina. It landed by accident at the Spanish mission of Santa Catalina, near the Savannah River. The Spanish there captured two Englishmen from the ship, William Carr and John Rivers. A small boat came from Charleston to get them back, and Joseph Bailey and John Collins carried a message ashore. The Spanish held them too and sent all four men to St. Augustine as prisoners.

Governor Manuel de Cendoya put the prisoners to work on the fort. On the Spanish payroll, Collins's name appears as Juan Calens. According to Manucy's history, Collins could burn more oyster shells into lime in a week than Spanish workmen could in two. The lime went into the mortar that held the coquina blocks together. As a prisoner he was paid 8 reales a day. A master workman was owed 20.

Collins rose from master of the lime kilns to master of the quarry. Later he ran the dugout boats, the food stores and the convict workers. At last he held the job of pilot, guiding ships between St. Augustine and Charleston. Officials of the Spanish king recognized his work after he had spent 19 years or more in the town. Neither Manucy's history nor the 1993 park handbook says when he was born or died, or whether he ever went home.

#### The oldest churches

San Miguel Chapel in Santa Fe, New Mexico, is often called the oldest church in the country. Its site and its foundations are that old, but most of the walls standing today date from a rebuilding in 1710. The chapel is built of adobe, bricks made of mud and straw and dried in the sun. It was built around 1620 as a church for the soldiers, servants and laborers of the town's Spanish officials, and it was in use before 1626.

The chapel was partly destroyed in 1680, when the Pueblo people of northern New Mexico rose up against Spanish rule. Spanish officials had been collecting tribute, payments of goods, from the Pueblos. They had also used their power to keep the Pueblo people from practicing their own religion. A religious leader named Popé planned the uprising from Taos. In the uprising, called the Pueblo Revolt, the Pueblo people drove the Spanish out of the region. The Spanish stayed out until 1692, when Diego de Vargas led them back. The histories of the chapel written for the National Park Service and the Historic Santa Fe Foundation do not say who damaged it. In 1710 Governor José Chacón had it rebuilt on the old foundations.

The Old Ship Meetinghouse in Hingham, Massachusetts, was built in 1681. The Puritans, a group of English Protestants who settled in New England, met in buildings like this one for church. It is the only Puritan meetinghouse from the 1600s still standing in the country. It is also the oldest church building in the United States that has been in use without a break. Its roof rests on a frame of heavy timbers, left open to view from inside. The frame reminded the people who worshiped there of the hull, or body, of a ship turned upside down. That is how the building got its name.

### 1700 to 1750

In the first half of the 1700s, colonists put up public buildings that are still landmarks today. The first lighthouse in what became the United States was lit in 1716, at the mouth of Boston Harbor. Boston's Old North Church went up in 1723. In 1732 builders in Philadelphia began a statehouse for Pennsylvania, a building where the colony's lawmakers would meet. It is now called Independence Hall. In Texas, Spanish priests ran a mission, a settlement where Native people lived and were taught the Catholic religion. There, at the place later known as the Alamo, the first stone of a stone church was laid in 1744.

#### The first lighthouse

Boston Light stands on Little Brewster Island, at the entrance to Boston Harbor. A lighthouse is a tower with a bright light at the top that warns ships away from rocks and guides them into harbor. Boston Light was first lit on September 16, 1716. It was the first lighthouse in what became the United States.

British forces blew up the tower in 1776. It was rebuilt in 1783, and the 1783 tower is the one that stands today.

<a id="story-george-worthylake"></a>

#### George Worthylake

> **Who:** The first keeper of Boston Light, the first lighthouse in what became the United States.
>
> **When and where:** Little Brewster Island, Boston Harbor, 1716 to 1718.

George Worthylake became the first keeper of Boston Light in 1716. He was paid £50 a year, 50 British pounds, to keep the light burning from sundown to sunrise. Worthylake lived on the island with his wife Ann and his daughter Ruth. He earned extra money guiding ships in and out of the harbor, and he kept a flock of sheep on Great Brewster Island, next door.

On November 3, 1718, the family had gone into Boston for a church sermon. Just after noon, on the way back to the island, their canoe tipped over. Worthylake, Ann and Ruth all drowned. Shadwell, a man Worthylake enslaved, drowned with them. So did George Cutler, a servant, and John Edge, a friend of the family.

Benjamin Franklin was 12 years old and working for his older brother, a printer in Boston. His brother had him write a ballad about the drowning called "The Lighthouse Tragedy." A ballad is a poem that tells a story and can be sung. Once it was printed, Franklin's brother sent him around the town to sell copies. Franklin later called his own verses "wretched stuff," and no copy survives. A few days after the Worthylakes died, the next keeper, Robert Saunders, drowned too.

#### A steeple and a statehouse

Old North Church in Boston, also called Christ Church, was built in 1723. It is the oldest church building still standing in Boston. Its steeple, the tall pointed tower on top, was finished in 1740 and is 191 feet high. On April 18, 1775, the church's sexton, or caretaker, Robert Newman, and Captain John Pulling Jr. hung two lanterns in the steeple. The lanterns were a signal, worked out by Paul Revere, that British troops were moving by water.

Work on the Pennsylvania State House in Philadelphia began in 1732 and ended in 1753, 21 years later. Andrew Hamilton designed it with Edmund Woolley, a master carpenter. Workers added its tower from 1750 to 1753. In 1753 a bell was hung in the new tower. Words on the bell read "Proclaim liberty throughout all the land." The building is now called Independence Hall.

#### The mission church later called the Alamo

Father Antonio de San Buenaventura y Olivares, a Spanish priest, founded Mission San Antonio de Valero in San Antonio, Texas, on May 1, 1718. Soldiers sent by Governor Martín de Alarcón came with him. The people who lived at this mission came from more than a hundred Native groups. Among them were the Payaya, the Pamaya, the Xarame, the Apache and the Karankawa. Diseases brought by Europeans had already killed many Native people in the region. Many came to the San Antonio missions for protection from their enemies and for a steadier supply of food.

As a rule, the Spanish forced no one to come in. Once people had joined a Texas mission, though, priests and soldiers used force to keep them. Soldiers went out to bring back people, and whole groups, who left. In 1739 an epidemic of smallpox and measles struck the mission. An epidemic is an outbreak of a disease that spreads to many people at the same time. In 1745 the mission had 311 residents.

The cornerstone of a stone church was laid on May 8, 1744. A cornerstone is the first stone set at a corner of a new building. That church fell down in the 1750s.
