Work on the church that stands today began in 1758. The missionaries never finished it. The bell towers and the dome they planned were never built. The records do not say who laid the church's stones.

In 1793 Spanish officials closed the mission and divided its lands among the Native people and other residents who were still there. The old mission church is known today as the Alamo.

### 1750 to 1800

Enslaved people worked at every stage of building the first buildings of the new national capital. Leaders of the United States began building the capital beside the Potomac River in the 1790s. Its two main buildings were the President's House and the Capitol. The officials in charge rented enslaved men from their owners, and the owners collected the pay. Two houses of the time that are landmarks today, Mount Vernon and Monticello, were also built by enslaved workers.

#### Raising the capital's buildings

The land chosen for the capital had been home to the Nacotchtank people. In 1608 the English captain John Smith traveled up the Potomac River and found their villages there. European settlers brought diseases that killed many of the Nacotchtank. In colonial times most of their groups joined other Native peoples, and some moved away.

The President's House, later called the White House, was designed by James Hoban, an architect born in Ireland. Its cornerstone was laid on October 13, 1792. A cornerstone is the first stone set at a corner of a new building, often in a ceremony. On September 18, 1793, George Washington laid the cornerstone of the Capitol, the building where Congress meets. Neither building was done by 1800. When John Adams moved into the President's House in November 1800, it was still unfinished. The Capitol had only one wing.

#### Enslaved men who built the capital

Enslaved people worked at every stage of building the President's House and the Capitol. They quarried sandstone, cut timber, made bricks, sawed boards, did carpentry and hauled loads. On December 2, 1791, the three commissioners in charge of the new District of Columbia bought a sandstone quarry for $6,000. It was on Aquia Creek, in Stafford County, Virginia. A quarry is a pit where stone is cut out of the ground. At the Government Island quarry, forty Black men worked beside free workers.

William C. Allen, a historian in the office of the Architect of the Capitol, studied the Capitol's payrolls for Congress in 2005. His report states that the commissioners rented enslaved men from their owners by the year. They called this "Negro hire." "Negro" was a word of that time for Black people. The Capitol's accounts list 385 payments for it between February 11, 1795, and May 17, 1801. The money went to the owners. At first an owner got $60 a year for each man. A white laborer with no special skills earned $70 a year. In 1797 the commissioners raised the owners' rate to $70. When a man missed work, the commissioners cut his owner's pay.

Two of the commissioners, Gustavus Scott and William Thornton, rented their own slaves to the project. Thornton also designed the Capitol. James Hoban was paid for enslaved men too, and so was the commissioners' treasurer, William Deakins. Other owners who were paid included Middleton Belt, who oversaw the Capitol's laborers, and a land developer named Thomas Law. Many Maryland slaveholders rented out men too, and several of them were women, such as Ann Digges and five women of the Brent family.

The commissioners told the overseers to keep the rented men at work "from sunrise to sunset," six days a week. The commissioners housed the men in huts. They gave them rations, a set share of food and drink, of salt meat and whiskey. Allen found that the commissioners' overseers probably kept the enslaved sawyers, men who sawed logs into boards, at work seven days a week. For work at night, on Sundays and on holidays, the men themselves got small extra wages.

Only a few of the men's names were written down, and only their first names. The payments name Dick and Tom, rented from Ann Digges in 1795. They also name Nace, Gerrard, David, Charles, Harry, Gabe and Sil, rented from the Brent women in April 1795. Allen wrote that "virtually nothing is known of their lives."

In 1793 a man named Jacob ran away from the work, and his owner offered a $6 reward for him. The historian Bob Arnebeck counts at least 200 known enslaved laborers on the Capitol and the President's House together. Richard Baker, the Senate Historian, and Kenneth Kato of the House history office introduced Allen's report. They wrote that no one will ever know how many enslaved people helped to build the Capitol.

<a id="story-white-house-enslaved-carpenters"></a>

#### Tom, Peter, Ben, Harry, and Daniel

> **Who:** Five enslaved carpenters who helped build the White House. They are known by name from the payroll for May 1795.
>
> **When and where:** The President's House building site, Washington, May 1795.

Tom, Peter, Ben, Harry and Daniel were enslaved carpenters who worked on the President's House in May 1795. The carpenters' payroll for that month lists them by their first names only. James Hoban, the architect of the building, held four of them in slavery. His assistant, Pierce Purcell, held the fifth.

The payroll records how many days the men worked that month. Peter and Ben each worked 28 days. Daniel worked 25 days, and Harry worked 9. Hoban signed for their wages. The pay went to the men's owners and not to the men. The payroll does not give their last names.

#### Landmark houses

Mount Vernon, George Washington's home in Virginia, was built and enlarged by enslaved workers. Monticello, Thomas Jefferson's home in Virginia, was too. Jefferson began building Monticello in 1769 and left it unfinished in 1784. From 1796 to about 1809 he redesigned it and had it rebuilt. Enslaved workers did much of the building and made much of its fine woodwork.

<a id="story-thomas-jefferson-landmarks"></a>

#### Thomas Jefferson

> **Who:** The owner of Monticello, who designed his own house and worked on the design for the Virginia State Capitol.
>
> **When and where:** Monticello, Virginia, 1769 to about 1809. The design for the Virginia State Capitol in Richmond, 1785.

Thomas Jefferson designed his own house at Monticello, and with a French draftsman, a man who drew building plans, he made the design for the Virginia State Capitol. The house at Monticello was under construction from 1769 to about 1809, a span of 40 years. The people he enslaved did much of the building.

In 1785 the Directors of Public Buildings of Virginia asked Jefferson for a design for a new state capitol in Richmond. Jefferson was then the United States minister to France, which means he represented the country to the French government. A French draftsman, Charles-Louis Clérisseau, persuaded him to model the outside of the building on the Maison Carrée. That is an ancient Roman temple in the city of Nîmes, in France. Clérisseau drew the final plans. A plaster model reached Richmond late in 1786 to guide the workmen, and Samuel Dobie built the capitol.

The Virginia General Assembly is the state's group of lawmakers. Its history of the building states that the capitol "introduced the Classical Revival temple style to the modern world." Classical Revival buildings copy the look of the temples of ancient Greece and Rome. The same history states that the capitol "has inspired countless public buildings for over 200 years."

At Monticello, the fine woodwork of the rebuilt rooms was made by enslaved craftsmen. One of them was John Hemmings, a joiner, or maker of fine woodwork.

### 1800 to 1850

Between 1800 and 1850, Americans began building monuments to the Revolution and to George Washington. A monument is something built to help people remember a person or an event. Two of them were tall stone pillars: the Bunker Hill Monument near Boston and the Washington Monument in the capital. The people raising both ran out of money and had to stop building. Workers finished the Bunker Hill Monument in 1842. Work on the Washington Monument stopped in 1854 at about 150 feet, and the stump stood unfinished for 25 years.

#### Two obelisks

Both monuments are obelisks. An obelisk is a tall stone pillar with four sides that narrows toward a pointed top.

The Bunker Hill Monument marks the Battle of Bunker Hill, fought on June 17, 1775. It stands on Breed's Hill in Charlestown, Massachusetts. In 1823 a group of leading citizens of the Boston area formed the Bunker Hill Monument Association to build it.

A cornerstone is the first stone set at a corner of a new building, often in a ceremony. Daniel Webster and the Marquis de Lafayette, a French general, led the ceremony that laid this one on June 17, 1825. That day was the 50th anniversary of the battle. About 40 men who had fought in the battle came, along with about 190 other men who had fought in the Revolutionary War.

The association bought a granite quarry, a pit where stone is cut out of the ground, in Quincy, Massachusetts. Horses pulled the granite blocks three miles to the Neponset River on a railway. A National Park Service article describes it as the first horse-drawn railway built to carry goods as a business. Ships then carried the blocks to Charlestown.

In December 1828, after 19 months of work, the association's money ran out and the work stopped. To pay off its debts, the association sold 10 acres of the old battlefield in 1839. Sarah Josepha Hale organized a Ladies' Fair at Quincy Market in Boston in 1840. The money taken in at the fair came to more than $30,000, about a quarter of the monument's cost. Workers finished the 221-foot granite obelisk in July 1842. It was dedicated, or opened with a public ceremony, on June 17, 1843, with President John Tyler there.

The Washington Monument was begun in the capital on July 4, 1848. About 20,000 people watched members of the Washington National Monument Society lay the cornerstone. By 1854 the society's money was gone, and work stopped at about 150 feet.

That same year, in March 1854, members of the Know-Nothing movement stole a block of marble meant for the monument. Pope Pius IX, the head of the Catholic Church, had given it. The Know-Nothings were people in a political movement who were against Catholics. By the usual account, the thieves threw the stone into the Potomac River. It was never found. From 1855 to 1858 Know-Nothings took control of the monument society. The stump of the monument stood unfinished until 1879.

From 1847 to 1855, workers in Washington put up the Smithsonian Institution Building, built of red sandstone. The architect James Renwick Jr. designed it. Its cornerstone was laid on May 1, 1847. People call it the Castle.

<a id="story-john-hemmings-landmarks"></a>

#### John Hemmings

> **Who:** An enslaved joiner who made the fine woodwork of Monticello's rebuilt rooms.
>
> **When and where:** Monticello and Poplar Forest, Virginia. Born 1776, died 1833.

John Hemmings was a joiner, a woodworker who makes the fine wooden parts inside a house, such as doors, trim and furniture. Thomas Jefferson held him in slavery at Monticello, Jefferson's home in Virginia. Hemmings was born in 1776. From the age of 17 he trained under white joiners whom Jefferson hired.

When Jefferson rebuilt Monticello, Hemmings made the fine woodwork of the remodeled rooms and much of the furniture. Hemmings also led the woodwork at Poplar Forest, Jefferson's other house in Virginia.

Jefferson enslaved more than 600 people during his life. In his will he freed five of them. Hemmings was one of the five, and he became free in 1826. Jefferson also left him the tools of the joiner's shop. Hemmings died in 1833.

### 1850 to 1900

When workers finished the Washington Monument in 1884, it was the tallest structure in the world, at 555 feet. In the same half century, workers raised a bronze statue onto the new dome of the Capitol. Others hung the Brooklyn Bridge from cables and set up the Statue of Liberty in New York Harbor. At least 21 workers died building the Brooklyn Bridge. As St. Louis grew, between 1850 and 1904, almost all of the Native mounds that had stood there for centuries were dug away.

#### The Statue of Freedom

On December 2, 1863, workers set the last section of a bronze statue called Freedom on top of the new dome of the Capitol. From 1860 to 1862 the statue was cast at the foundry of Clark Mills, a sculptor who had taught himself. A foundry is a workshop where metal is melted and poured into molds. One of the men who cast it was Philip Reid, whom Mills held in slavery.

<a id="story-philip-reid-landmarks"></a>

#### Philip Reid

> **Who:** An enslaved foundry worker who helped cast the Statue of Freedom for the dome of the Capitol, and who was free by the day it was raised.
>
> **When and where:** Clark Mills' foundry, Washington, 1860 to 1863.

Philip Reid worked out how to take apart the plaster model of the Statue of Freedom so it could be cast in bronze. He was born in slavery in Charleston, South Carolina, in about 1820. Clark Mills bought him there. Mills said he paid $1,200 for Reid "because of his evident talent for the business."

An Italian sculptor on the job refused to show how to take the model apart unless he got a raise in pay. Reid worked out how to separate the sections himself, using a pulley and tackle, a set of ropes and wheels for lifting heavy loads.

Reid earned $1.25 a day, but he kept only Sunday's pay. Mills collected the pay for the other six days of each week. On April 16, 1862, President Abraham Lincoln signed the District of Columbia Compensated Emancipation Act. Emancipation means setting enslaved people free, and compensated means paid. Counts of the people it freed in the capital differ. The government of the District of Columbia gives 3,100. The US Senate's history office gives 2,989, the number freed through the more than 930 requests that the officials in charge approved in the months after the law passed. Owners who had stayed loyal to the Union, the side of the United States government in the Civil War, could be paid up to $300 for each person. Reid received his freedom that day. When the last section of Freedom was set on the dome in December 1863, Reid was a free man. He later signed his name Philip Reed.

#### The Brooklyn Bridge

The Brooklyn Bridge, in New York, opened on May 24, 1883. It is a suspension bridge, which means its roadway hangs from cables strung between tall towers. At least 21 workers died building it, and the counts differ. The historian David McCullough counted 21 deaths. C. C. Martin, an assistant engineer on the bridge, told the *Brooklyn Eagle* newspaper that 27 men died in accidents. E. F. Farrington, the master mechanic, the head mechanic on the job, said the number could be as high as 40. Most of the dead were immigrants.

The towers stand on caissons. A caisson is a huge box, open at the bottom, sunk to the bottom of the river. Men worked inside it, digging out the riverbed in air pumped in under pressure to keep the water out. When men came up out of that air too quickly, bubbles of gas formed in their blood. The bubbles caused great pain in the joints. They could leave a man paralyzed, unable to move parts of his body, or kill him. This illness is called caisson disease, or the bends.

Dr. Andrew Smith, the bridge company's doctor, gave it the name caisson disease. Between January 25 and May 31, 1872, he treated 110 cases among the roughly 600 men who worked in the air under pressure. Three of them died of it.

Caisson disease killed John Myers on April 22, 1872, Patrick McKay eight days later, and Daniel Reardon within the month. After those deaths, Washington Roebling, the chief engineer, stopped digging the New York caisson any deeper.

Other workers died too. John French and Thomas Douglas died before the caisson deaths, and Neil Mullen died in 1877. In 1878 a strand of cable snapped at the Manhattan end and threw Thomas Blake and Harry Supple, two men from Newfoundland, to their deaths. Caisson disease also crippled many workers who lived.

<a id="story-roeblings"></a>

#### John, Washington, and Emily Roebling

> **Who:** The man who designed the Brooklyn Bridge, the son who took charge of building it, and the son's wife, who carried his instructions to the engineers for 11 years.
>
> **When and where:** New York, 1869 to 1883.
>
> **Movie:** *Brooklyn Bridge* (1981), Ken Burns' first documentary, narrated by David McCullough. It was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature. It is about the bridge and the Roeblings.

John A. Roebling designed the Brooklyn Bridge, but he died before building began. In June 1869 he was measuring the site for a tower when a ferry crushed his foot against the posts that held up the dock. Doctors told him the foot should be cut off. He refused and allowed only a water treatment, with cold water dripped steadily onto the wound. His crushed toes were cut off, and tetanus set in. Tetanus is an infection from a wound that makes the muscles tighten and lock. He died on July 22, 1869.

His son, Washington Roebling, took over as chief engineer. He went down into the caissons with the workers and got caisson disease. He collapsed in 1872 and was left partly paralyzed. For the next ten years he directed the work from a room in Brooklyn Heights, watching the bridge through a telescope.

His wife, Emily Warren Roebling, carried his instructions to the engineers for 11 years. She studied cable construction, the forces on a bridge and the mathematics of bridge building. That let her pass on his orders correctly and answer the engineers' questions. Trustees are people chosen to look after a project or a group's money. When the bridge's trustees tried to remove her husband, she defended him before them. Some writers today call her the bridge's "effective chief engineer," meaning she did much of that job in practice. Washington kept the title and made the engineering decisions from his sickroom. Emily was the person the engineers dealt with every day.

When the bridge opened in 1883, Emily Roebling was the first person to cross it by carriage. She carried a live rooster as a sign of victory.

#### The Washington Monument, finished

In 1876 members of Congress voted to have the federal government take over the unfinished Washington Monument. In 1879 Army engineers led by Lieutenant Colonel Thomas Lincoln Casey started work again. The workers finished the monument on December 6, 1884. On its point they placed a cast aluminum tip that weighed 100 ounces. Aluminum then cost about a dollar an ounce, roughly a day's wage for a laborer, and the whole tip cost $225.

The monument was dedicated on February 21, 1885. At 555 feet, it was the tallest structure in the world until the Eiffel Tower was built in Paris in 1889. About 150 feet up, the color of the marble changes. The stone laid after 1879 came from different beds of rock in the quarries than the stone laid from 1848 to 1854. The line shows where the work stopped for 25 years.

#### Building the Statue of Liberty

People in France gave the money for the Statue of Liberty, and Americans had to raise the money for its pedestal, the tall stone base it stands on. Édouard de Laboulaye proposed the statue in 1865. The sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi designed it.

The statue's finished arm and torch were shown at the Centennial Exhibition, a big fair in Philadelphia in 1876. Centennial means a 100th birthday, and the fair marked 100 years since 1776. From 1877 to 1882 the arm stood in Madison Square Park in New York to draw gifts of money for the pedestal. The engineer Gustave Eiffel joined the work in 1879 and designed the iron frame inside the statue. The statue's copper skin is 3/32 of an inch thick. In the words of the National Park Service, that is "about the thickness of two pennies placed together." The copper hangs on the iron frame.

The architect Richard Morris Hunt designed the pedestal, which was built from 1884 to 1886. Money for it came in slowly until 1885. That year Joseph Pulitzer, who published the *New York World* newspaper, ran a campaign in its pages. More than $100,000 came from about 120,000 donors. Most gave less than a dollar, and many of the gifts were coins from schoolchildren. Every donor's name was printed in the paper.

President Grover Cleveland led the dedication ceremony on October 28, 1886. The statue is 151 feet tall. With its pedestal it stands about 305 feet high.

<a id="story-frederic-auguste-bartholdi"></a>

#### Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi

> **Who:** The French sculptor who designed the Statue of Liberty.
>
> **When and where:** Paris, 1870 to 1885. New York Harbor, dedicated October 28, 1886.

Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi worked on the Statue of Liberty for more than 15 years, from 1870 to 1886. He was born in 1834 in Colmar, in the Alsace region of France, and he died in 1904.

In 1871 Bartholdi traveled to the United States. In a little under three months he chose Bedloe's Island in New York Harbor as the site and met many of the leading people in America. He and Laboulaye set up committees in both countries to raise money.

The statue's skin was made of thin copper sheets shaped by hammering, a method called repoussé. The arm and torch were finished in 1876, and the head and shoulders in 1878. That year the head and shoulders were shown at the Paris Universal Exposition, a world's fair. The whole statue was put together in Paris between 1881 and 1884.

Then it was taken apart again. The French ship Isère carried it across the Atlantic Ocean in 350 pieces packed in 214 crates. It arrived on June 17, 1885. Bartholdi came back to New York with a group sent from France for the dedication in 1886.

#### Mounds dug away for fill

St. Louis, Missouri, was once called the Mound City. It was built among about 40 mounds, hills of earth that Native people built between about the years 600 and 1300. As the city grew, people dug away most of them. One group of 25 mounds stood along the north riverfront. By the 1850s all of them were gone except part of the largest, Big Mound.

Big Mound stood about 30 to 34 feet high. In 1869 it was dug away completely, and its earth was sold to the North Missouri Railroad to build up the beds for its tracks. The workers who removed it found 32 burials, the graves of people, in two chambers inside it. No surviving record says what became of the bones. An archaeologist is a scientist who studies the past from the things people left behind, and no archaeologist is known to have recorded the digging. The history of the mounds written for the Landmarks Association of St. Louis does not name the men who dug the mound out or the person who sold its earth.

Before the World's Fair of 1904 in Forest Park, two more groups of mounds along the River des Peres were destroyed, 16 mounds in all. That same history does not name who destroyed them.

One mound is left in St. Louis, Sugarloaf Mound, on the south side of the city. In 1928 someone built a house on top of it. The Osage Nation, a Native American nation, bought that house and about a third of the mound in 2009 and tore the house down in 2017. In 2025 the Osage Nation, working with an arts group called Counterpublic, got the rest of the mound back. The Osage Nation's announcement describes Sugarloaf Mound as a sacred Osage site.

#### The largest private house

George W. Vanderbilt had Biltmore House built in Asheville, North Carolina, between 1889 and 1895. It has 250 rooms and covers about 179,000 square feet. It is still the largest privately owned house in the United States. Vanderbilt opened it to his family on Christmas Eve, 1895.

### 1900 to 1950

Many large structures in the country went up between 1913 and 1941. Among them were the Lincoln Memorial, Mount Rushmore, the Empire State Building, the Golden Gate Bridge and Hoover Dam. Workers died building three of them. Five died on the Empire State Building and 11 on the Golden Gate Bridge. At Hoover Dam the official count is 96. It does not include 42 more deaths that were listed as pneumonia. Mount Rushmore was carved into a mountain in the Black Hills of South Dakota. Members of Congress took that land from the Sioux in 1877, breaking a treaty, a written agreement between nations.

#### The Woolworth Building

Frank W. Woolworth paid the whole $13.5 million cost of the Woolworth Building in New York himself, in cash. Workers finished it in 1913. At 792 feet, it was then the tallest building in the world. Woolworth had made his fortune from stores that sold goods for five and ten cents.

#### The Lincoln Memorial

At the opening of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington in 1922, a white Marine ordered Black guests into a roped-off section, apart from white guests. William Howard Taft, who led the group in charge of the memorial, told the only Black speaker to cut his speech. The memorial honors Abraham Lincoln. Work began on February 12, 1914, Lincoln's 105th birthday. Joseph Blackburn broke the ground. He was a member of the Lincoln Memorial Commission, the group in charge of the building. He had also been an officer in the Confederate army, the army of the Southern states that fought to keep slavery in the Civil War. The architect Henry Bacon designed the building. The sculptor Daniel Chester French made the seated statue of Lincoln inside.

About 50,000 people came to the dedication on May 30, 1922. The crowd was segregated, which means Black people and white people were kept apart. A Smithsonian magazine account says the Marine sent the Black guests to their section "abrasively," which means roughly and rudely. Twenty-one of them left in protest.

Robert Russa Moton was the only Black speaker. A week before, on May 23, William Howard Taft sent him a telegram, a message sent by wire. Taft was the Chief Justice, the head of the US Supreme Court, and he was also the president of the Lincoln Memorial Commission. He wrote, "Shall have to ask you to cut five hundred words." Taft added, "I am sure you wish to avoid any insinuation of attempt to make the occasion one for propaganda." An insinuation is a hint. Propaganda means messages made to push people toward one side. Moton made the cuts. One passage he removed said that the work Lincoln died for was "still unfinished."

In 1939 Marian Anderson, a famous African American singer, sang from the memorial's steps after the Daughters of the American Revolution refused to let her sing in Constitution Hall. The group owned the hall, in Washington, and its rule allowed only white performers there. Eleanor Roosevelt, the president's wife, quit the group in protest. Harold Ickes, the Secretary of the Interior, got President Franklin D. Roosevelt's approval for a concert at the memorial. On Easter Sunday, April 9, 1939, Anderson sang from its steps to about 75,000 people of all races.

#### Mount Rushmore and the Black Hills

Mount Rushmore is carved on land that US officials promised to the Sioux in a treaty and that members of Congress later took. The Lakota, one of the Sioux peoples, call the mountain Tunkasila Sakpe, the Six Grandfathers. It stands in the Black Hills of South Dakota.

In the Fort Laramie Treaty of 1868, US officials set aside a large reservation for the Sioux, and the Black Hills were part of it. The treaty says the land was "for the absolute and undisturbed use and occupation" of the Sioux. It also says no part of it could be given up unless three-fourths of the adult Sioux men signed.

On July 2, 1874, Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer led close to 1,000 soldiers and teamsters, men who drove wagons, into the Black Hills. Lieutenant General Philip Sheridan had sent them. By the middle of August they had found gold. In August 1876, members of Congress passed a law saying no more money would be spent on food for the Sioux until they gave up the Black Hills. Under it, officials would give the Sioux no more food rations. The Sioux then depended on those rations to eat.

In September 1876 a group of officials led by George Manypenny brought the Sioux a paper that was already written. It gave up the Black Hills. Only about one in ten of the adult Sioux men signed it, far fewer than the three-fourths the treaty required. On February 28, 1877, members of Congress made that paper a law anyway. With it they took the Black Hills.

In 1980 the judges of the US Supreme Court, who are called justices, decided the case *United States v. Sioux Nation*. Justice Harry Blackmun wrote for the court that the taking had broken the treaty. The justices agreed with an earlier award of $17.1 million for the land, plus interest, extra money of 5 percent for every year since 1877. In 1980 the total came to between about $102 million and $106 million.

The Sioux nations have never taken the money. They say the Black Hills were never for sale. The money sits in a federal account held by the US Interior Department, and officials keep its balance sealed. Published estimates put it at more than $1 billion. Frank Star Comes Out, president of the Oglala Sioux Tribe, has said, "We will never sell out our holy lands, the Black Hills, to the United States for monetary compensation."

Workers carved the mountain from October 4, 1927, to October 31, 1941. According to the National Park Service, nearly 400 men and women worked there, among them drillers and blacksmiths. They did about 90 percent of the carving with dynamite. In all, they removed about 450,000 tons of rock. Then drillers made rows of holes close together, a method called honeycombing, and smoothed the faces with hand tools. Workers were lowered down the 500-foot face on steel cables, sitting in bosun chairs, which are seats hung from a cable. No worker died in the 14 years of carving. Today the memorial's staff consult with 21 Native nations connected to the site.

<a id="story-gutzon-borglum"></a>

#### Gutzon Borglum

> **Who:** The sculptor who designed Mount Rushmore. Before that, he carved a Confederate memorial at Stone Mountain, Georgia, a project the Ku Klux Klan helped pay for.
>
> **When and where:** Stone Mountain, Georgia, from 1923. The Black Hills of South Dakota, 1927 to 1941.

Before he carved Mount Rushmore, Gutzon Borglum went to meetings of the Ku Klux Klan and took a deep part in Klan politics, according to reports in the Washington Post and Smithsonian magazine. No record proves he was a member. Confederate veterans had started the first Klan in Pulaski, Tennessee, in December 1865. Its members whipped, burned the homes of and murdered freed Black people and the people who helped them. Federal officials put that Klan down in the early 1870s.

On Thanksgiving night in 1915, William J. Simmons and 16 other men climbed Stone Mountain in Georgia. They burned a cross there and announced that the Klan was born again. Members of the new Klan preached white supremacy, the belief that white people should rule over everyone else. They were also against Catholics and Jews, and they wanted fewer immigrants let into the country.

At Stone Mountain, Borglum designed a carving of three Confederate leaders on horseback, Robert E. Lee, Stonewall Jackson and Jefferson Davis. Klan money helped pay for it. Work began in 1923, and Borglum unveiled the head of Lee in 1924.

Borglum quarreled with the businessmen who ran the Stone Mountain project, and they fired him. He then destroyed his models to protect his design. That made the directors angry. A warrant, a court paper ordering his arrest, was issued, and he fled Georgia.

In 1927 Borglum began Mount Rushmore. He directed the carving from then until he died in 1941. He died in Chicago on March 6, 1941, after surgery, a few days before his 74th birthday. His son, Lincoln Borglum, finished the work that year.

<a id="story-nick-clifford"></a>

#### Nick Clifford

> **Who:** The youngest worker on Mount Rushmore, and the last of its carvers to die.
>
> **When and where:** Mount Rushmore, South Dakota, 1938 to 1940. Died in 2019, at 98.

Donald "Nick" Clifford was 17 when he was hired at Mount Rushmore in 1938. He was the youngest worker on the job. The Borglums hired him partly because they wanted him for the crew's baseball team, where he pitched.

Clifford earned 55 cents an hour. He ran the winch, a machine that winds a cable. The cable carried men up the face of the mountain. He also drilled holes for the dynamite. He worked there until 1940.

Clifford was the last of the carvers to die. He died on November 23, 2019, at the age of 98.

#### The Empire State Building and the Mohawk ironworkers

Builders took about 410 days to put up the Empire State Building in New York, from the first steel to the opening on May 1, 1931. Up to 3,400 workers were on the job each day. During the fastest stretch the steel frame rose about four and a half floors a week. The building has 102 stories and stands 1,250 feet tall, or 1,454 feet to the tip of today's antenna. It was the tallest building in the world until 1970, when the steel frame of the World Trade Center's North Tower rose higher.

Five workers died building it. That is the official count. A story that hundreds died is false. The photographer Lewis Hine took pictures of the men working on the steel for his book *Men at Work*.

Some of the riveting crews were Mohawk ironworkers from Kahnawake, a Mohawk community in Canada. The Mohawk are a Native nation. Riveters joined steel beams with rivets, hot metal pins that lock the beams together. Ironworkers put up the steel frames of buildings and bridges. Kahnawake men had done this work since the 1880s.

Kahnawake ironworkers had died on an earlier job, in 1907. On August 29 of that year, the south half of the Quebec Bridge fell while it was being built across the St. Lawrence River in Canada. James H. Marsh, writing in the Canadian Encyclopedia, gives 75 workers killed. Eve Cable, writing in *The Eastern Door*, the Kahnawake newspaper, gives 76. Thirty-three of the dead were Kahnawake men. A Royal Commission, a group set up to find the cause, blamed two engineers. Theodore Cooper was the consulting engineer, an expert brought in to oversee the design. He had made mistakes in the design and had lengthened the bridge to save money. John Deans, the chief engineer, kept the crews working after Cooper warned of danger.

After 1907, the women of Kahnawake made sure that the men of one family did not all work on the same job at the same time. *The Eastern Door* gives the rule this way: "If a lady had seven sons, they're not all going to the same job." Crosses made from the bridge's steel stand in the village cemetery. In 2007 a monument went up with a picture of each man who was killed and a 40-foot steel model of the bridge.

#### The Golden Gate Bridge

Eleven workers died building the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco, which opened in May 1937. On May 27, the first day, about 200,000 people walked across it. One died in October 1936. Ten died on February 17, 1937, when a falling work platform tore through the safety net under the bridge.

Joseph Strauss was the chief engineer. Charles Ellis, the engineer who worked out how the bridge's structure would hold its weight, did the detailed design and thousands of calculations from 1929 to 1931. Strauss fired Ellis before building began, and Ellis got no public credit for decades. In a 2007 report, officials of the Golden Gate Bridge District gave Ellis the main credit for the design.

<a id="story-joseph-strauss"></a>

#### Joseph Strauss

> **Who:** The chief engineer of the Golden Gate Bridge, who hung a safety net under the bridge while it was built.
>
> **When and where:** The Golden Gate Bridge, which opened in May 1937.

Joseph Strauss required hard hats on the Golden Gate Bridge job. He also spent about $130,000 on a safety net that hung under the bridge while it was built. It was the first large safety net used on an American bridge job.

The net caught 19 men who fell. They called themselves the Halfway to Hell Club.

<a id="story-al-zampa"></a>

#### Al Zampa

> **Who:** An ironworker who fell from the Golden Gate Bridge and lived. A bridge in California is named for him.
>
> **When and where:** The Golden Gate Bridge, October 19, 1936. From Crockett, California.

Alfred Zampa was an ironworker from Crockett, California. On October 19, 1936, he slipped on wet steel and fell into the safety net. He was near the shore, where the net sagged down onto the rocks, and he broke four bones in his back.

Zampa spent twelve weeks in the hospital and two years in a back brace. Then he went back to ironwork. He was one of the first members of the Halfway to Hell Club and later its unofficial spokesman, the man who spoke for the club without holding any title.

In 2003 California lawmakers named the new bridge over the Carquinez Strait the Alfred Zampa Memorial Bridge.

#### Hoover Dam

By the official count, 96 men died building Hoover Dam. The count comes from the Bureau of Reclamation, the federal agency that runs the dam. It covers deaths from falls, rock slides, machinery and drowning. It leaves out deaths from heat, heart trouble and pneumonia, a sickness of the lungs. The exact number of deaths is not known.

The main builder was a company called Six Companies Inc. The records list 42 more workers who died of pneumonia. Workers said these men really died of carbon monoxide poisoning. They said officials of Six Companies listed the deaths as pneumonia so the company would not have to pay compensation claims. Those are payments owed when a worker is hurt or killed on the job. Carbon monoxide is a gas with no color or smell that comes from burning fuel. When a person breathes it in, it stops the blood from carrying oxygen. The workers blamed the gasoline-powered vehicles running inside the diversion tunnels, which were dug to carry the river around the building site. The tunnels often reached 140 degrees Fahrenheit and filled with thick exhaust. In nearby Boulder City, no one who did not work on the dam was recorded as dying of pneumonia in those years.

The first deaths on the official list came in 1922, during the surveys for the dam. On December 20 of that year J. G. Tierney drowned, and Harold Connelly also died that year. The last death on the list came 13 years to the day after Tierney's. On December 20, 1935, his son, Patrick Tierney, an electrician's helper, fell from one of the dam's intake towers, the towers that take in water.

A story says that men are buried inside the dam's concrete. It is false. Workers poured the dam as many separate blocks, in shallow layers, with crews standing over each pour. A body could not have been left inside. President Franklin D. Roosevelt dedicated the dam on September 30, 1935. Its generators began making electricity in 1936.

### 1950 to 2000

The Vietnam Veterans Memorial, dedicated in Washington in 1982, is a black stone wall set into the ground. The names of more than 58,000 Americans who died in the Vietnam War are cut into it. Earlier, in the 1960s and 1970s, builders put up a steel arch in St. Louis and two towers in New York, one of which was for a few years the tallest building in the world. While the arch was going up, Black workers were kept out of the building trades unions and so off the job, Justice Department lawyers later charged in court. Two men climbed the arch in protest. Workers also restored older landmarks, including the Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island.

#### The Space Needle

Builders put up the Space Needle in Seattle in about 400 days for a world's fair called the Century 21 Exposition. It opened on April 21, 1962, the first day of the fair. The tower is 605 feet tall, with a restaurant on top that turns around.

#### The Gateway Arch

The Gateway Arch in St. Louis is 630 feet tall and 630 feet wide, and its outside is stainless steel. The architect Eero Saarinen won the contest to design it, and the winner was announced in February 1948. Saarinen died in 1961, before building began. Workers built the arch from February 12, 1963, to October 28, 1965. Insurers had predicted 13 deaths, and no worker died.

Black workers were kept out of the construction jobs on the arch, a federal monument. Unions are groups that workers join to bargain together for jobs and pay. In St. Louis, the building trades unions, the unions of carpenters, plumbers, ironworkers and other builders, had almost all white members. Justice Department lawyers later charged in court that the leaders and members of these unions kept Black men out of the unions and so out of the jobs.

On July 14, 1964, Percy Green and Richard Daly climbed a 125-foot construction ladder on the unfinished north leg of the arch. The two men were activists, people who campaign for a cause, and they climbed to protest. An article by the Gateway Arch Park Foundation states that they stayed up for 6 hours. A St. Louis Public Radio report by Kavahn Mansouri and Elaine Cha states that Green was up there for more than four hours. Police arrested both men. Green later helped start the Action Committee to Improve Opportunities for Negroes, called ACTION, a St. Louis group that worked for fair hiring. "Negroes" was a word of that time for Black people.

In 1966 two Black plumbers, Elijah Smith and Oliver Parker, were hired to work on bathrooms in the arch's visitor center. White union workers walked off the job to protest the hiring of the two Black plumbers. Lawyers in the US Justice Department then sued the St. Louis Building and Construction Trades Council and five of its unions. They sued under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Title VII is the part of that law that forbids employers and unions to treat workers unfairly because of their race, color, religion, sex or national origin. It was the department's first lawsuit under Title VII charging a "pattern or practice," which means unfair treatment by race as a regular habit. Officials of the St. Louis building trades unions signed an agreement to end "all practices that were discriminatory," meaning every rule and habit that kept Black workers out.

<a id="story-harold-mccomber"></a>

#### Harold McComber

> **Who:** A Mohawk ironworker from Kahnawake who built skyscrapers in New York.
>
> **When and where:** Manhattan and Kahnawake, filmed in 1965.
>
> **Movie:** *High Steel* (1965), a documentary by the National Film Board of Canada, directed by Don Owen. It is about McComber's working life.

Harold McComber was a Mohawk ironworker from Kahnawake. Like many Kahnawake men, he worked on the steel frames of skyscrapers in Manhattan. In 1965 the director Don Owen made a documentary film about his working life, called *High Steel*. The National Film Board of Canada produced it.

#### The World Trade Center

The architect Minoru Yamasaki designed the two towers of the World Trade Center in New York, each 110 stories tall. The ribbon-cutting was on April 4, 1973. The North Tower stood 1,368 feet. Its steel frame had passed the height of the Empire State Building in 1970, which made it the tallest building in the world. It kept that title until May 1973, about a month after the ribbon-cutting, when the steel frame of the Sears Tower in Chicago rose higher.

<a id="story-philippe-petit"></a>

#### Philippe Petit

> **Who:** A French high-wire walker who walked on a cable between the two towers of the World Trade Center.
>
> **When and where:** New York, August 7, 1974.
>
> **Movie:** *Man on Wire* (2008), directed by James Marsh. It won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature and is about the walk.

On August 7, 1974, Philippe Petit walked on a wire strung between the tops of the Twin Towers, about 1,350 feet above the ground. He and his friends had smuggled a cable up to the roofs and strung it from one tower to the other. Petit crossed eight times in 45 minutes.

Afterward police arrested him. The charges against him were dropped. In return, he put on a show for children in Central Park.

#### The Vietnam Veterans Memorial

Two long walls of polished black granite, set into the ground of the National Mall in Washington, form the Vietnam Veterans Memorial. The names of more than 58,000 Americans who died in the Vietnam War are cut into the stone, in the order they died. It was dedicated on November 13, 1982, and it became the most visited memorial in Washington.

Critics attacked the design before it was built. One veteran called it "a black gash of shame." Another critic said that burying the dead "in a black stone sarcophagus," a stone coffin, "is like spitting on their graves." Opponents of the design included Patrick Buchanan and Congressman Henry Hyde. The members of the US Commission of Fine Arts, a federal board that reviews designs in Washington, kept the wall. They also added a statue of three soldiers by Frederick Hart nearby, in 1984. Hart's design had won third place in the contest for the memorial.

<a id="story-maya-lin"></a>

#### Maya Lin

> **Who:** The 21-year-old college student whose design won the contest for the Vietnam Veterans Memorial.
>
> **When and where:** Yale University and Washington, 1981 to 1982.
>
> **Movie:** *Maya Lin: A Strong Clear Vision* (1994). It won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature and is about Lin.

Maya Lin was a 21-year-old architecture student at Yale University when she won the contest to design the Vietnam Veterans Memorial. She had first drawn the design for a class. She was born in Ohio, where her parents were professors. They had escaped from mainland China as young adults.

The contest was the biggest design competition held in the United States up to then. The judges looked at the entries without knowing who had made them. They chose entry number 1026 over 1,420 others. In May 1981 officials came to Lin's college room to tell her she had won the $20,000 first prize.

People who attacked the wall used Lin's age and her Chinese family background as reasons to change the design or drop it. At the dedication in 1982, no one spoke her name.

#### Restoring the old landmarks

From 1984 to 1986, workers restored the Statue of Liberty for its 100th birthday. They took down its original 1886 torch in 1984. It is now in the statue's museum. In its place they put a copy made of copper and covered in gold leaf, thin sheets of gold. The statue was dedicated again on July 4, 1986.

Ellis Island, in New York Harbor, was where federal officials checked arriving immigrants. On May 11, 1965, President Lyndon B. Johnson signed Proclamation 3656, a formal order from the president, which made Ellis Island part of the Statue of Liberty National Monument. Ellis Island's main building had opened in 1900. Workers restored it, and in 1990 it opened as a museum of immigration.

On the West Coast, from 1910, US officials held immigrants in barracks on Angel Island, in San Francisco Bay. Chinese immigrants held there had carved more than 200 poems into the barracks walls, and in 1970 the poems were found again. After that, people campaigned to save the barracks. In 1997 Angel Island Immigration Station became a National Historic Landmark.

### 2000 to Today

Since 2000, Americans have built memorials to people who were killed or enslaved: the victims of the September 11 attacks, the Black Americans murdered by lynch mobs, and the people held in slavery. In the same years, officials and work crews took down, moved or renamed hundreds of memorials to the Confederacy, the Southern states that fought to keep slavery in the Civil War. These memorials include statues and place names. In April 2025 researchers at the Southern Poverty Law Center, a group that campaigns for civil rights, counted 415 Confederate memorials removed, moved or renamed since 2015. By their count, 2,086 were still standing. In 2025 federal officials began putting some of the removed monuments back.

#### Ground Zero rebuilt

The National September 11 Memorial in New York stands where the Twin Towers stood. On September 11, 2001, hijackers took over four airliners. They crashed two of them into the North Tower and the South Tower, and fires from the crashes made both towers collapse. They crashed a third into the Pentagon, the headquarters of the US military, near Washington. The fourth, Flight 93, also crashed. The hijackers killed 2,977 people, not counting the 19 hijackers themselves, according to the 9/11 Memorial and Museum. Of those, 2,753 were killed in New York, 184 at the Pentagon and 40 on Flight 93.

The memorial opened on September 11, 2011, ten years after the attacks. It has two pools set into the footprints of the two towers. Each pool covers nearly an acre. Water falls 30 feet into each pool and then drops another 20 feet. Around the edges, bronze panels carry the names of 2,983 people. They are the people killed on September 11, 2001, and the six people killed in an earlier bombing of the towers in 1993.

The design, called *Reflecting Absence*, won a contest in 2004 against 5,201 entries from 63 countries. The museum under the memorial opened on May 21, 2014. On November 3, 2014, One World Trade Center opened nearby. It stands 1,776 feet to the tip of its spire. The height was chosen to match 1776, the year of the Declaration of Independence.

<a id="story-michael-arad"></a>

#### Michael Arad

> **Who:** The architect who designed the National September 11 Memorial.
>
> **When and where:** New York. He won the design contest in 2004, and the memorial opened in 2011.

Michael Arad was 34 years old and working as an architect for a New York City government agency when he entered the contest for the memorial. In his first sketches, he pictured two empty spaces cut into the surface of the Hudson River. His finished design put two pools where the towers had stood.

Arad worked with the landscape architect Peter Walker, who plans outdoor spaces such as parks. In 2004 the contest judges chose their entry from 5,201.

#### New memorials in Washington

In Washington, new memorials were built for Black Americans, among them the enslaved workers who helped build the Capitol. On February 28, 2012, members of Congress unveiled a marker in Emancipation Hall, the great hall of the Capitol Visitor Center. Emancipation means freeing people from slavery. The marker is a block of Aquia Creek sandstone taken from the Capitol's East Front, which was built from 1824 to 1826. Its plaque says the stone "was quarried by laborers, including enslaved African Americans, and commemorates their important role in building the Capitol." Quarried means cut out of the ground.

The Martin Luther King, Jr. Memorial was dedicated on October 16, 2011. It was the first memorial to an African American in the area of the National Mall. At its center is a 30-foot carving called the Stone of Hope.

The National Museum of African American History and Culture opened on September 24, 2016, beside the Washington Monument. It is part of the Smithsonian. The architect David Adjaye led its design. He based the building's outside, a bronze-colored shape in three levels called the corona, on the art of the Yoruba. The Yoruba are an African people. The pattern of its metal screen copies ironwork made by enslaved and free Black craftsmen in the South.

#### Memorials to lynching and slavery

The National Memorial for Peace and Justice, in Montgomery, Alabama, is a memorial to Black people who were lynched. Lynching is a killing by a mob, without a trial. The lawyer Bryan Stevenson founded the Equal Justice Initiative (EJI), a legal group that does not make a profit. EJI built the memorial and opened it on April 26, 2018, with a museum called the Legacy Museum.

The memorial holds 805 steel blocks, each six feet tall, hanging from above. Each one stands for a county in the United States where EJI researchers found a record of a lynching. In their study *Lynching in America*, EJI researchers counted almost 4,400 lynchings of Black people from 1877 to 1950. A copy of each county's block stands at the site. EJI offers each copy to groups in that county to set up at home. A team called MASS Design Group designed the memorial, and it cost about $20 million, paid by private foundations.

In March 2024 EJI opened the Freedom Monument Sculpture Park nearby, on 17 acres with nearly 50 sculptures. Its National Monument to Freedom lists more than 122,000 last names taken from the 1870 census, the government's count of everyone in the country that year. Nearly five million Black people took those names. The 1870 census was the first time people who had been enslaved could claim a last name that the government would recognize. The monument stands 43 feet tall and 155 feet long, and EJI dedicated it on Juneteenth, June 19, 2024. Juneteenth marks June 19, 1865, the day Major General Gordon Granger of the US Army reached Galveston, Texas, with the news that enslaved African Americans were free.

#### Confederate monuments coming down and going back up

In 2018 researchers at the Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC) reported that members of the United Daughters of the Confederacy had put up hundreds of Confederate statues at courthouses and other public places since the Civil War. The SPLC researchers found two main periods of building. The first began around 1900, while lawmakers in Southern states were passing Jim Crow laws. Lawmakers wrote these laws to force Black and white people apart and to take away Black people's rights. The second ran from the early 1950s through the 1960s, when segregationists, people who wanted to keep the races apart, fought the civil rights movement.

Hundreds of these memorials came down or were renamed after people were killed in three places: Charleston, Charlottesville and Minneapolis. On June 17, 2015, a 21-year-old white man named Dylann Roof sat in on a Bible study at the Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston, South Carolina. After about an hour he opened fire and killed nine Black worshippers. Roof had posted pictures of himself with Confederate flags on his website, and he had written racist views there. On December 15, 2016, a federal jury found Roof guilty of all 33 federal charges against him. On January 10, 2017, the federal court sentenced him to death.

In Charlottesville, Virginia, Paul Goodloe McIntire paid for a statue of the Confederate general Robert E. Lee, and it was dedicated in 1924. On February 6, 2017, the members of the city council voted 3 to 2 to remove it. White supremacists then organized a rally called Unite the Right around the statue. On August 12, 2017, James Alex Fields Jr. drove his car into a crowd of people protesting against the rally. He killed Heather Heyer, a 32-year-old paralegal, a worker who helps lawyers, and injured many others. Counts of the injured run from 19 to 29. In December 2018 a Virginia jury found Fields guilty of first-degree murder, the most serious kind of murder, done on purpose. In 2019 he pleaded guilty to 29 federal hate crimes, crimes against people chosen because of their race, religion or a similar trait, and a federal judge sentenced him to life in prison.

City workers took the Charlottesville statue down on July 10, 2021. City officials gave it to the Jefferson School African American Heritage Center. In October 2023 the staff of the center's Swords into Plowshares project had the statue melted down at a foundry, a workshop where metal is melted and poured into molds.

On May 25, 2020, Minneapolis police officer Derek Chauvin murdered George Floyd by kneeling on his neck, back and shoulder for about ten minutes. In 2021 a jury convicted Chauvin of murder. Protests followed Floyd's death. SPLC researchers counted at least 168 Confederate symbols removed in 2020 alone. In June 2020 Virginia Governor Ralph Northam ordered the removal of Richmond's Lee statue, a 12-ton monument put up in 1890. The judges of the Supreme Court of Virginia then refused to block the removal in two lawsuits. ABC News reporters Meredith Deliso and Emily Shapiro wrote that a crew led by Devon Henry, who owned the construction company doing the work, took the statue down on September 8, 2021.

In April 2025 SPLC researchers counted 2,086 Confederate memorials still standing in public places. In their count, memorials include place names and other symbols as well as monuments such as statues, and 685 of the 2,086 were monuments. Rivka Maizlish of the SPLC called the memorials "the results of a mass propaganda campaign."

In 2025 federal officials began putting some monuments back. In June 2020, protesters had pulled down a statue of the Confederate general Albert Pike in Washington and set it on fire. In October 2025 National Park Service workers put it back up. They cited a historic preservation law. They also cited an executive order, a written command from the president, that President Donald Trump had signed on restoring removed monuments.

The Confederate Memorial at Arlington National Cemetery was put up in 1914 by the United Daughters of the Confederacy. The sculptor, Moses Ezekiel, had fought for the Confederacy. The memorial shows "an enslaved man following his owner to war." It also shows an enslaved woman as a "mammy," holding a white officer's child. The "mammy" was a made-up picture of an enslaved Black woman who cared for a white family's children and seemed happy in slavery. The picture hid the truth that enslavers separated these women from their own children. A commission set up by Congress found that the memorial showed "highly sanitized depictions of slavery." That means pictures of slavery with the cruelty cleaned out. On that commission's advice, the memorial was taken down in December 2023. The *Stars and Stripes* report on it does not say who did the work. In August 2025 Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that it would return in 2027. The newspaper *Stars and Stripes* reported that the repairs would cost about $10 million.

#### Exhibits about slavery at the President's House

In 2026, National Park Service workers took down an exhibit about slavery in Philadelphia, and a federal judge ordered it put back. The President's House site marks where George Washington lived while he was president. Its exhibit panels described the lives of nine people Washington held in slavery there. The workers removed the panels in January 2026, following President Trump's executive order called "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History." Lawyers for the City of Philadelphia sued. On February 16, 2026, US District Judge Cynthia Rufe ordered the panels restored while the case went on, and workers began putting them back three days later. Lawyers for the federal government appealed, which means they asked a higher court to change the ruling. By July 2026, judges of the Third Circuit Court of Appeals had agreed that officials of the Trump administration had the power to replace the exhibit.

#### Old landmarks, new names and owners

Sugarloaf Mound, on the south side of St. Louis, is the only Native mound left in that city. Native people built about 40 mounds there between about the years 600 and 1300. As the city grew, people dug away all the others. In 1869 workers dug away Big Mound, the largest, and its earth was sold to a railroad to build up the beds for its tracks. Inside it the workers found 32 burials, the graves of people, in two chambers. No surviving record says what became of the bones. In 1928 someone built a house on top of Sugarloaf Mound. The Osage Nation bought that house and about a third of the mound in 2009, and tore the house down in 2017. In 2025, working with an arts group called Counterpublic, the Osage Nation got the last two pieces of the property transferred to it. Afterward Andrea Hunter, the Osage Nation's Historic Preservation Officer, said, "It has been a long 17-year journey, and I am thrilled to finally see the entire mound come under Osage Nation control." She said her office must now "remove all the structures from the properties and stabilize the mound." Osage leaders plan to build a center there to teach visitors about the mound.

In 2009 workers finished restoring the barracks of the Angel Island Immigration Station in California. On February 22, 2018, President Donald Trump signed a law that gave the Jefferson National Expansion Memorial in St. Louis, the grounds of the Gateway Arch, a new name, Gateway Arch National Park. It is the smallest national park in the country.

<a id="ch-elements"></a>

## Chapter 13: The Elements

### Before 1500

Native miners near Lake Superior were digging and shaping copper at least 9,500 years ago. A 2021 study places them among the first coppersmiths in the world. A coppersmith is a person who makes things out of copper. All the land that later became the United States was Native land before 1500, and no miner or metalworker from these thousands of years is known by name.

Copper is one of the chemical elements. Everything is made of tiny pieces called atoms, far too small to see. An element is a substance made of only one kind of atom. Copper, iron, gold and silver are all elements. Nobody anywhere on Earth yet knew what a chemical element was. People here mined copper, gathered salt and colored earth, and chose hard stone for tools. In some regions they also worked iron that had fallen from space. They turned these materials into tools, beads, ornaments and paint.

#### Copper from Lake Superior

Copper that lies in the ground as pure metal is called native copper. The Lake Superior country, in what are now Michigan, Wisconsin and Minnesota, has veins of it running through the rock. Native miners dug out this copper and hammered it into spear points, knives, fishhooks and ornaments. They also made awls, which are thin, pointed tools for punching holes.

In 2021 a team led by the geologist David Pompeani published new dates for this copper work in a journal called *Radiocarbon*. A journal is a magazine where scientists publish their studies. A geologist is a scientist who studies rocks and the Earth. Radiocarbon dating is a way to measure the age of things that were once alive, such as wood or bone. The team used 53 radiocarbon dates. They found that the copper work began at least 9,500 years ago, which is about 3,500 years earlier than scientists had thought. The work was busiest between about 7,000 and 5,000 years ago.

The oldest known copper work in the Middle East is a pendant about 8,700 years old. A pendant is an ornament that hangs from a cord. So the Lake Superior copper work is as old as the earliest known copper work in the Middle East, or older. Writers at the journal *Science* reported the 2021 study under the headline "Ancient Native Americans were among the world's first coppersmiths."

Traders carried Lake Superior copper hundreds of miles along Native trade routes. On the same routes they also carried turquoise, shells and obsidian. Turquoise is a blue-green stone. Obsidian is a natural glass that forms from the lava of volcanoes.

#### Iron from space

Before 1500, the only iron metal that people here could work came from meteorites. A meteorite is a piece of rock or metal from space that has fallen to Earth. Nobody here got iron out of rock by smelting yet. Smelting means heating rock until the metal inside it melts out.

In 1945, archaeologists dug 22 iron beads out of Hopewell burial mounds near Havana, Illinois. Archaeologists are scientists who dig up and study the things people left behind long ago. Hopewell is the name for a Native way of life in the woodlands of eastern North America from about 2,000 to 1,600 years ago. A burial mound is a hill of earth that people built over the graves of their dead. People made the beads about 2,000 years ago. In 2017, Timothy McCoy of the Smithsonian and four other scientists published a study of the beads in the *Journal of Archaeological Science*. They found that the iron came from the Anoka meteorite, an iron meteorite from Minnesota.

That means people had carried or traded the metal several hundred miles before anyone made it into beads. The beadmakers shaped the iron by hammering it. They used the same hammering skills that people used on copper.

#### Gold, silver, ochre, salt and stone

In some regions, metalworkers made ornaments of gold and silver. Red and yellow ochre, a colored earth, went into paint. The color of ochre comes from iron oxides. An iron oxide is a compound of iron and oxygen. A compound is a substance made of two or more elements joined together.

People gathered salt and traded it. Salt is a compound of two elements, sodium and chlorine. They made tools of flint and chert, two hard stones. Both are made of compounds that contain the element silicon.

### The 1500s

In the 1500s, Spanish expeditions came looking for gold and silver. An expedition is a long journey made by a group of people for a purpose. The Spaniards found no cities of gold in the lands that later became the United States. The land was still Native land from coast to coast. People here worked the same copper, gold and meteorite iron as before. Spaniards brought some metal of their own into their few outposts, the small forts and settlements they built.

#### Spanish gold hunters, 1539 to 1543

Hernando de Soto led a Spanish expedition across the Southeast from 1539 to 1543. Francisco Vázquez de Coronado led another across the Southwest from 1540 to 1542. Both men were following stories of cities full of gold. Neither man found one.

In the same century, Spaniards found large amounts of silver in Mexico and South America, not in the future United States. Nobody here or anywhere else yet had a science of elements. In Europe, the modern idea of an element had not been written down. People there who studied what things are made of still worked by alchemy, the older practice that came before chemistry. Alchemists tried to turn ordinary metals, such as lead, into gold by heating them and trying to make them purer. They kept most of their methods secret.

### The 1600s

English colonists built ironworks in Virginia and Massachusetts in the 1600s. An ironworks is a place where workers make iron out of ore, which is rock that contains a metal. Fighters of the Powhatan, a union of Native towns in eastern Virginia, destroyed the Virginia works in 1622. Building at Saugus, in Massachusetts, began in 1646, and the works there ran until about 1670. Scottish prisoners of war did forced labor at Saugus. People in Europe, Asia and Africa had already been smelting iron for thousands of years.

#### Falling Creek, 1619 to 1622

In 1619, English colonists began building an ironworks on Falling Creek, near present-day Richmond. They built it for the Virginia Company, the English business that King James I had allowed in 1606 to start a colony in Virginia. By March 1622 the furnace was ready to make iron, or close to it.

Opechancanough was the head chief of the Powhatan, a union of Native towns and nations in eastern Virginia. The English colony stood on Powhatan land. English colonists had been moving farther up the James River and settling more of that land. From 1618, Virginia Company officials gave land to new colonists, who planted it in tobacco. By 1620 colonists were taking the land they wanted from the Powhatan without asking or paying, according to the historian Betty Wood. Company officials, George Thorpe most of all, also pressed the Powhatan to send their children to live among the English. The English wanted to school the children and make them Christian.

Opechancanough planned attacks on many parts of the colony to drive the English out for good. On March 22, 1622, Powhatan fighters destroyed the ironworks at Falling Creek and killed twenty-seven people there. The colonists never managed to rebuild the works.

#### Hammersmith at Saugus

In 1646 Richard Leader began building an ironworks on the Saugus River near Boston. He worked for the Company of Undertakers of the Iron Works in New England. In the 1600s, an undertaker meant a person who took on a business project. People called the works Hammersmith. Its furnace was running by the next year.

Hammersmith was the first ironworks in North America where every stage of the work happened on one site. A blast furnace is a tall furnace with air blown into its fire, which makes it hot enough to melt iron out of ore. The iron that came out of it was called pig iron. A forge is a workshop where workers heat iron and hammer it. At the Saugus forge, workers hammered pig iron into wrought iron, a tougher iron that bends instead of breaking. The rolling and slitting mill had rollers that pressed the iron flat and blades that cut it into strips. The strips were the raw material for nails, tools and horseshoes. Seven waterwheels powered the machines.

The ore was bog iron. Workers collected it from swamps and ponds. The works ran until about 1668 to 1670. The site is now Saugus Iron Works National Historic Site.

#### Scottish prisoners at Saugus

Scottish prisoners of war did forced labor at Saugus. English soldiers under Oliver Cromwell took these Scottish soldiers prisoner at the Battle of Dunbar in 1650 and the Battle of Worcester in 1651. About 400 prisoners from the two battles reached New England in all, according to the National Park Service. The prisoners had no choice about going or about the work.

English soldiers led by Oliver Cromwell won the Battle of Dunbar in September 1650. Cromwell let more than 5,000 of the Scottish prisoners go. He marched about 3,900 of the fittest south to the English city of Durham. On the march their English captors gave the Scots no food and no shelter. The captors killed some of the prisoners for refusing to keep walking. At Durham the English locked the prisoners in the city's cathedral, a large church that was not in use at the time.

A group of English leaders called the Council of State decided to send most of the prisoners to the colonies. In November 1650 they ordered Sir Arthur Haselrig, the governor at Newcastle, to hand over 150 Dunbar prisoners. The prisoners went to agents of John Becx and Joshua Foote. Becx and Foote were two of the main investors in the Company of Undertakers, which had built the Saugus works. The prisoners sailed from England on a ship called the *Unity* and reached Boston in December 1650. The records do not show how many died on the voyage.

The men running the Company of Undertakers kept 62 of the prisoners for the ironworks, according to the historian Marsha Hamilton. They sent 36 to Saugus and 17 to a Boston warehouse run by William Aubrey, a manager for the company. Hamilton does not say where the other nine of the 62 went. The company's men sold the rest of the prisoners to farmers, merchants and other mills.

The men running the company forced many of the Scots to work five to seven years under indentures at the Saugus ironworks. An indenture was a written agreement that bound a person to work for a master for a set number of years. These men had no say in theirs. They had to work to pay back the cost of their voyage, food, shelter, care and clothing. National Park Service staff give the term at Saugus as seven years. There, most of the Scots cut wood, made charcoal or did heavy work that needed no special skill. The charcoal makers were called colliers. Other prisoners did hard and dangerous forced labor elsewhere in Massachusetts and in New Hampshire and Maine, for the farmers, merchants and mill owners who bought them.

#### Meanwhile in Europe

Chemistry is the science of what substances are made of and how they change. In Europe in the 1600s, chemists began to separate their work from alchemy. Robert Boyle published his book *The Sceptical Chymist* in 1661, and the book is one sign of that split. Every element discovery of this century happened in Europe. Phosphorus was found in the city of Hamburg in 1669.

### 1700 to 1750

By about 1750, colonists were shipping raw iron from their own furnaces to Britain. Raw iron meant iron not yet made into finished goods. Colonists had built ironworks in New England, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia and New Jersey. The owners of many ironworks forced enslaved people to do much of the labor. Nobody discovered an element anywhere in the Americas in these years, and element science still happened only in Europe.

#### Enslaved and indentured ironworkers

Owners held enslaved people as property and forced them to work without pay. Five rich Maryland planters, owners of large farms called plantations, founded the Baltimore Iron Works in 1731. They were Dr. Charles Carroll, his cousins Charles and Daniel Carroll, Daniel Dulany and Benjamin Tasker. The partners put up money and supplied enslaved workers. The works opened with 89 workers, and 42 of them were enslaved, according to the staff of the Mount Clare Museum House in Baltimore.

Workers at the Baltimore furnace hauled cartloads of charcoal, oyster shells and iron ore to its top in 12-hour shifts. The furnace ran day and night, six or seven days a week. Many of the workers were enslaved people. Others were convicts, people found guilty of crimes in Britain and shipped across the ocean as punishment. The owners did not give the workers enough food, according to the museum. Some enslaved and convict workers ran away, and others worked slowly or carelessly on purpose.

British investors set up the Principio Company in Maryland in 1719. Its Principio Furnace began with workers who were mostly indentured servants from Britain. By the middle of the 1700s, more of the workers there were enslaved African Americans, many of them in skilled jobs. Principio's owners gave their enslaved and indentured workers mostly corn and salt pork to eat. Some of these workers tried to escape. Historians at the University of Maryland and the Maryland Historical Trust surveyed the state's old industries. They wrote that escape attempts were "not uncommon."

#### The Iron Act of 1750

Parliament was the lawmaking body of Great Britain. In 1750 its members passed the Iron Act. They wrote it to encourage colonists to keep making raw iron and sending it to Britain. Raw iron meant pig iron and bar iron, which is iron hammered into bars. The act also stated that colonists could not build new mills to make finished ironware, meaning iron goods ready for use. The members of Parliament wanted that business kept in Britain.

Colonists ignored the ban. After 1750 they built more than sixty new ironworks, about twenty of them in Pennsylvania. By the American Revolution, colonists made more iron than people in England and Wales did. By a common ranking, the colonies were third in the world for iron.

Other elements turned up in colonial homes every day. Lead went into gunshot and into pewter, a gray metal made mostly of tin and used for plates, bowls, mugs and spoons. Kettles and buttons were made of copper or of brass, a metal made partly of copper. Silver and gold arrived in the colonies as Spanish coins.

### 1750 to 1800

Between 1750 and 1800, chemists in Europe turned chemistry into a modern science. Among them were the Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele and the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier. They worked out what an element is and found new ones. Nobody in the United States discovered an element in these years. Americans used elements in their coins and dug ores out of the ground.

Joseph Priestley collected the gas oxygen on its own in England in 1774 and moved to Pennsylvania twenty years later. In Maryland, owners of iron furnaces held hundreds of Black people in slavery. In North Carolina in 1799, a 12-year-old boy found the first gold in the United States that an expert confirmed was real.

#### Three elements in the new coins

A mint is a place where workers make coins. Lawmakers in Congress passed the Coinage Act, and it became law on April 2, 1792. Under it, government officials set up the United States Mint. The act also stated that the new country's coins would be made of three elements. Gold went into coins called eagles, silver into dollars and smaller coins, and copper into cents.

#### Enslaved ironworkers in Maryland

After the Revolution, Maryland officials took a one-fifth share of the Baltimore Iron Works from Daniel Dulany, a Loyalist. A Loyalist was a colonist who sided with Britain in the war. In 1785 they offered the share for sale in a newspaper advertisement, in the *Maryland Gazette*. The advertisement listed more than 200 enslaved Black people at the works, according to the Mount Clare Museum House. Their owners made them work without pay.

Four brothers, Thomas, James, Baker and Roger Johnson, built Catoctin Furnace in Maryland. It was making iron by 1776. Thomas Johnson later became the first governor of the state of Maryland. In 1803 Baker Johnson became the only owner. A Johnson owner enslaved more than 80 people at the furnace, according to the Catoctin Furnace Historical Society, which names him only as "Johnson." The society names some of the enslaved men, among them Collier Sam, Waggoner's Henry and Harvey. A collier made charcoal, and a waggoner drove wagons.

At least 271 enslaved people and an unknown number of free African Americans worked at Catoctin, according to a 2023 study in the journal *Science*. They mined ore, made charcoal, worked the forge, filled the furnace, drove wagons and cut wood. Others worked in the owners' houses and fields. The furnace had a cemetery for its African American workers, with burials from 1774. Between about 1825 and 1850, the owners switched to paid workers, most of them white.

On August 4, 2023, a team of scientists published a study in the journal *Science*. Three of them planned and led the work. They were David Reich of Harvard Medical School, Douglas Owsley of the Smithsonian and Joanna Mountain of the company 23andMe. They studied the DNA of 27 people buried in the Catoctin cemetery. DNA is the material inside the body's cells that parents pass down to their children. The team linked the 27 people to nearly 42,000 living relatives.

<a id="story-joseph-priestley"></a>

#### Joseph Priestley

> **Who:** The English chemist credited with discovering oxygen, who spent his last ten years as an immigrant in Pennsylvania.
>
> **When and where:** Isolated oxygen on August 1, 1774, in England. Moved to America in 1794. Lived in Northumberland, Pennsylvania, until his death on February 6, 1804.

On August 1, 1774, Joseph Priestley heated a substance called mercuric oxide with a burning lens. Mercuric oxide is a compound of the element mercury and oxygen. A burning lens is a glass lens that bends sunlight to one hot point. Priestley isolated a gas from the mercuric oxide, which means he collected it apart from everything else. The gas was later named oxygen.

Carl Wilhelm Scheele, in Sweden, had found the same gas earlier than Priestley did. Scheele published his work later. The French chemist Antoine Lavoisier gave oxygen its name.

Priestley invented carbonated water in Leeds in 1767. Carbonated water is water with bubbles of gas in it. In 1770 he gave rubber its English name, because he found it was good for rubbing out pencil marks.

Priestley was also a minister, a leader of a church. He preached outside the official Church of England, and many people in Birmingham, England, turned against him for his views on religion. In 1791 a mob there burned his home and his laboratory. In 1794 he left England for Pennsylvania and settled in Northumberland, where his house was finished in 1798. There he built what was then the best chemistry laboratory in the United States and identified the gas carbon monoxide.
