Snyder faced two counts of willful neglect of duty, which means knowingly failing to do his job. Lyon and Wells each faced nine counts of involuntary manslaughter. Earley faced three counts and Ambrose four counts of misconduct in office, which means breaking the law while doing a government job. Howard Croft, Nancy Peeler, Richard Baird and Jarrod Agen were charged too. In 2022 the judges of the Michigan Supreme Court ruled that the one-judge grand jury used to charge them broke the state constitution. A one-judge grand jury is a single judge who decides alone whether to charge someone with a crime. The 2021 cases ended on October 31, 2023, with no one found guilty.

Flint's people sued. On November 10, 2021, U.S. District Judge Judith Levy approved a settlement, an agreement to pay money to end the lawsuits, of $626.25 million for more than 90,000 Flint residents and businesses.

<a id="part-4"></a>

# Part 4: Work, Food, and Money

<a id="ch-work-workers"></a>

## Chapter 14: Work and Workers

### Before 1500

Before 1500, the people of North America farmed, hunted, fished and built canoes, but nobody worked for wages. A wage is pay from an employer for work done. No one hired another person for pay, set their hours or fired them. People planned their work around the seasons and the needs of their own households. Work for wages began here only after people from Europe arrived.

#### Work by season and by household

In Eastern Woodlands communities, in the forests of eastern North America, men and women did different work. Women farmed corn, beans and squash, and they gathered wild foods. Men hunted and fished.

On the biggest jobs, men and women worked together in larger groups. They did this at planting time and at harvest, for building canoes and for maple sugaring. Maple sugaring means boiling down the sap of maple trees to make sugar.

Where farmers grew enough food for whole towns, some people could spend their time on one kind of work. They became traders, stoneworkers or religious leaders.

### The 1500s

The first work that newcomers organized in this land was forced work. Spanish settlers in Florida and the Southwest made Native people work for them, with little pay or none. Spanish officials ran that forced work under two systems, the encomienda and the repartimiento.

#### The encomienda and the repartimiento

Under a system of the king of Spain called the encomienda, Spanish settlers could force Native people to work for them and to hand over tribute. Tribute is a payment of goods or labor that people are forced to give to those who rule them. In return the settlers were supposed to give the Native people "protection and religious instruction." Settlers used the encomienda from Florida across the Southwest.

From the middle of the 1500s, Spanish officials in the colonies also used a second system, called the repartimiento. Under it, the officials sent Native workers in groups, by turns, to work on Spanish projects. The officials were supposed to pay the workers. In New Mexico, Spanish governors used the repartimiento to farm and to trade. They also forced enslaved people to do the work, though Spanish law forbade it.

#### Acoma, 1599: forced work as a sentence

In February 1599 Juan de Oñate, the leader of the Spanish colony in New Mexico, sentenced the Acoma survivors to twenty years of forced labor. Forced labor means work a person is made to do and is not free to leave. Acoma Pueblo is the town of the Acoma people, with their fields around it.

In December 1598 Spanish soldiers led by Oñate's nephew, Juan de Zaldívar, came to Acoma to demand food. In the Acoma people's own account, the soldiers raped an Acoma woman. Rape means forcing a person into sex. The Acoma killed Zaldívar and eleven to fourteen of his men. Accounts differ on the number. In January 1599 Oñate sent about seventy soldiers back to Acoma, led by Vicente de Zaldívar. Over two or three days they killed Acoma men, women and children and burned much of the town. Nobody counted the dead, and estimates run from about 300 to about 1,500.

Oñate sentenced the men over 25 to have one foot cut off. He also sentenced them to work for Spanish households for twenty years, with no right to leave. Boys and men from 12 to 25, and girls and women over 12, got the same twenty years of forced labor. Whether anyone carried out the cutting of feet is disputed. In the Acoma people's own account, Oñate had the right feet of 24 captive men cut off. Two historians who studied the Spanish records for years, Marc Simmons and John Kessell, came to doubt it. Kessell points out that no record describes an Acoma man with one foot.

### The 1600s

Over the whole colonial period, between one-half and two-thirds of the European immigrants to the English colonies came as indentured servants. Under a contract, each of them had to work for a master for a set number of years, and most got no wages. They could not quit. Around Chesapeake Bay, masters worked them in the tobacco fields, and a sickness in the first summer killed more than half of the newcomers. Virginia judges had runaway servants whipped and added years to their time. In the same century, English colonists began to hold Africans in slavery for life.

#### Bound for years: indentured servants

An indentured servant was a person bound by a written contract, called an indenture, to work for a master for a set number of years. Most terms ran four to seven years, and the servant could not leave. Most servants got no wages. A skilled servant named Buckland was paid 20 English pounds a year on top of his food, drink, washing and a place to sleep, and his contract was unusual.

Counts of how many European immigrants came this way differ. Most estimates run from one-half to two-thirds of all European immigrants to the colonies. Some estimates go as high as three-quarters. In the colonies around Chesapeake Bay, about 50,000 servants arrived between 1630 and 1680. They made up three of every four newcomers. In the 1630s there were about six men for every woman among them.

Servants there worked tobacco "from dawn until dusk, six days a week through the growing season." Many newcomers fell sick in their first summer. People called this sickness the seasoning, and it killed more than half of the new arrivals. One writer of the time said immigrants died "like cats and dogs." Virginia's lawmakers also punished women servants who had a baby without being married. Such a woman had an extra year added to her term, or she had to pay her master 1,000 pounds of tobacco.

At the end of the term, a master owed the servant "freedom dues," goods to start a free life with. In Virginia a man got ten bushels of corn, thirty shillings and a musket. A bushel is a measure of grain, about eight gallons. A shilling was an English coin, and a musket was a long gun. A woman got fifteen bushels of corn and forty shillings.

Masters also took children and teenagers as apprentices. An apprentice worked for a master in order to learn a trade, such as printing or shoemaking.

At home, families did their own spinning, weaving, brewing and candle-making. Brewing means making beer.

#### Martin's Hundred, on the land of Tsenacomoco

Martin's Hundred was an English plantation on the James River in Virginia. Its main settlement was Wolstenholme Towne. The plantation stood inside Tsenacomoco, the land of the Powhatan chiefdom. The chiefdom was a union of many Native nations under one high chief. Tsenacomoco ran north from the James River to the Potomac River, and from Chesapeake Bay west to the places where the rivers drop in falls from higher ground. About 15,000 people lived there, and estimates run from 13,000 to just over 22,000.

On March 22, 1622, the Powhatan leader Opechancanough led an attack on most of the English settlements. Colony officials recorded 347 colonists killed. They got no report from some settlements, so the real number was probably higher. The Powhatan fighters killed at least 58 colonists at Martin's Hundred. They killed more colonists at Wolstenholme Towne, its main settlement, than at any other settlement.

<a id="story-richard-frethorne"></a>

#### Richard Frethorne

> **Who:** An indentured servant in Virginia, probably a young teenager, whose letters home to his parents survive.
>
> **When and where:** Martin's Hundred, Virginia, from December 1622 until his death, recorded by February 1624.

Richard Frethorne wrote home from Virginia to beg his parents to buy him out of his indenture. He had arrived at Martin's Hundred in December 1622 on a ship called the *Abigail*, nine months after the attack. He was probably a young teenager.

In March and April 1623 he wrote to his parents in England. He asked them to pay off his indenture, or else to send food. Since he left the ship, he wrote, he had eaten nothing but peas and loblollie. Loblollie was water gruel, a thin porridge boiled in water. He also wrote, "when we are sick there is nothing to comfort us."

By February 1624 a muster list had been made, a count of the living and the dead at each settlement. The list records Frethorne, spelled "Frethram," among the dead at Martin's Hundred.

#### Runaways, and a sentence for life

Servants who ran away and were caught faced the whip and more years of work. The governor of Virginia and his council sat together as the colony's highest court, called the General Court. On July 9, 1640, these judges heard the case of three runaway servants of Hugh Gwyn, a planter, or owner of a plantation. The judges ordered two of them, a Dutchman called Victor and a Scotsman named James Gregory, whipped with thirty lashes each. A lash is one stroke of the whip. Both men also had to serve extra years.

The third runaway was John Punch, a Black man. For the same escape, the same judges ordered him to serve his master "for the time of his natural Life," which meant for the rest of his life.

On July 22, 1640, the same judges ordered thirty lashes for other runaways. They also ordered three of them, Christopher Miller, Peter Wilcocke and a Black man named Emanuel, "to be Burnt in the cheek with the letter R." This punishment is called branding. To brand a person was to press a red-hot iron into the skin. The burn left the letter on the cheek as a scar for life. The court records name the letter R and the cheek, but they do not describe the iron used. They do not name the men who did the whipping and the branding. The judges also ordered Miller and Emanuel to work in shackles, iron rings locked around the legs, for a year or more.

In March 1643 Virginia's lawmakers wrote two punishments for runaways into law. A runaway had to serve double the time he had been gone. A servant who ran away a second time was to be "branded in the cheek with the letter R." The law did not say who was to do the branding.

### 1700 to 1750

A boy who learned a trade between 1700 and 1750 moved up through three ranks: apprentice, journeyman and master. A journeyman was a skilled worker paid by the day. Sailors and dock workers made up the other large group of people who worked for wages. Officers of the British navy could seize those men and force them to serve at sea. In the colonies around Chesapeake Bay and in the Lowcountry along the southern coast, colonists held more and more people in slavery. Slave traders brought about 8,600 enslaved Africans to Virginia between 1701 and 1710, about 6,200 between 1711 and 1720, and about 13,000 between 1721 and 1730.

#### The ladder of a trade

A trade such as printing, shoemaking, carpentry or blacksmithing had three ranks. A child or teenager started as an apprentice, bound to a master to learn the work. When the apprentice's time was up, he became a journeyman. A journeyman was a skilled worker who earned wages, paid by the day. A journeyman who set up a shop of his own became a master.

In the towns, enslaved men also worked at skilled trades. Owners "hired out" some of these men to other employers. The employers paid wages for the work, and the owners kept the wages.

<a id="story-benjamin-franklin-work-workers"></a>

#### Benjamin Franklin

> **Who:** A runaway apprentice. At 12 he was bound to work in his brother James's print shop, and at 17 he ran away.
>
> **When and where:** Boston, New York and Philadelphia, 1718 to 1723.
>
> **Movie:** *Benjamin Franklin* (2022), a two-part documentary by Ken Burns, shown on PBS in April 2022. It is about Franklin's life.

Benjamin Franklin ran away from his apprenticeship at 17. In 1718, when he was 12, he was bound as an apprentice to his brother James, a printer in Boston. Under his indenture he had to work in James's shop until he was 21. Only in the last year would he be paid a journeyman's wages.

Franklin later wrote that his brother beat him. He also admitted that he himself may have been "too saucy and provoking." He meant that he may have been rude to James and made him angry. In September 1723, with about four years left on his indenture, he ran away. He went first to New York and then to Philadelphia. He reached Philadelphia on October 6, 1723, with almost no money.

#### Sailors, press gangs and the Knowles Riot

Sailors and dock workers were paid wages. Officers of Britain's Royal Navy could also impress them. To impress a man was to seize him and force him to serve on a navy ship. The groups of men sent to grab them were called press gangs.

In November 1747, press gangs working for Commodore Charles Knowles seized 46 men in Boston. A commodore was a navy officer who commanded a group of ships. The men seized included boatmen, sailors and even carpenters. Beginning on November 17, a crowd made up mostly of working people rioted in Boston for three days. They took some of Knowles's officers as hostages. The crowd forced Knowles to free the seized men in exchange for his officers. The fight is called the Knowles Riot.

### 1750 to 1800

Hired workers in Philadelphia began to act together against their employers in the late 1700s. In 1786 journeymen printers there went on strike, stopping work together until their employers met their demands. They won pay of at least $6 a week. In 1794 journeymen shoemakers in the same city formed a trade union, a group of workers who bargain together with employers, and it lasted.

#### The printers' strike of 1786

In a strike, workers stop work together until the employer meets their demands. In 1786 the journeymen printers of Philadelphia struck against a cut in their wages. A U.S. Labor Department list of important events in labor history records the start of the strike as June 2, 1786. The printers won, and their employers agreed to pay at least $6 a week.

The printers also set up a fund of money to support one another during the strike, the first strike fund on record. The same Labor Department list describes theirs as "the earliest authenticated strike of workers in the United States in a single trade." Authenticated means proven by the records. Journeymen tailors in New York had struck earlier, in 1768, but New York was then a British colony and the United States did not yet exist. Records show other early times, too, when workers in the colonies stopped work together.

#### The shoemakers' union of 1794

Shoemakers in those days were called cordwainers. In May 1794, journeymen shoemakers in Philadelphia formed the Federal Society of Journeymen Cordwainers. A trade union is a group of workers in one trade who join together to bargain with employers over pay and hours. The Federal Society was the first trade union in the United States that lasted.

Its members called a "turn-out" to hold a standard wage, the same pay for the same work across the trade. A turn-out was their word for a strike.

### 1800 to 1850

In the first half of the 1800s, factory owners ran their workers' days by bells. In the mills of Lowell, Massachusetts, young women worked about 12 hours a day. Children tended machines, and Irish immigrants dug canals and railroads. In 1806 a jury in Philadelphia found shoemakers guilty of a crime for forming a union to raise their pay. A union is a group of workers who join together to bargain with employers, which means to talk with them to reach a deal on pay and hours. By 1842 a Massachusetts judge had ruled that a union could be lawful. Through these years workers fought for a working day of ten hours.

#### Unions on trial, 1806

In November 1805 the union shoemakers of Philadelphia, the cordwainers, held a turn-out, their word for a strike. In March 1806 lawyers led by Jared Ingersoll and Joseph Hopkinson put eight of them on trial. Judge Moses Levy heard the case in the Mayor's Court of Philadelphia, a city court. The jury found the eight men guilty "of a conspiracy to raise their wages." A conspiracy is a secret plan by two or more people to do something against the law. Each man had to pay a fine of $8 and the costs of the trial. After this verdict, prosecutors could take workers to court as criminals for forming a union to raise their pay.

#### Children, diggers and charcoal burners

Children worked in the mills, and that was legal. Children tended the machines and did the doffing. To doff was to take the full bobbins, the spools that held the spun thread, off a spinning machine and put empty ones on.

Gangs of laborers dug the new canals and graded the new railroad lines, which means they leveled the ground for the tracks. Many of these men were immigrants from Ireland.

At Hopewell Furnace, a place in Pennsylvania where workers made iron, the furnace burned charcoal. Charcoal is wood that has been burned slowly, with little air, until only a black fuel is left. More than 100 of the workers Hopewell paid from 1835 to 1837 were woodcutters. One count by the National Park Service lists 112 woodcutters out of 213 workers, and another lists more than 100 out of nearly 250. Most woodcutters worked part of the year, cutting and splitting hardwood through the winter with only axes. A woodcutter cut about two cords a day and was paid by the cord, a stack of cut wood of a set size.

About 20 colliers, the men who made the charcoal, worked there in the 1830s. Each tended 8 or 9 slowly burning mounds of wood, 24 hours a day for 10 to 14 days, and was paid by the bushel of charcoal. A bushel is a measure of about eight gallons. The colliers lived in huts beside the mounds.

#### Duffy's Cut, 1832

In late June 1832, 57 Irish immigrants arrived on the ship *John Stamp*. They came from Donegal, Tyrone and Derry in Ireland, and their average age was 22. A contractor named Philip Duffy hired them to dig a cut for the Philadelphia and Columbia Railroad. A cut is a channel dug through high ground so the tracks can run level. They also built up a bank of earth for the tracks. The site was at mile 59 of the line, in Chester County, Pennsylvania.

By early August the disease cholera had reached their camp. Cholera is an infection of the gut, spread by water or food that carries traces of a sick person's waste. In bad cases it causes watery diarrhea and vomiting, and the body loses water so fast that a person can go into shock and die. All 57 men died. Some died of cholera, and their remains later showed that someone killed others. Local people stayed away from the camp.

From 2009 to 2012, a team of researchers dug up some of the men's remains. Some of the skulls had been struck by blows at about the time of death. One man had a bullet in his skull, fired at close range. None of the remains the team dug up showed wounds from trying to defend themselves. Someone beat several of the men and shot one. The records do not say who, and no record shows that anyone was charged. To explain the killings, the historian who led the dig, William E. Watson, points to fear of cholera and perhaps to nativism, which is hatred of immigrants.

#### Lowell and the mill girls

The owners of the mills built the mill city of Lowell, Massachusetts, at Pawtucket Falls on the Merrimack River. The falls were a fishing and gathering place of the Pennacook people. In the 1600s two Pennacook towns, Pawtucket and Wamesit, stood where Lowell stands now. Their leaders were the sachems Passaconaway and his son Wannalancet. A sachem is a chief.

In 1675 and 1676 Native nations led by Metacom, a Wampanoag leader the English called King Philip, fought the English colonies of New England. About 9,000 people died in King Philip's War. Wannalancet kept peace with the English. In 1676, at Cocheco in New Hampshire, an English captain named Richard Waldron seized Native people who had come to him in peace. He sent them to Boston, where the governor and council of Massachusetts decided what to do with them. Officials in Boston hanged seven or eight of them. About 200 were enslaved for life and shipped to Barbados, an island in the Caribbean Sea. The records do not name the men who sold them. Wannalancet and his people moved north to St. Francis in Canada. By the end of the war they no longer lived in the lower Merrimack valley.

The Lowell mills belonged to a group of Boston merchants called the Boston Associates. Among them were Francis Cabot Lowell, Nathan Appleton and Patrick Tracy Jackson. Their mills spun cotton that enslaved people had grown in the South. The mills also made a cheap cloth that the owners sold to plantations to clothe enslaved people.

Most of the mill workers were young New England women, aged 15 to 25. They are known as the mill girls. Under the companies' rules they had to work at least a year, to live in a company boardinghouse and to go to church. On average a mill girl stayed about three years.

A report of the Massachusetts lawmakers in 1845 recorded the working day. From May through August, work began at 5 in the morning and ended at 7 at night. The workers had half an hour for breakfast and 45 minutes for the midday meal. From September through April, work began "as soon as they can see" and ran until 7:30 at night. Across the year, the mills ran an average of twelve hours and ten minutes a day. Bells rang the start and the end of work.

#### The Lowell turn-outs of 1834 and 1836

In February 1834 the mill managers announced wage cuts of 12 to 25 percent. About 800 women turned out, which meant they walked off the job together. The strike failed.

In October 1836 the women who ran the boardinghouses told the mill managers they could not make ends meet. The managers then took more money out of each woman's weekly pay for room and board. That was the same as a cut in pay. About 1,500 women struck and formed the Factory Girls' Association. They were better organized than in 1834, and this time they won part of what they asked for. Managers at the Boott and Merrimack mills took back the whole increase. At the Hamilton mill, managers took it back only for workers paid by the day.

<a id="story-harriet-hanson-robinson"></a>

#### Harriet Hanson Robinson

> **Who:** A child worker in a Lowell mill who led the girls of her room out on strike at age 11, and later wrote a book about the mill girls.
>
> **When and where:** Lowell, Massachusetts, 1835 to 1848. Born February 8, 1825. Died 1911.

Harriet Hanson was 11 years old when she led the girls of her room out on strike in October 1836. She had started work in a Lowell mill at 10, as a doffer.

On the day of the turn-out, the girls in her room could not decide whether to leave. She later remembered saying, "I don't care what you do, I am going to turn out, whether anyone else does or not." She walked out, and the others followed her.

Harriet stayed at the mills until 1848. In 1898 she published a book about her years there, called *Loom and Spindle, or Life Among the Early Mill Girls*, and in later life she worked for women's right to vote.

#### The ten-hour day

Workers in Philadelphia, in Lowell and on federal building jobs wanted a working day of ten hours. In 1835 coal heavers on the docks of the Schuylkill River in Philadelphia stopped work. A coal heaver moved coal on and off boats. Other workers joined them. By June 10, workers in more than forty trades, or kinds of skilled work, had struck, nearly 20,000 people in all. It was the first general strike in the United States. In a general strike, workers in many different trades stop work at the same time. Philadelphia's city officials agreed to the ten-hour day and to raises.

On March 31, 1840, President Martin Van Buren ordered a ten-hour day for laborers on building projects of the United States government. His order covered only workers paid by the federal government. It did not cover anyone who worked for a private employer.

#### Commonwealth v. Hunt, 1842

In 1842 the judges of the highest court in Massachusetts, the Supreme Judicial Court, heard a case called Commonwealth v. Hunt. Chief Justice Lemuel Shaw ruled that in Massachusetts a trade union was not a criminal conspiracy just for being a union. Workers there could lawfully form a union, and they could lawfully strike. In 1806 a Philadelphia jury had found union shoemakers guilty of a crime for doing the same thing.

#### Sarah Bagley and the ten-hour petition

In the winter of 1844 and 1845, Lowell mill workers formed the Lowell Female Labor Reform Association. Its president was Sarah Bagley. The women sent petitions to the Massachusetts lawmakers, asking for a ten-hour day. A petition is a written request signed by many people. After the petitions came in, the lawmakers looked into conditions in the mills.

In 1845 Bagley spoke to a committee of the Massachusetts House. She told them that she had "worked in the Lowell Mills eight years and a half." The committee's chairman was William Schouler. All the committee members agreed "that legislation is not necessary at the present time." They meant that no new law was needed. They turned down the ten-hour petition. Bagley said afterward that the committee had "misrepresented" what she told them.

### 1850 to 1900

From 1850 to 1900, working people in mines, mills, rail yards and sweatshops did dangerous work, and children worked beside adults. A sweatshop was a crowded workshop where people sewed clothing for long hours and low pay. In the cotton mills of the South, children worked 12-hour days, six days a week. Workers formed the first national unions to fight for higher pay and an eight-hour day. Police, private guards, state militia (the part-time soldiers of each state) and federal soldiers broke many of their strikes, and they shot and killed strikers.

#### The Chinese railroad strike, 1867

In the 1860s thousands of Chinese workers built the Central Pacific Railroad through the Sierra Nevada mountains of California. White workers on the line earned $40 a month. The Chinese workers earned $35. On June 25, 1867, several thousand of them went on strike. Estimates of their number run from 2,000 to 5,000.

They asked for the same pay as white workers, shorter hours and an end to whipping. The records do not name the men who whipped them. The company's managers cut off the food supply to their camps. After eight days the strike ended with no promises from the company, though pay later rose a little. It was the largest strike by workers in the country up to that time.

#### Avondale, 1869

On September 6, 1869, a fire broke out at the Avondale coal mine in Plymouth Township, near Wilkes-Barre, Pennsylvania. Above the mine stood the breaker, a tall wooden building where coal was broken up and sorted. The breaker stood over the mine's only shaft, the one way in and out. Sparks from the furnace that pushed air through the mine set the breaker on fire.

The men and boys below had no other way out. The fire killed 110 people. Among the dead were five boys and two men who tried to rescue the workers. In 1870 Pennsylvania's lawmakers passed a mine safety law that required more than one exit from every mine.

#### The Knights of Labor

On December 9, 1869, a tailor named Uriah Smith Stephens founded the Knights of Labor in Philadelphia. At first it was a secret society. Terence V. Powderly later led it and opened it up to the public. In 1879 the Knights had fewer than 10,000 members. By 1886 they had about 700,000.

The Knights let women join, and in some places Black workers too. Besides higher wages, they called for an eight-hour day, equal pay for equal work, and an end to child labor and to the work of prisoners leased to companies. They also wanted the public, not private owners, to own utilities, the companies that supplied things like gas and water.

#### Servants, children and sweatshops

The census is the count of all the people in the country that the United States government takes every ten years. The census of 1870 was the first to count women's work carefully. It found 867,354 domestic servants, people paid to cook, clean and care for other families' homes. They made up about half of all women who worked for pay. Domestic service stayed the largest job for women in every census from 1870 to 1940.

The same census found that about 1 in 8 children had jobs. By 1900 it was more than 1 in 5. From 1890 to 1910, at least 18 percent of all children aged 10 to 15 worked. In Philadelphia, the pay children brought home made up 28 to 46 percent of their family's income, depending on the family's ethnic group.

In the South, cotton mill owners hired children in growing numbers. In 1900, 25,000 of the nearly 100,000 textile workers in the South were children under 16. By 1904 there were 50,000 children in the mills, and 20,000 of them were under 12. They worked 12-hour days, six days a week. Mill owners said the fingers of adult farm workers were too "knotted and gnarled" for mill work.

In the hard-coal fields of Pennsylvania, breaker boys sat on benches in the breakers and picked slate, a kind of rock, out of the coal. In the cities, people sewed clothing in sweatshops set up in lofts, the open upper floors of buildings, and in tenements. A tenement was a cheap apartment building packed with families.

#### The Great Railroad Strike, 1877

In July 1877 John W. Garrett, the president of the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, cut his workers' wages by 10 percent. It was not the first cut. Workers at Martinsburg, West Virginia, walked off the job. The strike spread through West Virginia, Maryland, Pennsylvania, New York, Missouri and Illinois.

Governors called up their state militias, the part-time soldiers of each state. President Rutherford B. Hayes sent federal troops. He issued orders for West Virginia on July 18, Maryland on July 21 and Pennsylvania on July 23. In Pittsburgh on July 21, militiamen brought in from Philadelphia opened fire on a crowd. They killed more than twenty people, among them a woman and three small children. The official death count for Pittsburgh was 26, and the real number was likely higher. In Reading, Pennsylvania, on July 23, a crowd threw bricks and stones down on militiamen marching through a deep cut for the railroad. Some of the soldiers fired into the crowd, and at least ten people were killed. By September 1877, state and federal troops had broken the strike. The workers won nothing at the time.

#### The telephone operators

Telephone companies created a new job. Calls went through a switchboard, where an operator connected each caller to the person being called. The first operators were teenage boys. On September 1, 1878, a telephone company in Boston hired Emma Nutt as the first woman operator. Her sister Stella was hired the same day. Emma Nutt earned $10 a month for a 54-hour week. Telephone companies replaced the boys with women, and by the late 1880s nearly all operators were women.

#### The eight-hour day and Haymarket, 1886

On May 1, 1886, workers across the country went on strike for an eight-hour day. In Chicago about 35,000 workers struck. On May 3, Chicago police fired on strikers at the McCormick Harvesting Machine Company plant and killed at least two of them.

On May 4, workers held a meeting in Chicago's Haymarket Square to protest the killings. Inspector John Bonfield marched on the meeting with 176 police officers and ordered the crowd to break up. Then someone threw a dynamite bomb at the police. No one has ever proved who threw it. The police drew their guns and fired wildly. Counts of the dead differ. A Library of Congress history page lists seven police officers and at least four people in the crowd killed. A Chicago History Museum page lists eight police officers dead and sixty wounded, and states that an unknown number in the crowd were killed or wounded.

A Chicago jury convicted eight anarchists of conspiracy. Anarchists are people who believe there should be no government. The eight were Albert Parsons, August Spies, Louis Lingg, Samuel Fielden, Adolph Fischer, Michael Schwab, George Engel and Oscar Neebe. None was shown to have thrown the bomb. Judge Joseph E. Gary sentenced seven of them to death and Neebe to fifteen years in prison. On November 11, 1887, officials at the Cook County Jail hanged Parsons, Spies, Engel and Fischer. Lingg killed himself in his cell with a small bomb that someone smuggled in to him.

After Haymarket, most members left the Knights of Labor. By 1890 the Knights had about 100,000 members, down from about 700,000 in 1886.

In June 1893 Governor John Peter Altgeld of Illinois pardoned the three men still in prison. A pardon is an order that frees a person from punishment for a crime. Altgeld found that the trial had been unfair. He wrote that Judge Gary ran the trial with "malicious ferocity," meaning with cruel, spiteful anger. A court officer named Ryce, chosen at the suggestion of the state's attorney, the lawyer who brought the case, had called in a jury set against the men on trial. Altgeld wrote that "much of the evidence given at the trial was a pure fabrication," which means it was made up. He also wrote that some leading police officials had threatened men with torture and had offered money and jobs to anyone who would swear to what the police wanted.

#### The American Federation of Labor

On December 8, 1886, leaders of craft unions met in Columbus, Ohio, and founded the American Federation of Labor, the AFL. A craft union takes in the skilled workers of one trade, such as cigar makers or carpenters. The AFL's unions bargained with employers, talking with them to reach a deal, for higher wages and shorter hours. This way of running unions was called "pure and simple" unionism.

<a id="story-samuel-gompers"></a>

#### Samuel Gompers

> **Who:** A cigar maker who became the first president of the American Federation of Labor.
>
> **When and where:** Born in London, January 27, 1850. Worked in New York. President of the AFL from 1886 to 1924, except for 1895.

Samuel Gompers led the American Federation of Labor for almost forty years. He was its first president, and he served from 1886 to 1924, except for one year, 1895.

He was born on January 27, 1850, in Spitalfields, in London. He made cigars from boyhood. In New York he rolled cigars in tenement shops.

Gompers built the AFL around wages and hours. In 1886 its unions had about 140,000 members. By 1924 they had nearly 3 million.

#### Brakemen and the coupler

A brakeman on a railroad joined, or coupled, the cars of a train by hand. He stood between two cars as they moved together and guided an iron link into a socket. Brakemen's hands were crushed, and missing fingers were called "the badge of the experienced worker." Thousands of brakemen died.

A safer way already existed. In 1873 Eli Janney got a patent for an automatic coupler. A patent is a government paper that makes an inventor the only one allowed to make and sell an invention for a set time. The Westinghouse air brake, a brake worked by air pressure, had existed since 1869. Railroad owners did not put them on most of their cars. In 1893 members of Congress voted through the Safety Appliance Act, which required both on trains by 1900. Coupling accidents fell from about 11,000 in 1892 to about 2,000 in 1902, while the number of railroad workers grew.

#### Homestead, 1892

In 1892 steelworkers at Carnegie Steel's works in Homestead, Pennsylvania, were on strike, and they held the plant. On July 6, 300 agents of the Pinkerton detective agency, a private company, tried to land from barges and take the plant back. Henry Clay Frick had hired them for Carnegie Steel. Strikers and Pinkertons fought a gun battle. Seven workers and three Pinkerton agents were killed. Some accounts count more.

On July 12, 8,000 state militiamen, sent by the governor of Pennsylvania, arrived at Homestead. By November the strike had failed, and the steelworkers at Homestead no longer had a union.

#### Pullman, 1894

The Pullman Palace Car Company made and repaired railroad cars near Chicago. Its workers lived in Pullman, Illinois, a company town. In a company town, one company owns the houses and collects the rent. In 1893 and 1894 the company's managers cut wages by about 25 to 35 percent. They did not cut the rents.

The workers belonged to the American Railway Union, founded in June 1893. It was the first industrial union, which means it took in every kind of railroad worker in one union, not one craft at a time. In June 1894 the union's members held a convention, a big meeting of delegates sent by its branches. The delegates voted for a national boycott of Pullman cars. In a boycott, people refuse to buy from, use or work for a company. Railroad workers across the country refused to handle trains that carried Pullman cars. On June 28, 1894, while the boycott spread, President Grover Cleveland signed a law making Labor Day a federal holiday.

Attorney General Richard Olney, the federal government's top lawyer, took the union to court. On July 2, 1894, federal judges William Woods and Peter Grosscup issued an injunction. An injunction is a court order that tells people to stop doing something. The judges ordered Eugene V. Debs, the union's founder, and its other officers to stop anything that got in the way of the mail. They also had to stop anything that got in the way of trade between the states. On July 3, over the protest of Governor Altgeld, President Cleveland ordered federal troops into Chicago. More than 16,000 troops were called up across the country. The soldiers arrested boycotters and rioters and sometimes shot them.

About 30 people were killed across the country, and some counts reach 34. Accounts of the strike do not say who killed each of them. Federal judges and soldiers ended the boycott.

<a id="story-jennie-curtis"></a>

#### Jennie Curtis

> **Who:** A seamstress in the Pullman shops whose speech helped start the Pullman boycott.
>
> **When and where:** Pullman, Illinois, 1893 and 1894. Born 1871. Died 1917.

Jennie Curtis spoke to the American Railway Union's convention in June 1894. Her speech helped persuade the delegates to vote for the Pullman boycott.

She was a seamstress in the sewing room of Pullman's repair shops for five years. She told how the women there made "all the carpets, and all the silk, satin, plush, and velvet drapings for the dining cars." They also sewed the cloth covers for the seats. Before the depression of 1893, a time when many businesses failed and many people lost their jobs, she earned $1.50 to $2.25 a day. Then Pullman's managers cut her pay twice in one week in November 1893. Her pay fell to about 80 cents a day. Many of the girls she worked with averaged 40 to 50 cents.

Curtis was president of Local 269, the union's branch for young women workers, which had 125 members. In 1894 she told the United States Strike Commission, a panel that looked into the strike, about wages, rents and abusive supervisors. She said her father had worked for Pullman for 13 years. When he died, he owed back rent, and Pullman's managers collected it.

<a id="story-eugene-debs-work-workers"></a>

#### Eugene V. Debs

> **Who:** A locomotive fireman who founded the American Railway Union and went to jail for leading the Pullman boycott.
>
> **When and where:** Terre Haute, Indiana, and Chicago. Founded the union in June 1893.
>
> **Movie:** *American Socialist: The Life and Times of Eugene Victor Debs* (2017), a documentary directed by Yale Strom. It is about Debs's life.

Eugene V. Debs went to jail for six months for leading the Pullman boycott. As a young man in Terre Haute, Indiana, he was a locomotive fireman, the worker who shoveled coal into the engine's fire. He became an officer of the Brotherhood of Locomotive Firemen, a union for that one craft.

In 1893 he founded the American Railway Union, which took in all railroad workers. After the Pullman boycott, judges found him guilty of contempt of court, which means disobeying a court's order. For that, in 1895, he served six months in the jail at Woodstock, Illinois.

Debs later ran for president five times as a Socialist. Socialists wanted the public, not private owners, to own the big industries. In 1918 he gave a speech against the war, and he was sentenced to ten years in prison for it. He ran for president for the last time in 1920 from his prison cell, as Convict 2253. He got between 900,000 and 1 million votes. President Warren Harding shortened his sentence, and Debs went free at Christmas 1921.

#### Lattimer, 1897

On September 10, 1897, nearly 400 immigrant coal miners marched from Harwood to Lattimer, Pennsylvania, to support a strike. They carried no weapons. Luzerne County Sheriff James Martin had deputized nearly 90 men, which means he had given them the power to act as officers of the law. The deputies fired on the marchers. They killed 19 men, who were Polish, Slovak and Lithuanian, and wounded 38. Many were shot in the back.

Martin and his deputies were tried for murder from February 1 to March 2, 1898. The jury found every one of them not guilty. By 1900 the United Mine Workers, the coal miners' union, was the fastest-growing union in the country.

#### Convict leasing

In the South after the Civil War, state officials leased, or rented out, prisoners to mines, railroads and planters, who forced them to work. This was called convict leasing. Most of the prisoners were Black men. In Alabama, more than 90 percent of the state prisoners who were leased out were Black. Sheriffs arrested many of them for small offenses under the Black Codes. Southern lawmakers passed these laws from November 1865, and they made Black people prove they had work. In Alabama, contractors whipped prisoners who tried to escape or did not work hard enough. Every year 4 to 5 percent of Alabama's leased state prisoners died.

### 1900 to 1950

A federal law of 1938 set a minimum wage of 25 cents an hour. It also set a work week of 44 hours, falling to 40 by 1940, and banned most work by children under 16. Since 1935 workers had had the legal right to form unions, under a federal law that members of Congress passed that year. In the first years of the century, children still worked in mills and mines. In 1900, 1,489 coal miners were killed at work, and in 1907, 3,242. In 1911 a fire killed 146 workers in a New York garment factory. At Ludlow, Colorado, in 1914, National Guard soldiers burned a camp of striking miners' tents, and the fire killed 13 women and children hiding in a pit under one tent. In Chicago in 1937, police shot and killed ten people who were marching to support a steel strike.

#### The hard-coal strike, 1902

In May 1902, 147,000 hard-coal miners and breaker boys in Pennsylvania went on strike. Breaker boys were boys who picked waste rock out of the coal. They stayed out for about five months, until October. President Theodore Roosevelt stepped in. Earlier presidents had sent troops to break strikes, as in 1877 and 1894. Roosevelt acted as a mediator instead, a go-between who helps both sides reach a deal. It was the first time a president had done this in a strike.

Roosevelt set up a commission, a group of people chosen to look into the strike. The commission heard 558 witnesses. Some of them were breaker boys younger than nine. In March 1903 the commission's members ruled that the miners should get a 10 percent raise and a nine-hour day.

<a id="story-mother-jones"></a>

#### Mother Jones

> **Who:** Mary Harris Jones, a union organizer for coal miners whom a prosecutor called "the most dangerous woman in America."
>
> **When and where:** Baptized in Cork, Ireland. She said she was born in 1830, but her baptism record gives August 1, 1837. Organizing from the 1870s, and for the United Mine Workers from the 1890s. Died 1930.

Mary Harris Jones, known as Mother Jones, spent the last part of her long life organizing workers. In 1902 a prosecutor in West Virginia called her "the most dangerous woman in America."

She had worked as a dressmaker. In 1867, in Memphis, Tennessee, her husband and all four of her children died of the disease yellow fever. In 1871 she lost her home and her shop in the great fire in Chicago. After that she became a full-time organizer. From the 1890s she worked above all for the United Mine Workers, the coal miners' union.

In July 1903 she led the March of the Mill Children. Children who worked in textile mills in Philadelphia were on strike. Mother Jones marched with them from Philadelphia toward the home of President Theodore Roosevelt at Oyster Bay, New York. She wanted people across the country to look at child labor.

She said she was born in 1830, and on May 1, 1930, she celebrated her "100th" birthday. The record of her baptism in Cork gives August 1, 1837, which would have made her 92. She died in 1930.

#### Deaths in the coal mines

In 1900, 1,489 coal miners were killed at work. The worst year on record was 1907. That year 3,242 coal miners were killed out of 680,492 miners.

On December 6, 1907, explosions in two mines at Monongah, West Virginia, mines No. 6 and No. 8, killed hundreds of men and boys. Some of the boys were as young as eight. The official count was 362 dead. The West Virginia Mine Wars Museum and later estimates put the dead at more than 500. About 1,000 children lost their fathers. Accounts differ on which company ran the mines, the Fairmont Coal Company or the Consolidation Coal Company. The Fairmont company's president, C. W. Watson, blamed "the careless use of a mining lamp." No record shows that anyone was charged.

#### Lewis Hine photographs the children

Lewis Hine left his job as a teacher in 1908 to take photographs of working children. He worked for the National Child Labor Committee, a group trying to end child labor. From 1908 to 1917 he made thousands of pictures of children at work in mills, mines, food-canning plants and on city streets.

<a id="story-addie-card"></a>

#### Addie Card

> **Who:** A child spinner in a Vermont cotton mill whose photograph by Lewis Hine appeared on a United States postage stamp in 1998.
>
> **When and where:** North Pownal, Vermont, 1910. Died 1993.

In 1910 Lewis Hine photographed Addie Card at her spinning machine in the cotton mill at North Pownal, Vermont. She was 12 years old, according to Hine. The girls at the mill told him she was 10.

Hine wrote her name down wrongly as "Addie Laird." He called her an "anemic little spinner." Anemic means pale and weak because the blood is not carrying enough of what the body needs. In 1998 the picture appeared on a United States postage stamp.

In 2005 and 2006, a researcher named Joe Manning, working with the novelist Elizabeth Winthrop, found her real name and traced her life. In 1915, at 17, she married Edward Hatch. They split in 1925, and he won custody of their daughter. She married again, to Ernest Lavigne, and got another job in a mill in Cohoes, New York. In her last years she lived in a housing project in Cohoes. She died in 1993.

#### The shirtwaist makers and the Triangle fire

A shirtwaist was a woman's blouse. In New York City, many young immigrant women sewed shirtwaists in garment shops. On November 22, 1909, the shirtwaist makers held a meeting at Cooper Union, a hall in New York. Clara Lemlich, a shirtwaist maker, was still bruised from a beating by men hired by her company. She stood up and spoke in Yiddish, the language of many Jewish immigrants. "I have no further patience for talk," she said. "I move we go on strike." About 20,000 garment workers struck for eleven weeks. The strike is called the Uprising of the 20,000.

On March 25, 1911, a fire broke out on the top floors of the Triangle Waist Company's building near Washington Square in New York. The fire killed 146 workers. Most of them were young immigrant women, and some were only 14. On the ninth floor, the door to one stairway was locked. No record proves who locked it. Dozens of workers jumped from the building.

The owners of the company, Max Blanck and Isaac Harris, were tried for manslaughter. Manslaughter is the crime of killing someone without meaning to, through a wrongful act or through carelessness. On December 27, 1911, the jury acquitted them, which means it found them not guilty. The prosecutors could not prove that the owners knew the door was locked. New York's lawmakers then set up the Factory Investigating Commission, and they rewrote the state's factory safety laws.

<a id="story-rose-freedman"></a>

#### Rose Rosenfeld Freedman

> **Who:** A worker who survived the Triangle fire and spent the rest of her life telling what happened there.
>
> **When and where:** New York City, March 25, 1911. Died February 15, 2001, at 107, the last survivor of the fire.

Rose Rosenfeld was two days short of her 18th birthday when the Triangle fire broke out. She got out by following the company's executives up the stairs to the roof of the building, on the tenth floor. From the roof, rescuers pulled the survivors across.

She later said that the owners offered her money to keep quiet about the locked doors. She said she turned the money down. For ninety years she told people the truth about the locked doors.

Rose Rosenfeld Freedman died in Beverly Hills, California, on February 15, 2001. She was 107, and she was the last survivor of the Triangle fire.

<a id="story-frances-perkins-work-workers"></a>

#### Frances Perkins

> **Who:** A woman who watched the Triangle fire, later became the first woman in a president's Cabinet, and pushed for the law that set the country's first federal minimum wage.
>
> **When and where:** New York, 1911. Secretary of Labor in Washington, 1933 to 1945.
>
> **Movie:** *Summoned: Frances Perkins and the General Welfare* (2020), a documentary by Mick Caouette, shown on PBS. It is about Perkins's life.

Frances Perkins was having tea near Washington Square on March 25, 1911, when the Triangle fire broke out. She ran to the building and watched the workers jump. She later said the New Deal began on that day. The New Deal was the set of programs that President Franklin Roosevelt started in the 1930s.

After the fire, Perkins worked as an investigator for New York's Factory Investigating Commission. In 1933 President Roosevelt made her Secretary of Labor. She was the first woman in a US Cabinet, the group of top advisers who run the government's departments. She held the job until 1945. She pushed for the Fair Labor Standards Act and for Social Security, the government's program of payments to people who are old or cannot work.

#### Lawrence, 1912

In 1912 Massachusetts lawmakers cut the legal work week from 56 hours to 54. Mill owners in Lawrence, Massachusetts, then cut their workers' pay. On January 12, 1912, the workers struck. Most of them worked for the American Woolen Company. More than half of the mill workers were women and children, and they spoke more than a dozen languages. Leaders of a union called the Industrial Workers of the World sent organizers, who ran committees that gave out food and help.

In February the strikers began sending their children to live with families in other cities. On February 24, police at the Lawrence railroad station clubbed women and children who were trying to send children away. The police jailed 30 women. On March 12 the owners agreed to a 15 percent raise, double pay for overtime (extra hours of work) and no punishment for the strikers.

#### The assembly line

On October 7, 1913, managers at Henry Ford's plant at Highland Park, Michigan, started a moving line to build car frames, called chassis. The work moved past 140 assemblers along 150 feet of line. Each man did the same few motions over and over, at the speed of the line. Building a chassis had taken more than 12 hours. On the line it took about 93 minutes.

Many men could not stand the pace, and they quit. In 1913 worker turnover at the plant reached 370 percent. That means that for every job, Ford's managers had to hire nearly four men in a year. On January 5, 1914, Ford announced a pay of $5 for an eight-hour day. Before that, pay had been about $2.34 for nine hours.

The $5 day came with conditions. Ford's managers called part of the money "profit-sharing," and they paid that part only to men who passed inspections of their homes. Company investigators, from an office that Ford's managers called the Sociological Department, checked whether a man drank, whether he saved money and how clean his home was. They also checked whether he took in boarders, people who paid to live in a room of his home. The managers left out workers under 22 and, at first, most women.

#### Ludlow, 1914

Coal miners in Colorado went on strike in September 1913. They wanted the state's mining laws enforced. They also wanted the mine owners to recognize their union, the United Mine Workers, which means to accept it and bargain with it over pay and hours. Most of them worked for the Colorado Fuel and Iron Company. Its main owner was John D. Rockefeller Jr. The strikers and their families lived in tent colonies.

In October 1913 men in an armored car belonging to the company, called the "Death Special," fired on the tent colony at Forbes and killed one person. Governor Elias M. Ammons sent in the Colorado National Guard, the state's soldiers, and the mine owners paid for it.

On April 20, 1914, fighting broke out at the tent colony at Ludlow. Nobody knows who fired the first shot. Guardsmen burned the tents. At least 19 people were killed. One was a guardsman and five were miners. Thirteen were women and children who had hidden in a pit dug under a tent. They suffocated, which means they died because they could not get air. Guardsmen shot the strike leader, Louis Tikas, three times in the back.

After Ludlow, miners attacked mines across the region and killed supervisors and guards. Nobody knows exactly how many. On April 28 President Woodrow Wilson sent in the US Army. The strike ended in December 1914. The miners won none of their union's goals.

#### The first child-labor law, and the justices who threw it out

In 1916 members of Congress passed the Keating-Owen Act, the first federal law against child labor. Under it, a company could not ship goods to another state if it had used child workers to make them. It covered children under 14 in mills, food-canning plants and factories, and children under 16 in mines. Children aged 14 to 16 could not work more than 8 hours a day or 6 days a week, or at night.

Roland Dagenhart's sons worked in a cotton mill in North Carolina, and he sued to stop the law. On June 3, 1918, the justices of the Supreme Court ruled 5 votes to 4 in the case Hammer v. Dagenhart. They said the law broke the Constitution and could not be used. The majority ruled that Congress's power over trade between the states did not cover how goods were made. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes disagreed. Members of Congress passed a second child-labor law in 1919, and the justices threw that one out too.

<a id="story-grace-fryer-work-workers"></a>

#### Grace Fryer

> **Who:** A painter of glowing watch dials who was poisoned by radium at work and sued the company while she was dying.
>
> **When and where:** Orange, New Jersey. Worked from 1917 to 1920. Sued in 1927. Settled in June 1928.
>
> **Movie:** *Radium Girls* (2018), a drama inspired by the dial painters' case. Its main characters are two invented sisters, not Grace Fryer.

Grace Fryer painted watch dials with glowing paint at the United States Radium Corporation in Orange, New Jersey, from 1917 to 1920. The paint glowed because it contained radium. Radium gives off radiation, energy that damages the body from the inside. Their supervisors taught the women who painted the dials to shape the tip of the brush with their lips, so the radium paint went into their mouths. "Our instructors told us to point [our brushes] with our lips," Grace Fryer said later. The supervisors told the women the paint was safe.

Radium is in the same chemical family as calcium, so the body takes it into the bones and teeth. Almost all of it stays in the skeleton. Scientists who studied the dial painters found that it caused aplastic anemia, necrosis of the jaw and osteosarcomas. Aplastic anemia means the body stops making enough new blood cells. Necrosis means the bone dies, and the jawbone breaks down. An osteosarcoma is a cancer of the bone. In 1924 a dentist named Theodor Blum examined Grace Fryer and found that her jawbone was wasting away in a way he had never seen before.

As the dial painters fell sick and died, company officials played down and disputed the poisoning. In May 1927 a lawyer named Raymond Berry sued the company for five of the women. They were Grace Fryer, Katherine Schaub, Quinta Maggia Macdonald, Albina Maggia Larice and Edna Hussman. Reporters called them "the five women doomed to die." Some of them were too sick to travel to court.

In June 1928 the company's officials agreed to pay the women to end the lawsuit. This kind of deal is called a settlement. Each woman received $10,000 (some accounts say $15,000), $600 a year for as long as she lived and payment for her medical bills. A committee of three doctors had to approve the medical costs. The company's officials never admitted that the company was to blame.

#### Catherine Wolfe Donohue's case, 1938

At the Radium Dial Company plant in Ottawa, Illinois, a supervisor named Miss Murray also taught the dial painters to point their brushes with their lips. Catherine Wolfe Donohue was one of them. "We would first dip the brush into water, then into the powder, and then point the ends of the bristles between our teeth," she said. At a hearing on February 10, 1938, she brought a box of pieces of bone that she said had come from her jaw. When the judge asked her doctor about her chances, she collapsed. Several men carried her from the room. She weighed 71 pounds.

On April 5, 1938, the hearing officer, the official who ran the hearing, ruled that her illness came from her work at the plant. He awarded her $5,661, paid as $277 a year for life. The company's lawyers asked for a new ruling, which is called an appeal. On July 6, 1938, the members of the Illinois Industrial Commission, a state board that decided workers' claims, turned down the appeal and added $730. Donohue died later that month, at 35. The last appeal in her case ended in October 1938, after her death.

#### Hawks Nest tunnel, 1930 to 1932

From 1930 to 1932, managers of the Union Carbide company had workers dig a tunnel near Gauley Bridge, West Virginia, to carry water to a power plant. The plant was built to supply power to Union Carbide's alloy works, where metals were mixed. Union Carbide's managers hired the Rinehart and Dennis company of Charlottesville, Virginia, to do the digging. Almost 5,000 men worked on the tunnel. Most of them were Black men from the South.

The tunnel went through sandstone made mostly of silica, the hard mineral that sand is made of. A third of it was dug wider so that the silica could be mined. The men worked with no dust control and nothing to protect their breathing, in poor air underground.

Breathing silica dust causes silicosis. The dust forms scar tissue in the lungs, and the scarred lungs cannot take in enough oxygen. Silicosis cannot be cured, and in bad cases it kills.

The number of men who died is disputed. In 1936 members of a US House of Representatives committee held hearings and put the deaths at 476. In 1986 the scientist Martin Cherniack studied the records and found as many as 764. In 2002 scientists at the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health, the federal agency that studies workers' health, said close to 1,000. The workers and their families filed 538 lawsuits. They ended in a settlement of $200,000 in all. Single payments ran from $30 to $1,600.

#### Building the skyscrapers, the bridge and the dam

Up to 3,400 workers a day built the Empire State Building in New York. By the official count, five of them died. Lewis Hine photographed the ironworkers high on the open steel frame in 1931. Mohawk ironworkers from Kahnawake, a Mohawk community just south of Montreal in Canada, worked in the building crews.

At the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco, the chief engineer, Joseph Strauss, required workers to wear hard hats. He spent about $130,000 on a safety net under the bridge. The net caught 19 men who fell, and they called themselves the "Halfway to Hell Club." One of them, the ironworker Al Zampa, fell on October 19, 1936, and broke four bones in his back. He went back to ironwork. Eleven men died building the bridge. Ten of them died on February 17, 1937, when a falling platform tore through the net.

At Hoover Dam, the federal Bureau of Reclamation's official count is 96 deaths on the job. That count leaves out 42 deaths that were recorded as pneumonia, a disease of the lungs. Whether those men died of pneumonia or were poisoned in the tunnels by carbon monoxide, a gas from engines, is disputed. The true number of deaths at the dam is not known.

#### The right to organize and the sit-down strikes

During the Great Depression of the 1930s, many businesses closed and millions of people lost their jobs. At its worst, in 1933, about 12.8 million people, almost one worker in four, had no job. Federal officials hired people who were out of work through programs such as the Works Progress Administration and the Civilian Conservation Corps. In 1935 members of Congress passed the Wagner Act, which made it a legal right for workers to form unions.

That same year John L. Lewis and other union leaders formed a new group inside the American Federation of Labor, the AFL, to organize whole factories. The AFL was a large group of unions of skilled workers. The AFL's leaders threw them out, and the group became the Congress of Industrial Organizations, the CIO. Its unions took in every worker in a mass-production plant, such as a car factory or a steel mill.

In a sit-down strike, workers stop working but stay inside the plant, so the company cannot bring in other workers. On December 30, 1936, autoworkers in Flint, Michigan, sat down inside General Motors' Fisher Body plants. They stayed for 44 days, until February 11, 1937. The Women's Emergency Brigade, led by 23-year-old Genora Johnson, guarded the plants. When police fired gas at the men inside, the women broke windows. General Motors' managers agreed to recognize the United Auto Workers, which meant they would bargain with it over pay and hours.

#### The Memorial Day Massacre, 1937

Several hundred people marched toward the Republic Steel plant on Sunday, May 30, 1937. The plant stood on Chicago's far Southeast Side, and the marchers were supporting the steelworkers' strike there. They were white, Black and Latino men, women and children, and about 200 of them were women. There, 264 Chicago police met them.

The police threw tear gas, fired their guns and beat the marchers with clubs. They killed ten people and shot 40. More than 90 people were wounded in all. The Paramount company filmed it and at first held back the newsreel. Senators on a committee led by Senator Robert La Follette Jr. looked into the killings. They found that the police had used "excessive force," which means far more force than was needed. The police had also made "baseless allegations," claims with nothing true behind them. The senators said the police "did not carry out an honest investigation." No record names any police officer who was ever punished.

<a id="story-a-philip-randolph-work-workers"></a>

#### A. Philip Randolph

> **Who:** A union leader who organized the Pullman porters and won the first contract between a major American company and a union led by Black workers.
>
> **When and where:** Founded the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters in August 1925. Contract signed August 25, 1937. Washington, 1941.
>
> **Movie:** *10,000 Black Men Named George* (2002), a television drama with Andre Braugher as Randolph. Also *A. Philip Randolph: For Jobs and Freedom* (1996), a documentary shown on PBS.

A. Philip Randolph won the first contract between a major American company and a union led by Black workers. In August 1925 he founded the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters. Porters worked on the Pullman Company's sleeping cars on trains. All of the porters were Black men. The company required them to serve passengers with a smile, and passengers commonly called every porter "George."

On August 25, 1937, twelve years after the union began, the Pullman Company's officials signed a contract with it. The porters' working month had run to about 400 hours. Under the contract the working month fell sharply, and the porters got $1.25 million in raises.

In 1941 Randolph threatened to lead a march on Washington. On June 25, 1941, President Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 8802, an order from the president. It said there could be "no discrimination in the employment of workers in defense industries or government because of race, creed, color, or national origin." Defense companies made weapons and supplies for the military. Under the order, they and government offices could not refuse to hire people because of their race, religion or the country their families came from. In 1963 Randolph directed the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom.

#### The Fair Labor Standards Act, 1938

On June 25, 1938, President Roosevelt signed the Fair Labor Standards Act, and it took effect on October 24, 1938. The law set the first federal minimum wage at 25 cents an hour, rising to 40 cents by 1945, and a work week of 44 hours, falling to 40 hours by October 1940. The law also banned most work by children under 16 in the jobs it covered, but it did not cover farm work.

In 1941 the justices of the Supreme Court changed their minds about their earlier rulings. They ruled that Congress did have the power to limit child labor under the 1938 law.

#### War work and the braceros

During World War II, women took jobs in war plants in large numbers. In 1940 women made up 27 percent of the workforce. By 1945 they made up nearly 37 percent, and about 6.5 million more women were working. Before the war about 1 percent of aircraft workers were women. In 1943 more than 310,000 women built aircraft, about 65 percent of all the workers in that industry.

In 1942 US officials started the bracero program to bring Mexican men to work on American farms and railroads during the war. Bracero is Spanish for a man who works with his arms. Over 22 years, more than 4.5 million contracts were signed. From 1942 to 1946, American employers held back 10 percent of every bracero's pay. The money went through American banks to banks in Mexico, for a savings fund the braceros were to receive when they went home. Most braceros never got that money, and the records of where it went do not add up. In 2009 Mexican officials agreed to pay former braceros or their families 38,000 pesos each.

<a id="story-naomi-parker-fraley"></a>

#### Naomi Parker Fraley

> **Who:** A war worker at the Navy yard in Alameda, California, whom a scholar found to be the woman in a 1942 photograph linked to the "We Can Do It!" poster.
>
> **When and where:** Alameda, California, 1942. Died January 20, 2018, at 96.

Naomi Parker was a war worker at the Navy yard in Alameda, California. In 1942 a photographer took her picture at work. For decades, people said that the woman in that photograph was someone else.

The photograph is linked to a poster of a woman worker with the words "We Can Do It!" J. Howard Miller made the poster for the Westinghouse company, which put it on display in 1943. Few people knew the poster during the war. It became famous in the 1980s.

From 1984, the woman in the 1942 photograph was said to be Geraldine Hoff Doyle. Then a scholar named James J. Kimble found the original print of the photograph. Its caption named Naomi Parker. Nobody has proved that Miller used this photograph to make the poster. Naomi Parker Fraley died on January 20, 2018, at 96.

#### The strike wave of 1945 and 1946

When the war ended, workers struck in greater numbers than ever before. In 1945 there were 4,750 strikes involving 3.47 million workers. The Bureau of Labor Statistics, the federal office that counts jobs and workers, recorded 4,985 strikes involving 4.6 million workers in 1946. No other year in its records has more. Workers struck in steel, coal, railroads and car plants.

### 1950 to 2000

In 1954 about one American worker in three belonged to a union. After that the share fell for the rest of the century. By 1956 more Americans worked in offices, stores and schools than worked with their hands in factories, mines and building trades. The share of women with paid jobs rose from 34 percent in 1950 to 60 percent in 2000. New groups of workers organized: farmworkers, city garbage collectors, flight attendants and office clerks. After June 1979 the number of factory jobs fell, and by 2000 about 13 percent of workers belonged to a union.

#### Unions at their peak, and the move to the office

In 1954, 34.8 percent of Americans who worked for wages or salaries belonged to a union. That was the peak. On December 5, 1955, the AFL and the CIO joined into one big group of unions, the AFL-CIO, with about 15 million members. George Meany was its first president.

By 1956, for the first time, more Americans worked in white-collar jobs than in blue-collar jobs. White-collar workers work in offices, stores and schools. Blue-collar workers work with their hands in factories, mines and building trades.

Women also went to work for pay in growing numbers. In 1950, 34 percent of women were in the labor force, which means they had a paid job or were looking for one. By 2000 the figure was 60 percent. Over the same years, women's share of all workers rose from 30 percent to almost 47 percent.

#### The braceros at work

The bracero program went on after the war. Men who wanted contracts went through reception centers at the border. Officials of the federal agency that handled immigration ran them. One was the Rio Vista farm in El Paso, Texas. Men who went through Rio Vista remembered "poor food, humiliating medical examinations, and the fumigation." Officials had the men strip off their clothes, line up and be sprayed with DDT, a white powder that kills insects. The officials believed that Mexican workers carried insects and germs.

From 1948, growers could hire braceros right at the border. That let the growers skip the cost of moving the men and avoid government checks. Braceros worked six or seven days a week on farms and railroads in 26 states. Some were paid little and lived in poor housing. Supervisors cursed at some of them and attacked some of them physically. They worked with pesticides, chemicals that kill insects and weeds, and these were later found to be very harmful to farmworkers. The program ended in 1964, after pressure from unions, the spread of farm machines and public attention to the conditions.

#### The Mohawk ironworkers

Ironworkers from the Mohawk communities of Kahnawake, just south of Montreal, and Akwesasne, which lies across the border of the United States and Canada on the St. Lawrence River, worked high steel from the 1920s onward. Working high steel means building the steel frames of bridges and skyscrapers, walking on narrow beams far above the ground. Mohawk ironworkers helped build the Empire State Building, the Chrysler Building and Rockefeller Center in New York. Later they helped build the World Trade Center. The 9/11 Memorial and Museum has an exhibit about them called "Skywalkers."

<a id="story-chavez-huerta"></a>

#### Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta

> **Who:** Organizers who built the farmworkers' union, together with the Filipino American grape pickers led by Larry Itliong, who walked out first.
>
> **When and where:** Delano, California, 1965 to 1975.
>
> **Movie:** *Cesar Chavez* (2014), a drama directed by Diego Luna, with Michael Peña as Chavez. *Dolores* (2017), a documentary about Dolores Huerta directed by Peter Bratt.

Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta led farmworkers to win the first union contracts in the California grape fields. Filipino American workers started the strike that led to those contracts. On September 8, 1965, about 1,500 grape pickers, most of them Filipino American, walked out of the vineyards around Delano, California. They belonged to the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee, or AWOC, a union led by Larry Itliong. On September 16, members of Chavez and Huerta's National Farm Workers Association voted to join the strike.

From March 17 to April 11, 1966, strikers marched about 300 miles from Delano to Sacramento, the state capital. About 10,000 supporters were with them when they arrived. The two unions joined together and became the union now called the United Farm Workers. In February and March of 1968, Chavez went without food for 25 days as a call for nonviolence. Senator Robert Kennedy was with him when he ended the fast on March 10.

Across the country, people stopped buying California table grapes. This was the grape boycott. On July 29, 1970, 26 grape growers in Delano signed the first union contracts. Dolores Huerta negotiated the contracts. She also made up the union's slogan, "Sí, se puede," Spanish for "Yes, it can be done."

Since 1935 federal labor law had not covered farmworkers. In 1975 California's lawmakers passed the Agricultural Labor Relations Act. It was the first law in the United States to give farmworkers the right to collective bargaining, which means bargaining as a union with their employers.

In March 2026 the New York Times reported that Chavez had sexually abused two girls in the 1970s. The two women, Debra Rojas and Ana Murguia, are daughters of union organizers. They said the abuse began when they were 12 and 13. Rojas said Chavez raped her in a motel room when she was 15. Rape means forcing a person into sex. Dolores Huerta then said publicly that Chavez had pressured her into sex once and had raped her in a car in 1966, and that she became pregnant both times. She said she had kept the secret for 60 years because she believed the truth would hurt the farmworker movement. Chavez died in 1993, so no court has ever heard these accusations. The United Farm Workers canceled its events for Cesar Chavez Day. On March 26, 2026, California's lawmakers voted to rename the state holiday Farmworkers Day, and Governor Gavin Newsom signed the change into law.

#### Pesticides in the fields

Farmworkers who worked in fields sprayed with pesticides, chemicals that kill insects and weeds, had high rates of birth defects, cancer and burns. Cesar Chavez and Dolores Huerta campaigned to ban DDT on grape and lettuce ranches. In the 1980s, children in several towns of California's San Joaquin Valley had cancer at rates "800% above the norm."

#### The stewardesses' rules

Into the late 1960s, managers at US airlines fired stewardesses who married or who turned 32, and at some airlines 35. They also weighed the women and checked that they wore girdles, tight undergarments. Barbara "Dusty" Roads flew for American Airlines from 1950. She pressed members of Congress to change the rules and helped found the Association of Professional Flight Attendants, a union. The Civil Rights Act of 1964 banned treating workers unfairly in hiring and firing because they were women or men. Flight attendants brought cases under that law, and in those years airline managers dropped the age and marriage rules.

#### Memphis, 1968

On February 1, 1968, two Memphis garbage collectors, Echol Cole, 36, and Robert Walker, 30, took shelter from the rain inside the compactor of their garbage truck. The compactor is the part of the truck that crushes the garbage. The truck was not working properly, and the compactor crushed both men to death.

Eleven days later, 1,300 Black sanitation workers went on strike. They wanted the city's leaders to recognize their union, which means to accept it and bargain with it. They also wanted the work made safe and pay that was enough to live on. Many of them were paid so little that they were on welfare, and hundreds relied on food stamps to feed their families. The strikers carried signs that read "I AM A MAN."

On February 22 the members of the City Council voted to recognize the union. Mayor Henry Loeb rejected the vote. He said only the mayor could recognize a union, and he would not. He also kept the worn-out trucks on the streets and would not pay overtime for late-night shifts. On February 23 police sprayed Mace and fired tear gas at marchers walking to City Hall.

On March 28 violence broke out during a march, and some people looted downtown shops. Members of a young Black Power group called the Invaders were accused of starting it. Police followed the marchers back to Clayborn Temple, a church, fired tear gas inside and clubbed people lying on the floor. A Memphis police officer shot and killed Larry Payne, a 16-year-old student. The officer said Payne came at him with a knife. Most people who saw it said Payne came out of a basement with his hands up, and none of them saw a knife. The officer was never charged or disciplined.

Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. came to Memphis to support the strikers. On the evening of April 4, 1968, James Earl Ray shot and killed him on the balcony of the Lorraine Motel. On April 16, city negotiators agreed that the City Council would recognize the union and raise wages. The union was AFSCME Local 1733, part of a national union of city and state workers.

#### Coal dust and a new safety law

On November 20, 1968, an explosion in the Consol No. 9 mine at Farmington, West Virginia, killed 78 miners. Members of Congress then passed the Federal Coal Mine Health and Safety Act of 1969. Under it, federal inspectors had to inspect every underground coal mine four times a year. They could shut a mine down if it put lives in danger. The law also set up federal payments for miners with black lung.

Black lung is a disease caused by breathing coal dust. The dust scars the lungs. In the worst form, masses of scar tissue leave the miner "gasping for every breath." More than 76,000 miners have died of black lung since 1968. In 1968, 311 coal miners were killed at work. In 1980 the number was 133, and in 2000 it was 38.

On December 29, 1970, President Richard Nixon signed the Occupational Safety and Health Act, a federal law on safety at work. In 1970 about 14,000 workers were killed on the job each year, about 38 a day.

#### Office workers organize

In 1973 two office workers in Boston, Karen Nussbaum and Ellen Cassedy, founded 9to5. Its members were women who did clerical work, such as typing, filing and answering phones. They organized over pay, promotion and harassment on the job. Harassment means treating a worker in ways meant to upset, shame or frighten her.
