In an early lawsuit, they won $1.5 million in back pay, the pay the women were owed, from publishing companies in Boston.

The checkout job changed too. At 8:01 in the morning on June 26, 1974, cashier Sharon Buchanan at a Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio, scanned a ten-pack of Juicy Fruit gum. It was the first sale rung up by scanning a barcode. Cashiers no longer had to key in each price by hand. The scanners also gave managers records, hour by hour, of what sold, and managers later used those records to set workers' schedules.

#### The mills close

On September 19, 1977, the managers of Youngstown Sheet and Tube suddenly shut the company's Campbell Works steel mill in Youngstown, Ohio, and 5,000 workers lost their jobs. People in Youngstown remember that day as "Black Monday." Factory jobs in the United States reached their highest number, 19.6 million, in June 1979. After that the number fell for forty years.

In 1983, 20.1 percent of wage and salary workers belonged to a union. By 2000 the share was about 13.4 percent.

<a id="story-frank-lumpkin"></a>

#### Frank Lumpkin

> **Who:** A Black steelworker who lost his job, his last paycheck and his pension when his Chicago steel mill shut down, and who fought for 17 years to win the money back.
>
> **When and where:** Wisconsin Steel, South Deering, Chicago, from the 1950s. Born 1916. Died March 1, 2010.

Frank Lumpkin spent 17 years fighting to win back the pay and pensions that he and more than 3,000 other steelworkers lost when their mill closed in 1980. A pension is money paid to a worker after the worker retires. He was born in 1916 in Washington, Georgia, to a family of sharecroppers. Sharecroppers farm land that belongs to someone else and pay the owner with part of the crop. At 6 he hauled stone for an uncle. At 15 he left school to work on citrus plantations. He also boxed for money as "KO" Lumpkin.

In 1940 he moved north to Buffalo, New York. He worked in construction, in an aircraft factory and at Bethlehem Steel, and he served in the Merchant Marine, the crews of American cargo ships. In the 1950s he went to work at Wisconsin Steel in the South Deering neighborhood of Chicago. He worked in the mill for about 30 years.

International Harvester had owned the mill since 1902. In 1977 International Harvester's managers sold the mill to Envirodyne, a company with no experience in steel. They lent Envirodyne the money to buy it. In late March 1980, while Envirodyne owned it, the mill shut down without warning. The workers lost their jobs, their health benefits, their back pay and their pensions. In April, officers of Chase Manhattan Bank told them that their final paychecks were worthless.

Lumpkin and his wife, Bea Lumpkin, started the Wisconsin Steel Save Our Jobs Committee. Its members were Black, Mexican American and other steelworkers and their families. They helped families with food, medical care and utility bills. First the members tried to get the mill reopened. Then they fought to recover the lost pay and benefits, and they sued International Harvester and Envirodyne. In 1987 the committee counted 600 former workers who had died in the seven years since the closing.

In 1988 the lawyer Thomas Geoghegan won a settlement of $14.5 million from International Harvester. Over 17 years the committee won about $17 million in all. That was about a third of the $40 million the workers were owed. Lumpkin also ran to become an Illinois state lawmaker and lost. He died on March 1, 2010, at 93.

#### The air traffic controllers, 1981

On August 3, 1981, about 13,000 federal air traffic controllers, the workers who guide airplanes in and out of airports, went on strike. Federal law did not allow federal workers to strike. President Ronald Reagan gave them 48 hours to return to work. On August 5 he fired 11,345 of them. Their union was decertified, which means federal officials no longer accepted it as the workers' union. The historian Joseph McCartin, who wrote a book about the strike, argues that the firings showed private employers that they could fight strikes and beat their unions.

#### El Monte, 1995

On August 2, 1995, state and federal agents and El Monte police raided a fenced apartment complex in El Monte, near Los Angeles. Inside they found 72 Thai garment workers who had been forced to sew clothes and were not allowed to leave, and they freed them. Suni Manasurangkun and her sons ran the operation. Recruiters in Thailand had taken the workers' passports when they arrived. The workers owed about $5,000 for the trip.

A high fence topped with razor wire surrounded the buildings, and an armed guard sat in the courtyard. The workers sewed clothes 84 hours a week, from early morning to midnight, for about $1.60 an hour. One worker, Rotchana Cheunchujit, was paid five to seven cents a garment. The owners made the workers buy food at their own store at high prices. Some workers had not been outside the fence for as long as seven years.

One woman escaped through a second-story window. A letter in pencil with a hand-drawn map reached the authorities, and the raid followed. The clothes carried "Made in the USA" labels and were sold at chain stores including Miller's Outpost, Mervyn's and Montgomery Ward. In February 1996 Suni Manasurangkun, three of her sons and three other people pleaded guilty to federal crimes. That means they told the court they had broken federal law. Two of her sons fled and were never caught. In 1997 the companies that had sold the clothes agreed to pay the workers the wages they were owed, to end lawsuits against them. One account puts the total at more than $4.5 million, and another at $4 million. After the case, and partly because of it, members of Congress passed a federal law in 2000 against human trafficking, the buying, selling and moving of people to force them to work.

### 2000 to Today

About 11.9 million Americans worked as independent contractors in their main job in July 2023, outside most labor laws, including the minimum wage law. Some of them found work through apps on their phones. In 2025 one worker in ten belonged to a union, according to the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics. Workers at Starbucks coffee shops and at an Amazon warehouse voted in their first unions in 2021 and 2022. Workers still die on the job. In 2024, 5,070 workers were killed at work.

#### Unions and pay today

In 2025, 10.0 percent of wage and salary workers belonged to a union, 14.7 million people, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Union members were 32.9 percent of government workers and 5.9 percent of workers at private companies. In 1983 the share had been 20.1 percent, and in 1954 it had been about one worker in three.

The federal minimum wage has been $7.25 an hour since July 24, 2009, according to the Department of Labor. As of September 2026, members of Congress have not raised it.

#### Working through an app

An independent contractor is a person who works for themselves and sells their work to companies. Most labor laws, including the laws on the minimum wage and overtime pay, do not cover independent contractors. In July 2023, 11.9 million people, 7.4 percent of all workers, were independent contractors in their main job, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Some independent contractors find work through apps that send them rides to drive or food to deliver. The Pew Research Center is a research group. In a survey taken in August 2021, its researchers found that 16 percent of American adults had earned money through an online gig platform. A gig platform is an app or website that hands out short jobs one at a time. Nine percent had done so in the past year.

The managers of the app companies treat their drivers as independent contractors. In California, voters approved Proposition 22, a question put on the ballot, on November 3, 2020, with 58.63 percent of the vote. Under it, the app companies could keep treating drivers as independent contractors. They had to pay drivers at least 120 percent of the minimum wage for the time they spent on a ride or a delivery, plus pay for each mile.

<a id="story-raef-lawson"></a>

#### Raef Lawson

> **Who:** A food-delivery driver for Grubhub whose court case asked whether an app driver is an employee.
>
> **When and where:** Los Angeles, 2015 and 2016. A federal judge ruled on his case in 2018 and 2023, and approved a settlement in 2026.

Raef Lawson sued Grubhub for the minimum wage and overtime pay, which is extra pay for hours past 40 in a week, saying that he had been its employee. He was an actor, writer and director in Los Angeles who was trying to make a career. In August 2015 he signed up to deliver food for Grubhub, a company whose app takes food orders from restaurants.

He picked blocks of two to five hours around mealtimes, week by week. From October 2015 to February 2016 he signed up for blocks on 69 days and made deliveries on 59 of them. Grubhub paid him for 35 hours in November, 105 in December and 60 in January. It paid nothing toward his gas or his phone. In 2016 Grubhub had 4,000 delivery drivers in California, and its managers classed all of them as independent contractors.

On February 15, 2016, Grubhub's managers ended the company's agreement with him. They said he had not worked many of the blocks he signed up for. The judge at his trial also found that he sometimes "gamed" the app, which means he tricked it. He logged on late, and he switched his phone to airplane mode so no new orders came.

Lawson sued for the minimum wage, overtime and his costs. In 2018 Judge Jacqueline Scott Corley ruled that he had been an independent contractor. Three months later, the justices of California's Supreme Court set a new rule: a company must prove that a worker is not an employee. On September 20, 2021, a federal appeals court, a higher court that checks the rulings of lower courts, sent Lawson's case back to Judge Corley.

On March 30, 2023, Judge Corley ruled that under the new test Lawson had been an employee. She wrote that "food delivery is not outside the usual course of" Grubhub's business. She awarded him $65.11 in unpaid minimum wages for four months of work. In 2026 Grubhub agreed to pay $24.75 million to California drivers to end their claims, in a deal called a settlement. On July 30, 2026, the judge approved the deal. About 60,000 drivers are in the settlement, and each gets at least $25. Judge Corley called it "my oldest case."

#### The pandemic, 2020

In May 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, 35.4 percent of employed people, about 48.7 million, worked from home because of the pandemic, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. By April 2022 that share had fallen to 7.7 percent. Many office workers kept working from home for part of the week. Workers in grocery stores, warehouses, delivery and health care, called essential workers, kept going to work in person.

#### Unions at Starbucks and Amazon

Baristas, the workers who make the coffee drinks, at a Starbucks on Elmwood Avenue in Buffalo, New York, voted 19 to 8 to form a union on December 9, 2021. The Washington Post and ABC News reported that it was the first union at one of the company's roughly 9,000 US stores that Starbucks owned itself. Workers at hundreds of other stores followed.

Workers at Amazon's JFK8 warehouse on Staten Island, New York, voted 2,654 to 2,131 for the Amazon Labor Union. Officials of the National Labor Relations Board, the federal agency that runs union elections, announced the result on April 1, 2022. It was the first union at an Amazon warehouse in the United States.

<a id="story-chris-smalls"></a>

#### Chris Smalls

> **Who:** An Amazon warehouse worker who was fired and then organized the first union at an Amazon warehouse in the United States.
>
> **When and where:** The JFK8 warehouse, Staten Island, New York, 2020 to 2022.
>
> **Movie:** *Union* (2024), a documentary by Brett Story and Stephen Maing about the union campaign at JFK8. It won a Special Jury Award at the Sundance Film Festival in 2024.

Chris Smalls worked as a process assistant at Amazon's JFK8 warehouse on Staten Island. In March 2020 he led a walkout over safety from COVID-19, which means workers left their jobs together in protest, and Amazon's managers fired him.

Smalls and other workers then started the Amazon Labor Union. They organized at a bus stop across the road from the warehouse. They set up a table with food there and talked with workers as they came and went, thousands of conversations over many months. In April 2022 the workers won the vote.

#### Where the new unions stand in 2026

By June 2025 baristas at 600 Starbucks stores, about 12,000 workers, had joined the union Starbucks Workers United, according to the union. On November 13, 2025, they began a national strike. It grew to about 4,500 workers in more than 130 cities. The union called it the longest strike in the company's history. As of September 2026, the workers at no Starbucks store have voted to approve a first contract.

On April 2, 2026, members of the National Labor Relations Board ordered Amazon to begin talks with the union at JFK8 on a contract for pay and working conditions. They found that Amazon had "illegally and willfully" ignored the union, according to a Teamsters union press release. As of September 2026, no contract has been reported.

#### Injuries in the warehouses

Staff members working for Senator Bernie Sanders, who led a US Senate committee on labor, published a report on Amazon warehouses in December 2024. They were the staff of his party, which held most of the committee's seats, and not of the whole committee. They interviewed 135 workers. They found that Amazon warehouses recorded more than 30 percent more injuries than the average for warehouses in 2023. Amazon workers had been nearly twice as likely to be injured as other warehouse workers in each of the past seven years.

The report described the work. In 10- to 12-hour shifts, workers repeat the same movements "hundreds and thousands of times." A computer tracks how fast each worker goes. Workers who fall behind get penalties from the computer system automatically, and these can end in firing.

#### Children in the slaughterhouses

Managers at Packers Sanitation Services, a cleaning company based in Wisconsin, put 102 children aged 13 to 17 to work on night shifts. Officials of the US Department of Labor reported this in February 2023. The children worked at 13 meatpacking plants in 8 states, where animals are killed and cut up for meat, according to reporting by KCUR, a public radio station in Kansas City. The children cleaned back saws, brisket saws and head splitters, machines that cut up animals, using chemicals strong enough to burn skin. At least three of them were injured.

The JBS plant in Grand Island, Nebraska, had 27 of the children, and the Cargill plant in Dodge City, Kansas, had 26. The company paid $1.5 million, the most the law allowed. Jessica Looman of the Labor Department's Wage and Hour Division called the violations "systemic," which means built into the way the company worked, and "a corporate-wide failure."

On farms, federal law still allows children to work at younger ages than in other jobs. A child under 12 may work on a farm owned by a parent. Children of 12 and 13 may work on a farm with a parent's consent, and children of 14 and up may do farm work outside school hours.

#### Heat, floods and mines

From 1992 to 2006, 68 crop workers died of heat, according to a 2008 report by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Their death rate from heat was 0.39 for every 100,000 workers. For all civilian workers it was 0.02. In July 2005 a 56-year-old tobacco worker in North Carolina died with a body temperature of 108 degrees. He was in the United States on a temporary farmworker visa. The report does not name him.

From 2011 to 2019, 345 workers of all kinds died of heat on the job, 43 of them in 2019, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. On August 30, 2024, officials of the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, the federal job-safety agency, proposed a rule to protect workers from heat. A rule like this is a requirement that employers must obey by law. The officials held public hearings from June 16 to July 2, 2025. As of September 2026 there is no final federal rule on heat at work.

On September 27, 2024, floods from Hurricane Helene reached the Impact Plastics plant in Erwin, Tennessee. Five employees and a contractor who cleaned the offices drowned. One worker who survived and the families of some who died gave their account. They said no one told the workers they could leave until the flood had covered the road and the plant had lost power.

Inspectors from Tennessee's job-safety agency found that the company had "exercised reasonable diligence," which means it had taken reasonable care. They gave the company no citations, the official notices for breaking safety rules. In July 2025 the local chief prosecutor, District Attorney General Steven Finney, closed the case with no charges. He found "no evidence" that workers were told they could not leave or would be fired if they did. The family of Johnny Peterson, one of the men who died, filed a lawsuit.

On April 5, 2010, an explosion of gas and coal dust at the Upper Big Branch mine in West Virginia killed 29 miners. The mine belonged to Massey Energy. Its chief executive, Don Blankenship, was found guilty in December 2015 of conspiring, which means plotting with others, to break federal mine safety laws. On April 6, 2016, Judge Irene Berger gave him the longest sentence the law allowed, one year in prison and a fine of $250,000. He was not convicted of causing the deaths.

In 2024, 5,070 workers were killed by injuries at work, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That is one worker every 104 minutes, about 14 a day. Road crashes and other transportation accidents killed 1,937 of them. In 1970 about 38 workers a day had been killed on the job.

#### Wage theft and the tomato fields

Wage theft means that an employer does not pay workers all the money the law says they have earned. In 2017 researchers at the Economic Policy Institute, a research group that sides with labor unions, studied the ten states with the most people. They found that 2.4 million workers there were paid less than the minimum wage. Together they lost $8 billion a year. A worker who worked all year lost about $3,300, nearly a quarter of what they had earned.

In Immokalee, Florida, tomato pickers formed the Coalition of Immokalee Workers in 1993. The coalition's Fair Food Program has run since 2011. Big buyers such as McDonald's and Walmart pay a little extra for each pound of tomatoes. They buy only from growers who follow a code of conduct written by the workers. The code sets a lowest pay, requires shade and water and bans harassment. Checkers visit the farms, and workers can call a complaint line.

More and more farmworkers come to the United States on temporary H-2A visas, which allow them to do farm work for a season. According to the US Department of Agriculture, about 48,000 H-2A jobs were approved in fiscal year 2005 and about 385,000 in fiscal year 2024. A fiscal year is the government's budget year. More than 90 percent of the visas go to Mexican workers.

[Back to contents](#contents)

<a id="ch-food-farming"></a>

## Chapter 15: Food and Farming

### Before 1500

Farming in North America was thousands of years old by 1500. Native farmers had turned a wild grass into corn, and corn fed whole towns. People in each region also ate the foods that grew or lived best there, such as bison on the Plains and salmon in the Northwest.

Europeans later carried corn, beans and squash from these fields across the ocean to the rest of the world. Corn became an everyday food across Europe, Africa and Asia.

#### How corn was made

Corn did not grow wild. Native farmers bred it from a grass called teosinte. The seed head of teosinte holds only a few hard kernels. Farmers began changing it about 9,000 years ago in the Balsas River valley of southern Mexico. Scientists have confirmed that date and place in two ways. They studied the genes of corn and teosinte. Genes are the tiny instructions inside every living thing that parents pass on to their young. They also studied ancient corn dug from the ground.

Breeding a plant means choosing which plants to take seed from, year after year, so the crop changes over time. Native farmers bred teosinte for thousands of years, and the result was corn. Corn is so changed from the wild grass that it cannot reseed itself. It grows only where people plant it. Over thousands of years, Native farmers grew corn a little farther north at a time, until it reached what is now the United States.

#### The Three Sisters

Native farmers planted corn, beans and squash together in the same field, and each plant helped the other two grow. The three crops are called the Three Sisters.

The corn grew tall, and the bean vine climbed up the corn stalk. Bean roots hold tiny living things called bacteria. These bacteria take nitrogen, a gas in the air, and put it into the soil. Plants need nitrogen to grow, so the beans fed the soil that all three plants shared. The squash spread wide leaves over the ground. The shade kept water in the ground and blocked the sunlight that weeds needed.

The three crops also fed people well together. Protein is the part of food the body uses to build muscle. Corn and beans eaten in the same meal give the body a fuller mix of the protein it needs than either food gives alone.

#### Farming began in the East too

Native people in the eastern part of North America started farming on their own, long before corn reached them. They took wild plants and bred them into crops. About 5,000 years ago they had tamed a kind of squash. They also grew six plants for their seeds: sunflower, goosefoot, sumpweed, maygrass, little barley and erect knotweed. Sunflower and sumpweed seeds are rich in oil. The seeds of the other four are starchy, and maygrass and little barley are grasses whose grain can be ground into flour. People cooked and ate goosefoot's small seeds.

Scientists call this group of crops the Eastern Agricultural Complex. Eastern North America is one of the places in the world where people started farming on their own, without learning it from anyone else.

#### Foods by region

Cahokia was a Native town near where St. Louis is today. Around the year 1100, between about 10,000 and 20,000 people lived there, and corn farming fed them.

People in other regions lived mainly on other foods. On the Great Plains, hunters killed bison. By a widely used estimate, about 30 million bison still lived there in the early 1800s. Along the Northwest coast and its rivers, salmon was the main food. People on the coasts gathered shellfish. In the Northeast, people collected sap from maple trees.

Around the Great Lakes, people harvested manoomin, a wild rice that grows in shallow water. In Ojibwe, the word means "the good berry." People harvest it from canoes. The Ojibwe are one of the Anishinaabe peoples, a family of related nations that also includes the Odawa and the Potawatomi. In an Anishinaabe prophecy, a teaching about what was to come, the people were led to the place where they would find "the food that grows on water." Manoomin is still a central food of Ojibwe life today.

No farmer from before 1500 is known by name. Corn cannot reseed itself, so every generation of Native farmers had to save the seed and plant it again. Seed keepers in Native nations still grow these crops today.

### The 1500s

In the 1500s, Europeans began carrying crops and farm animals across the Atlantic Ocean in both directions, and Africans carried their own crops to the Americas. This movement is called the Columbian Exchange. The historian Alfred W. Crosby named it in his 1972 book *The Columbian Exchange*. Native people here still grew and ate their own foods.

#### What crossed the ocean

Europeans carried American crops and animals home to Europe. These included corn, potatoes, tomatoes, beans, squash, peanuts, peppers, cacao, vanilla and turkeys. Cacao is the bean that chocolate is made from. Corn and potatoes later became main foods across Europe, Africa and Asia.

Europeans brought wheat, rice, sugarcane, citrus fruit (the family of fruit that includes oranges and lemons), and honeybees to the Americas on their ships. They also brought cattle, pigs, sheep, goats and chickens. Columbus brought horses on his second voyage, in 1493. Spanish colonists founded St. Augustine, in Florida, in 1565, and began a colony in New Mexico in 1598. In both places they planted wheat and citrus and raised cattle.

The word exchange can sound like a friendly trade. It was not one. Europeans took American crops home from lands they were invading. Much of what arrived was grown to feed the colonists. Before long, planters were forcing enslaved people to grow sugarcane on plantations. Slave traders carried most of the Africans who came to the Americas across the ocean in chains. Those Africans brought their own crops and the skill to grow them. These included okra, watermelon, yams, sorghum, black-eyed peas and African rice.

#### De Soto's army and Apalachee corn

The Spanish soldier Hernando de Soto landed near Tampa Bay, in Florida, in May 1539, with an army of more than 600 people. He carried no food supplies except a small herd of pigs. Men who marched with him wrote accounts of the trip, and those accounts say the herd began with about 13 pigs. By 1542 the herd had grown to about 700. The army rarely killed the pigs for food. Pigs that escaped ran wild across the Southeast.

De Soto's army moved from town to town and took the corn that Native villagers had stored, and the soldiers ate it. Without that corn, the villagers were often at risk of starving. De Soto also seized dozens of Native men, women and children. His soldiers forced them to carry the army's equipment and supplies and to do the work of the camp.

Rodrigo Ranjel, de Soto's secretary, kept a diary of the march. An account written from it states that the Spaniards took the men "to have more slaves and servants." Some of the captives died and others ran away, so the soldiers seized more. The same account records that the soldiers wanted the women "for their lewdness and lust," which means they wanted them for sex. The women were prisoners and could not refuse. The soldiers raped them. Rape means forcing a person to have sex.

In October 1539, de Soto's army seized Anhaica, the main town of the Apalachee. Tallahassee, Florida, stands there today. The army lived in the town until March 1540. The Spanish took the town's stored food, which was enough to feed 600 men and 220 horses for five months. Archaeologists, scientists who study the past by digging up what people left behind, have found burned corncobs at the site. The Apalachee fought back with quick raids and ambushes, and they went after the Spaniards' horses.

### The 1600s

Native corn kept the first English colonists at Jamestown and Plymouth alive in the 1600s. The colonists bought some of that corn and grew some of it with Native teaching, and they took some by force. In Virginia, planters then grew tobacco, a crop that is not food, in place of food.

#### Jamestown: hunger, and corn the English took by force

The colonists at Jamestown, in Virginia, planned to live partly on food they traded from the Powhatan people and partly on supply ships from England. In the autumn of 1609, Powhatan leaders stopped trading food with them, and Powhatan warriors surrounded the fort. The winter of 1609 to 1610 is called the Starving Time. About 500 colonists were alive when it began. By spring, about 61 were still alive.

The colonists ate their horses, dogs and rats, and they ate leather. Some ate the bodies of people who had died. Archaeologists found the bones of a girl whom researchers call Jane. The bones show that colonists ate her body after she died. Scientists at the Smithsonian announced the finding in 2013.

English soldiers also took corn by force and destroyed Native fields. On August 10, 1610, George Percy led English soldiers against the Paspahegh town near Jamestown. They burned the houses, cut down the cornfields and took corn. Percy wrote that they killed 15 or 16 people. Other accounts put the number of villagers killed as high as 75.

The soldiers captured the wife and two children of Wowinchopunck, the Paspahegh weroance, or leader. When Percy hesitated, his men complained. Percy then agreed to kill the children. His soldiers threw the children overboard from a boat and shot them in the head in the water.

That night at Jamestown, Captain Davis told Percy that Lord De La Warr, the colony's governor, wanted the children's mother burned alive. Captain Davis and two soldiers took her into the woods and killed her with a sword. Percy wrote that he did not believe the order really came from the governor.

In March 1622 Powhatan warriors attacked the English settlements. After that, colonial soldiers marched out almost every summer for ten years to attack Powhatan towns and cornfields. In 1623 colonists at a peace meeting poisoned the Powhatans' wine, shot them, and then destroyed their cornfields.

#### Tobacco in place of food

John Rolfe grew Virginia's first successful tobacco crop in 1612. He planted a sweet kind of tobacco. Planters sold it for so much money that many of them grew it in place of food crops.

Members of Virginia's assembly, the colony's lawmaking body, passed laws again and again to make planters grow food. Under a tobacco law of 1629 and 1630, a family could grow 2,000 tobacco plants for each family member and no more. The lawmakers set the limit partly so that families would still plant food crops.

#### Plymouth: corn dug up, then corn planted

The first corn the Plymouth colonists ate was corn they took. In November 1620, men from the *Mayflower* went exploring on Cape Cod. There they found baskets of corn that the local people had buried in the ground. The owners were saving it as seed for the next spring. The Englishmen dug up about ten bushels of the corn and a bag of beans. A bushel is a measure of about 8 gallons. They wrote that they planned to "satisfy them for their corn," which meant to pay the owners later. They named the place Cornhill.

The same group of men dug up graves nearby. They opened bundles that held the bones of a man and a small child. They wrote that they "brought sundry of the prettiest things away," meaning they took several of the objects buried with the dead.

The owners of the corn were Nauset people. In the summer of 1621, the colonists met one of them and promised to pay him. They offered to bring the owners as much corn as they had taken. Later in 1621 the colonist Edward Winslow wrote that the owners had been given "full content," meaning they were fully satisfied. His letter does not say what they were given.

The colonists built their town on the land of Patuxet, a Wampanoag town. An epidemic, a disease that spreads quickly through many people, had killed most of the people of Patuxet between 1616 and 1619. The colonists listed as one reason for settling there the "good corn-ground ready to our hands." The Patuxet people had cleared those fields.

In the spring of 1621, the colonists planted about 20 acres of corn. The corn did well. Their first harvest, that autumn, fed them through their second winter.

<a id="story-squanto-food-farming"></a>

#### Squanto (Tisquantum)

> **Who:** A Patuxet man who taught the Plymouth colonists to plant corn, after an English captain had kidnapped him.
>
> **When and where:** Patuxet, where the colonists built Plymouth, in what is now Massachusetts. Kidnapped 1614, home 1619, taught the colonists in the spring of 1621, died 1622.
>
> **Movie:** *Squanto: A Warrior's Tale* (1994), a feature film that mixes his real story with invented events.

Squanto, also called Tisquantum, showed the Plymouth colonists how to plant corn in the spring of 1621. He also interpreted between the colonists and the Wampanoag, which means he put each side's words into the other's language.

In 1614 an English captain named Thomas Hunt kidnapped Squanto and took him to Spain to be sold as a slave. Squanto reached England and learned English there. In 1619 he came home with an English expedition. He found his town of Patuxet empty. An epidemic had killed most of its people.

The colonist Edward Winslow wrote about the corn planting in a letter of December 1621. He wrote that "according to the manner of the Indians, we manured our ground with herrings, or rather shads." To manure ground means to put something into the soil to feed the crops. Herring and shad are kinds of fish. The colonists buried fish in the ground with the corn seed. Squanto taught them to do this.

Scholars have argued for decades about where Squanto learned it. In 1975 Lynn Ceci, an anthropologist, or scientist who studies how people live, argued in the journal *Science* that burying fish with corn was a European method. She argued that Squanto probably learned it during his years among Europeans. She found little evidence that many Native farmers used fish this way. Other scholars defended the older account, and none of them has settled the question. Winslow himself called it "the manner of the Indians."

Squanto died in 1622.

#### What the colonists ate

The English colonists learned corn dishes from Native cooks. One was hominy, which is dried corn cooked in water. For samp, cooks pounded corn into coarse meal and boiled it into a mush. The name comes from the Narragansett word *nasàump*. Johnnycakes were flat cakes baked from cornmeal. Along with their corn, the colonists ate beans, and once their hogs had multiplied, they ate pork and drank cider made from apples. Americans went on eating these corn dishes for centuries.

### 1700 to 1750

Between 1700 and 1750, planters in the Carolina Lowcountry forced enslaved Africans to grow rice, and the planters became some of the richest people in the colonies. The Lowcountry is the flat, wet land along the coast of South Carolina. Enslaved Africans built the rice fields and did the work in them. Planters paid more for captives from West Africa who already knew how to grow rice.

Farther north, farmers in Pennsylvania, New York and New Jersey grew more wheat than they could eat and shipped flour to other places. New Hampshire's town histories say that settlers there planted the first potato patches in North America that lasted.

#### Carolina rice and African skill

English settlers first brought a small amount of rice to Charles Town, now Charleston, in 1670. No record shows that anything grew from it. By July 1699, samples of Carolina rice were on sale in London to test whether buyers wanted it. The first crops grew on dry, high ground. By the 1720s, planters had moved their rice into freshwater swamps inland. They had enslaved workers build dams to hold the water in ponds.

From 1698 to 1702, Carolina planters shipped out about 269,000 pounds of rice a year. From 1738 to 1742, they shipped out more than 30 million pounds a year. One kind of Carolina rice later became known as Carolina Gold.

Planters put out advertisements asking for captives from the part of West Africa known as the Rice Coast. That coast included Senegambia, the land along the Senegal and Gambia rivers, and Sierra Leone. Planters paid more for people from there because those people knew how to grow rice. Records from Carolina fields show African methods at work. Enslaved workers built earth banks around fields beside the tidal rivers so they could flood and drain them. They sowed seed by pressing it into the mud with the heel and toe. They separated the grain from its husks by tossing it in coiled baskets called fanner baskets.

Scholars disagree about how much of Carolina's rice farming came from African knowledge. In her 2001 book *Black Rice*, the geographer Judith Carney argued that African knowledge was the base of the whole rice business. A geographer is a scientist who studies the land and how people use it. In 2005 the historians David Eltis, Philip Morgan and David Richardson argued that she had made the African share too large. Records also show that in the early years of the colony, more captives came from Angola than from any other place. Angola is not on the Rice Coast. Most scholars now hold a middle view: planters built the rice business with their money and by force, and they also depended on African skill.

#### Whose land the rice grew on

The Kiawah, Etiwan and Stono people lived along the Ashley, Cooper and Stono rivers. They were still there in 1670, when English colonists settled among them at Charleston Harbor.

English colonists captured Kussoe people who fought back in 1671, and Stono people in 1674, and sold them into slavery in the Caribbean. The Kiawah left the Ashley River in the early 1680s and moved to the island now named for them. By the early 1680s no nation of the Lowcountry had more than fifty bowmen. The Stono had sixteen hunters. In the spring of 1684, leaders of eight nations signed away their land claims to the English who ran the colony.

Before 1720, English colonists in Carolina made their biggest profits from two kinds of goods they shipped out. One was ship supplies, such as tar made from pine trees. The other was Native people, whom they sold as slaves. In 1770 a colonist named William Bull wrote of the Native nations along the coast that "there remains now, except a few Catawbas, nothing of them but their names, within three hundred miles of our sea coast."

#### The rice workers, unnamed in the records

Planters' records list the enslaved rice workers by first name, age and price. They say almost nothing else about them. No single rice grower from these years can be followed through life in the records.

Planters gave each enslaved worker a set task every day. The usual task was to work a quarter of an acre of land. A worker who finished the task had the rest of the day. Workers labored in direct sun, standing in water or mud, among mosquitoes, horseflies, snakes and alligators. Enslaved Africans dug the banks and canals of the rice fields. Nic Butler, a historian at the Charleston County Public Library, has written that the earth they moved across the Lowcountry is about as much as all the great pyramids of Egypt put together.

Until the 1760s, more enslaved people died in the Lowcountry than were born there. Many of the dead were children. Planters kept buying new captives to replace them. In 1710 slave traders rarely landed more than 300 enslaved Africans a year at Charles Town. They landed more than 1,000 a year by 1720, and more than 3,000 a year by 1770. More than four of every ten Africans brought to North America in the slave trade came in through Charleston Harbor. By 1708 more Black people than white people lived in South Carolina.

<a id="story-eliza-lucas-pinckney"></a>

#### Eliza Lucas Pinckney

> **Who:** A planter's daughter who ran her family's South Carolina plantations as a teenager and made the colony's first successful indigo dye.
>
> **When and where:** Wappoo plantation, near Charleston, South Carolina. Indigo experiments from 1739, first successful dye in 1744.

Eliza Lucas produced the first successful indigo dye in South Carolina in 1744. Indigo is a plant, and dye made from it colors cloth blue. It is a farm crop but not a food.

In 1739 her father, George Lucas, went back to the island of Antigua, in the Caribbean, to serve as its lieutenant governor. Eliza was about 16. She took charge of Wappoo plantation and of the 20 enslaved people who worked it. She also oversaw the family's two other plantations, which were much larger.

That same year she began experimenting with indigo seed. Turning the plant into dye was skilled work done by experts. She first worked with an indigo maker from the island of Montserrat. Her best results came with an indigo maker of African descent whom her father hired from the French islands of the Caribbean.

She used her 1744 crop to make seed and gave the seed to other planters. Planters in South Carolina shipped out about 5,000 pounds of indigo in the shipping year 1745 to 1746. By 1748 they shipped out 130,000 pounds. She later married and took the name Pinckney.

#### Wheat, potatoes and everyday meals

Pennsylvania, New York and New Jersey were called the breadbasket colonies. Farmers there grew more wheat than their families needed. Merchants shipped the extra wheat as flour out of the ports of Philadelphia and New York.

In 1719 settlers known as the Scots-Irish planted potatoes at Londonderry, New Hampshire. The Scots-Irish were families of Scottish background who had lived in the north of Ireland. New Hampshire's histories count their patches as the first lasting potato fields in North America. The potato first grew as a crop in the Andes mountains of South America. People carried it to Europe, and settlers later brought it back across the ocean to North America.

Most colonial families ate corn, pork and bread, and drank cider. Rich families also bought tea, sugar and wine from overseas, and they ate bread made of wheat.

### 1750 to 1800

About nine of every ten working people in the United States were farmers when the country began, by a widely used estimate from the US Department of Agriculture. The first census, a count of the people, was taken in 1790. It counted about 4 million people.

Thomas Jefferson wrote that farmers were God's chosen people, while people he enslaved farmed his land. In 1796 Amelia Simmons became the first American to write a cookbook for American kitchens. Some of its recipes used American cornmeal.

<a id="story-matthew-patten"></a>

#### Matthew Patten

> **Who:** A New Hampshire farmer, carpenter and judge whose diary records what his family grew, caught and ate.
>
> **When and where:** Bedford, New Hampshire, on the Merrimack River. His surviving diary runs from 1754 to 1788.

Matthew Patten kept a diary that shows how one farm family in New Hampshire fed itself. He headed each little booklet of it "A Day Book continued." His entries for the year 1767 record the family's food through the seasons.

Patten was born in Ireland on May 19, 1719. He came to the colonies in 1728, when he was nine, and settled at the place later named Bedford in 1738. He was a joiner, a carpenter who does the finer woodwork in a house. He also farmed, worked as a judge, and surveyed land, which means he measured it and marked its borders.

On January 3, 1767, a neighbor, James Gilmore, paid Patten three pecks of corn for surveying his land. A peck is about 8 quarts. That same day Patten bought tea and 7 pounds of sugar, and he took corn and rye to a neighbor's mill to be ground into meal and flour. On January 30 he butchered the family's hogs. In February and March, other neighbors paid him in bushels of corn for surveying and for writing deeds, the papers that prove who owns a piece of land.

On March 4 he opened the pit where the family's potatoes had been buried for the winter. He wrote that they were "sound and good." In April and May the family sowed peas, then planted potatoes, corn, barley, hemp and flax. Hemp and flax are plants whose fibers are made into rope and cloth. He wrote that "the boys" planted the field behind the barn with corn and potatoes and spread manure from the barn on it.

In May, Patten helped haul a net in the Merrimack River from dark to sunrise. His share was 60 shad, a fish the family took from the Merrimack each spring. From May 28 to June 6 he fished at Amoskeag Falls and sent 354 fish home. The name Amoskeag comes from a Pennacook word that means roughly "good fishing place." Long before Bedford was a town, Pennacook people strung large nets across the river at the falls and caught sturgeon, salmon and a fish called the alewife. Bedford lies in Pennacook country.

In June and July Patten took salmon weighing from 6 to 19 pounds and split them with two neighbors. In August he reaped his rye and wrote, "I have 40 Stooks in all this year." A stook is a bundle of cut grain stood up to dry. Later that month he mowed his meadow and counted 205 piles of hay.

Patten died on August 27, 1795, in one of the town's fields. He had carried dinner out to the men who were mowing.

#### Jefferson's farmers and Monticello's rations

Thomas Jefferson believed that family farms made free citizens. He wrote about the idea in his book *Notes on the State of Virginia*, first printed in 1785: "Those who labour in the earth are the chosen people of God, if ever he had a chosen people." For about a hundred years afterward, American leaders wrote land laws meant to put land in the hands of family farmers.

People Jefferson enslaved did the farm work at Monticello, his plantation in Virginia. Jefferson owned more than 600 enslaved people during his adult life. In the years Jefferson had tobacco grown at Monticello, enslaved children picked worms off the tobacco plants.

Each week, Jefferson gave each enslaved worker at Monticello a set amount of food, called a ration: a peck of cornmeal, half a pound of pork or pickled beef, and four salted fish. Nursing mothers received extra, and workers got whiskey at harvest. Researchers who studied the Monticello records found that these rations were not enough food for a person to live on. So in their little free time, enslaved people hunted, fished, trapped, kept gardens and raised animals.

Enslaved families also sold chickens and vegetables from their own gardens and flocks to the Jefferson family. Jefferson's granddaughter Anne Cary Randolph wrote down these purchases in the household accounts. Most of the sellers she recorded were enslaved people who worked in the house, many of them members of the Hemings family.

#### Corn into whiskey

The backcountry was the land far from the coast, beyond the older farms and towns. Farmers there could not easily haul wagons of corn over the long roads to buyers. So they turned their extra corn into whiskey, which they could carry to market in jugs.

<a id="story-amelia-simmons"></a>

#### Amelia Simmons

> **Who:** The author of *American Cookery*, the first cookbook written by an American for American kitchens.
>
> **When and where:** Hartford, Connecticut, 1796.

Amelia Simmons wrote *American Cookery*, the first cookbook written by an American for American kitchens. It was printed in Hartford, Connecticut, in 1796. On the title page she called herself "an American orphan." Nothing else about her life is known.

Her book contains the first known printed recipes that used American cornmeal. Among them were johnnycake, "Indian slapjack" and Indian pudding. Colonists called corn "Indian corn" and cornmeal "Indian meal," so the word Indian in these names meant that the dishes were made with cornmeal.

Her book also contains the first printed recipe that used pearlash to make dough rise. Pearlash is a salt made from wood ashes. Bakers used it to make dough rise before baking powder existed. The book also contains some of the earliest printed uses of the words "cookey" (cookie) and "slaw" (a salad of shredded cabbage), which came into American English from Dutch settlers in America.

### 1800 to 1850

In the first half of the 1800s, Americans began to keep food fresh and sell it to strangers far away. Merchants sold food sealed in tin cans, and they shipped ice cut from frozen ponds. In the Deep South, planters, the owners of large farms worked by enslaved people, spread cotton fields over land that federal troops had forced Native nations to leave. On the prairie of the Midwest, farmers used a new steel plow to turn thick grassland into fields of wheat and corn.

#### Food in cans, and ice from ponds

Food spoils when it sits too long. In 1809 a Frenchman named Nicolas Appert proved that food sealed in a container and then heated would keep. The method is called canning.

Americans soon took up canning. William Underwood opened a cannery in Boston in 1820 or 1821. In New York, Thomas Kensett canned seafood, fruit and vegetables. In 1825 he received an American patent for tin cans. A patent is a government paper that gives an inventor the sole right to make and sell an invention for a set number of years. Food sealed in a can could be sold far from the farm where it grew, to people the grower never met.

Other merchants sold ice. Workers cut blocks of ice from frozen ponds in New England in winter, including Walden Pond. Merchants shipped the ice to cities. People used it to keep food, fresh fish and drinks cold. Families kept ice in a box called an icebox, which became a common piece of kitchen furniture.

<a id="story-frederic-tudor"></a>

#### Frederic Tudor

> **Who:** A Boston merchant, called the Ice King, who built a business shipping New England pond ice to warm places around the world.
>
> **When and where:** Boston. First cargo of ice to Martinique in 1806. Ice to India in 1833. Died 1864.

Frederic Tudor built a business selling New England pond ice in hot countries far away. His first cargo of ice left Boston in 1806, bound for the Caribbean island of Martinique. A Boston newspaper, the *Boston Gazette*, printed: "No joke. A vessel has cleared at the Custom House for Martinique with a cargo of ice. We hope this will not prove a slippery speculation." To clear at the Custom House meant to get permission from officials at the port to sail. A speculation is a risky business deal.

Much of the ice melted during the three-week voyage. Tudor sold what was left. He lost about $4,500 on the trip, though some accounts say $4,000. He kept at the business for years. In 1812 and 1813 he spent time in debtors' prison, a jail for people who could not pay what they owed.

On May 12, 1833, his ship, the *Tuscany*, sailed from Boston for Calcutta, in India. It carried 180 tons of ice cut the winter before. The ship reached India in September, about four months later. About 100 tons of the ice were still frozen. About 80 tons had melted on the way.

Tudor died in Boston on February 6, 1864.

#### Cotton fields on Native farms

Across the Deep South, planters spread cotton so widely that they pushed food crops to the edges of their land. Many planters bought corn and pork from Midwestern farms instead of growing enough food on their own plantations.

The new cotton fields were the farms and hunting grounds of the Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole nations. In 1830 President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act. Under it, federal troops forced these nations off their land and moved them west. The Cherokee removal of 1838 and 1839 is called the Trail of Tears. Soldiers under General Winfield Scott forced more than 16,000 people from their homes. Starting in May 1838, the soldiers rounded up most of the Cherokee and held them as prisoners in crowded, dirty camps. Measles, whooping cough and dysentery, a disease of the gut that causes bloody diarrhea, spread through the camps. People had too little food and water and no shelter from the weather. More than 4,000 Cherokee died of disease, hunger and cold in the camps and on the march west. That is the usual count. In 1984 the scholar Russell Thornton estimated that the number of dead may have been twice as high.

Enslaved people did the work in the cotton fields. They were held as property by the planters and forced to work without pay. They worked in groups called gangs, from sunup to sundown, six days a week.

#### Breaking the prairie

Farmers moving onto the prairie of Illinois found thick, sticky sod. Sod is the top layer of soil, held together by the tangled roots of grass. Prairie sod stuck to iron plows and stopped them.

John Deere was a blacksmith, a worker who shapes iron and steel by heating and hammering it, in Grand Detour, Illinois. In 1837 he made a plow of polished steel. The sod slid off its smooth blade instead of sticking, so the plow could cut through the prairie. By 1846 Deere was selling nearly a thousand plows a year.

In 1831, six years before Deere made his plow, Cyrus McCormick had shown his reaper at Steele's Tavern, Virginia. A reaper is a machine that cuts grain. Before it, farmers cut wheat by hand, with tools such as the sickle, a curved blade. A reaper cut grain many times faster than a person with hand tools, so a family could plant far more wheat. Within one generation, farmers had turned the prairie into fields of wheat and corn.

Deere's plows broke land that Native nations had lived on. Early settlers at Grand Detour saw signs of a Ho-Chunk village inside the bend of the river.

In 1832 US soldiers and militia, citizens called up to fight, went to war against Sauk and Meskwaki people led by Black Hawk. On August 1 and 2, 1832, at Bad Axe on the Mississippi River, Black Hawk's band of perhaps 500 men, women and children tried to cross the river. Soldiers on the army steamboat *Warrior* fired on them. About 1,300 soldiers and militia under General Henry Atkinson attacked the people still on the east bank. The soldiers shot some of the Sauk and Meskwaki before they could reach the far shore, and others drowned trying to get across. Thomas Ford, a governor of Illinois, later estimated that 150 were killed and as many drowned. Others have disputed his count.

In September 1832, Ho-Chunk leaders signed a treaty with General Winfield Scott and Illinois governor John Reynolds. A treaty is a written agreement between nations. In it the Ho-Chunk gave up their lands south and east of the Wisconsin River and the Fox River of Green Bay, with a border running up the Rock River. US officials agreed to pay them $10,000 a year for 27 years.

In 1833, at a treaty meeting in Chicago, Potawatomi leaders sold the last of their land in northern Illinois and all of their land in southeastern Wisconsin to the United States. In return they received 5 million acres in Iowa, $100,000 in goods and supplies, and $14,000 a year for 20 years. They had to leave Wisconsin by 1838.

#### The potato blight

In 1843 a potato disease called late blight broke out near the ports of Philadelphia and New York. It is caused by a water mold, a tiny living thing that destroys potato plants. The blight spread through potato fields in the eastern United States. American farmers lost potato crops, but they had other food to eat.

By 1845 the blight had reached Europe. In Ireland, poor families depended on potatoes and had no other food. The blight destroyed their crop. A famine is a time when there is so little food that people starve. During the Great Famine in Ireland, from 1845 to 1852, about 1 million people died.

### 1850 to 1900

By 1900, food was grown, packed and shipped as a big business, from Texas ranches to Chicago meatpacking plants to the cities of the East. Under the Homestead Act, families claimed millions of acres of free farmland that US officials and soldiers had taken from Native nations. Cowhands drove millions of cattle north from Texas, and meatpackers in Chicago shipped their beef east in cold railroad cars. Starting in 1867, farmers formed groups of their own to buy supplies together and to speak up against the rates railroad companies charged them.

#### Homestead farms on taken land

The Homestead Act became law on May 20, 1862. Under it, a person could claim 160 acres of public land for free. To keep the land, the person had to live on it and farm it for five years. Women could claim land. After 1868 Black Americans could claim land too. Most Native people could not.

Over the years the law was in force, people filed about 4 million claims. About 1.6 million of them finished the five years and received a land patent, the government paper that made the land theirs. Together they received about 270 million acres, close to one tenth of all the land in the United States.

All of this land had belonged to Native nations. US officials and soldiers had taken it by treaty, by purchase and by war. In 1887 members of Congress passed the Dawes Act. Under it, federal officials broke up land that each Native nation held together into separate plots for single families. Officials then sold the land they called surplus, meaning left over, and much of it went to white farmers. Native nations held about 138 million acres in 1887. By 1934 they held about 48 million. Through the plots and the sales, federal officials had taken about 90 million acres from them, two of every three acres they had held. In 1889 federal officials opened land in Oklahoma to settlers. US officials had taken that land from Native nations. Settlers raced in to claim it.

<a id="story-oblinger-family"></a>

#### Uriah and Mattie Oblinger

> **Who:** A homesteading family whose letters describe the food and work of a Nebraska farm claim.
>
> **When and where:** Fillmore County, Nebraska. Uriah filed his claim in 1872. Mattie and their baby, Ella, arrived in May 1873. The family letters run from 1862 to 1911.

The letters of Uriah and Mattie Oblinger describe what one homestead family in Nebraska grew and ate in the 1870s. The Library of Congress and the Nebraska State Historical Society keep the family's letters. The Library of Congress collection holds 318 of them, written from 1862 to 1911. Uriah and Mattie married on March 25, 1869.

In the fall of 1872, Uriah went ahead from Indiana to Nebraska. He filed a claim about eleven miles west of the town of Geneva, in Fillmore County. He broke the prairie sod and built a house out of blocks of sod. On December 1, 1872, he wrote about the other young families starting out around him. "We will all be poor here together," he wrote. The Otoe-Missouria and the Pawnee had signed over most of their land in this part of Nebraska in treaties of 1854 and 1857. Homesteaders began filing claims in the county in 1866.

Mattie and their baby daughter, Ella, joined Uriah in May 1873. On June 16, 1873, Mattie wrote a letter about the garden and the crops. She spelled words her own way. "Uriah has 23 acres of sod corn planted it looks real well," she wrote. Sod corn was corn planted straight into newly plowed prairie sod. In 1902 an Iowa settler, L. S. Coffin, described how it was done. A man struck an axe deep into the sod, and a boy or girl dropped three or four kernels into the slot and stamped it shut with one foot. "We have a nice lot of Squashes and Cucumbers & Mellons & Beans comeing on." She was growing tomato plants too. She bought milk and butter from a neighbor, Mrs. Furgison, and paid twelve cents a pound for the butter. "I like the sod house the best," she wrote. She also wrote that "every lick we strike is for our selves and not half for some one else."

Over the next years the family lived through blizzards, drought, swarms of grasshoppers and low prices for their crops. In February 1880 Mattie died giving birth, and her newborn son died with her. She was 36. She left three daughters, Ella, Stella and Maggie. Uriah moved the family to Minnesota that year. The family later lived in Nebraska, Kansas and Missouri, and came back to Nebraska in 1894.

#### Sharecropping: growing a crop someone else sold

After the Civil War, most freedpeople, the men, women and children who had been freed from slavery, had no land of their own. Many became sharecroppers. A landowner gave a sharecropping family food, seed, tools and a cabin on credit, which meant the family would pay for them later. This was called the furnish. The family usually worked about twenty acres.

At harvest the landowner sold the crop and took out the cost of the furnish plus interest, an extra charge for paying later. Then the landowner paid the family its share. The share was usually half of the crop's value or less. The landowner held a lien on the crop, which meant the landowner had a legal claim to it until the debt was paid. The landowner also kept the account books. Most sharecropping families stayed in debt to the landowner year after year. They grew food and cotton but did not control the money from selling it.

#### The bison killed, the cattle driven north

About 30 million bison lived on the Great Plains in the early 1800s. By 1900 fewer than 1,000 were left. One count in 1884 found 325. Hunters killed bison to sell their hides. Railroad building, disease and drought also shrank the herds. US Army commanders encouraged the killing, because the herds were the food supply of the Plains nations. By 1881 the people of the Lakota leader Sitting Bull were starving, because the bison herds were nearly gone. They surrendered at Fort Buford in July 1881.

Ranchers put cattle on the grasslands where the bison had lived. Between 1866 and 1884, cowhands drove about 5.2 million Texas cattle north to railroad towns. In 1867 Joseph McCoy built a market for cattle at Abilene, Kansas, where the railroad line reached. Herds came up to it along the Chisholm Trail. In Texas, as many as one cowhand in four was Black. Many others were Mexican or Mexican American.

The open range was grassland with no fences, where cattle could graze and travel freely. The long drives ended as barbed wire fences and quarantine lines closed the open range. Joseph Glidden received a patent for barbed wire on November 24, 1874. A quarantine line was a border that cattle from some areas were not allowed to cross. Under a Kansas quarantine law of 1885 and 1886, Texas cattle could not enter Kansas. Herds could no longer use the trails that crossed those lines.

<a id="story-charles-goodnight"></a>

#### Charles Goodnight

> **Who:** A Texas cattleman who invented the chuckwagon, the kitchen on wheels that fed cowhands on cattle drives.
>
> **When and where:** Texas, 1866.

Charles Goodnight invented the chuckwagon in 1866. A cattle drive crossed open grassland for months, and its crew had to eat every day. Goodnight took a leftover Army wagon and built a hinged pantry box onto it. Part of the box dropped down flat to make a table where the cook could work.

The chuckwagon carried the food for the trail, such as beans, bacon, biscuits and coffee. On a drive, the cook ranked second only to the trail boss, the man in charge of the whole drive. Some characters in the novel *Lonesome Dove* are partly based on Goodnight.

#### Beef from the Plains to a city plate

The Union Stock Yards opened in Chicago on December 25, 1865. Stock yards are pens where cattle, hogs and sheep are held until they are sold. The Chicago yards became the largest market for farm animals in the world.

Gustavus Swift was a meatpacker, a businessman who ran a plant where animals were killed and cut up into meat for sale. He shipped beef east from Chicago already butchered, instead of shipping live animals. In 1878 an engineer named Andrew Chase designed a railroad car for Swift that was cooled with ice. Beef packed in it stayed cold all the way to the cities of the East. A steer, one of the male cattle raised for beef, could now be raised in Texas, killed in Chicago and eaten in New York.

#### Farmers join together

In 1867 Oliver Hudson Kelley founded the Patrons of Husbandry, better known as the Grange. Husbandry is an old word for farming. Kelley was a Minnesota farmer and a clerk in the federal Department of Agriculture. The Grange was the first large farmers' group with members across the whole country. Grange members met in their own halls and bought supplies together to get lower prices. They also spoke up together against the rates the railroad companies charged to carry their crops.

In 1862 members of Congress passed the Morrill Act. Under it, federal officials gave each state 30,000 acres of public land for each of the state's members of Congress. That land had been taken from Native nations. State officials sold the land and used the money to start colleges that taught farming and the skills of working with machines. These schools are called land-grant colleges. In 1887 members of Congress passed the Hatch Act, named for William Hatch, a member of the US House of Representatives from Missouri. Hatch led the House committee on farming. Under the act, each state's land-grant college received $15,000 a year at first to run a farm experiment station. At these stations, scientists studied soil, seed and farm animals and sent their results to farmers. There are stations today in all 50 states.

### 1900 to 1950

Between 1900 and 1950, federal officials took on new jobs in how Americans got their food. Federal inspectors went into the meatpacking plants in 1906. In the 1930s, federal officials paid farmers to grow less, bought up extra food and gave it to hungry families. During World War II, officials limited how much sugar, meat and coffee each person could buy. In 1946 President Harry Truman signed a law that made school lunch a permanent federal program. On the farms, tractors took the place of horses, and new kinds of seed corn and chicken farming began.

#### What was in the meat: the 1906 food laws

On June 30, 1906, President Theodore Roosevelt signed two food laws on the same day. Under the Pure Food and Drug Act, no one could sell adulterated or mislabeled food and medicine from one state to another. Adulterated food is food that has been made impure, or mixed with something that should not be in it. Scientists at the Bureau of Chemistry, part of the Department of Agriculture, enforced this law. In 1927 federal officials handed that work to a new office in the Department of Agriculture. In 1930 they renamed the office the Food and Drug Administration, or FDA.

The second law was the Meat Inspection Act. Under it, federal inspectors worked inside the packing plants and checked the meat. Members of Congress passed both laws within a few months after a novel about Chicago's meatpacking plants came out.

<a id="story-upton-sinclair-food-farming"></a>

#### Upton Sinclair

> **Who:** A novelist whose book about the Chicago meatpacking plants came out months before the 1906 food-safety laws.
>
> **When and where:** Chicago, 1904. His novel *The Jungle* came out as a book in February 1906.

Upton Sinclair wrote *The Jungle* to show how immigrant workers in Chicago's meatpacking plants lived. In 1904 he spent about seven weeks working undercover in the plants. His novel was printed in parts in 1905 and came out as a book in February 1906.

Readers fixed instead on what Sinclair described going into the meat. Within months, Roosevelt signed the two food laws of June 30, 1906. Later that year Sinclair wrote about how readers had taken his book: "I aimed at the public's heart, and by accident I hit it in the stomach."

<a id="story-george-washington-carver-food-farming"></a>

#### George Washington Carver

> **Who:** A scientist who taught poor Southern farmers how to rebuild worn-out cotton land and grow their own food.
>
> **When and where:** Born enslaved near Diamond, Missouri, about 1864. Taught at Tuskegee Institute, Alabama, from 1896 until his death in 1943.
>
> **Movie:** *George Washington Carver: An Uncommon Life* (Iowa PBS, 2018), a documentary.

George Washington Carver taught Southern farmers to plant crops that rebuilt their soil. He was born near Diamond, Missouri, in about 1864. No record gives the exact date. Moses and Susan Carver enslaved his mother, Mary, and so they claimed him as their property too. When he was a few months old, a band of men kidnapped him and his mother from the farm to sell them. A neighbor got the baby back. His mother was not brought back. Moses and Susan Carver raised him and his older brother, Jim. He was the first Black student at Iowa State, and later he taught there. In October 1896 he took charge of farming studies at Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, and he stayed until he died in 1943.

Year after year of cotton had worn out the soil on many Southern farms. Carver taught crop rotation, which means changing the crop planted in a field from one year to the next. A farmer planted peanuts, cowpeas (a kind of bean) or sweet potatoes, which built the soil back up, and then went back to cotton, which wore it down.

Carver wrote 44 practical bulletins and gave them to farmers for free. A bulletin is a small printed booklet. He also sent out the Jesup wagon, a wagon pulled by a mule that was used to show farmers new ways of farming. His best-known bulletin came out in 1916 and was reprinted for decades. It was called *How to Grow the Peanut and 105 Ways of Preparing It for Human Consumption*. In his laboratory he made hundreds of test products from peanuts and sweet potatoes.

Many people believe that Carver invented peanut butter. He did not. The Aztecs of Mexico made peanut paste centuries earlier. Marcellus Gilmore Edson received a patent for a peanut paste in Canada in 1884, and John Harvey Kellogg received one in 1895. A patent is a government paper that gives an inventor the sole right to make and sell an invention for a set number of years.

#### Pellagra: a disease from a corn diet

Pellagra is a disease caused by a diet missing a vitamin called niacin. Between 1900 and 1940, about 3 million Americans got pellagra, and about 100,000 died of it. Those hit hardest were poor farmers, sharecroppers and cotton-mill workers in the South. Sharecroppers were families who farmed land owned by someone else in return for a share of the crop. They lived mostly on cornmeal, molasses and dried pork, with few fresh vegetables and little meat or milk. Many mill owners paid workers in scrip, a kind of paper money that could be spent only at the company's own store. Those stores sold mostly cornmeal, dried meat and molasses.

A person with pellagra got skin rashes, diarrhea and dementia, which means confusion and loss of memory. The disease could end in death.

In 1915 Joseph Goldberger, a doctor with the US Public Health Service, tested the diet on prisoners. Mississippi's governor, Earl Brewer, agreed to the test. Starting on April 19, 1915, Goldberger fed eleven volunteer prisoners at the Rankin State Prison Farm the corn-based meals poor Southerners ate. They got biscuits, mush, grits, gravy, cornbread, sweet potatoes, cane syrup and coffee. In return, the men were promised pardons, meaning they would be let out of prison. Accounts of the results differ. About half of the eleven men got pellagra, and the others showed some signs of it. The men had skin rashes and stomach illness. The men who got pellagra recovered. In 1916 Goldberger injected himself, his wife and other volunteers with blood from pellagra patients, to show that the disease did not spread from person to person.

In 1937 a scientist in Wisconsin found that the missing nutrient was niacin, also called vitamin B3. Federal and state laws passed during World War II required that niacin be added to bread.

#### Sugar and pineapple from Hawaii

Sugar plantations made up most of the business of the Hawaiian Islands. In 1901 James Dole started the Hawaiian Pineapple Company. Workers at his company canned pineapple in huge amounts for kitchens on the mainland. The United States had taken over the islands three years before, in 1898.

Hawaii was a kingdom with its own queen until 1893. On January 17 of that year, a group of mostly American businessmen moved to overthrow Queen Liliuokalani. John L. Stevens, the top US official in Hawaii, had 162 US sailors and Marines brought ashore from the warship USS *Boston*. The queen gave up her power under protest. In 1897 Native Hawaiians signed 21,269 names on petitions, written requests, asking that Hawaii not be joined to the United States. On July 7, 1898, President William McKinley signed the Newlands Resolution, a measure to annex Hawaii. To annex a place means to take it over and make it part of a country.

#### Tractors, hybrid corn and chickens

In 1917 Henry Ford's company began selling a cheap tractor called the Fordson. In 1920 American farms had 246,000 tractors and about 26 million horses and mules. Most of the pulling was still done by animals. In 1924 the International Harvester company brought out the Farmall. The Farmall could also cultivate row crops, meaning it could work the soil between rows of growing plants. That had been the last big farm job that still needed horses.

A farm horse ate crops too. It took about five acres to grow the feed for one horse. When a farmer sold a horse or stopped using it, the farmer could plant those acres with food for people.

In 1926 Henry A. Wallace founded Pioneer Hi-Bred, the first company that sold hybrid seed corn. Hybrid seed comes from crossing two different parent plants.

<a id="story-cecile-steele"></a>

#### Cecile Steele

> **Who:** A Delaware farmer who began the business of raising chickens for meat after a hatchery sent her 500 chicks by mistake.
>
> **When and where:** Ocean View, Delaware, 1923. She lived from 1900 to 1940.

In 1923 Cecile Long Steele ordered 50 chicks for her farm in Ocean View, Delaware. The hatchery made a mistake and sent her 500. She raised them indoors. At 16 weeks old she sold them for 62 cents a pound.

She ordered 1,000 chicks on purpose in 1924, and by 1926 she was raising 10,000. The Delmarva Peninsula is the land where Delaware, Maryland and Virginia meet. By 1928 about 500 farms there were raising broilers. A broiler is a young chicken raised for its meat.

Chicken later became the meat Americans eat most, by weight. The National Chicken Council is a group that speaks for chicken companies. Its staff add up how much meat each American eats in a year. By their count, each American ate about 32 pounds of chicken in 1965. Their figures for 2025 put each American at about 103 pounds of chicken, 59 pounds of beef and 49 pounds of pork.

#### Dust, pigs and food stamps in the 1930s

During World War I, wheat sold for high prices. Farmers on the southern Great Plains plowed up the grassland to plant it. A drought began in 1931, and the wheat died. The bare, dry soil blew away in dust storms. The storm of April 14, 1935, is called Black Sunday. Crops failed year after year. Farm families lived on vegetables from their gardens, canned food, food handed out by federal officials, and jackrabbits.

No one kept an official count of the people the dust killed. In Kansas alone, dozens of people died of dust pneumonia in 1935. Dust pneumonia happened when dust settled deep in a person's lungs. It stopped the cilia, the tiny hairs that sweep the airways clean, from moving. The person had fever, chest pain, coughing and trouble breathing.

Under the Agricultural Adjustment Act of May 1933, federal officials paid farmers to grow less, so that crop prices would rise. In 1933 farmers plowed under about 10 million acres of cotton that was already growing, which means they plowed the young plants back into the ground. Federal officials bought about 6 million pigs and had them killed. At the same time, hungry people across the country stood in breadlines, long lines for free food. In 1936 judges threw out the farm law, and members of Congress wrote a new one in 1938. Federal payments to farmers have continued ever since.

Many Americans were angry that federal officials were having food destroyed while people went hungry. Federal officials set up the Federal Surplus Relief Corporation to give extra farm food to families on relief, meaning families getting government help. On May 16, 1939, the first Food Stamp Program began in Rochester, New York. Mabel McFiggin was the first buyer. People bought orange stamps that paid for food. With them came free blue stamps, which could buy only foods that federal officials listed as surplus, meaning extra.

#### Who got the cotton money

Under the cotton contracts of 1934 and 1935, federal officials paid landowners to take land out of cotton. Sharecroppers, the families who farmed that land for a share of the crop, were supposed to get a part of the payment. Under the contracts, their share was only about 11 percent. A landowner could keep the whole payment by evicting the sharecroppers, meaning forcing them off the land, and hiring day laborers, workers paid one day at a time, instead. Planters were the owners of big farms. When planters cut their cotton land by 40 or 50 percent, they cut the number of families working it by the same share.

In July 1934, seven Black men and eleven white men met at the Sunnyside School in Poinsett County, Arkansas. They started a union, a group of workers who join together to demand better pay and treatment. They called it the Southern Tenant Farmers' Union, and they started it to fight the evictions. A tenant farmer is a farmer who works land that someone else owns. Planters and lawmen answered with force. In January 1935 a white organizer, Ward Rodgers, was arrested and jailed at Marked Tree. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas account of the union does not say who arrested him.

At a union meeting in Gilmore, four armed white men broke in. They ordered the Black members to leave. They told them they would be lynched, meaning killed by a mob, if they were caught at another union meeting. Many members were beaten and threatened with guns. The same account does not name the men who did it. On March 15, 1935, at Birdsong, about forty armed planters, their riding bosses and lawmen broke up a union crowd. Riding bosses were men on horseback who watched over the field workers. Later that month a mob attacked the home of the union's lawyer, Cornelius Tyree Carpenter.

The Agricultural Adjustment Administration was the federal office that ran the farm payment program. Some of its lawyers, led by Jerome Frank, decided that landowners had to keep the same tenant families. In February 1935 the agency's head, Chester Davis, had Secretary of Agriculture Henry Wallace fire them.

#### Ration books and victory gardens

During World War II, federal officials rationed food, which means they limited how much of it each person could buy. Every person got a ration book of stamps, even babies. Sugar was the first food rationed, in May 1942. Coffee followed that November. In March 1943 meat, cheese, fats and canned foods were added. Sugar was also the last food to come off the list, in June 1947.

Federal officials allowed each person 26 pounds of sugar a year, about 8 ounces a week. In 1945 they cut the amount to as little as 4.5 ounces a week. Every month each person got 64 red points for meat and fats and 48 blue points for processed foods, such as canned goods. A shopper had to hand over the right points, along with money, to buy these foods.

Americans also grew their own food. They planted about 20 million victory gardens, home vegetable gardens grown to help feed the country during the war. By 1943 and 1944, these gardens grew about 40 percent of the country's fresh vegetables, roughly 9 to 10 million tons. Accounts differ on which of the two years was the peak.

Frozen food was already on sale by the war years. Clarence Birdseye's quick-frozen foods first went on sale on March 6, 1930, in 18 stores in Springfield, Massachusetts.

<a id="story-adelaide-wisdom-benjamin"></a>

#### Adelaide Wisdom Benjamin

> **Who:** A girl whose family grew a victory garden and shopped with ration stamps during World War II. She told her story in an oral history for the National WWII Museum in 2013.
>
> **When and where:** New Orleans, Louisiana, and El Paso, Texas, 1941 to 1945. She was born in New Orleans in 1932.
