Adelaide Wisdom grew up in New Orleans. During the war her father tried to join the Army and the Navy but did not meet their requirements. He was accepted by the Marines. After boot camp he was posted to El Paso, Texas, as a Marine recruiter, and the family moved with him.

At the store, the family could buy sugar, butter and some vegetables only with the right ration stamps. Beef and lamb were hard to find. With so little to serve, the family could not have guests over for meals.

The family grew a victory garden in New Orleans and in El Paso. "We grew mirlitons, and string beans and tomatoes in our backyard," she said in 2013. A mirliton is a pale green squash. The crops grew well in New Orleans. They did not grow well in El Paso. She collected scrap metal with her brother, including old coat hangers and bicycle tires. She put 10 cents of her 25-cent weekly allowance into war savings stamps.

When Germany surrendered in 1945, she bought a chocolate soda, a comic book and bubble gum. She later graduated from Tulane University Law School. With her husband, Eddie Benjamin, she practiced law for 55 years.

#### Farms taken from Japanese Americans

On February 19, 1942, President Franklin Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, an order from the president that has the force of law. In March and April, General John L. DeWitt ordered about 120,000 people whose families came from Japan forced out of their homes on the West Coast. Under his orders, US officials sent both citizens and noncitizens away and locked them up in prison camps behind barbed wire.

Many of these families were farmers. Lawrence Hewes ran the Farm Security Administration in the region. His agency was the federal office put in charge of handing their farms to new farmers. He said his agents had registered 6,000 Japanese American farms, covering about 200,000 acres. In March 1942 alone, Japanese American families lost more than 1,000 of those farms, about 50,000 acres, and new farmers took them over. That same month, leaders of the California Farm Bureau, a farmers' group, said Japanese American farmers grew 40 percent of the state's vegetables. Those included nearly all of its tomatoes, celery, strawberries and peppers. In April 1942 officials of the federal Wartime Civil Control Administration estimated that the crops on 21 percent of the land might be lost. The families who farmed it had been forced out, and no one had been found to take their place.

Inside the camps, the people held there farmed. About 15,000 people were sent to the camp at Tule Lake, California, alone.

#### Braceros in the fields

In 1942 US officials started the bracero program to bring Mexican workers into the country for farm and railroad work. The workers were called braceros. Over 22 years, workers signed more than 4.5 million contracts. Braceros picked much of the country's fruit and vegetables until the program ended in 1964.

From 1942 to 1949, US employers held back 10 percent of each bracero's pay. They sent the money through two US banks, Wells Fargo and the Union Trust Company of San Francisco, to banks in Mexico. Under the program's rules, the workers were to get the money back when they went home. Many braceros never got it. A Mexican report of 1946 said $8 million had been paid back to braceros that year, and no one could say where another $6 million had gone. Former braceros sued to get the money. In 2009, under a settlement, an agreement that ends a lawsuit, former braceros, or the families of braceros who had died, received a one-time sum of 38,000 pesos, about $3,500.

#### School lunch

Towns and charities had run school meal programs for decades. In the 1930s, federal officials gave these programs extra food that they had bought from farmers. During World War II, many young men called up to serve in the military failed their physical exams because of malnutrition. Malnutrition means a person has not had enough of the right food. General Lewis Hershey ran the draft, the system that called men into the military. After the war he told members of Congress that malnutrition put the country's safety at risk. On June 4, 1946, President Harry Truman signed the National School Lunch Act. The law states that Congress passed it "as a measure of national security," a way to keep the country safe, and to protect the health of the nation's children. Under it, federal money for school lunches became permanent.

### 1950 to 2000

After 1950, American farms grew fewer and bigger, and each acre grew more food. Farmers used tractors, hybrid seed, fertilizer and pesticides. Swanson sold 25 million frozen TV dinners in 1955, and fast-food stands served hamburgers in seconds. In the 1980s, after land prices fell and interest rates rose, about 300,000 farms could not pay their loans. At the same time, some farmers and cooks began to grow food by organic methods and to serve food from nearby farms.

#### Tractors outnumber horses, and farms grow bigger

The Census of Agriculture is the federal government's count of the country's farms. The 1954 Census of Agriculture was the first count in which American farms had more tractors than horses and mules. Farms had about 4.6 million tractors that year and about 4 million horses and mules. In 1920 there had been about 25 to 26 million horses and mules.

The number of farms fell too. In 1935 the country had 6.8 million farms, the most it ever had. After that the number kept dropping, toward 2 million. The farms that were left were bigger. Many of them grew only a few kinds of crops and relied on chemical fertilizers and pesticides.

By the 1950s nearly all the corn in the country grew from hybrid seed. For about a hundred years, farmers had grown roughly 25 to 30 bushels of corn on an acre. A bushel is a measure that holds about 8 gallons. By the 1970s farmers were growing more than 100 bushels an acre.

#### Fast food and the TV dinner

Richard and Maurice McDonald opened a drive-in restaurant in San Bernardino, California, in 1940. In 1948 they rebuilt it around what they called the Speedee Service System, with a menu cut down to 15-cent hamburgers, french fries and milkshakes. The carhops, the servers who had carried food out to people's cars, lost their jobs. Workers made the food on a kind of assembly line, where each worker did one job over and over, and customers got their food in seconds.

In 1953 the Swanson company put a frozen turkey dinner in an aluminum tray on sale and called it a TV dinner. It cost about 98 cents. The company sold more than 10 million in 1954 and 25 million the next year. According to company stories, Swanson had too many turkeys left over after Thanksgiving. Who thought of the TV dinner is disputed. For decades a salesman named Gerry Thomas said the idea was his. The company's owners were the brothers Gilbert and Clarke Swanson. Their relatives, and a Swanson scientist named Betty Cronin, said the brothers came up with it at the company and that Thomas took the credit. Frozen meals had been sold before either claim. In 1945 the Maxson company made frozen "Strato-Plates" to serve on airplanes.

<a id="story-ray-kroc"></a>

#### Ray Kroc

> **Who:** A milkshake-machine salesman who became the McDonald brothers' franchise agent and then bought them out.
>
> **When and where:** Visited San Bernardino, California, in 1954. Opened his first McDonald's in Des Plaines, Illinois, on April 15, 1955. Bought out the brothers in 1961.
>
> **Movie:** *The Founder* (2016), a drama based on his story and the brothers'.

Ray Kroc sold milkshake machines. In 1954 he went to see the McDonald brothers' stand in San Bernardino. He became the brothers' franchise agent. A franchise is a deal in which a business owner lets other people open stores under the owner's name and system, in return for fees.

On April 15, 1955, Kroc opened his own McDonald's in Des Plaines, Illinois. In 1961 he bought the brothers out for $2.7 million. The brothers said Kroc had made a handshake promise to keep paying them royalties, a share of the money from every sale, and never kept it. Kroc also opened a McDonald's near their original stand, in competition with it. The movie *The Founder* is a drama based on these events.

<a id="story-norman-borlaug"></a>

#### Norman Borlaug

> **Who:** An Iowa-born plant scientist whose wheat helped poor countries grow far more grain, in what was called the Green Revolution.
>
> **When and where:** Mexico from 1944. India and Pakistan in the 1960s. Nobel Peace Prize in 1970.
>
> **Movie:** *The Man Who Tried to Feed the World* (PBS American Experience, 2020), a documentary.

Norman Borlaug bred wheat that grew more grain on the same land. Starting in 1944, he worked in Mexico for a program run by the Rockefeller Foundation, a charity started by the Rockefeller family. He crossed thousands of kinds of wheat. The result was a semi-dwarf wheat, with short stems, that resisted plant diseases. By 1956 Mexico grew all the wheat it needed.

In the 1960s, experts predicted famines in India and Pakistan. A famine is a time when there is so little food that people starve. Farmers there planted Borlaug's wheat, and the famines they predicted did not happen. In 1970 Borlaug won the Nobel Peace Prize. He is the only farm scientist to have won it. Many writers credit his work with saving as many as a billion lives. That number is a common estimate, not a count. The rise in grain harvests in poor countries that followed is called the Green Revolution.

Farmers grew his wheat together with chemical fertilizer and irrigation, water brought to the fields by pipes and ditches. This made farmers depend on bought chemicals. Many farmers also stopped planting old kinds of crops, so fewer kinds were grown.

#### Pesticides in the fields

Farmers sprayed their crops with pesticides, chemicals that kill insects and weeds. DDT, a chemical that kills insects, was in wide use from the mid-1940s. It made the shells of eagles' eggs thin. By 1963 only 417 pairs of bald eagles were nesting in the lower 48 states. In September 1962 Rachel Carson's book *Silent Spring* had described what these long-lasting pesticides did to birds, soil, water and people. Officials at the Environmental Protection Agency banned DDT in 1972.

Farmworkers in steady contact with pesticides had high rates of burns, cancer and children born with birth defects. In the 1980s, children in several towns of California's San Joaquin Valley had cancer at rates "800% above the norm," according to the Walter P. Reuther Library at Wayne State University. Cesar Chavez, Dolores Huerta and the United Farm Workers organized the people who picked the crops. They are known for the grape strike in Delano, California, when grape pickers refused to work until growers met their demands.

In March 2026 the New York Times reported that Chavez had sexually abused two girls in the 1970s, beginning when they were 12 and 13. The two women, Debra Rojas and Ana Murguia, are daughters of union organizers. Rojas said Chavez raped her in a motel room when she was 15. Rape means forcing a person into sex. Dolores Huerta then said publicly that Chavez had pressured her into sex once and had raped her in a car in 1966, and that she became pregnant both times. Chavez died in 1993, so no court has ever heard these accusations. On March 26, 2026, California's lawmakers voted to rename the state holiday Cesar Chavez Day as Farmworkers Day, and Governor Gavin Newsom signed the change into law.

#### Black farmers and their land

In 1920 Black farmers ran more than 900,000 farms, about 15 percent of all the farms in the United States. Between 1910 and 1997, the amount of farmland Black Americans owned fell by nearly 90 percent. In 2022 five economists published a study that put the value of the land lost from 1920 to 1997 at about $326 billion in today's dollars. By 2007 about 1.5 percent of the country's farms, 32,938 of them, were run by Black farmers.

Researchers at the Union of Concerned Scientists, a science group, named two of the causes in a 2023 report. Lloyd Wright once ran the civil rights office of the US Department of Agriculture, or USDA. He called the department "the last plantation," because its officials had kept Black farmers from getting the loans and grants that would have kept them on their land. Plantations were the big farms where enslaved people had been forced to work. The second cause was heirs' property. A will is a paper that says who gets a person's things after the person dies. When a landowner died without a will, the land passed to the landowner's heirs, the family members who inherit it. All the heirs owned the land together. Each owned a share of the whole farm, not a piece of land of their own. Any one of them could ask a court to force a sale of the whole farm. A land buyer could buy one heir's share and then ask a court to sell the farm at auction. Farms sold that way went for far less than they were worth. USDA officials have called heirs' property "the leading cause of Black involuntary land loss," meaning land lost when the owners did not choose to sell.

Black farmers took the USDA to court. The case was called *Pigford v. Glickman*. The farmers showed that from 1983 to 1997, USDA officials treated Black farmers worse than white farmers because of their race. The officials also failed to look into the farmers' complaints. Members of local county committees made the decisions on USDA farm loans. Black farmers said committee members turned down their loans, or made them wait longer for approval than white farmers. The Congressional Research Service report on the case does not name the committee members. On April 14, 1999, Judge Paul L. Friedman approved a settlement. Under it, 15,645 farmers had their claims approved, out of 22,721 who qualified. Farmers whose claims were approved under the part of the settlement called Track A each received $50,000, and USDA officials canceled what they owed on their USDA loans. The payments and debt relief came to about $1.06 billion. On February 18, 2010, a second settlement of $1.25 billion was announced for farmers who had missed the first deadline.

#### Organic farming rules become law

Organic farmers grow food without man-made chemical fertilizers and pesticides. They build up their soil with compost, which is rotted plant and animal matter. In 1942 J.I. Rodale began a magazine called *Organic Farming and Gardening* in Emmaus, Pennsylvania. He spent decades urging farmers and gardeners to farm this way. In 1990 members of Congress passed the Organic Foods Production Act. It required national rules for what could be sold as organic. The USDA organic seal, a label for food that meets those rules, came into use on October 21, 2002.

<a id="story-alice-waters"></a>

#### Alice Waters

> **Who:** A cook who built her restaurant around food from nearby farms and started a school garden where children grow and cook their own food.
>
> **When and where:** Chez Panisse restaurant, Berkeley, California, opened in 1971. The Edible Schoolyard, Berkeley, started in 1995.
>
> **Movie:** *Alice Waters and Her Delicious Revolution* (PBS American Masters, 2003), a documentary.

In 1971 Alice Waters opened a restaurant called Chez Panisse in Berkeley, California. She cooked with food that was fresh, grown nearby, in season and organically grown. Chez Panisse was one of the first restaurants of the style later called California cuisine, cooking built on fresh food from local farms. Waters helped start the farm-to-table idea, which means buying food straight from local farms.

In 1995 Waters started the Edible Schoolyard at Martin Luther King Jr. Middle School in Berkeley. Students there grow a garden, cook what they grow and eat it.

#### The farm crisis of the 1980s

In the 1970s, American farmers sold large amounts of grain to other countries. They planted "fencerow to fencerow," every acre up to the fences. Interest is the extra money a borrower pays back on top of a loan. In the early 1980s, interest on loans rose high. At the same time, the price of farmland fell. In parts of the Midwest, farmland lost as much as 60 percent of its value between 1981 and the mid-1980s. By 1984 American farmers owed about $215 billion, twice what they had owed in 1978.

During the 1980s, an estimated 300,000 farms defaulted, meaning they could not pay back their loans. About 300 banks in farm country failed, meaning they ran out of money and closed. On September 22, 1985, Willie Nelson, John Mellencamp and Neil Young held a concert called Farm Aid in Champaign, Illinois. About 80,000 people came, and the concert raised more than $7 million for farm families. Farm Aid concerts still take place.

<a id="story-jordan-family-farm"></a>

#### Russel and Mary Jane Jordan

> **Who:** An Iowa farm couple who sold their machinery, livestock and household goods at auction to pay their bank. Their daughter filmed it.
>
> **When and where:** Iowa. The family had owned its farm for 125 years. Their bank was in Atlantic, Iowa.
>
> **Movie:** *Troublesome Creek: A Midwestern* (1995), a documentary about the family. It won the Grand Jury Prize at the Sundance Film Festival and was nominated for an Academy Award.

Russel and Mary Jane Jordan owned a farm in Iowa that had been in their family for 125 years. A company called Norwest, which owned banks in several states, bought their bank in Atlantic, Iowa. A man from the company's headquarters, Tim Wolf, took over their loans. The bank's officers called in a debt of $70,000 that had built up over the years, meaning they demanded it be paid. Each year the Jordans also took out a loan of $150,000 to pay for that year's farming. Together the old debt and the yearly loan came to about $220,000.

The Jordans held an auction. They sold all their machinery, their livestock and even their household goods. The Jordans kept only the land. The sale raised about $300,000, more than enough to pay the back debt. Russ and Mary Jane moved to a rented house in Atlantic. Their son Jim took over farming the home place with his own equipment. Later the crop land was rented out to neighbors.

Their daughter, Jeanne Jordan, and the filmmaker Steven Ascher made the film about the family.

### 2000 to Today

Since 2000, Americans have argued over what goes into their food, who picks it and who can get enough of it. The 2022 Census of Agriculture, the USDA's count of the country's farms, found 1.9 million farms in the United States. That was 7 percent fewer than in 2017. It was the first count below 2 million since before the Civil War. In 1935 there had been 6.8 million.

#### Weight, hunger and food stamps

Researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or CDC, measure obesity, which means a body weight high enough to raise the risk of illness. By their count, 30.5 percent of American adults had obesity in 1999 and 2000. The share rose to 41.9 percent in the years 2017 to March 2020. It was 40.3 percent from August 2021 to August 2023. Doctors link type 2 diabetes and heart disease to diet. Type 2 diabetes is an illness in which the body cannot keep the sugar in the blood at a healthy level.

Some Americans live far from a place to buy fresh food. USDA officials map low-income areas that are far from a supermarket. In a city, far means more than 1 mile away. In the country, it means more than 10 miles. An area counts when at least 500 people, or a third of the people who live there, are that far away. People call these areas food deserts. By that measure, USDA data for 2019 put about 19 million people, about 6 percent of the population, in them. A broader measure used for 2015 counted 39.4 million. The number depends on which measure is used.

Since 1995, USDA economists had counted households that did not always have enough food. In September 2025, USDA officials under Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced that they would end the count. They called it "redundant, costly [and] politicized." The last report came out on December 30, 2025. It found that in 2024, 13.7 percent of households did not always have enough food. Nearly 48 million people lived in those households, including more than 14 million children.

The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, is the program once called food stamps. On July 4, 2025, President Donald Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The law cuts federal spending on SNAP. Economists at the Congressional Budget Office, which works out costs for Congress, figured that the cut will come to $186.7 billion over ten years.

#### Farmers' markets and the 2020 pandemic

Farmers' markets, where farmers sell their own crops straight to shoppers, grew in number. USDA counted 1,755 of them in 1994 and 8,771 in 2019. The number grew about 7 percent a year until about 2011, and then it stopped growing much.

In 2020 the disease COVID-19 spread through plants that process meat and poultry, which means chickens and turkeys. In April and May 2020, 23 states reported 16,233 cases of COVID-19 among workers in 239 plants, and 86 of those workers died. This count comes from a CDC report of July 2020. Of the sick workers whose race was recorded, 87 percent were members of racial or ethnic minority groups.

#### Changed seeds and new kinds of meat

Genetic engineering means scientists change a plant's DNA, the chemical instructions inside every cell, in a laboratory. In 2025, about 92 percent of the country's corn acres, 96 percent of its soybean acres and 93 percent of its cotton acres were planted with genetically engineered seed, according to USDA economists. Scientists had changed that seed so the plants survive sprays that kill weeds.

In 2016 the National Academies of Sciences, a group of leading American scientists, reviewed about 1,000 studies. The scientists wrote that they found no convincing proof that eating these foods harms people's health. Many Americans still argued against them. Under federal rules in force since January 2022, foods that contain changed DNA that tests can detect must carry a "bioengineered" label. Industry histories name the Flavr Savr tomato, sold in 1994, as the first engineered food sold in stores.

Companies also began selling new kinds of meat. The Impossible Burger, made from plants, came out in 2016. Beyond Meat also makes meat from plants. In 2019 the public could buy its shares, small parts of the company, for the first time. Their price rose more on the first day than that of any other company's new shares that year. In June 2023 USDA officials gave two companies, UPSIDE Foods and GOOD Meat, the first approval in the United States to sell chicken grown from animal cells instead of from a live bird. People call it lab-grown meat.

Other companies grew vegetables indoors on shelves stacked high, called vertical farms. Investors put money into them, and the business grew fast. In June 2023 AeroFarms, an early company of this kind, filed for bankruptcy, a court process for a business that cannot pay its debts. The company later reorganized and stayed in business.

#### Who picks the food

USDA economists report that most hired crop workers in the United States were born in other countries. In recent years about 15 percent of crop-farm jobs have gone to workers on H-2A visas. A visa is a paper that lets a person from another country enter the United States. An H-2A visa lets a farmworker come for one season of farm work. More than 90 percent of H-2A workers come from Mexico. By the USDA economists' figures, officials at the US Department of Labor approved about 48,000 H-2A jobs in 2005 and about 372,000 in 2022. The Labor Department's own count for 2025 was 398,258 jobs.

From 1992 to 2006, 68 crop workers died from heat, according to a CDC report of 2008. Crop workers died of heat at about 20 times the rate of all American workers. One of them was a 56-year-old H-2A worker harvesting tobacco by hand in North Carolina in July 2005. It was his third day on the job, and no one had trained him about heat. His body temperature reached 108 degrees Fahrenheit, and he died of heat stroke, which happens when the body cannot cool itself. The report does not give his name.

Federal law lets children work on farms at younger ages than in other jobs. Outside school hours, a child under 12 may work on a farm owned or run by a parent. With a parent's permission, a child under 12 may also work on a small farm that does not have to pay the minimum wage, the lowest pay the law allows. Children of 12 and 13 may work with a parent's permission or on a farm where a parent works. At 14, a child may do farm jobs outside school hours.

<a id="story-lucas-benitez"></a>

#### Lucas Benitez

> **Who:** A tomato picker who helped start the Coalition of Immokalee Workers and its Fair Food Program.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Guerrero, Mexico. Moved to Immokalee, Florida, at 17. The coalition began in 1993, and the Fair Food Program began in 2011.
>
> **Movie:** *Food Chains* (2014), a documentary about the coalition. Benitez appears in it.

Lucas Benitez came to Immokalee, Florida, from the state of Guerrero in Mexico when he was 17. He picked tomatoes in the fields there. In 1993 he helped start the Coalition of Immokalee Workers, a group of farmworkers.

In November 2010 the coalition and Florida's tomato growers announced an agreement, and the Fair Food Program began running in 2011. Under it, large buyers of tomatoes, such as McDonald's and Walmart, agree to pay a premium, an extra amount of money, for the tomatoes. People often call it an extra "penny per pound," and it raises the pickers' pay. The buyers also agree to hold growers to a code of conduct, a written set of rules. The code sets a lowest pay rate and requires shade, water and protection from abuse for the pickers. The code also bans forced labor, sexual assault and putting children to work as a regular practice. Sexual assault means any sexual touching or attack against a person's will, and it includes rape. When any of these happens on a farm, the program's managers suspend the farm from the program until its owners fix the problem. Checkers called auditors make sure growers follow the code.

In October 2023 Benitez received the University of Michigan's Wallenberg Medal, an award for people who defend human rights. Benitez had helped investigate cases of slavery on farms, where workers were held and forced to work. In one case alone, he helped free about 700 workers, according to WGCU, a public radio station in Florida.

#### Black farmers in the new century

The 2022 Census of Agriculture counted 46,738 Black farmers on 32,653 farms, according to a USDA report of June 2024. They made up 1.4 percent of all the country's farmers and worked 5.3 million acres. The number of farms run by Black farmers was 8 percent lower than in 2017.

On July 31, 2024, USDA officials paid about $2 billion to more than 43,000 farmers, ranchers and forest owners who had faced discrimination in USDA farm loans. Discrimination means treating people worse because of who they are, such as their race. The NAACP Legal Defense Fund reported the payments that day. The money came from a section of the Inflation Reduction Act, a law that members of Congress passed in 2022.

#### The first farmers, still farming

Native nations are working to control their own food. This is called food sovereignty. Tribes run bison herds, seed banks that save the seeds of old crops, and programs that bring back traditional foods. Native chefs and seed keepers are rebuilding the ways their nations cooked and ate. Among the Ojibwe of the Great Lakes, manoomin, or wild rice, is harvested by canoe and is still a central food.

<a id="story-nephi-craig"></a>

#### Nephi Craig

> **Who:** A White Mountain Apache and Diné (Navajo) chef who opened a café built around Apache foods.
>
> **When and where:** Café Gozhóó, Whiteriver, on the White Mountain Apache Reservation in Arizona, opened in 2021.
>
> **Movie:** *Gather* (2020), a documentary about Native food sovereignty that features him.

Nephi Craig is a chef. In 2021 he opened Café Gozhóó, a café built around Apache foods, in Whiteriver, Arizona, on the White Mountain Apache Reservation. Apaches who are recovering from addiction to alcohol or drugs work in the café's kitchen through a job-training program run by the tribe's Rainbow Treatment Center. In 2026 Craig said he had been sober himself for 15 years. That year he published a book about his life and his cooking, *Our Knives Will Save Us*. He also founded the Native American Culinary Association, a group for Native cooks. The 2020 documentary *Gather* follows him and others who are bringing back Native foods. Among them are Twila Cassadore, a San Carlos Apache woman who gathers wild foods, and Elsie DuBray, a student scientist from the Cheyenne River Sioux.

<a id="ch-economy"></a>

## Chapter 16: Economy

### Before 1500

Before 1500, Native people here had economies of their own. An economy is the way people make, share and trade the things they need. People here had no coins and no wages, and nothing had a set market price. They traded by barter, which means swapping one good for another, and by giving gifts between people and between nations. Goods such as stone tools, shells and copper traveled hundreds of miles. No record names any one person who took part in this trade.

#### Cahokia and its hoe blades

Cahokia stood near what is now St. Louis. It was the largest city north of Mexico, and it was at its biggest from about 1050 to 1150. Its farmers grew more corn than they ate. That extra corn, called a surplus, fed specialists. A specialist is a person who spends most of their time on one kind of work, such as making tools, instead of growing food.

The people of Cahokia controlled the making and trading of hoe blades. A hoe is a farm tool for breaking up soil. The blades were chipped from Mill Creek chert, a tough stone found only in southern Illinois. Workers dug it out of quarries, open pits for stone. Some of the pits were 10 to 20 feet deep. Archaeologists are scientists who study the past from the things people left behind. They have found these blades more than 400 miles away, in places from Louisiana to Minnesota and in the Arkansas River valley.

#### Shell, copper and obsidian

People carried whelk shells north from the coast of the Gulf of Mexico. A whelk is a large sea snail. Traders also moved copper from the land around Lake Superior. At Cahokia, workers made shell beads in large numbers, and families on small farms made them as well.

In the West, people traded obsidian across their own trade networks. Obsidian is a natural glass that forms in volcanoes. Archaeologists have traced pieces found in western Canada back to Obsidian Cliff, in what is now Wyoming, and Bear Gulch, in what is now Idaho. Some pieces had traveled as far as 750 miles from where the stone formed.

### The 1500s

The kings and queens of Spain, France and England paid for voyages to this coast in the 1500s to find gold and silver. In the land that became the United States, their explorers found none. The Spanish silver came from mines in Mexico and South America. Fishing was the first steady European business in these waters. Some ship crews also traded with Native people on the coast, and some of that trade was for furs. Almost no Europeans settled here yet, so there was no colonial economy.

#### Fish, furs and a rope from a cliff

European fishing crews worked the cod waters off the northeast coast all through the 1500s. They dried their catch on shore. The Spanish town of St. Augustine in Florida began in 1565 as a military post. The Spanish king's government paid its costs. Unlike the English colonies that came later, it was not set up to make a profit.

In 1524 the crew of Giovanni da Verrazzano's ship met Abenaki people on the coast of what is now Maine. The Abenaki would not let the crew come ashore. Instead they traded from the top of a cliff, lowering baskets of goods to the ship on a rope. Crews of earlier European ships had already taken Native people from the Maine coast to sell as slaves. That is why the Abenaki kept this crew off the land. Verrazzano called the place "the land of bad people." The records do not say whether the baskets held furs.

In July 1534, at Chaleur Bay, north of Maine in what is now Canada, Mi'kmaq traders held up beaver furs on sticks to the crew of Jacques Cartier. They traded the furs for knives and other iron goods. Cartier wrote the trade down in his own account of the voyage. It is one of the earliest recorded trades of furs between Europeans and Native people on the Atlantic coast of North America. The fur trade reached the land that became the United States in the next century.

### The 1600s

Tobacco became Virginia's main business in the 1600s. Indentured servants from England did the early work in the tobacco fields. They had signed contracts to work for a master for a set number of years. Near 1700, the planters who owned the fields switched to buying enslaved Africans, whom they could hold for life. Dutch traders shipped beaver skins to Europe. Lawmakers in London wrote rules that required colonists to ship their main crops only to England or its colonies.

#### Tobacco in the Chesapeake

The first colonists at Jamestown hoped to find gold. John Smith wrote that there was "no talk, no hope, no work but dig gold, wash gold, refine gold, load gold." They found none. Colony officials tried glassmaking and other small businesses, and none of them made money. Then Virginia's planters began to grow tobacco as a cash crop. A cash crop is a crop grown to sell rather than to eat. Planters in Virginia shipped about 2,300 pounds of tobacco in 1615 and 1616. By 1617 they shipped about 20,000 pounds, and by 1629 and 1630 about 1.5 million pounds.

By 1700, planters in Virginia and Maryland together sent about 22 million pounds of tobacco a year to England. These two colonies, around Chesapeake Bay, are called the Chesapeake colonies. Planters there also used tobacco as money.

<a id="story-john-rolfe-economy"></a>

#### John Rolfe

> **Who:** A Jamestown colonist whose tobacco shipments to London began Virginia's trade in its main crop.
>
> **When and where:** Jamestown, Virginia, 1612 to 1614.

John Rolfe began Virginia's export trade in tobacco. An export is a good sent away to be sold in another place.

Rolfe lived at Jamestown, the English colony in Virginia. By July 1612 he was growing tobacco from seed brought in from the West Indies, the islands of the Caribbean Sea. He sent his first shipments of tobacco to London in 1614.

#### Indentured servants

For most of the 1600s, the tobacco work was done by indentured servants. An indentured servant signed a contract, called an indenture, to work for a master for a set number of years. In return, the master paid for the servant's trip across the ocean and gave food, clothing and a place to sleep. Adults usually served four to seven years. Children sometimes served much longer. At the end of the term, the master owed the servant "freedom dues." Depending on the contract and the colony, these could be land, tools, clothes or farm animals.

Counts of servants are estimates made from ship records and court records. About 50,000 servants came to the Chesapeake colonies between 1630 and 1680. They were about three out of every four people who arrived there. Of about 120,000 English people who moved to Virginia and Maryland in the 1600s, about 90,000 came as servants. The historian Abbot Emerson Smith made an estimate for all the British colonies. From the 1630s to the Revolution, he found, one-half to two-thirds of the white people who moved there came as indentured servants.

Planters gained from each servant in two ways. Under Virginia's headright rule, whoever paid for a person's passage, the cost of the ocean trip, received 50 acres of land for that person. A planter who paid a servant's passage got the servant's years of work and 50 acres as well. The large tobacco planters built their estates, their large holdings of land, this way.

#### What servants went through

Masters could whip their servants. When a servant ran away, judges in the colony's courts added years to the servant's term. They also added years when a woman servant had a child outside marriage. Under a Virginia law of March 1662, she served two more years or paid her master 2,000 pounds of tobacco. Some of the fathers were the masters themselves. Virginia's lawmakers wrote a second law in December 1662 about a woman servant "gott with child by her master." When her years ran out, officers of the local church, called churchwardens, sold her to work two more years "for the good of the parish," the church district where she lived. Under this law the churchwardens sold the woman, not the master who was the father. Some masters also forced women servants into sex. Julie Richter, a historian of colonial Virginia, writes that some masters "physically and sexually abused their servants." She gives no count of how many. A Virginia law required masters to give servants "Competent Dyet, Clothing & Lodging," which meant enough food, clothes and shelter. The same law required masters not to "exceed the Bounds of moderation in correcting them." Correcting meant punishing.

The Virginia Company of London, a group of investors in England, started Jamestown in 1607 and ran the colony until 1624. That year the king of England took the colony away from the company and put it under his own control. Under the company's first form of contract, used from 1609 to 1619, its officers in Virginia could hang, burn to death or shoot runaway servants they caught.

Many servants died of disease before their contracts ended. Most of those who lived to the end of their terms stayed poor.

#### From servants to enslaved Africans

By 1650, about 300 Africans lived in Virginia, next to about 4,000 white servants. In the 1660s, members of Virginia's assembly, the colony's lawmakers, passed the colony's first laws that treated Africans as slaves for life. The first came in March 1661. Under it, an English servant who ran away together with Africans had to serve extra time for the Africans' missing time as well as his own. Judges punished runaway servants by adding years to their terms, but the law's words said the Africans were "incapable of makeing satisfaction by addition of time." No years could be added to their time, because they were already held for life.

In Bacon's Rebellion of 1676 and 1677, an armed uprising in Virginia, servants and enslaved Africans fought on the same side. After it, the planters who ruled Virginia passed new laws. Historians at the College of Charleston describe the purpose of those laws as "to harden Virginia's racial caste system." A caste system sorts people into ranks at birth, and they cannot leave their rank. In 1705 the members of Virginia's assembly gathered the colony's slave laws into one slave code. Under it, enslaved people were property, and being baptized did not free anyone. Being baptized means going through the church ceremony that makes a person a Christian. A master who killed an enslaved person while "correcting" them faced no punishment.

Near 1700, the planters chose to buy enslaved Africans instead of servants. Fewer English servants were coming by then, because life in England had improved. In the same years, the Atlantic slave trade grew. Ship crews in that trade carried captive Africans across the ocean to be sold. The economist David Galenson explains the planters' choice in money terms. A servant worked for a master for about five years. A planter who bought an enslaved person held that person, and that person's children, for life. So the planter got a whole lifetime of unpaid work, and the work of the children too, instead of five years.

#### Beaver skins, and rules from London

In 1626, one ship of the Dutch West India Company, the *Arms of Amsterdam*, carried 7,246 beaver skins to Amsterdam in a single cargo. It also carried the skins of otters, minks, lynxes and muskrats. The cargo is listed in a letter known as the Schaghen letter. People in Europe bought hats made of felt from beaver fur, and those buyers were the reason traders wanted the skins.

English leaders followed an idea called mercantilism. They held that colonies existed to make the home country richer. Colonists were to send raw goods, such as tobacco, to England and buy back finished goods, things already made in England. Members of Parliament, England's lawmakers, wrote this idea into laws called the Navigation Acts. The act of 1651 required colonists to ship their trade goods only in English or colonial ships. The act of 1660 listed "enumerated goods," a phrase that means listed goods. Colonists could ship these only to England or to other English colonies. The list included tobacco, sugar, cotton, indigo and ginger. Indigo is a plant used to make blue dye.

### 1700 to 1750

By 1774, free colonists earned more on average than the people of England. The economic historians Peter Lindert and Jeffrey Williamson published that finding in 2016. They also found that income among free colonists was spread more evenly than in any other place they could measure at that time. Much of the colonies' wealth, most of all in the South, came from the work of enslaved people. Their owners paid them nothing. From 1718, British judges also sent about 50,000 convicts across the ocean to be sold as laborers.

#### What the colonies sold

Tobacco came from the Chesapeake colonies, wheat and flour from the middle colonies, such as Pennsylvania, New York and New Jersey, and fish, rum and ships from New England. In the Lowcountry of South Carolina, the low land along the coast, enslaved workers grew rice and indigo and prepared them for sale.

Timber cost little in the colonies, so colonial shipbuilders could build ships for less than builders in England. By the Revolution, about one-third of the British merchant fleet had been built in America. A merchant fleet is all the ships that carry a country's goods for trade.

#### Rice, and the people who knew how to grow it

The rice fields of the South Carolina Lowcountry were built and worked by enslaved Africans. Rice was the Lowcountry's main cash crop from the early 1700s. From about 1708, enslaved Africans were a majority of the people in South Carolina. By 1740 they were about two out of every three.

Nic Butler of the Charleston County Public Library writes that enslaved people "moved earth on a massive scale" to build the rice fields. By the 1720s, Carolina planters were asking slave traders for Africans from the region called the Rice Coast. The planters wanted them because people from there already knew how to grow rice.

The wealth from rice, Butler writes, "remained concentrated in the hands of a small minority of white planters." Historians at the College of Charleston record that enslaved children in the Lowcountry died at especially high rates. Their account gives no count of those children's deaths in the early 1700s. The number of enslaved people there did not grow through births until the 1760s.

<a id="story-eliza-lucas-pinckney-economy"></a>

#### Eliza Lucas Pinckney

> **Who:** A young woman who ran her father's three South Carolina plantations from the age of 16 and directed the colony's first successful indigo dye crop.
>
> **When and where:** South Carolina, 1744 to the 1750s.

Eliza Lucas directed the first successful crop of indigo dye in South Carolina, in 1744. Enslaved workers on her father's plantations did the growing and the work of making the dye. Indigo is a plant used to make blue dye. She later married and became Eliza Lucas Pinckney.

From the age of 16, she ran her father's three plantations. Her 1744 crop made 17 pounds of dye, and she shared the seed with neighboring planters. South Carolina's indigo exports grew from about 5,000 pounds in 1745 and 1746 to about 130,000 pounds by 1748. By the middle of the 1750s, planters there shipped more than a million pounds a year. Indigo became the colony's second biggest export after rice. By the Revolution, it made up more than a third of the value of the colony's exports.

Other people did the work of making the dye. Her father sent skilled dye-makers from the Caribbean, and enslaved workers did the processing, the work of turning the plant into dye. She relied on their knowledge and their labor.

#### Convicts sold at the dock, 1718 to 1775

From 1718 to 1775, British judges sent about 50,000 people convicted of crimes to the North American colonies, where merchants sold them as laborers. In 1718 members of Parliament passed the Transportation Act. Transportation here meant sending convicts away across the ocean as a punishment. A felony is a serious crime. Under the act, a judge could send a person convicted of one of the less serious felonies to the colonies for seven years instead of hanging them. For worse crimes, a judge could send a person for fourteen years instead of hanging them. The convicts were about one in four of all the people who moved from Britain to colonial America in those years.

Most convicts went to Maryland and Virginia. There, merchants sold them at the dock as bound laborers, people who had to work for whoever bought them until their term ended. In the records of four Maryland counties, about 82 of every 100 convicts were men and 18 were women. On two ships of 1721 and 1724, most convicts were between 20 and 29 years old, and about half were laborers with no trade.

British government officials paid a London merchant named Jonathan Forward £3 for each convict he carried, and later £5. The pound, written £, was British money. A Maryland firm, Stevenson, Randolph and Cheston, sold convicts in Maryland from 1767 to 1775. The firm's own sales books record that most men sold for £11 to £14 and most women for £9 to £10. The planters who bought them got years of work without paying wages.

Convicts died on the crossing. On 38 voyages from London between 1718 and 1736, the ships carried 3,599 convicts, and 385 of them died. That is about 11 of every 100. The historian A. Roger Ekirch points out that the records of some of these voyages list no deaths at all. If those blanks are gaps in the clerks' records, the true count was about 15 of every 100. On 12 voyages from Bristol in the 1770s, 23 of 990 convicts died.

#### Rhode Island's slave ships

Merchants in Rhode Island sent out at least 1,000 slaving voyages in the century before 1807. That year members of Congress made a law that banned bringing captive Africans into the United States, starting on January 1, 1808. The Rhode Island ships carried more than 100,000 Africans into slavery. About 60 of every 100 slaving voyages that left North America sailed from Rhode Island, and in some years more than 90 of every 100 did. These numbers come from a 2006 report by Brown University called *Slavery and Justice*.

The merchants who sent out these ships made their money by buying and selling human beings. Their crews sailed a loop around the Atlantic Ocean. Colonists turned molasses from the Caribbean into rum. Molasses is a thick, dark syrup left over when sugar is made. Captains carried the rum and other goods to West Africa and traded them for captive people. Crews then carried the captives across the ocean, on the crossing called the Middle Passage, to be sold in the Caribbean and on the mainland. The ships brought sugar and molasses back north.

#### Parliament's molasses and iron laws

In 1733 members of Parliament passed the Molasses Act. Under it, colonists had to pay a duty, a tax on goods brought in, on molasses from colonies that did not belong to Britain. The duty was sixpence, six British pennies, for each gallon. Many colonists dodged the duty by smuggling, which means bringing goods in secretly.

Under the Iron Act of 1750, raw iron from the colonies could enter Britain with no duty. The act forbade colonists to build new steel furnaces, rolling and slitting mills or plating forges. Those were the works that turned raw iron into finished goods. Colonists built them anyway.

### 1750 to 1800

Americans paid for the Revolution with paper money and debt. In 1790, the new national government and the states still owed about 79 million dollars for the war. Alexander Hamilton wrote the plan to pay those debts in full. Members of Congress taxed whiskey to help pay them, and in 1794 farmers in western Pennsylvania rose up against that tax. Both before and after the war, Rhode Island merchants sent ships to Africa to buy captive people.

#### The Browns and the slave ship Sally

In 1764 four merchant brothers of Providence, Rhode Island, sent their ship *Sally* to West Africa to buy people. They were Nicholas, John, Joseph and Moses Brown. By that year the colony had about 30 rum distilleries, places where rum is made, and 22 of them were in Newport. The distillers made the rum from molasses shipped from the Caribbean. The *Sally* carried 17,274 gallons of rum, along with chains, shackles and guns. Shackles are metal rings locked around a person's wrists or ankles.

The captain, Esek Hopkins, bought 196 Africans. Hopkins kept the ship on the African coast for more than nine months while he bought them. Nineteen died before the ship left Africa. They included several children and a woman who hanged herself below deck. On the day the ship sailed, another woman was "left for dead," in the report's words. The report does not say who left her or what became of her. Four more, a woman and three children, died in the first week at sea. Sixty-eight people died during the whole crossing, and 20 more died soon after the ship reached the West Indies. One more captive died on the way to the Brown brothers in Providence. The report's stage counts of 19, 68 and 20 add up to 107, but the report gives the total at that point as 108. With the death on the way to Providence, the historians who wrote Brown University's report count at least 109 deaths among the 196. The captives died from disease and starvation, by killing themselves, and in an uprising.

When the captives rose up, Hopkins's crew fired on them. Hopkins wrote in his account book: "Slaves Rose on us was obliged fire on them and Destroyed 8 and Several more wounded badly." By "Destroyed 8" he meant that his crew killed eight people. The survivors were so sick that buyers paid only £5 for some of them.

John Brown kept trading in people. In 1795 the crew of his ship *Hope* took 229 Africans from the Gold Coast of Africa, and 198 of them lived to be sold in Cuba. A law of 1794 already banned Americans from owning, equipping, putting money into or working on ships that carried captive people to other countries. Members of the Providence Abolition Society, a group working to end slavery, took Brown to a United States court for breaking that law. On August 5, 1797, he became the first American tried under it. A jury found him not guilty, and the court ordered the men who had charged him to pay his court costs. He did not get the *Hope* back.

#### Paying for the war with paper money

Members of the Continental Congress had almost no power to tax. From 1775 they paid for the war by printing paper money called Continental dollars. The paper dollars quickly lost their value. By the end of 1777, it took about 4 paper dollars to buy what 1 silver dollar bought. By 1781 it took about 100, and the paper money was close to worthless. The saying "not worth a Continental," meaning worth nothing at all, comes from this money.

<a id="story-alexander-hamilton-economy"></a>

#### Alexander Hamilton

> **Who:** The author of the plan to pay the Revolution's debts in full.
>
> **When and where:** The new United States government, 1790 and 1791.
>
> **Movie:** Alexander Hamilton (American Experience, 2007), a two-hour documentary shown on PBS, with Brían F. O'Byrne as Hamilton.

Alexander Hamilton planned how the new United States would pay the debts of the Revolution. In January 1790 he set out the plan in his First Report on Public Credit. He counted the national debt at about 54 million dollars. The states owed about 25 million dollars more for the war.

Hamilton proposed that the national government pay every debt in full. He also proposed that it take over the states' war debts, a step called assumption. The people who were owed money would then look to the new government to be paid. They would want it to last, so that they got their money. Paying in full would also build the government's credit. Credit means that lenders trust a borrower to pay back what it borrows.

In June 1790, assumption did not have enough votes to pass in the House of Representatives. Thomas Jefferson invited Hamilton and James Madison to dinner, and the three men made a deal. After it, members of Congress voted assumption through, and they placed the country's permanent capital on the Potomac River.

Hamilton's Report on Manufactures is dated December 5, 1791. In it he laid out a plan to grow American manufacturing, the making of goods in workshops and mills, with tariffs and subsidies. A tariff is a tax on goods brought in from other countries. A subsidy is money paid to help a business grow. Members of Congress never brought the plan to a vote. Hamilton also helped found the Society for Establishing Useful Manufactures. Through it, he and the other founders started an industrial town at the falls of the Passaic River, which is Paterson, New Jersey.

#### The whiskey tax

In 1791 members of Congress passed a national excise on distilled spirits, such as whiskey, to help pay the war debt. An excise is a tax on goods made and sold inside the country. The tax was 7 cents a gallon. Farmers in western Pennsylvania sent their corn to market as whiskey, so the tax fell on the crop they sold.

The farmers fought the tax. In September 1791 a gang in disguise caught a tax collector named Robert Johnson and tarred and feathered him. That means they coated him with hot tar and stuck feathers to it. In July 1794, about 600 armed men attacked the house of John Neville, the tax inspector, at a place called Bower Hill. When their leader, James McFarlane, stepped into the open, someone inside the house shot and killed him. The accounts do not say who fired. The attackers then set the house on fire. This uprising is called the Whiskey Rebellion.

President George Washington called up about 13,000 militia, soldiers drawn from the states. The rebels broke up without a battle. On November 13, 1794, troops under General Henry Lee broke into houses at night, pulled people from their beds and arrested about 150 of them. They held the prisoners in animal pens and basements. For years afterward, people in the area called it "the Dreadful Night." The troops took 20 of the prisoners to Philadelphia for trial. Two men, Philip Wigle and John Mitchell, were found guilty of treason, the crime of making war against their own country. Washington pardoned them both, which means he set aside their punishment.

### 1800 to 1850

Cotton grown by enslaved people was the country's biggest export in these years. An export is a good sold to other countries. By 1860, enslavers valued the people they held at 3 billion dollars or more. In 1800 most American families grew and made most of what they used. By 1850 far more of them grew crops and made goods to sell, and bought what they needed. The name for this change is the market revolution. In the panics of 1819 and 1837, many people rushed to get their money out at once, and businesses closed. In 1819 about 50,000 people in three big cities had no steady work. By one estimate, a third of all workers had no jobs by the fall of 1837.

#### From household to market

Farm families and workshops could sell goods far from home once moving them got cheaper. Before the Erie Canal opened in 1825, it cost about 100 dollars to haul a ton of goods by road from Buffalo to New York City. By canal boat the same ton cost about 10 dollars. The trip took about ten days instead of twenty.

The owners of the new cotton mills in New England hired young women from farm families and paid them wages in cash. These women were among the first large groups of Americans who worked for cash wages.

In 1843 a rush for copper began on the Keweenaw Peninsula of Michigan, a point of land with water on three sides. It began after Douglass Houghton, the state geologist, reported on the copper there. A geologist is a scientist who studies rocks. By 1849 miners there dug 96 of every 100 pounds of copper mined in the United States.

Gold was found at Sutter's Mill in California early in 1848. About 80,000 people went to dig for it in 1849, and about 300,000 people came to California between 1848 and 1855. The merchants who sold the miners their supplies made steadier money than most of the miners did.

#### King Cotton

Cotton was the most valuable American export, and enslaved people did the work of growing it. They planted it, picked it and got it ready for sale. In 1840 cotton made up 51.6 percent of the value of everything the United States sold to other countries. It stayed above half almost every year until the Civil War. About three of every four pounds grown here were sent abroad. From 1820 to 1860, about 80 of every 100 pounds of cotton used in the world came from the United States. The crop was known as King Cotton.

The cotton crop more than doubled in six years. Enslaved people grew about 300 million pounds of cotton in 1831 and more than 600 million pounds in 1837. To grow it, enslavers forced people out of the older slave states and into the new cotton states. They moved about 155,000 enslaved people this way in the 1820s and at least 250,000 in the 1830s. Between about 1790 and 1860, enslavers moved more than 1 million people from the Upper South to the Deep South. The Upper South means the older slave states farther north, such as Virginia. The Deep South means the cotton states farther south.

#### People counted as property worth billions

Enslavers counted the people they held as capital. Capital is money or property that an owner uses to make more money. In 1860 census takers, the government workers who count every person in the country, counted 3,953,760 enslaved people in the United States. Enslavers valued them at 3 billion dollars or more. That is the price enslavers put on human beings as property. It was more than all the money invested in American railroads and factories put together.

Enslavers used enslaved people as capital in two ways. The people grew the cotton and were paid nothing for it. Enslavers could also borrow money by promising the people themselves to a lender. If the loan was not repaid, the lender could take the people and sell them.

#### Banks and bond sellers

In the 1830s, planters in Louisiana and Mississippi set up their own banks. The banks lent planters money on mortgages. A mortgage is a loan in which the borrower promises property to the lender. These mortgages covered land and enslaved people. The banks then sold bonds, which are paper promises to repay a loan with interest, to investors in Europe and in the Northern states. The mortgages on land and people backed those bonds.

The historian Edward E. Baptist of Cornell University names the banks and the firms that sold their bonds. Baring Brothers of London sold 2.5 million dollars in bonds for the Consolidated Association of the Planters of Louisiana. Baring Brothers and its New York partners, Prime, Ward and King, sold 7 million dollars in bonds for the Union Bank of Louisiana in 1832. Hope and Company of Amsterdam sold 12 million dollars in bonds for the Citizens' Bank of Louisiana in 1833. The Mississippi Union Bank sold 15.5 million dollars in state bonds. By 1836 the banks of New Orleans held 64 million dollars in capital, more than the banks of any other American city.

In January 2005 the bank JPMorgan Chase reported on two of the older banks it grew out of. The two were Louisiana banks, the Citizens Bank and the Canal Bank. The report states that they had taken about 13,000 enslaved people as collateral on loans to planters. Collateral is property a borrower promises to hand over if the loan is not repaid. When planters failed to pay, the two banks came to own about 1,250 of those people. JPMorgan Chase's leaders apologized and set up a 5-million-dollar scholarship fund for students in Louisiana. They made the report because a 2003 law in Chicago required companies that did business with the city to search their records for ties to slavery.

#### Insurers, cotton traders and Northern mills

Northern insurance companies sold enslavers policies on the lives of enslaved people. A policy is a written deal. The enslaver paid the company a fee, and when an enslaved person died, the company paid the enslaver. From 1846 to 1848, New York Life, then called Nautilus Insurance, insured the lives of 520 people who appear to have been enslaved. It paid 15 claims, which means it paid out money for 15 deaths. In March 2000, leaders of the insurer Aetna apologized for policies the company sold on enslaved people's lives in the 1850s. They said Aetna would pay no reparations, which are payments made to make up for a wrong.

The brothers Henry, Emanuel and Mayer Lehman sold goods in Montgomery, Alabama. They took raw cotton grown on slave-labor plantations as payment for goods, and then they began trading in cotton. The 1860 census lists Mayer Lehman as the owner of seven enslaved people. Their firm, Lehman Brothers, lasted until it failed in 2008.

Northern mill owners also made money from slave-grown cotton. Francis Cabot Lowell, Nathan Appleton, Patrick Tracy Jackson and the other Boston merchants who built the Lowell mills were called the Boston Associates. In 1813 they founded the Boston Manufacturing Company. Their mills spun cotton grown by enslaved people in the South. The mills also made a cheap, rough cloth known then as "negro cloth." Negro was the word white Americans of that time used for Black people. The mill owners sold the cloth to planters, who used it to clothe the people they enslaved. By 1845, 31 textile companies tied to the Boston Associates, in Massachusetts, New Hampshire and southern Maine, made one-fifth of all the cotton and wool cloth in the United States. Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts called the tie between planters and mill owners an "unholy union ... between the lords of the lash and the lords of the loom." The lash is a whip. A loom is a machine that weaves thread into cloth.

#### The Panic of 1819

The Panic of 1819 was the first major depression that the American public lived through. A panic happens when many people try to get their money out, or to sell what they own, at the same time. A depression is a long stretch of hard times, when businesses close and many people lose their work. This one lasted from about 1819 to 1822.

Several things caused it. The prices that buyers paid for cotton fell sharply. Officers of the Second Bank of the United States called in loans, which means they asked borrowers to pay back money right away. Under an 1817 order from Congress, buyers of land from the national government had to pay in gold or silver coin. American factories closed because buyers chose cheaper goods from Britain.

During the panic, employers let workers go, and judges jailed people who could not pay their debts. In New York, Philadelphia and Baltimore, about 50,000 people had no work or only odd jobs. One observer from abroad estimated that half a million people across the country had no work. Nobody made a real count. In those years, a person who was owed money could sue, and a judge could order the borrower arrested and locked in a debtors' prison, with no set date for release. In Philadelphia, judges sent 1,808 people to debtors' prison this way. In Boston, judges sent 3,500. Farmland in Pennsylvania fell from 150 dollars an acre in 1815 to 35 dollars in 1819. Property in Richmond, Virginia, lost half its value. In New York City, the number of paupers, people too poor to feed themselves without help, rose from 8,000 in 1819 to 13,000 in 1820. The city had about 120,000 people. Mathew Carey, a publisher and economist in Philadelphia, estimated that 3 million people, about one-third of the nation, were hurt by the panic.

Small cotton planters went bankrupt in 1819, and again in 1837. Going bankrupt means being unable to pay one's debts, so that the lenders can take what the borrower owns. Larger planters bought up the small planters' land and the enslaved people those planters had held.

#### The Panic of 1837

A depression began with the Panic of 1837 and lasted until about 1843. In the years before it, buyers speculated in western land and in cotton. To speculate is to buy something in the hope of selling it later at a higher price. Then British lenders made loans harder to get, and the price of cotton fell. In New Orleans cotton prices fell by half. On May 10, 1837, the bankers of New York City stopped paying out gold and silver. People who brought in the banks' paper money could no longer trade it for coins.

Counts of the banks that failed differ. One count says that of about 850 banks in the country, 343 closed and 62 more partly failed. That is about 4 of every 10 banks. A college textbook, *U.S. History I*, says that 200 banks closed. It adds that the governments of seven states and one territory did not pay back their loans.

Nobody counted how many workers lost their jobs in 1837. All the figures are later estimates. One widely repeated estimate says that a third of all workers had no jobs by the fall of 1837. The same estimate says that within two years, employers cut the pay of people who kept their jobs by 30 to 50 percent. Unemployment is the share of people who want work and cannot find it. Other estimates put New York's unemployment at about 25 or 30 percent in 1837 and 1838.

Food had already grown costly before the banks stopped paying. Between 1836 and 1837, a barrel of flour in New York rose from 7 dollars to 12. On February 13, 1837, about 5,000 New Yorkers met in City Hall Park to protest the price of food and fuel. Part of the crowd broke into the store of the flour merchants Eli Hart and Company. They took or destroyed 500 to 600 barrels of flour and 1,000 bushels of wheat. A bushel is a measure of grain. A bushel of wheat weighs about 60 pounds.

Mississippi planters owed 33 million dollars to the banks of New Orleans. Their 1837 cotton crop sold for only 10 million dollars. Lawmakers in Mississippi and Florida later refused to pay the bonds their states had backed. The planters kept their land and the people they enslaved. The investors in Europe and the North who had bought the bonds lost their money.

When debtors could not pay, their creditors seized the people the debtors enslaved and sold them. A creditor is a person who is owed money. Judges ordered the property of debtors taken. Many debtors fled to Texas at night and took the people they enslaved with them. When a debtor failed to pay, a single creditor's claim could force the sale of a whole enslaved community. Its people were sold to different buyers and scattered. Sales like these split families. The Equal Justice Initiative, a group that studies the history of slavery, counts that the trade in enslaved people inside the country separated nearly half of the people it moved from a husband, a wife or a parent.

<a id="story-philip-hone-economy"></a>

#### Philip Hone

> **Who:** A New York merchant whose diary recorded the Panic of 1837 as it happened.
>
> **When and where:** New York City. He kept the diary from 1828 to 1851.

Philip Hone wrote down how business in New York City stopped during the Panic of 1837. He lived from 1780 to 1851. He sold goods at auction, and he served as the city's mayor in 1826 and 1827.

Hone kept a diary from 1828 until 1851. During the panic, he wrote: "No goods are selling, no business stirring, no boxes encumber the sidewalks of Pearl Street." Encumber means to crowd or block. Hone lost part of his own fortune in the crisis years. His diary was printed in 1889, after his death, as *The Diary of Philip Hone*.

### 1850 to 1900

Between 1850 and 1900 the United States became an industrial country. In an industrial country, much of the work is done in mines, mills and factories. Railroad track grew from about 9,000 miles in 1850 to 193,346 miles by 1900. In 1900 American mills made 11.4 million tons of steel, more than Britain and Germany together. After slavery ended, Southern landowners farmed with sharecroppers, families who worked a landowner's land for a share of the crop and stayed in debt to him. Officials in Southern states leased prisoners, which means they rented them out, to private companies. In Alabama, 90 or more of every 100 prisoners were Black. After the Panic of 1873, by estimates of the time, about one in four workers in New York City lost their jobs. After the Panic of 1893, estimates for the whole country run from about 17 to 25 percent of workers. The era is called the Gilded Age.

#### The Gilded Age

The name Gilded Age comes from a novel of 1873 by Mark Twain and Charles Dudley Warner, *The Gilded Age: A Tale of Today*. In it, the two writers made fun of their own time. Gilded means covered with a thin layer of gold. The name means a thin shine of gold over serious problems underneath.

#### Steel, rails, cattle and metal

Steel rails got cheap in these years. According to histories of the steel industry, a ton of steel rails cost about 140 dollars in 1872, about 35 dollars in 1882 and about 20 dollars by 1900. American mills made more steel than Britain's by about 1889 or 1890.

Cattle ranchers in Texas drove herds north to the railroads in Kansas. A Texas longhorn worth up to about 5 dollars at home could sell for up to about 40 dollars at a Kansas railroad town. From 1866 to 1884, cowboys drove more than 5 million cattle north. The open range was land with no fences, where cattle grazed wherever they wandered. Four things ended the open-range cattle business. Barbed wire fences went up across the range, and more railroads were built. Officials put a quarantine on cattle in 1885 and 1886. A quarantine keeps animals apart from others to stop the spread of a disease. Then came the winter of 1886 to 1887.

In 1862 members of Congress passed the Homestead Act. Under it, a settler could claim up to 160 acres of land and own it after living on it and farming it for five years. Settlers filed about 4 million claims. About 270 million acres, about a tenth of the country's land, became private farms. US officials had taken that land from Native nations.

The Comstock Lode, found near Virginia City, Nevada, in 1859, was the richest body of silver in North America. A lode is a long vein of metal running through rock.

Copper from Michigan, and later from Butte, Montana, became the wire for electric lights and telephones.

On February 23, 1886, Charles Martin Hall, a 22-year-old college graduate, made aluminum by a new method in his family's woodshed in Oberlin, Ohio. His sister Julia helped him. The Pittsburgh Reduction Company began making the metal by his method in 1888, and a new industry began. A pound of aluminum cost about 12 dollars in the early 1880s and less than 1 dollar by the middle of the 1890s.

#### The panics of 1857 and 1873

On August 24, 1857, the Ohio Life Insurance and Trust Company failed. Its manager in New York had stolen from it, and its officers had made bad loans. News of the failure went out by telegraph. People in many places rushed to take their money out of banks. This rush is called a bank run. A depression followed. It was short but deep.

The Panic of 1873 began on September 18, when the investment bank Jay Cooke and Company failed. An investment bank sells bonds and shares to raise money for businesses such as railroads. Jay Cooke and his partners had put too much money into bonds of the Northern Pacific Railroad. The New York Stock Exchange, where people buy and sell shares of companies, closed for ten days. It had never closed like this before. About 18,000 businesses failed. Economists study how people make, buy and sell things. Economists at the National Bureau of Economic Research set the dates when hard times begin and end. By their count, this depression lasted 65 months, until March 1879. It was the longest stretch of hard times on their record until the 1930s.

By the winter of 1873 to 1874, about one of every four workers in New York City had lost their jobs, according to estimates drawn from newspapers of the time. The historian Howard Zinn wrote that more than 90,000 homeless workers, almost half of them women, slept in New York police stations.

On January 13, 1874, about 7,000 people with no work met in Tompkins Square Park in New York City. They wanted Mayor William F. Havemeyer to create public jobs. Soon after 10 in the morning, New York police, some of them on horseback, charged into the crowd. Abram Duryée was the police commissioner, the official in charge of the city's police. The police beat people with clubs, and men, women and children ran. The accounts give no count of the people who were hurt. Men from a German workers' club fought back, and someone hit one policeman on the head with a hammer. The police drove the crowd out of the square and arrested 46 people.

#### Farmers and the railroads

Farmers were angry about what railroads and grain elevators charged them. A grain elevator is a tall building where grain is stored before it is shipped. In 1867 Oliver Hudson Kelley founded the Patrons of Husbandry, known as the Grange. Husbandry is an old word for farming. By the middle of the 1870s it had about 800,000 members.

Grange members pushed state lawmakers to pass the Granger laws, which set the highest rates that railroads and grain elevators could charge. In *Munn v. Illinois* in 1877, the justices of the Supreme Court ruled that those laws were allowed under the Constitution.

#### The Panic of 1893 and Coxey's Army

In the Panic of 1893, about 500 banks and 15,000 businesses failed. More than 150 railroad companies later went bankrupt. Nobody counted the people out of work at the time. Later estimates for the worst of it run from about 17 to 25 percent of workers. The economic historian Stanley Lebergott estimated that unemployment rose from about 3 percent in 1893 to 18.4 percent in 1894.

In 1894 a businessman named Jacob Coxey led a march of men without work from Massillon, Ohio, to Washington, D.C. About 100 men left on March 25. About 500 arrived on May 1, and a crowd of about 30,000 watched them. The marchers, called Coxey's Army, asked the national government for a 500-million-dollar program of public works. Under it, the government would have hired people without jobs to build public projects. When Coxey tried to speak at the Capitol, police arrested him for walking on its grass. He served 20 days in jail. His was the first large protest march on Washington.

#### Sharecropping and debt

After the Civil War, most freedpeople in the South had no land. Freedpeople were the people freed from slavery. Many families went to work as sharecroppers. Sharecropping was a way of farming someone else's land in return for a share of the crop.

A landowner gave a family a plot of land, usually about twenty acres. He also "furnished" the family with food, seed, tools and a cabin on credit, which means the family would pay later. This was called the furnish. Interest is a fee a borrower pays for borrowing. On the furnish, landowners charged interest far above a fair rate. At harvest the landowner sold the crop and took out the cost of the furnish and the interest. Then he gave the family its share, usually half of what was left or less.

Landlords held a lien on the crop. A lien is a legal claim on property until a debt is paid. Landlords also kept the account books. So most sharecroppers were still in debt when the landlord settled the yearly accounts, year after year. A landlord could put a sharecropping family off the land whenever he chose.

Sharecropping lasted into the 1930s. In 1930 census takers counted 1,831,470 tenant farmers in the South. Tenant farmers farmed land they did not own, and they were about half of all farmers in the South. About 700,000 of them were share tenants, who owned mules or tools and kept two-thirds to three-quarters of the crop. By 1935, 77 of every 100 Black farmers in the country owned no land. Nearly half of white farmers owned none. In 1937 members of the President's Committee on Farm Tenancy counted about 775,000 sharecroppers in the South, almost equal numbers of white and Black.

#### Debt peonage and Alonzo Bailey

Peonage means forcing a person to work to pay off a debt. Members of Congress banned it in the Peonage Abolition Act of 1867. Lawmakers in Southern states then wrote laws that had the same effect. Peonage was most common in the turpentine camps of southern Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia and the Florida panhandle, and in the cotton belt, the part of the South where cotton was grown. In turpentine camps, workers collected sap from pine trees to make turpentine, a liquid used in paint.

Alonzo Bailey was a Black farm laborer in Montgomery County, Alabama. On December 26, 1907, he signed a work contract with H. C. Borden, the manager of the Riverside Company, a company that ran a farm. Bailey received 15 dollars before he started work, to be paid back out of wages of 12 dollars a month. He quit after about a month. Under Alabama law, a worker who quit without paying back money he got this way was a criminal. In an Alabama court, Bailey was found guilty. He was fined 30 dollars and sentenced to 136 days of hard labor, heavy work done as a punishment.

A Montgomery lawyer, Edward S. Watts, and a city judge, William H. Thomas, helped Bailey take his case to the United States Supreme Court. Booker T. Washington helped in secret. On January 3, 1911, in *Bailey v. Alabama*, the justices ruled that the Alabama law broke the Thirteenth Amendment, the part of the Constitution that bans slavery. Other states' peonage laws stayed in force until the justices struck down Georgia's and Florida's in the 1940s.

#### Convict leasing in Alabama

The Thirteenth Amendment bans slavery "except as a punishment for crime." Under that exception, state and county officials in the South rented out prisoners to private companies. This was called convict leasing. The companies paid the government a fee for each prisoner. The companies' bosses made the prisoners work in mines, on farms and in lumberyards.

Officials in Alabama leased prisoners from 1846 to July 1, 1928. After a money crisis in the state government in 1875, the warden John G. Bass leased state prisoners to coal mines, farms and lumberyards for monthly fees. A warden is the official in charge of a prison. From 1883, under the warden John Hollis Bankhead, most state prisoners went to three coal companies. These were the Pratt Coal and Iron Company, the Tennessee Coal, Iron and Railroad Company, called TCI, and the Sloss Iron and Steel Company. In 1888 TCI signed a ten-year contract for every state prisoner able to work. It paid the state 9 to 18.50 dollars a month for each prisoner.

More than 95 of every 100 county prisoners in Alabama were Black, and so were 90 of every 100 state prisoners. The companies' bosses whipped prisoners to make them work. Coal company officials wrote false reports of "bad conduct" so that the prisoners would have to serve longer sentences.
