Alabama's state officials collected money from leasing prisoners. Fees for leased prisoners were about 10 of every 100 dollars the state took in during 1883. In 1898 they were nearly 73 of every 100 dollars.

Leased prisoners died in the mines. In 1896, 1,710 state prisoners worked in the mines, and 233 state prisoners had died in the two years before. That year 745 county prisoners worked in the mines, and 181 had died in the two years before. In 1895 Dr. Thomas D. Parke, the health officer of Jefferson County, reported that 90 of every 1,000 prisoners at Sloss's Coalburg mine died each year. According to Digital History, a history website of the University of Houston, 25 of every 100 Black leased prisoners in Alabama died in 1873. The same source says that death rates for leased prisoners were about ten times the rates for prisoners in states that did not lease them.

In 1924 a prisoner named James Knox, from Mobile, was killed at Sloss's Flat Top mine. Men there whipped him with a steel wire and lowered him into a vat of boiling water. The published accounts of his death do not name the men who did it. His death was first reported as a suicide by poison. An autopsy, an examination of a dead body by doctors, found that his heart had stopped and that the poison had been put into his body after he died. Investigators found that the whipping and the boiling water caused the injuries that killed him. His death led to an investigation. The Sloss company kept county prisoners working in its mines until 1928. In 1928 Alabama's officials ended convict leasing. Alabama was the last state to end it, about five years after Florida.

TCI also used leased prisoners in Tennessee, where officials leased prisoners from 1871 to 1896. A TCI official told the *New York Times* that "one of the chief reasons" the company took up convict leasing "was the chance it offered for overcoming strikes." In a strike, workers stop working until their employer agrees to better pay or conditions. The official said free miners would not want to strike once they saw the company had plenty of prisoners to put to work. The account of the interview does not give his name. A union is a group of workers who join together to bargain with their employer, and TCI's managers used prisoners to keep unions out of the mines.

<a id="story-andrew-carnegie-economy"></a>

#### Andrew Carnegie

> **Who:** A Scottish immigrant who started work as a mill boy, built a steel company, sold it for 480 million dollars and gave away more than 350 million dollars.
>
> **When and where:** Scotland and Pennsylvania, 1835 to 1919. He built steel mills from the 1870s and sold his company in 1901.
>
> **Movie:** The Richest Man in the World: Andrew Carnegie (American Experience, 1997), a documentary about him shown on PBS.

Andrew Carnegie went from a job paying 1.20 dollars a week to selling his steel company for 480 million dollars. He was born in Dunfermline, Scotland, in 1835. In 1848 his family moved to Allegheny, Pennsylvania. At about 13 he went to work in a cotton mill as a bobbin boy, changing the spools that held the thread.

Carnegie worked as a telegraph messenger and then as a manager for the Pennsylvania Railroad. From the 1870s he built steel mills, among them the Edgar Thomson works. In 1889 he wrote an essay called "The Gospel of Wealth." In 1901 he sold Carnegie Steel to a group led by J. P. Morgan for 480 million dollars. He gave away more than 350 million dollars, including money for about 2,500 public libraries. Counts of the libraries vary, and some go above 2,800 around the world.

In 1892 workers went on strike at Carnegie Steel's works in Homestead, Pennsylvania, which means they stopped working. Henry Clay Frick, one of the men running Carnegie's company, hired 300 armed agents from the Pinkerton detective agency, a private company that hired out guards and detectives, to take back the plant. On July 6, 1892, the Pinkertons came up the river on barges, and they and the strikers fought a gun battle. Seven workers and three Pinkertons were killed, and some accounts count more. No record names the men who fired the shots that killed them. Governor Robert E. Pattison of Pennsylvania sent about 8,000 state soldiers. By November the strike had failed, and Frick and the company's other managers had broken the steelworkers' union at Homestead. A union is a group of workers who join together to bargain with their employer.

<a id="story-john-d-rockefeller-economy"></a>

#### John D. Rockefeller

> **Who:** The founder of Standard Oil, which by 1880 controlled about 90 percent of oil refining in the United States.
>
> **When and where:** Cleveland, Ohio, from 1870. He lived from 1839 to 1937.
>
> **Movie:** The Rockefellers (American Experience, 2000), a documentary shown on PBS about four generations of his family, not about him alone.

John D. Rockefeller built the company that controlled most of America's oil refining. Refining is the work of turning crude oil from the ground into fuels people can use. He founded the Standard Oil Company in Cleveland in 1870. By 1880 his company controlled about 90 percent of the oil refining in the United States.

Kerosene was the fuel that ordinary families burned in their lamps. In 1870 a gallon of kerosene cost about 26 cents. It cost about 9 cents by 1880 and about 7 cents by 1890. Lamp light became cheap for ordinary homes.

Rockefeller became the richest man in the country. Later he gave large sums of money to universities and to medical research.

### 1900 to 1950

In these fifty years Americans lived through a stock boom, the Great Depression and the Second World War. A stock is a share in the ownership of a company. After stock prices crashed in October 1929, about one of every four workers had no job by 1933. In Chicago and Pittsburgh, more than half of Black workers had no job in 1932, by later estimates. In 1935 members of Congress and President Franklin D. Roosevelt set up old-age pensions and unemployment insurance in the Social Security Act. A pension is a regular payment to a person too old to work, and unemployment insurance pays workers who have lost their jobs. The law left out farmworkers and domestic workers, people who cleaned, cooked and cared for children in other people's homes. Most Black workers did those two jobs. Two accounts disagree about who made that choice. In 1944, with factories making goods for the war, unemployment fell to 1.2 percent.

<a id="story-henry-ford-economy"></a>

#### Henry Ford

> **Who:** The carmaker who roughly doubled his workers' pay in 1914 and cut the price of his Model T car from 825 dollars to 260 dollars.
>
> **When and where:** Ford's Highland Park car factory. He announced the five-dollar day on January 5, 1914.
>
> **Movie:** Henry Ford (American Experience, 2013), a documentary about him shown on PBS.

Henry Ford roughly doubled his workers' pay in 1914. He did it to stop workers from quitting, and workers who earned more could also buy the cars they built. An assembly line moves each car past a row of workers, and each worker does one step over and over. After Ford's managers put in the assembly line, the work never let up and was dull. In 1913 turnover at the Highland Park factory reached 370 percent. Turnover counts the workers who quit and had to be replaced. At 370 percent, managers had to hire almost four new workers in a year for every job.

On January 5, 1914, Ford announced five dollars for an eight-hour day. Before, a Ford worker earned about 2.34 dollars for a nine-hour day. The new rate began on January 12.

The raise came with conditions. Ford paid the extra money as profit-sharing, a share of the company's profits, and a worker qualified only after six months. Staff of the company's Sociological Department inspected workers' homes before granting the full rate. They checked whether workers saved their money and whether they drank alcohol. They also checked for what they called "proper" living. Ford left out men under 22, and at first most women.

After the raise, fewer workers quit. The price of the Model T kept falling, from 825 dollars in 1908 to 260 dollars by 1925.

Ford fought unions for decades. A union is a group of workers who join together to bargain with their employer. Ford owned a newspaper, the *Dearborn Independent*, and he published antisemitic articles in it through the 1920s. Antisemitic means hateful toward Jewish people. Ford later apologized in public for the articles.

#### The crash and the Great Depression

The Dow Jones average fell by 89 percent between September 1929 and July 1932. The Dow is a number built from the stock prices of a group of large companies. It rose from 63 in August 1921 to 381 on September 3, 1929. Prices fell hard on Black Thursday, October 24, 1929, and again on Black Tuesday, October 29. By July 8, 1932, the Dow stood at 41.

The hard times of the 1930s are called the Great Depression. By 1933 about 25 percent of workers, one in four, had no job. Government officials and scholars made that estimate later, because nobody counted the jobless every month at the time.

GDP is the total value of all the goods and services made in the country in a year. It fell from about 104 billion dollars in 1929 to about 56 billion dollars in 1933. Prices fell too. From October 1929 to April 1933, the prices of the things people bought every day dropped by about 27 percent. Counted as the amount of goods and services, with the fall in prices taken out, output fell by about 30 percent. About 9,000 of the country's 25,000 banks failed and closed by 1933.

Hungry people stood in breadlines, which are lines for free food. Some people lived in shantytowns, groups of shacks, which people called Hoovervilles.

#### The Bonus Army

In the summer of 1932, veterans of the First World War camped in Washington, D.C., to ask for a bonus they were owed for their war service. The bonus was not due until 1945, and the veterans asked to be paid early in cash. Estimates of their number run from about 10,000 to more than 20,000. Many had their families with them. On June 17, members of the Senate voted the payment down.

On July 28, police tried to clear veterans out of some buildings in the city. Police shot and killed two veterans, William Hushka and Eric Carlson. Hushka had come from Lithuania. He sold his butcher shop to join the army in the First World War and became a citizen while he served. He was buried at Arlington National Cemetery less than a week after he was shot.

President Hoover then ordered the Army to clear the camps. General Douglas MacArthur sent in infantry, who are soldiers on foot, and cavalry, who are soldiers on horseback, with tanks and tear gas. Tear gas stings the eyes, nose and throat, so people cough and their eyes stream with tears. MacArthur's soldiers burned the main camp.

Members of Congress later voted to pay the bonus over the veto of President Franklin D. Roosevelt. A veto is a president's refusal to sign a bill. The payments began in June 1936.

<a id="story-benjamin-roth-economy"></a>

#### Benjamin Roth

> **Who:** A lawyer in Youngstown, Ohio, who kept a diary of the Great Depression for more than ten years.
>
> **When and where:** Youngstown, Ohio. He began the diary in June 1931.

Benjamin Roth, a lawyer in Youngstown, Ohio, kept a record of the Depression from June 1931 for more than ten years. He lived from 1894 to 1978.

In his diary Roth wrote about the banks that closed and the stocks that became worthless. He wrote down prices, and what lawyers and workers earned. In 2009 his son, Daniel B. Roth, and James Ledbetter edited the diary, and the publisher PublicAffairs printed it as a book, *The Great Depression: A Diary*.

#### Last hired, first fired

Black workers lost their jobs first and at higher rates than white workers. Employers hired Black workers last and fired them first, a pattern called "last hired, first fired." By 1932 nearly half of all Black Americans had no work, according to the National Museum of African American History and Culture.

History.com, drawing on the Library of Congress, reports that in 1932 more than half of Black workers in Chicago and Pittsburgh had no job. About a quarter of white workers in Northern cities had none. In Atlanta in 1934, nearly 70 percent of Black workers had no job. These numbers are all later estimates, because nobody kept an official count by race.

From 1929, government officials and private employers forced people whose families came from Mexico to leave for Mexico. In 2005 California's lawmakers found that about 400,000 American citizens and legal residents had been forced to go from California alone. They estimated that about two million people were forced out across the country, and that about 1.2 million of them had been born in the United States. Local officials sold some families' property to pay for sending them away.

#### The New Deal

Before 1933, the federal government, the national government in Washington, paid no unemployment insurance and no old-age pensions. Members of Congress set up both in the Social Security Act of 1935. President Roosevelt and his officials started many programs from 1933 on, including the CCC, the WPA and Social Security. Together they are called the New Deal.

President Roosevelt set up the Civilian Conservation Corps, or CCC, on March 31, 1933. It was a federal jobs program for young men. About 3 million young men worked in it over the years it ran. They earned 30 dollars a month and sent about 25 dollars of it home.

The Works Progress Administration, or WPA, ran from 1935 to 1943. About 8.5 million people worked for it. WPA workers built about 650,000 miles of roads, 125,000 public buildings and 75,000 bridges.

On August 14, 1935, President Roosevelt signed the Social Security Act. The first monthly old-age check went to Ida May Fuller of Ludlow, Vermont, on January 31, 1940. It was for 22.54 dollars. She had paid a total of 24.75 dollars in Social Security taxes.

<a id="story-frances-perkins-economy"></a>

#### Frances Perkins

> **Who:** The Secretary of Labor who chaired the committee that planned Social Security, and the first woman in a United States Cabinet.
>
> **When and where:** Secretary of Labor from 1933 to 1945. She lived from 1880 to 1965.
>
> **Movie:** Summoned: Frances Perkins and the General Welfare (2020), a documentary about her.

As chair of the Committee on Economic Security, Frances Perkins led the planning of Social Security. She was Secretary of Labor from 1933 to 1945. She was the first woman in a United States Cabinet, the group of the president's top officials.

President Roosevelt set up the committee on June 29, 1934. Its members planned old-age pensions and unemployment insurance. They sent their report to President Roosevelt on January 15, 1935. He signed the Social Security Act on August 14, 1935.

According to the historian Larry DeWitt, Perkins wanted farmworkers and domestic workers covered by the new law, and so did Harry Hopkins, the official in charge of aid to the jobless. Those workers were not in the law as it passed.

#### Who Social Security left out

Under the Social Security Act of 1935, farmworkers and domestic workers could not get old-age pensions or unemployment insurance. Domestic workers cleaned, cooked and cared for children in other people's homes. In 1930, 65 of every 100 Black workers did one of these two kinds of work. So about two-thirds of Black workers could get neither payment, and in the South the share was higher. Derrick Johnson, president of the NAACP, a civil rights group, gave these figures in 2020.

At the hearings on the bill in 1935, Charles Hamilton Houston spoke for the NAACP. He said the bill would leave out "Negro sharecroppers and Negro cash tenants, who are just about at the bottom of the economic scale." Negro was a common word for Black people at that time. A sharecropper farmed a landowner's land and paid with part of the crop. A cash tenant rented land and paid in money. Houston called the law "a sieve with the holes just big enough for the majority of Negroes to fall through." A sieve is a strainer full of holes.

Two accounts disagree about who made the choice to leave these workers out. Jon Dubin, in a 2024 article in a Stanford law journal, points to Southern members of Congress. Senator Harry Byrd of Virginia opposed a rule that payments be high enough for "decency and health." He said that rule "might serve as an entering wedge for federal interference with the handling of the Negro question." An entering wedge is a first step that opens the way to more. Byrd did not want federal officials to have a say in how matters touching Black people were handled.

Edwin Witte, executive director of the Committee on Economic Security, reported that Byrd's position was "supported by nearly all of the southern members of both committees," the two committees in Congress that worked on the bill. Representative Howard Smith of Virginia argued for keeping Black sharecroppers and domestic workers dependent on their employers.

Larry DeWitt, a historian at the Social Security Administration, gave a different account in 2010. He found that Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau asked for the changes to the bill that left these workers out. DeWitt said Morgenthau's reasons had to do with collecting the tax. DeWitt wrote that the charges of "racial bias in the founding of the Social Security program" did "not hold up under detailed scrutiny." Racial bias means unfair treatment because of race. Scrutiny means close study.

Members of Congress changed the law in 1950 to cover farm and domestic workers who worked regularly for one employer. In 1954 they covered the rest. Representative Smith opposed these changes too. Of eight House members who voted against them, six were Southern Democrats. Senators John Stennis of Mississippi and Harry Byrd also opposed them.

#### Farm payments and evicted sharecroppers

Federal farm payments in the 1930s went to landowners, and many sharecroppers lost their places on the land. The landowners are also called landlords, or planters. In May 1933 members of Congress passed the Agricultural Adjustment Act. Under it, officials of the Agricultural Adjustment Administration, or AAA, ran a farm program under Agriculture Secretary Henry Wallace. They paid farmers to grow less. That year farmers plowed under about 10 million acres of growing cotton, which means they turned the plants back into the soil. AAA officials bought about 6 million pigs and had them killed.

Under the AAA's cotton contracts of 1934 and 1935, officials paid landowners to take land out of cotton. Agriculture Secretary Henry Wallace "rented" about three-eighths of the country's cotton land in this way. Sharecroppers got only about 11 percent of the payments. A landlord could keep the whole check by evicting the sharecroppers and hiring day laborers, who were paid by the day. Evicting means putting people off the land or out of their homes. When planters cut their cotton land by 40 or 50 percent, they cut the number of their tenants, the families who farmed their land, by the same share.

More than two-thirds of Black sharecroppers made no profit or went into debt, according to the National Museum of African American History and Culture.

In July 1934, seven Black men and eleven white men met at the Sunnyside School in Poinsett County, Arkansas, and founded the Southern Tenant Farmers' Union to protest the evictions. Planters and the men who worked for them attacked the union. In January 1935 lawmen at Marked Tree arrested and jailed a white organizer, Ward Rodgers. At a union rally at Gilmore, four armed white men broke in. They ordered the Black members to leave and told them they would be lynched, killed by a mob, if they were caught at another union meeting. Many union members were beaten and threatened with guns. The accounts do not name the men who beat them. On March 15, 1935, at Birdsong, about forty armed planters, their riding bosses and local lawmen broke up a union crowd. Riding bosses were men on horseback who watched over the field workers for the planters. Later that month a mob attacked the home of the union's lawyer, Cornelius Tyree Carpenter.

A group of AAA lawyers, led by Jerome Frank, ruled that landlords had to keep the same tenants. In February 1935, AAA administrator Chester Davis had Wallace fire those lawyers. This firing is called the AAA purge.

In 1936 the justices of the Supreme Court ruled the AAA unconstitutional, which means against the Constitution. Members of Congress wrote a new version in 1938. Federal officials have paid farmers ever since.

#### War work ends mass unemployment

During the Second World War, factory workers made war goods. Unemployment fell from 14.6 percent in 1939 and 1940 to 1.2 percent in 1944. The figure for 1939 and 1940 was estimated later. The official yearly records begin in 1944, and 1.2 percent is the lowest rate in them.

Workers in American factories built 299,230 military aircraft from January 1940 to August 1945. Real GDP counts output with the changes in prices taken out. It rose about 72 percent from 1940 to 1945. By 1945 the United States made about half of all the manufactured goods in the world.

### 1950 to 2000

The income of the typical American family roughly doubled between 1947 and 1973, even after counting the rise in prices. Families who were poor, in the middle and rich all gained. In the 1970s prices and unemployment rose at the same time. Factory jobs peaked at 19.6 million in June 1979. By the 2000s, more than 80 of every 100 jobs outside farming were in services, in places such as stores, offices, hospitals and schools. In the Mahoning Valley around Youngstown, Ohio, about 50,000 people lost jobs in steel and related work within about five years of 1977. In the 1980s about 300,000 farms could not repay their loans. From March 1991 to March 2001, the country went 120 months in a row without a downturn.

#### The postwar boom

For about twenty-five years after the Second World War, pay rose for families at every level of income. Between 1947 and 1973, the median family income roughly doubled, counted with the rise in prices taken out. The median is the middle one. Half of all families earned more than the median family, and half earned less. A general rise in prices is called inflation. Inflation means each dollar buys less than before.

The economists Claudia Goldin and Robert Margo studied the gap between high wages and low wages. They found that the gap narrowed sharply in the 1940s and stayed narrow into the 1970s. They named this the Great Compression. To compress means to squeeze together.

Under the G.I. Bill, veterans of the Second World War could use federal money for school or job training, and federal officials backed their home loans. By July 1956, when the first version ended, 7.8 million of the 16 million veterans had used its money for education or job training. From 1944 to 1952, officials of the VA, the federal agency for veterans, backed about 2.4 million home loans. Backing a loan means promising to repay the lender if the borrower cannot.

In the Employment Act of 1946, members of Congress made "maximum employment, production, and purchasing power" a stated duty of the federal government. Purchasing power means how much people can buy with their money. Under the same act they created the Council of Economic Advisers, a group of economists who advise the president. The ideas behind the act came from the British economist John Maynard Keynes. Keynes argued that government spending could fight slumps, the times when business falls off. Members of Congress took a promise of full employment out of the bill before they passed it.

On April 26, 1956, Malcom McLean's ship *Ideal X* carried 58 large shipping boxes, called containers, from Port Newark to Houston. By the economist Marc Levinson's calculation, loading loose cargo onto a ship by hand cost about 5.86 dollars a ton in 1956. Loading it in containers cost about 16 cents a ton.

#### Stagflation in the 1970s

In the 1970s prices and unemployment rose together. Most economists had thought this could not happen. The mix of inflation and a stagnant economy, one that is not growing, was called stagflation.

In October 1973, leaders of Arab oil-selling countries stopped the sale of their oil to the United States. Such a ban on trade is called an embargo. The price of oil roughly quadrupled in six months. Consumer prices, the prices of the things people buy for daily life, rose about 11 percent in 1974. Unemployment reached 9.0 percent in May 1975.

Inflation passed 13 percent in 1979 and 1980. In 1980 prices rose 13.5 percent. In November and December 1982, unemployment reached 10.8 percent. That was the highest rate since the Great Depression.

#### Factory jobs fall

After 1950, a shrinking share of American workers had jobs in manufacturing, the making of goods in factories. In 1955, 30.6 of every 100 jobs outside farming were in manufacturing. By 2005 about 11 of every 100 were, and by the 2020s about 8. The number of factory jobs peaked at 19.6 million in June 1979. By the 2000s, more than 80 of every 100 jobs outside farming were in service industries.

On September 19, 1977, the managers of Youngstown Sheet and Tube announced that they would close the company's Campbell Works steel mill in Youngstown, Ohio. About 5,000 workers lost their jobs at once. The day became known as Black Monday. Within about five years, about 50,000 people in the Mahoning Valley around Youngstown lost jobs in steel and related work. These numbers come from later news reports.

<a id="story-gerald-dickey-economy"></a>

#### Gerald Dickey

> **Who:** A Youngstown steelworker who proposed that the workers and the town buy their closed mill and reopen it.
>
> **When and where:** Youngstown, Ohio, 1977 to 1979.

After the Campbell Works closed, Gerald Dickey proposed that the steelworkers and the people of Youngstown buy the mill and reopen it. From 1976 to 1979 he was the recording secretary of Local 1462 of the United Steelworkers union. A union is a group of workers who join together to bargain with their employer. A local is a union's branch in one place. A recording secretary keeps the written record of its meetings.

Church leaders led the Ecumenical Coalition of the Mahoning Valley, and its members took up Dickey's plan. Ecumenical means bringing together people of different churches.

The plan needed about 100 million dollars in federal loan guarantees. A loan guarantee is a promise that the government will repay a loan if the borrowers cannot. Officials in President Carter's government first signaled that they supported the guarantees. In 1979 officials of the Economic Development Administration, a federal agency, turned the guarantees down, and the mill stayed closed. Accounts differ a little on when officials first signaled support. All of them agree on the refusal and the closing.

Dickey and the coalition spread the idea of workers owning their own workplaces through the labor movement.

#### The farm crisis of the 1980s

In the 1980s about 300,000 farms defaulted, which means their owners could not repay their loans. About 300 farm banks failed.

In the 1970s farmers sold more crops abroad, planted more of their land and borrowed at low rates of interest. Interest is the extra money a borrower pays a lender for a loan. Then officials of the Federal Reserve raised interest rates under their chairman, Paul Volcker. The Federal Reserve is the country's central bank, the government's bank that sets interest rates for other banks. On January 4, 1980, President Jimmy Carter stopped many sales of American farm goods to the Soviet Union after Soviet troops invaded Afghanistan. The Soviet Union was a large country, ruled from Moscow in Russia, and the main rival of the United States. Carter's order canceled contracts for about 17 million metric tons of wheat, corn and soybeans. A metric ton is about 2,205 pounds. Under this grain embargo, farmers lost some sales abroad, and exports fell. Farmers had borrowed against the value of their land. In parts of the Midwest, farmland lost up to 60 percent of its value from 1981 to 1986. Farm debt reached about 215 billion dollars by 1984, double the debt of 1978.

On September 22, 1985, Willie Nelson, John Mellencamp and Neil Young played the first Farm Aid concert, at Memorial Stadium in Champaign, Illinois. About 80,000 people came. The concert raised more than 7 million dollars for farm families.

#### The 1980s and 1990s

Income tax rates on the highest incomes fell in the 1980s. Under the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981, President Reagan's tax cut, the top income-tax rate fell from 70 percent to 50 percent. Under the Tax Reform Act of 1986, it fell to 28 percent. The top rate is the tax on each dollar of income above a high level.

Inflation fell from 13.5 percent in 1980 to between 3 and 4 percent by the middle of the 1980s. The national debt roughly tripled during the 1980s. The national debt is the total that the federal government owes on money it has borrowed.

From March 1991 to March 2001, the country went 120 months in a row without a downturn. A stretch of growth like this is called an expansion. It was the longest expansion on record until then, according to the National Bureau of Economic Research. That group of economists dates the country's booms and downturns. Unemployment fell to 3.9 percent in the fall of 2000. In the government's budget years of 1998 through 2001, federal tax money coming in was more than federal spending. A year like that is called a budget surplus.

The NASDAQ is an index, a single number built from the stock prices of many companies, including many technology companies. It rose about 600 percent from 1995 to March 2000.

### 2000 to Today

Since 2000 the country has gone through three recessions. A recession is a stretch of months when output falls and people lose their jobs. The longest of the three ran from December 2007 to June 2009, after home prices crashed. In the crash, lenders took homes from Black and Latino families at higher rates than from white families. This is called foreclosure: a lender takes a home because the borrower cannot keep up the loan payments. In August 2026 the unemployment rate was 4.1 percent, and about 86 of every 100 jobs outside farming were in services. From April to June 2026, the richest tenth of households held 68.9 percent of all household wealth, and the poorer half held 2.3 percent.

#### The dot-com crash

Technology stock prices crashed from 2000 to 2002. The NASDAQ index peaked at 5,048 on March 10, 2000. By October 2002 it had fallen about 78 percent. The boom and the crash are called the dot-com bubble, after companies that did business on the internet. A bubble is a time when prices climb far above what things are worth and then fall.

A recession followed, from March to November 2001. It lasted eight months.

#### The crash of 2008

The Great Recession, from December 2007 to June 2009, began with a crash in home prices. Home prices rose for years before the crash. Lenders made home loans, called mortgages, that many borrowers could not repay. Bankers bundled many of these mortgages together into investments and sold the investments as safe. When home prices fell, the investments failed, and some of the biggest financial firms began to fail too.

The financial firm Lehman Brothers failed on September 15, 2008. It owed about 619 billion dollars. It was the largest bankruptcy in the country's history. Bankruptcy is a court process for a person or a company that cannot pay its debts.

In October 2008 members of Congress passed a rescue plan for financial firms, the Troubled Asset Relief Program, or TARP, worth up to 700 billion dollars. Treasury officials paid out about 443 billion dollars under it, and the firms that got the money paid most of it back.

Employers cut about 8.7 million jobs in the Great Recession. Unemployment peaked at 10.0 percent in October 2009. Lenders foreclosed on about 3.8 million homes from 2007 to 2010. Estimates for the whole crisis run from 7.7 million to 10 million homes.

#### Who lost homes and wealth

Black and Latino homeowners lost their homes at higher rates than white homeowners, and they lost more of their wealth. Latino and Hispanic both name Americans whose families came from Spanish-speaking countries. African American is another name for Black Americans.

The Center for Responsible Lending, a research group that campaigns on lending, studied people who took out home loans from 2005 to 2008. By 2010, lenders had foreclosed on about 8 percent of the African American borrowers and 8 percent of the Latino borrowers. For non-Hispanic white borrowers the figure was 4.5 percent. Counting all homeowners, 17 percent of Latino homeowners and 11 percent of African American homeowners had lost a home or were close to losing one. For white homeowners the figure was 7 percent. White families still made up about 56 percent of all completed foreclosures, because there were more white borrowers.

Lawyers at the Justice Department said that from 2004 to 2008, Countrywide Financial, a mortgage lender, charged at least 200,000 qualified Black and Latino borrowers higher fees and rates or steered them into subprime loans. A subprime loan has a higher interest rate and is meant for borrowers that lenders think are more likely to fall behind. Bank of America had bought Countrywide. In December 2011 its officers agreed to pay 335 million dollars to settle the case. It was the largest settlement up to that time in a case about lenders treating borrowers unfairly because of their race. A settlement is an agreement to pay money to end a legal case.

On July 12, 2012, officers of the bank Wells Fargo agreed to pay at least 175 million dollars. Of that, 125 million dollars went to borrowers, and 50 million dollars went to help with down payments. A down payment is the part of a home's price that the buyer pays at the start. The Justice Department's lawyers said Wells Fargo charged Black and Latino borrowers higher rates and fees, and steered some into subprime loans when they qualified for regular ones. The lawyers reviewed 2.7 million loans made from 2004 to 2009. They said at least 34,000 borrowers in 36 states and Washington, D.C., were treated this way.

Assistant Attorney General Tom Perez said that a Black borrower in the Chicago area with one kind of Wells Fargo loan paid on average 2,937 dollars more than a similar white borrower. Wells Fargo's officers denied that the bank discriminated, which means treating people unfairly because of their race. They said they settled to avoid a fight in court.

Wealth, or net worth, is what a household owns minus what it owes. The Pew Research Center, a research group, reported in 2011 on wealth from 2005 to 2009, using surveys by the Census Bureau. With inflation taken out, the median wealth of Hispanic households fell 66 percent. For Black households it fell 53 percent, and for white households 16 percent.

In 2009 the typical Black household had 5,677 dollars in wealth, and the typical Hispanic household had 6,325 dollars. The typical white household had 113,149 dollars. The typical white household's wealth was 20 times that of the typical Black household and 18 times that of the typical Hispanic household. These were the largest gaps since the government began collecting the numbers in 1984. About 35 percent of Black households and 31 percent of Hispanic households owned nothing or owed more than they owned. For white households the figure was 15 percent.

<a id="story-ed-neufeldt-economy"></a>

#### Ed Neufeldt

> **Who:** A worker who built cabinets for recreational vehicles in Elkhart, Indiana, lost his job in 2008 and introduced President Obama in 2009.
>
> **When and where:** Elkhart, Indiana, from 2008 into the middle of the 2010s.

In the fall of 2008, after 32 years of building cabinets at Monaco Coach, an RV plant in Elkhart, Indiana, Ed Neufeldt lost his job. An RV, or recreational vehicle, is a home on wheels. Elkhart was known as the "RV capital of the world." As the RV plants shut, unemployment in Elkhart's county went from about 5 percent to nearly 20 percent in about a year.

On February 9, 2009, Neufeldt introduced President Obama at a town hall meeting in Elkhart. Obama was on his first trip to promote the stimulus bill, a plan to spend federal money to bring back jobs.

Reporters from ProPublica, NPR and NBC News followed Neufeldt for years. He worked three low-wage jobs. Later he got a factory job again. NPR reporters visited him again in 2015 and 2016.

#### The long recovery and the shift to services

The recovery after 2009 was slow at first, with years of high unemployment. It then became the longest expansion in the country's records, which go back to 1854. It lasted 128 months, from June 2009 to February 2020. The National Bureau of Economic Research announced these dates on June 8, 2020.

By August 2021, 16 percent of American adults had earned money at some time through an online gig platform, according to the Pew Research Center. A gig platform is an app or a website that connects workers with short, one-time jobs.

In August 2026 there were 159.1 million jobs outside farming. About 12.6 million of them, about 8 percent, were in manufacturing. About 137.5 million, about 86 percent, were in services, counting government jobs. The Bureau of Labor Statistics, the government office that counts jobs and prices, gave these numbers. They are early figures that the bureau can still change.

#### 2020 and the price rises after

The shortest recession on record lasted two months, from February to April 2020, as the COVID-19 pandemic began. A pandemic is a disease that spreads around the world. Unemployment reached 14.8 percent in April 2020.

On March 27, 2020, members of Congress passed the CARES Act, a relief law of about 2 trillion dollars. It was the largest relief law up to that time. From April to June 2020, GDP fell at a yearly rate of 31.4 percent. A yearly rate shows how far output would fall in a full year at that speed. From July to September, output rose at the fastest rate on record.

Consumer prices rose 9.1 percent in the 12 months to June 2022, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That was the largest rise since November 1981. Economists disagree about the causes. Some blame breakdowns during the pandemic in supply chains, the chains of factories, ships and trucks that bring goods to stores. Others point to federal relief spending, or to higher energy prices after Russian forces invaded Ukraine. By the middle of 2023, prices were rising near 3 percent a year.

#### The economy in 2026

In August 2026 the unemployment rate was 4.1 percent, the same as in July. That was about 7.0 million people. Unemployment was 3.7 percent for white workers, 6.0 percent for Black workers, 4.8 percent for Hispanic workers and 3.2 percent for Asian workers. Employers added 162,000 jobs that month. The Bureau of Labor Statistics released these figures on September 4, 2026.

Consumer prices rose 3.4 percent in the 12 months to August 2026. Leaving out food and energy, they rose 2.4 percent. Energy prices rose 16.3 percent, and food prices rose 2.7 percent. The Bureau of Labor Statistics released these figures on September 11, 2026.

Real GDP grew 2.1 percent in 2025, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis, the government office that measures the country's output. From April to June 2026, real GDP grew at a yearly rate of 1.5 percent, by the bureau's estimate of August 26, 2026. As of September 2026, the National Bureau of Economic Research had announced no recession since the two months in 2020.

Economists at the Federal Reserve, the country's central bank, publish figures on who holds the country's wealth. From April to June 2026, American households held about 185.7 trillion dollars in net worth. The richest 10 percent of households held 68.9 percent of it. Within that group, the richest one household in every thousand held 15.0 percent. The next 40 percent of households held 28.8 percent. The poorer half of all households together held 2.3 percent. Households that Federal Reserve economists count as white held 82.4 percent of household wealth. Black households held 3.2 percent, and Hispanic households held 2.4 percent.

<a id="ch-money"></a>

## Chapter 17: Money

### Before 1500

Before 1500, nobody in this land used money. People here had no coins, paper bills, banks or prices. They got what they needed by barter, which means trading one thing straight for another. They also gave gifts and owed each other duties, both between neighbors and between nations.

Some goods went a long way. People carried shells from the Gulf coast, copper from Lake Superior and obsidian from the West hundreds of miles along rivers and trails. Obsidian is a black glass that forms in volcanoes and can be chipped into sharp blades.

#### Wampum

Wampum was not money before Europeans came. People used it to keep records, to make agreements between nations, in ceremonies and as gifts.

Wampum is beads made from shell. The white beads came from the shells of whelks, which are large sea snails. The purple-black beads came from the shells of quahogs, a hard-shelled clam of the Atlantic coast. People strung the beads on cords or wove them into belts.

The Haudenosaunee are a league of Native nations in what is now New York State. Among them, the beads of a belt recorded spoken agreements and histories. People presented the belts at meetings of leaders, called councils, and read them there.

Wampum first passed as money in the 1600s, after colonists arrived. Colonists and Native traders used it that way in their dealings with each other.

### The 1500s

In the 1500s, far to the south in lands ruled by the king of Spain, Spanish officials forced Native men to dig silver. A mint is a workshop where coins are made. Workers at Spanish mints struck the silver into a coin called the piece of eight. Almost none of those coins reached the land that became the United States during the 1500s. This land still had no mint of its own.

#### The piece of eight

The piece of eight was a silver coin worth 8 reales. A real was a Spanish unit of money. In English the coin was also called the Spanish dollar. Workers at Spanish mints in the Americas made it from silver dug at Potosí, in what is now Bolivia, and at Zacatecas, in Mexico. Silver was found at Potosí in 1545.

Native men of the Andes, the high mountains of South America, did the digging at Potosí. In 1573 Francisco de Toledo began forcing thousands of them to work in the mines, in turns. Toledo was the viceroy, the man who governed Peru for the king of Spain. His system was called the mita. Toledo took the name and the idea of turns of work from an older system used by the Inca.

Toledo's rules covered Native men aged 18 to 50 in the highland provinces between Potosí and Cuzco. Each year about one man in seven from those villages had to go to the mines. That came to more than 11,000 men a year.

The men worked in shifts, one week in the mines and then two weeks of rest. Many brought their families and carried most of their own food. They were paid a little, and most of that pay went to the tax they owed the colonial government. The work was dangerous and unhealthy. By sending the men away from their home villages, Toledo also broke up life there. Across the Andes, disease killed far more Native people than work in the mines did. No reliable count shows how many of the forced workers died from the work at Potosí.

Writers on the history of money, among them Alejandra Irigoin and Bridget Millmore, call the piece of eight the first money used around the whole world. Traders carried it from South America to Europe, and across the Pacific Ocean to Asia.

Almost none of that coin reached this land. Some did reach St. Augustine, in Florida, a town where Spanish soldiers were posted. Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded it in September 1565 at Seloy, a Timucua village, in the homeland of the Timucua-speaking peoples. The Spanish soldiers there were paid from Spanish colonial funds, with the coin of a foreign empire.

Later, Thomas Jefferson and members of Congress based the United States dollar on the piece of eight. Spanish coins stayed legal tender in the United States until February 21, 1857. Legal tender is money that the law says must be accepted to pay a debt. Americans still call a quarter "two bits." The piece of eight was divided into eight parts called bits, so two bits made a quarter of a dollar.

### The 1600s

The English colonies were short of coins from the start. Little English coin reached them. Colonists spent the coins they did get on goods shipped in from overseas, and those coins went back across the ocean. To trade with each other, colonists paid in tobacco, corn, beaver skins and wampum. Massachusetts leaders opened a mint of their own without England's permission. In 1690 they printed paper money, the first printed by any government in Europe or the lands Europeans had settled.

#### Money made of goods

Colonists called payment in goods "country pay." Colonial lawmakers set how much each kind of goods was worth when it was used to pay a debt. Money of this kind is called commodity money, because the money is a useful thing in itself.

English money counted in pence, shillings and pounds. Twelve pence made a shilling, and twenty shillings made a pound.

In Virginia, lawmakers set a value on tobacco so it could be used as money from the 1620s, and in 1642 they made it legal tender. People in Virginia, Maryland and North Carolina used tobacco as money through much of the colonial period. In the northern colonies, beaver pelts and corn also passed as money.

New England colonists used wampum for small payments. The nations that made wampum had not used it as money before colonists came. Members of the Massachusetts General Court, the colony's lawmakers, voted on November 15, 1637, to accept wampum. The rate was 6 beads a penny, for sums under 12 pence. Thirteen years later, on October 18, 1650, they set the rate at 8 white beads or 4 black beads a penny. They also made wampum legal tender for debts up to 40 shillings, but not for taxes. They canceled the law on May 22, 1661.

#### The pine-tree shilling, 1652

In 1652 members of the Massachusetts General Court voted to set up a mint in Boston. They did not ask anyone in England first. By English law, only the king could make coins. In 1652 England had no king. Supporters of the king had fought a civil war against supporters of Parliament, England's lawmakers. Afterward the judges of a court set up by Parliament found King Charles I guilty of making war on Parliament and on the people of England. Their sentence called him a "traitor" and a "murderer." Fifty-nine of the judges, Oliver Cromwell among them, signed the order for his death. On that order the king was beheaded in London on January 30, 1649. Workers at the Boston mint struck silver coins worth threepence, sixpence and a shilling.

The mint's coins included the pine-tree shilling, named for the tree stamped on it. Workers at the mint struck pine-tree shillings from about 1667 to 1682. But nearly all of the colony's silver coins carry the date 1652.

Coin experts who write in the magazine CoinWeek and in older books on early American coins explain the date as a cover. Charles II became king of England in 1660. A coin dated 1652 could pass as a leftover from the years without a king. A coin with a later date would show that the men of Massachusetts were still making coins without the king's permission.

The mint closed in 1682. A charter is a legal paper that gives a colony or a company the right to exist and states what it may do. In 1684 officials acting for King Charles II canceled the Massachusetts charter. The illegal mint was one of their complaints against the colony.

<a id="story-john-hull"></a>

#### John Hull

> **Who:** A Boston silversmith who ran the colony's mint against English law and struck the pine-tree shilling.
>
> **When and where:** Boston, Massachusetts. Mintmaster from 1652 until the mint closed in 1682. Lived 1624 to 1683.

John Hull ran the Massachusetts mint from 1652 until it closed in 1682, without permission from England. He was born on December 18, 1624, in Market Harborough, England, the son of a blacksmith. He came to Boston with his parents in 1635, when he was 11. He trained as a silversmith, a craftsman who makes things out of silver.

In 1652 members of the Massachusetts General Court named him mintmaster, the man in charge of the mint. He was 27. His appointment was dated May 27, 1652. Robert Sanderson worked with him as his partner. Hull's contract paid him a share of every batch of coins he struck.

Hull's share of the coins made him one of the richest men in New England. He later became the colony's treasurer, the official in charge of its money.

A story says Hull gave his daughter Hannah her weight in pine-tree shillings as her dowry. A dowry is money or goods that a bride's family gives when she marries. The story is a legend. The writer Nathaniel Hawthorne retold it in his book *Grandfather's Chair* and added details of his own.

#### 1690: the first government paper money

In 1690, soldiers from Massachusetts attacked the French city of Quebec, in Canada, during King William's War. The attack failed. When the soldiers came home, the colony's treasury held too few coins to pay them. According to accounts from the time, the troops were close to mutiny, which means rising up against their officers.

Massachusetts lawmakers decided to pay the soldiers in paper. They began voting on it in December 1690. The first bills totaled 40,000 pounds. The paper bills were called bills of credit. Each bill stated that the colony's treasurer would accept it "in all Public payments." It also stated that the bill could later be exchanged for coins.

These bills were the first paper money printed by any government in the Western world. The Western world means Europe and the lands that Europeans settled. China had used paper money centuries earlier.

People took the bills and passed them from hand to hand. By 1714 Massachusetts lawmakers had put out 240,000 pounds in paper money. By 1718 lawmakers in the other New England colonies were printing their own.

### 1700 to 1750

In the early 1700s lawmakers in more colonies began printing paper money, and in time lawmakers in every colony printed their own. Some of that paper kept its value and some lost it, depending on how much the lawmakers printed. Benjamin Franklin argued for paper money in Pennsylvania and then printed it. In South Carolina, which had no banks, enslavers borrowed money by pledging land and the people they enslaved. If a loan was not paid back, the lender could take the land or the enslaved people who had been pledged.

#### Paper that held its value and paper that lost it

Economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland compared the paper money of the colonies. Economists are people who study how money and trade work. The Cleveland bank is one of twelve Federal Reserve banks, which serve as banks for the nation's banks. In Pennsylvania, New York and New Jersey, lawmakers printed limited amounts, and the bills held their value. In New England and the Carolinas, lawmakers printed large amounts. Prices counted in paper money rose there, and each bill was worth less silver than before.

In Virginia, people began to pass paper receipts for tobacco as money. Virginia lawmakers set up public warehouses for tobacco, with government inspectors, in the 1720s and 1730s. A planter, a farmer who grew tobacco to sell, brought his tobacco to a warehouse. An inspector checked it, and it stayed in the warehouse. The inspector then wrote a receipt, called a tobacco note, for the inspected tobacco. People passed tobacco notes from hand to hand as money.

<a id="story-benjamin-franklin-money"></a>

#### Benjamin Franklin

> **Who:** A Pennsylvania printer who argued for paper money, then printed it with leaf patterns that were almost impossible for counterfeiters, people who make fake money, to copy.
>
> **When and where:** Pennsylvania, from 1729.
>
> **Movie:** *Benjamin Franklin* (2022), a documentary by Ken Burns, shown on PBS. It is about his whole life, not only his work on money.

Benjamin Franklin printed paper money for three colonies and made it hard to fake. In 1729, when he was 23, he published a pamphlet, a short printed booklet. Its title was *A Modest Enquiry into the Nature and Necessity of a Paper-Currency*, which means a modest look at what paper money is and why it is needed. In it he argued that Pennsylvania needed more paper money. Partly because of the pamphlet, Franklin won the contract to print Pennsylvania's bills in his shop. His firm printed money for Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware.

A counterfeiter is a person who makes fake money. To stop counterfeiters, Franklin printed the shapes of real leaves on the bills. Every leaf has its own pattern of veins. A counterfeiter could almost never carve that pattern into a printing plate by hand. The method is called nature printing. Franklin almost certainly worked it out from leaf prints he made with his friend Joseph Breintnall. The printing plates were probably cast in metal from plaster molds of real leaves.

In 2023 scientists at the University of Notre Dame studied 600 notes printed by Franklin's firm. They found the leaf prints. They also found tiny shiny flakes of a mineral called mica in the paper, and colored fibers mixed into it. Printers kept putting leaf prints like Franklin's on colonial money into the Revolution.

Colonial bills carried the words "To Counterfeit is Death." Under colonial laws, a court could sentence a counterfeiter to death.

#### Paper money lent against land and people

In colonial South Carolina, enslavers used the people they enslaved as security to borrow money. Security is something a borrower promises to hand over if the loan is not paid back. The colony had no banks, and its paper money lost most of its value between 1703 and the late 1720s.

South Carolina's colonial lawmakers began printing paper money in 1703. At first, 1.5 South Carolina pounds were worth one English pound. By the late 1720s it took about 7 South Carolina pounds to equal one English pound.

With no banks, people borrowed through private agreements called mortgages and bonds. A bond was a written promise to pay back a loan. A mortgage is a loan in which the borrower pledges property as security. If the borrower does not pay, the lender can take that property. A mortgage could be on land. It could also be on movable property, called chattel. In these loan papers, enslavers and lenders listed enslaved people as chattel. So when an enslaver did not pay, the lender could take the people he had pledged.

Nic Butler of the Charleston County Public Library described in 2024 how these loans worked. He wrote: "A slave owner could mortgage their human chattel to a slave broker to secure credit used to purchase more slaves, then use their collective labor to satisfy the debt." A slave broker was a dealer in enslaved people. The enslaver pledged the people he enslaved to get a loan. He used the loan to buy more people. Then he paid off the debt with what the people's forced work earned.

Hundreds of colonial land mortgages survive in the Charleston County Register of Deeds, the county office that keeps records of land. Thousands of early chattel mortgages survive in the South Carolina Department of Archives and History.

### 1750 to 1800

Members of the British Parliament banned new paper money as legal tender in New England in 1751 and in all thirteen colonies in 1764. Colonists added the ban to their complaints against Britain. During the Revolution, members of the Continental Congress paid for the war with paper money, and by 1781 that paper was close to worthless. After the war, Thomas Jefferson, Alexander Hamilton and members of Congress planned a new money system. Members of Congress chose a dollar divided into tenths and hundredths in 1785. They set up a national bank in 1791 and created a mint in 1792.

#### The Currency Acts

Parliament is the lawmaking body of Britain. In the Currency Act of 1751, its members barred Massachusetts Bay, Rhode Island, Connecticut and New Hampshire from printing new paper bills as legal tender. They passed the act because New England's paper money had lost so much of its value.

Thirteen years later, on April 19, 1764, members of Parliament passed a second Currency Act. It extended the ban to all thirteen colonies. Colonists were already short of coins. Without new legal-tender paper, they had even less money to pay debts and buy goods. Colonists listed the Currency Acts among their complaints against Britain.

#### Not worth a Continental

The Continental Congress was the group of men the colonies sent to lead the Revolution. Its members had no power to tax. From June 1775 its members paid for the war by printing paper money, called Continental currency. In all, they put out $241,552,780 in Continental bills.

People working for the British side printed fake Continental bills on purpose, so that the real bills would lose their value faster. Most of this faking was done in New York City, which the British army held for most of the war. On April 14, 1777, an advertisement in the *New York Gazette* asked people going into the other colonies to take fake bills with them. In January 1780 General Henry Clinton, the British commander, wrote about the plan in a letter. It went to Lord George Germain, the official in London in charge of the American colonies. Stuart Hatfield, who wrote about the British faking of Continental bills in the *Journal of the American Revolution* in 2015, calls that letter the clearest sign that British leaders approved the plan.

In Philadelphia, one silver dollar was worth about 4 paper dollars at the end of 1777. At the end of 1778 it was worth about 8. By 1781 a silver dollar was worth about 100 paper dollars, and people stopped using the paper. In North Carolina the rate reached 210 paper dollars to one silver dollar.

Continental bills with about $226 million printed on them ended up worthless. Counted in silver, the loss was about $40 million. Whoever was holding the bills as they lost value lost that money, and most of them were ordinary people. Americans began to call anything worthless "not worth a Continental." By the late 1800s people in Britain were using the saying too.

#### Counterfeiting was a hanging crime

Officials in New York hanged Owen Sullivan, whose name was also spelled Syllavan, in 1756 for faking that colony's paper money. Colonial bills carried the warning "To Counterfeit is Death," and New York officials carried it out.

Sullivan was born in Ireland in about 1720. He was an engraver, a man who cuts designs into metal plates for printing. He had also worked as an armorer, someone who makes and repairs weapons, for colonial soldiers. He ran gangs of counterfeiters who passed fake colonial bills from New England to New York.

Before that, officials in Rhode Island had punished Sullivan for faking that colony's bills. On October 9, 1752, the *Boston Evening Post* printed a report from Providence, Rhode Island. The report states that he had "lately had both his Ears crop'd, and been branded on both his Cheeks with the Letter C." Cropping meant cutting off part or all of each ear. Branding meant burning the letter C, for counterfeiter, into the skin of each cheek with a hot iron. The C marked him as a counterfeiter to anyone who saw his face. The report does not name the officials who carried out the punishment.

Sullivan went on counterfeiting. At a session of the Supreme Court for the City and County of New York, he was found guilty of faking and passing New York's bills of credit from 1737. He was hanged on Monday, May 10, 1756. A pamphlet about his life, which says it was "taken from his own mouth," was printed the same year.

#### Building the dollar

In 1784 Thomas Jefferson wrote notes on what the new nation's money should be. He proposed the Spanish dollar as the basic unit. He wanted it divided into tenths and hundredths. The English system of pounds, shillings and pence did not divide by tens.

On July 6, 1785, members of Congress voted "that the money unit of the United States of America shall be one dollar." They also voted that the coins should "increase in decimal ratio," which means counting up by tens. With that vote, the United States became the first nation whose coins were fully based on tens.

Members of Congress set up the United States Mint in Philadelphia with the Coinage Act of April 2, 1792. The Mint's building was the first building the national government put up under the Constitution. The act defined the dollar as the unit of money. Under the act, the decimal system of dollars, dimes, cents and mills became law. A dime is one tenth of a dollar, and a mill is one tenth of a cent.

The act listed coins in three metals: gold coins, including a ten-dollar coin called the eagle, silver coins from the dollar down to the half-dime, and copper coins, the cent and the half-cent.

<a id="story-alexander-hamilton-money"></a>

#### Alexander Hamilton

> **Who:** The first Secretary of the Treasury. He planned the national bank and the United States Mint.
>
> **When and where:** Secretary of the Treasury, 1789 to 1795. Lived 1757 to 1804.
>
> **Movie:** *Alexander Hamilton* (2007), a documentary in the PBS series *American Experience*.

Alexander Hamilton planned the national bank and the Mint in reports he wrote for Congress. On September 11, 1789, President George Washington chose him to be the first Secretary of the Treasury, the head of the government department in charge of money. He served until 1795.

In December 1790 Hamilton sent Congress his *Report on a National Bank*. He proposed a bank that would hold the government's money and put out banknotes that people could trust. A banknote is paper money printed by a bank.

Lawmakers in Congress then passed a bill to charter the First Bank of the United States, in Philadelphia, for twenty years. A charter is a legal paper that allows a company to exist and states what it may do. Thomas Jefferson and James Madison argued that the Constitution did not give Congress the power to create a bank. In the House, Madison asked whether starting a bank was "among the powers" the Constitution gave to Congress. President Washington asked Hamilton to answer the objections, so that he would have "the arguments for and against the measure." Then Washington signed the bill, on February 25, 1791. Twenty years later, in 1811, a new charter lost by one vote in each house of Congress.

In January 1791 Hamilton sent Congress his *Report on the Establishment of a Mint*. In it he defined the dollar in both silver and gold, with 15 ounces of silver worth 1 ounce of gold. Members of Congress built the Coinage Act of 1792 on his plan and set up the Mint under it.

### 1800 to 1850

The United States had a national bank twice before 1850, and both banks lost their federal charters. A charter is a legal paper that allows a bank or company to exist and states what it may do. The First Bank's charter ran out in 1811. President Andrew Jackson vetoed, or refused to sign, a new charter for the Second Bank in 1832, and its federal charter ran out in 1836. From 1836 until 1862 the country had no national paper money. Americans paid with gold and silver coins and with paper notes printed by state banks. A bank's notes were worth less the farther from that bank a person tried to spend them.

#### Banknotes lent against enslaved people

By the 1830s, planters in Louisiana had set up banks that lent out their own paper money against mortgages on enslaved people. Planters were the enslavers who ran large farms. A mortgage is a loan in which the borrower pledges property, and the lender can take that property if the loan is not paid back. The paper notes people carried in their pockets in Louisiana had been lent out against enslaved human beings.

At the Consolidated Association of the Planters of Louisiana, an enslaver pledged "slaves and cultivated land" to the bank in a mortgage. He could then borrow up to half of what the bank's officers judged those people and that land to be worth. He received the loan in the bank's own paper notes.

To raise money to lend, the banks put out bonds. A bond is a paper that promises to repay a loan with interest. Louisiana lawmakers backed $2.5 million of the Consolidated Association's bonds, at 5 percent interest. Backing them meant the state promised to pay the bonds if the bank did not. Baring Brothers, bankers in London, paid the money up front and sold the bonds to investors in Europe. The Union Bank of Louisiana, founded in 1832, put out $7 million in state bonds. The Citizens' Bank of Louisiana, chartered in 1833, had $12 million in bonds that Hope and Company of Amsterdam agreed to sell.

A typical bond was for $1,000. Edward E. Baptist wrote in 2010 that this was "roughly the price of a field hand," an enslaved man who worked in the fields. An investor in Europe could own a share of a debt backed by thousands of enslaved people without owning any one person.

In 1824 the merchant Vincent Nolte lent $48,000 to the Louisiana enslaver Alonzo Walsh. Walsh pledged "from 90 to a 100 head of first rate slaves." Head is the word used to count cattle. The account of the loan gives no names for these people. At New Orleans auction prices they were worth up to $80,000.

Many enslavers had placed several mortgages on the same person. Then cotton prices fell, from 18 cents a pound in 1834 to under 10 cents by late 1836. By March 1837 ten large New Orleans cotton firms had failed. The enslavers owed the New Orleans banks alone $33 million. They could expect to make no more than $10 million from the 1837 crop. When they could not pay, the people they had mortgaged were sold in forced sales to pay their debts. The accounts of the crash do not name who ran each sale. Buyers spent what little cash they had at the first sales, and then the prices of land and of enslaved people fell sharply.

In Mississippi and Florida, state officials refused to pay bonds that their states had backed. In Baptist's account, the bondholders in Europe and the northern states lost their money, and the enslavers kept the people they held. In January 2005 officials of the bank JPMorgan Chase published a report on two Louisiana banks it grew out of, Citizens Bank and Canal Bank. Officers of those two banks had accepted about 13,000 enslaved people as collateral, which is property pledged for a loan. After borrowers failed to pay, the two banks came to own about 1,250 of those people.

#### The Bank War

The Bank War was the fight over whether the country should keep a national bank. A national bank is a bank chartered by the national government to hold the government's money. Members of Congress chartered the Second Bank of the United States in 1816, for twenty years, after the money troubles of the War of 1812. Its main office was in Philadelphia.

Nicholas Biddle became president of the Bank in 1823. Under him the Bank held the government's deposits, the money the government kept in the Bank's care, and moved money across the country. Its officers also collected the notes of state banks and presented them to those banks for payment in gold and silver coins. A state bank had to hold enough coins to pay, so its owners could not print as many notes as they wanted.

Andrew Jackson and his supporters argued that the Bank was a private company with public power, with owners in other countries and no control by voters. They said its officers gave favors to rich people with connections. Biddle and the Bank's defenders argued that the Bank kept the country's money the same everywhere and kept its value sound. They said that without it, nothing would stop state banks from printing too much paper.

Henry Clay was running against Jackson for president in 1832. In July of that year, four years before the old charter ran out, Clay led the push for a new one. Members of Congress passed it. Jackson vetoed the charter on July 10, 1832. A veto is a president's refusal to sign a bill into law. In his veto message he called the Bank "unauthorized by the Constitution, subversive of the rights of the States, and dangerous to the liberties of the people." Subversive means working to weaken something from the inside. That fall Jackson beat Clay and won a second term.

In 1833 Jackson ordered the government's deposits moved out of the Bank and into state banks he chose. His opponents called them "pet banks." Two Treasury secretaries would not move the money, and Jackson replaced them. Roger Taney, the third, moved it. Biddle struck back in 1833 and 1834 by cutting the Bank's lending to force a new charter. Borrowing became hard, and Biddle lost supporters.

On March 28, 1834, members of the Senate censured Jackson, which means they voted to blame him officially for what he had done. The Bank's federal charter ran out in 1836. In 1837 senators voted to remove the censure from the record. The Bank went on as a Pennsylvania state bank and failed for good in 1841. Biddle died in 1844, facing lawsuits.

<a id="story-andrew-jackson-money"></a>

#### Andrew Jackson

> **Who:** The president who vetoed the Second Bank's new charter and moved the government's money out of it.
>
> **When and where:** The United States. Veto in 1832, removal of the deposits in 1833.
>
> **Movie:** *Andrew Jackson: Good, Evil and the Presidency* (2007), a two-hour PBS documentary narrated by Martin Sheen. It covers his whole presidency, not only the Bank War.

Andrew Jackson distrusted banks and paper money after a land deal left him with debts that took him about 15 years to pay off. In August 1795, at 28, he sold 68,000 acres of land to David Allison. The accounts of the sale do not say where the land lay or which Native nation had lived on it. Jackson was selling for himself, for John Overton and for others.

Allison paid with promissory notes, which are written promises to pay money later. Jackson used the notes to buy supplies for a trading post. In 1797 Allison could not pay his debts, and his notes were worth nothing. The people holding the notes came to Jackson for payment instead. It took him about 15 years to pay his way out. Allison's creditors, the people he owed, had him put in debtors' prison in Philadelphia. A debtors' prison held people who could not pay what they owed. Allison died there on September 28, 1798.

A 2001 article in *American Heritage* magazine described what Jackson took from all this. By the end, the article states, he had settled ideas about "debt, paper money, and speculation: He hated them all." Speculation means buying something only to sell it later at a higher price.

As president, Jackson vetoed the Second Bank's new charter in 1832 and ordered the government's money moved out of it in 1833. No national bank replaced it. From 1836 until 1862, American paper money was whatever the state banks printed.

#### State banknotes and counterfeit detectors

From 1836 until 1862, paper money meant notes printed by banks that state lawmakers had chartered. Each bank printed its own designs. A note was worth only as much as people trusted the bank that printed it. Far from that bank, people would take its notes only for less than the amount printed on them. The difference was called a discount.

Store owners checked notes against a printed guide before they took them. The guides were called bank note reporters and counterfeit detectors. A counterfeit is a fake made to pass as the real thing. Publishers put them out weekly or monthly from about 1826 to 1866. Each issue listed the discount on each bank's notes and described the fake notes going around. Shopkeepers kept them by the cash drawer.

Some banks were called wildcat banks. They were set up under state laws, called free-banking laws, with few rules for opening a bank. The story went that some stood so far out in the woods that only wildcats lived nearby, so nobody could get there to trade the notes for coins. Economists today, among them Gerald Dwyer and the team of Rolnick and Weber, have found that the story is somewhat exaggerated. Most free banks were not frauds. The people holding their notes did lose money, but less than the legend says.

#### Whose land the Michigan banks lent against

In the late 1830s, Michigan's wildcat bankers lent money against land in the southeast of the state, around Ann Arbor. Until 1807 that land belonged to the Potawatomi, Ojibwe, Odawa and Wyandot nations.

A treaty is a written agreement between nations. In the Treaty of Detroit, on November 17, 1807, leaders of those four nations signed the land over to the United States. William Hull, the governor of Michigan Territory, signed for the United States. The land included the place that later became Ann Arbor. The treaty page of the Nottawaseppi Huron Band of the Potawatomi states that the land came to about 8 million acres. A history page of the Ann Arbor District Library states 5,611,532 acres. United States officials paid as little as 1.2 cents an acre, $57,717.32 in all. The library's page states the land's estimated value as $6,400,000.

<a id="story-alpheus-felch-money"></a>

#### Alpheus Felch

> **Who:** A Michigan bank commissioner who inspected the state's new banks and found boxes of nails and glass under a top layer of coins.
>
> **When and where:** Michigan, 1838 and 1839. Born September 28, 1804. Died June 13, 1896.

Alpheus Felch was one of three officials who inspected Michigan's banks in 1838, and he wrote down the frauds he found. He was a lawyer in Monroe, Michigan, from 1833. As a state lawmaker, he was one of four who voted against Michigan's free-banking law.

Michigan lawmakers passed that law on March 15, 1837. Before it, Michigan had 9 banks. Within months there were 18, and then 40. On December 30, 1837, three bank commissioners were appointed to inspect the banks. Felch served as one of them in 1838.

Felch described the inspections in 1880. Some banks kept "grossly insufficient books," meaning records far too poor to show what the bank held. One bank had nothing of value at all. At another, bankers showed the commissioners boxes of coin. Under a top layer of coins, the boxes were filled with nails and glass. At three banks in a row, the bankers showed the commissioners the same coins as their own. Local accounts say the bankers sent word ahead of the commissioners' route and carried the coins from bank to bank.

The commissioners could close a bank by court order. They could also hand it to a receiver. A receiver is an official who takes over a failed bank and pays its debts from what is left. After the commissioners' reports, many banks closed and criminal cases followed in the courts. Michigan lawmakers suspended the free-banking law in 1838. By September 1839 only 9 banks were left. Felch resigned as commissioner in 1839. In 1845 the judges of the Michigan Supreme Court ruled that the law broke Michigan's constitution, the state's basic set of laws.

Michigan bank notes lost an estimated 60 percent of the amount printed on them, according to the Ann Arbor District Library. In 2014 the economists Dove, Pecquet and Thies found that the true wildcat period lasted less than a year and involved "perhaps a dozen" banks. They put the noteholders' losses from those wildcat banks at about $350,000. In 1985 the economist Hugh Rockoff gave a larger figure, for all of Michigan's failed free banks. He estimated that their losses would have come to about $1 million if the state Supreme Court judges had not stopped the closing-down of those banks. Dove, Pecquet and Thies also argued that when the judges threw out the law in 1845, many notes became worthless.

Felch went on to serve as a justice of the Michigan Supreme Court from 1842 to 1845, as governor of Michigan from 1846 to 1847 and as a United States senator from 1847 to 1853.

#### The Panic of 1837: the runs

A panic, in money, is a time when fear spreads and many people rush to get their money out of banks. A bank run happens when many people rush to a bank at once to trade its notes or their deposits for coins. A bank keeps only part of its money in coin, so it cannot pay everyone at the same time.

On May 10, 1837, the officers of New York City's banks stopped paying out gold and silver for their notes and deposits. Bank officers across the country did the same. This was called suspending specie payments. Specie means coins of gold and silver. People who lined up at the banks got paper promises or nothing.

The country had about 850 banks. By about 1843, roughly 4 in 10 of them had failed, wholly or in part. No surviving record counts the depositors who lost their savings. The records give only the number of banks that closed.

### 1850 to 1900

By 1860 more than 10,000 different kinds of banknotes were in use in the United States. Federal officials today estimate that from one-third to nearly one-half of that paper money was fake. During the Civil War, members of Congress created a national paper money in 1862. Then they taxed state banknotes until banks stopped printing them. For the rest of the century Americans argued over what should stand behind a dollar, gold alone or gold and silver together.

#### Greenbacks

On February 25, 1862, members of Congress passed the Legal Tender Act to help pay for the Civil War. Under the act, they approved $150 million in paper money called United States Notes. Nobody could trade these notes at the Treasury for gold or silver. They were money because members of Congress made them legal tender, which means the law said people had to accept them to pay debts. Later acts raised the total to $450 million. The backs of the notes were printed in green ink, so people called them greenbacks.

Salmon P. Chase, the Treasury Secretary, managed the new paper money. He put his own portrait on the first $1 United States Note, in 1862.

In the National Banking Acts of February 25, 1863, and June 3, 1864, members of Congress created national banks, which got their charters from the national government. These banks put out national bank notes of one design, backed by government bonds. In 1865 members of Congress put a tax of 10 percent on state banknotes. Bankers stopped printing their own notes. The state notes still in use fell from $143 million in 1865 to $4 million by 1867. By then, people everywhere in the country used the same national paper money.

The words "In God We Trust" first appeared on American coins in these same years. In November 1861 a Pennsylvania minister, the Reverend M. R. Watkinson, wrote to Chase asking that God be named on the coins. His letter survives in Treasury records. Chase told officials at the United States Mint, the government's coin-making office, to prepare a motto. In the Coinage Act of April 22, 1864, members of Congress approved a two-cent coin. It was the first United States coin to carry the words IN GOD WE TRUST. The motto became the national motto in 1956. It first appeared on paper money in 1957, after a law passed in 1955.

#### Counterfeiters and the Secret Service
