History pages of the U.S. Marshals Service and the Secret Service state that about one-third of the paper money in use in the 1860s was counterfeit. A 2025 release from the Department of Homeland Security puts it at nearly one-half. Nobody made a full count at the time, so these figures are estimates.

On July 5, 1865, Treasury officials formed the Secret Service Division, as part of the Treasury Department, to catch counterfeiters. Its first chief was William P. Wood. Treasury Secretary Hugh McCulloch swore him in.

Guarding presidents was not part of the job at first. On September 6, 1901, Leon F. Czolgosz shot President William McKinley at a public event in Buffalo, New York. McKinley died on September 14. Afterward, members of Congress asked the Secret Service to protect presidents. In 1902 its agents took on full-time protection of the president.

<a id="story-emanuel-ninger"></a>

#### Emanuel Ninger

> **Who:** A sign painter who drew fake money by hand and was caught when his ink ran on a wet bar top.
>
> **When and where:** New Jersey and Manhattan, 1883 to 1896. Lived 1845 to 1924.

Emanuel Ninger drew fake banknotes by hand for thirteen years, until his ink smudged on a wet bar. He was a sign painter, born in Germany, who lived in New Jersey. He drew United States banknotes, mostly $50 and $100 bills, with a pen, a pencil and a brush made of camel's hair.

To make a bill, Ninger laid a real note against glass and traced over it. He used colored inks for the parts printed in color. One bill took him weeks. From 1883 to 1896 he spent his fakes in Manhattan.

On March 28, 1896, Ninger laid one of his bills on a saloon bar. The bar was wet, and the ink smudged. A man working for the bartender followed him and had him arrested. The tellings of the story differ a little on how the arrest happened. All of them include the smudged ink on the wet bar.

Ninger pleaded guilty in May 1896, and a judge sentenced him to six years in prison. Newspaper writers and experts at the time marveled that each fake had cost him more work than honest sign painting would have paid.

#### The Freedman's Savings Bank, 1865 to 1874

The Freedman's Savings Bank held the savings of people freed from slavery. It failed in 1874, and about 31,000 of its depositors never got any of their money back.

President Abraham Lincoln signed the law that created it, its charter, on March 3, 1865. The full name was the Freedman's Savings and Trust Company. By 1871 it had about 37 branches in 17 states and Washington, D.C. About 70,000 people opened accounts over the bank's life. Accounts ranged from about $5 to $50. Deposits over those years added up to more than $57 million.

At first the bank could hold only safe government bonds. In 1870 members of Congress changed its charter to let it make loans on land and buildings, and other loans. Henry D. Cooke sat on the bank's board and also served his family's banking business. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency is the government office that oversees national banks. A history it published states that Cooke used the Freedman's Bank's money and property "to benefit the latter," meaning his family's business. The bank's headquarters, on Lafayette Square across from the White House, cost more than $200,000. Charles Meigs, a bank examiner, an official who inspects banks, reported the bank's problems in February 1873. Then came the Panic of 1873, a time of fear when at least 100 banks failed, and many of the Freedman's Bank's loans went bad. Meigs reported the bank's problems again in 1874.

Frederick Douglass became the bank's president in March 1874. He put $10,000 of his own money into the bank to restore trust in it. Then he saw that it could not be saved. The bank closed on June 29, 1874.

When the bank closed, it owed 61,144 depositors nearly $3 million, by the count in the Comptroller's history. Between 1875 and 1883 the commissioners who closed out the bank's business paid back 62 percent of what was owed, in five payments. Of the 61,131 depositors who could claim, 29,996 turned in their passbooks, the small books that recorded their savings. About 31,000 never collected anything. The records do not say why they did not.

The bank's signature books and deposit records from 29 branches survive at the National Archives. They list depositors' names, ages, jobs and family members. Black families today use them to trace their history.

#### Bank runs of 1873 and 1893

There was no deposit insurance in the 1800s. Deposit insurance is a promise, backed by the government, to repay people's savings if their bank fails. Without it, every depositor in a failed bank waited for whatever the receiver, the official who took over the failed bank, could collect from the bank's leftover property.

At least 100 banks failed in the Panic of 1873. Banks failed in Washington, D.C., Pennsylvania, New York, Virginia, Georgia, Indiana, Illinois and Ohio. The New York Stock Exchange is the market in New York City where people buy and sell shares of companies. On September 20, 1873, the exchange closed for ten days, the first time it had ever closed.

In 1893 the gold the Treasury held fell to about $100 million, from $190 million in 1890. Writers for the Federal Reserve's history website count more than 100 banks that suspended in June 1893. To suspend meant to shut the bank's doors or stop paying out cash. Between mid-July and mid-August, 340 more banks suspended. Some of them later reopened, so counts differ. An Encyclopedia.com article puts the banks that failed in 1893 at about 500.

No surviving record counts how many depositors lost savings in 1873 or 1893, or how much they lost.

#### Gold against silver

Americans argued over whether gold alone or gold and silver should stand behind the dollar. Farmers and others who owed money were on one side, and bankers on the other.

With the dollar tied to gold, the supply of money grew slowly. Prices fell through most of the years from 1865 to 1896. A farmer's crop brought fewer dollars each year, but his mortgage payment, the money he owed each year on a loan against his farm, stayed the same. Supporters of "free silver" wanted the government to coin all the silver brought to it, at 16 ounces of silver to 1 ounce of gold. That would have put more money in use and raised prices, which would have made debts easier to pay. Debtors and many people in the states that mined silver wanted silver. Bankers and bondholders wanted gold alone. Bondholders were people who had lent money by buying bonds.

In the Coinage Act of February 12, 1873, members of Congress dropped the standard silver dollar from the list of coins. After that, in practice, the dollar was tied to gold alone and not to silver, just as western mines were producing more and more silver. People on the silver side called the act "the Crime of '73."

Two later laws required the government to buy some silver. The Bland-Allison Act of 1878 required the Treasury to buy $2 million to $4 million of silver each month and coin it into silver dollars. Lawmakers passed it over President Hayes's veto. Under the Sherman Silver Purchase Act of 1890, the purchases rose to 4.5 million ounces a month. Treasury officials paid for the silver in notes that could be traded for gold. As holders traded the notes in, the government's gold shrank. In 1893, during the panic, members of Congress canceled the Sherman Act because President Cleveland insisted on it.

<a id="story-william-jennings-bryan"></a>

#### William Jennings Bryan

> **Who:** A 36-year-old former congressman from Nebraska whose speech for silver made him the Democratic Party's candidate for president.
>
> **When and where:** The Democratic convention in Chicago, July 9, 1896.

William Jennings Bryan became the Democratic Party's candidate for president in 1896 with a speech for silver. On July 9, 1896, at the Democratic convention in Chicago, he gave the last speech in the debate over the party's platform, its list of positions. Bryan was 36 years old and a former congressman from Nebraska.

He ended the speech with words aimed at the supporters of gold. "You shall not press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns," he said. Then he said, "you shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold." To crucify means to put someone to death by nailing them to a cross. Both pictures come from the Bible's account of the death of Jesus. Bryan was comparing that suffering to the gold standard, which means a dollar backed by gold alone. Under it prices fell, and farmers and working people found their debts harder to pay each year. After the speech, the delegates, the party members sent to the convention, chose him as their candidate for president on the fifth round of voting.

Republicans wrote support for the gold standard into their platform. The Republican candidate was William McKinley. Bryan's votes came mostly from the South, the rural Midwest and the Rocky Mountain states. McKinley was strongest in the cities and in the Northeast, the Upper Midwest and the Pacific Coast.

Each state had a number of electoral votes, set by its seats in Congress, and a candidate needed more than half of them to become president. McKinley won 271 electoral votes to Bryan's 176. He won 7,112,138 votes from the people, 51.0 percent, to Bryan's 6,510,807, 46.7 percent. Bryan ran against McKinley again in 1900 and lost again.

### 1900 to 1950

Between 1900 and 1950, members of Congress and two presidents set up two guards for people's savings. One was the Federal Reserve, a bank for the nation's banks. The other was deposit insurance, a government promise to pay savers back if their bank fails. Both are still in place to guard against bank runs, times when many people rush to take their money out of a bank at once. In the Gold Standard Act of March 14, 1900, members of Congress made gold the only metal behind the dollar, at $20.67 an ounce. After that, silver was no longer a standard in law. Members of Congress created the Federal Reserve in 1913, six years after the Panic of 1907, and deposit insurance in 1933, after thousands of banks had failed. In 1933 President Franklin Roosevelt also ordered Americans to turn in their gold coins. From 1934 on, a dollar in an American's hand was paper that could not be traded for gold.

#### The Panic of 1907

In October 1907 depositors, the people who kept money in banks, rushed to pull their money out of New York's trust companies. A trust company was a kind of bank that took deposits and managed people's money. The country had no central bank, a bank for the country's banks, to stop the run, so a private banker, J.P. Morgan, organized the rescue.

The trouble began with a failed attempt to corner the stock of United Copper. To corner a stock means to buy up so much of it that the buyers can set its price. When the attempt failed, the banks of the men behind it were ruined, and depositors grew afraid of other banks linked to those men.

On October 22, 1907, so many depositors demanded their money from the Knickerbocker Trust Company that its officers stopped paying out money. It was one of the largest trust companies in New York. Depositors then ran on the Trust Company of America and others, standing in lines around the block. Some hired people to hold their place in line. Charles T. Barney, the Knickerbocker's former president, shot himself on November 14, 1907.

A central bank holds the cash other banks keep on hand, called their reserves, and lends to them in a crisis.

<a id="story-jp-morgan-money"></a>

#### J.P. Morgan

> **Who:** A New York banker who ran the rescue in the Panic of 1907 from his own library.
>
> **When and where:** New York City, October and November 1907.

J.P. Morgan was 70 years old when he took charge of stopping the Panic of 1907. He worked from his private library at 36th Street and Madison Avenue in New York City.

Under Morgan's rescue, teams of examiners went through the books of the trust companies. They decided which ones were sound enough to save. Officials of the Treasury, the government department in charge of its money, deposited $25 million of the government's money with Morgan's group of banks. Morgan also got the presidents of banks and trust companies to promise money to shared rescue funds.

On the night of November 2 to 3, 1907, Morgan gathered the presidents of the trust companies in his library and had the doors locked. In the account told by the Morgan Library & Museum and others, he kept the key in his pocket. He kept the presidents in the room until they agreed to put up $25 million to save the weakest trusts. They signed the deal near 5 in the morning. Memoirs differ on small details, such as who held the key and the exact hour. Today the exhibition on the panic at the Morgan Library & Museum describes the locked-door meeting.

People at the time drew a lesson from the panic: the country's money system had depended on one 70-year-old private banker. In 1908 members of Congress passed the Aldrich-Vreeland Act. In it they created the National Monetary Commission to design a better system.

#### Jekyll Island and the Federal Reserve, 1913

The Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, began with a secret meeting in November 1910. Six men traveled to the Jekyll Island Club, on an island off Georgia. To keep the trip secret, they traveled as a duck-hunting party. They were Senator Nelson Aldrich, Treasury official A. Piatt Andrew, the bankers Henry Davison, Frank Vanderlip and Paul Warburg, and Aldrich's secretary, Arthur Shelton. On the island they wrote a plan for a central bank.

The men who were there did not admit to the meeting in public until the 1930s. Today the Federal Reserve's published history describes the trip. Members of Congress never passed their plan, called the Aldrich Plan. Three years later they used much of its design in the law they did pass.

President Wilson signed the Federal Reserve Act on December 23, 1913. The act provided for twelve Reserve Banks in different parts of the country, run under a board in Washington. The Reserve Banks opened on November 16, 1914.

The Federal Reserve is a bank for banks. It holds their reserves, which are the money a bank keeps on hand instead of lending it out, and it moves money between them. Its officers can lend to a sound bank that is facing a run, so the bank can pay its depositors and stay open.

#### Black-owned banks, and Greenwood's losses

In the early 1900s Black Americans started their own banks, among them Maggie Lena Walker in Richmond and Jesse Binga in Chicago. Black depositors and business owners later lost money when banks failed and when a white mob burned Tulsa's Black district in 1921.

Maggie Lena Walker opened the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank in Richmond, Virginia, in November 1903, and became its first president. She was the first Black woman to found a bank in the United States. On the first day, people deposited more than $8,000, in amounts from 31 cents to over $100. During the Great Depression of the 1930s, Walker merged it with other Black-owned banks into the Consolidated Bank and Trust Company. That bank lasted into the 2000s as the longest continuously run Black-owned bank in the country. Walker lived from 1864 to 1934.

Jesse Binga opened a private bank in Chicago in 1908, mainly for Black customers, because many bank managers turned them away. In 1921 he opened the Binga State Bank. Binga lived at 5922 South Park Avenue, in a white neighborhood. His home and his offices were bombed at least five times. The records do not say who set the bombs.

In 1930 Illinois state officials closed the Binga State Bank when it could not meet a requirement to hold $400,000 in cash. Accounts date the closing to June or to July 31, 1930. Binga lost his own fortune. Many depositors lost their savings, and the records do not count them. In 1933 a jury found Binga guilty of embezzlement, which means taking money a person was trusted to look after. A judge sentenced him to ten years in prison. Governor Dwight H. Green of Illinois pardoned him in 1941. A pardon is an official act that forgives a crime and ends the punishment.

On May 31 and June 1, 1921, a white mob attacked Greenwood, the Black district of Tulsa, Oklahoma, where about 10,000 people lived. The mob included men whom the Tulsa police had deputized, which means sworn in as temporary officers. National Guard units took part in the attack. The attackers destroyed more than 1,000 homes and businesses. Estimates of the number of people killed run from 50 to 300. The count is uncertain because many of the dead were never identified and lie in unmarked graves. Most Black Tulsans lost their homes, and thousands lived in tents through the winter of 1921 to 1922. No white person went to prison for the murders or the burning. An all-white grand jury blamed Black Tulsans. A grand jury is a group of citizens who decide whether to charge people with crimes.

Greenwood's residents filed more than $1.8 million in damage claims with the city of Tulsa between June 1921 and June 1922. All but one of the claims were turned down. A 2021 Brookings study of the claims does not name the officials who turned them down. The one claim paid went to a white shop owner, for guns taken from his store. Officers of the insurance companies refused to pay for the burned property. They called the attack a "riot," and their policies did not cover riot damage. No rebuilding money came from the city, the state or the federal government.

Greenwood's residents rebuilt the district. In 1925 the National Negro Business League held its national meeting in Greenwood. "Negro" was a common word for Black people at the time. By the 1940s Greenwood had 242 Black-owned businesses.

#### 1930 to 1933: the runs, the holiday and deposit insurance

From 1930 to 1933 more than 9,000 American banks failed, and their depositors lost about $1.34 billion. Federal deposit insurance did not begin until 1934, so the losses fell on the depositors.

Banks had failed at a rate of more than 600 a year even in the 1920s, mostly small banks in farm country. The count grew after 1929. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, or FDIC, is the government agency that insures bank deposits. Its later records list 1,350 banks that suspended, meaning they closed their doors or stopped paying depositors, in 1930. They list 2,293 in 1931, 1,453 in 1932 and 4,000 in 1933. That makes 9,096 in all. A fact sheet from the Franklin D. Roosevelt Presidential Library gives the number as about 9,000 of the country's 25,000 banks. By an estimate on the history website ushistory.org, about nine million savings accounts had been lost by March 1933.

On December 11, 1930, the Bank of United States in New York City failed. It was the largest bank failure in the country up to then. It had about 400,000 depositors. Many were immigrants who worked in the clothing factories, and small savers in the Bronx and Brooklyn.

A history published by the FDIC in 1998 states that Federal Reserve officials "did little to ease the liquidity problems of banks." Liquidity means having cash on hand to pay depositors. Most of the banks that failed in 1930 had not joined the Federal Reserve system, and its officials felt no responsibility for them.

On February 14, 1933, the governor of Michigan closed every bank in the state for eight days. That left 900,000 depositors unable to reach their money. Runs then spread from state to state.

Franklin Roosevelt became president in March 1933. On March 6, two days after he took office, he closed every bank in the country. This was called the bank holiday. On March 9 members of Congress passed the Emergency Banking Act. On the night of Sunday, March 12, Roosevelt gave the first of his radio talks called fireside chats. About 60 million people listened. He explained in simple terms how banks work, and he said money was safer in a reopened bank than under the mattress. Banks reopened from March 13 to 15, after federal officials reviewed them. When they opened, people put in more money than they took out.

On April 5, 1933, Roosevelt signed Executive Order 6102, a written order from the president. It required Americans to turn in their gold coins, gold bars and gold certificates to the government at $20.67 an ounce. A gold certificate was a paper note that could be traded for gold. Americans could keep small keepsakes and collections. In the Gold Reserve Act of January 30, 1934, members of Congress moved all the gold the country used as money to the Treasury. They set a new price of $35 an ounce. From then on, Americans could not trade their dollars for gold. Foreign governments still could.

Between those two gold measures, on June 16, 1933, members of Congress created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the FDIC, in the Banking Act. Its insurance began on January 1, 1934, and covered each depositor up to $2,500. In July 1934 the limit rose to $5,000. If an insured bank failed, its depositors would be paid back from the insurance fund, up to the limit. With that promise, depositors no longer had a reason to rush to the bank to get their money out first.

<a id="story-lydia-lobsiger"></a>

#### Lydia Lobsiger

> **Who:** The first depositor in the United States to be paid back by federal deposit insurance.
>
> **When and where:** East Peoria, Illinois, 1934. Her grave record gives her life as 1870 to 1956.

Lydia Lobsiger received the first federal deposit insurance check ever paid. It was for $1,250 and dated July 3, 1934.

Her bank was the Fond du Lac State Bank of East Peoria, Illinois. It failed in the spring of 1934. It was the first bank with FDIC insurance to fail. The insurance had begun only a few months earlier, on January 1, 1934.

From 1930 to 1933, before the insurance began, depositors in failed banks had lost about $1.34 billion. When Lobsiger's bank failed, reporters at newspapers across the country wrote that a depositor with a small account had not lost her savings.

#### War bonds

During World War II, about 85 million Americans, roughly half the country, lent money to the government by buying war bonds. Together they paid in about $185.7 billion.

One kind was the Series E bond. A buyer paid $18.75 for it and got back $25 ten years later. Children bought war stamps for 10 cents or 25 cents each and saved them toward a bond.

From 1942 to 1945, officials of the Treasury and the Office of Education ran a program called Schools at War. Students bought stamps and bonds toward goals set at their schools. About 200,000 schools and 30 million students took part. They raised more than $2 billion. Their money paid the price of at least 90,000 jeeps and several thousand airplanes for the armed forces. Eleanor Roosevelt spoke in support of the program on the radio on September 25, 1942.

### 1950 to 2000

The dollar lost its last link to gold in 1971. In the same years Americans began to pay with plastic cards and take cash from machines. On August 15, 1971, President Nixon ended the right of foreign governments to trade dollars for gold. Since then no metal has stood behind the dollar. Prices rose fast for about seventeen years, from about 1965 to 1982, and a dollar saved in 1965 bought about a third as much in 1982. Paul Volcker, head of the Federal Reserve, stopped that rise in the early 1980s by letting interest rates rise past 20 percent.

#### Plastic: the charge card and the credit card

The first card that people could use to pay at many different businesses was the Diners Club card, in 1950. Frank McNamara started the company with Ralph Schneider and other partners. The first cards were made of cardboard. At first a couple dozen restaurants in New York took them. The first use was at Major's Cabin Grill in February 1950.

The Diners Club card was a charge card. The holder had to pay the whole bill each month. A story often told says that McNamara had the idea in 1949 after he forgot his wallet at dinner. Matty Simmons, the company's first publicity man, was there. He said later that the story was made up for publicity. According to Simmons, McNamara simply had the idea and worked on it.

In September 1958, officers of Bank of America mailed about 60,000 ready-to-use cards, called BankAmericards, to people in Fresno, California. None of those people had asked for a card. The BankAmericard was a true credit card. The holder could pay part of the bill and owe the rest later. About 22 percent of the accounts fell behind on payments, against the 4 percent the bank's officers had planned for. There was also fraud, which means cheating to get money or goods. The bank lost millions of dollars in the card's first years. In 1970 members of Congress banned mailing credit cards to people who had not asked for them. Officers of Bank of America licensed the card to other banks across the country, and in 1976 it was renamed Visa.

Until 1974, a lender who turned down a woman for credit because she was a woman broke no federal law. A blog post by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, a federal agency, states that "discrimination against women applying for credit was common." Lenders who made mortgages, or home loans, "often discounted a married woman's income, especially if she was of childbearing age." That means they counted her pay as worth less when they decided whether to lend to her. Lenders were more likely to turn down single women. In October 1974 members of Congress passed the Equal Credit Opportunity Act. Under the act, it became illegal for lenders to treat people differently because of their sex or whether they were married. In March 1976 members of Congress added race, color, religion, national origin, age, and receiving public assistance. Public assistance is money from a government aid program.

#### The ATM

The first automated teller machine in the United States, a machine that pays out cash without a bank clerk, opened on September 2, 1969. It stood at a Chemical Bank branch in Rockville Centre, New York. Docutel, a company in Dallas, built the machine, called the Docuteller, from an idea by Don Wetzel. The bank's advertisement said, "On September 2, our banks will open at 9:00 and never close again."

#### August 15, 1971: the last tie to gold

After 1934, Americans could not trade dollars for gold, but foreign governments still could, at $35 an ounce. This deal was part of an agreement among countries made after World War II, called the Bretton Woods system. By 1971 far more dollars were held outside the country than the United States had gold to pay for them. Foreign governments were trading in dollars for American gold, and the country's gold was running down. It was a run on the nation's gold.

President Nixon spent a weekend at Camp David with his advisers. They included Arthur Burns, the chairman of the Federal Reserve, John Connally, the Treasury Secretary, and Paul Volcker, a Treasury official. On Sunday night, August 15, 1971, Nixon announced that Treasury officials would no longer trade gold for the dollars foreign governments turned in. He called the change temporary. No president has reversed it.

Since that night the dollar has been fiat money. Fiat money is money backed by no metal. It is worth what it can buy. People accept it because it is legal tender, which means the law says it must be accepted to pay a debt, and because they trust the government that prints it. The greenbacks of 1862 worked the same way.

#### The Great Inflation

From about 1965 to 1982, prices in the United States rose fast year after year. Economists call this the Great Inflation. Inflation means prices going up, so that each dollar buys less.

In the early 1960s prices had risen 1 or 2 percent a year. Food prices rose more than 20 percent over the year to late 1973. Prices overall rose about 11 percent in 1974. That year President Ford started a campaign called "Whip Inflation Now," with buttons that said WIN. Prices went on rising. At the peak, in 1979 and 1980, they rose more than 1 percent a month, and for all of 1980 they rose 13.5 percent.

A dollar saved in 1965 bought about a third as much in 1982, so savings put aside in 1965 had lost about two-thirds of their buying power. Borrowing became costly. In October 1981 the average interest rate on a 30-year home mortgage, a loan to buy a house, was 18.63 percent. That is the highest rate ever recorded in the Freddie Mac survey of home loan rates.

<a id="story-bruce-bent-henry-brown"></a>

#### Bruce Bent and Henry Brown

> **Who:** Two men who met at a pension company and set up the first money market fund, a way for small savers to earn more than the legal limit on bank interest.
>
> **When and where:** The United States, 1969 to 1973. Bent was born in 1937. Brown lived from 1926 to 2008.

Bruce Bent and Henry Brown set up a fund that let ordinary savers earn the higher interest that only large investors could get before.

Since 1933 a federal rule called Regulation Q had forbidden banks to pay more than a set rate of interest on a savings account. Federal Reserve officials first put it in place in September 1933. In July 1973 Federal Reserve officials raised the limit on an ordinary bank savings account from 4.5 percent to 5 percent. Most banks paid exactly the limit. In 1974 prices rose about 11 percent. Money in a savings account at 5 percent lost about 6 percent of its buying power that year.

Large investors could earn more by buying short-term debt from the government and from large companies, such as Treasury bills, which are short loans to the government. Only large investors could buy that debt directly. Bent and Brown met while working at TIAA-CREF, a pension company. In August 1969 Bent proposed a fund that would pool the money of many small savers and buy that debt for them.

They set up the Reserve Fund in 1970. A saver needed $1,000 to start, and each share cost $100. The fund opened to savers in 1971 or 1972, depending on the source. Bent and Brown had no sales staff. They phoned financial advisers and handed out brochures. On January 7, 1973, the reporter Robert D. Hershey Jr. wrote an article about the fund in the *New York Times*. By the end of 1973 it held $100 million.

Federal Reserve History counts 1 money market fund in 1972, 36 in 1975, 90 in 1980 and 649 in 1990. The limits of Regulation Q were phased out by 1986 under a law members of Congress passed in 1980. The Reserve Fund later grew into the Reserve Primary Fund, which held about $62 billion in 2008.

<a id="story-paul-volcker"></a>

#### Paul Volcker

> **Who:** The chairman of the Federal Reserve who brought down the Great Inflation with interest rates above 20 percent, at the cost of a recession with 10.8 percent unemployment.
>
> **When and where:** Washington, D.C., 1979 to 1983.

Paul Volcker stopped the Great Inflation by letting interest rates rise past 20 percent. He was six feet seven inches tall and known for smoking cheap cigars. President Jimmy Carter appointed him chairman of the Federal Reserve in August 1979. In 1979 and 1980 prices were rising more than 1 percent a month.

On Saturday night, October 6, 1979, Volcker announced a new policy. He and the other Federal Reserve officials would control how much money was in the economy. They would let interest rates rise as high as that took them. The federal funds rate, the rate banks charge one another for overnight loans, passed 20 percent in 1981.

In the recession of 1981 and 1982, unemployment reached 10.8 percent, the highest since the 1930s. A recession is a time when business shrinks and people lose jobs. Farmers drove tractors to the Federal Reserve's building in protest. Home builders in debt mailed sawed-off pieces of two-by-four lumber to the Federal Reserve.

Inflation fell from 13.5 percent in 1980 to 3.2 percent in 1983. Prices next rose as fast as in late 1981 in the 12 months to June 2022, when they rose 9.1 percent.

#### The savings and loan crisis

From 1989 to 1995, federal officials closed 747 failed savings and loans. Kenneth Robinson, writing for the Federal Reserve's history website, estimates that taxpayers paid as much as $124 billion of the cost. A savings and loan, also called a thrift, took in people's savings and made long-term home loans at fixed interest rates.

When interest rates climbed in the late 1970s and early 1980s, the thrifts lost money. Under Regulation Q, thrifts could not pay savers the rates they could get elsewhere. The old fixed-rate home loans they held lost value. By 1983 closing the thrifts that could not pay their debts would have cost about $25 billion. Their insurance fund, the Federal Savings and Loan Insurance Corporation, or FSLIC, held only $6 billion. In the Garn-St Germain Act of 1982, members of Congress let thrifts make new kinds of loans beyond home mortgages. Many of those loans carried more risk.

In 1989 members of Congress passed a law. In it they closed the FSLIC and moved thrift deposit insurance to the FDIC. They also created the Resolution Trust Corporation to shut down failed thrifts. By the end of 1995 its officials had closed the 747 savings and loans, which together held more than $407 billion in loans and other property. Savers with insured accounts were paid in full.

Banks failed in the same years. FDIC records count 120 failed insured banks in 1985, 145 in 1986, 203 in 1987 and 280 in 1988. In 1984 federal officials rescued Continental Illinois National Bank, which held $45 billion in loans and other property, instead of letting it fail.

### 2000 to Today

Most American payments today are made by credit or debit card. In 2024 cards made up 65 percent of payments, according to the Federal Reserve's yearly payment diary, and in 2025 Americans used cash for 14 percent. Runs came back. In 2008 savers ran from money market funds, and in 2023 depositors ran from Silicon Valley Bank and other banks. Both times, federal officials promised to cover money that no insurance protected. Since 2009 people have also used digital coins, such as bitcoin, that no government and no bank puts out.

#### 2008: the run comes back

In September 2008 savers ran on money market funds, the kind of fund Bruce Bent and Henry Brown had started. In a money market fund, the managers pool many people's money to buy short-term loans to the government and to large companies. Many people treated these funds like bank accounts. A share was meant to stay worth exactly $1. The funds had no deposit insurance.

On September 15, 2008, the large financial firm Lehman Brothers failed. The next day, the Reserve Primary Fund "broke the buck," which means its shares fell below $1, to 97 cents. The fund held $62.5 billion, and $785 million of it was in Lehman's debt. According to a study in the *Journal of Financial Crises*, published by Yale University, investors pulled more than $40 billion out of the fund in two days. On September 17 alone they pulled about $144.5 billion out of money market funds across the country.

On September 19, 2008, Treasury officials announced a guarantee for money market funds. President George W. Bush approved it, and Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson put up to $50 billion of the Treasury's Exchange Stabilization Fund behind it. The guarantee worked like deposit insurance, set up within a week, and the run stopped. Later, officials of the Securities and Exchange Commission charged Bruce Bent and his son with fraud over the Reserve Primary Fund's collapse. On November 12, 2012, a jury cleared them of the fraud charges.

Banks failed too. From 2008 through 2013, 489 insured banks failed, according to a history the FDIC published in 2017. Their failures cost the deposit insurance fund about $73 billion. IndyMac failed on July 11, 2008, with losses of about $12 billion, the most costly failure in the FDIC's history. Washington Mutual failed on September 25, 2008. It held $307 billion in loans and other property, which made it the largest bank failure in the country's history. On October 3, 2008, members of Congress raised the deposit insurance limit from $100,000 to $250,000. In 2010 they made the $250,000 limit permanent.

#### Money issued by nobody

Bitcoin is a digital coin that no government and no bank puts out. It runs on a public record of who owns which coins, kept by many computers that check one another's work.

On October 31, 2008, a person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto published a paper describing Bitcoin. On January 3, 2009, Nakamoto started the system by creating its first block of records. The code of that first block includes a headline from that day's *Times* of London: "Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks." The Chancellor is the British government's top money official, and a bailout is government money given to businesses in trouble. No one has shown who Nakamoto is.

People hold bitcoin as an investment, hoping its price will rise, and others use it to pay for things. Economists disagree about whether it is money, property owned for its value, or a bet on a price.

<a id="story-laszlo-hanyecz"></a>

#### Laszlo Hanyecz

> **Who:** A programmer who made the first recorded purchase with bitcoin: two pizzas for 10,000 coins.
>
> **When and where:** Florida, May 22, 2010.

On May 22, 2010, Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 bitcoins for two pizzas. It was the first recorded time anyone traded bitcoin for a real thing.

Hanyecz was a programmer in Florida who had worked on Bitcoin's code. He wrote the first version of the Bitcoin program for Apple's Mac computers, and he was the first to use a computer's graphics card to create new bitcoins, which is called mining. In May 2010 he posted an offer on the Bitcoin forum, a website where users wrote to one another. He would give 10,000 bitcoins to anyone who got two large pizzas delivered to him. A forum user named jercos took the deal and ordered the pizzas. The pizzas cost jercos about $25. At the time of the offer, the 10,000 bitcoins were worth about $41, according to the bitcoin.it wiki.

The same wiki estimates that at the high point of May 2025, those 10,000 coins would have been worth about $1.1 billion. In a 2019 interview, reported by the news site CoinDesk, Hanyecz said, "A trade happens because both parties think they're getting a good deal." May 22 is now marked each year as Bitcoin Pizza Day.

#### Payday loans

A payday loan is a small loan meant to be paid back from the borrower's next paycheck. Researchers at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, a federal agency, released a study of these loans on April 24, 2013. They found that a $350 payday loan with the typical fee of $15 for every $100 borrowed cost an annual percentage rate of 391 percent. An annual percentage rate is the cost of a loan over a full year, written as a share of the amount borrowed.

Storefront payday lenders charged fees of $10 to $20 for every $100 borrowed, the study found. Nearly half of payday borrowers took out more than 10 loans in a year, and 14 percent took out 20 or more. The typical borrower was in debt to a payday lender 199 days of the year.

#### Inflation returns, 2021 to 2026

Prices rose fast again from 2021 to 2023, and Federal Reserve officials raised interest rates faster than at any time since Volcker. In the 12 months to June 2022, prices rose 9.1 percent, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That was the largest rise since November 1981. Energy prices rose 41.6 percent that year and food prices 10.4 percent. Federal Reserve officials raised their main interest rate from near zero in March 2022 to more than 5 percent in 2023. By the middle of 2023, prices were rising at close to 3 percent a year.

Economists still disagree about the causes, as a report by the Congressional Research Service, which does research for members of Congress, describes. The causes they name include broken supply chains (the network of factories, ships and trucks that moves goods), federal spending on pandemic relief and higher energy prices.

In the 12 months to August 2026, prices rose 3.4 percent, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported. Energy prices rose 16.3 percent, and food prices 2.7 percent.

#### FTX and stablecoins

FTX was a company where people bought, sold and kept cryptocurrency, digital money such as bitcoin. In November 2022 it went bankrupt, which means it could not pay what it owed and went to court to settle its debts. Its founder was Sam Bankman-Fried. According to the *Washington Post*, he had used customers' money to buy luxury real estate, to make investments and to give political donations.

In November 2023 a federal jury found him guilty of wire fraud, conspiracy to commit fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering. Wire fraud is cheating people using phones, email or the internet. A conspiracy is a plan by two or more people to commit a crime. Money laundering is hiding where money from a crime came from. On March 28, 2024, Judge Lewis Kaplan sentenced him to 25 years in prison and ordered him to give up more than $11 billion.

The people running the bankruptcy paid customers back what their accounts were worth on the day FTX filed for bankruptcy in November 2022. On that day one bitcoin sold for $16,080. By May 2024 it sold for close to $62,675, according to CBS News. Customers who had held bitcoin did not get back that later value. Another payment went out to customers on July 31, 2026. An FTX press release in 2026 states that, after it, customer claims had received 105 percent of their value in all, and small claims 120 percent. Payments above 100 percent were interest added to the claims. FTX's chief executive, John Ray, described the plan in 2024 as "100% of bankruptcy claim amounts plus interest."

On July 18, 2025, President Trump signed the GENIUS Act, a law with rules for stablecoins. A stablecoin is a digital coin that the company behind it promises to trade for a fixed amount, such as one dollar. Under the law, a company that puts out stablecoins must hold at least one dollar of approved reserves, such as cash, insured bank deposits or Treasury bills, for every coin. The law states that stablecoins are not federally insured, according to a 2025 report by the Congressional Research Service. In the 1800s, before national paper money, banks chartered by the states printed their own notes. Each note was only that bank's promise to pay in coin. A stablecoin works the same way: a private promise to pay, backed by what the company holds, with no federal insurance behind it.

#### 2023: the run on Silicon Valley Bank

In March 2023 federal officials protected every depositor at two failed banks, including money above the insurance limit. On March 9, 2023, depositors took $42 billion out of Silicon Valley Bank in California in a single day. About 88 percent of the bank's deposits were above the $250,000 insurance limit. If the bank failed, the owners of that money stood to lose it. On March 10, officials of California's Department of Financial Protection and Innovation closed the bank. On Sunday, March 12, officials of New York's Department of Financial Services closed Signature Bank. About 90 percent of its deposits were uninsured.

Also on March 12, Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen, after consulting the president, used an emergency power. She protected every depositor at both banks, insured or not. On March 27, 2023, FDIC Chairman Martin Gruenberg told Congress that FDIC officials estimated the cost at about $20 billion for Silicon Valley Bank and $2.5 billion for Signature Bank. They planned to collect that money from other banks through special fees, not from taxpayers. On May 1, 2023, California officials closed First Republic Bank, and JPMorgan Chase took over all its deposits.

#### Cash fades, and the penny ends

In 2025 cash was the third most used way to pay in the United States, after credit cards and debit cards. Federal Reserve researchers track this with the Diary of Consumer Payment Choice, in which people record the payments they make.

In 2016 cash was the most used way to pay, at about a third of all payments. In 2024 cash was used for 14 percent of payments, credit cards for 35 percent and debit cards for 30 percent. Adults aged 18 to 24 paid by phone 45 percent of the time that year. In 2025 people made about 47 payments a month, according to the diary's report released in May 2026. Cash was 14 percent of them, about 6 a month. It was the sixth year in a row that cash came third. People aged 55 and older paid cash about 10 times a month, against about twice for people aged 18 to 24. In the countryside the count was about 9 a month, and in cities and suburbs about 6. Ninety percent of people said they planned to keep using cash.

In the 2024 budget year, each penny cost the U.S. Mint 3.69 cents to make and ship. The Mint's losses on pennies came to about $85 million that year. On February 9, 2025, President Trump said he had told the Treasury Secretary to stop making new pennies. A PBS and Associated Press report at the time said it was unclear whether he had that power, because members of Congress set the rules for coins. On November 12, 2025, at a ceremony at the Philadelphia Mint, the last pennies made for everyday use were struck. The first federal cents had been made 232 years earlier, in 1793. The expected savings were about $56 million a year. Pennies already made are still legal tender.

On September 14, 2026, members of the House of Representatives passed the Common Cents Act, and senators passed it on September 28, 2026. The bill would end penny production in law. When a customer paid cash and exact change was not available, the total would round up or down to the nearest five cents. Payments by card or check would not round. As of October 2, 2026, the bill was waiting for President Trump's signature.

<a id="ch-marketplace"></a>

## Chapter 18: Marketplace and Consumer Life

### Before 1500

People in this land got goods from far away long before 1500. They had no stores. They traded one thing for another. At some places, people from many nations gathered to fish and to trade. One of the biggest was on the Columbia River in the Northwest. Goods passed from one person to the next, sometimes across hundreds of miles.

#### The Dalles and Celilo Falls

The biggest trading place in the Northwest was a ten-mile stretch of the Columbia River. It ran from Celilo Falls down to a place called The Dalles, on the border of what are now Oregon and Washington. People fished and lived there. Archaeologists, scientists who study the past from what people left behind, date the first human use of the site to at least 10,000 years ago. Some newspaper and museum writers give 15,000 years.

Traders came from as far north as what is now British Columbia and as far south as California. The Oregon Historical Society reports that, by some accounts, traders came from as far east as the Great Lakes. Northern traders brought coiled baskets, skins and berries. Traders from the south carried obsidian, a black volcanic glass that makes sharp blades, along with bows and captives. Captives were people seized by force and then traded away with the other goods. The accounts of the trade do not name who seized them. Camas root and buffalo hides arrived from the east, and wapato root, whale oil and dentalium shells from the coast. Camas and wapato are roots that people dug up and ate.

Horses came later. Spanish colonists had brought horses to the Americas. In the early 1700s, Native traders passed horses north to this part of the river.

Dentalium shells are the shells of a small sea animal. Each one is shaped like a tiny elephant tusk and can grow a few inches long. Most of them came from the sea off Vancouver Island. People passed them from hand to hand over a wide area. So many people accepted them that traders used them to measure what other goods were worth.

In October 1805, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark reached this stretch of river. Clark wrote in his journal that it was the "Great Mart of all this Country." A mart is a market. People had been trading there long before his visit.

The trading place is now under water. Workers for the US Army Corps of Engineers, the part of the army that builds dams and other large works, built The Dalles Dam eight miles downstream. At 10 o'clock on the morning of March 10, 1957, the dam's floodgates were closed. The written account of that day does not name who gave the order. Four and a half hours later, Celilo Falls lay under the lake behind the dam. The villages of Wyam, on the Oregon side, and S'kin, on the Washington side, went under too. US government officials later paid the Warm Springs, Yakama, Umatilla and Nez Perce nations $26.8 million for the fishing sites they lost.

#### Goods that traveled without a store

Archaeologists have found copper from Lake Superior, shells from the Gulf of Mexico, obsidian from the West and turquoise from the Southwest hundreds of miles from where each was dug up or gathered. People carried and traded these goods over those distances, one exchange at a time.

Cahokia was a city near what is now St. Louis. It was at its largest from about 1050 to 1150. Around 1100, about 10,000 to 20,000 people lived there. People at Cahokia controlled the trade in hoe blades made from Mill Creek chert, a hard stone that holds a sharp edge. Archaeologists have found those blades more than 400 miles away. People that far from Cahokia got the blades by trading for them.

No trader from before 1500 is known today by name.

### The 1500s

In the 1500s, Native people in what is now eastern Canada traded with the crews of European whaling and trading ships. Native traders passed the metal they got far inland, as far as the Great Lakes. There were still no stores. Native traders chose which European goods they wanted. Archaeologists can see those choices in the kettles that the traders cut up and made into new things.

#### What Native customers chose

In the late 1500s, Native buyers in the Northeast and around the Great Lakes traded for copper and brass kettles. Kettles were among the European goods they wanted most. Basque, French and Dutch traders carried the kettles across the ocean because those buyers asked for them. The Basques come from the Basque Country, a region in the mountains on the border of Spain and France. Basque ship crews crossed the ocean to hunt whales. They traded with the Beothuk of Newfoundland, the Innu of Labrador and the Mi'kmaq.

Many of these kettles were not used for cooking. Archaeologists dig them up cut into flat sheets. Native craftspeople turned the sheets into beads, tubes, arrow points and pendants, which are ornaments that hang from a cord. For a long time, people in these nations had made the same shapes from copper found as pure metal in the ground. Buyers like these used a kettle as a supply of metal.

Pieces of Basque copper kettles from the late 1500s and early 1600s turn up from the Canadian Maritimes, on the Atlantic coast, to the lower Great Lakes. Native traders passed the metal along among themselves, far inland. Basque kettles and axes reached the lands of the Huron and their neighbors in what is now Ontario.

Native traders chose carefully what they took in trade. They were skilled bargainers who asked for useful tools and for fine goods alike. In the fur trade of later years, Native customers also traded for wool cloth, linen shirts, glass beads, iron knives, awls, axes, fish hooks, blankets, guns and gunpowder. An awl is a pointed tool for punching holes in leather. The Hudson's Bay Company, a fur-trading company, began in 1670. Its Native customers demanded good guns. The men running the company sent gunsmiths to its trading posts to check the guns and repair them.

### The 1600s

English colonists in the 1600s paid for goods with crops, with other goods and with work, as well as with coins. At John Pynchon's shop in Springfield, Massachusetts, customers seldom paid in coins at all. A shopkeeper wrote down what each customer owed and let the debt run for months. Public markets and trading posts also opened in the English colonies in this century.

#### Market days

A market day was a set day when farmers brought meat, milk, butter, cheese, fruit and vegetables into town to sell. Town people could not travel out to the farms for these foods, so the farmers came to them.

In 1634, Governor John Winthrop of Massachusetts ordered a market for Boston. It is the first public market of the European kind recorded by officials in the English colonies. Hartford, in Connecticut, had a market in 1643. New York had one by 1686, and Philadelphia had one in 1693.

#### Trading posts

A trading post was a building where colonists traded goods with Native people and with other traders. In 1627, the colonists of Plymouth Colony built one at Aptucxet, on the Manomet River on Cape Cod. It was about 20 miles from Plymouth. The post stood on land of the Wampanoag people, who used the place as summer fishing grounds. The name Aptucxet meant "little trap in the river."

At Aptucxet the Plymouth colonists traded with the Wampanoag for corn and beans. They also traded with Dutch traders. That same year, Isaack de Rasieres, the secretary of the Dutch colony, brought wampum into Plymouth's trade. Wampum is small beads made from shells and strung together.

#### The ledger

A colonial shopkeeper kept two books. The first, the journal, listed every sale and every purchase in the order it happened. The second, the ledger, gave each customer a page of their own. The customer's purchases went on the left side of the page and the customer's payments on the right.

Buying without paying at once is called buying on credit. The amount still owed is the debt. A shopkeeper usually let a customer's debt run for up to a year. Customers paid in crops, in other goods, in work and sometimes in coins.

John Pynchon kept a shop in Springfield, Massachusetts. The town and the shop stood on land that the Agawam people had sold to his father. On July 15, 1636, William Pynchon bought land from the Agawam on both sides of the Connecticut River. He took a deed for it, a signed paper that records who owns a piece of land. The deed names Commucke and Matanchan, "ancient Indians of Agaam," acting for the community, and Cuttonus as "the right owner." Pynchon paid 18 fathoms of wampum, 18 coats, 18 hatchets, 18 hoes and 18 knives. A fathom is six feet, here a length of strung beads. The deed states that the Agawam kept their planted fields and their right to take fish, deer, ground nuts, walnuts and acorns. It also states that they would be paid if English cattle damaged their corn.

Seven of John Pynchon's account books survive, covering 1651 to about 1702. Almost every adult in Springfield bought goods at his shop. The editors who printed the books found only a few payments in coins. Books like these record what ordinary colonists bought, item by item.

<a id="story-john-stewart-marketplace"></a>

#### John Stewart

> **Who:** A Scottish soldier, captured in war and sold into forced labor, who became the blacksmith of Springfield and bought on credit at John Pynchon's shop for more than thirty years.
>
> **When and where:** Springfield, Massachusetts, 1653 to 1689.

John Stewart bought his own freedom on credit. He was a Scottish soldier. Soldiers of Oliver Cromwell's army captured him at the Battle of Dunbar, in Scotland, in 1650. The men on the council that ruled England ordered Sir Arthur Haselrig, the governor at Newcastle, to hand over 150 of the Dunbar prisoners to the agents of John Becx and Joshua Foote. These two men had put money into an ironworks in Massachusetts, a works that made iron. In his own recorded words, Stewart was "sold for eight years service." That meant he was forced to work for whoever owned his service until the eight years ran out. As prisoners in the hands of Becx and Foote's agents, Stewart and the other men boarded a ship called the *Unity*, whose master was Augustine Walker. Stewart arrived in New England in December 1650. He worked at the ironworks at Lynn, in Massachusetts. Then the merchant John Pynchon bought his service and took him to Springfield.

On December 29, 1653, Pynchon wrote in his account book that Stewart owed him £30 "for releasing him from my Service." The sign £ stands for pounds, the main English unit of money. Shillings and pence were smaller units. Stewart agreed to pay an extra 12 shillings a year for three years while Pynchon waited for the £30. He paid that extra in blacksmith's work, "in mending or making of Iron worke."

Stewart became the Springfield blacksmith. His page in Pynchon's ledger lists what he bought, item by item. A forge is the fire where a blacksmith heats iron to shape it. For his forge he bought 241 pounds of iron by weight in one purchase, then more bars of iron every few weeks, bars of steel and a coal basket. He also bought a sword and belt, a grindstone, a pair of boots, wool cloth, silk and buttons, a bushel of apples, soap, a comb, pepper and ginger. Pynchon charged him for using Pynchon's tools at the shop and for an old bellows, the air pump that blows on a forge fire.

Almost none of it was paid in coins. By December 23, 1654, Stewart had paid in two lots of wampum and in smith's work, including work on Pynchon's mill. Neighbors also paid wheat to Pynchon for him. He still owed £13 6s. The letter s stands for shillings. Later he paid in land and in a day of haymaking.

The editors of the account books explain that in 1660 he was fined for striking a man named William Morgan and breaking his nose. In 1662 he was fined for playing cards at his house. The books do not say who set the fines. By 1664, ten years after his first purchases, he was still buying on the book: sugar again and again, salt, gunpowder, scissors, pins, a knife for "the Boy," and iron for the troopers' horseshoes. Troopers were soldiers on horseback. On February 20, 1666, he owed £11 17s 1d. The d stands for pence. The same page charges him £1 as a fine for himself and his wife for "unseasonable night meetings."

Pynchon's books list his purchases until 1689. He died at Springfield on April 21, 1691. The Scottish Prisoners of War Society, a group that traces the Dunbar prisoners, knows of no family he left when he died.

### 1700 to 1750

In the 1700s, colonial families began buying British-made goods in large amounts. Goods made in Britain became cheap enough for them. Shops in the port towns sold these goods, and in Philadelphia Benjamin Franklin made advertisements pay for much of his newspaper. Colonists also bought and sold enslaved people. In New York, city officials set up a market where enslaved people were sold. Printers, Franklin among them, ran advertisements offering enslaved people for sale.

#### The consumer revolution

A consumer is a person who buys goods to use them. The words "consumer revolution," meaning a big change in buying, name what happened in the colonies during the 1700s. Colonists had made many of their own clothes, tools and kitchen things. Now they began buying them instead, mostly from Britain.

In Britain, makers found better ways to make goods. Merchants got better at shipping goods across the ocean and at selling them on credit. Prices fell. At the same time, colonial families earned more. Goods that only rich families had owned became ordinary.

Tea came with a whole set of goods: a teapot, cups, sugar and a table to set them on. Buying goods like these became a sign that a family was respectable.

#### A market where people were sold

In New York, colonists bought and sold enslaved people at a market that city officials set up. The Common Council was the group of men who ran New York City, and its members were called aldermen. On November 30, 1711, the aldermen passed a law that set up the market at the bottom end of Wall Street, near Pearl Street and Water Street.

Slaveholders sold enslaved Africans at this market and rented them out to others as workers. They sold and rented out Native people held in slavery there too. The law required owners who rented out enslaved people as workers by the day to do it at this market. Buyers also inspected the people for sale there, looking them over before buying. The accounts of the market do not describe how the inspections were done. The market was a wooden building with a roof and open sides. It held about 50 men. Slaveholders used it for 51 years, until 1762.

In 2015, Jim O'Grady, a reporter for the New York radio station WNYC, wrote that thousands of people were sold at the market: men, women, shiploads of children and captured Native people. In 1700, New York had about 5,000 people. At least 750 of them were enslaved. The city's aldermen chose the place for the market. The accounts of the market do not name the men who bought and sold people there.

In 2015, Jumaane Williams, a member of the New York City Council, asked for a sign to mark the place where the market stood. In June of that year, Mayor Bill de Blasio officially opened the sign at Wall Street and Water Street.

#### Newspaper advertising begins to pay

An advertisement is a notice that a seller pays to have printed, so that people will buy what the seller offers. On October 2, 1729, Benjamin Franklin bought a newspaper in Philadelphia, the *Pennsylvania Gazette*, from a printer named Samuel Keimer. Under Franklin, the money that sellers paid for advertisements became one of the paper's main sources of income.

Franklin changed the way the advertisements looked. He put more empty space around them and used letters of different sizes. The *Gazette* grew from two pages to four, partly to make room for more advertisements.

<a id="story-benjamin-franklin-marketplace"></a>

#### Benjamin Franklin

> **Who:** The Philadelphia printer who made advertising pay for a newspaper, and who ran advertisements in it selling enslaved people.
>
> **When and where:** Philadelphia, from October 2, 1729.
>
> **Movie:** *Benjamin Franklin* (2022), a documentary by Ken Burns, shown on PBS. It covers Franklin's whole life.

Benjamin Franklin made his fortune as a printer partly by selling space in his newspaper to advertisers. When he took over the *Pennsylvania Gazette* in 1729, it had about 90 subscribers, the people who paid to get every copy. By 1748 it had more than 1,500. It was the most widely read newspaper in the colonies.

Some of the advertisements Franklin ran offered enslaved people for sale. Franklin published the *Gazette* for 37 years, counting the years after 1748 when he was David Hall's partner in the paper. In those 37 years, the *Gazette* printed at least 277 advertisements offering at least 308 enslaved people. Franklin ran these notices. He took the fees for these notices and acted as the go-between for the buyers and the sellers. He printed notices about servants who had run away from the people they were bound to work for.

In 1748, when he was 42, Franklin stepped back from printing. He made a partnership with a printer named David Hall. Hall ran the shop, and Franklin kept a share of the profits. Much of the money that let Franklin stop working at his trade early came from the paper's advertising.

#### Shops and shopkeepers in the port towns

Shops in the port towns sold cloth and other goods brought in from London. Some sold haberdashery, which means small sewing goods such as thread, ribbons and buttons. Shopkeepers ordered their goods from London. Colonists who bought on credit could end up in debt to a local shopkeeper or to a merchant in London.

Women ran some of these shops. Elizabeth Murray came to Boston from Scotland in 1749, when she was 23. She opened a shop that sold cloth and other goods from Britain. Her brother's business friends helped her get started. She traveled to London to choose the goods for her shop, and she earned enough to support herself. Later she helped other women open shops.

### 1750 to 1800

From 1767 to 1770, many colonists refused to buy British goods as a protest against British taxes. Merchants promised not to bring the goods in, and families made their own cloth instead of buying it. Members of merchants' committees warned shopkeepers who kept selling British goods. The men at Boston's town meeting voted to write two of those shopkeepers' names into the town record. At a shop door in Boston, Ebenezer Richardson shot and killed a boy, Christopher Seider. Away from the ports, a single storekeeper sold a whole farming neighborhood its goods on credit until the next harvest.

#### Non-importation

In 1767, members of Parliament, the lawmaking body in London, passed a tax law called the Townshend Revenue Act. It set duties, which are taxes on goods brought into the colonies from Britain. Colonists who opposed the duties answered by refusing to buy British goods. Refusing to buy something as a protest is called a boycott.

The seniors at Harvard College in Massachusetts voted in the autumn of 1767 not to drink tea or wear imported British clothes at their graduation. It was a protest against the Townshend duties. Imported goods are goods brought in from another country. At the next year's graduation, the seniors' printed theses were on paper made in New England. The theses were a printed sheet of the ideas the graduates were ready to argue for in public at the ceremony.

On August 1, 1768, about 60 Boston merchants and traders signed the Boston Non-Importation Agreement. They promised not to import most British goods from January 1, 1769, to January 1, 1770. Within two weeks, all but 16 of the town's merchants had joined.

The value of British goods brought into Boston fell from about £420,000 in 1768 to about £208,000 in 1769. That is about half. In 1770, members of Parliament took back most of the Townshend taxes. The agreement in Boston ended that year.

#### Spinning instead of buying

If families did not buy British cloth, they had to make their own. Cloth made at home was called homespun. To make it, women first spun wool or flax into yarn on a spinning wheel. Flax is a plant whose stems give the threads for linen. Then the yarn was woven into cloth.

Women in New England held at least 46 spinning meetings between 1768 and 1770, where they spun together in public. In all, 1,644 women took part. Ministers held 30 of the meetings, and those 30 drew 94 out of every 100 of the spinners.

In August 1769, women in Brookfield, Massachusetts, met at the minister's house from 5 o'clock in the morning. The young woman who did best on the linen wheel spun 70 knots. A knot was a measured length of yarn. One married woman did her morning work at home and made cheese first. Then she rode more than two miles carrying her wheel, spun from 9 in the morning to 7 at night, and finished 53 knots. After that she went home to do the milking.

Members of a society in Hartford, Connecticut, offered a prize of 12 pounds to whoever made the most yards of woolen cloth in a year. Printers ran newspaper stories about the meetings. Only six of those stories called the spinners "Daughters of Liberty," a name for women on the side of the protest.

<a id="story-cuming-sisters"></a>

#### Ame and Elizabeth Cuming

> **Who:** Two sisters who kept a shop in Boston, refused to join the boycott and were named in the newspaper and the town record for it.
>
> **When and where:** Boston, 1765 to 1776, then Halifax, Nova Scotia.

Ame and Elizabeth Cuming sold imported goods in Boston and would not stop when the town's merchants told them to. The sisters were not married and were in their middle thirties. Their parents were from Scotland, and they grew up in Concord, Massachusetts. By 1765 they lived in Boston and earned their own living. They sold fashionable goods from London, taught embroidery, which is sewing pictures and patterns with colored thread, and took in young women who paid to live with them. Elizabeth Murray had helped them start their business.

In late 1769, a shipment of silk and haberdashery worth £300 reached them from London. In the middle of November, men from the merchants' committee came to the shop. They warned the sisters of "consequences" if they sold the goods. The sisters refused. They said they had never entered into any agreement not to import. They called themselves "two industrious Girls" who were trying "in an honest way" to earn their bread.

A notice in the *Boston Gazette* described them as "enemies to their country" who "preferred their own little private Advantage to the Welfare of America." On March 19, 1770, the men at Boston's town meeting voted to write the sisters' names into the town record. The wording of the vote states that this was so that "POSTERITY may know" they had "opposed their Country." Posterity means the people who live later.

In March 1776, the Cuming sisters left Boston with the Loyalists, the colonists who sided with Britain in the Revolutionary War, and went to Halifax, Nova Scotia. By 1780 they were "more prosperous than ever they were in Boston."

#### A killing at a shop door, 1770

In February 1770, a Boston man named Ebenezer Richardson shot and killed a boy, Christopher Seider, during a protest at a shop door. Theophilus Lillie kept the shop, in Boston's North End. He went on selling imported goods during the boycott. On February 22, 1770, a carved head on a long pole was set up in front of his shop door. Some accounts say it was a sign that read "Importer." Thomas Hutchinson's letter about that day does not name who put it there. A crowd of boys and young men gathered and let no one go into the shop.

Richardson was Lillie's neighbor. He was a customs informer. Customs officials collected the taxes on goods brought in by ship, and they paid informers like Richardson to report smugglers. Richardson tried to pull the pole down. The crowd threw stones and sticks at him, chased him into his house and broke his windows. From inside the house, Richardson fired a musket at the boys. The shot hit Christopher Seider in the chest, and he died soon after. Christopher was 10 and a half years old in the letters of Thomas Hutchinson, and 11 in most other accounts. Hutchinson was the acting governor of Massachusetts, running the colony for the king while the governor was away in England. Hutchinson wrote that Richardson "killed one & wounded another." The second boy was hit in the thigh.

Christopher Seider's funeral was on February 26, 1770. A funeral procession is the line of people who walk behind the coffin. Hutchinson wrote that people said Christopher's procession "reached from the Town House to Liberty Tree," two places in Boston. The modern editors of his letters call it the largest procession ever seen in Boston, as people reported it at the time. Richardson was tried for murder on April 20, 1770. The next day the jury found him guilty. The judges believed he was innocent, and they put off his sentence.

#### The country store and the crop ledger

Away from the port towns, one country storekeeper sold goods to a whole farming neighborhood. Customers paid in crops, in work and in promises to pay later.

The storekeeper wrote each family's debt in a ledger. A farm family bought goods all through the year and paid after the harvest. When a harvest failed, the family could not pay, and the debt carried into the next year.

Some of these account books survive, and they name the customers. Robert Townsend kept a shop in Oyster Bay, on Long Island, and kept account books there and in New York. His surviving books cover 1773 to 1785. Staff at the East Hampton Library have copied them out and published them. One book runs from April 1, 1773, to November 15, 1779. In 1773 it lists tea at 4 shillings 8 pence a pound, stockings, calico, which is a cotton cloth, linen cloth, gloves, packs of pins, molasses, and large barrels of spirits, a strong liquor.

Townsend's customers paid mostly in cash. Library staff counted the payments in his book from 1773 to 1779. In their count, 73 out of every 100 were cash, 22 were farm goods and 5 were notes, which are written promises to pay. Some customers also paid in work.

### 1800 to 1850

Peddlers carried goods from house to house in the first half of the 1800s, selling to farm families in the country. P.T. Barnum sold tickets to his shows with posters and newspaper advertisements, and he lied in them. His first show was an enslaved woman, Joice Heth, whom he advertised as 161 years old. In 1846, A. T. Stewart opened a store in New York with several floors of goods and a set price on each one.

#### The peddler's trade

A peddler traveled a route through the countryside and sold goods at people's doors. Some went on foot. Others drove a wagon. They carried tinware, clocks, pins, needles, combs, books and patent medicines, which were bottled remedies sold under a brand name. Tinware means pots, pans, cups and other things made of thin sheets of metal coated with tin. The tin peddlers from Connecticut were the best known.

<a id="story-james-guild"></a>

#### James Guild

> **Who:** A Vermont farm boy who set out to peddle with a trunk of goods and wrote down what happened to him.
>
> **When and where:** Tunbridge, Vermont, and the roads beyond it, 1818 to 1824.

James Guild peddled goods from a trunk in 1818 and wrote down what happened to him. He lived in Tunbridge, Vermont, and from the age of 9 he was bound out to work on a farm. Being bound out meant he had to work for a farmer until he turned 21. In the opening pages of his journal, Guild does not say who bound him out. He turned 21 on July 9, 1818. In his own words, "My disposition would not allow me to work on a farm." Disposition here meant his nature, the kind of person he was.

Guild held a note, a written promise that someone would pay him money. He could not turn the note into cash, so he traded it for "a trunk of goods." The first entry in his journal is headed "Tunbridge Oct, 5th 1818." Tunbridge is a town about thirty miles from Montpelier. He felt ashamed of the work. He wondered why he "should stoop so low as to follow so mean a calling." Here mean meant low, and a calling was a trade.

At the houses he visited, he asked, in his own spelling, "do you wish to by some harecombs, needles, buttons, buttonmolds, sewing silk." Customers who wanted to buy "would want to banter until they could get it for nothing." To banter here meant to haggle, or argue over the price.

At first he sold very little. On the road toward the Dog River, he wrote, "I think I traveled 3 days and selling but 30 cent worth of goods." At poor houses that wanted "a needle or a few pins," he gave them away, and he believed he gave away more than he sold. He killed a partridge with a stone and traded it for "a dish of bread and milk." A flood had carried off a bridge, so he crossed the river on a log and fell in with his trunk.

Over the next six years, Guild went from peddling to mending pots and pans as a tinker, then to teaching school, then to painting portraits. In the end he went to London. In 1937 an editor at the Vermont Historical Society printed his journal as *From Tunbridge, Vermont, to London, England*.

<a id="story-pt-barnum-marketplace"></a>

#### P.T. Barnum

> **Who:** A showman who sold tickets through advertising, and whose first paid show was an enslaved woman he put on show under a false claim.
>
> **When and where:** New York City and towns across the Northeast, from 1835.
>
> **Movie:** *The Circus* (2018), a two-part documentary in the *American Experience* series on PBS. It is about the American circus and tells a large part of Barnum's story.

Phineas Taylor Barnum started his career in show business by showing an enslaved woman named Joice Heth to paying crowds. He lied about her age. In 1835 a man named R. W. Lindsay of Kentucky signed a contract to sell Barnum possession of Heth. Possession meant that Barnum now held her. Under the contract, Barnum could show her for ten months. Heth was Black, elderly and blind. Barnum advertised her as George Washington's nurse and said she was 161 years old.

For seven months, Barnum and his partner, Levi Lyman, showed Heth to paying crowds in cities and towns across the Northeast. The two men put her on show in taverns and inns, which were places where people drank, ate and stayed the night, and in museums, railroad buildings and concert halls. To bring in the crowds, they used posters and advertisements in the *New York Sun*. When fewer people came, Barnum wrote a letter to a Boston newspaper without signing his name. In it he claimed that Heth was a machine made of whalebone and old leather, and not a person. People came back to see for themselves.

Joice Heth died in February 1836. Barnum then sold tickets to a dissection of her body. A dissection is the cutting open of a dead body to look at its insides. On February 25, 1836, at the City Saloon in New York, 1,500 people paid 50 cents each to watch. Dr. David L. Rogers, a surgeon, cut open her body. Doctors and medical students were in the crowd. Rogers examined her heart, her lungs, her brain and the places where the bones of her skull join. He decided that she had been no more than 75 years old, or at the most 80.

A humbug is a trick or a false claim made to fool people. Barnum called himself the "Prince of Humbug." He wrote a book called *The Humbugs of the World*. Its copyright is dated 1865, and its title page says 1866. In it he wrote that humbug did not include crimes or swindles, which are tricks to cheat people out of their money.

In 2017 a musical movie about Barnum came out, called *The Greatest Showman*. Its story is mostly made up, and it leaves out Joice Heth.

#### Barnum's American Museum

In 1841 Barnum bought John Scudder's American Museum, at Broadway and Ann Street in New York. A day's ticket cost 25 cents.

In 1842 Barnum showed the Feejee Mermaid there. His advertisements showed pictures of a beautiful creature, half woman and half fish. The object in the museum was the head and upper body of a monkey sewn to the tail of a fish. Large crowds came to see it in New York for about a month.

#### The Marble Palace

Alexander Turney Stewart opened a dry goods store at 280 Broadway in New York on September 21, 1846. Dry goods means cloth, clothing and sewing supplies. The building was faced with Tuckahoe marble, and it became known as the Marble Palace.

Stewart sold goods to shoppers on several floors, and that was new. Before, stores sold to shoppers only on the ground floor. The upper floors were used for wholesale, which is selling goods in bulk to other sellers, or as living space. Stewart also set a standard price on his goods, so that customers did not haggle. He held sales to bring in women customers.

Many writers call the Marble Palace the first American department store. A department store is a large store with many kinds of goods, each kind in its own section, called a department. Definitions of a department store differ, so other writers name Macy's or Wanamaker's as the first. The Marble Palace building still stands. It is now called the Sun Building.

### 1850 to 1900

Between 1850 and 1900, city shoppers and farm families both got new ways to buy. Department store owners such as John Wanamaker made price tags and money-back promises common. Mail-order sellers mailed catalogs to farm families, who could then order goods by mail. The A&P, a chain of stores, started in 1859, and N. W. Ayer & Son, usually called the first advertising agency in the country, started in 1869. Edward Clark, a partner in the Singer sewing machine business, began selling the machines across the whole country on monthly payments.
