Sellers also used advertisements to sell medicines that harmed people. In 1859 a slave dealer advertised the largest recorded sale of people in the United States.

#### Paying a little each month

In 1856 Edward Clark began selling Singer sewing machines on installments. Buying on installments means taking the goods home now and paying for them in small amounts over time. Isaac Singer's company made the machines, and Clark, a lawyer, was Singer's business partner.

In February 1856, Clark announced that customers could trade in any old sewing machine, even a worthless one, for $50 off a new Singer. In September 1856 he began the installment sales. Furniture makers in New York and clock makers in New England had already sold goods this way. Peter Lyon, who wrote the history of Singer's machine for the magazine *American Heritage* in 1958, calls Clark's plan the first time a business selling across the whole country did it. A writer for the magazine *Scientific American* said that a woman "would rather pay $100 for a machine in monthly installments of five dollars" than pay $50 all at once.

A Singer machine that sold for $110 could cost as little as $23 to make.

#### The department store

Macy's department store began as a small dry goods store. Rowland Hussey Macy opened it at Sixth Avenue and 14th Street in New York on October 28, 1858. On the first day he took in $11.06, according to most accounts, or $11.08, according to others. In his first year he took in about $85,000.

John Wanamaker opened a store called the Grand Depot in Philadelphia in 1876. The store stood at Thirteenth Street and Market Street, in a building that had been a freight station of the Pennsylvania Railroad. A freight station is a building where trains load and unload goods.

Wanamaker gets the credit for making three practices common: one price for every customer, a printed price tag on the goods and a promise of money back on anything returned. He was not the first to use all of them. A. T. Stewart had set fixed prices in 1846, and histories of the Wanamaker stores call Wanamaker "one of the first" to use the other two.

With a money-back promise, a customer who bought something poor could return it and get the money back. Montgomery Ward, a mail-order seller, made the same promise to customers who bought goods without seeing them first.

<a id="story-john-wanamaker"></a>

#### John Wanamaker

> **Who:** A Philadelphia merchant who gets the credit for spreading the price tag and the money-back guarantee in American stores.
>
> **When and where:** Philadelphia, from 1861, and the Grand Depot from 1876.

John Wanamaker gets the credit for spreading the one-price rule: every customer paid the price marked on the goods. A. T. Stewart had already set fixed prices in New York in 1846. Before stores like these, customers bargained over prices, as James Guild's customers did when he peddled in Vermont. He opened a store selling men's clothes in Philadelphia in 1861, with his brother-in-law Nathan Brown. In 1876 he turned a railroad freight building into the Grand Depot.

A guarantee is a promise. Wanamaker promised customers their money back on anything they returned. In 1879 he bought a whole page of a newspaper for one advertisement. It was the first full-page newspaper advertisement bought by an American department store.

From 1889 to 1893, Wanamaker was the US Postmaster General, the official in charge of the national mail service. He pushed for rural free delivery, a service in which postal workers carried mail to farm families' homes. Later, mail carriers on those rural routes brought catalogs from mail-order companies, his competitors, to the same farms.

#### People sold at auction: Savannah, 1859

Slave dealers advertised sales of people in the newspapers, the same way sellers advertised goods. Pierce Mease Butler held people in slavery on Georgia plantation land. On March 2 and 3, 1859, he sold between 429 and 436 of them, men, women and children, to pay his gambling debts. The sale took place at the Ten Broeck Race Course, a racetrack near Savannah, Georgia. It was the largest single sale of enslaved people recorded in the United States.

Joseph Bryan, a slave dealer in Savannah, ran the sale. He advertised it for weeks in the Savannah newspapers and in papers in Charleston, Macon, Augusta, Mobile, New Orleans, Memphis and Richmond. The sale brought Butler $303,850. It rained hard on both days.

The terms of the sale stated that people would be sold in families, but only as far as the terms allowed. Under those terms, some husbands and wives could not be bought together. Different buyers bought the husband and the wife, and each buyer took away the person he had paid for. Black Georgians remembered the two days as "the weeping time."

Mortimer Thomson, a reporter for the *New York Tribune*, went to the sale pretending to be a buyer. He wrote a long account of what he saw, and the *Tribune* printed it under the title "What Became of the Slaves on a Georgia Plantation?"

#### Chain stores and the five-cent store

In 1859, George Gilman started a business in New York selling tea and coffee. Most company histories name George Huntington Hartford as his partner from the start. Other accounts say Hartford began by working for Gilman and rose to run the business later. In 1869 the owners named it the Great Atlantic and Pacific Tea Company, to mark the finishing of the first railroad across the country. People called it the A&P. It became a chain store, one of many stores that belong to the same owners and sell the same kinds of goods. The A&P had 70 stores by 1878 and nearly 200 by 1900.

Frank Winfield Woolworth opened a store in Utica, New York, on February 22, 1879. Everything in it cost five cents. The store did well for about two weeks and then failed. On June 21, 1879, he opened another five-cent store in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, and that one succeeded.

#### Advertising agencies and patent medicines

Francis Wayland Ayer started an advertising agency in Philadelphia in 1869, when he was 21. An advertising agency is a business that plans advertisements for sellers and buys space for them in newspapers and magazines. His father, Nathan Wheeler Ayer, gave him $250, and Francis named the business after his father: N. W. Ayer & Son. It is usually called the first advertising agency in the country. Ayer showed his customers what each newspaper charged for space. That way the sellers knew he was working for them and not for the newspapers.

Lydia E. Pinkham's Vegetable Compound, a patent medicine, went on sale in the middle of the 1870s. Its advertisements stated that it cured almost any "female complaint," meaning a health problem of women. Smithsonian museum records and other histories give the mixture as 18 to 20 percent alcohol. Its label stated that the alcohol was there to dissolve and preserve the other ingredients. Pinkham's sons put her picture in the newspaper advertisements. She asked customers to write to her personally, and she used their letters to sell more of the compound.

Jeremiah Curtis and his partner, Benjamin A. Perkins, began selling Mrs. Winslow's Soothing Syrup in 1849. They sold it to mothers to give to babies who were teething, or growing their first teeth. The syrup held alcohol and morphine, about 65 milligrams of morphine in each ounce. Morphine is a strong painkilling drug. It slows a person's breathing, and too much can kill, especially a child. One teaspoon of the syrup held enough morphine to kill an average child. The makers advertised it on recipe cards, in newspapers, on calendars and on trade cards, which were small printed cards given out to customers.

In 1906, members of Congress passed a food and drug law that required makers to list the drugs in their medicines on the label. Some time after that law, the makers of Mrs. Winslow's syrup took out the morphine and dropped the word "soothing" from its name. In 1911, the American Medical Association, the national organization of doctors, printed a book called *Nostrums and Quackery*. A nostrum is a fake cure, and quackery is selling fake medicine. The book listed Mrs. Winslow's syrup under the heading "Baby Killers." No one counted how many children the morphine in the syrup killed.

#### Mail order reaches the farm

On August 18, 1872, Aaron Montgomery Ward mailed his first catalog from Chicago. Mail order means choosing goods from a printed list, called a catalog, and ordering them by mail. Ward's first catalog was one sheet of paper. According to the Chicago History Museum, it listed 163 items. The reference work Encyclopedia.com gives about 150.

Late in 1872, leaders of the Illinois Grange, an organization of farmers, made Ward their buyer. His catalog grew to 32 pages in 1874 and to 152 pages in 1876, with about 3,000 items.

In 1886 Richard Warren Sears, a railroad station agent in Minnesota, began selling watches. A station agent was the railroad worker in charge of a station. He moved his watch business to Chicago. There he worked with a watchmaker, Alvah Roebuck. In 1893 their company became Sears, Roebuck and Company, and that year its catalog ran to 196 pages.

Many city people had their mail brought to their homes for free from 1863. Before 1896, farm families had to pick up their mail at the post office. A Postal Service history describes farmers who had to unhitch the horse from the plow and go five or six miles into town to get it. On October 1, 1896, postal workers began bringing mail to farm families' homes in West Virginia. The first three routes started from Charles Town, Halltown and Uvilla. This service was called rural free delivery. Within a year, 44 routes were running in 29 states.

<a id="story-aaron-montgomery-ward"></a>

#### Aaron Montgomery Ward

> **Who:** A traveling salesman who worked out that a farm family could buy from a printed list instead of from a country store.
>
> **When and where:** Chicago, from August 18, 1872.

Aaron Montgomery Ward built his mail-order business on a complaint he heard from farmers about their country stores. From 1865 he worked as a clerk at the Chicago store that later became Marshall Field's. Then he worked for a wholesale dry goods company, Willis, Gregg and Brown. After that he traveled as a salesman for Walter M. Smith and Company, a St. Louis company that sold goods in bulk to stores.

On the road, Ward heard the farmers' main complaint. Country general stores charged high prices and had few goods to choose from. The farmers also blamed the middlemen, the sellers between the maker and the buyer, for taking too much profit. Ward's plan was to buy straight from the factories, pay cash and sell straight to customers by mail.

The Chicago Fire of 1871 destroyed Ward's savings. In 1872 he started over with $1,600 of his own and $800 from his brother-in-law, George R. Thorne.

On November 8, 1873, the *Chicago Tribune* printed an article headed "Grangers, Beware!" The article described Montgomery Ward & Co. as a "swindling firm" that hid behind a post-office box. Ward sued the *Tribune* for libel and asked for $20,000. Libel is printing something false that harms a person's name. On December 24, 1873, the editors of the *Tribune* printed a notice taking back the charge. In it they called Ward's company "a bona fide firm, composed of respectable persons, and doing a perfectly legitimate business." Bona fide means real.

Ward promised that customers could send goods back for their money. His 1875 catalog included the words "satisfaction guaranteed or your money back." The Encyclopedia.com entry on Ward dates the promise a year earlier, to 1874. When he died in 1913, his company sold $40 million worth of goods a year and had 6,000 workers.

<a id="story-richard-sears"></a>

#### Richard Sears

> **Who:** A railroad station agent who started by selling watches and went on to build the Sears catalog.
>
> **When and where:** Minnesota in 1886, then Chicago.
>
> **Movie:** *Mr. Sears' Catalogue* (1989), a documentary in the *American Experience* series on PBS, about Richard Sears and his catalog.

Richard Sears began his business with a shipment of watches that someone else refused. He was born on December 7, 1863, in Stewartville, Minnesota. In 1886 he was a station agent for the Minneapolis and St. Paul Railroad, at North Redwood, Minnesota. That is the station *Encyclopaedia Britannica* names. The Encyclopedia.com entry names Redwood Falls, the town next to North Redwood. He was 22 when the year began and 23 by its end.

That year a jeweler refused a shipment of watches that came to Sears's station. Sears got permission to sell the watches himself. He sold them to other station agents along the line for $14 each. Then he quit the railroad and started the R. W. Sears Watch Company in Minneapolis. He moved the business to Chicago, where he hired a watchmaker, Alvah C. Roebuck, to repair watches that customers sent back.

Sears wrote the words in the catalog himself. At its biggest, the Sears catalog ran to about 1,500 pages and listed about 100,000 items. The documentary *Mr. Sears' Catalogue* states that it went to about 20 million people at its height. The company's own counts and later accounts differ, so these figures are estimates.

Sears resigned as president of the company in 1908 or 1909. *Encyclopaedia Britannica* gives 1908, and Encyclopedia.com gives 1909. He died on September 28, 1914.

<a id="story-persis-albee"></a>

#### Persis Foster Eames Albee

> **Who:** The first woman to sell door to door for the company that later became Avon.
>
> **When and where:** Winchester, New Hampshire, and across the Northeast, from 1886.

Persis Foster Eames Albee was 50 years old in 1886 when David McConnell hired her to sell perfume door to door. McConnell had sold books from house to house. He gave away perfume as a free gift with the books, and he found that customers liked the perfume more than the books. He started a perfume company, the California Perfume Company. It later became Avon.

Albee lived in Winchester, New Hampshire. She became the company's first General Traveling Agent. She sold the Little Dot Perfume Set, which held five scents: violet, white rose, hyacinth, lily of the valley and heliotrope, a small purple flower. She sold it from house to house in Cheshire County, New Hampshire, and then across the Northeast. She also found other women to sell for the company and trained them.

Most of what is known about Albee comes from Avon's own history of itself.

In 1886, women in most of the United States could not vote. Women did vote in three western territories, lands that were not yet states: Wyoming from 1869, Utah from 1870 and Washington from 1883. In 1887, lawmakers in Congress took the vote away from women in Utah, and judges on Washington's highest court struck down that territory's law. Wyoming became a state in 1890, and its women kept the vote.

In 1920, 34 years after Albee started selling, the Nineteenth Amendment became part of the Constitution. An amendment is a change added to the Constitution. This one states that no state and no federal official may keep a citizen from voting because of whether the citizen is a man or a woman.

### 1900 to 1950

Chain stores grew fast between 1900 and 1950. A chain is a group of stores with the same owners and the same name. One grocery chain, the A&P, went from about 200 stores in 1900 to about 15,000 in 1930. Grocers began letting customers take goods off the shelves themselves. Families bought cars and radios on monthly payments. Sellers began paying radio and television stations to carry their advertisements into people's homes. In coal towns, coal companies paid miners in their own company money, which only the company's own store took at full value. During the Second World War, shoppers needed ration stamps from the government as well as money to buy many foods.

#### The chain store at full size

The A&P had 1,600 stores by 1915. By 1930 it had about 15,000 stores and sold $2.9 billion worth of goods a year. That made it the largest retailer in the world. A retailer is a seller who sells goods to the people who use them. The A&P was the largest grocery seller in the United States from 1915 to 1975.

Woolworth's stores had lunch counters, where customers sat and ate. In the South, the people who ran these counters served white customers only. Later, on February 1, 1960, four Black students from North Carolina A&T, a college in Greensboro, North Carolina, sat down at the Woolworth counter there and asked to be served. They were Ezell Blair Jr., Franklin McCain, Joseph McNeil and David Richmond. The counter staff refused to serve them. Hundreds of people joined their protest over the next six months. On July 25, 1960, the manager of the lunch counter picked three Black workers from the store's kitchen. He told them to get dressed, walk around the store like customers and then sit at the counter. One of them, Geneva Tisdale, ordered an egg-salad sandwich. In Tisdale's own telling, the three of them were chosen as the first Black people to eat at that counter.

<a id="story-frank-woolworth"></a>

#### F. W. Woolworth

> **Who:** The storekeeper who built a national chain of five-cent and ten-cent stores and paid cash for the tallest building in the world.
>
> **When and where:** Utica and Lancaster, 1879, and New York, 1911 to 1913.

Frank Winfield Woolworth turned his five-cent stores of 1879 into the largest store company in the world. On November 12, 1911, he signed agreements to join his chain with four rival chains. They were the Knox, Kirby, Charlton and C. S. Woolworth chains. The new F. W. Woolworth Company started with 596 stores and $65 million in capital, which is the money put into a business to run it. The new company was formally set up in 1912, so some histories give that year as its start.

In 1913 the Woolworth Building was finished in New York. At 792 feet, it was the tallest building in the world at the time. It cost $13.5 million, and Woolworth paid for it himself, in cash.

#### Self-service

In a self-service store, customers pick goods off the shelves themselves instead of asking a clerk to fetch them. Clarence Saunders opened the first Piggly Wiggly store at 79 Jefferson Street in Memphis, Tennessee, on September 6, 1916. Some accounts give the date as September 11. Customers came in through a turnstile, a gate with turning arms that lets one person through at a time. Then they had to follow a single fenced path past every shelf in the store before they reached the place where they paid.

Saunders asked the government for a patent on his "Self-Serving Store" on October 21, 1916. A patent is a government paper that lets only the inventor use an invention for a number of years. He received Patent 1,242,872 on October 9, 1917.

King Kullen opened in Jamaica, in Queens, New York, on August 4, 1930. Michael J. Cullen started it. He had worked for the Kroger grocery company and had sent its managers a plan for a supermarket, which they ignored. By the account of the Smithsonian, the national museum in Washington, King Kullen was the first supermarket. It met the museum's five tests: separate departments, self-service, low prices, many stores under one name and buying goods in huge amounts. Cullen's slogan, a short phrase repeated in advertising, was "Pile it high. Sell it low."

<a id="story-clarence-saunders"></a>

#### Clarence Saunders

> **Who:** The Memphis grocer who started self-service shopping and then lost his company fighting traders on Wall Street.
>
> **When and where:** Memphis, Tennessee, 1916 to 1923, and later stores. He died in 1953.

Clarence Saunders built Piggly Wiggly into a chain of 1,268 stores and then lost it in a fight over its stock. By 1923 the stores sold $100 million worth of groceries a year. Piggly Wiggly was the third-largest grocery business in the country. Saunders had put the company's stock up for sale on the New York Stock Exchange, a market where people buy and sell shares. A share of stock is a small piece of ownership in a company.

The Tennessee Encyclopedia and writers on the history of money and business tell the fight this way. In early 1923, some Piggly Wiggly stores in New York that other owners ran under the Piggly Wiggly name failed. Traders then began selling Piggly Wiggly stock short. Selling short is a bet that a stock's price will fall. The trader sells borrowed shares and plans to buy them back later at a lower price.

Saunders fought back. He borrowed about $10 million from bankers in the South, added his own money and kept buying shares. In the end he held orders for 196,000 of the 200,000 shares that existed. Then the men who ran the Stock Exchange stopped trading in the stock and gave the short sellers more time to pay. Within months Saunders was bankrupt, which means he could not pay his debts, and he was out of the company.

He started again with a new chain called the "Clarence Saunders, Sole Owner of My Name" stores. They did well until the 1930s, when they failed during the Great Depression, the years of hard times that began in 1929. Later he built the Keedoozle, a grocery store that worked like a vending machine. It never made a profit. Saunders died on October 15, 1953.

#### The company store

Many coal companies in Appalachia owned the store in their mining towns and paid their miners mostly in scrip instead of dollars. Scrip was the company's own money, made as metal coins or paper. A miner could draw scrip against pay he had already earned. The company store took it at full value, but the company would not trade it for cash. Other merchants nearby took scrip only at a discount of 10 to 30 percent. That meant a miner who spent $1 of scrip at another store got only 70 to 90 cents' worth of goods.

In 1922 researchers for the US Coal Commission, a government group that studied the coal industry, checked prices in coal towns. In southern West Virginia, company stores charged 4.2 percent more for food than independent stores. In Alabama they charged 7 percent more. The economist Price Fishback later studied these numbers. An economist is a scholar who studies how money, work and business fit together. He found that most companies did not let a miner's store debt run longer than two weeks.

A page by the West Virginia Mine Wars Museum describes scrip differently. It states that scrip "created a kind of debt bondage that kept coal miners and their families tied to their employer for almost everything they needed to survive." Debt bondage means being forced to keep working to pay off a debt. Fishback found small price gaps and short debts. The museum calls the system debt bondage.

In 1891, West Virginia lawmakers passed a law that let companies give out scrip only as pay for work already done or as an advance on wages. In 1925 they made it against the law to pass scrip from one person to another. Scrip disappeared when the coal industry collapsed in the 1950s.

#### The catalog under Jim Crow

Jim Crow is the name for the laws and customs in the South under which white lawmakers and officials kept Black people apart from white people in schools, railroad cars, waiting rooms, courtrooms and cemeteries, and at water fountains. White mobs enforced it with murder. Between 1877 and 1950, white mobs lynched more than 4,400 Black people, by the count of the Equal Justice Initiative. To lynch means for a mob to kill a person without any trial. Louis Hyman, a historian at Cornell University, argued in 2018 that mail-order catalogs helped Black farm families in the South get around Jim Crow at the store. His argument was reported by NPR, the *Washington Post* and America's Black Holocaust Museum.

According to Hyman, many Black farm families had to buy on credit, taking goods now and paying later, at a white-owned country store, often owned by the landlord whose land they farmed. The storekeeper set the prices and made Black customers wait until white customers were served. A catalog order cost the same national price for everyone, and no clerk decided who was served first. The family could also buy on the mail-order company's credit instead of the landlord's.

Hyman also says that some Southern storekeepers held bonfires to burn catalogs, and told white customers that Sears was owned by Black people to keep them from buying there. These are Hyman's claims.

#### Buying on time

In the 1920s, buying on installments, which means paying for goods a little at a time, spread from sewing machines to cars, radios, furniture and household machines. By the end of the 1920s, about 60 percent of cars and about 80 percent of radios were bought on installments, according to the reference site Encyclopedia.com. The number of cars registered in the United States grew from about 9 million in 1920 to nearly 27 million by 1929.

In 1924 members of the National Association of Finance Companies, a group of lending companies, adopted standard terms for car buyers. A buyer paid one-third of the price at the start for a new car and two-fifths for a used car. The buyer then had no more than twelve months to pay the rest.

#### Advertising on radio and television

The first paid radio advertisement went on the air on August 28, 1922, on the station WEAF in New York. The Queensboro Corporation paid $50 for about ten minutes of air time to promote the Hawthorne Court apartments in Jackson Heights, Queens.

Television stations were not allowed to sell advertising until officials of the Federal Communications Commission, the government office that licenses stations, gave licenses to 10 stations on May 2, 1941. The licenses let the stations sell advertising from July 1, 1941. Two years earlier, people at NBC had shown test advertisements for three companies. The first commercial allowed under the new licenses ran on the station WNBT in New York on July 1, 1941, before a Brooklyn Dodgers baseball game against the Philadelphia Phillies. For about ten seconds it showed the face of a Bulova watch over a map of the United States, while a voice said, "America runs on Bulova time." It cost Bulova $9: $4 for the air time and $5 in station charges. There were about 4,000 television sets in the New York area at the time.

Mary Frances Gerety wrote advertisements at N. W. Ayer & Son, the advertising agency. For the diamond company De Beers, she wrote the slogan "A Diamond Is Forever." Accounts of the slogan date it to 1947 or to 1949. In 1999 the magazine *Ad Age* named it the most memorable slogan of the 1900s.

#### Shopping under rationing

During the Second World War, officials of the US government's Office of Price Administration ran rationing. To ration means to limit how much of something each person may buy. Sugar, meat, cheese, fats, canned and other processed foods, shoes and gasoline were among the rationed goods. At the start, each person could buy 26 pounds of sugar a year, about 8 ounces a week. Every person in the country, babies included, got a ration book full of stamps.

War Ration Book Two came into use on March 1, 1943. Its blue stamps bought processed foods, which are canned, dried or frozen foods. Its red stamps bought meat, cheese, fats and oils. Each person got 48 blue points and 64 red points a month, so a family of four had 192 blue points a month for processed food. Every cut of almost every kind of meat had its own point value.

At the store a shopper paid with stamps and with money together. The price could not go above the ceiling price, the highest price government officials allowed. Point values changed often. Newspaper editors printed them, radio announcers read them out and members of local ration boards posted them. By the end of the war, more than 100,000 volunteers were running the program through about 5,600 local boards.

<a id="story-emilia-lundberg"></a>

#### Emilia Ruth Palmquist Lundberg

> **Who:** A widowed mother of six in Jersey City who shopped for her family with ration books during the Second World War.
>
> **When and where:** Jersey City, New Jersey, about 1942 to 1943.

Emilia Lundberg fed six children on a small, fixed income, and during the war she also had to count ration stamps. She was born in Göteborg, Sweden, in 1894. In 1930 her husband was killed in an explosion at the dry-cleaning plant where he was in charge. As her son Donald remembered it, his father left her with six children, no relatives to turn to and no money.

She raised the children on workmen's compensation of $100 a month. Workmen's compensation is money paid to a worker's family after the worker is hurt or killed on the job. The rent was $35 a month. Her oldest daughter, 16, moved to night school and took a job keeping accounts for $12 a week. Donald packed and delivered groceries at a store after school and on Saturdays for $5 a week.

Before the war, the family ate a roast on Sunday after church and potatoes and macaroni the rest of the week. Under rationing, everyone in the family had a ration book with stamps for meat and other goods. They took the books to the store and bought what the stamps allowed. The ration was counted for each person, so a large family got more in all than a small one. They bought meat for Sunday and ate macaroni, spaghetti and mashed potatoes the rest of the week. Shoes were rationed too. Each child had one good pair for school and one pair of sneakers for play.

Emilia had a 1933 Plymouth. Donald remembered the family's gasoline ration as about a gallon and a half. When they told the ration board they were driving to visit his older brother, a soldier at Camp Kilmer in New Jersey, they got a coupon for about two more gallons. Donald described all of this in an interview for the Rutgers Oral History Archives in 2008, about 65 years later.

### 1950 to 2000

The first fully enclosed shopping mall in the United States opened in Minnesota in 1956. Plastic cards issued by banks let shoppers buy on credit in any store that took the card. Kmart, Target and Wal-Mart all opened their first stores in 1962. In 1974 a cashier in Troy, Ohio, made the first sale with a scanner that read a printed code on a package. By 2000, people could shop at home on television shopping channels, and from 1995 on a computer.

#### The enclosed mall

Southdale Center opened in Edina, Minnesota, on October 8, 1956. It was the first fully enclosed shopping mall in the United States with its own heating and cooling. A mall is a group of stores under one roof or around one walkway. It had 72 stores on two levels around a brightly lit central court. Its two biggest stores were the department stores Dayton's and Donaldson's.

The Dayton family owned department stores in Minneapolis. In 1952 they hired the architect Victor Gruen and his firm, Victor Gruen & Associates, to design the mall. Building began in 1954. Southdale cost $20 million.

<a id="story-victor-gruen"></a>

#### Victor Gruen

> **Who:** The architect who designed the first enclosed American mall and later rejected what developers built from his idea.
>
> **When and where:** Vienna, then New York and Minnesota. Southdale opened October 8, 1956.
>
> **Movie:** *The Gruen Effect: Victor Gruen and the Shopping Mall* (2009), a documentary by Anette Baldauf and Katharina Weingartner, about Gruen and the malls he started.

Victor Gruen designed Southdale as the center of a new neighborhood, and developers copied only the mall. Gruen was a Jewish architect from Vienna, in Austria. In March 1938 the leaders of Nazi Germany, the Germany ruled by Adolf Hitler's Nazi Party, took over Austria and made it part of Germany. The takeover was called the Anschluss. In the weeks after, Austrian Nazis and others beat, attacked and humiliated Jews. In Vienna, Nazis forced Jews to scrub the city's streets while crowds jeered at them. Soon Nazi officials put Austria's Jews under the same laws that already took away Jewish rights in Germany. Gruen fled Vienna that year. He reached New York on the ship *Statendam* with an architect's degree, eight dollars and no English.

One of his early jobs was a shop front on Fifth Avenue in New York, for Ludwig Lederer's leather-goods shop. Gruen designed its entrance as an arcade, a covered walkway, meant as a "customer trap" to draw people inside.

For Southdale, the Dayton company bought about 500 acres of land in Edina. Gruen's plan for the land around the mall had apartment buildings, houses, schools, a medical center, a park and a lake. He said he wanted "the Minneapolis downtown you would get if you started over and corrected all the mistakes." The medical center opened in 1965. The Daytons sold the rest of the land for housing.

In a speech in London in 1978, Gruen rejected the malls that American developers had built. He said he refused to pay alimony for those developments, and he used a rude word to describe them. Alimony is money that a person pays to a former husband or wife after a divorce. He went back to Vienna and objected to a shopping center built there.

#### Plastic at the counter

A credit card lets a person buy now and pay the bank or the card company later. A charge card is a card whose holder has to pay the whole bill every month. Diners Club, started in February 1950, was the first charge card that many different businesses accepted. It was made of cardboard. The first place it was used was Major's Cabin Grill, a restaurant in New York. The company's first publicity man, Matty Simmons, later admitted that the famous story of how the card began, with a founder who forgot his wallet, was made up for publicity.

In September 1958, officers of Bank of America mailed about 60,000 BankAmericards to people in Fresno, California, who had not asked for them. The cards were ready to use. Each cardholder got $300 to $500 of credit at once. Stores that took the card paid the bank 6 percent of each sale. The bank's officers had expected about 4 percent of cardholders to fall behind on paying. About 22 percent did. The bank's officers later licensed the card across the country, and in 1976 it was renamed Visa.

In 1970, members of Congress passed a law that banned mailing credit cards to people who had not asked for them.

Before 1974, lenders often turned women down for credit because they were women, or because they were married or single. Mortgage lenders, who lend money to buy houses, often counted only part of a married woman's pay, especially if she was young enough to have children. They were also more likely to turn down single women. Lawmakers in Congress passed the Equal Credit Opportunity Act in October 1974. Under it, lenders could no longer treat people differently because of their sex or whether they were married. Two years later, in March 1976, the lawmakers added more reasons lenders could not use: race, color, religion, national origin, which means the country a person or their family came from, age, and getting money from government aid programs.

#### 1962: the discount stores

A discount store is a store that sells goods at prices below what other stores charge. Four discount chains began in 1962. The first Kmart store opened in Garden City, Michigan, on March 1, 1962, and reports said 4,000 customers waited in line on the first day. Target's first store followed on May 1, in Roseville, Minnesota. On July 2, Sam Walton opened the first Wal-Mart in Rogers, Arkansas. Woolco's first store opened that year too.

Kmart grew out of the S. S. Kresge chain of five-and-dime stores, which sold small goods for 5 and 10 cents, and Woolco out of F. W. Woolworth's company. Target grew out of the Dayton Company's department stores, run by the same Dayton family that had hired Victor Gruen to design Southdale.

<a id="story-sam-walton"></a>

#### Sam Walton

> **Who:** The Arkansas storekeeper who put discount stores in small towns and built the largest retailer in the United States.
>
> **When and where:** Rogers, Arkansas, from July 2, 1962.
>
> **Movie:** *Wal-Mart: The High Cost of Low Price* (2005), a documentary by Robert Greenwald. It argues against the company and is not a life story of Walton.

Sam Walton built Walmart, spelled Wal-Mart at first, by opening discount stores in small towns. The heads of the large chains had judged those towns too small to bother with. Before 1962 Walton ran Ben Franklin variety stores in Arkansas, which sold many kinds of small, cheap goods. He bought goods in huge amounts and priced them below the stores nearby. Walmart became the largest retailer in the United States and the largest private employer, which means it had more workers than any other company.

Economists have measured what Walmart did to shoppers and to towns. Jerry Hausman of MIT and Ephraim Leibtag of the US Department of Agriculture reported in 2007 that shoppers gained a great deal from Walmart's low prices, most of all households with lower incomes.

David Neumark, Junfu Zhang and Stephen Ciccarella reported in 2008 that when a Walmart opened, the county around it lost about 150 retail jobs, or 2.7 percent. By their count, each Walmart worker replaced about 1.4 workers at other stores. Kenneth Stone, an economist at Iowa State University, has studied Walmart in Iowa since 1988. In a 2012 study, Stone and a co-author found that retail sales in Iowa towns with fewer than 2,500 people fell 30 percent in the years after Walmart stores opened in Iowa. That was about $1.5 billion. Towns of 3,000 to 20,000 people that got a Walmart saw their total retail sales rise.

#### The franchise

A franchise is a deal in which the owner of a business name and its way of working sells other people the right to run a business under that name, following the owner's rules. Roy Allen bought a recipe for root beer in 1919. He began selling A&W franchises in 1924, or in 1925 by some accounts. Histories of franchising often call A&W the first successful food franchise. J. Willard Marriott was one of its early franchise owners.

The Howard Johnson's restaurant business sold its first franchise to Reginald Sprague in 1935. By the end of 1936 there were 41 Howard Johnson's restaurants. By 1939 there were 107, with about $10.5 million in sales.

#### The barcode

The Universal Product Code, or UPC, is the barcode printed on packages in stores. A barcode is a pattern of printed stripes that a scanner at the checkout can read.

The people who planned the first scan chose a small pack of gum on purpose. They wanted to show that the code could be printed clearly on a package that size. The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History keeps one of the first ten scanners, a Spectra-Physics Model A.

<a id="story-sharon-buchanan"></a>

#### Sharon Buchanan

> **Who:** The supermarket cashier who made the first sale ever scanned with a barcode.
>
> **When and where:** Marsh Supermarket, Troy, Ohio, 8:01 a.m., June 26, 1974.

Sharon Buchanan was the cashier at the first sale ever made with a barcode scanner. At 8:01 in the morning on June 26, 1974, she was working at the Marsh Supermarket in Troy, Ohio. The customer was Clyde Dawson, the head of research and development at Marsh. He bought a ten-pack of Wrigley's Juicy Fruit gum. Buchanan passed it over the scanner. The price was 67 cents.

#### Stamps, television selling and the end of the big catalog

In the 1960s and 1970s, about 80 percent of American households collected S&H Green Stamps. Trading stamps were small stamps that grocery stores, gas stations and other stores gave out with purchases. Shoppers pasted them into books. They traded full books for goods at a Green Stamps store or from a catalog. In the 1960s more S&H stamps were printed than US postage stamps, and about 35 million S&H catalogs went out each year.

The Home Shopping Network began with a radio station. In 1977 a company that advertised on Lowell "Bud" Paxson's radio station paid him in electric can openers instead of money. The station's host, Bob Circosta, sold them on the air for $9.95 each. In 1982 Paxson and Roy Speer started the Home Shopping Club on cable television in Pinellas County, Florida. It went national on July 1, 1985. Joe Segel founded QVC, another shopping channel, in 1986. It first went on the air that November, and the first thing it sold was a radio made to be used in the shower.

On January 25, 1993, Sears officials announced that they were closing the company's catalog business. They also said they would cut 50,000 jobs and close 113 stores. The last general catalog went out that spring. News reports said the catalog was 97 years old. Other accounts say 101 or 105 years, because they count from different starting dates.

#### Buying on a computer begins

On July 5, 1994, Jeff Bezos filed papers to start a company called Cadabra, Inc. He worked from a rented house with a garage in Bellevue, Washington. The company became Amazon. Amazon.com opened for orders on July 16, 1995. The first book it sold was *Fluid Concepts and Creative Analogies*, by Douglas Hofstadter. In its first week it took in about $12,000 in book orders.

Pierre Omidyar started a website called AuctionWeb, where people sold goods at auction to whoever offered the most money. He started it over Labor Day weekend, on September 3, 1995. It later became eBay. The first thing sold on it went for $14.83. According to eBay, it was a broken laser pointer. Some accounts say it was a broken printer.

### 2000 to Today

From April to June 2026, about one dollar in six of all American retail spending went to online sales, by the count of the US Census Bureau. Since 2005, members of Amazon Prime have paid a yearly fee for two-day shipping. Drivers carry the orders to people's doors, including on days of summer heat. Sellers now buy the right to show advertisements to one person at a time, chosen from records of what that person has done online.

#### How big online shopping is

Every three months, workers at the US Census Bureau publish a count of online sales. In 2025, online sales were 16.4 percent of all retail sales in the United States. In the second quarter of 2026, from April through June, they were 17.1 percent. That came to $340.2 billion in three months. It was 12.2 percent more than in the same months of 2025. The bureau's staff released those numbers on August 18, 2026. By those numbers, more than four dollars in five were still spent in stores.

Researchers at the Federal Reserve, the central bank of the United States, which acts as a bank for other banks, ask people to keep diaries of how they pay. In 2024, credit cards were the most-used way to pay in the United States, used for 35 percent of all payments. Cash was used for 14 percent.

<a id="story-jeff-bezos"></a>

#### Jeff Bezos

> **Who:** The founder of Amazon, which began as an online bookstore and grew into a store selling books, music, movies and many other kinds of goods.
>
> **When and where:** Bellevue and Seattle, Washington, from July 1994.
>
> **Movie:** *Amazon Empire: The Rise and Reign of Jeff Bezos* (2020), a documentary by James Jacoby and Anya Bourg in the PBS series *Frontline*. It is an investigation that argues a case against Amazon's power.

Jeff Bezos left a job in New York in 1994 to sell books online. He was a vice president at D. E. Shaw, an investment company. In 1994 he read that use of the web had been growing by 2,300 percent a year that spring, and he quit. He and his wife, MacKenzie Bezos, moved from Manhattan to the Seattle area. They chose it because software engineers lived and worked there, at Microsoft and the University of Washington, and because of its taxes. Bezos studied which product would sell best online, and he chose books. Music and DVDs were the next goods Amazon added.

Amazon Prime began on February 2, 2005. According to Amazon's announcement, members paid $79 a year and got two-day shipping on their orders at no extra charge. By 2021, more than 200 million people around the world were members. In 2026 a year of Prime in the United States cost $139, or $14.99 a month, the same as since February 2022, according to the shopping news site dealnews.

Senate committee staff, drivers and a union have complained about how Amazon treats the people who pack and deliver its orders. In December 2024, the staff of a Senate committee led by Senator Bernie Sanders reported that in 2023 Amazon had recorded more than 30 percent more injuries at its warehouses than the average for the warehouse industry. A union is a group that workers form to bargain together with their employer. In June 2023, Amazon ended its contract with a delivery company two months after the company's drivers joined a union. The union and the company's owner said Amazon was punishing the drivers for it. Amazon's representatives said the contract ended over safety violations and missed insurance payments.

#### Malls empty out

Nobody keeps an official government count of malls, and the private counts disagree, because people define a mall in different ways. One industry count lists about 700 enclosed malls in 2023. A broader count, which includes open-air shopping centers, lists about 1,150 for 2024.

One company counts store closings every year. Researchers at Coresight Research, a company that studies stores, counted 7,325 store closings in the United States in 2024 and later raised that count to 8,825. They had predicted about 15,000 closings for 2025. Their count for 2025, published in January 2026, was 8,270 closings and 5,270 openings.

As shoppers moved online or to newer outdoor shopping centers, the anchor department stores of many malls closed. An anchor store is a big store that draws shoppers to the smaller shops around it. The smaller shops that had depended on the department stores' crowds lost customers. Mall owners could not find new stores to fill the empty space. Owners and builders have turned some empty malls into apartments, clinics, colleges and warehouses.

#### Advertising aimed at one person

When a person visits a website, the company that runs the site can save small files and codes on the person's device that record what the person looked at. Companies called data brokers collect records like these and combine them with records from outside the internet, such as store purchases, warranty cards and property records. Then they sell what they have gathered, including the chance to show an advertisement to a chosen group of people.

In May 2014 the staff of the Federal Trade Commission, the government office that protects shoppers, published a report called *Data Brokers: A Call for Transparency and Accountability*. The commission's staff found that data brokers held "billions of data elements," meaning billions of separate facts, about nearly every American shopper. They gathered most of it without people knowing. The report describes how brokers attached offline records to the files in a person's web browser. That way the person could be followed from site to site and shown advertisements chosen for them. The commissioners asked Congress to pass a law letting people see the information held about them.

Website and app owners use money from this advertising to keep their services free to use. The advertisements can also show a person something they want to buy. And companies the person has never heard of buy and sell records of what the person reads and buys. As of 2026, members of Congress had passed no general federal privacy law. By June 29, 2026, lawmakers in 24 states had passed their own, according to the law firm Husch Blackwell.

#### Selling to children inside a game

Fortnite is a video game made by Epic Games that came out in 2017. It is free to play. Epic sells V-Bucks, game money that players buy with real money to get costumes and dance moves for their characters. By 2022, the game had more than 400 million players around the world, according to the Federal Trade Commission.

On December 19, 2022, officials of the Federal Trade Commission announced that Epic had agreed to pay $520 million. Of that, $275 million was a penalty under the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act. That law requires a company to get a parent's permission before it collects personal information from a child under 13. The commission's officials said Epic had collected personal information from children under 13 who played Fortnite without telling their parents or getting their permission. They also said Epic let children buy V-Bucks just by pressing buttons, with no parent or card owner agreeing. The other $245 million went back to customers as refunds. The officials said Epic had used "dark patterns," confusing buttons and screens that led players into charges they did not mean to make. For example, Epic's game could charge a player who was only waking it from sleep mode. The officials cited "hundreds of millions of dollars in unauthorized charges," meaning charges that players had not agreed to. Lina Khan was the head of the commission at the time.

#### Payday loans

A payday loan is a small loan from a storefront lender that the borrower is supposed to pay back on the next payday. In April 2013, researchers at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, a government office that watches over lenders, published a study of these loans. They found that storefront payday lenders charged $10 to $20 for every $100 borrowed. The typical loan lasted 14 days. A borrower who took the typical $350 loan, with a fee of $15 for each $100, had to find more than $400 in two weeks. Counted as a yearly rate, the way the cost of a loan is measured, that fee comes to 391 percent a year.

They also found that nearly half of payday borrowers took out more than 10 loans in a year. Fourteen percent took out 20 or more. The typical borrower was in debt 199 days of the year, more than half of it.

#### Buying secondhand clothes

The staff of ThredUp, a company that sells used clothes online, publish a yearly report on the market for secondhand clothes. Because ThredUp sells used clothes, its report is a company's estimate, not a government count.

By ThredUp's 2025 report, the market for used clothes in the United States grew 14 percent in 2024, and online sales of used clothes grew 23 percent. In 2024, 58 percent of shoppers bought something secondhand, up from 52 percent in 2023. The firm GlobalData did the research for ThredUp's 2026 report, which found that in 2025 used clothing sales grew almost four times as fast as all clothing sales. GlobalData's researchers forecast that the US secondhand market will reach $78.8 billion by 2030.

#### The last step: heat in the delivery truck

The drivers who make fast delivery possible keep delivering in summer heat. In July 2023, the NPR reporter Danielle Kaye reported that injury records kept by OSHA, the government's workplace safety office, showed at least 40 UPS drivers taken to the hospital for heat illness since 2015.

José Cruz Rodriguez was 23. He died of heat illness during a UPS delivery shift in Waco, Texas, in August 2021, according to OSHA. Heat illness happens when the body gets too hot and cannot cool itself down. His family sued UPS for causing his death, and the case was settled.

Esteban Chavez Jr., a UPS driver for four years, died after he was found unconscious in his truck. It was June 25, 2022, the day after his 24th birthday, and he was on his route in Pasadena, California. The temperature that day reached the upper 90s. UPS trucks had no air conditioning then. His family said at least 20 minutes went by before anyone noticed him and called for help. The medical examiner, the doctor whose job is to find out why a person died, found that his heart stopped working. His family believes the heat caused it.

In June 2023, UPS managers and leaders of the Teamsters union, which represents UPS drivers, agreed that every small delivery truck UPS bought after January 1, 2024, would have air conditioning. The trucks would also get heat shields and fans.

The packages are packed in warehouses first. In December 2024, Senator Bernie Sanders released a report by staff of the Senate committee he led. These staff members work for the party that holds the most seats in the Senate. They found that in 2023 Amazon recorded more than 30 percent more injuries at its warehouses than the average for the warehouse industry. For seven years in a row, Amazon warehouse workers were nearly twice as likely to be hurt as workers at other warehouses. The report said Amazon had drawn up plans to lower injuries and chose not to use them because the plans would slow down work.

<a id="story-renica-turner"></a>

#### Renica Turner

> **Who:** A driver who delivered Amazon packages in the California desert for a small delivery company, and who joined a union to push for protection from the heat.
>
> **When and where:** Palmdale and Victorville, California, about 2022 to 2023.

Renica Turner delivered Amazon packages for a company called Battle Tested Strategies. It was one of about 3,000 small companies under contract to deliver Amazon's packages. Its vans were leased from Amazon, and its drivers worked out of an Amazon building in Palmdale, California.

In a July 2023 story by the NPR reporter Danielle Kaye, Turner described a day in Victorville, California, when the temperature reached 110 degrees. The van's air conditioning and fans were not working, she said. When she rolled the windows down, hot air came in. Her body began to tingle, and she thought she might pass out. She told the Amazon dispatcher, the worker who sends drivers out and keeps track of them. The dispatcher gave her a 20-minute break. In her words, "They never sent no one out to help me with the rest of the route." The route was 300 packages, and she was expected to deliver 25 every hour. She finished it herself, feeling woozy and numb.

Amazon's representatives told NPR that its vans had working air conditioning and that any van without it was taken off the road at once. They also said the delivery companies were in charge of fixing the vans, and that Amazon had changed some routes the year before so drivers could take more breaks to cool down. The owner of Battle Tested Strategies, Johnathon Ervin, said Amazon regularly failed to fix broken air conditioning, sometimes for weeks or months.

In April 2023, Turner and 83 other drivers at the company joined the Teamsters union and bargained a contract with Battle Tested Strategies. NPR reported that they joined the union in large part to push for protection from the heat. In June 2023, Amazon ended its contract with the company. The union and the company's owner said Amazon was punishing the drivers for joining a union. Amazon's representatives said Amazon ended the contract over safety violations and missed insurance payments by the company. The drivers went on strike, which means they stopped working as a protest.

Lawyers for the National Labor Relations Board, the government office that enforces labor law, brought a case against Amazon over the drivers. The case turned on whether Amazon was a joint employer of the drivers, a company that shares an employer's legal duties toward workers another company hired. In April 2026, lawyers for the board settled the case with Amazon. A settlement is an agreement that ends a case. Each of the roughly 84 drivers who worked there from April to June 2023 would get two weeks of pay, about $250,000 in all. Under the settlement, Amazon did not admit that it was the drivers' employer. In late May 2026, G. Rebekah Ramirez, a judge who hears labor cases for the board, approved the settlement. The Teamsters objected and asked to appeal.

<a id="ch-big-business"></a>

## Chapter 19: Big Business and Its Power

### Before 1500

No company existed in this land before 1500. A company is a group of people who put their money together to run a business and share what it earns. A corporation is a kind of company that goes on after its first owners are gone. To start one, people needed a written grant from a government.

Native nations did trade goods over long distances. Archaeologists have found copper from Lake Superior, shells from the Gulf of Mexico and turquoise from the Southwest hundreds of miles from their sources. People at Cahokia, in what is now Illinois, traded stone hoe blades that have turned up more than 400 miles away. The traders belonged to many different nations. None of them organized that trade as a company whose owners each held a part of it.

### The 1500s

The Europeans who reached this coast in the 1500s came on voyages paid for by kings and queens. No chartered company traded on this coast during that century. At the same time, merchants in London were forming joint-stock companies. Companies of that kind later paid for the first lasting English colonies here.

#### The joint-stock company, an English idea

In the 1500s, merchants in London began forming joint-stock companies. In a joint-stock company, many investors each buy a share. A share is one part of the ownership. Each investor gets a part of the profit that matches the number of shares he owns. The money he paid in is called stock.

In 1555 the explorer Sebastian Cabot and a group of London merchants formed the Muscovy Company. The company held a monopoly on English trade with Russia. A monopoly is the right to be the only seller of something, or the only trader in a place. Earlier investors had taken their money back after each voyage. The Muscovy Company kept its investors' money in the business from one voyage to the next. It was the first English joint-stock company to work that way.

On 11 September 1592, Sir Edward Osborne founded the Levant Company by joining two older companies, the Venice Company and the Turkey Company. Its merchants traded in the eastern Mediterranean Sea. The Levant Company's merchants did not trade in North America. On 31 December 1600 Queen Elizabeth I gave a charter to the East India Company of London. The Earl of Cumberland, a nobleman, and 218 other men had asked her for one. A charter is the written grant from a government that creates a company and lists its rights.

### The 1600s

Investors in English companies paid for the first lasting English colonies in this land. The companies' officers sent the settlers who founded them. A king signed each company's charter. Investors bought shares in each company, hoping the colony would earn them a profit. The kings who signed the charters gave the companies land where Native nations already lived. The Virginia Company and the Massachusetts Bay Company both lost their charters.

Other companies made money by owning enslaved people and by shipping enslaved Africans across the ocean. The Dutch West India Company owned the enslaved men who dug the trench for a wall at New Amsterdam. The historian William Pettigrew judged that the Royal African Company, chartered in 1672, shipped more enslaved Africans to the Americas than any other single company or group in the whole history of the slave trade.

#### The Virginia Company, a colony run as a business

In 1606 King James I of England gave a charter to the Virginia Company of London. It allowed the company to start a colony in North America. The company's settlers founded Jamestown on 13 May 1607. They built it inside Tsenacomoco, the land of the Powhatan chiefdom. A chiefdom is a group of towns under one leading chief.

A share in the company cost 12 pounds and 10 shillings, and it lasted seven years. A shilling was a coin worth one twentieth of a pound. The first sale of shares may have raised as much as 10,000 pounds. In 1616 the company paid its shareholders in land alone.

Under a second charter, dated 23 May 1609, the king gave up some of his power over the company. From then on the investors elected a treasurer to run it. Under a third charter, dated 12 March 1612, the company's lands included the island of Bermuda, and the company could run lotteries. A lottery is a game in which people buy tickets and a few tickets win prizes. By May 1620 lotteries had brought in 7,000 pounds of the company's 9,831 pounds in cash for the year. In February 1621 members of the House of Commons attacked the lotteries in a debate. The House of Commons is one of the two groups of lawmakers in England's Parliament. King James I banned the lotteries soon after.

Of the 4,270 people counted in Virginia from 1619 to 1622, only 1,240 were alive at the end. In 1619 about 700 settlers lived in the colony. Over the next three years the company shipped 3,570 more men, women and children there, for a total of 4,270. English settlers had been taking Powhatan land to grow tobacco. On 22 March 1622 an alliance of Virginia Indians led by Opechancanough attacked the English settlements. Opechancanough was the leading chief of the Powhatan. The attackers killed as many as 347 colonists.

Besides the 347 killed in the attack, 2,683 people were gone. An investor named Samuel Wrote asked what had happened to them. Encyclopedia Virginia's history of the company states that most of them died of disease.

In May 1623 King James I's advisers on his Privy Council, the king's inner council, set up a royal commission, a group of officials named to look into the company's business. On 24 May 1624 the king took away the company's charter. From then on Virginia was a royal colony, run by officials the king chose.

The first Africans known to reach English Virginia came in 1619, while the company ran the colony. Earlier that summer the crews of two privateer ships had attacked a Portuguese slave ship, the *São João Bautista*, off the coast of Campeche, in what is now Mexico. They seized 50 to 60 Africans from it. A privateer was a ship's captain with a government's permission to attack and rob enemy ships. One ship, the *White Lion*, had sailed from the Netherlands, and its captain, John Colyn Jope, carried Dutch papers giving him that permission.

In late August 1619 the *White Lion* landed "20. and odd" Africans, in the words of the colonist John Rolfe, at Point Comfort in Virginia. The other ship, the English *Treasurer*, arrived three or four days later with more of the stolen people. Its owners were Robert Rich, Lord Warwick, a nobleman, and Samuel Argall, Virginia's deputy governor. Governor George Yeardley and the merchant Abraham Peirsey bought the enslaved people from the *White Lion* and paid for them with food.

<a id="story-edwin-sandys"></a>

#### Sir Edwin Sandys

> **Who:** The treasurer the Virginia Company's investors elected in 1619, the year its shipments of settlers grew.
>
> **When and where:** London, 1619 to 1624.

The investors of the Virginia Company elected Sir Edwin Sandys their treasurer on 28 April 1619. From 1619 to 1622, most of the people counted in the company's colony died or were killed.

Under Sandys, the company's officers used a plan called the headright to draw settlers. They promised 50 acres of land for each person whose trip to Virginia someone paid for. The payer got the land, whether he paid for his own trip or for another person's. The settler then paid the company a quitrent of one shilling a year. A quitrent is a small yearly rent paid on land. The land the company handed out this way was Powhatan land.

Sandys and the company's officers shipped 3,570 more men, women and children to Virginia from 1619 to 1622. Of the 4,270 people counted in the colony in those years, 1,240 were still alive at the end. The historian Edmund S. Morgan studied these years in a book published in 1975. Encyclopedia Virginia's history of the company sums up what Morgan and later scholars showed: "any responsible monarch would have been obliged to stop the reckless shipment of his subjects to their deaths." A monarch is a king or a queen. Obliged means bound by duty, and subjects are the people a monarch rules. The king at the time was James I. He took the company's charter away in 1624.

#### The Dutch West India Company

On 3 June 1621, members of the States General, the lawmaking assembly of the Netherlands, gave a charter to the Dutch West India Company. For 24 years, no one else from the Netherlands could sail to or trade with the Americas. The same rule covered the coast of Africa from the Tropic of Cancer to the Cape of Good Hope. The Tropic of Cancer is a line on maps that circles the earth north of the equator. The Cape of Good Hope is near the southern tip of Africa.

In 1624 men working for the company built a trading post called Fort Orange, where Albany, New York, stands today. It was the first lasting Dutch settlement in New Netherland, the colony along the Hudson River. The upper Hudson was the country of the Mohican people. The company's settlers then moved onto Manhattan Island, the home of the Lenape people. Company officials said they bought Manhattan in 1626 for trade goods worth 60 guilders, which were Dutch coins. A guide to Lenape history from the Pratt Institute Libraries says the Dutch likely misunderstood what the Lenape meant by that exchange.

The company owned people as well as ships and forts. In 1653 enslaved men owned by the company dug the trench for a wall at New Amsterdam, the town on Manhattan. Three of them are known by name: Paulo d'Angola, Simon Congo and Anthony Portuguese. In 1644, after 18 or 19 years of forced work, the company's director and council had given these three, eight other men and their wives what the officials called "half-freedom." The men could own land. Their children stayed the company's property, and the men still had to pay the company a yearly fee of grain or beans and a hog. They also had to work for the company whenever it called them.

#### The Massachusetts Bay Company

The colony of Massachusetts was started by a company of investors, the Massachusetts Bay Company, and the company's leaders governed the colony under its charter. King Charles I signed the charter of the Massachusetts Bay Company in March 1629. In late August 1629, twelve men signed a paper called the Cambridge Agreement. Among them were John Winthrop, Richard Saltonstall and Thomas Dudley. They promised to sail to New England if the company's charter and its government moved there with them.

In 1630 Winthrop and about 1,000 Puritan settlers arrived at the Shawmut Peninsula. Puritans were English Protestants who wanted to "purify" the Church of England, the king's official church. The land around the peninsula belonged to the Massachusett people, whose leading chief was Chickataubut. According to the West End Museum in Boston, about 100,000 people had lived in the region. An epidemic from 1616 to 1618 had killed about 75,000 of them. An epidemic is a disease that spreads quickly through many people. Winthrop renamed the peninsula Boston. In 1633 Chickataubut agreed to a treaty with Winthrop that gave up his rights to the peninsula. A treaty is a written agreement between nations or their leaders. Chickataubut died of smallpox that same year.

On 23 October 1684 English judges cancelled the company's charter for three reasons. Colonists had traded with other countries against English trade laws. The colony's leaders had made their own coins, without the king's picture on them. The colony's lawmakers had passed laws against Quakers and against members of the Church of England. Quakers belong to a Christian group, also called the Society of Friends, that began in England in the 1600s.

#### The Hudson's Bay Company

King Charles II gave a charter to the Hudson's Bay Company on 2 May 1670. Prince Rupert, the king's cousin, had persuaded the king and a group of merchants and noblemen to back the company. The charter gave the company the only right to trade in all the lands whose rivers flow into Hudson Bay. Those lands are in what is now Canada. In the charter they are called Rupert's Land.

The Hudson's Bay Company was an English company. In 1821 it took over the trading posts of its rival, the North West Company, in the Pacific Northwest. On 19 March 1825 the company's governor, George Simpson, and the trader Dr. John McLoughlin opened Fort Vancouver on the Columbia River, in what is now Washington state. Chinookan people had lived along that river for thousands of years. They called the place where the fort stood Skatcutxat, which means "Mud Turtles."

#### The Royal African Company

The Royal African Company was an English company whose investors made money from shipping enslaved Africans to the Americas. King Charles II gave it a charter in 1672, and his brother James, Duke of York, led it. Duke of York was James's royal title. It held the only English right to trade with West Africa. That trade included gold, silver and enslaved people. James later became King James II.

Between 1672 and 1731, ships that the company put money into carried 186,748 enslaved people on 652 voyages to English colonies in the Americas. Of those people, 16,077 died on the way. The count comes from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, a record of known slave voyages. From 1680 to 1686, the company's ships carried about 5,000 people a year. Most of them went to English colonies in the Caribbean and to Virginia.

Thousands of the people the company shipped arrived with the company's initials branded on their chests. To brand a person means to press a red-hot metal stamp against the skin. The heat burns the letters into the flesh and leaves a raised scar for life. Many of the brands read DoY, for Duke of York, the company's leader. Others read RAC, for Royal African Company. The accounts of the branding name the company but not the men who pressed the hot stamps into people's skin.

The historian William Pettigrew wrote in his 2013 book *Freedom's Debt* that the company "shipped more enslaved African women, men and children to the Americas than any other single institution during the entire period of the transatlantic slave trade." An institution here means a company or any other organization. Transatlantic means across the Atlantic Ocean. He also wrote that its investors knew what the company did and meant to make money from it.

### 1700 to 1750

From 1700 to 1750 almost no business in the colonies was a corporation. The historian Robert E. Wright counts only 8 business corporations chartered in the colonies before independence. He writes, "Before the Revolution, American business corporations were few, small, and largely inconsequential." Inconsequential means unimportant. Under British rules, Wright writes, a charter cost a lot to get and gave its owners little in return. So most colonists in business chose other ways to organize.

#### Partners, and the trade in people

Many colonial businesses were partnerships. In a partnership, two or more men put their money together and shared the profits. Under the law of the time, each partner was liable for all of the firm's debts. Liable means that a person has to pay. If the firm failed, the people it owed could make any one partner pay all of it from his own property.

The Royal African Company lost its monopoly in practice in 1689, after King James II lost his throne. The company's own leaders admitted it that year. In 1698 members of the English Parliament passed a law that opened the African trade to every English merchant. Under that law any English merchant could carry enslaved people from Africa. He had to pay the company a fee of 10 percent on the goods he shipped out of Africa. The Royal African Company itself stopped trading in enslaved people in 1731.

Boston merchants bought and sold people. From 1719 to 1781 the *Boston Gazette*, a newspaper, ran about 2,300 advertisements for about 2,000 enslaved people. Charles Apthorp, a Boston merchant born in Britain, ran a firm that imported enslaved people and sold them along with other goods. By 1746 he was one of the richest men in Boston. In the 1730s and 1740s he placed advertisements in the *Boston Gazette* for "a parcel of likely negros just imported." A parcel meant a group. Sellers used likely as a word of praise. It meant fit for work, healthy and good-looking. Negro was a word used then for a Black person. In 1742 Apthorp offered a reward of five pounds for the return of "a negro man named Jack about 35 years old." Jack had escaped from his enslaver, Stephen Eastwick. Apthorp was also a business partner of Thomas Hancock, one of the richest merchants in New England.

<a id="story-thomas-hancock"></a>

#### Thomas Hancock

> **Who:** A Boston merchant who built one of the largest fortunes in New England. With his partner Charles Apthorp, he rented out the ships that carried the Acadians away from their homeland in 1755.
>
> **When and where:** Boston, from about 1724 until his death in 1764.

Thomas Hancock built one of the largest fortunes in New England. Part of his firm's business was carrying people whom British officials had forced from their homes. He was born in Lexington, Massachusetts, on 17 July 1703. At 13 or 14 (accounts differ), he was apprenticed to a bookseller in Boston. An apprentice works for a master for a set number of years to learn a trade. Hancock opened his own bookshop in 1723 or 1724. In 1730 he married Lydia Henchman. She was the daughter of Daniel Henchman, a Boston bookseller who was Hancock's business partner.

Hancock traded in many goods, and with different partners he made paper. His ships took codfish, whale oil, logwood and potash to other countries. Logwood is a tree whose wood gives a dye, and potash is a salt made from wood ashes. He sold rum and molasses to the crews of the fishing fleet off Newfoundland, and he controlled a group of fishing boats of his own.

Smuggling was part of the business too. Smuggling means moving goods in or out of a place in secret, against the law. Under English trade laws, colonial merchants could buy and sell only where those laws allowed. Hancock's ships carried tea and paper from Amsterdam to the West Indies. When his ships brought French molasses into Boston, he hid it.

Hancock's partner Charles Apthorp worked as a paymaster and agent for the British army and navy. A paymaster is the man who pays out an army's or a navy's money. Apthorp supplied goods and money to British forces in Nova Scotia and in Boston. In the autumn of 1755, British officials forced the Acadians out of Nova Scotia and took their houses and farms. The Acadians were French-speaking Catholic farm families. The officials who gave the orders were Governor Charles Lawrence of Nova Scotia and Governor William Shirley of Massachusetts.

Lawrence and Shirley hired about 24 sailing ships from the firm of Apthorp and Hancock to carry the Acadians away. They paid by the month, and they paid a fixed fee for each person carried. The partners charged 40 to 48 pounds a month for each ship. In Boston the partners' ships were rebuilt inside to hold two people for every ton of cargo the ship could carry. Some ships held 300 to 500 people. The historian Mark Peterson writes that the ships were "fitted out in the manner of slave ships." The ships carried the Acadians to British colonies along the Atlantic coast, among them Maryland and South Carolina.

The ships that Apthorp and Hancock supplied were in poor condition. On board, Acadians went without enough food, caught diseases and died. The ships carried no passenger lists, so no record shows which Acadians died at sea or how many.

In 1763 Hancock made his nephew John Hancock his equal partner. Thomas Hancock died of a stroke on 1 August 1764, as he entered the council chamber in Boston. He left property and money worth about 70,000 pounds.

### 1750 to 1800

In 1773 colonists in Boston destroyed tea that belonged to the East India Company of London. British lawmakers had just given that company the right to sell its tea straight to the colonies. After independence, American lawmakers began chartering companies of their own. Most of the charters went to banks, to insurance companies, to companies that piped water to towns, and to companies that built bridges, canals and toll roads. An insurance company takes a regular fee from people and pays them back if they suffer a loss, such as a fire. A toll is a fee that people pay to use a road or to cross a bridge. Robert E. Wright counts 319 business corporations chartered in the United States before 1801. Only 8 of them came from the colonial years, and 21 more from 1776 to 1789. The rest were chartered from 1790 to 1800.

#### The Tea Act and the East India Company

Members of the British Parliament passed the Tea Act on 10 May 1773. The East India Company of London, the company chartered in 1600, held about 17 million pounds of tea, by weight, that it could not sell. Under the Tea Act the company could ship tea straight to the American colonies. Its own agents could sell the tea there at a lower price. Under the Act, the tax on tea that members of Parliament had set in 1767 still had to be paid on the company's tea in the colonies. The Act added no new tax. The company's agents could sell tea more cheaply than colonial merchants, so the merchants who sold tea in the colonies lost business.

Ships carrying the company's tea reached Boston in late 1773. Thomas Hutchinson was the royal governor of Massachusetts. He refused to let the *Beaver*, the *Dartmouth* and the *Eleanor* leave the harbor until they had unloaded. On 16 December 1773, members of a protest group called the Sons of Liberty boarded the three ships. Some were dressed as Mohawk men. They smashed open 340 chests of tea with axes and dumped them into Boston Harbor. The tea weighed more than 92,000 pounds, about 46 tons. Many accounts say 342 chests, but the company's own papers say 340.

In February 1774 the company's directors sent a bill to the Earl of Dartmouth, a British lord who was the minister in charge of the American colonies. They asked to be paid back for the tea. The bill came to 9,659 pounds, 6 shillings and 4 pence. A penny was a coin worth one twelfth of a shilling, and "pence" means more than one penny.

#### Americans start chartering companies

The Bank of North America was the first commercial bank in the United States. A commercial bank keeps people's money safe and lends money to merchants and businesses. Robert Morris planned the bank, and members of the Continental Congress approved his plan on 26 May 1781. The Continental Congress was the meeting of leaders from the 13 states that ran the country during the Revolution. Its members granted the charter on 31 December 1781. The bank opened on 7 January 1782 on Chestnut Street in Philadelphia.

Morris used a shipment of French silver worth $450,000, which had been sent to Congress, to start the bank. The bank then lent the money back to Congress. Ninety-nine Philadelphians and members of Congress bought shares.

Pennsylvania's lawmakers had given the bank a second charter of their own in 1782. In March 1785 members of the Pennsylvania assembly, the state's lawmakers, received petitions asking them to cancel that charter. A petition is a written request signed by many people. The bank's critics said its officers favored their friends, charged too much interest on loans, and had too much power over trade and politics. They pointed to the 14 percent dividends the bank paid its shareholders. A dividend is a share of the profits paid out to the owners. The lawmaker William Findley called the bank "a monopoly." That September the lawmakers voted to cancel the charter. In 1787 they gave the bank a narrower charter. It lasted 14 years, and under it the bank's capital, the money its owners put in, could be no more than $2 million. The bank could own no property beyond what its business needed.
