Only 7 of the 319 corporations that Wright counts before 1801 were for making goods. From 1786 to 1798, lawmakers in the Northeast chartered 59 private companies to build toll bridges. The first was the Charles River Bridge in Boston. In its first six years, its investors earned an average of 10.5 percent a year on their money.

Getting a charter cost money. Wright found that people who wanted one paid for signatures and for help getting a bill passed by the lawmakers. Some paid lobbyists and bribes. A lobbyist is a person paid to persuade lawmakers. A bribe is money paid to someone in power to get them to do something.

In a corporation, each owner risks the money he paid for his shares. Limited liability is the rule that owners cannot also be made to pay the company's debts from their own property. The historians Oscar and Mary Handlin found only 16 early charters that spelled out a promise of limited liability. Wright argues that owners' risk was limited anyway. A company could not charge its shareholders more than the price of their shares.

<a id="story-robert-morris"></a>

#### Robert Morris

> **Who:** The merchant who ran the country's finances near the end of the Revolution and planned its first commercial bank. He bought almost all of the Seneca Nation's remaining land in New York, and he was later locked in a prison for people who could not pay their debts.
>
> **When and where:** Philadelphia, 1781 to 1801. Born 1734, died 1806.

Robert Morris ran the finances of the United States near the end of the Revolution, and later he went to prison for his debts. As Superintendent of Finance, the man the Continental Congress put in charge of its money, he wrote the charter of the Bank of North America. He used the bank to keep the value of the country's money steady and to keep the national government from running out of money.

After the war, Morris bought land with borrowed money. Starting in 1793, he and his partners John Nicholson and James Greenleaf bought thousands of building lots in the new District of Columbia. They also bought millions of acres in Pennsylvania, New York, Kentucky, Virginia, Georgia and the Carolinas.

Morris's land in western New York was Seneca land. From 20 August to 16 September 1797, his son Thomas Morris and his agent Charles Williamson met Seneca leaders at Geneseo, New York. Nearly 3,000 Seneca and other Haudenosaunee people came. The Haudenosaunee are a union of Native nations: the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca, later joined by the Tuscarora. The Seneca leaders at Geneseo included Cornplanter, Red Jacket and Handsome Lake, along with the clan mothers. Clan mothers are women leaders who choose their clan's chiefs and can remove a chief who acts badly. At this meeting the Seneca leaders signed the Treaty of Big Tree. Under it they gave up almost all of their remaining land in New York, nearly 3.5 million acres. They kept 12 small pieces of land.

Morris paid $100,000. Federal officials held the money and put it into shares of the Bank of the United States, which paid the Seneca up to $6,000 a year. Morris asked that the $100,000 go back to his own heirs, the family members who would inherit from him, if the Seneca nation should "become extinct," meaning if every Seneca died. The heads of the federal Treasury and State departments refused. Most of the land went on to the Holland Land Company.

By 1797 Morris and Nicholson together owed their creditors about $12 million. A creditor is a person owed money. In February 1798 officers arrested Morris at his home. They took him to the Prune Street debtors' apartment, next to the Walnut Street Prison in Philadelphia. Morris was held there because he could not pay his debts. He stayed there about three and a half years.

In 1800 members of Congress passed a bankruptcy law. Bankruptcy is a legal process for a person who cannot pay his debts. A court divides what he owns among the people he owes, and he is freed from the rest of the debt. Accounts differ about whether Morris's time in prison helped get that law passed. He was released under it in August or October 1801 (accounts differ). At his release, three bankruptcy commissioners, officials who handled his case, found that he himself owed $2,948,711.11.

### 1800 to 1850

Americans formed corporations by the thousands between 1800 and 1850. A corporation is a company that the law treats as one body. Its owners hold shares, which are parts of the ownership, and it goes on after its first owners are gone. A corporation needs a charter, the written grant from state lawmakers that creates it. At the start of the century, state lawmakers had to pass a special law for each charter. Under a Connecticut law of 1837, people could start a corporation for any lawful business by following set steps. Merchants in Boston used corporations to build cotton mills, and by 1850 their group controlled a fifth of the country's cotton cloth making. In 1819 the justices of the Supreme Court ruled that a state could not change a charter it had already granted. In the 1830s President Andrew Jackson fought the Second Bank of the United States, one of the largest companies in the country. Jackson blocked the renewal of its federal charter, and the charter ran out in 1836.

#### From special charter to general law

Before 1811, a group that wanted a corporation had to ask lawmakers to pass a special law just for them. On 22 March 1811, New York's lawmakers passed the first general incorporation law in the country. A general incorporation law lets any group form a corporation by following set steps, without a special vote.

The New York law covered only makers of goods. It named goods of wool, cotton or linen, and goods of iron, steel, copper, lead and similar metals. Any five or more people could form such a company. The charter lasted 20 years, and the company could raise no more than $100,000. In 1972 the historian Seavoy wrote in the *Business History Review* that the law was "essentially an emergency measure." Under two federal laws, the Embargo of 1807 and the Non-Intercourse Act of 1809, cloth from Europe had stopped coming in. An embargo is a government ban on trade, and non-intercourse here means no trade. New York's lawmakers wanted thread made at home so that families could weave their own cloth.

In 1837 Connecticut's lawmakers passed a law that let people incorporate, or form a corporation, for "any other lawful business." It was the first such law that did not list which trades were allowed or set a time limit on the corporation's life. Banks still needed a special act.

In some Southern states, lawmakers shut particular groups out of their general incorporation laws, most often people who were not white. The economic historian Eric Hilt describes these rules. In those states a Black American could not form a corporation under the general law.

The economic historians Richard Sylla and Robert E. Wright count 22,419 business corporations that state lawmakers created by special laws, one charter at a time, from 1790 to 1860. Together their charters allowed their owners to raise at least $4.5 billion. Several thousand more corporations formed under general laws.

#### Dartmouth College v. Woodward, 1819

In 1819 the justices of the Supreme Court ruled that a charter is a contract, and that a state cannot change it at will. The case was about a college's charter. Because the justices treated any charter as a contract, business corporations could rely on the same rule to protect their own charters.

King George III had granted Dartmouth College its charter in 1769. In 1815 the college's trustees, the board that ran it, removed its president, John Wheelock. Wheelock then persuaded the governor of New Hampshire to change the college's charter. In 1816 New Hampshire's lawmakers rewrote it. Under the new charter the governor chose trustees and a state board could overrule them. The lawmakers also renamed the college Dartmouth University. The old trustees sued William Woodward, who served as secretary under the new plan.

Daniel Webster argued the trustees' case before the Supreme Court. He said, "It is, sir, as I have said, a small college, and yet there are those who love it!" Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the Court's decision and its reasons. He ruled that the 1769 charter was a contract. The Constitution states that no state may pass a law "impairing the obligation of contracts." Impairing means weakening. New Hampshire's lawmakers had broken that rule.

After the ruling, state lawmakers could not take back a charter that lawmakers had granted in an earlier year. Justice Joseph Story, in his own written opinion in the case, pointed to a way around this. Lawmakers could write into a charter, at the start, a power "to alter, modify, or repeal" it, which means to change it or cancel it. State lawmakers began writing such lines into new charters. Dartmouth College's own history of the case calls it a basis for the Constitution's protection of corporations. Supreme Court justices still cite it, among other places in their opinions in *Citizens United v. FEC*, a 2010 case about money spent on elections, and *Burwell v. Hobby Lobby*.

#### The Boston Associates and the mills

A group of Boston merchants, known today as the Boston Associates, built cotton mills with far more money behind them than their rivals had. In 1813 Francis Cabot Lowell, Patrick Tracy Jackson and Nathan Appleton organized the Boston Manufacturing Company. It started with $400,000 in capital, the money its owners put in. That was more than ten times the money behind the average cotton mill in Rhode Island. By 1820 the owners had put in $200,000 more. By 1850, the National Park Service counts, the Boston Associates controlled a fifth of the country's cotton cloth making.

In 1814 they built a mill at Waltham, on the Charles River. It was the first mill in the world to spin cotton into thread and weave it into cloth under one roof. Every step, from raw cotton to finished cloth, happened in one building. Within six years the mill ran 5,376 spindles and 175 power looms. A spindle is the rod that twists cotton fibers into thread, and a power loom is a weaving machine driven by water power. The mill used 450,000 pounds of cotton a year. A typical Rhode Island mill ran fewer than 1,000 spindles. By 1820 the Waltham mill used all the power the Charles River could give.

The same investors then built mills at Pawtucket Falls, on the Merrimack River. The falls were a fishing place of the Pennacook people. In the 1600s the Native towns of Pawtucket and Wamesit stood there, under the leaders Passaconaway and his son Wannalancet. On 1 March 1826 the mill village became a town named Lowell. It had 2,500 people in 1826 and 6,477 in 1830.

Enslaved people in the South grew the cotton the mills spun. The mills also made a cheap cloth that planters bought to clothe the people they enslaved. People at the time called it "negro cloth." Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts spoke of the tie between the mill owners and the slaveholders. He called it an "unholy union" between the lords of the loom and the lords of the lash. The lash is a whip.

<a id="story-nicholas-biddle"></a>

#### Nicholas Biddle

> **Who:** The president of the Second Bank of the United States, one of the largest companies in the country, during President Andrew Jackson's fight to end it.
>
> **When and where:** Philadelphia, from 1822 or 1823 to 1839.

Nicholas Biddle ran the Second Bank of the United States while President Andrew Jackson fought to end its federal charter. President James Madison signed the bank's charter into law on 10 April 1816. The charter ran for 20 years. The bank had $35 million in capital, the money its owners put in. That was three and a half times the $10 million of the first national bank. The federal government owned a fifth of the bank's stock, its shares of ownership. The president chose 5 of its 25 directors, the board that ran the bank. The bank opened in Philadelphia in January 1817. The Federal Reserve's own history of the bank describes it as "one of the largest U.S. corporations."

Biddle became the bank's president in 1822 or 1823 (accounts differ). By the end of the 1820s the bank had 29 branches, by one count, and did about $70 million of business a year. Another count gives 25 branches. The Federal Reserve's history states that Biddle "was not above allowing the Bank to make loans to his friends while denying loans to those less friendly."

Andrew Jackson became president in 1829. That year he called the bank unconstitutional, which means against the Constitution, and he said it was corrupt. On 6 January 1832 members of Congress brought in bills to recharter the bank, which means to renew its charter, four years before it ran out. Thomas Cadwalader, a director of the bank and Biddle's close friend, had counted votes in Congress and advised asking early. Biddle agreed. Most accounts say he did so unwillingly, under pressure from the political leaders Henry Clay and Daniel Webster. Majorities in both houses of Congress voted yes: 28 to 20 in the Senate and 107 to 85 in the House. Jackson vetoed the bill, which means he refused to sign it. The bank's supporters could not get the two-thirds vote needed to pass the bill over his veto.

Jackson won a second term in 1832. He then ordered the government's money moved out of the bank and into banks chartered by the states. By late 1833 most of it was gone. Biddle answered by cutting the bank's lending and by calling in loans, which means he told borrowers to pay back what they owed. He believed that the shortage of credit, or money to borrow, might turn people against Jackson. In April 1834 a majority of the House of Representatives voted against renewing the charter.

The federal charter ran out in 1836. Pennsylvania's lawmakers chartered the bank again as a state bank. In 1839 the bank's officers suspended payment, which means they stopped handing out coins to people who brought in its paper notes. Biddle resigned that year.

In 1841 the bank's stockholders, the people who owned its shares, chose a committee to look into its books. The committee members reported that Biddle had used the bank's money to buy cotton, tobacco and other crops and ship them to Europe. The bank closed for good on 4 April 1841.

On 10 December 1841 a grand jury charged Biddle and two other bank officers, Samuel Jaudon and John Andrews, with a crime. A grand jury is a group of citizens who decide whether there is enough proof for a trial. The charge stated that the three men had cheated the stockholders out of $400,000 in 1836 and had tried to cover it up with false records in 1841. Biddle was arrested. Judges later dropped the charges. Biddle paid the bank's creditors, the people it owed money, with what was left of his own fortune. He faced lawsuits until he died in 1844. One suit asked for nearly $25 million. The histories of the bank do not name who brought it.

### 1850 to 1900

A few companies came to control whole industries between 1850 and 1900. In 1880 the capital of one railroad, the Pennsylvania, was larger than everything the federal government took in that year. John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil refined 90 to 95 percent of the country's oil by 1880. By 1895 one company controlled about 98 percent of the country's sugar refining.

Members of Congress wrote the first federal rules for business in 1887 and 1890. In the 1890s the justices of the Supreme Court let the sugar trust stand under those rules, and federal lawyers used the second rule to get a court order against a railroad strike. When workers struck, owners and officials answered with armed guards, court orders and soldiers. Henry Clay Frick hired the Pinkerton guards who fought steelworkers at Homestead in 1892. Governor Robert Pattison sent the Pennsylvania National Guard there. In 1894 President Grover Cleveland sent federal troops against the Pullman strike.

#### The railroads

In 1880 the largest corporation in the country was a railroad. That year the Pennsylvania Railroad had 30,000 workers and $400 million in capital. It carried 10 percent of all the freight in the United States and 20 percent of the passengers. The federal government collected about $334 million in all in the year that ended on 30 June 1880, less than the railroad's capital. By 1882 the Pennsylvania was the largest corporation in the world.

Federal and state officials also gave the railroads land. A land grant is a gift of land from a government. From 1850 to 1871, federal officials granted about 129 to 131 million acres to railroad companies. State lawmakers granted about 51 million acres more. Counts of the federal grants differ by a few million acres.

The first federal grant went to the Illinois Central in 1851, under a law passed the year before. Of the 3.75 million acres in that law, nearly 2.6 million went to the Illinois Central.

The granted land came from land that federal officials had taken, or were taking, from Native nations. The Pacific Railroad Act of 1 July 1862 states: "The United States shall extinguish as rapidly as may be the Indian titles to all lands falling under the operation of this act." Indian titles meant the Native nations' rights to their own land. To extinguish them meant to end them. In that law, members of Congress told federal officials to end the Native nations' rights to the land along the railroad as fast as they could.

<a id="story-john-d-rockefeller-big-business"></a>

#### John D. Rockefeller

> **Who:** The Cleveland businessman who built Standard Oil and set up the first large trust.
>
> **When and where:** Cleveland and New York, 1870 to 1911.
>
> **Movie:** *The Men Who Built America* (2012), a History Channel series about Rockefeller, Carnegie, J. P. Morgan and others. It is a docudrama: actors play the real people in scripted scenes.

John D. Rockefeller used secret deals with the railroads to take over nearly all of the country's oil refining. Refining is the work of cleaning crude oil from the ground and separating it into products that people can use.

On 10 January 1870 Rockefeller formed the Standard Oil Company in Ohio. His partners were his brother William Rockefeller, Samuel Andrews, Henry M. Flagler and Stephen V. Harkness. The company had $1,000,000 in capital. Its refineries in Cleveland could handle about 1,500 barrels of crude oil a day. All the refineries in Cleveland together handled about 10,000 to 12,000 barrels a day.

Rockefeller and his partners controlled 900 of the 2,000 shares of the South Improvement Company. Thomas A. Scott of the Pennsylvania Railroad had set it up late in 1871. It was a secret deal between a few refiners and the railroads. Under the deal, the railroads would charge $2.56 a barrel to carry crude oil to New York. South Improvement members got back $1.06 on every barrel they shipped. That payment was called a rebate. The members also got $1.06 in cash on every barrel that their rivals shipped. That payment was called a drawback. A rival refiner paid the full price, and part of what he paid went to his own competitors.

Oil producers in western Pennsylvania learned of the plan and fought it. They organized and raided the shipments of the scheme's members. They also asked Pennsylvania's lawmakers and Congress for help. On 2 April 1872 Pennsylvania officials suspended the South Improvement Company's charter. The company never shipped any oil.

While the scheme stood, in early 1872, Rockefeller bought out 21 or 22 of the 26 refiners in Cleveland. Accounts give both numbers. One account puts the buying between mid-February and mid-March. Ida Tarbell says it took three months. One refiner later testified that "our establishment was worth $150,000, and we sold it for about $65,000." That was about forty or forty-five cents for each dollar his business was worth. Rockefeller told the sellers, "Take Standard Oil Stock, and your family will never know want." In three months Standard Oil went from refining about 1,500 barrels a day to 10,000. According to Ida Tarbell, it then held more than a fifth of the country's refining capacity.

Rockefeller kept buying out rivals and making deals with railroads for lower rates. By 1880 Standard Oil refined 90 to 95 percent of all the oil produced in the United States.

#### What a trust was

A trust was a way to run many companies as one business, with one small group in charge. The Standard Oil Trust was the first large one. On 2 January 1882, the people who owned shares in Standard Oil signed the Standard Oil Trust Agreement. Accounts differ on how many signed: 41 in one count, and about 50 in Ida Tarbell's. They handed over their shares in about 40 companies to nine trustees. A trustee is a person who holds and manages property for others. Rockefeller was one of the nine, and the nine trustees themselves owned most of the stock. The trust was valued at about $70 million. In time the trustees ran some 40 corporations, 14 of them fully owned.

Owners in other industries copied the plan. Laws against such combinations of companies are still called antitrust laws.

In 1892 the justices of the Ohio Supreme Court ruled that the Standard Oil Trust was a monopoly that broke Ohio law. A monopoly is a business that has no real rivals, so it alone sells something. Rockefeller moved the property to companies in other states. Ida Tarbell later wrote of the trust, "You could argue its existence from its effects, but you could not prove it."

On 31 January 1890 James B. Duke's tobacco firm, W. Duke, Sons and Company of Durham, North Carolina, joined four other firms. Together they formed the American Tobacco Company. Duke had gone into the cigarette business in 1881. He leased new machines that rolled cigarettes, advertised heavily and bought up smaller rivals. The new company was the largest tobacco business in the world. In sugar, the American Sugar Refining Company controlled about 98 percent of the country's sugar refining by 1895.

<a id="story-franklin-tarbell"></a>

#### Franklin Tarbell

> **Who:** An independent oil producer in western Pennsylvania who fought Standard Oil from 1872 into the 1890s. He was the father of Ida Tarbell, the reporter who later investigated Standard Oil.
>
> **When and where:** Oil Creek and Titusville, Pennsylvania, from 1859 until his death in 1905.

Franklin Tarbell joined the oil producers' fight against Standard Oil in 1872. In 1893 he had to mortgage his family's home to pay a ruined partner's debts. His daughter Ida Tarbell wrote about him in her memoir, published in 1939.

He was born in Oxford, New York, on 21 October 1829. In 1859 he was on his way home to Iowa when he heard about the oil well at Titusville, Pennsylvania. He guessed that oil men would need tanks to hold their oil. He believed he could build a wooden tank that held 500 barrels or more. He was told, "Show me a model that won't leak, and I'll give you an order." He made the model and got the order. He built the first large round wooden tank on Oil Creek, and he built tanks for ten years.

In 1867 he began to produce oil himself, on farms near Rouseville. In 1870 he moved his family into a new house he had built in Titusville. His daughter Ida was thirteen.

In 1872 the oil producers learned of the South Improvement scheme. Ida remembered her father coming home one night with a grim look on his face. He told the family that he and scores of other producers had signed a pledge. They would not sell oil to Standard Oil, the one company that had gained from the scheme. Ida was fifteen. She later wrote that in 1872 "there was born in me a hatred of privilege, privilege of any sort."

The fight between the independent producers and Standard Oil went on for twenty years. The producers waited for slow decisions from the Interstate Commerce Commission, the federal board set up in 1887 to watch over the railroads. Some of their businesses failed while they waited. Between 1891 and 1893, while Ida was living in Paris, one of her father's business partners lost everything in this fight and shot himself. Ida's memoir does not state the man's name. The partner left Franklin Tarbell owing money on notes, which are written promises to repay loans. To pay them, during the money panic of 1893, he mortgaged the family's home. A mortgage is a loan that a person gets by pledging a house. If the loan is not repaid, the lender can take the house.

Ida Tarbell spent most of five years investigating Standard Oil. According to a 2012 account in *Smithsonian* magazine, her father warned her that Rockefeller and Standard Oil could crush her, just as, in his view, they had crushed her home town of Titusville. Franklin Tarbell died in Titusville on 1 March 1905.

<a id="story-andrew-carnegie-big-business"></a>

#### Andrew Carnegie

> **Who:** The Pittsburgh steelmaker whose company owned each step of making steel, from the iron ore to the finished steel. His general manager broke the steelworkers' union at Homestead in 1892.
>
> **When and where:** Pittsburgh, until he sold his company in 1901.
>
> **Movie:** *Andrew Carnegie: The Richest Man in the World*, an American Experience documentary shown on PBS on 20 January 1997.

Andrew Carnegie cut his costs and raised his profits by owning every step of making steel. This way of running a business is called vertical integration. It means that one company owns each stage of making a product, from the raw material to the finished goods.

By 1888 Carnegie already owned 73.5 percent of Henry Clay Frick's coke company. Coke is a fuel made by baking coal, and steel makers burn it to melt iron ore. In the 1890s Carnegie leased newly found iron ore deposits in the Mesabi Range of Minnesota. The name Mesabi comes from the Ojibwe name for the range, Misaabe Wajiw, which means Big Man Mountain. It was Ojibwe country. In a treaty of 1854, Ojibwe bands gave up northeastern Minnesota to the United States. A treaty is a written agreement between nations. Federal officials wanted a vein of copper on the north shore of Lake Superior. In a treaty of 1855, Ojibwe bands gave up most of north-central Minnesota, where federal officials wanted land for logging and mining.

Carnegie also bought ships on the Great Lakes to carry his ore. He bought a railroad and extended it to link his steel works to Lake Erie. He no longer had to buy coke, ore or shipping from other companies, and that cut his costs.

By the end of the 1890s Carnegie Steel was the largest steel maker in the world. It made a quarter of all the steel produced in the United States. In 1900 it earned $40 million in profits.

Carnegie was in Scotland in the summer of 1892. In the words of the encyclopedia Britannica, he gave his general manager, Henry Clay Frick, "carte blanche to break the union" at the Homestead works. Carte blanche means full freedom to act.

#### Homestead, 1892

In 1892 Henry Clay Frick broke the steelworkers' union at the Homestead works near Pittsburgh. He used a fence, a lockout and about 300 armed Pinkerton men. Frick was the general manager of Carnegie Steel. That year he became its chairman, and he owned 11 percent of it, as much as Carnegie's longtime partner Henry Phipps. The workers' union was the Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers, and its contract ran out on 1 July 1892.

Frick cut wages. He had a fence built around the plant, topped with barbed wire. The workers called it "Fort Frick." In late June he locked the workers out, which means he closed the plant to them. On 2 July he fired all 3,800 workers.

Frick signed a contract with William and Robert Pinkerton, who ran the Pinkerton National Detective Agency. They agreed to send 300 armed men, at five dollars a day for each man. The agency gathered 316 men in New York and Chicago. Some were Pinkerton regulars. Others had no jobs, some were criminals on the run, and a few were college students earning money for the summer. Their crates held 250 Winchester rifles and 300 pistols. Early on 6 July 1892, tugboats towed two barges carrying the men up the Monongahela River to the plant. A gun battle followed.

Accounts give different death counts. The encyclopedia Britannica lists at least 7 workers and 3 Pinkerton men killed in the battle and the days after it. The historian Leon Wolff counts about 9 strikers and 7 Pinkerton men dead from bullets, beatings, drowning and suicide. He writes that about 40 strikers and 20 Pinkerton men were shot. By the time the strike ended in November, he counts 35 men dead from the battle and the violence that followed.

Wolff names some of the dead. A Pinkerton guard named Klein died on the gangplank, shot through the head. Joseph Sotak went to help a wounded worker, Martin Murray, and was shot in the mouth and killed. A worker named Streigle was shot through the throat and died at once. Neither Wolff nor Britannica names the men who fired the shots that killed them.

After the battle, Frick asked Governor Robert Pattison of Pennsylvania for help. Pattison sent about 8,500 soldiers of the state National Guard. Another count gives 8,000. The soldiers took over the plant on 12 July. By 15 July Carnegie Steel's managers had the plant running again, with replacement workers. Many of them were Black men from the South. The union did not let Black workers join it. In November 1892 about 2,000 white workers attacked Black workers and their families, and gunfire badly wounded several people. The accounts do not say who fired. The union gave up on 21 November.

Officials charged scores of union leaders and workers with crimes. Almost all of them were acquitted, which means found not guilty.

Carnegie Steel's managers cut wages in all of Carnegie's mills by about half. A heater's helper, one of the workers who heated the steel, was paid by the ton of steel. He earned 4.85 cents a ton in February 1892 and 2.22 cents a ton in February 1894. The managers enforced the twelve-hour workday. The members of the union's advisory committee were blacklisted for life. A blacklist is a list of workers that employers agree never to hire. The historian Leon Wolff does not name the employers who kept the list.

Members of Congress investigated the use of private armed guards at Homestead, and Frick testified before them.

<a id="story-john-w-holway"></a>

#### John W. Holway

> **Who:** A 23-year-old medical student hired as a Pinkerton guard for the Homestead job.
>
> **When and where:** Chicago to Homestead, Pennsylvania, July 1892.
>
> **Movie:** *The River Ran Red* (1993), a documentary about the Homestead lockout, directed by Steffi Domike and Nicole Fauteux. It tells the story from the workers' side.

John W. Holway was hired to guard the Homestead works, and a crowd there kicked him and beat him with stones. He was 23 years old and studying to be a doctor. Henry Clay Frick had signed the contract for the guards with William and Robert Pinkerton. Holway was one of the college students who signed up with the Pinkerton agency for summer work at five dollars a day.

The agency's Chicago superintendent, the man in charge of its Chicago office, would not tell the men where they were going. He told them, "The element of danger which is usually found in such expeditions will be here entirely lacking." After dark, agency men put Holway and the other Chicago men on a train at the Lake Shore depot. Pinkerton detectives stood guard to stop anyone from getting off, even at the stops in Toledo and Cleveland. The thought struck Holway, Wolff writes, that he was "a sort of prisoner." He also had a feeling that there would be shooting.

On 6 July he was on the barges at Homestead. According to Wolff, he does not seem to have fired a shot all day. After the Pinkerton men surrendered, they walked to the town through a crowd that beat them. Three strikers knocked Holway down. One of them said, "You have killed two men this morning. I saw you!" As they pushed him up the hill, a stone hit him in the head.

Holway described what happened next under oath to the congressional committee. "I ran about half a mile, I suppose, but was rather weak and had had nothing to eat or drink, and my legs gave out, could not run any further, and some man got hold of me by the back of my coat, and about 20 or 30 men came up and kicked me and pounded me with stones." He said, "I thought I was about going and commenced to scream." About going meant about to die. Two or three strikers with rifles then ran up and kept the crowd off him.

#### The first federal rules, and how they were used

Members of Congress passed the first federal laws to control big business in 1887 and 1890. In the 1890s the justices of the Supreme Court let the sugar trust stand, and federal officials used the second law to break a railroad strike.

The Interstate Commerce Act became law on 4 February 1887. Under it, a five-member board called the Interstate Commerce Commission watched over the railroads. Interstate commerce means trade between states. The railroads became the first industry under federal regulation, which means rules made and enforced by the national government. The commission was the first federal regulatory board.

The Sherman Antitrust Act became law on 2 July 1890. It was named for Senator John Sherman of Ohio. Under it, every contract or combination "in restraint of trade" became illegal. That means any deal that blocks free buying and selling between the states. Trying to monopolize, or to become the only seller of something, also became a crime. A person found guilty could be fined $5,000 and sent to jail for a year. People harmed could sue for three times their losses. The law did not define the words "trust," "combination," "conspiracy" or "monopoly."

In 1895, in *United States v. E. C. Knight Co.*, the justices of the Supreme Court ruled on the sugar trust. The American Sugar Refining Company controlled about 98 percent of all sugar refining in the United States. The justices ruled that the company had not broken the law. They reasoned that making sugar was manufacturing, and that manufacturing was not trade.

In 1893, during a depression, managers of the Pullman Palace Car Company laid off more than 2,000 workers and cut wages by 25 percent. A depression is a long period when many businesses fail and many people lose their jobs. The company owned the town where its workers lived, and its managers did not lower the rents. Company president George M. Pullman refused to meet the workers' representatives. In 1894 between 125,000 and 250,000 railroad workers in 27 states joined a boycott of Pullman cars, refusing to handle trains that carried them.

That year federal officials used the Sherman Act against the workers. Edwin Walker was a special lawyer working for Attorney General Richard Olney. Walker claimed that the strike broke the Sherman Act. On 2 July 1894 federal judges William Woods and Peter S. Grosscup granted him an injunction. An injunction is a court order that tells people to stop doing something. Anyone who breaks it can be jailed. President Grover Cleveland used the injunction as his reason to send federal troops. The soldiers arrested boycotters and rioters and sometimes shot them, according to the Federal Judicial Center's history of the case. About 30 people were killed across the country during the strike.

### 1900 to 1950

Between 1895 and 1904, owners and bankers joined more than 1,800 manufacturing firms into 157 large corporations. Federal lawyers and judges then began to break some of the biggest apart. The largest, U.S. Steel, issued more than a billion dollars in stock in 1901. Stock is the shares, or parts of ownership, that a company sells to investors. Presidents Theodore Roosevelt and William Howard Taft had their lawyers sue the biggest combinations. In 1911 the justices of the Supreme Court ruled that Standard Oil and the American Tobacco Company had broken the law, and under court orders both were split apart.

Members of Congress passed two more antitrust laws in 1914. Antitrust laws are laws against trusts, which are giant combinations of companies run as one business, and against other deals that block competition. After the stock market crash of 1929, members of Congress passed a law in 1934 that made companies selling stock report their finances to the public. During the Second World War, federal officials gave about two-thirds of the value of their main war contracts to 100 companies.

#### The great merger movement and U.S. Steel

In a merger, two or more companies join into one. The 157 large combinations formed between 1895 and 1904, and more than 60 of them formed in 1899 alone. Naomi Lamoreaux, in her book *The Great Merger Movement in American Business*, names the causes. Factories cost a great deal to build, and industries grew fast after 1887. A depression is a long time when many businesses fail and many people lose their jobs. After the depression of 1893 began, rival owners cut their prices against each other in price wars. The owners had made agreements, called pools, to hold prices up. The price wars went on anyway.

Lamoreaux writes that "there was nothing natural or inevitable" about these combinations. Inevitable means certain to happen. Most of them used more money and work to make the same goods than the new rivals that soon appeared did, and in her words they "quickly lost their positions of market dominance," which means they lost their lead in their markets. The firms that built barriers against rivals, such as U.S. Steel through its control of iron ore, kept their lead longer.

U.S. Steel was set up as a corporation in New Jersey in February 1901. The banker J. P. Morgan put it together. Morgan bought Carnegie Steel for Andrew Carnegie's asking price of $480 million. Other companies went in with it, among them Federal Steel, National Steel, National Tube and American Bridge. So did the Lake Superior Consolidated Iron Mines, whose ore came from Ojibwe land in Minnesota. Charles M. Schwab was president from 1901 to 1903, and Elbert H. Gary was chairman from 1901 to 1927.

The new company issued stock with a stated value of about $1.4 billion. Accounts give figures from $1.403 billion to $1.466 billion. It was the first company in the world with more than a billion dollars in stock. Government investigators at the federal Bureau of Corporations put the real value of what the company owned at about $682 million, about half the stock issued. Stock issued for more than the property behind it is called watered stock. According to the financial data firm Finaeon, when the shares first traded in 1901, buyers valued them at about $765 million in all. The market value of the stock did not pass $1 billion until 1916.

U.S. Steel made about two-thirds of all the steel in the United States at the start. Kenneth Warren, in his book *Big Steel*, counts 65.7 percent in 1901. Another count gives 67 percent in 1902. EBSCO's reference entry gives a lower figure for the start, 44.8 percent, which no other count matches. That year the company employed 168,000 people. By 1911 its share had fallen to between 40 and 50 percent, depending on who counts.

<a id="story-jp-morgan"></a>

#### J.P. Morgan

> **Who:** The Wall Street banker who put companies together, among them U.S. Steel in 1901 and the Northern Securities Company.
>
> **When and where:** New York, 1901 to 1904.

J. P. Morgan was a banker on Wall Street, in New York City, who joined rival companies into single giant ones. Around 1900 he led a wave of these mergers.

In December 1900 Charles M. Schwab, then president of Carnegie Steel, gave a speech at the University Club. The speech led Morgan to the steel deal. Carnegie named a price of $480 million for his company, and Morgan accepted it at once. Morgan then formed U.S. Steel in 1901 and sat on its finance committee.

In 1901 Morgan and the railroad owner James J. Hill also formed the Northern Securities Company. It was a holding company, which is a company that owns controlling shares in other companies and does little else. Northern Securities controlled three railroads: the Great Northern, the Northern Pacific, and the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy. In 1902 President Theodore Roosevelt's Justice Department lawyers sued to break it up.

<a id="story-ida-tarbell-big-business"></a>

#### Ida Tarbell

> **Who:** The reporter whose history of Standard Oil, built from court records and sworn testimony, showed how John D. Rockefeller built Standard Oil.
>
> **When and where:** New York and the Pennsylvania oil region, 1900 to 1904.

Ida Tarbell spent most of five years, by her own count, tracing from public records how John D. Rockefeller built Standard Oil. Her family moved into Titusville in 1870, when she was 13. In 1872 her father, Franklin Tarbell, signed a pledge with other oil producers not to sell oil to Standard Oil. She began the work in 1900.

Tarbell read hundreds of thousands of documents from across the country. She used court records and depositions. A deposition is sworn testimony that is taken outside a courtroom and written down. She also interviewed employees and lawyers. The writer Mark Twain arranged for her to meet Henry H. Rogers, an officer of Standard Oil, and she interviewed him too.

Her *History of the Standard Oil Company* came out in 19 parts in *McClure's* magazine, from November 1902 to October 1904. In 1904 it was published as a book in two volumes.

In one part, Tarbell told the story of a Cleveland widow, Mrs. Backus, who sold her late husband's plant for making oil for machines to Rockefeller in 1878. Tarbell wrote that he paid her next to nothing. Rockefeller's biographer Ron Chernow gives a different account. He says the plant was out of date, that the widow asked for as much as $200,000, and that Rockefeller paid $79,000, which included $10,000 added on top. The two accounts of that sale do not agree. Chernow calls Rockefeller's buyouts of his Cleveland rivals in 1872 "one of the most shameful episodes in his career."

Rockefeller called Tarbell "That poisonous woman." He told his advisers, "Not a word about that misguided woman."

<a id="story-theodore-roosevelt-big-business"></a>

#### Theodore Roosevelt

> **Who:** The president known as the trust-buster. Lawyers in his Justice Department won the Northern Securities case and brought 44 antitrust suits in seven and a half years.
>
> **When and where:** Washington, 1901 to 1909.
>
> **Movie:** *TR: The Story of Theodore Roosevelt*, an American Experience documentary first shown on PBS in October 1996.

Theodore Roosevelt is known as the trust-buster, but the president after him brought more antitrust suits. In 1902 Roosevelt's Justice Department lawyers sued the Northern Securities Company, J. P. Morgan and James J. Hill's railroad holding company, under the Sherman Act. The Sherman Act is the federal law of 1890 against deals that block trade and against attempts to become the only seller of something.

On 14 March 1904 the justices of the Supreme Court ruled 5 to 4 for the government and upheld the order to break the company up. Justice John M. Harlan wrote for the majority. Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes disagreed. He wrote, "Great cases like hard cases make bad law."

Roosevelt's lawyers brought 44 antitrust suits in seven and a half years. William Howard Taft, the next president, had his lawyers bring more in four years. One count gives 75 and another gives 99. In 1911 Taft's lawyers sued U.S. Steel. Roosevelt then accused Taft of being unable to tell the good trusts from the bad ones.

#### Standard Oil and American Tobacco are broken up, 1911

In May 1911 the justices of the Supreme Court ruled against Standard Oil and the American Tobacco Company, and both companies were split apart. On 15 May they ruled that Standard Oil of New Jersey had broken the Sherman Act. Chief Justice Edward D. White wrote the court's decision and its reasons. He wrote that the Sherman Act banned only "unreasonable" limits on trade. This test is called the rule of reason. The justices gave the company six months to break itself up. Standard Oil was split into 34 separate companies.

Rockefeller was worth about $300 million in May 1911 and more than $900 million by the end of 1913. According to Chernow, Roosevelt said that Wall Street's prayer was now, "Oh Merciful Providence, give us another dissolution." Providence means God's care, and a dissolution is the breakup of a company. In 1916 newspaper headlines called Rockefeller the world's first billionaire. Companies that grew out of Standard Oil later became Exxon, Mobil and Chevron.

On 29 May 1911 the justices ruled against the American Tobacco Company. They found that James B. Duke, Benjamin N. Duke, George W. Watts, R. J. Reynolds and others had broken the Sherman Act "by seeking to monopolize practically all sectors of the tobacco industry." To monopolize means to become the only seller, with no real rivals. In November 1911 federal judges in New York divided the company's property among a new American Tobacco Company, Liggett and Myers, P. Lorillard, R. J. Reynolds and others. James B. Duke's tie to American Tobacco ended that year.

#### Two new laws, 1914

In 1914 members of Congress passed two laws that added to the Sherman Act. The second one named business practices the Sherman Act had left vague. President Woodrow Wilson signed the Federal Trade Commission Act on 26 September 1914. Under it, "unfair methods of competition" became illegal, and a new Federal Trade Commission had the power to make companies obey that rule. The commission opened on 16 March 1915.

Wilson signed the Clayton Antitrust Act on 15 October 1914. It banned several practices by name. One was price discrimination, which means charging different buyers different prices for the same goods. Others were deals that tied a buyer to one seller, mergers that cut down competition, and the same people sitting on the boards of competing companies. The Clayton Act also stated "that the labor of a human being is not a commodity or article of commerce." A commodity is a thing that is bought and sold. Under that section, federal lawyers and judges could no longer treat unions as illegal combinations. In 1894 they had used the Sherman Act that way against the railroad workers of the Pullman boycott.

#### Ludlow, 1914

At Ludlow, Colorado, on 20 April 1914, soldiers of the Colorado National Guard, the state's part-time army, burned the tent camp of striking coal miners. The mine owners were paying the Guard's costs. At least 19 people were killed, 13 of them women and children. Most of the strikers worked for the Colorado Fuel and Iron Company, whose main stockholder, the person who owned the most shares, was John D. Rockefeller Jr.

The miners struck in September 1913. In October men in a company armored car known as the "Death Special" fired on their tent camp at Forbes and killed one person. Governor Elias M. Ammons sent the Colorado National Guard.

On 20 April 1914 fighting broke out at the tent camp at Ludlow. Nobody knows who fired the first shot. Guardsmen set the tents on fire. Thirteen women and children had hidden in a pit dug under a tent, and they suffocated there. Suffocate means to die from lack of air. One guardsman and five miners were also killed. Guardsmen shot the strike leader Louis Tikas three times in the back. President Wilson sent the U.S. Army on 28 April. The strike ended in December 1914, and the union won none of its goals.

#### Leaded gasoline, 1924 to 1926

In the 1920s, three of the largest companies in the country kept selling a lead fuel additive after workers who made it died. Tetraethyl lead is a liquid made with lead. Researchers at General Motors added it to gasoline to stop engines from knocking. In August 1924 General Motors and Standard Oil of New Jersey formed the Ethyl Gasoline Corporation to sell it. DuPont made it.

Workers died at plants and a laboratory of all three companies. In October 1924, seven men died and 33 went to the hospital after working at Standard Oil's Bayway refinery in Elizabeth, New Jersey. A refinery is a plant that turns crude oil into fuel. Bill Kovarik, who wrote a history of leaded gasoline in 2005, gives those counts. Other accounts count five dead. Kovarik counts ten more dead at a DuPont plant and at least two dead at General Motors' laboratory in Dayton, Ohio. Poisoned workers at Bayway were "black and blue from uncontrolled muscle spasms." Some had to be tied into straitjackets, which are coats that hold a person's arms tight against the body.

On 20 May 1925 the Surgeon General, the head of the federal public health service, called a meeting about the additive. Frank Howard of Standard Oil said the industry could not give up "what has come to the industry like a gift from heaven." The companies kept selling it. Robert Kehoe, a scientist paid by the Ethyl company, then set out a theory of a "safe level" of lead that the companies relied on for decades.

#### Who controlled the corporations, 1932

In 1932 two writers showed that the 200 largest corporations outside banking held about half of the country's corporate wealth, and that hired managers, not owners, ran them. In their book *The Modern Corporation and Private Property*, Adolf Berle and Gardiner Means counted the 200 largest corporations outside banking. By 1930 those 200 held 49.2 percent of the country's corporate wealth. The scholar Gerald F. Davis later worked out that if that trend had continued, they would have held all of it by 1959.

Berle and Means also found that ownership of these companies was split among many scattered shareholders, the people who owned their shares, so the managers made the decisions.

#### The Securities and Exchange Commission, 1934

After the stock market crash of 1929, members of Congress passed a law that made companies selling stock report their finances to the public. President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the Securities Exchange Act on 6 June 1934. Under it, the members of a new Securities and Exchange Commission, or SEC, watched over the stock markets. The yearly and quarterly reports that such companies still file with the SEC began with this law.

Roosevelt made Joseph P. Kennedy the first chairman of the SEC in the summer of 1934. Accounts give June or 1 July. Kennedy had made money in the stock market using the same practices the new law banned. He had given, lent and raised money for Roosevelt's 1932 campaign. Newspaper writers said the choice was "like putting the fox in the hen house." In private, Roosevelt answered, "set a thief to catch a thief." Both sayings meant the same thing: Roosevelt had put a man who had used those practices in charge of stopping them. Kennedy resigned in September 1935.

#### Spies, guns and company police, 1936 to 1940

From 1936 to 1940, senators on a committee led by Senator Robert M. La Follette Jr. of Wisconsin held hearings on how employers fought unions. Witnesses told the senators that company managers had planted spies inside unions. Company managers had stored up weapons, among them submachine guns, rifles and tear gas. They had also hired their own police forces.

On Memorial Day, 30 May 1937, during a steel strike, several hundred men, women and children marched toward the Republic Steel plant in Chicago to support the strikers. Republic Steel's chairman was Tom M. Girdler. At the plant, 264 Chicago police threw tear gas at the marchers, fired their guns and beat them with clubs. The police killed 10 people and shot 40, and more than 90 people were hurt in all. The senators on the La Follette committee found that the police had used "excessive force."

#### Hawaii's Big Five

In Hawaii, five companies known as the Big Five controlled about 94 percent of the islands' sugar crop by 1920. They were C. Brewer and Company, Theo H. Davies and Company, H. Hackfeld and Company, Castle and Cooke, and Alexander and Baldwin. The historian Carol MacLennan gives the 94 percent figure. The same people sat on the boards of several of the firms, and together they controlled shipping, banking and stores in the islands. Four of the firms together owned nearly three-quarters of the Matson shipping line, which carried 80 percent of the cargo between the mainland and Hawaii.

In 1893 members of a group called the Committee of Safety organized the overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom. They pressed for the United States to annex the islands, which means to take them over. Some children of Big Five partners were members of that committee. The Big Five's plantations stood on the land of Native Hawaiians, the Kanaka Maoli. From 1893 into the 1950s, the owners of the Big Five dominated Hawaii's economy and government.

#### War contracts, 1940 to 1944

During the Second World War, a small number of large companies received most of the government's war business. Robert Higgs, writing for the Independent Institute in 1995, gives the figures for prime contracts from 1940 to 1944. A prime contract is a contract made directly between the government and a company. The 100 companies with the most contract money received about two-thirds of the value of those contracts. The top 10 received about 30 percent. General Motors alone received nearly 8 percent.

Federal officials also paid for new factories and rented them to private companies. As of 30 June 1944, just 26 companies had the use of half the value of all those government-paid factories.

### 1950 to 2000

The largest American companies of these years had workers by the hundreds of thousands. General Motors was the largest private employer in the country in 1979. The Bell telephone system had about a million workers in the early 1980s. From the 1970s, business leaders organized to win influence in Washington, and by 1982 more than 2,400 firms had registered lobbyists there. A lobbyist is a person paid to persuade lawmakers.

Some companies kept selling products that studies linked to disease and death. In 1954 tobacco companies paid for advertisements in which they disputed studies linking smoking to lung cancer. In 1994 heads of tobacco companies told a House hearing that they did not believe nicotine is addictive. AT&T's leaders agreed with federal lawyers to split up the Bell System, and the split took effect in 1984. In 1999 federal lawyers won a ruling that Microsoft held a monopoly. In 2001 an appeals court agreed that Microsoft had broken the law to keep it.

#### General Motors

In the 1950s General Motors was the country's largest car maker, and in 1953 it sold more to the armed forces than any other company. In 1954 it sold 54 percent of new cars, by the Associated Press's count. The encyclopedia Britannica lists GM at 40 to 45 percent of all car sales through the 1950s and 1960s. In 1955 GM became the first company to earn more than a billion dollars in profit in one year. In the first three quarters of 1955 alone it made $912,887,537 in profit. *TIME* magazine wrote, "Never before in history has one corporation made so much in so short a time." GM's workforce in the United States peaked at 618,365 in 1979. That made it the largest private employer in the country.

In January 1953 President Dwight D. Eisenhower chose GM's president, Charles E. Wilson, as Secretary of Defense. He gave up a salary of $600,000 a year for one of $22,000. Wilson owned 40,000 shares of GM stock, and GM sold more to the armed forces than any other company. As Secretary of Defense he could make decisions that helped or hurt GM, so at his hearing senators pressed him on that conflict. Senator Robert C. Hendrickson asked whether Wilson could make a decision that went strongly against GM's interest. Wilson answered, "Yes, sir, I could. I cannot conceive of one because, for years, I thought what was good for our country was good for General Motors, and vice versa." Vice versa means the other way around. People soon repeated his words as "What is good for General Motors is good for the country."

In 1965 Ralph Nader wrote a book called *Unsafe at Any Speed*. In it, Nader criticized the safety of GM's Corvair car. GM managers hired private detectives to look into Nader's private life. In 1966 GM's president, James M. Roche, apologized to a Senate committee. That same year members of Congress passed the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act, the first federal rules for how cars must be built. Nader sued GM for invading his privacy and settled for $425,000. He used the money to start groups that work for consumers. GM stopped making the Corvair in 1969.

#### Eisenhower's warning, 1961

On 17 January 1961, in his farewell speech, President Dwight D. Eisenhower warned the country about the power of the arms makers and the armed forces together. He said, "in the councils of government, we must guard against the acquisition of unwarranted influence, whether sought or unsought, by the military-industrial complex." The councils of government are the places where leaders make decisions. Acquisition means getting, and unwarranted means without good reason. By the military-industrial complex he meant the ties between the armed forces and the companies that made their weapons. Those were the same kinds of large companies that had received most of the war contracts of 1940 to 1944.

#### The conglomerate

A conglomerate is one company that owns many businesses that have nothing to do with each other. Harold Geneen ran the company ITT from 1959 to 1977. In those years ITT bought between 250 and 350 companies, depending on the count, in more than 80 countries. They included the Sheraton hotel chain, Avis car rental, the Hartford insurance company and Continental Baking, the maker of Wonder Bread. ITT's yearly sales grew from about $700 million to $17 billion, and it became the eleventh-largest corporation in the country. Geneen believed that good managers could make a success of any business.

In 1966 ITT's leaders tried to buy the ABC television network for $700 million, and federal antitrust officials stopped the deal. In Chile, officials under President Salvador Allende took over ITT's company there. ITT later admitted that it had given the CIA, the American spy agency, $350,000 for "political" purposes in Chile.

#### Business organizes in Washington

In the 1970s, heads of large companies built up their own political power in Washington. On 23 August 1971 the lawyer Lewis F. Powell Jr. sent a private memo to Eugene B. Sydnor Jr. of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, a national group of businesses. Its title was "Attack On American Free Enterprise System." Powell wrote that critics of business now came from "the college campus, the pulpit, the media" and from politicians. The pulpit here means preachers in churches. He urged business leaders to keep "constant surveillance," or a close watch, on textbooks and television programs. On 21 October 1971, less than two months later, President Richard Nixon nominated Powell to the Supreme Court. The newspaper columnist Jack Anderson made the memo public in September 1972. That year the Chamber's leaders set up a 40-person working group on the memo. In late 1973 they approved plans for business to act in education, in communications, in politics and in the courts.

On 13 October 1972 three groups of company heads joined to form the Business Roundtable. Its founders included John D. Harper of Alcoa and Roger Blough, the retired head of U.S. Steel. They set out to fight the growing power of unions, especially construction unions.

Company heads opened offices in Washington and hired lobbyists. Corporations with public affairs offices in Washington went from 100 in 1968 to more than 500 in 1978. Firms with registered lobbyists went from 175 in 1971 to 2,445 in 1982. Companies also set up political action committees. A political action committee, or PAC, collects money and gives it to candidates. Officials of the Federal Election Commission counted 89 company PACs at the end of 1974, 294 in May 1976 and 1,206 at the end of 1980.

From 1978 to 1980 members of Congress voted to remove federal rules on three industries. President Jimmy Carter signed each law: for airlines on 24 October 1978, for banks on 31 March 1980 and for trucking on 1 July 1980.

#### Products that hurt people, and what the companies said

From 1954 to 1994, heads of tobacco companies publicly disputed the evidence that smoking causes disease and that nicotine is addictive. On 4 January 1954 the major American tobacco companies ran an advertisement called "A Frank Statement to Cigarette Smokers" in more than 400 newspapers. It reached about 43 million people. In it, the companies disputed new scientific studies that linked smoking cigarettes to lung cancer. The public relations firm Hill and Knowlton, a company paid to shape what the public thinks of its clients, designed it.

Addison Yeaman, the chief lawyer of the Brown and Williamson tobacco company, wrote a memo on 17 July 1963. In it he said that to protect its earnings, the industry must "either a) disprove the theory of causal relationship or b) discover the carcinogen or carcinogens...and demonstrate our ability to remove or neutralize them." A causal relationship here meant that smoking causes cancer. Disprove means to show that something is false. A carcinogen is a substance that causes cancer, and to neutralize something is to make it harmless.

At a hearing in the House of Representatives on 14 April 1994, Representative Ron Wyden asked seven tobacco company heads whether nicotine is addictive. William Campbell of Philip Morris answered, "I believe nicotine is not addictive, yes." James Johnston of R. J. Reynolds said cigarettes "clearly do not meet the classic definition of addiction." Joseph Taddeo of U.S. Tobacco said, "I don't believe that nicotine or our products are addictive."

Four cigarette makers, Philip Morris, R. J. Reynolds, Brown and Williamson and Lorillard, signed an agreement with the attorneys general of 46 states on 23 November 1998. An attorney general is a state's chief lawyer. The states had sued to get back what they spent treating sick smokers. The companies agreed to pay at least $206 billion over the first 25 years and to limit their advertising.

Asbestos is a mineral that separates into thin, strong fibers. Builders used it to fireproof and insulate buildings. When people breathe asbestos fibers in, the fibers can stay in the lungs for years. They scar the lungs and can cause asbestosis, a lung disease that brings shortness of breath, coughing and lasting lung damage. They can also cause mesothelioma, a cancer of the thin linings of the chest and belly. The illness can take 10 to 40 years or more to show. Johns-Manville was once the largest maker of asbestos products in the country. In 1981 it faced 9,300 lawsuits brought by 12,800 people who sued over illness from asbestos. In August 1982 the company's leaders filed for bankruptcy, a court process for a company that cannot pay its debts. The filing put all the injury lawsuits against the company on hold. By the end of 1988, a fund set up in the bankruptcy to pay injury claims had paid more than 12,600 claims, for almost $500 million in all.

On 3 December 1984 more than 40 tons of a poison gas called methyl isocyanate leaked from a pesticide plant in Bhopal, India, a factory that made poisons to kill insects. Union Carbide India Limited ran the plant. It was part of the American company Union Carbide. Union Carbide's leaders had first planned to close the plant, which was losing money. Instead they cut many jobs, including maintenance engineers, to run it for less, according to a report by France's environment ministry. The same report says that on 2 December 1984 the plant's senior managers ordered the cleaning of pipes that led to a machine meant to clean escaping gas. According to a 2005 medical review by Edward Broughton, a broken valve let about a ton of water used for cleaning pipes into a tank of the gas.

That gas-cleaning machine had been turned off. Broughton's review says that happened three weeks before the leak. The French report dates it to 23 October 1984, about six weeks before. The same report says the plant's cooling unit had been shut down since June 1984 to cut its use of electricity by 18 percent. Neither report names the people who turned off the machine or shut down the cooling unit.

The gas damaged people's eyes, causing redness and sores, and it filled their lungs with fluid. According to Britain's Health and Safety Executive, a government safety agency, the gas killed about 2,000 people in the first hours. Broughton's review gives about 3,800 dead at once, and 15,000 to 20,000 early deaths reported over the next twenty years. At first Union Carbide's leaders tried to keep the company free of legal blame. Later they said the company accepted "moral responsibility," and it paid $470 million to the government of India.

#### The Bell System is split, 1984

In the early 1980s AT&T's Bell System held about $150 billion in property and employed about a million people. Justice Department lawyers sued AT&T in 1974. In January 1982 AT&T's leaders and the Justice Department's lawyers agreed that AT&T would give up its local telephone companies. Judge Harold H. Greene approved the deal with changes, and the case was closed on 24 August 1982.

On 1 January 1984 the local companies became seven regional companies, called the Baby Bells. AT&T kept its long-distance service, its research center, Bell Labs, and its equipment maker, Western Electric. It kept $34 billion of the $149.5 billion in property it had held the day before, and it had 636,000 fewer workers.

<a id="story-bill-gates"></a>

#### Bill Gates

> **Who:** The head of Microsoft when federal and state lawyers sued it for keeping an illegal monopoly on the software that runs personal computers.
>
> **When and where:** Redmond, Washington, and Washington, D.C., 1998 to 2001.
>
> **Movie:** *Inside Bill's Brain: Decoding Bill Gates* (2019), a Netflix series directed by Davis Guggenheim.

Bill Gates founded Microsoft and ran it as its chief executive until January 2000, so he was in charge when a federal judge found that it held an illegal monopoly. Microsoft made Windows, the operating system that ran most personal computers. An operating system is the main program that runs a computer and the other programs on it.

On 18 May 1998 lawyers for the Justice Department, the attorneys general of twenty states and the District of Columbia sued Microsoft. The main question in the case was whether Microsoft could bundle its web browser, Internet Explorer, with Windows. A web browser is the program people use to look at websites. To bundle it meant to build it into Windows, which made it harder for rival browsers such as Netscape Navigator to win users.

Gates answered the government lawyers' questions in a deposition that was filmed on videotape. A deposition is sworn testimony taken outside a courtroom. A person who was there called him "evasive and nonresponsive." According to *Businessweek* magazine, the government lawyers used snippets of emails to show that many of his denials were false.

On 5 November 1999 Judge Thomas Penfield Jackson found that Microsoft held a monopoly. On 7 June 2000 he ordered the company split into two, one for Windows and one for its other software. On 28 June 2001 seven judges of the federal appeals court upheld the finding that Microsoft had illegally kept its monopoly. They threw out the breakup order, partly because Jackson had talked about the case to reporters while it was still going on.

On 6 September 2001, Attorney General John Ashcroft announced that the Justice Department would no longer seek a breakup. On 1 November 2001 the government's lawyers settled with Microsoft. Microsoft's leaders agreed to share some of its technical information with other companies. They also accepted a panel of three investigators with full access to its systems.

<a id="story-steve-young-vlasic"></a>

#### Steve Young

> **Who:** A Vlasic pickle executive who described what it was like to sell to Walmart.
>
> **When and where:** The late 1990s to January 2001. His account was published in December 2003.
>
> **Movie:** *Is Wal-Mart Good for America?* (FRONTLINE, PBS, 2004), a documentary about Walmart.

Steve Young watched Walmart's buyers push his company's pickles to a price that left almost no profit. He was vice president of grocery marketing for pickles at Vlasic. The reporter Charles Fishman told his story in *Fast Company* magazine in December 2003.

In the late 1990s a Walmart buyer saw Vlasic's gallon jar of pickles. The buyer began talking about it with Pat Hunn, the head of Vlasic's Walmart sales team. The jar went into every Walmart, about 3,000 stores, at $2.97. At that price Vlasic and Walmart each made a penny or two a jar, if that. Young said each store sold about 80 jars a week, which came to 240,000 gallons of pickles a week.

Walmart was 30 percent of Vlasic's business. Young says shoppers who used to buy Vlasic's pickle spears and chips at supermarkets bought the cheap gallon jar instead. He says Vlasic's profits from pickles fell by 25 percent or more.

Young says Vlasic asked to raise the price. He remembers the Walmart buyers' answer: "If you do that, all the other products of yours we buy, we'll stop buying." He called it "a clear threat." Hunn remembers the buyers saying, "We want the $2.97 gallon of pickles. If you don't do it, we'll see if someone else might." Later, Walmart's buyers let Vlasic shrink the jar to just over half a gallon, at $2.79. Vlasic filed for bankruptcy in January 2001. Everyone involved agrees the gallon jar was not a critical factor in that failure.

### 2000 to Today

In September 2026 three American companies, Nvidia, Apple and Alphabet, were each worth more than $4 trillion, according to the investment website The Motley Fool. In the same years federal lawyers took four of the largest technology companies to court over monopoly power. Walmart employed about 1.6 million people in the United States in 2026, by its own count. That is about 2.6 times General Motors' American workforce at its peak in 1979.

A federal jury convicted Enron's former chief executives of fraud in 2006. Lehman Brothers failed in 2008, and members of Congress set aside $700 billion that year to rescue banks and other companies. The four technology companies taken to court were Google, Meta, Amazon and Apple. By September 2026 judges had ruled twice that Google broke the law and once for Meta, and the Amazon and Apple cases had not come to trial.

#### How big, in numbers

A company's market value is the price of one share times the number of shares. It changes every day the stock market is open. On 29 October 2025 Nvidia became the first company worth $5 trillion, according to the business news network CNBC. On 7 September 2026, The Motley Fool listed the three most valuable companies in the world. Nvidia was worth about $5.6 trillion, Apple about $4.7 trillion and Alphabet about $4.1 trillion.

Walmart reported $713.2 billion in revenue, the money it took in, for the year that ended on 31 January 2026. Its 2026 annual report records about 2.1 million workers around the world, about 1.6 million of them in the United States. About 92 percent of its American workers were paid by the hour. At that time it had more than 10,900 stores in 19 countries. Amazon's yearly report to the government for 2025 states that it employed about 1,576,000 people at the end of that year. It also used independent contractors, who are paid for each job and are not employees, and temporary workers. Neither group is counted in that number.

#### Fraud and harm at the top

Courts found that leaders of several large companies of these years had deceived the public, and Purdue Pharma's leaders admitted it in guilty pleas. Enron was an energy company in Houston, Texas. On 2 December 2001 it filed for bankruptcy. Enron's workers had much of their retirement savings in Enron stock. At the end of 2000, 62 percent of the money in the company's retirement plan was in its own shares, according to the Congressional Research Service, which does research for Congress. The shares fell from more than $80 each in January 2001 to less than 70 cents in January 2002.

A lawsuit claimed that Enron had blocked its workers from moving their retirement money out of Enron stock while the price fell. On 25 May 2006 a federal jury in Houston convicted Enron's former chief executives, Kenneth L. Lay and Jeffrey K. Skilling, of conspiracy and fraud, according to the Justice Department. Conspiracy means planning a crime together with others. Fraud means lying or cheating to get money.

On 17 August 2006 federal Judge Gladys Kessler ruled that the major tobacco companies had broken the federal racketeering law. Racketeering here means running a business through a pattern of fraud. She found that the companies had "defrauded the American people by lying for decades about the health risks of smoking and their marketing to children." She wrote that they had "marketed and sold their lethal products with zeal, with deception, with a single-minded focus on their financial success, and without regard for the human tragedy or social costs that success exacted." Zeal means great eagerness, and exacted means took as its price. She ordered them to publish statements about the harm of smoking and about how addictive nicotine is.

Purdue Pharma made OxyContin, a pain pill. OxyContin is an opioid, a drug from the same family of chemicals as heroin. According to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the first wave of opioid overdose deaths, from 1999, came from prescription opioids, after doctors wrote more opioid prescriptions in the 1990s. CDC researchers count about 806,000 Americans who died of opioid overdoses from 1999 to 2023, from all kinds of opioids.

In May 2007 the company pleaded guilty to misleading the public about the risk of becoming addicted to OxyContin, and it agreed to pay $600 million. Its president, Michael Friedman, its top lawyer, Howard R. Udell, and its former chief medical officer, Paul D. Goldenheim, also pleaded guilty. They admitted to misbranding, which means selling a drug with false or misleading claims about it, and together they paid $34.5 million. On 24 November 2020 the company pleaded guilty to three federal felonies, which are serious crimes. When Purdue pleaded guilty in 2020, no member of the Sackler family, which owned Purdue, was charged with a crime.

On 16 June 2025, 55 state and territorial attorneys general joined a $7.4 billion settlement with Purdue and the Sacklers, according to the New York attorney general's office. On 28 April 2026 federal Judge Madeline Cox Arleo sentenced Purdue to pay $5.5 billion, as CNBC and Reuters reported. She said she could not send Purdue's executives or owners to prison, because the Justice Department had charged only the company. More than 40 people spoke at the sentencing. Judge Arleo said, "Your government failed you." On 1 May 2026 New York's attorney general announced that Purdue had shut down. A new company, Knoa Pharma, took over, with no role for the Sacklers.

#### The 2008 rescue

In 2008 the investment bank Lehman Brothers failed, and members of Congress voted public money to rescue banks and other companies. On 15 September 2008 Lehman Brothers filed the largest bankruptcy in the country's history. It had about $639 billion in property and $619 billion in debts, according to the reference publisher EBSCO. Its chief executive was Richard S. Fuld Jr. Investigators later looked into whether Lehman's executives, Fuld among them, had moved money and raised their own pay just before the bankruptcy. EBSCO's entry states that Fuld "walked away with $480 million" but does not say over what years he received it.

In March 2010 Anton R. Valukas, an investigator named by the bankruptcy court, reported on deals that Lehman called Repo 105. Lehman's managers had used them to make the firm's books look stronger at the end of each quarter, the three-month periods for which companies report their results. In 2011 officials of the Securities and Exchange Commission reported that it would be hard to prove that Lehman had broken the law. No Lehman executive was charged with a crime.

On 3 October 2008 members of Congress passed the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act, which allowed up to $700 billion to rescue banks and other companies. Federal officials paid out $443.5 billion in all, and most of it was paid back. In December 2023 auditors at the Government Accountability Office, which checks federal spending for Congress, put the final cost at $31.1 billion. The Capital Purchase Program, which put money into banks, made a profit of $16.3 billion. The rescue of the insurance company AIG cost $15.2 billion, the loans to car makers cost $12.1 billion and the housing programs cost $31.4 billion. The car loans began with $13.4 billion that President George W. Bush announced in December 2008.

#### Antitrust returns

In the 2020s, government lawyers brought monopoly cases against four of the largest technology companies. By September 2026 they had won two cases against Google and lost one against Meta, and two more were waiting for trial.

Federal Judge Amit P. Mehta ruled on 5 August 2024 that Google had illegally kept monopolies in general internet search and in search advertising. On 2 September 2025 he refused to make Google sell its Chrome browser or its Android phone software. Then, on 5 December 2025, he ordered Google to share its search index and some user data with rival companies. A search index is the huge list of web pages that a search engine keeps. A committee of five technical experts was to oversee it. Google's lawyers appealed. In late July 2026 Justice Department lawyers filed a brief, a written argument, with the appeals court, according to the news service Courthouse News. They asked the court to keep the ruling. They also asked it to ban Google's large payments to companies such as Apple. Those payments make Google the search engine that the companies' products use unless the user changes it.

In a second case, federal Judge Leonie Brinkema ruled in April 2025 that Google had illegally monopolized the tools that websites use to sell advertising space. On 16 September 2026 the court made public her opinion on what Google must do. She refused to make Google sell its advertising exchange, the online market where websites sell ad space to advertisers. She ordered new rules for how the tools work. The National Law Review reported the opinion in an article by a writer for Chamber of Progress, a group funded by the technology industry.

The Federal Trade Commission's case against Meta was about its purchases of Instagram in 2012 and WhatsApp in 2014. The trial began on 14 April 2025. On 18 November 2025 Judge James Boasberg ruled for Meta. He found that Meta did not hold a monopoly, because TikTok and YouTube competed with it. FTC lawyers appealed on 20 January 2026, and in August 2026 the appeals court had not yet set a date to hear the case.

FTC lawyers and 17 state attorneys general sued Amazon on 26 September 2023 for keeping an illegal monopoly. Judge John H. Chun set the trial for 29 March 2027. He will decide the case himself, without a jury. Apple was sued on 21 March 2024 by Justice Department lawyers and 16 state attorneys general, for monopolizing the market for smartphones. On 30 June 2025 Judge Julien Neals refused Apple's request to throw the case out.

<a id="story-lina-khan"></a>

#### Lina Khan
