They were on probation, which is supervision in place of prison, or on parole, which is early release from prison under supervision, or they had finished their sentences. State lawmakers and state constitutions set these rules. Under the laws of Maine and Vermont, people in prison can vote.

#### A senator convicted, 2024

On September 22, 2023, federal prosecutors in Manhattan charged Senator Bob Menendez of New Jersey, his wife, Nadine Menendez, and others with bribery. According to news reports of the case in 2023, agents had found $480,000 in cash and more than $100,000 in gold bars in the Menendez home. On July 16, 2024, a jury found him guilty on all counts, or charges, including acting as a foreign agent of Egypt, meaning acting on behalf of Egypt's government. He resigned from the Senate in August 2024. On January 29, 2025, a judge sentenced him to 11 years in prison. He reported to prison in June 2025.

#### Immigration law after 2001

In the Homeland Security Act of 2002, members of Congress created the Department of Homeland Security. Its officials began work in 2003. Under the act, the old Immigration and Naturalization Service was split into three agencies: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Customs and Border Protection (CBP). On June 15, 2012, officials of the Department of Homeland Security began a policy called Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, or DACA. Under it, certain people brought to the country as children could get protection from being deported, or sent out of the country, and permission to work. Lawsuits over DACA went on for years.

<a id="ch-crime-justice"></a>

## Chapter 21: Crime, Police, and Justice

### Before 1500

Before 1500, no nation north of Mexico kept its laws in writing. When one person killed another, the families of the two people settled it between them, and a life was owed for a life. Among the Cherokee, the dead person's clan had the duty to take that life from the killer's side. In accounts of other nations, the killer's relatives had the duty to give up a life in exchange. Some families took a payment instead, such as wampum, furs or other goods. Wampum is strings or belts of beads made from shells.

Everything known about these rules comes from later sources. Some are the nations' own spoken traditions, written down long afterward. Others are accounts by Native and European writers after about 1600. No written record names a person tried or punished before 1500. What is known is the rules, which the nations remembered and later wrote down.

#### The Cherokee law of blood

Among the Cherokee, a killing was settled between two clans. A clan is a large family group. The Cherokee had seven clans, among them the Wolf, the Deer and the Paint, and a child belonged to the mother's clan.

In 1829 the editors of the *Cherokee Phoenix*, the Cherokee Nation's own newspaper, printed an article on the old rules. The article states that the Cherokee "as a nation, had nothing to do with murder." The nation's leaders did not punish a killing. The clans did. The clan of the dead person had the duty to take revenge by killing the killer. If the killer ran away, his brother or his nearest relative "was liable to suffer in his stead," in the article's words. That meant the clan could kill the brother or the relative in the killer's place. Every killing counted as murder, so a person who killed someone by accident could be killed in return. A man who killed his own brother answered to no law and no clan.

The same article states that about twenty years before 1829, the Cherokee held a council, a large meeting to decide the nation's business, and ended these rules. From then on, murder was a crime against the Cherokee government.

#### Condolence and the Great Law

The Haudenosaunee are five nations in what is now New York: the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca. Their own tradition says the five nations were once caught in feuds. A feud is a long run of killings in which each side takes revenge for the last death. A man named Hiawatha, whose daughters had been murdered, strung shells into wampum. He used the strings to speak words of comfort instead of words of revenge. These words of condolence, meaning comfort for people in grief, became central to the Great Law of Peace. The five nations joined together under the Great Law.

The Haudenosaunee told the Great Law aloud for generations. By 1910 two written versions existed at a Haudenosaunee community in Ontario called Six Nations of the Grand River. Seth Newhouse, a Mohawk, wrote one, and the chiefs of that community wrote the other. Arthur C. Parker printed them in English in 1916, for the New York State Museum.

In that version, a chief who committed murder lost his title, and the other chiefs removed him. A war chief then ordered him to leave the land of the five nations and never come back. An outsider adopted into one of the nations who did wrong got a warning from a war chief the first time. After a second wrong, the written law says, the person was to be sent out of the land of the five nations for good. It does not say who was to send the person away.

#### Forgiveness at the Green Corn

The Muscogee, also called the Creek, and other nations of the Southeast held the Green Corn Ceremony each midsummer, when the first corn ripened. Its Muscogee name, the busk, comes from their word for "to fast." People fasted, and they lit the sacred fire again in the town square. At that time the people of each town forgave every crime except murder.

The trader James Adair wrote about the ceremony in the middle 1700s. William Bartram, a naturalist, and Benjamin Hawkins, a government agent, also described it. A naturalist is a person who studies plants and animals. A government agent is an official sent to deal with a nation for a government. The most detailed descriptions were written in the late 1800s and early 1900s.

### The 1500s

In the 1500s, the only European courts in this land were at a few Spanish outposts. Spanish settlers founded St. Augustine, in Florida, in 1565. Juan de Oñate led a Spanish colony into New Mexico in 1598. In a Spanish colony the same officials governed the settlers, commanded the soldiers and judged the cases. Everywhere else, the Native nations kept their own laws.

In a Spanish town, an official called an alcalde acted as the judge. His power covered smaller crimes and quarrels, but in practice he heard most of the cases in his area. A person who lost could appeal, which means asking a higher official to change the decision. The appeal went to a higher judge or to the governor himself.

#### Killed without a trial, 1565

In September and October of 1565, the Spanish commander Pedro Menéndez de Avilés had French Protestants killed after they surrendered to him. Protestants are Christians outside the Catholic Church. The men had no trial. The National Park Service's handbook for Fort Matanzas lists 111 killed the first time and 134 the second, about 245 in all. It states that 16 men were spared each time. Chuck Meide, speaking on the PBS program *Secrets of the Dead*, gives wider ranges for the two killings, from 110 to 200 and from 70 to 150.

#### The Acoma trial, 1599

In February 1599, Juan de Oñate, the leader of the Spanish colony in New Mexico, put about 500 Acoma people on trial. He had ordered the attack on their town a month before, and he sat as their judge.

The trial followed a fight at Acoma Pueblo, the Acoma people's town. In December 1598, Spanish soldiers under Juan de Zaldívar came to Acoma and demanded food. Acoma people killed Zaldívar and eleven or twelve of his soldiers. The Acoma people's own account says the soldiers had also raped an Acoma woman. Rape means forcing a person into sex.

On December 28 Oñate opened an inquiry, an official hearing to find out what had happened. He asked the Franciscan friars with the colony whether a war on Acoma would be just, meaning right and fair. Friars are Catholic religious brothers. They said yes. In January 1599 Vicente de Zaldívar led about 70 soldiers against Acoma. His soldiers broke into the town, killed Acoma men, women and children, and burned it. Counts of the Acoma dead differ. New Mexico's state historian gives about 600. The Pueblo leaders of the All Pueblo Council of Governors give 800, and a National Park Service page gives about 1,500.

The trial of the captives began on February 9, 1599, and lasted three days. Oñate named a defender for the prisoners, and the defender asked for mercy. Acoma witnesses said many of their people had been working in their fields during the first fight. They said that "some wanted to surrender but some refused, and so they fought."

Oñate gave his sentence on February 12. He sentenced no one to death. Every man over 25 was to have one foot cut off and to be made a slave for twenty years. He would be forced to work for Spanish colonists with no pay and no right to leave. Boys and young men from 12 to 25, and women and girls over 12, were also to be made slaves for twenty years. Oñate sentenced the old people to be handed over as slaves to the Plains Apache. Two Hopi men were to have their right hands cut off and be sent home to tell their people.

Oñate declared the Acoma children under 12 innocent. He still ordered them taken from their families and handed to the friars. A National Park Service page states that about 70 girls were sent to convents in Mexico, houses where nuns live. It states that in all probability none of them ever came home. The PBS program *POV* states that some scholars believe the children were later sold as slaves. The Pueblo leaders of the All Pueblo Council of Governors give the number of children taken as 60.

The Spanish record states the order, the ages of the prisoners, the twenty-year terms and the taking of the children. On those points the accounts agree. The record states Oñate's order to cut off a foot. It does not say how the cutting was to be done, or whether it was done to each man. The Acoma people's own history says that 24 men had a foot cut off. Reporters for the Associated Press and NPR give the same number. The historian Marc Simmons first wrote that the feet were cut off, and he later came to doubt it. The historian John L. Kessell doubts it too. Kessell wrote that "the historical record makes no mention of a one-footed Acoma slave."

### The 1600s

Judges in the English colonies of the 1600s punished crime on the body and in public. They ordered whippings, brandings and cut-off ears, and they sent people to sit in the stocks where their neighbors could see them. In Massachusetts Bay, ordinary settlers took turns walking a watch to keep order at night. A jail held people waiting for a trial or a punishment, people who had done small wrongs, and people who owed money. Locking people in a prison for years as the punishment itself began in the 1790s.

Colonial judges in Massachusetts Bay and Plymouth also tried Native people who lived near the colonists. In Virginia in 1669, lawmakers passed a law under which a master was not charged with a crime when an enslaved person resisted him and died while he was beating the person. In 1692 judges in Massachusetts had 19 people hanged for witchcraft.

#### Jamestown under martial law, 1610 to 1619

From 1610 to 1619, the leaders of the Jamestown colony in Virginia ruled it under martial law. Martial law means rule by army officers instead of by ordinary courts. Jamestown stood in Tsenacomoco, the land of the Powhatan people.

Sir Thomas Gates issued the first orders on May 24, 1610. Thomas West, Lord De La Warr, an English nobleman, confirmed them and added more on June 12, 1610. Sir Thomas Dale added military rules on June 22, 1611. William Strachey printed the whole set in 1612 as the *Lawes Divine, Morall and Martiall*.

The historian Brent Tarter lists the punishments in the *Encyclopedia Virginia*. The punishment was death for murder, for robbery and for blasphemy, which means insulting God. It was also death to speak treason, meaning words against the king's rule, to speak against the company that ran the colony, or to trade with Indians without permission. The printed laws of 1612 also set death for any man who would "ravish or force any woman, maid or Indian," which means rape. They set death for "the horrible, and detestable sins of Sodomie" too, and they do not say which acts that word covered.

The punishment was a whipping for gambling, for missing church, for sex between two unmarried people, for killing farm animals without need, and for stealing crops or farm tools. Tarter lists adultery, sex between a married person and someone outside the marriage, among the crimes punished by whipping. The printed laws of 1612 set death for it. Rule under these laws ended when Sir George Yeardley arrived in Virginia on April 18, 1619.

In 1625 a colonist named George Percy wrote an account of the colony's early years. He wrote about the building of a fort at Henricus in 1611, and about colonists there who ran away to live with the Native people nearby. When they were caught, Dale had them put to death: "Some he apointed to be hanged some burned some to be broken upon wheles others to be Staked and some to be shott to deathe." Breaking on the wheel was a way of putting a person to death in Europe. The executioner broke the person's arms and legs with a heavy bar or club and tied the body to a large wooden wheel. Percy does not describe how it was done at Jamestown, and he does not explain what "Staked" meant. He wrote that Dale did these things "To terrefy the reste," meaning to frighten the other colonists.

Percy also wrote that Dale had men who robbed the colony's storehouse tied to trees and left there until they starved to death. He gives no names and no count. Percy wrote his account partly to defend his own record in Virginia.

#### Oñate convicted, 1614

Spanish officials later put Juan de Oñate on trial in Mexico City for what he had done in New Mexico. They charged him with 30 crimes in 1612 or 1613, and accounts differ on the year. In 1614 they found him guilty of 12. Among them were using too much force against the Acoma and hanging two Indians without cause.

The officials banished Oñate from New Mexico for life, which means they ordered him to leave and never return. They also barred him from Mexico City for four years, though one source says five, and fined him 6,000 ducats. A ducat was a Spanish coin. Whether he was later pardoned, meaning officially forgiven and freed from the punishment, is not settled. No record shows that any Acoma person was asked to testify.

#### The watch and the whipping post in Massachusetts

The court records of the Massachusetts Bay Colony from the early 1630s show who kept order and how the colony's judges punished people. The colonists had settled among the Massachusett people and the Pawtucket, who belonged to a larger group of nations led by Massachusett sachems. In 1631 the judges fined the Massachusett sachem, or leader, Chickatabut one beaver skin for shooting a pig that belonged to Sir Richard Saltonstall. Governor John Winthrop wrote in his journal that Chickatabut paid it right away. From the colony's first year, its judges tried Native people who lived near the colonists.

The settlers themselves kept watch at night. On April 12, 1631, the judges ordered a watch of four men every night at Dorchester and four more at Watertown, "to begin att sunsett." Anyone who fired a gun after the watch was set had to pay a fine of 40 shillings, which was English money, or be whipped. In July the judges ordered a watch of six men and an officer every night at Boston. The watchmen were settlers taking turns. The judges fined Daniel Abbott "for refuseing to watch" and Richard Norman for "negligence in watching."

Whipping meant being struck on the bare back with a whip, often at a post in a public place. Bartholomew Hill got a whipping for stealing a loaf of bread from John Hoskins, and John Baker got one for shooting at birds on the Sabbath, the day of rest and worship. The records state "whipped" or "severely whipt" and do not say how many strokes anyone received.

John Goulworth confessed to a felony, a serious crime, and the judges had him whipped and then set in the stocks. The stocks were a wooden board with holes that locked a person's ankles while the person sat in a public place. For helping in a crime, John Boggust and John Pickryn had to sit in the stocks at Salem for four hours.

The pillory was a wooden frame on a post, set on a platform in a public place. It locked a person's neck and wrists while the person stood. Britannica's account for students states that it was meant to expose people to "public scorn and ridicule," and to cause "bodily discomfort," meaning the body ached from standing locked in place. The bilboes were iron rings locked around the ankles and joined to a bar, so the person could not walk away. Edward Seale, punished for drunkenness, sat in the bilboes until the court day ended, "& then to bee severely whiped."

Richard Hopkins sold guns, powder and shot to Indians. In September 1632 the court sentenced him to be whipped and "branded with a hott iron on one of his cheekes." Branding meant pressing a red-hot iron into the skin. It burned a mark into the flesh that stayed for life. Robert Scarlett, "a knowen theife," got a whipping in 1635 and the letter T, for thief, branded on his forehead. Then his master, Benjamin Felton, had to send him out of the colony.

Officers of the colony also cut off ears. In September 1658 three Quakers, Christopher Holder, John Copeland and John Rous, were held in the Boston prison. Quakers are members of a Christian group also called the Society of Friends. Their sentence stated that each man's right ear was to be "cut off by the Hangman." The marshal was the colony's officer who carried out the court's orders. On September 16 the marshal's deputy came to the prison with a group of men and shut the door. They cut off the right ear of each of the three men. George Bishop, a Quaker, recorded it in his book *New England Judged* in 1661. He does not say which of the men did the cutting, and he does not name the tool.

<a id="story-philip-ratcliffe"></a>

#### Philip Ratcliffe

> **Who:** A servant whose ears were cut off for speaking against the Massachusetts government and the church at Salem.
>
> **When and where:** Boston, June 1631.

Philip Ratcliffe was punished for words. Governor John Winthrop's journal calls him a servant of a Mr. Cradock. On June 14, 1631, the judges of the Massachusetts Bay court at Boston ordered that he "shalbe whipped, haue his eares cutt of, fyned 40£, & banished." In today's spelling, he was to be whipped, have his ears cut off, pay a fine of 40 pounds, and leave the colony for good.

His crime was "vttering mallitious & scandulous speeches against the govmt & the church of Salem." That means he had said hateful and shameful things about the colony's government and about the church at Salem. The record says what he said was "proved vpon oath," which means people swore in court that he said it.

Governor John Winthrop wrote in his journal that the sentence "was presently executed," which in his day meant it was carried out right away. Neither the court record nor Winthrop says who cut off Ratcliffe's ears, or how. The same judges that day ordered Philip Swaddon whipped for running away from his master, Robert Seely, to go to Virginia. Both orders are in the colony's printed court records, the *Records of the Governor and Company of the Massachusetts Bay*.

#### When killing an enslaved person was no crime, 1669

In October 1669 the members of Virginia's assembly, the colony's lawmakers, passed "An act about the casuall killing of slaves." Sir William Berkeley was the governor. An enslaved person was a person owned by another person as property and forced to work for no pay.

Under the act, if an enslaved person resisted and died under "correction" by the master, or by someone the master sent, the death "shall not be accompted felony." Correction meant a beating. The lawmakers gave their reason in the act. They wrote that no one would kill on purpose when the enslaved person was his own "estate," meaning his property. Under this law, a master who beat an enslaved person to death, after the person resisted him, was not charged with any crime. The act is printed in William Waller Hening's collection of Virginia's old laws, the *Statutes at Large*.

#### A murder trial at Plymouth, 1675

In 1675 the judges of Plymouth Colony tried three Native men for killing another Native man. Plymouth stood in the country of the Wampanoag. On January 29, 1675, John Sassamon died at Assawompset Pond. In March, Tobias, the sachem Tuspaquin and Tuspaquin's son William pledged their land, worth 100 pounds, as a promise that Tobias would come to court in June.

In June the judges tried Tobias, his son Wampapaquan, and Mattashunannamo for Sassamon's murder. The charge stated that they had struck him or twisted his neck until he died, then pushed his body through a hole in the ice of the pond. The three men said they were innocent.

The jury was twelve English colonists. The judges added six Native men, Hope, Maskippague, Wannoo, George, Wampye and Acanootus, to advise the jury. They had not taken the jurors' oath, but the record states that they "fully concurred," meaning they agreed with the verdict. The jury found all three men guilty, and the judges sentenced them to hang.

Plymouth officials hanged Tobias and Mattashunannamo on June 8, 1675. The judges put off Wampapaquan's hanging for a month. Within that month he was shot to death, and the colony's court record does not say who shot him. Later that June, King Philip's War began at Swansea.

#### Salem, 1692

In 1692 and 1693, colonial judges in Massachusetts tried people for witchcraft, which meant using the Devil's power to hurt others. Accusers named more than 200 people, Smithsonian magazine reports. The judges had 19 of them hanged, and Sheriff George Corwin carried out the hangings. Corwin also had one man pressed to death under stones. At least five more accused people died in jail.

English settlers built Salem on Naumkeag, a home of the Pawtucket people. The City of Salem's tourism office states that between 1616 and 1619 a plague brought by English traders "devastated" the Pawtucket, meaning it killed many of them.

The first accusers were three girls in Salem Village: Betty Parris, who was 9, Abigail Williams, 11, and Ann Putnam Jr., about 12. They said three women were hurting them by witchcraft. The three were Tituba, a woman enslaved in the house of the minister Samuel Parris, and Sarah Good and Sarah Osborn. The magistrates John Hathorne and Jonathan Corwin questioned them on March 1, 1692. A magistrate is a local judge. Tituba denied it. The magistrates kept at her with questions again and again, and then she confessed. Members of the Putnam family later made accusations in dozens of cases.

On May 27, 1692, Governor William Phips set up a special court to try the accused. It was called a Court of Oyer and Terminer, words that mean "to hear and to decide." William Stoughton was its chief judge. The judges accepted spectral evidence. That was an accuser's word that the spirit of the accused person had come to her in a dream or a vision and hurt her. Only the accuser could say what she had seen. Stoughton was sure such evidence could be used. The minister Increase Mather wrote: "It were better that ten suspected witches should escape than one innocent person be condemned."

Giles Corey was 71 or 81 years old, and accounts of his age differ. He refused to plead guilty or not guilty. Under English law, a court could force a plea by pressing. The prisoner lay on the ground under a wooden board, and officers piled heavier and heavier stones on it until the prisoner answered or died. Sheriff Corwin made Corey strip naked and lie face up on the ground. Then Corwin placed large rocks on the board one at a time. The pressing went on for two days, and Corey died on the third, September 19, 1692. Because he was never convicted, his children could keep his land under the law. The Massachusetts Historical Society gives that as his reason for refusing to plead.

Sarah Good's daughter Dorothy was a small child when the magistrates had her jailed with her mother in March 1692. The warrant, the written order for her arrest, calls her four years old, her father later said four or five, and one archive says six. In 1710 her father, William Good, wrote that she was kept in prison seven or eight months and "chain'd in the dungeon." He wrote that she was "so hardly used and terrifyed," meaning treated so harshly and frightened so badly. He said she had been a heavy cost to care for ever since. Sarah Good gave birth in jail, and her baby died there. Sarah Good was hanged on July 19, 1692. The University of Virginia's *Salem Witch Trials Documentary Archive* holds the papers of her case.

In October 1692, after accusers named Phips's own wife, Phips shut the special court. The judges of the new court that replaced it would not allow spectral evidence, and they condemned 3 of 56 defendants. By May 1693 Phips had pardoned everyone still held. In October 1711 the governor and lawmakers of Massachusetts passed an act that cancelled the convictions of many of the condemned, and they granted 600 pounds to the heirs. In 1957 the state's lawmakers made a formal apology.

<a id="story-rebecca-nurse"></a>

#### Rebecca Nurse

> **Who:** A member of the Salem church whom a jury found not guilty of witchcraft, and who was then convicted and hanged.
>
> **When and where:** Salem, Massachusetts, March to July 1692.

A jury found Rebecca Nurse not guilty of witchcraft. The judges objected, the jury changed its verdict to guilty, and she was hanged. On March 23, 1692, Edward and Jonathan Putnam filed a complaint against her. They said she had hurt Ann Putnam Sr., Ann Putnam Jr. and Abigail Williams by witchcraft. The magistrates John Hathorne and Jonathan Corwin signed the warrant, and Marshal George Herrick arrested her the next day. She had been sick for eight or nine days and could not leave the house.

At her questioning on March 24 she said, "I am as clear as the child unborn." When she moved her hands, the record states, the accusers fell into fits. Thirty-nine of her neighbors signed a statement that they had never had "Any: cause or grounds to suspect her."

Women searched her body for a mark of the Devil. The most experienced of them found nothing that could not come from a natural cause. On June 28 Nurse asked the court, in a petition, for other women to examine her again, two of them midwives. A petition is a written request. A midwife is a woman who helps other women give birth. Nurse signed the petition with her mark, because she could not write her name.

At her trial the jury found her not guilty. The judges objected. They pointed to something she had said about two other accused women, Goodwife Hobbs and her daughter: "they used to come among us." Goodwife was the title for a married woman, the way "Mrs." is used today. The jury went out again. Back in court she did not answer, and one juror, Thomas Fisk, took her silence as evidence against her. The jury then found her guilty.

Afterward Nurse explained that she had meant the two women were fellow prisoners. She wrote that she was "something hard of hearing, and full of grief," and that no one had told her how the court took her words. Governor Phips pardoned her. Several men from Salem then persuaded him to take the pardon back. On July 3 the minister Nicholas Noyes led the members of the Salem church in putting her out of the church, "by unanimous vote." That is called excommunication. Sheriff George Corwin had her hanged on July 19, 1692. Her house in Danvers still stands. Her case file, number 94, is in the University of Virginia's *Salem Witch Trials Documentary Archive*.

### 1700 to 1750

Between 1700 and 1750, an enslaved person accused of a crime faced a different kind of trial from a free white person. In Virginia, under a law of 1723, a panel of local justices tried an enslaved person accused of a crime that carried death, with no jury. In New York in 1741, a white defendant could turn away up to twenty jurors without giving a reason. Two enslaved men, Quack and Cuffee, went to trial with no lawyer. In South Carolina, from 1704, white men rode on slave patrols to watch and control enslaved people.

In Virginia, a county court of local justices met about once a month to settle quarrels over land and debts. In the colonies a lender could have a person who could not pay a debt locked in jail. British judges also sent about 52,200 convicts across the ocean to work in the colonies.

#### The county court and the debtors' jail

By 1622 the Virginia settlements had local courts made up of local judges called commissioners of the peace, later called justices of the peace. The justices met, usually once a month. In 1642 the members of Virginia's assembly named these courts county courts. By the end of the colonial years Virginia had 61 counties.

The justices gave out licenses to marry and to keep taverns, recorded deeds and wills, and settled quarrels over land and over debts. A deed is a paper showing who owns land. Emily Salmon, writing in the *Encyclopedia Virginia*, calls serving as a justice "the logical stepping stone" to a seat in the House of Burgesses, Virginia's assembly.

A jail in these years held people waiting for a trial or a punishment, and people who owed money. From the first colonies until the middle 1800s, a lender could have a person who could not pay a debt locked in jail. Under English law, which the colonists brought with them, the prisoner even paid the cost of being kept there. Robert C. Voigt, writing in the *Encyclopedia of North Carolina*, explains that jailing a debtor gave the lender "a forceful means" of collecting the money. A person in jail could not work to earn the money.

#### Convicts shipped from Britain

Between 1700 and 1775, British judges sent about 52,200 convicts by ship to the American colonies. This punishment was called transportation. More than 20,000 of the convicts went to Virginia, and about 80 percent of all of them went to Maryland or Virginia. Emily Jones Salmon gives these numbers in the *Encyclopedia Virginia*.

In 1718 the members of Parliament, Britain's lawmaking body, passed the Transportation Act. Under it British officials paid merchants to carry convicts across the ocean. Jonathan Forward was the first merchant to hold the contract. The convicts were sold as soon as they landed, and Salmon does not name the sellers. Most of them were forced to work for their buyers for seven to fourteen years, mostly in tobacco fields. Others went to tradesmen, shipbuilders and ironworks.

Virginia's lawmakers tried to stop the shipments. In 1722 they passed a law meant to make shipping convicts too expensive. Forward complained, and the members of the Board of Trade, a group of officials in London who watched over the colonies, overturned the law. In 1751 Benjamin Franklin wrote against the shipments. The last convict ship reached the James River in Virginia in 1776.

#### Slave patrols and courts without juries

White South Carolinians set up official slave patrols in 1704, copying the island colony of Barbados. A slave patrol was a group of white men who rode out to watch and control enslaved people. The patrollers were the same men who served in the militia, the colony's part-time citizen army. At first wealthy men, called gentlemen, rode alongside poorer white farmers. From 1734 to 1737 the patrollers were paid for the work.

In 1739 enslaved people at Stono, in South Carolina, rebelled against the people who enslaved them. After that, the members of the South Carolina assembly ordered "constant, regular patrols" in the Negro Act of 1740. In Charleston, the town's night watch patrolled the streets. A patrol's route ran 10 to 15 miles. In later years a typical patrol was a few men on horseback. They searched the cabins where enslaved people lived, broke up their gatherings and guarded the roads. The *South Carolina Encyclopedia* states that this patrol system lasted until the end of the Civil War.

In Virginia, a law of 1723 states how enslaved people were to be tried for crimes that carried death. Justices named for each case tried the accused person at the county courthouse. They could convict on a confession or on the oath of one witness. They could also convict on the word of Black or Native witnesses if it "shall seem convincing" to them. The law calls these witnesses "Negroes, Mulattos, or Indians." Those were old words for Black people, for people with one Black and one white parent or ancestor, and for Native people. All of this was done "without the solemnity of a jury," which means with no jury at all. If they found the person guilty, they ordered the execution. The owner of the accused person could come and speak in the person's defense.

The same law states a punishment for any Black or Native witness found to have lied. Under the law, the person's ear was to be nailed to the pillory, and the person was to stand there for an hour. Then the ear was to be cut off. An hour later the other ear was to be nailed and cut off the same way. Then the person was to get 39 lashes of the whip, "well laid on, on his or her bare back, at the common whipping-post." The justices had this warning read aloud to every such witness. The law states the punishment and not the officer who was to carry it out, and it does not say how often it was done.

#### The New York trials of 1741

In 1741 New York judges tried about 200 people for a plot to burn the city, after a string of fires that began in March. The judges were James De Lancey, Daniel Horsmanden and Frederick Philipse. Officials burned 13 Black men at the stake and hanged 17 more. They also hanged four white people, two men and two women. John and Sarah Hughson and Peggy Kerry were hanged on June 12.

Burning at the stake meant chaining a person to an upright post with wood piled around it. Then the wood was set on fire, so the person burned to death.

A grand jury is a group of citizens who decide whether a person should be charged with a crime. The first witness before the grand jury was Mary Burton, a 16-year-old servant of the tavern keeper John Hughson. At first she refused to talk. She began to talk as she was being taken to the dungeon at City Hall. Enslaved witnesses named Sandy and Fortune testified after being promised their lives. The grand jury told Sandy that enslaved people who confessed and named others "were certainly pardoned, and shipped off."

Judge Horsmanden questioned suspects himself before he sent them to the grand jury. White defendants had more protection under New York law. Each could turn away up to twenty jurors without giving a reason, which is called a peremptory challenge. Quack and Cuffee, two enslaved men, had no lawyer. Douglas Linder wrote an account of the trials for the Famous Trials project at the University of Missouri-Kansas City. He writes of "grave questions about the contours of the suspected conspiracy," meaning serious doubts about what the supposed plot really was and who was in it.

<a id="story-quack-and-cuffee"></a>

#### Quack and Cuffee

> **Who:** Two enslaved men in New York City who were burned at the stake in the trials of 1741.
>
> **When and where:** New York City, tried and burned in May 1741.

Quack and Cuffee were burned at the stake after a trial in which they had no lawyer. Quack was enslaved by a painter named Roosevelt. Cuffee was enslaved by Adolph Philipse.

On May 12 the undersheriff, the sheriff's deputy, put Cuffee in a cell with a white prisoner, Arthur Price. He gave the two men "a tankard of punch now and then," a large cup of a mixed drink, so that Price could draw Cuffee into talking. Price then swore that Cuffee had spoken about the fires.

Attorney General Richard Bradley, the colony's chief lawyer, led the case against the two men. His side called eleven witnesses. Quack and Cuffee had to defend themselves. They called ten witnesses, and most of them said the two men had been somewhere else when the fires started. The men said they were innocent. The jury, Horsmanden wrote, was "soon returned" and found them guilty. Judge Horsmanden sentenced them to be "chained to a stake, and burnt to death" on Saturday, May 30, 1741.

At about three o'clock that afternoon, the sheriff brought them to the stake, with piles of wood around them. Horsmanden wrote that the crowd "were very impatient" for the fire. The deputy secretary, a Mr. Moore, and Quack's owner, Mr. Roosevelt, told each man that the other had already confessed. Both men then confessed and named other people. Moore asked the sheriff to wait while someone asked the governor for a reprieve, an order to put off the burning. The sheriff said he could not take the men back through the crowd without a strong guard. Horsmanden called the governor's answer "conditional and discretionary," which means it came with conditions and left room for choice. He wrote that "the execution proceeded." He does not name the men who lit the fire.

Their confessions at the stake named other people and led to more trials. Horsmanden told the story in his own book, *A Journal of the Proceedings*, in 1744.

### 1750 to 1800

In 1790 Pennsylvania's lawmakers turned the Walnut Street Jail in Philadelphia into the country's first state prison. Before then, a convict in Pennsylvania could be fined, made to pay back what he took, whipped, branded or hanged. From 1786 he could also be put to hard labor in the streets. After 1790, a judge in Pennsylvania could send a convict to prison for years, to work there, and to spend part of that time alone in a cell.

In 1791 lawmakers in enough states approved the Bill of Rights, the first ten additions to the Constitution, and four of them list rights for accused people. In 1763 armed settlers in Pennsylvania killed twenty Conestoga people, and no one was ever charged.

#### Counterfeiting was a hanging crime

Counterfeiting means making fake money. Colonial paper money carried the warning "To Counterfeit is Death." Owen Sullivan was an engraver, a person who cuts designs into metal for printing, and he was born in Ireland. He ran gangs that passed fake bills from New England to New York.

On October 9, 1752, the *Boston Evening Post* printed a report from Providence, Rhode Island. It said that Sullivan "has lately had both his Ears crop'd, and been branded on both his Cheeks with the Letter C." Cropping meant cutting off part of the ear. The C was for counterfeiting. He had been punished for faking Rhode Island's paper money. The newspaper does not name who cut and branded him. Later, New York judges convicted him of faking and passing New York's bills, and he was hanged on May 10, 1756.

#### The Conestoga killings, 1763

In December 1763, armed white settlers from Paxton Township and nearby places in Pennsylvania killed all twenty people of the Conestoga town. No one was ever charged with the killings. The Conestoga were descendants of the Susquehannock people. Their town stood near Lancaster, on land that the Penn family had set aside for them. The land was supposed to be under the Penn family's protection.

In 1763 Native nations to the west were at war with the British, in what is called Pontiac's War. The killers claimed that the unarmed Conestoga were hiding spies for the enemy. The historian Michael Goode calls that charge "a fabrication," which means a lie. Earlier in the war, Lieutenant Governor James Hamilton had offered a reward of 25 pounds for each Native scalp. A scalp is the skin and hair cut away from the top of a person's head.

Benjamin Franklin wrote about the killings in a pamphlet in 1764. He counted twenty people in the town: seven men, five women and eight children. At daybreak on December 14, 1763, fifty-seven men rode in with guns, short swords and hatchets. They found six people at home, three men, two women and a boy. The men shot them, stabbed them and killed them with hatchets. Shehaes was a very old man who had been at a treaty meeting with William Penn in 1701. A treaty is a written agreement between nations. He was in his bed, and they cut him to pieces there. The attackers scalped all six. Then they burned the houses.

Lancaster's magistrates put the other fourteen Conestoga people in Lancaster's workhouse to keep them safe. A workhouse was a building where poor people were made to work. On December 27 about fifty of the Paxton men broke open the workhouse door. Franklin wrote that the families knelt, with the children holding on to their parents, and said they were innocent. The men killed all fourteen with guns and hatchets, among them children about a year old and babies still nursing. Will Soc was shot at the door. A company of British soldiers stationed nearby did nothing to stop the attack.

Franklin named some of the dead. They included Shehaes, his daughter Peggy, and her husband John Smith, a Cayuga, with their child of about three. They also included Betty and her son Peter, and Sally, whose Native name was Wyanjoy. Governor John Penn offered a reward for the killers' names. A modern introduction to Franklin's pamphlet, published by Miami University, states that no one came forward and no one was ever prosecuted. In January 1764 as many as 200 of the Paxton men marched toward Philadelphia and stopped at Germantown. Franklin met with them. Afterward their leader, Matthew Smith, published their complaints.

#### Three trials in Boston, 1770

In 1770, judges in Boston heard three murder trials. One was of a customs informer who had shot a boy. The other two were of a British captain and of eight British soldiers.

On February 22, 1770, Ebenezer Richardson fired a gun from his house into a crowd of boys and killed Christopher Seider, who was 10 or 11. Richardson was a customs informer, a man who told the customs officials about smugglers. Customs officials collected taxes on goods brought in by ship. A jury found Richardson guilty of murder on April 21. The judges thought he was innocent, and they put off sentencing him.

On March 5, 1770, British soldiers fired into a crowd and killed five people. Crispus Attucks, Samuel Gray and James Caldwell died that night. Samuel Maverick, 17, died the next morning, and Patrick Carr died nearly two weeks later. Captain Thomas Preston and eight soldiers were arrested and jailed. No lawyer in Boston would defend them until John Adams agreed, with Josiah Quincy and Robert Auchmuty. Adams later wrote that in a free country, a lawyer "ought to be the very last thing that [an] accused Person should want." In his day, want meant lack. He meant that an accused person must never be left without a lawyer.

A jury found Preston not guilty on October 30. The soldiers' trial began on November 27. After two and a half hours, the jury acquitted six soldiers, which means it found them not guilty. It found Hugh Montgomery and Mathew Kilroy guilty of manslaughter, which means killing someone without planning to. Manslaughter could be punished by death. The two men used an old English rule called benefit of clergy. It let a first-time offender who could read escape a death sentence once.

Instead of being hanged, each man was branded on the hand, at the base of the right thumb. On December 14, 1770, Sheriff Stephen Greenleaf pressed a red-hot iron onto each man's thumb in the courtroom, and it burned a mark into the skin that stayed for life. John Adams remembered in 1822 that when the sheriff came near, the two soldiers "burst into tears." The *Boston Gazette* reported that after the branding they were "discharged," which means let go.

#### From street work to the cell, Philadelphia

Between 1786 and 1790, Pennsylvania's lawmakers tried two new punishments in place of hanging. The historian Louis Masur found that in the ten years before 1786, Pennsylvania officials had hanged about 40 people for robbery or burglary.

In 1786 the lawmakers passed a law under which judges sentenced convicts to "continued hard labour publicly and disgracefully imposed." People called the prisoners "wheelbarrow men." Ann Warder wrote in her diary on March 30, 1787, that the convicts cleaned the streets with "an iron collar around their neck and waist to which a long chain is fashioned and at the end a heavy ball." Their heads were shaved, and a guard went with each gang. She wrote that at first the prisoners "preferred death" to being shown in public this way. Thirty wheelbarrow men escaped in one night in October 1788. The lawmakers ended the law by 1790.

In 1787, 37 Philadelphians formed the Philadelphia Society for Alleviating the Miseries of Public Prisons, a group to improve the prisons. Alleviating the miseries means easing the suffering. Among them were the doctor Benjamin Rush, Benjamin Franklin and Bishop William White. They drew on the ideas of John Howard, an English prison reformer. In the city's old jail, men, women and children were held together, whatever their crime. Annie Anderson, writing in the *Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia*, states that the sheriff there forced money out of prisoners, sold them liquor from a bar and held back their food.

In April 1790 Pennsylvania's lawmakers passed a new law. Under it the Walnut Street Jail became the Walnut Street Prison, a state prison for convicts from all of Pennsylvania. The lawmakers ordered a separate building of cells, called a penitentiary house. It was for "the more hardened and atrocious offenders," meaning the convicts who had done the worst crimes. The word penitentiary comes from penitence, which means being sorry for wrongdoing. Each cell was six feet wide, eight feet long and nine feet high, and thirty-six of them were built. Judges could sentence a prisoner to time alone in one of these cells. Keeping a prisoner alone in a cell is called solitary confinement.

The law professor David Shapiro studied the prison's records for the *Harvard Law Review* in 2019. Between 1795 and 1800, he found, judges sent 748 people to the prison, and they sentenced 29 of them to time in solitary confinement. Margaret Price, convicted of counterfeiting in 1795, got four years with four months in solitary. Prisoners worked in a nail factory inside the prison. Caleb Lownes wrote in 1799 that a prisoner who refused to work was locked in a cell for "some weeks, without labour, bed, or furniture, of any kind, except a vessel to hold his drink, and another his mush, and a blanket." Lownes does not name the keepers who locked the prisoner in.

#### Rights for the accused, 1791

On December 15, 1791, lawmakers in enough states approved the first ten amendments to the Constitution, called the Bill of Rights. An amendment is an addition or change to the Constitution. Four of them list rights of people accused of crimes.

The Fourth Amendment requires officers to have a warrant, a judge's written order, to search a home. A judge may give one only when there is good reason to believe a crime took place. The Fifth forbids forcing anyone to be a witness against himself. The Sixth requires, for an accused person, "a speedy and public trial, by an impartial jury" and the help of a lawyer. An impartial jury is one whose members favor neither side. The Eighth forbids "cruel and unusual punishments" and bail set too high. Bail is money paid to the court so an accused person can go free until the trial.

At first these rules applied only to the federal government and its courts. State courts did not have to follow them.

<a id="story-patrick-lyon"></a>

#### Patrick Lyon

> **Who:** A Philadelphia blacksmith held three months in the Walnut Street Prison for a bank robbery he did not commit.
>
> **When and where:** Philadelphia, 1798 to January 1799.

Patrick Lyon spent three months in the Walnut Street Prison for a bank robbery that other men had done. He was a blacksmith, born in Scotland, who came to Philadelphia in 1793.

In 1798 Lyon did a rush job for the Bank of Pennsylvania. He changed the locks on two of its iron vault doors. It was his last job before he left the city. He told the bank's carpenter that the doors were not right for a bank and the locks were not safe. A stranger came to his shop with the carpenter and spent a long time looking at the doors, keyholes and locks. Then a yellow fever outbreak struck Philadelphia, and about 1,300 people died of it. Lyon left the city by boat for Lewes, Delaware, with his 19-year-old apprentice, a young man learning his trade. The apprentice died of the fever there.

On the night of August 31, while Lyon was away, someone took $162,821 from the bank's vault without breaking in. Lyon heard that he was the main suspect, and he walked back to Philadelphia to clear his name. "I had come 150 miles to surrender myself," he wrote. High Constable John Haines, the chief of the city's constables, wanted the $2,000 reward. He and the bank's officers questioned Lyon. The bank's officers were sure that the man who changed the locks had made an extra key. A magistrate sent him to the Walnut Street Prison and set his bail at $150,000.

Lyon called the prison "cold, damp, unwholesome and solitary." His cell was 12 feet by 4 feet. "I read until I was tired and walked until I was weary," he wrote. He caught yellow fever there and lived.

The robbers were Isaac Davis, a carpenter, and the bank's porter, Thomas Cunningham, who died of the fever. Davis was the stranger who had studied the locks. He confessed and gave back the money, and the governor promised him a pardon. Davis seems never to have spent a day in prison. The bank's officers still said Lyon had helped by making a key. He stayed in prison until January 1799, when a grand jury refused to charge him.

Lyon wrote a book about what had happened to him. He sued the bank's officers and the constable for keeping him in prison without cause. In 1805 a jury awarded him $12,000. The men he sued appealed, and in 1807 they paid him $9,000 to settle the case. The painter John Neagle later painted him as *Pat Lyon at the Forge*. Ron Avery tells the story for the Carpenters' Company of Philadelphia, drawing on Lyon's own 1799 *Narrative*.

### 1800 to 1850

Between 1800 and 1850, officials in New York and Pennsylvania built prisons where convicts, people found guilty of crimes, were locked alone in cells, at night in New York and all day and night in Pennsylvania. Officials in Boston and New York hired full-time police. Prison keepers in the two states ran two different kinds of prison, and both kept prisoners silent. Pennsylvania's lawmakers moved hangings inside jail walls in 1834, and twelve years later Michigan's lawmakers voted to end the death penalty.

In the South, white men still policed enslaved people. South Carolina's slave patrols, small groups of white men on horseback, searched the places where enslaved people lived and broke up their gatherings. Virginia's local judges, called justices, tried enslaved people with no jury. White mobs also killed people with no trial at all. A white mob in St. Louis burned Francis McIntosh to death in 1836, and no one was charged.

#### The Cherokee Nation's police, 1808

Leaders of the Cherokee Nation set up their own police in 1808. The Cherokee lived then in their own country, in parts of what are now Georgia, Tennessee, Alabama and North Carolina. On September 11, 1808, at Brooms Town, the leaders on the Cherokee national council, who made the nation's laws, passed a written law. Under it, they set up "regulating parties," companies of men who made sure people obeyed those laws. The law was signed by the principal chief, or head leader, Black Fox, with Path Killer, Toochalar, and Charles Hicks, the council's secretary.

Each company of regulators had six men: a captain, a lieutenant who was second in command, and four privates, the ordinary members. The law set the pay: fifty dollars for the captain, forty for the lieutenant and thirty for each private. The regulators went after horse thieves and robbers. They also protected what children got from their dead parents and what widows owned. A man found guilty of stealing a horse got "one hundred stripes on the bare back," which means one hundred blows of a whip. Blows like these cut the skin and leave welts, raised stripes of swollen skin, and scars. The law does not name the men who were to strike the blows. If a regulator killed a man who fought back with a weapon, "the blood of him or them shall not be required." That meant the dead man's clan could not kill in return. A clan was a large family group, and a Cherokee child belonged to the mother's clan.

On April 10, 1810, at Oostanallah, the clans agreed to an "act of oblivion for all lives." Oblivion means forgetting. Under the act, a person who killed someone "without malice intended," meaning by accident, would no longer be held guilty. With this act, the clans ended the old rule that an accidental killing had to be paid for with a life. The editors of the *Cherokee Phoenix*, the Cherokee Nation's own newspaper, printed both laws on March 13, 1828.

#### Two kinds of prison: Auburn and Eastern State

In the 1820s, prison keepers in New York and Pennsylvania ran two different kinds of prison. In both, they kept prisoners from talking to each other.

At Auburn Prison in New York, prisoners worked together in groups during the day and slept alone in cells at night. They were not allowed to speak at any time. Elam Lynds became the head keeper in 1821. He had prisoners flogged for breaking even small rules. Flogging means beating a person's bare back with a whip. The whip cuts the skin and leaves welts and scars. No record of Auburn gives the number of blows or names the keepers who swung the whip. Lynds and John D. Cray made prisoners march in step with their arms locked together, a way of marching called the lockstep. Lynds also dressed them in striped uniforms.

New York's officials used the same plan at Sing Sing, their third state prison. By 1829 officials in Connecticut, Massachusetts, Maryland and Washington, D.C., had taken up the Auburn plan. Officials in most other states chose it later.

In Philadelphia, Pennsylvania's officials opened Eastern State Penitentiary, a prison, in October 1829. The building's designer, the architect John Haviland, laid out seven blocks of cells joined to a center hall. He said he designed it for "watching, convenience, economy and ventilation." Economy meant saving money, and ventilation meant fresh air. Each prisoner lived and worked alone in a cell about 8 feet wide and 12 feet long, with its own small exercise yard. A Bible was the only thing he was allowed to keep. Prisoners made shoes and wove cloth in their cells. Whenever a prisoner left his cell, a guard put a hood over his head so that no other prisoner could see his face.

Guards punished prisoners who broke the rules. They gave them cold showers. One account states that guards apparently did this once outdoors in winter. They also used the iron gag. The guards clamped an iron piece over the prisoner's tongue, like the bit in a horse's mouth, and chained it to his hands, which were held behind his back. With his hands chained to it, he could not take it out. In 1833 prison officials put a prisoner named Mathias Maccumsey in the iron gag as a punishment for talking, and he died. The prison doctor gave the cause as apoplexy, an old word for a sudden stroke. The historian Jennifer Lawrence Janofsky, writing in the *Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia*, states that the prison's leaders tried to cover up the death. The warden, a man named Wood, was investigated and was not found guilty of cruel and unusual punishment.

The English writer Charles Dickens visited Eastern State in 1842. He wrote that he believed the system "in its effects, to be cruel and wrong." He also wrote: "I hold the slow and daily tampering with the mysteries of the brain to be immeasurably worse than any torture of the body." He meant that keeping a person alone and silent for years did more harm to the mind than any torture does to the body.

Pennsylvania's prison officials gave up keeping prisoners alone in 1913. Eastern State was built for 250 prisoners, and by the middle 1920s it held about 1,700.

<a id="story-charles-williams"></a>

#### Charles Williams

> **Who:** The first prisoner at Eastern State Penitentiary.
>
> **When and where:** Philadelphia, October 1829 to October 1831.

Charles Williams, an 18-year-old Black farmer, was the first prisoner at Eastern State Penitentiary. He had been found guilty of breaking into a house and stealing a silver watch, a gold seal and a gold key, worth $25 in all. A seal was a small stamp, often hung on a watch chain, for pressing a mark into wax. His sentence was two years alone and in silence, with work. Jane Brox, who tells his story in the *Public Domain Review*, does not name the judge or jury who convicted and sentenced him.

In October 1829 guards led him into the new prison with a hood over his head. From then on he was Prisoner Number 1, and Brox writes that he was not called Charles again while he was there. His cell was twelve feet by eight. *Smithsonian* magazine reports that prisoners there spoke to the guards through a small feeding hole and worked alone in their cells. He was let out in October 1831, two years to the day after he went in.

#### After Nat Turner's revolt, 1831

In August 1831 Nat Turner, an enslaved man, led a revolt in Southampton County, Virginia. Turner and the rebels who joined him killed 55 white men, women and children, by the count of the historian Patrick Breen. A Library of Virginia article gives the number as 57.

In the days after the revolt, white people from Southampton and beyond killed Black people with no trial. Breen writes that they killed about three dozen in Southampton County. He also writes that armed units formed "to put down the revolt and in many cases get revenge." A Library of Virginia article states that they killed hundreds, with no exact count.

The county's justices tried the accused rebels in a court of oyer and terminer. In Virginia that meant local justices judged enslaved people with no jury. Breen counts thirty enslaved people and one free Black man sentenced to death. Nineteen were put to death on the justices' orders. Breen does not name the men who carried out the executions. Governor John Floyd changed the sentences of the other twelve so they would not die.

Turner hid for two months. He gave himself up on October 30, 1831. The justices tried him on November 5 and ordered him "hanged by the neck until he be dead" on November 11. He was hanged that day, as the justices had ordered. The Library of Virginia's account of the trial does not name the man who hanged him. In the same court record, the justices set his value as property at $375. Virginia officials paid that sum to his owner.

#### Hangings move inside the jail

In 1834 Pennsylvania's lawmakers became the first in any state to ban public executions, hangings in front of crowds. The Death Penalty Information Center, a group that collects facts about the death penalty, records this. After that, officials hanged prisoners who had been sentenced to death inside the county prisons.

On May 18, 1846, Michigan's lawmakers voted to end the death penalty. An article by the news outlet Michigan Public states that Michigan was the first English-speaking government in the world to do so.

#### Francis McIntosh, St. Louis, 1836

On April 28, 1836, a white mob in St. Louis, Missouri, burned Francis McIntosh alive, and no one was ever charged. McIntosh was a free Black man, 26 years old, from Pittsburgh. He worked on the steamboat *Flora* as a cook and as a porter, who carried passengers' bags.

That day Deputy Constable William Mull, a local law officer, arrested McIntosh for getting in the way of officers who were arresting two sailors. Deputy Sheriff George Hammond, a county law officer, helped take him to jail. McIntosh was told he would get five years in prison. He stabbed both officers with a knife. Hammond bled to death. Mull was badly wounded, and accounts differ on whether he died later.

A crowd of several hundred white people gathered, and a city alderman, a member of the city council, was among them. Men from the crowd broke into the jail and took McIntosh out. They chained him to a locust tree near Seventh and Chestnut Streets, then piled wood around his knees and set it on fire. The crowd cheered as he burned, according to a history written at the University of Missouri-St. Louis. He died within about twenty minutes. By one report, he asked to be shot.

Judge Luke Lawless then spoke to the grand jury, a group of citizens who decide whether to charge someone with a crime. He told the jurors to charge any person they could identify. But he said the killing might be the act of a whole crowd moved by one feeling. If it was, he said, it was beyond the reach of the law. He also blamed the writings of abolitionists, people who worked to end slavery. The jurors, led by their foreman, or head juror, John O'Fallon, charged no one.

Elijah Lovejoy, the editor of the *St. Louis Observer*, wrote against the killing and against the judge. In November 1837 a mob of people who were against ending slavery killed Lovejoy in Alton, Illinois. In January 1838 a young lawyer named Abraham Lincoln spoke about the McIntosh killing in Springfield, Illinois. He said McIntosh had been "chained to a tree, and actually burned to death." He added that it was "all within a single hour from the time he had been a freeman, attending to his own business, and at peace with the world." Lincoln's words left out the stabbing and Hammond's death.

#### Police take over from the night watch

The people of Boston had kept a town watch since 1631. A watch was a group of men who walked the streets at night to keep order.

In 1838 a small day police began work in Boston, with officers on duty full time beside the night watch. The crime historian Gary Potter calls this the first organized police force paid for with public money and with officers on duty full time. A 2017 *TIME* article reports his view. In 1854 Boston's city officials replaced the watch and the day police with one Police Department of 250 officers, the City of Boston's own history states.

Before 1845, New York had about 320,000 people. A night watch and 182 other officers guarded them: 100 city marshals, 31 constables and 51 city police officers. All three were kinds of local law officers. On May 7, 1844, New York's state lawmakers passed a Municipal Police Act, a law for a city police force. Under it, city officials were to end the night watch. The mayor and the city council argued over who would choose the officers. Mayor William Havemeyer and the council finally adopted the law for the city on May 23, 1845. Accounts differ on the size of the force. The website CultureNow states that the 1844 law allowed 1,200 officers. Another count gives 800. After a long argument, the officers first wore a navy blue uniform in 1853.

### 1850 to 1900

After the Civil War, white mobs in the South killed Black people without any trial. A killing like this, by a mob, with no trial, is called a lynching. In 2017 the Equal Justice Initiative, a group in Montgomery, Alabama, founded by the lawyer Bryan Stevenson, published a report called *Lynching in America*. It records 4,075 Black people lynched in twelve Southern states between 1877 and 1950, and more than 4,400 in all. It states that the people who took part "were celebrated and acted with impunity," meaning with no fear of punishment. It also states that state and federal officials mostly let the killings happen. Mobs in the West also killed Chinese immigrants.

In the same years, private detectives such as Allan Pinkerton's men worked for railroads and factory owners. Officials in Alabama and other states rented prisoners to mining companies and farm owners. In Alabama, more than 95 percent of the county prisoners and 90 percent of the state prisoners were Black. In New York, state senators on a committee that met in 1894 and 1895 estimated that police officers took more than $10 million a year in payments from people breaking the law.

#### Vigilance committees in San Francisco, 1851 and 1856

A vigilance committee was a group of private citizens who arrested, tried and punished people themselves, outside the courts. About 700 San Francisco men formed one on June 9, 1851. The next day they held their own trial and hanged John Jenkins, a man from Sydney, Australia, for stealing a safe. At that time California law allowed a death sentence for that kind of theft.

In 1851 the committee's members hanged four men and whipped one. They sent fourteen men back to Australia and ordered fourteen others to leave California. They handed fifteen to the police and courts and let forty-one go. The members held and questioned people at their headquarters without due process, the rules a court must follow to give an accused person a fair trial.

On May 14, 1856, after James Casey shot the newspaper editor James King of William, San Francisco men formed the committee again, led by William Tell Coleman. The leaders claimed 6,000 members. Its members hanged four more men that year, among them Casey and Charles Cora. The boxer James "Yankee" Sullivan killed himself after being held in one of the committee's cells. The members broke up the committee on August 11, 1856. Members of the two committees hanged eight people in all.

#### The Dakota trials, 1862

After the war between the United States and the Dakota in Minnesota in 1862, US Army officers tried 392 Dakota men and hanged 38 of them together at Mankato. The Minnesota River valley was the Dakota homeland.

On September 28, 1862, Colonel Henry Sibley set up a military commission, a court of army officers, to try Dakota prisoners. The officers held the trials at a place called the Lower Agency, in François LaBathe's summer kitchen, one of the only buildings there still standing. Some trials lasted no longer than five minutes. The law professor Carol Chomsky of the University of Minnesota wrote that "the evidence was sparse," meaning thin, and that the officers were "biased," meaning they had taken a side before they heard the cases. She wrote that the men on trial had no lawyers, and that the trials were held in a language they did not know. The officers sentenced 303 men to death and 16 to prison.

President Abraham Lincoln and his lawyers read all 303 trial records. Lincoln first looked for men found guilty of rape, which means forcing a person into sex, and he found two. Next he added men found to have taken part in "massacres," the killing of many civilians, people who were not soldiers. He approved 39 hangings. One of those men was later reprieved, which means spared from hanging.

On December 26, 1862, army officers hanged 38 Dakota men together at Mankato. About 4,000 people watched, and 2,000 soldiers stood guard. An article by the Death Penalty Information Center states that it was the largest mass execution in United States history. The officers hanged two of the men by mistake. One was Caske, whose Dakota name was Wicaŋȟpi Wastedaŋpi. The other was Wasicuŋ, a white man the Dakota had adopted, whom the officers had found not guilty.

The bodies were cut down and put together in one shallow grave on a sandbar between Mankato's main street and the Minnesota River. Before morning, doctors had dug up most of them to use as cadavers, dead bodies that doctors and medical students cut open to study the human body. The Minnesota Historical Society records this and does not name the men who buried the bodies or the doctors who took them. A year later, the army's chief lawyer found that Sibley had never had the power to set up the trials.

#### Police against the draft riots, 1863

From July 13 to 16, 1863, mobs in New York City attacked the police, burned buildings and killed Black New Yorkers. The rioters were fighting the new Civil War draft, a law that required men to serve in the army when called. The state militia, the state's part-time soldiers, had been sent to Gettysburg, so at first the Metropolitan Police were the only force in the city.

On the first day, rioters beat Police Superintendent John Kennedy, the head of the city's police officers, until he was nearly unconscious and cut his hand with a knife. Police Commissioners Thomas Acton and John Bergen, two of the officials who ran the police, took command. Their officers kept the rioting out of Lower Manhattan, below Union Square. Rioters burned two police station houses. They also burned the Colored Orphan Asylum, a home for Black children, and the more than 200 children inside all got out.

Rioters beat, tortured and killed Black New Yorkers. Village Preservation, a New York history group, records that William Jones, a Black cart driver, had gone out to buy a loaf of bread. A mob chased him on Clarkson Street, beat him, hanged him and set him on fire. Another Black man was attacked by a crowd of 400, hanged from a tree and set on fire. Hundreds of Black New Yorkers left the city, among them the doctor James McCune Smith and his family.

Secretary of War Edwin Stanton sent five regiments, units of soldiers, from Gettysburg to stop the riot, and it ended on July 16. By the official count, 119 or 120 people were killed in the riots. A New-York Historical Society article records the official count of 119 and states that it may be too low.

#### Mobs that killed Chinese immigrants

In the West, white mobs killed Chinese immigrants. After the killings at Los Angeles in 1871 and at Rock Springs in 1885, every man who was charged or arrested went free. In 1854 the justices of the California Supreme Court had ruled that Chinese people could not testify against white people in court.

In Los Angeles on October 24, 1871, a white man named Robert Thompson was killed during a gunfight between two Chinese groups. A crowd of about 500 people, one tenth of the city, then attacked the Chinese part of town. They killed 18 Chinese men and boys, by the count of the Los Angeles Public Library, or 19 in the list of names the historian Scott Zesch published in 2008. Among the dead was a doctor, Gene Tong. The mob hanged seven of them from the crossbar of Goller's wagon shop and three from a freight wagon. The next morning seventeen bodies lay in the jail yard.

In Los Angeles, grand jurors brought 25 charges of murder. Only ten men were tried, and seven or eight of them were found guilty of manslaughter, which means killing a person without planning to kill. Judges later threw out the verdicts on a technical point of law. The Los Angeles Public Library's account does not name the judges. District Attorney Cameron Thom chose not to try the men again, and they went free in 1873.

Rock Springs was a town in Wyoming, which was then a territory, land under the federal government that was not yet a state. On September 2, 1885, between 100 and 150 armed white miners, railroad workers and townspeople attacked the Chinese miners there. They killed 28, wounded 15, and robbed and burned all 79 homes in the town's Chinatown. Federal troops arrived nearly a week after the killings and stayed for 13 years. Sixteen white miners were arrested and let out on bail, which means they paid money as a promise to come back for trial. The historian Tom Rea, writing for WyoHistory.org, a Wyoming history website, states that "though the killing had been done in daylight, in front of other people, no one could be found who would swear to having seen any crimes." No charges were filed. Chinese diplomats, officials who spoke for China's government, listed nearly $150,000 in losses. Under pressure from the president, members of Congress agreed to pay.

#### Prisoners rented out: convict leasing

After the Civil War, state and county officials in Alabama and other states rented prisoners to private companies. This was called convict leasing. The companies' bosses made the prisoners work in mines, on farms and on railroads. The companies' owners paid the state or the county, not the prisoners.

The historian Mary Ellen Curtin gives the Alabama numbers in the *Encyclopedia of Alabama*. Officials there leased prisoners from 1875 to 1928. More than 95 percent of the county prisoners and 90 percent of the state prisoners there were Black. Most county prisoners had been found guilty of misdemeanors, small crimes such as being drunk in public. They had to work longer to pay off their court costs. The companies' bosses whipped prisoners who tried to escape or talked back, and they whipped others to make them work harder.

Each year, four or five of every hundred state prisoners died. Of the 745 county prisoners in the mines in 1896, 181 had died in the two years before. At the Coalburg mine, 90 of every 1,000 prisoners died. On April 8, 1911, an explosion at the Banner mine killed 123 Black county prisoners.

In 1924 James Knox, a prisoner from Mobile, was killed at the Flat Top mine. His death was first reported as a suicide by swallowing poison. A City of Birmingham history states that the autopsy, the doctors' examination of his body, showed he had died of heart failure, and that the poison had been put into his body after he was dead. His deadly injuries came from being whipped with a steel wire and put into hot water. Curtin describes it as being lowered into "a vat of boiling water." Neither account names the men who did it. After his death, Alabama's lawmakers ended convict leasing on June 30, 1928. Alabama was the last state to end it.

<a id="story-allan-pinkerton"></a>

#### Allan Pinkerton

> **Who:** A Scottish barrel maker who started a private detective agency in Chicago.
>
> **When and where:** Chicago and across the country, 1850 to 1884.

Allan Pinkerton ran a private detective agency whose men were paid by the companies that hired them. They were not police officers. He was born in Glasgow, Scotland, in 1819. He was a cooper, a barrel maker, and in 1843 he settled in Dundee, Illinois. His house there was a hiding place for people escaping slavery. While cutting wood one day he found a gang of counterfeiters, people who made fake money, and told the sheriff, who arrested them.

In 1850 Pinkerton and the lawyer Edward Rucker started a detective agency in Chicago. It became the Pinkerton National Detective Agency. Its sign was an open eye with the words "We never sleep." The men who ran express companies, which carried money and packages by train, hired his detectives to catch criminals, and so did the men who ran the railroads. His men kept photographs of known criminals. Some of them joined gangs in disguise. In February 1861 Pinkerton guarded Abraham Lincoln on his way to Washington, against what Pinkerton said was a plan to kill him in Baltimore.

In January 1875 Pinkerton's detectives and local helpers raided the Missouri farm of the family of the outlaw Jesse James, a robber on the run from the law. They threw a firebomb into the house. It exploded and killed Jesse's eight-year-old half-brother, Archie. It wounded his mother, Zerelda Samuel. Jesse was not there. Afterward, many people took the side of the James family and blamed the agency for the raid.

After the Civil War, factory owners also hired Pinkerton men as armed guards against workers on strike, workers who had stopped work together to press their employers for changes, the PBS series *American Experience* states. Pinkerton died in Chicago in 1884.

#### The Haymarket trial, 1886

On May 4, 1886, someone threw a bomb at police at a workers' meeting in Haymarket Square in Chicago. Seven officers were killed and sixty were hurt. The bomb thrower was never identified.

Prosecutors charged eight anarchists, people who wanted to do away with all government. They tried the eight as accessories, people who help a crime happen without doing the act. The prosecutors said the men's speeches had led to the bombing. A jury found all eight guilty in three hours. The judge sentenced seven to hang and Oscar Neebe to 15 years in prison.

On November 11, 1887, Albert Parsons, August Spies, George Engel and Adolph Fischer were hanged. The PBS account of the trial does not name the men who carried out the hangings. Louis Lingg had already killed himself in his cell with an explosive someone had smuggled in. Governor Richard Oglesby changed the sentences of two men to life in prison. In June 1893 Governor John Peter Altgeld pardoned the three men still in prison, Samuel Fielden, Oscar Neebe and Michael Schwab. The pardon freed them and cancelled their punishment. Altgeld wrote that their trial had been unfair.

#### The first electric chair, 1890

William Kemmler became the first person put to death in an electric chair, on August 6, 1890, at Auburn Prison in New York. He had killed Matilda Ziegler in Buffalo in 1889 with a hatchet, or with an axe by one account. Electrocution means killing a person by sending a strong electric current through the body. The current stops the heart and burns the skin where the metal touches it.

A Buffalo dentist, Dr. Albert Southwick, had first suggested it in 1881. He argued that it was kinder than hanging, in which a person sentenced to death could hang for up to 30 minutes before dying. Kemmler's lawyers argued that the electric chair was a cruel and unusual punishment, which the Constitution forbids. The justices of the US Supreme Court turned them down.

Kemmler's chair had two metal plates covered with damp sponges, one on his head and one on his back. Warden Charles Durston, the head of the prison, gave the order, with 17 witnesses in the room. The first shock lasted 17 seconds. It was about 700 volts by one account, or 1,000 by another. A volt is a measure of how strongly electricity pushes through a wire or a body. The first shock did not kill him. The witnesses smelled burning cloth and burning flesh. A second shock of about 1,030 volts went on for about two minutes, until smoke rose from his head, and Kemmler died. Doctors who examined the body found that the plate on his back had burned through to his spine, the HISTORY.com account states.

The chair ran on alternating current, a kind of electricity that flows back and forth many times a second. Harold Brown, whom New York State hired to build the chair, used it. *Smithsonian* magazine reports that Thomas Edison, whose company sold the other kind, direct current, was secretly paying Brown to use alternating current. George Westinghouse's company built electric systems that used alternating current. After Kemmler's death Westinghouse called it "a brutal affair" and said: "They would have done better with an axe."

#### Eleven men killed in a New Orleans prison, 1891

A mob in New Orleans broke into the city's prison on March 14, 1891, and killed eleven Italian American men. Five months earlier, the police chief, David Hennessy, had been shot. Nineteen Italian Americans were charged with his murder, among them a 14-year-old boy. Nine were tried. The jury found six not guilty, and the trial of the other three ended in a mistrial, with no verdict. A *Smithsonian* magazine article states that "there was no solid evidence against them."
