In 1748 British and French diplomats signed the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle. British diplomats gave Louisbourg back to France. In exchange French diplomats gave back Madras, a city in India that French forces had taken from Britain. British officials did not ask the colonists, and New Englanders were furious.

### 1750 to 1800

American leaders began reaching out to other countries in November 1775, early in the war for independence from Britain. They looked in secret for people in other countries who might help them fight Britain. French and American diplomats signed an alliance in 1778. In 1783 American diplomats in Paris signed the peace that ended the war.

After the war the country had almost no navy and little money. Rulers in North Africa seized American ships, and their officials enslaved the crews. In the 1790s, when France and Britain went to war with each other, American leaders tried to keep the United States out of it. President Washington accepted a treaty that favored Britain because he judged the country too weak to fight the British. From 1798 to 1800 American sailors fought an undeclared war at sea against France.

#### A committee for secret letters, 1775 to 1789

On November 29, 1775, members of the Second Continental Congress set up the Committee of Secret Correspondence. The Congress was the meeting of delegates, the men each colony chose to speak for it. The committee's job was to make secret contact with people in other countries who might help. Its first members were Benjamin Franklin, Benjamin Harrison, Thomas Johnson, John Dickinson and John Jay.

On April 17, 1777, the delegates renamed it the Committee for Foreign Affairs. The delegates later set up a Department of Foreign Affairs. Accounts disagree on whether that happened on January 10, 1780, or January 10, 1781. On August 10, 1781, they chose Robert R. Livingston of New York as the first Secretary for Foreign Affairs.

Under the new Constitution, members of Congress set up the department again in a law of July 27, 1789. In a second law, on September 15, 1789, they renamed it the Department of State, because they had also given it record-keeping work at home as well as foreign affairs. It still has that name.

#### Morocco, 1777 and 1786

Encyclopaedia Britannica describes Sultan Mohammed III, the ruler of Morocco, as the first ruler of any country to recognize the United States. To recognize a country is to accept officially that it exists. On December 20, 1777, he declared that ships flying the American flag could enter Moroccan ports freely. He did this about six weeks before French officials signed their treaties with the Americans. His declaration named ships of several other nations too. It was part of his plan to trade in peace with Christian countries, and it was not aimed at the Americans alone.

A treaty with Morocco followed nine years later. The American agent Thomas Barclay reached Marrakesh on June 19, 1786. Moroccan officials approved the agreement on June 23, and Barclay signed it on June 28. Thomas Jefferson signed it in Paris on January 1, 1787, and John Adams signed it in London on January 25, 1787. Delegates to Congress ratified it on July 18, 1787. To ratify is to give final, formal approval.

It was the first treaty the United States made with an African country or a Muslim one. Officials of the two countries rewrote parts of it in 1836 (some accounts say 1837), and it is still in force. No other treaty relationship in United States history has lasted as long without a break.

#### The French alliance, February 6, 1778

France's foreign minister, the Comte de Vergennes, a French nobleman, agreed to an alliance only after the Americans won a major battle. Benjamin Franklin sailed to France in late 1776. His ship reached Auray, in Brittany, on December 3 or 4, 1776, and he was in Paris by December 21. He, Silas Deane and Arthur Lee were the American commissioners, the men sent to bargain for the United States.

A British army surrendered to American forces after the Battle of Saratoga, in New York. The State Department's own historians write that Vergennes "finally decided in favor of an alliance" when that news reached him in December 1777.

On February 6, 1778, the Americans and the French signed two treaties. Amity means friendship, and commerce means trade. In the Treaty of Amity and Commerce, the French formally recognized American independence. In the Treaty of Alliance, the two sides promised that neither would make peace with Britain on its own, without the other. A secret section stated that other countries in Europe could join.

On June 21, 1779, Spain's leaders took their country into the war against Britain, as France's ally. They did not sign a treaty with the United States, and they did not recognize American independence during the war.

<a id="story-benjamin-franklin-america-world"></a>

#### Benjamin Franklin

> **Who:** An American commissioner and then minister to France, and one of the three Americans who made the peace with Britain.
>
> **When and where:** Paris, December 1776 to May 1785.
>
> **Movie:** *Franklin* (2024), an eight-part drama series on Apple TV+, with Michael Douglas as Franklin. It is about his time in France and is based on Stacy Schiff's book *A Great Improvisation*. It is a drama, not a documentary.

Benjamin Franklin represented the United States in France for more than eight years, from December 1776 to May 1785. In Paris he wore plain clothes and a fur cap instead of a wig. His biographer Walter Isaacson identifies the fur as marten. The French took the cap as a sign that Franklin was a plain, rugged American. Augustin de Saint-Aubin made an engraving of Franklin in the cap in 1777. The print is in the Philadelphia Museum of Art.

Delegates to Congress named Franklin Minister Plenipotentiary to France on September 14, 1778. A minister plenipotentiary is an official with full power to act for his country in another country. He presented his credentials, the letters that proved his position, to the French government on March 23, 1779.

Delegates to Congress also named him minister to Sweden, on September 28, 1782. Franklin never went to Sweden, but worked out a treaty with it from Paris and signed it on April 3, 1783. In the same years he was one of the three Americans who made the peace with Britain. His mission in France ended on May 17, 1785.

#### The Treaty of Paris, 1783

In the Treaty of Paris, British diplomats accepted that the United States was independent. They also handed the United States Britain's claim to land that Native nations lived on. Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and John Jay negotiated for the United States. They signed the first version of the peace terms on November 30, 1782. French diplomats signed their own first version on January 20, 1783. The final Treaty of Paris was signed on September 3, 1783.

The British negotiators accepted a western border for the United States at the Mississippi River. Under the treaty, Americans could fish off Newfoundland. British lenders could still collect the debts Americans had owed them since before the war. The American negotiators promised Loyalists, colonists who had sided with Britain, payment for property that Americans had taken from them. British troops had to leave the thirteen states. Franklin asked the British to hand over Canada as well, and they refused.

Members of the Confederation Congress, meeting at Annapolis, Maryland, ratified the treaty on January 14, 1784. British officials ratified it on April 9, 1784. The two sides traded signed copies in Paris on May 12, 1784.

The land inside that western border was the home of Native nations. Among them were the Haudenosaunee in what is now New York and Pennsylvania. In about 1722 the Tuscarora had joined their league, and after that the league was called the Six Nations. The Six Nations were the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca and Tuscarora. No Native nation was invited to Paris.

In 1763 the British king had set aside much of that land for Native nations, in a royal order called the Royal Proclamation. In 1783 British diplomats handed it to the United States. They also ignored many earlier British treaties with Native nations.

At Fort Stanwix in 1784, American negotiators backed by a strong force of soldiers treated the Six Nations as nations they had beaten in war. They took huge parts of Six Nations land.

<a id="story-john-adams-america-world"></a>

#### John Adams

> **Who:** The first United States minister to Great Britain.
>
> **When and where:** London. Presented to King George III on June 1, 1785.

On June 1, 1785, John Adams met King George III as the representative of the United States. In August 1775 the same king had declared the colonies to be in open rebellion against him. The next year Adams signed the Declaration of Independence.

Adams bought a new coat for the meeting. Two days later, on June 3, 1785, he wrote to Thomas Jefferson about the meeting. He wrote that the king had received him with more kindness than he had expected. The Library of Congress holds that letter.

#### Americans enslaved in Algiers, 1785 to 1796

From 1785 to 1796, officials of the ruler of Algiers held American sailors as slaves, and American leaders could not free them. Algiers, Tunis, Tripoli and Morocco were states on the coast of North Africa, called the Barbary states. Many of their rulers sent armed ships to seize the ships of weaker countries, to make those countries pay them money for safe passage. They held the captured sailors for ransom, a price paid to set a prisoner free.

In 1784 Moroccan ships seized an American merchant ship, and a treaty with Morocco followed in 1786. In 1785 Muhammad, the Dey of Algiers, declared war on the United States. The Dey was the ruler of Algiers. His ships captured several American ships. On July 25, 1785, an Algerian warship took the schooner *Maria* of Boston about three miles off Cape St. Vincent, in Portugal. A schooner is a sailing ship with two or more masts. The *Maria* reached Algiers on August 4, and the Dey's officials enslaved its crew. More American crews followed.

The United States had almost no navy and very little money. American leaders could not free the sailors by force, and for years they could not pay what the Dey asked for them. In 1795 American officials sent Joel Barlow, Joseph Donaldson and Richard O'Brien to North Africa. They made treaties with Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli. The treaty with Algiers was signed on September 5, 1795. The American ratification is dated March 7, 1796.

Accounts disagree on what the treaty cost. The State Department's historians say it freed 83 American sailors. Treasury officials estimated the total cost at about $992,463. That total began with a first payment of about $585,000. The money reached Algiers late, and the Dey demanded more. Editors of George Washington's papers at the University of Virginia give $642,500 paid at once, plus $21,600 a year in supplies for ships. The counts of captives also differ, from 83 freed in 1796 to 115 held in 1793.

The Dey's officials released the surviving sailors on July 8, 1796. Six captives had died shortly before. Several others carried lasting injuries from their years of captivity.

<a id="story-james-leander-cathcart"></a>

#### James Leander Cathcart

> **Who:** An Irish-born American sailor, enslaved in Algiers for eleven years, who rose to be the chief Christian clerk to the Dey and helped put the 1795 treaty into English.
>
> **When and where:** Born June 1, 1767, in County Westmeath, Ireland. Captured July 25, 1785, off Cape St. Vincent, Portugal. Held in Algiers until May 1796. Died October 6, 1843.

James Leander Cathcart was 18 when an Algerian warship captured his ship, and he spent eleven years as a slave in Algiers. He had come to America as a boy. During the Revolution he served as a midshipman, a young officer in training, on the frigate *Confederacy*, a fast warship. The British captured him and held him on prison ships at New York until he escaped.

In 1785 he was one of six crewmen on the Boston schooner *Maria*. An Algerian warship with 14 guns took the *Maria* on July 25, 1785. Cathcart later gave his own reason for the timing. Spain had just made peace with Algiers, and the British consul, Charles Logie, told the Algerians they could take any ship that lacked a certain British pass. A consul is an official who looks after his country's trade and citizens in a foreign port.

The Algerian crew drove the six Americans into a boat and took their hats, handkerchiefs and shoes. On the voyage the captors locked all 42 of their prisoners every night in the sail room in the ship's hold. The drinking water was so foul, Cathcart wrote, that "we were, literally, obliged to strain through our teeth." The *Maria* reached Algiers on August 4. On August 12 the *Dauphin* of Philadelphia arrived with 15 more American captives, which made 21 in all.

Dey Muhammad chose some of the captives to work in his palace and garden. His officials sent others to the slave prisons and to hard labor at the harbor. A man at hard labor got one suit of clothes, worth about a dollar and a half, and two rough blankets meant to last his whole captivity.

About four months after he arrived, Cathcart was beaten on the orders of the officials who ran the Dey's household. Four men threw him down, tied his arms and legs, and beat the soles of his bare feet with sticks. This punishment was called the bastinado. In the usual method, the guards threw the man face down and tied his ankles to a pole. Two men held up the pole, and a guard sat on his shoulders. Cathcart took 28 blows and lost four toenails. He wrote that all fourteen slaves in the garden got the same beating, "old men of sixty and children of ten years of age" among them.

Cathcart rose step by step. He served coffee to the minister of the harbor, then became clerk of the harbor, then clerk of a slave prison. At last he became chief Christian clerk to the Dey. Foreign ambassadors who could not get a meeting with the Dey went through him. He helped the American negotiator Joseph Donaldson, and he translated the Turkish text of the 1795 treaty into English.

By Cathcart's own list, 9 of the 21 Americans taken in 1785 died in Algiers, most of them of plague, a disease that spread quickly and killed many people. The other 12 went home at different times. Family or friends bought some of them free before 1796, and the rest were freed in 1796. Cathcart left Algiers on May 8, 1796, carrying dispatches, official letters for the American government.

He married Jane B. Woodside in Philadelphia in 1798. In January 1799 he sailed from Philadelphia as the American consul for Tunis and Tripoli. From 1807 to 1817 he was the chief American consul at Cádiz, in Spain. His daughter, J. B. Newkirk, published his account, *The Captives: Eleven Years a Prisoner in Algiers*, in 1899.

#### Staying out of Europe's war, 1793 to 1796

In 1793 France and Britain went to war with each other again, and President George Washington decided to keep the United States out of it.

On April 8, 1793, Edmond-Charles Genêt, France's new minister, landed at Charleston, South Carolina. On April 22, 1793, Washington issued the Proclamation of Neutrality. It stated that the United States would take neither side. Genêt hired American privateers to attack British ships. A privateer was a privately owned armed ship that had permission from a government to attack enemy ships. When Washington would not do as Genêt wished, Genêt threatened to go over the President's head to the American people. Washington demanded that the French government replace him.

John Jay signed a treaty with Britain on November 19, 1794. Senators approved it on June 24, 1795, by 20 votes to 10. Under it, British troops were to leave the forts in the Northwest that British diplomats had promised to give up in 1783. British officials agreed to give American traders terms as good as those of any other country. They also put heavy limits on trade with the British islands in the Caribbean.

The two sides sent several quarrels to arbitration, a way of settling a dispute by letting a neutral panel decide. These included the border between Maine and Canada, the old debts, and British seizures of American ships. British officials kept the right to seize American cargo bound for France, with payment, and to take French goods off American ships without paying. The State Department's historians sum it up this way: the treaty "addressed few U.S. interests, and ultimately granted Britain additional rights." It was very unpopular with Americans. Washington signed it anyway, because he judged that the country was too weak to fight Britain.

Thomas Pinckney signed a treaty with Spain on October 27, 1795. He negotiated it with Manuel de Godoy, a Spanish minister. Senators approved it on March 7, 1796. Under it, the border with Spanish West Florida was set at the 31st parallel, an east-west line on the map. Americans got free use of the Mississippi River and the right to use the port of New Orleans without paying tax. Farmers in Kentucky and Tennessee could not haul their crops over the mountains to sell them. They floated the crops down the rivers to New Orleans, which Spanish officials controlled. Under Pinckney's Treaty they could sell them there.

On September 19, 1796, Washington's Farewell Address was printed in the *American Daily Advertiser*, a Philadelphia newspaper. Alexander Hamilton had helped him write it. In it Washington said he would not run for a third term. He also argued that American leaders should not make permanent alliances with any foreign country.

#### The XYZ Affair and a war at sea, 1798 to 1800

From 1798 to 1800 American navy crews fought French ships in the Caribbean in a war that neither government declared. The war followed a failed attempt at talks. President John Adams sent three commissioners to France: Elbridge Gerry, Charles Cotesworth Pinckney and John Marshall.

French agents told the three Americans that talks could not begin until the United States met their demands. The agents asked for a low-interest loan to France and for the United States government to pay the money American merchants said France owed them. On top of that, they wanted "a substantial bribe" for the French foreign minister, Talleyrand. A bribe is money paid to get someone to do something dishonest. Adams made the Americans' reports public, with the agents' names replaced by the letters W, X, Y and Z. The agents were Nicholas Hubbard, Jean Hottinguer, Pierre Bellamy and Lucien Hauteval.

The fighting at sea that followed is called the Quasi-War. Quasi means "almost." The State Department's historians call it "a limited, undeclared war." American and French negotiators ended it with an agreement called the Convention of 1800, also called the Treaty of Mortefontaine. In the same agreement the negotiators ended the alliance of 1778 between France and the United States. Senators did not ratify it until December 18, 1801.

### 1800 to 1850

Between 1800 and 1850 American leaders pushed the country's borders from the Mississippi River to the Pacific Ocean. American leaders bought land from France, took Florida from Spain, split the Oregon country with Britain and took the Southwest from Mexico in a war. Native nations lived across all that land, and none of them signed the sales and treaties. In the same years American sailors fought wars against rulers on the coast of North Africa. In 1823 President James Monroe told Europe's rulers to start no new colonies in the Americas.

#### Tribute and the Barbary wars, 1801 to 1815

American leaders had been paying tribute to the rulers of the Barbary states, four states on the coast of North Africa: Algiers, Tunis, Tripoli and Morocco. Tribute here means protection money. American officials paid the rulers so that the rulers' ships would not seize American ships. The crews of seized ships could be held for ransom, a price paid to free a prisoner.

When American officials would not raise the payments, the pasha of Tripoli declared war on the United States on May 14, 1801. Pasha was the title of Tripoli's ruler. The fighting ended with a treaty signed on June 10, 1805. A treaty is a written agreement between countries. Under this one, American officials paid no more yearly tribute to Tripoli. They did pay a ransom to free the crew of the *Philadelphia*, an American warship that Tripoli's forces had captured. A second Barbary war followed in 1815.

#### The Louisiana Purchase, 1803

On April 30, 1803, American envoys signed a treaty to buy about 828,000 square miles of land west of the Mississippi from France. An envoy is a person sent to bargain for a government. The price was $15 million, and the purchase roughly doubled the size of the United States.

The envoys had been sent to buy only the port of New Orleans. French officials offered them all of Louisiana instead. The people enslaved in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, now called Haiti, had risen against French rule. Napoleon, the ruler of France, had sent an army to put them down. The attempt failed, and he lost the army he sent. With a war against Britain coming, Napoleon sold Louisiana to raise money and to keep the British from taking it.

Article III of the treaty states that the people living in the territory would be "incorporated in the Union of the United States." It also states that they would be admitted to "all the rights, advantages and immunities of citizens of the United States." To be incorporated in the Union meant to be made part of the country. Immunities here are the protections the law gives every citizen. So in 1803, land the United States bought came with a written promise that its people would become full citizens. A century later, judges on the Supreme Court ruled that no such promise covered Puerto Rico, Guam or the Philippines.

Native nations lived across those 828,000 square miles, but they were not part of the sale and no one asked them. The promise of citizenship in Article III did not include them.

#### Florida, 1818 and 1819

In 1818 General Andrew Jackson led American troops into Spanish Florida. They attacked the Seminole people and people who had escaped slavery. American officials who approved the raid saw these people as a threat to Georgia. Jackson's troops seized the Spanish forts at Pensacola and St. Marks. Jackson had two British citizens put to death, on charges of stirring up the Seminoles and the escaped slaves.

President James Monroe and his advisers seriously thought about speaking out against Jackson. The Secretary of State, John Quincy Adams, defended him. The Secretary of State is the official who runs the country's dealings with other countries. Adams then used Jackson's raid to put a choice to Spain: control the people of East Florida, or hand it over to the United States.

In 1819 Adams and the Spanish minister, a diplomat named Luis de Onís, signed the Adams-Onís Treaty. Under it, Spain's leaders handed East Florida to the United States and gave up their claim to West Florida. Spanish officials received no payment. Instead, American officials agreed to take on the bill for $5 million in damage that American citizens had done when they rebelled against Spanish rule. The treaty also fixed the western edge of the Louisiana Purchase. Spain's leaders gave up their claims to the Pacific Northwest, and American officials accepted Spanish rule over Texas. Leaders in both countries ratified the treaty in 1821. To ratify is to give a treaty final approval.

<a id="story-john-quincy-adams-america-world"></a>

#### John Quincy Adams

> **Who:** Secretary of State under President James Monroe, 1817 to 1825.
>
> **When and where:** Washington, D.C.

John Quincy Adams got Florida from Spain for the United States, and the State Department's historians credit him with writing the statement now called the Monroe Doctrine. He was Secretary of State from 1817 to 1825. The Secretary of State is the official who runs the country's dealings with other countries.

Adams negotiated the 1819 treaty with Spain's minister, Luis de Onís, and it carries both their names. Before that, he used Jackson's raid to press Spain to give up Florida.

In that statement, President Monroe told Europe's rulers to start no new colonies in North or South America. Monroe had thought of making the statement jointly with Britain. Adams talked him out of it, so the United States made the statement alone.

#### The Monroe Doctrine, 1823

On December 2, 1823, President James Monroe told Europe's rulers to start no new colonies in North or South America. He said it in his yearly message to Congress. His words were that "the American continents, by the free and independent condition which they have assumed and maintain, are henceforth not to be considered as subjects for future colonization by any European powers." Henceforth means from now on. Colonization means starting colonies.

The State Department's historians credit John Quincy Adams with writing it. In 1823 the United States Navy was too small to enforce the warning. British leaders also wanted other European powers kept out of Latin America. Under Spain's colonial trade rules, Spanish officials had blocked British merchants from trading there, and British leaders wanted the new Latin American countries open to British trade. British warships kept those powers' fleets away.

#### Texas, Oregon and the land taken from Mexico, 1845 to 1848

In the 1840s American leaders took Texas and the Southwest, and they split the Oregon country with Britain. On March 1, 1845, members of Congress passed a joint resolution, a measure voted on by both the House and the Senate, to annex Texas, and Texas joined the United States on December 29. To annex a place is to take it and make it part of a country. The Oregon country stretched from the Pacific coast to the Rocky Mountains. It covered what is now Oregon, Washington and most of the Canadian province of British Columbia. On June 15, 1846, American and British negotiators set the border there at the 49th parallel. Negotiators are officials sent to bargain. The 49th parallel is an east-west line on the map. The United States got the part of the Oregon country south of that line. The two sides settled it by treaty, without a war.

The land in the Southwest came from a war with Mexico, fought from 1846 to 1848. On February 2, 1848, American and Mexican negotiators signed the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. They signed it at Guadalupe Hidalgo, a city north of Mexico City where Mexico's leaders had fled. Mexican officials, whose army had lost the war, signed over more than 525,000 square miles. American officials agreed to pay $15,000,000. The land became all or part of California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, New Mexico, Colorado and Wyoming.

Between about 80,000 and 100,000 Mexican citizens lived on that land, depending on the count. Without moving, they found themselves living in the United States. As signed, Article IX of the treaty said that Mexicans who became American citizens would keep "the free enjoyment of their liberty and property." They would also keep the free practice of their religion. Senators then rewrote Article IX and cut its last two paragraphs.

When senators voted to approve the treaty on March 10, 1848, they struck out Article X completely. Article X was the part that kept Spanish and Mexican land grants valid under American law. A land grant was a legal title to land given by Spanish or Mexican officials. American negotiators then wrote a side agreement, the Protocol of Querétaro. In it they told Mexican officials that deleting Article X had not canceled those land titles. American judges did not treat the Protocol as equal to the treaty.

In 1851 a new law made Mexican landowners in California prove their deeds before officials of the United States government. A deed is the paper showing that someone owns land. The cases took an average of 17 years. Many families sold most of their land during those years to pay English-speaking lawyers and land taxes. The Peralta family of San José and the East Bay kept only 700 of their 49,000 acres.

English-speaking American squatters, newcomers who settled on land that was not theirs, took more. In some cases, as with the Suñol and Berryessa families, squatters lynched the Mexican landowners, killing them without any trial, and stayed on the land. Many Mexican American families lost their land or fell into debt.

In 1850 California's new lawmakers passed the Foreign Miners' Tax, $20 a month for each miner born outside the country. The lawmakers aimed it at Chinese and Latino miners, and officials collected it mostly from them. Thousands of foreign-born miners left the mining towns. Lawmakers ended the tax the next year. The historians William Carrigan and Clive Webb counted at least 597 Mexicans whom mobs in the United States lynched between 1848 and 1928.

In northern New Mexico and southern Colorado, some land grants belonged to whole villages together. The families of a village shared its common land, including forest on the nearby mountains. In the late 1800s American officials and judges broke up these shared grants, and the villages lost most of their common land. From 1891 a special Court of Private Land Claims judged these grants. Its judges, and United States land officials before them, often recognized a grant only up to the foot of the mountains. They left out the forests. In 1897 the judges of the Supreme Court decided a case called *United States v. Sandoval*. They agreed with government lawyers that a village's common lands belonged to the United States government. Seven grants lost between 95 and 99 percent of their land under that ruling. Other villages lost their common land in lawsuits that split it into private pieces, or because they could not pay the taxes on it.

Article XI of the treaty describes the Native nations who lived on the land as "savage tribes," an insulting name. It states that "a great part" of the land was "now occupied" by them. Its words are that they "will hereafter be under the exclusive control of the Government of the United States." The article also states that the United States government would "forcibly restrain" their raids into Mexico. Among the nations on that land were the Tohono O'odham. No Native nation signed the treaty.

<a id="story-nicholas-trist-america-world"></a>

#### Nicholas Trist

> **Who:** The American diplomat who made peace with Mexico after President James K. Polk ordered him home.
>
> **When and where:** Mexico, 1847 and 1848.

Nicholas Trist signed the treaty that ended the war with Mexico after the president had already ordered him to come home. President James K. Polk sent Trist to Mexico to bargain for an end to the war. Then Polk recalled him in October 1847.

Trist ignored the order. He kept bargaining with no authority to do so. In February 1848 he signed the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo.

Polk sent the treaty to the Senate anyway, because it gave him what he wanted, including California. Then he fired Trist. Polk refused to pay Trist's expenses or his salary for his last months of work.

### 1850 to 1900

In the second half of the 1800s, American leaders began taking lands across the oceans and keeping them. Americans claimed small islands for their fertilizer, and American officials bought Alaska from Russia. In Hawaii, a group of mostly American businessmen overthrew the queen with the help of American Marines. More than half of the Native Hawaiian people signed a petition against annexation. A petition is a paper that many people sign to ask leaders for something or to object to something. In 1898 members of Congress annexed the islands. That same year, after a war with Spain, American leaders took Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines. No one asked the people who lived in these places.

These places became territories of the United States. A territory is land that belongs to the United States but is not a state.

#### Perry's warships in Japan, 1853 and 1854

Commodore Matthew Perry opened two Japanese ports to American ships by bringing warships to Japan. A commodore is a navy officer in charge of a group of warships. In July 1853 Perry sailed a group of American warships into Edo Bay, the bay beside the city of Edo, now called Tokyo. He came back in 1854. On March 31, 1854, Japanese and American officials signed the Convention of Kanagawa, a written agreement that opened the two ports to American ships. The Japanese officials signed it under the threat of Perry's warships.

#### Islands claimed for bird droppings, 1856

Americans first claimed land overseas for the United States in 1856, forty-two years before the war with Spain. The reason was fertilizer. Guano, the droppings of seabirds, makes crops grow.

On August 18, 1856, members of Congress passed the Guano Islands Act. Under it, an American citizen who found an island with guano on it could take the island for the United States, unless another country already claimed it. Americans claimed about a hundred islands under this law. In 1890, in a case called *Jones v. United States*, the judges of the Supreme Court ruled that the law was valid. Lawmakers have never ended it, and it is still part of United States law today.

#### Alaska, 1867

In 1867 American officials bought Alaska from Russia. The diplomats who wrote the treaty left Alaska's Native peoples out of American citizenship by name. American and Russian diplomats signed the treaty on March 30, 1867. The price was $7,200,000. On October 18, 1867, at a ceremony on Castle Hill in Sitka, Russian officials formally handed over the territory. Then the United States flag went up.

Russian officials sold land that they did not really control. Alaska Native nations lived on it, and they had no part in the sale. Castle Hill itself was Tlingit land. In 1804 Alexander Baranov, the first Russian governor, had attacked the hill to take it from the Kiksadi clan of the Tlingit people. After a six-day battle, the Russians seized the Kiksadi fort and burned it. In 1867 a Tlingit village still stood beside the Russian town of Sitka.

Article III of the treaty states who would become an American citizen. People living in Alaska who stayed would be admitted to "the enjoyment of all the rights, advantages, and immunities of citizens of the United States." The article then leaves out "uncivilized native tribes," an insulting name for Alaska's Native peoples. They would instead be "subject to such laws and regulations as the United States may from time to time adopt."

Alaska had no civil government, one run by elected or appointed civilians, until 1884. For 17 years American officers ruled it, first from the Army, then from the Treasury Department, then from the Navy. The historian Rebecca Poulson, writing for the Alaska Historical Society, says that American officials considered Native people "savages," an insulting word, and did not allow them to be citizens.

Under Russian rule, officials of the Russian company that ran Alaska had paid compensation when a Tlingit person was killed. Compensation is a payment to the dead person's family. Under Tlingit law, a death was settled with a payment, not with punishment. American officers refused to pay. In early 1869 an army guard at Sitka killed two men from the village of Kake. Poulson calls the deaths accidental. Army officers at Sitka refused to pay compensation for their deaths. Relatives of the dead men then killed two white men.

General Jefferson C. Davis ordered the American warship USS *Saginaw* to attack Kake. It was winter. The crew fired exploding shells from the ship's guns at the Kake villages. They burned 28 of the villages' 29 clan houses, the houses of the Kake clans, which are large family groups. They also burned the villagers' canoes, totem poles and stored food. In 2024 reporters at KTOO, a public radio station in Juneau, wrote that the number of deaths that followed has not been worked out. Kake oral history, the accounts the Tlingit of Kake passed down by word of mouth, records many, especially among elders and children.

#### Hawaii: a kingdom overthrown, 1887 to 1893

In January 1893 a group of mostly American businessmen overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani of Hawaii, and American Marines and sailors helped them. Two of their leaders had already used armed men to force a Hawaiian king to do what they wanted. On June 30, 1887, a group of haole lawyers and sugar planters forced King Kalākaua to sign a new constitution. Haole is the Hawaiian word for white people who are not Native Hawaiian. An armed militia, a force of armed citizens, backed them. Their leaders were two lawyers, Sanford B. Dole and Lorrin Thurston. The document became known as the Bayonet Constitution. A bayonet is a blade fixed to the end of a rifle.

That month members of the Annexation Club, Thurston among them, contacted John L. Stevens. He was the United States Minister to Hawaii, the top American diplomat there. The club's men wanted to know whether the Americans would back them. On January 15, 1893, the group, calling itself the Committee of Safety, began to move against the queen. On January 17 Stevens had 162 American sailors and Marines landed from the warship USS *Boston*. The queen's government had several hundred soldiers and police, and they did not fight. Dole became president of the new provisional government, a government set up for a short time until a lasting one is formed.

Queen Liliʻuokalani gave up her throne under protest. She addressed her protest to the United States, not to the men who had taken power. She wrote that she yielded "to the superior force of the United States of America, whose Minister Plenipotentiary, His Excellency John L. Stevens, has caused United States troops to be landed at Honolulu." She meant that Stevens, the top American diplomat in Hawaii, had brought American troops ashore.

#### Two American reports that disagree, 1893 and 1894

Two American investigations of the overthrow reached opposite findings. President Grover Cleveland sent James H. Blount to Hawaii to find out what had happened. Blount reported that Stevens had landed the Marines on a false excuse to help the plotters. On December 18, 1893, Cleveland sent Congress a message about it. He said the "military demonstration on the soil of Honolulu was of itself an act of war." A military demonstration is a show of armed force. He also said that "the provisional government owes its existence to an armed invasion by the United States." Albert S. Willis, the new American minister in Hawaii, apologized for "the reprehensible conduct of the American minister and the unauthorized presence on land of a military force." He meant Stevens. Reprehensible means deserving blame.

Cleveland could not get the queen put back on her throne. In 1894 members of a Senate committee made their own investigation, called the Morgan Report, and they cleared everyone involved. On July 4, 1894, the men who had taken power declared the Republic of Hawaii.

<a id="story-queen-liliuokalani-america-world"></a>

#### Queen Liliʻuokalani

> **Who:** The last queen of the Kingdom of Hawaii, and the writer of the song "Aloha ʻOe."
>
> **When and where:** Honolulu. Overthrown January 17, 1893. Held prisoner in ʻIolani Palace in 1895.

Queen Liliʻuokalani lost her throne to an armed takeover backed by American troops. Two years later officials of the Republic of Hawaii put her on trial in her own palace. On January 17, 1893, she yielded under protest. She asked American leaders to undo what their own minister had done. President Cleveland agreed that Stevens had acted wrongly, but he could not get her put back on the throne.

In January 1895 Hawaiians loyal to the queen, among them Robert Wilcox and Prince Kūhiō, tried to restore her by force. Within 36 hours officials of the Republic of Hawaii had caught the rebels and jailed them. The Republic's officials then arrested the queen. On January 24, 1895, they forced her to sign a paper giving up her throne for good.

They tried her before a military court in the throne room of ʻIolani Palace, where she had ruled. The charge was misprision of treason, which means knowing about a plot against the government and not reporting it. The officers who sat on the court found her guilty, fined her $5,000, and sentenced her to five years in prison at hard labor, which means forced heavy work. The Republic's officials later reduced the sentence. For nearly eight months they held her prisoner in an upstairs bedroom of the palace. They allowed her no visitors except one woman companion. She spent her days praying, reading, writing music, crocheting and quilting.

#### 21,269 names against annexation, 1897

Native Hawaiians defeated a treaty to annex their islands by signing their names against it. Between September 11 and October 2, 1897, two Hawaiian groups held meetings on the five main islands. The groups were Hui Aloha ʻĀina, which had separate branches for men and for women, and Hui Kālaiʻāina. They gathered 21,269 signatures of Native Hawaiians against annexation. That year about 39,000 Native Hawaiian and part-Hawaiian people were counted, so more than half of them signed.

Four men carried the petition to Washington: James Kaulia, David Kalauokalani, John Richardson and William Auld. They arrived on December 6 and presented it to the Senate on December 9, 1897. A treaty needs the votes of two-thirds of the senators. When the four men left Washington on February 27, 1898, only 46 senators were still willing to vote for the annexation treaty, short of the two-thirds it needed. The treaty failed.

Supporters of annexation in Congress then used a method that did not need the Senate votes the Hawaiians had blocked. A joint resolution passes when more than half of the House and more than half of the Senate vote for it. Their joint resolution was called the Newlands Resolution, and under it the United States took Hawaii. Members of the House voted for it on June 15, 1898, and senators on July 6. President William McKinley signed it on July 7, 1898.

#### 1898: Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines

After a war with Spain in 1898, American officials ruled Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines. On February 15, 1898, the American battleship USS *Maine* blew up in the harbor of Havana, in Cuba. In April members of Congress declared war on Spain. On June 21, 1898, Juan Marina, the Spanish governor of Guam, surrendered the island to officers of the American warship USS *Charleston*. American troops landed in Puerto Rico at Guánica on July 25.

Spanish and American diplomats signed the Treaty of Paris on December 10, 1898. Spanish diplomats gave up Cuba and signed Puerto Rico and Guam over to the United States. They sold the Philippines to the United States for $20 million.

No one from Puerto Rico, Guam or the Philippines took part in the talks in Paris. Several million people in those places got new rulers without being asked. Among them on Guam were the CHamoru, the island's Native people. In the Philippines, Filipinos had already declared their own independence.

#### The Philippine-American War begins, 1899

War between American troops and the Philippine Republic began on February 4, 1899, because American officials had decided to keep the islands. Filipinos had been fighting Spain before the Americans arrived. On June 12, 1898, they declared their independence. American officials kept the islands instead of recognizing the new republic, and the two sides went to war.

The war lasted until 1902. About 4,200 Americans and about 20,000 Filipino soldiers were killed. Counts of Filipino civilians, the people who were not soldiers, who died do not agree, and they are far apart. The State Department's historians say as many as 200,000 died "from violence, famine, and disease." Encyclopaedia Britannica gives more than 200,000. Other estimates run from 250,000 to 1,000,000, and the Philippine-American War Centennial Initiative gives 510,000. Much of the civilian toll came from hunger and from a cholera epidemic in 1902, which killed more than 200,000 people by itself. Cholera is a disease of the gut spread by dirty water, and an epidemic is an outbreak that spreads to many people at once. The epidemic was worse because the fighting had broken up daily life in the islands.

The State Department's historians also record what American troops did. In their words, "U.S. forces at times burned villages, implemented civilian reconcentration policies, and employed torture on suspected guerrillas." Reconcentration meant forcing civilians out of their homes into camps or zones that soldiers guarded. Guerrillas are fighters in small bands who hide among the people and attack by surprise. One kind of torture American soldiers used was called the water cure. To make a prisoner talk, they held his throat so that he had to swallow water until it filled his stomach. Then they forced the water out by pressing on his stomach.

<a id="story-emilio-aguinaldo-america-world"></a>

#### Emilio Aguinaldo

> **Who:** The Filipino leader who declared the Philippines independent from Spain and then led the war against the United States.
>
> **When and where:** Born March 22 or 23, 1869, near Cavite, on the island of Luzon. President of the Philippine Republic from January 1899. Captured at Palanan on March 23, 1901. Died February 6, 1964.

Emilio Aguinaldo led Filipino fighters against Spain, then led the Philippine Republic against the United States until American officers captured him by a trick in 1901. In 1896 he was the mayor of his town, Cavite Viejo, and a local leader of the Katipunan. The Katipunan was a secret society fighting Spanish rule.

In December 1897 Aguinaldo made a deal with the Spanish governor. He agreed to leave the islands in return for money and a promise of reforms. From Hong Kong and Singapore he made plans with American consuls and with officers of Commodore George Dewey's fleet. A consul is an official who looks after his country's trade and citizens in a foreign port. He would come back and help the Americans fight Spain. He landed in the Philippines again on May 19, 1898.

On June 12, 1898, Filipinos declared independence with Aguinaldo at the head of their government. Six months later Spanish diplomats sold the islands to the United States in the Treaty of Paris. On January 23, 1899, Filipinos proclaimed a constitution and elected Aguinaldo president of the Philippine Republic. The fighting with American troops began on February 4, 1899. From November 1899 his forces fought as guerrillas.

On March 23, 1901, General Frederick Funston captured him at Palanan, in northern Luzon. Macabebe scouts, Filipinos who served the United States Army, dressed as rebel soldiers. Funston and a few other American officers went along, pretending to be their prisoners. Fake letters sent ahead to Aguinaldo said that more of his own soldiers were coming and were bringing American prisoners to him. At Palanan the scouts opened fire on his guards, killed two and seized him.

Aguinaldo swore loyalty to the United States. On April 19, 1901, he called on his fighters to lay down their weapons and accept American rule. He lived until 1964 and saw the Philippines become independent in 1946.

#### Samoa divided, 1899

On December 2, 1899, in an agreement called the Tripartite Convention, diplomats divided the Samoan islands between the United States and Germany. Tripartite means having three sides. The three sides that signed it were the United States, Germany and Great Britain. The chiefs of the island of Tutuila signed a paper handing their island to the United States on April 17, 1900. Tui Manuʻa Elisala, the ruler of the Manuʻa islands, signed his islands over on July 16, 1904.

### 1900 to 1950

In the first half of the 1900s American officials ruled lands overseas, and judges of the Supreme Court ruled that the people living there did not get the whole Constitution. American troops finished a war in the Philippines and occupied Haiti, the Dominican Republic and Nicaragua. Workers, most of them from islands in the Caribbean, built the Panama Canal for the United States, on a strip of land that American officials held forever under a treaty. A treaty is a written agreement between countries. Americans fought in two world wars. After the first, senators refused to join the League of Nations that President Woodrow Wilson had proposed. After the second, American leaders helped found the United Nations and the NATO military alliance.

#### Finishing the war in the Philippines, 1900 to 1902

American soldiers in the Philippines tortured Filipinos and killed civilians. Of the officers who ordered it, one was suspended for a month and fined, one was scolded and forced to retire, and one went free. One method of torture was called the water cure.

At Igbaras on November 27, 1900, a group of five or six American soldiers tied up Tobeniano Ealdama, the town's mayor. They held his throat so he could not stop himself from swallowing, and they poured water into him until his stomach filled. Then they forced the water out by pressing on his stomach with a foot or with their hands. They did it to make him talk. Captain Edwin F. Glenn, an Army lawyer, directed it, along with a doctor working for the Army. After a second round, Ealdama said he was a captain among the Filipino fighters. That night Glenn ordered the whole town burned, 400 to 500 houses.

On September 28, 1901, at Balangiga on the island of Samar, townspeople and Filipino fighters attacked a company of American foot soldiers at breakfast. They killed about 48 soldiers. It was the Army's worst loss in a single fight since the Little Bighorn in 1876.

General Jacob H. Smith gave the orders for the American answer on Samar. His orders survive in the record: "I want no prisoners. I wish you to kill and burn." "The more you kill and burn, the better it will please me." He said the inside of Samar "must be made a howling wilderness." Someone asked Smith how young a target could be. He said any Filipino male over ten, because in his words a boy that age could carry a weapon. On Samar, Marine Major Littleton Waller had eleven Filipino guides and carriers shot without a trial.

How many people American troops killed on Samar is disputed, and the counts are far apart. An American soldier who was there said 39. A British researcher, Bob Couttie, studied it for ten years and put it at about 2,500. Most estimates fall between 2,000 and 2,500. Other counts reach 5,000. An old figure of 50,000 is now traced to misread documents.

#### What happened to the officers

The torture came out in the Senate. Senator George Frisbie Hoar asked for an investigation. Senator Henry Cabot Lodge kept it inside his own Committee on the Philippines. On April 14, 1902, Charles S. Riley, a former sergeant, told the committee what he had seen at Igbaras.

Secretary of War Elihu Root ordered Glenn court-martialed, which means tried in a military court. Army officials moved the trial from San Francisco to Catbalogan, in the Philippines, far from the witnesses. The officers on the court found Glenn guilty. They suspended him for one month and fined him fifty dollars. He retired in 1919 as a brigadier general. Ealdama was then serving a prison sentence as a "war traitor."

Waller told his court-martial that he had followed Smith's orders, and the officers on the court found him not guilty. Another court-martial found Smith guilty of "conduct to the prejudice of good order and military discipline." That means behaving in a way that harmed order and discipline in the armed forces. Its officers asked only that he be formally scolded. President Theodore Roosevelt went further and forced Smith to retire, two years before he was due to leave the Army. Smith was not sent to prison. In a private letter, Roosevelt called the water cure "the old Filipino method of mild torture." He wrote that "nobody was seriously damaged." In the same letter he also wrote, "torture is not a thing that we can tolerate."

Roosevelt declared the war over on July 4, 1902. American troops kept fighting in the Moro provinces of the southern Philippines until 1913.

#### The Insular Cases, 1901 to 1922

The judges of the Supreme Court are called justices. Between 1901 and 1922 they decided that the islands taken in 1898 belonged to the United States but were not fully part of it. The decisions are called the Insular Cases. Insular means having to do with islands.

The justices decided *Downes v. Bidwell* on May 27, 1901. They held that Puerto Rico "belongs to, but is not a part of, the United States." From these cases came the idea of the "unincorporated territory." That is a place the United States owns and rules, where the people do not get the whole Constitution unless Congress chooses to give it to them. In *Balzac v. Porto Rico* in 1922, the justices held that Puerto Ricans had no constitutional right to a trial by jury at home. By then Puerto Ricans were American citizens.

The justices who decided these cases believed the people of the islands were not fit for full constitutional government. In 2022 Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote about the Insular Cases. In his words, they "have no foundation in the Constitution and rest instead on racial stereotypes." A stereotype is a fixed, unfair idea about a whole group of people. He added, "They deserve no place in our law." The justices of the Supreme Court have never overturned them. In 2026 they are still the law for the people of Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands.

#### Who became a citizen, and when

Members of Congress decided, island by island, whether the people of each territory would be American citizens. The answers came at different times. People born in American Samoa are still not citizens at birth.

Under the Foraker Act, signed on April 12, 1900, members of Congress set up a government for Puerto Rico. The law called the island's people "citizens of Porto Rico," under the protection of the United States but not citizens of it. On March 2, 1917, President Wilson signed the Jones-Shafroth Act, and under it Puerto Ricans became American citizens. One month later Americans entered the First World War. Two months after that, Wilson signed the law for the draft, which required young men to serve in the military. Accounts disagree on how many Puerto Ricans were drafted. The figure usually given is about 18,000, and History.com gives 20,000. Their citizenship came from a law passed by Congress, not from the Constitution. It did not come with a vote for president.

Hawaii's territorial government came from the Hawaiian Organic Act, signed on April 30, 1900. In a treaty signed on August 4, 1916, Danish officials agreed to sell the Danish West Indies to the United States for $25 million in gold. The islands changed hands on March 31, 1917, and became the U.S. Virgin Islands. Members of Congress did not make their people American citizens until 1927.

Officers of the United States Navy governed Guam from 1899. Its people did not become citizens until President Harry Truman signed the Organic Act of Guam on August 1, 1950. That was fifty-two years after Navy officers took the island. Under the act, Guam got a government run by civilians and stayed an unincorporated territory.

The chiefs of Tutuila, in Samoa, signed a deed, a paper handing their island to the United States, on April 17, 1900. Tui Manuʻa Elisala signed one for the Manuʻa islands on July 16, 1904. Members of Congress did not approve either deed until 1929. Navy officers governed American Samoa until 1951. Under federal law its people are American nationals, not citizens, and that is still true. A national can live in the United States and carry an American passport but is not a citizen. American Samoa is the only territory with people living on it where they do not become citizens at birth.

Under laws Congress passed in 1902 and 1916, American officials ran a colonial government in the Philippines, with a promise of independence someday. Under the Tydings-McDuffie Act, signed on March 24, 1934, the Philippines would become independent on July 4, 1946, after ten years of self-rule. In the same act, members of Congress put Filipinos in a different group under immigration law, so far fewer could move to the United States. The Philippines became independent on July 4, 1946.

Filipinos served in the American armed forces in the Second World War, at the call of the United States. In 1946 members of Congress passed the Rescission Act. It stated that their service "shall not be deemed to have been active military, naval, or air service" for most veterans' benefits. Under it, they could not get benefits that other veterans of the same war received.

#### The Panama Canal, 1903 to 1914

American officials backed Panama's break from Colombia in 1903. Philippe-Jean Bunau-Varilla, a Frenchman, signed the Hay-Bunau-Varilla Treaty for Panama on November 18, 1903. Under the treaty American officials got a strip of land 10 miles wide across Panama, forever. Panama got $10,000,000 at once and $250,000 a year, starting nine years later.

The canal opened on August 15, 1914. The official count of the dead during the American building of the canal is 5,609, out of about 56,000 workers. Most of the workers came from Barbados, Jamaica and other islands of the Caribbean. The historian Caroline Lieffers, writing for The Conversation, says many historians think the real number was several times higher.

#### Marines in Haiti, the Dominican Republic and Nicaragua

American presidents sent the Marines to occupy three nearby countries for years at a time. To occupy a country is to hold it with troops and control its government.

In December 1914 American Marines took $500,000 from Haiti's national bank and moved it to New York. In July 1915 Haitian President Jean Vilbrun Guillaume Sam was killed. The State Department's historians do not name who killed him. President Woodrow Wilson then sent the Marines into Haiti. They stayed for nineteen years, until 1934. Under a treaty of 1915, American officials took full control of Haiti's money. They set up a Haitian police force, the Gendarmerie, commanded by Marines. American officials forced the election of Philippe Sudré Dartiguenave as Haiti's president in August 1915.

American officials wanted a new Haitian constitution that let foreigners own land in Haiti. When Haiti's lawmakers resisted it, American officials forced President Dartiguenave to send the lawmakers home, and they did not meet again until 1929. The new constitution, written under American direction, went to a public vote on June 12, 1918. The official count recorded it as approved by 99 percent of the votes, with fewer than 5 percent of Haitians voting. Marines and the Gendarmerie brought back the corvée, a system of forced labor. They made Haitians build roads without pay.

Haitian fighters called cacos rose against the occupation. By some estimates the Marines and the Gendarmerie killed more than 2,000 cacos, according to a report by the Congressional Research Service. American forces lost 10 killed and 26 wounded. The report gives no count of other Haitians killed. On December 6, 1929, Marines fired on about 1,500 protesters at Les Cayes and killed at least 12 Haitians. President Franklin D. Roosevelt pulled the Marines out in 1934.

Charlemagne Péralte led the armed resistance from 1917. Marine officers ordered their men to "get Charlemagne." Sergeant Herman H. Hanneken went into Péralte's camp in disguise and shot him dead near Sainte-Suzanne on November 1, 1919. The Marines photographed the body and passed the picture around. Accounts give his birth year as 1885 or 1886.

Marines landed in the Dominican Republic in May 1916, and American officers declared a military government that November. From 1917 to 1921 they fought guerrillas in the east, fighters in small bands called gavilleros. The Library of Congress's country study describes the Americans' methods as "often brutal." It gives no count of the Dominicans killed. Dominicans took back control when President Horacio Vásquez took office on July 13, 1924.

In Nicaragua, American officials encouraged a revolt against President José Santos Zelaya in 1909, and Marines landed at Bluefields. In 1912 Marines came to support President Adolfo Díaz. A guard of 100 Marines stayed at the American embassy until 1925. In 1927 about 2,000 more Marines arrived.

Augusto César Sandino fought them for as long as they stayed. The Marines trained a Nicaraguan National Guard and left in January 1933, with Anastasio Somoza García in command of the Guard. In 1934 Somoza and other high officers agreed to kill Sandino. On February 23, 1934, Sandino came to what looked like a peace meeting, and National Guardsmen seized him and murdered him. Somoza became president on January 1, 1937, and ruled for about twenty years. No reliable count exists of the Nicaraguans killed in the fighting with the Marines.

<a id="story-woodrow-wilson-america-world"></a>

#### Woodrow Wilson

> **Who:** President of the United States during the First World War. He proposed the League of Nations.
>
> **When and where:** Washington, D.C., 1915 to 1920.

Woodrow Wilson proposed a League of Nations, and the United States never joined it. He was president when the United States entered the First World War on April 6, 1917. On January 8, 1918, he set out his terms for peace, called the Fourteen Points. One of them was a League of Nations, a group of countries that would settle quarrels by talking instead of fighting. Senators voted against the peace treaty and the League in November 1919 and again in March 1920.

Wilson also sent the Marines into Haiti in 1915, and they stayed until 1934. In 1917 he signed both the law that made Puerto Ricans American citizens and the draft law that followed it.

#### Puerto Rico under an appointed governor, 1937

In 1937, under Governor Blanton Winship, police in Puerto Rico shot marchers at Ponce, and officials began using public money to sterilize Puerto Rican women, which means operating on them so they could never become pregnant again. Winship was an American general. The President of the United States appointed him to govern the island. Puerto Ricans did not elect him.

On Palm Sunday, March 21, 1937, members of the Nationalist Party marched in Ponce. They marked the end of slavery in Puerto Rico and protested the jailing of their leader, Pedro Albizu Campos. The Insular Police were under Winship's direct military command. The police opened fire on the marchers. Accounts give the dead as between 19 and 21 and the wounded as between about 150 and 235. A human rights commission that looked into it found that all the dead had been shot by police. The killings are known as the Ponce Massacre.

Also in 1937, under Winship, Law 116 took effect. Under it, officials set up a Eugenics Board, and public money paid for sterilizations. Eugenics was a set of beliefs, now rejected, that some groups of people should be kept from having children. Sterilization is an operation after which a woman can never become pregnant again. In Puerto Rico the usual method was tubal ligation, which Puerto Ricans called *la operación*. In it a doctor cut or tied the two tubes that carry eggs from the ovaries to the womb. Some women instead had a hysterectomy, in which a surgeon removed the womb.

From 1937 until the law was repealed in 1960, members of the Eugenics Board forced 97 sterilizations. Many thousands more women had the operation under pressure. Some women were told, falsely, that it could be undone, or that employers would not hire them unless they were sterilized, and accounts do not name who told them. Employers did favor hiring sterilized women. Hospital staff turned away some pregnant women unless they agreed to be sterilized after giving birth. Clarence Gamble, an heir to the Procter and Gamble fortune who believed in eugenics, set up clinics on the island. By 1968 about one Puerto Rican woman in three of childbearing age had been sterilized. A 1982 study found 41 percent of married women in Puerto Rico sterilized.

The record on consent is mixed. Some women chose the operation because it was the only birth control offered to them. The doctor Helen Rodríguez-Trías said, "Women make choices based on alternatives, and there haven't been many alternatives in Puerto Rico."

<a id="story-pedro-albizu-campos-america-world"></a>

#### Pedro Albizu Campos

> **Who:** A United States Army officer in the First World War who became the leader of the movement for Puerto Rican independence.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Ponce, Puerto Rico, on September 12, 1891.

Pedro Albizu Campos was an American citizen who could be drafted into the American army but could not vote for the president who commanded it. He was born in Ponce on September 12, 1891. He was the first Puerto Rican to graduate from Harvard Law School.

In the First World War he served in the United States Army and rose to second lieutenant. Army officers assigned him to the 375th Infantry Regiment, which was all Black. The Army kept Black and white soldiers in separate units, which is called segregation. The segregation he met there shaped his politics.

In 1930 he became president of the Puerto Rican Nationalist Party, which wanted independence from the United States. He was later convicted of sedition, the crime of urging people to rise against the government, and sent to prison. In 1937 Nationalists marched in Ponce partly to protest his imprisonment, and police shot them.

#### The St. Louis, 1939

In 1939 American officials refused to let a ship full of Jewish refugees land. Refugees are people who flee their country to escape danger. The ship *St. Louis* sailed from Hamburg, in Germany, on May 13, 1939, with 937 passengers. Almost all of them were Jews escaping Nazi Germany.

Cuban officials let 28 of them land. American and Canadian officials refused them. The ship carried the rest back to Europe. Officials in Great Britain let in 288 of them, in the Netherlands 181, in Belgium 214 and in France 224. According to the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, 254 of the passengers were later killed in the Holocaust, the Nazis' mass murder of the Jews of Europe.

#### Guam under Japanese occupation, 1941 to 1944

The people of Guam lived through two and a half years of Japanese occupation as people of the United States who were not American citizens. Japanese forces invaded Guam on December 8, 1941, hours after the attack on Pearl Harbor. Japanese soldiers beat CHamoru people, forced them to work without pay and put some of them to death. By the spring of 1944 Japanese officers had put every able-bodied man into a labor battalion, working without pay. In the last weeks, Japanese troops force-marched the people to concentration camps, where soldiers held civilians under guard. The largest camp was at Manenggon. American forces landed on July 21, 1944. People on Guam mark that day as Liberation Day.

#### The United Nations, the Marshall Plan and NATO, 1945 to 1949

After the Second World War, American leaders helped build the kind of world organization that senators had refused in 1920. Delegates from many countries signed the United Nations Charter in San Francisco on June 26, 1945. It took effect on October 24, 1945.

In March 1948 members of Congress passed the law for the Marshall Plan, under which American officials sent money to rebuild Western Europe after the war. The money eventually rose to more than $12 billion. On April 4, 1949, twelve countries signed the treaty that created NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, a military alliance. The State Department's historians call it "the first peacetime military alliance the United States entered into outside of the Western Hemisphere."

### 1950 to 2000

For forty years after 1950, American leaders shaped their dealings with the world around a rivalry with the Soviet Union, called the Cold War. With that rivalry in mind, American presidents and their advisers chose where aid, weapons and troops went, and they sent troops to fight in Korea and Vietnam. American officials secretly helped overthrow elected governments in Iran, Guatemala and Chile. In these same years Alaska and Hawaii became states. Puerto Rico got a new name but stayed a territory. American officials set off nuclear bombs on Pacific islands whose people the United States had taken charge of protecting for the United Nations.

#### The Cold War

The Cold War was a long rivalry between the United States and its allies on one side and the Soviet Union and its allies on the other. American leaders chose their allies with the rivalry in mind. They also decided with it in mind whom to give aid and weapons to, and where to send troops. American troops fought in Korea from 1950 to 1953 and later in Vietnam, as part of this contest.

On November 9, 1989, the Berlin Wall, which had divided the city of Berlin, was opened. The Soviet Union broke apart on December 26, 1991, and the Cold War was over.

#### The Cuban Missile Crisis, October 1962

In October 1962 American and Soviet leaders came closer to nuclear war than at any other time. In July 1962 Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev and Cuban leader Fidel Castro secretly agreed to put Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba. Before that, a force backed by the United States had tried and failed to overthrow Castro in the Bay of Pigs invasion.

On October 14, 1962, an American U-2 spy plane took pictures of missile sites being built in Cuba. On October 22 President John F. Kennedy ordered American warships to stop ships carrying weapons to Cuba. He called it a quarantine, and he told the country about it on television. American forces went on alert for war. On October 27 a U-2 was shot down over Cuba.

Kennedy then offered to promise not to attack Cuba if the missiles were removed. His brother Robert Kennedy secretly told the Soviet ambassador, Anatoly Dobrynin, that American missiles in Turkey would also be taken out, though not as part of any public deal. On October 28 Khrushchev announced that the Soviet missiles would leave Cuba. The American Jupiter missiles left Turkey in April 1963.

#### The Peace Corps, 1961

On March 1, 1961, President Kennedy created the Peace Corps by an order he signed. It is a program for American volunteers to serve in other countries. Sargent Shriver was its first director. The first volunteers went to Ghana, in Africa, that same year.

<a id="story-lillian-carter-america-world"></a>

#### Lillian Carter

> **Who:** A nurse from Plains, Georgia, who joined the Peace Corps at 68. Mother of President Jimmy Carter.
>
> **When and where:** India, 1966 to 1968.
>
> **Movie:** *Miss Lillian: More Than a President's Mother* (2021), a documentary film about her directed by Vivian Winther.

Lillian Carter joined the Peace Corps at the age of 68 and worked as a nurse in India from 1966 to 1968. She told the recruiter she wanted to go "where it's warm, people have dark skins and need a nurse's service."

She was sent to the Godrej Colony, about 30 miles from Mumbai, and she turned 70 there. After she came home, her son Jimmy Carter became president. She died in 1983. In 1986 Peace Corps officials created the Lillian Carter Award for volunteers who serve at the age of 50 or older.

#### Governments overthrown with American help

In Iran, Guatemala and Chile, American officials secretly helped overthrow elected governments. A coup is the sudden overthrow of a government by a small group, often by the army.

**Iran, 1953.** Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh had taken control of Iran's oil industry away from British companies. In June 1953 President Dwight Eisenhower approved a secret American and British plan to overthrow him. CIA Director Allen Dulles oversaw the planning. The CIA is the Central Intelligence Agency, the American government's spy service. Kermit Roosevelt of the CIA ran the plan in Iran. CIA officers paid journalists, religious leaders and politicians to attack Mosaddegh as corrupt and power-hungry.

On August 19, 1953, General Fazlollah Zahedi replaced Mosaddegh, and the Shah, Iran's king, took back power. The Shah had Mosaddegh convicted of treason. Mosaddegh served three years in prison and lived the rest of his life under house arrest. Officials of the Shah's government put to death one of his advisers and more than a dozen military officers and student leaders on his side. In 2013 CIA officials released the agency's own history, which states that the agency "planned and helped implement the coup."

**Guatemala, 1954.** On June 27, 1952, President Jacobo Árbenz began a land reform, a plan to share out farmland, with a law called Decree 900. Under it his officials took land from owners and gave about 1.5 million acres to about 100,000 families. The owners were paid more than $8 million in all. The United Fruit Company was one of the landowners. Árbenz's officials offered United Fruit $2.99 an acre for its land. State Department officials demanded $75 an acre.

In August 1953 Eisenhower approved a CIA operation to overthrow Árbenz. CIA officers ran what they called "psychological warfare and political action" against Árbenz's government. Psychological warfare means using fear, rumors and false stories to turn people against their leaders. The officers also drew up lists of Guatemalan officials to be killed. One list had 58 names. On June 18, 1954, a force under Carlos Castillo Armas invaded from Honduras, after planes had harassed the capital. On June 27 Árbenz resigned. Castillo Armas became president, and his officials gave the land back to the companies and broke up the labor unions. Human rights groups estimate that between 1954 and 1990, the forces of Guatemala's military governments murdered more than 100,000 civilians.

**Chile, 1970 to 1973.** Salvador Allende was elected president of Chile in September 1970. On September 15, 1970, President Richard Nixon met CIA Director Richard Helms and ordered him to stop Allende. Helms wrote down Nixon's words in his notes. One line was "make the economy scream." Another was "$10,000,000 available, more if necessary." CIA officers then ran a plan they called Track II. Its stated aim was "a firm and continuing policy that Allende be overthrown by a coup." CIA officers gave weapons to men who planned to kidnap the head of Chile's army, General René Schneider. A different group of plotters killed Schneider on October 22, 1970.

On September 11, 1973, General Augusto Pinochet led the army coup that overthrew Allende. An American military attaché, an officer posted to the American embassy, called the coup "close to perfect." Pinochet ruled Chile until 1990. Chile's official commissions count 3,216 people killed or disappeared by Pinochet's forces between 1973 and 1990, and 38,254 people who survived political imprisonment, torture or both. To be disappeared means to be taken by the government's forces and never seen again.

#### Alaska and Hawaii become states, 1959

Alaska became the 49th state on January 3, 1959, and Hawaii became the 50th on August 21, 1959. Hawaii's voters could only say Yes or No to becoming a state right away. On June 27, 1959, the ballot asked: "Shall Hawaii immediately be admitted into the Union as a State?" The only answers were Yes and No.

Independence was not on the ballot. In 1953 members of the United Nations General Assembly had passed Resolution 742. It stated that votes like this one should offer a free choice among several futures, including independence. A large majority of Hawaii's voters chose statehood. Hawaii and Alaska were then taken off the United Nations list of territories that did not govern themselves.

#### Puerto Rico: a new name, and armed revolt, 1950 to 1954

In 1950 Puerto Ricans got the right to write their own constitution, but the island stayed a territory under the Insular Cases. Members of Congress passed Public Law 600 that year. Puerto Rico's voters approved the law in 1951 and the constitution in 1952. On July 25, 1952, Governor Luis Muñoz Marín proclaimed the Commonwealth, the *Estado Libre Asociado*. Under that new name, the island was still a territory of the United States. The date was the anniversary of the American landing at Guánica in 1898. On November 27, 1953, members of the United Nations General Assembly voted to take Puerto Rico off the list of territories that did not govern themselves. American officials then stopped sending the United Nations reports about the island.

Some Puerto Ricans fought the new arrangement with guns. On October 30, 1950, Nationalists rose up in several towns. Soldiers and pilots of the Puerto Rico National Guard, under Major General Luis R. Esteves, attacked the towns of Jayuya and Utuado with P-47 Thunderbolt warplanes, artillery, mortars and grenades. Pilots in American military aircraft fired on and bombed towns full of American citizens. On November 1, 1950, two Nationalists, Griselio Torresola and Oscar Collazo, attacked Blair House in Washington, where President Harry Truman was living. Torresola shot a White House guard, Leslie Coffelt, three times. Coffelt was dying, but he got up and shot Torresola dead. Coffelt died of his wounds. Collazo was sentenced to death, and in 1952 Truman changed the sentence to life in prison.

On March 1, 1954, four Puerto Rican Nationalists went into the visitors' gallery of the House of Representatives. They were Lolita Lebrón, Rafael Cancel Miranda, Andrés Figueroa Cordero and Irvin Flores Rodríguez. They unfurled a Puerto Rican flag and fired down onto the floor. They wounded five members of the House, and all five recovered. All four Nationalists were convicted and sent to prison.

#### The Pacific: a trust, nuclear tests and one vote to join

After the Second World War, members of the United Nations placed more than 2,000 Pacific islands under American rule. The islands were the Marianas, the Carolines and the Marshalls. The arrangement was called the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, and it lasted from 1947 to 1986. A trust territory is land that one country governs for the United Nations, with a duty to look after its people.

Between 1946 and 1958 American officials set off 67 nuclear tests at Bikini and Enewetak, two atolls in the Marshall Islands. An atoll is a ring of small coral islands around a lagoon. American officials moved the people off those atolls before the tests.

The largest test was Castle Bravo, on March 1, 1954. Its explosive force was 15 megatons, equal to 15 million tons of TNT. That was about two and a half times what its designers had predicted. Fallout, the radioactive dust from the blast, came down on islands where people lived. On Rongelap, about 110 miles away, the fallout looked like snow, and children played with the flakes. All 64 people on Rongelap took in radiation from it. American officials moved the people of Rongelap and Utirik away about 72 hours after the blast. Rongelap could no longer be lived on. Officials of the Atomic Energy Commission, the government agency in charge of nuclear weapons, then ran a study of the exposed people, called Project 4.1. Radioactive iodine from fallout collects in the thyroid, a gland in the neck. In later years thyroid disease, including thyroid cancer, was the most common lasting harm among the people exposed.
