A screening from 1993 to 1997 found 57 Marshallese born before 1954 who had thyroid cancer or had had it removed. Twenty-three Japanese fishermen on the boat *Lucky Dragon* were also caught in the fallout, and one of them died.

The people of the Northern Mariana Islands voted to join the United States. Of today's five territories with people living in them, it is the only one whose people voted to come in. A Covenant, a formal agreement, between the islands and the United States was signed on February 15, 1975. On June 17, 1975, 78.8 percent of the people who voted approved it. The Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands began in 1978, and its people became American citizens in 1986. The Marshall Islands and the Federated States of Micronesia became independent countries in 1986, tied to the United States by agreements called Compacts of Free Association. Free association means a separate country tied to the United States by a formal agreement. Palau's compact took effect in 1994.

#### The capital, the canal and an apology

Washington, D.C. is not a state, and the people living there could not vote for president at all until 1961. That year enough states ratified, or approved, the Twenty-third Amendment to the Constitution, and it took effect on March 29, 1961. In 1971 the city got back a delegate in the House, who can speak there but cannot vote on bills. Under the Home Rule Act of 1973, its people elected their own mayor from 1975. Members of Congress passed an amendment in 1978 to give the city full seats in Congress. Lawmakers in too few states approved it, and it ran out of time in 1985.

On September 7, 1977, American and Panamanian leaders signed the Torrijos-Carter Treaties. Under them, American officials handed the Panama Canal to Panama on December 31, 1999.

In 1993 members of Congress passed, and President Bill Clinton signed, the Apology Resolution, Public Law 103-150. It is about the overthrow of the Kingdom of Hawaii a hundred years earlier. On January 17, 1893, a group of mostly American businessmen had overthrown Queen Liliʻuokalani. John L. Stevens, the top American diplomat in Hawaii, had landed 162 American sailors and Marines to back them. The resolution states that Stevens "conspired," or plotted in secret, with "a small group of non-Hawaiian residents of the Kingdom of Hawaii, including citizens of the United States." It names the men who took power as a Committee of Safety that "represented the American and European sugar planters, descendents of missionaries, and financiers."

The resolution states that the overthrow was illegal. In it, members of Congress apologized to Native Hawaiians "on behalf of the people of the United States" for the overthrow, carried out "with the participation of agents and citizens of the United States." It also states that the Native Hawaiian people never directly gave up their claims to sovereignty, the right to govern themselves. Its last section states that it does not settle any claims against the United States.

### 2000 to Today

Since 2001 American leaders have sent troops to wars in Afghanistan, Iraq and, in 2026, Iran. They have argued over trade and over the Paris agreement on climate. More than 3.6 million people live in the five American territories with people on them. They still live under the Insular Cases, and none of them can vote for president while living at home.

#### September 11, 2001, and the wars after it

On September 11, 2001, 19 hijackers attacked the United States and killed 2,977 people. The count does not include the 19 hijackers. The next day, representatives of NATO's member countries called on Article 5 of their treaty for the first and only time. Article 5 is the promise that an attack on one member is an attack on all of them.

American forces went into Afghanistan on October 7, 2001. The last American troops left on August 30, 2021. On March 20, 2003, American forces invaded Iraq. American leaders said Iraq had weapons of mass destruction, meaning nuclear, chemical or biological weapons. None were found.

Researchers count the dead of these wars in different ways, and their counts are far apart. Researchers on the Costs of War project at Brown University count more than 940,000 people killed directly by war violence in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Yemen and Pakistan from 2001 to 2023. More than 432,000 of them were civilians. The same researchers estimate that another 3.6 to 3.8 million people died from hunger, destroyed hospitals and disease caused by the wars. That makes at least 4.5 to 4.7 million deaths in all.

For Iraq, counts built from deaths recorded one by one come out much lower than estimates built from surveys of households. Workers at Iraq Body Count, a group that records deaths one at a time, had counted more than 187,000 civilians killed from 2003 to 2024. A survey published in the medical journal *The Lancet* in 2006 estimated about 600,000 violent deaths in Iraq in just the first three years of the war. American and Iraqi officials disputed it at the time. A survey by the World Health Organization and Iraq's health ministry estimated about 151,000 violent deaths over the same three years.

On January 11, 2002, American officials began holding prisoners at the navy base at Guantánamo Bay, in Cuba. Most of them were never tried in court. According to the journalist Andy Worthington, who tracks the prison, 779 men had been held there by January 2025, and 15 were still held.

#### Trade and the climate agreement

On November 10, 2001, members of the World Trade Organization approved China's entry into the organization. The WTO is a body of countries that sets rules for trade between them. China joined at the end of that year. On July 1, 2020, according to the Office of the United States Trade Representative, a new agreement among the United States, Mexico and Canada took effect. It replaced the North American Free Trade Agreement, called NAFTA.

American presidents have joined and left the Paris climate agreement twice. In that agreement, countries promise to cut the gases that are warming the earth. American presidents took the country out of it in November 2020 and brought it back in February 2021. On January 20, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an order to leave again. Researchers at the Congressional Research Service, which studies issues for Congress, report that the United States was out of the agreement as of January 27, 2026.

#### Strikes at sea, Venezuela and Iran, 2025 and 2026

Starting on September 2, 2025, American forces struck boats in the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean. Officials in President Trump's government said the boats were carrying drugs. By September 19, 2026, the strikes had killed at least 231 people in 69 strikes, the Associated Press reported. In at least one strike, military officers gave no evidence that the boat was carrying drugs. Lawyers for the ACLU, a group that defends civil rights in court, are suing for the families of two men from Trinidad, Chad Joseph and Rishi Samaroo. American forces killed the two in a strike on October 14, 2025. The ACLU's lawyers say the men were fishermen and farm workers.

On January 3, 2026, American special operations troops captured Venezuela's president, Nicolás Maduro, and his wife and took them out of Caracas, Venezuela's capital. American officials had charged them with crimes involving drugs. According to the Brookings Institution, a research group, the raid went ahead without approval from Congress beforehand.

On February 28, 2026, a war with Iran began with American and Israeli bombing. Workers at the Human Rights Activists News Agency, a rights group that tracks Iran, counted 3,636 people killed in Iran by April 7, 2026, and 1,701 of them were civilians. The Pentagon is the headquarters of the American military. Its public count showed 19 American service members dead on September 22, 2026, and more than 820 wounded. That same day, five American officials told the *Washington Post* that at least 22 service members had died in the Middle East since the war began. A sixth official said 23. Not all of those deaths came from the fighting.

#### The territories today

In 2020 more than 3.6 million people lived in the five American territories with people on them. The census is the government's count of everyone who lives in the country and its territories. In the 2020 census, Census Bureau workers counted 3,285,874 people in Puerto Rico, 11.8 percent fewer than in 2010. They counted 153,836 in Guam, about 87,146 in the U.S. Virgin Islands, 49,710 in American Samoa and 47,329 in the Northern Mariana Islands. Every one of the five lost people between 2010 and 2020.

People born in Puerto Rico, Guam, the U.S. Virgin Islands and the Northern Mariana Islands are American citizens. People born in American Samoa are American nationals. Their passports say so, and to vote they must go through naturalization, the process a person from another country uses to become a citizen. No one living in a territory can vote for president. Voters in each territory elect one delegate to the House of Representatives. The delegate can speak and work on committees but cannot vote on whether a bill passes. Puerto Rico's delegate is called the Resident Commissioner.

By 2016 Puerto Rico's government owed more than $72 billion. It also owed more than $55 billion in pensions, the money it had promised to pay its workers after they retired. Puerto Rico's leaders had no legal way to change the terms of the debt. On June 30, 2016, members of Congress passed a law called PROMESA. Under it, a board of seven members, appointed in Washington, has power over Puerto Rico's budget. Puerto Ricans call it *la junta*. The people whose budget the board controls did not elect its members. By the board's own account, its members have changed the terms of about 80 percent of the debt, cutting it from more than $70 billion to about $37 billion.

On August 5, 2025, President Trump fired several members of the board. CBS News named five of them. Under PROMESA a president may remove a member "only for cause," which means for a real reason such as wrongdoing. Three of the fired members, Arthur J. González, Andrew G. Biggs and Betty A. Rosa, went to court. On October 3, 2025, Judge María Antongiorgi-Jordán of the federal court in Puerto Rico put them back on the board. In 2026 she made that order permanent and called the firings "plainly contrary to law," according to the Democracy Defenders Fund, a group that campaigns on political causes.

Puerto Ricans have voted on their island's status several times, and Congress has not acted on any of the results. In 2020 statehood won 52.52 percent. On November 5, 2024, statehood won 58.61 percent, free association 29.57 percent and independence 11.82 percent, according to the island's certified results. Free association means a separate country tied to the United States by a formal agreement, as the Marshall Islands are. Some voters stayed away from these votes in protest. Members of Congress do not have to follow the results, and only Congress can change Puerto Rico's status.

Washington, D.C. had about 690,000 people in the 2020 census, more than the state of Wyoming, which had 576,851, or Vermont. It has one delegate in the House who cannot vote on bills, and no senators. On April 22, 2021, members of the House of Representatives voted 216 to 208 to make it a state. Senators did not take up the bill.

<a id="story-john-fitisemanu-america-world"></a>

#### John Fitisemanu

> **Who:** A man born in American Samoa who lives in Utah. He is an American national, not an American citizen.
>
> **When and where:** Utah. His case was decided by a federal appeals court in 2021.

John Fitisemanu lives in Utah. Because he was born in American Samoa, he is an American national, not a citizen, and a national must become a citizen before he can vote. He sued the United States to be recognized as a citizen by birth. A federal judge in Utah agreed with him. In 2021 judges of a higher federal court, the Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit, overturned that decision. They held that the Insular Cases were still the law. On October 17, 2022, the justices of the Supreme Court refused to take his case.

American Samoa's own elected leaders opposed his lawsuit. They argued that citizenship ordered by a court could put *faʻa Sāmoa* at legal risk. *Faʻa Sāmoa* is the Samoan way of life, which includes land held in common by families and the matai system of chiefs. Fitisemanu wants to be a citizen. The leaders of his home territory did not want citizenship granted to Samoans that way.

<a id="story-jose-luis-vaello-madero-america-world"></a>

#### José Luis Vaello Madero

> **Who:** A man the United States government sued for $28,081 after he moved to Puerto Rico.
>
> **When and where:** New York, then Puerto Rico. His case was decided by the Supreme Court on April 21, 2022.

José Luis Vaello Madero moved from New York to Puerto Rico, and lawyers for the United States government sued him to get back $28,081 in benefits. While he lived in New York, he lawfully received Supplemental Security Income, a federal payment for people with very low incomes who are elderly, blind or disabled. Members of Congress have not made that benefit available to people living in Puerto Rico. After he moved, the payments kept coming, and he did not know he was no longer allowed to get them.

His case went to the Supreme Court. On April 21, 2022, the justices ruled 8 to 1 that the Constitution does not require Congress to pay that benefit to people in Puerto Rico. Justice Neil Gorsuch agreed with the result. He also wrote a separate statement of his own in this case, and in it he called for the Insular Cases to be overturned.

<a id="part-6"></a>

# Part 6: Freedom and Fairness

<a id="ch-slavery-freedom"></a>

## Chapter 24: Slavery and Freedom

### Before 1500

Before 1500, some Native nations in North America took captives in war. In most of those nations, a captive could become a member of a family. A captive's children did not automatically become captives too. On the Northwest Coast, the Tlingit, the Haida and their neighbors held people as slaves. They bought and sold them, and the children of slaves were slaves too.

Holding a person as property for life, and passing that status on to the person's children, is called chattel slavery. Chattel is an old word for property. Later, Europeans wrote chattel slavery into the laws of the colonies they set up here.

#### Captives and slaves

Warriors in some Native nations took captives in raids on their enemies. Among the Haudenosaunee, the nations also called the Iroquois, a family that had lost someone in war could adopt a captive to take the dead person's place. This practice is called the mourning war. Of all these customs of captive-taking, it is the one the records describe most fully. In most of these nations, a captive could stop being a captive. The captive's children did not automatically become captives.

The Northwest Coast was different. There, among the Tlingit, the Haida and the nations near them, slaves were property. Their owners traded them, and a slave's children were born slaves. Leland Donald studied this system in a 1997 book and found that it was slavery in the full sense of the word.

### The 1500s

The first people enslaved by Europeans in what is now the United States were Native people. From the early 1500s, Spanish raiders took Native people captive on the coasts of Florida and the Carolinas. In 1526 a Spanish colonist brought about 100 enslaved Africans to a colony on the Atlantic coast. That October they rebelled and escaped, in the first known revolt of enslaved Africans in what became the United States.

#### Spanish slavery and the first revolt

In their colonies, the Spanish ran a system called the encomienda. Under it, Spanish colonists forced Native people to work for them and to hand over goods. On November 20, 1542, King Charles I of Spain issued the New Laws. They said that no one could enslave Native people, and that an encomienda ended when its holder died. Spanish colonists opposed the New Laws and kept forcing Native people to work.

In 1526 Lucas Vázquez de Ayllón founded a colony called San Miguel de Gualdape on the coast of what is now Georgia or South Carolina. Nobody knows the exact spot. Between 600 and 700 colonists came with him, and about 100 of them were enslaved Africans. Ayllón died, and the colonists fought among themselves. In October 1526 the enslaved Africans rose up and escaped. Where they went is not certain. The accounts say they most likely found shelter with Native people nearby, probably the Guale. Within months the surviving colonists gave up the colony.

On September 8, 1565, Pedro Menéndez de Avilés and about 800 Spanish colonists founded St. Augustine, in Florida. They moved into the Timucua town of a chief named Seloy and made his council house their first fort. Africans were among St. Augustine's first residents, some free and some enslaved. They worked as craftsmen, farmers and house servants. Spanish slave law, set down in an old code called the *Siete Partidas*, listed rights for enslaved people that English colonial law later left out. Under it, owners were not to split up families. Enslaved people could join the Catholic Church and marry in it, and the code listed ways for them to become free.

<a id="story-estevanico-slavery-freedom"></a>

#### Estevanico

> **Who:** An enslaved man from North Africa who survived a Spanish shipwreck, crossed the south of the continent on foot, and was killed while guiding a Spanish expedition.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Azemmour, Morocco. Shipwrecked on the Texas coast in 1528. Reached Mexico in 1536. Killed at the Zuni town of Hawikuh in 1539.

Estevanico was an enslaved man who guided Spanish expeditions through North America. He was born in about 1500 in Azemmour, in Morocco. In 1522 a Spanish nobleman named Andrés Dorantes de Carranza bought him as a slave.

In 1528 Dorantes and Estevanico were part of a Spanish expedition that was wrecked on the coast of Texas. Native people on that coast held the survivors, Estevanico among them, as slaves for several years. In 1534 four of the survivors escaped: Estevanico, Dorantes, Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca and Alonso del Castillo Maldonado. They walked west, working as healers along the way, and reached Mexico City in July 1536.

After that, the Spanish official who ruled Mexico, Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza, got Estevanico from Dorantes. He either bought him or received him as a gift. Some evidence suggests Mendoza freed him. On March 7, 1539, Estevanico set out as the guide for Marcos de Niza, who was heading north. Marcos was a friar, a member of a Catholic religious order. Estevanico went ahead of the friar with Native men from Sonora. The people of Hawikuh, a Zuni town, killed him there in 1539. Several accounts of his death survive, and they do not agree about why the people of Hawikuh killed him. The Spanish commander Coronado wrote in 1540 that they killed him because he had "killed and assaulted their women." Another Spaniard, Pedro de Castañeda, wrote that they killed him for demanding turquoise and women. Hernando de Alarcón reported that they killed him after he boasted that armed men were coming behind him. Zuni tradition does not agree with the Spanish accounts.

### The 1600s

In the 1600s, English colonists built slavery into their laws step by step, through court cases and new laws. When about twenty Africans reached Virginia in 1619, Virginia's law had no category for a person held as property for life. Between 1640 and 1705, judges and elected lawmakers in Virginia, Massachusetts and Carolina created that category. In 1662 Virginia's lawmakers ruled that a child born to an enslaved mother was enslaved for life, whoever the father was.

Over the whole Atlantic slave trade, ship crews loaded about 12.5 million captive Africans onto ships bound for the Americas. About 1.8 million of them died on the way.

#### Point Comfort, 1619

In late August 1619, an English ship called the *White Lion* landed at Point Comfort, in Virginia. It carried "20. and odd Negroes," in the words of the colonist John Rolfe. Negro was the word English writers of the time used for Black Africans. The *White Lion* was a privateer, a privately owned armed ship that attacked the ships of enemy countries. Its crew had taken these Africans from a Portuguese slave ship. They came from the Ndongo and Kongo region of West Central Africa. Sources give different days for the landing. The National Park Service says late August. Some writers give August 20, and the Hampton historian Beth Austin argues for about August 25.

Point Comfort was Native land. It belonged to the Kecoughtan, one of the Powhatan nations. They lived where the city of Hampton stands today. Their language belonged to the Algonquian family, a large group of related Native languages. English colonists built a fort beside their main village in 1609. On July 9, 1610, soon after Lord De La Warr arrived, the colonists seized the village. They drew the people out with a man playing a tambourine and then attacked them. The records do not say how many Kecoughtan they killed. The survivors fled to other towns of the Powhatan nations.

In 1619 Virginia's law did not yet have a category for slaves. Accounts still differ about whether the colonists held the Africans of 1619 as servants for a set number of years or as slaves for life. The records that survive do not settle it.

#### The Middle Passage

Ship crews took captive Africans across the Atlantic Ocean to the Americas. That crossing is called the Middle Passage. Over the whole history of the trade, ship crews loaded about 12.5 million Africans onto slave ships. About 10.7 million lived through the crossing. About 1.8 million died at sea. These figures come from the SlaveVoyages database of slave-ship voyages.

The average voyage took just over two months. The trip from Upper Guinea, in West Africa, took about three weeks. Crews chained the captives below the deck, in spaces too low for a person to stand up. They held the women apart from the men and kept the men in chains for long periods so they could not revolt. Crew members often raped the women and children. Rape means forcing a person into sex. About one captive in four was a child.

People died of disease and of thirst, and some killed themselves. The crew threw the bodies of the dead into the sea. Historians at the College of Charleston report that 13 to 19 percent of the people on board died during a crossing.

Ship crews landed most of the captives who survived in the Caribbean and in Brazil. Fewer than 4 percent came to mainland North America. Crews brought about 305,000 people there straight from Africa. Counting those who came by way of the Caribbean, the total is close to 388,000.

#### One survivor's account

Slave traders carried Olaudah Equiano across the ocean on a slave ship when he was a child. In 1789 he published a book in London about his life, *The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano*. In it he described the crossing.

The crew put Equiano below deck, and he was too sick to eat. Two white crewmen tied him across the windlass, the winch that pulled up the anchor chain, and flogged him for refusing food. Flogging means that a person is tied down and struck over and over on the bare body with a whip. Each stroke cuts the skin, and deep or repeated flogging leaves raised scars for life. Equiano wrote that captives were "hourly whipped for not eating."

He wrote that the hold was "so crowded that each had scarcely room to turn himself." The heat and the foul air made people sick, "of which many died." Children fell into the tubs the captives used as toilets and nearly smothered. One day two men who were chained together broke through the netting around the deck and jumped into the sea. A third man followed them. The crew lowered a boat. The two chained men drowned. The crew pulled the third man out "and afterwards flogged him unmercifully."

The ship landed at Barbados, an island in the Caribbean. From there, traders sold him on to Virginia. In 2005 the historian Vincent Carretta reported two records that give Equiano's birthplace as Carolina: a 1759 baptism record in London and a 1773 Royal Navy crew list. Equiano's own book says he was born in Africa. The two cannot both be right, and the question is still open.

<a id="story-john-punch"></a>

#### John Punch

> **Who:** The first African known to have been sentenced by a Virginia court to serve for life.
>
> **When and where:** Virginia. Sentenced on July 9, 1640.

On July 9, 1640, the judges of the General Court of Virginia sentenced John Punch to serve his master for the rest of his life. The same judges gave the two white men who had run away with him four more years. Punch was the only African among the three.

The three men were servants of a man named Hugh Gwyn. The court record calls them "Victor, a dutchman, the other a Scotchman called James Gregory, the third being a negro named John Punch." They ran away together toward Maryland and were caught.

The judges ordered that "the said three servants shall receive the punishment of whipping and to have thirty stripes apiece." A stripe is one stroke of the whip. Victor and James Gregory then had to finish their time with their master, serve him one more year, and serve the colony for three years after that.

The judges ordered that John Punch "shall serve his said master or his assigns for the time of his natural Life here or elsewhere." His assigns meant anyone the master sold or handed him to. It is the first known sentence of lifetime slavery in Virginia.

#### From servant to slave for life, 1640 to 1705

In the early years of Virginia, many workers were indentured servants. An indentured servant was bound by a contract to work for a master for a set number of years and then went free. Between 1640 and 1705, judges and lawmakers made a different rule for Africans. They could be held for life.

In 1654 Anthony Johnson went to court in Northampton County, Virginia. Johnson was an African who had arrived in about 1621, gained his freedom and become a landowner on the Eastern Shore. He sued his white neighbor Robert Parker over a Black man named John Casor. Casor said the time on his contract had run out and he was free. In 1655 the county judges ruled that Casor was Johnson's servant for life. That made Casor Johnson's slave. It was the first court ruling in the English mainland colonies that a person who had committed no crime could be held for life.

Lawmakers in New England wrote slavery into law too. The lawmakers of the Massachusetts Bay colony were called the General Court. On December 10, 1641, they adopted a code of laws named the Body of Liberties. In it they wrote that slavery was allowed for "lawful captives taken in just wars, and such strangers as willingly sell themselves or are sold to us." That meant people captured in a war the colonists called fair could be held as slaves. So could outsiders who sold themselves or were sold to the colonists. The Massachusetts Bay lawmakers were the first in any English colony on the mainland to put slavery into a written law.

In 1662 the members of Virginia's House of Burgesses, the colony's elected assembly, passed a law about children. Under the old rule in English law, a child's place in the law, free or bound, came from the father. Virginia's lawmakers broke with that on purpose. They ruled that a child's place followed the mother's. A child born to an enslaved mother was enslaved for life, whoever the father was. Lawyers called the rule by a Latin phrase, *partus sequitur ventrem*, which means "the child follows the womb."

Some colonists were unsure whether baptism, the ceremony that made a person a Christian, set an enslaved person free. In September 1667, Virginia's lawmakers, who met as the General Assembly, passed a law that said the opposite. It stated that "the conferring of baptisme doth not alter the condition of the person as to his bondage or ffreedome." In other words, being baptized as a Christian did not set an enslaved person free. The lawmakers gave their reason in the law. With that doubt gone, they wrote, masters would be more willing to let enslaved people be baptized.

#### The slave codes

A slave code is a set of laws about enslaved people: what they could not do, how they could be punished, and what their owners could do to them. In 1705 the same lawmakers gathered the colony's earlier slave laws into one code. Under it, enslaved people counted as real estate, the same kind of property as land. The code said that baptism did not free anyone. A master who killed an enslaved person while "correcting" him, which meant punishing him, faced no penalty.

Carolina's lawmakers, who met as the colony's assembly, passed their first slave law in 1690. The Lords Proprietors, the English noblemen who owned the colony, struck that law down. The assembly's members passed a new code in 1696. They based both laws on the slave code that lawmakers in Barbados, an English island in the Caribbean, had written in 1661.

The 1690 Carolina law already allowed branding, nose-slitting and castration as punishments. Branding meant pressing a metal iron, heated red-hot, into the person's skin. The iron burned a mark, often a letter, that stayed on the body as a scar for life. Nose-slitting meant cutting the person's nose open. Under the Barbados code, an enslaved person who hit a Christian a second time was to be whipped hard, have the nose slit and be burned on the face with a hot iron. Castration meant cutting off a man's testicles, which left him unable to father children.

The slave codes of the 1600s set rules for enslaved people's bodies and for who could be held for life. They said nothing about reading or writing. South Carolina's lawmakers passed the first law against teaching enslaved people to write in 1740.

### 1700 to 1750

Between 1700 and 1750, colonial lawmakers wrote slave codes that ordered whipping, branding and cutting off ears as punishments. Enslaved people rose up in both the South and the North. South Carolina planters grew rice to sell overseas, a crop that enslaved West Africans already knew how to grow. In 1739 about 20 enslaved men near Charleston took up arms and marched toward Spanish Florida. The king of Spain had promised freedom to people who escaped there from the English colonies.

The English colonists enslaved Native people as well as Africans. In New York City in 1712, about one person in five was enslaved.

#### Carolina's trade in Native captives

English traders in Carolina ran a large business in enslaved Native people. Between 1670 and 1715, they enslaved between 24,000 and 51,000 Native people of the Southeast. That range comes from the historian Alan Gallay. The traders shipped many of the captives to the Caribbean. In those years, traders shipped more enslaved Native people out of Charleston than slave ships brought enslaved Africans in.

#### The ships from Rhode Island

Merchants in the northern colonies sent out slave ships too. Rhode Island merchants paid for about 1,000 slaving voyages, and about half of all the slave ships that left mainland North America sailed from Rhode Island ports. The historian Jay Coughtry counted 934 of these voyages, which carried about 106,000 Africans. In the 1700s, Rhode Island merchants controlled between 60 and 90 percent of the American trade in African captives.

The DeWolf family of Bristol, Rhode Island, sent out about twice as many slaving voyages as the families closest behind them. Bringing captives into the United States from abroad became illegal in 1808. George DeWolf kept sending out slave ships anyway, against the law, until 1825.

#### New York, 1711 and 1712

In 1700 New York City had about 5,000 people, and at least 750 of them were enslaved. On November 30, 1711, the city's aldermen, the men who governed the city, set up a market at the foot of Wall Street. There, enslaved people were sold, rented out and inspected by buyers. The market stood from 1711 to 1762. The accounts of the market do not name the men who bought and sold people there.

On April 6, 1712, more than 20 enslaved people in New York City set fire to a building on Maiden Lane. Accounts describe most of them as Coromantee, Akan people from the Gold Coast of West Africa, which is Ghana today. When white people came to fight the fire, the rebels attacked them. They killed 8 or 9 white people and wounded 6 or 7. Six of the rebels killed themselves before they could be captured.

Governor Robert Hunter called out the militia, the colony's armed citizens. Officials arrested more than 70 Black people. They put 27 on trial, found 21 guilty and put all 21 to death. One account says 20 were burned alive and one was broken on the wheel. Breaking on the wheel was a public execution. The person was tied to a large wheel, and the executioner broke the person's arms and legs with an iron bar and left the person to die. Other accounts say only that the punishments ran from burning alive to breaking on the wheel. Afterward, the members of the colony's assembly made it illegal for enslaved people to gather in groups of more than three or to own guns.

#### Rice and the Lowcountry

The Lowcountry is the coast of South Carolina around Charleston. Rice planters there relied on the skill and the labor of West Africans from rice-growing parts of Africa. Planters paid more for captives from those coasts. Rice shipped out of Carolina rose from about 268,602 pounds a year around 1700 to more than 30 million pounds a year around 1740. Charleston became the largest port on the mainland where slave ships landed their captives.

Ships arriving at Charleston stopped first at Sullivan's Island, in the harbor. The island had a quarantine station, called the pest house, where captives who might carry disease were held apart from everyone else. Many accounts say about 40 percent of all the enslaved Africans brought to mainland North America passed through the island itself. The Charleston historian Nic Butler and others say that figure is too high, because many ships landed elsewhere in the harbor. Their doubt is about the island's share only.

The rice plantations stand on Native land. When English colonists settled Charleston in 1670, about fifteen Native groups lived in the Lowcountry. Among them were the Stono, the Kiawah, the Etiwan, the Edisto and the Combahee. By the middle 1700s these groups were nearly gone. Many of their people had died of disease or been killed in wars, and English colonists had taken their land.

In June 1712, the members of South Carolina's assembly passed a law that listed punishments for people who ran away. The law applied to any enslaved person who stayed away for twenty days or more. For a first escape, it ordered a public whipping of up to forty lashes. A lash is one stroke of the whip. For a second escape, it ordered the person "branded with the letter R, on the right cheek." For a third, it ordered forty lashes and one ear cut off. A man caught a fourth time was to be castrated. A woman caught a fourth time was to be whipped, branded with an R on the left cheek, and have her left ear cut off. The 1712 law does not name the people who carried out these punishments.

For a fifth escape, the law let two justices of the peace and three landowners decide. A justice of the peace was a local judge. They could order the person killed. Or they could order the person's Achilles tendon, the cord just above the heel, cut through. After that the person could not run. From 1723 on, South Carolina's lawmakers dropped these lists from their codes and left punishment to the enslaver.

#### Fort Mose, 1738

Florida belonged to Spain. In 1693 the king of Spain promised freedom to enslaved people who escaped from the English colonies and reached Florida, if they became Catholics. Men also had to serve in the militia.

In 1738 Florida's governor, Manuel Montiano, set up a town for these free people about two miles north of St. Augustine. Its Spanish name was Gracia Real de Santa Teresa de Mose. People call it Fort Mose. It was the first free Black town in what is now the United States to be recognized by law. About 100 people lived there, in more than 20 households.

In 1740 British forces surrounded St. Augustine and attacked it. Fort Mose was destroyed in the fighting, which people remember as the battle of Bloody Mose. The people rebuilt it in 1752. In 1763, when the Spanish left Florida, the people of Mose left with them for Cuba. The site is now Fort Mose Historic State Park.

<a id="story-francisco-menendez"></a>

#### Francisco Menéndez

> **Who:** A man from West Africa who escaped slavery in Carolina and became captain of the free Black militia at Fort Mose.
>
> **When and where:** Born in the Gambia region of Africa. Enslaved in Carolina. Led the militia at Fort Mose, Florida, from 1738.

Francisco Menéndez commanded the free Black militia at Fort Mose, the town of people who had escaped slavery in the English colonies. He was a Mandinga man, born in the Gambia region of West Africa. Slave traders carried him to Carolina, where he was enslaved.

He escaped south to Spanish Florida. There he was baptized as a Catholic and took the name Francisco Menéndez. From 1738 he led the militia at Mose, the armed men who defended the town. Spanish colonial records document his life. Of all the people who lived at Mose, he is the one the records describe most fully.

#### The Stono Rebellion, 1739

On September 9, 1739, about 20 enslaved men rose up at the Stono River, south of Charleston. It was the largest uprising of enslaved people in the mainland colonies before the American Revolution. Their leader was a man named Jemmy. A report written in 1739 describes them as Angolan and says "one who was called Jemmy was their Captain." They seized weapons and marched south toward Spanish Florida. Others joined them along the way. The same report says they were "calling out Liberty" and marched "with Colours displayed, and two Drums beating." The rebels killed about 25 white colonists.

Lieutenant Governor William Bull met the rebels on the road that day. He rode off to warn the planters and raised the militia, which attacked the rebels the same day. Bull also hired Chickasaw and Catawba men, and some enslaved men, to hunt down those who got away. About a week later, the militia fought a group of rebels again, about 30 miles from the first fight.

The militia killed between 35 and 50 rebels in the first fight. A historical marker says at least 54. The 1739 report gives its own count: "about 40 Negroes and 20 whites were killed." The report says the militia "shot on the Spot" rebels they took in the field. Colonists cut off the heads of rebels and set them on stakes along the main roads as a warning to others. The colonists put most of the captured rebels to death. One account says the militia took 43 rebels who had no weapons and hanged them. The colonists sold the survivors to the West Indies, the islands of the Caribbean.

#### The Negro Act of 1740

On May 10, 1740, the members of South Carolina's assembly passed the Negro Act in answer to Stono. Under it, enslaved people could not gather in groups, grow their own food, earn money or move about freely. Teaching an enslaved person to write became a crime. That was the first law in what became the United States against teaching enslaved people. It named writing, not reading.

Under the Negro Act, a white person who murdered an enslaved person was guilty only of a misdemeanor, a minor crime punished by a fine. Any white person, not only an owner, could arrest and punish a Black person who broke the act. Under the act, a court could put an enslaved person to death for plotting a revolt, running away, setting fires, or teaching others about poisonous plants.

#### New York, 1741

In March 1741, a string of fires began in New York City with a fire at Fort George, the governor's home. City officials claimed that enslaved people and poor white people had plotted to burn the city. Three judges of the colony's Supreme Court heard the cases: James De Lancey, Daniel Horsmanden and Frederick Philipse. The trials began on May 11, 1741.

The main witness was Mary Burton, a young servant bound to a tavern owner named John Hughson. Judge Horsmanden offered her an end to her contract and a reward in money.

About 200 people were tried. The New York courts' historical society counts 30 people sentenced to death and 70 sentenced to be sold into slavery in the Caribbean. The historian Jill Lepore counts 34 put to death between May 11 and August 29, 1741. By her count, officials burned 13 Black men at the stake and hanged 17 Black men, two white men and two white women. John Hughson, his wife Sarah and their daughter Sarah were among the white people put to death. In 1744 Horsmanden published his record of the trials.

### 1750 to 1800

In 1776 the Declaration of Independence stated "that all men are created equal." In 1790 officials made the first census, a count of every person in the United States. They counted 697,681 people held in slavery. Some enslaved people went to court and used the words of the new state constitutions to win their freedom. Elizabeth Freeman won hers in a Massachusetts court in 1781. About 20,000 Black people joined or fled to the British during the war, after Virginia's royal governor promised freedom to enslaved men who fought for Britain. In 1796 Ona Judge escaped from President George Washington's household.

Between 1777 and 1804, lawmakers and judges in Vermont and six northern states began to end slavery. Most of their laws freed no one right away. They freed only children born after a set date, and only once those children grew up. The men who wrote the Constitution in 1787 protected slavery in three of its clauses without once using the word. A clause is one part of a written law or constitution.

<a id="story-phillis-wheatley-slavery-freedom"></a>

#### Phillis Wheatley

> **Who:** A girl kidnapped from West Africa who became the first African American to publish a book of poetry.
>
> **When and where:** Landed in Boston in 1761. Her book was published in London on September 1, 1773. Freed by November 1773. Died in 1784, at about age 31.

Phillis Wheatley was the first African American to publish a book of poetry. She was about seven years old when slave traders kidnapped her from West Africa. In 1761 she landed in Boston on a slave ship called the *Phillis*. When she arrived, John Wheatley, a Boston merchant, and his family bought her. Her first name came from the ship that carried her. Her last name came from the family who bought her.

Her book, *Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral*, was published in London on September 1, 1773. The Wheatleys freed her by November 1773, shortly after it appeared.

In 1778 she married John Peters. She died poor in 1784, at about 31 years old.

#### Two promises of freedom in the Revolution

On March 5, 1770, British soldiers fired on a crowd of colonists in King Street, in Boston. People call it the Boston Massacre. Crispus Attucks was the first person killed. He was a sailor with African and Wampanoag ancestors. Most accounts say he had escaped from slavery in Framingham, Massachusetts, around 1750. Accounts differ about whether he was legally free by 1770 or still an escaped slave.

On November 7, 1775, Virginia's royal governor, Lord Dunmore, made a promise to the men enslaved by Virginians who were fighting the British. Any of them who joined the British army would be free. About 300 men joined his Ethiopian Regiment within a month, and it grew to about 800. Over the whole war, by the estimates of the Gilder Lehrman Institute and the American Battlefield Trust, about 20,000 Black people joined or fled to the British. About 9,000 served the American side, the Patriots. About 5,000 of those fought as soldiers. Both sides promised freedom to some of the enslaved men who fought for them, and neither side kept those promises to all of them.

#### The first states to end slavery

In 1777 Vermont's constitution banned holding adults in slavery. Vermont then governed itself as its own country, and it joined the United States in 1791. It was the first constitution to ban slavery.

On March 1, 1780, Pennsylvania's lawmakers passed the Act for the Gradual Abolition of Slavery. To abolish something means to end it. Gradual means step by step, over many years. No elected lawmakers anywhere in the world had passed a law to end slavery before. No enslaved person went free on the day it passed. Children born after it were to go free when they turned 28.

In Massachusetts, juries and judges ended slavery in court cases decided between 1781 and 1783. Lawmakers in Connecticut and Rhode Island passed gradual laws, which ended slavery step by step, in 1784. New York's lawmakers passed one in 1799, and the last enslaved people in New York were freed in 1827. New Jersey's lawmakers passed theirs last, in 1804. Under these gradual laws, people in the North stayed enslaved for decades.

On July 13, 1787, the members of Congress passed the Northwest Ordinance, a law for the lands north of the Ohio River. It banned slavery there.

<a id="story-elizabeth-freeman"></a>

#### Elizabeth Freeman ("Mum Bett")

> **Who:** An enslaved woman who sued for her freedom under the new Massachusetts constitution and won.
>
> **When and where:** Sheffield and Great Barrington, Massachusetts. Jury verdict in August 1781. Died in 1829.

Elizabeth Freeman went to court in 1781 and won her freedom. Before that she was known as Bett, or Mum Bett. She was enslaved in the household of Colonel John Ashley in Sheffield, Massachusetts.

The new Massachusetts constitution of 1780 states that "all men are born free and equal." Bett and an enslaved man named Brom sued Ashley for their freedom. Their lawyer, Theodore Sedgwick, argued that those words in the constitution made slavery illegal.

In August 1781, a jury in Great Barrington set them free. The jury also ordered Ashley to pay them 30 shillings for the harm done to them. The case was called *Brom and Bett v. Ashley*, which means Brom and Bett against Ashley. The juries and judges in that case and in the court cases of an enslaved man named Quock Walker, decided from 1781 to 1783, ended slavery in Massachusetts.

Bett took the name Elizabeth Freeman. For the rest of her life she worked for pay as a housekeeper and a nurse. She died in 1829.

#### Sally Hemings and Thomas Jefferson

Thomas Jefferson was the main author of the Declaration of Independence. Over his lifetime he owned more than 600 enslaved people. One of them was Sally Hemings. Jefferson owned her and used her for sex from the time she was a girl, and she had his children.

Sally Hemings was born enslaved in 1773. Her mother, Elizabeth Hemings, was enslaved. Her father was most likely John Wayles, the man who owned her mother. By law Wayles owned Elizabeth Hemings, and she had no legal right to refuse him sex. Wayles was also the father of Jefferson's wife, Martha. That made Sally Hemings the half-sister of Jefferson's wife.

In 1787 Jefferson was the United States minister to France, the man who spoke for his country in Paris. That year Sally Hemings went to Paris with his daughter Polly. Sally was 14 and enslaved by Jefferson. He was 44. By law he owned her, and she could not refuse him. He had the legal power to sell her or her family. Her son Madison Hemings said in 1873 that in Paris she "became Mr. Jefferson's concubine." A concubine, in the old meaning of the word, was a woman a man kept for sex without marrying her. Madison Hemings said she was pregnant when they came back to Virginia. In 2026 Jessica Marie Johnson, a historian of slavery at Johns Hopkins University, wrote that Jefferson was a rapist.

Under French law she could have claimed her freedom in Paris. Madison Hemings said Jefferson promised that her children would be freed at age 21 if she went back with him. She had children from 1790 to 1808. Four lived to be adults: Beverly, Harriet, Madison and Eston.

In 1998 scientists compared DNA and found that a man of the Jefferson family was the father of Eston Hemings. In January 2000 the Thomas Jefferson Foundation, which runs Jefferson's home at Monticello, concluded that Jefferson "was probably the father" of her children. By 2018 the foundation's historians treated this as a fact. In September 2026 a study paid for by the Smithsonian tested DNA from a lock of Jefferson's hair, cut on the day he died. Descendants of Madison and Eston Hemings carried more of Jefferson's DNA than the scientists expected, and the scientists concluded that Jefferson fathered her children. Jefferson died in 1826. Neither he nor anyone after him ever legally freed Sally Hemings. His daughter Martha Jefferson Randolph let her live in Charlottesville with her sons. The census of 1833 listed her as free. She died in 1835.

#### The Constitution's protections for slavery, 1787

The men who wrote the Constitution in 1787 put three protections for slavery into it. None of the three clauses uses the word slave.

Under the three-fifths clause, each enslaved person counted as three-fifths of a person. The number of seats a state got in the House of Representatives depended on that count. Enslaved people could not vote, but their owners' states got extra seats for them. In 1793 the slave states held 47 of the 105 seats in the House. Counting only their free people, they would have had 33. The fugitive clause said that a person "held to Service or Labour" who escaped to another state had to be "delivered up," handed back to the person who claimed that person's work. The slave-trade clause barred Congress from ending the import of enslaved people before 1808.

#### Enslaved builders of the capital

Enslaved people worked at every stage of building the White House and the Capitol in Washington. The cornerstone of the White House was laid on October 13, 1792, and that of the Capitol on September 18, 1793. Enslaved men cut sandstone at the quarries on Aquia Creek, the open pits where the stone was dug. They also cut timber, made bricks, sawed lumber and did carpentry. The officials in charge of the building hired them from their owners, and the owners kept the pay.

The payroll of the President's House for May 1795 names five enslaved carpenters: Tom, Peter, Ben, Harry and Daniel. The architect James Hoban owned four of them, and his assistant Pierce Purcell owned one. The payroll records the days four of the men worked that month: Peter 28, Ben 28, Daniel 25 and Harry 9. Hoban signed for their wages.

<a id="story-ona-judge"></a>

#### Ona Judge

> **Who:** An enslaved woman who escaped from President George Washington's household and was never caught.
>
> **When and where:** Walked out of the President's House in Philadelphia on May 21, 1796. Lived free in New Hampshire. Died in 1848.

Ona Judge escaped from President George Washington and his wife, Martha, and lived the rest of her life free. She was enslaved as Martha Washington's personal servant.

On May 21, 1796, while the Washingtons were eating dinner in the President's House in Philadelphia, Ona Judge walked out. She boarded a sloop, a small sailing ship, called the *Nancy*, and sailed to Portsmouth, New Hampshire.

On May 24, 1796, a runaway advertisement ran in the *Philadelphia Gazette*. It offered ten dollars for her capture. George Washington tried for years to get her back. She refused an offer to return. She married and lived in New Hampshire until she died in 1848.

In the 1840s she told her own story to newspaper interviewers, including one from *The Granite Freeman* in 1845. She told them that she was poor and that she was free.

### 1800 to 1850

On January 1, 1808, it became illegal to bring enslaved people into the United States from abroad. The number of people held in slavery kept growing anyway, mostly through children born into it. Government officials regularly counted everyone in the country, in a count called the census. They counted 697,681 enslaved people in 1790 and 3,953,760 in 1860. Slave traders moved more than a million people from the older slave states of the Upper South, such as Virginia, to the new cotton states of the Deep South and sold them to planters there. Traders and buyers split families by selling husbands, wives and children to different owners.

Enslaved people resisted every day, and some rose up in armed revolt. Thousands escaped to the free states and to Canada. In most of the slave states, lawmakers made it a crime to teach an enslaved person to read.

#### Cotton

In 1793 Eli Whitney built a cotton gin, a machine that pulls the seeds out of cotton. With the gin, planters could make money growing upland cotton, the kind that grows away from the coast. Enslavers took enslaved people west to clear and plant new cotton lands. A bale is a big pressed bundle of cotton. Cotton growers in the United States produced fewer than 9,000 bales a year around 1790. By 1800 they produced more than 200,000 bales, and by 1860 about 4 million. The number of slave states grew from six in 1790 to fifteen in 1860. By 1860 enslaved people on Southern plantations grew about 75 percent of the world's cotton. Cotton made up more than half of everything Americans sold to other countries, measured in dollars.

By 1860 the people who held four million people in slavery valued them at $3 billion or more. That was more than all the money invested in the country's railroads and factories put together. Enslavers bought, sold and priced people as property. They also mortgaged them, which means they borrowed money and promised to hand the enslaved people over to the lender if they could not pay it back.

The cotton land of these years was Native land. On September 27, 1830, Choctaw leaders signed the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek, a written agreement with the United States. In it they signed away more than 10 million acres in Mississippi and Alabama. It was the first treaty signed after members of Congress passed the Indian Removal Act of 1830. The Chickasaw signed away their land in the Treaty of Pontotoc Creek in 1832. Under the Removal Act, United States officials then forced both nations west to Indian Territory, today's Oklahoma. They moved the Choctaw in groups in 1831, 1832 and 1833. By the Choctaw Nation's own count, more than a quarter of the Choctaw people removed in those years died. Enslavers then brought in enslaved people to clear and plant the land the Choctaw and Chickasaw had lost. Mississippi's cotton crop grew from about 20 million pounds in 1820 to 193.2 million pounds in 1839. The number of enslaved people in Mississippi grew from 65,659 in 1830 to 195,211 in 1840.

#### The slave trade inside the country

Between about 1790 and 1860, slave traders moved more than one million people from the Upper South to the cotton lands of the Deep South. From 1820 on, they moved about 200,000 people every ten years. They marched people overland in coffles, lines of people chained together. They also shipped people along the coast to New Orleans, which had the largest slave market in the country.

The biggest trading firm belonged to Isaac Franklin and John Armfield. From 1828 to 1836 they ran it from 1315 Duke Street in Alexandria, Virginia. Their compound took up half a city block, with separate pens for men and for women. At their busiest they moved between 1,000 and 1,500 people a year, and about 8,500 in the nine years of the partnership. They marched people to Natchez, in Mississippi, and shipped others to New Orleans on their own ships. Franklin and Armfield also sold enslaved women and teenage girls to men who bought them in order to rape them. Rape means forcing a person into sex. This was known as the "fancy" trade, and the traders charged much higher prices for these women and girls. The historian Joshua Rothman read the partners' own letters. He found that Franklin, Armfield and their partner Rice Ballard also raped some of these women themselves, and joked about it in their letters.

Traders and buyers broke families apart as a matter of routine. The Equal Justice Initiative, a group that studies racial injustice, has added up the effects. Its researchers found that traders separated nearly half of the people they moved from a husband, a wife or a parent. About one enslaved marriage in three ended because an owner sold the husband or the wife away. Traders sold children away from their mothers.

#### Work, food and home

Enslaved people worked from sunup to sundown, six days a week. On cotton and sugar plantations, an overseer, a man the owner paid to run the work, drove them in gangs, row by row across the fields. This was called the gang system. On the rice plantations of the Lowcountry, the coast around Charleston, South Carolina, the overseer gave each person a set task for the day. When it was done, the rest of the day was the person's own. This was called the task system.

Solomon Northup picked cotton in Louisiana in the 1840s. In his book *Twelve Years a Slave* (1853), he wrote: "An ordinary day's work is two hundred pounds." Every night each person's cotton was weighed at the gin-house, the building where the cotton gin stood. When a person's cotton came up short, the owner or the overseer whipped that person. On the plantation where Northup was held, the owner, Edwin Epps, did the whipping himself in the yard. A lash is one stroke of the whip. Northup wrote that "Twenty-five are deemed a mere brush," fifty lashes were "the ordinary penalty," and "one hundred is called severe."

Frederick Douglass lived as an enslaved child on a plantation in Maryland. In his *Narrative* (1845), he recorded the food allowance there for one month: eight pounds of pork, or the same amount of fish, and one bushel of cornmeal. A bushel is a measure about the size of a big basket. The enslaver gave out clothing once a year, and it was so thin that small children too young for field work often had only a long shirt to wear. Enslaved people added to their food with gardens, fishing and trapping where their owners allowed it.

Formerly enslaved people interviewed in the 1930s remembered cabins of one room, with dirt floors and beds made of boards. Under the law, their marriages did not count. An owner could sell a husband, a wife or a child on any day.

#### Punishment

Owners and overseers flogged enslaved people for picking too little cotton, for arriving late and for running away. A flogging meant being tied and struck again and again on the bare body with a whip. The whip named most often in Southern sources is the cowskin, also called the cowhide. It was a whip made of dried, twisted cow's hide. Each stroke cut the skin. Deep or repeated whipping left raised scars for life.

Frederick Douglass described a flogging he saw as a child. His enslaver, Aaron Anthony, stripped Douglass's Aunt Hester from her neck to her waist. He tied her crossed hands to a hook in a ceiling beam, so that she stood on her toes. Then he whipped her with "the heavy cowskin" until her blood dripped to the floor.

In 1839 Theodore Weld published *American Slavery As It Is*, a collection of reports from eyewitnesses and of advertisements from Southern newspapers. Weld was an abolitionist, one of the people working to end slavery. One witness saw an overseer whip a man named Joe "with a heavy cow-hide full six feet long" for arriving five minutes late.

The advertisements were written by the enslavers themselves. On July 18, 1838, Micajah Ricks of Nash County, North Carolina, placed one in the Raleigh *Standard*. It began: "Ranaway, a negro woman and two children." Negro was an old word for a Black person. The ad went on: "a few days before she went off, I burnt her with a hot iron, on the left side of her face, I tried to make the letter M." The advertisement does not give the woman's name. In another advertisement that Weld printed, Robert Nicoll of Mobile, Alabama, offered ten dollars for "my woman Siby, very much scarred about the neck and ears by whipping."

#### Sexual violence

By law, an enslaved woman or girl had no right to refuse the man who owned her, and no right to defend herself from him. Harriet Jacobs later wrote a book about what one of those men tried to do to her.

Jacobs was born enslaved in Edenton, North Carolina, in 1813. In 1825 she was left in a will to a three-year-old girl, Mary Matilda Norcom. That put her under the control of the girl's father, Dr. James Norcom. From her early teens, Norcom tried again and again to rape her. He held her as property, and for years she could not get away from him. To protect herself she began a relationship with a white lawyer, Samuel Tredwell Sawyer, and had two children with him, Joseph and Louisa.

In 1835 she ran away. She hid in a crawl space above a storeroom in her grandmother's house for seven years. The space was so small she could barely sit up. In 1842 she escaped north by boat. Ten years later the wife of her employer, Cornelia Grinnell Willis, bought her freedom. Jacobs told her story in *Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl*, dated 1861 and published under the name "Linda Brent." Historian Jean Fagan Yellin later proved from Jacobs's letters that she wrote it herself. She died in Washington, D.C., in 1897.

#### Churches and hush harbors

Richard Allen was born enslaved. In Philadelphia, he founded the African Methodist Episcopal Church, known as the AME Church. It was formally organized in 1816, and it was the first Black church denomination in the country. A denomination is a group of churches that share the same beliefs and leaders.

In the slave states, enslaved people also worshipped out of their owners' sight. They met in brush arbors, shelters built of branches, which they called "hush harbors." They sang spirituals, religious songs that expressed their faith and also had hidden messages in them.

#### Reading made a crime

South Carolina's lawmakers had banned teaching enslaved people to write in 1740, and Georgia's followed in 1755. After 1829 lawmakers in more slave states passed such laws or made them harsher. Georgia's lawmakers passed a new law in December 1829. Lawmakers in Louisiana and North Carolina followed in 1830, in Virginia in 1831 and in Alabama in 1832. South Carolina's lawmakers made their law harsher in 1834. Most of the slave states had such a law, but not all of them.

The punishments depended on who broke the law. A white person who taught was fined. In North Carolina the fine was $200. The laws of Georgia and other states added jail. For Black teachers and learners, the laws ordered whipping. North Carolina's law set the punishment at 39 lashes, and in Virginia a person caught at a school could get up to 20 lashes. Several of these laws covered free Black people as well as the enslaved.

Enslavers had several fears. With writing, an enslaved person could forge, or fake, a pass, a note from an owner that allowed an enslaved person to travel. Readers could get the newspapers of the abolitionists, and they could read the Bible without an owner choosing which parts they heard. After Nat Turner's revolt in 1831, enslavers feared organized revolt most of all.

Enslaved people learned to read anyway. Estimates reported by Encyclopedia Virginia and History.com say about 5 to 10 percent of enslaved people could read by 1860. Some estimates for the last years of slavery run as high as 20 percent.

<a id="story-frederick-douglass-slavery-freedom"></a>

#### Frederick Douglass

> **Who:** A man born enslaved in Maryland who taught himself to read against the orders of the man who held him, escaped, and became the most photographed and most heard abolitionist of his century.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Talbot County, Maryland, in February 1818. Escaped on September 3, 1838. Died in 1895.
>
> **Movie:** *Becoming Frederick Douglass* (2022), a documentary by Stanley Nelson, shown on PBS. It is about Douglass's life.

Frederick Douglass learned to read while he was enslaved, after Hugh Auld, the man who held him in Baltimore, forbade anyone to teach him. He was born in Talbot County, Maryland, in February 1818. No record gives the exact day. He chose February 14 as his birthday.

As a boy he lived in Baltimore, in the household of Hugh and Sophia Auld. Sophia Auld began to teach him the alphabet. Hugh Auld stopped her. Douglass wrote in his *Narrative* (1845) that hearing Auld forbid it was "the first decidedly antislavery lecture" he ever heard.

He kept learning in secret. He traded bread with hungry white boys for reading lessons. At about age twelve he bought a book of speeches called *The Columbian Orator*.

On September 3, 1838, Douglass escaped. He rode a train north through Baltimore, dressed in a sailor's clothes and carrying a sailor's papers that he had borrowed. Anna Murray, a free Black woman, helped him, and he married her.

In 1845 he published *Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass*. In 1847 he started a newspaper, the *North Star*. For the rest of the century he spoke and wrote against slavery, and more people heard him speak than any other abolitionist. He was also photographed more than any other abolitionist. He died in 1895.

<a id="story-milla-granson"></a>

#### Milla Granson (Lilly Ann Granderson)

> **Who:** An enslaved woman who ran a secret night school in Natchez, Mississippi, and by her own count taught hundreds of people to read and write.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Petersburg, Virginia, about 1816. Enslaved in Kentucky, then near Natchez, Mississippi. Died in 1889.

Milla Granson ran a school at night in Natchez, Mississippi, while she was enslaved. Her pupils were enslaved people who came after a full day's work. In March 1864, she told her story to Laura Haviland, a teacher who belonged to the Quakers, a Christian group. Haviland printed it in a book in 1881. It is the only record of the school.

Granson was born in Petersburg, Virginia, in about 1816. She was enslaved in Kentucky, where the children of her enslaver taught her to read and write. When that enslaver died, she was sold south to an owner near Natchez and put to work in the fields. She could not keep up with the field hands, and the overseer whipped her. She told Haviland: "sometimes I thought I would die from such cruel whippings upon my bared body." The record does not give the overseer's name.

The school opened "at eleven or twelve o'clock at night, and closed at two o'clock A. M." Every door and window was shut so no one would find out. Her pupils came into a back alley, "each with a bundle of pitch-pine splinters for lights." She taught twelve at a time. When those twelve could read and write, she sent them off and took twelve more, "until she had graduated hundreds." Some of her pupils wrote their own passes and set out for Canada. She never heard from them again, and she believed they got away.

After slavery ended, she pushed for the founding of Natchez Seminary, the school that became Jackson State University. She married Oliver Granderson. She died in 1889 and is buried in the Natchez City Cemetery.

#### Resistance and revolt

Enslaved people resisted slavery in small ways every day. They worked slowly, broke tools, pretended to be sick and took food. Most of all, they ran away. Southern newspapers were full of advertisements for runaways, placed by enslavers who wanted them back. Some of the ads warn that the person "can read," or "can write and may forge a pass." Researchers at Cornell University, in a project called Freedom on the Move, are putting thousands of these ads online.

In 1800 an enslaved blacksmith named Gabriel planned to lead a march on Richmond, Virginia. On August 30, the day it was to begin, two enslaved men, Pharoah and Tom, who belonged to members of the Sheppard family, told Mosby Sheppard about the plan. Sheppard told Governor James Monroe. A storm that day scattered those who had gathered. Virginia judges, sitting in special courts with no juries, found 26 men guilty, Gabriel among them. On the judges' orders, all 26 were hanged. Encyclopedia Virginia's account does not name the men who carried out the hangings.

In January 1811, Charles Deslondes led an uprising on the German Coast of the Territory of Orleans, upriver from New Orleans. Between 64 and 125 enslaved people began it, and accounts put the number who joined at 200 to 500. They marched about twenty miles down the river road toward New Orleans and killed two white men, Gilbert Andry and François Trépagnier.

Governor William C. C. Claiborne, General Wade Hampton and a militia, a band of armed local men, put the uprising down. Hampton led U.S. Army troops and Navy sailors. Manuel Andry and Charles Perret led the militia, which was made up of planters. On January 10, in about half an hour of fighting, they killed 40 to 45 rebels. They killed others without any trial as they caught them. Over the next two weeks, planters sat as judges in special courts called tribunals. Planters and U.S. officials put 44 more captured rebels to death. About 95 rebels were killed in all. The militia cut off the heads of the dead. They set nearly 100 of them on poles along the levee, the river wall, from New Orleans upriver. Deslondes was captured on January 11 and given no trial. Militiamen cut off his hands, shot him several times and burned him alive.

In 1822 white officials in Charleston, South Carolina, accused Denmark Vesey, a free Black carpenter, of planning a revolt to free thousands of enslaved people. No revolt ever took place, and no white person was harmed. Officials in Charleston put Vesey and 34 other men to death. They claimed the city's African Methodist Episcopal church had helped plan the revolt. They ordered its members to scatter and destroyed the church. The Equal Justice Initiative says they burned it to the ground. Other accounts say it was torn down. Black Charlestonians rebuilt their church. In 1834 Charleston's white city leaders outlawed independent Black churches, the historian Manisha Sinha writes. The accounts do not name the officials who passed that ban. The congregation later became the church known today as Mother Emanuel.

<a id="story-nat-turner"></a>

#### Nat Turner

> **Who:** An enslaved preacher who led the deadliest slave revolt in United States history.
>
> **When and where:** Southampton County, Virginia, August 21 to 23, 1831. Hanged on November 11, 1831.
>
> **Movie:** *The Birth of a Nation* (2016), a feature film about Turner's revolt. It is a different film from a 1915 film with the same title.

Nat Turner was an enslaved preacher in Southampton County, Virginia. From August 21 to 23, 1831, he led a revolt in which the rebels killed at least 55 white people.

After the revolt, militias and bands of armed white men killed more than 100 Black people. Many of them had nothing to do with the revolt. Some estimates put the number killed at 200.

Turner hid until he was caught on October 30. Judges in Southampton County put about 30 people on trial. Virginia officials put to death 19 of those found guilty. They hanged Turner on November 11, 1831. While he was in jail, a lawyer named Thomas R. Gray took down his account, and Gray published it that year as *The Confessions of Nat Turner*.

Lawmakers in Virginia and other slave states answered the revolt with new laws against teaching enslaved people to read and against their gathering in groups.

<a id="story-sengbe-pieh"></a>

#### Sengbe Pieh (Joseph Cinqué)

> **Who:** A Mende man who led the captives of the ship *Amistad* in taking control of it, and who won freedom for them in the United States Supreme Court.
>
> **When and where:** From the Mende country, in the region of Sierra Leone in West Africa. Took the ship on July 1, 1839. Freed by the Supreme Court in 1841. Home in 1842.
>
> **Movie:** *Amistad* (1997), a feature film about the case.

Sengbe Pieh led 53 kidnapped Africans in taking over the ship that held them, and they won their freedom in an American court. Spanish slave traders had carried them, most of them Mende people from the region of Sierra Leone, to Cuba. There the 53 were bought for a Cuban plantation and put aboard a sailing ship, the *Amistad*. On July 1, 1839, they rose up and took control of the ship. Pieh is also known as Joseph Cinqué.

In late August 1839, the U.S. Navy ship *Washington*, commanded by Lieutenant Thomas R. Gedney, seized the *Amistad* off Long Island. Officials took the Africans to New London, Connecticut, and jailed them. Some died at sea or in prison while they waited for trial.

Their lawyers took the case all the way to the Supreme Court. Former president John Quincy Adams argued part of it for them. On March 9, 1841, the justices set them free. In 1842, 35 of the survivors sailed home to Sierra Leone. They had never been enslaved on American soil.

<a id="story-solomon-northup"></a>

#### Solomon Northup

> **Who:** A free man from New York who was kidnapped and held in slavery in Louisiana for twelve years, and who named the people who did it.
>
> **When and where:** Kidnapped in Washington, D.C., in 1841. Freed on January 4, 1853. Where and when he died is not known.
>
> **Movie:** *12 Years a Slave* (2013), directed by Steve McQueen. It won the Academy Award for Best Picture.

Solomon Northup was born free and was kidnapped into slavery. He was born in 1808 in Minerva, New York. He was a farmer and a fiddler. In 1841 two white men who called themselves Merrill Brown and Abram Hamilton offered him work playing music for a circus. They took him to Washington, D.C. There they gave him a drink that left him "insensible," or unconscious. He woke up "alone, in utter darkness, and in chains."

He was in Williams's slave pen, called the Yellow House, near the U.S. Capitol. A slave pen was a building where traders locked up enslaved people until they sold them. A slave trader named James H. Burch held him there. When Northup said he was a free man, Burch beat him. Northup described the paddle Burch used: "a piece of hard-wood board, eighteen or twenty inches long." Burch also used a cat-o'-nine-tails, a whip of rope with many strands, each with a knot tied at the end. Burch told Northup that if he ever again said he was free, what came next would be worse. "He swore that he would either conquer or kill me."

In New Orleans, Burch's partner Theophilus Freeman sold him under the name Platt to William Ford. Ford sold him to a carpenter, John Tibeats, in the winter of 1842. Edwin Epps held him for almost ten years on a cotton plantation on Bayou Boeuf, in Louisiana.

A Canadian carpenter named Samuel Bass mailed letters for Northup to people he knew in Saratoga Springs, New York. Two storekeepers there sent one on to Northup's wife, Anne. She went to Henry B. Northup, a lawyer who had been Solomon's friend since childhood. Henry's family had once enslaved Solomon's father, Mintus, and freed him in a will. Henry B. Northup got help from the governor of New York, Washington Hunt. Solomon Northup was freed on January 4, 1853.

That year he published *Twelve Years a Slave*, which sold about 30,000 copies. Burch was tried in Washington in 1853 and found not guilty. The law did not allow Northup, a Black man, to testify against a white man. In May 1857 the New York case against the kidnappers ended without a trial, in a dispute over which court had the power to hear it. No one was ever convicted. After about 1857, Northup disappears from the records. Where and when he died is not known.

#### The Underground Railroad and the abolitionists

The Underground Railroad was a network of people who helped enslaved people escape to the free states and to Canada. It had guides and safe houses. Much of the work was done by free Black communities and their churches. By an estimate the National Park Service uses, it helped about 100,000 people escape over several decades. Many more tried to escape and were caught.

In the free states, Black people started their own churches, newspapers and groups. On March 16, 1827, Samuel Cornish and John Russwurm published the first issue of *Freedom's Journal* in New York. It was the first newspaper in the United States owned by Black people. Free Black communities in the North ran vigilance committees, groups that hid people who had escaped and helped them move on.

<a id="story-sojourner-truth-slavery-freedom"></a>

#### Sojourner Truth

> **Who:** A woman who walked away from slavery in New York, then sued to get back her son, who had been sold south against the law, and won.
>
> **When and where:** Ulster County, New York. Walked to freedom in 1826. Won her son's return in 1828. Died in 1883.

Sojourner Truth went to court to get her son back and won. She was born enslaved in about 1797 in Ulster County, New York, and her name then was Isabella Baumfree. In 1826 she walked away from her enslaver, carrying her baby daughter. One year later, on July 4, 1827, New York's law ending slavery took effect.

Her son Peter was five years old. Her enslaver, John Dumont, sold him for $20 to Eleazar Gedney. Eleazar sold him to his brother, Solomon Gedney, who sent the boy to his own brother-in-law in Alabama. Selling a child out of the state that way was against New York law. She sued, and in 1828 she won his return. The Historical Society of the New York Courts says she was the first Black woman to win a case of this kind against a white man in an American court.

In 1843 she took the name Sojourner Truth. Her life story, the *Narrative of Sojourner Truth*, was published in 1850.

<a id="story-harriet-tubman"></a>

#### Harriet Tubman

> **Who:** A woman who escaped slavery in Maryland and went back about 13 times to lead about 70 people out.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Dorchester County, on Maryland's Eastern Shore, in March 1822. Escaped in September 1849. Died in 1913.
>
> **Movie:** *Harriet* (2019), a feature film about her life, with Cynthia Erivo as Tubman.

Harriet Tubman escaped from slavery and then went back into Maryland about 13 times to lead others out. She brought out about 70 people, most of them family and friends, among them her parents, Rit and Ben. An old story says she made 19 trips and freed 300 people. The National Park Service says that story is a legend. The numbers 13 and 70 come from her own statements and the records.

She was born in March 1822 in Dorchester County, on Maryland's Eastern Shore. Her name then was Araminta Ross. In 1835, when she was 13, she was at a store when an enslaved person tried to escape. An overseer threw a two-pound weight. It hit her in the back of the head and broke her skull. For the rest of her life she had pain and "sleeping spells," times when she fell asleep suddenly. The accounts of her injury do not name the overseer.

In September 1849, she escaped to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Between 1850 and 1860 she made her trips back. During the Civil War she worked as a scout for the Union army, the army of the United States. She died of pneumonia in 1913, at about 91 years old, in a home for elderly Black people.

### 1850 to 1900

In 1850 the members of Congress passed a law that forced people in the free states to help catch those who had escaped slavery. Fifteen years later, after the Civil War, slavery became illegal under the 13th Amendment to the Constitution, and about four million people became free.
