Many of them had already freed themselves by escaping to the Union army, the army of the United States, during the war.

Freed people searched for family members who had been sold away. They married in law, chose their own names, built churches and schools, voted and served in Congress. White men answered with new laws that forced Black people to work, with whippings and burnings, and with massacres, the killing of many people who could not defend themselves. In April 1877 President Rutherford B. Hayes ordered the last federal troops out of the Southern statehouses. That ended the period of rebuilding called Reconstruction.

#### The Fugitive Slave Act, 1850

On September 18, 1850, the Fugitive Slave Act became law. A fugitive is a person who has escaped. Under the act, federal officials, who worked for the national government, decided whether a captured person was a runaway slave. These officials were called commissioners. There was no jury, and the captured person was not allowed to testify, which means to speak as a witness in court. A commissioner was paid $10 for ruling that a person was a slave and $5 for ruling that the person was free. Officials could force bystanders to help catch people. Its rules held in the free states too, and free Black people in the North fled to Canada.

Anthony Burns escaped from slavery in Virginia by stowing away on a ship. Charles F. Suttle, the man who held him in slavery, came to Boston with William Brent to claim him. On May 24, 1854, the two men had Burns arrested there. After a hearing that lasted a week, federal troops marched him through the city on June 2, 1854, to a ship that took him back to Virginia. He passed crowds draped in black, the color of mourning.

#### Celia, 1855

In 1855 a Missouri judge refused to tell a jury that an enslaved woman had the right to fight off a man who was raping her. Her name was Celia. In 1850 Robert Newsom, a farmer in Callaway County, Missouri, bought her when she was 14 years old. From 1850 to 1855 he raped her again and again. She had two children, and at least one was his. In 1855 she was pregnant again.

On the night of June 23, 1855, Newsom told Celia he would come to her cabin. She had put a large stick in the corner. When he came, she struck him on the head with it twice, and the second blow killed him. She burned his body in her fireplace.

Missouri's law made it a crime to force "any woman" into sex against her will, and it allowed a woman to use force to resist. Celia's trial began in October 1855. Her lawyer, John Jameson, asked Judge William Hall to tell the jury that Celia could be found not guilty if she had been resisting rape. Hall refused. That left the jury no way to treat the killing as self-defense. A jury of twelve white men found her guilty of murder. Her defense appealed, which means it asked a higher court to look at the case again. On December 14, 1855, the judges of the Missouri Supreme Court turned the appeal down. Celia was hanged in Fulton, Missouri, on December 21, 1855. The accounts of her death do not name the officials who hanged her. On December 20, 2024, at the request of her descendants, Missouri's governor, Mike Parson, pardoned her. A pardon is an official act that forgives a person for a crime.

<a id="story-dred-harriet-scott"></a>

#### Dred and Harriet Scott

> **Who:** An enslaved couple who sued for their freedom and lost in the United States Supreme Court, whose justices ruled that no Black American could be a citizen.
>
> **When and where:** Suit filed in St. Louis, Missouri, in 1846. Supreme Court decision on March 6, 1857. Freed in May 1857.

Dred and Harriet Scott sued for their freedom in 1846 and lost in the Supreme Court eleven years later. Dred Scott was born enslaved in Virginia in about 1800. Peter and Elizabeth Taylor Blow held him. The Blows moved to St. Louis in 1830 and sold him to Dr. John Emerson, an army surgeon.

Emerson took Scott to Fort Armstrong, in Illinois, in 1833, and then to Fort Snelling, in Wisconsin Territory, in 1836. Slavery was banned in both places. At Fort Snelling, Dred Scott married Harriet Robinson, who was also enslaved. They had two daughters, Eliza and Lizzie. Eliza was born on a steamboat in free waters. After Emerson died in 1843, his widow, Irene Emerson, claimed the family as her property.

On April 6, 1846, the Scotts sued for their freedom in St. Louis. They argued that living where slavery was banned had made them free. On January 12, 1850, a jury ruled in their favor. On March 22, 1852, the judges of the Missouri Supreme Court reversed that ruling, and Irene Emerson held the Scotts as her property again.

The Scotts and their lawyers took the case to the United States Supreme Court. On March 6, 1857, the justices ruled against the Scotts, 7 votes to 2. Chief Justice Roger Taney wrote that Black Americans were not and could never be citizens. He wrote that Black people "had no rights which the white man was bound to respect." The justices also ruled that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories of the West.

Irene Emerson's second husband, Calvin Chaffee, handed ownership of the family to Taylor Blow. Taylor Blow freed them on May 26, 1857. Dred Scott worked as a porter, a man who carried guests' bags, at Barnum's Hotel in St. Louis, and he helped Harriet with her laundry work. He died of tuberculosis, a disease of the lungs, on September 17, 1858.

#### Sold and smuggled, 1858 to 1860

On March 2 and 3, 1859, Pierce Mease Butler sold between 429 and 436 men, women and children at a racetrack near Savannah, Georgia, to pay his gambling debts. The National Park Service describes it as the largest single sale of people in the United States. The slave dealer Joseph Bryan ran it. He advertised it for weeks in newspapers from Charleston to Richmond. The sale brought in $303,850. A reporter from the *New York Tribune*, Mortimer Thomson, went disguised as a buyer. He wrote a long article about the sale for the *Tribune*, "What Became of the Slaves on a Georgia Plantation?" Black Georgians remembered those two days as "the weeping time."

Bringing captives from Africa had been against the law since 1808, but some men kept doing it. In 1858 Charles A. L. Lamar led a group of investors who paid for a ship called the *Wanderer* to bring captives from Africa. Its captain, William R. Corrie, bought 487 Africans at the Congo River. About 409 of them were still alive when the ship landed at Jekyll Island, Georgia, on November 29, 1858. The others died on the voyage. Six trials followed. None of them ended in a conviction.

In 1860 Timothy Meaher, a businessman and shipbuilder in Mobile, Alabama, bet that he could sneak a ship full of captives into Mobile Bay. Captain William Foster sailed the ship *Clotilda* to West Africa. He bought 125 people and carried 110 of them across the ocean. On July 8, 1860, the ship entered the Gulf of Mexico. Later that month Foster anchored it near Twelve-Mile Island and set it on fire to destroy the evidence. The only punishment anyone received was a $1,000 fine charged to Foster.

<a id="story-oluale-kossola"></a>

#### Oluale Kossola (Cudjo Lewis)

> **Who:** A man carried to Alabama on the *Clotilda*, the last known slave ship to reach the United States, who helped found the town of Africatown after he was freed.
>
> **When and where:** Born about 1841 in what is now Benin, in West Africa. Landed near Mobile, Alabama, in July 1860. Freed in 1865. Died in 1935.
>
> **Movie:** *Descendant* (2022), a documentary by Margaret Brown about the *Clotilda*, Africatown and the families of the survivors.

Oluale Kossola was one of the people carried to Alabama on the *Clotilda* in 1860, and he lived long enough to tell his story to a writer in the 1920s. He was born in about 1841 in what is now the country of Benin, among the Yoruba Isha people.

In April 1860, the army of Ghezo, the King of Dahomey, attacked his town. Kossola was captured and held in a barracoon, a pen for captives, at the port of Ouidah. There he was sold to William Foster, the *Clotilda*'s captain. The crossing took 45 days. He was one of 110 people on board.

In Mobile, James Meaher, Timothy Meaher's brother, enslaved him. Kossola worked on a steamship and lived with others from the *Clotilda* under Meaher's house, which stood high off the ground. In 1865 he was freed. He took the name Cudjo Lewis and married Abile, a woman who had also been on the *Clotilda*.

The people from the *Clotilda* could not afford to sail home. They chose Kossola to speak for them and asked Timothy Meaher for land. Meaher refused. So they bought land from him and from others, and about 30 of them founded Africatown, north of Mobile. Kossola and Abile had six children, and all six died young. In 1902 he was hurt in a train accident and sued the railroad company. He became the caretaker of the Africatown church.

In 1927 the writer Zora Neale Hurston interviewed him. Her book about his life, *Barracoon*, was not published until 2018. Kossola died on July 26, 1935, at about 94. In May 2019 officials of the Alabama Historical Commission announced that the burned wreck of the *Clotilda* had been identified in the Mobile River.

#### Freedom taken during the war

On May 23 and 24, 1861, three enslaved men rowed to Fort Monroe, a Union fort at Old Point Comfort in Virginia. Their names were Frank Baker, Shepard Mallory and James Townsend. It was the same ground where the *White Lion* had landed Africans in 1619. They were about to be taken south to build batteries, gun positions, for the Confederate army, the army of the Southern states that had broken away from the United States. General Benjamin Butler refused to send them back. He called them "contraband of war," meaning property of the enemy that an army may seize.

Word spread, and enslaved people walked, rowed and rode to Union lines across the South. By the end of the war, about half a million people had freed themselves by reaching the Union army. The people who escaped to Fort Monroe called it "Freedom's Fortress."

Union army officials, and later officials of the Freedmen's Bureau, the federal office set up to help freed people, ran camps for people who had escaped slavery. These were called contraband camps. The camps were crowded and dirty. Between 1862 and 1868, more than 60,000 freed people died of smallpox, according to the historian Jim Downs. Smallpox is a disease caused by a virus that spreads from person to person. It brings a fever and a rash that spreads over the skin and turns to scabs. About 3 in every 10 people who caught it died, and many who lived had scars for life, most of all on their faces. Doctors knew how to prevent it. They could vaccinate people, giving them a shot that protects against the disease, and they could keep the sick away from the well. Keeping sick people apart is called quarantine. The quarantine tents for freed people were made of old, ripped army cloth.

Philip Reid was an enslaved craftsman at the foundry of Clark Mills in Washington, D.C. A foundry is a workshop where metal is melted and cast. Mills owned him. Mills's workers were casting the Statue of Freedom for the top of the Capitol dome. The paid foreman demanded more money before he would take apart the plaster model. Reid worked out how to separate it with a pulley and tackle. He was paid $1.25 a day, but he kept only the pay for Sundays. Mills took the rest. Members of Congress passed a law that freed the enslaved people of Washington, D.C., on April 16, 1862, and Reid was one of them. The government of the District of Columbia counts 3,100 people freed there, and the US Senate's history office counts 2,989. Under the law, owners loyal to the Union could be paid up to $300 for each person freed. The statue was set on the dome on December 2, 1863. In his later life Reid signed his name Reed.

<a id="story-robert-smalls"></a>

#### Robert Smalls

> **Who:** An enslaved harbor pilot who sailed himself, his family and his crew out of slavery on a Confederate ship, and later served five terms in Congress.
>
> **When and where:** Charleston, South Carolina, before dawn on May 13, 1862. Later Beaufort, South Carolina. Died in 1915.

Robert Smalls freed himself, his family and his crew by taking a Confederate ship out of Charleston harbor. He was 23 years old and enslaved. He worked as the pilot, the man who steered the ship, on a Confederate transport ship called the *Planter*.

Before dawn on May 13, 1862, Smalls took the *Planter* out with an enslaved crew and their families aboard. Smalls wore the captain's straw hat, and he gave the right signals as they passed Fort Sumter. Out at sea he surrendered the ship to the Union navy ships that were blockading, or closing off, the harbor.

Smalls went on to become a ship's captain in United States service. After the war he served as one of South Carolina's state lawmakers. He was elected to the United States House of Representatives five times. He died in 1915.

#### The Emancipation Proclamation, 1863

President Abraham Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation in two steps. He announced it on September 22, 1862, and it took effect on January 1, 1863. Emancipation means setting people free from slavery.

In the proclamation, Lincoln declared free the enslaved people in the states that were fighting against the United States. Wherever the Union army advanced after that, its soldiers freed the enslaved people they reached. In the proclamation, Lincoln also opened the army to Black men.

Lincoln's proclamation did not free everyone. Lincoln left out the slave states that had stayed loyal to the Union: Delaware, Maryland, Kentucky and Missouri. He also left out Tennessee and the parts of Virginia and Louisiana that the Union army already held. Enslaved people in those places had to wait for their state's lawmakers to end slavery, or for the 13th Amendment.

#### Black soldiers and the scourged back

About 180,000 Black men served in the Union army in the regiments called the U.S. Colored Troops. By the end of the war, about one Union soldier in ten was Black. About 19,000 more Black men served in the navy. On September 29, 1864, at the Battle of New Market Heights in Virginia, fourteen Black soldiers earned the Medal of Honor, the highest award for bravery in battle.

In March 1863, a man named Peter escaped from the 3,000-acre plantation of Captain John Lyons in St. Landry Parish, Louisiana. He reached Union troops at Baton Rouge. Army doctors examined him before he joined the army. His back was covered in thick raised scars, called keloid scars, which grow over a healed wound. Peter said the overseer, Artayou Carrier, had whipped him in October 1862. He said he lay in bed for two months, sore "from the whipping and salt brine" that was poured on the wounds. The accounts do not say who poured it.

About April 2, 1863, the photographers William D. McPherson and J. Oliver photographed his back. The picture became known as "The Scourged Back." Scourged means whipped. *Harper's Weekly* printed pictures made from the photograph on July 4, 1863, under the name "Gordon." Later accounts of Peter's life say the *Harper's* story mixed up three different men. No record shows what became of Peter after he joined the Union army.

<a id="story-william-harvey-carney"></a>

#### William Harvey Carney

> **Who:** A man born enslaved in Virginia who carried the flag at Fort Wagner with the 54th Massachusetts, a Black regiment. His actions there were the earliest act of bravery by a Black American to be recognized with the Medal of Honor.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Norfolk, Virginia, on February 29, 1840. Fort Wagner, South Carolina, July 18, 1863. Died on December 9, 1908.

William Harvey Carney carried the flag of the United States through a battle while badly wounded, and he did not let it fall. He was born enslaved in Norfolk, Virginia, on February 29, 1840. Accounts differ about how he became free. Some say he escaped on the Underground Railroad. Others say his father escaped and then bought his freedom. The family settled in New Bedford, Massachusetts.

In February 1863 Carney joined Company C of the 54th Massachusetts, a regiment of Black soldiers. He became a sergeant in March. On July 18, 1863, the 54th attacked Fort Wagner, in South Carolina. The soldier carrying the flag was shot. Carney took the flag and went forward with several serious wounds. He planted it on the wall of the fort and then carried it back to the Union lines. The National Park Service quotes his words afterward. He said, "Boys, I did but my duty," and then, "the dear old flag never touched the ground!" The attack appears in the film *Glory* (1989), which is about the 54th Massachusetts.

He received the Medal of Honor in May 1900. The National Park Service says his actions were "the earliest act of African American bravery to be recognized with the medal." He was one of 22 African Americans to receive it for service in the Civil War. He died at Boston City Hospital on December 9, 1908.

#### Combahee Ferry, Juneteenth and the 13th Amendment

On the night of June 2, 1863, Harriet Tubman guided Union gunboats and soldiers of the 2nd South Carolina Volunteers up the Combahee River in South Carolina. More than 700 enslaved people escaped to freedom on the boats that night.

On January 31, 1865, the members of Congress passed the 13th Amendment. Its text forbids slavery everywhere in the United States, "except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted." That exception still allowed forced labor for people convicted of crimes.

On June 19, 1865, Major General Gordon Granger arrived in Galveston, Texas, with about 2,000 federal soldiers. He issued General Order No. 3. It said that "all slaves are free," with "absolute equality of personal rights." More than 250,000 people were still enslaved in Texas, two and a half years after the Emancipation Proclamation, because the Union army had not been there to enforce it. June 19 became a day of celebration, called Juneteenth.

The 13th Amendment became part of the Constitution on December 6, 1865, when lawmakers in enough states had approved it.

Some Native nations had also held Black people in slavery. The Cherokee, Muscogee (Creek), Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole nations were known as the Five Tribes. At emancipation the Cherokee Nation held as many as 2,500 enslaved people. In 1866 the leaders of each of these nations signed treaties with the United States. In them the leaders agreed to free the people their nations had enslaved and to make them citizens of the nation. In Article 9 of the Cherokee treaty, Cherokee leaders promised the freed people, called Freedmen, "all the rights of native Cherokees."

#### Freedom, day to day

For decades after slavery ended, freed people searched for family members who had been sold away. They placed advertisements in Black newspapers, under headings such as "Information Wanted," asking for news of mothers, children, husbands and wives. The searches ran into the 1900s. Few ended in a reunion, and when one did, people wrote about it with joy. Researchers at Villanova University and Mother Bethel AME Church in Philadelphia, in a project called "Last Seen: Finding Family After Slavery," have put more than 5,000 of these ads online.

Enslaved people's marriages had never counted in law. After the war, officers of the Freedmen's Bureau, the federal office set up to help freed people, recorded thousands of marriages. Couples who had been together for decades stood up to be married in law. The Bureau's marriage registers survive at the National Archives.

Freed people chose and registered their own last names. Some kept a former owner's name, so that family members who had been sold away could find them. Others chose new names. Freeman was one.

Congregations that had met in hush harbors built their own churches. Within ten years of the war, freed people had joined or founded AME and AME Zion churches across the South. Freed people used their churches as schools, as meeting halls and as places to organize for elections.

Members of Congress set up the Freedman's Savings Bank by law to hold the savings of freed people, and President Lincoln signed the law on March 3, 1865. The bank's managers ran it badly and lost money on risky deals. It failed in June 1874. About 61,000 people had nearly $3 million saved in it. Between 1875 and 1883, the officials in charge of closing the bank, called commissioners, paid back 62 percent of what was owed. Only about 30,000 depositors turned in their bank books to collect, and about 31,000 never got anything back.

<a id="story-thornton-copeland"></a>

#### Thornton Copeland

> **Who:** A freed man who placed a newspaper advertisement in 1865 searching for his mother, from whom he had been sold away 21 years earlier.
>
> **When and where:** The *Colored Tennessean*, a newspaper in Nashville, Tennessee, October 1865. He had been sold in Richmond, Virginia, in 1844.

Thornton Copeland was sold away from his mother in 1844. The buyer was Samuel Copeland, in Richmond, Virginia. The ad does not say who sold him. In October 1865, after slavery ended, he placed an advertisement in the *Colored Tennessean*, a Black newspaper in Nashville, to look for her. Her name was Betty.

His advertisement reads: "INFORMATION is wanted of my mother, whom I left in Fauquier county, Va., in 1844, and I was sold in Richmond, Va., to Saml. Copeland." He had been held before that by a man named Robert Rogers.

His advertisement is item 918 in the "Last Seen" collection. No record shows whether he ever found his mother.

#### Schools, the moment freedom came

People who had been forbidden to read started schools as soon as the Union lines reached them. They opened schools in churches, in army camps and in buildings the Union army had taken over. Grandparents and grandchildren learned in the same rooms. Grown men and women came to night classes after a full day's work.

Freed people paid for schools themselves wherever they could. They paid school fees out of their first wages, and they gave land and their own labor to build schoolhouses. Northern aid societies helped, the American Missionary Association most of all. Thousands of teachers came south, many of them women, and a growing number of them Black. By 1870 Freedmen's Bureau officials had counted more than 2,600 day and night schools with about 150,000 students. Counts that include every kind of school are higher.

New colleges opened for freed people. Fisk, in Nashville, opened in January 1866. Members of Congress passed a law that set up Howard University in 1867. By 1872 there were about 25 colleges for freed people.

In 1868 and 1869, delegates in the Southern states wrote new state constitutions. Their conventions were the first public bodies in United States history with many Black members. The delegates created the South's first statewide systems of free public schools, open to white children too.

<a id="story-susie-king-taylor"></a>

#### Susie King Taylor

> **Who:** A girl who learned to read in secret schools in Savannah, escaped at 13, and became the first Black teacher of freed children in a school working openly in Georgia.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Liberty County, Georgia, on August 6, 1848. Taught on St. Simons Island, Georgia, in 1862. Died in 1912.

Susie King Taylor was a teacher of freed people at 14, while the Civil War was still going on. As a child in Savannah, Georgia, she went to two secret schools run by Black women. Two white young people also taught her, breaking the law to do it.

In April 1862, at 13, she escaped with others to St. Simons Island, which the Union army held. She turned 14 that August. There she became the first Black teacher of freed students in a school for freed people working openly in Georgia. She taught about 40 children by day and grown people at night, until the Union army moved everyone off the island in October 1862.

She married Edward King, a Black noncommissioned officer in the army, a soldier who had risen through the ranks to lead other soldiers. She served with the 33rd U.S. Colored Troops as a nurse and laundress, and she taught soldiers to read. In 1902 she published a book about those years, *Reminiscences of My Life in Camp*. She died in 1912.

#### Memphis and New Orleans, 1866

In early May 1866, white mobs in Memphis, Tennessee, attacked the city's Black neighborhoods. The mobs included city policemen, firemen and some businessmen. The attacks began after a clash between the police and Black Union soldiers who had just left the army. General George Stoneman had taken the soldiers' guns away. The mobs killed 46 Black people. Two white people also died.

Members of Congress formed a committee to look into the killings. Its members counted 75 people injured, 100 robbed and five women raped. The mobs burned 91 homes, 4 churches and 8 schools. That was every Black church and school in the city. No one was ever punished for the killings, as far as the records show.

Frances Thompson testified to the committee. She said that on May 1, 1866, seven white men broke into her home and raped her and her roommate, 16-year-old Lucy Smith. Accounts of her testimony differ on whether two or three of the men were police officers. The men also stole about $300. In July 1876, Memphis police arrested Thompson for wearing women's clothing. Dr. Joseph Nuttall, who worked for the city, and three other doctors examined her body against her will and declared that she was a man. She could not pay the fine, and she was sentenced to 100 days on the chain gang, cleaning streets. A chain gang was a crew of prisoners chained together and forced to work. Her opponents used the arrest to attack her testimony about the rapes. She died of dysentery, a disease of the gut, in the city hospital on November 1, 1876.

On July 30, 1866, delegates met at the Mechanics' Institute in New Orleans. They wanted to reopen a meeting that was rewriting Louisiana's constitution and give Black men the vote. Mayor John T. Monroe had declared the meeting unlawful. About 200 unarmed Black men, most of them Union veterans, marched in support. Sheriff Harry T. Hays had given police powers to many men, a lot of them former Confederate soldiers. These police attacked, with white mobs and firemen. They killed 34 Black people and wounded 119. They killed 3 white delegates and wounded 17. The official report counts 38 killed and 146 wounded in all. General Philip Sheridan called it "an absolute massacre by the police."

#### Black political power

The 15th Amendment became part of the Constitution on February 3, 1870. It states that the right to vote "shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude." Abridged means cut down. Servitude means slavery. In the ten years that followed, 16 Black men served in Congress, 14 in the House and 2 in the Senate. All of them were Republicans from the South. Joseph Rainey of South Carolina became the first Black member of the House of Representatives on December 12, 1870. Robert Smalls served five terms in the House.

Across the South, about 2,000 Black men held public office during Reconstruction, some elected and some appointed. The historian Eric Foner has found more than 1,500 of them by name and listed them in his book *Freedom's Lawmakers*.

<a id="story-revels-bruce"></a>

#### Hiram Revels and Blanche K. Bruce

> **Who:** The first two Black United States senators. Revels was the first to serve. Bruce, born enslaved, was the first to serve a full six-year term.
>
> **When and where:** Both represented Mississippi. Revels served from 1870 to 1871. Bruce served from 1875 to 1881.

Hiram Revels became the first Black United States senator on February 25, 1870. Blanche K. Bruce became the first Black senator to serve a full term, from 1875 to 1881. Both men represented Mississippi.

Revels was born free on September 27, 1827, in Fayetteville, North Carolina. He was a minister in the African Methodist Episcopal Church and a teacher. During the Civil War he served as a chaplain, a minister to soldiers, for Black regiments. In 1869 he won a seat in the Mississippi state senate. On January 20, 1870, Mississippi's state lawmakers voted 85 to 15 to send him to the United States Senate. Democrats in the Senate argued against seating him. Some said he had not been a citizen until the 14th Amendment was adopted in 1868, so he had not been a citizen long enough to serve. The senators voted 48 to 8 to seat him. He served until March 3, 1871. In 1871 he became the first president of Alcorn University. He died in 1901.

Bruce was born enslaved on March 1, 1841, near Farmville, Virginia. Pettus Perkinson held him in slavery. When the Civil War began, Bruce escaped to Lawrence, Kansas, where he taught school. After the war he moved to Mississippi. He was a sheriff and a tax collector in Bolivar County and the county's superintendent of education. On February 4, 1874, he was elected to the Senate. He served from March 4, 1875, to March 3, 1881. Later he served as Register of the Treasury, an office in the federal government. He died in Washington, D.C., in 1898.

#### The promises broken

Within a year of the war's end, President Andrew Johnson and Southern lawmakers had taken back much of what freed people had been promised.

On January 16, 1865, the Union general Sherman issued Special Field Orders No. 15. In it, Sherman set aside about 400,000 acres of coastal land, from Charleston to northern Florida, for freed families in plots of forty acres. About 40,000 people settled on the land. In the fall of 1865, President Andrew Johnson reversed the order and gave the land back to its former owners. The phrase "forty acres and a mule" comes from this broken promise.

In November 1865, Mississippi's lawmakers passed the first Black Codes, and lawmakers in other Southern states followed. Vagrancy means having no job or home. Under the new vagrancy laws, officials could arrest a Black person who could not prove he had a job. Under apprenticeship laws, officials could force Black children to work for white employers. Other laws required licenses to work in certain jobs. Officials hired out the people they arrested under these laws to work for others. The members of Congress answered with the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and the 14th Amendment, which became part of the Constitution on July 9, 1868.

Without land of their own, many freed families became sharecroppers. A sharecropper farmed a landlord's fields in exchange for a share of the crop. The landlord lent the family tools, seed and food, charged at the plantation store's prices, and took the cost out of the family's share. The debt carried over from year to year, and families could not leave the land until it was paid.

#### Convict leasing

The 13th Amendment allowed forced labor as a punishment for crime. Southern officials used that exception. Sheriffs arrested Black men, often for vagrancy or small crimes under the new codes, and county judges sentenced them. State officials then leased the prisoners, or rented them out, to planters, mine owners and railroads. The prisoners worked without pay. This was called convict leasing.

Alabama officials leased the state's prisoners to companies from 1875 to 1928. State officials signed the leases, and company managers ran the prison camps. Officials sent most of the prisoners to coal mines run by companies such as the Tennessee Coal, Iron and Railroad Company, Sloss Iron and Steel, and Pratt Coal and Iron. More than 95 percent of the county prisoners and 90 percent of the state prisoners were Black. In one count from the 1890s, 181 of 745 county prisoners in the mines died within two years. County prisoners also had to work off their court costs, which made their sentences longer. In 1912 Alabama's state government took in more than $1 million from prison mining.

#### Terror

In December 1865, Confederate veterans founded the Ku Klux Klan in Pulaski, Tennessee. Klansmen, armed and in disguise, whipped freed people and the white people who worked with them, burned their homes and murdered them. They attacked mostly at night.

Klansmen went after schools and teachers. In late 1869, at Greensboro, Georgia, they drove away a teacher named R. H. Gladding. Abram Colby, a Black man, had just been elected to Georgia's state lawmaking body, and he supported the school. Klansmen took him out of his house and beat him nearly to death. In Alabama, Klansmen burned many Black schools and churches. On July 11, 1870, at Cross Plains, Alabama, they killed a teacher of freed people, William Luke, a preacher from Ontario in Canada. Accounts say six or eight people were killed there.

Under the Enforcement Acts of 1870 and 1871, federal officials broke up the Klan for a time.

On Easter Sunday, April 13, 1873, white men carried out a massacre at Colfax, Louisiana. A massacre is the killing of many people who cannot defend themselves. The historian Eric Foner calls it the bloodiest single act of racial violence in Reconstruction. After a disputed election, Black militiamen and Republicans held the courthouse of Grant Parish. In Louisiana a parish is what other states call a county. Christopher Columbus Nash, who claimed to be the sheriff, led more than 150 armed white men against them. Other accounts say about 300. The attackers fired a small cannon, set the courthouse on fire and shot the men who came out. That night some of the attackers killed their prisoners, most of them with shots to the head. Estimates of the number of Black men killed run from about 60 to 153. Two white men died.

A jury found three of the attackers guilty of conspiracy, which means planning a crime together. On March 27, 1876, in the case *United States v. Cruikshank*, the justices of the Supreme Court threw out the convictions. They ruled that the rights at stake protected people only against actions by governments, not against private men. No one was ever punished for the killings. In 1950 Louisiana officials put up a marker calling it a riot in which "three white men and 150 Negroes were slain." Negroes was an old word for Black people. It was taken down in 2021.

#### The end of Reconstruction, 1877

The presidential election of 1876 ended in dispute. Five senators, five representatives and five Supreme Court justices decided it. They voted 8 to 7, Republicans against Democrats, to give the Republican, Rutherford B. Hayes, every disputed vote. Democrats in Congress then stopped blocking the count. In return, Republicans agreed to end the army's control over the South. No written copy of this deal has ever been found. It is called the Compromise of 1877. President Hayes then ordered the last federal troops out of the Southern statehouses. The last ones left the Louisiana statehouse in New Orleans on April 24, 1877. The 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments stayed in the Constitution, but federal officials stopped enforcing them in the South.

On May 18, 1896, in the case *Plessy v. Ferguson*, the justices of the Supreme Court ruled 7 to 1 that states could keep Black and white people separate by law, under the rule known as "separate but equal." Justice Harlan was the only one to disagree. Separating people by race is called segregation. With that ruling, the justices upheld the segregation laws that Southern lawmakers had already passed.

### 1900 to 1950

Slavery was against the law after 1865, but in the first half of the 1900s, Southern lawmakers, sheriffs, judges and company managers built a system that took its place. Lawmakers passed laws that kept Black and white people apart, and they took the vote from most Black men. Sheriffs arrested Black men for small crimes, judges sentenced them, and state officials rented them to mine companies, whose managers worked them without pay. White mobs lynched Black people by the thousands. Researchers at the Equal Justice Initiative have counted more than 4,400 such killings between 1877 and 1950.

By the 1930s, the people who had been born into slavery were old. From 1936 to 1938, writers paid by the federal government wrote down the life stories of more than 2,300 of them.

#### Segregation and the stolen vote

In 1896 the justices of the Supreme Court decided the case *Plessy v. Ferguson*. They ruled that a state could keep Black and white people apart by law, under a rule called "separate but equal." After that ruling, lawmakers across the South passed laws that kept Black and white people apart in schools, railroad cars, waiting rooms, courtrooms and cemeteries, and at water fountains. Keeping people apart by race is called segregation. These laws became known as Jim Crow laws.

Southern lawmakers also took away the vote from Black men. A state's constitution is its set of basic laws. The men who wrote Mississippi's constitution of 1890 set the pattern, with three rules for voters. A poll tax was a fee a man had to pay before he could vote. A literacy test was a reading test. A clause is one part of a written law or constitution. Under the understanding clause, a man had to be able to read any part of the state constitution. A man who could not read could still sign up to vote if he understood a part when someone read it to him, or gave "a reasonable interpretation" of it. Henry Williams had been found guilty of murder in Mississippi by an all-white jury. In 1898 his lawyer told the justices of the Supreme Court that the local officer who signed up voters was "the sole judge" of each test. The officer could turn away any man he chose. The justices ruled against Williams.

Much later, the justices decided another case about the same rules, in 1965. In it, lawyers for the United States government told the Supreme Court that Black men had once been more than half of Mississippi's qualified voters. By 1899 they were about 9 percent.

In 1898 the men who wrote Louisiana's new constitution added a grandfather clause. It let a man vote if his father or grandfather had voted before January 1, 1867. At that time most Black Southerners had been enslaved. So the clause let white men who could not pass the tests vote anyway.

In 1896 about 130,000 Black voters were registered in Louisiana. By 1900 there were 5,320. By 1904, by the count of Equal Justice Initiative researchers, there were about 1,000.

#### Lynching

A lynching is the killing of a person by a mob, with no trial. Researchers at the Equal Justice Initiative have documented more than 4,400 lynchings of Black people carried out as racial terror between 1877 and 1950. Other counts, which use different years and different rules for what counts, give different totals. Mobs hanged people and shot them. In Chattanooga, Tennessee, in 1906, an all-white jury found a Black man named Ed Johnson guilty of rape, though about a dozen witnesses said he was somewhere else. Rape means forcing a person into sex. Johnson's lawyers appealed, which means they asked a higher court to look at the case again. The justices of the Supreme Court stopped his execution while they looked at his appeal. That night the sheriff, Joseph F. Shipp, took away the jail's usual guard and left only the night jailer. A mob broke into the jail, took Johnson to a bridge over the Tennessee River, hanged him from a beam and shot him. In 2000 a Tennessee judge threw out the guilty verdict.

White mobs used lynching to frighten Black people into staying in low-paid work and into obeying white Southerners. Black Southerners left the South to get away from the terror, in a movement known as the Great Migration.

#### Forced labor after slavery

Sheriffs, judges, state officials and company managers kept Black people working without pay well into the 1900s, through convict leasing and debt peonage. Under convict leasing, state officials rented prisoners out to companies, and company managers worked them without wages. Sheriffs arrested Black men, often for having no job or for small crimes, and county judges sentenced them. Debt peonage meant forcing a person to work to pay off a debt. Douglas Blackmon told this history in his book *Slavery by Another Name*, which won the Pulitzer Prize, one of the top American prizes for writing. In 2012 PBS showed a film made from the book.

Alabama officials leased the state's prisoners to coal companies from 1875 to 1928, among them the Tennessee Coal, Iron and Railroad Company. More than 95 percent of Alabama's county prisoners were Black. In one count from the 1890s, 181 of 745 county prisoners working in the mines died within two years. In 1911, 123 Black county prisoners whom officials had leased to the Banner Mine were killed in an explosion there. In 1924 a prisoner named James Knox, from Mobile, died at the Flat Top mine. His death was first reported as a suicide by poison. An autopsy, an examination of the body after death, then showed that he had died of heart failure and that poison had been put into his body with a needle after he died. A City of Birmingham article states that his fatal injuries came from being whipped with a steel wire and lowered into hot water. The historian Mary Ellen Curtin describes a vat, a large tub, of boiling water. Neither account names who first called his death a suicide, who put in the poison, or who whipped him and put him in the water. Alabama officials ended convict leasing on June 30, 1928. Alabama was the last state to end it.

On January 3, 1911, the justices of the Supreme Court ruled that an Alabama law punishing farm workers who quit after taking an advance broke the 13th Amendment. An advance is money paid before the work is done. The 13th Amendment is the part of the Constitution, added in 1865, that forbids slavery. The case began with Alonzo Bailey, a farm worker in Alabama. He signed on to work for the Riverside Company for $12 a month and took $15 in advance. After about a month he left. Under Alabama law, leaving a job after taking an advance was a crime, and the law barred him from telling the court why he had left. He was fined $30 and sentenced to 136 days of hard labor. In *Bailey v. Alabama*, the justices ruled 7 to 2 that the law broke the 13th Amendment. Booker T. Washington secretly helped pay for Bailey's lawyers. Lawmakers in other Southern states kept laws like it for decades. The justices of the Supreme Court struck down Georgia's law in 1942 and Florida's in 1944.

#### The last voices

From 1936 to 1938, federal officials running the Federal Writers' Project, a government program that gave jobs to writers, sent interviewers to talk with people who had been born into slavery. The interviewers worked in 17 states, wrote down more than 2,300 life stories and took 500 photographs. The Library of Congress keeps them in a collection called "Born in Slavery."

The Library of Congress also keeps sound recordings of people who were born into slavery, made between 1932 and 1975. The collection is called "Voices Remembering Slavery."

<a id="story-fountain-hughes"></a>

#### Fountain Hughes

> **Who:** A man born into slavery in Virginia, one of the few people born enslaved whose own voice survives on a recording.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Charlottesville, Virginia. Recorded by the Library of Congress in Baltimore, Maryland, on June 11, 1949.

Fountain Hughes was recorded talking about slavery in 1949, and the recording still exists. On June 11, 1949, in Baltimore, Hermond Norwood of the Library of Congress interviewed him. Hughes began: "My name is Fountain Hughes. I was born in Charlottesville, Virginia." He said he was 101 years old, which would mean he was born in about 1848. Some reference books give 1854, and other accounts argue for a later year.

His grandfather, Wormley Hughes, was the enslaved head gardener at Monticello, Thomas Jefferson's plantation. Fountain Hughes said his father "got killed in the Army," and that left the children "to live on whatever people choose to give us."

He was never sold, he said, because "I was too young to sell." But he described how others were sold: "They'd sell us like they sell horses and cows and hogs and all like that. Have an auction bench, and they'd put you on up on the bench and bid on you." He could not go anywhere without his enslaver's permission: "I couldn't go from here across the street, or I couldn't go through nobody's house without I have a note or something from my master."

He said of being enslaved: "You're nothing but a dog. You're not a thing but a dog!"

### 1950 to 2000

An amendment is a change added to the Constitution. The 14th Amendment, added in 1868, says that no state may deny any person "the equal protection of the laws," which means the same protection the laws give everyone else. The 15th, added in 1870, says that no one may be kept from voting because of race. For almost a hundred years, federal officials did not enforce those amendments in the South. In 1954 the justices of the Supreme Court ruled that public schools kept separate by race were against the Constitution. In 1964 and 1965, members of Congress passed two laws that gave federal officials the power to enforce the amendments. After Alex Haley's book *Roots* came out in 1976 and ABC showed it on television in 1977, many Black families began tracing their ancestors back to slavery.

#### The amendments enforced

On May 17, 1954, in *Brown v. Board of Education*, the justices of the Supreme Court all agreed that "separate educational facilities are inherently unequal." Inherently means by their very nature. With that ruling, the justices threw out the "separate but equal" rule of *Plessy v. Ferguson* for public schools.

The Civil Rights Act became law on July 2, 1964, and the Voting Rights Act on August 6, 1965. Under the Civil Rights Act, hotels, restaurants and other places open to the public could no longer turn people away or keep them apart because of race, and employers could no longer refuse people jobs because of race. Under the Voting Rights Act, no state or county could use any rule to keep a citizen from voting because of race. With these laws, the members of Congress who voted for them gave federal officials the power to enforce the 14th and 15th Amendments. They came about a hundred years after the 13th Amendment forbade slavery.

In 1995 Mississippi's state lawmakers voted to approve the 13th Amendment, 130 years after it became part of the Constitution. No one filed the paperwork that would have made their vote official.

#### Roots and the search for family

In 1976 Alex Haley published *Roots*, a book about his family, which he traced back to an African man enslaved in America. In January 1977 the ABC television network showed *Roots* as a miniseries, a story told over several nights. An estimated 130 million people watched it, the largest audience a television series had ever had. Afterward, many Black families began searching for their own ancestors.

Parts of Haley's work were later challenged. In 1978 Haley agreed to pay the writer Harold Courlander $650,000 to settle a lawsuit claiming that Haley had copied passages from Courlander's novel *The African*. Professional genealogists, people who trace family histories from records, have challenged links in the chain of records behind Haley's family story.

<a id="story-alex-haley"></a>

#### Alex Haley

> **Who:** A writer who traced his family back to an enslaved African ancestor in the book *Roots*, and whose work led many Black Americans to search for their own families. Parts of his research and writing have been challenged.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Ithaca, New York, in 1921. *Roots* published in 1976. Died in Tennessee in 1992.
>
> **Movie:** *Roots* (1977), a television miniseries on ABC based on Haley's book. It tells his family's story as drama. It is not a documentary about Haley.

Alex Haley wrote *Roots*, a book about his family's history from Africa through slavery. He was born in Ithaca, New York, on August 11, 1921. He spent part of his childhood in Henning, Tennessee, his mother's hometown. There his aunts and grandmothers told the family's stories. One story was about an African ancestor named Toby, who "insisted that his real name was Kin-te."

Haley served twenty years in the United States Coast Guard, and he became a writer while he was in it. Later he traveled to Gambia, in West Africa. There a griot, a keeper of history who tells it from memory, told him the story of "his ancestor Kunta Kinte, captured by slave traders."

*Roots* came out in 1976. It won a special Pulitzer Prize in 1977. The television miniseries ran on eight nights in a row in January 1977 and won 145 awards, including nine Emmys, the top awards for television.

In 1978 Haley agreed to pay Harold Courlander $650,000 to settle Courlander's lawsuit. Genealogists have questioned whether the records support every link Haley drew between his family and Kunta Kinte. Haley died in a Tennessee hospital in February 1992, of problems caused by diabetes.

### 2000 to Today

Since 2000, Americans have built museums about slavery and opened its records to the public. Lawmakers and city leaders have argued over whether to make payments or other repairs to the descendants of enslaved people. The Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture opened in Washington in 2016. In a project begun in 2015, volunteers made about 1.8 million names from the records of the Freedmen's Bureau searchable online. The Freedmen's Bureau was the federal office set up after the Civil War to help freed people. In 2025 and 2026, federal officials removed or changed exhibits about slavery at some national parks, and judges were still deciding in September 2026 whether that was lawful.

#### Museums, a holiday and a late vote

The Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture opened in Washington, D.C., on September 24, 2016. Its history galleries begin with the slave trade. Among the things on display is a cabin where enslaved people lived. The International African American Museum opened in Charleston, South Carolina, on June 27, 2023. It stands at Gadsden's Wharf, one of the main places where slave ships landed their captives.

Members of Congress passed the Juneteenth National Independence Day Act, and President Joe Biden signed it on June 17, 2021. Under it, June 19 is a federal holiday. It marks the day in 1865 when Union soldiers announced freedom in Galveston, Texas.

In 2012 two Mississippi residents found that the paperwork for the state's 1995 vote approving the 13th Amendment had never been filed. It was officially recorded on February 7, 2013.

On December 20, 2024, at the request of her descendants, Missouri's governor, Mike Parson, pardoned Celia. A pardon is an official act that forgives a person for a crime. Celia was the enslaved woman hanged in 1855 for killing Robert Newsom. The accounts of her death do not name the officials who hanged her. He had bought her at 14 in 1850 and raped her again and again from 1850 to 1855.

#### The records opened

For millions of Black Americans, the records of the Freedmen's Bureau are the first papers in which their ancestors appear by name, according to FamilySearch and the Smithsonian. The records include marriage registers, work contracts and school lists. In a project begun in 2015, volunteers for FamilySearch, a genealogy group, typed up about 1.8 million names from these records so that people could search them. The names can be searched at discoverfreedmen.org.

In 1838 the Maryland Jesuits, priests of a Catholic religious order, sold 272 enslaved people to plantations in Louisiana. They sold them in part to keep Georgetown College, now Georgetown University, from running out of money. It is one of the best-documented mass sales of people in American history. The people sold are now called the GU272. In 2016 Georgetown's leaders announced that descendants of the GU272 would get an advantage when they applied to the university. They also renamed buildings. Genealogists have traced thousands of descendants, according to the Georgetown Memory Project in 2021. In 2021 the Jesuits and leaders of the descendants set up the Descendants Truth and Reconciliation Foundation. Reconciliation means making peace after a wrong. The Jesuits promised to give $100 million to it. The Boston Globe reported that it is the largest pledge of its kind by a religious group in the United States.

When slavery ended, Cherokee slaveholders held as many as 2,500 Black people in slavery. In a treaty of 1866, a written agreement with the United States, Cherokee leaders promised these people, called Freedmen, "all the rights of native Cherokees." In 2017, in the case *Cherokee Nation v. Nash*, a federal judge ruled that the treaty still bound the Cherokee Nation. Descendants of Cherokee Freedmen had a right to full citizenship in the nation. Cherokee leaders accepted the ruling. In 2021 the justices of the Cherokee Nation's own Supreme Court struck the words "by blood" out of its rules on citizenship.

<a id="story-melisande-short-colomb"></a>

#### Mélisande Short-Colomb

> **Who:** A descendant of two people sold by the Maryland Jesuits in 1838, who enrolled at Georgetown University at the age of 63.
>
> **When and where:** From New Orleans. Entered Georgetown University in Washington, D.C., in the fall of 2017.

Mélisande Short-Colomb enrolled at Georgetown University in 2017, at 63 years old. That was 179 years after the Jesuits of Maryland sold her ancestors to keep the college going. She was a retired chef from New Orleans.

She descends from Abraham Mahoney and Mary Ellen Queen. Both were among the 272 people the Jesuits sold in 1838. She grew up hearing family stories from her grandmother and her great-aunts. In the summer of 2016 she learned that Mahoney and Queen had been part of the 1838 sale. In April 2017 Georgetown's leaders held a Liturgy of Remembrance, a religious service honoring the people who were sold. After that, she applied to the university.

At Georgetown she wrote a play, *Here I Am*, about her ancestors and the university.

#### Repair debated

Reparations are payments or other actions meant to make up for a wrong. Since 1989 members of Congress have argued over whether the United States should pay reparations for slavery.

Representative John Conyers first introduced a bill called H.R. 40 in 1989. It would set up a commission, a group of people chosen to study slavery and its effects and to recommend ways to repair them, including a formal apology and payments. The number 40 comes from the forty-acre plots that General William T. Sherman set aside for freed families in January 1865. President Andrew Johnson took the land back that fall and returned it to its former owners. In 2021 the members of the House Judiciary Committee voted to move it forward for the first time. On January 3, 2025, Representative Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts introduced it again. As of September 2026, neither the full House nor the full Senate had voted to pass it, according to the records of Congress.

In 2019 the members of the city council of Evanston, Illinois, voted to create the first reparations program paid for by a city. Council member Robin Rue Simmons led the effort. City officials set aside $10 million and in March 2021 approved its first grants of $25,000 for housing. The program is for Black residents who lived in Evanston between 1919 and 1969. In those years Evanston's city officials used city laws to separate where Black and white people could live. In January 1921 the members of the city council passed Evanston's first zoning law, a law that sets what may be built in each part of a city. Mayor Harry P. Pearsons signed it. The law marked almost every block where Black people lived outside the west side of town for stores and businesses. As those blocks were turned over to businesses, the Black families living there were pushed out to the west side, the historian Andrew Wiese writes.

By August 2026, according to the Evanston RoundTable newspaper, 137 people had received a total of $3.47 million. In May 2024 a conservative group called Judicial Watch sued the city, arguing that paying people based on race breaks the 14th Amendment. On June 16, 2026, lawyers for the U.S. Department of Justice asked to join the lawsuit against the city. The case was still open in September 2026.

In California, a state task force, a group the state set up to study reparations, delivered its final report on June 29, 2023. According to the state's Department of Justice, it made more than 115 recommendations, including a formal apology. Governor Gavin Newsom signed the state's apology in September 2024. On October 10, 2025, he signed a law creating a state Bureau for Descendants of American Slavery. The bureau is to check who qualifies, handle claims and recommend forms of repair. The law provides for no payments.

In Maryland, Governor Wes Moore vetoed a bill for a state reparations commission in May 2025, which means he refused to sign it into law. On December 16, 2025, Maryland's state lawmakers passed it over his veto, 31 to 14 in the Senate and 93 to 35 in the House. The 23-member commission is to study state and local policies from 1877 to 1965.

#### Slavery exhibits in the national parks, 2025 and 2026

On March 27, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an executive order, a written command from the president to the people who run the federal government. It was called "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History." Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who is in charge of the national parks, then ordered a review of how the signs and exhibits in the parks present the history of the United States.

In September 2025, reporters for the Washington Post and the New York Times wrote that officials had ordered a copy of an 1863 photograph removed from an exhibit. The exhibit was at Fort Pulaski National Monument, near Savannah, Georgia. The photograph shows the back of Peter, a man who escaped slavery in Louisiana in 1863, covered in scars from whipping. On September 16, 2025, Elizabeth Peace, who spoke for the Interior Department, told The Hill newspaper that park sites "were not asked to remove the photo." The two accounts differ. In January 2026, officials removed the exhibits about slavery at the President's House site in Philadelphia. That was the house where President George Washington lived, and where Ona Judge, an enslaved woman, walked out to freedom in 1796. On February 16, 2026, Judge Cynthia M. Rufe ordered the exhibits put back. Government lawyers appealed, and the judges of an appeals court, a higher court that hears appeals, later ruled that the administration had the power to replace that exhibit.

In a separate case, Judge Angel Kelley of the federal court in Massachusetts ruled on June 12, 2026, that the order could not be carried out at any of the park system's 433 sites. She ordered the removed exhibits put back by July 3. On July 2, 2026, the judges of the First Circuit Court of Appeals paused her order, so removals could go on while the case continued. By the government's own count, in court papers filed in June 2026, exhibits had been removed or changed at 37 park sites. The case was still undecided in September 2026.

<a id="story-joycelyn-davis"></a>

#### Joycelyn Davis

> **Who:** A descendant of Charlie and Maggie Lewis. Charlie Lewis was one of the Africans smuggled into Mobile, Alabama, as captives on the *Clotilda* in 1860.
>
> **When and where:** Africatown, in Mobile, Alabama, where she has lived all her life.
>
> **Movie:** *Descendant* (2022), a documentary by Margaret Brown about the *Clotilda*, Africatown and the survivors' families. Joycelyn Davis appears in it.

Joycelyn Davis descends from people who survived the last known slave ship to reach the United States, and she organizes gatherings in their honor in the town they founded. Her ancestors Charlie and Maggie Lewis were among the 110 Africans whom Captain William Foster carried from West Africa and smuggled into Mobile on the *Clotilda* in 1860. Bringing captives into the country had been against the law since 1808. She has lived in Africatown all her life. As a child she visited her great-grandmother in Lewis Quarters, one of the first pieces of land the *Clotilda* survivors bought. It was named for Charlie and Maggie Lewis.

She went to the school and the church that her ancestors founded. In 2017 she sued the International Paper Company over pollution from its old mill near Mobile. She is a cancer survivor.

Early in the search for the wreck of the *Clotilda*, she said: "Our community is suffering, and you're asking about a ship?" After the wreck was confirmed in 2019, she came to see the ship as a way to bring money and attention to Africatown. In 2019 she organized a reunion of *Clotilda* descendants. Of the crowd that came, she told National Geographic: "I never in a million years thought it would be that big." A yearly festival she organizes is called Spirit of Our Ancestors. The 2021 festival, the third, honored the women who survived the *Clotilda*.

She appears in *Descendant*, the documentary by Margaret Brown. It won a special jury award at the Sundance Film Festival in January 2022 and was released in theaters and on Netflix on October 21, 2022.

<a id="ch-rights-movements"></a>

## Chapter 25: Rights and Movements

### Before 1500

A rights movement is a group of people who organize together to change a rule that denies them something. No record shows a movement of that kind in this land before 1500. In 1492 about six hundred Native nations lived in North America north of the Rio Grande, the river that now runs along part of the border with Mexico. Each nation governed itself in its own way. In at least one of them, the Haudenosaunee, a union of five nations in what is now New York, women held power in government. Each clan, a group of related families, had a leading woman called the clan mother, and she chose the man who led for the clan. When he did not do his job, she warned him, and his clan could then remove him.

#### The clan mothers of the Haudenosaunee

The Haudenosaunee Confederacy is a union of nations. Its five founding nations are the Seneca, the Cayuga, the Onondaga, the Oneida and the Mohawk. The Onondaga Nation's own account states that the founding took place on the shores of Onondaga Lake, in what is now central New York. The Onondaga still describe how their women choose leaders.

A clan is a group of related families. Each clan has a clan mother. She chooses the man who speaks for her clan in council, the meeting where the chiefs talk and decide together. His title is Hoyane, which means chief. The Onondaga Nation records that a figure called the Peacemaker placed deer antlers on the headdress of every Hoyane. The antlers show that the man is a chief.

The clan mother can also start the removal of a chief. If the chief stops speaking for his clan, she warns him that he is not following the ways of the Great Peace and must change. The Great Peace, also called the Great Law of Peace, is the set of laws that the people of the five nations agreed to live by when they joined together. If he still does not change, the clan removes him in council. The clan takes his antlers off, and the Onondaga say that he has been "de-horned."

The National Park Service is the part of the US government that runs the country's national parks and historic sites. An article on its website records more of the women's powers. Haudenosaunee women grew the food and shared it out. Through that work, the article states, the women "controlled the economy" of their nations, meaning the food and goods their people lived on. They also held "the final authority over land transfers and decisions about engaging in war." That means the women had the last word on whether land was handed to anyone else and on whether their nation went to war. When a husband and wife separated, the wife took with her all the property she had brought into the home, and the children went with her.

Nobody can prove when the five nations agreed to the Great Law of Peace. The Haudenosaunee keep their own account of it in spoken history and in wampum, belts and strings of shell beads that record agreements. By that account, the date falls between about the year 1000 and 1400. The encyclopedia Britannica reports that scholars working from written records mostly date it around 1450, and that some date it to the late 1100s.

#### What the records can and cannot show

Almost everything written down about how these nations governed themselves was written after Europeans arrived, by Europeans. The nations kept their own records in spoken accounts and in wampum. Wampum is beads cut from the white and purple parts of clam shells and woven into strings and belts. The Onondaga Nation describes how it works: a speaker puts the words of an agreement into the wampum while the belt is woven. Every speaker after that uses the belt to remember the agreement and what has happened since. The Onondaga have been the wampum keepers of the Confederacy since its founding.

No record from before 1500 in this land names a single person who claimed a right that others denied.

### The 1500s

Spanish settlers in the 1500s forced Native people to work for them under Spanish law. No group organized to change that law. In Spain, a Spanish priest named Bartolomé de Las Casas argued that Native people had rights. People also fought back in this century. In October 1526, enslaved Africans at San Miguel de Gualdape, a Spanish settlement on the coast of what is now Georgia or the Carolinas, rose up and escaped. It is the first rebellion of enslaved Africans on record in what became the United States.

#### The encomienda

One Spanish system for forcing Native people to work was the encomienda. It was a grant from the Spanish king that gave a settler the labor of a named group of Native people. On paper, the settler had to protect them and teach them Christianity. In practice, he forced them to work for him and took the food and goods they produced. The historians who wrote the open textbook *The American Yawp* call it "an exploitive feudal arrangement in which Spain tied Indigenous laborers to vast estates." Exploitive means using people for your own gain. "Feudal" refers to the old system in Europe in which farm workers were bound to a lord's land. "Indigenous" means Native, and the estates were huge farms. Under these grants, Spanish settlers held Native workers on their land. The same historians write that the settlers who held these grants "brutalized their laborers," meaning they beat and hurt the people who worked for them.

Las Casas came to the Caribbean in 1502. He later wrote that he saw Spaniards "cut off the Hands, Noses, and Ears, both of Indians and Indianesses," meaning Native men and women. They did it, he wrote, "for no other reason, but only to gratify their bloody mindedness," meaning for the pleasure of hurting people.

The Caribbean island of Hispaniola was one of the places where Spanish settlers forced Native people to work this way. The Native people of the islands were the Taíno. Spaniards enslaved them and made them dig for gold. When the gold ran out, the Spaniards forced them to work on the encomienda farms. The Native population of Hispaniola fell from 60,000 in 1508 to fewer than 20,000 ten years later. The authors of *The American Yawp* write of the Spaniards' "casual violence and dehumanizing exploitation." Dehumanizing means treating people as if they were not human. Within a few generations, the same authors write, the whole island had been emptied of its Native people.

In 1542 King Charles I of Spain ended the encomienda with a set of rules called the New Laws. Spanish officials replaced it with another forced-labor system, the repartimiento, and Spanish settlers went on forcing Native people to work for them.

#### Bartolomé de Las Casas

In 1513 Las Casas went to Cuba as a chaplain, a priest who travels with soldiers. He served with the Spanish forces who were taking the island from the Taíno. In his *History of the Indies*, he later wrote what he saw at the town of Caonao. The Spanish soldiers were under the command of Captain Narváez. The Taíno there had made cassava bread and fish for them. About two thousand people sat in the town square, and more than five hundred were in a large house nearby. One Spaniard drew his sword. Then the whole hundred soldiers drew theirs. In Las Casas's words, they began "to rip open the bellies, to cut and kill" the men, women, children and old people, who were all sitting down. They went into the large house and killed the people there too. Some escaped by climbing to the top of the house. Las Casas had stepped away to another part of the town shortly before.

For serving with the soldiers, Las Casas received land and an encomienda. In 1514 he told the people of his church that the whole encomienda system was wrong. He freed the Native people he held and began arguing for them to the Spanish officials on the island.

In 1516 he asked the Spanish king to bring enslaved Africans to the Indies, the Spanish name for Spain's islands and lands across the Atlantic, to take the place of Native workers. He believed Africans were better suited to hard physical labor. Slave traders had already been carrying enslaved Africans across the Atlantic for about sixteen years. On 18 August 1518, King Charles I of Spain, later Emperor Charles V, gave a man named Lorenzo de Gorrevod a charter, a written permission, to ship enslaved Africans across the Atlantic.

Las Casas wrote a short book about what Spanish settlers did to Native people. Its Spanish title is *Brevísima relación de la destrucción de las Indias*, in English *A Brief Account of the Devastation of the Indies*. Soon after he wrote it, King Charles issued the New Laws of 1542.

In 1550, Charles V called Las Casas and a scholar named Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda to the town of Valladolid, in Spain. The question was whether the Spanish had the right to make war on Native people and rule them by force. Sepúlveda argued that they did. Las Casas argued that they did not. They spoke in front of a panel of churchmen and royal officials, among them the church scholars Domingo Soto and Melchor Cano. On the first day Sepúlveda spoke for three hours. The panel held its final meeting in 1551. Andrea Daher, a scholar writing for an encyclopedia of Sorbonne University in Paris, records no ruling by the panel.

Later in life, Las Casas changed his mind about enslaving Africans. In his *History of the Indies* he wrote at length against the African slave trade and the slave markets of Spain and Portugal. He did not publish that book while he was alive, so his change of mind was not public while the trade grew.

### The 1600s

English colonists brought English law with them. Under one of its rules, a married woman did not count in law as a person separate from her husband. Nobody organized against that rule in this century. The men in charge punished people who spoke against them, and the records name those people. In November 1637 the men who ran Massachusetts, sitting as a court, banished Anne Hutchinson, which means they ordered her out of the colony for good. They did it because of what she taught at religious meetings in her house. In 1660 Massachusetts officials hanged Mary Dyer on Boston Common for coming back to the colony as a Quaker, a member of a new religion that the colony's leaders had outlawed. In 1688 four men in Pennsylvania signed a protest against slavery together and sent it to their church.

#### Coverture: what marriage did to a woman in law

The rule was called coverture. In law, a married woman was "covered" by her husband. The legal name for her was *feme covert*, which means a covered woman. She had no legal standing of her own.

In law, that meant she did not control property, even property she had brought into the marriage. Her husband had full rights to any money or wages she earned. She could not sign a contract, a written deal that a court can make people keep. Nobody could take her to court, and she could not bring a case to court in her own name.

An adult woman who had never married, or whose husband had died, was a *feme sole*, a woman on her own. She could buy and sell property, sign contracts and go to court in her own name. Under English law, a woman lost those rights on the day she married.

In daily life, wives ran businesses beside their husbands, and for husbands who were away. Some married women traded in their own names under a legal exception, and the people of their town held everyone to the deal. Under the law, whatever a wife held, she held because her husband allowed it.

<a id="story-anne-hutchinson-rights-movements"></a>

#### Anne Hutchinson

> **Who:** A Boston woman put on trial for what she taught at religious meetings in her own house, and banished from Massachusetts for it.
>
> **When and where:** Boston and Newtown, Massachusetts Bay Colony. Meetings from 1636, trial in November 1637, put out of her church in March 1638.

In November 1637 the leaders of Massachusetts put Anne Hutchinson on trial for heresy, which means teaching against the church's beliefs. They banished her, which means they forced her to leave the colony and forbade her to return. The charge grew out of the religious meetings she held in her home for men and women, and out of what she taught there. The colony's governor told her that such meetings were not fitting for a woman.

She was born about 1591 at Alford, in England. In the fall of 1634 she crossed the Atlantic on the ship *Griffin* with her husband, William, and their children. They followed their minister, John Cotton, to Boston, a town the English had built on Massachusett land.

From 1636 she held a weekly meeting in her house to go over the Sunday sermons. At first only women came. Then men came too, including some of the most important men in the colony. Like the colony's leaders, she was a Puritan, one of the English Protestants who had come to Massachusetts to worship God in their own way. In Puritan teaching, grace meant God's gift of being saved, which means going to heaven after death. She said she could tell which ministers and which neighbors had received God's grace. She taught that God saved people by grace alone, and not because they behaved well.

In November 1637 the colony's lawmakers, sitting as judges, tried her at Newtown, the town now called Cambridge. These men were called the General Court. They made the colony's laws, and they also judged cases. The trial lasted two days.

Governor John Winthrop opened it by telling her she was "called here as one of those that have troubled the peace of the commonwealth." The commonwealth meant the colony. He called her meetings "a thing not tolerable nor comely in the sight of God nor fitting for your sex." He meant that the meetings should not be allowed, were not proper in God's eyes and were not fitting for a woman. She answered his Bible verses with Bible verses of her own. At the end of the trial she said God had spoken to her directly, by "an immediate revelation," a message straight from God. She said God would curse the Puritans and their families for all the generations after them if they harmed her. The men judging her called that blasphemy, which means speaking against God.

She told the judges, "You have power over my body, but the Lord Jesus hath power over my body and soul."

The trial record states the sentence: "Mrs. Hutchinson, the sentence of the court you hear is that you are banished from out of our jurisdiction as being a woman not fit for our society." A jurisdiction is the area that a government rules. She asked, "I desire to know wherefore I am banished?" Wherefore means why.

Colony officials held her through the winter. In March 1638 the leaders of the Boston church tried her a second time and put her out of the church. Their charge said she had "rather been a Husband than a Wife and a preacher than a Hearer." The charge went on, "and a Magistrate than a Subject." A magistrate is an official with the power to judge cases and enforce the laws.

In the spring of 1638 the family moved to Aquidneck Island, in what became Rhode Island. The minister Roger Williams helped them buy land there from the Narragansett. One of the first written rules of their new town, Portsmouth, stated that no person should be punished or "called into question on matter of religion ... so long as he keeps the peace."

After her husband died, she moved in 1642 to Dutch-held land on Long Island Sound. It was the country of the Siwanoy, a Native people. The Dutch governor, Willem Kieft, had started a war with the Native people there. On the night of 25 February 1643, armed Dutch settlers murdered Munsee people at Corlaer's Hook, on Manhattan. Dutch soldiers did the same at Pavonia, across the Hudson River. Together they murdered at least eighty Munsee people, and perhaps as many as 120. The Munsee were a Native people of that region. Kieft and his council had approved both attacks. In August or September 1643, Siwanoy warriors killed Anne Hutchinson, her servants and all but one of the children who were with her. One daughter survived.

#### Massachusetts leaders outlaw Quakers, then hang four of them

In 1660, Massachusetts officials hanged a woman named Mary Dyer because she kept coming back to the colony as a Quaker. The Quakers followed George Fox, an Englishman who had founded a new religion. Fox taught that men and women were equal in God's eyes. Quakers refused to take their hats off to people of higher rank, because they believed all people were equal, and they refused to swear oaths, solemn promises made in God's name, to any government. Massachusetts Governor John Endecott called them a "pernicious sect," meaning a harmful religious group.

The men of the General Court passed a series of laws against Quakers. In late 1656 and 1657 they outlawed "the cursed sect of heretics commonly called Quakers." They fined ship captains who brought Quakers to the colony and people who owned Quaker books. In October 1657 they set punishments for Quakers who came back after being sent away. Their law stated that a man who came back once should have one ear cut off with a blade, and a man who came back a second time should lose the other ear. For a third return, the law stated, "they shall have their tongues bored through with a hot iron." That means a hole burned through the tongue with a heated iron rod. For women who came back, the law set whipping, which means being struck on the bare back with a whip.

In 1658 the colony's leaders used that law against a Quaker named Christopher Holder and two other Quaker men. One of the two was John Rous. Governor John Endecott sent Rous to prison, and on 7 September 1658 Rous was sentenced to have his right ear cut off. A British reference book, the *Dictionary of National Biography*, states that the cutting was done inside the prison, although the law called for it to be done in public. A chronology by the law professor Douglas Linder gives a different date, 3 June 1658, for the cutting of the three men's ears. Linder's chronology adds that the men were also whipped, and then beaten twice a week for nine weeks. Neither account names the judges or the men who did the cutting, the whipping and the beating.
