On 19 October 1658 the men of the General Court voted 12 to 11 to banish Quakers "upon pain of death." Under that law, a Quaker who came back after being sent away could be hanged.

Mary Dyer had lived in Boston in the 1630s. She was a close friend of Anne Hutchinson, and when leaders of the Boston church put Hutchinson out in March 1638, Dyer walked out of the church beside her. Around 1650 she met George Fox in England. She came back to Boston as a Quaker in 1657. Officials jailed her as soon as she landed, and she spent two and a half months in a dark cell with its windows boarded up. Her husband got her out by promising she would not preach, and the family moved to Rhode Island. She kept going back to Massachusetts to stand by Quakers who were in prison there.

On 20 October 1659, Governor Endecott sentenced Mary Dyer and two Quaker men to death. The men were William Robinson, a merchant from London, and Marmaduke Stephenson, a farm worker from Yorkshire. Dyer's son, William Dyer, asked the governor to spare her. On 26 October Endecott signed an order giving her 48 hours to leave the colony. The same order said she must first be taken to the gallows, the wooden frame used for hangings, and stand there with a rope around her neck while the two men were hanged. On 27 October 1659, officials hanged Robinson and Stephenson in front of her. Then they took her back to prison and sent her out of the colony.

She came back to Massachusetts in 1660. Her husband asked for her life, and she refused to say she was sorry. On 1 June officials hanged Mary Dyer near the Frog Pond on Boston Common, on the sentence of Governor Endecott and the General Court. About 200 soldiers stood around the gallows with guns, swords, long spears called pikes, and flags.

In 1661 officials hanged a fourth Quaker in Boston, William Leddra, a cloth maker and Quaker minister from Cornwall, in England. An English Quaker named Edward Burrough counted what had been done to Quakers in Massachusetts between 1656 and 1660. His count lists 64 jailings and 25 banishments. On 9 September 1661, King Charles II of England ordered the punishments stopped and said accused Quakers must be sent to England instead. By 1677, Quakers could meet openly in Massachusetts.

#### Four men sign a protest against slavery, 1688

On 18 April 1688, four men at Germantown, in Pennsylvania, signed a paper against owning enslaved people. Their names were Garret Hendericks, Francis Daniel Pastorius, Derick op de Graeff and Abraham op de Graeff. They sent it up through the meetings of their Quaker church. A National Park Service page calls it the first protest against African slavery made by a religious body in the English colonies.

Germantown stood on the land of the Lenape, the Native people of the Philadelphia region. Pastorius had bought the land in 1683 from William Penn, a Quaker to whom King Charles II had given a charter for Pennsylvania in 1681. The surviving records of that sale do not name the Lenape families who lived on it.

The protest rested on the Golden Rule, the teaching that people should treat others as they want to be treated. In the paper's own spelling, the rule was "that we shall doe to all men licke as we will be done ourselves."

A Quaker meeting is a group of Quakers who worship together and make decisions together. A monthly meeting is a local group. A quarterly meeting joins several local groups, and a yearly meeting joins the Quakers of a whole region. The members of four meetings, one after another, read the paper and passed it on without acting. The first was Germantown Monthly Meeting, then Dublin Monthly Meeting, then Philadelphia Quarterly Meeting. The last was Burlington Yearly Meeting, in New Jersey, and its members voted to take no stand either way. Nothing changed because of the protest.

The Quakers put the paper aside and forgot it. Abolitionists, people working to end slavery, found it again in 1844. Then it went missing a second time. In March 2005 it turned up in a vault at the Arch Street Meetinghouse in Philadelphia. It is now kept at Haverford College, in Pennsylvania.

### 1700 to 1750

Between 1700 and 1750, a few men, each on his own, printed arguments against slavery, and the Quakers began to argue about it among themselves. There was still no organized group working for anyone's rights. The Quaker leaders punished the members who raised the question first. By 1776, the Quakers of Philadelphia had changed their own rules anyway and banned slaveholding among their members.

#### A Boston merchant writes a pamphlet against slavery, 1700

In 1700 Samuel Sewall, a Boston merchant and magistrate, an official with the power to judge cases and enforce the laws, wrote a three-page pamphlet called *The Selling of Joseph*. A pamphlet is a short printed booklet. A Massachusetts Historical Society page calls it the first antislavery pamphlet published in America. Bartholomew Green and John Allen printed it in Boston.

Sewall argued that taking people and selling them is the crime the Bible calls man stealing, and he pointed to the verse Exodus 21:16. Then he went through the usual arguments in favor of slavery and answered each one.

Sewall wrote it because of a case in Boston. In 1700 a petition, a written request signed by people, went around Boston asking for the freedom of an enslaved man named Adam and his wife, who were "unjustly held in Bondage" by a merchant named John Saffin. Saffin had promised Adam his freedom after seven years of good behavior. When the seven years were up, Saffin would not free him.

Saffin printed an answer to Sewall in 1701, defending slavery and his own treatment of Adam. Adam went to court, and in 1703 he won his freedom. Sewall answered Saffin again in 1705 by reprinting an English attack on the slave trade.

#### Quakers who spoke first, and what their church did to them

Among the Quakers, an argument about slavery kept going in these years. Their own church leaders spoke out against the first Quakers who pressed it.

Ralph Sandiford published *A Brief Examination of the Practice of the Times* in Philadelphia in 1729. It argued against owning slaves. Quaker leaders spoke out against it in public.

Benjamin Lay was born in Essex, in England, in 1682. From 1718 he and his wife spent about eighteen months in Barbados, an island in the Caribbean. By 1660, enslaved Africans there already outnumbered the white settlers, about 27,000 to 26,000. He later wrote that there he "saw and heard of such very great Barbarity used toward the Slaves, Night and Day." Barbarity means cruelty. A man named Richard Parrot whipped the people he enslaved "very severely" every Monday morning. One of them, a barrel maker, told Lay he would not be whipped on Monday morning, and he killed himself on a Sunday. Hungry enslaved workers came into the Lays' shop to buy, to beg, and sometimes to steal food. Lay wrote that when he caught them he sometimes whipped them, "but I have been sorry for it many times."

Then Lay settled near Philadelphia. He was just over 4 feet tall, with a hunched back and thin arms and legs. For a time he lived in a cave with a library of about 200 books. His wife, Sarah Lay, was also small and had a curved spine. She was a recorded Quaker minister, a speaker her meeting officially recognized.

In 1737 Lay published a book against slaveholding with a long title: *All Slave-Keepers That Keep the Innocent in Bondage, Apostates*. An apostate is a person who has abandoned their faith. Benjamin Franklin printed it and left his own name off it. Quaker leaders spoke out against the book, and the Quakers of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting disowned Lay. Disowning was a formal statement that a member no longer shared an essential part of the faith. The member's name came off the membership list, and he could no longer hold certain offices, though he could still come to worship. Sarah Lay stayed a member all her life.

In 1738, at the yearly meeting's gathering in Burlington, New Jersey, Lay stood up in front of the Quakers there. His words began, "Oh, all you negro masters, who are contentedly holding your fellow-creatures in a state of slavery during life." Negro was a word then used for Black people. He threw off his plain Quaker cloak. Underneath he wore a soldier's uniform, in front of people who were committed to peace. He said that holding people as slaves would be as right, or "as justifiable," as "if you should thrust a sword through their hearts, as I do through this." Then he drove a sword into a hollowed-out book. Inside it he had hidden an animal bladder filled with pokeberry juice, and the red juice sprayed the people near him. The Quakers carried him out and laid him on the doorstep. He lay there for the rest of the day, so everyone leaving had to step over him. Lay died in 1759.

#### The Quaker meetings change their rules, 1754 to 1778

Quakers changed their rules step by step after 1750. In 1754 the Quakers of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting published a paper that called slavery a sin, and sent it to other meetings. In 1758 the members of the yearly meeting spoke out against buying and selling people, but still allowed members to keep the people they already held.

In 1776 the members of Philadelphia Yearly Meeting banned slaveholding among themselves, 88 years after the four men at Germantown signed their protest. A Quaker who held people in slavery could now be disowned. Philadelphia Quakers disowned the first members for it in 1778. Quakers in other regions made the same change in those years. The members of New England Yearly Meeting made slaveholding a reason to disown a member in 1773. New York Quakers spoke out against slaveholding in 1774, and North Carolina Quakers made it a reason to disown a member in 1776.

### 1750 to 1800

In 1775 a group of men in Philadelphia formed a society to help free people who had been seized and held as slaves against the law. On 4 July 1776 the delegates to the Continental Congress voted to adopt the Declaration of Independence, which states that "all men are created equal." The men who wrote the other new state constitutions of 1776 kept women from voting. New Jersey's did not. Some of the people left out of those rights answered with the Revolution's own words. Black taxpayers in Massachusetts asked why they paid taxes without a vote. In New Jersey, some women and some free Black men could vote for thirty-one years, until the state's lawmakers took the vote away in 1807.

#### Dinah Nevil and the first antislavery society, 1775

The Philadelphia antislavery society of 1775 started because of one woman's claim that she was free. Her name was Dinah Nevil, and the records call her an Indian woman, meaning a Native American. In 1773 a Virginia man named Benjamin Bannarman bought Nevil and her four children from Nathaniel Lowry of New Jersey. When they were delivered in Philadelphia, Nevil said in public that she and her children were "free people."

The mayor of Philadelphia sent Nevil and her children to the city's Work House, a building where the city held people, to wait for a hearing. A group of Quakers led by Israel Pemberton brought a lawsuit for her. The case ran for two years. At the end, the judges ruled that Dinah Nevil and her children were slaves. The society's records do not name the judges.

On 14 April 1775, after that ruling and others like it, a group of men met at the Rising Sun Tavern in Philadelphia. They formed the Society for the Relief of Free Negroes Unlawfully Held in Bondage. Sixteen of the 24 first members were Quakers. Thomas Harrison was the secretary, and Anthony Benezet was a member. A Historical Society of Pennsylvania page calls it the first abolition society in the western world. Its first work was helping free people of color, people who were not white, who had been seized and held as slaves.

The members stopped meeting in November 1775. Most of them were Quakers, who refused to fight in the war with Britain, and they believed that refusal would turn people against the society.

Dinah Nevil did not win her case. In 1781 Thomas Harrison, who had been caring for her and her children, used his own money to buy the family from the man who claimed them. Then he freed them. Judges had kept rejecting her claim, and buying her was the only way left. Eight years had passed since she first said she was free.

The society began meeting again on 23 April 1787 and let in members who were not Quakers. Its members elected Benjamin Franklin president. Later members included Benjamin Rush, Thomas Paine and John Jay. People in other states set up societies like it. New York had one by 1785, two years before the Philadelphia society met again. In 1787 Richard Allen, Absalom Jones and other Black Philadelphians formed their own group, the Free African Society. In 1789 the Philadelphia members got a charter, an official paper from the Pennsylvania government that recognized the society. They also took a longer name: the Pennsylvania Society for Promoting the Abolition of Slavery, for the Relief of Free Negroes Unlawfully Held in Bondage, and for Improving the Condition of the African Race. By 1790 Delaware, Maryland and Connecticut had societies too.

<a id="story-abigail-adams"></a>

#### Abigail Adams

> **Who:** A Massachusetts woman who wrote to her husband while he was helping lead a new country, and asked him to "Remember the Ladies" in its laws.
>
> **When and where:** Braintree, Massachusetts. Letters of 31 March, 14 April and 7 May 1776.
>
> **Movie:** John Adams (2008 HBO miniseries). The series is about John Adams and his family. Abigail is a lead character, not the subject.

In the spring of 1776, Abigail Adams asked her husband, John, to limit a husband's power over his wife in the new country's laws. He wrote back that he could only laugh at the idea.

John Adams had been away at the Continental Congress in Philadelphia since 1774. That summer he helped draft the Declaration of Independence. Abigail Adams stayed at home in Braintree, the town now called Quincy, Massachusetts. She ran the family farm and its money. The couple wrote to each other often, and their letters are kept at the Massachusetts Historical Society.

On 31 March 1776 she wrote, in her own spelling, "I long to hear that you have declared an independency." She went on: "and by the way in the new Code of Laws which I suppose it will be necessary for you to make I desire you would Remember the Ladies, and be more generous and favourable to them than your ancestors. Do not put such unlimited power into the hands of the Husbands. Remember all Men would be tyrants if they could. If perticuliar care and attention is not paid to the Laidies we are determined to foment a Rebelion, and will not hold ourselves bound by any Laws in which we have no voice, or Representation." To foment a rebellion means to stir one up. Tyrants are rulers who use their power cruelly.

In 1776 the rule of coverture still governed marriage in the colonies. Under it, a husband controlled everything his wife owned and earned. An English lawyer, William Blackstone, had written the rule down a few years earlier, in his *Commentaries on the Laws of England*, published from 1765 to 1769. "By marriage, the husband and wife are one person in law," he wrote, "that is, the very being or legal existence of the woman is suspended during the marriage, or at least is incorporated and consolidated into that of the husband." While she was married, a wife did not exist in law as her own person. Her legal self was folded into her husband's. Blackstone did not invent the rule. It was already centuries old.

Her last sentence used the same complaint that the colonists were making against Britain. In the Declaration of Independence that July, the delegates accused the British king of "imposing Taxes on us without our Consent." They also called "the right of Representation in the Legislature," the right to have a say in the body that makes the laws, "a right inestimable to them," meaning too precious to measure.

John Adams answered on 14 April 1776: "As to your extraordinary Code of Laws, I cannot but laugh." He wrote, "We have been told that our Struggle has loosened the bands of Government every where." He listed who had grown bold: "That Children and Apprentices were disobedient," and "that schools and Colledges were grown turbulent," meaning rowdy. He added "that Indians slighted their Guardians and Negroes grew insolent to their Masters." Slighted means treated without respect. By "Negroes" and "their Masters" he meant enslaved Black people and the men who enslaved them. Insolent means rude to someone in charge. He would not give up the men's power, he wrote, because that "would compleatly subject Us to the Despotism of the Peticoat." Despotism means rule by a tyrant, and a petticoat was a woman's underskirt. He meant rule by women.

She wrote back on 7 May 1776: "I can not say that I think you very generous to the Ladies, for whilst you are proclaiming peace and good will to Men, Emancipating all Nations, you insist upon retaining an absolute power over Wives." She added that "Arbitary power is like most other things which are very hard, very liable to be broken." Emancipating means setting free. Arbitrary power is power used however the ruler likes, with no rules to limit it.

No lawmakers in any state changed a law for women because of these letters. The letters were private. In 1840, more than twenty years after she died, her grandson Charles Francis Adams published a book of her letters called *Letters of Mrs. Adams, the Wife of John Adams*.

#### Some women and free Black men vote in New Jersey, 1776 to 1807

From 1776 to 1807, unmarried women and free Black men who owned enough property could vote in New Jersey. New Jersey's constitution of 1776 gave the vote to "all inhabitants of this colony, of full age, who are worth fifty pounds ... and have resided within the county ... for twelve months." It did not say male, and it did not say white. The other states' constitutions of 1776 limited the vote to a "freeman," a "man" or a white man, and every one of them left women out.

Because of coverture, only unmarried women and widows could meet New Jersey's property test. A married woman could not own fifty pounds of anything, because in law everything she had belonged to her husband. In 1800 members of the state assembly said so: "Our Constitution gives this right to maids or widows black or white." Maids meant unmarried women. Some losing candidates later complained that married women had voted anyway.

The state's election laws of 1790 and 1797 described the voter as "he or she." Researchers at the Museum of the American Revolution have found 163 women's names on nine lists of voters from 1800 to 1807. That count is the lowest possible number, because only nine lists survive. Sarah Eoff, Margaret McDonald and Eleanor Boylan are on the 1800 list for Bedminster Township. Eleanor Boylan was a widow of about 51 when she voted. In October 1801, four women of one family, Rebecca, Ann, Catherine and Sarah VanDike, voted together. The 1801 list for Montgomery Township holds at least 46 women and at least four free Black men, among them Caesar Trent of Princeton.

The men who made New Jersey's laws took the vote away in November 1807. Earlier that year, in February, Essex County held a vote on whether to build a new courthouse in Newark or in Elizabeth. People on both sides broke the rules and brought in voters who had no right to vote. In Elizabeth the number of votes counted came to 279 percent of the people allowed to vote, nearly three votes for every person allowed to vote. The new law limited the vote to "free, white, male citizens." Under it, the lawmakers took the vote away from women, from free Black men and from recent immigrants. In the law's opening paragraph, the lawmakers wrote that there were "doubts" about letting "aliens, persons of color, or negroes" vote. Aliens meant people from other countries who were not citizens. An exhibit by the Museum of the American Revolution says that in this way the lawmakers blamed women, people of color and newcomers for all the cheating. The museum calls it scapegoating, which means putting the blame on people who were not at fault.

Writers for the National Park Service, the New Jersey Historical Commission and the Museum of the American Revolution all say the lawmakers acted for party reasons, not out of a debate about women's rights. The museum's historians also link the law to the cheating in the courthouse vote. The three disagree about which party women's votes had helped. The two parties of the time were the Federalists and the Democratic-Republicans, two groups that ran candidates against each other. A National Park Service page says women often voted for the Federalist Party, and the law helped the rival Democratic-Republicans before the 1808 presidential election. A New Jersey Historical Commission teaching sheet says Federalists had come to believe that women's votes helped the Democratic-Republicans.

#### No vote, no taxes: Paul and John Cuffe, 1780

In February 1780, seven free Black men of Dartmouth, Massachusetts, told the state's lawmakers that they should not be taxed if they could not vote. They were John Cuffe, Adventur Child, Paul Cuffe, Samuel Gray, Pero Howland, Pero Russell and Pero Coggeshall. John and Paul Cuffe were brothers. Gray, Howland and Russell signed with a mark instead of a written name.

The petition said that "by reason of long bondage and hard slavery, we have been deprived of enjoying the profits of our labor or the advantage of inheriting estates from our parents." They were taxed all the same, although "we are not allowed the privilege of freemen of the State, having no vote or influence in the election of those that tax us." It pointed out that "many of our colour (as is well known) have cheerfully entered the field of battle in the defence of the common cause," meaning they had fought in the Revolution.

The new Massachusetts constitution of March 1780 contained nothing that answered their complaint. The Cuffe brothers wrote to the county court and to the town's leaders, calling themselves both "Indian men" and "free Negroes." They refused to pay their taxes, and Dartmouth's town officials put them in jail for it.

#### Prince Hall asks for schools, 1787

In 1787 Prince Hall and other Black Bostonians asked the Massachusetts lawmakers for schools for their children. No law barred Black children from Boston's free schools, but the National Park Service records that Black students there "found themselves at the mercy of hostile teachers and fellow students." The petition said they "receive no benefit from the free schools in the town of Boston, which we think is a great grievance, as by woful experience we now feel the want of a common education." A grievance is a wrong that people complain about.

The lawmakers turned the petition down. They turned down a second petition in 1796. In 1798 the families opened their own school, the African School. It met in the home of Primus Hall, Prince Hall's son.

#### Judith Sargent Murray argues that women's minds are equal, 1790

In 1790 Judith Sargent Murray published an essay called "On the Equality of the Sexes." She was born on 1 May 1751 in Gloucester, Massachusetts. The essay ran in the *Massachusetts Magazine* under the pen name "Constantia," a made-up name for signing her writing. She argued that men and women have equal minds, and that women fell behind only because girls did not get the education that boys got. One line of the essay asks "in what the minds of females are so notoriously deficient, or unequal." Unlike Abigail Adams's private letters, the essay was printed where anyone could read it.

### 1800 to 1850

Between 1800 and 1850, many groups of Americans organized to change rules that held them back. Women formed antislavery societies, gathered signatures on petitions, which are written requests to people in power, and sent them to Congress. They also spoke to crowds. Ministers, lawmakers and mobs attacked them for doing it. Some of those women then turned the same methods to their own rights. In July 1848, more than 300 people met at Seneca Falls, New York. One hundred of them signed a declaration that listed the wrongs men had done to women, and the people at the meeting voted to demand the vote. Black families in Boston campaigned to get their children into the city's schools. In 1817 teachers at a new school in Hartford, Connecticut, began teaching deaf children together in sign language.

#### Deaf children taught together, 1817

The American School for the Deaf opened at Hartford, Connecticut, on 15 April 1817, in a building called Bennett's City Hotel. Seven pupils came full time in the first classes. Teachers taught them in sign language, using a method from France.

Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet founded the school with Laurent Clerc, a deaf French teacher whom Gallaudet brought back from Paris. A Hartford doctor, Mason Fitch Cogswell, and ten other Hartford men backed them. Cogswell's deaf daughter, Alice Cogswell, was one of the first pupils.

Public money came early. In October 1816, before the school opened, Connecticut's lawmakers voted the school $5,000. An essay by John Crowley for the Disability History Museum calls that grant the first public money for educating Americans with disabilities. In 1819 members of Congress voted to give the school 23,000 acres of public land in Alabama, after a motion by Henry Clay. It was land the United States had taken from Native nations. The surviving accounts do not say which nation's land it had been. The school's leaders sold the land to build up an endowment, a sum of money kept and invested so that its earnings pay for the school's work.

#### Girls ask for the same lessons as boys

Some of the first organized demands for women between 1800 and 1850 were about schooling. Girls' schools usually taught manners and fine arts. A few women opened schools that taught girls the subjects boys learned.

In 1819 Emma Willard wrote *A Plan for Improving Female Education* and addressed it to New York's lawmakers. She argued that young women needed the same subjects young men were taught. With the support of Governor DeWitt Clinton, she opened the Troy Female Seminary in Troy, New York, in 1821. A seminary was a school for older girls or young women.

Catharine Beecher and her sister Mary opened the Hartford Female Seminary in Connecticut on 20 May 1823. Their pupils studied geography, world history, Latin, rhetoric (the art of speaking and writing well), philosophy and the natural sciences. Within three years the school had 100 full-time pupils.

Mary Lyon began raising money in 1834 for a school for women. She opened Mount Holyoke Female Seminary at South Hadley, Massachusetts, in 1837. Gifts ran from six cents to $1,000. Women's sewing circles sent quilts and bedding, and the school's trustees, the people in charge of its money and buildings, gave stoves and furniture. Tuition was $60 a year. A history page by Mount Holyoke College says Lyon "endured ridicule from those who felt her ambitious undertaking would be 'wasted' on women." It adds that "The idea of a college for women was horrifying to many people in the 1830s."

At Oberlin, in Ohio, women won the chance to earn a college degree in two steps. Oberlin stands on land that the college's own art museum calls "unceded ancestral lands" of the Erie, Wyandotte, Mingo and other Native nations. Unceded means never given up by treaty or agreement.

Women studied beside men at Oberlin from its opening in 1833, but in a Ladies Course that ended with a diploma, not a degree. In 1837 four women entered the course that led to a bachelor's degree: Mary Kellogg, Mary Caroline Rudd, Mary Hosford and Elizabeth Prall. Rudd, Hosford and Prall graduated in 1841. Kellogg ran out of money, left, and came back later. Oberlin was the first college to give bachelor's degrees to women in classes with men.

In 1835 Oberlin also became the first college with a rule of admitting Black students.

#### Boston's Black families and the city's schools

Boston's Black families opened the African School in 1798, in Primus Hall's house. In 1808 they moved it into the basement of the African Meeting House. In the mid-1830s it moved into the Abiel Smith School. The Smith School became the segregated school where most of Boston's Black pupils were taught. Segregated means kept apart by race. The members of Boston's Primary School Committee kept separate schools for Black and white children.

In the late 1840s William Cooper Nell and others organized a boycott of the Smith School, which means families kept their children out of it in protest. They also gathered signatures on petitions against it. A father, Benjamin Roberts, asked the Primary School Committee four times to let his five-year-old daughter, Sarah, into the school nearest their home. To reach the Smith School she had to walk past five schools for white children. The committee's members refused each time, and in 1848 he sued the city of Boston.

#### Women petition Congress, 1829 to 1830

A petition is a written request to people in power, signed by the people who are asking. Women had no vote, and petitions were the way they first spoke to Congress about national questions. The House of Representatives' own historian says women first petitioned on political issues in 1829 and 1830.

The question was Indian removal, the plan to force the Cherokee and other Native nations off their land. On 31 December 1829, Catharine Beecher wrote a *Circular Addressed to Benevolent Ladies of the United States*. "It may be, that female petitioners can lawfully be heard, even by the highest rulers of our land," she wrote. More than 1,500 women signed petitions to Congress against removal. On 15 February 1830, women of Steubenville, Ohio, called themselves "the feeblest of the feeble" in theirs.

Members of Congress mocked the women in public. Senator Thomas Hart Benton of Missouri told "these ladies" to "sit down on the way side, and wait for the coming of the conquerors." In 1830 a majority in Congress voted for the Indian Removal Act.

#### Maria W. Stewart speaks in Boston, 1832

In September 1832, Maria W. Stewart, a free Black woman, spoke at Franklin Hall in Boston to an audience that included men. A National Park Service page calls it one of the first recorded times an American woman of any race spoke in public.

Stewart was born in 1803 in Hartford, Connecticut. In her own words she "was left an orphan at five years of age" and "was bound out in a clergyman's family," meaning she was sent to work as a servant in a minister's house. In Boston she and her husband, James W. Stewart, lived among the city's free Black families. In 1831 William Lloyd Garrison printed her essay "Religion and the Pure Principles of Morality" in his antislavery newspaper, *The Liberator*. In her speeches she asked, "How long shall the fair daughters of Africa be compelled to bury their minds and talents beneath a load of iron pots and kettles?" She urged her listeners, "Sue for your rights and privileges."

Audiences turned against her. She scolded Black men in public for drinking too much, and some people objected that it was improper for a woman to speak in front of men. On 21 September 1833 she gave a farewell speech. She asked, "What if I am a woman," and said it was "no use for me as an individual, to try to make myself useful among my color in this city." In 1834 she moved to New York and taught school. She later worked as matron, the woman in charge of housekeeping and care, at the Freedmen's Hospital in Washington, where she died on 17 December 1879.

<a id="story-prudence-crandall"></a>

#### Prudence Crandall and Sarah Harris

> **Who:** A young Black woman who asked to be taught, and the white teacher who was arrested, tried and attacked for teaching her and other Black girls.
>
> **When and where:** Canterbury, Connecticut, 1832 to 1834.

In 1832 Prudence Crandall let a young Black woman, Sarah Harris, into her school for girls in Canterbury, Connecticut. For the next two years the men of the town and the state fought to close the school, and in the end armed men attacked it.

Sarah Harris had finished primary school. Her father handed out *The Liberator*, Garrison's antislavery newspaper. She wanted enough schooling to teach Black children in the town of Norwich. She told Crandall, "I want to get a little more learning, if possible enough to teach colored children." Colored was a word then used for Black people. She added, "If you think it will be the means of injuring you, I will not insist on the favor."

Crandall admitted her. The white families took their daughters out of the school.

In the spring of 1833 Crandall went to Boston to see Garrison. Then she traveled around New England asking Black families to send their daughters. Her advertisements said the school would reopen on 1 April 1833 for "young ladies and little misses of color." About 24 pupils came, and most of them boarded in the house.

The man who led the fight against the school was Andrew T. Judson, a lawyer and politician who lived next door. He told the minister Samuel J. May, "we mean there shall not be such a school set up anywhere in our State." He also said, "They are an inferior race of beings, and never can or ought to be recognized as the equals of whites."

On 24 May 1833 the lawmakers of the Connecticut General Assembly passed what people called the Black Law. Under it, a school in the state that took Black pupils from outside Connecticut without the town's permission was breaking the law. They wrote it to close Crandall's school.

Connecticut officials arrested Crandall on 27 June 1833, and she spent a night in jail. Judson led the case against her. At her first trial the jury could not agree. At the second, in October 1833, Judge David Daggett told the jury that Black Americans were not citizens, so the protections her lawyers pointed to did not cover her pupils. The jury found her guilty. On 26 July 1834 the judges of the Connecticut Supreme Court threw out the guilty verdict on a technical point. The judges did not rule on the law itself, so the Black Law still stood.

Canterbury's town officials went after the pupils too. Ann Eliza Hammond was a 16-year-old pupil from Providence, Rhode Island, who arrived in April 1833. The town officials used the state's vagrancy law against her, a law against people with no home or work in the town. Its punishment was whipping "on the naked body not exceeding ten stripes," which means up to ten lashes of a whip on bare skin. Crandall paid so that no one whipped her.

Shopkeepers would not sell to the school, and people threw stones and eggs at the pupils. Someone hung a dead cat at the school door. In January 1834 a fire set by an unknown person damaged the building.

On the night of 9 September 1834, a mob of armed men broke the windows of the house and went through it with weapons while Crandall and her pupils were inside. A National Park Service page states that the mob broke more than ninety windows. Another account, in the Online Review of Rhode Island History, says the armed men broke five main windows on the first floor. No one was ever charged, and no record names the attackers. Crandall closed the school the next morning.

Crandall married a minister of the Baptist church, Calvin Philleo, and moved west to Illinois and then Kansas. In 1886 Connecticut's lawmakers voted her a pension of $400 a year. She died in Kansas in 1890, aged 87. Sarah Harris became an abolitionist, a person working to end slavery, and a conductor on the Underground Railroad, helping people escape from slavery. In 1877 she traveled to Kansas to visit Crandall, and the two women wrote to each other about their old pupils.

#### Mobs attack the organizers, 1835 to 1838

Between 1835 and 1838, white mobs in Boston, Alton and Philadelphia attacked people who organized against slavery. The mobs broke up meetings, destroyed printing presses, burned a hall and killed a newspaper editor. No one was convicted for any of the three attacks.

On 21 October 1835, a mob of about 5,000 men surrounded a meeting of the Boston Female Anti-Slavery Society at its room on Washington Street, in Boston. Maria Weston Chapman, her sisters Caroline, Anne and Deborah Weston, and eight other women had founded the society in 1834. Deborah Weston called it "the day when 5,000 men mobbed 45 women." A report in the *Hampshire Gazette* of 28 October 1835 described the crowd as citizens "calling themselves 'respectable.'"

When Mayor Theodore Lyman asked the women to leave, Maria Weston Chapman answered, "If this is the last bulwark of freedom, we may as well die here as anywhere." A bulwark is a strong wall that protects. The women walked out through the hissing crowd and finished their meeting at the Chapman house. The mob caught William Lloyd Garrison and dragged him through the streets at the end of a rope. Mayor Lyman and other men took him to the Leverett Street Jail and kept him there overnight so the mob could not reach him. No record names a man in the mob or shows that anyone was charged.

A mob in Alton, Illinois, shot and killed Elijah Lovejoy on 7 November 1837. He was a minister of the Presbyterian church, a Protestant church, and he printed an antislavery newspaper. After threats to hurt him, he had moved from St. Louis to Alton, 25 miles away, for safety. Mobs in Alton smashed three of his printing presses. On the night of 7 November, Lovejoy and a group of men guarded a fourth press in a warehouse. About 20 or 30 men of the town surrounded the building. Men in the armed mob shot Lovejoy five times as he stood in an open doorway. He died within the hour, two days before his 35th birthday.

In January 1838 Judge William Martin and a jury in Alton's city court tried the men who had defended the press, for riot. A riot is a violent disturbance by a crowd. The jury found the warehouse owner, Winthrop Gilman, not guilty in about fifteen minutes, and the prosecutor dropped the charges against the other eleven defenders. Then eleven men of the mob, among them John Solomon, Levi Palmer and James M. Rock, were tried for riot for breaking in and destroying the press. On 20 January 1838 the jury found them not guilty. No one was charged with killing Lovejoy, and the court record does not name who fired the shots.

In Philadelphia, on 17 May 1838, a mob burned down Pennsylvania Hall, a new meeting hall where antislavery groups met. The Pennsylvania Hall Association had raised about $40,000 to build it, and the Philadelphia Female Anti-Slavery Society raised much of that money. The hall opened on 14 May 1838. That week the Anti-Slavery Convention of American Women met in it. A convention is a large organized meeting. Three days after it opened, the mob set the hall on fire, using its own gas lights. Between 10,000 and 15,000 people watched, and 200 to 300 of them took part in the attack.

Mayor John Swift made what one history of the city calls "half-hearted efforts" to clear the crowd. Sheriff John G. Watmough arrested about a dozen men that night, and the crowd took them away from him. In all, officials arrested dozens of men and investigated five, and no court found any of them guilty. The same history records the rioters only as "dock workers and white rioters," and names none of them. In 1847 the judges of the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ordered the county to pay $27,942.27 for the damage.

<a id="story-grimke-sisters"></a>

#### Sarah and Angelina Grimké

> **Who:** Two sisters from a South Carolina slaveholding family who spoke against slavery to crowds of men and women, and were condemned from the pulpit for speaking at all.
>
> **When and where:** Charleston, then Philadelphia and New England. Their speaking tour ran in 1837 and 1838.

Sarah and Angelina Grimké were the first women to work as agents, or organizers, for the American Anti-Slavery Society. In 1837 ministers of the Congregational church, a Protestant church, in Massachusetts condemned them because they were women speaking in public, and the sisters answered with arguments for the rights of women.

Sarah was born on 26 November 1792 and Angelina on 20 February 1805. Their father, John Faucheraud Grimké, was a judge and cotton planter in Charleston, South Carolina, who held people in slavery. Both sisters became Quakers, members of a Christian group that taught that men and women were equal before God. Angelina left Charleston for Philadelphia in November 1829. In 1835 the sisters joined the American Anti-Slavery Society.

In July 1835 a mob in Charleston broke into the post office and burned antislavery papers. Angelina wrote a letter to William Lloyd Garrison about it, and he printed it in *The Liberator*. After that the sisters were not welcome in South Carolina.

At Poughkeepsie, New York, they spoke to a crowd of men and women together. In 23 weeks across 1837 and 1838 they spoke at 88 or more meetings in 67 towns, to more than 40,000 people.

In July 1837 the Congregational ministers of Massachusetts issued a Pastoral Letter, a message from church leaders to the members of their churches, and ministers read it aloud from their pulpits. The letter states that women like the sisters put "the female character" in danger of "wide spread and permanent injury." It criticizes "females" who take "an obtrusive and ostentatious part in measures of reform." Obtrusive and ostentatious mean pushing forward to be seen. The ministers attacked the sisters for being women who spoke in public.

Sarah Grimké answered the same month. The first of her "Letters on the Equality of the Sexes" ran in the *New England Spectator* in July 1837. At a convention of antislavery women in 1837, Angelina proposed that "the right of petition is natural and inalienable," meaning a right that nobody can take away.

At that time the House of Representatives had a rule, which its members adopted in 1836, that set aside every antislavery petition without reading it. People called it the gag rule. On 14 February 1838 women of Brookline, Massachusetts, petitioned the House to end it. They called the rule "an assumption of authority, at once dangerous and destructive to the fundamental principles of republican government, to the rights of minorities, to the sovereignty of the People." They meant that the rule went against the idea that the people hold the final power in their government, and against the rights of the smaller side in a vote. The first two names on the petition were Sarah M. Grimké and Angelina E. Grimké. Members of the House voted to renew the gag rule each time a new Congress met, every two years, until 1844.

On 21 February 1838, Angelina Grimké went to the Massachusetts State House in Boston. She gave a committee of the state's lawmakers antislavery petitions signed by about 20,000 Massachusetts women. She spoke to the committee in front of an overflowing crowd. The House of Representatives' historian calls her "the first woman in the United States to speak before a legislative body," meaning a group of lawmakers. She told the lawmakers, "I stand before you as a southerner, exiled from the land of my birth by the sound of the lash and the piteous cry of the slave." Exiled means driven away from home, and piteous means full of pain. She also said, "We are citizens of this republic and as such our honor, happiness, and well-being are bound up in its politics, government, and laws."

Both sisters lived to see the end of slavery in the United States. Sarah died in 1873 and Angelina in 1879, before American women won the vote.

<a id="story-dorothea-dix"></a>

#### Dorothea Dix

> **Who:** A Massachusetts woman who visited every jail and poorhouse in her state, wrote down how the people who ran them held people with mental illness, and handed the record to the state's lawmakers.
>
> **When and where:** Massachusetts, 1841 to 1843. Born 1802, died 1887.

Dorothea Dix went to see how people with mental illness were kept in the jails, poorhouses and houses of correction of Massachusetts, and what the people who ran those places did to them. Then she wrote down what she saw and put it in front of the state's lawmakers. The word used then was *insane*. It meant a person whose mind worked in ways that their family or their town could not manage.

On 28 March 1841 Dix went to the jail at East Cambridge, Massachusetts, to teach a Sunday school class. She found women with mental illness locked in with convicted criminals, in "a bare, foul-smelling, unheated jail room." The jail officials denied her account. Then they improved the women's conditions.

Between 1841 and 1843 Dix visited every jail, poorhouse and house of correction in Massachusetts. A poorhouse was a building where a town kept people who had no money. A house of correction was a kind of jail for people found guilty of small crimes. She wrote down what she saw in each one. In January 1843 she gave the Massachusetts lawmakers a memorial, a formal written statement, of what she had found.

"I come as the advocate of the helpless, forgotten, insane men and women held in cages, closets, cellars, stalls, pens!" she wrote. "Chained, naked, beaten with rods, and lashed into obedience!" A stall and a pen are enclosures built for animals. A rod is a stick used for beating, and lashed means whipped. Her notes named places. At Lincoln she found a woman in a cage. At Medford she found one person "chained, and one in a close stall for seventeen years."

Printers reprinted the memorial as a pamphlet, and newspapers printed parts of it. The lawmakers voted money to make the state hospital at Worcester bigger. In 1843 the United States had 13 hospitals for people with mental illness. By 1880 it had 123, and Dix had helped found 32 of them.

#### Coverture begins to break, 1837 to 1848

Coverture was the old English rule, still in force in 1848, that a married woman had no legal existence apart from her husband. She did not control property, even what she brought into the marriage. The first law in any state that let a married woman own property in her own name passed in Mississippi in 1839. It came out of a court case about a Chickasaw woman, and the property in that case was an enslaved man.

Betsy Love was Chickasaw, through her mother, Sally Colbert. She had inherited an enslaved man named Toney from her father, Thomas Love, and had given him to her daughter, Susan. Betsy Love's husband owed money to a man named John Fisher. Fisher went to court to have Toney sold at auction to pay the husband's debt. In 1837 the judges of the Mississippi Supreme Court ruled that Betsy Love was the legal owner, and that her husband had no rights over her property. They gave three reasons. Chickasaw families trace their family lines and pass on property through the mother. Since 1830, contracts made under Chickasaw law, including marriage contracts, had counted as binding in Mississippi. The third, in the words of the National Park Service's account, was that "Property in the Chickasaw Nation was owned by the women of the tribe."

In 1839 Mississippi's lawmakers passed the Married Women's Property Act. A married woman could now own property she got by gift, will, purchase or inheritance, as long as it did not come from her husband.

New York's lawmakers passed their own Married Women's Property Act in 1848, months before the Seneca Falls convention. Under it, the property a woman owned when she married stayed hers. Her husband could not sell it, and the people he owed money to could not take it to pay his debts. Lawmakers in other states copied New York's law. Under it, one part of coverture no longer applied in New York: the part about property a wife brought into a marriage. The rest of coverture stayed the law.

#### Sojourner Truth takes her name, 1843

The woman born Isabella Bomfree in Ulster County, New York, in 1797 changed her name in 1843. She said the Spirit had called her to preach the truth, and she named herself Sojourner Truth. A sojourner is a traveler who stays in a place for a while. She traveled through Long Island, Connecticut and Massachusetts, speaking and singing.

In 1844 she joined the Northampton Association of Education and Industry in Massachusetts. Abolitionists had founded it as a community. Its members supported women's rights and religious tolerance and opposed war, and the community was a stop on the Underground Railroad. It broke up in 1850. Her formal lecture tour began the next year, in 1851.

<a id="story-stanton-mott"></a>

#### Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott

> **Who:** Two women who were refused seats as delegates at an antislavery meeting in London because they were women, and who called the first women's rights convention eight years later.
>
> **When and where:** London, 1840. Waterloo and Seneca Falls, New York, July 1848.

In July 1848, Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucretia Mott led the first women's rights convention in the United States, at Seneca Falls, New York. The people at the meeting voted to demand that women be allowed to vote. James Gordon Bennett, publisher of the *New York Herald*, printed their declaration in his paper to make fun of it.

Lucretia Mott was born on Nantucket, Massachusetts, in 1793. She was raised a Quaker and went to a Quaker boarding school called Nine Partners. In 1833 she helped found the Philadelphia Female Anti-Slavery Society. Elizabeth Cady Stanton was born at Johnstown, New York, on 12 November 1815.

The two women met in London in 1840, at the World Anti-Slavery Convention. American antislavery groups had elected women as delegates. In the words of a National Park Service account, the women "were refused admission because of their sex." That account does not name the men who refused them. After an argument, the men at the convention decided that the women "would sit at the rear of the hall, but not participate." Stanton was in London on her honeymoon. She found Mott in the women's section, and the two agreed to hold a women's rights convention when they got home.

Stanton moved to Seneca Falls in 1847. The town is on Cayuga land. In 1789 the Cayuga Nation kept a 64,000-acre reservation there by a treaty, a written agreement, with New York. New York officials bought almost all of it in 1795 and the last three square miles in 1807. In 2017 a federal judge in western New York ruled that Congress had never approved those purchases, as a law of 1790 required.

Stanton later wrote about what pushed her to act: "The general discontent I felt with women's portion as wife, mother, housekeeper ... impressed me with a strange feeling that some active measures should be taken."

On 9 July 1848 five women met for tea at Waterloo, New York, and decided to hold the convention. They were Stanton, Mott, Mary Ann M'Clintock, Martha Coffin Wright and Jane Hunt. They put a notice in the local paper calling people to "a Convention to discuss the social, civil and religious rights and condition of woman."

The convention, a large organized meeting, met on 19 and 20 July 1848 at the Wesleyan Chapel in Seneca Falls, three miles east of Waterloo. More than 300 people came. The first day was meant for women only. Men took part on the second day. Lucretia Mott's husband, James Mott, chaired the convention, which means he ran the meeting. Mary M'Clintock was the secretary.

Stanton wrote a Declaration of Sentiments with the M'Clintock family. She modeled it on the Declaration of Independence. It listed, one by one, the wrongs men had done to women. "He has never permitted her to exercise her inalienable right to the elective franchise," meaning the right to vote. "He has taken from her all right in property, even to the wages she earns." That was coverture, still the law in 1848. "He has denied her the facilities for obtaining a thorough education," it went on, "all colleges being closed against her."

The people at the convention voted on a set of resolutions, written statements of what they wanted. Eleven passed with no one against them. The resolution demanding the vote met opposition and passed only narrowly. Frederick Douglass stood with Stanton and argued for it. He had escaped from slavery in Maryland ten years before and now published an antislavery newspaper, the *North Star*. One hundred people signed the Declaration of Sentiments, 68 women and 32 men. A Library of Congress exhibition states that seventy-two years of organized campaigning for women's votes followed that resolution, up to the Nineteenth Amendment in 1920.

The signers had written that they expected "misconception, misrepresentation, and ridicule," and it came. Bennett printed the whole declaration in the *Herald*. Some signers later took their names off after people criticized them harshly for signing. The records do not say how many.

### 1850 to 1900

Americans who were denied rights learned, in the second half of the 1800s, to plan court cases on purpose. They chose a law to challenge, raised money, hired a lawyer and found a person willing to be arrested or refused. Susan B. Anthony voted in 1872, the Tape family sued a school board in 1884, and Black men on a committee in New Orleans arranged an arrest on a train in 1892. The judge at Anthony's trial told the jury to find her guilty. The Tapes won in court, and school officials still kept their daughter out of the white school. Homer Plessy, the man the committee's members chose, lost in the Supreme Court.

After the Civil War, members of Congress and state lawmakers added three amendments, or changes, to the Constitution. The 13th bans slavery, the 14th states that people born in the country are citizens, and the 15th bars states from denying the vote because of race. In 1869 the leaders of the women's movement split over whether Black men or women should get the vote first. Women first voted under territorial law in Wyoming and Utah. Members of Congress voted for laws that shut Chinese immigrants out, and Chinese Americans fought those laws in court. In Memphis, the newspaper editor Ida B. Wells began counting the people killed by lynch mobs, crowds that killed people outside the law, with no trial.

<a id="story-sojourner-truth"></a>

#### Sojourner Truth

> **Who:** A woman born into slavery in New York who spoke in public for more than thirty years for the rights of Black people and of women.
>
> **When and where:** Akron, Ohio, May 1851. Washington, D.C., 1864. Died at Battle Creek, Michigan, 26 November 1883.

Sojourner Truth spoke for women's rights and Black Americans' rights from 1851 on. Her most famous speech survives in two versions, and the famous one was written by Frances Dana Gage twelve years after the speech.

In 1850 she published *The Narrative of Sojourner Truth: a Northern Slave* and bought a house in Northampton, Massachusetts. She paid for part of it by selling photographs of herself. On them she printed the words "I sell the shadow to support the substance."

On 28 May 1851 she spoke at the Ohio Women's Rights Convention in the Old Stone Church at Akron, Ohio. She had not been invited. (One account gives the date as 29 May. The convention ran for two days.)

Marius Robinson, one of the convention's secretaries, printed a report of her speech in the *Anti-Slavery Bugle* on 21 June 1851, about three weeks later. Truth was staying with Robinson and his wife, Emily, at the time. A National Park Service page says it is believed he went over the text with her. His version begins, "May I say a few words? I want to say a few words about this matter. I am a woman's rights. I have as much muscle as any man, and can do as much work as any man. I have plowed and reaped and husked and chopped and mowed, and can any man do more than that?" Later she said, "You need not be afraid to give us our rights for fear we will take too much, for we can't take more than our pint will hold." She ended, "But man is in a tight place, the poor slave is on him, woman is coming on him, and he is surely between a hawk and a buzzard." Robinson wrote that it was "impossible to transfer it to paper, or convey any adequate idea of the effect it produced upon the audience."

The famous version, with the question "And ain't I a woman?" repeated through it, was written by Frances Dana Gage, who had run the convention. Gage published it in 1863, twelve years after the speech. She wrote it while she was in South Carolina, in land held by the Union Army during the war. She did not check it with Truth. She called it "but a faint sketch of her speech." Gage's version gives Truth a Southern way of speaking.

Sojourner Truth grew up in Ulster County, New York, nearly 100 miles north of New York City. She spoke only Dutch until she was nine, and she was never enslaved in the South. Gage's version also has her say she bore thirteen children. She had five. A National Women's History Museum exhibit says Gage "fabricated" her version, which means she made it up. Robinson's version is the one written down that summer.

After 1857 Truth lived in Michigan. During the Civil War she recruited Black men for the Union Army, among them her grandson James Caldwell, who joined the 54th Massachusetts regiment, an Army unit, in April 1863. In 1863 officials in Indiana arrested her under a state law that barred Black people from entering the state, and held her for ten days.

In 1864 she worked in Washington, D.C., for the National Freedmen's Relief Association, which helped people who had just been freed from slavery. She rode the city's streetcars to force the streetcar companies to carry Black passengers. When a streetcar conductor tried to stop her from riding by force, she had him arrested and won her case. On 29 October 1864 she met President Abraham Lincoln at the White House.

From 1870 she campaigned for the federal government to give land in the West to people freed from slavery. The campaign failed. In 1872 she went to the polls in Battle Creek, Michigan, to vote, and election officials turned her away. That same year, Susan B. Anthony voted in Rochester, New York, and was arrested for it.

Sojourner Truth died at Battle Creek on 26 November 1883, about 86 years old. She believed she was 105.

#### Massachusetts lawmakers outlaw segregated schools, 1855

In Boston, William Cooper Nell and other Black Bostonians kept up their boycott of the segregated Smith School and their petition drives. In 1787 Prince Hall and other Black Bostonians had asked the state's lawmakers for schools for their children. In 1855, 68 years after that first petition, Massachusetts lawmakers voted to outlaw segregated public schools. A National Park Service page records that race-based segregation policies continued in Boston's public schools for decades afterward, even though state and federal laws forbade them.

#### A wife's wages, New York, 1860

Until 1860, a married woman in New York did not own the money she earned. Under coverture, her wages belonged to her husband. Women's rights campaigners in New York organized to change that. They carried petitions to every county in the state. They held conventions in 40 of its 60 counties and gave talks in 150 towns. Frances D. Gage, Antoinette Brown Blackwell and Susan B. Anthony were among the speakers.

Anthony gave a draft bill, a proposed law, to a state senator, Andrew J. Colvin, and he brought it to the state's lawmakers. State senators passed it on 28 February 1860, and members of the assembly on 20 March. Governor Edwin D. Morgan signed it. One newspaper of the time printed the date of passage as 30 March. The law states that "the earnings of any married woman, from her trade, business, labor or services, shall be her sole and separate property, and may be used or invested by her in her own name."

#### Three amendments, and the violence around them

Members of Congress and state lawmakers added three amendments to the Constitution after the Civil War. An amendment becomes part of the Constitution when lawmakers in enough states vote to approve it, which is called ratifying it. The 13th, ratified on 6 December 1865, bans slavery. The 14th, part of the Constitution from 9 July 1868, states that "All persons born or naturalized in the United States" are citizens. Naturalized means made a citizen after coming from another country. It also says no state may "deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws," meaning a state must apply its laws the same way to everyone. The 15th, ratified on 3 February 1870, states that the right to vote cannot be denied "on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude." Servitude means slavery.

In these same years white men attacked Black Americans who were living as free people. In May 1866, mobs that included Memphis police officers, firemen and businessmen killed 46 Black residents of the city. By the count of a committee of Congress, the mobs also burned 91 homes, 4 churches and 8 schools and raped five women. Rape means forcing a person into sex. On 13 April 1873, at Colfax, Louisiana, more than 150 armed white men led by Christopher Columbus Nash killed between 62 and 153 Black men. In April 1877 President Rutherford B. Hayes ordered federal soldiers out of the Louisiana state house, the last state house in the South that they guarded.

In 1875 members of Congress voted for a Civil Rights Act. Under it, no one could lawfully deny anyone "the full and equal enjoyment of any of the accommodations, advantages, facilities, and privileges of inns, public conveyances on land or water, theaters and other places of public amusement." Public conveyances are trains, boats and coaches for hire. In 1883 the justices of the Supreme Court struck the law down. They held that the 14th Amendment did not let Congress stop private individuals from treating people unfairly because of race.

#### The women's movement splits, 1869

In 1869 the people who had worked together against slavery split over who should get the vote next. The 14th Amendment was the first place the Constitution used the word "male." Under its second section, the number of seats a state got in Congress depended on the number of its "male inhabitants" who could vote. The 15th Amendment, which members of Congress passed on 26 February 1869, bars denying the vote because of race. It says nothing about sex.

The break came on 12 May 1869, at the third annual meeting of the American Equal Rights Association. People working to end slavery and women's rights campaigners had formed that group together in 1866. At the 1866 meeting, the Black campaigner Frances Ellen Watkins Harper had told the white women there, "You white women speak here of rights. I speak of wrongs."

At the 1869 meeting, Frederick Douglass argued that Black men needed the vote first. "I do not see how any one can pretend that there is the same urgency in giving the ballot to woman as to the negro," he said. Negro was a word then used for Black people. "With us, the question is a matter of life and death, at least, in fifteen States of the Union." He described Black families "in danger of having their homes burnt down over their heads," and children "not allowed to enter schools."

Susan B. Anthony answered, "If you will not give the whole loaf of suffrage to the entire people, give it to the most intelligent first." Suffrage means the right to vote. Elizabeth Cady Stanton said, "If intelligence, justice, and morality are to have precedence in the government, let the question of women brought up first and that of the negro last." A National Park Service page records that Stanton used racist language in this fight. She called Black Americans "ignorant of the laws and customs" of the country. Stanton and Anthony argued that educated white women should vote before Black men. Their words angered Black campaigners, among them Douglass and Harper.

Two rival groups formed in 1869. Stanton and Anthony started the National Woman Suffrage Association, which worked for a change to the Constitution. Lucy Stone, Henry Blackwell and Julia Ward Howe started the American Woman Suffrage Association, which worked state by state and supported the 15th Amendment. Members of the two groups stayed apart until 1890, when they joined as the National American Woman Suffrage Association. Two daughters of the founders, Alice Stone Blackwell and Harriot Stanton Blatch, helped bring them together.

#### Women vote first in the West, 1869 and 1870

The lawmakers of Wyoming Territory passed the first law in United States history that openly gave women the vote, and they had mixed reasons for it. William H. Bright, a Democrat from South Pass City, brought the bill to the territory's first group of lawmakers. Governor John Allen Campbell approved it on 10 December 1869. Under the act, women could vote and hold office. A National Park Service page records that some of the lawmakers also wanted to draw more women to a territory that had very few.

South Pass City was a gold-mining camp that grew up after gold was found in 1867. It stood in country that United States officials had recognized as the Eastern Shoshone's in an 1863 treaty, a homeland of about 44 million acres. White prospectors, men searching for gold, had been slipping into that country since the 1850s, in spite of the treaties. In the 1868 treaty of Fort Bridger, United States officials left the Shoshone only a reservation of about 3.2 million acres on the Wind River.

The lawmakers of Utah Territory passed a women's vote law two months later, and the acting governor signed it on 12 February 1870. Two days after that, on 14 February 1870, a Salt Lake City schoolteacher named Seraph Young voted in the city election. She was the first woman in the United States to vote under a law that gave women the vote on the same terms as men.

On 17 February 1870, Esther Hobart Morris was appointed justice of the peace at South Pass City, a local judge for small cases. She was the first woman in the country to hold that office. In the spring of 1870, women in Laramie were called to serve on juries, the first women in the country to do so. Later, the jury rule was read to cover only "male citizens over 21 years of age." The Wyoming State Museum, which records this, does not say who read it that way. Under that reading, no women sat on Wyoming juries until 1949. In Wyoming, Louisa Swain of Laramie voted on the morning of 6 September 1870.

In the Edmunds-Tucker Act of 1887, members of Congress voted to take Utah women's vote away, as part of a federal campaign against the Mormon church. Utah women got the vote back in the state constitution when Utah became a state on 4 January 1896. When Wyoming became a state in 1890, its women kept the vote, so Wyoming was the first state where women could vote.

<a id="story-susan-b-anthony"></a>

#### Susan B. Anthony

> **Who:** One of fifteen women who voted in Rochester, New York, in 1872, and the only one put on trial for it.
>
> **When and where:** Rochester, New York, 5 November 1872. Trial at Canandaigua, New York, 17 to 19 June 1873.

Susan B. Anthony voted in 1872 to test whether the Constitution gave women the vote. She was arrested and tried, and the judge told the jury to find her guilty.

In 1871 the leaders of the National Woman Suffrage Association had decided that women should try to register to vote, be refused, and then sue in federal court. Their argument was that the 14th Amendment made voting one of the rights of every citizen. Anthony went to register in Rochester, and the officials let her. On election day she went back, and the officials let her vote.

On 5 November 1872, in the first district of Rochester's Eighth Ward, Anthony and fourteen other women voted in the national election. A poll watcher, a man watching the voting for one party, named Sylvester Lewis challenged her. The three election inspectors did what New York law required. They put her under oath and asked whether she was a citizen, whether she lived in the district and whether anyone had paid her. Her answers satisfied them, and they put her ballots in the boxes.

Nine days later, a federal official, Commissioner William Storrs, issued warrants, papers ordering an arrest, for all fifteen women. On 18 November 1872 a deputy marshal, a federal officer who makes arrests, came to Anthony's house. She told the story many times. "'What for?' I asked. 'To arrest you,' he said. 'Is that the way you arrest men?' 'No.' Then I demanded that I should be arrested properly." He took her downtown on the streetcar, and the government paid her fare.

All fifteen women were arrested, and only Anthony was tried. The charge stated that she had voted "without having a lawful right to vote," being "then and there a person of the female sex." At a hearing on 29 November 1872, the assistant prosecutor, John Pound, asked the election inspectors, "Was Miss Anthony dressed in the apparel of a woman and had she the appearance of a woman?" Her lawyer objected. The inspectors answering that question had been arrested themselves for letting the women vote.

Federal courts at that time did not let a person on trial for a crime speak to the jury. So in March and April 1873 Anthony spoke to the people the jurors would come from. She gave a lecture, "Is It a Crime for a U.S. Citizen to Vote?", in twenty-nine villages and towns of Monroe County. The federal prosecutor, Richard Crowley, then had the trial moved to Ontario County. Anthony scheduled a speech in every village there too.

The trial opened at Canandaigua on 17 June 1873, before a jury of twelve men. The judge was Ward Hunt, a justice of the Supreme Court who was also hearing cases in that part of New York. When the prosecution finished, Hunt read out an opinion he had already written. He said voting was not one of the rights the 14th Amendment protected, and that Anthony had known New York let only men vote. Then he told the jury to bring in a verdict of guilty. Her lawyer, Henry Selden, asked for each juror to be polled, which means asked one by one for his own verdict. The clerk refused. The jury never talked the case over.

On 19 June Selden asked for a new trial, because Hunt had taken the decision away from the jury. Hunt refused. Then he asked the question a court asks before it sets a punishment. Three reports of what Anthony said next survive, and none comes from the court's own record of the trial. The words below are from the version she published herself.

Hunt asked, "Has the prisoner anything to say why sentence shall not be pronounced?" Anthony answered, "Yes, your honor, I have many things to say, for in your ordered verdict of guilty, you have trampled under foot every vital principle of our government." She went on, "Robbed of the fundamental privilege of citizenship, I am degraded from the status of a citizen to that of a subject."

"The Court cannot allow the prisoner to go on," Hunt said. She kept going. "May it please the Court to remember that since the day of my arrest last November, this is the first time that either myself or any person of my disfranchised class has been allowed a word of defense before judge or jury." Disfranchised means denied the vote. "The prisoner must sit down," said Hunt. "The Court cannot allow it."

She said that every man who had judged her was her "political superior," whether "native or foreign born, white or black, rich or poor, educated or ignorant, awake or asleep, sober or drunk." Hunt answered, "The Court must insist." He said she had been tried "according to the established forms of law." She replied, "Yes, your honor, but by forms of law all made by men, interpreted by men, administered by men, in favor of men, and against women."

Hunt fined her $100 and the costs of the trial. "May it please your honor, I shall never pay a dollar of your unjust penalty," she said. Hunt answered, "Madam, the Court will not order you committed until the fine is paid." If he had jailed her for not paying, she could have appealed to the Supreme Court. In July 1873 the deputy marshal sent to collect reported that he could "find no goods or chattles land or tenements" to take. Chattels are belongings, and tenements are buildings. Federal officials dropped the matter, and she never paid.

The three election inspectors were tried after her, found guilty and fined $25 each. They refused to pay too, and on 25 February 1874 the marshal put them in jail. Anthony sent telegrams to Representative Benjamin Butler and Senator Aaron Sargent. On 3 March 1874 President Ulysses S. Grant pardoned the inspectors, which means he canceled their punishment. The same day, the voters of the Eighth Ward elected all three to their posts again.

#### The Comstock Act, 1873

On 3 March 1873 members of Congress voted for "An Act for the Suppression of, trade in, and circulation of obscene literature and articles of immoral use," known as the Comstock Act. Under it, sending certain things by mail became a federal crime. They included anatomy books, some novels, photographs of boxing matches and information about contraception, which means ways to prevent pregnancy. Under the act, it was a crime to mail a woman the information she needed about her own body.

Obscene means indecent or shocking, but the act never said what counted as obscene. Anthony Comstock had pushed members of Congress to pass it, and he was appointed a special agent of the Post Office. In practice, he decided what the word meant. In court he often refused to let jurors see the item he had seized, saying it was too vile to show them. He claimed that over his life he seized 150 tons of books, made 4,000 arrests and drove 15 people to suicide.

#### A Harvard doctor says school will harm girls, 1873

In 1873 Edward H. Clarke, a professor at Harvard Medical School, published a book that said studying would damage girls' bodies. The book was *Sex in Education*, with the subtitle *A Fair Chance for the Girls*. Clarke argued that a girl's body spends the teenage years building the organs used to carry a pregnancy. Studying the way boys studied, he said, would take the energy that work needed. "Unless the work is accomplished at that period, unless the reproductive mechanism is built and put in good working order at that time, it will never be perfectly accomplished afterwards," he wrote. He warned that the result would be "monstrous brains and puny bodies."

A Smith College history page lists the harms Clarke said would follow. They were atrophy of the uterus and ovaries, the organs a woman's body uses to carry a pregnancy. Atrophy means those organs shrinking and stopping working. The list also named masculinization, which means a girl's body taking on a man's traits, and sterility, which means being unable to have children, and insanity and death. He said women should study no more than four hours a day, and not at all during their monthly bleeding. He described a patient he called Miss A: "She graduated at nineteen, the first scholar, and an invalid." An invalid is a person too sick to live a normal life.

Leaders of the new women's colleges answered him. Smith College opened in 1875, and its first president, Laurenus Clark Seelye, said, "It is to preserve her womanliness that this College has been founded." Smith's leaders built supervised houses for its students in answer to worries like Clarke's.

Mary Putnam Jacobi answered with evidence. She had earned a pharmacy degree, a degree in preparing medicines, in 1863, the first woman in the country to do so. She earned a medical degree in 1864 and a second medical degree in Paris in 1871. Jacobi sent out a thousand printed lists of questions through women's rights groups and collected answers from hundreds of women, rich and poor, in towns and on farms. Her essay *The Question of Rest During Menstruation* won Harvard's Boylston Prize in 1876, and she was the first woman to win it. She found no evidence that monthly bleeding made women unfit to study or work.

#### Supreme Court justices rule that the Constitution gives no one the vote

Virginia Minor, a woman in St. Louis, Missouri, used the same argument Anthony had used. The registrar, Reese Happersett, refused to register her to vote, and she sued him. She argued in court that she was a citizen and that citizens have the right to vote.

The Supreme Court justices ruled against her, all of them, in *Minor v. Happersett*, decided in the court term that began in October 1874. They held that "the Constitution of the United States does not confer the right of suffrage upon any one," and that a state could give the vote to men only. Women were citizens, but in the justices' reading, being a citizen did not include a right to vote. After that ruling, the only way left to win the vote everywhere at once was a new amendment to the Constitution.

#### Getting into college, and into court as a lawyer

Colleges for women opened in these years. Matthew Vassar founded Vassar College at Poughkeepsie, New York, in 1861, and it opened on 26 September 1865 with 353 students. Smith, founded in 1871, opened in the fall of 1875 with 14 students. Pauline and Henry Fowle Durant founded Wellesley in 1870, and it opened on 8 September 1875 with 314 students. Bryn Mawr, a Quaker college for women, opened in September 1885.

Spelman began on 11 April 1881 in the basement of Friendship Baptist Church in Atlanta, Georgia. Two New England teachers, Sophia B. Packard and Harriet E. Giles, founded it with help from the church's pastor, Frank Quarles. Its first class was eleven students: ten women, some of them formerly enslaved, and one girl.

Some state universities opened to women too, though admitting women and letting them finish a degree often came years apart. A University of Iowa history page says women were admitted from its founding, and "on an equal basis with men" from 1860. In February 1870 Madelon Stockwell enrolled at the University of Michigan, the first woman there since it opened in 1817. The first woman to enter Cornell, Jennie Spencer of Cortland, came in 1870. She had won a state scholarship, and she left because there was nowhere near the campus for a woman to live. Women entered Cornell regularly from 1872.

Rebecca Lee Crumpler received the degree "Doctress of Medicine" from the New England Female Medical College on 1 March 1864. She was the first African American woman in the United States to earn a medical degree. After the war she moved to Richmond, Virginia, and worked with the Freedmen's Bureau, the federal office that helped people freed from slavery. She treated patients who had no other doctor.

Women who studied law could pass the examination and still be refused a license. Arabella Mansfield passed the Iowa bar examination on 15 June 1869 and became the first woman admitted to a state bar. The bar is the body of lawyers allowed to practice in a court. Iowa's law described "any white male citizen" as eligible, and she argued that nothing in it forbade a woman. Charlotte E. Ray graduated from Howard University School of Law in 1872 and was admitted to the District of Columbia bar, the first Black woman lawyer in the country. A page by the District of Columbia attorney general's office says she later had to close her law office because, as a woman of color, she could not get enough clients.

Myra Bradwell passed the Illinois bar examination in 1869. The judges of the Illinois Supreme Court refused her a license because she was married.
