They were survivors of a Spanish expedition, a group sent out to explore and conquer, led by a commander named Narváez. One of them, Cabeza de Vaca, later wrote an account of what happened. He wrote that the people of the island spoke two languages, and he called them the Capoque and the Han.

Only 15 of the 80 Spaniards stayed alive. Five Spaniards camped on the coast grew so desperate that they ate the bodies of their own dead as each one died. Their names were Sierra, Diego López, Corral, Palacios and Gonçalo Ruiz. Nobody ate the body of the last one to die. Cabeza de Vaca wrote that the islanders were in an uproar when they learned of it.

After that, a disease of the bowels killed half of the island's people, Cabeza de Vaca wrote. The bowels are the long tube in the belly that food passes through after the stomach. He did not name the disease. The islanders believed the Spaniards had caused the deaths, and they planned to kill the survivors. The Native man who had charge of Cabeza de Vaca talked them out of it. He pointed out that the Spaniards had not been able to save their own men from dying.

The islanders then told the Spaniards to heal the sick, and they gave them no food until they did. Cabeza de Vaca described how the island's own healers worked. A healer made small cuts in the skin over the place that hurt and sucked at the cuts. Healers also burned the skin at the painful spot on purpose, a treatment called cautery, and then blew on it. Cabeza de Vaca tried the burning on himself and wrote that it helped him. The Spaniards blessed the sick, breathed on them, and said two Christian prayers, the Lord's Prayer and the Hail Mary.

Years later, on a long walk west, people brought Cabeza de Vaca a man with an arrowhead lodged in his chest above the heart. The year and the place are not certain, because accounts of the route differ. Cabeza de Vaca cut open the man's chest with his knife and pulled the arrowhead out. He closed the cut with two stitches, using a deer bone as a needle, and stopped the bleeding with hair from an animal skin. He wrote that the next day he cut the stitches and the man was well.

#### Empty towns at Cofitachequi, 1540

In the spring of 1540, the army of the Spanish commander Hernando de Soto reached Cofitachequi. It was a town on a river in what is now South Carolina or Georgia. Accounts place it in different spots.

A Portuguese member of the army, known only as the Gentleman of Elvas, wrote that there were large empty towns nearby, grown over with grass. People at Cofitachequi told the Spaniards that a disease had struck the land two years before. The people of those towns had moved away to other towns. The Gentleman of Elvas did not name the disease, and he did not say how many people died.

That disease arrived before de Soto's army did. No record shows where it came from. Accounts differ about whether de Soto's own army carried new diseases inland. The records do show that de Soto's men killed and enslaved Native people and took their food.

#### Roanoke, 1585 and 1586

English colonists sent by Sir Walter Raleigh lived on Roanoke Island, in what is now North Carolina, in 1585 and 1586. The island lay in the land of the Carolina Algonquian peoples. The colonists visited Algonquian towns, and within a few days after they left a town, people there began to die quickly.

The scientist Thomas Harriot, who was with the colonists, wrote down the deaths. In some towns about 20 people died, in some 40, in some 60, and in one town 120. Harriot wrote that, as far as he could learn, the deaths happened only in towns the English had visited. The oldest people told him nothing like it had ever happened before. During the same months, he wrote, no English colonist died or became seriously sick.

Harriot did not name the disease. In 1994 Peter Mires, writing in the journal *Historical Archaeology*, compared Harriot's report with John Smith's later accounts. Smith had heard about an epidemic among the Accomac, a people the Roanoke colonists visited in the winter of 1585 to 1586. Mires concluded that the English colonists carried the disease, and that it was probably influenza. He called influenza probable, not certain.

<a id="story-thomas-harriot"></a>

#### Thomas Harriot

> **Who:** An English mathematician and scientist who wrote down, town by town, an epidemic among the Carolina Algonquians. His name is also spelled Hariot.
>
> **When and where:** Roanoke Island and the Carolina Algonquian towns, 1585 and 1586. His report was printed in London in 1588.

Thomas Harriot recorded what the Carolina Algonquians believed was killing them in 1585 and 1586. Some believed the English God was killing people for the English. Others believed that more English people were still to come, to kill them and take their places. These coming English were already in the air, invisible and without bodies, and they were shooting "invisible bullets" into people at the English colonists' request. Algonquian healers sucked what they called "strings of blood" out of the sick. They said these were the strings tied to the invisible bullets.

Harriot was born in about 1560 and finished his studies at Oxford University in 1580. He taught how to find the way across the open ocean at Sir Walter Raleigh's house in London. He sailed with the colony that reached Roanoke Island on June 26, 1585. There he and the artist John White mapped the area.

Wingina was the wiroans, or chief, of the people the English lived among. Twice he was so sick that he nearly died, and he sent for the English to pray for him. Wingina and others also asked the English to pray that their enemies would die of the same disease. Harriot wrote that he told them such prayers were ungodly. When their enemies did die, they came to thank the English anyway.

Harriot explained the deaths as "the special work of God" for the English. He also described how the Algonquians used a plant they called uppowoc, which is tobacco, as a medicine. They breathed in its smoke through clay pipes. Harriot believed it kept them healthy. He died in 1621.

### The 1600s

Epidemics killed Native people along the Atlantic coast in the 1600s, sometimes years before colonists settled beside them. English colonists also died in large numbers in their first years, from disease and hunger. The people who treated the sick in the colonies included a weaver with no known medical training and a minister. In New Amsterdam, surgeons worked for a Dutch trading company, and the company paid the town's midwives. In 1693 yellow fever reached Boston. The virus that causes it and the mosquito that carries it had crossed the Atlantic on the ships of the slave trade.

#### Jamestown, 1607

In 1607, 104 English men and boys built a fort at Jamestown, in Virginia. The fort stood in the land of the Paspahegh, one of the nations led by the Powhatan paramount chief. A paramount chief was a leader over the chiefs of many nations. By the end of September 1607, half of the 104 colonists were dead, most of them from sickness.

George Percy, one of the colonists, wrote down each death with its date and cause. John Asbie died of the "bloudie Flixe," Percy's spelling of bloody flux, on August 6. Flux was the old word for diarrhea, and a bloody flux was diarrhea with blood in it. Percy also listed "Swellings" and "Burning Fevers," and deaths from wounds in fighting.

Percy blamed hunger most of all. Each day, five men shared one small can of barley boiled in water. They drank from the river. At high tide its water was salty, and at low tide it was "full of slime and filth." Many nights three or four men died. Then Native people of the area, whom Percy called "our mortall enemies," brought bread, corn, fish and meat to the fort in great plenty. Percy wrote that "divers Kings," meaning several Native leaders, brought more. He did not name them.

In 1979 the geographer Carville Earle pointed to the river. At Jamestown the river water was part salt and part fresh, so the colonists' waste stayed in it instead of washing away. Tree rings show a drought that lasted seven years, from 1606 to 1612. The historian Dennis Blanton wrote that colonists who were hungry and thirsty from the drought were the most likely to fall sick. In the winter of 1609 to 1610, only about 60 of about 240 colonists in the fort survived. That winter is called the Starving Time.

#### An epidemic on the New England coast, 1616 to 1619

From 1616 to 1619, a disease killed Native people along about 200 miles of the coast of southern New England, as far as Cape Cod. As far as the records show, the European fishermen and traders nearby did not catch it.

No count of the dead exists. Estimates of the share who died rest on weak records, and they run from one third to nine tenths of the people in the area. Before the epidemic, the Wampanoag Nation had about 21,000 to 24,000 people, and the Patuxet town had about 2,000. In 1674 the colonist Daniel Gookin wrote down what Native people told him about the sick. "The bodies all over were exceedingly yellow," they said, both before the people died and after.

No one has settled what the disease was. The ideas put forward include yellow fever, smallpox, plague, typhus and several other diseases. In 2010 two researchers, John Marr and John Cathey, proposed leptospirosis. Leptospirosis is an infection by bacteria that rats carry in their urine. They suggested that rats from European ships spread it into the water and soil. They called their idea a proposal for others to test, not an answer.

When the Plymouth colonists arrived in 1620, the Patuxet town was empty. The colonists built Plymouth on its site. Governor William Bradford wrote that so many had died that the living could not bury the dead. He wrote that in many places in the area, skulls and bones still lay above the ground where houses had stood. Squanto, also called Tisquantum, was one of the few Patuxet survivors. Bradford wrote that Squanto told other Native people the English kept the plague buried in the ground. Squanto said the English could send it among them whenever they wished.

#### Plymouth's first winter, 1620 and 1621

In two or three months of their first winter, about half of the roughly 100 Mayflower passengers at Plymouth died. Sometimes two or three died in one day. Bradford blamed the cold, the lack of houses, and scurvy and other diseases from the long voyage. Scurvy is a disease caused by too little vitamin C. The gums swell and bleed, the teeth loosen, and the person grows too weak to work.

At the worst, only six or seven people were well enough to care for everyone else. They cut wood, made fires, cooked, made beds and washed the sick people's clothes. William Brewster and Myles Standish were two of them.

<a id="story-samuel-fuller"></a>

#### Samuel Fuller

> **Who:** A wool weaver with no known medical training who came on the Mayflower and became the doctor for Plymouth and its neighbors.
>
> **When and where:** Plymouth, Salem and Charlestown, in Massachusetts, 1620 to 1633.

Samuel Fuller treated the sick of Plymouth and the towns near it for about thirteen years, although no record shows he ever trained as a doctor. He was baptized in 1580 in Norfolk, England. Before the voyage he lived in Leiden, in the Netherlands, where he wove woolen cloth. He came to Plymouth on the Mayflower in 1620. His brother Edward and Edward's wife died in Plymouth's first winter.

In 1629 settlers at Salem fell sick with scurvy and with a fever that had spread on their ships. Their leader, John Endicott, asked Governor Bradford to send Fuller. Endicott had heard that Fuller had cured people "by letting blood and other means."

Letting blood, or bloodletting, meant cutting open a vein, most often in the arm, and letting blood run out into a bowl. Doctors of the time believed it balanced the fluids of the body. It does not cure scurvy or fever, and it left sick people weaker. In 1630 Fuller let blood from about 20 newly arrived colonists at Charlestown.

In 1633 a fever killed more than 20 men, women and children at Plymouth, and many Native people nearby. Fuller treated the sick. Then he died of the same fever, sometime between August and late September 1633. The colonist Nathaniel Morton later wrote that Fuller "was their surgeon and physician, and did much good in his place."

#### Smallpox on the Connecticut River, 1634

In the winter of 1633 to 1634, about 1,000 Native people closed themselves inside a fort on the Connecticut River, upriver from Plymouth's trading house. A disease struck them, and more than 950 of them died, Bradford wrote. Many of the bodies lay rotting above the ground, unburied. Bradford did not name the nation or the disease.

That spring, smallpox struck the Native people living near Plymouth's trading house on the Connecticut River. Smallpox is a disease caused by a virus, a germ even smaller than bacteria. It spread from person to person through close contact, face to face. It caused a fever and a rash, and the rash turned into blisters and then scabs. In general, about 3 of every 10 people who caught smallpox died. Many survivors had scars for life, most of all on their faces.

Bradford described the sick lying on hard mats. The blisters broke open and ran, and the skin stuck to the mats. When a sick person turned over, the skin of a whole side came off at once. So many were sick that no one could make a fire, fetch water or bury the dead. Some crawled on their hands and knees to get water and died on the way.

The English at the trading house brought the sick wood, water and food, and buried the dead. None of the English there caught the disease. Very few of the Native people survived. Their chief sachem, or leader, died, and so did almost all of his friends and relatives. Bradford did not write down his name. No record shows who brought the disease to the river.

#### Midwives and surgeons in New Amsterdam

Officials of the Dutch West India Company, a trading company, ran the colony of New Netherland. Its town of New Amsterdam stood on Manhattan, in the homeland of the Munsee Lenape. Company officials appointed and paid the town's midwives. A midwife is a woman who helps other women give birth. In 1638 the midwife Lysbert Dircksen lived in a house built for her with public money.

Surgeons worked in the town too. Hans Kierstede arrived in 1638 and worked in the town for nearly 30 years. Under a rule of 1652, barbers from the ships could not treat wounds on shore without permission. Under a rule of 1657, surgeons had to report how each wounded person had been hurt.

In 1658 the Company surgeon Jacob Hendrichsen Varvanger asked for a place to care for sick patients. Members of the colony's council agreed. They made Hilletje Wilbruch the matron, the woman in charge, and paid her 100 florins, which were Dutch coins, a year. Richard Amerman, in a 1957 article on medicine in New Netherland, called it the first hospital.

<a id="story-tryntje-jonas"></a>

#### Tryntje Jonas

> **Who:** A midwife from Amsterdam who served as an official midwife of New Amsterdam.
>
> **When and where:** New Amsterdam, now New York City, by 1644.

By 1644 Tryntje Jonas was the official midwife of New Amsterdam. Officials of the Dutch West India Company appointed her and paid her, and she had her own house on Pearl Street. She came from Amsterdam. Her daughter Anneke Jans arrived in New Netherland in 1630.

On July 7, 1644, Tryntje Jonas swore to the colony's secretary what a mother had said about her baby's father. She had been called to help a woman named Hillegont Joris give birth. Hillegont Joris first named "Jan, the pilot" as the father of the child. Afterward she named Laurens Cornelisz. The secretary copied the statement into the colony's record book, where it survives. The record does not say why the midwife was asked to report this.

After Tryntje Jonas died, her daughter Anneke Jans collected the pay that the Company still owed her mother for her work. The date of her death is not known.

#### Smallpox advice and yellow fever, 1677 to 1693

After smallpox spread through Boston in 1676 and 1677, the minister Thomas Thacher of the Old South Church wrote a guide for families. It was printed in 1677 or 1678 on a single large sheet called a broadside. Librarians at Harvard University's medical library call it the first medical paper published in the American colonies.

Thacher told families not to put a smallpox patient under heavy bedclothes, in a hot room, or give strong hot drinks. He told them to give weak beer, a thin porridge of cornmeal and water, and boiled apples. He warned that bloody or black urine, and diarrhea, were danger signs.

Yellow fever came from Africa. It is a disease caused by a virus, and a mosquito called Aedes aegypti carries the virus from one person to another when it bites. The virus and the mosquito both crossed the Atlantic aboard the ships of the slave trade, a team of scientists led by Juliet Bryant reported in 2007. Nobody knew about the mosquito's part until the early 1900s.

In 1693 yellow fever struck Boston. The makers of the PBS history series *American Experience* call Boston the first British colony in North America to have a yellow fever epidemic. That June a fleet of English warships arrived in Boston. The first Boston death from the fever came on June 25. No surviving count gives the number of dead. Charleston and Philadelphia had yellow fever soon after.

#### Smallpox along the slave-raiding paths, 1696 to 1700

In 1696 smallpox broke out in Virginia and spread south and west along the trading paths. It spread with Native slave raiders and the captives they took for the colonial slave trade. By 1699 it had reached the Tunica people, in what is now Louisiana. It came back in waves until 1715.

By one estimate, some Native nations lost more than 60 of every 100 people. A South Carolina colonist wrote that smallpox had killed so many Native people that there was "little reason to believe they will be capable of doing any harm to us for several years to come."

### 1700 to 1750

Between 1700 and 1750, doctors in Boston and Charleston began protecting people against smallpox by inoculation. Inoculation meant giving a healthy person a small case of smallpox on purpose, so that the person would not catch it again. In Boston the minister Cotton Mather first heard of the method from Onesimus, an African man Mather enslaved. Epidemics still killed thousands of people. Diphtheria killed about 5,000 people in New England, most of them children. Smallpox killed about half of the Cherokee Nation.

#### Smallpox and inoculation in Boston, 1721

On April 22, 1721, the ship *Seahorse* arrived in Boston from the island of Barbados with sailors sick with smallpox. Boston had about 10,600 people. Close to 5,800 of them caught smallpox that year, and 844 died.

The minister Cotton Mather led the Boston ministers who backed inoculation. He had first heard of it from Onesimus, a man he enslaved. To inoculate someone, a doctor took pus from a smallpox sore and dried it. Then the doctor rubbed or scratched the pus into a cut in a healthy person's skin. Almost all of Boston's doctors feared that inoculation would spread the disease. Zabdiel Boylston was the one Boston doctor who tried it, starting in June 1721.

By the end of the epidemic, about 287 people in Boston had been inoculated, and 6 of them died. That is about 2 in every 100. Among people who caught smallpox the ordinary way, about 14 or 15 in every 100 died.

The doctor William Douglass led the people who opposed inoculation. He called inoculation a "poisonous humor." Humor was an old word for a fluid of the body. James Franklin printed attacks on inoculation in his newspaper, the *New-England Courant*. The town's selectmen, its elected officials, ordered Boylston to stop. He started again two days later.

On November 14, 1721, someone threw a bomb through a window of Mather's house. The note that came with it ended with the words "I will inoculate you with this, with a pox on you!" The records do not name who threw it.

<a id="story-onesimus"></a>

#### Onesimus

> **Who:** An enslaved African man who described inoculation to Cotton Mather years before Boston first tried it.
>
> **When and where:** Boston, enslaved by Cotton Mather from 1706 to 1716.

Onesimus told Cotton Mather how people in Africa protected themselves against smallpox. Mather later used that knowledge to back inoculation during Boston's smallpox epidemic of 1721.

In December 1706, members of Mather's North Church gave Onesimus to Mather as a gift. Another account gives the year as 1707. Mather named him Onesimus, after an enslaved man in the Bible. The name he was born with is not recorded. He was probably Coromantee, one of the Akan peoples of the Gold Coast, which is now Ghana.

In 1716 Mather wrote to the Royal Society in London, a group of leading scientists. He wrote that he had asked Onesimus whether he had ever had smallpox. Onesimus answered "both, Yes, and No." He had "undergone an Operation, which had given him something of the Small-Pox, and would forever preserve him from it." He showed Mather the scar on his arm. Mather wrote down the method in Onesimus's words: people "take Juice of Small-Pox" and "Cut the Skin, and put in a drop." Mather wrote that he heard this from Onesimus months before he read of the same method in reports from Europe.

Onesimus married and had two children. Both died before they were ten. His son Onesimulus died in 1714. His daughter Katy died of tuberculosis.

In 1716 Onesimus paid money toward buying another enslaved man, Obadiah, to take his place. Mather then freed him, but with conditions. Onesimus still had to work for Mather's household, shoveling snow and chopping wood, whenever Mather called for him. He also had to repay five pounds that Mather said he had stolen. Few records of his life after 1716 survive.

<a id="story-zabdiel-boylston"></a>

#### Zabdiel Boylston

> **Who:** The one Boston doctor who tried inoculation in 1721, when almost all the others feared it.
>
> **When and where:** Boston, 1721 and 1722. Born 1679, died 1766.

On June 26, 1721, Zabdiel Boylston inoculated three people. One was his son Thomas, who was about six. The other two were people Boylston enslaved: Jack, a man of 36, and Jack's son Jackey, who was two and a half. By law Jack and Jackey were Boylston's property, so they could not refuse. The accounts of that day do not say whether Jack agreed.

Boylston wrote down how each one's illness went. Thomas and Jack each had about "an hundred" blisters full of pus. On the ninth day Boylston gave them a medicine to make them vomit. All three recovered.

He went on to inoculate between 242 and 248 people, by different counts. Six of them died. When the selectmen ordered him to stop, he started again two days later. For a time he stayed on his farm, because he could not leave it without risk of being attacked.

Later he sailed to London, where the scientists of the Royal Society made him a member. In 1726 he published a book about his inoculations, *An Historical Account of the Small-Pox Inoculated in New England*.

<a id="story-elizabeth-phillips"></a>

#### Elizabeth Phillips

> **Who:** A licensed midwife from London who delivered babies in Boston for more than forty years.
>
> **When and where:** Boston and Charlestown, Massachusetts, 1719 to 1761.

Elizabeth Phillips helped deliver more than 3,000 babies in and around Boston, according to her gravestone. She was born in Westminster, in London, in about 1685. In 1718 the Bishop of London gave her a license to work as a midwife.

She came to Boston in 1719 and worked there until she died in 1761. Her gravestone stands in the Phipps Street Burying Ground in Charlestown. It says she "brought into this world above 3000 Children."

#### The throat distemper, 1735 to 1740

In May 1735 a disease began in Kingston, New Hampshire. It spread along the coast into Maine and Massachusetts. People called it the throat distemper, an old word for a sickness. Doctors today identify it as diphtheria, an infection by bacteria.

The bacteria killed the living tissue of the throat and nose. The dead tissue formed a thick coating across the throat, until the child could no longer breathe.

About 5,000 people in New England died of it by 1740, and more than three quarters of them were children. That count comes from Ernest Caulfield's 1939 book on the epidemic. In the town of Hampton Falls, New Hampshire, 210 people had died by July 1736, and 160 of them were under ten. The treatments printed in the *Boston Gazette* newspaper were bloodletting, borax or honey on the throat, and drinks made from herbs. Borax is a white powder made from a mineral.

In Ipswich, Massachusetts, Mark and Hephzibah Howe lost eight children in November 1736. They were Abijah (1), Mark (2), Aaron (5), Mary (7), Lucy (9), Moses (11), Love (12) and Hannah (13).

#### Smallpox among the Cherokee and Catawba, 1738 and 1739

Smallpox struck the Cherokee towns in the southern Appalachian Mountains in 1738 and 1739. Between 7,000 and 10,000 Cherokee people died, about half of the nation. About half of the Catawba Nation died too.

How the disease reached them is disputed. The trader James Adair wrote in 1775 that it came into Charleston on slave ships from West Africa. Historians writing for NCpedia, a North Carolina encyclopedia, give two other routes. In one, traders brought it. In the other, Cherokee warriors carried it home after fighting beside the British against the Spanish in Florida.

Cherokee healers treated the sick in sweat houses and then plunged them into icy streams. The NCpedia historians write that this only added to the number who died. Adair wrote that some survivors whom the disease had scarred killed themselves.

In Charleston, during the same epidemic, the doctor James Kilpatrick inoculated 800 to 1,000 people. Eight of them died.

### 1750 to 1800

Philadelphia doctors opened a hospital for the sick poor in 1752 and a medical school in 1765. Smallpox spread through the colonies and the Native nations during two wars. In 1763 the British commander at Fort Pitt and a trader tried to spread it on purpose. In 1793 yellow fever killed about 4,000 to 5,000 people in Philadelphia, about one person in ten. In 1798 members of Congress passed, and President John Adams signed, a law under which federal officials took money from sailors' pay for their medical care.

<a id="story-doctor-caesar"></a>

#### Caesar

> **Who:** An enslaved healer whose cure for poison led South Carolina's lawmakers to pay his enslaver for his freedom.
>
> **When and where:** St. Paul's Parish, South Carolina, near the Edisto River. Freed in 1750. Died in 1754.

In 1750 the lawmakers of South Carolina bought Caesar's freedom in exchange for his cure for poison. Caesar was enslaved by John Norman of Beach Hill, near the Edisto River. He was known for curing people of poisoning and of rattlesnake bite.

White South Carolinians feared that the enslaved people who cooked their food would poison them. In 1740 the colony's lawmakers had made poisoning a crime punished by death. In November 1749 the members of the Commons House, the colony's lawmaking body, voted to pay Norman 500 pounds for Caesar's freedom. They made the payment final on May 31, 1750. The lawmakers also promised Caesar 100 pounds a year for life. He received his first payment in 1751.

The *South Carolina Gazette* newspaper printed Caesar's cure in May 1750. It was made by boiling plantain roots, horehound and goldenrod with rum, sugar, tobacco and lye made from wood ash.

In 1751 the same lawmakers passed a law aimed at enslaved healers, "commonly called doctors." Under it, enslaved healers could not give anyone medicine without permission from white people.

Caesar died in early 1754, at about 77 years old. His wife Lilly and his daughter Hannah were never freed by the lawmakers. They were still enslaved by John Norman. When Caesar died, he owned an enslaved woman himself.

#### Pennsylvania Hospital and the first medical school

On May 11, 1751, Dr. Thomas Bond and Benjamin Franklin founded Pennsylvania Hospital in Philadelphia. They founded it to care for "the poor, sick and insane." Franklin's petition, a written request, described people "deprived of their rational Faculties," meaning they had lost their reason. It stated that they could be "contained and confined" there.

The first patients came on February 6, 1752, to a house on Market Street that the hospital used until its own building was ready. Writers for the Mütter Museum, a museum of medical history in Philadelphia, give the year as 1753. The permanent building opened in 1756. Its basement held rooms for patients with mental illness. The first floor was for men, and the second floor was for women.

Older places in the colonies also housed people in need. Philadelphia's almshouse, a home for the poor, opened in 1732. A New York workhouse of 1736, a place where poor people lived and were put to work, later became Bellevue Hospital. The Dutch hospital in New Amsterdam was older than both.

In 1765 Dr. John Morgan founded a medical school at the College of Philadelphia, now the University of Pennsylvania. The museum's writers call it the first medical college in the colonies. Students learned at the bedsides of the hospital's patients.

#### Smallpox as a weapon at Fort Pitt, 1763

In 1763 two British men at Fort Pitt gave two Delaware men blankets from a smallpox hospital, hoping to spread the disease. Fort Pitt was a British fort where Pittsburgh stands now. That year Delaware, or Lenape, and Shawnee and Mingo warriors surrounded the fort, during the war led by the Ottawa leader Pontiac. Smallpox had broken out among the soldiers inside.

On June 24, 1763, Captain Simeon Ecuyer, the fort's commander, and the trader William Trent met two Delaware men, Turtle's Heart and Mamaltee. Most accounts give that date. Ecuyer and Trent gave them two blankets and a handkerchief taken from the fort's smallpox hospital. Trent wrote in his journal, "I hope it will have the desired effect." One copy of Trent's journal dates this entry May 24. Ecuyer signed the bill that charged the army for the blankets.

In July, General Jeffery Amherst, the British commander in North America, wrote to Colonel Henry Bouquet. He asked: "Could it not be contrived to send the Small Pox among those disaffected tribes of Indians?" Contrived means arranged, and disaffected means unfriendly. Bouquet answered that he would "try to inocculate the Indians by means of Blankets." Amherst also wrote of trying "to extirpate this Execrable Race." Extirpate means to wipe out completely, and execrable means hateful. Ecuyer and Trent had given away the blankets in June, before these letters, and on their own.

In 1764 a man named Gershom Hicks reported that smallpox had been spreading among the Native nations. He said about 100 people died of it between the spring of 1763 and April 1764. The historian Elizabeth Fenn writes that no one can know whether the attempt to spread smallpox worked. A month after the meeting, Turtle's Heart and Mamaltee showed no sign of smallpox.

#### Smallpox in the Revolution, 1775 to 1782

In 1775 Virginia's royal governor, Lord Dunmore, promised freedom to people enslaved by the rebels if they joined his army. In the spring and summer of 1776, smallpox and other fevers spread through his camps. An estimated 500 Black soldiers of his Ethiopian Regiment died on Gwynn's Island, in Virginia, along with about 150 white soldiers.

On February 6, 1777, General George Washington ordered the Continental Army to be inoculated. He wrote that if smallpox spread through the army, "we should have more to dread from it, than from the Sword of the Enemy." Dr. William Shippen ran the inoculations in secret, in winter, at Morristown, New Jersey, and in Philadelphia. He kept them secret so the British would not learn of them.

#### The Doctors' Riot, New York, 1788

To learn how the body is built, medical students cut open dead bodies and studied the parts. This is called dissection. In New York, students dug up bodies for dissection from the Negroes Burial Ground, where Black New Yorkers buried their dead. "Negro" was a word for Black people used at the time. The students also dug up bodies from the paupers' graveyard, where the poor were buried.

In February 1788, free and enslaved Black New Yorkers asked the city's Common Council, the group that ran the city, to stop it. Their petition described "young gentlemen in this city who call themselves students of the physic," meaning students of medicine, who were digging up "bodies of our deceased friends and relatives." The council members took no action to stop the digging.

In April 1788, boys outside New York Hospital saw a human arm from the dissecting room. Crowds attacked the hospital. The mayor had a doctor and medical students taken to the city jail to protect them. About 5,000 people then gathered at the jail. Militiamen, ordinary citizens called up to serve as soldiers, had orders not to fire. A rock hit the politician John Jay in the head, a brick hit General Baron von Steuben, and the militiamen opened fire. The accounts of the riot do not name an officer who gave the order. As many as 20 people were killed, among them at least 3 rioters and 3 militiamen.

In 1789 New York lawmakers banned grave robbing. The same law let judges order that the bodies of executed murderers, arsonists and burglars be dissected.

#### Yellow fever in Philadelphia, 1793

From August to November 1793, yellow fever killed 4,041 people in Philadelphia, by the count of Mathew Carey, who wrote a book about the epidemic. Other counts run to about 5,000, which was about one person in every ten in the city. About 20,000 people left the city. Nobody in 1793 knew that mosquitoes carried the disease.

Dr. Benjamin Rush treated patients by bleeding them heavily and giving them purges. A purge was a medicine that emptied the bowels. Rush's purges were made with mercury, a metal. Losing that much blood could send a weak patient into shock, which happens when too little blood is left in the body. A person in shock becomes confused, the heart beats fast, and the blood pressure drops. A French doctor, Jean Devèze, used milder treatment at the Bush Hill hospital.

Mayor Matthew Clarkson issued a public order about the epidemic on September 10, 1793. From September 14, a committee of 26 citizens worked with him to run the city's response. After the elders of the African church asked, some prisoners were let out of jail on the condition that they nurse the sick at Bush Hill. Two thirds of those prisoners were Black. Jones and Allen's account does not name the officials who let them out.

<a id="story-benjamin-rush"></a>

#### Benjamin Rush

> **Who:** A Philadelphia doctor who treated patients in the 1793 yellow fever epidemic, and a signer of the Declaration of Independence.
>
> **When and where:** Philadelphia, 1793. He worked at Pennsylvania Hospital from 1783 to 1813.

Benjamin Rush told Philadelphians that Black people could not catch yellow fever, and he printed that belief in the newspapers. In fact Black Philadelphians caught the fever and died of it while they nursed the sick.

During the 1793 epidemic, Rush bled his patients heavily and gave them purges made with mercury. Several doctors died, and most of the rest were worn out by sickness or work. Then Rush asked Absalom Jones and Richard Allen, who both knew how to bleed a patient, to care for the sick. He told them where to get medicine, how to give it, and at what stage of the fever to bleed. When they could not tell what to do, he came himself or sent his student Edward Fisher.

At Pennsylvania Hospital, Rush moved patients with mental illness out of the basement and onto hospital floors with windows.

<a id="story-jones-and-allen"></a>

#### Absalom Jones and Richard Allen

> **Who:** Two Black Philadelphians who led Black volunteers to nurse the sick and bury the dead.
>
> **When and where:** Philadelphia, September to November 1793. Their account was printed in 1794.

Absalom Jones and Richard Allen led members of the Free African Society, a group of Black Philadelphians, in nursing the sick and burying the dead in 1793. In early September a notice in the newspapers asked "the people of colour" to help the sick. It stated that they could not catch the fever. Jones, Allen and a few others met to talk over how to act. The next day they asked the mayor how they could help.

They carried away and buried the dead, several hundred poor people and strangers in all, and never asked for pay. Five men they hired helped them, and two of those men were Allen's brothers. Rush taught them when to bleed a patient, and they bled more than 800 people.

The fever killed Black Philadelphians too. In 1792, 67 Black people were buried in the city. In 1793 the number was 305. When some Black nurses fell sick, the families they worked for put them out of their houses. Jones and Allen knew of one who died in a stable.

Mathew Carey wrote that Black nurses had overcharged the sick and stolen from them. In 1794 Jones and Allen printed their own account to answer him. In it they named Mary Scott, a Black nurse who refused to take more than her wage from a Mrs. Mason. Mrs. Mason then gave her six pounds a year for life.

#### Medical care for sailors, 1798

On July 16, 1798, President John Adams signed the Act for the Relief of Sick and Disabled Seamen, which members of Congress had passed. Under it, federal officials took 20 cents a month out of every merchant sailor's pay to pay for sailors' medical care. For a time, the first marine hospital, a hospital for sailors, stood on Castle Island in Boston Harbor. Today's United States Public Health Service began as this program.

### 1800 to 1850

A new protection against smallpox, called vaccination, reached the United States in 1800. Doctors scratched matter from cowpox, a mild disease of cows, into the skin. It was safer than the older method, inoculation, which put pus from a real smallpox sore into a cut. Cholera, a disease spread in dirty water, killed thousands of people in the growing cities in 1832 and 1849. Smallpox killed at least nine in ten Mandan people on the upper Missouri River in 1837, after a federal official had left them out of a vaccination program. From 1845 to 1849 an Alabama doctor, J. Marion Sims, operated again and again on enslaved women to work out a new surgery, and he gave them nothing to stop the pain. A Boston dentist showed surgeons in 1846 that a drug called ether, breathed as a vapor, could keep a patient from feeling an operation. Elizabeth Blackwell became the first woman in the United States to earn a medical degree in 1849.

#### Vaccination arrives, 1800 and 1802

Smallpox is a disease caused by a virus. It covers the body with a rash of blisters, and about 3 of every 10 people who caught it died. To vaccinate a person, a doctor scratched fluid from a cowpox sore into the skin. Cowpox is a mild disease of cows. It protected the person against smallpox. In the older method, inoculation, doctors put pus from a real smallpox sore into a cut in the skin, and some inoculated people died of smallpox.

On July 8, 1800, Dr. Benjamin Waterhouse of Cambridge, Massachusetts, vaccinated his young son Daniel Oliver and a servant, Samuel Carter. He used cowpox matter on threads sent from England. It is the first recorded vaccination in the United States. Doctors in other places claimed earlier ones, but Waterhouse kept official records. He then vaccinated three more of his children and a second servant, Kesiah Flag.

Waterhouse sent vaccine to other doctors and to President Thomas Jefferson. Jefferson vaccinated his family, the enslaved people at his plantation, Monticello, and his neighbors. The enslaved people were Jefferson's property by law, so they could not refuse. The accounts of these vaccinations do not say whether they agreed.

On August 16, 1802, Waterhouse and six other doctors vaccinated nineteen boys. That fall the boys, whom the record calls volunteers, were exposed to smallpox to test the vaccine. The Harvard medical library's account of the test does not say who exposed them, whose sons they were, or whether their parents agreed. The members of Boston's Board of Health then reported that cowpox was "a complete preventive against all the effects of the Small-pox." That meant it kept a person from getting smallpox at all.

#### Smallpox on the upper Missouri, 1832 and 1837

On May 5, 1832, President Andrew Jackson signed a law that members of Congress had passed. It set aside $12,000 to vaccinate Native people. Secretary of War Lewis Cass designed the program and ran it through federal Indian agents, the government officials sent to deal with each Native nation. By February 1833, more than 17,000 Native people had been vaccinated. Some Army doctors refused to take part because the pay was too low. Cass left the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara nations on the upper Missouri River out of the program. The accounts of the program do not give his reason.

On June 18, 1837, the American Fur Company's steamboat *St. Peters* stopped at Fort Clark, beside the Mandan villages in what is now North Dakota. A deckhand had shown signs of smallpox weeks earlier, and three Arikara women who had caught it had boarded to go home to their village. The fort's trader, Francis Chardon, learned from the captain that people on the boat had smallpox. The crew unloaded goods and loaded furs in less than a day, and the boat went on upriver. The historian R. G. Robertson blames the captain, Bernard Pratte Jr., who would not keep the sick apart from other people. Robertson calls that "criminal negligence," a failure to take care so serious that it should count as a crime.

On July 14 Chardon wrote that a young Mandan had died that day of smallpox. Later he wrote that the Mandan "die so fast that it is impossible" to keep count. About 2,000 Mandan lived in the villages in the spring. By October only 23 to 138 were alive, and the counts differ. The Arikara lost between half and two thirds of their people, by different counts. The Hidatsa lost many people too. Along the Missouri River more than 17,000 people died. About two thirds of the Blackfoot died, about half of the Assiniboine, about one third of the Crow and about one quarter of the Pawnee.

The Mandan leader Four Bears caught smallpox. Before he died he spoke about white people, as Chardon recorded it: "I have loved the Whites ... and how have they repaid it! With ingratitude!" Ingratitude means giving no thanks in return for kindness.

#### Cholera in the river cities, 1832 and 1849

Cholera is an infection of the gut. People catch it from food or water that carries its germ. A germ is a living thing too small to see that can cause disease. It causes diarrhea that can start two hours after a person swallows the germ. The body loses so much water and salt that the person can die. Cholera first reached the United States in 1832, and it killed about 3,500 of New York City's roughly 250,000 people that year.

On January 2, 1849, two steamboats from New Orleans reached St. Louis, on the Mississippi River, with 66 passengers sick with cholera. In the spring more boats and gold seekers headed for California came through, and deaths rose. St. Louis had grown from about 5,000 people in 1830 to 77,000 by 1850, and it had no sewers. About three of every four people drank from shallow wells, often dug near outhouses. Pigs rooted through the garbage in the streets.

Doctors did not know what caused cholera. They blamed night air, bad food and alcohol, and told people to stop eating vegetables and then meat. At night they lit fires to clean the air. Some bled their patients: they cut a vein, most often in the arm, and let blood run out into a bowl, which left the sick person weaker.

On June 13, 1849, 65 people died of cholera in St. Louis, and on June 21, 85 died. In early July more than 100 a day died. On June 27 the city's lawmakers gave a Committee of Public Health $50,000. The committee members stopped steamboats at a quarantine station on an island in the river. A quarantine station is a place where people who may carry a disease are kept apart from others. The city engineer drained standing water, and city officials banned hogs from the city. By late July, deaths had dropped to about 10 a day.

Reports from 1849 give 4,557 cholera deaths in St. Louis that year. Many deaths were never reported, so the real number was higher. About 7 of every 10 of the dead were Irish and German immigrants. In 1854 two researchers identified the germ that causes cholera and showed that it spreads in dirty water.

#### Ether, 1842 and 1846

Anesthesia means using a drug so that a patient does not feel pain during an operation. Before it, surgeons worked as fast as they could, because a long operation could send a patient into shock. Shock is a sudden collapse in which the heart and blood can no longer keep the body going.

On March 30, 1842, Dr. Crawford Long of Jefferson, Georgia, cut a tumor from the neck of James Venable while Venable breathed ether. A tumor is a lump of tissue that grows where it should not. Long had noticed that people who breathed ether for fun at parties felt little pain when they got hurt. He did not publish what he had done until 1849.

On October 16, 1846, at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, the dentist William T. G. Morton gave ether to Edward Gilbert Abbott, a young house painter. Abbott breathed the vapor through an inhaler, a breathing device, that Morton had made. Dr. John Collins Warren cut a tumor from Abbott's neck. Abbott said afterward that he had not been fully asleep but "had felt no sensation of pain."

#### J. Marion Sims's operations on enslaved women, 1845 to 1849

From 1845 to 1849, Dr. J. Marion Sims of Montgomery, Alabama, operated again and again on enslaved Black women and girls to work out a new surgery. He gave them nothing to stop the pain.

The women had an injury called a vesicovaginal fistula. It is a hole torn through the wall between the bladder, where urine is held, and the vagina, the passage a baby is born through. A long, blocked childbirth crushes the tissue and makes the hole. Afterward urine runs out of the woman's body all the time. Her skin becomes sore and infected, and she smells of urine. Some women also had a hole into the bowel, so stool leaked too.

The women's enslavers sent them to Sims. The enslavers paid for their clothes and taxes, and Sims fed and housed them in a small hospital behind his office. He named three of the women, Anarcha, Betsey and Lucy. One count gives twelve women and girls in all. A museum of the history of anesthesia counts six or seven women whose names Sims did not write down. Another doctor, Nathan Bozeman, later named four more: Ann McRee, 16, Lavinia Boudurant, 13, Delia, 23, and Julia McDuffie, 20. Sims wrote that he promised to operate only with "the full consent of the patients." An enslaved woman had no power to refuse.

Ether was shown in Boston in 1846, partway through these years. Sims still used nothing to stop the pain during any of the operations. He wrote that the operations were "not painful enough to justify the trouble, and risk attending their administration." He meant the trouble and risk of giving a drug against the pain. Many white doctors of the time wrongly believed that Black people felt less pain. After the operations Sims often gave the women opium, a drug that dulls pain and brings sleep.

For each operation Sims had the woman placed naked on her knees and elbows so that he could see inside her. Sims operated on Lucy, who was about 18, for about an hour while about twelve doctors watched. Sims left a sponge inside her bladder to draw off urine. She nearly died of an infection that spread through her blood. Sims wrote: "Lucy's agony was extreme."

In 1849 Sims closed the hole in Anarcha on about the thirtieth operation. He sewed it shut with silver wire, which caused fewer infections than silk thread. A sponge or a tube drained urine from her bladder while it healed. He published the method in 1852.

Sims also operated on enslaved babies sick with neonatal tetanus, an infection in newborn babies that locks the jaw and other muscles in spasms. He believed the bones of the baby's skull had been pushed in on the brain. In 1847 he kept the baby son of an enslaved woman named Ann at his home. He cut through the baby's scalp with the point of a knife and pried a skull bone outward.

Over the next two months he did it again with the point of a crooked awl, a pointed tool for punching holes. He did the same to the baby of another enslaved woman, Frances, and her baby died twelve hours later. Sims then cut open the body. He blamed Ann for holding her baby with its head on her arm.

In his reports, every baby he operated on or cut open after death was enslaved. When a white baby, the daughter of Wyatt Peters, had the same disease, Sims gave no medicine and had her laid on her side on a pillow. Sims's two articles on the disease report 27 cases, 17 of them from his own notes. The historian Stephen Kenny studied those articles, and his study does not give a total of how many enslaved babies Sims operated on or how many died.

In April 2018 New York City officials voted to take down Sims's statue in Central Park.

<a id="story-anarcha"></a>

#### Anarcha

> **Who:** An enslaved young woman on whom J. Marion Sims operated about thirty times, with nothing to stop the pain, to work out his fistula surgery.
>
> **When and where:** Montgomery, Alabama, 1845 to 1849.

Sims operated on Anarcha about 30 times over about four years before his surgery worked. He gave her no drug to stop the pain. Each time, Sims had her placed naked on her knees and elbows.

Her childbirth had been long and blocked. It tore holes from her vagina into her bladder and into her rectum, the end of the bowel. Urine and stool leaked from her body all the time. The accounts of her age differ. Some give 17 when she gave birth. One estimate says she was 13 when Sims first treated her.

Her enslaver sent her to Sims. She lived in his small hospital in Montgomery during the years of operations. In 1849 the operation closed the hole into her bladder. The records do not show what happened to Anarcha, Betsey and Lucy after Sims finished with them.

<a id="story-elizabeth-blackwell"></a>

#### Elizabeth Blackwell

> **Who:** The first woman to earn a medical degree in the United States.
>
> **When and where:** Geneva, New York, 1847 to 1849, then New York City. Born in Bristol, England, in 1821. Died in Hastings, England, in 1910.

On January 23, 1849, Elizabeth Blackwell graduated at the head of her class from Geneva Medical College in New York. She was the first woman in the United States to earn a medical degree.

About 29 medical schools had turned her down. In 1847 the men studying at Geneva Medical College voted to let her in. Two accounts explain the vote. In one, the students thought the question was a joke by their teachers. In the other, they thought it would be funny to have a woman in the class.

Later in 1849 she worked at La Maternité, a hospital in Paris. She caught an eye infection from a baby she was treating and lost the sight of that eye. She had to give up her plan to become a surgeon.

In 1857 she opened the New York Infirmary for Indigent Women and Children with her sister, Dr. Emily Blackwell, and Dr. Marie Zakrzewska. Indigent means poor. In 1868 she added a medical college for women beside it.

### 1850 to 1900

Disease killed more soldiers than fighting did in the Civil War. From 1862 to 1868 smallpox killed more than 60,000 people who had just been freed from slavery. Officers of New York's new health board ordered filth cleared from the streets in 1866, and cholera killed a smaller share of the city than in earlier years. Yellow fever killed about 20,000 people along the Mississippi River in 1878. Most American doctors did not yet kill germs on their hands and tools. When President James Garfield was shot in 1881, his doctors probed his bullet wound with unwashed fingers, and he died weeks later with his body full of infection. By 1900 women were training as nurses and doctors. Among them were the first Black woman to earn a nursing license and the first Native American woman to earn a medical degree.

#### Disease in the Civil War armies, 1861 to 1865

Between about 620,000 and 850,000 soldiers died in the Civil War, and the count is disputed. For every three soldiers killed in battle, about five died of disease.

The diseases that killed them included diarrhea and dysentery, which are infections of the gut. Others were typhoid fever, an infection spread by food and water that has touched human waste, and pneumonia, an infection of the lungs. Measles, malaria and scurvy killed soldiers too. Malaria is a fever spread by mosquitoes. Scurvy is a sickness caused by too little vitamin C, found in fresh fruit and vegetables.

Soldiers dug latrine trenches, the ditches they used as toilets, too shallow, and they did not cover the waste with dirt. Waste could then wash into the water the soldiers drank. One army surgeon found a camp's latrine uphill of "the stream, from which all water in the camp is obtained."

<a id="story-clara-barton-health"></a>

#### Clara Barton

> **Who:** A clerk at the US Patent Office who took supplies to Civil War battlefields and later founded the American Red Cross.
>
> **When and where:** Antietam, Maryland, September 17, 1862. Born in North Oxford, Massachusetts, on December 25, 1821.

Clara Barton brought a wagon of bandages and supplies to the battlefield at Antietam, Maryland, on September 17, 1862. She had spent a year collecting them. At a farmhouse she held wounded men's heads, gave them water and cooked for them. The lanterns she brought let surgeons keep operating after dark.

A bullet passed through her sleeve and killed a soldier while she was giving him a drink. She wrote that it cut "through his chest from shoulder to shoulder." A surgeon there, Dr. James Dunn, called her "the angel of the battlefield."

Before the war Barton had been a teacher and then a clerk. On May 21, 1881, she and others formed the American Association of the Red Cross, the group now called the American Red Cross, in Washington, D.C. She was its president until 1904, when she resigned after growing criticism.

<a id="story-hannah-ropes"></a>

#### Hannah Ropes

> **Who:** The head nurse of a Civil War hospital in Washington, who reported a thief on the staff to the Secretary of War and died of typhoid caught at work.
>
> **When and where:** Union Hotel Hospital, Georgetown, Washington, D.C., 1862 and 1863. Born in 1809 in New Gloucester, in what is now Maine.

Hannah Ropes ran the nurses at a Civil War hospital in Washington until typhoid killed her in January 1863. Her son Edward was a Union soldier. In 1862 she volunteered as a nurse. She became matron, the woman in charge of the nurses, at the Union Hotel Hospital. It was an old hotel turned into a hospital for 300 to 400 patients.

The writer Louisa May Alcott nursed under her from December 1862. Alcott wrote in her diary: "A more perfect pestilence-box than this house I never saw." A pestilence is a deadly disease that spreads.

Ropes found that the hospital steward, the man in charge of supplies, was stealing supplies meant for the wounded. The chief surgeon ignored her complaints. She took them to the Secretary of War, Edwin Stanton, and the steward and the surgeon were both arrested. The accounts of her life do not say who arrested them.

She caught typhoid in late December 1862 and died on January 20, 1863. Alcott fell sick in the same outbreak and went home on January 21, 1863. Ropes's diary and letters were printed as a book in 1980.

#### Smallpox among freed people, 1862 to 1868

From 1862 to 1868, smallpox killed more than 60,000 people who had just been freed from slavery, the historian Jim Downs counts. Women and children died at higher rates than men.

During the war, people who escaped slavery came to camps the Union army set up for them. The army called them contraband camps. Contraband is a word for goods taken from an enemy in war. The camps were crowded and dirty, and many people in them lacked the basic things they needed to stay alive. Smallpox broke out in Washington, D.C., in 1862 and spread to nearby Alexandria, Virginia.

Doctors already knew how to stop smallpox. They could vaccinate people and keep the sick apart from the healthy. Union army officers and officials of the Freedmen's Bureau, a federal office set up to help people freed from slavery, ran the camps. They put sick freed people in tents made of old, ripped army tarps, with blankets full of insects. Sick white soldiers went to army hospitals. The accounts of the epidemic do not name the men in charge.

Harriet Jacobs, who had escaped slavery herself, came to Alexandria to open a school and worked against the epidemic.

#### Health boards and yellow fever, 1866 to 1879

In February 1866, New York State lawmakers passed a law and Governor Reuben Fenton signed it. Under it, New York City got a Metropolitan Board of Health. The doctor Stephen Smith had worked to get it passed. By April its officers had given 7,000 orders to clear away piled horse manure, dead animals and heaps of garbage. Crews spread chloride and lime, chemicals that kill germs, where cholera struck. Cholera killed 1,137 New Yorkers in 1866. That was a smaller share of the city than in 1832 or 1849.

In 1878 yellow fever spread up the Mississippi River from New Orleans. Yellow fever is a disease caused by a virus. It brings a high fever and can kill. It began after the ship *Emily B. Souder* arrived in New Orleans in late May, and crew members fell ill and died. The first official yellow fever death in the city that year was a four-year-old girl, in July. Along the river about 120,000 people caught the fever and about 20,000 died.

In Memphis, Tennessee, about 25,000 to 27,000 of the city's 47,000 people fled. More than 5,000 people died in the city. Annie Cook ran a brothel, a house where men paid women for sex. She turned it into a hospital, nursed the sick, and died of the fever.

That a mosquito spreads yellow fever was not proved until 1900. In 1879 members of Congress set up a National Board of Health.

#### Germs and the death of President Garfield, 1881

Germs are living things too small to see, such as bacteria, and many of them cause disease. The English surgeon Joseph Lister urged doctors to kill germs on their hands and tools, to stop wounds from getting infected. Most American doctors thought this was too much trouble.

On July 2, 1881, Charles Guiteau shot President James Garfield at a railroad station in Washington, D.C. Doctors pushed their unwashed fingers and unwashed tools into the wound to search for the bullet. Dr. Willard Bliss, who took charge, probed the wound several times a day and never cleaned his hands first. One doctor punctured Garfield's liver while probing. The accounts of Garfield's care do not name him.

Garfield died on September 19, 1881. Doctors who examined his body found pneumonia in both lungs and his body full of pus. A medical paper of 2013 argues instead that a burst artery near his spleen killed him. An artery is a large tube that carries blood from the heart, and the spleen is an organ beside the stomach. Candice Millard, who wrote a 2011 book about Garfield's death, said in an interview that Garfield "would have been better off if they had just left him alone."

#### Women become nurses and doctors

The New England Hospital for Women and Children in Boston had only women doctors. Its nursing course took 16 months. Of 42 students who began in 1878, four finished in 1879. One of them was Mary Eliza Mahoney, who had worked at the hospital for 15 years before she started the course. She became the first Black woman in the United States to earn a professional nursing license. In 1908 she helped found a group for Black nurses, the National Association of Colored Graduate Nurses. "Colored" was a word then used for Black people.

<a id="story-susan-la-flesche-picotte"></a>

#### Susan La Flesche Picotte

> **Who:** An Omaha woman who became the first Native American woman to earn a medical degree, and went home to be the doctor for her own nation.
>
> **When and where:** The Omaha Reservation, Nebraska. Born 1865, graduated 1889, died 1915.

In 1889 Susan La Flesche became the first Native American woman in the United States to earn a medical degree. She was born in 1865 on the Omaha Reservation in northeastern Nebraska. Her father was Chief Joseph La Flesche, and her mother was Mary, also called One Woman.

As a child she watched a sick Native woman die because the local white doctor would not treat her. She studied at the Woman's Medical College of Pennsylvania. She finished its three-year course in two years and graduated first in her class.

Back on the reservation she cared for more than 1,300 people spread over 450 square miles. In 1913 she opened a hospital at Walthill, Nebraska, on the reservation. She died in 1915.

#### Typhoid in the army camps, 1898

During the war with Spain in 1898, soldiers in army camps in the United States caught typhoid. There were 20,738 cases and 1,590 deaths in the camps. Typhoid caused 87 of every 100 deaths from disease in those camps. Major Walter Reed and two other army doctors, Victor Vaughan and Edward Shakespeare, studied the camps. They found that the disease spread mostly from man to man, and some of it by flies.

### 1900 to 1950

Army doctors proved in 1900 that a mosquito spreads yellow fever. An influenza epidemic, a flu that spread to huge numbers of people at once, killed about 675,000 people in the United States in 1918. In 1932 doctors of the United States Public Health Service began a study of 399 Black men in Alabama who had syphilis. For 40 years the doctors kept the men from being treated, while telling them they were being treated. A medicine mixed with a poison killed more than 100 people in 1937. In 1938 a new law required drug makers to prove a drug safe before selling it. Penicillin, which kills many kinds of bacteria, reached patients from 1942. Public Health Service doctors exposed 1,308 people in Guatemala to diseases passed during sex, on purpose, from 1946 to 1948.

#### Proving the mosquito, 1900 and 1901

In 1900 four army doctors near Havana, Cuba, proved that mosquitoes pass yellow fever from sick people to healthy ones. Yellow fever is a disease caused by a virus. It brings a high fever and can kill. Major Walter Reed led the four, and the others were James Carroll, Jesse Lazear and Aristides Agramonte. Lazear raised mosquitoes and let them feed on yellow fever patients. A mosquito that had fed on a patient at least 12 days before passed the disease on when it bit someone else. Carroll and a soldier who volunteered caught yellow fever from these bites in late August. Lazear was probably bitten by an infected mosquito himself, and he died of yellow fever on September 25, 1900.

In November 1900 the doctors tested two buildings. In one, volunteers slept in bedding soiled by yellow fever patients, and they stayed well. In the other, a clean building, infected mosquitoes bit volunteers, and several caught yellow fever. All of them recovered. The volunteers signed written contracts that named the danger, and they were paid. After workers killed the mosquitoes in Havana, yellow fever there nearly stopped.

<a id="story-clara-maass"></a>

#### Clara Maass

> **Who:** A New Jersey nurse who died after letting infected mosquitoes bite her in a yellow fever experiment.
>
> **When and where:** Havana, Cuba, 1901. Born in East Orange, New Jersey, in 1876.

Clara Maass died of yellow fever at 25, after she let infected mosquitoes bite her in Havana in 1901. She came from a poor German immigrant family in East Orange, New Jersey. She started training as a nurse at 17, at the Newark German Hospital, and she was its head nurse by 21. She nursed soldiers in the 1898 war with Spain and then in the Philippines.

In Havana volunteers were paid $100, and $200 if they caught the fever. In March 1901 Maass let infected mosquitoes bite her. She had a mild case and got well. In August 1901 she volunteered again, caught yellow fever, and died on August 24. Soon after her death, the yellow fever commission was ordered to break up. The museum account of her life does not name who gave the order.

#### Mary Mallon, held on an island

Mary Mallon was a cook in New York who carried typhoid germs in her body without being sick herself. Typhoid is a fever caused by bacteria that spread through food and water. Health officials counted 47 people infected through her cooking, and 3 of them died.

Officials of the New York City Board of Health held her on North Brother Island, in the East River, from 1907 for more than two years. In a letter in June 1909, she wrote that they kept her "a prisoner without being sick nor needing medical treatment." She also wrote, "I have been in fact a peep show for everybody." Officials took her back to the island in 1915. She stayed there until she died on November 11, 1938. She became known as "Typhoid Mary."

#### Fewer medical schools, 1910

In 1910 Abraham Flexner published a survey of the country's 148 medical schools. Leaders of the Carnegie Foundation had hired him to do it. He called several schools "beyond repair." In the years after, the number of medical schools fell to 66. Writers at JSTOR Daily, a history magazine, say that members of the American Medical Association, most of them white men, used the report to close schools and protect their own jobs and earnings. Seven medical schools had trained Black doctors. Only two were left: Howard University in Washington, D.C., and Meharry Medical College in Nashville, Tennessee.

#### Polio in New York, 1916

Polio is a disease caused by a virus that can attack the nerves in the spine. It can leave a person unable to move the arms, the legs or the muscles used for breathing. This loss of movement is called paralysis.

In the summer of 1916 polio spread through New York City. More than 9 of every 10 of the city's cases were in children five or younger. One count gives more than 27,000 cases and more than 6,000 deaths across the whole country. Accounts of New York City alone differ, from about 2,000 deaths to about 6,000.

Dr. Haven Emerson was the city's health commissioner. Every day the names and addresses of the sick appeared in the newspapers. Signs went up on their houses. The accounts of the epidemic do not say who put them up. A team of Health Department workers led by Dr. Simon Blatteis kept the families shut inside. Under Health Department rules, a family that could not give the sick child a separate room, a separate toilet and a nurse had to let the department take the child to a hospital, free of charge. Police stood at the railroads, roads and rivers to turn back anyone trying to leave the city. Writers in the *New York Times* blamed Italian immigrants for the disease. Italian immigrants were shunned, cursed and beaten up, and the accounts of the epidemic do not name who beat them.

#### The 1918 influenza

Influenza, or flu, is a disease caused by a virus that infects the nose, throat and lungs. In 1918 a new kind of influenza spread around the world. About 500 million people caught it, and at least 50 million died. About 675,000 of the dead were in the United States. Many of them were healthy adults between 20 and 40. There was no vaccine against it. A vaccine is a medicine that trains the body to fight off a germ before the germ can make a person sick. There was no antibiotic either, a medicine that kills bacteria. A navy nurse in Illinois later described patients with nosebleeds so strong that the blood shot across the room. Many died of pneumonia, a sickness in which the lungs fill with fluid.

In Philadelphia, Dr. Wilmer Krusen, the city's director of public health, let a parade to sell war bonds go ahead on September 28, 1918. People bought the bonds to lend money to the government for the war. About 200,000 people crowded onto Broad Street. Krusen said in public that the flu was not a threat, although army camps nearby were full of it. Within three days every bed in the city's 31 hospitals was full. City officials closed schools, churches and theaters on October 3. More than 12,000 people in Philadelphia died within weeks.

In 1918 the flu reached Brevig Mission, an Alaska Native village. Within five days, 72 of the 80 villagers were dead. Miners from the town of Nome thawed the frozen ground with steam and dug one grave for all of them.

<a id="story-josie-mabel-brown"></a>

#### Josie Mabel Brown

> **Who:** A Navy nurse from Missouri who worked the influenza wards at Great Lakes, Illinois, and described them in an interview when she was about 100.
>
> **When and where:** Great Lakes Naval Training Station, Illinois, fall 1918 to 1919. Born on a Missouri farm in 1886.

Josie Mabel Brown nursed sailors dying of influenza at the Great Lakes Naval Training Station in Illinois in 1918. At the worst of the epidemic, 6,000 of the 173,000 men there were in the hospitals.

Brown was born on a farm in southwestern Missouri in 1886. She finished nurse training in 1917 and was called into the Navy. In the fall of 1918 she was ordered to Great Lakes.

On her first ward, one man lay dying on the bed and another lay on the floor. A third waited on a stretcher for the bed. The nurses wrapped each dead man in a sheet and tied a shipping tag to one big toe. The ambulance brought four sick men and took away four dead ones.

The nurses had no time to take temperatures. Patients had nosebleeds so strong that "the blood would just shoot across the room," she said. In some men, air leaked from torn lungs into the body, and she could see bubbles under the skin of their arms.

She worked 16 hours a day until just before Christmas 1918. In March 1919 she caught a fever of 104 or 105 herself, and she recovered. She told her story to her niece in 1986 and died at 104.

#### Radium in the body, 1917 to 1932

Radium is a metal that gives off radiation, a stream of energy that damages living cells. Radium belongs to the same family of elements as calcium, so growing bones take it up as if it were calcium. There it keeps giving off radiation from the inside.

From 1917, women painted watch dials with glowing radium paint at the U.S. Radium factory in Orange, New Jersey. They shaped their brushes into a point with their lips. The radium destroyed their bone marrow, the soft tissue inside bones that makes blood, so their bodies could not make enough blood. Their jaw bones died and broke apart. Some grew cancers of the bone. In 1924 a dentist, Theodor Blum, examined the dial painter Grace Fryer. Her jaw bone was wasting away, and he called the damage "radium jaw."

Grace Fryer, Katherine Schaub, Edna Hussman, Albina Larice and Quinta McDonald sued. Judge William Clark worked out an agreement under which the company paid the women. The five women signed it on June 8, 1928. Each woman received $10,000, though some accounts give $15,000, plus $600 a year for as long as she lived, and her medical costs. The company's officers never admitted that the company was to blame.

William Bailey sold radium dissolved in water as a medicine called Radithor. He falsely claimed to have medical training and paid doctors to tell their patients to take it. Eben Byers, a Pittsburgh businessman, drank about 1,400 bottles from 1927 to 1930. In 1931 a government investigator found that the bone in Byers's body was falling apart and holes were forming in his skull. He died on March 31, 1932, of a cancer of the jaw bone caused by the radium.

#### Native health, 1928

In 1928 a team of investigators led by Lewis Meriam reported on the lives of Native people on reservations and in government boarding schools. They wrote that "the health of the Indians as compared with that of the general population is bad." They wrote that the share of Native people who died each year was high, and so was the share of babies who died.

The investigators found tuberculosis "extremely prevalent," which means very common. Tuberculosis is a disease caused by a germ, usually in the lungs, and it spreads by coughing. They found trachoma, an eye disease that "produces blindness," to be "a major problem." In the government boarding schools the children's food was "deficient in quantity, quality, and variety." That means there was not enough of it, and it was poor and the same every day. "The medical service rendered the boarding school children is not up to a reasonable standard," they wrote. That means the care doctors gave the children was not good enough.

#### The Tuskegee study, 1932 to 1972

From 1932 to 1972, doctors of the United States Public Health Service watched hundreds of Black men in Alabama live with syphilis, and they kept the men from being treated. They wanted to see what the disease did to a body when no one treated it.

Syphilis is a disease caused by bacteria. It is passed during sex, or from a mother to her unborn baby. Left untreated, it goes through stages. At first the person gets a painless sore where the germ entered. Weeks later the person gets a rash, a fever and a sore throat. Then the germ can hide in the body for years with no signs. After 10 to 30 years it can damage the heart and the large blood vessels, the brain and the nerves. It can cause blindness, and it can cause dementia, which is the loss of memory and reason. It can kill, and a baby born with syphilis can die.

In 1932 Dr. Taliaferro Clark began the study. He was head of the Public Health Service's office for diseases passed by sex. The study took place in Macon County, Alabama, near the town of Tuskegee. Dr. Raymond Vonderlehr ran it there and later took Clark's place. Most of the men were poor farmers. Many were sharecroppers, who farmed someone else's land for a share of the crop. The doctors chose 399 men who had syphilis and 201 men who did not, to compare them. They planned no treatment at all for the infected men. The study was planned to last six months, and it ran for 40 years.

The doctors told the men they had "bad blood" and that they were being treated for it. They did not tell the men that the disease was syphilis, and they never asked whether the men agreed to be studied. The men got free exams, hot meals on exam days and rides. From 1935 they were also promised about $50 toward their burials, if they let doctors cut open their bodies after death to study them. Eunice Rivers, a Black nurse, kept in touch with the men for all 40 years. She gave them aspirin and a "spring tonic" that did nothing against syphilis. Dr. Oliver Wenger, who ran the clinic in the region, wrote, "we have no further interest in these patients until they die."

The exams also included spinal taps. In a spinal tap a doctor pushes a needle between the bones of the lower back and draws out fluid from around the spinal cord. The doctors wanted to see whether syphilis had reached the brain and nerves. A spinal tap often causes a lot of pain and other harm. The doctors' letter to the men called it their "Last Chance For Special Free Treatment."

Keeping treatment away from the men was part of the study. Its doctors gave local doctors lists of the men's names and asked them not to treat them. In 1941 army officials drafted some of the men and told them to start treatment. Public Health Service officers gave the draft board, the group that chose men for the army, a list of 256 names to leave untreated, and the board members did as they asked. Accounts differ on when penicillin became the usual cure for syphilis: 1943, by 1947, or the early 1950s. The study doctors never offered it to the men. Vonderlehr later wrote, "I hope that the availability of antibiotics has not interfered too much with this project."

Reports that the study doctors printed show what the disease did to the men. In 1936 the doctors reported that the infected men had much more disease of the heart and blood vessels than the men without syphilis. Only 16 of every 100 infected men showed no sign of illness, against 61 of every 100 of the uninfected men. About ten years later, nearly twice as many infected men as uninfected men had died. The doctors worked out that the disease had cut the men's lives by about a fifth. In 1955 they reported on the infected men whose bodies they had cut open after death. More than 30 of every 100 had died because syphilis destroyed their heart and blood vessels or their brain and spinal cord.

A news story revealed the study in 1972. By then, by one count, at least 28 of the men had died of syphilis itself and 100 more of problems it caused. Forty of their wives had caught it. Nineteen of their children were born with it.

<a id="story-charles-pollard"></a>

#### Charles Pollard

> **Who:** An Alabama farmer who was kept in the Tuskegee study for 40 years without being told he had syphilis, and who then brought the lawsuit for the men.
>
> **When and where:** Near Tuskegee, Macon County, Alabama, 1932 to 1972.

Charles Pollard learned from the news in July 1972 that he had had syphilis for 40 years. He was 66. He farmed 66 acres of land he had inherited, about three miles from Tuskegee. His father was the son of two enslaved people.

In 1932 men from the study told Pollard he could get a free physical exam at a one-room school the next afternoon. "So I went on over and they told me I had bad blood," he said. "And that's what they've been telling me ever since." For 40 years doctors came around "from time to time and check me over."

Pollard went to Fred Gray, a lawyer in Tuskegee. Their lawsuit, *Pollard v. United States*, ended in a settlement of $10 million. In 1997 Pollard was one of the survivors at the White House when President Bill Clinton apologized to them.

#### A poison sold as medicine, and a new law, 1937 and 1938

In 1937 a poison in a new medicine killed more than 100 people. In 1938 a new law required drug makers to prove a drug safe before selling it. The S. E. Massengill Company of Bristol, Tennessee, sold a liquid medicine called Elixir Sulfanilamide for strep throat. Its chemist, Harold Watkins, dissolved the drug in diethylene glycol, a chemical used in antifreeze. Diethylene glycol is a poison. No law required the company to test the medicine for safety before selling it.

In September and October 1937 the medicine killed more than 100 people in 15 states, many of them children. It shut down their kidneys. They stopped passing urine and had strong stomach pain, vomiting and seizures before they died. A mother wrote to President Franklin Roosevelt about her daughter Joan: "we can see her little body tossing to and fro and hear that little voice screaming with pain." The owner, Dr. Samuel Massengill, said, "I do not feel that there was any responsibility on our part." Watkins killed himself.

On June 25, 1938, President Roosevelt signed the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, which members of Congress had passed. Under it, a company had to prove to officials of the Food and Drug Administration that a new drug was safe before it could sell the drug.

#### Penicillin, 1942
