Penicillin is a drug made from a mold. It kills many kinds of bacteria, the germs behind infections such as blood infections and syphilis. It was the first antibiotic made in large amounts.

In March 1942 Anne Miller of New Haven, Connecticut, had an infection of the blood after a miscarriage, which is the loss of a baby before it can live outside the womb. For weeks her fever stayed at 103 degrees or higher. Her doctors got 5.5 grams of penicillin, half of all the penicillin in the United States at the time. She got her first dose on March 14. By the next morning her temperature was back to normal. She was the first patient in the United States whose life was saved by penicillin.

#### Exposed on purpose in Guatemala, 1946 to 1948

From 1946 to 1948, doctors of the United States Public Health Service, led by Dr. John Cutler, gave people in Guatemala syphilis, gonorrhea and chancroid on purpose, or tried to. All three are diseases passed during sex. The doctors infected people without asking whether they agreed.

The doctors exposed 1,308 people to these diseases: prisoners, soldiers and patients in the national mental hospital. They ranged from 10 to 72 years old. The records show some kind of treatment for 678 of them. The doctors used women who were paid for sex to pass on the diseases. They infected most of these women first, then sent them to the prisoners. They also rubbed pus from sick men painfully onto people's genitals and into the opening where urine leaves the body. They injected germs into people's spinal fluid.

For tests, the doctors also took blood or spinal fluid from 5,128 people, among them children in orphanages and schools and people with leprosy. Leprosy is a disease caused by bacteria that damages the skin and nerves.

The money came from the Public Health Service, the National Institutes of Health and the Pan American Sanitary Bureau. Guatemalan officials supplied staff and buildings. Cutler's records note 83 deaths while the experiments went on. A presidential commission studied the experiments in 2011 and found it unclear how many of those deaths the experiments caused. The doctors never published their results. The public learned of the experiments in 2010.

#### Federal money for hospitals, 1946

On August 13, 1946, the Hospital Survey and Construction Act became law. People call it the Hill-Burton Act, after the two senators who put it forward, Lister Hill of Alabama and Harold Burton of Ohio. Over the years, federal lawmakers set aside $3.7 billion under it to build hospitals, and states and towns added $9.1 billion.

Under the law, the people who ran hospitals built with the money could keep Black and white patients apart, as long as the separate care was called equal. Accounts differ on who asked for that rule. Judges struck it down in 1963.

#### Pellagra, silica dust and forced sterilization

Pellagra killed about 100,000 Americans between 1900 and 1940, out of about 3 million who had it. Pellagra is a disease caused by too little niacin, a vitamin, in the diet. Most of the sick were poor farmers, sharecroppers and cotton-mill workers in the South who lived on little but cornmeal, molasses and dried pork. Scientists identified niacin in 1937.

From 1930 to 1932, almost 5,000 workers dug the Hawks Nest tunnel in West Virginia. It was the Union Carbide company's tunnel, and the contractor was Rinehart and Dennis. Most of the workers were Black men who had come from other parts of the South. The rock was full of silica, the mineral in sand. The men drilled through it with no masks and no way to control the dust. The West Virginia Encyclopedia's account of the tunnel does not name the company men who made that choice. Breathing silica's fine dust scars the lungs until a person cannot breathe, a disease called silicosis. Death counts run from 476 to close to 1,000.

In Puerto Rico, under a law that took effect in 1937, members of a government Eugenics Board ordered 97 women sterilized by force. Sterilized means that a person can never become pregnant. Doctors did it by cutting or tying the tubes that carry eggs to the womb, or by removing the womb. Eugenics was the false idea that a country could improve its people by stopping some people from having children.

Many thousands of other women were pressured into the same operation. Clarence Gamble, an heir to the Procter and Gamble soap fortune, set up birth control clinics in Puerto Rico with money from the Puerto Rico Reconstruction Administration, a federal office. Gamble made sterilization a rule in his clinics. A woman with three living children could be seen there only if she agreed to be sterilized, historians on the history podcast DIG report. Some women were told the operation could be undone. Factory owners hired sterilized women first. Some women were told they would not get a job unless they were sterilized. Some employers opened clinics inside their factories where workers could be sterilized. Some pregnant women were turned away from hospitals unless they agreed to be sterilized right after giving birth. The historians' accounts do not name the factories or the hospitals.

### 1950 to 2000

Doctors reported more than 21,000 Americans paralyzed by polio in 1952. A vaccine tested on about 1.8 million children was announced in 1955. The last polio case caught inside the United States came in 1979. In 1965 President Lyndon Johnson signed Medicare, health insurance for people 65 and older, and Medicaid, for people with little money. A reporter exposed the Tuskegee study in 1972, and a federal health official announced its end that November. In the 1970s doctors in federally paid clinics sterilized poor Black women and girls. Doctors in the Indian Health Service sterilized Native women. Many of these women and girls never gave permission. In 1981 doctors reported the first cases of the disease later named AIDS. By the end of 2000, 448,060 Americans had died of it.

<a id="story-henrietta-lacks"></a>

#### Henrietta Lacks

> **Who:** A Black woman whose cancer cells doctors took without asking her. Her cells were the first human cells to keep growing in a laboratory.
>
> **When and where:** Johns Hopkins Hospital, Baltimore, 1951. Born Loretta Pleasant in Roanoke, Virginia, on August 1, 1920.
>
> **Movie:** *The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks* (2017), a drama made for HBO about her and her daughter Deborah.

In 1951 doctors at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore cut cells from Henrietta Lacks's body without her permission or knowledge. Her cells were the first human cells to keep growing and dividing in a laboratory. At that time no rule required doctors to ask.

She grew up in Clover, Virginia, in a log cabin that had been slave quarters on a plantation. Her white great-grandfather and great-uncle had owned it. In January 1951 she went to Johns Hopkins with a lump in her womb. Doctors found cancer of the cervix, the opening of the womb. They treated her with radium placed inside her body, and then with X-rays. During her treatments, doctors cut two samples from her cervix.

Dr. George Gey grew the cells. They kept dividing, and they were named HeLa, from the first two letters of her first and last names. By 1954 Jonas Salk's team used HeLa cells in its polio vaccine work. Another doctor, Chester Southam, injected HeLa cells into cancer patients, prisoners and healthy people to see whether cancer could be passed on.

She died on October 4, 1951, at 31, after the cancer spread through her body. Her family did not learn about the cells until 1975. In 2021 her family sued a company, Thermo Fisher Scientific, for making money from HeLa cells without her permission, and the two sides settled in 2023.

#### The polio vaccine, 1952 to 1979

In 1952 doctors in the United States reported more than 21,000 people paralyzed by polio. Fewer than 1 in 100 children who catch polio are paralyzed. When polio paralyzes the muscles used for breathing, the person needs a machine to breathe. The iron lung was a metal tube about seven feet long, and the patient lay inside it. Bellows, a pump with folding sides, changed the air pressure inside the tube to pull air into the lungs.

Jonas Salk of the University of Pittsburgh made a vaccine from polio virus that had been killed. The money for his work came from the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis, a charity that later became the March of Dimes.

Dr. Thomas Francis Jr. of the University of Michigan ran the test in 1954. About 1.8 million children in the United States, Canada and Finland took part, counting children who got no shot and were only watched. From April 26 to July 10, 1954, more than 443,000 children got at least one shot of vaccine. More than 210,000 got a placebo, a shot with no medicine in it. Neither the child nor the nurse knew which one it was. The children were called Polio Pioneers, and their parents signed permission forms. On April 12, 1955, at the University of Michigan, the results were announced: the vaccine was 80 to 90 percent effective. It was approved for use the same year.

That April, Cutter Laboratories in Berkeley, California, made 120,000 doses that still held live virus. About 40,000 children who got it had a mild form of polio. Fifty-six were paralyzed, and five died. The children passed the virus to others, and 113 more people were paralyzed and 5 more died. Cutter's managers took the vaccine off the market on April 27, 1955. At a hearing that June, members of Congress said the staff of the federal laboratory that was supposed to check the vaccine were mostly to blame, because they had not checked it closely.

Albert Sabin's vaccine, which people swallowed instead of getting a shot, was approved for use from 1961 to 1963. The last case of polio caught inside the United States was in 1979. Between 15 and 40 years after they got sick, 25 to 40 of every 100 people paralyzed by polio as children get new muscle pain and new weakness. This is called post-polio syndrome.

<a id="story-jonas-salk"></a>

#### Jonas Salk

> **Who:** The doctor who made the first polio vaccine and did not patent it.
>
> **When and where:** University of Pittsburgh, 1947 to 1955. Born in New York City in 1914.

Jonas Salk made the polio vaccine that was approved for use in 1955, and he never took out a patent on it. A patent is a legal right to be the only one who may make and sell an invention.

He started work at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine in 1947. In 1952 he made a vaccine from polio virus that had been killed, so that it could not cause the disease.

Thomas Francis Jr. ran the 1954 test. Salk had first learned about viruses in Francis's laboratory in 1941. At first Salk did not want some children to get a dummy shot, because the dummy shot could not protect them against polio. He gave way, because only that kind of test could prove the vaccine worked.

The television reporter Edward R. Murrow asked Salk who owned the patent. Salk answered, "Could you patent the sun?" People at the charity that paid for the work and at the university had looked into a patent. They judged that the method was probably not new enough to patent. Salk died in La Jolla, California, in 1995.

<a id="story-paul-alexander"></a>

#### Paul Alexander

> **Who:** A Dallas boy paralyzed by polio at six who lived in an iron lung for more than 70 years and became a lawyer.
>
> **When and where:** Dallas, Texas, 1952 to 2024. Born in Dallas on January 30, 1946.

Paul Alexander lived in an iron lung for more than 70 years after polio paralyzed him in 1952. He was six, and there was an outbreak of polio in Dallas. Within days he could not move below his neck or breathe on his own. Doctors saved him with a tracheotomy, an operation that cuts an opening in the front of the neck into the windpipe so that air can get in. Then they put him in an iron lung.

From 1954 he learned to breathe outside the machine for hours at a time by swallowing air into his lungs. Every night he went back into it.

He held a stick in his mouth to turn pages, to paint, and later to type. He studied at Southern Methodist University and the University of Texas, earned a law degree in 1984, and worked as a lawyer in Dallas. In 2020 he published a book about his life, *Three Minutes for a Dog*.

"I've never thought of myself as a cripple," he said in 2017. Cripple is an old, unkind word for a person who cannot use part of the body. "I'm Paul Alexander, human being." Guinness World Records named him the longest-surviving iron lung patient. He died in Dallas on March 11, 2024, at 78.

#### The Indian Health Service, 1954 to 1976

In 1954 President Dwight Eisenhower signed the Indian Health Transfer Act. Under it, Public Health Service officials took over health care for Native people from the Bureau of Indian Affairs, the federal office that ran the government's dealings with Native nations. The new office was called the Indian Health Service. That same year Dr. Thomas Parran reported to the Interior Department on the health of Alaska Natives. He wrote that they suffered "sickness, crippling conditions and premature deaths to a degree exceeded in very few parts of the world." That means people in very few places anywhere were sicker or died younger. Health care for Alaska Natives moved to the Indian Health Service in 1955, and its staff led the work against tuberculosis.

Under a 1959 law, Public Health Service workers could bring clean water and ways to get rid of sewage to reservations, and tribes took part in the decisions. In 1976 President Gerald Ford signed the Indian Health Care Improvement Act. Under it, Medicare and Medicaid could pay the Indian Health Service for the care its staff gave.

#### New operations and new pictures of the body, 1954 to 1963

On December 23, 1954, at a Boston hospital, Dr. Joseph Murray moved a healthy kidney from Ronald Herrick into his identical twin brother, Richard. Richard was dying of kidney disease. The body's defenses attack an organ from almost anyone else, which is called rejection. Because the twins were identical, Richard's body accepted the kidney. He lived eight more years, married and had two children.

In 1958 scientists at Brookhaven National Laboratory in New York built the first machine to make technetium-99m, a radioactive chemical. A doctor injects a tiny amount into a patient. It gives off rays that a camera outside the body picks up, to make pictures of the bones, the heart and other organs. Doctors in the United States first reported scans with it in 1963. Doctors around the world now use it in tens of millions of scans a year.

#### Fallout on Rongelap, 1954

On March 1, 1954, United States scientists set off a hydrogen bomb called Castle Bravo at Bikini Atoll in the Marshall Islands. It was nearly three times as strong as they expected. Fallout, the radioactive dust and ash that falls after a nuclear blast, came down on Rongelap, an island of the Marshallese people about 110 miles away. It looked like snow, and children played in it. Twenty-three Japanese fishermen on the boat *Lucky Dragon* got sick, and one died.

More than 230 people were moved off Rongelap, Rongerik and Utirik. The Rongelap and Utirik people were moved about 72 hours after the blast. The accounts of the evacuation do not name who moved them or who decided when. Radioactive iodine from the fallout collected in their thyroid glands, which sit in the neck. In the years after, doctors found more thyroid lumps and thyroid cancers among them. Staff of the Atomic Energy Commission, the federal office in charge of nuclear weapons and nuclear power, studied the exposed people. Doctors working for the United States government later gave them follow-up medical care.

#### Radiation tested on people, 1944 to 1974

In 1994 President Bill Clinton appointed a committee to investigate radiation experiments paid for by the federal government. He acted after reports that doctors had injected plutonium, a radioactive metal, into hospital patients who did not know it. In its 1995 report the committee counted nearly 4,000 such experiments from 1944 to 1974. Researchers paid by the federal government had also run experiments on children and on prisoners.

The committee wrote that in the 1940s and 1950s it was common for doctors to use patients in research "without their awareness or consent." In some studies on children, the radioactive doses raised the children's lifetime risk of thyroid cancer. The committee also found studies in which patients died soon after receiving radiation doses as large as those given to treat disease.

Miners who dug uranium underground breathed radon, a radioactive gas that comes off uranium ore. At least several hundred of them died of lung cancer. The committee found that federal officials neither required the mines to be ventilated, which means fresh air pumped in, nor properly warned the miners. Under a 1990 law, the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act, some of the miners get payments from the government.

#### Thalidomide, 1960 to 1962

In 1960 the drug company Richardson-Merrell asked the Food and Drug Administration for permission to sell thalidomide. It was a sleeping pill that doctors also gave pregnant women for morning sickness. It was already sold in more than 20 other countries. Dr. Frances Kelsey, a new FDA reviewer, refused to approve it because the company's evidence was weak. For more than a year, under steady pressure from the company, she kept asking for more.

In November 1961 doctors in Europe linked thalidomide to babies born with arms and legs that were very short or missing. Around the world more than 10,000 babies were born harmed by it, and about 40 of every 100 died at birth or soon after.

Richardson-Merrell staff had already given more than 2.5 million tablets to more than 1,000 American doctors to "test." Nearly 20,000 patients took them, and several hundred of those patients were pregnant. At least 17 American babies were born with thalidomide damage. Company officials withdrew the application in March 1962. In October 1962, members of Congress passed the Kefauver-Harris Amendments with no votes against. Drug makers then had to prove that a drug worked, report its harms to the FDA, and get people's permission before testing drugs on them.

#### Smoking and asbestos, 1954 to 1998

On January 11, 1964, Surgeon General Luther Terry released a report on smoking by ten experts who had read more than 7,000 articles. The surgeon general is the country's top public health doctor. The ten experts found that smokers died at a rate 70 percent higher than non-smokers. The average smoker was 9 to 10 times as likely to get lung cancer, and a heavy smoker at least 20 times. Smoking was the main cause of chronic bronchitis, a long-lasting swelling of the air passages, and was linked to emphysema, a lung disease, and to heart disease.

Ten years earlier, in January 1954, the big tobacco companies had paid for an advertisement in more than 400 newspapers that disputed the studies linking cigarettes to lung cancer. In 1957 Surgeon General Leroy Burney said the evidence showed that smoking caused lung cancer.

Lung cancer grows in the cells that line the air passages of the lungs. It causes a cough that does not go away, trouble breathing, and coughing up blood. Smoking causes about 9 of every 10 lung cancers in men and 8 of every 10 in women. In emphysema, the thin walls between the lungs' tiny air sacs break down, so the person cannot get enough air.

Under a 1965 law, every pack of cigarettes had to carry a health warning. From 1970 cigarette ads were banned from television and radio. On April 14, 1994, the heads of seven tobacco companies told Congress that nicotine is not addictive. In a 1998 settlement, a deal to end lawsuits, the tobacco companies agreed to pay 46 states at least $206 billion over 25 years.

Asbestos is a group of minerals that split into thin fibers. Workers used it to insulate buildings and ships. Its fibers, breathed in, stay in the lungs and scar them. They cause lung cancer and mesothelioma, a cancer of the thin lining of the chest and belly. The sickness can start 10 to 40 years or more after the person breathed the dust. Shipyard workers, insulation workers, miners and firefighters were among those who breathed it. Johns-Manville, the biggest maker of asbestos, went bankrupt in 1982 while facing thousands of lawsuits.

#### Medicare and Medicaid, 1965 and 1966

In 1950 two thirds of Americans over 65 had incomes below $1,000 a year, and only 1 of every 8 had health insurance. Health insurance is a plan that pays doctor and hospital bills.

On July 30, 1965, President Lyndon Johnson signed Medicare and Medicaid into law at the Truman Library in Independence, Missouri. Former President Harry Truman was with him. Truman had asked Congress for national health insurance 20 years earlier. Medicare is health insurance for people 65 and older. Medicaid is health insurance for people with little money. Nearly 20 million people signed up for Medicare in its first three years.

Many hospitals still kept Black and white patients apart. In the South, the people who ran hospitals mostly put Black patients in separate basement wards or separate buildings, or turned them away. In many northern cities, hospital care was just as segregated through unwritten rules. In 1963, in the case *Simkins v. Moses H. Cone Memorial Hospital*, judges of a federal appeals court ruled that hospitals built with Hill-Burton money could not keep patients apart by race. In 1964 the justices of the Supreme Court refused to take up the case.

The Civil Rights Act of 1964 barred federal money for any place that treated people differently by race. Medicare was to begin paying hospitals on July 1, 1966. Before then, almost 1,000 federal workers volunteered to inspect about 6,000 hospitals. They checked beds, waiting rooms, lunch rooms and hiring. Inspectors drove at high speed to get away from local Klan groups. Some inspectors were jailed on false charges. Bullets were fired at their rental cars, and crosses were burned on the lawns of at least two of them. Several hospital workers who helped the inspectors had their homes bombed, and one may have been murdered, the historian David Barton Smith wrote. Smith's account does not name who jailed the inspectors, who fired, who burned the crosses or who set the bombs. By July 1, hospitals holding 97 of every 100 beds for short-term care in the country had met the rule.

#### Hepatitis experiments at Willowbrook, 1956 to 1971

Willowbrook State School on Staten Island, New York, was a state home for children with intellectual disabilities. It was built for 4,000 children and held 6,000 by 1965.

From 1956 to 1971, Dr. Saul Krugman of New York University and Dr. Robert McCollum of Yale ran hepatitis experiments on children at Willowbrook. Hepatitis is a disease that inflames the liver. In one study they fed 60 healthy children live hepatitis virus taken from other people's stool, their solid waste. The children's skin and eyes turned yellow, their livers swelled, and they vomited and would not eat. Every one of them became ill, some badly.

Parents signed permission letters, often because signing got their child a place in the crowded school. Critics said the letters played down that the children would be infected on purpose. At times the only beds open were in the study ward.

In 1972 the television reporter Geraldo Rivera filmed the school's crowded wards and filthy bathrooms, and staff who beat and sexually abused the residents. That March, parents of 5,000 residents sued the State of New York. The last children left Willowbrook in 1987.

#### The Tuskegee study ends, 1972 to 1997

The Tuskegee study ended in November 1972, four months after a reporter made it public. In 1966 Peter Buxtun, a Public Health Service worker in San Francisco, had written to the head of the service's office for diseases passed by sex, saying the study was wrong. Officials of the CDC, the federal disease agency, ran the study by then. They decided to keep it going until every man had died. They also decided that doctors should then cut open each man's body and examine it. Members of local chapters of two doctors' groups, the National Medical Association and the American Medical Association, backed that decision. At a review in 1969 CDC officials decided again to keep it going.

In the early 1970s Buxtun went to the press. Jean Heller, a reporter for the Associated Press, wrote the story. It ran in the *Washington Star* on July 25, 1972, and on the front page of the *New York Times* the next day. At the start of that year, 74 of the untreated men were still alive. In October a government panel advised stopping the study. In November 1972 Dr. Merlin DuVal, the top health official in the federal health department, announced the end of the study.

In 1973 Senator Edward Kennedy held hearings, and federal officials began paying for the survivors' medical care. Their wives, widows and children were added in 1975. The men's lawsuit ended in a $10 million settlement out of court in 1974. Some accounts date it 1973. In 1974 members of Congress passed the National Research Act. Since then, a study on people that uses federal money must be approved by a review board. Every person in it must first be told what will be done and what the risks are, and must agree. This is called informed consent.

On May 16, 1997, President Bill Clinton apologized at the White House to five of the survivors, Charles "Charlie" Pollard, Herman Shaw, Carter Howard, Fred Simmons and Frederick Moss. "What the United States government did was shameful, and I am sorry," he said.

#### Sterilized without consent, the 1970s

To sterilize a person is to operate so that the person can never have a baby. In an operation called a tubal ligation, a surgeon cuts or ties the two tubes that carry eggs from the ovaries to the womb. In a hysterectomy, a surgeon cuts out the womb.

In the Relf sisters' case, a federal judge found in 1974 that doctors in programs paid for by the federal government were sterilizing an estimated 100,000 to 150,000 poor people a year. Some doctors told women on welfare, government money for poor families, that they would lose it unless they agreed. The judge barred both practices.

In 1976 investigators of the General Accounting Office, which checks how federal money is spent, reported on the Indian Health Service. In four of its 12 regions, its doctors had sterilized 3,406 Native women from 1973 to 1976. Writers for the National Library of Medicine and the National Archives describe the operations as done without the women's permission. Thirty-six of the women were under 21, although a federal judge had ordered that women that young not be sterilized. The investigators' report does not name the doctors. In 1974 Dr. Connie Pinkerton-Uri, who is Choctaw and Cherokee, had found in her own study that 1 in 4 Native women had been sterilized without consent.

Norma Jean Serena, who was Shawnee and Creek, gave birth in Armstrong County, Pennsylvania, on August 16, 1970. Two days later Drs. Donald Carter and James Houston cut out her fallopian tubes, the tubes that carry eggs to the womb. She said no doctor ever told her. A welfare caseworker, Jean Burgess, had advised the operation. Burgess later said, "This was a burden on society. I felt that Mrs. Serena should have no further children." Burgess and two other county child welfare workers, Patricia Walker and Natalie Leezer, had also taken three of Serena's children from her in 1970. Serena sued in 1974. The jurors found that the welfare workers had given a false picture of the children's health and of how long the children would stay in foster homes. They awarded her $17,000. The same jurors found that she had agreed to the operation.

In Puerto Rico, about 1 in 3 women of child-bearing age had been sterilized by 1968, and 37.4 of every 100 by 1976, historians on the history podcast DIG report. Some chose it because it was the only birth control offered to them. Others were told it could be undone, or were pushed into it by their employers.

<a id="story-relf-sisters"></a>

#### Minnie Lee and Mary Alice Relf

> **Who:** Two Black sisters in Alabama who were surgically sterilized as children through a federally paid clinic, after their mother was told they would get birth control shots.
>
> **When and where:** Montgomery, Alabama, June 1973.

In June 1973 surgeons in Montgomery, Alabama, sterilized Minnie Lee and Mary Alice Relf. The girls were 12 and 14. Accounts differ on which sister was older. The surgeons tied or cut the tubes that carry eggs to the womb, so the girls could never have children. No record names the surgeons.

Nurses from a family planning clinic had told their mother, Minnie Relf, that her daughters would get birth control shots. Montgomery Community Action ran the clinic with federal money. She could not read or write, and she signed the form with an X. Both girls had intellectual disabilities. The family lived in public housing that the same agency had found for them in 1971. In all, 11 children from the same clinic's program were sterilized, and 10 of them were Black.

Their father, Lonnie Relf, saw the scars when the girls came home from the hospital. The same day a nurse asked their sister Katie, who was 17, to agree to be sterilized. Katie locked herself in her room.

Lawyers from the Southern Poverty Law Center sued for the family. The federal officials they sued included Caspar Weinberger, the Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare, and Alvin Arnett of the Office of Economic Opportunity. The judge barred federal money for sterilizing people against their will, and barred doctors from threatening to cut off welfare money.

#### AIDS, 1981 to 2000

On June 5, 1981, CDC doctors reported a rare kind of pneumonia in five young gay men in Los Angeles. Two of them had died. The disease was later named AIDS. It is caused by HIV, a virus that destroys the white blood cells that fight infection. As those cells die, other infections and cancers kill the person. HIV passes through blood, semen and other body fluids, not through touch.

In 1985 more Americans were diagnosed with AIDS than in all earlier years together. By early 1986 about half of the adults ever diagnosed had died, and patients died about 15 months after they were diagnosed. People with hemophilia, whose blood does not clot, took a clotting medicine made from blood given by many donors. Of those treated with it between 1979 and 1984, nearly 9 in 10 caught HIV, hepatitis C or both.

In March 1987 the writer Larry Kramer started ACT UP, the AIDS Coalition to Unleash Power, in New York. That month FDA officials approved AZT, the first drug for AIDS. On October 11, 1988, more than 1,000 ACT UP members shut down FDA offices in Maryland, and police made 176 arrests. Eight days later FDA officials announced rules to approve drugs faster.

In 1994 AIDS was the leading cause of death for Americans aged 25 to 44. From 1996, doctors gave several drugs together, and the next year AIDS deaths fell by 47 percent. By the end of 2000, 774,467 Americans had been reported with AIDS, and 448,060 of them had died.

<a id="story-ryan-white"></a>

#### Ryan White

> **Who:** An Indiana teenager who caught HIV from his hemophilia medicine, was kept out of school, and then spoke across the country about AIDS.
>
> **When and where:** Kokomo and Cicero, Indiana, 1984 to 1990. Born in Kokomo on December 6, 1971.
>
> **Movie:** *The Ryan White Story* (1989), a film made for ABC television. Ryan White had a small part in it.

Ryan White was 13 when doctors told him, on December 17, 1984, that he had AIDS. They gave him six months to live. He had hemophilia and took a clotting medicine made from blood given by many people. Some of it carried HIV.

In 1985 James O. Smith, the head of his school district, refused to let him back into Western Middle School. 117 parents and 50 teachers signed a petition, a written request, to keep him out. Health officials of the state and the CDC said he was no danger to anyone. When he went back for one day in February 1986, 151 of the school's 360 students stayed home. After he returned, school staff made him use throwaway forks and spoons and a separate bathroom. Someone fired a bullet through his family's living room window while no one was home.

The family moved to Cicero, Indiana. On his first day at Hamilton Heights High School, the principal, Tony Cook, and students who had learned about AIDS shook his hand. In 1988 he spoke to a presidential commission on AIDS. He died on April 8, 1990, at 18. That August, members of Congress passed the Ryan White CARE Act. Under it, federal money pays for care for people with HIV.

### 2000 to Today

COVID-19 killed 1,245,791 people in the United States from 2020 to September 19, 2026, by the early count of the CDC, the federal disease agency. Drug overdoses killed more than 100,000 Americans a year in 2022 and 2023. Life expectancy, the average age a newborn would reach if that year's death rates held, fell from 78.8 years in 2019 to 76.4 in 2021. It was back to 79.0 in 2024, federal health officials who count births and deaths reported in January 2026. In 2010 President Barack Obama signed the Affordable Care Act. In 2025, 26.7 million people had no health insurance all year, the Census Bureau reported in September 2026. Doctors can now edit the genes in a patient's own cells to treat sickle cell disease.

#### Reading and editing genes, 2003 to 2023

A genome is the full set of DNA instructions in a person's cells. Scientists of the Human Genome Project, begun in 1990, finished the first reading of the human genome in April 2003.

Sickle cell disease bends red blood cells into a curved shape like a sickle, a farm tool with a curved blade. The bent cells slow the flow of blood in small blood vessels and carry less oxygen. That causes attacks of severe pain, and it can disable or kill a person. About 100,000 people in the United States have it, the Food and Drug Administration reported in 2023. It is most common in African Americans.

On December 8, 2023, FDA officials approved Casgevy, the first treatment made with the gene-editing tool called CRISPR that the FDA has approved. Doctors take some of the patient's blood-making cells and edit their DNA. Then the patient gets high doses of chemotherapy, strong drugs that kill the cells left in the bone marrow. Doctors put the edited cells back in a single drip into a vein.

#### The Affordable Care Act and the uninsured, 2010 to 2026

In 2010, 49.9 million people in the United States had no health insurance, which was 16.3 percent of everyone, the Census Bureau counted.

On March 23, 2010, President Obama signed the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act. Members of the House had passed it 219 to 212. Most of its parts started in January 2014. Lawmakers in many states opened Medicaid to more adults with low incomes, and people could buy insurance on new insurance marketplaces, websites where people compare plans and sign up. By 2016, about 20 to 24 million more people had insurance, and the share without it had fallen by about half.

In 2025, 26.7 million people, or 7.9 percent, had no insurance for the whole year. The Census Bureau reported this on September 15, 2026. Census Bureau staff changed their survey questions in 2013, so the 2010 and 2025 counts were not measured in exactly the same way.

On July 4, 2025, President Donald Trump signed a budget law with new rules for keeping Medicaid. From 2027, adults who got Medicaid when their state widened it under the Affordable Care Act must show 80 hours a month of work or similar activity to keep it. They can instead show a reason they are excused. In July 2025 staff of the Congressional Budget Office, which estimates the cost of laws for Congress, estimated that 10 million more people would have no insurance in 2034 because of the law.

Extra federal help with the price of marketplace insurance ended after 2025. In 2026, sign-ups fell by more than a million, to 23.1 million, the health research group KFF reported. The average monthly payment rose from $113 to $178.

Rural hospitals have also closed. Since 2005, 197 rural hospitals have closed or stopped keeping patients overnight, by the December 2025 count of the Sheps Center at the University of North Carolina.

#### COVID-19, 2020 to 2026

COVID-19 is an illness caused by a coronavirus. It spreads when an infected person breathes out droplets and tiny particles that carry the virus. It causes fever, cough, shortness of breath and loss of taste or smell. In severe cases the person has trouble breathing and pain or pressure in the chest, becomes confused, and the lips or skin turn pale, gray or blue.

The first case in the United States was confirmed in a laboratory on January 20, 2020. On March 11, 2020, officials of the World Health Organization declared a pandemic, a disease spreading around the world. FDA officials allowed the first vaccine on December 11, 2020. Recorded deaths in the United States passed 500,000 on February 21, 2021, and 1 million on May 12, 2022. The federal health emergency ended in May 2023.

The CDC's early count, as of September 24, 2026, is 1,245,791 COVID-19 deaths from 2020 to September 19, 2026. The year with the most deaths was 2021, with 463,267. In 2025 there were 20,682. These early counts rise as late death records come in.

For American Indian and Alaska Native people, life expectancy fell from 71.8 years in 2019 to 65.2 in 2021. That was a drop of 6.6 years, federal health officials who count births and deaths reported in 2022. That was the same as the life expectancy of all Americans in 1944. COVID-19, accidents and liver disease caused most of that drop.

<a id="story-sandra-lindsay"></a>

#### Sandra Lindsay

> **Who:** A nurse who led the intensive care nurses at a hospital in Queens through the pandemic, and was the first American outside a vaccine trial to get a COVID-19 vaccine.
>
> **When and where:** Long Island Jewish Medical Center, Queens, New York, 2020 and 2021. She came from Jamaica.

On Monday, December 14, 2020, Sandra Lindsay got the first COVID-19 vaccine given in the United States outside a trial. She directed the nurses who cared for the sickest COVID-19 patients at Long Island Jewish Medical Center in Queens, New York.

She had questions about the vaccine at first. She did her own research and listened to experts before she decided. "We needed a more powerful tool," she said.

During the pandemic her aunt died, and she could not be with her mother. Her grandson Avery was born too soon, in March 2020, and spent about four and a half months in a hospital unit for newborns. Lindsay could not sleep or focus, and she began to meditate.

On July 2, 2021, President Joe Biden gave her the Outstanding Citizen By Choice award, which honors immigrants who became citizens. Her hospital scrubs and her ID badge went to the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History.

#### Opioids and overdose deaths, 1999 to 2026

Opioids include strong painkillers such as oxycodone and fentanyl, and the illegal drug heroin. Too much of one slows a person's breathing, and the person can die. Fentanyl is 50 to 100 times stronger than morphine. A drug called naloxone reverses an overdose if someone gives it quickly.

The CDC describes three waves of deaths. The first came from pain pills, after doctors began writing more prescriptions for opioids in the 1990s. A prescription is a doctor's written order for a medicine. The second came from heroin, from 2010. The third came from fentanyl made illegally, from 2013. From 1999 to 2023, about 806,000 Americans died of opioid overdoses, the CDC counted in 2026.

In 2007 Purdue Pharma, the maker of the pain pill OxyContin, pleaded guilty to misleading the public about how easily people became addicted to it. It paid $600 million. Three of its leaders, Michael Friedman, Howard Udell and Paul Goldenheim, pleaded guilty too. Purdue pleaded guilty to federal crimes again in 2020. On June 16, 2025, 55 attorneys general joined a $7.4 billion settlement with Purdue and the Sackler family, who owned it. An attorney general is the top lawyer of a state or territory government. In the settlement, Purdue and the Sacklers agreed to pay money to end lawsuits against them.

On March 29, 2023, FDA officials approved a naloxone nasal spray for sale in stores without a doctor's order. Overdose deaths from all drugs peaked at about 112,000 in the 12 months ending August 2023. The CDC's early count for the 12 months ending April 2026 is about 67,000. About 42,000 of those deaths involved opioids.

#### Smoking, measles and vaccines, 2006 to 2026

US District Judge Gladys Kessler ruled on August 17, 2006, that the big tobacco companies had "defrauded the American people by lying for decades about the health risks of smoking and their marketing to children." Defrauded means cheated. Smoking and breathing other people's smoke still kill more than 480,000 Americans a year, by the CDC's count last updated in 2024. That is nearly 1 of every 5 deaths in the country.

Measles is a disease caused by a virus. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and a person can catch it in a room up to 2 hours after the sick person has left, CDC doctors write. It starts with a high fever, a cough and red, watery eyes, and then a rash spreads down from the face. As many as 1 of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common way measles kills young children. About 1 child in 1,000 gets a swelling of the brain. By 2000 measles had stopped spreading nonstop inside the United States for at least a year. Health officials call that elimination. In 2025 there were 2,289 confirmed cases and 3 deaths, by the CDC's count. In an early count of 2,144 of those cases, 93 of every 100 were in people who had not been vaccinated. In 2026, by September 24, the CDC had counted 3,659 cases and 1 death.

On June 9, 2025, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the Secretary of Health and Human Services, removed all 17 members of the panel of experts that advises the CDC on vaccines. He wrote that the panel had become "little more than a rubber stamp for any vaccine." He meant that the panel approved every vaccine it was shown. Leaders of the American Medical Association said the move "upends a transparent process that has saved countless lives." They meant that it threw out an open way of deciding about vaccines.

#### The last of the Tuskegee men

The last man from the Tuskegee study died in January 2004. The last widow in the benefit program died in January 2009. CDC officials report that 10 of the men's children receive medical care through the program.

<a id="ch-disasters"></a>

## Chapter 27: Disasters and Rescue

### Before 1500

Volcanoes, earthquakes and droughts that lasted for decades struck this land long before anyone wrote them down. The people who lived through them belonged to Native nations. What is known about these disasters comes from three kinds of evidence. Scientists study layers of ash in the ground and the growth rings of old trees. The nations kept their own accounts and told them to each new generation.

#### Two volcanoes

Mount Mazama is a volcano in the Cascade Range of southern Oregon, about 60 miles north of the California line. About 7,700 years ago it erupted, and its top fell in. The eruption lasted only a few days. Scientists estimate that it was more than forty times as powerful as the eruption of Mount St. Helens in 1980. Its ash fell as far away as what is now central Alberta, in Canada.

Over several hundred years, rain and snow filled much of the hole that the collapse left behind. The water became Crater Lake. It is 1,943 feet deep, the deepest lake in the United States. In the Klamath language its name is *giiwas*.

People had lived in the region for about 1,500 years or more before the eruption. In 1938 an archaeologist named Luther Cressman dug in Fort Rock Cave, in Lake County, Oregon. An archaeologist studies the past from the things people left behind. Under a layer of ash from Mount Mazama, Cressman found dozens of sandals woven from sagebrush bark. Radiocarbon dating is a test that measures how much of one kind of carbon is left in something that was once alive. It later showed that the sandals were more than 9,000 years old. Sandals of the same kind from half a dozen sites date from between about 10,500 and 9,100 years ago. The families who wore them lived there long before the mountain erupted.

The Klamath Tribes say that they have lived in the Klamath Basin for 13,000 years. They tell the eruption as a battle between Llao, chief of the Below World, and Skell, chief of the Above World. In their account, Llao attacked the people with fire after a chief's daughter refused him. Skell defended the people, and two holy men gave up their lives. Skell drove Llao back into Mount Mazama, the mountain fell in, and water filled the basin.

Around the year 1085, Sunset Crater erupted near what is now Flagstaff, Arizona. Scientists fixed the date from chemical changes in the growth rings of trees that were alive then. Ash fell on land 12 to 15 miles away and buried people's homes. Crops cannot grow in ash deeper than about 6 to 8 inches.

People who lived near the volcano had to leave because of the eruption. The Sinagua farmers who lived closest to the volcano were ancestors of today's Pueblo peoples. National Park Service scientists think they had to leave their fields and move farther away. Where the ash lay thin, it worked as a mulch, a covering that keeps soil from drying out, and crops there grew better. No record counts any dead. The people of the area told stories of the eruption, and those stories are still told today.

#### Droughts that lasted decades

A drought is a long stretch of time with too little rain for crops. A tree adds one ring of new wood each year, and in a dry year the ring is thin. Scientists read those rings in very old trees and wooden beams to find out which years were dry.

The rings show that the Colorado Plateau, in the dry Southwest, had too little rain from about 1130 to 1180. From 1140 to 1162 there were 23 dry years in a row. Susan Ryan, a researcher at the Crow Canyon Archaeological Center in Colorado, calls it the greatest drought recorded for North America. The Colorado River carried less water in the middle 1100s than at any other time in the past 1,200 years. At Chaco Canyon, in present-day New Mexico, builders had stopped putting up large stone buildings called great houses by about 1130. In the decades after that, the people of the Chaco towns moved away.

A second drought, called the Great Drought, lasted from 1276 to 1299. Ryan found it less severe than the drought of the 1100s. By about 1300 the Pueblo people of the Mesa Verde region, in present-day southwestern Colorado, had moved south. They went to the Rio Grande valley, to Zuni and Acoma, and to the Hopi mesas, where rain came more reliably.

Archaeologists at Crow Canyon count the drought as one cause of that move among several. Other causes on their list are changes in how the communities got along, how they were ruled and how they made a living. In their view, the drought probably caused food shortages in a region crowded with people, and the hard times that followed may have led to quarrels and fighting.

Around 1280, attackers killed at least 41 people at Castle Rock Pueblo and at least 8 at Sand Canyon Pueblo. Both places are in the Mesa Verde region. Kristin Kuckelman and two other scientists studied the skeletons. They found that someone had cut the bodies apart and broken, crushed and burned the bones, during or after the fighting. They also found signs that people probably ate human flesh there. No evidence shows who the attackers were, or who cut up the dead.

#### A fault under the northwest coast

The outer layer of the earth is broken into huge slabs called plates. Off the coast of present-day Washington, Oregon and northern California, one plate slides under another. The line where they meet is a fault, a crack in the earth's crust where the rock on each side can move. This one is called the Cascadia Subduction Zone. Subduction means one plate sliding down under another.

When the rock along a fault moves suddenly, the ground shakes. Scientists have found signs of 19 great earthquakes on this fault in the last 10,000 years. The most recent one struck in January 1700.

### The 1500s

Spaniards who sailed to this land in the 1500s wrote down the disasters they lived through. Hurricanes sank their ships. A hurricane is a very large storm that forms over warm ocean water, with winds that spin in a circle and heavy rain. Droughts left Native towns short of corn, and one drought was among the causes of an English colony's end. What is known about them comes from tree rings and from letters that Spaniards wrote.

#### A hurricane wrecks a colony, 1559

A hurricane in September 1559 sank most of the ships of the largest Spanish colony yet sent to the Southeast. Nearly all of the colony's food went down with them. The colonists had landed on August 15, 1559, at Pensacola Bay in present-day Florida. The Native name of the bay was Ochuse. They came from Veracruz, in Mexico, on 11 ships, towing a 12th, smaller ship behind them.

About 1,500 people made the voyage. They included an army of 500 soldiers and about 200 Aztec warriors and craftsmen from Mexico City. Servants, enslaved Africans, and some wives and children came too. For five weeks they unloaded people and tools and began building a town on high, flat ground above the bay. They left the food for all 1,500 people on board the ships, because they thought it was safer there than on land.

One of the 11 ships, a galleon, had already sailed back to Mexico in late August or early September. On the night of September 19 to 20, 1559, a hurricane came into the bay. It sank six ships and pushed a seventh a short way onto the land. Three of the 11 ships came through the storm. The small towed ship later carried supplies on relief voyages. Nearly all the food for 1,500 people went down with the ships. The people who drowned were mostly the sailors and passengers still on board. No record gives their number.

After the storm the colonists did not have enough to eat. One ship came from Havana, in Cuba, with supplies soon after the hurricane. Relief ships from Mexico came after that, one every five to seven months. The colonists sent about 200 men inland to look for towns with food to spare. The men found a large town called Nanipacana, on the Alabama River in present-day central Alabama. Its people left before the Spaniards arrived. As they went, they destroyed the food they had stored.

Many colonists grew sick and died from lack of food. Native people attacked and killed others. The records do not state which Native people attacked them. The colonists shipped many survivors back to Mexico. By September 1560, 362 people were left at the bay, and another 200 were far inland. Most of the rest sailed away in April 1561 with a new commander, Ángel de Villafañe. Two small ships of his fleet later sank in another storm off Cape Hatteras, with everyone aboard. The last Spanish soldiers left the bay in August 1561. In February 1562 the viceroy, the Spanish king's governor in Mexico, gave up the colony.

<a id="story-tristan-de-luna-disasters"></a>

#### Tristán de Luna y Arellano

> **Who:** A Spanish noble and soldier who led the colony at Pensacola Bay when the hurricane of 1559 destroyed its ships and food.
>
> **When and where:** Pensacola Bay, Florida, and the Alabama River, 1559 to 1561.

Tristán de Luna y Arellano led the colony at Pensacola Bay. It was the largest Spanish attempt up to that time to settle the Southeast, and the one with the most money behind it. He was born to a noble family in Borobia, in Spain. Years before, he had marched with the Spanish explorer Coronado. The colonists he led landed in August 1559. The hurricane of September 19 to 20 sank or wrecked seven of his ships with the food still on board.

From February to June 1560, Luna moved most of his people inland to the town of Nanipacana. In April he sent 200 men under Mateo del Sauz farther north, to Coosa, a chiefdom in present-day northwestern Georgia. A chiefdom is a group of towns under one head chief. The men were looking for food. They stayed there until November.

In late summer 1560, Luna ordered 100 soldiers and 50 servants to march to Coosa on short rations, meaning with less food than they needed. All of his soldiers refused, and the march never took place.

In early April 1561, Ángel de Villafañe arrived at the bay with a small fleet. He dismissed Luna and ordered him back to Spain. Villafañe took most of the roughly 150 settlers still at the bay to Havana. Luna died in New Spain, the Spanish colony in Mexico, on September 16, 1573.

#### The droughts behind the Lost Colony

Tree rings from old bald cypress trees on the border of Virginia and North Carolina show two long droughts in the 1500s. A team of scientists led by David Stahle published the record in 1998. The first drought lasted from 1562 to 1571 and was worst from 1565 to 1569. In September 1570 a Spanish priest in the Chesapeake Bay region, Father Juan Batista de Segura, wrote about it. He wrote that the region had gone six years with too little corn and wild fruit, with hunger, death and dry soil.

From 1587 to 1589 came the driest three years in the whole 800-year record. English colonists on Roanoke Island, in present-day North Carolina, disappeared during those years. They are known as the Lost Colony. The Stahle team counts the drought as one of several causes of the colony's end. An earlier English colony on Roanoke had come in wetter years, 1585 and 1586. Only 4 of its 108 people died.

The Croatan people were allies of the English colonists. In 1587 their crops were poor. The same year, the people of the town of Dasemunkepeuc killed George Howe, an adviser to the English governor, John White. They spoke an Algonquian language, one of a large family of Native languages along the coast. They killed him in revenge for the killing of their leader, Wingina. Men under Ralph Lane, leader of the earlier colony, had attacked Wingina and killed him in June 1586. After Howe's death the people of Dasemunkepeuc left their town.

Before daylight on August 8, 1587, White led his soldiers in an attack on Dasemunkepeuc. The people they found there were Croatan, who had come to the empty town looking for food. White's men killed one of them and wounded many before they saw their mistake. The Stahle team writes that the shooting happened partly because the Croatan needed food.

#### St. Augustine burns and floods

St. Augustine, in present-day Florida, was burned, raided or flooded again and again in its first 35 years. Spanish soldiers and colonists founded it in 1565 at Seloy, a town of the Timucua people. The Timucua were tired of the Spaniards living in their town. In 1566 Timucua warriors shot flaming arrows at the fort. On April 1, 1566, the fort was half burned, and all its supplies were lost. The records do not state whether the arrows started that fire.

The colonists moved the town across the bay to Anastasia Island that year. In 1570 soldiers there rose against their officers and destroyed the fort. The sea was washing away the rebuilt fort by 1572. Native people attacked the town in 1577 and burned many houses. Then, in 1586, the English privateer Francis Drake and his men burned the whole town and its fort. A privateer was a ship captain who raided enemy ships and towns with his own government's permission.

In March 1599 a fire swept through the town, which was built of wood with roofs of thatch, meaning dried plants. In September of the same year a hurricane flooded the buildings that the townspeople had not yet repaired.

### The 1600s

The English colonies on the Atlantic coast were small in the 1600s. One dry summer or one storm could kill a large share of the people in them. Colonists built their towns mostly of wood, so a fire in one house could spread to the next. Governors and ordinary colonists wrote down the storms, fires and earthquakes they lived through, in letters and journals full of detail.

#### Jamestown: drought, a hurricane and the Starving Time

English colonists landed at Jamestown, in present-day Virginia, in April 1607. They built their fort inside Tsenacomoco, the land of the Powhatan people. Tsenacomoco was a paramount chiefdom, a group of many towns and chiefs under one head chief. Its head chief was Powhatan.

Tree rings show that the colonists arrived during the driest seven years in 770 years, from 1606 to 1612. The drought hit the Powhatan towns as well as the English. The colonists' drinking water came from the lower James River, where fresh water mixes with salt water from the sea. In the dry years the water was salty and foul, and colonists fell sick from it. Of the 104 colonists who landed in 1607, only 38 were alive a year later. Malnutrition, which means the body does not get enough food, was a leading cause of death.

On June 2, 1609, the leaders of the Virginia Company of London, the business that ran the colony, sent nine ships and about 600 people to the colony, with farm animals and enough food to last a year. It was the largest English fleet yet to sail west. On July 24, 1609, a hurricane struck the fleet about seven days from land. It drove the lead ship, the *Sea Venture*, away from the others. The ship began to leak so badly that one passenger wrote, "we almost drowned within."

The *Sea Venture* reached Bermuda, an island in the Atlantic. All 150 people on board got ashore, among them the colony's new governor, Sir Thomas Gates. Before the ship sank, the crew saved many of the supplies. The castaways stayed on Bermuda for ten months and built two small ships, the *Patience* and the *Deliverance*. The playwright William Shakespeare drew partly on their story for his play *The Tempest*. The other eight ships reached Jamestown in late August 1609. Many passengers were sick, and the crews had thrown many of their supplies overboard in the storm.

#### The Starving Time, 1609 to 1610

In the winter of 1609 to 1610, most of the people at Jamestown starved to death. That winter is called the Starving Time. The colonists had not farmed, hunted or fished to feed themselves. They lived on supplies from England and on food they bargained for from the Powhatan people, or often stole from them. In the drought the Powhatan towns had little food to spare.

In the autumn of 1609 the killing began on both sides. The colonist Francis West cut off the heads of two warriors of the Patawomeck people while he was trading with them. In November 1609 warriors ambushed a party of colonists led by John Ratcliffe at Orapax. They tortured Ratcliffe to death. That same month Powhatan ordered his people to surround Jamestown and cut off its food.

Counts of the colonists differ. The historian Martha McCartney counts 240 people at Jamestown at the start of the winter. Other counts record about 500 in the colony. By May 1610 about 60 were alive. Some survivors dug up and ate the bodies of dead colonists and of Native people the colonists had killed.

The *Sea Venture* castaways reached Jamestown in their two small ships on May 24, 1610. Gates decided to give up the colony and sail home with the survivors. On the river they met Thomas West, Lord De La Warr, an English nobleman. He was bringing a year's supply of food, and everyone went back to Jamestown. Between 1607 and 1625, the company's leaders sent about 6,000 people to Jamestown. About 4,800 of them died.

#### The Great Colonial Hurricane, August 1635

A hurricane struck New England on August 15, 1635. The English then used an older calendar that ran ten days behind the one used today. By today's calendar the date was August 25. William Bradford, the longtime governor of Plymouth Colony, wrote that no one living there, "either English or Indeans, ever saw" a storm like it. *Indeans* is his spelling of Indians.

South of Plymouth the sea rose more than 20 feet above its normal height. Bradford wrote that many Native people climbed into trees to escape the water. No record gives the number of Native people who drowned. The wind blew down houses and, in Bradford's words, "many hundered thowsands of trees." The worst of the storm lasted five or six hours.

The same storm wrecked the *Angel Gabriel*, a ship full of English settlers, at Pemaquid, in present-day Maine. Three or four passengers and one sailor died. Off Cape Ann, in Massachusetts, it wrecked a small boat carrying two families.

<a id="story-anthony-thacher"></a>

#### Anthony Thacher

> **Who:** An English colonist who survived the wreck of a small boat in the hurricane of 1635 and described it in a letter to his brother Peter.
>
> **When and where:** Off Cape Ann, Massachusetts Bay Colony, August 11 to 15, 1635.

Anthony Thacher and his wife, Elizabeth, were the only two of 23 people who lived through the wreck of their boat off Cape Ann. Days later he wrote down what happened in a letter to his brother Peter.

On August 11, 1635, Thacher and his family left Ipswich, in Massachusetts, for the town of Marblehead. With them went his cousin John Avery, a minister, and Avery's family. The people of Marblehead had asked Avery to be their minister, and they sent a pinnace, a small sailing ship, to carry the two families. Thacher's letter lists 23 people on board: 11 in Avery's family, 7 in his own, a man named William Elliot, and four sailors.

At about 10 on the night of August 14, the wind split the pinnace's old sails. Before daylight the hurricane struck. The anchor dragged along the bottom, and the storm drove the boat onto the rocks of a small island. A wave threw Thacher onto a rock with his oldest daughter, Mary. His cousin Avery and Avery's oldest son joined them there. The next wave broke the boat to pieces. It carried his wife toward the shore on a piece of the deck. All the others still on board drowned. Thacher's letter names four of his children who died. They were his oldest daughter Mary, his son William, his daughter Edith, and baby Peter, whom Edith was holding in her arms.

Another wave swept all four off the rock. He was in the water for at least a quarter of an hour before he crawled ashore. On the island he and his wife found a knapsack with a flint, a piece of steel for striking sparks from it, and dry gunpowder. They also found a drowned goat, two cheeses, some butter, a hat and his son William's coat. He struck a fire and they cooked some of the goat. They had only salty water to drink. He found the body of Avery's oldest daughter on the shore. She is buried on the island.

On the following Monday a passing boat picked them up. Thacher named the island "Thatchers Woe" and the rock "Avery's Fall." On September 3, 1635, the colony's lawmakers, meeting as the Massachusetts General Court, voted him 40 marks from the treasury toward his losses. A mark was an English unit of money. In March 1637 they gave him the island. It is still called Thacher Island.

#### An earthquake, 1638

An earthquake shook New England on about June 1, 1638, by the old calendar. Bradford wrote that people heard it before they felt it. He compared the sound to faraway thunder. Dishes rattled and fell from shelves. People outdoors could not stand without holding on to posts. Native people felt it inland, and ships along the coast shook.

Scientists today measure an earthquake's strength with a number called its magnitude. Each step up the scale, such as from 6 to 7, means the ground moves about ten times as far, and the quake lets out about 32 times as much energy. Scientists at Boston College's Weston Observatory estimate the 1638 earthquake at about magnitude 6.5. They think it was centered in central New Hampshire, but the few reports of the time make that uncertain. People felt the aftershocks, smaller quakes that follow a large one, for 20 days. No deaths were recorded.

Bradford wrote that the shaking looked like a sign that God was displeased. He added that for years afterward the summers were not warm enough for the corn to ripen well. He left the cause, in his words, "to naturallists to judge," meaning people who study nature.

#### Boston burns, and the town buys a fire engine

A fire in Boston on January 14, 1653, destroyed many buildings and killed three children. After it, town officials hired the owner of a water engine, a pump that sprays water, to bring it to fires. They bought six long ladders, four strong iron hooks and fire buckets. They required every property owner to keep a ladder and a swab pole, a long pole with a mop on the end for putting out sparks on roofs.

On November 27, 1676, a fire in Boston's North End destroyed 45 buildings. Among them were several warehouses, the North Meeting House, a church, and the home of its minister, Increase Mather. In 1678 town officials brought a fire engine from England and hired men to run it. A Boston Public Library guide calls them the first paid fire department in what is now the United States. Officials also made a law that roofs be slate or tile and walls be brick. Large fires burned parts of Boston again in 1679, 1682 and 1691.

### 1700 to 1750

Fires burned large parts of Boston and Charleston between 1700 and 1750, and townspeople began to organize to fight them. In 1722 about two-thirds of Boston's nearly 3,000 houses were built of wood. A fire that started in one building could spread across a neighborhood in a night. Boston got its first fire wardens after a fire in 1711, and neighbors in Boston and Philadelphia formed fire companies. On the coasts, an earthquake struck the Pacific Northwest in 1700, and a hurricane wrecked a Spanish fleet off Florida in 1715. In New York, officials blamed a series of fires in 1741 on enslaved people and poor white people, and put at least 30 people to death.

#### The Cascadia earthquake, January 1700

The Cascadia fault broke along about 620 miles of the Pacific coast at about 9 at night on January 26, 1700. The break ran from Vancouver Island, in present-day Canada, to northern California. Scientists at the Pacific Northwest Seismic Network call it one of the largest earthquakes known anywhere in the world. They put its size at about magnitude 9.

The coast dropped when the fault broke. Salt water flooded forests of cedar trees that had grown above the reach of the tides. The salt water killed the trees. Their dead trunks, called ghost forests, still stand along rivers and bays in Washington and Oregon.

The earthquake also set off a tsunami, a series of huge waves that can cross a whole ocean. The waves reached Japan the next day. At Miyako the water destroyed 13 houses, and a fire afterward burned 20 more. Near Nakaminato the waves drove a ship carrying rice onto rocks, and two sailors died. The Japanese records describe the waves but no shaking. In 1996 scientists used those Japanese records to work out the day and the hour of the earthquake. Tree rings from the ghost forests confirmed the year.

No one counted the dead on the American coast. The Native nations there had no written records then. In their accounts, whole villages were lost. The Makah, in present-day Washington, tell of a great earthquake at night. The Quileute tell of a flood that carried canoes far inland. Archaeologists have found Native villages on the coasts of Washington and Oregon that sank, flooded and were left empty after 1700.

In 1933 Annie Miner Peterson, a Coos woman from Oregon, told what her grandfather had seen. Melville Jacobs, a scholar who was writing down Coos stories, recorded her words. Her grandfather had seen an old woman who survived the "raised water." When she was a girl, the water had left her hanging high in a tree. She tied her pack line, the rope she used to carry loads, to a branch to climb down, and she fell. The fall broke her back, and she had a humped back for the rest of her life. Scientists who studied the account date the flood she described to between 1690 and 1805.

#### A hurricane sinks the Spanish treasure fleet, 1715

Early on July 31, 1715, a hurricane drove eleven Spanish treasure ships onto the reefs of Florida's east coast. At least 1,000 people died. The fleet of twelve ships had left Havana, in Cuba, a few days before, bound for Spain. The 1715 Fleet Society gives the day it sailed as July 24, and a NOAA writer gives July 27. The eleven Spanish ships carried silver and gold from Spain's colonies in the Americas. They were wrecked along the coast from present-day Fort Pierce to Wabasso, north of Vero Beach. The twelfth ship, the French *Grifon*, escaped, because its captain had sailed farther from shore.

About 2,500 people were on board the fleet. Scientists at NOAA, the US government's ocean and weather agency, count about 1,000 dead. The 1715 Fleet Society, a group that studies the wrecks, says well over 1,000. Spanish records from Cuba state about 1,500. The fleet's commander, Juan Esteban de Ubilla, was among the dead.

The survivors camped on the beach in the land of the Ais people. The Ais lived along the coast from Cape Canaveral to the Indian River. On August 6, Admiral Francisco Salmón sent the pilot Nicolás de India and 18 men in a small boat to Havana for help. They reached it 11 days later. Ships from Havana and from St. Augustine brought emergency supplies, officials, soldiers and tools for salvage, which means bringing up goods from a wreck. By late October 1715 the salvagers had raised more than 5 million pieces of eight, the silver coins of Spain.

A man the records call Captain Barrett came for the silver too. Ned Grant was an enslaved man, and his enslaver hired him out to Barrett. Barrett took Grant to the wrecks to work as a diver.

In the winter of 1715 to 1716, the pirates Henry Jennings and John Wills attacked the Spanish salvage camp. The 1715 Fleet Society dates the raid to early January 1716 and says the pirates took about 120,000 pieces of eight. Other accounts put the raid in December 1715, name the pirate Charles Vane beside Jennings, and give the haul as about 87,500 pounds in English money.

#### Boston burns, 1711

Boston's fire of 1711 began in a building of rented rooms off Cornhill on the evening of October 2. A Scottish woman named Mary Morse was working with oakum there. Oakum is old rope fiber, picked apart and used to seal the seams of ships. A flame nearby set it on fire. By 2 in the morning the fire had burned about 100 buildings. Among them were the Town House, where the colony's government met, and the town's first meeting house, a building used as a church. The fire left 110 families without homes.

Four sailors climbed the meeting house steeple to save its bell. The roof fell in, and they died. Other people died when they went too close to the fire. Still others died in gunpowder blasts. People fighting the fire blew up houses in its path so that it would have nothing to burn. The full count of the dead is not known.

Members of Boston's churches raised 700 pounds, in English money, for the families who lost their homes. A few months after the fire, 12 men became Boston's first board of fire wardens. Each was in charge of the firefighting tools in one part of the town. Bostonians rebuilt the Town House and the meeting house in brick. The new Town House is known today as the Old State House.

#### Charleston: a hurricane in 1700 and a fire in 1740

On September 3, 1700, a hurricane struck Charleston, South Carolina. It knocked down thousands of trees and dozens of buildings. The Scottish ship *Rising Sun* sank at anchor. It carried people from a failed Scottish colony at Darien, in Panama. About 100 people on board drowned, including the captain.

On November 18, 1740, at 2 in the afternoon, a fire broke out in Charleston. A strong wind from the northwest carried burning pieces across the town. In less than a day the fire destroyed more than 300 houses and shops and several docks. The officers and crews of British navy ships in the harbor pulled down and blew up houses to stop it. The records that survive do not say whether anyone died.

Lieutenant Governor William Bull ordered every townsman to fight the fire, "by themselves and slaves." Townsmen were to send the people they enslaved to fight it as well. He called out the militia, the colony's armed citizens, to stop people from stealing from the ruins.

Most of the help from London after the fire went to the rich. Officials in London promised 20,000 pounds, in the king's name, for the people "most affected." They paid it out by the size of each person's losses. Most of it went to wealthy merchants, whose losses were large. Poorer people depended on gifts and loans from the vestry, the governing board of St. Philip's Church.

Mary Bedon, an innkeeper with three children, and Catharine Joor, a shopkeeper, lost their businesses in the fire and opened again in rented houses. By February 1741 the two women needed aid from the St. Philip's vestry to get through the winter.

#### New York, 1741: fires and blame

In March and April 1741, 13 fires broke out in lower Manhattan. The first, in March, burned the governor's house and its chapel inside Fort George. Accounts give its date as March 8 or March 18. New York officials said that enslaved Black people and poor white people had plotted together to burn the city. A witness named Mary Burton told the court that the fires were such a plot.

Three judges, James De Lancey, Daniel Horsmanden and Frederick Philipse, tried about 200 people. Officials burned 13 Black men alive at the stake, which means they tied each man to a post and set a fire around him. They hanged 17 Black men and 4 white people, two men and two women. Counts of the people put to death range from 30 to 34. Officials shipped 70 to 84 more people to the Caribbean islands to be sold into slavery there.

#### An earthquake in New England, 1727

An earthquake shook New England at about 10:40 on the night of October 29, 1727. By today's calendar the date was November 10. Scientists at the Weston Observatory estimate it at about magnitude 5.6. At Newbury, Massachusetts, it knocked down many stone walls and the tops of almost all the chimneys. Some solid ground turned to mud, and some marshes dried up. People felt it from Maine to the Delaware River, and smaller shocks went on for months. The records that survive show no one badly hurt.

In Boston the minister Cotton Mather heard "a horrid rumbling like the noise of many coaches." Ministers in New England preached that God had sent the earthquake to show his anger. Writers blamed it on sins such as swearing and failing to keep the Sabbath, the day of rest. Towns such as Medford, Massachusetts, held a day of fasting, when people went without food and prayed. John Barnard, a minister at Marblehead, came to a different view. He decided that the surface of the earth had moved because of shocks deep underground.

#### Fire companies

In Boston, groups of neighbors formed mutual fire societies. Members promised to help save one another's houses, and only those. On December 7, 1736, Benjamin Franklin and about 25 other men in Philadelphia signed the articles, or rules, of the Union Fire Company. Every Union member kept six leather buckets for water and two linen bags for carrying goods out of burning houses. They promised to come to every fire in the town, not only to the houses of members.

### 1750 to 1800

From 1750 to 1800, people who lost their homes in fires got help from lawmakers, and sometimes from other colonies and from people far away. After fires in Boston and Charleston, lawmakers voted public money for the families who lost their homes. Lawmakers in other colonies, and people as far away as London, sent money and gifts to Boston. In 1752 Philadelphians started a company to insure houses against fire. During the Revolutionary War, hurricanes sank Spanish warships and troop ships on the Gulf Coast, and a fire burned a large part of New York while British troops held it.

#### Charleston under water, 1752

A hurricane pushed the sea more than 10 feet above the normal high-water mark at Charleston, South Carolina, on the morning of September 15, 1752. The water covered the whole town. People fled to the upper floors of their houses. Before 11 o'clock nearly every ship in the harbor had been thrown onto land. Only one, the British warship *Hornet*, rode out the storm.

About 500 buildings were destroyed. No one kept an exact count of the dead. Many people drowned, and others died when houses fell apart around them. A second storm on September 30 ruined crops and killed farm animals. Officials then limited how much corn, peas and rice could be shipped out of the colony, to keep food prices down.

#### Fire insurance, 1752

Fire insurance means that many owners each pay a small amount into a shared fund. The company that keeps the fund pays any owner whose house burns. In 1752 Benjamin Franklin organized the Philadelphia Contributionship, a fire insurance company, in Philadelphia. Its inspectors looked at each house before insuring it. They set the price by how likely the house was to burn. Insured houses carried a sign showing four hands.

Owners who insured with the Contributionship had to remove the trees from their land, because trees got in the way of firefighters. A rival company, the Mutual Assurance Company, let its customers keep their trees. People called it the Green Tree.

#### The Cape Ann earthquake, 1755

An earthquake centered in the ocean about 25 miles off Cape Ann, Massachusetts, shook New England at about 4:30 in the morning on November 18, 1755. Scientists estimate it at about magnitude 6.2. In Boston the shaking lasted more than a minute. It threw down about 100 chimneys and damaged as many as 1,500 more. Some church steeples were left leaning. People felt it from Nova Scotia, in present-day Canada, to South Carolina. No deaths were recorded in the Boston area.

After the quake, a Boston minister and a Harvard professor argued in public over what had caused it. Seventeen days before the Cape Ann quake, a large earthquake had struck Lisbon, in Portugal. New England ministers held prayer services, and officials named days of fasting. Writers in New England published at least 27 sermons, poems and accounts about earthquakes after the one at Cape Ann. A sermon is a talk given in church. A lightning rod is a metal rod on a building that carries lightning into the ground. The Boston minister Thomas Prince wrote that Boston had more lightning rods than any other New England town. He argued that the rods had drawn electricity into the ground and made the shaking worse. John Winthrop, a professor at Harvard College, answered him in lectures. He said that heat and gases deep in the earth had caused the earthquake.

#### Boston burns, and other colonies send help, 1760

A fire started in a house on Cornhill in Boston at about 2 in the morning on March 20, 1760. No one ever found the cause. The fire burned 349 buildings, 174 of them homes. It left 220 families, more than 1,000 people, without homes. No one was killed. A Boston Public Library guide describes it as the worst fire in the American colonies up to that time.

Lawmakers in Massachusetts voted 3,000 pounds for the families who lost their homes. Lawmakers in Pennsylvania and New York voted to send money too.
