People in Nova Scotia raised money for Boston, and people as far away as London sent gifts. Afterward Massachusetts lawmakers passed a law that any building more than 7 feet high had to be made of brick or slate.

#### Fires in wartime: New York, 1776, and Charleston, 1778

British troops under General William Howe took New York City in September 1776, during the Revolutionary War. On the night of September 20, a fire broke out near the southern tip of Manhattan. Accounts differ on the exact spot. John Joseph Henry, an American prisoner on a British ship, said it began in the Fighting Cocks Tavern, near Whitehall Slip. Dry weather and strong winds spread it north and west. By morning it had burned between 400 and 1,000 buildings. That was between one tenth and one quarter of the city. Trinity Church burned.

British commanders blamed rebel arsonists, people who set fires on purpose. British soldiers and sailors killed a few men they suspected of setting the fire. They killed them on the spot, without a trial. The records do not give the men's names or an exact number. British officers questioned more than 200 suspects and charged none of them.

Historians still disagree about how the fire started. The historian Barnet Schecter found that no accusation of arson holds up. The historian Benjamin Carp argued in 2023 that rebels most likely set the fire on purpose. Gene Procknow, who reviewed Carp's book, wrote that Carp's evidence is not strong enough to prove it for certain.

In Charleston, people found a fire in a bakery at 4 in the morning on January 15, 1778. By noon it had destroyed more than 250 houses and killed six people, both Black and white. People who had lost their homes got beds and food in the city's public buildings, paid for with public money. The next day South Carolina's lawmakers, meeting as the General Assembly, voted 20,000 pounds to help them.

#### Hurricanes and the war on the Gulf Coast, 1779 and 1780

Spain's leaders joined the war against Britain on June 21, 1779. In 1779 Bernardo de Gálvez, the Spanish governor of Louisiana, was getting ships ready to attack the British fort at Baton Rouge. A hurricane destroyed the ships in less than three hours. Gálvez had to put off his attack for ten days.

On October 20, 1780, another hurricane struck a Spanish fleet of 64 ships under Admiral José Solano. The fleet was carrying Gálvez and 4,000 soldiers from Havana to attack the British town of Pensacola, in Florida. An unknown number of the ships sank. A NOAA writer counts half of the soldiers, about 2,000, as lost. The NOAA account does not say how many of them drowned. The attack on Pensacola did not go ahead that year.

A different storm that same month crossed the islands of the Caribbean. It is called the Great Hurricane of 1780. About 22,000 people died in the Lesser Antilles, the chain of small islands at the eastern edge of the Caribbean, from October 10 to 16. The storm also struck Puerto Rico. Scientists at NOAA count 1780 as the deadliest Atlantic hurricane season on record.

#### New Orleans burns twice, 1788 and 1794

New Orleans was a Spanish town in 1788. On March 21 of that year, a fire started at about 1:30 in the afternoon in the house of Vicente José Núñez, the army treasurer. That day was Good Friday, the Christian holy day before Easter. Church bells were the town's fire alarm, but the priests refused to let the bells ring on Good Friday. The fire burned 856 of the town's 1,100 buildings. Governor Esteban Miró set up tents for the people who lost their homes.

On December 8, 1794, another fire burned 212 more buildings. Spanish officials then required new buildings to be built with thick brick walls. Builders rebuilt the town in brick, with courtyards and iron balconies.

#### Charleston, 1796

On the afternoon of June 13, 1796, a fire started in Lodge Alley in Charleston and burned until nearly dawn. It burned the buildings on more than 250 lots and left at least 300 families without homes. A committee of church leaders and town leaders handed out the money that other townspeople gave, according to what each family needed. The fire reached the roof of St. Philip's Church. An enslaved man named Will climbed up and saved it.

<a id="story-will-st-philips-church"></a>

#### Will

> **Who:** An enslaved man in Charleston who put out the fire on the roof of St. Philip's Church, and whom the church's leaders then bought and freed.
>
> **When and where:** Charleston, South Carolina, June to September 1796.

Will put out the fire on the bell tower of St. Philip's Church during the Charleston fire of June 13 to 14, 1796. He climbed to the very top of the tower and tore off the burning wooden shingles of its roof. In 1854 the writer Charles Fraser wrote that he did it "at the risk of his life."

Will was enslaved by Charles Lining. Lining was a member of the vestry, the board that ran St. Philip's Church. On August 14, 1796, two months after the fire, the vestry's members voted to reward Will by making him free.

The next month they bought Will from Charles Lining for $707.14. Then they freed him with a deed of manumission. Manumission means freeing an enslaved person by a legal paper.

The vestry's records include only his first name. A later history of the church describes the man who saved it as a Black boatman.

### 1800 to 1850

Steamboats became a new cause of sudden death between 1800 and 1850. Steamboat boilers exploded on rivers and at sea, and the steamboat *Erie* burned on Lake Erie. In 1838 members of Congress passed the first federal law to inspect steamboats. A federal law is one made by Congress for the whole country. Earthquakes, a city fire and a tornado also killed hundreds of people. After the New Madrid earthquakes of 1811 and 1812, members of Congress voted to give land to people whose farms the quakes had ruined.

#### The New Madrid earthquakes, 1811 and 1812

Three strong earthquakes shook the middle Mississippi Valley in the winter of 1811 to 1812. The first struck northeast Arkansas at about 2:15 in the morning on December 16, 1811. The others came on January 23 and February 7, 1812. An earthquake's strength is given as a number called its magnitude. Experts at the U.S. Geological Survey estimate these quakes at about magnitude 7.3 to 7.5. The seismologist Susan Hough, a scientist who studies earthquakes, has argued that they were closer to magnitude 7.0. The quakes are named for New Madrid, Missouri, the largest town on the Mississippi River between St. Louis and Natchez.

The shaking threw down log cabins and chimneys as far away as Cincinnati and St. Louis. The first quake woke people in New York City, Washington, D.C., and Charleston, South Carolina. The Encyclopedia of Arkansas states that the shaking rang church bells in Boston. No story about it appeared in Boston's newspapers of the time. Susan Hough thinks the story began with bells that rang in Charleston, South Carolina, and that someone mixed up Charleston with Charlestown, a part of Boston.

On the Mississippi River, high banks and whole islands fell into the water. Huge waves sank boats or threw them onto the shore. The river ran backward. Most accounts say it did so for a few minutes, and others say for up to three days. Land sank near the St. Francis River in Arkansas. In the northwest corner of Tennessee the ground sank and formed Reelfoot Lake, about 18 miles long and 5 miles wide. Aftershocks, the smaller quakes that follow a large one, went on into 1816.

Reports of the time counted fewer than 100 deaths on land. No one counted the dead on the river or in the Native towns of the region. The historian William E. Foley writes that recent scholars believe the real number of deaths was far higher. Groups of Cherokee people who had already moved west from their homelands farmed along the St. Francis River. The earthquakes ruined their land. They left their farms and cattle and moved west again, where the Osage people living there resisted them.

Missouri was then a territory, land that belonged to the country but was not yet a state. In 1814 its governor, William Clark, and two other leaders asked Congress for help. In February 1815 members of Congress passed a law for people whose land the quakes had ruined. Each owner could claim the same amount of public land somewhere else, up to 640 acres. It was one of the country's earliest laws to help people after a disaster. Speculators, people who buy things cheaply to sell them later for a profit, learned of the law first. In the spring of 1815 they hurried to New Madrid. They bought the ruined land at low prices from owners who had not yet heard of the law. Most Missourians came to believe that the speculators got most of the benefit. The records do not identify them by name.

#### Fire in the cold: New York, 1835

On the night of December 16, 1835, a gas pipe burst in New York's business district. A coal stove lit the gas. The temperature that night fell as low as 17 degrees below zero. The rivers were frozen. Firefighters cut holes in the ice to reach water, and the water froze again in their hoses. They had fought two large fires two days before, and the city's water tanks were nearly empty.

The fire burned 17 blocks and between 530 and 700 buildings in New York's business district. Two people died. At about 3 in the morning, U.S. Marines and sailors brought gunpowder from the Brooklyn Navy Yard. They blew up buildings in the fire's path so that it had nothing left to burn. The damage came to about 20 million dollars. Twenty-three of New York's 26 insurance companies went out of business. The people who investigated the fire blamed no one.

#### Steamboat boilers explode, 1838

A steamboat's boiler is a large metal tank where a fire turns water into steam to drive the engine. A boiler can burst if the steam pressure grows too high. It can also burst if the water inside runs low and someone then lets cold water in on the hot metal.

On April 25, 1838, all four boilers of the steamboat *Moselle* burst at once as it pulled away from a landing just east of Cincinnati. The captain, Isaac Perin, had kept the boilers at full steam during the stop, to impress people watching from shore. Many witnesses said he was racing another boat, the *Ben Franklin*. The blast threw Perin onto the riverbank and killed him. A committee of Cincinnati citizens met the next day. Its members counted at least 280 passengers on board and estimated about 150 dead. Later accounts give 160.

The steamship *Pulaski* ran between Savannah, Georgia, and Baltimore, Maryland. On June 14, 1838, it left Charleston, South Carolina, for Baltimore. At about 11 that night, about 40 miles off the coast of North Carolina, its starboard boiler exploded. Starboard is a ship's right side. The ship broke in two and sank in about 45 minutes. About 128 people died, and 59 were saved. The records of the numbers do not agree. One record lists 168 people on board, 37 crew and 131 passengers. Yet 128 dead and 59 saved add up to 187.

Investigators at the end of 1838 found that the engineers had run the boilers wrongly. An account written with the help of two survivors identifies the cause. The second engineer let the water boil away in the boiler and then let a full load of cold water in on the hot copper. The account does not include his name.

Families on the *Pulaski* brought enslaved people with them. The passenger list does not name them. It puts the word "servant" after the family's name. The list also names three Black women, Jenny, Priscilla and Sallie Middleton, and does not say whether they were enslaved or free. The records do not say how many enslaved people died.

<a id="story-rebecca-lamar"></a>

#### Rebecca Lamar

> **Who:** A survivor of the *Pulaski* explosion who lived on a floating piece of the wreck from Thursday night until the next Tuesday, and later wrote down what happened.
>
> **When and where:** Off the coast of North Carolina, June 14 to 19, 1838.

Rebecca Lamar survived on a floating piece of the *Pulaski* from Thursday night, June 14, until the next Tuesday, and later wrote down what happened there. She was traveling north with her brother, the Savannah banker Gazaway Bugg Lamar. With them were his wife, Jane, and their six children. Another niece of hers was also on board. Her brother owned shares in the ship.

The explosion woke her in her cabin. Her bed had jammed the door, so she began to climb out through the small window above it. Her brother put her and a niece into a small boat. A moment later something struck her, and she was in the sea. She caught hold of a piece of wood and pulled herself onto a floating section of the ship. Her niece Martha and her nephew Charles reached her there. A stranger brought her nephew Thomas to her.

The people on that section of the wreck had almost no food or water. They saved the wine and peppermint for the children. Rebecca Lamar tore strips from her dress into squares. She wet them and laid them on the children's heads during the day, to keep the children from getting thirsty. On the second day six men who could swim took the best small boat to row for help. Her brother was one of them. They reached the beach 40 miles above Wilmington, North Carolina.

People on the wreck died one by one. A man named Mr. Brown drank sea water. In a storm a woman named Mrs. Woart died, and a wave carried off her body and her husband, the Reverend Woart. Two men became delirious, which means confused and out of their minds, and walked into the sea. A man named Mr. Smith set off on a raft he had built and was never heard from again. On the Monday night her nephew Thomas died in her lap.

On the following Tuesday the schooner *Henry Cameron*, under Captain Eli Davis, found them. A schooner is a sailing ship with two or more masts. The *Pulaski*'s sailing master, the officer in charge of sailing the ship, Captain Pearson, was already on board, rescued from another piece of the wreck. That group numbered 23 people in all. He asked Davis three times to search for more survivors. The third search found Rebecca Lamar's group.

Her brother's wife, five of their six children and a niece died. Her brother and his son Charles, age 14, lived. In 1858 Charles Lamar led a group of investors who paid for the ship *Wanderer* to smuggle captive Africans into Georgia as slaves. Federal law had banned bringing enslaved people into the country since 1808. The *Wanderer*'s captain, William Corrie, bought 487 captive Africans at the Congo River. About 409 of them lived through the voyage, and the rest died on the way. Six trials were held in 1859 and 1860, and no one was convicted.

Rebecca Lamar later married Hugh McLeod. She wrote her account of the wreck without planning to publish it. The *Georgia Historical Quarterly* later printed it.

#### The first steamboat safety law, 1838

On July 7, 1838, members of Congress passed a law "to provide better security of the lives of passengers" on steamboats. It was the first federal law that required steamboats to be inspected. Under it, federal judges named engineers as inspectors. The inspectors checked each boat and gave the owner two certificates, signed papers the owner needed to get a license to run the boat. Owners paid 5 dollars for each inspection, repeated every 6 or 12 months. No federal officer enforced the law. Only a person who sued the owner in court could make an owner obey it. After 1838 steamboat disasters came more often and killed more people.

#### A tornado at Natchez, 1840

At about 1 in the afternoon on May 7, 1840, a tornado struck the Mississippi River at Natchez, Mississippi, and Vidalia, Louisiana, across the river. A tornado is a spinning column of wind that reaches down from a storm cloud to the ground. At the Natchez landing it threw 116 of the 120 flatboats into the river. Flatboats were large, flat-bottomed boats that carried farm goods and people downriver. Their crews and passengers drowned.

At least 317 people died, 269 of them on the river and 48 on land. The courthouse at Vidalia fell and killed Judge Keeton. Many bodies were never identified. By that count it is the second deadliest tornado in the country's history.

The count of 317 leaves out the enslaved people killed on plantations in Louisiana. P. M. Lapice reported that on his plantation below Vidalia the tornado blew down all the houses of the enslaved workers. Four or five people were killed outright. About twenty were badly hurt, and some of them had wounds so bad that they were dying. The *Mississippi Free Trader*, a Natchez newspaper, printed reports of hundreds of enslaved people killed on plantations up to 20 miles away, but no one made an exact count.

After the storm Stephen Duncan, a planter, paid to turn the Tremont House hotel into a hospital. A planter was the owner of a plantation, a large farm worked by enslaved people. Doctors and several thousand dollars came from New Orleans. Other slaveholders in the area sent large groups of enslaved people to clear the ruins and pull out the bodies.

#### The steamboat Erie burns, 1841

The steamboat *Erie* carried passengers between Buffalo, New York, and Chicago. On the evening of August 9, 1841, it left Buffalo with about 340 people on board. The boat had just been painted and varnished. A group of six painters, hired by William G. Miller of Buffalo, planned to ride only to the first stop, in Pennsylvania. They had left jugs of paint, varnish and turpentine, a paint thinner that burns easily, on the deck, near the boiler's vent pipe. That spot on the deck had caught fire three times before.

At about 8 p.m., off Silver Creek, New York, on Lake Erie, the turpentine exploded. Fire spread over the freshly painted boat within seconds. Two of the lifeboats turned over. The third carried the captain, Thomas Jefferson Titus, and four others. At 10 p.m. the crew of another steamboat, the *DeWitt Clinton*, arrived and pulled survivors from the lake. Fewer than 100 people were saved. The first counts put the dead at about 170. Later counts found as many as 254. All six painters died.

### 1850 to 1900

The country's deadliest shipwreck, its deadliest wildfire and its deadliest dam failure all happened between 1850 and 1900. Each one killed more than 1,000 people. After the *Sultana* sank and the Johnstown dam broke, survivors and investigators blamed named men, and no court punished any of them. In the same years Americans built new groups whose job was to warn people or help them. Under a law of 1870, Army soldiers took on the job of warning people about storms, and Clara Barton founded the American Red Cross in 1881.

#### A stronger steamboat law, 1852

Steamboat explosions and fires went on after the law of 1838. From 1847 to 1852, boiler explosions caused a long run of disasters. On August 30, 1852, members of Congress passed a stronger law, the Steamboat Act. Under it, officials of the Treasury Department enforced the rules through supervising inspectors, who were in charge of the local inspectors. Under the old law, only a lawsuit could make an owner obey.

Inspectors had to test every boiler by filling it with water under pressure, to see whether it leaked or burst before it was used with steam. Owners had to fit each boiler with a safety valve, a part that lets steam out before the pressure gets too high. Pilots and engineers had to earn a license from the inspectors. The law left out freight boats, ferries and tugboats. A law of 1871 covered all steam vessels and their crews.

#### The Sultana, 1865

The worst shipwreck in the country's history happened on the Mississippi River in April 1865, just as the Civil War was ending. The steamboat *Sultana* was built to carry 376 passengers. At Vicksburg, Mississippi, Union Army officers crowded more than 2,000 Union soldiers onto it. Most of the soldiers had just been freed from Confederate prison camps at Cahaba, Alabama, and Andersonville, Georgia.

Army officials paid boat owners for each soldier they carried home. They paid 2 dollars and 75 cents for each enlisted soldier, meaning one who was not an officer, and 8 dollars for each officer. Captain Reuben Hatch was the Army's chief quartermaster, or supply officer, at Vicksburg. He offered the *Sultana*'s captain, J. Cass Mason, a full load of about 1,000 soldiers. In return Hatch wanted a kickback, a secret payment for the favor. One of the boat's boilers was leaking. Mason had it patched instead of making the longer repairs a full fix would take. Captain George Williams, the officer in charge of loading, put every man at the Vicksburg parole camp, where freed prisoners waited to go home, on board. He believed there were fewer than 1,500.

At about 2 in the morning on April 27, 1865, about seven miles north of Memphis, Tennessee, the boilers exploded. The boat caught fire. Investigators blamed low water in the boilers while the overloaded boat leaned to one side, along with the patched boiler. Men who were thrown into the river floated past Memphis in the dark. Crews of other steamboats and of U.S. Navy ships pulled survivors from the water. On the Arkansas shore, the Fogelman family tied logs into a raft and took 25 soldiers off the burning boat. Franklin Hardin Barton, a Confederate soldier of the 23rd Arkansas Cavalry, was among the rescuers. The *Sultana* burned and sank at about 7 a.m.

Almost everyone on board was a Union soldier. Counts of the dead range from about 1,100 to about 1,800. General William Hoffman investigated for the Army and counted 1,238 in May 1865. Officials of the Customs Service, who kept records of ships, counted 1,547. The researcher Jerry Potter estimates about 1,800. About 200 of the men pulled out alive later died of their burns. Mason and most of the boat's officers died.

Captain Frederic Speed of the Army was tried and found guilty of overcrowding the boat. The Army's top lawyer, the Judge Advocate General, overturned the verdict. He found that Speed had spent the whole day at the camp and had not put a single soldier on board. Hatch quit the Army and refused three orders to come and testify. No one was punished.

#### Fire on October 8, 1871: Chicago and Peshtigo

On the evening of October 8, 1871, two fires began that together killed well over a thousand people. The smaller one burned the city of Chicago. The larger one burned the forests and towns of northeastern Wisconsin and Michigan's Upper Peninsula.

The Chicago fire started at about 8:30 p.m. in or near a small barn that belonged to Catherine O'Leary's family. More than two-thirds of the buildings in Chicago were made entirely of wood, and most had roofs of tar or wooden shingles, which burn easily. Only 1 inch of rain had fallen since early July. Strong winds from the southwest carried burning pieces toward the center of the city. The fire burned until October 10. It destroyed about 17,500 buildings over more than 3 square miles and left 90,000 to 100,000 people without homes. Searchers found 120 bodies. The county coroner, the official who looks into deaths, said that an exact count was impossible. The death toll may have been as high as 300.

A newspaper reporter, Michael Ahern, wrote that Catherine O'Leary's cow and a lantern had started the fire. She was a poor Irish Catholic immigrant, which made her an easy person to blame. In 1893 Ahern admitted that he had made the story up. In 1997 the members of the Chicago City Council voted to clear her name. The historian Richard Bales has suggested that a man named Daniel Sullivan started the fire.

Mayor Roswell B. Mason put the city under martial law, rule by the army, and placed General Philip Sheridan in charge from October 11 to 24. He also gave a private charity, the Chicago Relief and Aid Society, control of the relief. Donors in New York City gave $450,000 and donors in St. Louis $300,000. Money came from London too.

The fire in Wisconsin began with people who were clearing forest for farms and railroads. They set small fires to burn away the brush. On October 8 a cold front, the edge of a large mass of cold air, moved east and made the wind stronger, and the wind joined several of those fires into one. It burned about 1.2 million acres. It destroyed Peshtigo, Wisconsin, a town of about 1,700 people, and 16 other towns. People jumped into the Peshtigo River, into wells and into other water nearby to escape the flames. Some drowned, and others died of cold in the water.

The fire burned the town's records, so no one knows exactly how many people died. Estimates run from 1,200 to 2,400. In 1873 a report to Wisconsin's lawmakers listed 1,182 names of people who died or went missing. More than 350 bodies were buried in one grave, because no one was left alive who could name them. It is the deadliest wildfire in the country's recorded history.

Peshtigo stood on forest land that had belonged to the Menominee Nation. In 1836 Henry Dodge, the governor of Wisconsin Territory, signed a treaty with the Menominee at a place called The Cedars, on the Fox River. A treaty is a written agreement between nations. Under the Treaty of the Cedars, the Menominee handed over about 4 million acres to the United States, and United States officials agreed to pay $700,000. Loggers and white settlers then moved onto the land.

#### The Red Cross, 1881, and an earthquake in Charleston, 1886

Clara Barton and a group of supporters founded the American Red Cross in Washington, D.C., on May 21, 1881. On September 5, 1881, forest fires burned more than a million acres in the Thumb, the part of Michigan shaped like a thumb. The fires killed 282 people and left thousands without homes. Red Cross workers sent money, clothes and furniture to about 14,000 people in need there. It was the Red Cross's first disaster relief.

At about 9:50 on the night of August 31, 1886, an earthquake of about magnitude 7 shook Charleston, South Carolina. It killed 60 people and damaged about 2,000 buildings. Most of the damage, 81 percent of it, was to brick buildings. Wooden buildings were damaged much less than brick ones.

#### Storm warnings and the blizzards of 1888

On February 9, 1870, President Ulysses S. Grant signed a law. Under it, a national weather service began inside the Army's Signal Service, the branch that handled signals and telegraph messages. The law required the Secretary of War to have weather readings taken and to send notice of coming storms, by telegraph and signals, to the northern lakes and the seacoast.

On January 12, 1888, a blizzard struck the northern Great Plains without warning. A blizzard is a snowstorm with very strong wind and bitter cold. The morning had been warm, near 50 degrees. In Huron, Dakota Territory, many children left for school without winter coats. About 235 people died in Dakota Territory, Nebraska, Minnesota and Iowa, by one count. Other estimates range from 250 to 500, and some go as high as 1,000. People call it the Schoolchildren's Blizzard.

Near Ord, Nebraska, the wind tore the door and the roof off the schoolhouse of Minnie Freeman, a teacher of 19. The schoolhouse was made of sod, blocks of earth held together by grass roots. Freeman tied her students together with twine and carried the youngest in her arms. She led them to a farmhouse about half a mile away, and all of them lived. In Plainview, Nebraska, the teacher Loie May Royce tried to lead three students to her home, less than 90 yards from the school. The wind-driven snow blinded them, and they lost their way. Searchers found them the next morning. The three children were dead. Royce's arms and legs were frostbitten, which means the cold had frozen and damaged the flesh. In Turner County, in present-day South Dakota, five boys were found dead four days after the storm. They were John Albrecht, Peter Graber, and Henry, John and Elias Kaufman.

In March 1888 another blizzard struck the Northeast and killed about 400 people. Forecasters of the Signal Service had predicted brisk winds and rain, then fair weather. After the two storms, members of Congress passed a law on October 1, 1890. Under it, weather forecasting moved from the Army to a new Weather Bureau in the Department of Agriculture. The bureau's forecasters were civilians, people who were not in the army.

#### The Johnstown Flood, May 31, 1889

The dam that broke above Johnstown, Pennsylvania, belonged to a private club of wealthy Pittsburgh men. The changes they made had weakened it. The South Fork Dam was 69 feet high and held back a lake 14 miles up the valley from Johnstown. Henry Clay Frick led a group of Pittsburgh businessmen who bought the lake for the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club. The club had more than fifty members, most of them steel, coal and railroad owners.

Workers the club hired lowered the top of the dam by as much as 3 feet to make room for a road for carriages. They put a screen across the spillway, the channel that lets extra water out, to keep the club's fish in the lake. Someone had removed the pipes at the bottom of the dam, which could let water out, before the club bought it, and club members never replaced them. The club's members had no way to lower the lake in an emergency.

On May 30 and 31 the heaviest rain ever recorded in that part of the country fell on western Pennsylvania. Army weather officers estimated 6 to 10 inches in 24 hours. The dam broke in the afternoon of May 31, 1889. Earlier that day the club's president, Elias Unger, had twice sent a man named Parke on horseback to a telegraph office to warn Johnstown. The people who received the warnings did not pass them on to the town's leaders, because there had been many false alarms before.

The water rushed down the valley. The railroad engineer John Hess drove his engine backward toward East Conemaugh with the whistle blowing the whole way. His warning saved many people. At the Stone Bridge in Johnstown, the wreckage piled up against the bridge and caught fire. At least 80 people died there, and the fire burned for three days.

The count of the dead was 2,209. Eleven years later one man counted as dead, Leroy Temple, turned up alive, which made it 2,208. Ninety-nine whole families died. National Park Service staff count 396 children under the age of 10 among the dead. Of all the dead, 777 were never identified. The flood left 124 women and 198 men widowed. It left 98 children orphaned, and by the Park Service's count 568 children lost one or both parents.

In 1891 the American Society of Civil Engineers, a group of engineers, released a report. It stated that the dam would have failed even if the club had kept it as first built. The group's president in 1890, William Shinn, had been a business partner of Andrew Carnegie. The report was kept from the public for two years. The authors of a study published in 2016 found that the club's changes cut the amount of water the dam could safely let out by half.

Survivors sued the club. Two of its members, the lawyers Philander Knox and James Hay Reed, defended it in court. They argued that the flood was an "act of God," a natural event that no person could be blamed for. The survivors lost, and no one ever paid them for their losses. Frick and about half of the club's members gave money to help the survivors. Andrew Carnegie built the town a new library.

<a id="story-victor-heiser"></a>

#### Victor Heiser

> **Who:** A 16-year-old who rode the Johnstown Flood on a barn roof, lost both his parents, and later became a doctor.
>
> **When and where:** Johnstown, Pennsylvania, May 31, 1889.

Victor Heiser was 16 when the Johnstown Flood destroyed his home and killed his parents. As the river rose that afternoon, his father sent him to the barn to untie the horses. He heard what he called a "dreadful roar." He looked back and saw his parents at a window of the house. His father waved at him to climb onto the barn roof.

From the roof he saw his house "crushed like an eggshell." He noted the time: 4:20 p.m. The barn floated away with him on its roof. When it was about to hit a neighbor's house, he jumped onto that house. It began to fall in, and he fell back onto the barn roof. The water carried him down to the Stone Bridge.

He spent the night in a house with 19 other people. The next day he went looking for his parents. He tried to help people trapped in the burning wreckage at the bridge. For two weeks he searched among the bodies of the dead. He found the body of his mother, Mathilde Heiser. He was never able to identify his father, George.

Heiser later studied at Jefferson Medical College and became a doctor. He worked in many countries against diseases such as leprosy, cholera and malaria. In 1936 he told his story in a book, *An American Doctor's Odyssey*. He was born on February 5, 1873, and died on February 27, 1972.

#### The Sea Islands hurricane, 1893

On August 27, 1893, a hurricane came ashore near Savannah, Georgia. It drove the sea over the low Sea Islands of South Carolina. Between 1,000 and 2,000 people died, most of them drowned. Most people on the islands were Black. On St. Helena Island about 6,000 Black people lived, and most of them owned their land. Many of their houses stood no more than 2 feet above the ground.

Red Cross workers arrived on October 1, more than a month after the storm, and ran a relief effort for 10 months. The historian Caroline Grego wrote about the relief work in 2019. She found that South Carolina politicians and newspaper writers pushed Red Cross leaders to send supplies to white farmers instead of to Black islanders. The records do not identify those politicians or newspaper writers by name. The Democratic Party leaders who ran the state government worked against the efforts of Black islanders to earn a steady living again.

<a id="story-clara-barton-disasters"></a>

#### Clara Barton

> **Who:** The founder of the American Red Cross, who led its relief work after fires, floods and hurricanes.
>
> **When and where:** Michigan, 1881. Johnstown, Pennsylvania, 1889. The South Carolina Sea Islands, 1893. Galveston, Texas, 1900.

Clara Barton founded the American Red Cross in 1881, when she was 59, and led its relief work after disasters for more than 20 years. Its first disaster relief went to the people who lost their homes in the Michigan forest fires that September.

She reached Johnstown on June 5, 1889, five days after the flood. She was 67. About 50 Red Cross workers came with her from Washington, D.C., and they stayed five months. Her workers built "Red Cross hotels" where people who had lost their homes could stay. Most of the people who rented rooms in them were merchants and businessmen. Red Cross workers gave out supplies worth $211,000 and helped about 25,000 people.

A separate Red Cross group from Philadelphia ran a hospital in Johnstown. The historian David McCullough wrote that Barton "spoke her mind once or twice" to the head of that group. Within a few days neither group would have anything to do with the other.

In 1893 she led relief for about 30,000 people left homeless by the Sea Islands hurricane, most of them Black. Her last relief work came after the Galveston hurricane of September 1900. She resigned as president of the Red Cross on May 14, 1904, after growing criticism.

Her house in Glen Echo, Maryland, was built partly from lumber of the Red Cross buildings at Johnstown. She lived there from 1897 to 1912.

### 1900 to 1950

Between 1900 and 1950, many people died in disasters because of choices other people made. In New York, witnesses said the owners of a blouse factory kept an exit door locked. Near Los Angeles the city's chief engineer and his assistant judged a leaking dam safe, and in Texas members of a school board piped waste gas into a school to save money. After the Triangle fire, the sinking of the *Titanic*, the Cocoanut Grove fire and the New London school explosion, lawmakers wrote new safety rules for factories, ships, nightclubs and gas lines. The deadliest disaster came first. The Galveston hurricane of September 1900 killed between 6,000 and 12,000 people, more than any other natural disaster in the country's history. In three disasters, leaders and officials treated Black survivors and Black victims worse than white ones. In Galveston, members of an armed militia forced Black workers at gunpoint to bury the dead. In the 1927 Mississippi flood, the local leaders who ran many relief camps gave supplies to white people first and forced Black people to work. After the 1928 hurricane in Florida, officials saved the few coffins for white victims. The bodies of Black victims were burned in piles or thrown into mass graves.

#### Galveston, September 8, 1900

A hurricane flooded Galveston, Texas, on September 8, 1900, and killed more people than any other natural disaster in the country's history. Galveston was a port city of about 38,000 people on an island in the Gulf of Mexico. At about 6:30 that evening, a storm wave put the city under as much as 15 feet of water. The highest water mark was 15.7 feet.

Between 6,000 and 8,000 people died in the city. Estimates for the whole island and the nearby coast run from 10,000 to 12,000. In early October the *Galveston News* printed a final list of 4,263 dead. The storm destroyed a third of the city. Counts of the homes destroyed run from 2,636 to about 3,600.

Searchers found about 70 bodies a day during the first month. The last body was found on February 10, 1901. Galveston's leaders put the city under martial law, which means soldiers or armed guards take over from the police and courts. A volunteer militia, a group of armed citizens, patrolled the streets against looters, people who steal from damaged buildings. Some accounts say that men accused of looting were shot, but the records do not give their names or a count.

Too few volunteers came forward to handle the dead, so armed men rounded up other men at gunpoint or bayonet point to do it. The writer Elizabeth Blasius found that members of the volunteer militia did this, and that many of the men they forced were Black workers. About one fifth of the people of Galveston were Black. Even before the storm, the city's segregation rules kept Black Galvestonians from drinking at the public fountains or going to the public schools. Segregation means keeping people apart by race. At first, workers loaded bodies onto barges, tied heavy rocks to them and dropped them into the Gulf. Days later, some of the bodies floated back to shore. After that, workers burned the dead in large fires. The fires burned into November.

Clara Barton, 78, arrived with Red Cross workers on September 17, nine days after the storm. Mayor Walter C. Jones led a Central Relief Committee that included the banker John Sealy. The committee's members spent its money on 483 new houses and on partial help toward 1,114 more. Afterward, workers built a seawall that stood 17 feet above the low-tide line. Its first section ran three and a half miles. Workers then raised the ground under the city by as much as 17 feet. They lifted about 2,000 buildings on jacks first. St. Patrick's Church, which weighed 3,000 tons, went up five feet.

<a id="story-isaac-cline"></a>

#### Isaac Cline

> **Who:** The chief of the U.S. Weather Bureau office in Galveston, whose pregnant wife died in the 1900 hurricane.
>
> **When and where:** Galveston, Texas, September 8, 1900.

Isaac Cline was Galveston's chief weather forecaster, and nine years before the storm he had written that a hurricane could never do serious harm to the city. He was born near Madisonville, Tennessee, in 1861 and took charge of the Galveston office in 1889. His brother Joseph joined him there in 1892.

In 1891 Cline wrote an article for the *Galveston Daily News*. In it he called the thought of a hurricane seriously harming Galveston "a crazy idea." Many people in the city had asked for a seawall. His article was one reason no seawall was built before the storm.

On September 8, 1900, water began flooding the low parts of the city. Around noon, Cline raised the hurricane warning flags without waiting for approval from the Weather Bureau's main office in Washington. Weather Bureau rules required that approval.

Cline later wrote that he drove a horse-drawn cart along the beach and warned people to leave. No eyewitness ever reported seeing him do it. The writer Erik Larson argued that Cline warned no one before his office sent out its official warning.

Cline's wife, Cora, was pregnant with their fourth child, and she died in the storm. Cline nearly drowned. He saved his youngest daughter, Esther, who was 6. Joseph saved the two older girls, Allie May, 12, and Rosemary, 11.

In 1901 Cline moved to New Orleans. Between 1900 and 1924 he charted the paths of 16 storms. He retired in 1935 and died in 1955, at 93.

#### San Francisco, April 18, 1906

Fire did most of the damage after the San Francisco earthquake of April 18, 1906. The earthquake struck at 5:12 in the morning. Scientists measure an earthquake's strength with a number called its magnitude. This one had a magnitude of about 7.9 and shook the city for about 42 seconds. It broke gas pipes, and within three days more than 30 fires had spread across the city. Between 80 and 95 percent of the damage came from the fires.

Firefighters tried to blow up buildings with dynamite to make empty gaps the fire could not cross. They had no training with dynamite, and some of their blasts started new fires. The city's fire chief, Dennis T. Sullivan, had been hurt in the earthquake itself, when a building next door fell onto the fire station where he lived. He died four days later. General Frederick Funston sent in Army soldiers. Some building owners set fire to their own damaged buildings, because their insurance paid for fire damage and not for earthquake damage.

More than 80 percent of the city was destroyed. Between 227,000 and 300,000 people lost their homes, out of about 410,000. The first counts of the dead ran from 375 to more than 500. Those counts left out hundreds of deaths in Chinatown that no one recorded. In 2005 the members of the Board of Supervisors, San Francisco's city lawmakers, voted to accept more than 3,000 as the official count. They voted for a written statement by the novelist James Dalessandro and the city historian Gladys Hansen.

On the day of the earthquake, Mayor Eugene Schmitz announced that he had authorized soldiers and police "to kill any and all persons found engaged in Looting or in the Commission of Any Other Crime." Authorized means he gave them permission. The records do not say how many people they killed. People also accused soldiers themselves of looting.

About 15,000 Chinese people lived in Chinatown, and they lost nearly everything. Even before the earthquake, some city officials had wanted to move the Chinese out of Chinatown to Hunters Point. After it, they tried to use the ruins to take Chinatown's land for business buildings. The Chinese were the only group that officials kept apart in the camps for people who had lost their homes. Army officers moved the Chinese survivors to camps farther and farther from Chinatown. Most Chinese survivors left for Oakland, and only about 400 stayed in the city. The officials' plan to move Chinatown failed. Chinese residents rebuilt Chinatown.

<a id="story-hugh-kwong-liang"></a>

#### Hugh Kwong Liang

> **Who:** A 15-year-old in San Francisco's Chinatown who lived through the 1906 earthquake and fire.
>
> **When and where:** San Francisco, April 1906.

Hugh Kwong Liang was 15 when the earthquake woke him in Chinatown. He is one of the few Chinese survivors whose own account of the earthquake has lasted to today. He remembered seeing "pieces of plaster falling down like water." He ran out into Washington Street, and the building across from his home fell down.

As the fire spread, city officials who were directing the people fleeing told him and his family to go to the open ground of the Presidio. The Presidio was an Army post by the Golden Gate, the entrance to San Francisco Bay. He remembered the moment he left: "I turned away from my dear old Chinatown for the last time."

At the Presidio, Army officers kept the Chinese survivors apart from everyone else. They moved them from camp to camp. The last camp stood in a cold, windy corner of the Presidio near Fort Point.

#### The Triangle fire, March 25, 1911

On March 25, 1911, a fire at the Triangle Waist Company in New York City killed 146 workers. Witnesses said the owners kept one of its exit doors locked. The company made women's blouses on the top three floors of the ten-story Asch Building. Most of its workers were young immigrant women, and many were teenagers. The youngest who died, Kate Leone and Rosaria Maltese, were 14.

The fire started on the eighth floor just before the 4:45 p.m. quitting time. Workers ran down the Greene Street stairs, crowded into the elevators, and climbed onto the one fire escape, which collapsed. On the ninth floor, the door to the Washington Place stairs would not open. Other witnesses told the court that the owners, Max Blanck and Isaac Harris, kept it locked so workers could not leave with stolen blouses. Harris later admitted that all the blouses ever stolen were worth less than 25 dollars.

The firefighters' ladders reached only to the seventh floor. Workers trapped on the ninth floor could not get past the fire, and many jumped from the windows. A crowd in the street watched 62 people jump or fall to their deaths. Joseph Flecher, who worked in the company office, watched from the roof and saw his workers "hit the sidewalk spread out and still." On the tenth floor, workers climbed to the roof. A law professor at New York University, Frank Sommer, and his students found ladders that painters had left and set them across to the school's roof. Workers climbed over them to safety.

Blanck and Harris were put on trial for manslaughter, the crime of killing a person without meaning to, through carelessness. Judge Crain told the jury it had to find that the owners knew the door was locked. On December 27, 1911, after less than two hours, the jury found them not guilty. One juror, Victor Steinman, said he believed the door was locked, "but we couldn't find them guilty unless we believed they knew the door was locked." On March 11, 1914, the families in 23 lawsuits against the building's owner settled, which means they agreed to take money and end the lawsuits. They got an average of 75 dollars for each life.

New York lawmakers set up a nine-member Factory Investigating Commission. From 1911 to 1914 they passed 36 new laws to change the state's rules for workplaces. A state law already in force at the time of the fire had required factory doors to open outward where possible and to stay unlocked during working hours.

<a id="story-kate-alterman"></a>

#### Kate Alterman

> **Who:** A worker who escaped the Triangle fire and told the jury how another worker, Margaret Schwartz, died at the locked door.
>
> **When and where:** New York City, March 25, 1911, and the trial in December 1911.

Kate Alterman saw another worker, Margaret Schwartz, catch fire at the locked Washington Place door, and she told the jury what she saw. Margaret died in the fire. Kate worked on the ninth floor. She had lived in Philadelphia for nine years, and she had been in New York and worked at the Triangle factory for four months.

When the fire reached the ninth floor, the two women ran to the Washington Place door. The manager's brother, whose last name was Bernstein, tried it and could not open it. Margaret tried next. Then Kate pulled the handle "in and out, all ways," and it still would not open.

Kate saw Margaret kneel down by the door. She saw the hem of Margaret's dress and the ends of her loose hair start to burn. Margaret screamed, "Open the door! Fire! I am lost, there is fire!"

Kate turned her coat inside out and put it over her head with the fur against her face. She covered her head with a bunch of dresses. Then she ran out through the flames. "The whole door was a flame right to the roof," she said.

At the trial the prosecutor, Charles Bostwick, used her account to show that the locked door caused Margaret Schwartz's death. The owners' lawyer, Max Steuer, made her tell the story again and again. She used almost the same words each time. In this way Steuer made her story seem less believable without ever saying she was lying. She said she told it the same way "because he asked me the very same story over and over."

#### Ships: the Titanic, 1912, and the Eastland, 1915

The *Titanic* carried lifeboats for only some of the people on board, and United States senators blamed British officials for that. The *Titanic* was a British passenger ship. It hit an iceberg in the North Atlantic and sank on April 15, 1912. More than 1,500 passengers and crew died. The ship *Carpathia* picked up about 710 survivors.

The ship had too few lifeboats for everyone, but it met the rules of the British Board of Trade, the government office in charge of British ships. Senator William Alden Smith of Michigan led a Senate investigation. It began in New York on April 19, four days after the sinking. The senators found that Captain Edward Smith's "indifference to danger" was one of the direct causes of the deaths. They blamed the Board of Trade's officials for the missing lifeboats. They called for ships to slow down near ice, to carry enough lifeboats for all on board, and to keep a radio operator on duty day and night. In March 1915, after the *Titanic* sinking, members of Congress passed the Seamen's Act, pushed by Senator Robert La Follette of Wisconsin.

On July 24, 1915, the Great Lakes passenger ship *Eastland* rolled over while it was tied to a dock in the Chicago River. It was taking workers of the Western Electric Company and their families to a company picnic in Indiana, and it had already filled to its limit of 2,500 passengers. The ship had tipped badly before, including in 1906. Under the new law, its owners had added a full set of lifeboats so it could carry more people. That added weight may have made the ship more dangerous. At 7:28 a.m. it rolled onto its side and settled on the river bottom, only 20 feet down. In all, 844 people died. Many of the dead were immigrants, and 220 of them were Czech.

A deckhand, Peter Boyle, drowned while saving people. A nurse, Helen Repa, led much of the rescue work on shore. A grand jury is a group of citizens who decide whether there is enough evidence for a trial. An Illinois grand jury charged the president of the steamship company and three other company officers with manslaughter. It charged the captain and the engineer with criminal carelessness. The men were outside Illinois, and a federal court refused to send them there for trial. The court found "barely a scintilla of proof," meaning almost no evidence, because the four company officers had not been on the ship. None of the men was ever tried in Illinois.

#### The Mississippi flood of 1927

About 637,000 people had to leave their homes in the Mississippi River flood of 1927. In the relief camps, local leaders gave supplies to white people first and forced Black people to work. In the spring the river broke through its levees in at least 145 places. A levee is a wall of earth built along a riverbank to hold the water in. Water covered 27,000 square miles, as deep as 30 feet. About 500 people died.

On April 29 a group of New Orleans bankers arranged to set off about 30 tons of dynamite on the levee at Caernarvon, Louisiana, below their city. They wanted to let the river out there to keep it from badly damaging New Orleans. The water flooded St. Bernard Parish and part of Plaquemines Parish. A parish is what Louisiana calls a county. Blowing up the levee turned out to be unnecessary. The New Orleans businessmen never paid the people whose homes and land they flooded.

About 325,000 people lived in relief camps, and 69 percent of them were Black. Near Greenville, Mississippi, more than 13,000 people escaped to the top of a levee that had held. Many of them were stranded there for days without food or clean water. Local leaders from the countryside ran many of the camps. They gave supplies and boats to white people first, and Black people got what was left. A Black person got supplies only by giving the name of a white employer. Black people in the camps were forced to work and were not allowed to leave. The records do not name the camp leaders who gave these orders. A white police officer ordered a Black man at gunpoint to unload a relief boat. The man refused, and the officer shot and killed him. The records do not give the name of the man who was killed. Near Helena, Arkansas, a plantation overseer, the man who bossed the workers, tried to force a Black man, Owen Flemming, to rescue the plantation owner's mules. Flemming killed the overseer. Then he was lynched, which means he was killed by a mob without a trial. The records do not name the men who killed him.

Herbert Hoover, the Secretary of Commerce, led the national government's relief work. A group of Black leaders headed by Robert Russa Moton studied the camps and reported what was happening in them. Hoover asked that their reports be kept out of the newspapers, and they were. After the flood, members of Congress passed the Flood Control Act of 1928.

#### Two disasters of 1928: the St. Francis Dam and Lake Okeechobee

The St. Francis Dam in northern Los Angeles County broke just before midnight on March 12, 1928. That same day its builder had looked at a new leak and judged it safe. William Mulholland was the chief engineer of the city's Bureau of Water Works and Supply. His workers had built the dam from 1924 to 1926. Leaks and cracks showed up in 1927 and 1928. That morning the dam keeper, Tony Harnischfeger, found a new leak. Mulholland and his assistant, Harvey Van Norman, looked at it and decided it was not dangerous.

The dam gave way at about 11:57 that night. Harnischfeger and his family were probably among the first people killed. The flood ran 54 miles to the Pacific Ocean and killed at least 431 people. Among them were 84 workers of the Southern California Edison company at a construction camp beside the river. At the investigation afterward, the *Express* newspaper reported that Mulholland said, "the only ones I envy are those who are dead." The *Los Angeles Times* printed his words as "on an occasion like this I envy the dead."

On April 12, 1928, a coroner's jury, a group of citizens who decide how people died, ruled on the collapse. The jurors found an error in engineering judgment about the rock under the dam, and they put that blame on Mulholland's bureau and its chief engineer. They found a second error, in the rules meant to keep the public safe. They put that blame on three groups: the city's water and power commissioners, the lawmakers of the city and the state, and the public. The jurors wrote that a great dam should never be left "to the sole judgment of one man, no matter how eminent," meaning no matter how famous and respected. They found no crime and recommended that no one be charged. Mulholland's career as chief engineer ended after the dam broke.

Six months later, early on September 17, 1928, a hurricane came ashore near West Palm Beach, Florida. It had already killed 312 people in Puerto Rico. The storm pushed the water of Lake Okeechobee over the low dike at the lake's south end. A dike is a bank of earth built to keep water back. Floods more than 20 feet deep covered the farm towns of Belle Glade, Canal Point, Chosen, Pahokee and South Bay.

At least 2,500 people died in the United States. For many years the official count was the Red Cross estimate of 1,836. About three out of four of the dead were migrant farm workers, people who moved from farm to farm to pick crops. Most of them were Black. Black workers did most of the cleanup after the storm. Officials saved the few coffins they had for the bodies of white people. White victims were buried with a service, in a shared grave at Woodlawn Cemetery in West Palm Beach. The bodies of Black victims were burned in piles or thrown into mass graves. One mass grave at Port Mayaca holds 1,600 bodies. The records do not name the officials who made these decisions.

Robert Hazard of West Palm Beach started a group to win recognition for the Black victims buried in the city's mass grave. The city bought the grave site back in 2000. In 2003 a state historical marker was put up there.

#### Black Sunday, April 14, 1935

On April 14, 1935, a wall of blowing dirt swept across the southern Great Plains, with winds of up to 60 miles an hour. It reached Beaver, Oklahoma, at about 4 p.m. and Boise City, Oklahoma, at about 5:15 p.m. For a short time the sky was so black that people could not see their own hands in front of their faces. The day became known as Black Sunday. An Associated Press reporter, Robert Geiger, and a photographer, Harry Eisenhard, were caught in the storm six miles from Boise City. The next day Geiger wrote a news story that began, "Residents of the southwestern dust bowl marked up another black duster today." A duster was a dust storm. His story is generally accepted as the first use of the words "dust bowl."

#### The New London school explosion, March 18, 1937

A gas explosion destroyed a school in New London, Texas, on March 18, 1937, and killed about 298 people, most of them children. Members of the school board had piped in the gas to save money. Early that year, board members canceled the school's contract for natural gas. They had plumbers connect the school to a pipe of leftover waste gas from a nearby company, the Parade Gasoline Company. Natural gas that has not been treated has no smell and no color. Gas leaked from the new connection and built up in the closed crawlspace, the low space under the floor, which ran the whole 253-foot length of the building's front. Students had been complaining of headaches for some time, but few people paid attention.

About 500 students and 40 teachers were in the building that afternoon. At 3:17 p.m. Lemmie R. Butler, who taught shop, turned on an electric sander. A spark from its switch probably set off the gas. The *Handbook of Texas*, published by the Texas State Historical Association, records about 298 dead. Other counts run from 294 to more than 400, and the exact number is not known.

More than 70 lawsuits were filed. Judge Robert T. Brown dismissed the ones that came to trial, for lack of evidence, and no one was ever found responsible. The school superintendent, W. C. Shaw, whose son was killed, resigned. Texas lawmakers gave the state's Railroad Commission the power to require a chemical with a strong smell in natural gas, so that people can smell a leak. Within weeks of the explosion, that chemical was being mixed into the gas.

#### The Hindenburg, 1937, and the Cocoanut Grove, 1942

On May 6, 1937, the German passenger airship *Hindenburg* caught fire as it came in to land at the Naval Air Station in Lakehurst, New Jersey. An airship is a giant aircraft held up by a gas lighter than air, with engines to push it and a cabin for passengers. The *Hindenburg* was filled with hydrogen, a gas that burns very easily. Of the 97 people on board, 35 died. A man working on the ground, Allen Hagaman, died too. Cameramen from four newsreel companies were filming the landing and filmed the fire. Newsreels were short news films shown in movie theaters. None of them caught the moment the fire started. The radio reporter Herbert Morrison recorded what he saw as it happened. What caused the first spark has never been settled. Passenger travel by giant airship ended after the fire.

On November 28, 1942, at about 10:15 p.m., fire spread through the Cocoanut Grove nightclub in Boston and killed 492 people. Many of them were trapped behind doors that were locked, hidden or blocked. More than 1,000 people were inside a club that was allowed to hold 460. The owner, Barnett Welansky, had locked some exits, hidden others behind curtains, and bricked one up. The main entrance was a single revolving door. Bodies piled up on both sides of it and jammed it until it broke. Other doors opened inward, so people could not open them against the crush of the crowd. Fire officials later told the court that if the doors had swung outward, at least 300 lives could have been saved. How the fire started is not known.

Welansky was found guilty of manslaughter and spent nearly four years in prison. Lawmakers then passed new laws that banned decorations that burn easily. The laws required emergency exits to stay unlocked, and a revolving door could no longer be a building's only exit.

#### Explosions at the docks: Port Chicago, 1944, and Texas City, 1947

On July 17, 1944, two ships being loaded with ammunition blew up at the Port Chicago Naval Magazine in California, a Navy base for storing explosives. The blast killed 320 men, and 202 of them were Black sailors. Navy officers had given Black sailors the job of loading the ships without enough training or equipment.

On the morning of April 16, 1947, a fire broke out in the cargo of the French ship *Grandcamp* at the docks of Texas City, Texas. The ship carried about 2,300 tons of ammonium nitrate, a chemical used as fertilizer that can explode. The ship's captain ordered his crew not to use water on the fire, so that the cargo would not be ruined. The crew closed the hatches and pumped in steam. The unusual smoke drew a crowd of about 500 people to the shore to watch, many of them children.

At 9:12 a.m. the ship exploded. Flying pieces of metal set fire to oil refineries and chemical tanks along the waterfront. The Monsanto chemical plant beside the ship took the worst of the blast, and seven broken oil tanks at the Republic Refinery caught fire. Another ship, the *High Flyer*, which carried 961 tons of ammonium nitrate, blew up at 1:10 the next morning. At least 581 people died. The first explosion killed 26 of the town's volunteer firefighters, all but one member of the fire department, and destroyed all of the city's firefighting equipment. The anchor monument in Texas City lists 576 people known to have died. Sixty-three of them were buried without names.

More than 8,000 people sued the United States government. They used a 1946 law that let people sue the government for harm caused by the carelessness of its workers. In 1953 the justices of the Supreme Court ruled against them, 4 to 3. In 1955 members of Congress voted to pay the claims anyway. The government paid 1,394 awards, worth nearly 17 million dollars in all.

### 1950 to 2000

Between 1950 and 2000 forecasters began giving hurricanes names, and a president put most of the national government's disaster help under one office. Choices made by owners and engineers still killed hundreds of people. Weather Bureau forecasters began giving hurricanes human names in 1953 and warned the Louisiana coast a day before Hurricane Audrey struck in 1957. In 1979 President Jimmy Carter put much of the government's disaster work under the Federal Emergency Management Agency, called FEMA. In 1972 a coal company's waste dam in West Virginia broke and killed 125 people. In 1981 two hotel walkways in Kansas City fell and killed 114, after an engineer approved a design change without checking the math. News reporters broadcast the rescue after a plane crash in Washington, D.C., live as it happened. After Hurricane Andrew in 1992, a single building code, a set of rules for how strong buildings must be, was set up for the whole state of Florida.

#### Hurricanes with names: Audrey, 1957, and Camille, 1969

Hurricane Audrey killed at least 416 people in 1957. Forecasters warned the Louisiana coast a day before it struck, but the storm sped up and arrived sooner than forecasters or residents expected. By then, hurricanes had names. In 1953 forecasters of the U.S. Weather Bureau began giving human names to storms. In 1956 Weather Bureau officials opened a hurricane center in Miami.

At 10 a.m. on June 26, 1957, forecasters warned the whole Louisiana coast that a hurricane was coming. About 75,000 people left. Audrey came ashore the next day near Cameron, about 24 hours after the warning. It moved faster as it neared land, which surprised both forecasters and the people who lived there. Its storm surge rose as high as 12 feet. A storm surge is the wall of seawater that a hurricane's winds push onto land. The water did damage as far as 25 miles inland. Audrey killed at least 416 people in the United States, most of them in Cameron Parish. The final count may never be known.

Late on August 17, 1969, Hurricane Camille came ashore near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, with winds of 175 miles an hour. The water rose 24.6 feet at Pass Christian, Mississippi. Camille killed 172 people in Mississippi and 9 in Louisiana. As the storm moved north, its rain caused floods in Virginia that killed more than 153 people there. At least 343 people died in all.

#### The Alaska earthquake, March 27, 1964

The strongest earthquake ever recorded in North America struck southern Alaska at 5:36 p.m. on March 27, 1964. Most of the people it killed drowned in the giant waves it caused. The earthquake had a magnitude of 9.2 and lasted four minutes and 38 seconds. The shaking and underwater landslides sent tsunamis into the coast. A tsunami is a series of giant waves set off by an earthquake or a landslide under the sea. Scientists of the U.S. Geological Survey count 131 dead: 122 killed by the tsunamis and 9 by the shaking. Other counts reach 139. At Valdez, 32 people died when the town's harbor and docks collapsed. Tsunamis also reached Oregon and California. In Crescent City, California, one killed 10 people.

Chenega was a village of Chugach Alutiiq people, also called Sugpiaq, on an island in Prince William Sound. Their people had lived there since before Russians came to Alaska. About four minutes after the shaking began, a wave 27 feet high struck the village. It knocked down every building except the school and one house. Between 23 and 26 of the roughly 70 people who lived there died, by different counts. Scientists of the Geological Survey found that Chenega lost a larger share of its people than any other town. The survivors outran the wave and climbed to high ground.

Rescuers took the survivors to Cordova. Officials of the federal Bureau of Indian Affairs later moved them for good to the village of Tatitlek. In 1971 members of Congress passed the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act. Under it, Alaska Natives received 44 million acres and $962.5 million, held by companies that Alaska Natives own. Former Chenega residents formed one of them, the Chenega Corporation, and won the right to choose 76,093 acres of land. People began living in a new village, Chenega Bay, in 1984.

President Lyndon Johnson declared all of Alaska a disaster area the day after the earthquake. Army engineers of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers led the work of rebuilding roads, clearing wreckage and laying out new town sites, at a cost of 110 million dollars. The people of Valdez moved their town to higher ground four miles to the west. In 1967 federal scientists of the Coast and Geodetic Survey opened a tsunami warning center at Palmer, Alaska.

#### Floods of 1972: Buffalo Creek and Rapid City

The Pittston Company's coal waste dam above Buffalo Creek, West Virginia, broke at about 8 a.m. on February 26, 1972, and the flood killed 125 people. The Buffalo Mining Company, part of Pittston, owned and ran three dams made of coal waste on the creek's Middle Fork. The third dam sat on a layer of soft coal mud instead of solid rock. Neither Pittston nor the mine's earlier owner had sent the dams' plans to the state for approval. Four days before the flood, a federal mine inspector called the dam "satisfactory."

The dam gave way and let out 132 million gallons of water, coal waste and mud. The flood ran down the narrow valley through 16 coal towns. It killed whole families, injured about 1,000 people, and destroyed 507 houses and 44 mobile homes. About 4,000 of the 5,000 people who lived along the creek lost their homes.

Pittston officials blamed three days of rain and called the flood "an act of God," meaning a natural event that no person could have prevented. Members of the governor's commission that investigated wrote that "the Pittston Company, through its officials, has shown flagrant disregard for the safety of residents of Buffalo Creek." Flagrant disregard means ignoring something openly and on purpose. Members of a separate commission formed by citizens said the company was guilty of murdering at least 124 people. The records show no Pittston official charged with a crime.

In 1974 Pittston paid 13.5 million dollars to settle a lawsuit by survivors and family members. One count gives 645 of them, and another gives 625. That came to about 13,000 dollars each after the lawyers were paid. Governor Moore settled the state's own lawsuit in 1977 for 1 million dollars. Members of Congress and West Virginia lawmakers passed new laws on how such dams must be built and kept up.

On June 9 and 10, 1972, less than four months later, about 15 inches of rain fell on part of the Black Hills of South Dakota. Rapid Creek flooded Rapid City, where people had built houses and businesses on the creek's flood plain. A flood plain is the low land beside a river that the river covers when it floods. The flood killed 238 people. Afterward, new zoning rules set what could be built where, and most of the flood plain was rebuilt as parks.

#### FEMA and Three Mile Island, 1979

In 1979 President Jimmy Carter put much of the national government's disaster work under one new office, the Federal Emergency Management Agency, or FEMA. Before then, officials of more than 100 separate federal offices could each claim a part in the response to a single disaster. On April 1, 1979, Carter signed two executive orders, written orders from the president, that started FEMA. In July he signed another order that moved disaster relief into it. In 1988 members of Congress passed the Stafford Act. It set the rules for when a president may declare a disaster, so that federal money and help can be sent.

Four days before FEMA started, the worst accident in the history of the country's nuclear power plants began at Three Mile Island, near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. A nuclear reactor makes heat from uranium fuel in its core, and water must keep flowing around the core to cool it. At 4 a.m. on March 28, 1979, a small fault in the cooling system of the Unit 2 reactor set off a chain of failures. A relief valve stuck open and let cooling water escape. The operators had no instrument that showed them the valve was open. They thought the system held too much water, so they cut the flow of new water. The core overheated, and at least 45 percent of it melted.

The operators at the plant, officials of Metropolitan Edison, the power company that ran it, and state and federal officials gave the public unclear and conflicting reports. Station manager Gary Miller declared an emergency at the plant. Federal nuclear officials had no power to order people to leave. On March 30, Governor Richard Thornburgh advised pregnant women and small children within five miles to leave. He told people within ten miles to stay indoors. About 140,000 people left on their own. In at least 12 studies since 1981, scientists have found no deaths and no health harm that can be measured from the radiation that escaped. A commission of 12 members, led by John G. Kemeny, reported on the accident on October 31, 1979.

#### Mount St. Helens, 1980, and the Hyatt Regency walkways, 1981

Mount St. Helens, a volcano in Washington State, blew out its north side at 8:32 a.m. on May 18, 1980, and killed about 57 people. An earthquake loosened the side of the mountain, and the whole weakened north face slid away. Hot gas and shattered rock blasted north toward Spirit Lake. The blast turned hundreds of square miles into wasteland. Most of the people who died were suffocated, and a few died of burns. Among the dead were Harry R. Truman, who owned a lodge at Spirit Lake, the photographers Reid Blackburn and Robert Landsburg, and David Johnston, a volcano scientist of the U.S. Geological Survey. Johnston was on duty at a lookout post about six miles north of the mountain.

On the evening of Friday, July 17, 1981, two walkways fell onto a crowd in the lobby of the Hyatt Regency Hotel in Kansas City, Missouri. Engineering mistakes caused the fall. About 1,600 people had come to a dance in the lobby. The two walkways hung over the lobby. They killed 114 people and injured 216.

Engineers at Jack D. Gillum and Associates, the firm of the engineer Jack D. Gillum, designed the walkways. Their first design was already too weak. It could hold only 60 percent of the weight that Kansas City's building code required. Then the makers of the steel parts, at a company called Havens Steel, proposed a change in how the walkways hung. The engineer Daniel M. Duncan accepted the change in a phone call without doing the math to check it. The change doubled the load on the walkway beams on the fourth floor. Investigators found that the walkways would have failed under one third of the weight they held that night.

Members of a Missouri state board found the engineers to blame for gross negligence, which means a serious failure to take the care their job required. They also found them guilty of misconduct and unprofessional conduct, meaning they had broken the rules of their profession. Gillum's company lost its engineering licenses in Missouri, Kansas and Texas. The engineers were cleared of the crimes they were first charged with, and no one was convicted of a crime.

#### Air Florida Flight 90, January 13, 1982

On the snowy afternoon of January 13, 1982, Air Florida Flight 90 took off from Washington National Airport with snow and ice on its wings. It crashed into the Potomac River. The captain, Larry Wheaton, 34, and the first officer, Roger Pettit, 31, had not turned on the engines' ice protection. The jet hit the 14th Street Bridge, struck seven cars with people in them, and fell through the ice of the river. Of the 79 people on the plane, 74 died. Four drivers on the bridge died too.

Six people held on to the wreck in water of about 34 degrees. The rescuers who reached the riverbank had no equipment that could reach them. Roger Olian, the boss of the sheet-metal workers at St. Elizabeths Hospital, was the first to jump into the water to try. A U.S. Park Police helicopter arrived at about 4:20 p.m. and pulled most of the survivors out. One passenger, Arland D. Williams Jr., 46, was a bank examiner, a person who checks that banks follow the rules. He was strapped into the wreckage and could not free himself. Twice he passed the rescue line to others. When the helicopter crew came back for him, the wreckage had rolled and he was under the water. The coroner, the official who finds out how people died, found that he was the only passenger who drowned. The bridge span was later renamed for him. The Carnegie Hero Fund gives medals for bravery. It says that its staff could not firmly establish who the sixth person in the water was. The coroner and the renamed bridge name Williams.

A passenger, Priscilla Tirado, was badly hurt and blinded by jet fuel, and she was too weak to grab the line when the helicopter came back to her. Lenny Skutnik, an assistant at the Congressional Budget Office, took off his coat and boots, swam out in short sleeves and pulled her to shore. "Somebody had to go into the water," he told *Time* magazine. News reporters recorded the rescue and broadcast it live.

Investigators of the National Transportation Safety Board, the federal office that looks into crashes, found that the pilots caused the crash. The investigators blamed the pilots' failure to use the engines' ice protection and the pilots' decision to take off with snow or ice on the wings. The captain did not listen when the first officer told him the engine readings looked wrong. He did not stop the takeoff while there was still room on the runway. Both pilots died in the crash.

<a id="story-melvin-windsor"></a>

#### Melvin Windsor

> **Who:** A U.S. Park Police officer who stood on a helicopter's skid over the frozen Potomac River to pull a survivor out.
>
> **When and where:** Washington, D.C., January 13, 1982.

Melvin E. "Gene" Windsor, 41, pulled the last survivor of Air Florida Flight 90 out of the Potomac while standing on the skid of a flying helicopter with no safety line. A skid is one of the long metal bars a helicopter lands on. Windsor was born in Washington, D.C., in 1940 and grew up in Rockville, Maryland. He had managed a carpet store, among other jobs, before he joined the Park Police in 1971. By 1982 he was a rescue technician.

He flew with the chief pilot, Donald W. Usher, 31. Earlier that day Usher had decided that no routine flights would go up. At about 4:09 p.m. a radio call came in. They took off at 4:16 and reached the river at about 4:20. Usher steered by watching the highway below through the windows in the helicopter's floor.

Six people were holding on to the wreck, in water up to their shoulders and necks. Windsor dropped life jackets and lines to them while Usher flew so low that the skids went under the water.

The last survivor out of the water was Patricia Felch. She had been in the river for 30 minutes. Windsor unbuckled his seat belt and stepped out onto the right skid, which was under the water. He grabbed her with one arm and held the back of her head with the other.

They went back for the man who had passed the line to others, and could not find him. "In a mass casualty, you'll find people like him, but I've never seen one with that commitment," Windsor told *Time*. A mass casualty is an event in which many people are hurt or killed at once. Windsor, Usher, Skutnik and Olian each received the Carnegie Medal for bravery. Windsor served 22 years with the Park Police. He died on August 24, 2014, at 74.

#### 1989: Hurricane Hugo and the Loma Prieta earthquake

Hurricane Hugo hit two U.S. territories before it reached the mainland in September 1989. On St. Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands, it damaged more than 90 percent of the buildings and killed three people. In Puerto Rico it killed eight people and left nearly 28,000 without homes. On September 22 it came ashore on Sullivan's Island, South Carolina. The storm surge reached 20.2 feet near McClellanville, and 13 people died in South Carolina.

At 5:04 p.m. on October 17, 1989, an earthquake of magnitude 6.9 struck about 10 miles northeast of Santa Cruz, California, and killed 63 people. A World Series baseball game was about to begin at Candlestick Park in San Francisco. In Oakland, the upper deck of the Cypress Street Viaduct fell onto the lower deck, and 42 people were crushed to death in their cars. The viaduct was a two-level section of the Nimitz Freeway, a highway raised above the ground. A section of the San Francisco-Oakland Bay Bridge also fell, and a 23-year-old woman, Anamafi Moala, died there.

#### Hurricane Andrew, August 24, 1992

Hurricane Andrew struck Florida on August 24, 1992, and destroyed more than 63,500 houses. Help from the national government was slow to come. Andrew came ashore at Homestead with winds as high as 165 miles an hour. It damaged more than 124,000 other houses and wrecked 99 percent of the mobile homes in Homestead.
