It killed 44 people in Florida. Fifteen died in the storm itself and 29 from its effects afterward. In all, the storm left 65 people dead.

Three days after the storm, Dade County's emergency management director, Kate Hale, went on national television. "Where in the hell is the cavalry on this one?" she asked. "They keep saying we're going to get supplies. For God's sake, where are they?" The cavalry were soldiers on horseback, and she meant the rescuers and supplies that had not come. Many people criticized FEMA for the slow start. Some critics blamed Florida's governor, Lawton Chiles, instead. FEMA officials believed they could not act until he sent a formal request for federal help. By that account, he waited five days to send it.

Engineers who surveyed the damaged roofs found that concrete roof tiles had been glued to felt paper and shingles stapled on the wrong way. A single building code for the whole state of Florida was set up in 1998, and it took effect in 2002.

#### Northridge, 1994, and the Chicago heat wave, 1995

At 4:30 a.m. on January 17, 1994, the Northridge earthquake, magnitude 6.7, struck Los Angeles. The official count of the dead is 57, and other counts run from 60 to 72. Sixteen people died when the Northridge Meadows apartment building collapsed. Buildings with parking on the bottom floor held up poorly in the shaking.

A heat wave in Chicago in mid-July 1995 killed 739 more people in one week than usually die in a week. Most of the dead were poor, old people. Many had no air conditioning, or had it and could not afford to run it. Many kept their windows shut and would not sleep outside, because they were afraid of crime. Black residents were more likely to die than white residents.

City officials did not issue a heat emergency warning until the last day of the heat wave. The records do not say who made that choice. Few people used the city's five cooling centers. A medical examiner is a doctor who examines the dead to find out how they died. The morgue run by the medical examiner, Edmund Donoghue, could hold 300 bodies, and it filled. Refrigerated trucks were parked outside to hold the rest. Donoghue said later that his office was not allowed to hold press conferences, and that Mayor Richard M. Daley was not told until the weekend. A later study counted 692 deaths above normal over the summer. In August, 41 victims whose bodies no one claimed were buried together in one grave in Homewood, Illinois.

### 2000 to Today

In three disasters after 2000, Hurricane Katrina, Hurricane Maria and the Eaton Fire, many of the dead were old or sick. Hurricane Katrina killed 1,392 people in 2005, by the National Hurricane Center's count as corrected in 2023. Most of them died in Louisiana, many of them in New Orleans, where floodwalls broke. Investigators found that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers was responsible for those floodwalls. After Hurricane Maria struck Puerto Rico in 2017, officials of the island's government counted 64 dead. In 2018 they raised the official count to 2,975, after a study of deaths in the months after the storm. Power lines owned by utility companies started deadly fires in California in 2018 and 2025 and in Hawaii in 2023.

#### September 11, 2001, and the illnesses afterward

On September 11, 2001, 343 members of the New York City Fire Department died in the attacks on the World Trade Center, and by 2026 more of its members had died from breathing the dust of the ruins. That morning 19 hijackers from the group al-Qaeda took over four passenger jets by force. They flew two into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center in New York City and one into the Pentagon, near Washington, D.C. On the fourth plane, United Airlines Flight 93, passengers and crew fought back, and it crashed into a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. The attacks killed 2,977 people, not counting the 19 attackers. Seventy-one police and other law officers also died in New York.

For months afterward, firefighters, police officers, construction workers and volunteers dug through the ruins. They breathed dust of crushed concrete, glass fibers, asbestos, lead and mercury. Asbestos is a mineral whose tiny fibers lodge in the lungs and can cause cancer years later. Fires in the ruins burned for three months. Many of the workers later got cancer or lung disease. In September 2026 leaders of the Fire Department reported that 453 more of its members had died of illnesses tied to the dust. That is more than the 343 it lost on the day of the attacks.

In December 2010 members of Congress passed the James Zadroga 9/11 Health and Compensation Act. President Barack Obama signed it on January 2, 2011. It set up the World Trade Center Health Program, which gives medical checkups and treatment to responders and survivors with illnesses tied to the attacks. Members of Congress renewed it in December 2015.

#### Hurricane Katrina, August 29, 2005

Most of the people Hurricane Katrina killed died in Louisiana, where New Orleans flooded after its floodwalls broke. On August 28, 2005, Mayor Ray Nagin ordered the first mandatory evacuation in the city's history, meaning everyone was ordered to leave. Governor Kathleen Blanco opened all lanes of the highways to traffic leaving the city, and about one million people left. Between 100,000 and 150,000 people stayed in the city. City officials opened the Superdome stadium as a "refuge of last resort," a place to go when there was nowhere else.

Katrina came ashore on August 29. The levees and floodwalls broke in more than 50 places, and water covered 80 percent of the city. In the Lower Ninth Ward, a neighborhood where most homeowners were Black, the water was more than 10 feet deep. Members of Congress had put the Corps of Engineers in charge of the city's flood protection in a law of 1965. Investigators found that the Corps was responsible for the floodwalls that broke, and that the flood protection system the national government built had engineering flaws. Judges of a federal appeals court later ruled that, under a law of 1928, the Corps could not be made to pay for the damage.

In 2023 scientists at the National Hurricane Center lowered their count of the dead from 1,833 to 1,392, after new studies. Other studies found that most of the dead in New Orleans were old people who lived near the broken levees, in the Lower Ninth Ward and Lakeview neighborhoods. Coast Guard crews rescued more than 33,500 of the roughly 60,000 people stranded in the city. People waited for days at the Convention Center, which had no food, water or medical help. Early news reports of mass crime at the Superdome later turned out to be false or exaggerated. Federal officials did not begin to act in earnest to help the people at the Convention Center until September 2. Michael Brown, the head of FEMA, lost charge of the relief work to Vice Admiral Thad Allen and resigned on September 12.

Some police officers turned their guns on survivors. On September 1, police from the city of Gretna and from the Crescent City Connection bridge police, with deputies of the Jefferson Parish sheriff, blocked the bridge over the Mississippi River. They turned back people walking out of New Orleans at gunpoint. Gretna's police chief, Arthur Lawson, made that decision with the sheriff's office and the bridge police. On September 4, New Orleans police officers shot six unarmed Black people on the Danziger Bridge. They killed James Brissette, 17, and Ronald Madison, 40, a man with a mental disability. Madison was shot seven times, five times in the back. Among the officers were Kenneth Bowen, Robert Gisevius, Anthony Villavaso and Robert Faulcon. Police officers then tried to cover up the killings. In 2016 five former officers pleaded guilty and were sentenced to between 3 and 12 years in prison.

At Memorial Medical Center, 45 bodies were found after the storm. In July 2006, the office of Charles Foti, Louisiana's attorney general and top lawyer, finished an investigation of nearly a year. A judge then ordered the arrest of a doctor, Anna Pou, and two nurses, Lori Budo and Cheri Landry, for murder, which Louisiana law called second degree murder. They were accused of giving deadly doses of morphine and midazolam to four patients: Emmett Everett Sr., 61, Hollis Alford, 66, Ireatha Watson, 89, and Rose Savoie, 90. Morphine is a strong painkiller, and midazolam is a drug that makes people calm and sleepy. In large doses, both slow and then stop a person's breathing. In 2007 a grand jury refused to charge any of the three. The state later paid Pou's legal bills of more than 450,000 dollars.

<a id="story-herbert-freeman-jr"></a>

#### Herbert Freeman Jr.

> **Who:** A New Orleans man who took his 91-year-old mother, Ethel Freeman, out of their flooded home by boat, then stayed beside her body outside the Convention Center after she died waiting for help.
>
> **When and where:** New Orleans, August 31 to early September 2005.

Herbert Freeman Jr. rescued his mother from their flooded house, and she died the next day outside the New Orleans Convention Center, where police had sent them to wait for a bus. Ethel Mayo Freeman was 91. She had a pacemaker for her heart and a feeding tube, and she used a wheelchair. She was often sick, and she decided to stay home when Katrina came.

The floodwater filled her house several feet deep. On August 31, Herbert, 58, borrowed a friend's boat. He put his mother in her wheelchair, lifted her into the boat and took her to dry ground. New Orleans police officers there sent them to the Convention Center. Herbert told officers his mother needed a doctor. They told him a bus would come.

The Convention Center had no food, no water, no medical help and no way out. "She was calling out for a doctor or a nurse, but there was nothing there," Herbert said. Ethel Freeman died at the Convention Center on September 1. Her body stayed outside for days, slumped in the chair and covered with a poncho. Pictures of it were shown on national television.

Herbert watched over his mother's body for nearly four days, until he was ordered onto a bus. The NBC News report of his story does not say who gave the order. Before he left, he put a note with his name and phone number in her pocket. It took him seven weeks to find her body, at a morgue in St. Gabriel, Louisiana. Her funeral was held in New Orleans in November 2005.

He and the families of two other people who died sued the national government. In 2009 federal appeals judges ruled that, under the Stafford Act, the government could not be sued over decisions like these in a disaster, and they threw out the case.

#### Hurricane Maria in Puerto Rico, September 20, 2017

Hurricane Maria left all 3.4 million people in Puerto Rico without electricity on September 20, 2017, and thousands died in the months that followed. Puerto Rico is a U.S. territory, and its people are U.S. citizens. Maria struck two weeks after Hurricane Irma crossed the region. It caused the worst blackout in U.S. history. Some customers did not get their power back until August 2018, 11 months later.

After Irma, FEMA officials had shipped many of the supplies they kept in Puerto Rico to the U.S. Virgin Islands. After Maria, they admitted to failures in moving supplies, too few staff and poor communication. On September 29, 2017, the mayor of San Juan, Carmen Yulín Cruz, said of the national government's relief work: "We are dying and you are killing us with the inefficiency." On October 3, President Donald Trump compared the count of dead at that time, 16, with "a real catastrophe like Katrina."

Officials and researchers gave very different counts of the dead. Officials of Governor Ricardo Rosselló's government counted 64 dead for months. Researchers found that many more people than usual died in the months after the storm. People who needed dialysis could not reach emergency care for long stretches of time. Dialysis is a treatment that cleans the blood of people whose kidneys have failed. In 2018 researchers at Harvard University estimated 4,645 extra deaths from September to December 2017. Their range was very wide, from 793 to 8,498. Researchers at George Washington University estimated between 2,658 and 3,290 extra deaths from September 2017 to February 2018. On August 28, 2018, Rosselló's officials accepted their study and raised the official count to 2,975. On September 13, 2018, Trump wrote on Twitter that "3000 people did not die" and blamed Democrats for the number. He gave no evidence.

<a id="story-jesse-vazquez"></a>

#### Jesse Vazquez

> **Who:** A retired veteran in Bayamón, Puerto Rico, who lived for months without electricity after Hurricane Maria with his 89-year-old mother, Mercedes Mercado.
>
> **When and where:** Calle Alameda, Bayamón, Puerto Rico, September to December 2017.

Jesse Vazquez and his mother, Mercedes Mercado, went 96 days without electricity after Hurricane Maria. Maria cut the power to their house on Calle Alameda in Bayamón on September 20, 2017. For weeks the family ran electric fans and charged their phones from the battery of Jesse's car.

A small generator cost about 600 dollars on sale, more than Jesse could afford. In October his son, also named Jesse, and his daughter, Megan, flew in from New York to bring him a generator. "It's basically cheaper to buy a flight, get a generator and bring it down here," his son said. Running it five hours a day took about 80 dollars of gasoline a month. Exhaust from a neighbor's generator blew into the family's living room. Megan said they needed a carbon monoxide detector. Carbon monoxide is a poison gas in engine exhaust that has no smell.

By Christmas the house had been without power for 96 days. Jesse and his mother used the generator to run the refrigerator, and fans at night so they could sleep. A FEMA inspector told Jesse he could not get help to fix his damaged roof. "It's kind of humiliating," he said. With his son's help he bought four solar panels. He and his mother decided to stay in Puerto Rico.

#### Floods: Harvey, 2017, Helene, 2024, and the Texas Hill Country, 2025

Hurricane Harvey struck Texas in late August 2017 and dropped more rain than any other hurricane or tropical storm in U.S. records. Scientists at the National Hurricane Center recorded 60.58 inches near Nederland, Texas. Rescuers made more than 17,000 rescues. Their report records at least 68 people killed by the storm's direct effects in Texas and about 35 more by causes such as electric shock, car crashes and being cut off from medical care.

Hurricane Helene came ashore in Florida, near Perry, late on September 26, 2024. The next day its rain fell on North Carolina and Tennessee. Busick, North Carolina, got 30.78 inches of rain, and the rain set off more than 2,000 landslides. Scientists at the National Hurricane Center count at least 250 dead in the United States, 107 of them in North Carolina.

In Erwin, Tennessee, six people died at the Impact Plastics factory as the Nolichucky River rose on September 27. The flood swept 11 people away, and five were rescued. A worker who survived and the families of the dead spoke out. They said the workers were not told they could leave until floodwater had covered the road to the plant and the power had gone out. Five employees and a contractor who cleaned the offices were killed. In April 2025 inspectors of Tennessee's workplace safety agency found that the deaths were not work-related. They issued no citations, which are official notices that a company broke a safety rule. In July 2025, after a review by the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation, District Attorney General Steven Finney filed no charges against the company's president, Gerald O'Connor. The investigators said they found no evidence that workers were told they could not leave or that they would be fired for leaving, and that the workers had a little more than an hour to get out. The family of Johnny Peterson, one of the dead, sued the company.

Early on July 4, 2025, as much as 20 inches of rain fell on the Texas Hill Country, and the Guadalupe River rose about 26 feet in 45 minutes. The flood killed 136 people, 117 of them in Kerr County, by counts reported in July 2026. At Camp Mystic, a Christian summer camp for girls, 25 campers, two counselors, Chloe Childress and Katherine Ferruzzo, and the camp's owner and director, Dick Eastland, died. The first flash flood warning for Kerr County went out at 1:14 a.m. At 4:03 a.m. a flash flood emergency, a more urgent alert, told people in the towns of Hunt and Ingram to "seek higher ground now!"

Kerr County had no warning system built just for floods. In 2016 the county sheriff had asked for one, with sirens. County Commissioner H. A. "Buster" Baldwin said, "I think this whole thing is a little extravagant for Kerr County, with sirens and such." After appeals from the camp, FEMA officials took 15 of its buildings on the Guadalupe River off the federal map of land likely to flood in 2013. They took 15 buildings at a newer camp site off the map in 2019 and 2020, the Associated Press reported. On June 18, 2026, members of the Texas Senate and House investigating committees released a report. The lawmakers found that the camp had no written emergency plans, which state rules required. They also found that the camp's leaders did not move the campers out in time even though they had chances to. In September 2025, at an extra meeting called a special session, Texas lawmakers had passed new camp safety laws, among them the Heaven's 27 Camp Safety Act. In the week before July 18, 2026, officials used three of Kerr County's six new sirens, an official of the Upper Guadalupe River Authority said.

#### Fires started by power lines: Paradise, 2018, Lahaina, 2023, and Los Angeles, 2025

On the morning of November 8, 2018, a single metal hook broke on a power line tower owned by Pacific Gas and Electric, called PG&E. The tower was poorly maintained. The line started a fire. The tower was part of a line built in the early 1900s. The Camp Fire burned through the town of Paradise, California. It killed 85 people and destroyed more than 18,000 buildings. On June 16, 2020, the company pleaded guilty in court to 84 counts of involuntary manslaughter, the crime of killing people through carelessness.

On August 8, 2023, a wildfire destroyed the town of Lahaina on the island of Maui, Hawaii, and killed 102 people. That is the most people killed in a U.S. wildfire since 1918. High winds knocked down power lines of Hawaiian Electric, and the lines started a fire that morning. Maui firefighters declared that fire under control and left. Less than an hour later, embers from it started the fire again. Firefighters lost water pressure in the hydrants. Many people died in their cars. Some jumped into the ocean to escape the flames.

Maui has more than 80 outdoor warning sirens, and none of them sounded. Herman Andaya, the head of the Maui County Emergency Management Agency, said the sirens would have sent people toward the mountains and into the fire. He resigned the next day. In an October 2024 report, federal fire investigators and the Maui Fire Department called the fire accidental and blamed no person or company. Lahaina had been the capital of the Kingdom of Hawaii for 35 years. Many Native Hawaiian families could afford to live there only because they had inherited homes that were already paid for. Under a settlement of the survivors' lawsuits, Hawaiian Electric, Maui County and others agreed to pay 4 billion dollars. As of August 2026, none of that money had been paid, because of a court fight over the lawyers' fees, the *Honolulu Star-Advertiser* reported.

In January 2025, fires pushed by winds of up to 100 miles an hour burned parts of Los Angeles. They killed at least 31 people and destroyed more than 18,000 homes and other buildings. The Eaton Fire in Altadena killed 19 people. In August 2026 Los Angeles County and state fire investigators reported that it started from electric sparks on an unused Southern California Edison tower. Seventeen of the 19 died in west Altadena, a neighborhood with a long history as a Black community. Reviewers from the firm Citygate Associates found in May 2026 that county officials' orders to leave reached west Altadena hours after the fire turned toward it. The records do not name the officials who made those decisions. The dead had an average age of 77. California's attorney general, Rob Bonta, opened an investigation into whether race, age or disability affected how officials warned people.

The Palisades Fire killed 12 people. In October 2025 Jonathan Rinderknecht, 29, was arrested and charged with starting it. Prosecutors say he set a small fire on January 1, and that strong winds rekindled it, or started it burning again, on January 7 as the Palisades Fire. Firefighters had thought the January 1 fire was out. A Los Angeles Fire Department battalion commander ordered crews to leave that site, although they reported that the ground was still burning slowly. Rinderknecht's federal trial ended on June 26, 2026, when the jury could not agree. Ten jurors voted not guilty and two voted guilty. Prosecutors then charged him again with two charges of arson, the crime of setting a fire on purpose, and dropped a third charge. On August 19, 2026, he pleaded not guilty. A judge set a last hearing before trial for October 21 and his second trial for November 2, 2026. As of October 3, 2026, he had not been convicted of any crime.

#### Cold, a collapse and FEMA's future: 2021 to 2026

In February 2021 a winter storm struck Texas, and more than 4.5 million homes and businesses lost power, some of them for days. Officials of the Texas Department of State Health Services counted 246 deaths from the storm. Almost two-thirds of the dead died of hypothermia, which means the body gets so cold that it stops working. Some estimates run as high as 702 deaths. Cristian Pavón Pineda, 11, died of carbon monoxide poisoning in his family's mobile home in Conroe, Texas. The home had no power.

At 1:22 a.m. on June 24, 2021, part of Champlain Towers South, a 12-story apartment building in Surfside, Florida, fell down and killed 98 people. Each family owned its own apartment. For years, water had seeped into the concrete and steel supports of the parking garage under the pool deck, and the steel had rusted. In 2018 engineers of the firm Morabito Consultants reported the damage. They warned that if the waterproofing was not replaced soon, the damage to the concrete would spread fast. On April 9, 2021, Jean Wodnicki, the president of the owners' board, wrote to the residents that "the concrete deterioration is accelerating," meaning the concrete was breaking down faster. A 15-million-dollar repair had been approved, but the main work had not started.

President Trump called for getting rid of FEMA. On February 17, 2025, officials of the Trump administration fired more than 200 FEMA workers. On March 24, 2025, Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said she would move to eliminate FEMA. The acting head of FEMA, Cameron Hamilton, told members of Congress: "I do not believe it is in the best interest of the American people to eliminate the Federal Emergency Management Agency." He was removed from his job the next day. In August 2025 more than 180 current and former FEMA workers signed a public statement of protest they called the "Katrina Declaration." On May 7, 2026, a review council the president had set up approved a report with ten recommendations. On September 15, 2026, members of a House committee voted for one bill to change FEMA, the Post-Disaster Protection Act. In late September 2026, FEMA still existed, and members of Congress were still debating its future.

<a id="ch-drugs-alcohol"></a>

## Chapter 28: Drugs and Alcohol

### Before 1500

For thousands of years before 1500, people in this land used plants that change how the body and the mind feel. The oldest one found so far is tobacco. Many of the uses in the records were part of prayer and ceremony. In later accounts, Native people offered tobacco in prayer, men in the Southeast drank Black Drink to make themselves pure, and the O'odham drank cactus wine at a rain ceremony. The Apache drank their corn beer mostly at everyday social times.

Before Europeans came, people made beer and wine mainly in the Southwest, and people in other parts of the land used alcohol here and there. Nobody in this land made distilled liquor, such as rum or whiskey. To distill a drink, people heat it and catch the steam, which cools into a liquor stronger than beer or wine.

#### Tobacco for prayer

The oldest known sign of people using tobacco in the Americas is about 12,300 years old. Scientists found burned tobacco in a hearth, a place where people made a fire, at the Wishbone site, in the desert of western North America. It is 9,000 years older than any earlier evidence of tobacco use. The scientists first published the find online in October 2021. How the people at the hearth used the tobacco is not known.

A pipe found in central Washington State is about 1,430 years old. Chemists found nicotine inside it. Nicotine is the drug in tobacco. The pipe also held traces of a wild tobacco that grows here, mixed with a plant called smooth sumac.

Today the "Keep It Sacred" program of the Inter-Tribal Council of Michigan describes tobacco used as an offering, which it calls traditional tobacco. It is grown or gathered for ceremony or for medicine, and it is the plant known by its Latin name, *Nicotiana rustica*. People offer it to the Creator, or to another person, place or being. They burn it in a fire or smoke it in a pipe. In the program's words, the smoke carries "thoughts and prayers to the spirit world." The smoke is generally not breathed into the lungs.

The program's writers state that traditional tobacco used in this way is not linked to addiction or to harm to health. Addiction means that a person's body and mind come to need a drug, so that stopping is very hard. The writers separate traditional tobacco from commercial tobacco, the kind sold in stores. The ways people used tobacco differed from one nation to another.

#### Black Drink, cacao, peyote and datura

Black Drink was a tea made from the leaves of yaupon holly or dahoon holly, two kinds of holly bush. It contains caffeine, the drug in coffee that keeps people awake. Chemists found traces of it inside beaker cups from Cahokia, in what is now Illinois, dated from 1050 to 1250. These hollies grow far to the south of Cahokia, so people carried the leaves north. Records from later centuries describe men in the Southeast drinking Black Drink in a ceremony to make themselves pure.

Cacao is the bean that chocolate is made from. It grows in Mexico and Central America. At Pueblo Bonito, in Chaco Canyon in New Mexico, jars from about 1000 to 1125 held traces of a cacao drink. The beans came north by trade. It is the first known use of cacao drinks north of the Mexican border. Drinks made from cacao or holly turn up at 18 sites in the Southwest and northern Mexico, from about 750 to 1400.

Peyote is a small cactus. Its top holds mescaline, a drug that causes visions. Two dried peyote tops kept at the Witte Museum in San Antonio are about 5,700 years old. They were probably found in Shumla Cave, on the Rio Grande in Texas. When chemists tested them, they still held mescaline. The chemists wrote that Native North Americans knew what peyote does as long as 5,700 years ago.

Datura is a flowering plant that holds two drugs, scopolamine and atropine. These drugs cause hallucinations, which means seeing and hearing things that are not there. In Pinwheel Cave in California, people chewed wads of datura and pressed them into the painted ceiling. Records from later times show Native Californians using datura to enter a trance, a state like a dream while awake. People used the cave from before 1500 into the years after Europeans arrived, so the wads have no exact date.

#### Beer and wine in the Southwest

In 1996 Patrick J. Abbott, a doctor, wrote a study of how Native nations used alcohol before Europeans came. He found that alcohol was used mainly by nations in the Southwest, with scattered use elsewhere. The drinks were beer and wine. Most Native people first met alcohol when Europeans brought it in the 1500s and 1600s.

The Akimel O'odham and the Tohono O'odham made wine from a cactus. Older books list them as the Pima and the Papago. Each late summer the women gathered the red fruit of the saguaro cactus. They made most of it into jam and the last of the harvest into wine. People drank the wine at the rain ceremony held at their New Year, late in the summer. When Abbott wrote in 1996, many Tohono O'odham villages still held that ceremony.

The Apache made a corn beer called tiswin, which they learned to make from peoples of northern Mexico. People drank it mostly in everyday dealings with one another, and only sometimes in ceremony. The Apache reached the Southwest sometime between 1000 and 1550. For that reason, nobody knows whether they made tiswin here before 1500.

### The 1500s

In the 1500s Europeans learned to use tobacco from the peoples of the Americas and carried it home. In 1560 a French official sent tobacco seeds to the queen of France with a letter about its uses as a medicine, and the next year he showed her how to sniff the powdered leaves for headaches. Spanish colonists also brought wine with them to Florida.

Most Native people in this land first met alcohol when Europeans arrived, in the 1500s and 1600s. The historian Peter C. Mancall writes that some Europeans surely offered it as a gift when they met Native people, though no record from this century names a case. A regular trade in alcohol with Native nations did not begin until about 1650.

#### Tobacco reaches Europe

Jean Nicot was the French ambassador to Portugal, the official who spoke for the king of France there. In 1560 he sent tobacco seeds to Queen Catherine de Médicis of France. With them he sent a letter about the plant's uses as a medicine. In 1561 he gave her tobacco leaves and showed her how to grind them into a powder to sniff for headaches. The powder then caught on among the people around the French king and queen, who sniffed it too.

The word nicotine comes from Nicot's name. In 1753 the Swedish scientist Carl Linnaeus named the tobacco plants *Nicotiana*, also after Nicot.

Tobacco reached England in 1565, perhaps brought from Florida by Sir John Hawkins. By 1588 English men and women of high rank were using it, and so were some well-trained doctors.

<a id="story-thomas-hariot-drugs-alcohol"></a>

#### Thomas Hariot

> **Who:** An English mathematician who smoked tobacco the Algonquian way at Roanoke and wrote down how the Algonquian people used it.
>
> **When and where:** Roanoke Island, in what is now North Carolina, 1585 to 1586. London until his death in 1621.

Thomas Hariot and the other English at Roanoke smoked tobacco the way the Algonquian people of the Outer Banks did. In a book printed in 1588, he described how the Algonquian people used the plant.

Hariot was born in about 1560. He studied mathematics and the stars. In 1585 he sailed to Roanoke Island with a group of English ships and men sent to start a colony. Most of the colonists were soldiers. Hariot and the artist John White were the best-known of the few who were not. The island was the land of the Roanoke, Secotan and Croatoan peoples. Their leading werowance, or chief, was Wingina. Wingina let the English build a fort on the north end of the island. Hariot learned the Algonquian language from two Native men of the region, Manteo and Wanchese.

In that book, *A Briefe and True Report of the New Found Land of Virginia*, he described a plant the people called uppowoc. The people planted it in plots of its own, dried the leaves and ground them to powder, and drew the smoke through clay pipes. In their belief, the smoke opened the passages of the body and kept them healthy. As an offering, they threw the powder into sacred fires, and onto the water in storms and after escaping a danger.

Hariot wrote that the English "vsed to suck it after their maner" while they were on the island. In today's words, they smoked it the way the Algonquian people did. They went on smoking it after they came home.

On 1 June 1586, men under the English commander Ralph Lane attacked Wingina's village. They shot Wingina, chased him down, and an Irishman named Edward Nugent cut off his head. A week later the English sailed home.

Hariot died in London on 2 July 1621, of cancer of the nose. The writers of Encyclopedia Virginia state that the cancer was "probably caused by heavy tobacco use."

#### Spanish wine in Florida

On 8 September 1565, Pedro Menéndez de Avilés and his Spanish colonists founded St. Augustine in Florida. They built it at Seloy, a town of the Timucua people. Historians at the Florida Museum of Natural History write that wine and olive oil were perhaps even more important to the Spanish than wheat and beef. Both came by ship in big Spanish storage jars called olive jars. The museum's historians write that the Spanish soon turned to the Timucua for food, cooking pots and wives. Their account does not say whether the Timucua women chose these marriages.

The historian Peter C. Mancall writes that some Europeans surely offered alcohol to Native people when they first met, but that the real trade in alcohol did not begin until about 1650. No record from the 1500s describes the Spanish trading wine to Native nations as a regular business.

### The 1600s

The first drinks English colonists made in the 1600s were cider and beer. They believed alcohol kept the body warm and strong. Colony leaders licensed taverns and punished people who got drunk with fines, shackles, the stocks and public shame. In Virginia, planters grew tobacco to sell in England, and the smoking habit spread.

From about 1650, English traders sold rum and French traders sold brandy to Native nations in exchange for furs. Colony leaders passed laws against these sales, and traders kept breaking them.

#### Beer, cider and bad water

The first drinks the colonists made were cider and beer. They brewed beer from corn, wheat, oats, persimmons and green cornstalks. They tried to grow grapes for wine, but the vines they brought from Europe died of American pests and diseases.

Colonists believed that alcohol warmed the body, helped digestion and made people strong. The land here had plenty of clean water, but some colonists drank from dirty sources and got sick. At Jamestown, George Percy wrote that the settlers drank river water that was salty at high tide and "full of slime and filth" at low tide. He called it "the destruction of many of our men." In Europe, where rivers were often dirty, people drank alcohol in place of water, and the colonists kept that habit.

In 1622 officials of the Virginia Company of London wrote to Governor Francis Wyatt. They complained that the colonists' drinking was harming the colony.

#### Laws about drinking

In 1619 the members of Virginia's first General Assembly, the colony's first lawmaking body, passed a law against drunkenness. The first time a man was found drunk, the minister scolded him in private. The second time, the minister scolded him in public. The third time, he had to lie in bolts for 12 hours. Bolts were iron shackles. He lay in them in the house of an officer called the provost marshal, and he had to pay the marshal's fees. If he still kept drinking, the governor and his council, the men who advised him, could give him whatever harsh punishment they chose.

In Massachusetts, the colony's lawmakers passed a set of drinking laws between 1633 and 1647. Nobody could run a tavern without a license from the county court. A tavern keeper could not serve one person more than half a pint of wine at a time. Nobody could sit drinking for more than half an hour, or stay after nine at night.

A person found drunk in Massachusetts paid a fine of 10 shillings. English money was counted in pounds, shillings and pence. Twelve pence made a shilling, and 20 shillings made a pound. The law defined drunk as unable to think clearly, which showed in the way the person talked or moved. The law ordered that a person who could not pay the fine be jailed, or be set in the stocks for up to three hours. The stocks were a wooden frame that locked a person's ankles while the person sat in a public place.

The lawmakers also set prices. In 1634 an innkeeper in Boston could charge sixpence for a meal and a penny for a quart of beer. If he charged more, he paid a fine of 10 shillings. A traveller named John Josselyn reported that a constable, a town officer who kept order, would stop a stranger in a Boston tavern from ordering more drink than the constable thought right.

<a id="story-samuel-cole-drugs-alcohol"></a>

#### Samuel Cole

> **Who:** A maker of sugar-coated sweets who kept the earliest tavern in Boston known to have had a license.
>
> **When and where:** Boston, in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, 1634 to 1638.

Samuel Cole kept the earliest tavern in Boston known to have had a license. The historian Samuel Adams Drake wrote a book on Boston's taverns, first printed in 1886. Its enlarged edition of 1917 dates the opening to 4 March 1634. A tavern was then called an ordinary.

Cole was a comfit-maker, a maker of sugar-coated sweets. He came to Boston in 1630, in the fleet of ships that brought Governor John Winthrop. His ordinary stood on Washington Street. The house had a brew-house, a building for making beer.

In 1636 the English and the Narragansett people made a peace agreement, and Governor Henry Vane hosted Narragansett leaders in Boston. The Narragansett leader Miantonomi and two sons of the leader Canonicus ate at the governor's house. About twenty other Narragansett men ate their meal at Cole's inn.

In 1638 the colony's judges let Cole sell his house as an inn. He sold it to Robert Sedgwick. Cole died in 1666.

<a id="story-robert-coles-drugs-alcohol"></a>

#### Robert Coles

> **Who:** A colonist whom judges in Massachusetts punished again and again for drunkenness, the last time by making him wear a red letter D.
>
> **When and where:** Roxbury and Agawam, now Ipswich, in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, 1631 to 1634.

Judges in Massachusetts punished Robert Coles for drunkenness four times between 1631 and 1634. The last time, in 1634, the judges ordered him to wear a red letter D around his neck for a year.

Coles was born in England in about 1600. He came to Massachusetts in 1630 with Governor John Winthrop's fleet. In 1631 the colony's judges fined him five marks, about 3 pounds, 6 shillings and 8 pence in English money, for being drunk on the ship *Friendship* and at Winnisimmet, now Chelsea. The *Friendship* was carrying a spiced wine made from honey.

In 1633, at Agawam, he was charged with drunkenness for the third time. The judges fined him 10 pounds. He had been drunk, had encouraged John Shatswell's wife to drink, and had urged her to be unfaithful to her husband. They also made him stand in public with a paper on his back. On it the word drunkard was written in large letters.

In 1634 he was drunk again, at Roxbury. The judges ordered him to wear a D made of red cloth, set on a white background, hanging from his neck over his clothes. He had to wear it for a year, whenever he was among other people. They also took away his right to vote. Governor Winthrop wrote in his journal that Coles, "having been oft punished for drunkenness, was now ordered to wear a red D about his neck for a year." Oft means often.

About two months later he got back his right to vote. The records show no later charge of drunkenness against him. Records of the Roxbury church show that he was later put out of the church.

Coles moved to Providence, a town built on land that Roger Williams got in 1636 from the Narragansett leaders Canonicus and Miantonomi. In 1640 Coles helped write the Providence Combination, a written plan for governing the town. He died in Warwick, Rhode Island, in 1655.

#### Selling alcohol to Native nations

In September 1609, Henry Hudson's ship lay near what is now Albany, in the land of the Mahican people. There Hudson and his mate took some Mahican leaders into the ship's cabin. They gave them "so much Wine and Aqua vitae," a strong liquor like brandy, "that they were all merrie." Robert Juet, who kept a journal on the ship, wrote why. Hudson and the mate wanted to find out whether the leaders were planning "treacherie," a plan to betray them. In the end one of the men got drunk. Juet wrote that this was strange to the Mahican, "for they could not tell how to take it." The next day the people came back with tobacco and beads for Hudson, and a platter of venison.

The historian Peter C. Mancall dates the start of a regular trade in alcohol to about 1650. Some liquor was already being sold earlier: the Dutch order of 1643 states that liquor was sold to Native people "daily." In the regular trade, English traders sold rum to Native nations, and French traders sold brandy, in exchange for furs. Mancall writes that young men who controlled the furs from a season's hunt traded them for liquor, and more families became poor.

Native and colonial witnesses both wrote down what happened when Native people drank the trade liquor. Drinkers fought each other and members of their own families. Some fell into fires or off cliffs, some drowned, and some killed other people. No one counted the deaths.

The leaders of the colonies passed laws against the trade. In New Netherland, the Dutch colony that is now New York, Director General Willem Kieft, the colony's governor, and his council banned selling liquor to Native people on 18 June 1643. Their order said that "large quantities of strong liquors are daily sold to the Indians." The fine was 25 guilders, and a guilder was a Dutch coin. They passed the ban again in 1645. In 1647 the next Director General, Petrus Stuyvesant, and his council passed it a third time. They raised the fine to 500 guilders, plus the cost of any damage. The laws of the colonies name the officials who banned the trade. They rarely name the traders who broke the bans.

Mancall writes that Native people organized against the trade themselves. Some colonists came to believe that Native people were born more likely to become alcoholics, people who cannot stop drinking. Mancall states that no evidence supports that belief.

#### Tobacco and rum

In 1604 King James I of England attacked smoking in *A Counterblaste to Tobacco*. He called it "lothsome to the eye, hatefull to the Nose, harmefull to the braine, dangerous to the Lungs." Lothsome means disgusting. He mocked the English for copying "the barbarous and beastly maners of the wilde, godlesse, and slauish Indians." Maners means manners, the ways people act. Those words show the king's scorn for Native people.

The tobacco that the Powhatan people grew tasted dark and bitter to the English. John Rolfe, a colonist at Jamestown who smoked heavily, got seeds of a milder Spanish tobacco from Trinidad and Caracas. He was growing it by July 1612. In 1617 the colonists shipped 20,000 pounds of it to England. In 1622 they grew 60,000 pounds. After 1622 English planters took over land that the Powhatan had already cleared, to grow more tobacco.

In 1633 Massachusetts officials told constables to report "tobacco takers" as idle people. The lawmakers had canceled their earlier laws against tobacco. In 1638 they wrote that since then smoking was "more abused than before." So they banned smoking near any house, barn, corn or haystack, because a pipe that close might set those things on fire. They also banned smoking outdoors in the streets and fields, except on a journey or at a meal, and in the public rooms of an inn. They passed these rules again in 1647, and that version put the distance from buildings and crops at about 330 feet.

Rum is a strong liquor made from molasses. Molasses is the thick syrup left over when sugar is made from sugarcane. The first known name for rum comes from the island of Barbados, in about 1651. A planter there called it "Kill-Divill" and "a hott hellish and terrible liquor." In the 1600s New England merchants began shipping fish and lumber to the islands of the West Indies. They traded them for molasses and made the molasses into rum at home.

### 1700 to 1750

Between 1700 and 1750, rum was the colonists' favorite strong drink, and it was cheap. In Philadelphia in 1740, a gallon of rum made in the colonies cost 1 shilling 8 pence. People drank in taverns, and they also met there to do the town's business. Colony leaders controlled drinking with tavern licenses and with rules for elections.

In Georgia, the colony's leaders banned strong liquor for seven years, from 1735 to 1742. A Yamacraw leader named Tomochichi had asked them to stop the sale of rum. Nobody counted how much colonists drank in these years. The first estimates come from the 1770s.

#### Rum, molasses and tobacco

Colonial distillers made rum from molasses shipped in from the sugar plantations of the Caribbean. Some of the molasses came in legally, and some was smuggled, which means merchants brought it in secretly without paying the tax on it. In Philadelphia in 1740, a gallon of colonial rum cost 1 shilling 8 pence. A gallon of rum from the Caribbean cost 2 shillings 5 pence.

At the urging of large sugar planters on the British islands in the Caribbean, members of the British Parliament, the lawmakers of Britain, passed the Molasses Act in 1733. It put a tax of sixpence a gallon on molasses from the French islands. Colonial merchants kept smuggling French molasses anyway, much of it from Saint Domingue, now Haiti. The tax should have brought in 25,000 pounds in British money each year. In 1735 British officials collected 259 pounds.

Rum was part of a trade in people. New England ships carried rum to Africa, enslaved Africans to the West Indies, and molasses back to New England. Distillers made an extra-strong rum for this trade, so that ships could carry more of it in less space. When the ships reached Africa, the captains added water to the rum. They traded it for people to sell into slavery.

By 1700, enslaved Africans outnumbered white indentured servants on Virginia's tobacco farms. An indentured servant was a worker bound to work for a master for a set number of years. In 1709 Virginia planters grew 29 million pounds of tobacco, the most the colony ever grew.

#### Drinks for voters

In colonial Virginia, only white men aged 21 or older who owned land could vote. Enslaved people, free Black people, Native people, servants, white men with no land and all women could not vote. Each voter said his choice out loud in front of the crowd. Voters expected the men running for office to give them liquor and food.

In 1705 Virginia's lawmakers passed a law that limited these gifts, called treats. Candidates could give treats before the sheriff read out the notice of an election, and again after the voting. The weeks in between were supposed to be "dry," with no treats. Some candidates got around the rule. They stayed away and had a friend, a servant or even a wife hand out the drinks.

#### The tavern as the town's meeting place

In Boston, men used taverns as meeting places for a lodge, for the colony's lawmakers, and for signing up sailors in wartime. Francis Holmes kept the Bunch of Grapes on King Street, now State Street, from 1712. One traveller called it the best punch house in Boston. Punch was a mixed drink made with liquor. On 30 July 1733, Henry Price, a Boston tailor, organized a grand lodge of Freemasons there. The Freemasons were a society of men who met in lodges, and a grand lodge was a head lodge over the others.

Luke Vardy kept the Royal Exchange tavern. In the winter of 1747, Boston's town-house burned. The colony's lawmakers then finished their meetings at Vardy's.

In July 1728 two young men quarrelled at Vardy's over their cards or their wine. They fought with swords on Boston Common, and one of them killed the other, a man named Woodbridge. The killer's friends put him on a ship that sailed at once. The historian Samuel Adams Drake, who told the story in 1886, does not give the killer's name.

In 1745, during a war between Britain and France, notices posted in Boston stated that sailors who wanted to join a privateer should report to the Widow Gray's Crown Tavern. A privateer was a privately owned ship allowed to attack enemy ships. Women kept several of Boston's taverns. Drake's list includes the Widow Gray, the Widow Anna Swords, a Mrs. Wardwell and a Mrs. Glover.

#### Georgia bans rum, 1735 to 1742

In February 1733 James Oglethorpe and the first colonists of Georgia settled on Yamacraw Bluff, where Savannah stands today. Tomochichi, the leader of a Yamacraw town of about 200 Creek and Yamasee people, gave them the land on the bluff.

Tomochichi saw more of his people drinking heavily. In 1734 he asked Oglethorpe and the Trustees to ban the sale of rum. The Trustees were a board of men who met in London and ran the colony from there. In 1735 the Trustees banned rum and brandy in Georgia, and King George II and his council approved the law. The law described these liquors as "hurtful and pernicious to Man's Body." Pernicious means harmful. The Trustees named an officer to enforce the ban and set fines that grew larger with each offense. Taverns could still sell beer and wine with a license.

Colonists soon accused the officials who ran the ban of being dishonest, and they protested the ban. A group of colonists known as the Malcontents, a word for people who are unhappy and complain, argued that the ban hurt trade. They said Georgia merchants needed rum to trade for timber and other goods, which they then shipped to the British islands in the Caribbean. On 29 September 1742 the Trustees ended the ban and let rum in again for use in the lumber trade. Oglethorpe disagreed with their decision.

Traders from South Carolina kept carrying rum up the Savannah River, against the Trustees' order. In a letter of 1737, Oglethorpe wrote that the Creek had learned drunkenness "from our Traders."

<a id="story-alexander-hamilton-physician-drugs-alcohol"></a>

#### Dr. Alexander Hamilton

> **Who:** A Scottish-born doctor from Annapolis, Maryland, who kept a diary of the taverns and drinking clubs he saw on a long ride north. He is not the Alexander Hamilton who later ran the Treasury.
>
> **When and where:** From Maryland to York, Maine, and back, 30 May to 27 September 1744.

Dr. Alexander Hamilton kept a diary in 1744 that records how people drank in the taverns of the colonies. He rode 1,624 miles, from Maryland to Maine and back.

Hamilton was born near Edinburgh, Scotland, in 1712. In 1738 he moved to Maryland and worked as a doctor in Annapolis. He was very sick in 1743. On 30 May 1744 he set out on horseback, mainly to get his health back. He reached home on 27 September.

On 31 May, at Tradaway's inn in Maryland, he met "a drunken Club" leaving. Most of the men had climbed onto their horses and sat on them crooked. On 5 June, at an inn near Philadelphia, the landlady did all the work because the landlord was drunk. Hamilton wrote that the liquor had taken away "the use of his tongue." The landlord sat without moving in a corner, smoking his pipe.

On 15 June he ate supper in New York with the Hungarian Club at Todd's tavern. After supper the men drank "bumpers," glasses filled to the brim and drunk off at once, at each round. Hamilton did not want to drink and drank only three. He left at ten, "pretty well flushed with my three bumpers." Flushed meant red in the face from the drink. Some of the men, he wrote, thought nothing was finer than being able "to pour down seas of liquor, and remain unconquered, while others sank under the table." He wrote that some members were "very fond of making a stranger drunk."

In Boston he met with a club of doctors at the Sun Tavern. "We drank punch, smoaked tobacco, and talked of sundry physical matters," he wrote. Sundry means various, and physical matters meant medicine. In 1745 he started a club of his own in Annapolis, the Tuesday Club. He died on 11 May 1756.

### 1750 to 1800

By 1770 the colonies had more than 140 rum distilleries, making about 4.8 million gallons of rum a year. Ship captains from Rhode Island carried rum to Africa and traded it for African people to sell into slavery. After the Revolution, Americans switched from rum to whiskey made from their own corn and rye.

From the 1750s, Native leaders asked colonists to stop selling them liquor. The Philadelphia doctor Benjamin Rush argued in 1785 that heavy drinking was a disease. Members of Congress voted a tax on whiskey in 1791. Three years later armed men in western Pennsylvania burned a tax inspector's house. President George Washington called up nearly 13,000 militiamen, part-time citizen soldiers, against them. In 1799 Handsome Lake, a Seneca religious leader, stopped drinking and preached against it.

#### How much people drank

Nobody measured how much colonists drank before the 1770s. The estimates made since then each measure something different. The writer Ed Crews, in the *Colonial Williamsburg Journal*, reports an estimate that in the 1770s the average grown man may have drunk as much as three pints a week. The writer Ian Williams gives 3.7 gallons of rum a year for each colonist by the time of the Revolution. The historian Peter C. Mancall cites an estimate of perhaps seven shots of liquor a day by 1770.

In 1790, government figures showed that the average American over the age of 15 drank 34 gallons of beer and cider, 5 gallons of liquor and 1 gallon of wine.

People believed alcohol was good for the body. They took whiskey for stomach pain and for a sore throat. They took hot brandy punch for cholera, a disease that causes severe diarrhea. Pregnant women and women in labor drank a shot of liquor to ease the pain. Benjamin Franklin collected more than 200 words that meant drunk.

#### Rum and the slave trade

By 1764 Rhode Island had about 30 rum distilleries, 22 of them in the town of Newport. Rhode Island merchants traded the rum on the coast of West Africa for African people to enslave. In the hundred years before 1807, Rhode Islanders made at least 1,000 voyages to buy and carry enslaved people. They carried more than 100,000 Africans into slavery.

In 1764 the brothers Nicholas, John, Joseph and Moses Brown of Providence sent their ship *Sally* to West Africa. Its captain was Esek Hopkins. The ship carried 17,274 gallons of rum to trade, along with chains, shackles and guns. Hopkins used the rum to buy 196 people. At least 109 of them died. According to Brown University's report on the voyage, 19 died before the ship left Africa, several of them children. One of the 19 was a woman who hanged herself below deck. Four more, a woman and three children, died in the first week at sea. When the captives rose up against the crew at sea, Hopkins's men fired on them. The ship's account book records that the crew "Destroyed 8," which means they killed eight people. After that, the account book says, "Some Drowned themselves Some Starved and others Sickened & Dyed." In all, 68 people died during the crossing. Twenty more died in the days after the ship reached the West Indies, and one more died on the way to the Brown brothers in Providence. The report's stage counts of 19, 68 and 20 add up to 107, but the report gives the total at that point as 108. With the death on the way to Providence, it gives 109 in all.

The same year, members of the British Parliament cut the tax on foreign molasses to threepence a gallon, in a law called the Sugar Act. Under it, British navy officers who caught smugglers could seize half of the smuggled goods they found.

During the Revolution, British warships stopped much of the shipping, and molasses became costly and hard to get. Scotch-Irish farmers in Pennsylvania, Maryland, western Virginia and western North Carolina made whiskey from rye and corn instead. Before 1800, distillers in Kentucky were shipping whiskey down the rivers to New Orleans.

#### Native leaders against the liquor trade

In 1754 Hagler, a leader of the Catawba people in the hill country of the Carolinas, spoke to officials sent by North Carolina. He told them, "You Rot Your grain in Tubs, out of which you take and make Strong Spirits." Hagler and other Native leaders asked the colonists to stop the liquor trade, because it brought violence and despair.

The British official in charge wanted the trade to go on. Sir William Johnson was the British superintendent of Indian affairs for the northern colonies, the official who handled dealings with Native nations. In 1764 he wrote to his bosses in London, the Lords of Trade, that rum could cause problems. He also wrote that "the Trade will never be so extensive" without rum. After the Revolution, traders carried liquor farther west. They added water to it so they had more to sell.

In 1779 United States troops burned the villages of the Haudenosaunee, also called the Iroquois, in New York. After the war, at Fort Stanwix in 1784, American negotiators backed by soldiers took huge sections of land from the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee. By 1799 the Haudenosaunee had lost most of their land in New York and Pennsylvania. Many of them drank heavily. One was Handsome Lake, a Seneca man from the Genesee River. In 1799, sick after many years of heavy drinking, he had visions. Soon after, he stopped drinking and began preaching against drunkenness. His teaching became the Longhouse Religion, which Haudenosaunee people still practice today.

<a id="story-benjamin-rush-drugs-alcohol"></a>

#### Benjamin Rush

> **Who:** A Philadelphia doctor who signed the Declaration of Independence and wrote that heavy drinking was a disease.
>
> **When and where:** Philadelphia, 1785 to 1790.

Benjamin Rush argued that heavy drinking was a disease and an addiction. Before him, most Americans thought a drunkard simply lacked the will to stop. Rush was a Philadelphia doctor, and he had signed the Declaration of Independence.

In 1785 he published *An Inquiry into the Effects of Ardent Spirits Upon the Human Body and Mind*. Some records date the first printing to 1784. Ardent spirits meant strong liquor such as rum, gin and whiskey.

Rush wrote that a person begins drinking by free choice, and the habit then becomes a need. In his words: "The use of strong drink is at first the effect of free agency. From habit it takes place from necessity." He said the only cure was to stop drinking completely. His advice to heavy drinkers was "Taste not, handle not."

An edition of 1790 added a chart that Rush called "A Moral and Physical Thermometer." Water and milk stood at the top. Lower down, punch led to "idleness, sickness and debt." At the bottom, gin, brandy and rum taken every day led to "murder, madness" and the gallows.

Few people changed their drinking at the time. The historian Mark Lender says that "the conception we have of addiction today can generally be traced back to Benjamin Rush."

#### Whiskey as money, and the Whiskey Rebellion

In western Pennsylvania, farmers turned their grain into whiskey, and they used the whiskey as money. They farmed land that the Shawnee, Delaware and Mingo peoples had used. In 1768, at Fort Stanwix in New York, representatives of the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee had signed that land over to Britain. The Shawnee and Delaware, who lived on much of the land, were at the meeting but did not sign. The roads over the mountains to the east were bad, and grain spoiled on the way. Whiskey kept, and it was easier to carry. Coins were scarce on the frontier, so people paid for goods and paid their workers in whiskey.

In January 1791 Alexander Hamilton, the Treasury Secretary in charge of the country's money, asked for a tax on whiskey made in the United States, to pay the debt from the Revolutionary War. Members of Congress voted it into law. The law specified a tax of 7 cents a gallon. Large distillers could instead pay a flat fee for each still, the equipment used to distill liquor. For them the fee came to as little as 6 cents a gallon. A farmer with a small still paid about 9 cents a gallon. The law required payment in coin, which the farmers rarely had.

On 6 September 1791, a gang of armed men in disguise caught Robert Johnson, a new tax collector, at Pigeon Creek in Washington County, Pennsylvania. Some records give the date as 11 September. They tarred and feathered him, cut off his hair and took his horse, so he had to walk a long way. Tarring and feathering meant pouring hot tar on a person's skin and then sticking feathers to the tar. Hamilton's 1794 report on the attacks names none of the men. Officials sent a man to serve court papers on Johnson's attackers. Someone whipped that man, then tarred and feathered him too. No surviving record names who did it.

On 15 July 1794, John Neville, the regional tax inspector, went with David Lenox, a United States marshal, to serve court papers. A marshal was an officer who carried out the orders of the national courts. At a farm about 10 miles south of Pittsburgh, men fired warning shots at them. The next day, at least 30 men from the Mingo Creek militia surrounded Neville's house, called Bower Hill. Neville shot and killed one of them, Oliver Miller. Neville had the people he enslaved help him defend the house. They could not refuse.

On 17 July the men came back, this time between 400 and 600 of them. Their leader was Major James McFarlane, who had fought in the Revolution. After about an hour of shooting, McFarlane called a stop. When he stepped into the open, someone in the house shot and killed him. The records do not say who fired. The attackers burned Neville's house and the quarters where the enslaved people lived. How many men died at Bower Hill is not clear. The dead included McFarlane, one or two other militiamen, and perhaps one soldier.

Washington called up 12,950 militiamen from New Jersey, Maryland, Virginia and Pennsylvania. He went with them as far as Bedford, Pennsylvania, and Fort Cumberland, Maryland, then went back to Philadelphia. He left Henry Lee, the governor of Virginia, in command, and Hamilton went along as an adviser. The rebels scattered without a battle. About 12 soldiers died of illness or accidents.

On the night of 13 November 1794, soldiers under Lee broke into houses and seized people, rebels and witnesses alike. The soldiers drove the prisoners barefoot, in their nightclothes, over muddy roads and through streams, and locked them in animal pens and in cellars with no floors. The soldiers ruined the health of some of the prisoners, and at least one prisoner died. The night became known as "the Dreadful Night." In all, the soldiers arrested about 150 men during the march west.

Soldiers marched twenty of the prisoners to Philadelphia. On Christmas Day 1794 the soldiers paraded them down Broad Street as trophies of the march. Ten of the prisoners were tried for treason, the crime of making war against one's own country. Two were found guilty. In 1802 members of Congress voted to end the whiskey tax.

<a id="story-philip-vigol-drugs-alcohol"></a>

#### Philip Vigol

> **Who:** A man from western Pennsylvania, one of the first two Americans found guilty of treason against the United States, for attacking whiskey-tax officers.
>
> **When and where:** Westmoreland and Fayette counties, Pennsylvania, 1794. Philadelphia, 1795.

Philip Vigol and John Mitchell were the first two Americans found guilty of treason against the United States. Vigol's crime was attacking two officers who collected the whiskey tax. The court report spells his name Vigol. Other records spell it Wigle, Weigel or Wigal.

During the rebellion, Vigol went with an armed party, carrying guns and beating drums, to the house of Reigan, a tax officer in Westmoreland County. They forced Reigan to hand over his official papers. They made him swear never to collect the tax again.

The same party then rode to the house of Wells, the tax officer in Fayette County. They swore to destroy Wells and his house. Wells had run and hidden. The men ransacked his house, which means they tore through it and wrecked it. Then they burned it, with everything inside, including the tax records. Later they found Wells. They locked him up and made him swear to quit his job.

In 1795 a jury in the United States court in Philadelphia found Vigol guilty of treason. The judges sentenced him to death by hanging. At the trial, Justice William Paterson told the jury that fear excused a crime only when a person's life was in real danger at that moment.

In November 1795 President Washington pardoned Vigol and Mitchell, which means he freed them from their punishment. The records differ on the day, 2 November or 14 November. In his yearly message to Congress, Washington wrote, "The misled have abandoned their errors."

#### George Washington's rum and whiskey

George Washington used alcohol to win votes and to keep soldiers working, and he handed it out to the people he enslaved on the days they worked. At the end of his life he owned one of the largest whiskey distilleries in the country.

In 1758 Washington ran for the Virginia House of Burgesses, the colony's elected lawmaking body, in Frederick County. He gave the voters 28 gallons of rum, 50 gallons of rum punch and 82 gallons of wine, beer and cider. He won the seat.

In June 1779, as commander of the Continental Army, he wrote that he wanted "a pretty good stock of rum" at the forts for soldiers on work duty. At his plantation, Mount Vernon, he gave the people he enslaved an allowance of liquor for each day's work. They could not refuse the work. Once he accused his overseer, James Butler, the man who ran their work, of giving the enslaved people 36 pints of rum. Butler answered that he had given "no more than a pint of rum & a pound of Meat to each man."

In 1797 his farm manager, James Anderson, advised him to build a whiskey distillery at Mount Vernon. It made 600 gallons that first year. In 1799 it made almost 11,000 gallons, worth $7,500. The average distillery in Virginia made about 650 gallons. Anderson's son, John, ran the distillery with an assistant distiller and six enslaved workers. Their names were Hanson, Peter, Nat, Daniel, James and Timothy. Washington died in December 1799.

### 1800 to 1850

The average American of drinking age drank 7.1 gallons of pure alcohol in 1830. In 2023 the figure was 2.48 gallons. Americans drank at breakfast, in the fields and at work. From 1826, ministers and reformers asked people to sign a pledge, a written promise not to drink. More than a million people signed. In the 1840s and 1850s, drinking fell to about 3.5 gallons, half the 1830 figure.

Anyone could buy laudanum, a medicine made of opium, a painkilling drug from the poppy plant, mixed with alcohol, without a doctor's order. Doctors gave it to adults and to children. Among Native nations, leaders such as Little Turtle of the Miami asked members of Congress to stop the traders who sold liquor to their people.

#### How much Americans drank

Beer, cider, whiskey and rum hold different amounts of alcohol. The usual way to compare them is to count only the pure alcohol inside the drinks. In 1790 Americans of drinking age drank an average of 5.8 gallons of pure alcohol each in a year. By 1830 the figure was 7.1 gallons. Bruce Bustard, writing in the National Archives magazine *Prologue*, gives these figures, which come from the counts of the historian W. J. Rorabaugh. In 2023 Americans aged 14 and older drank an average of 2.48 gallons each. That figure comes from the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism.

In the early 1800s, men, women and even children drank "a healthful dram" with breakfast. A dram was a small drink of liquor. Farmers took cider, beer or whiskey into the fields. Employers stopped work in the middle of the morning so their workers could drink. When people got sick, a doctor's first medicine was often a drink of alcohol.

Between 1840 and 1860 drinking fell to about 3.5 gallons of pure alcohol a person each year. Those were the years when the temperance societies were most active.

#### Temperance and the pledge

Temperance means drinking little or no alcohol. By 1808, people in Connecticut, Virginia and New York had formed temperance societies. In 1825 Lyman Beecher, a minister in Connecticut, began giving talks against all drinking of liquor.

On 13 February 1826, reformers in Boston founded the American Temperance Society. Its members signed a pledge not to drink liquor, such as whiskey and rum. The pledge still allowed beer, wine and alcohol taken as medicine. Within five years the society had 2,220 local groups and 170,000 members. By the late 1830s it had more than 8,000 groups and more than 1,250,000 members.

In the late 1830s the reformers split. Many moved to total abstinence, which means no alcohol at all, not even beer or wine. Some stopped trying to talk people out of drinking and began asking lawmakers to ban the sale of liquor.

In 1838 Massachusetts lawmakers banned selling hard liquor, such as whiskey and rum, in amounts of less than 15 gallons. Only people with money could buy 15 gallons at once, so under this law only the rich could buy hard liquor. The lawmakers canceled the law within two years. In the 1840s, lawmakers in many states let voters in each town or county decide on liquor licenses. A license was a paper from the government that allowed a person to sell liquor.

Sailors in the Navy got a daily ration of liquor, a set share handed out each day. In 1843 almost 400 people signed a petition to members of Congress asking them to end it. A petition is a paper that people sign to ask for something. The petition was more than 10 feet long.

#### The Washingtonians, 1840

On 2 April 1840, six drinkers met at Chase's Tavern on Liberty Street in Baltimore and began keeping each other sober. They were William K. Mitchell, John F. Hoss, David Anderson, George Steers, James McCurley and Archibald Campbell. They called their group the Washington Temperance Society.

The members stayed sober by telling each other the stories of their own drinking. Then they went looking for other drinkers and told them the same stories. Estimates of how many people joined run from tens of thousands up to 600,000. Within a few years the group faded away.

On 22 February 1842, Abraham Lincoln, then 33 years old, spoke to the Washingtonians of Springfield, Illinois. He said that people had blamed and scolded drinkers and the men who sold them liquor too much, and that this was both unwise and unfair. "If you would win a man to your cause," he said, "first convince him that you are his sincere friend." He also said that "a drop of honey catches more flies than a gallon of gall." Gall is a bitter liquid.

<a id="story-john-b-gough-drugs-alcohol"></a>

#### John B. Gough

> **Who:** An English-born bookbinder, a worker who sews and covers books, whose drinking cost him his work. His wife and baby died while he was drunk. He signed the temperance pledge and spent his life asking others to sign it.
>
> **When and where:** New York, and Worcester, Massachusetts, 1829 to 1845.

John B. Gough drank until he lost his work, and his wife and baby died while he was drunk. Then he signed the temperance pledge and spent the rest of his life asking others to sign it. He told his story in *An Autobiography*, printed in 1845.

Gough was born in Sandgate, England, on 22 August 1817. At the age of 12 he came to America. He arrived in New York in August 1829 and later learned bookbinding, the trade of sewing pages together and putting covers on books, in New York City. After his mother died, he began drinking heavily. He lost one job after another and sang comic songs in theaters.

Once, when he stopped drinking all at once, he had delirium tremens. This is an illness of heavy drinkers who suddenly stop. The body shakes and the mind is confused, and the person sees things that are not there. The illness can kill. Gough wrote: "Hideous faces appeared on the walls, and on the ceiling, and on the floors." He saw "millions of monstrous spiders" around him.

When his wife fell sick, the women nursing her sent him to buy two quarts of rum. He drank it himself. Ten days later his wife and their baby both died. Gough wrote that the whole town learned "that my wife and child were lying dead, and that I was drunk!"

In late October 1842, in Worcester, Massachusetts, a stranger touched his shoulder and asked, "Why do you not sign the pledge?" The man was Joel Stratton, a waiter at the town's temperance hotel. The next evening Gough told his story to a meeting at the Worcester town hall. Then he signed the pledge.

About five months later he drank again. Then he signed the pledge a second time, in public. Between May 1843 and January 1845, he wrote, he traveled more than 12,000 miles and gave 605 talks. At those talks, 31,760 people signed the pledge.

#### Whiskey and enslaved people at Christmas

In the 1830s, Frederick Douglass was enslaved in Maryland. In his book of 1845 he wrote that slaveholders used whiskey to control the people they enslaved. Enslaved people had the days between Christmas and New Year's off work. Slaveholders wanted them to spend those days drunk.

"It was deemed a disgrace not to get drunk at Christmas," Douglass wrote. Deemed means thought to be. Slaveholders made "bets on their slaves, as to who can drink the most whisky without getting drunk." In this way, Douglass wrote, they got "whole multitudes to drink to excess," which means far too much.

Douglass wrote that the slaveholders did this to keep enslaved people from rising up in an armed revolt. He wrote that he and the others felt "that we had almost as well be slaves to man as to rum."

#### Liquor and Native nations

Little Turtle, also called Michikinikwa, was a leader of the Miami people. He urged members of Congress to stop traders from selling liquor to Native nations. In 1802 Congress members gave the president the power to stop those sales. War Department officials then made rules that banned traders from bringing liquor onto Native land. The officials did little to enforce the rules.

Traders kept selling because they made more money on liquor than on other goods. They also watered it down. In 1834 members of Congress made it a crime, with a fine of up to $300, to bring liquor onto Native land.

Native leaders worked against drinking among their own people. The Shawnee religious leader Tenskwatawa and a Delaware woman named Beate told their followers to give up alcohol. Pawnee leaders limited drinking in their towns.

In 1827, leaders of the Mohican-Stockbridge people wrote to Congress. They had been living on part of the Oneida Reservation in New York. They wrote that one reason they had agreed to move to what is now Wisconsin was to "flee from" liquor in their community. The land in Wisconsin was the homeland of the Menominee people.

#### Opium sold as medicine

Opium is a drug made from the opium poppy. It stops pain and brings sleep. A person who takes it every day comes to need it. Laudanum was opium dissolved in alcohol. Until the early 1900s, anyone could buy laudanum without a doctor's order.

Doctors gave laudanum for colds, for heart disease and for pain, to adults and to children. Nurses fed it to babies with a spoon. In the late 1700s and early 1800s, patients having surgery got laudanum and alcohol first. Then the surgeon's helpers held them down while the surgeon cut.

In 1804, in Germany, a pharmacist named Friedrich Sertürner took a drug called morphine out of opium. A pharmacist is a person who makes and sells medicines. In 1817 he tested morphine on himself and three boys, and all four nearly died. In 1827 a German pharmacy that later became the drug company Merck began making morphine for sale.

#### Chewing tobacco

The English writer Charles Dickens visited the United States in 1842. In his book *American Notes*, he complained about how common it was in Washington to chew tobacco and spit out the juice. In the courts of law, he wrote, "the judge has his spittoon, the crier his, the witness his, and the prisoner his." A spittoon is a bowl for spitting into, and the crier was the officer who called the court to order.

In hospitals, Dickens saw signs asking medical students to spit their tobacco juice into boxes and not onto the stairs. On a steamboat, he watched two young men chew and spit on the deck for a quarter of an hour before breakfast.

### 1850 to 1900

In 1851 lawmakers in Maine banned the sale of liquor, and by 1855 lawmakers in twelve more states had passed bans. In Portland, Maine, in 1855, soldiers fired on a crowd at the mayor's order and killed a young sailor. In the Civil War, surgeons gave wounded soldiers morphine and opium, and thousands of veterans came home addicted, which means their bodies had come to need the drug.

Drugstores sold medicines with opium, morphine, cocaine, a drug made from coca leaves, and alcohol in them, and the labels did not have to say so. City, state and federal lawmakers passed laws against opium. A federal law of 1887 named Chinese people outright. Accounts differ about whom San Francisco's opium law of 1875 was aimed at. Women marched into saloons to pray, and in 1874 they founded the Woman's Christian Temperance Union. In 1880 Kansas voters approved a ban on liquor in their state constitution, the state's highest set of laws.

#### The Maine Law and the Portland Rum Riot

On 2 June 1851, lawmakers in Maine banned the sale of all alcoholic drinks. The law still allowed alcohol for medicine and for use in factories. Neal Dow, the mayor of Portland, had helped write it. By 1855, lawmakers in twelve more states had passed bans of their own. Judges threw out some of these laws, and lawmakers passed them again.

For years Dow had ordered police raids on saloons in Portland. A saloon was a bar, mostly for men, that sold drinks by the glass. Many of the saloons Dow raided were run by Irish immigrants, and he gave speeches about "rum-swilling foreigners." In 1850 about one in nine of Portland's 21,000 people was an Irish immigrant.

In 1855 Dow was mayor again. He had city officials buy $1,600 worth of liquor for medicine and for use in workshops and factories, and he stored it at City Hall. The law required a city committee to make such a purchase, and no committee had been named. Under the Maine Law, any three voters could ask a judge for a search warrant, a paper from a judge that allows a search. On 2 June 1855, three men got a warrant to search City Hall. The police would not let them in. By evening a crowd of between 1,000 and 3,000 people, most of them Irish, stood outside. Some threw stones at the door.

Dow called out the militia, a force of part-time soldiers, and ordered them to fire. John Robbins, a 22-year-old sailor from Deer Isle, Maine, broke a hole in the door of the room where the liquor was kept. The soldiers shot him dead. He had planned to marry the next day. The soldiers kept firing as the crowd ran and wounded seven more people. The New England Historical Society's account of the riot does not name the soldiers who fired or their officers.

Dow was tried for buying the liquor improperly and found not guilty. Voters turned him out of office. In 1856 Maine lawmakers ended the ban.
