On June 1, 1956, an Alabama judge banned the NAACP, a national civil rights organization, from working anywhere in the state. Four days later, on June 5, about a thousand people met at Sardis Baptist Church and started the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights. Shuttlesworth said that officials could outlaw an organization but not a movement. He said the word "Christian" set the group apart from groups being called Communist. Communists wanted the government to own the land and the businesses. He also said the word gave the group "a foundation and Christian orientation." Members met every Monday night in churches around the city. The National Park Service describes the meetings as "emotional testimony, soul-lifting music, impassioned preaching, and fundraising." By 1958 weekly meetings were being held in 55 other working-class churches in Birmingham.

On Christmas night, December 25, 1956, someone set off twelve sticks of dynamite in the space between the church and the parsonage, the pastor's house. The blast destroyed the parsonage. Shuttlesworth was inside talking with a deacon, a member who helps run the church, and his family was watching television. He had a minor head injury. The bomb went off the night before the movement's members had said they would ride Birmingham's segregated buses, where Black riders had to sit apart from white riders. The next day 250 people rode the buses, and police arrested 22 of them.

A second bomb came on June 29, 1958, and a third in 1962, which broke the church's windows. The 1958 bombing was not solved until 1980, when J. B. Stoner was convicted of it. No one is recorded as convicted of the 1956 bomb or the 1962 bomb.

Other Black churches were bombed and burned in these years. On September 15, 1963, a bomb at the 16th Street Baptist Church in Birmingham killed four girls: Addie Mae Collins, 14, Denise McNair, 11, Carole Robertson, 14, and Cynthia Wesley, 14. Robert Chambliss was convicted of the bombing in 1977, Thomas Blanton in 2001 and Bobby Frank Cherry in 2002. Jason Wollschleger of Whitworth University is a sociologist, a scholar who studies how groups of people live together. He and his research team have mapped about 145 attacks on Black churches across the South from about 1954 to 1970. It is one team's count, not an official one. In Albany, Georgia, in 1961 and 1962, four Black churches connected with the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, a civil rights group of young people, were burned to the ground. Among them were Shady Grove Baptist and High Hope Baptist. Wollschleger's account does not name who set the fires.

<a id="story-revis-family-bethel"></a>

#### The Revis family of Bethel Baptist Church

> **Who:** A church deacon and his two daughters, whose front porch became the guard post for a church that kept being bombed.
>
> **When and where:** Collegeville, Birmingham, Alabama, 1956 to the early 1960s.

The Revis family turned their own front porch into a guardhouse so that armed volunteers could watch Bethel Baptist Church day and night. James Revis was a deacon of the church, a member who helps run it, and sat on the executive committee of the Alabama Christian Movement for Human Rights. His house stood across the street from the church.

After the bomb of Christmas night 1956 destroyed the pastor's house, members of the church and the movement volunteered to guard the church and the new parsonage. In 1957 the Revis family closed in their porch to make a room for the guards. His daughter Robbie Revis Smith described it years later: "with our house sitting on the corner, it gave a very good view several ways that they could see because they had the glass out there and they put a little gas heater out there so they wouldn't be too cold sitting up. They did this year round." Her sister Laverne Revis Martin said their parents made the room "just so the guards would be able to watch."

The volunteers were called the Civil Rights Guards. They worked in two shifts, from six in the evening to midnight and from midnight to six in the morning. They carried rifles, which they called their "nonviolent Winchesters." Women of the movement took a weekly shift, among them Desta Brooks, a florist, and Minnie Eaton, a schoolteacher.

At about half past one in the morning on Sunday, June 29, 1958, Laverne was coming home from work when she saw a bomb smoking beside the church. She told the guards. They carried it into the street, where it went off. It blew a hole in the road and broke church windows, and the building stood. Afterward Birmingham police came to the Revis house and took four rifles from the guards on the porch.

Robbie Revis Smith said of coming home in those years: "So it was kind of a good feeling coming home because you never came home without a person out there watching you, so you didn't have to worry about that."

<a id="story-billy-graham"></a>

#### Billy Graham

> **Who:** A Southern Baptist preacher who held large public revival meetings, which he called crusades, from 1949 to 2005.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Charlotte, North Carolina, November 7, 1918. Died at Montreat, North Carolina, February 21, 2018.

Billy Graham held revival meetings from 1949 to 2005, and in 1957 Martin Luther King Jr. gave the opening prayer at one of them. He grew up on a dairy farm near Charlotte, North Carolina. In 1934, after hearing a traveling preacher in Charlotte, he decided to give his life to God. Southern Baptist leaders ordained him in 1939, which means they made him a minister. He earned a degree in theology, the study of religious belief, at the Florida Bible Institute in 1940 and a degree from Wheaton College in Illinois in 1943. That August he married Ruth Bell.

From 1944 to 1948 he traveled the country speaking at rallies for a group called Youth for Christ. In 1949 he held a campaign in Los Angeles that was planned for three weeks and ran for seven. He then started the Billy Graham Evangelistic Association and a film company. A weekly radio program, *Hour of Decision*, and a daily newspaper column followed. He preached for twelve weeks in London in 1954, and every night for sixteen weeks at Madison Square Garden in New York in 1957.

On July 18, 1957, at the New York crusade, Martin Luther King Jr. gave the opening prayer. Graham and King had spoken by telephone, and on July 5 the evangelist Leighton Ford, a traveling preacher, had sent King a telegram asking him to come. King asked for help "for a warless world and for a brotherhood that transcends race or color." Then he led the crowd in the Lord's Prayer.

On August 31, 1957, King wrote to Graham: "You have courageously brought the Christian gospel to bear on the question of race." On July 23, 1958, King wrote again, this time to object. Graham had shared a platform with Governor Price Daniel of Texas, and King called that an "endorsement of racial segregation and discrimination." At Easter in 1964, Graham held crusades in Birmingham, Alabama, that Black and white people attended together.

In 1996 members of Congress voted Billy and Ruth Graham a gold medal, which was presented to them in the Capitol Rotunda on May 2. In the law, members of Congress wrote that his crusades had reached 100 million people in person and more than 2 billion on television. He stepped down from his association in 2000 and held a last crusade in Queens, New York, in 2005. He died on February 21, 2018, aged 99. On February 28 his body lay in honor in the Rotunda, the round hall under the dome of the Capitol, where people could come to pay their respects. According to the House of Representatives, he was the fourth private citizen to be given that honor.

#### Dynamite at an Atlanta synagogue, 1958

In the early hours of October 12, 1958, fifty sticks of dynamite exploded in the entrance of the Hebrew Benevolent Congregation in Atlanta, called The Temple. It was the congregation Leo Frank had belonged to. No one was hurt. Its rabbi, the congregation's religious leader, was Jacob Rothschild. He had preached against segregation in his sermons since 1947.

Within days police arrested five men, all members of anti-Semitic groups, groups that spread hatred of Jews. Only one of them, George Bright, was tried. His first trial ended in a mistrial, a trial stopped without a verdict, because the jury split 9 to 3. At his second trial the jury found him not guilty. The charges against the other four men were dropped. No one was ever convicted of the bombing.

#### Prayer and the Bible in public schools, 1962 and 1963

In 1962 and 1963 the justices of the Supreme Court ended official prayer and Bible reading in public schools. The families who brought the cases came from several faiths, and some had none. On June 25, 1962, in *Engel v. Vitale*, the justices ruled that New York's public schools could not have pupils say a prayer written by the New York State Board of Regents, the state officials in charge of its schools. On June 17, 1963, in *School District of Abington Township v. Schempp*, they ruled that public schools could not open the day with Bible reading as a religious exercise.

The parents of ten pupils brought the New York case. They said the official prayer went against their own beliefs and their children's. Judges in a New York court had already found that the prayer did not fit the teachings of Jewish, Unitarian or Ethical Culture groups. Unitarians belong to a church that does not teach the Trinity, the belief that God is three persons in one. The Ethical Culture society is a group that meets to teach right conduct. One parent was an agnostic, a person who holds that no one can know whether God exists.

The Schempps, who brought the 1963 case, went to church. Edward and Sidney Schempp and their children Roger and Donna were members of the Unitarian church in Germantown, Philadelphia, and so was their son Ellory, who had started the case. Under Pennsylvania law, public schools had to read ten verses from the Bible each morning. A child could be excused if a parent asked. Edward Schempp decided not to ask. He testified that teachers and classmates would label his children "odd balls" every school day. He said classmates would lump every religious difference together as "atheism," and in 1962 atheism was tied to communism and called un-American. An atheist is a person who believes there is no God. He also said that an excused child had to stand in the hall outside the homeroom, which looked like a punishment for bad behavior.

Two scholars testified about the Bible itself. Solomon Grayzel, for the families, said the Jewish scriptures have no New Testament. He said that from the standpoint of Jewish faith, calling Jesus the Son of God is "practically blasphemous," which means close to an insult against God. Read to children without explanation, he said, parts of the New Testament had been "psychologically harmful to the child." Luther A. Weigle, for the school district, said the Bible was "non-sectarian," meaning it belonged to no single religious group. He later said he meant non-sectarian among Christian churches.

A second case was decided with the Schempps'. In Baltimore, schools opened each day with a chapter from the Bible or the Lord's Prayer. Madalyn Murray and her son William J. Murray III were atheists. They argued that the rule threatened their religious liberty "by placing a premium on belief as against non-belief," which means it rewarded believers over people who do not believe.

#### The day after, and the years after

The day after the 1962 ruling, a member of Congress introduced an amendment, a change to the Constitution, to undo it, and others were drafting more. The *Evening Star* newspaper of Washington, D.C., reported on June 26, 1962, that Representative Taylor of North Carolina was first. The paper noted that Billy Graham was one of his constituents, the people he represented. Senator Beall of Maryland had one ready for the Senate. Representative Chelf of Kentucky said that if he could not get a law passed, he would try to limit Supreme Court justices to a set number of years instead of life. In Washington, D.C., the school board's rules required a Bible reading and the Lord's Prayer to open the school day. Superintendent Carl F. Hansen said that "on the surface it appears that it does invalidate the board's rule," which means that the ruling seemed to cancel the board's rule. None of the proposed amendments became part of the Constitution.

The justices had set some limits before 1962. In 1948, in a case brought by a mother named Vashti McCollum, the justices ruled against a program in Champaign, Illinois. There, Catholic, Protestant and Jewish teachers came into the public school buildings once a week to teach religion for thirty to forty-five minutes. Children whose parents asked had to attend. In 1952 the justices allowed a program in New York City in which children left the school buildings to go to a church or synagogue for the lesson. The justices ruled out religion lessons inside the school building. They allowed lessons that children left the building to attend.

In the 1963 ruling, Justice Clark also wrote that teaching *about* religion was allowed. He wrote that "it might well be said that one's education is not complete without a study of comparative religion or the history of religion and its relationship to the advancement of civilization." He wrote that the Bible "is worthy of study for its literary and historic qualities."

After 1963 Alabama's lawmakers tried a moment of silence. They passed a law in 1978 for one minute of silence "for meditation." In 1981 they changed it to "for meditation or voluntary prayer," and in 1982 they let teachers lead "willing students" in a prayer to "Almighty God." In 1985, in *Wallace v. Jaffree*, the justices struck down the 1981 law because its purpose was to support religion. They left the 1978 law for plain silence in place.

In 1980, in *Stone v. Graham*, the justices struck down a Kentucky law that required the Ten Commandments to be posted in every public classroom.

In 1992 the justices ruled that a principal could not invite a member of the clergy, such as a minister or a rabbi, to pray at a school graduation. Principal Robert E. Lee of Nathan Bishop Middle School in Providence, Rhode Island, had invited Rabbi Leslie Gutterman of Temple Beth El to pray at Deborah Weisman's graduation. The principal gave the rabbi a pamphlet of guidelines and told him to keep the prayers non-sectarian. The rabbi began, "God of the Free, Hope of the Brave." Deborah's father, Daniel Weisman, sued. In *Lee v. Weisman*, the justices held that by handing over the pamphlet and the instruction, the principal "directed and controlled the content of the prayers."

#### Evolution in court again, 1968 and 1987

Two state laws about teaching evolution reached the Supreme Court, in 1968 and 1987. The justices struck down both, and both times they named the religious belief behind the law. Susan Epperson had gone to school in Arkansas and earned a master's degree in zoology. In the autumn of 1964 Little Rock school officials hired her to teach tenth-grade biology at Central High School. For the 1965 to 1966 school year, school officials adopted a new biology textbook with a chapter on evolution. Teaching that chapter was a crime under the Arkansas law of 1928. She sued, and H. H. Blanchard, a parent of children in the public schools, joined her case.

On November 12, 1968, in *Epperson v. Arkansas*, the justices struck the law down. They wrote that "fundamentalist sectarian conviction was and is the law's reason for existence," meaning that the law existed because of one group's religious belief. They also wrote that the First Amendment requires the government to be neutral "between religion and religion, and between religion and nonreligion." No justice voted to keep the law. They did not all agree on the reasons, and Justice Black wrote separately that he doubted the Court's reading of why Arkansas had passed it.

Louisiana's lawmakers passed a different kind of law. It stated that a public school that taught evolution also had to teach "creation science," and a school that taught creation science also had to teach evolution. Creation science was the teaching that a supernatural being created humankind. The people who sued to stop the law included Louisiana parents, Louisiana teachers and religious leaders.

Religious groups stood on both sides. Groups may send the Court a friend-of-the-court brief, a written argument from people who are not in the case. The Catholic League for Religious and Civil Rights, the Christian Legal Society and Concerned Women for America sent briefs asking the justices to keep the law. The New York Committee for Public Education and Religious Liberty sent one asking them to strike it down. The Rabbinical Alliance of America sent its own brief, and so did a group led by the Reverend Bill McLean. On June 19, 1987, in *Edwards v. Aguillard*, the justices struck the law down by 7 votes to 2. They held that "the preeminent purpose of the Louisiana Legislature was clearly to advance the religious viewpoint that a supernatural being created humankind." The justices meant that Louisiana's lawmakers passed the law mainly to promote one religious belief.

<a id="story-jonas-and-frieda-yoder"></a>

#### Jonas and Frieda Yoder

> **Who:** An Old Order Amish father who would not send his daughter to high school, and the daughter, who told the court that the decision was her own religion too.
>
> **When and where:** Green County, Wisconsin, 1968 to 1972.

Frieda Yoder was the only child who testified in her family's case, which went to the Supreme Court and asked whether Amish parents could keep their children out of high school. Her father, Jonas Yoder, belonged to the Old Order Amish, a Christian church whose members keep apart from the outside world. They lived in Green County, Wisconsin.

Wisconsin law required children to stay in school until they turned sixteen. Frieda was fifteen and had finished the eighth grade at the public school. Her father did not send her on to high school.

His reason was one line from the Bible. In his letter to the Romans, Paul, an early leader of the Christian church, wrote, "be not conformed to this world." The Amish take that line as a rule for daily life. They did not object to the first eight grades, because a child needs to read the Bible, farm and deal with people outside the community. They saw the high school as the world they were told not to join.

Jonas Yoder was charged, tried and convicted in the Green County Court along with two other fathers, Wallace Miller and Adin Yutzy. Miller was also Old Order Amish, and Yutzy belonged to the Conservative Amish Mennonite Church. On May 15, 1972, in *Wisconsin v. Yoder*, the justices of the Supreme Court decided for the three fathers.

Frieda testified that her own religious beliefs were the reason she had stopped going to school after the eighth grade. Neither side called the other children. Justice Douglas agreed with the ruling for her father. He disagreed with it for the other two fathers, because no one had asked their children, Barbara Miller and Vernon Yutzy, what they believed. He said the Court had never answered whose religion counts when a family's religion decides a child's schooling, the parents' or the child's.

#### Ministers on both sides of a textbook fight, 1974

In 1974 ministers spoke up on both sides of a fight over schoolbooks in Kanawha County, West Virginia. During the protests people fired guns, and attackers firebombed and dynamited schools. The county had 46,000 pupils in 124 public schools. In April 1974 the five members of the county school board voted to adopt 325 language-arts textbooks and other books.

The next month a board member, Alice Moore, objected to what some of the books said and taught. She was the wife of a minister, and she had been elected in 1970 after campaigning against sex education. She and several ministers campaigned against the books. Twenty-seven ministers condemned them as immoral and indecent, and petitions carried 12,000 signatures. Another minister, Jim Lewis of Charleston, spoke out most strongly for the books. In June the board voted 3 to 2 to accept most of them.

When school opened on September 3, 1974, a fifth of the pupils stayed home in a boycott, a refusal to take part. Picket lines, groups of protesters standing outside with signs, spread from the schools to businesses and coal mines, and 3,500 miners walked off the job in support. The West Virginia Encyclopedia lists gunfire, firebombs and dynamite attacks on schools, and it does not name who carried them out. Police made 11 arrests. The schools were closed for four days starting September 12. The records of the protest give no count of the injured.

The protests went on into 1977, and outside groups joined them, among them the Ku Klux Klan and the John Birch Society, a political group. The Reverend Marvin Horan was tried for plotting to bomb schools, and the violence ended with his trial. Board members set up committees that gave parents a part in choosing textbooks.

#### The law that said Native religion was allowed, 1978 to 1997

On August 11, 1978, members of Congress passed the American Indian Religious Freedom Act. In it they declared that it was the policy of the United States to protect the right of Native people "to believe, express, and exercise the traditional religions of the American Indian, Eskimo, Aleut, and Native Hawaiians." That included the right to visit sacred sites, to have sacred objects, and to worship "through ceremonials and traditional rites." It came ninety-five years after the 1883 rules that made the Sun Dance, a sacred ceremony of the Plains nations, a crime.

The members of Congress wrote down what had been happening. Federal laws and policies "often deny American Indians access to sacred sites required in their religions, including cemeteries." They wrote that "traditional American Indian ceremonies have been intruded upon, interfered with, and in a few instances banned." Federal officials had done this, as Price's rules of 1883, Jones's order of 1902 and Burke's circular of 1921 show. Since 1962, for example, a Native person had needed a federal permit to hold an eagle feather for worship. Without one, the penalty was up to $500 or six months in prison.

The 1978 Act stated a policy. In 1988 the justices of the Supreme Court ruled that it created no right a court could enforce. They ruled it in the case *Lyng v. Northwest Indian Cemetery Protective Association*. Officials of the U.S. Forest Service planned to build a six-mile paved road through the Chimney Rock area of Six Rivers National Forest in California. They also planned to allow logging there. The Yurok, Karuk and Tolowa had long used this high country for worship. Justice Brennan, who disagreed with the ruling, wrote that they had held it sacred "for at least 200 years and probably much longer." It is land of the Yurok, Karuk and Tolowa that the Forest Service holds as federal land. The authors of a study that the Forest Service itself paid for found that the road "would cause serious and irreparable damage to the sacred areas" and advised against building it. In 1982 Forest Service officials chose a route through Chimney Rock anyway.

The justices ruled 5 to 3 that the Constitution did not stop the road. Justice O'Connor wrote: "Even assuming that the Government's actions here will virtually destroy the Indians' ability to practice their religion, the Constitution simply does not provide a principle that could justify upholding respondents' legal claims." She meant that even if the road nearly destroyed their religion, the Constitution gave the courts no rule for stopping it. The justices' opinion also records that the Native people of the area did not all oppose the road.

In 1990 the justices decided *Employment Division v. Smith*. Alfred Smith and Galen Black were members of the Native American Church. Their employer, a private drug treatment program, fired them because they ate peyote at a church ceremony. Peyote is a small cactus that causes hallucinations, which means it makes a person see or feel things that are not there. Members of the church take it as a sacrament, a sacred act of worship. Oregon officials refused to pay the men unemployment money. The justices ruled 6 to 3 that Oregon could ban peyote even for worship and deny the payments. Justice Scalia wrote that leaving such questions to lawmakers "will place at a relative disadvantage those religious practices that are not widely engaged in."

Members of Congress answered twice. In 1993 they passed the Religious Freedom Restoration Act. It stated that government officials could not put a heavy burden on a person's religion. They needed a reason of the highest importance, and they had to choose the way that restricted religion least. On October 6, 1994, members of Congress also amended, or changed, the 1978 Act. They wrote that 28 states protected the peyote ceremony and 22 did not. They made it lawful everywhere in the country for a Native person to use peyote in traditional religious ceremonies. In 1997, in a case brought by Archbishop Patrick Flores of San Antonio, the justices ruled that the 1993 act went beyond Congress's power over the states. That ruling did not touch the 1994 peyote law.

#### Jonestown, 1978

On November 18, 1978, Jim Jones, the leader of an American congregation called Peoples Temple, ordered its members at its settlement in Guyana, in South America, to take poison. More than 900 people died. Jones had founded Peoples Temple in Indianapolis in the 1950s and moved it to San Francisco in 1971. Members then moved to a settlement they called Jonestown.

That day Temple members shot and killed Congressman Leo Ryan of California and four other people at the Port Kaituma airstrip, among them an NBC cameraman and a newspaper photographer.

At Jonestown, at Jones's order, parents and nurses used syringes to squirt a mix of cyanide, sedatives and powdered fruit drink into the children's mouths. Cyanide is a poison that stops the cells of the body from using oxygen, so the cells cannot make the energy they need to live. Sedatives are drugs that make a person calm and sleepy. More than 200 children were killed this way, according to the Association for Diplomatic Studies and Training, an organization of former American diplomats. The children could not choose, and the association calls them murdered. Then the adults drank the mix while armed guards surrounded the pavilion, the large roofed meeting place where they had gathered. In all, 909 members died at Jonestown, all but two of them from what appeared to be cyanide poisoning. One or two people there, among them Jim Jones, had bullet wounds instead.

#### Houses of worship attacked, 1991 to 2000

On August 10, 1991, gunmen shot nine people dead at Wat Promkunaram, a Thai Buddhist temple near Phoenix, Arizona, during a robbery of the monks. Johnathan Doody and Alessandro Garcia were later convicted of the killings. The dead were six monks, a nun, a novice, who is a person training to become a monk, and a boy who helped at the temple. Each was shot in the head. Doody was 17 at the time. His first conviction was thrown out because federal appeals judges found that his confession had been coerced, which means forced out of him. At his third trial he was convicted of nine counts of first-degree murder, one for each person killed. First-degree murder is a killing planned ahead of time. On March 14, 2014, he was sentenced to 249 years in prison. Alessandro Garcia pleaded guilty and was sentenced to life, NBC News reported.

In the middle of the 1990s people set fire to churches across the country. On July 3, 1996, members of Congress passed the Church Arson Prevention Act. They wrote that fires set at places of worship had increased, "especially in the context of places of religious worship that serve predominantly African-American congregations," which means mostly Black congregations. Arson is the crime of setting a fire on purpose. Agents of a federal task force from the Justice and Treasury departments counted 297 arsons, bombings or attempted bombings at houses of worship in 1996, 209 in 1997, 165 in 1998 and 140 in 1999. Between January 1995 and August 2000 they arrested 431 suspects, and courts found 305 people guilty in connection with 224 of the arsons and bombings. On July 11, 2000, Jay Scott Ballinger pleaded guilty to setting fire to 26 churches in eight states between 1994 and 1999.

#### Mount Carmel, near Waco, 1993

In 1993 a standoff between federal agents and a religious community near Waco, Texas, ended when some of the Davidians set fire to their own building. More than 70 people died in it, 22 of them children, according to a report by members of Congress. A Special Counsel, an outside lawyer appointed to investigate, later found that some of the Davidians had spread fuel through their building and set it on fire. The Branch Davidians lived at a property called Mount Carmel, outside Waco. Their leader was Vernon Howell, who called himself David Koresh.

On February 28, 1993, 76 agents of the federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms (the ATF) stormed the building. They had warrants, papers from a judge that allowed them to arrest people and search the building. The Davidians had learned of the raid in advance. The gun battle lasted almost 90 minutes. The Special Counsel found that Davidians shot and killed four ATF agents, Conway C. LeBleu, Todd W. McKeehan, Robert J. Williams and Steven D. Willis, and wounded 20 others. Six Davidians were killed that day, by the Special Counsel's count. The House report says that ATF agents killed at least two of them.

Who fired first is disputed. ATF agents testified that the Davidians did. The Davidians' lawyers said they believed an ATF gun went off by accident. In their 1996 report, members of two House subcommittees, small groups of members of the House of Representatives, found that the question could not be settled for certain, and that "It appears more likely, however, that the Davidians fired first."

Agents of the FBI then took over and talked with the Davidians for 51 days. By March 23, 35 people had come out. The House majority report records 21 of them as children, and the minority report records 14. After March 23 no one else left. A six-year-old girl, Melissa Morrison, told an FBI negotiator that she could not leave because "David won't let me." She died in the fire.

On April 19, 1993, at about 6 in the morning, FBI agents in armored vehicles began punching holes in the walls and spraying tear gas inside, and Davidians fired on the vehicles. At about 12:07 in the afternoon a fire broke out in the building. Two more began within two minutes, and within eight minutes the whole building was burning.

Former Senator John C. Danforth was the Special Counsel. The Attorney General, the head of the Justice Department, appointed him, and he studied the case for ten months. In 2000 he reported that government agents did not start or spread the fire and did not shoot at the Davidians. He found that some of the Davidians spread fuel through the building and set it on fire in at least three places. Danforth placed the responsibility for the deaths on "certain of the Branch Davidians and their leader, David Koresh." He counted at least 80 dead in all, including the six Davidians killed on February 28.

Danforth found that some Davidians shot and killed their own people, among them at least five children. At least twenty Davidians were shot dead on April 19, many of them in the head or mouth at close range. A three-year-old, Dayland Gent, was stabbed in the chest and died. Danforth's report does not name who stabbed him.

Danforth also reported that an FBI agent had fired three tear-gas rounds of a kind that can start fires at 8:08 that morning, toward a pit about 75 feet from the living quarters. Government officials did not reveal this until August 1999. Danforth found that those rounds did not start the fire four hours later. A Texas jury later found eight Davidians guilty of gun crimes.

### 2000 to Today

A smaller share of Americans has belonged to a congregation since 2000, and the share who say they have no religion has grown. In a survey taken in 2023 and 2024, 29 percent of American adults said they had no religion. People attacked worshippers inside gurdwaras (Sikh houses of worship), churches and synagogues and killed them where they prayed.

Records made public in these years showed that more than 10,000 people had told Catholic officials that priests sexually abused them as children. A grand jury in Pennsylvania, a group of citizens who hear evidence gathered by prosecutors, found that church leaders in six dioceses, the regions led by bishops, had hidden the abuse there. A report on the Southern Baptist Convention found that its leaders had pushed back against people who reported abuse, and sometimes met them with outright hostility. Families and teachers kept going to court over what a public school may teach about religion and whether public money may pay for religious schools.

#### How many people say they have no religion

The Pew Research Center is a polling organization, not a government office. Between July 17, 2023, and March 4, 2024, its researchers asked 36,908 American adults about their religion. Pew published the results on February 26, 2025. Sixty-two percent said they were Christian, compared with 71 percent in Pew's study of 2014 and 78 percent in 2007. Twenty-nine percent said they had no religion, compared with 23 percent in 2014 and 16 percent in 2007. This group, often called the "nones," includes atheists, agnostics and people who answer "nothing in particular."

In the same 2023 to 2024 study, 1.7 percent of adults said they were Jewish, 1.2 percent Muslim, 1.1 percent Buddhist and 0.9 percent Hindu. Pew's own report states that the fall in the Christian share had slowed and may have stopped, because it had stayed about the same for four or five years.

Gallup's pollsters ask a different question: whether people belong to a church, synagogue or mosque. Seventy percent said they did in 1999. Fifty percent said so in 2018 and 47 percent in 2020. That was the first time since Gallup began asking in 1937 that fewer than half said yes. Gallup published those figures in March 2021. In the years 2018 to 2020, 66 percent of Americans born before 1946 belonged to a congregation, compared with 36 percent of those born between 1981 and 1996.

#### Killed where they were worshipping, 2001 to 2025

The FBI counts crimes that police report as motivated by hatred of a group. The FBI's report for 2001, the year of the September 11 attacks, records 481 incidents aimed at Muslims, with 554 victims. That was more than 1,600 percent higher than in 2000. Crimes aimed at Jews were still the largest group, at more than half of all religious hate crimes that year.

On Sunday morning, August 5, 2012, a white supremacist carrying a loaded gun walked into the gurdwara, the Sikh house of worship, at Oak Creek, Wisconsin, and killed six people. A white supremacist is a person who believes white people are better than others and should rule over them. Paramjit Kaur was sitting for morning prayers when he shot her. The others killed were Sita Singh, Ranjit Singh, Prakash Singh, Suvegh Singh Khattra and Satwant Singh Kaleka, the gurdwara's president, who was killed fighting the gunman. Santokh Singh and Punjab Singh were shot. In 2022 Senator Tammy Baldwin of Wisconsin introduced a resolution in the United States Senate that counts Punjab Singh as the seventh person killed. The resolution also names Lieutenant Brian Murphy, a police officer who was shot 15 times at close range.

<a id="story-harpreet-singh-saini"></a>

#### Harpreet Singh Saini

> **Who:** A young man whose mother was shot dead at morning prayers, and who asked the United States Senate to start counting crimes against Sikhs.
>
> **When and where:** Oak Creek, Wisconsin, and Washington, D.C., August and September 2012.

Harpreet Singh Saini asked the United States Senate to count crimes against Sikhs, forty-five days after a gunman killed his mother at prayer. His parents brought him and his brother, Kamaljit, from India to the United States in 2004, when he was ten. "Like many other immigrants," he said, "they wanted us to have a better life, a better education."

On Sunday, August 5, 2012, a white supremacist carrying a loaded gun walked into their gurdwara at Oak Creek, Wisconsin. He killed Harpreet's mother, Paramjit Kaur, while she sat for morning prayers. He also killed five men, all of whom wore turbans, as Harpreet does.

Two days later Harpreet and his brother ate the last rotis, a kind of flatbread, that their mother had made from scratch the night before she died. He said that with the last bite he understood it was the last food made by her hands that they would ever eat. He had just started college, and she was not there to send him off.

On September 19, 2012, he testified before a subcommittee of the United States Senate. He said: "I want to tell the gunman who took her from me: You may have been full of hate, but my mother was full of love."

He told the senators what his mother's faith taught her. "My mother was a devout Sikh. Like all Sikhs, she was bound to live in Chardi Kala," which he described as "a state of high spirits and optimism." He said, "She was also taught as a Sikh to neither have fear of anyone nor strike fear in anyone."

Then he asked for one thing. "I came here today to ask the government to give my mother the dignity of being a statistic. The FBI does not track hate crimes against Sikhs. My mother and those shot that day will not even count on a federal form. We cannot solve a problem we refuse to recognize."

The FBI's report for 2015 was the first to list crimes against Sikhs. It counted 6 offenses against Sikhs that year.

#### Charleston, Sutherland Springs and Pittsburgh, 2015 to 2018

On Wednesday evening, June 17, 2015, a 21-year-old man named Dylann Roof killed nine members of Mother Emanuel church in Charleston, South Carolina, at their weekly Bible study. Mother Emanuel is an African Methodist Episcopal church. That denomination, a group of churches sharing one set of teachings, was formed in 1816 by Richard Allen and other Black Methodists. Twelve members were meeting in the fellowship hall. Roof came in at about 8:16. Judges of a federal appeals court later described what happened next: "The parishioners welcomed Roof, handing him a Bible and a study sheet. For the next 45 minutes, Roof worshipped with the parishioners. They stood and shut their eyes for closing prayer. Roof then took out his gun and started shooting." He fired about seventy-four shots.

The nine killed were the Reverend Sharonda Coleman-Singleton, Cynthia Hurd, Susie Jackson, Ethel Lee Lance, the Reverend DePayne Middleton-Doctor, the Reverend Clementa Pinckney, Tywanza Sanders, the Reverend Daniel Simmons Sr. and the Reverend Myra Thompson. Roof told the FBI that he had looked up African American churches in Charleston, visited this one beforehand, and learned from a member that the Bible study met on Wednesday nights. A federal jury convicted him on 33 counts, among them nine counts of obstructing religion resulting in death. That federal crime means using force to stop people from practicing their religion, in a way that kills someone. He was sentenced to death. Appeals judges upheld the sentence on August 25, 2021.

On Sunday, November 5, 2017, Devin Patrick Kelley walked into the First Baptist Church of Sutherland Springs, Texas, and opened fire. He killed twenty-six people and wounded twenty-two more, then died of his own gunshot after fleeing. Among the dead were Emily Hill, 11, and Megan Hill, 9. Kelley had been convicted of a crime of domestic violence while he was in the U.S. Air Force. In 2012 a military court found him guilty of attacking his wife at the time, Tessa Brennaman, and his stepson.

Air Force agents and jail staff never sent his fingerprints or his conviction to the FBI. A gun store must run a background check, a search of national criminal records, before it sells a gun, and a reported conviction like his would have stopped the sale. Without the record, Kelley passed the check each time he bought a gun from a store. In 2021 Judge Xavier Rodriguez, a federal judge, found that federal officials had failed "to exercise reasonable care" in sending his criminal record to the FBI. He held the United States government 60 percent responsible for the harm. He wrote that if the government had reported the record, it was "more likely than not" that Kelley would have been deterred, or put off, from the shooting.

On Saturday morning, October 27, 2018, three Jewish congregations, Tree of Life, Dor Hadash and New Light, were at prayer in one building in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. Twelve Tree of Life members were in the chapel, partway through the opening prayers. Audrey Glickman had begun the service. David Rosenthal, who could not read but had memorized every prayer and song, was helping to lead it, and his brother Cecil was one of the greeters. In Dor Hadash's room, three men were setting out prayer books and copies of the Torah, the Jewish scriptures. They were Jerry Rabinowitz, a doctor, Daniel Leger, a hospital chaplain, a minister who serves patients, and Martin Gaynor. Downstairs, Richard Gottfried and Daniel Stein of New Light were in the kitchen making a meal for a breakfast the next day.

Robert Bowers came in with three handguns and a rifle and killed eleven people: Jerry Rabinowitz, David Rosenthal, Cecil Rosenthal, Rose Mallinger, Bernice Simon, Sylvan Simon, Joyce Fienberg, Irving Younger, Richard Gottfried, Daniel Stein and Melvin Wax. The youngest was 54, and Rose Mallinger was 97. Two more worshippers were badly wounded, and five police officers were injured going in after him. Federal prosecutors charged him with eleven counts of obstructing the free exercise of religious beliefs resulting in death, among other crimes. He was sentenced to death on August 3, 2023.

#### Two attacks on churches in 2025

On Wednesday, August 27, 2025, children at the Church of the Annunciation in Minneapolis were at an all-school Mass, the Catholic worship service, in the first week of school. A shooter fired through the church windows at them in the pews. Two children were killed. Twenty-six children and three adults were wounded by gunfire, and one more person was hurt in another way, according to the City of Minneapolis. NPR reported that the shooter was Robin Westman, 23, who then fatally shot themself at the scene, according to police. NPR reported that FBI officials called it an act of domestic terrorism, an attack meant to frighten people inside the country. They said it was driven by a "hate-filled ideology," a set of hateful ideas.

On Sunday, September 28, 2025, members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints were at services in their meetinghouse in Grand Blanc Township, Michigan. Thomas Jacob Sanford, 40, of Burton, Michigan, drove his pickup truck through the front doors. He opened fire and set the building on fire. He killed four people: Craig Hayden, Pat Howard, John Bond and Thelma Armstrong. Nine others, aged 6 to 78, were wounded. Police shot him dead within 3 minutes and 43 seconds of the first 911 call, the television station WNEM reported. The reports of the attack give no settled reason for it.

In August 2026 the FBI released its count of hate crimes for 2025. By the Anti-Defamation League's reading of those figures, police reported 2,408 hate-crime incidents based on religion, and 1,528 of them, or 63 percent, were aimed at Jews. The Anti-Defamation League is a group that speaks out against anti-Semitism, the hatred of Jews. Staff of the Sikh Coalition, a group that speaks up for Sikhs, counted 177 incidents aimed at Sikhs in the FBI's figures for 2025, up from 142 in 2024.

#### What priests did to children, and what bishops did about it

Between 1950 and 2002, more than 4,000 Catholic priests in the United States were accused of sexually abusing children. Sexual abuse of a child means an adult using a child's body for sex. Church officials reported few of these priests to the police, and in Pennsylvania a grand jury, a group of citizens who hear evidence gathered by prosecutors, found that church leaders in six dioceses had hidden the abuse. In 2002 the Catholic bishops of the United States asked John Jay College of Criminal Justice, in New York, to study how many of their priests had done it. Researchers at the college published their report in February 2004. It was based on surveys covering 98 percent of the country's diocesan priests, the priests who serve in a bishop's region.

The report records accusations against 4,392 priests for the years 1950 to 2002, about 4 percent of all the priests who served in those years. These were accusations that had not been withdrawn and were not known to be false. In all, 10,667 people said they had been abused. Half of them were between 11 and 14 years old when it happened. Sixteen percent were between 8 and 10, and nearly 6 percent were younger than 7. Eighty-one percent were boys.

The acts reported most often were touching the child over or under the clothes. Next came the priest putting his mouth on the child's sex organs, the child being undressed, and rape or attempted rape. Rape means forcing sex on a person. Rape or attempted rape was reported in 22.4 percent of the cases. Most of the accused priests were said to have done more than one of these things to the same child. It happened most often in the priest's own home or the parish house, the house beside the church where priests live, and next most often inside the church.

Only 384 of the 4,392 priests were ever charged with a crime. Victims reported fifteen percent of the priests to the police. The report says that dioceses and religious orders, the groups of priests, brothers or sisters who live under shared religious promises, reported "a much smaller number." Before 1993, church officials knew of only a third of the cases at all. The dioceses and religious orders reported that they had already paid $472 million for victims, for treating priests and for lawyers, and 14 percent of them gave no figure.

Accusations kept coming after the report. The Center for Applied Research in the Apostolate at Georgetown University counts the accusations made since 2004 by the years in which the abuse is said to have happened. It counts 4,216 for the ten years of the 1960s. For five-year spans it counts 2,813 for 1970 to 1974, 2,712 for 1975 to 1979, 2,113 for 1980 to 1984 and 266 for 1995 to 1999. For the three years 2020 to 2022 it counts 36. These are accusations made years afterward. They are not a count of everything that happened in each period, and one priest can be accused by more than one person.

In August 2018 a grand jury in Pennsylvania released a report on six of the state's Catholic dioceses. The jurors read half a million pages of the dioceses' own internal records. They found believable accusations against more than three hundred priests. They identified more than one thousand children from the church's own records, and they wrote that they believed the real number was in the thousands. They wrote that most of the victims were boys and some were girls, some were teenagers, and many were young children whose bodies had not yet begun to grow into adult bodies. Some were raped. "But all of them were brushed aside, in every part of the state, by church leaders who preferred to protect the abusers and their institution above all."

The grand jury set out what it called a playbook for hiding the truth. Its first item was to use mild words instead of real ones in church documents: never to write "rape," but "inappropriate contact" or "boundary issues" instead. In the grand jury's account, church officials let fellow priests ask the questions rather than trained investigators. When they removed a priest, they told his parish he was on "sick leave," or said nothing. They kept paying for his housing and living costs. If people found out, they moved him to a new place "where no one will know he is a child abuser." The last item was "Finally and above all, don't tell the police." Because of this hiding, the jurors wrote, "almost every instance of abuse we found is too old to be prosecuted."

In May 2026 the bishops released their own yearly audit, a check of their records, for July 2024 to June 2025. It records 1,070 new accusations made by 973 people, OSV News, a Catholic news service, reported. Only 24 of them came from people who were still children. Most of the rest concerned abuse that had happened decades earlier. Diocesan officials reported $389.9 million in costs connected with abuse that year.

Members of the Executive Committee of the Southern Baptist Convention, a large group of Baptist churches, hired an outside firm, Guidepost Solutions, to look at how they had handled abuse. The firm published its report in May 2022. It states that people who reported abuse "were met, time and time again, with resistance, stonewalling, and even outright hostility." Stonewalling means refusing to answer or act. The firm's investigators found that two former leaders, D. August Boto and Roger Oldham, had kept a private list of ministers accused of abuse. On May 26, 2022, the committee released the list, 205 pages long, NBC News reported.

#### A sacred place traded to a mining company, 2014 to 2026

Members of Congress ordered in 2014 that Oak Flat, a place where Apache people pray, be traded to a mining company, and in March 2026 the trade was completed. Oak Flat, called Chí'chil Biłdagoteel in Western Apache, is a place in the Tonto National Forest in Arizona where Apache people hold ceremonies, among them the Sunrise Ceremony. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2016. The company is Resolution Copper, owned by the mining companies Rio Tinto and BHP. Members of Congress put the order into the yearly bill that pays for the armed forces. With the exchange of about 2,400 acres in March 2026, the land became private property. Company officials expect the mine to leave a crater about two miles wide within about forty years, the radio station KJZZ reported.

#### A church divides, 2019 to 2024

More than a quarter of the United Methodist Church's American congregations left it between 2019 and the end of 2023. Its members had argued over gay members and gay ministers since at least 1984, when the church banned making gay people ministers. Gay means attracted to people of the same sex. In 2019, at a special General Conference, delegates added a rule. The General Conference is the gathering where delegates write the church's rules. Under the rule, a congregation could leave the denomination, the whole group of United Methodist churches, and keep its buildings for "reasons of conscience" over the church's decisions about homosexuality, another word for being gay. The rule ran out on December 31, 2023. By then more than 7,600 congregations in the United States had left under it, about 26 percent of the church's American congregations.

On May 1, 2024, at the General Conference in Charlotte, North Carolina, the delegates voted 692 to 51 to remove a ban that had been in the church's rule book since 1984. It had banned making gay people ministers, in the rule's words "self-avowed practicing homosexuals," meaning gay people who said so openly and lived as gay people. Delegates at the same conference also removed the ban on ministers and churches holding weddings for same-sex couples.

#### A prisoner's dreadlocks, 2020 to 2026

Damon Landor was a prisoner at the Raymond Laborde Correctional Center in Louisiana. In 2020, on the warden's order, guards there handcuffed Landor to a chair and shaved off his dreadlocks. Landor had grown them for decades under a Rastafarian vow, a religious promise not to cut his hair. He showed the guards a court decision, and they threw it away. He had three weeks left to serve. Landor sued under the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act, a federal law that protects the religious practice of people held in prisons. On June 23, 2026, the justices of the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that he could not sue the individual officers for money under that law. Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote for the majority. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson dissented, joined by Justices Sotomayor and Kagan. Published accounts of the case do not name the guards.

#### Worship on a screen

By November 2022, 27 percent of American adults were watching religious services on a screen. Between November 16 and 27, 2022, researchers at the Pew Research Center asked 11,377 adults how they took part in worship. Pew published the answers in June 2023. Sixteen percent were regularly going to services in person only, 10 percent were regularly watching only on a screen, and 17 percent were doing both. In all, 43 percent were attending or watching at least once a month, and 57 percent were doing neither. Among those who did both, 76 percent said they would rather be in the room. The reason people gave most often for watching on a screen was that it was convenient.

#### The churches answer for the boarding schools, 2022 to 2024

Catholic leaders apologized between 2022 and 2024 for the church's part in the boarding schools for Native children. Religious groups ran 210 of the 417 federal Indian boarding schools in the United States. At the 417 schools, staff cut children's hair, forbade their languages and beat them, and at least 973 children died, by the count of investigators at the Department of the Interior. On July 25, 2022, in Canada, Pope Francis asked forgiveness "for the ways in which many members of the Church and of religious communities cooperated, not least through their indifference, in projects of cultural destruction and forced assimilation." Forced assimilation means making people give up their own ways of life. He was speaking of Canada's schools.

On March 30, 2023, officials at the Vatican, the headquarters of the Catholic Church in Rome, rejected the Doctrine of Discovery. Catholic News Service described it as a set of old writings by popes that "appeared to bless the efforts of explorers to colonize and claim the lands of any people who were not Christian." The Vatican officials said it "is not part of the teaching of the Catholic Church." On June 14, 2024, the bishops of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops voted 181 to 2 to adopt a document called "Keeping Christ's Sacred Promise." It is a formal apology for the Catholic Church's part in the schools in the United States. The Interior Department's 2024 report on the schools states that its authors know of no support from the bishops' conference for a Pope's apology for the schools in the United States.

#### Prayer at a football game, 2000

Families went to court again and again from 2000 on over religion in public schools and public money for religious schools. One case, decided on June 19, 2000, was about football. Before 1995, at Santa Fe High School in Texas, a student elected as chaplain of the student council said a prayer over the loudspeakers before every home game of the school's top football team. The chaplain was the student who said the prayers. District officials then set up two student elections. One decided whether to have prayers at the games, and the other chose who would give them. Two families sued. One was Mormon and one was Catholic. On June 19, 2000, in *Santa Fe Independent School District v. Doe*, the justices of the Supreme Court struck down the policy.

#### Public money and religious schools, 2022

The justices of the Supreme Court ruled in 2022 that Maine's officials could not refuse to pay for a child's schooling because the school taught religion. Under Maine law, the state pays the fees for children who live in towns with no high school of their own. Since 1981 it had paid only for schools that were nonsectarian, meaning not tied to any religious group.

David and Amy Carson of Glenburn, Maine, sent their daughter to Bangor Christian Schools, which Bangor Baptist Church had founded in 1970. They paid her fees themselves. Troy and Angela Nelson of Palermo, Maine, sent their son to Temple Academy, a school connected with Centerpoint Community Church. They could not afford its fees for their daughter too, so she went to a private school that was not religious. On June 21, 2022, in *Carson v. Makin*, the justices ruled 6 to 3 for the families.

Justice Breyer, who disagreed, quoted the two schools' own descriptions of their teaching. One of Bangor Christian's goals is "lead[ing] each unsaved student to trust Christ as his/her personal savior." "Unsaved" meant a student who did not yet believe in Christ. School officials said there was no way to separate its religious teaching from its other teaching. Temple Academy said the Bible is used in every subject it teaches. In mathematics that meant teaching that a creator made the universe so that "one plus one is always going to be two."

<a id="story-joseph-kennedy-bremerton"></a>

#### Joseph Kennedy

> **Who:** A high school football coach who was put on paid leave over his prayers on the field after games, and who won his case in the Supreme Court.
>
> **When and where:** Bremerton, Washington, 2008 to 2022.

Joseph Kennedy was put on paid leave from coaching over prayers he said on the football field, and in 2022 the justices of the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that the school district's officials could not punish him for his prayers. He spent nearly twenty years in the Marine Corps. In 2008 he began coaching football at Bremerton High School in Washington State. After each game, once the players and coaches had shaken hands, he knelt at the 50-yard line and prayed for about thirty seconds.

At first he prayed alone. Then players asked whether they could join him, and he told them, "This is a free country. You can do what you want." After some games most of the team knelt with him. Sometimes players from the other team were invited to join. He began adding short speeches to encourage the players when others were there. No one complained for more than seven years.

In September 2015 an employee of another school praised the practice to Bremerton's principal, and the district's superintendent found out. On September 17, 2015, district officials wrote to Kennedy. On October 16 they wrote again, forbidding "any overt actions" while he was on duty that could look like the school supporting prayer. He prayed after the games of October 16, 23 and 26. On October 16 most of his players were singing the school fight song, and players from the other team and people from the crowd joined him before he finished. On October 23 no one joined him. On October 26 other adults gathered around him while he knelt. After that game, district officials put him on paid leave and barred him from the football program.

On June 27, 2022, in *Kennedy v. Bremerton School District*, the justices ruled for him, 6 to 3. Justice Gorsuch wrote for the majority that the First Amendment protects "an individual engaging in a personal religious observance from government reprisal," which means punishment by government officials.

Justice Sotomayor, who disagreed, described what happened differently. She wrote: "To the degree the Court portrays petitioner Joseph Kennedy's prayers as private and quiet, it misconstrues the facts." A petitioner is the person who brings a case to the Court. She wrote that the record showed that he "consistently invited others to join his prayers and for years led student athletes in prayer at the same time and location." The nine justices read the same record and described the events in two different ways.

#### The Ten Commandments in the classroom, 2024 to 2026

Louisiana's lawmakers passed a law requiring every public school classroom to display the Ten Commandments, and Governor Jeff Landry signed it on June 19, 2024. Families of several faiths sued to stop it. In 1980, in *Stone v. Graham*, the justices of the Supreme Court had struck down a Kentucky law that required the same thing. Louisiana's law requires a poster or framed copy at least 11 inches by 14 inches, with the Commandments as its "central focus" in large print. The law sets out the exact wording, which begins "I AM the LORD thy God."

The parents who sued include ministers and Jewish parents. The case is named for one of them, the Reverend Darcy Roake. A Jewish parent swore that the law "misappropriates a Jewish text, ripping it from its Jewish context." Misappropriates means takes and misuses something that belongs to others. The parent said it then requires the changed text to be shown to non-Jews, "in violation of core Jewish tenets that oppose proselytizing." Tenets are the main rules of a faith. Proselytizing means trying to convert people to a religion. Another Jewish parent objected that Louisiana's version leaves out the freeing of the Jews from slavery in Egypt, "a key piece of the Ten Commandments and of the Jewish story." A Presbyterian minister who is also a parent objected to the state putting its "stamp of approval" on one version.

A federal judge blocked the law, and on June 20, 2025, three judges of the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals, the federal appeals court for Louisiana, Texas and Mississippi, agreed. Then all the judges of the Fifth Circuit reheard the case, and on February 20, 2026, they lifted the order blocking the law. The law is called House Bill 71, or H.B. 71. The judges wrote that the question before them was "not whether H.B. 71 is constitutional, but whether that issue is fit for judicial resolution at this time." They held that it was too early to decide. Three judges wrote dissents. As of September 2026, no court had decided whether Louisiana's law breaks the Constitution.

Texas's lawmakers passed a similar law. Rabbi Mara Nathan is one of the parents suing over it. She objects that the required text "erases this foundational Jewish tenet and historical context." On April 21, 2026, the full Fifth Circuit's judges ruled 9 to 8 that the Texas law does not violate the First Amendment's religion clauses, the two parts of the amendment about religion. On August 17, 2026, the Texas families asked the Supreme Court to hear their case. As of late September 2026 the Court had not said whether it would.

#### Storybooks and parents' faith, 2025

Members of the school board of Montgomery County, Maryland, added five storybooks with LGBTQ+ characters for children from kindergarten to fifth grade in the 2022 to 2023 school year. LGBTQ+ stands for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer people and others. At first board members let parents take their children out of those lessons. Then they ended that choice.

Parents of several faiths sued. Tamer Mahmoud and Enas Barakat are Muslims. Jeff Roman is Catholic and Svitlana Roman is Ukrainian Orthodox. Chris and Melissa Persak are Catholics. On June 27, 2025, in *Mahmoud v. Taylor*, the justices of the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 that the parents were entitled to have their children excused while the case went on. Justice Alito wrote for the majority. He relied on the 1972 Amish case, *Wisconsin v. Yoder*, and its holding that parents have a right "to direct the religious upbringing of their children."

Justice Sotomayor wrote for the three who disagreed. She wrote that public schools "offer to children of all faiths and backgrounds an education and an opportunity to practice living in our multicultural society." She warned that this "will become a mere memory if children must be insulated from exposure to ideas and concepts that may conflict with their parents' religious beliefs."

#### Fewer sisters to teach in the Catholic schools

Members of religious orders built and staffed the Catholic school system of the 1800s, and by 2025 there was about one Catholic sister in the United States for every five there had been in 1965. Sisters, also called nuns, are women who belong to Catholic religious orders, groups whose members make religious promises and live and work together. The Center for Applied Research in the Apostolate at Georgetown University takes its figures from the Catholic Church's own yearly directory. Its researchers counted 178,740 religious sisters in the United States in 1965, 79,814 in 2000, and 33,135 on January 1, 2025.

Over the same sixty years, Catholic elementary schools fell from 9,366 to 4,606, and Catholic high schools from 1,986 to 1,178. Priests fell from 59,426 to 33,462. In 1965, 530 parishes had no priest living there as pastor. In 2025, 3,674 did not. The same center estimates from surveys that 54.9 percent of Catholics went to Mass every week in 1970, and 17.6 percent in 2025.

#### Teaching religion at home

Some parents teach their children at home so that they can teach them religion. The National Center for Education Statistics, part of the U.S. Department of Education, surveyed parents of homeschooled children aged 5 to 17 about the 2022 to 2023 school year. It published the answers in September 2024. Fifty-three percent said that wanting to give religious instruction was an important reason for homeschooling, and 11 percent said it was the most important reason. More parents named a concern about the environment of other schools. That was important to 83 percent and the most important reason for 28 percent.

<a id="ch-education"></a>

## Chapter 30: School and Education

### Before 1500

Before 1500, the children of the Native nations in this land learned from their own families and communities. There were no school buildings, no grades and no school year. Nobody taught as a full-time job. Children learned skills by working beside the adults who had them. They learned their nation's history from the spoken words of adults who kept it in memory.

#### Learning by doing and by listening

The Blackfeet are one nation whose way of teaching is described in a National Park Service account. It states that "Blackfeet children learned by doing, by example, and through apprenticeship to their elders." An apprentice is a young person who learns a skill by working next to someone who already has it. Elders are the older people of a community. The same account states that on long winter evenings, adults passed on the nation's history and ways of life around a fire the whole group shared.

Teaching by the spoken word is called oral tradition. A teaching page from the Smithsonian's National Museum of the American Indian states that "the oral tradition continues to be an integral part of Indigenous teaching and learning." Integral means a necessary part of the whole. Indigenous means belonging to the first peoples of a land. Native families and teachers still teach this way today.

#### Memory in place of writing: wampum

No writing system was in use in this land before 1500. The first one made for a language spoken in what is now the United States was the Cherokee syllabary, in 1821. A syllabary is a set of written signs in which each sign stands for one syllable. Without writing, a nation kept its agreements and its history in people's memories, in speech, and in objects made to help people remember. Some people were trained to hold those memories and recite them.

The Haudenosaunee Confederacy is a union of five nations: the Seneca, Cayuga, Onondaga, Oneida and Mohawk. Its people record agreements and history in wampum. Wampum is beads cut from the white and purple parts of clam shells, strung on strings or woven into belts. The Onondaga Nation says it was made the Wampum Keeper, the nation that looks after the belts, at the founding of the Great Law of Peace, when the five nations joined. The Onondaga Nation's own account describes how a speaker puts a record into a belt: "The speaker puts the words of the agreement into the wampum as the strings or belts are woven together." After that, "each speaker thereafter uses the wampum to remember the initial agreement and the history that has happened to date." The Onondaga call the belts "our living history."

So a speaker had to hold the agreement in memory and recite it, with the belt as the reminder. People still disagree about when the Great Law of Peace was agreed, and no record shows which date is right. In the Haudenosaunee people's own oral tradition, it was founded between about 1000 and 1400. Accounts based on written records put it at about 1450, and some put it in the late 1100s.

#### No names survive

No pupil or teacher from this land before 1500 is known by name. With no writing system, no one made a written list of the people who taught or learned. No count exists either, of children taught or of people who could recite a record.

### The 1500s

No schoolhouse stood in this land in the 1500s. The only European teaching was done by Spanish priests at their missions. A mission was a settlement where priests worked to make Native people into Catholics. Spanish priests set up missions in Florida. In Virginia a mission lasted a few months, in 1570 and 1571. In New Mexico the first missions came at the very end of the century. The priests taught reading at some missions, but their purpose was conversion, which means changing a person's religion. Outside the missions, Native children went on learning from their families by the spoken word, the oral tradition that Native teachers still use today.

#### Mission teaching in Florida

In September 1565 Pedro Menéndez de Avilés and about 800 Spanish colonists came to the Timucua town of a chief named Seloy. The group included 26 women and an unknown number of enslaved Africans. They made their first settlement in Seloy's town and used his council house as their first fort. That settlement became St. Augustine. The Florida Museum of Natural History's account of the settlement does not say what happened to Seloy's people afterward.

Spanish priests began trying to convert Native people in Florida within a few years. By the 1580s, friars of the Franciscan order had missions across Florida. A friar is a member of a Catholic religious order who has promised to live in poverty. One of the largest missions, San Juan del Puerto, stood on Fort George Island among the Mocama, a coastal people who spoke Timucua. The National Park Service's history of the mission states only that it began "sometime in the 1570s."

At a mission the friars taught Catholic doctrine, meaning the beliefs of the church. They also taught European customs, farming, and reading and writing. They taught in Spanish and in Timucua, the local language.

Father Francisco Pareja, the friar who did the teaching at San Juan del Puerto, wrote this report of his own pupils: "many Indian men and women have learned to read in less than six months, and they write letters to one another in their own language."

#### New Mexico, 1598

Juan de Oñate led a Spanish expedition of colonists to the upper Rio Grande in 1598. Franciscan missions in New Mexico, and the religious teaching at them, began that year.

<a id="story-paquiquineo-don-luis"></a>

#### Paquiquineo (Don Luís de Velasco)

> **Who:** A young man from the Chesapeake Bay country who was taught by Spanish priests for years and came home with a Jesuit mission.
>
> **When and where:** 1561 to 1572. The Chesapeake, Spain, Mexico, and back.

Paquiquineo is the one person of the 1500s whose schooling by Europeans is recorded by name and by date. That schooling led to a Spanish mission to this land. No pupil of a 1500s mission school in Florida or New Mexico is known by name.

He was about seventeen when he left the Chesapeake on a Spanish ship in late June 1561. Whether he went willingly or was kidnapped is disputed, and the record does not settle it. Spanish captains of the time regularly captured boys and young men to serve as interpreters, people who translate between two languages. He came from the Powhatan chiefdoms, groups of towns each led by a chief. He may have come from a Paspahegh, Kiskiack or Kecoughtan family, and the record does not show which.

He reached Seville, in Spain, on September 9, 1561, was in Madrid by the end of October, and met King Philip II. In 1562 he sailed to Mexico. He fell so ill there that he was close to death, and he was baptized in Mexico City. Baptism is the Christian ceremony of joining the church. He took the name of the viceroy of New Spain, the king's ruler in Mexico: Don Luís de Velasco.

From 1566 to 1570 he studied in Seville with the Jesuits, an order of Catholic priests. No surviving record says what they taught him in those four years.

Paquiquineo had promised Father Juan Bautista de Segura, the Jesuit leader in Florida, that many people in his homeland would become Christians. Segura planned a mission there on that promise. In September 1570 Paquiquineo landed on the James River with Segura's party of Jesuits, and his own people welcomed them. Encyclopedia Virginia states that soon after, he "appears to have left the missionaries" and gone back to his own family.

In February 1571 Segura sent Father Quirós and two Brothers, Gabriel de Solís and Juan Baptista Méndez, to meet him. A Brother was a Jesuit who was not a priest. On February 4, 1571, Paquiquineo killed the three Jesuits. Then he and his companions surrounded the mission house and killed Father Segura and the other Spaniards. The only one left alive was the altar boy, Alonso de Olmos, a boy who helped the priests during church services.

In August 1572 the Spanish governor of Florida, Pedro Menéndez de Avilés, sent soldiers to the James River. They captured some of Paquiquineo's people in a fight. Spanish soldiers hanged several of them from the yardarms of their ship, the wooden beams that cross the masts. One of the hanged men wore a paten around his neck, the metal dish the priests used in their main church service, the Mass. The Spanish records do not give the names of the men they hanged. The Powhatan people handed Alonso de Olmos back. The soldiers did not find Paquiquineo, and no European record mentions him again.

### The 1600s

In the 1600s the English colonists of Massachusetts made teaching children to read a duty under law. The men who wrote the laws gave a religious reason: children had to be able to read the Bible for themselves. Schooling was not free. Parents or masters paid the teacher, and the Latin schools took only boys. Outside New England, children learned at home, as apprentices, or at a few schools such as a Dutch one in Manhattan. In New England, colonists also opened schools and a college building for Native students, with the aim of making them Christian.

#### Boston Latin School, 1635

Boston Latin School opened on April 23, 1635, and it is still open. It is the oldest public school in the country. A public school is one that a town or a state runs for its children. Boston stood on the Shawmut peninsula, which the Massachusett people called Mushauwomuk, "the boat landing place." It was part of the land of the Massachusett nation, whose chief sachem, or leader, was Chickataubut. Between 1616 and 1618 an epidemic swept the region. An epidemic is a disease that spreads fast through a population. By the West End Museum's count, it killed about 75,000 of the region's 100,000 people. In 1630 John Winthrop and about 1,000 English settlers arrived on the peninsula.

On April 13, 1635, the townsmen of Boston met and agreed to ask Philemon Pormort to teach. The town record states that he "shall be intreated to become scholemaster for the teaching and nourtering of children with us." Intreated means asked, and nourtering means bringing up. The record gives the date as "the second month," which was April, because the English year then began on March 25. The first classes met in Pormort's own house. The boys learned Latin and Greek.

The leaders of Collegiate School in New York City say their school is the oldest in the country. Dutch colonists founded it. In 1982 the school's leaders moved its founding date back from 1638 to 1628, the year the minister Jonas Michaelius began teaching in Manhattan. The two schools' claims to be oldest of all have never been settled.

#### The two Massachusetts school laws

In 1642 the men of the Massachusetts General Court passed the first law in this land that ordered children to be taught to read. The General Court was the colony's group of lawmakers. Under the law, parents and masters had to teach their children and apprentices to "read the English tongue." A master was the adult an apprentice lived with and worked for. Children also had to know the "Capital Lawes," the colony's list of crimes that were punished by death. The lawmakers set up no school and hired no teacher. Selectmen, the men elected to run a town's business, visited homes to check. A family that failed could be fined. The selectmen could also take a child or an apprentice away and place the child with another master who would do the teaching.

Many families ignored that law, so the men of the General Court passed a second one in 1647. Its opening words state the reason. It is "one of the chief projects of that old deluder Satan to keep men from the knowledge of the Scriptures." A deluder is someone who tricks people, and the Scriptures are the Bible. For that reason people call it the Old Deluder Satan Act. The lawmakers wanted every child able to read the Bible without help.

Under the 1647 law, the men of every town of 50 households had to choose someone to teach children to read and write. The parents or masters paid that teacher's wages. The men of every town of 100 families also had to set up a grammar school, a school that taught Latin, to prepare boys "for the university." That meant Harvard College, founded in 1636. If a town's men did not obey the law, the town had to pay 5 pounds, in English money, every year to the nearest school until they did. Lawmakers in the other New England colonies passed similar laws. Rhode Island's did not.

#### The New England Primer

A primer is a first reading book. The English printer Benjamin Harris made *The New England Primer* for buyers in the colonies sometime between 1687 and 1690. That range comes from the American Antiquarian Society. The records of how the book was first printed are lost, so the Society's dates rest only on advertisements by printers and booksellers. The first of them is one Harris placed in 1690. No copy printed before 1727 is known to survive. The Society holds a copy of that 1727 edition.

The book contained lessons in reading, spelling and religious rules for behavior, all mixed together. Each letter of the alphabet had a small woodcut, a picture printed from a carved block of wood. After the alphabet, the 1727 edition gives this instruction: "let him learn these and such like Sentences by Heart." Children were expected to memorize the sentences and recite them.

<a id="story-ezekiel-cheever"></a>

#### Ezekiel Cheever

> **Who:** A schoolmaster who taught Latin and Greek for 70 years, the last 38 of them as head of the Boston Latin School.
>
> **When and where:** Born in London in 1615. Died in Boston on August 21, 1708. Taught at New Haven, Charlestown and Boston.
