Ezekiel Cheever taught Latin and Greek for 70 years without a break. The Database of Classical Scholars, kept at Rutgers University, states that this is longer than anyone else in the history of this country.

He was born in London on January 25, 1615. Some sources give 1614, because the English calendar then began the year on March 25, so January fell in the old year. He ran the schools at New Haven from 1638 and taught at Charlestown from 1661. On December 29, 1670, he was invited to head the Boston Latin School. He was still teaching there when he died at 93.

Accounts of his classroom describe a smoky fireplace, poor light, and "a bundle of birch rods beside his desk." A birch rod is a thin stick or bundle of twigs cut from a birch tree, used to beat a child.

Cotton Mather had been one of his pupils. He preached at Cheever's funeral and called him a teacher "than whom New England had known no better." Cheever's Latin textbook, *A Short Introduction to the Latin Tongue*, was printed in Boston in 1708, the year he died. Schools used it for nearly 200 years, longer than any other Latin textbook printed in this country.

#### Beaten at school: John Barnard

In the 1600s the rod was standard equipment in a schoolroom. One of Ezekiel Cheever's pupils wrote down what it was like. John Barnard was born in Boston on November 6, 1681. In the spring of 1689, when he was seven, he was sent to Cheever's school. He left after a few weeks and came back about a year and a half later. He stayed until he entered Harvard at fifteen.

Cheever told Barnard openly that he played too much and kept his classmates from their lessons. Cheever said that "if any of them cannot perform their duty, I shall correct you for it." To correct a child, in the words of that time, meant to beat him. When one classmate did not know his lesson, "our master beat me," Barnard wrote. The other boy saw this and neglected his book on purpose, "for which I was still corrected, and that for several days." Barnard beat that boy after school, and the boy never came back.

Barnard wrote that he was "often beaten for my play." Once Cheever set the class to turn the stories called Aesop's fables into Latin verse. Barnard could not do it. Cheever beat him for it "two or three days going," until Barnard told him he had tried his hardest. Then Cheever stopped asking it of him. Barnard does not say what Cheever hit him with, or how many times. He wrote his account as an old man, in the late 1760s, and it was printed in 1836.

The saying "spare the rod and spoil the child" is not in the Bible, though it comes close to one verse. Proverbs 13:24 says that whoever spares the rod hates their children, but the words "spoil the child" are not in it. Ælfric of Eynsham, an English monk, wrote the oldest known English version. A monk is a man who lives in a religious community and has given his life to God. Ælfric lived from about 950 to about 1010 and wrote: "He who spareth his rod hateth his child." Spareth means spares, and hateth means hates. The wording people use now comes from a comic poem, *Hudibras*, by Samuel Butler: "Then spare the Rod, and spill the Child." Later speakers changed "spill" to "spoil." Accounts give 1662, 1663 and 1664 for the part of the poem with that line.

#### Natick's school, and Deer Island

In 1651 the English minister John Eliot and a group of Native leaders founded Natick, in Massachusetts, on a bend of the Charles River. Waban and Cutshamekin of the Massachusett nation and John Speen of the Nipmuc nation worked on it with him. Natick was the first of more than a dozen "praying towns," towns set up for Native people who had become Christians. Natick had a meetinghouse with a school inside it. The schoolmaster was a Massachusett man named Monequassun.

Eliot printed schoolbooks in the Massachusett language: a catechism in 1653 and an *Indian Primer* in 1669. A catechism is a list of religious questions and answers that a pupil learns by heart. In each of these schoolbooks, the reading lessons were also lessons in Christian belief.

In 1675 war began between the English colonists of New England and a group of Native nations led by Metacom, a sachem, or leader, of the Wampanoag. The English called him King Philip, so they called it King Philip's War. On October 13, 1675, the men who governed the Massachusetts colony ordered the Christian Native people of the praying towns taken to Deer Island in Boston Harbor and held there as prisoners. Colonists set up the prison camp. They started with the people of Natick. The surviving accounts do not name the men who voted for the order. The National Park Service's page on the island states that about 500 to 1,100 people were held there that winter, most of them women and children.

On Deer Island the prisoners starved and froze through the winter without shelter. The Park Service page states: "Due to starvation, freezing temperatures and lack of shelter, very few survived internment." Internment means being held prisoner in a camp. Members of a Boston history group, the Partnership of Historic Bostons, estimate that more than half of them died. Colonists released the survivors in May 1676. An unknown number of people were smuggled off the island and sold into slavery in the West Indies or in Tangier, in North Africa. No record names the men who took them off the island and sold them. No record says what became of Monequassun, the Natick schoolmaster. Every year, descendants of the Native nations of that war hold a remembrance of their ancestors on Deer Island.

#### Harvard, the Indian College, and the people Harvard men enslaved

A charter is an official paper from a government that creates or recognizes a school or another group. Harvard's charter of 1650 included a promise of "the education of the English and Indian youth of this Country." A building called the Indian College stood in Harvard Yard from 1655. Accounts differ on when it came down. Harvard Magazine says it fell down in 1695, and Harvard's Native American Program says it stood until 1698. A printing press kept inside it printed the first Bible published in North America, in 1663, in the Algonquian language.

Only a handful of Native students came to the Indian College. Caleb Cheeshahteaumuck graduated in 1665. His classmate Joel Iacoomes drowned in a shipwreck just before the graduation ceremony. Two more students died of disease before they finished, and one left to become a sailor.

Harvard's leaders and staff also enslaved people. In April 2022 the members of a Harvard committee led by Tomiko Brown-Nagin reported records of "at least 79 people who were enslaved by Harvard presidents, overseers, and faculty and staff members" before slavery was outlawed in Massachusetts in 1783. Overseers were the men on one of Harvard's governing boards. A woman named Jane was enslaved by the college steward Andrew Bordman, who enslaved at least eight people. A steward is the man in charge of a household's food and supplies. A woman named Cicely was enslaved by William Brattle, who taught students at the college and kept its money. Titus, Venus, Juba and Bilhah were enslaved at Wadsworth House, where they were made to live and work for two Harvard presidents.

<a id="story-caleb-cheeshahteaumuck"></a>

#### Caleb Cheeshahteaumuck

> **Who:** A Wampanoag student from Martha's Vineyard, the first Native American to graduate from Harvard.
>
> **When and where:** Graduated in 1665 in Cambridge, Massachusetts. Died in 1666.

Caleb Cheeshahteaumuck was the first Native American to graduate from Harvard. He took his degree in 1665. He came from a Wampanoag community on Martha's Vineyard, an island off the coast of Massachusetts.

One piece of his own writing survives. It is a short letter in Latin to the English donors who paid for the Indian College. It begins "Honoratissimi benefactores," which means "most honored benefactors." A benefactor is a person who gives money to help. The letter is often described as the earliest surviving writing by a Native person on this continent.

He died in 1666, within a year of his graduation, of a disease people then called consumption. One account says he died at Watertown, Massachusetts, when he was about twenty. Martha's Vineyard Magazine states that the disease was "presumably" tuberculosis, a disease of the lungs. Presumably means the writer judged it likely. No record from his time gives a diagnosis of tuberculosis.

Of the Native students who came to the Indian College in his time, he was the only one who finished.

#### Timucua in print

In Florida, Father Francisco Pareja wrote the Timucua language down in books printed in the early 1600s. He published three catechisms, a grammar, and a book of questions for confession, dated 1613. In confession a person tells a priest their sins. A grammar is a book that explains how a language works. Those books are now the only record of the Timucua language. Nobody speaks it today.

About 200,000 people who spoke Timucua lived in what is now northern Florida and southern Georgia in the 1500s, by the estimate of the historian Matthew Holt Jennings. Nobody counted them. By the 1650s about 2,000 were left. Most died in epidemics of diseases the Spanish had brought. After the English founded Charles Town in Carolina in 1670, Carolina slave traders and Native groups allied with them raided the Spanish missions again and again to capture people and sell them. In 1763, at the end of a war, Spain's rulers gave Florida to Britain, and Spanish officials shipped the last Timucua people to Cuba. The last Timucua of full descent died there in 1767.

### 1700 to 1750

In 1740 the lawmakers of South Carolina made it a crime to teach an enslaved person to write. It was the first law in these colonies that punished someone for teaching. Most other children in these fifty years learned at home, at a small school in a neighbor's kitchen, or as apprentices. The schools that did exist mostly took boys whose families could pay. Church societies in London paid for charity schools and for schoolmasters to cross the Atlantic. Two traders brought four captive Native boys to a college in Virginia to be its first Native pupils.

#### The law against teaching, 1740

On May 10, 1740, South Carolina's lawmakers passed "An Act for the Better Ordering and Governing Negroes and Other Slaves in This Province." In that title, "Negroes" is an old word for Black people. They passed it the year after the Stono Rebellion of 1739. In that uprising about 20 enslaved men near Charleston took up weapons and marched toward Spanish Florida, where they hoped to be free. They killed about 25 white colonists. William Bull, the lieutenant governor, or deputy governor, called out armed planters, who killed about 35 to 50 of the rebels. Colonists cut off the heads of some rebels and set them on stakes along the roads. The act names the men who made it law. They were Bull, who was acting as the colony's head, the King's Council, and the Commons House of Assembly. The Council and the Commons House were the colony's two groups of lawmakers. The act does not name the members who drafted it.

Section 45 of the act states its reason in these words: "the having of slaves taught to write, or suffering them to be employed in writing, may be attended with great inconveniences." It then states that anyone who teaches an enslaved person to write, or has one taught, or uses one as a scribe, "shall, for every such offense, forfeit the sum of one hundred pounds current money." A scribe is a person who writes documents for someone else. To forfeit means to lose as a punishment.

The teacher owed the fine, not the pupil. Under another section of the act, a person could collect the fine by suing the teacher in court. Half the money went to the colony. The other half went to whoever reported or sued. That gave anyone a reason to watch for a teacher and turn the teacher in.

Under the act, teaching writing was a crime and teaching reading was not. The act gives only "great inconveniences" as its reason. An enslaver's own words, from later in the century, show one danger enslavers saw in writing. A pass was a note from an enslaver that let an enslaved person travel. A person who could write could forge a pass, which means write a fake one, and escape with it. In 1774 one enslaver, Lewis Burwell, advertised for Isaac Bee, a young man who had run away from him, and warned that he "may easily get some One to forge a Pass for him."

#### Harry and Andrew's school in Charleston

About three years after the law, a school for Black pupils opened in Charleston, South Carolina. The historian Carter G. Woodson wrote about it in 1915. The Society for the Propagation of the Gospel was a group in London run by members of the Church of England, England's own Protestant church. In Woodson's account, the Society's leaders bought two young Black men named Harry and Andrew, and from then on the Society owned them as slaves. Woodson does not say who sold them. The Society's leaders bought them in order to train them as teachers "to their people." Alexander Garden, a Church of England official in Charleston, had a schoolhouse built for about 308 pounds. Harry and Andrew taught in it.

Accounts give 1743 or 1744 for the opening. The school began with about sixty young pupils. It also ran in the evenings for people who worked in the day. Woodson judged it "highly probable" that after the 1740 law only free Black people attended. The school closed in 1763, by Woodson's account in a later book, and some accounts give 1764. One of the two teachers had died, and the men who ran the Society judged that the other was not doing the job well.

#### Where a small child started: the dame school and the hornbook

In New England a small child usually learned to read first from a woman in her own home. This was called a dame school. Dame was an old word for a woman. The teacher took children from about three or four years old for a few hours a day, for a small fee. Often she was a widow or an unmarried woman who needed the money, and families paid her in eggs, firewood, or washing and ironing instead of cash. Her lessons covered the letters, reading, the catechism and the Lord's Prayer, and sewing for girls.

The town schools of New England would not take a boy until he could "stand up and read words of two syllables and keep their places." Somebody had to teach him that first, and that somebody was usually a woman in her kitchen. Women were already teaching, for very little pay, before a woman could hold a teaching job in a town school.

A child's first reading tool was often a hornbook. A hornbook was a wooden paddle about the shape of a table-tennis bat, with one printed sheet tacked to it. A thin, clear sheet of animal horn covered the paper so that it would not wear out. A leather cord through the handle let a child hang it from a belt. The sheet showed a cross, then the alphabet in capital and small letters, then the vowels joined to consonants, then the Lord's Prayer. Because of the cross at the top, the alphabet row was called the "Christ's Cross row," later shortened to "crisscross row." The Smithsonian Institution holds a hornbook made in the 1700s.

#### Charity schools

Some schools in the colonies were paid for from London. King William III gave a charter to the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in Foreign Parts on June 16, 1701. The minister Thomas Bray pushed for it, along with Bishop Henry Compton and others. The Society's stated job was to send priests and schoolmasters to the colonies. Across the 1700s its members paid for more than 300 of them to cross the Atlantic. Members of a separate group, the Associates of Dr. Bray, founded in 1724, set up schools of their own.

These were charity schools. A society in London paid the teacher. The men who ran the societies paid so that pupils could read the catechism and the Bible. These were not town schools, and the town did not run them.

#### How many people could read and write

Nobody surveyed how many colonists could read. Historians such as Kenneth Lockridge count signatures on wills and deeds instead. A will is a paper saying who gets a person's belongings after death, and a deed is a paper showing who owns land. A person who could write signed a name. A person who could not made a mark, such as an X. This method undercounts readers, because many children were taught to read and never taught to write. That was common for girls.

Lockridge counted men's signatures in New England. About 60 percent of white men could sign their names between 1650 and 1670. About 85 percent could sign between 1758 and 1762, and about 90 percent between 1787 and 1795. Lockridge's counts, and later counts built on his method, also cover women's signatures. For women, the figures follow the years they were born. Of women born between 1650 and 1669, 27 percent could sign. The share rose to 48 percent for women born between 1690 and 1709, and 81 percent for women born between 1730 and 1749. More people could sign in New England and the middle colonies than in the South, and more in towns than in the countryside.

An article in Encyclopedia Virginia gives an estimate: by 1775 as many as 5 percent of enslaved people in Virginia could read. One check on that number comes from enslavers themselves. Between 1736 and 1776 enslavers placed about 1,000 advertisements in the *Virginia Gazette*, a newspaper, to hunt for people who had run away. Fifty-five of the advertisements said the person could read or write.

#### Girls' schools: New Orleans and Pennsylvania

In 1727 a group of Ursuline nuns came to New Orleans from France and started a school for girls. A nun is a woman who lives in a religious community and has given her life to God, and the Ursulines are an order, or group, of Catholic nuns. New Orleans was then a French colony. It became part of the United States in 1803. The school's own history states that it is the oldest Catholic school in the United States and the oldest school for girls that has run without stopping. It also states that the nuns taught the first classes for enslaved Black women, free women of color and Native women.

In May 1742 Countess Benigna von Zinzendorf started classes for twenty-five girls at Germantown, near Philadelphia. She belonged to the Moravian Church, a Protestant church. Protestant churches are Christian churches that broke away from the Catholic Church. The school moved to Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, in 1745 and settled there in 1748. It took in mainly the daughters of traveling Moravian church workers. The Moravian schools' own histories describe it as the first Protestant boarding school for girls in what became the United States. A boarding school is one where pupils live as well as study.

#### Franklin's plan for an academy, 1749

In October 1749 Benjamin Franklin published *Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth in Pensilvania*. He argued for a school that taught in English instead of Latin and Greek. He wanted it to teach geography, natural history and modern languages. People called this kind of school an academy. An academy was a school for older pupils, a step above the town school and a step below a college.

#### What a school day was like, and what is not known

The one-room school with a stove, slates to write on, and a bench where pupils stood to recite is described in records of the 1800s. For 1700 to 1750 the records contain less. The men of a town appointed one man to teach, the parents or masters paid him, and children of every age sat in the same room because there was only one teacher.

#### The Indian school at William & Mary

The College of William & Mary in Virginia received its royal charter in 1693. The charter lists three purposes for the college. The third was to teach Native students "in the Christian Religion." Rents from a country estate in Yorkshire, England, bought in 1695 with 5,400 pounds from the estate of the scientist Robert Boyle, paid for this Indian school.

Governor Francis Nicholson tried to recruit Native pupils in 1700 and failed. So about 1702 two traders, Robert Hicks and John Evans, "purchased or acquired four young Indian captives from the Catawba Nation." William & Mary's own history states this. The traders got the boys along with deerskins and furs. The same history states that the boys were "likely destined to be sold by the Catawba as forced laborers." The four boys became the school's first Native pupils. The college's published records do not give their names. The Meherrin Nation's account states that the college "resorted to buying their pupils from local Native Americans who captured the boys from other tribes."

By 1712 the college had twenty Native pupils besides the four captive boys. That was a third to a half of all the pupils in the college. In 1723 a building for the Indian school, called the Brafferton, was finished. Enslaved workers built it. More than 125 Native students from at least 26 nations lived and studied there between 1723 and 1776. They learned reading, writing, arithmetic and the prayers of the Church of England. The published records do not say how many of them died at the school.

The college's leaders also bought people. In 1718 they bought a tobacco plantation of 2,119 acres in Virginia for 150 pounds. They paid 476 pounds more for seventeen enslaved people to work the plantation.

<a id="story-christopher-dock"></a>

#### Christopher Dock

> **Who:** A Mennonite schoolmaster in Pennsylvania who wrote the first book about how to teach written in this country.
>
> **When and where:** Skippack and Salford, Pennsylvania, from no later than 1718 until his death in 1771.

Christopher Dock wrote the first book about how to teach written in this country. Most of what he wrote down is about how he punished children and how he rewarded them. He was a member of the Mennonite church, a Christian church.

He came to Pennsylvania between 1710 and 1714. His schools were on Lenape land. The Lenape homeland covered southeastern Pennsylvania, central and southern New Jersey and Delaware. Between 1682 and 1684 William Penn bought land for his colony in southeastern Pennsylvania from the Lenape, paying at least 1,200 pounds in goods.

Dock opened a school at Skippack no later than 1718. He taught for ten years, then farmed for about ten more. In 1738 he went back to teaching and taught for the last 33 years of his life. He ran two schools, at Skippack and at Salford, on alternate days.

On August 8, 1750, he finished a book called *Schul-Ordnung*, which is German for "school management." He did not want it printed while he was alive. The printer Christopher Saur printed it anyway. Accounts differ on the date. Brumbaugh gives 1769 for the first printing and 1770 for the second, and other reference works give 1770 for the first. It was still being printed in English in the 1900s.

Dock sorted children by what worked on each one. He gave praise to children who wanted it, a penny for hard study to children who wanted money, and a sugar pretzel for good learning to children who wanted sweets. In the words of the historian Martin Brumbaugh, who wrote Dock's life in 1908, "The ill-intentioned, who were not affected by the promise of a penny or a cooky, he threatened with whipping." Whipping means hitting a person again and again with a whip, a rod or a strap. Brumbaugh names the rod: "With some he had to use the rod." When a child failed at a task, Dock would say "I no longer love you," and in Brumbaugh's words the children "wept until he comforted them." Dock also put a yoke, a wooden frame worn over the neck and shoulders, on a child who swore. He made some children sit alone. Dock was milder than the schoolmasters around him, and he still used whipping and the threat of it.

One evening in the autumn of 1771 Dock did not come home from school at the usual time. In Brumbaugh's account, people went to look for him, and "he was found in his schoolroom on his knees," dead.

### 1750 to 1800

The men who founded the United States argued that the new country needed schools, and they mostly did not pay for them. Thomas Jefferson wrote a plan for public schools in Virginia, and Virginia's lawmakers never passed it. The new schools of these fifty years included private academies, the first school for girls with a charter from a government, church charity schools, and a charity school and a college meant for Native students. At a charity school in Williamsburg, Virginia, Black children learned to read. The men who ran the London charity that paid for it wanted them taught that slavery was God's will.

#### Jefferson's plan, and who was left out

Thomas Jefferson wrote "A Bill for the More General Diffusion of Knowledge." Diffusion means spreading. The bill went to the Virginia House of Delegates, the lower house of the state's lawmakers, on June 18, 1779. Jefferson described the plan in his book *Notes on the State of Virginia*. Each county would be divided into districts five or six miles square, called hundreds, with a school in each one. Every free family could send its children for three years free, and longer if they paid. The district schools would teach reading, writing and arithmetic. Above them, grammar schools would teach Greek, Latin, geography and harder arithmetic.

Jefferson also set out how poor boys would be chosen for more schooling. Each year, officials called visitors would "chuse the boy, of best genius in the school, of those whose parents are too poor to give them further education." In this way, he wrote, "twenty of the best geniusses will be raked from the rubbish annually." Chuse is an old spelling of choose, genius here means unusual ability, and annually means each year. Rubbish is Jefferson's word for the children of poor families.

The plan in *Notes on the State of Virginia* does not mention girls. Every reference is to boys. Enslaved children are not in it either, because it was a plan for free children only. Virginia's lawmakers never passed the bill. James Madison brought it forward again while Jefferson was in Paris, and it failed again. In 1796 the lawmakers passed a much-changed version, an "Act to Establish Public Schools." Under that act the men who sat on each county's court chose whether to open schools, and in most counties they did nothing.

#### The Land Ordinance of 1785: school money from Native land

In 1785 the members of Congress set aside land to pay for public schools. US commissioners had taken that land from Native nations by a treaty that the Shawnee and other nations refused to accept. On May 20, 1785, they passed the Land Ordinance. An ordinance is a law. Under it, surveyors were to cut the western land into townships six miles square. Each township was split into 36 numbered sections of one square mile. The law states: "There shall be reserved the lot N 16, of every township, for the maintenance of public schools, within the said township."

Section 16 sat near the middle of each township. Under the law it was not to be sold to a settler. The money it earned was to pay for a school. US officials sold the rest of the land to settlers.

The first land surveyed under the Ordinance was in what is now eastern Ohio. Wyandot, Lenape, Ojibwe, Odawa and Shawnee people lived there. On January 21, 1785, at Fort McIntosh, US commissioners signed a treaty with Wyandot, Lenape, Ojibwe and Odawa leaders. The commissioners' terms stated that most of the Ohio nations had to stay inside a reserve, an area set aside for them, between the Cuyahoga and Maumee rivers. In September 1785 surveyors began measuring the land, guarded by troops from Fort McIntosh. George Knepper, an Ohio historian, writes that the Ohio nations, especially the Shawnee, refused to obey the treaty. In his words, it had been "negotiated under duress by minor tribal chiefs who lacked authority to speak for their people and for other tribes." Negotiated under duress means worked out under threat or pressure. Knepper means that the chiefs who signed were lesser leaders with no right to speak for everyone else.

#### The academies

Franklin's academy, the Academy and Charity School of Philadelphia, opened in 1751. Thomas and Richard Penn, the owners of the colony, granted it a charter in 1753. The College of Philadelphia was chartered two years later.

Samuel Phillips founded Phillips Academy at Andover, Massachusetts, on April 25, 1778. It opened five days later. Paul Revere cut its seal. John and Elizabeth Phillips signed the papers founding Phillips Exeter Academy in New Hampshire on April 3, 1781. That school opened on May 1, 1783, with one teacher and 56 students.

#### Girls' academies, and the first with a charter

John Poor founded the Young Ladies' Academy of Philadelphia on June 4, 1787. On January 7, 1792, the school was granted a charter. That made it the first school for the higher education of women in the country to be recognized by a government. Its pupils studied reading, writing, English grammar, mathematics, geography, composition, chemistry and natural philosophy. Natural philosophy was the old name for physics and the other sciences of how nature works. Benjamin Rush was among the men who backed it.

Sarah Pierce, born in 1767, opened the Litchfield Female Academy in Connecticut in 1792. She ran it for 41 years. More than 2,000 girls attended over about 30 of those years, from 17 states and territories and from Canada and the West Indies. Researchers at the Litchfield Historical Society have found 1,848 of them by name. More than 8 in 10 came from other towns and boarded with Litchfield families. They studied history, geography, arithmetic and composition, and later Latin, logic and natural philosophy. Girls who finished the whole course received diplomas.

Sarah Pierce took up an argument made after the Revolution: that mothers gave children their first moral training and their first lessons, and that the new country depended on it. In this argument, girls needed schooling because of the children they would raise. Pierce herself believed girls and boys were equally able. She did not argue that women should enter the men's colleges or professions.

#### The Williamsburg Bray School, 1760 to 1774

From 1760 to 1774 enslaved and free Black children in Williamsburg, Virginia, learned to read at a charity school. The men who paid for it also meant to teach them to accept slavery as God's will. The Associates of Dr. Bray, a church charity in London, set up the school on Benjamin Franklin's advice. Thomas Dawson, the president of the College of William & Mary, backed it. One teacher, Ann Wager, taught there for all fourteen years.

The pupils were three to ten years old, and thirty or more might crowd into the room on an ordinary day. They learned to spell and to read aloud clearly. They worked up through *The Child's First Book*, the Psalms, the New Testament, the Book of Common Prayer and the Bible. The Psalms are songs from the Bible, and the Book of Common Prayer was the Church of England's prayer book. Lessons began with the pupils reciting the Apostles' Creed, a short statement of Christian belief, the Lord's Prayer and the catechism from memory. Girls were also taught to sew.

The count of pupils is not settled. Colonial Williamsburg's history of the school states that "hundreds of students attended." William & Mary's Bray School Lab states 300 to 400, and an Encyclopedia Virginia article states about 200. The names of more than 80 pupils survive on three school lists, from 1762, 1765 and 1769. One of them is a child named Locust, sent by the Armistead family, who enslaved people near Williamsburg.

William & Mary's own account states that the school's "faith-based curriculum justified slavery." A curriculum is the set of lessons a school teaches, and faith-based means built on religious belief. From those same lessons, the children learned to read.

The school closed in 1774, when Ann Wager died. A second Bray school, at Fredericksburg, Virginia, ran from 1765 to about 1769 under the merchant Fielding Lewis, with 40 to 50 pupils. It closed because fewer pupils came and local enslavers opposed it.

The Williamsburg schoolhouse still stands. In 2020 researchers at Colonial Williamsburg and William & Mary confirmed that a building on the William & Mary campus, later a private home and then student housing, was the building where the school began. The school met there from 1760 until 1765, when it moved to a larger building. On February 10, 2023, it was moved to Colonial Williamsburg. William & Mary's Bray School Lab and *Smithsonian* magazine describe it as the oldest surviving schoolhouse for Black children in the United States.

<a id="story-ann-wager"></a>

#### Ann Wager

> **Who:** The only teacher the Williamsburg Bray School ever had. The men who ran the charity that paid her wanted Black children taught to read and taught that slavery was God's will.
>
> **When and where:** Williamsburg, Virginia, 1760 to 1774.

Ann Wager taught every class the Williamsburg Bray School ever held. She was born in about 1716. Her husband, William Wager, died in 1748, and she began teaching to support herself.

From 1760 she was the Bray School's only teacher. She was paid 20 pounds a year, and her rent was paid too. Colonial Williamsburg's history of the school describes that as "roughly equivalent to a journeyman worker's yearly wage." A journeyman was a skilled worker who had finished an apprenticeship and worked for wages. She taught at the school until she died on August 20, 1774, and the school closed with her death.

Her pupils were enslaved and free Black children of Williamsburg. She taught them to spell, to read aloud, and to recite prayers and the catechism. The men who ran the charity in London wanted the children taught that being enslaved was God's plan for them. The children came out of her lessons able to read.

One of her pupils, on the 1765 list, was a boy named Isaac Bee. In the summer of 1774, when he was eighteen or nineteen, he ran away from Lewis Burwell, the man who claimed to own him. In September 1774 Burwell placed an advertisement in the *Virginia Gazette*. He wrote that Isaac Bee believed he had a right to be free, because his father was a free man. He offered a reward of 40 shillings, a shilling being one twentieth of a pound, for Isaac Bee's return. He warned that Isaac Bee could read, and that "he may easily get some One to forge a Pass for him." Bray School researchers at William & Mary matched the runaway to the pupil on the 1765 list. The Associated Press report on the researchers' work does not say whether he was caught or what became of him.

#### Georgia copies South Carolina's ban

In 1755 the members of Georgia's colonial House of Assembly passed the colony's first slave code, a set of laws for controlling enslaved people. Following South Carolina's act of 1740, they made it a crime to teach an enslaved person to write, or to use one as a scribe. The members passed another slave law in 1770. The records disagree on whether the 1770 law also banned teaching enslaved people to read, or whether that ban came only in 1829.

#### Moor's school, Samson Occom and Dartmouth

In 1754 Eleazar Wheelock, a Connecticut minister, opened Moor's Indian Charity School at Lebanon, Connecticut, for Native students. From 1761 he took girls as well. Students past and present complained that Wheelock made the Native students do more manual labor, hard work with the hands, than was fair. He quarreled with many of his best students, including Samson Occom, a Mohegan man who had been one of his pupils. In 1769 Oneida families took all their children out of the school. The Dartmouth scholars who edit Wheelock's papers write that the Oneida acted "perhaps due to concerns about corporal punishment." Corporal punishment means hitting a child as a punishment.

From 1766 to 1768 Occom preached across England and Scotland to raise money for the school. He raised 12,026 pounds. Wheelock used the money to start a college in New Hampshire instead. The royal governor of New Hampshire, John Wentworth, signed Dartmouth College's charter in 1769. The charter stated its purpose as "the education and instruction of youth of the Indian tribes in this land," for "civilizing and christianizing children of pagans." In the charter, pagans meant people who were not Christian. Only two Native students went with Wheelock to New Hampshire. Occom never set foot on the campus of the college his tour paid for. About 75 Native students enrolled at Dartmouth before 1972.

Wheelock enslaved people. Dartmouth's own researchers have found papers naming at least seventeen people he enslaved, among them Exeter, Chloe, Hercules, Peggy and Caesar. Between 1743 and 1769 his papers record that he bought six men and two women.

<a id="story-noah-webster"></a>

#### Noah Webster

> **Who:** A schoolteacher who wrote the spelling book American children learned from for more than a hundred years, and later a dictionary.
>
> **When and where:** Born in West Hartford, Connecticut, on October 16, 1758. Died in New Haven on May 28, 1843.

Noah Webster wrote the spelling book that American children learned from for more than a hundred years. He was born on October 16, 1758, in the part of Hartford, Connecticut, that is now West Hartford.

He finished Yale in 1778. He taught school in Glastonbury, Hartford and West Hartford, and in 1782 in Goshen, New York. He believed the new country needed its own schoolbooks and one settled way of spelling to hold it together.

In 1783 he published the first part of *A Grammatical Institute of the English Language*. People called it the Blue-Backed Speller. In it Webster kept most spellings as they were. He used, every time, many spelling changes that earlier dictionaries had used only some of the time.

Families and schools used the speller from 1783 into the early 1900s. By one estimate it had sold 15 million copies by 1837 and about 60 million by 1890. Other estimates run as high as 100 million copies in all. Nobody kept an exact count.

#### Teaching as a job

Noah Webster taught in four schools in about four years on his way to law and writing. That is one recorded pattern. Other men made teaching their life's work. Ezekiel Cheever taught for 70 years and Christopher Dock for more than 40. No count of teachers from the 1700s is known, so which pattern was more common is not known.

### 1800 to 1850

Between 1800 and 1850, Horace Mann argued in Massachusetts for schools that were free to the family and paid for by taxes. Members of school boards hired more and more women to teach, because they could pay a woman far less than a man. In Massachusetts in 1838 a woman teacher earned $6.49 a month and a man $23.10. The first school paid for by a state to train teachers opened in 1839. Deaf children and blind children got schools of their own. In the South, lawmakers made teaching an enslaved person to read a crime and wrote whipping into the punishment. In Boston, school officials kept a five-year-old Black girl out of the school nearest her home. Judges on the state's highest court ruled that the city could keep her out.

#### Horace Mann and the common school

In 1837 Massachusetts lawmakers set up a state Board of Education to look after the common schools. A common school was a school meant for all the children of a town, paid for by the town's taxes instead of fees from parents. Horace Mann, a lawyer and state senator, became the board's first secretary. Under the law, the board's members could not make any town do anything. Mann's job was to gather facts, write reports and argue. He did it for eleven years, until 1848.

Mann wrote twelve yearly reports, and in 1838 he started a magazine, the *Common School Journal*. He made the same three arguments again and again. Every child had a right to an education. Taxes on everyone should pay for schools, instead of fees charged to parents. Teachers should be trained before they taught.

The free school Mann argued for was in practice a school for white children. While he was secretary, Boston's school officials ran separate schools for Black children. Two years after he left the board, Chief Justice Lemuel Shaw of the state's highest court ruled that the city could keep them separate.

<a id="story-horace-mann"></a>

#### Horace Mann

> **Who:** The first secretary of the Massachusetts Board of Education. For eleven years he argued that schools should be free and paid for by taxes.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Franklin, Massachusetts, on May 4, 1796. Died in 1859.

Horace Mann spent eleven years arguing that every child should have a free school. As a boy he had spent only a few weeks a year in school himself. He was born on May 4, 1796, into a poor farming family in Franklin, Massachusetts. His father died when he was thirteen. He braided straw for the hat-makers of Franklin to earn money. Until he was about fifteen he spent no more than about ten weeks a year in school. A different retelling of his own memories puts it at no more than six weeks a year between the ages of ten and twenty.

A traveling teacher named Barrett taught him Latin and Greek, and he got into Brown University. He graduated first in his class in 1819. He became a lawyer, and then a member of the Massachusetts House of Representatives from 1827 and the state Senate from 1835. He became president of the Senate.

In 1837 he became secretary of the new state Board of Education. In 1843 he visited schools in Prussia and Saxony, two German states, and in Holland. He wrote about that trip in his seventh report, and thirty-one schoolmasters of Boston attacked it in print.

In 1848 he was elected to the US House of Representatives, in the seat left empty when John Quincy Adams died. There he spoke against slavery and against letting it spread. In 1853 he became the first president of Antioch College, in Yellow Springs, Ohio. He died in 1859.

#### The one-room school and the school day

A country school of these years had one room and one teacher. Pupils of every age, from small children to nearly grown young men and women, sat together. A wood stove stood in the middle of the room. Children wrote on slates, thin boards of dark stone, with slate pencils, and wiped them clean to use again. At the front stood a recitation bench. A pupil came up to the bench and said a lesson out loud to the teacher while the others worked at their desks. Many children walked to school.

Accounts of country schools from before about 1900 describe a school year of two terms. A summer term, roughly May to August, was for the younger children, and women taught it. A winter term, roughly November to April, was for the older boys, who could be spared from farm work then. Men were often hired for the winter term to keep order. Children stayed home to plant in the spring and to harvest in the autumn.

Part of a teacher's pay was room and meals. The teacher lived in the house of each family in the district in turn, one family after another, through the term. This was called boarding round.

#### The first school for teachers, 1839

The first school paid for by a state to train teachers opened at Lexington, Massachusetts, on July 3, 1839. Three students came on the first day. Schools like it were called normal schools. The name comes from the French *école normale*, a school that taught the norms, or rules, of teaching. The principal was Cyrus Peirce, a minister whom Horace Mann had persuaded to come from Nantucket. By 1842 the school had 42 students. It moved twice and is now Framingham State University.

Members of the Massachusetts Board of Education set the entry rules for the state's normal schools. A man had to be at least 17 years old and a woman at least 16. Every student had to pass a test in spelling, geography and arithmetic. The course lasted one year and was free to a student who promised to teach in the state's schools.

In 1843 Mary Elizabeth Miles graduated from the Lexington normal school. She was the first African American to graduate from any public teachers college in the United States. She married Henry Bibb, a man who had escaped slavery, and worked with him in Ontario, in Canada, in the movement to end slavery.

<a id="story-mary-swift-education"></a>

#### Mary Swift

> **Who:** A seventeen-year-old in the first class of the first state school for teachers in America. She kept a journal of it.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Nantucket, Massachusetts, on June 22, 1822. Died in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on March 2, 1909.

Mary Swift was one of the first people in America trained to teach at a state school for teachers, and her journal of it survives. She entered the new normal school at Lexington in 1839, three weeks after her seventeenth birthday. Her class graduated on April 4, 1840.

She wrote in her journal through the school's first term. The principal, Cyrus Peirce, kept a journal of the same days. Both survive, and in 1926 they were printed together as one book, *The First State Normal School in America: The Journals of Cyrus Peirce and Mary Swift*.

In 1841 she became the teacher of Laura Bridgman, a deaf and blind girl at the Perkins Institution in Boston. Swift spoke to her by spelling words letter by letter into her hand. She kept the job until she married Edwin Lamson in 1846. In 1878 she published a book about Bridgman, built mostly from her teachers' journals. It was called *Life and Education of Laura Dewey Bridgman, the Deaf, Dumb, and Blind Girl*. In that title, "dumb" meant unable to speak.

#### Why school boards hired women

Members of school boards hired women because they could pay them far less. School journals of the time printed the monthly wages, and a teacher usually got her room and meals on top of the wage. In Connecticut in 1838, with about as many men as women teaching, men were paid $14.50 a month and women $5.75. In Massachusetts that year, 2,411 men and 3,826 women taught. The men were paid $23.10 a month and the women $6.49. The gap was smaller in Pennsylvania, where many more men than women taught: men got $18.50 a month and women $11.30.

The officials who made the savings said so in writing. Samuel Lewis, the Superintendent of Common Schools, or official in charge of Ohio's common schools, wrote in his report of 1839 that counties that hired women "are able to do twice as much with the same money." He went on: "As the business of teaching is made more respectable, more females engage in it, and the wages are reduced." In his fourth report, in 1841, Horace Mann welcomed the "change . . . rapidly taking place" in the hiring of women teachers.

<a id="story-catharine-beecher-education"></a>

#### Catharine Beecher

> **Who:** She ran a school for girls, then spent decades arguing that teaching was women's work.
>
> **When and where:** Born in East Hampton, New York, on September 6, 1800. Died in Elmira, New York, in 1878.

Catharine Beecher spent decades arguing that teaching was women's work, and she helped send hundreds of women out to teach. She was the eldest child of the preacher Lyman Beecher and a sister of Harriet Beecher Stowe. In 1822 the man she was engaged to marry, a Yale mathematics professor named Alexander Metcalf Fisher, drowned when the ship *Albion* wrecked off the coast of Ireland. She never married. She went into teaching.

Accounts differ on when she opened the Hartford Female Seminary in Hartford, Connecticut. Today in Connecticut History and the National Women's History Museum give May 20, 1823, and say she opened it with her sister Mary. Connecticut History, a state history website, gives 1824 and her sister Isabella. The girls there studied geography, world history, Latin, rhetoric, philosophy and the sciences. Most girls' schools of the time taught manners and fine arts instead. Within three years the school had 100 full-time pupils. In 1831 she moved west and opened the Western Female Institute in Cincinnati. It ran out of money after a money crisis called the Panic of 1837.

In 1835 she published *An Essay on the Education of Female Teachers*. In it she argued that teaching was part of a mother's work and that women were the right people to raise the next generation. If the country's leading women became "refined, well educated, pious and active," she wrote, "the salt is scattered through the land to purify and save." Pious means devoted to religion. By the salt she meant women like these, spread across the country as teachers, making it better. In 1847 she founded the Board of National Popular Education. Its members trained women in Hartford and sent them to teach in the West and the South. By 1857 the board's own reports counted 452 teachers sent. In 1852 she founded the American Woman's Educational Association.

She opposed giving women the vote. She believed a woman's proper places were the home and the schoolroom.

#### Hitting children, and an argument about it

In his seventh report, in 1843, Horace Mann argued against beating children as the ordinary way to keep order in a classroom. He also argued for teaching reading by whole words, instead of letter by letter. In 1844 thirty-one Boston schoolmasters answered him in print, in a pamphlet called *Remarks on the Seventh Annual Report of the Hon. Horace Mann*. They attacked his plan to train teachers, and they defended beating. Mann answered them in a second pamphlet that same year, and in 1845 they answered him again. All three pamphlets survive, and the Library of Congress holds copies.

A novel of the time describes the tools of punishment in a village schoolroom. Charles Dickens, an English writer, published *The Old Curiosity Shop* in 1840 and 1841. In it, a cane and a ruler hang on hooks on the schoolroom wall. Near them, on a shelf, sits "the dunce's cap, made of old newspapers." A dunce's cap was a pointed paper hat that a teacher made a pupil wear to shame him. This English novel is one of the earliest written descriptions of a dunce's cap kept in a schoolroom. Nobody counted how often American teachers made a pupil wear one.

The word dunce comes from the name of John Duns Scotus, a thinker who died in 1308 and was admired in his own lifetime. Later scholars who disliked his way of arguing used his followers' name as an insult, and dunce came to mean a stupid person. A popular story says his followers wore pointed hats to funnel knowledge into their heads. No record supports that story.

#### The books children learned from

William Holmes McGuffey taught at Miami University in Ohio from 1826 to 1836. A Cincinnati publishing firm, Truman and Smith, paid him to make a set of reading books. The First and Second *Eclectic Readers* came out in 1836, the Third and Fourth in 1837, the Fifth in 1844 and the Sixth in 1857. Eclectic means chosen from many sources. The readers mixed proverbs, grammar and passages from Shakespeare with lessons about patriotism, religion, good behavior, games and sports. Librarians at Miami University keep more than 300 editions of the readers. They estimate that the readers sold more than 150 million copies over about a hundred years, most of them in the Midwest.

Children still learned spelling from Noah Webster's speller. In 1828 Webster published *An American Dictionary of the English Language*, with 70,000 words, their meanings and where they came from. A set cost $20.

#### Schools for deaf children and blind children

In 1815 Dr. Mason Fitch Cogswell and other Hartford men asked Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet to go to Europe and learn how teachers there taught deaf children. In Paris he studied at a school for the deaf, and he came back with Laurent Clerc, a deaf French teacher. With Cogswell and ten other Hartford men behind them, they opened the American School for the Deaf in Hartford, Connecticut, on April 15, 1817. The first classes met in a hotel building, with seven full-time pupils. One of them was Cogswell's deaf daughter, Alice. Lessons were in sign language, a language made with the hands.

In 1819 Connecticut's lawmakers voted the school a yearly grant of money. The school's own history describes this as the first state aid to a school in America. In 1820 members of Congress gave the school land in the Alabama Territory.

The first school for blind children in the United States was set up in Boston on March 2, 1829. Dr. John Dix Fisher started it after he saw a school for blind children in Paris. Samuel Gridley Howe became its first director in 1831. The school opened in 1832 in his father's house, with six pupils. In 1839 Thomas Handasyd Perkins gave money for a larger building, and the school was named for him. It is Perkins School for the Blind today.

Laura Bridgman was born in Hanover, New Hampshire, on December 21, 1829. When she was two, scarlet fever, a disease that causes a high fever and a rash, left her deaf and blind. She came to the Boston school on October 12, 1837, two months before her eighth birthday. Howe taught her by touch. He gave her raised letters and objects together, again and again. After about two months she understood that the letters stood for the things. She was the first deaf and blind person in the United States to receive a formal education.

#### A Catholic school system begins

In the public schools of Philadelphia, the school day began with a reading aloud from the King James Bible, the Bible used by Protestants. The Catholic Church used a different English Bible, the Douay-Rheims. In New York, Catholic families said the public schools were Protestant schools that mocked their religion.

The first free Catholic school in the country was older than this fight. In 1810 Elizabeth Ann Seton and her Sisters of Charity, a group of Catholic nuns, opened Saint Joseph's Academy and Free School at Emmitsburg, Maryland. They taught the poor girls of the parish, the area served by their church, for no charge.

In New York City a private group called the Public School Society ran the public schools with state money. In June 1840 John Hughes, a Catholic bishop in New York, challenged the Society. A bishop is a church leader in charge of the priests and churches of a whole area. Governor William Seward suggested that Catholics ask for a share of the school money, and New York Catholics asked for it, to run schools of their own. In April 1842 state lawmakers shut down the Society. They put elected school boards in its place and banned religious teaching in public schools, which was not what Hughes had asked for. Protestants still controlled the elected boards. Hughes set out to build a separate system of Catholic schools. Someone threw stones at his house.

In Philadelphia the fight ended in killings. In 1842 Bishop Francis Patrick Kenrick asked the city's Board of Controllers of Public Schools to let Catholic children read their church's Bible. He also objected that Catholic children had to sing Protestant hymns in school. In February 1844 a school director in Kensington, Hugh Clark, suggested stopping the Bible readings until the board could agree on a rule. A rumor spread that he had ordered the Bible out of the schools.

On May 6, 1844, nativists held a meeting in Kensington, and a fight began. A nativist was someone who opposed immigrants. George Shiffler, a young nativist, was shot dead. The Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia's account of the riots does not say who shot him. By the end of the day a second man had been killed, and that account says he was apparently only watching. Several more people were wounded, and two of them later died.

On May 8 mobs burned houses, a Catholic seminary, which is a school for priests, and two Catholic churches, St. Michael's and St. Augustine's. Hugh Clark's house was among the houses burned. The Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia does not name the people in the mobs.

In July, in Southwark, a Catholic priest's brother stored guns in the basement of the Church of St. Philip Neri. Crowds gathered and demanded the guns, and the sheriff called in the militia, the state's citizen soldiers. From July 5 to 7 the crowd and the militia fought each other with guns. At least two people in the crowd were killed at once. By the next morning four militiamen and probably about a dozen people in the crowd were dead. Counts that add up the dead from May and July put the total at about twenty or more.

#### Teaching an enslaved person to read becomes a crime

Between 1819 and 1834, lawmakers in six Southern states made it a crime to teach enslaved people to read. The states were Virginia, North Carolina, Georgia, Louisiana, Alabama and South Carolina. The lawmakers wrote the punishments into the laws. The South Carolina law of 1740 had banned only the teaching of writing. The new laws banned reading too, and some reached free Black people as well.

Virginia's lawmakers widened their laws in three steps. On January 24, 1804, they barred enslaved people from meeting at night at churches, meetinghouses or anywhere else. On March 2, 1819, they banned enslaved people from "any school or schools for teaching them reading or writing, either in the day or night." On April 7, 1831, they reached free Black people too: "All meetings of free negroes or mulattoes, at any school house...for teaching them reading or writing...shall be considered as an unlawful assembly." An unlawful assembly was a meeting the law banned, which officials could break up. Negro was a word used then for a Black person, and mulatto for a person with one Black parent and one white parent.

North Carolina's lawmakers passed their law in the session of 1830 and 1831. Its opening words state their reason. Teaching enslaved people to read and write "has a tendency to excite dissatisfaction in their minds, and to produce insurrection and rebellion." An insurrection is an armed uprising. The law set the punishments by who the teacher was:

- A white person who taught an enslaved person to read or write was fined between $100 and $200, or jailed.
- A free Black person who did it could be whipped, with no fewer than 20 and no more than 39 lashes, or else fined or jailed, as the court chose.
- An enslaved person who taught another enslaved person got 39 lashes on the bare back.

A lash is one blow with a whip. A whipping under these laws meant blows across the bare back with a leather whip or a switch, a thin stick cut from a tree, hard enough to break the skin. Thirty-nine was the usual highest number of lashes in Southern law. Under the same North Carolina law, judges had to instruct grand juries to enforce it. A grand jury is a group of citizens who decide whether a person should be charged with a crime.

The other states set their own punishments. Georgia's lawmakers passed their law in 1829. A Black person who taught another to read or write was fined and whipped. A white person was fined up to $500 and could be jailed. Louisiana's lawmakers in 1830 set one to twelve months in prison for anyone who taught an enslaved person to read or write. Alabama's lawmakers in 1832 set a fine of $250 to $500 for teaching any Black person, enslaved or free. Under Virginia's law of 1831, any judge or justice of the peace, a local judge, could break up a school for free Black people. He could also order up to twenty lashes for each person caught there. A white person found guilty of teaching Black people to read or write was fined $50 and could be jailed for two months. Teaching an enslaved person carried a fine of $10 to $100. South Carolina's lawmakers widened their old law in 1834.

Only the North Carolina, Georgia and Virginia laws set the whip, and only for Black people. Louisiana's and Alabama's laws set the same prison term or fine for every teacher, whatever the teacher's race.

Two events fell in the middle of these years. In 1829 David Walker published his *Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World*. Walker was a free Black man from North Carolina who ran a used-clothing store in Boston. His *Appeal* urged Black people to resist slavery, and sailors carried copies into the South. The Georgia, Louisiana and North Carolina laws, and Virginia's law of 1831, all came after it. In August 1831 Nat Turner, an enslaved preacher, led a revolt of enslaved people in Southampton County, Virginia. They killed at least 55 white people. Afterward, militias and other armed white men killed more than 100 Black people, and some estimates run to 200. Many of them had no part in the revolt. A county court led by Judge Jeremiah Cobb sentenced Turner to death, and the sheriff hanged him in Jerusalem, Virginia, on November 11, 1831. Alabama's law of 1832 and South Carolina's of 1834 came after the revolt. Virginia's laws of 1804 and 1819 came before both events.

Enslaved people learned to read anyway. About 5 percent of enslaved people in Virginia could read by 1775. In the decades before the Civil War, while these laws were in force, the share doubled to about 10 percent.

#### Federal money for schooling Native children, from 1819

Federal officials began paying for the schooling of Native children in 1819. On March 3, 1819, the members of Congress passed the Civilization Fund Act. Under it, the lawmakers set aside $10,000 a year to hire people to teach Native nations farming and to teach their children "reading, writing, and arithmetic." The law states its purpose as "providing against the further decline and final extinction of the Indian tribes" and "introducing among them the habits and arts of civilization." Extinction here meant the Native nations dying out completely. Government officials gave much of the money to churches and other religious groups. Lawmakers in Congress kept paying into the fund until 1873. In a report published in 2022, investigators for the US Department of the Interior date the start of the federal Indian boarding school system to 1819.

The Choctaw Academy in Kentucky was one of these schools. It opened in November 1825 on the farm of Richard Mentor Johnson, a US senator who later became Vice President. Twenty-one Choctaw boys came first. Its first head was a Baptist minister, Thomas Henderson. It was paid for with the Choctaw Nation's own money. Under a treaty of 1825, a written agreement between the United States and the Choctaw Nation, the US government owed the Choctaw $6,000 a year for schooling, and that money went to Johnson's school. Choctaw leaders tried to break with the academy and take back control of the money in 1829 and again in 1833. They failed.

More than 600 students from 17 Native nations went to the Choctaw Academy. Johnson enslaved at least sixty people. Among them were Julia Chinn and the two daughters she had with him, Adaline and Imogene. By law he owned Chinn, and she could not refuse him. Enslaved people did most of the farming, building and cleaning at the school. Inspectors who visited in 1840 "confirmed the many complaints of poor living conditions, inadequate education, food, and clothing, as well as forced manual labor." Inadequate means not good enough. In 1842 the Choctaw leader Peter Pitchlynn took every Choctaw student out of the school. The last thirteen Chickasaw students left in 1848.

#### A school open to Black and white students dragged away: Canaan, 1835

In 1835 men in Canaan, New Hampshire, drove Black students out of their school. Noyes Academy in Canaan had opened in March 1835 with 28 white students and 14 Black students. Its trustees, the people in charge of the school, had voted in 1834 to admit students of every race. The Black students included Henry Highland Garnet, Alexander Crummell, Thomas S. Sidney and Julia Williams.

In July 1835 the voters at a Canaan town meeting declared the school a public nuisance, meaning a harm to the town. On August 10, 1835, men from Canaan and the towns around it hitched teams of oxen to the school building with chains. They pulled it off its foundation and dragged it down the road. The town's own history says it took two days, and the building ended as a heap near the meeting house. One account counts about seventy-five men and nearly a hundred oxen. Another gives a hundred yoke of oxen. A yoke is a pair of oxen joined by a wooden frame, so a hundred yoke would be two hundred animals. Garnet fired a shotgun from a window, and the crowd drew back. The townspeople drove the Black students out of Canaan. No record shows that anyone was ever punished for it. Garnet, Crummell and Sidney went on to study at the Oneida Institute, near Utica, New York.

<a id="story-sarah-roberts-education"></a>

#### Sarah Roberts

> **Who:** A five-year-old Black girl put out of the Boston school nearest her home. Her father sued the city.
>
> **When and where:** Boston, Massachusetts, 1848 to 1850.

Sarah Roberts was five years old when members of Boston's school committee kept her out of the school nearest her home, because she was Black. She lived on Andover Street in Boston. The school city officials let her attend was the Abiel Smith School, the school for Black children. To get there she had to walk past five schools for white children.

Her father, Benjamin F. Roberts, asked the Boston Primary School Committee four times to let her into the nearest school. Each time the committee members refused. In 1848 he sent her to the nearest school anyway, and she was put out of it. The National Park Service's account of the case does not name the person who put her out. He sued the city under a Massachusetts law of 1845. That law let a child who had been wrongly shut out of a public school claim damages, a payment of money for the harm.

Her lawyers were Charles Sumner and Robert Morris. Morris was twenty-five and one of the first Black lawyers in the United States. The judges of the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court, the state's highest court, heard the case in 1849. In 1850 Chief Justice Lemuel Shaw ruled for the city. He wrote that the school committee "have come to the conclusion, that the good of both classes of school will be best promoted, by maintaining the separate primary schools for colored and for white children." Colored was a word used then for Black people.

Black Bostonians kept up the fight. In 1855 Massachusetts lawmakers outlawed separate public schools by race.

### 1850 to 1900

In these fifty years, state lawmakers began to order children to go to school, starting with Massachusetts in 1852. Lawmakers in Congress gave states public land, which the United States had taken from Native nations, to found colleges. Nearly four million people had been enslaved in 1860. Once freed, they built schools, and by 1869 they paid for all or part of 1,094 of them, by the count of a federal inspector. White men burned some of those schools, whipped their teachers and killed at least one teacher, and the same inspector wrote that down too. Southern lawmakers made separate schools for Black and white children the law. In 1896 the justices of the Supreme Court called separate schools lawful in a case about train cars. In 1899 they refused to stop a Georgia school board that had closed a Black high school and kept paying for white ones. From 1879 federal officials sent Native children to boarding schools far from home, where staff cut their hair, took their clothes and forbade their languages. More than 180 children died at Carlisle, the first federal boarding school built away from the reservations, the lands set aside for Native nations.

#### Laws that made children go to school

A compulsory attendance law is a law that requires children to go to school. Massachusetts lawmakers passed the first one in 1852. It covered children from 8 to 14 years old. Each child had to attend at least twelve weeks a year, six of them in a row. By 1900, 32 states had such a law. By 1918 every state had one. Mississippi was the last. How strictly officials enforced the early laws is not known.

#### Colleges built with Native land: the Morrill Acts

On July 2, 1862, the Morrill Act became law. Under it, each state received 30,000 acres of public land for each of its senators and representatives in Congress. State officials sold the land and used the money to found colleges that taught agriculture and the mechanic arts, which means engineering and machine work. These were called land-grant colleges. At them, the children of farmers and working people could go to college.

The United States had taken the land from Native nations. In 2020 two journalists, Robert Lee and Tristan Ahtone, traced it through land records. By their count it came to about 10.7 million acres, taken from nearly 250 tribes, bands and communities. US officials took it through more than 160 land cessions. A land cession was an agreement in which a nation gave up land, and Lee and Ahtone write that these were backed by violence. US officials paid less than $400,000 for that land. Its sale raised $17.7 million for 52 colleges.

In 1890 members of Congress passed a second Morrill Act. Under it, states got money instead of land. The law required each state's lawmakers either to admit Black students to the land-grant college the state already had or to set up a separate one for them. Lawmakers in most Southern states set up separate colleges. Some of today's historically Black colleges and universities, the colleges first founded for Black students, began that way. Alcorn State University in Mississippi, founded in 1871, is the oldest public historically Black land-grant college.

#### The schools freed people built

In March 1865 members of Congress set up the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands, called the Freedmen's Bureau, inside the War Department. Its officials helped people who had just been freed from slavery. John W. Alvord was its inspector of schools. He wrote a report on the schools every six months, from 1866 to 1870.

In the half year that ended on December 31, 1869, Alvord counted 4,027 schools of all kinds, 8,907 teachers and 210,018 pupils. He explained what his own count meant. A person who went to more than one kind of school was counted more than once. So the total showed "the amount of tuition furnished, rather than the exact number of persons taught." He meant that the total measured how much teaching was given, not how many different people were taught.

Freed people paid for all or part of 1,094 of the day and night schools. In Alvord's words, they "sustained wholly or in part 1,094" of them, and they owned 554 of the school buildings. Bureau officials supplied 635 buildings.

Many children had to pick cotton in the autumn, so many schools did not open until December. Many others ran right through the summer. In July 1869, 1,020 schools were open. In August the number was 1,048, and in September 1,482. In that half year, 34,320 pupils were advanced readers, 27,471 studied geography, 30,749 studied arithmetic and 39,437 studied writing. Another 3,834 were in high schools and normal schools, training for professions.

Alvord estimated that in its five years the Bureau's schools had given "an elementary education to about one million of pupils." That did not count the parents and other adults who had learned to read at home, many of them from their own children. Bureau officials stopped paying for schools in 1870.

#### Attacks on the freed people's schools

White men burned freed people's schools, whipped their teachers and killed at least one of them, and Alvord recorded the attacks in his reports. In his report of January 1868 he wrote: "Teachers were proscribed and ill-treated, school-houses burned, and threats so strong that many schools could not be opened." Proscribed means openly condemned and shut out. In the Oxford district of Mississippi, "A Mr. Borum started a school about twelve miles from this place and it was immediately burned." The report does not say who burned it.

His report of January 1870 names places and people. In Georgia late in 1869, bands of "armed and disguised men," which the report calls "K. K. K.," attacked people in county after county. K. K. K. stands for the Ku Klux Klan. The Confederacy was the group of Southern states that broke away and fought the United States in the Civil War. Men who had fought for it started the Klan in Pulaski, Tennessee, in December 1865. Its members whipped, burned and murdered freed people and the people who helped them. At Greensboro, Georgia, men drove the teacher R. H. Gladding out of town. The white man he boarded with was "taken out of his own house in the night and unmercifully whipped." Abram Colby had backed the school, and he had just been elected as one of the state's lawmakers. He was a Black man, and he "was also taken out of his house and beaten nearly to death." The report does not name the men who did any of this. The mayor told Gladding that the town's officials could not protect him.

In Dresden, Tennessee, two students from Fisk University ran a school of about fifty children. On the night of September 2, 1869, "men masked and armed" took them from their boarding house into the woods. The men "severely whipped" them and told them to stop teaching and leave or be killed. The report states that local officials were told about it and "nothing was done in the matter." At Slaughter Neck, Delaware, drunken white men burned the school. The report states that the evidence was given to the state's attorney and the governor was told, "yet nothing was done to bring the parties to justice." It does not say who gave the evidence. Black families there rebuilt the school with help from a Delaware charity and some Bureau money.

In May 1866 white mobs and police in Memphis, Tennessee, killed 46 Black people. They burned every Black church and school in the city, 8 schools in all, by the count of a committee of Congress. On July 11, 1870, members of the Ku Klux Klan lynched William Luke at Cross Plains, Alabama. To lynch someone is to kill the person without any trial. Luke was a preacher from Flesherton, Ontario, in Canada, who taught freed people for Talladega College. The Klansmen killed Black men with him. One count gives six dead in all, and another gives eight.

<a id="story-charlotte-forten-education"></a>

#### Charlotte Forten

> **Who:** The first Black graduate of the Salem Normal School and the first Black teacher in Beaufort County, South Carolina.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Philadelphia in 1837. Died in Washington, D.C., on July 23, 1914.

Charlotte Forten went south in 1862, while the Civil War was still being fought, to teach people who had just been freed from slavery. She was the first Black teacher in Beaufort County, South Carolina.

She was born in Philadelphia in 1837, into a well-off Black family that worked to end slavery. Philadelphia's school officials would not take her, so her family had her taught at home by tutors. In 1853 she moved to Salem, Massachusetts, to live with the Remond family and go to school there. In 1856 she graduated from the Salem Normal School, its first African American graduate. She had studied subjects from algebra and Latin to optics, the science of light. Her principal, Richard Edwards, found her a job at the Epes Grammar School. She became the first African American teacher in Salem's public schools, teaching white children.

In her journal she wrote that her time in Salem was "the happiest of my life." She also wrote: "I wonder that every colored person is not a misanthrope. Surely we have everything to make us hate mankind." A misanthrope is a person who hates other people.

In October 1862, in the middle of the war, Forten sailed to St. Helena Island, off South Carolina, to teach at the Penn School with Laura Towne and Ellen Murray. The school had opened that year with 41 pupils. By 1865 it had 436 pupils in four buildings. She taught there until the war ended and kept a journal the whole time. In May and June 1864 she published an account of it, "Life on the Sea Islands," in the *Atlantic Monthly*, a magazine.

After the war she taught in Boston and in Charleston, South Carolina. By 1872 she was teaching in Washington, D.C., at the school that became Dunbar High School.

#### A teacher jailed in Norfolk, 1854

Officials in Virginia used the 1831 law against a white teacher. Margaret Douglass, a white woman in Norfolk, and her daughter Rosa opened a school for free Black children in June 1852. A Mr. Robinson, whose two daughters Margaret Douglass had begun to teach, asked her to do it. The Douglasses charged three dollars for each quarter of a year. Twenty-five boys and girls came, and the school ran openly for about eleven months.

On the morning of May 9, 1853, the city constable, Cherry, came to the house with a second officer, Cox. A constable was a town officer who kept order and made arrests. Mayor Simon S. Stubbs had sent them. The officers wrote down the name of every child and every parent. They marched the two teachers and the children to the mayor's office. The mayor read out the Virginia law and told them its highest penalty was a fine of one hundred dollars and six months in jail. A grand jury charged the two women with meeting with Black children "for the purpose of instructing them to read and to write." Rosa left Norfolk for New York before the trial.

In November 1853 a jury found Margaret Douglass guilty and set her fine at one dollar. On January 10, 1854, Judge Baker of the Norfolk court added a month in the city jail. He said the jail term was "an example to all others in like cases disposed to offend." She served the month. Afterward she published her own account of the case, with the court papers printed in it.

#### Separate schools by law, upheld by the courts

After the Civil War, Southern lawmakers wrote the separation of Black and white pupils into law. Tennessee is one example. Its lawmakers passed a school law that separated the races just after the war. The state's new constitution, of 1870, forbade mixed schools. In 1873 Tennessee's lawmakers wrote the rule out in full: "white and colored persons shall not be taught in the same school, but in separate schools." In much of the North, members of city school boards kept Black children apart by their own rules. In San Francisco, school officials opened a separate school for Black children in 1854 and one for Chinese children in 1859. In 1870 they closed the Chinese school, and Chinese American children were left with no public school at all.

In 1896 the justices of the United States Supreme Court decided *Plessy v. Ferguson*, a case about train cars. In 1890 Louisiana's lawmakers had required railroads to seat Black and white passengers in separate cars. In 1892 Homer Plessy, a shoemaker in New Orleans, sat in a car for white passengers. He had arranged his arrest ahead of time, to test the law in court. The justices ruled 7 to 1 that the law was allowed. In their ruling they called separate schools "the most common instance" of lawful separation by race. The first case they cited was Sarah Roberts's case from Boston. They also cited state court rulings from Ohio, Missouri, California, Louisiana, New York, Indiana and Kentucky. They pointed out that laws passed by Congress required separate schools in Washington, D.C.

In 1899 the justices refused to stop a Georgia school board that had closed a Black high school. Since 1880 the members of the school board of Richmond County, in Augusta, Georgia, had run the Ware High School for Black students. On July 10, 1897, the board members closed it and said they needed the money for Black primary schools. They kept paying for high schools for white students. Three Black parents, J. W.
