Prince Edward County closed its schools for years. On April 23, 1951, Barbara Johns, who was 16, had led the Black students of Robert Russa Moton High School in Farmville out of their school to protest its condition. Their case became one of the five cases the justices decided together as *Brown*.

Local leaders spent years getting ready to keep the county's schools separate. From 1954, J. Barrye Wall, the editor of the *Farmville Herald*, and Robert Crawford, a laundry owner and former school board chairman, built a group called the Defenders of State Sovereignty and Individual Liberties. On May 31, 1955, hours after the second *Brown* ruling, the county supervisors, the officials who ran the county, passed a motion by Supervisor John Bruce to give the schools only the legal minimum of $150,000, a fraction of what they needed. On June 7, 1955, at a meeting in Longwood College, 1,250 people voted, against 25, for a plan by Mayor W. C. Fitzpatrick. It set up a private fund to pay white teachers if the public schools closed.

On May 1, 1959, two courts ordered the county to integrate its schools. The supervisors then voted to stop paying for public schools at all. Accounts of that vote differ. Two date it June 26, 1959, and a third gives June 2. The schools did not open that September. Roy Pearson of Farmville organized private schools for the white children. They went to Prince Edward Academy, a new private school, paid for partly by tuition grants from the state.

Between 1,700 and 2,000 Black children had no school. One account gives about 1,750, and another gives nearly 2,000. Some children went to live with relatives in other counties or states. Some were taught in church basements. For one year, starting on September 16, 1963, private donors, backed by President John F. Kennedy's government, paid for free classes for about 1,500 children. On May 25, 1964, in *Griffin v. County School Board of Prince Edward County*, the justices of the Supreme Court ordered the county to reopen its schools. About 1,500 children went back on September 8, 1964.

In 2003 Virginia's lawmakers voted for a statement of "profound regret" for the closings. A news report in *Education Week* stated that some lawmakers would not vote for an apology because they thought an apology could lead to demands for payment. In 2004 the lawmakers set up a scholarship fund for people who had lost those years of school. They put in $50,000. John Kluge, a rich donor, then gave $1 million on the condition that the lawmakers match it. They did, and the fund reached $2,050,000.

<a id="story-ruby-bridges"></a>

#### Ruby Bridges

> **Who:** At six she walked into an all-white school in New Orleans, and for months she was the only pupil in it.
>
> **When and where:** New Orleans, Louisiana, 1960 and 1961.

On November 14, 1960, four federal marshals walked six-year-old Ruby Bridges into William Frantz Elementary School in New Orleans. Marshals are officers who carry out the orders of federal courts. For the rest of that school year, one teacher taught her in a classroom by herself. She was born on September 8, 1954, in Tylertown, Mississippi, the eldest child in her family. She grew up in New Orleans and went to a segregated kindergarten in 1959.

In 1960 a federal judge, J. Skelly Wright, ordered New Orleans to desegregate its public schools one grade at a time, starting with first grade. Members of the Orleans Parish School Board made Black children take an entrance test and checked their families. White children moving the other way had to do neither. Six children passed the test, and two of them chose to stay at their own school.

On the morning of November 14, Ruby Bridges walked in with the marshals and her mother, Lucille. That same morning Leona Tate, Gail Etienne and Tessie Prevost, also six, went into McDonogh No. 19 school nearby with marshals of their own. The four girls were the first Black children in white public schools in Louisiana.

Louisiana's leaders fought the order. That summer the lawmakers had made it a crime, punished by fines and jail, to challenge the state's control over the schools. Under one of their laws, Governor Jimmie Davis took over every decision about desegregation in New Orleans. Leaders of the White Citizens' Council, a group of white people who wanted the schools kept separate, held a rally of 5,000 people and told white parents to defy the court. On November 16 a riot broke out in front of the school board building.

A crowd stood outside Frantz and screamed at her. A group of young white women who called themselves the Cheerleaders came back day after day. They blocked the children and their parents, spat at the children, shouted racial insults and slashed tires. One protester threatened to poison her lunch. No record names the woman who made the threat.

White parents took their children out. By the end of November, fewer than ten white children attended the two schools together. From January to May 1961, Ruby Bridges was the only pupil at Frantz. Every teacher but one refused to teach her. Barbara Henry, a white teacher from Boston, taught her alone for the year. Ruby Bridges did not miss a day.

Her father lost his job. Grocers refused to serve her mother. Her grandparents had sharecropped a farm for 25 years, and they were thrown off it. Sharecroppers farm land that someone else owns and pay the owner with part of the crop. The National Park Service's account does not name the owner who made them leave. Her parents later separated.

Robert Coles, a child psychiatrist, which is a doctor who treats problems of the mind, met with her through that year and had her draw and talk about what was happening. In 1964 Norman Rockwell painted her walk to school and called it *The Problem We All Live With*. On July 15, 2011, she saw the painting hanging in the White House. Five years after she walked into Frantz, 96 of every 100 Black elementary pupils in New Orleans were still in schools more than 90 percent Black.

She finished elementary school at Frantz and worked in travel for about fifteen years. In 1999 she started the Ruby Bridges Foundation. On November 14, 2015, fifty-five years to the day after she first went in, a bronze statue of her was unveiled at the school.

#### A university, 1962: two men killed

Two men were killed on the night federal marshals brought James Meredith, the first Black student at the University of Mississippi, onto its campus. Meredith was an Air Force veteran. He applied on January 20, 1961, and university officials turned him down after he wrote that he was Black. Medgar Evers helped him, and Constance Baker Motley and Jack Greenberg, lawyers for the NAACP, a civil rights organization, took his case. On September 10, 1962, Justice Hugo Black ordered the university to admit him. Governor Ross Barnett worked for weeks to stop it.

On the evening of September 30, 1962, about 500 federal marshals brought Meredith to the campus at Oxford and put him in a dormitory, Baxter Hall. At about 7:25 that evening, State Senator George Yarbrough sent the Mississippi Highway Patrol away from the crowd, and at 7:30 a riot began. The crowd grew to more than 2,500 people by one count and about 3,000 by another, students and people from off the campus. A former Army general, Edwin Walker, helped lead them. They threw rocks, bottles and firebombs at the marshals and fired guns.

Paul Guihard, 30, a reporter for a French news agency, was shot in the back within about ten minutes of reaching the campus. Ray Gunter, 23, a jukebox repairman from Oxford, was dead when he reached the hospital. Nobody was ever charged with killing Guihard, and no record names who killed Gunter. The counts of the injured run from at least 75, in the first news report, to more than 300 in a later account, many of them marshals and soldiers. About 3,000 federal soldiers took control of the campus by the next morning, and 108 people were arrested.

On October 1, 1962, Meredith registered as a student and walked to his first class, a lesson in American colonial history. People shouted at him, "Was it worth two deaths?" Marshals went with him everywhere, and some students walked out of his classes. He graduated in August 1963.

#### Prayer and Bible reading in the school day

In 1962 and 1963 the justices of the Supreme Court ruled that public school staff could not lead pupils in official prayers or Bible readings. In New Hyde Park, New York, the members of the school board of Union Free School District No. 9 had told each class to say a prayer at the start of every day. Members of the New York State Board of Regents had written it. The whole prayer is 22 words: "Almighty God, we acknowledge our dependence upon Thee, and we beg Thy blessings upon us, our parents, our teachers and our Country." On June 25, 1962, in *Engel v. Vitale*, the justices struck it down, six votes to one. Justice Hugo Black wrote that "it is no part of the business of government to compose official prayers for any group of the American people to recite as a part of a religious program carried on by government."

A Pennsylvania law said that "at least ten verses from the Holy Bible shall be read, without comment, at the opening of each public school on each school day." At the high school in Abington Township, the verses and the Lord's Prayer went out over the school's loudspeakers. In Baltimore a rule from 1905 required a reading from the King James Bible and the Lord's Prayer. On June 17, 1963, the justices struck down both, eight votes to one, in *School District of Abington Township v. Schempp*. Justice Tom Clark wrote that government must keep "strict neutrality, neither aiding nor opposing religion." It made no difference that a child could ask to be excused.

In 1972 the justices let Amish parents, members of a Christian church called the Old Order Amish, take their children out of school after the eighth grade. Wisconsin required children to attend school until 16. Jonas Yoder, Wallace Miller and Adin Yutzy kept their children, Frieda Yoder and Barbara Miller, both 15, and Vernon Yutzy, 14, at home. Each father was fined $5. On May 15, 1972, in *Wisconsin v. Yoder*, Chief Justice Warren Burger wrote that the state could not force the parents to send the children to high school.

#### Federal money for poor children's schools, 1965

In 1965 members of Congress began paying for schools where poor children studied, and for classes for children too young for school. President Lyndon Johnson signed the Elementary and Secondary Education Act on April 11, 1965. He signed it on the front lawn of the old Junction school in Johnson City, Texas, the one-room school he had started at when he was four. His first teacher, Kate Deadrich Loney, sat beside him. He told her, "I started school when I was 4 years old, and they tell me, Miss Kate, that I recited my first lessons while sitting on your lap." Members of the House had voted for the law 263 to 153, and senators had voted for it 73 to 18.

Johnson said the law would "bridge the gap between helplessness and hope for more than 5 million educationally deprived children." Under Title I, one part of the law, federal officials send money to schools with poor children. By the end of 1965, the first 100 Title I projects were reaching 347,047 children in 12 states.

Head Start began the same year. Sargent Shriver, who ran the federal Office of Economic Opportunity, put together the group that designed it. Johnson announced it on May 18, 1965. It was a summer program to prepare young children for school in September, and it also gave them "medical and dental attention that they badly need." On that day Johnson spoke of about 530,000 children in 11,000 centers, at a cost of $112 million. By August 31 he reported nearly 560,000 children in 13,400 centers in 2,500 communities.

On June 23, 1972, President Richard Nixon signed a new education law with a part called Title IX. Title IX states that "no person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance." That means a school or college that gets money from the federal government may not shut anyone out or treat anyone worse because the person is male or female.

#### College for millions, and borrowing to pay for it

Over these fifty years, going to college changed from something a few Americans did to something millions did, and by the end most graduates had borrowed money to pay for it. In the fall of 1950, 2,281,298 people were enrolled in American colleges and universities. In 1960 there were 3,639,847, and in 1970 there were 8,580,887. In 2000 there were 15,312,289, about seven times as many as in 1950.

Much of the growth was paid for with federal money. Federal loans for students began under the 1958 defense education law. On November 8, 1965, President Johnson signed the Higher Education Act at Southwest Texas State College in San Marcos, Texas. Under the law, students in need could get grants, money that does not have to be paid back, of up to $1,000 a year, part-time jobs on campus worth about $400 a year, and loans backed by the government that a student did not have to start paying back until after graduating. Johnson said that 140,000 young people would be in college the next year who otherwise would not.

In the same speech he spoke of the year he had taught at the Welhausen Mexican School in Cotulla, Texas, for $125 a month. "I shall never forget the faces of the boys and the girls in that little Welhausen Mexican School," he said, "and I remember even yet the pain of realizing and knowing then that college was closed to practically every one of those children because they were too poor."

The cost of college rose faster than other prices. Measured in dollars of the same value, a year at a public four-year college, with tuition, fees, a room and meals, cost about $7,745 in 1963 to 1964 and about $12,572 in 1999 to 2000. At private four-year colleges the cost rose from about $15,093 to about $31,509, more than double.

More students borrowed. Of the people who finished a four-year degree in 1992 to 1993, 49 in every 100 had borrowed, an average of $12,100. Of those who finished in 1999 to 2000, 65 in every 100 had borrowed, an average of $19,300. Among students from the richest families, the share who borrowed roughly doubled, from 24 to 46 in every 100.

#### What students could say and wear

Public school students have a right to free speech at school, the justices of the Supreme Court ruled in 1969. Four years later the justices let stand a school rule that punished Native boys for wearing braids. In December 1965 John Tinker, 15, and Christopher Eckhardt, 16, students at high schools in Des Moines, Iowa, and Mary Beth Tinker, 13, in junior high, planned to wear black armbands to protest the Vietnam War. On December 14, 1965, the Des Moines principals made a rule that any student who wore an armband would be told to take it off and suspended for refusing. Mary Beth and Christopher wore armbands on December 16, and John wore his the next day. All three were suspended until after New Year's Day.

On February 24, 1969, in *Tinker v. Des Moines*, the justices ruled for the students, seven votes to two. Justice Abe Fortas wrote that students do not "shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate." He also wrote that the case did not concern rules about "the length of skirts or the type of clothing, to hair style, or deportment." Deportment means how a person behaves.

At Pawnee Junior High School in Oklahoma, Pawnee boys wore their hair parted in the middle with a long braid on each side, to follow "the old traditional ways." On April 24, 1972, school officials suspended them with no end date, under a rule that a boy's hair could not reach his shirt collar or his ears. Federal appeals judges upheld the rule. On December 10, 1973, the justices of the Supreme Court refused to hear the case, *New Rider v. Board of Education*. Justice William O. Douglas disagreed. He wrote that the boys "were in fact attempting to broadcast a clear and specific message to their fellow students and others, their pride in being Indian."

#### Black teachers lose their jobs, and the bus

When officials in Southern districts joined Black and white schools, school board members pushed Black teachers out of their jobs. The economist Owen Thompson counted teachers in 781 school districts in the eleven states that had formed the Confederacy. In 1964, 30.6 percent of their teachers were Black. By 1972 the share was 24.2 percent. The number of Black teachers fell by almost a third in eight years.

As districts joined schools together, the school board members let Black teachers go far more often than white ones, and they hired white teachers, many with less experience. Officials in the districts with the fewest Black pupils cut their Black teachers the hardest. Thompson estimates that about half of the teachers who lost their jobs went into work that needed less training, and the rest left the South to teach somewhere else.

Then came the buses. On April 20, 1971, in *Swann v. Charlotte-Mecklenburg Board of Education*, the justices ruled unanimously that a federal judge could order children carried by bus to end separate schools. The Charlotte-Mecklenburg district in North Carolina had more than 84,000 pupils in 107 schools, and about 24,000 of them were Black. Its officials already bused children. The year before, its buses carried 26,600 pupils an average of 15 miles each way, a trip of more than an hour. Under the plan, elementary pupils would ride about seven miles, "not over 35 minutes at the most." The justices wrote that an objection to busing counted only when the trip was long enough to risk the children's health or to harm their schooling.

In Boston, fourteen families sued the city's School Committee in 1972. On June 21, 1974, Judge W. Arthur Garrity ruled that "the entire school system of Boston was unconstitutionally segregated." Under his order, buses began carrying Black students from Roxbury to South Boston High School on September 9, 1974. Of the 800 Black students assigned there, 56 came on the first day. Protesters threw rocks and bottles at the buses.

Phyllis Ellison was one of the Black students bused to South Boston High, and she later described that year. People shouted racial insults at the bus and held up bananas at the students inside. In the school, she said, there were "anywhere between ten and fifteen fights" on an ordinary day. Black and white students sat on opposite sides of the classrooms, the lunchroom and the washrooms.

On December 11, 1974, a white student, Michael Faith, was stabbed during a shoving match outside a classroom. Police arrested a Black student from Roxbury, James White. A crowd gathered at the school gates shouting racial abuse, and it threw bricks and bottles and turned over a police car. Boston police and 125 state troopers pushed the crowd back. The Black students were locked in their classrooms while the white students were let out, Ellison said. She did not say who gave that order. Then four empty buses pulled up to the front door as decoys, while the Black students were put on buses at the back and driven home. *Time* magazine reported the decoy buses but did not say who planned them. South Boston High and seven other Boston schools were then closed for a time, and *Time*'s report does not say who closed them. Phyllis Ellison graduated in 1977.

#### The boarding schools: largest in the 1970s

Enrollment in the boarding schools for Native children reached its highest point about forty-five years after the Meriam Report. Children still died trying to get home from them. By the Heard Museum's count, enrollment peaked at about 60,000 children in 1973. The government's own counts were lower. In 1969 the Bureau of Indian Affairs ran 77 boarding schools holding about 35,000 children, and nearly 9,000 of them were under nine years old. On the Navajo Reservation, 7,476 children aged nine and younger lived at 48 boarding schools because no day school was near their homes. One of them, at Tuba City, housed 1,200 elementary pupils.

In January 1968 three brothers ran away from the Crownpoint Boarding School in New Mexico, just after the Christmas holiday. They were trying to walk about 50 miles home to Chaco Canyon, and they wore jeans, shorts and light jackets. That night the temperature fell to about 10 degrees below zero. On January 13, searchers found Ronald Yazzie, who was 9, and Willie B. Yazzie, who was 13, frozen to death about 30 miles from the school. Their brother Ray, 12, lived, with frostbite. Frostbite is damage to skin and flesh from freezing. A Navajo police officer, Stewart Silentman, said, "They were lonesome for home and just took off."

In November 1969 a subcommittee of the Senate published a report, *Indian Education: A National Tragedy, A National Challenge*. It describes the policy behind the schools as "coercive assimilation," which means forcing people to give up their own ways and take on another people's ways. It includes a letter from a teacher at Tuba City. At that school, parents could take a child home for a weekend only if staff judged the child's behavior good. A child who had run away could be kept from going home for up to a month. The report also includes the account of an anthropologist, a scientist who studies how groups of people live, of a Navajo boarding school where "Children are beaten" and where "teachers advocate the free labor of Navajo girls in their homes." The report does not name that school or the anthropologist. The senators who issued the report asked that Native nations run their own schools.

The Navajo Nation opened Navajo Community College in 1968. The college states that it was the first community college in the country run by a tribe. It is now Diné College. In January 1975 members of Congress passed the Indian Self-Determination and Education Assistance Act, which let Native nations sign contracts to run schools themselves. Many federal boarding schools closed in the 1980s.

Officials took Native children from their families in other ways too. Surveys by the Association on American Indian Affairs in 1969 and 1974 found that 25 to 35 of every 100 Native children had been separated from their families and put in foster homes, adoptive homes or institutions. State welfare workers, courts, private agencies and officials of the Bureau of Indian Affairs, through their boarding schools, removed them. In 16 states surveyed in 1969, about 85 of every 100 Native children in foster care were living with non-Native families. The Bureau of Indian Affairs census of 1971 counted 34,538 children living in its boarding schools and dormitories instead of at home. On November 8, 1978, the Indian Child Welfare Act became law. Its purpose was to keep Native children with Native families.

#### Punished for speaking Spanish

In much of the Southwest, school staff punished Mexican American children for speaking Spanish, and in 1972 a federal commission printed how. The U.S. Commission on Civil Rights published *The Excluded Student* in May 1972. It covered schools in Arizona, California, Colorado, New Mexico and Texas with many Mexican American pupils. Of about 5,800 schools, about a third had rules that discouraged children from speaking Spanish in class, and about 15 in every 100 discouraged it on the playground too.

The rule was most common in Texas. Two-thirds of the Texas schools surveyed had rules that discouraged Spanish in class, at least twice the rate of most other states. In California fewer than a fifth did. The rule was also most common in poor neighborhoods. In 5 of every 10 schools serving poor barrios, or Mexican American neighborhoods, there was a "No Spanish" rule in class. In schools serving rich families, about 15 in every 100 had one.

The commission's staff asked schools how they enforced the rule. In 48 of every 100, staff were asked to correct children who spoke Spanish, and in 12 of every 100 they were required to. In 7 of every 100, staff encouraged other children to correct them. In 3 of every 100, school staff said they punished children who kept speaking Spanish. No principal admitted hitting a child for it, but witnesses at the commission's hearing in San Antonio in December 1968 said children were hit. At that hearing a principal from El Paso testified that children caught speaking Spanish were sent to a Spanish detention class for an hour after school. The report includes a copy of the slip used to send a child there.

In October 1964 a class of Mexican American seventh graders in Texas wrote about their elementary schools. A Texas teacher, Alonzo Perales, sent the essays to the commission. The report does not name the children. One wrote: "If we speak Spanish we had to pay 5 cents to the teacher or we had to stay after school." Another wrote: "In the first through the fourth grade, if the teacher caught us talking Spanish we would have to stand on the 'black square' for an hour or so." A third had to "write three pages saying, 'I must not speak Spanish in school'." A fourth wrote: "In the sixth grade, they kept a record of which if we spoke Spanish they would take it down and charge us a penny for every Spanish word. If we spoke more than one thousand words our parents would have to come to school and talk with the principal."

Texas law had required teaching in English only since 1918. In October 1970 a Mexican American teacher in Crystal City, Texas, was charged with a crime for teaching a high school history class in Spanish. The charge was later dropped. On June 3, 1973, Governor Dolph Briscoe signed a law that ended the English-only rule, 55 years after it began.

Some districts kept Mexican American children apart and called it language teaching. In Driscoll, Texas, officials of the school district made Mexican American children spend four years getting through the first two grades. Linda Pérez, who spoke only English, was put in the "Mexican" first grade to learn English. In 1957 a federal court called the system "arbitrary and unreasonable" and ordered it stopped.

The Blackwell School in Marfa, Texas, taught Mexican American children from September 1909 until 1965. It started in the old school building that the district had left them in 1892, when it built a new school for white children. The National Park Service states that schools like it ran in more than 120 Texas school districts in 59 counties, with a "no Spanish in the classroom" rule. Blackwell closed in 1965, when Marfa opened one elementary school for all children. In October 2022 it became a national historic site.

From March 1 to 8, 1968, about 15,000 students walked out of seven schools in East Los Angeles. Mexican American students there faced a dropout rate of 60 percent in high school, bans on speaking Spanish, and being pushed into trade classes instead of classes that prepared them for college. They asked for bilingual teaching, classes taught in both Spanish and English, and for Mexican American school leaders. Members of the Board of Education turned them down and said there was no money. Later that spring, Los Angeles police arrested thirteen of the organizers on felony conspiracy charges, which means they were accused of planning a serious crime together. One of those arrested was the teacher Sal Castro, and school officials took away his teaching job. After months of sit-ins at the Board of Education, he got his job back. About two years later, a California appeals court threw out the charges against him and the others.

On January 2, 1968, President Johnson signed the Bilingual Education Act, which became Title VII of the 1965 school law. In 1974 the justices of the Supreme Court ruled on children placed in classes they could not understand. In San Francisco about 2,856 pupils of Chinese descent did not speak English. About 1,000 were getting extra lessons in English, which left about 1,800 with none. One of the children was Kinney Kinmon Lau. On January 21, 1974, in *Lau v. Nichols*, Justice William O. Douglas wrote that leaving those children without help "denies them a meaningful opportunity to participate in the public educational program." The ruling does not require schools to teach in Chinese. It states that a school may not put a child in a class taught only in a language the child did not understand and call that an equal education.

#### Hawaiian comes back into the schools

In 1896 Hawaii's lawmakers required schools to teach in English. In practice children were stopped from speaking Hawaiian at school. The history written by the Pūnana Leo teachers' group does not say who stopped them. In January 1983 a group of Hawaiian-language teachers met to plan how to keep the language alive. In August 1984 they opened the first Pūnana Leo preschool, at Kekaha on the island of Kauaʻi. *Pūnana leo* means "nest of voices." In 1986 they worked with the state's lawmakers to end the 90-year ban on teaching in Hawaiian. In 1987 immersion classes, where children are taught in Hawaiian, opened at Keaukaha Elementary in Hilo and Waiau Elementary in Pearl City. The group's own history describes them as the first elementary classes in the United States taught through a Native language.

#### New kinds of school

Several new kinds of school began in these years. Two of them, the magnet school and the segregation academy, came out of the fight over desegregation. The magnet school came first. At a magnet school, officials offer special teaching to draw families from across a district. McCarver Elementary in Tacoma, Washington, opened as one in the fall of 1968. Before that, 91 of every 100 of its pupils were Black. Nobody was assigned to go there. School officials used a $200,000 federal grant, moved in the district's best teachers, and let children work through their lessons at their own speed. Counselors visited families at home to ask them to choose the school. On the first day, about 200 white children enrolled where there had been about 50. By 1970 fewer than half of McCarver's pupils were Black, and there was a waiting list. The second magnet school opened in Boston in 1969. By 1981 there were about 1,000 in the country, and by 1991 more than 2,400.

White families in the South also started private schools, which were called segregation academies. A segregation academy was a private school started so that white children would not have to sit in class with Black children. Mississippi had only three private schools not run by a church before 1954. In 1964 the state's lawmakers voted grants of $185 for each child to attend such a school. In the school year 1964 to 1965, more than 500 children received more than $80,000. One new school was Citizens' Council School No. 1 in Jackson. The Citizens' Council was a group founded in Indianola, Mississippi, in 1954, months after *Brown*. By the mid-1960s its leaders were promoting private schools as a way to avoid public schools with Black and white pupils together.

In 1969 the justices of the Supreme Court ruled that Mississippi's school districts had to desegregate by 1970. Between 1966 and 1970 the number of private schools in the state rose from 121 to 236, and the number of pupils in them tripled. In 1970 almost every white student in Canton left the public schools for a private academy, and more than 40 of every 100 white students in Jackson left. The historian Michael Fuquay found that the academies got books, supplies, sports equipment, buildings and money straight from the public school systems. His account does not name the officials who handed them over. In Tunica and Clay counties, private school teachers stayed on the public school payroll. In Forrest County, private school pupils rode public school buses. William J. Simmons led the Mississippi Private School Association. He took the minutes of its board meeting on January 23, 1971. They record the board's decision that its schools would stay members "until such a time as they accept a Negro student or faculty member." At that point, the minutes say, a school would be asked to leave the association. "Negro" was the usual word for Black people at the time.

Catholic schools shrank in the same years. Their enrollment was highest in the school year 1964 to 1965, when 5,601,000 children attended 13,249 Catholic schools. By 1990 to 1991 there were 2,475,439 pupils. In 26 years the number of pupils fell by more than half. The number of schools fell from its high point of 13,292, in 1965 to 1966, to 8,587.

The charter school came last. A charter school is a public school run by its own board under an agreement, called a charter, instead of by the school district. In 1991 Minnesota's lawmakers passed the country's first charter school law, and Governor Arne Carlson signed it. The charter bill had failed in the state House in 1989, in 1990 and earlier in 1991. Lawmakers then put it into a larger bill that paid for the state's schools. They also cut it back. Only school districts could grant a charter, and the state could have only eight charter schools. It passed the House by one vote. The first charter went to Bluffview Montessori in Winona in December 1991. The first charter school to open was City Academy in St. Paul, in the fall of 1992. Milo Cutter founded it. In 1993 the lawmakers raised the limit from eight schools to twenty.

#### Disabled children get a right to school

Until 1975 the officials of an American public school could refuse to take a disabled child. The federal Department of Education states that in 1970 American schools taught only one disabled child in five, and that more than 1 million children with disabilities were shut out of school altogether.

In 1971 lawyers sued the school board of Washington, D.C., for seven children who had been kept out of school. George Liddell was eight. Staff at Maury Elementary School had turned down his application because he needed a special class, and he had never been to school at all. Janice King was thirteen, with weakness down one side of her body. She had been refused a place since she was old enough for school, because there was no program for her, and she had never been to school either. Jerome James was twelve and, in the court's words, "totally excluded from public school." Duane Blacksheare had been put out of Giddings Elementary School in October 1967, in the third grade, as a "behavior problem." He was out of school for about four years. Steven Gaston had been out of Taylor Elementary since September 1969. Michael Williams, 16, had epilepsy, which means he had seizures. A seizure is a sudden burst of activity in the brain that can make a person shake or pass out. He had been out of the Sharpe Health School since October 1969. The seventh child was Peter Mills.

The counts in the case did not agree, and the court's opinion lists all of them. The families said about 22,000 children in the city had disabilities and perhaps 18,000 of them were getting no special teaching. School board members said they were teaching at least 3,880. The city's own report for 1971 stated that an estimated 12,340 disabled children would not be served in the coming school year.

On November 29, 1975, President Gerald Ford signed the Education for All Handicapped Children Act. Under it, every disabled child in every state had the right to a free public education suited to that child.

The number of children in special education had begun to rise before the law. It went from 356,000 in 1947 to 1948, 1.5 of every 100 pupils, to 2,677,000 in 1969 to 1970, 5.9 of every 100. After the law, it reached 3,692,000 in 1976 to 1977 and 4,641,000 in 1989 to 1990, more than 1 child in 9. More than half of the rise in the number of children came before the law. After 1975, schooling was their right under federal law.

The groups children were sorted into changed too. The federal count had no group for children with learning disabilities until 1976 to 1977, when it counted 796,000 of them. By 1989 to 1990 it counted 2,050,000, nearly half of all children in special education. Over the same years, the number the government counted as "mentally retarded," its word then for children it judged to learn much more slowly than others, fell from 830,000 in 1969 to 1970 to 548,000 in 1989 to 1990.

<a id="story-peter-mills-education"></a>

#### Peter Mills

> **Who:** A twelve-year-old put out of his Washington school and kept out, whose name is on the 1972 case that gave disabled children a right to public school.
>
> **When and where:** Washington, D.C., 1971 and 1972.

Peter Mills was put out of Brent Elementary School in Washington, D.C., on March 23, 1971, and no public school took him in after that. He was in the fourth grade. School staff called him a "behavior problem," in words the court record keeps.

He was twelve. He was a ward of the District of Columbia, which means the city government was legally responsible for him. In the court's words, he was "excluded from any publicly-supported education," and he stayed that way.

On September 24, 1971, lawyers filed a case for him and six other children who had been shut out of Washington's schools. It was called *Mills v. Board of Education of the District of Columbia*. Part of the school board's answer was that it did not have the money to teach them.

Judge Joseph C. Waddy decided the case on August 1, 1972. He ruled that the District had to give a publicly supported education to every child of school age, whatever the child's disability. Lack of money was no excuse. He wrote that if there was not enough money for everything, it had to be spent "in such a manner that no child is entirely excluded from a publicly supported education." Before school officials could put a child out or move the child, they had to tell the family why and hold a hearing, a meeting where the family could answer.

In 1975 members of Congress applied the same rule to every state in a federal law. The federal Department of Education names two court cases as the ones that established that states had to teach disabled children, and *Mills* is one of them. The court record does not say what happened to Peter Mills afterward.

#### The paddle, in court and in the states

A public school could paddle a child without any hearing first, the justices of the Supreme Court ruled in 1977. After that ruling, state lawmakers banned school paddling one state at a time. Until 1971, hitting schoolchildren was lawful in every state except New Jersey. In American schools the usual method was a paddle, a wooden board that an adult swung against the child's buttocks.

In October 1970 James Ingraham was an eighth grader at Charles R. Drew Junior High School in Dade County, Florida. The Supreme Court's opinion states: "Because he was slow to respond to his teacher's instructions, Ingraham was subjected to more than 20 licks with a paddle while being held over a table in the principal's office." The beating left a hematoma, a pool of blood under the skin from a blow. He needed a doctor, and he missed several days of school. Roosevelt Andrews, a ninth grader at the same school, was paddled several times for small things. He was also hit on the arms, and one blow left him unable to use his arm fully for a week.

The rules allowed paddling but set limits on it. Florida law allowed punishment that was not "degrading or unduly severe." Dade County's own rule described the paddle as "less than two feet long, three to four inches wide, and about one-half inch thick." It set the usual punishment at "one to five 'licks' or blows with the paddle." James Ingraham was hit more than twenty times.

The families sued. On April 19, 1977, in *Ingraham v. Wright*, the justices ruled against the children, five votes to four. Justice Lewis Powell wrote that "the Eighth Amendment does not apply to the paddling of children as a means of maintaining discipline in public schools." The Eighth Amendment forbids cruel and unusual punishment. Powell also wrote that the Constitution did not require "notice and a hearing prior to the imposition of corporal punishment." He meant that school staff did not have to tell a child why, or hold a hearing, before they hit the child. Justice Byron White wrote for the four who disagreed. The record, he wrote, showed "beatings so severe that if they were inflicted on a hardened criminal for the commission of a serious crime, they might not pass constitutional muster." He meant that the Constitution might forbid beating even a criminal that hard.

State lawmakers ended school paddling instead, one state at a time. Massachusetts was the first state after New Jersey, in 1971. Hawaii followed in 1973, Maine in 1975, and Rhode Island and the District of Columbia in 1977. New Hampshire banned it in 1983, New York and Vermont in 1985 and California in 1986. Eight states banned it in 1989 and four in 1993. By 1994, 27 states and the District of Columbia had banned it. Then no state banned it again until 2003. When the century ended, school staff could still lawfully hit children in 23 states.

In 1978, 4 of every 100 American schoolchildren were hit at school. The districts' own reports to the federal government counted about 1.5 million children paddled in 1976, 613,514 in 1990 and 342,038 in 2000. District officials counted the children themselves, and nobody checked their numbers. In 2009 the law professor Deana Pollard Sacks wrote that some researchers had found the true numbers may be twice as high as reported.

#### Teaching at home

In the 1970s and 1980s some parents began to teach their children at home, and in several states officials took them to court. Many state attendance laws said that a child had to be taught in a school, or by a teacher with a state certificate. The historian Milton Gaither, who wrote a history of American homeschooling, says the old laws in many states made it "either illegal or dubious." Dubious means open to doubt. Six states required parents to hold a teaching license.

Two men who knew each other started the movement for different reasons. John Holt was a writer on school reform. He argued that ordinary schooling trained children to obey, and he told parents to take their children out of school. In August 1977 he started a newsletter, *Growing Without Schooling*, and he made up the word "unschooling." He died in 1985. Raymond Moore was a researcher on education and a Seventh-day Adventist, a member of a Christian church. He and his wife, Dorothy Moore, argued that school before about age eight or nine harmed children and that they should be taught at home until then. Their book *Better Late Than Early* came out in 1975, and *Home Grown Kids* in 1981.

In Harrison County, West Virginia, Bobby and Esther Riddle taught their children, Tim and Jill, at home. They were convicted of breaking the state's school attendance law and fined ten dollars each. On December 11, 1981, the West Virginia Supreme Court upheld the convictions, although its ruling said, "By all accounts in the record below, the Riddles did an excellent job." Larry Delconte moved to North Carolina in March 1981 with his wife, Michelle, and their four children and taught them at home. A state appeals court ruled that the attendance law forbade it. On May 7, 1985, the North Carolina Supreme Court reversed that ruling.

Lawmakers and judges in state after state changed the rules through the 1980s. Some states wrote detailed homeschooling laws, some added a sentence to an old law, and in some a court made the change. By 1989 most states had settled with homeschooling families, and a few held out into the early 1990s.

<a id="story-dejonge-family-homeschool"></a>

#### Mark and Chris DeJonge

> **Who:** Parents in rural Michigan who were convicted of a crime for teaching their own children at home, and who appealed for about ten years.
>
> **When and where:** Western Michigan, 1984 to 1993.

Mark and Chris DeJonge were convicted in 1985 for teaching their own children at home, and the Michigan Supreme Court overturned the conviction in 1993. They began teaching their children in August 1984, in rural western Michigan. They used a course from the Church of Christian Liberty and Academy of Arlington Heights, Illinois. Neither parent held a Michigan teaching certificate, the state's license to teach. A certified teacher is one who holds that license.

Chris DeJonge was in her second week of teaching when officials from the state Department of Social Services came to the house and told the family that the children were truants, children missing school without permission. Michigan law said a child between 6 and 16 had to be taught in a public school, or in an approved private school by a certified teacher.

They were charged and convicted in the Ottawa County District Court in 1985. The trial judge had a "very, very favorable report on the education of the children." He convicted them anyway, because the law was about who did the teaching and not about how well it was done. Each parent got two years of probation, which means living under a court's watch. Each was also fined $200. The judge ordered them to have the children tested and to arrange for a certified teacher. The sentence was put on hold while they appealed.

Their reason was religious. They wanted what they called a "Christ centered education," because, as the court's opinion records, "the major purpose of education is to show a student how to face God, not just show him how to face the world."

The Michigan Court of Appeals ruled against them on August 8, 1989. The Michigan Supreme Court sent the case back on October 17, 1990, and the Court of Appeals ruled against them again in 1991. On May 25, 1993, the Michigan Supreme Court ruled for them, four votes to three. Justice Riley wrote that the state had a strong interest in children being educated, but that Michigan had not shown that a certified teacher was necessary for it. The majority of the justices held that the rule could not be applied to a family with a sincere religious objection to it.

The case took them to court nine times over about ten years. In 2008 Mark DeJonge said, "We're glad we went through it. We grew as a family and we grew as a couple."

#### A Nation at Risk, 1983

In April 1983 a federal commission published a report that said American schools were failing, and it began the argument about testing and school standards that followed. On August 26, 1981, Secretary of Education T. H. Bell had set up the National Commission on Excellence in Education, led by David P. Gardner. After 18 months it published *A Nation at Risk*.

Its best-known sentences compared weak schooling to an attack by an enemy country: "If an unfriendly foreign power had attempted to impose on America the mediocre educational performance that exists today, we might well have viewed it as an act of war. As it stands, we have allowed this to happen to ourselves." It also stated that the foundations of American schooling were "being eroded by a rising tide of mediocrity." Mediocrity means work that is only average or poor.

The report lists the commission's reasons. On 19 tests given in many countries, American students were never first or second, and compared with other industrial countries they were last seven times. It stated that some 23 million American adults could not read, write and understand well enough for everyday life. It stated that about 13 of every 100 seventeen-year-olds could not either, and as many as 40 of every 100 among minority youth. Average SAT scores had fallen almost every year from 1963 to 1980, by more than 50 points in reading and nearly 40 in math. Of seventeen-year-olds, nearly 40 of every 100 could not draw conclusions from something they read, and only about one in three could solve a math problem that needed several steps.

These are the commission's own figures, and other researchers disputed several of them. In 1993 researchers at Sandia National Laboratories, a federal laboratory, published their own study of the same kinds of measures. On most of them, including test scores, dropout rates and college enrollment, they found steady or slight improvement.

#### Teachers strike, and their pay

In this era teachers in New York City and in Florida joined unions and went on strike. A union is a group of workers who join together to bargain with an employer over pay and working conditions. On November 7, 1960, Election Day, the new United Federation of Teachers held the first teachers' strike in New York City's history. It lasted one day. The union said it had about a quarter of the city's 39,000 teachers, *Time* magazine reported. In June 1961 New York teachers voted to bargain as a group, and in December they chose the union to bargain for them. Later accounts call it the first big-city teachers' union in the country to win that right.

On February 19, 1968, more than 27,000 Florida teachers and school officials handed in letters resigning their jobs and walked out. The Zinn Education Project, a group that makes history lessons for teachers, calls it the first strike by teachers across a whole state in the United States. The teachers had asked for better pay and more money for schools, and Governor Claude Kirk had refused. The strike ended on March 8, when members of the state board of education agreed to more money for schools. Afterward, officials refused to rehire thousands of the teachers because they had gone on strike.

Measured in dollars of the same value, the average public school teacher earned about $58,700 a year in 1969 to 1970, about $52,900 in 1979 to 1980, and about $63,500 in 1989 to 1990. In 1999 to 2000 the figure was still about $63,500, so real teacher pay did not grow in the 1990s. The economist Sylvia Allegretto compares teachers' weekly pay with that of other college graduates of the same age and schooling. By her count, teachers earned about 7 percent less in 1979, about 5 percent less in 1993 and about 6 percent less in 1996. After 1996 the gap grew.

#### The last one-room schools

The one-room school nearly disappeared in these years. The federal count of one-teacher public schools was 59,652 in 1949 to 1950, 20,213 in 1959 to 1960 and 1,815 in 1970 to 1971. By 1990 to 1991 there were 617. The number of school districts kept falling. There were 83,718 districts in 1949 to 1950, 40,520 in 1959 to 1960 and 17,995 in 1970 to 1971.

### 2000 to Today

After 2000 the arguments about American schooling were over which school a child attended, what was taught there and how learning was measured. In 2002 President George W. Bush signed a law that ordered every state to test every child in reading and math each year from third grade to eighth. The yearly tests began in the school year 2005 to 2006. More families chose charter schools, private schools paid for with state money, or teaching at home. In the spring of 2020 officials closed the school buildings because of the coronavirus pandemic, a disease spreading around the world, and children were taught over the internet for the rest of that school year. Gunmen killed children and teachers inside schools. Federal officials counted the children who had died at the government's own Indian boarding schools, and a president apologized. In 2025 President Donald Trump ordered his Secretary of Education to begin closing the federal Department of Education. Federal officials publish their school counts years after the school year they describe.

#### Testing every child: No Child Left Behind

Under a federal law signed in 2002, every state had to test every child in reading and math every year from third grade through eighth grade. President George W. Bush signed the No Child Left Behind Act on January 8, 2002, at Hamilton High School in Hamilton, Ohio. The law is called the act "of 2001" because members of Congress passed it in 2001. The first lines of the law state its purpose: "to close the achievement gap with accountability, flexibility, and choice, so that no child is left behind." The achievement gap is the difference between the test scores of different groups of children, such as rich and poor children.

At the signing Bush said, "The fundamental principle of this bill is that every child can learn, we expect every child to learn, and you must show us whether or not every child is learning." The yearly tests in grades 3 through 8 began in the school year 2005 to 2006. Science had to be tested at least once in grades 3 to 5, once in grades 6 to 9 and once in grades 10 to 12. States had to be able to report the scores separately for boys and girls, for each main racial and ethnic group, for children still learning English, for children of migrant farm workers, for disabled children and for children from poor families.

The law also set a deadline. By the end of the school year 2013 to 2014, "all students in each group" were to "meet or exceed the State's proficient level of academic achievement." Proficient means good enough to meet the standard that each state set. So every child in the country was to reach that level in reading and math by 2014.

On December 10, 2015, President Barack Obama signed a new law, the Every Student Succeeds Act. The federal Department of Education's own description states that No Child Left Behind's "prescriptive requirements became increasingly unworkable for schools and educators." Prescriptive means telling people exactly what to do. Under the new law the yearly tests in grades 3 through 8 stayed, along with one test in high school. The single national deadline went away. Officials in each state now set their own "long-term goals" for all their pupils and for each group of them. Both laws are rewritten versions of the 1965 school law that President Lyndon Johnson signed at his old one-room school in Texas.

Children in big cities took many tests. The Council of the Great City Schools, a group of big-city school districts, studied the tests in 66 of those districts in the school year 2014 to 2015. The districts had more than 7 million students in about three dozen states. According to the Associated Press report of the study, a student took about 112 required standardized tests between pre-kindergarten and twelfth grade. A standardized test is the same test, given and scored the same way, for every child who takes it. Students spent 20 to 25 hours a year taking these tests. For the average eighth grader that was about 2.3 percent of class time. Eighth and tenth grade had the most required tests.

The researchers Thomas Dee and Brian Jacob called the law's effect on learning "a highly controversial but centrally important question." In 2011 they studied national test scores from before and after the law. They found that the law raised fourth graders' math scores, and eighth graders' math scores to some degree. They found no sign that it raised fourth graders' reading.

#### Choosing a school: charters, private schools and state money

In these years more families sent their children to schools other than the local public school, and state lawmakers paid for some of those choices with public money. The federal count of every public school records the growth of charter schools. In the school year 2012 to 2013 there were 6,079 charter schools, with 4.6 percent of all public school pupils. In 2022 to 2023 there were 7,998, with 3,717,857 pupils, or 7.6 percent. Federal statisticians published that table in February 2024. As of September 2026, 2022 to 2023 was still the newest year in the federal count of charter schools.

About 1 American child in 11 went to a private school. In the fall of 2021, 4.7 million children from kindergarten through twelfth grade were in private schools, 9 percent of all schoolchildren. Catholic schools had 1.7 million of them. Other religious schools had 2.0 million, and schools with no church behind them had 1.1 million. Ten years earlier, in the fall of 2011, the total was 4.5 million. Catholic schools had lost about 200,000 children over those ten years, and other religious schools had gained about 300,000. The National Center for Education Statistics, the federal office that counts schools, published those figures in May 2024. As of September 2026, they were still the newest full federal count of private schools. Catholic schools had 5,601,000 pupils in 1964 to 1965, their highest year. The 1.7 million of 2021 was less than a third of that.

State lawmakers created three main ways to pay for private schooling with public money. A voucher is a payment from the state that a family can use toward a private school's fees instead of sending the child to the local public school. An education savings account, called an ESA, is state money set aside for one child. The family can spend it on private school fees, a tutor, books or an online course. A tax-credit scholarship works through taxes. A person or a company gives money to a scholarship fund, and the state takes the same amount off their tax bill.

EdChoice, a group that supports these programs, keeps the national count. It listed 69 programs for the school year 2024 to 2025. By its count, 488,736 children used education savings accounts, 349,923 used vouchers, 217,194 had tax-credit scholarships, and 106,442 in Florida had a tax-credit ESA. Together that is about 1,162,000 children. Patrick Wolf, a researcher at the University of Arkansas, has said that studies of the programs open to all children find that about two of every three children using them had never gone to a public school. In Florida, which opened its programs to all children in 2023, *Politico* reported that 69 percent of the new students were already in private schools.

The two sides disagree about the money. EdChoice states that its aim is "advancing educational freedom and choice for all," and it quotes the economists Milton and Rose Friedman's idea that "every family could choose the learning environment that best fits their child." The National Education Association, a teachers' union, states that "vouchers take scarce funding from students in public schools and give those resources to unaccountable private schools." Studies of one program, Louisiana's vouchers, found different things about the children who used them and about the public schools nearby. In 2016 the researchers Jonathan Mills and Patrick Wolf studied the program's first two years. Children who used a voucher to go to a private school scored lower in math than similar children who did not. The researcher Anna Egalite found that the public schools that stood to lose the most pupils to the program did the same or slightly better.

#### Teaching at home: the 2020 jump

The share of children taught at home rose in this era and jumped in 2020. The federal survey that counts homeschooling found 1.7 percent of children aged 5 to 17 taught at home in 1999 and 3.4 percent in 2012. In 2019 it was 2.8 percent, about 1.5 million children. Another 1.2 percent were in full-time online school.

Parents gave reasons in the 2019 survey. For 80 in every 100 homeschooled children, a parent named worry about the school environment. For 75 in every 100, a parent wanted to give moral teaching, and for 75 in every 100, a parent wanted more family life together. For 73 in every 100, a parent was unhappy with the teaching at other schools.

Then the school buildings closed. The Census Bureau asked households the same question twice in 2020. Between April 23 and May 5, 5.4 percent of households with school-age children said they were homeschooling. Between September 30 and October 12, the figure was 11.1 percent. Among Black households it went from 3.3 percent to 16.1 percent. The Census Bureau published those figures in March 2021. It worded the question so that children taking public school lessons over a screen were not counted.

Most of the rise stayed after the schools reopened. The researchers Genevieve Smith and Angela R. Watson studied the Census Bureau's surveys from September 2022 to August 2023. They found 5.82 percent of school-age children reported as homeschooled in the school year 2022 to 2023, 10.06 percent in private schools and 84.12 percent in public schools. They wrote that education experts had predicted the number would fall once schools reopened, and it did not. The figure was about twice what it had been before 2020. It was highest in Alaska, at 12.6 percent, and lowest in Rhode Island, at 2.9 percent.

Lawmakers in each state make their own rules for homeschooling, and the rules range from almost none to many. The Coalition for Responsible Home Education, a group that argues for more checks on homeschooling, counted the rules in March 2026. In 12 states a family does not have to tell anyone that it is homeschooling. In 29 states no one ever has to check a homeschooled child's progress, and only 3 states require a check for every homeschooled child. In 22 states a family does not have to keep any school records. Texas requires no notice, no check and no records. New York requires all three. A parent there must send the local school superintendent a written notice by July 1 each year. Then the parent must send a teaching plan for the child. Every three months the parent sends a report giving the hours taught and what was covered in each subject. Once a year the parent sends an assessment, a test or written review of how the child is doing.

#### Special education now

By the 2020s about 1 public school student in 7 received special education. The 1975 law under which disabled children have a right to school is now called the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, or IDEA. In the school year 2022 to 2023, 7.5 million students aged 3 to 21 received special education or related services under it. That was the same as 15 percent of all public school students, according to the National Center for Education Statistics in May 2024. The largest group, 32 in every 100, had specific learning disabilities, such as trouble learning to read or to do math. In 1989 to 1990 the count had been 4,641,000, or 11.4 percent.

#### How separate the schools are now

In the school year 2020 to 2021, about 1 American student in 7 went to a school where at least 90 of every 100 students were of one race or ethnic group. The Government Accountability Office, the office that checks federal programs for Congress, counted this in a report released in July 2022. More than a third of students, about 18.5 million, went to schools where at least 75 of every 100 students were of one race or ethnic group. That report covers only 2014 to 2021.

Researchers at the Civil Rights Project at the University of California, Los Angeles, measure a longer stretch. In a report of April 2024, they counted schools where 90 to 100 of every 100 students were not white. In 1988, 7.4 percent of American public schools were like that. In 2021, 19.8 percent were. In 2021, 78 of every 100 students in those schools were poor. Their series starts in 1988, so it cannot be compared with the years before.

The same researchers measured the South further back. In a 2017 report they counted Black students in the South who went to schools where 90 to 100 of every 100 students were not white. The share fell from nearly 80 percent to 23 percent during the years of desegregation, and it was back up to 35.8 percent in 2014. The share of Southern Black students in schools that were mostly white was highest, about 43 percent, in the mid-1980s. By 2021 it was about 16 percent.

The students themselves had changed. In 1968, 80.7 of every 100 American public school students were white, 14.7 were Black and 4.7 were Latino. In 2021, 45.3 were white, 14.9 were Black and 28.2 were Latino.

In New Orleans, the McDonogh No. 19 school building, where Leona Tate, Gail Etienne and Tessie Prevost walked in with federal marshals on November 14, 1960, reopened on May 4, 2022, as the Tate, Etienne and Prevost Center.

#### The school year and the school day

In most states that set a minimum, school must run at least 180 days a year, and a few districts have tried other calendars. Researchers at the Pew Research Center checked state laws in 2023. Of the 38 states that set a minimum number of school days, the laws of 27 states and Washington, D.C., required 180. The laws of seven states set a lower minimum, and Colorado's 160 days was the lowest. The laws of four states set a higher one, and Kansas was highest, at 186 days for kindergarten through grade 11.

Year-round school spreads about the same number of days across the whole year, with shorter breaks. It became less common. The federal count found 4.4 percent of public schools with all their pupils on a year-round calendar in 2007 to 2008, 3.2 percent in 2011 to 2012 and 2.5 percent in 2017 to 2018.

The four-day school week spread instead. In September 2023 Paul Thompson, an economist at Oregon State University, counted about 2,100 schools in almost 900 districts in 26 states on a four-day week. He said that was about double the number ten years before and almost 40 percent more than in 2019. In Missouri, by the count of Jon Turner of Missouri State University, 105 districts had a four-day week in 2020 and 128 in 2022, a quarter of the state's districts. His count and the state's list differ, so both are estimates.

In a 2014 policy statement, the American Academy of Pediatrics, a group of children's doctors, said that middle and high schools "should aim for a starting time of no earlier than 8:30 am," because teenagers who start earlier lose sleep. In the school year 2020 to 2021 the average American public high school started at 8:07 in the morning. More than 7 of every 10 started before 8:30.

California's lawmakers wrote a start time into law, and the governor approved it on October 13, 2019. Under Senate Bill 328, middle schools may begin no earlier than 8:00 a.m. and high schools no earlier than 8:30 a.m. Schools had to change by July 1, 2022, or, where a teachers' contract in force on January 1, 2020, ended later, when that contract ended. The law does not apply to rural districts. Florida's lawmakers passed a similar law in 2023, to begin in 2026. District officials said they did not have enough buses or drivers to do it. On March 27, 2025, Florida senators voted for Senate Bill 296 with no votes against. Under the bill, the requirement ended. Instead, any district that kept early start times had to file a report on what stood in the way. Governor Ron DeSantis signed it on May 21, 2025.

By 2021 staff at nearly every public school gave a tablet or other device to any pupil who needed one. In the spring of 2020, 45 percent of public school principals said their school gave pupils a computer or other device to use at home. In September 2021, 96 percent of public schools said they gave devices such as tablets to pupils who needed them, and 70 percent supplied internet service at home.

#### The paddle and the suspension

In 2026 the laws of 15 states still let an adult at school hit a child as a punishment. In American schools the usual method is the paddle. At the end of the 1990s, 23 states had no ban on it. From 2003 to 2011 lawmakers in four more states banned it: Delaware in 2003, Pennsylvania in 2005, Ohio in 2009 and New Mexico in 2011. In August 2026 reporters at NPR, the public radio network, counted 15 states whose laws allow it and 30 states plus Washington, D.C., whose laws ban it in all public schools. The other five states neither allow it nor ban it outright. Some have other laws that have been interpreted as bans, and some have no law about it. Other groups count differently for that reason, and they say so.

Federal officials count the children who are hit, in a survey that every public school district must answer, called the Civil Rights Data Collection. In the school year 2021 to 2022, about 24,500 public school students were hit at school as a punishment. NPR counted almost 32,000 reported paddlings in the same data, because some children were hit more than once. Not every district reports it. Almost all the reported cases were in eight states, most of them in the South. Mississippi had the highest rate in the country and Arkansas the second highest. Officials posted the next survey, for 2023 to 2024, in September 2026, about eight months late. They posted it as raw data files with no national totals, so as of September 2026, 2021 to 2022 was the newest national count.

The same survey shows which children were hit. White boys were 23 of every 100 public school students and 47 of every 100 children hit. Black boys were 8 of every 100 students and 20 of every 100 children hit. American Indian and Alaska Native boys were fewer than 1 of every 100 students and 2 of every 100 children hit. Girls of every group were hit less often than their share of students.

School staff suspend children far more often than they paddle them. A suspension keeps a child out of class for a set number of days, either in a separate room at school or at home. In 2021 to 2022, about 2.3 million children, 5 percent of public school students, were suspended at least once inside school. About 2.4 million were suspended at least once out of school. Black boys were 8 of every 100 students. They were 18 of every 100 children suspended in school, 22 of every 100 suspended out of school and 21 of every 100 expelled, which means put out of the school altogether. The federal report states that "Black boys were disciplined at higher rates, compared to boys of other races." Black girls were 7 of every 100 students and 13 of every 100 children suspended out of school. Children with disabilities were 17 of every 100 students and 29 of every 100 suspended out of school.

School officials also call the police. In 2021 to 2022 districts reported about 220,000 children to the police, and about 17 of every 100 of those reports ended in an arrest at school. Black children were 15 of every 100 students, 28 of every 100 children reported to the police and 33 of every 100 children arrested at school.

School staff suspended and expelled even preschool children. In 2021 to 2022, out of 1.4 million children in public preschool, about 2,700 were suspended out of school and about 370 were expelled. Black children were 18 of every 100 preschool children and 38 of every 100 of those suspended. Preschool children with disabilities were 23 of every 100 preschool children and 74 of every 100 of those expelled.

#### Shootings at school

In these years gunmen shot and killed children and teachers inside American schools. Statisticians at the National Center for Education Statistics count every time a gun is fired or shown at a school, or a bullet hits school property, whether anyone is hurt or not. In the school year 2000 to 2001 they counted 30 shootings, with 18 people killed and 29 hurt. In 2021 to 2022 they counted 327 shootings, with 81 people killed and 269 hurt. Both counts include the people who fired. The statisticians warned that 2021 to 2022 was far above every earlier year. As of September 2026, it was the newest year the federal count covered. Reporters at Education Week, a newspaper about schools, count a narrower set. They count only shootings on school grounds, during school or a school event, in which someone other than the shooter was hit. By their count, 7 people were killed in 2025, the fewest since 2020. The two counts use different rules and cannot be joined into one list.

Adam Lanza, who was 20, shot and killed his mother in her bed at their home in Newtown, Connecticut, on December 14, 2012. Then he went to Sandy Hook Elementary School with a rifle and shot his way into the building. In a hallway he killed the principal and the school psychologist. He went into two first-grade classrooms. He killed the two adults in each room, 15 children in one room and 5 in the other, and then he shot himself. Stephen Sedensky, the prosecutor for that part of Connecticut, investigated. A prosecutor is a lawyer who brings criminal charges for the government. He wrote that "in fewer than 11 minutes twenty first-grade pupils and six adults had lost their lives." Lanza also wounded two other adults. The report does not print the children's names. Sedensky found no one else criminally responsible.

On February 14, 2018, Nikolas Cruz, a 19-year-old former student, shot and killed 14 students and 3 staff members at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, and wounded 17 others. He fired inside one building for about six minutes, from 2:21 to 2:27 in the afternoon. A state commission investigated. Its members found that Scot Peterson, the sheriff's deputy assigned to the school, "fled to a position of personal safety while Cruz shot and killed ... students and staff." Prosecutors charged Peterson with felony child neglect, a serious crime of failing to protect children, and with other crimes. On June 29, 2023, a jury found him not guilty.

In Uvalde, Texas, an 18-year-old gunman went into Robb Elementary School with a rifle at 11:33 in the morning on May 24, 2022. He went into two joined classrooms and killed 19 children and 2 teachers. At least 17 others were wounded. Within 3 minutes, 11 police officers were inside the school. The gunman fired at them, and they pulled back. The school district's police chief, Pete Arredondo, told officers several times to wait while they looked for keys, and he tried to talk to the gunman. Justice Department officials counted at least 380 officers from 24 agencies at the school. A committee of the Texas House of Representatives counted 376. Children in the classrooms called 911, and within four minutes of the officers' arrival the dispatchers knew that class was in session. At about 12:50 p.m. a team of Border Patrol agents and sheriff's deputies went in and killed the gunman. That was 77 minutes after the first officers entered the school.

Officials of the U.S. Justice Department published their review on January 18, 2024. The review states that the officers' "most significant failure" was how they saw the gunman. They treated the gunman as a "barricaded subject," a person shut in a room, instead of an "active shooter," a person who is still attacking people. The report does not name the gunman. In June 2024 a grand jury charged Arredondo and a former school police officer, Adrian Gonzales, with abandoning and endangering children. A grand jury is a group of citizens who decide whether there is enough proof for a trial. They were the only officers charged. On January 21, 2026, a jury found Gonzales not guilty. Arredondo's trial on 10 counts was set for February 22, 2027.

At Apalachee High School in Winder, Georgia, on September 4, 2024, Colt Gray shot and killed two 14-year-old students and two teachers. He pleaded guilty, and on July 27, 2026, a judge sentenced him to life in prison with no chance of ever being let out. His father, Colin Gray, had given him the rifle as a Christmas present. On March 3, 2026, a jury found Colin Gray guilty of two counts of second-degree murder. Under Georgia law, that crime means causing a death while, through criminal carelessness, causing a child under 18 "cruel or excessive physical or mental pain." It does not require meaning to kill, and it carries 10 to 30 years in prison. The jury also found him guilty of two counts of involuntary manslaughter, which means causing a death without meaning to, and of reckless conduct and cruelty to children. On July 30, 2026, he was sentenced to 15 years.

#### The school buildings close, 2020

In the spring of 2020 state and local officials closed nearly every school building in the country because of COVID-19, an illness caused by a virus. On March 11, 2020, the World Health Organization had declared it a pandemic, a disease spreading around the world. On March 17, 2020, Governor Laura Kelly of Kansas ordered every school building in her state closed for the rest of the school year. Kansas was the first state to do that. Reporters at Education Week tracked the closures from March 6 to May 15, 2020. By their count, at their peak the closures kept at least 55.1 million students out of 124,000 public and private school buildings. Nearly every state's officials ordered or advised that schools stay closed until the end of the school year.

Teachers taught over the internet, and not every child had a computer at home. In a Census Bureau survey in September 2020, 59 percent of adults with a child in school said the school or district had given the child a computer.

<a id="story-tabatha-rosproy-2020-teaching"></a>

#### Tabatha Rosproy

> **Who:** A preschool teacher named National Teacher of the Year in the spring her classroom was shut by the pandemic.
>
> **When and where:** Winfield, Kansas, 2020.

Tabatha Rosproy kept teaching her preschool class from a distance after Kansas closed its school buildings in March 2020, and in May 2020 she was named National Teacher of the Year. She was the first early childhood teacher to win the award.

She taught for the Winfield Early Learning Center in Winfield, Kansas. Her classroom was not in a school. It was inside Cumbernauld Village, a retirement community and nursing home in the town, and the program was called Little Vikes. Children with disabilities and children without them were in her class together, and residents of the home joined in with the children every day.

When the Kansas school buildings closed, Rosproy was a co-chair of the state task force of teachers that wrote the guidance for teaching children at home. She recorded her lessons and put them on an app called Seesaw. Once a week she held a video call with each child, one at a time. When a family could not get online, she called them, texted them, or delivered the materials to their home. For the families of her pupils with disabilities, she prepared materials that showed the parents how to use the methods she used in the classroom. She mailed each child a bin of sensory toys, the part of the classroom they liked best, and she put pinwheels in their yards.

"At first, I was nervous to be named National Teacher of the Year during this pandemic," she told Education Week, "because I wondered if I was able to make a difference." On May 22, 2020, she told the news site Chalkbeat, "Nothing will replace what we are able to do in person. But we are surviving through this and we are looking for the small victories when we have them."

#### Test scores after 2020

National test scores fell after the school closures and had not recovered by 2024. The National Assessment of Educational Progress, often called the Nation's Report Card, is the same federal test given to a sample of American children decade after decade. It was given from January to March 2022, the first time since the closures. Compared with 2019, the average math score had fallen 5 points in fourth grade and 8 points in eighth grade. The report on the test called these the largest drops in math since those tests began in 1990.

It was given again from January to March 2024. The average fourth-grade reading score was 5 points below 2019. Thirty-one of every 100 fourth graders reached the level the test calls Proficient, 4 fewer than in 2019. Fourth-grade math was 3 points below 2019. In twelfth grade, reading and math were each 3 points below 2019. The National Assessment Governing Board, which oversees the test, released those twelfth-grade results on September 9, 2025.
