It called them "the lowest ever reported on each assessment," which means the lowest since each of these tests began, not the lowest in all of history. Forty-five of every 100 high school seniors scored below the lowest level the test names, called Basic, in math, and 32 of every 100 in reading.

The test does not measure why scores fell. Reading scores had already begun to drop between 2017 and 2019, before the closures.

#### Teachers: hard to hire, and paid less than other graduates

In 2023 and 2024 most public schools reported trouble filling teaching jobs, and teachers earned less than other college graduates. In August 2024 the National Center for Education Statistics asked 1,392 public schools in every state how their hiring was going. Seventy-four of every 100 said they had trouble filling at least one teaching job for the school year 2024 to 2025. On average each school had six teaching jobs open, and it had filled 79 of every 100 of them with fully certified teachers. The reason schools gave most often was a lack of qualified people, at 64 of every 100 schools. Next was too few people applying, at 62 of every 100. A year earlier, 86 of every 100 schools had reported trouble hiring teachers.

The National Education Association, a teachers' union, keeps the pay figures. By its count the average public school teacher earned $74,495 in the school year 2024 to 2025, up from $71,985 the year before. A new teacher started at $48,112 on average. Once rising prices are counted, the union reports, teachers were earning about 5 percent less than teachers had ten years earlier.

The economist Sylvia Allegretto compares the weekly pay of public school teachers with that of other college graduates of about the same age, schooling and state. By her count, in 2024 teachers earned 26.9 percent less a week than those other graduates, the widest gap she had measured. In 1996 the gap had been about 6 percent.

#### Paying for college

In these years a year at college cost tens of thousands of dollars, and 42.3 million Americans owed money on federal student loans. The National Center for Education Statistics gives the full average cost of a year for a new full-time student living at a four-year college in the school year 2022 to 2023. At a public college it was $27,100. At a private college run for profit it was $33,600, and at a private college not run for profit it was $58,600.

Fewer new students borrowed than ten years before. In 2020 to 2021, 38 of every 100 new full-time students received a loan, down from 50 of every 100 in 2010 to 2011. Students who finished a four-year degree in 2015 to 2016 with federal loans still owed an average of $45,300 in 2020.

In August 2022 officials in President Joe Biden's Department of Education announced a plan to cancel some federal student loans. A borrower who earned less than $125,000 a year could have up to $10,000 canceled, and some could have up to $20,000. About 43 million borrowers qualified. The Congressional Budget Office, which works out costs for Congress, estimated the plan would cancel about $430 billion. On June 30, 2023, in *Biden v. Nebraska*, the justices of the Supreme Court struck the plan down, six votes to three. Chief Justice Roberts wrote that the law the officials relied on did not let them cancel "$430 billion of student loan principal." The principal is the money borrowed, not counting interest. Justice Kagan wrote for the three who disagreed: "Emergencies, after all, are emergencies, and more serious measures must be expected in response to more serious problems."

On June 30, 2026, according to the federal office that runs student aid, 42.3 million people owed more than $1.7 trillion in federal student loans. More than 9.3 million of them were in default. Under federal law a loan is in default when the borrower has gone 270 days, about nine months, without making a payment on time.

#### The boarding schools investigated, and an apology

Between 2021 and 2024 federal officials investigated the government's own Indian boarding schools, and in 2024 President Joe Biden apologized for them. On June 22, 2021, Secretary of the Interior Deb Haaland ordered the investigation. She is a citizen of Laguna Pueblo and was the first Native person in a president's cabinet, the group of the president's top officials who each run a department. Her order asked for a report on the government's records of the schools, "with an emphasis on cemeteries or potential burial sites." Her department's announcement said the order followed news from Canada. There the Tk'emlúps te Secwepemc First Nation had reported 215 unmarked graves at the former Kamloops Indian Residential School.

Investigators published a first report in May 2022 and a final report in July 2024, under Bryan Newland, the Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs. The final report counted 417 federal boarding schools between 1819 and 1969 and at least 973 children who died at them. It named 18,624 children who had attended. Investigators found burial sites at 65 of the schools. The first report lists what staff did to children as punishment. Staff locked children alone in a room, which the report calls solitary confinement, and kept food from them. Staff also flogged children, which means beating them with a whip or a rod, and whipped, slapped and cuffed them. To cuff means to hit with an open hand. Staff sometimes made older children punish younger ones.

On October 25, 2024, Biden spoke at the Gila Crossing Community School in the Gila River Indian Community in Arizona, and Haaland introduced him. "I formally apologize today as President of the United States of America for what we did," he said. He also said, "After 150 years, the government eventually stopped the program but never formally apologized." On December 9, 2024, by proclamation, a formal written order from the president, he made about 24.5 acres of the old Carlisle Indian Industrial School grounds in Pennsylvania into a national monument. The proclamation states that "nearly 1,000 Native youths died in schools across the system, but the actual number of lives lost is likely much higher."

Members of Congress proposed a commission to study the boarding schools. Senator Lisa Murkowski introduced her bill on February 26, 2025, and Representative Tom Cole introduced his on February 3, 2026. By September 2026 neither the Senate nor the House had voted to pass either one.

Four federal boarding schools for Native students, away from reservations, were still open in 2026, according to the Bureau of Indian Education: Chemawa Indian School in Salem, Oregon, Flandreau Indian School in South Dakota, Riverside Indian School in Anadarko, Oklahoma, and Sherman Indian High School in Riverside, California.

#### Books taken off the shelves, and limits on teaching

In the 2020s school board members and state officials removed thousands of books from school libraries. Lawmakers or officials in 18 states limited what teachers could say about race and sex. Each side described the removals differently. PEN America, a writers' group that defends free speech, calls a school book ban any removal of a book, or any limit on reading it, because of what is in it. The removal can follow a complaint from parents or community members, a decision by school officials, or an order or threat from government officials. By PEN America's count there were just under 3,000 bans a year in the school years 2021 to 2022 and 2022 to 2023, 10,046 in 2023 to 2024, and 6,870 in 2024 to 2025. In 2024 to 2025 Florida had the most, 2,304, then Texas with 1,781 and Tennessee with 1,622.

In January 2025 officials of the U.S. Department of Education sent out a memo calling book bans a "hoax." They also canceled earlier advice that removing books could break civil rights law. In July 2025 Defense Department officials removed nearly 600 titles from the schools the department runs for children on military bases. According to PEN America, the reason given was that the books did not fit the president's orders on diversity, race and what the orders called "gender ideology extremism."

The American Library Association, the national group for librarians, counts school, public and college libraries together. For 2025 it recorded 4,235 different titles that people tried to have removed. By its count, pressure groups, government officials and other decision makers started 92 of every 100 of those attempts.

Education Week, a newspaper about schools, reported in March 2024 that lawmakers or officials in 44 states had considered limits since 2021 on how race and gender could be taught, and that 18 states had put such limits in place. In Florida, Governor Ron DeSantis signed the Parental Rights in Education law on March 28, 2022. It banned classroom teaching about sexual orientation or gender identity from kindergarten through third grade. Sexual orientation means which sex a person is attracted to. Gender identity means a person's own sense of being a boy or a girl, a man or a woman. DeSantis said that parents "should be protected from schools using classroom instruction to sexualize their kids as young as 5 years old." Opponents called it the "Don't Say Gay" bill. U.S. Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona said the governor was targeting "some of Florida's most vulnerable students and families, all while under the guise of 'parents' rights.'" A guise is a false cover.

In the school year 2022 to 2023 members of the Montgomery County school board in Maryland added five storybooks with LGBTQ characters for kindergarten through fifth grade. LGBTQ stands for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer. These are words for people who are attracted to people of their own sex, or whose sense of being male or female differs from the body they were born with. At first board members let parents take their children out of those lessons. Then they ended that choice. Parents of several religions sued, among them Tamer Mahmoud and Enas Barakat, who are Muslims, and Jeff and Svitlana Roman and Chris and Melissa Persak, who are Christians. On June 27, 2025, in *Mahmoud v. Taylor*, six justices of the Supreme Court ruled that the parents were entitled to have their children excused while their case went on. Justice Alito, writing for the six, relied on *Wisconsin v. Yoder*, the 1972 Amish case, and wrote that parents have a right "to direct the religious upbringing of their children." Justice Sotomayor wrote for the three who disagreed that public schools "offer to children of all faiths and backgrounds an education and an opportunity to practice living in our multicultural society."

#### The federal Department of Education, 2025 and 2026

In 2025 President Donald Trump ordered his Secretary of Education to begin closing the federal Department of Education. In 2026 his officials announced that they would move its special education and civil rights offices to other departments. The people who work in that department send federal money to schools and enforce the laws against discrimination in them. Staff in the department, or paid by it, also collect the civil rights survey, the national test and the other federal school counts in this era.

On March 11, 2025, Secretary of Education Linda McMahon announced layoffs that would cut the department's staff from 4,133 people to 2,183. On March 20, Trump signed an order telling her to "take all necessary steps to facilitate the closure of the Department of Education and return authority over education to the States and local communities." The order gave his reasons. It cited the 2024 national test, by which "70 percent of 8th graders were below proficient in reading, and 72 percent were below proficient in math." Below proficient includes children who reached the Basic level.

In a lawsuit later called *McMahon v. New York*, a federal judge in Massachusetts blocked the layoffs on May 22, 2025. On July 14, 2025, a majority of the justices of the Supreme Court, in an order that no justice signed, let the layoffs go ahead while the case continued. Justice Sotomayor, joined by Justices Kagan and Jackson, disagreed. She wrote that the case "arises out of the President's unilateral efforts to eliminate a Cabinet-level agency established by Congress nearly half a century ago." Unilateral means done by one person alone.

In June 2026 officials announced that the office for special education would move to the Department of Health and Human Services. The Office for Civil Rights, which investigates discrimination in schools, would move to the Justice Department. *Education Week* reported in June 2026 that "only Congress can formally close a cabinet agency." By then members of Congress had passed no law closing it.

<a id="ch-news-communication"></a>

## Chapter 31: News and Communication

### Before 1500

Before 1500, people carried the news themselves. Runners carried messages from one nation to another. Nations that spoke different languages talked with their hands. Most of what is known about how they did it comes from two places. One is the accounts that Native nations and Europeans gave later. The other is the old objects that archaeologists, scientists who study the past by digging, have found in the ground.

#### Runners and wampum

The Haudenosaunee have lived for a thousand years and more in what is now central New York. They are also called the Iroquois, or the Six Nations. Five nations joined together before Europeans came, and the Tuscarora became the sixth in 1722. Haudenosaunee runners called the nations to council, a meeting of their leaders. The runners also carried news from nation to nation and warned of danger. A runner carried a string of wampum to show that his message was official. Wampum is small beads cut from the white and purple parts of a clam shell. His pouch held pounded, dried corn mixed with maple sugar.

The Onondaga Nation keeps the wampum records of the Haudenosaunee. Its people describe how a council is called. Each nation receives a string of wampum that stands for the topic the leaders will meet about. A wooden stick is tied to the end of the string. Its notches count the days until the meeting. As each day passes, someone cuts a notch off the stick.

Shell beads as old as 4,500 years have been found in the Northeast. Earlier bead makers drilled their beads with stone drill bits. Drilling with stone was hard, so their beads were larger than later wampum, and there were fewer of them. After Europeans arrived, Native bead makers drilled with iron awls and nails. An awl is a thin, pointed tool for making holes.

#### Hand signs and trade

People in this land spoke many different languages. Near the Gulf coast and in what is now Texas, nations that could not understand each other's speech talked with their hands. The first and fullest written accounts of this sign language come from the Spanish expedition of Cabeza de Vaca, which sailed in 1527. Its survivors noted which groups spoke the same language and which groups could understand each other only through signs. Jeffrey E. Davis, a scholar who studies sign languages, writes that scholars who study these accounts think the sign language was in use across that region well before the Spanish came.

Trade goods moved hundreds of miles. Copper from Lake Superior and shells from the Gulf of Mexico have been found far from where they came from. No record survives of what news the traders passed along with the goods.

### The 1500s

In the 1500s, Spanish, French and English newcomers sent their news home across the ocean in letters and books. A Spanish commander wrote to his king about the Frenchmen his soldiers had killed. A French survivor wrote a book about the same killings, and a printer in France published it. On the plains in 1541, Native people made themselves understood in hand signs, as a member of a Spanish expedition later recorded.

#### A letter to a king and a book by a survivor, 1565 and 1566

In September 1565 the Spanish commander Pedro Menéndez de Avilés and his soldiers killed French Protestants at Fort Caroline, in Florida. Protestants are Christians who do not belong to the Catholic Church. The fort stood in the homeland of Timucua-speaking peoples. Menéndez's men then killed more of the French at Matanzas Inlet, south of the fort, in two groups. Both groups had given up before they were killed. The National Park Service counts 111 men killed there in late September and 134 more, with their leader Jean Ribault, on October 11 or 12. Matanzas is Spanish for "slaughters." Menéndez gave his reason himself: the Frenchmen were Protestants.

On October 15, 1565, Menéndez reported the killings in a letter to King Philip II of Spain. By his own count, his men cut the throats of 132 men at the fort. The next day they cut the throats of 10 more, prisoners they had caught in the woods. At the inlet, he wrote, the first group of Frenchmen gave up their weapons. "I had their hands tied behind them and put them to the knife." He meant that his men killed them with knives. He spared sixteen.

Nicolas Le Challeux was a carpenter who escaped from Fort Caroline. He wrote the French account of the killings, and a printer in Dieppe, France, published it in 1566. Its title describes the killings as the cruelty of the Spaniards against the French king's subjects.

#### Hand signs on the plains, 1541

In 1541 Francisco Vázquez de Coronado and his Spanish expedition met a Native nation on the plains of what is now the Texas Panhandle. The Spaniards called them Querechos. Pedro de Castañeda was a member of the expedition who later wrote its history. He recorded that "although they conversed by means of signs they made themselves understood so well that there was no need of an interpreter." An interpreter is a person who puts one language into another.

#### A message carved in a post, Roanoke, 1587 to 1590

In 1587 John White left 117 English colonists on Roanoke Island, in what is now North Carolina, and sailed to England for supplies. The island and the coast around it were the land of peoples who spoke Algonquian languages, a family of related languages. Among them were the Roanoke, the Secotan and the Croatoan. Before White left, he and the colonists agreed on a signal. If they moved, they would carve the name of their new place on a tree or a doorpost. If they left because they were in danger, they would carve a cross above the name.

White could not sail back for three years. In 1588 England's queen took every English ship for her navy, to fight the Spanish Armada, a great fleet of warships sent from Spain. On August 18, 1590, he found the houses gone and a fence of posts standing around the empty site. The letters CROATOAN were carved on one post "in fayre Capitall letters," which is old spelling for neat capital letters. The letters CRO were cut into a tree. There was no cross.

White wrote that Croatoan was "the place where Manteo was borne," and he called the people of that island "our friends." Manteo was an Algonquian man who had learned English and interpreted for the English. A hurricane blew White's ship out to sea before he could search there. White never found the colonists.

Readers in Europe learned about this coast from printed books. Thomas Harriot came to Roanoke Island with the English in 1585, and he and John White explored and mapped the area. In 1588 Harriot published *A Briefe and True Report of the New Found Land of Virginia* in London. In 1590 the engraver Theodor de Bry printed it again in four languages. An engraver cuts pictures into metal plates for printing. De Bry made his pictures from John White's watercolor paintings.

<a id="story-manteo-news-communication"></a>

#### Manteo

> **Who:** An Algonquian man, born on Croatoan by John White's account, who learned English and interpreted for the English.
>
> **When and where:** The Outer Banks of North Carolina, and London, 1584 to 1590.

Manteo crossed the ocean to England in 1584 and sailed home the next year able to speak English. In 1584 the English captains Philip Amadas and Arthur Barlowe spent six weeks on the Outer Banks. When they sailed home, Wingina, a leader of the Algonquian people there, chose two men to go with them. They were Manteo and Wanchese.

Both men began to learn English from the sailors during the voyage. The ship reached England in mid-September. In London they met Sir Walter Raleigh, who sent the voyages. By the end of 1584 Manteo could speak enough English to interpret. On April 9, 1585, he sailed home on the *Tyger*, the lead ship of Raleigh's fleet.

In 1587 Manteo helped the new colonists set up a village near the old English fort on Roanoke Island. On August 13, 1587, the English baptized him into their church, a Christian ceremony with water that made him a member. They also named him Lord of "Dasamongueponke." In 1590 White wrote that the colonists had gone to Croatoan, "the place where Manteo was borne." When White came back, he found neither the colonists nor Manteo. The National Park Service's account of his life states that what happened to him is unknown.

### The 1600s

The English colonies got their first mail services and their first newspaper in the 1600s. The men who governed the colonies decided who could print news and who could not. In 1683 Virginia's governor, Thomas Culpeper, and his council, a small group of men who advised him, ordered the printer William Nuthead to stop printing. Seven years later, in Massachusetts, Governor Simon Bradstreet and his council shut down the first newspaper four days after it appeared. In New Mexico in 1680, Pueblo runners carried the plan for a revolt against Spanish rule from town to town.

#### Letters by ship, by tavern and by planter

Most letters in the early colonies crossed the ocean, between the colonies and the countries in Europe that ruled them. In 1639 the lawmakers of Massachusetts, who met as the General Court, named Richard Fairbanks's tavern in Boston as the place to leave and collect letters sent "beyond the seas." Inside the colonies, people sent letters with friends, with merchants and with Native messengers.

In Virginia, around the middle of the 1600s, officials wrote "for public service" on the outside of government letters. Virginia's rulers required each planter to send such a letter on to the next plantation. A planter who failed to do it had to give up a hogshead of tobacco as a fine. A hogshead is a large barrel. Postal Service historians write that on the big plantations of the South, the messengers were usually enslaved people.

#### The first post rider, 1673, and a mail service for all the colonies, 1692

A post rider is a man on horseback who carries the mail along a set route. On January 22, 1673, the first post rider left New York for Boston. The ride was about 250 miles, through New Haven, Hartford, Springfield and Worcester. Governor Francis Lovelace of New York set up the route with John Winthrop Jr. of Connecticut. The rider was to make the trip once a month. The ride took about two weeks.

The monthly service did not last long. The rider's trail became known as the Boston Post Road, and part of it is now US Route 1. In 1683 William Penn set up the first post office in Pennsylvania.

In 1692 a man named Thomas Neale got the right to run a mail service for all the colonies for 21 years. The right came from the English Crown, which means the king or queen of England and the royal government. Neale never came to America. Andrew Hamilton, the governor of New Jersey, ran the service for him.

#### Virginia: no printing allowed, 1671 to 1730

William Berkeley was the governor of Virginia. In 1671 he wrote to the king's officials in London: "I thank God, there are no free schools nor printing, and I hope we shall not have these hundred years." He gave his reason. Printing, he wrote, had spread new religious groups, disobedience and attacks on the government.

In 1682 a merchant named John Buckner brought a printer, William Nuthead, to Virginia. By February 1683 Nuthead had printed the laws that Virginia's lawmakers had just passed. Governor Thomas Culpeper and his council ordered both men to stop printing. Nuthead moved on to Maryland. The next governor, Francis Howard, arrived in 1684 with orders from King Charles II that barred printing in Virginia. The first printing press that Virginia's rulers allowed arrived in 1730, when William Parks opened a print shop in Williamsburg.

#### The first newspaper, 1690, closed after one issue

From 1667 on, printers in Massachusetts printed single sheets of news, one at a time, with no plan for a next issue. A single printed sheet like this is called a broadside. On September 25, 1690, Benjamin Harris printed *Publick Occurrences, Both Forreign and Domestick* in Boston. It was the first newspaper in the English colonies. Harris marked it "Numb. 1," which means number one, and planned to print it once a month. It had three printed pages and a blank fourth page. Harris's notice suggested that readers could write more news on the blank page and pass the paper on.

Four days later, on September 29, Governor Simon Bradstreet and the men of his council ordered the paper "Suppressed and called in." That meant it was stopped, and every copy had to be handed back. They said Harris had printed it without their permission. They also objected to what he had printed. Harris had accused Native allies of the English of "barbarous" cruelty to French prisoners, and he had complained that colonial officials told the Mohawks, one of the Six Nations of the Haudenosaunee, too much about the colonists' war plans. The paper also carried a rumor that King Louis XIV of France was having sex with his son's wife.

Bradstreet and his council then ordered that no one could print news in the colony without a license from the government. A license is written permission. There was never a second issue of *Publick Occurrences*. One copy is known to survive, in London.

<a id="story-benjamin-harris-news-communication"></a>

#### Benjamin Harris

> **Who:** The London printer who printed the first newspaper in the English colonies.
>
> **When and where:** London, then Boston, 1679 to 1695.

English officials had jailed Benjamin Harris for his printing before he ever came to Boston. He was born about 1647. In London in the 1670s and 1680s he printed pamphlets for Protestants who had broken away from the Church of England. A pamphlet is a short printed booklet. Harris was a Baptist, a member of one of those Protestant groups, and he spoke out against King Charles II.

In 1679 Harris printed a newspaper without a license, *The Domestick Intelligence*. English officials jailed him twice. After a third arrest in 1685 he fled to the Netherlands. A year later he sailed to Boston and opened a print shop.

On September 25, 1690, he printed *Publick Occurrences*. His opening notice said he wanted to stop the "many False Reports, maliciously made, and spread among us." The paper reported a fire that burned about 20 houses. It also reported an outbreak of smallpox, a disease that spreads from person to person and kills many of the people who catch it. On September 29 the governor and his council ordered every copy called in and forbade Harris to print any newspaper in the colony again.

Harris obeyed. In 1692 Massachusetts officials named him the colony's official printer. He went back to England in 1695 and started a London paper, the *London Post*, in 1699. He died in 1720.

#### Knotted cords and the Pueblo Revolt, 1680

In 1680 the Pueblo peoples of New Mexico planned to drive out the Spanish. Spanish soldiers and settlers had come in 1598 under Juan de Oñate to take Pueblo land, labor and food. In 1675 the Spanish governor Juan Francisco Treviño ordered the arrest of 47 Pueblo religious leaders for "practicing sorcery," which means using magic. Spanish officials sentenced four of them to hang. They hanged three, and the fourth man killed himself. They whipped the others in public and put them in prison. Pueblo people went to Santa Fe and demanded that the prisoners be let go, and the Spanish released them. One of the men released was Po'pay, a Tewa leader from Ohkay Owingeh.

Po'pay planned the revolt with towns that spoke at least five different languages. All of them had to rise on the same day. To set that day, he sent runners with knotted cords. Each town untied one knot a day. When the last knot was untied, the revolt would begin. The accounts differ on the day planned. The National Museum of the American Indian gives August 11, and the Indian Pueblo Cultural Center gives August 13.

The Spanish learned of the plan and caught two of the runners on August 9. The revolt began a day early, on August 10, 1680. Pueblo fighters killed about 400 people, including 21 of the 33 Spanish priests in New Mexico. On August 21 Governor Antonio de Otermín led about 2,000 Spanish settlers out of Santa Fe and south to El Paso. The Spanish did not return until 1692.

<a id="story-catua-and-omtua"></a>

#### Nicolás Catua and Pedro Omtua

> **Who:** Two young runners from Tesuque Pueblo who carried the knotted cords of the Pueblo Revolt.
>
> **When and where:** New Mexico, August 8 and 9, 1680.

Pedro Omtua and Nicolás Catua carried the knotted cords of the Pueblo Revolt, and Spanish officials hanged them for it. On the morning of August 8, 1680, the two young men set out from Tesuque Pueblo with cords for the Tano towns. Tesuque is Tewa for "village of the narrow place of the cottonwood trees." The first town they reached was Pecos.

After they left Pecos, Christian Pueblo people told Fernando de Velasco that two Tewa messengers had visited the war chief's house. Velasco was a leader of the Franciscan missionaries, Catholic priests sent to turn the Pueblo people Christian. Two Pueblo leaders from the Galisteo Basin who sided with the Spanish also sent word of a revolt to Governor Antonio de Otermín. Otermín ordered the messengers arrested, and on August 9 the Spanish caught them.

Spanish officials tortured Catua and Omtua to make them explain the knotted cord. Torture means hurting a person's body on purpose to force him to talk. The surviving accounts do not say how the two young men were hurt. The historian Charles W. Hackett, working from Otermín's own records, wrote in 1911 that on August 9 the two told Otermín they had been given a cord with two knots, to carry to the chiefs of the Tano towns, San Marcos and La Cienega. The two knots stood for the two days left before the revolt. Then the Spanish hanged them. The accounts do not name the men who tortured and hanged them.

When Po'pay heard that the runners had been caught, he ordered the revolt to start a day early. It began on August 10.

### 1700 to 1750

Between 1704 and 1750, printers and postmasters started newspapers in Boston, Philadelphia, New York, Charleston and Williamsburg. Several of those printers were also postmasters, who ran the post office in their town. Colonial governors and lawmakers still had printers jailed when the printers offended them. The newspaper owners made money from advertisements. According to the International Printing Museum, by the 1750s nearly a quarter of the advertisements in Benjamin Franklin's paper in Philadelphia offered enslaved people for sale or asked for help catching people who had escaped from slavery.

#### The Boston News-Letter, 1704

On April 24, 1704, John Campbell, the postmaster of Boston, published the first issue of the *Boston News-Letter*. It was one small sheet printed on both sides, and it came out once a week. The words "Published by Authority" appeared in its title from 1704 to 1720, and again from 1723 to 1725. "Authority" means the people with the power to rule. A printer named Bartholomew Green printed the paper for Campbell.

Most of the first issue was copied from London newspapers of mid-December, more than four months old. Local news filled one column. The *News-Letter* came out every week until February 1776. It was the first newspaper in the colonies to keep going. Boston had no other newspaper until the *Boston Gazette* began on December 21, 1719. The *American Weekly Mercury* started in Philadelphia the next day.

#### The Courant: a paper the government did not approve, 1721 to 1726

James Franklin started the *New-England Courant* in Boston on August 7, 1721, during an epidemic of smallpox. An epidemic is a disease spreading to many people at once. The minister Cotton Mather and the doctor Zabdiel Boylston urged people to try inoculation. In inoculation, a doctor put a little pus from a sick person into a cut in the skin of a healthy person. The healthy person usually got a mild case of smallpox and soon got well. Mather had learned of the method from Onesimus, an African man, and from other enslaved Africans. Mather had owned Onesimus as a slave since 1706.

Almost every doctor in Boston except Boylston opposed inoculation. James Franklin printed attacks in the *Courant* on the people who supported it. On November 14, 1721, someone threw a lit bomb through a window of Mather's house. A note with it read: "Cotton Mather, You Dog, Dam You: I'll inoculate you with this, with a Pox to you." The fuse came off, and the bomb did not explode. No record names the person who threw it.

Nearly 6,000 people caught smallpox in the epidemic, and 844 of them died. Boylston inoculated 248 people, and 98 out of every 100 of them lived. Among people who caught smallpox the ordinary way, 85 out of every 100 lived.

In June 1722 James Franklin printed a short item in the *Courant*. It said Massachusetts officials were fitting out a ship to chase pirates, which would sail "some time this Month, if Wind and Weather permit." Massachusetts officials read it as a hidden attack on them. The members of the General Court, the colony's lawmakers, had James Franklin jailed for a month. His younger brother Benjamin, then 16, ran the paper while James was locked up. James was let out on July 2, 1722.

Early in 1723 the members of the General Court forbade James Franklin to print the *Courant* unless officials checked each issue first. Checking and cutting what a printer may print before it comes out is called censorship. James then put the paper in Benjamin's name, and it came out that way until it closed in 1726.

#### The Weekly Journal and the Zenger trial, 1733 to 1736

For years New York had one newspaper, the *New-York Gazette*. Its printer, William Bradford, printed for the government and supported Governor William Cosby. In 1733 Lewis Morris, the chief judge of New York, wrote a dissent in a court case of Cosby's called Cosby v. Van Dam. A dissent is a judge's written disagreement with the other judges. Cosby removed Morris from office.

Morris and two lawyers, James Alexander and William Smith, then started the *New-York Weekly Journal* on November 5, 1733. Alexander edited it. In the *Journal*, Alexander accused Cosby and his officials of tyranny, which means cruel and unjust rule. John Peter Zenger, a printer born in Germany, printed it. Cosby had copies of the *Journal* burned by the hangman.

Officials arrested Zenger on November 17, 1734, for seditious libel. Under the law of that time, seditious libel meant printing blame of any official, of the law, or of anything the law had set up, without a lawful excuse. Whether the words were true did not matter. The court set Zenger's bail at £400. Bail is money paid to a court so that a prisoner can go free until his trial. Zenger stayed in jail for more than eight months. His wife Anna kept the *Journal* coming out.

On August 4, 1735, a jury found Zenger not guilty. The verdict changed no law. In New York, a printer could not defend himself by showing that his words were true until 1805. That year the state's lawmakers passed a law that allowed it. In 1736 an account of the trial came out as a pamphlet, *A Brief Narrative of the Case and Tryal of John Peter Zenger*. Printers reprinted it many times.

<a id="story-anna-zenger-news-communication"></a>

#### Anna Catharina Zenger

> **Who:** The printer's wife who kept the *New-York Weekly Journal* coming out while her husband was in jail, and who ran the print shop after he died.
>
> **When and where:** New York City, 1734 to 1748.

Anna Catharina Zenger ran the *New-York Weekly Journal* for more than eight months while officials held her husband in jail. She was born Anna Catharina Maulin. She married John Peter Zenger on September 11, 1722. When officials jailed him on November 17, 1734, she took charge of the shop and kept the *Journal* coming out. The writer Ann T. Keene reports the story that Zenger gave her his instructions "through the hole of the door of the prison."

After the trial, in 1737, Zenger became New York's official printer. He died on July 28, 1746. Anna Zenger then ran the family print shop for more than two years. In December 1748 their eldest son, John, took it over.

#### Printers who were postmasters, and papers in German

A printer who was also the postmaster got the letters and newspapers from other towns first, and so got the news first. He could also stop the post riders from carrying a rival's newspaper. Andrew Bradford printed the *American Weekly Mercury* in Philadelphia and also kept the town's post office. Bradford forbade the post riders to carry Benjamin Franklin's paper. Franklin wrote that he got his papers carried only by bribing the riders to take them in secret. Alexander Spotswood, a former governor of Virginia, was in charge of the post office for the colonies. In 1737 he was unhappy with how carelessly Bradford kept the post office's accounts. Spotswood took the job away from Bradford and gave it to Franklin, who was 31.

Franklin also set up partners as printers in other towns. In November 1733 he made Lewis Timothy the printer of the *South-Carolina Gazette* in Charleston.

In Virginia, William Parks printed the first issue of the *Virginia Gazette* in Williamsburg on August 6, 1736. Virginia's lawmakers allowed only one printing office in the colony, and they wanted it to print what the government needed first.

Franklin tried a German-language paper, the *Philadelphische Zeitung*, in May and June 1732, and it failed. On August 20, 1739, Christopher Sauer, a German printer in Germantown, started a German-language paper. His family printed it, under changing names, until 1777. Each month sixteen newspapers from Europe reached Sauer, and he took his news of Europe from them.

<a id="story-elizabeth-timothy"></a>

#### Elizabeth Timothy

> **Who:** A widow born in Holland who ran the *South-Carolina Gazette*. The *South Carolina Encyclopedia* names her the first woman in the American colonies to own and publish a newspaper.
>
> **When and where:** Charleston, South Carolina, 1738 to 1746.

Elizabeth Timothy took over a newspaper as a widow with six small children, and within a year she owned it. The *South Carolina Encyclopedia* states that she was the first woman in the American colonies to own and publish a newspaper. Franklin wrote that she was "born and bred in Holland." Her husband, Lewis Timothy, printed the *South-Carolina Gazette* in Charleston under a six-year partnership with Franklin. He died in December 1738 after what was described at the time as "an unhappy Accident," meaning an unlucky one. He left her with six small children and a seventh about to be born.

Their eldest son, Peter, was too young to run the shop, so Elizabeth Timothy ran it herself. She printed the next issue on January 4, 1739. She promised to make the paper "as entertaining and correct as may be reasonably expected." By the end of 1739 she had bought out Franklin's share. Franklin praised how exactly she kept her accounts.

She handed the shop to Peter when he came of age in 1746, and she opened a bookstore next to it. She died in 1757. In her will she left her children eight enslaved people, along with her other property.

#### Advertisements for people as property

Newspaper owners made much of their money from advertisements, and some of those advertisements were for human beings. Franklin printed advertisements in the *Pennsylvania Gazette* that slave owners and slave traders paid for. Some offered enslaved people for sale. Others were notices about enslaved people who had escaped, so that readers would help catch them. Franklin was paid for printing them. According to the International Printing Museum, by the 1750s these made up nearly a quarter of the paper's advertisements.

Franklin himself owned enslaved people. According to the Benjamin Franklin House museum in London, he and his household held enslaved people from about 1735 until 1790 and bought at least seven people. Their names were Joseph, Jemima, Peter, King, Othello, George and Bob. Peter and King went with Franklin to London.

In 1740 lawmakers in South Carolina made it a crime to teach an enslaved person to write.

<a id="story-benjamin-franklin-news-communication"></a>

#### Benjamin Franklin

> **Who:** A Boston printer's apprentice who became a Philadelphia newspaper owner and the town's postmaster.
>
> **When and where:** Boston, 1718 to 1723, and Philadelphia, 1723 to 1753.
>
> **Movie:** *Benjamin Franklin* (2022), a documentary by Ken Burns about his life, shown on PBS.

Benjamin Franklin grew rich as a printer, and much of his money came from the advertisements in his newspaper. He was born in Boston in 1706. In 1718 he became an apprentice to his older brother James, a printer. An apprentice is a young worker bound to a master for years to learn a trade. Benjamin carried copies of the *New-England Courant* through the streets to the people who paid for it. In 1722, at 16, he wrote letters to the paper under the made-up name "Silence Dogood." He later wrote that his brother "had often beaten me." When James was jailed in 1722, Benjamin ran the paper. In 1723, at 17, he broke his apprenticeship and ran away. He landed at the Market Street wharf in Philadelphia on a Sunday morning.

On October 2, 1729, Franklin bought the *Pennsylvania Gazette* from the printer Samuel Keimer. Advertising became the paper's main source of money. Franklin grew the paper from two pages to four, partly to hold more advertisements. In 1732 he began *Poor Richard's Almanac*, which he wrote under the made-up name Richard Saunders. An almanac is a book that comes out once a year with a calendar and other useful facts. He wrote that he sold "near ten thousand" copies a year, and that ordinary people "bought scarcely any other books."

In 1737 Franklin became the postmaster of Philadelphia. He wrote that the post office "facilitated the correspondence that improv'd my newspaper." He meant that the job helped him get the letters and news that made his paper better. With it he gained more readers and more advertisements. In 1753 British officials named him and William Hunter to run the royal post office for all the colonies together.

### 1750 to 1800

From 1765 to 1800, printers, letter writers and post riders spread the arguments and the news that led to the American Revolution. Supporters of independence also wrecked the press of a New York printer who took Britain's side. In 1791 lawmakers in three-fourths of the states approved the First Amendment to the Constitution, which protects freedom of the press. Seven years later, in 1798, the Federalist members of Congress passed the Sedition Act. Federal judges then jailed newspaper editors who had criticized President John Adams.

#### The Stamp Act and the printers, 1765

In March 1765 the members of Parliament in London passed the Stamp Act. Parliament is Britain's group of lawmakers. The act took effect on November 1, 1765. Under it, colonists had to pay a tax on newspapers, pamphlets, almanacs and legal papers. They had to pay a halfpenny on each copy of a newspaper printed on half a sheet of paper, and a penny on each copy printed on a whole sheet. A halfpenny and a penny were small British coins. They had to pay two shillings on each advertisement in a newspaper, and one shilling was worth twelve pennies. Printers had to print on stamped paper made in London, which showed that the tax was paid.

On October 31, 1765, the day before the tax began, the Philadelphia printer William Bradford printed his *Pennsylvania Journal* with thick black borders, like a tombstone. In the place for the official stamp he printed a skull and crossbones. Across the top of the front page he printed that the paper was "EXPIRING: In Hopes of a Resurrection to LIFE again." Expiring means dying. This William Bradford was born in 1722 and was a different man from the New York printer of the same name. He never actually stopped printing. He put out the next issue on November 7.

John Hughes had the job of handing out the stamps in Philadelphia. Opponents of the tax threatened him with violence and with destroying his property. He then promised not to enforce the act. In 1766 the members of Parliament repealed the Stamp Act, which means they canceled it.

#### Committees of correspondence, 1772 to 1774

A committee of correspondence was a small group of men chosen to write letters to other towns or colonies and share news. Samuel Adams proposed one for Boston. On November 2, 1772, Boston's town leaders voted to set up a Committee of Correspondence of 21 men. They set it up in answer to news that the colony's judges would now get their pay from the royal treasury, the king's own money. The 21 men wrote a set of reports on the colonists' rights and on how Parliament had broken them. Their reports were printed as the Boston Pamphlet and sent to every town in Massachusetts.

On March 12, 1773, Dabney Carr asked the members of Virginia's House of Burgesses, the colony's elected lawmakers, to set up an 11-man committee, and they did. Patrick Henry and Thomas Jefferson were two of its members. The 11 men wrote to the lawmakers of the other colonies. They asked them to share news of laws from London and of what each colony planned to do about them. Within a year, lawmakers in eleven colonies had set up their own committees. North Carolina and Pennsylvania were the two that did not.

#### The news of Lexington, April 1775

On the morning of April 19, 1775, British soldiers fired on the militia at Lexington, Massachusetts. A militia is a group of ordinary men trained to fight when they are called. At about 10 o'clock that morning, in Watertown, Joseph Palmer wrote a letter "To all the Friends of American liberty." It said the soldiers had killed six men and wounded four. Palmer was a member of the Massachusetts Committee of Safety. The colonists' own congress had set up this committee to gather supplies for a fight with the British army in Boston and to spread the alarm if the army marched.

Palmer gave the letter to a rider, Isaac Bissell, to carry toward Connecticut. At Worcester the town clerk, Nathan Baldwin, copied the letter, wrote that the copy was true and signed it. Someone made another copy at Springfield. Other riders then carried copies on, and the alarm reached Philadelphia five days and seven hours after it left Watertown. Seven months earlier, in September 1774, thousands of militiamen had turned out for nothing after false rumors of a British attack. Palmer took care to make his letter believable for that reason.

<a id="story-isaac-bissell"></a>

#### Isaac Bissell

> **Who:** A 26-year-old blacksmith from Suffield, Connecticut, who carried a written report of the killings at Lexington from Massachusetts toward Connecticut.
>
> **When and where:** From Watertown, Massachusetts, to Connecticut, April 19 and 20, 1775.

Isaac Bissell carried a written report of the killings at Lexington west from Watertown. He was a blacksmith from Suffield, a town on Connecticut's northern border. On April 19, 1775, he was in Watertown, Massachusetts. At about 10 in the morning, Joseph Palmer handed him the letter about the killings. The letter said that "the Bearer Mr. Isaac Bissell" was "charged to alarm the country quite to Connecticutt," which meant his job was to warn people all the way to Connecticut. It asked people along the way to give him the horses he needed.

Bissell reached Worcester in the early afternoon. The town clerk, Nathan Baldwin, copied the letter and signed the copy. At Springfield someone made another copy. On the morning of April 20 the letter reached Connecticut's leaders.

In Wethersfield, Silas Deane wrote in his journal that the news "was discredited, from the suddeness of its arrival." Discredited means people did not believe it. Wethersfield was the home town of Governor Jonathan Trumbull. After men from Massachusetts confirmed the news, Trumbull agreed to call Connecticut's lawmakers together.

Bissell then joined the siege of Boston, where colonial soldiers surrounded the British army in the town. He served as a private in Captain Elihu Kent's company from Suffield. In July 1775 the members of the Massachusetts committee of safety approved his bill as a post rider, two pounds and one shilling. The colony's treasurer then would not pay it without a signed approval from the colony's congress.

Many books call the rider "Israel Bissell" and say he rode all the way to Philadelphia. The historian J. L. Bell found that his name was Isaac, that he carried the letter only as far as Connecticut, and that the long ride to Philadelphia is a story that grew up later. Many riders, most of them unnamed, carried the news the rest of the way.

#### Common Sense and the Declaration in print, 1776

On January 10, 1776, the printer Robert Bell published *Common Sense*. It was a pamphlet by Thomas Paine that argued for independence from Britain. Printers printed it at least twenty-five times, sixteen of them in Philadelphia. In April 1776 Paine claimed that 120,000 copies had sold, and later he claimed 150,000. In 1892 Moncure Conway, who wrote a book about Paine's life, guessed half a million.

No sales records survive, so nobody knows the real number. The historian Trish Loughran put the highest possible number at 75,000, and she thinks the real number was much lower.

Members of the Continental Congress declared independence on July 4, 1776, in Philadelphia. The Continental Congress was the meeting of men sent by each colony to act for all of them. Over that night the Philadelphia printer John Dunlap printed about 200 copies of the Declaration of Independence as broadsides. The members of Congress ordered the copies sent to the new states and to the soldiers, read aloud, and put up in public places. On July 9 George Washington's soldiers in New York City heard it read aloud. Twenty-six of Dunlap's copies are known to survive.

<a id="story-thomas-paine"></a>

#### Thomas Paine

> **Who:** An English-born writer whose pamphlet *Common Sense* argued that the colonies should declare independence.
>
> **When and where:** Philadelphia, 1774 to 1776, and with the army, 1776.

Thomas Paine wrote *Common Sense*, the pamphlet that argued for independence, and he took no money from its sales. He was born in Thetford, England, on January 29, 1737. He met Benjamin Franklin in London, and Franklin gave him letters of introduction to people in America. Paine arrived in Philadelphia on November 30, 1774. He helped edit the *Pennsylvania Magazine* and wrote articles under pen names, made-up names that hid who the writer was. For a long time Paine was named as the writer of "African Slavery in America," an essay printed in March 1775 under the name "Justice and Humanity." The essay describes slavery as unjust. Gary Berton of the Thomas Paine National Historical Association later concluded that a Rhode Island minister, Samuel Hopkins, most likely wrote it, so the accounts differ.

*Common Sense* came out on January 10, 1776. Paine soon fell out with its first printer, Robert Bell. Paine later wrote that he gave the right to print it to every state.

On December 19, 1776, Paine published *The American Crisis*. It began, "These are the times that try men's souls." Washington ordered it read to all his troops. Paine died in New York City on June 8, 1809.

#### A Loyalist printer's press wrecked, 1775

Supporters of independence also attacked printers who took Britain's side. A colonist who stayed loyal to Britain was called a Loyalist. The New York printer James Rivington printed the *New-York Gazetteer*, one of the most widely read newspapers in the colonies, and he used it to back the British government.

In November 1775 Isaac Sears led a group of Sons of Liberty from New Haven, Connecticut, to Rivington's shop in New York City. The Sons of Liberty were colonists who organized against British taxes and rule. The men wrecked Rivington's press and his type. Type is the set of metal letters that a printer puts together by hand to print a page, and it was a printer's most valuable possession. Rivington left for England a few weeks later.

After British soldiers captured New York, Rivington came back with the title of King's Printer, the official printer for the British government there. He printed his paper on the British side until the British left in November 1783.

#### A postal service for the new country, 1774 to 1792

In 1774 British officials fired Benjamin Franklin from his job running the royal post office in the colonies. In the words of the Postal Service's own history, he was "too much of an American." The printer William Goddard set up a rival mail service, which he called the Constitutional Post. He warned that letters could be stopped and opened on the orders of the king's ministers, the men who ran Britain's government, and that what the letters said could be twisted into proof of treason. Treason is the crime of betraying one's own government. By 1775 Goddard's service had nearly 50 post offices from Maine to Virginia.

On July 26, 1775, the members of the Continental Congress made Franklin their postmaster general, the head of their post office, at $1,000 a year.

The Constitution, approved in 1788, lists among the powers of Congress the power "To establish Post Offices and post Roads." In 1789 the country had 75 post offices and about 2,400 miles of post roads, for almost four million people. On February 20, 1792, the members of Congress passed a new law about the mail. Under it, printers could send newspapers through the mail at very low rates, some for free. The law also forbade postal officials to open people's letters.

<a id="story-mary-katharine-goddard"></a>

#### Mary Katharine Goddard

> **Who:** A printer and newspaper publisher who ran Baltimore's post office for 14 years and printed the first copies of the Declaration that listed the signers.
>
> **When and where:** Baltimore, Maryland, 1774 to 1789.

The first printed copies of the Declaration of Independence to show the signers' names came from Mary Katharine Goddard's press in Baltimore. Goddard was born on June 16, 1738. In the 1760s she learned printing in her brother William's shop in Providence, Rhode Island. In 1774 she moved to Baltimore. She ran his print shop and his newspaper, the *Maryland Journal*, during his many trips away. She reprinted *Common Sense* in the *Journal*.

In 1775 she became the postmaster of Baltimore. Postal Service historians call her the first known woman postmaster in the colonies. Postmasters then earned a share of the postage instead of a salary. The members of Congress often failed to pay her, so she paid the post riders and the high rent of the office herself. In 1778 she let readers pay for the newspaper in beeswax, flour, lard, butter, beef or pork.

In January 1777 the Continental Congress was meeting in Baltimore. Its members ordered new copies of the Declaration of Independence, and Goddard printed them on January 18, 1777. Hers were the first printed copies to show the signers' names. At the bottom she printed "Baltimore, in Maryland: Printed by Mary Katharine Goddard." Nine of her copies are known to survive.

In January 1784, Smithsonian Magazine reports, her brother William "apparently forced his sister out" of the *Maryland Journal*. In October 1789 the new postmaster general, Samuel Osgood, replaced her with a man. Osgood's assistant, John Burrell, said the job might need "more travelling ... than a woman could undertake." More than 200 people in Baltimore signed a letter asking Osgood to give her the job back. She wrote to President George Washington and to the Senate. Neither helped her. She ran a bookshop in Baltimore until about 1810, and she died there on August 12, 1816.

#### The First Amendment and the party papers, 1789 to 1793

The First Amendment took effect on December 15, 1791. An amendment is a change or addition to the Constitution. The First Amendment states that "Congress shall make no law ... abridging the freedom of speech, or of the press." Abridging means cutting back.

Newspaper editors took sides in the quarrels inside Washington's government. John Fenno used his *Gazette of the United States* to push the plans of Alexander Hamilton, the head of the Treasury. Secretary of State Thomas Jefferson called Fenno's paper "a paper of pure Toryism." Tory was a name for the colonists who had sided with Britain's king during the Revolution. Jefferson hired Philip Freneau as a translating clerk at the State Department, paid $250 a year, even though Freneau knew only English and French. Freneau started the *National Gazette* on October 31, 1791. It came out twice a week and had about 1,700 subscribers, people who paid to get each issue. Freneau closed it on October 26, 1793.

Benjamin Franklin's grandson, Benjamin Franklin Bache, printed a paper in Philadelphia called the *Aurora*. In it he attacked Washington and John Adams.

#### The Sedition Act, 1798 to 1801

In 1798 American and French warships began fighting each other in the Caribbean Sea. President John Adams's party, the Federalists, held a majority in Congress. The Federalist members voted the Sedition Act through, and Adams signed it on July 14, 1798. Sedition means stirring people up against their government. Under the act, it was a crime to write or print "any false, scandalous and malicious writing" against the federal government, Congress or the President. The punishment was a fine of up to $2,000 and up to two years in prison.

Under the act, unlike the law in the Zenger trial, a person charged could try to prove that his words were true, and the jury could decide what the law meant as well as what the facts were.

Federal prosecutors and judges used the act mostly against editors of newspapers that supported Jefferson's party, the Democratic-Republicans. Peter McNamara, writing in the First Amendment Encyclopedia, gives the count that scholars long used: 17 formal criminal charges under the act, and 10 people found guilty. The legal historian Wendell Bird later found 11 more court cases against 16 more people. Writers for the National Constitution Center, a museum about the Constitution, count more than two dozen people found guilty. Most of them were publishers who opposed Adams's party.

Among those charged were Congressman Matthew Lyon of Vermont, William Duane of the *Aurora*, Ann Greenleaf of New York's *Argus*, and Anthony Haswell of the *Vermont Gazette*. Luther Baldwin and Brown Clark of Newark, New Jersey, were charged for words they spoke against President Adams in a tavern.

Federalist supporters physically attacked Benjamin Franklin Bache in Philadelphia. Jonathan Dayton of New Jersey, a Federalist, was Speaker of the House of Representatives, the member chosen to run its meetings. Dayton barred Bache from the floor of the House, the room where its members met, so that he could not report its debates. The Federalists held a majority there. On June 24, 1798, more than two weeks before the Sedition Act became law, Judge Peters, a federal judge in Philadelphia, signed an order for Bache's arrest. The charge was seditious libel against President Adams, the same crime that officials had charged Zenger with in 1734. Peters let Bache out on bail, and his trial was set for October.

Bache kept printing the *Aurora* through an epidemic of yellow fever, a disease carried from person to person by mosquitoes. He died of the fever on September 10, 1798, at 29, a month before his trial date. His widow kept the paper going, with William Duane as editor. The text of the Sedition Act stated that it would stay in force only until March 3, 1801.

<a id="story-matthew-lyon"></a>

#### Matthew Lyon

> **Who:** An Irish-born congressman and newspaper owner, the first person tried under the Sedition Act.
>
> **When and where:** Vermont, 1798 to 1799.

In 1798 Matthew Lyon became the first person tried under the Sedition Act. He came to America from Ireland and fought in the Revolutionary War. In 1797 he went to Congress for Vermont. He also owned a newspaper.

In a letter that a newspaper printed, Lyon wrote of seeing the public good "swallowed up in a continual grasp for power, in an unbounded thirst for ridiculous pomp, foolish adulation, or selfish avarice." Adulation means too much praise, and avarice means greed. At campaign meetings he also read aloud a letter by the poet Joel Barlow. It said Adams should be sent to a "madhouse."

On October 5, 1798, a federal grand jury in Vermont charged Lyon with three crimes under the Sedition Act. A grand jury is a group of citizens who decide whether there is enough evidence to charge someone. A deputy marshal, an officer who made arrests for the federal courts, arrested him the next day. At his trial in Rutland on October 9, Lyon defended himself. He pleaded not guilty, and in a second plea he stated that the Sedition Act broke the Constitution.

Justice William Paterson of the Supreme Court told the jury that its job had "nothing whatever to do with the constitutionality or unconstitutionality of the sedition law." He meant that the jurors must not decide whether the law broke the Constitution. The jurors came from towns that supported Adams's party. They found Lyon guilty within an hour. Paterson sentenced him to four months in jail and a $1,000 fine.

Lyon was held in the jail at Vergennes. He ran for Congress again from his cell, and the voters of his district re-elected him. He was let out on February 9, 1799.

### 1800 to 1850

The number of American newspapers grew from about 900 in the 1830s to 2,526 in 1850. In 1850 American newspapers printed half a billion copies, for a population of about 23 million. From 1833 a New York printer sold a daily paper for one cent, when most daily papers cost six cents. From 1844 news could travel along a telegraph wire, faster than any horse or train.

Free Black New Yorkers started the first Black-owned newspaper in 1827, and Cherokee leaders started the first Native American paper a year later. Men who defended slavery attacked antislavery editors. In 1835 men of the Georgia Guard, a militia of armed men from the state of Georgia, seized the Cherokee press. That same year Amos Kendall, the Postmaster General, who ran the post office, let Southern postmasters hold back antislavery papers. In Illinois in 1837, a mob killed an editor who was defending his press.

#### The last Sedition Act trials, 1800

The Sedition Act of 1798 made it a crime to print "false, scandalous and malicious" writing against the government, Congress or the President. It was still the law in 1800, and federal judges used it that year against two more writers. On May 24, 1800, in the federal court at Richmond, Virginia, a grand jury charged the writer James Callender with a crime. A grand jury is a group of citizens who decide whether there is enough proof to put someone on trial. The charge was over his pamphlet, a short printed booklet, called *The Prospect Before Us*. In it Callender wrote words that harmed the good name of President John Adams. The trial began on June 3, and the jury found him guilty the same day. Justice Samuel Chase sentenced him to nine months in prison and a fine. The Federal Judicial Center's history of the trials states the fine as $400 in one place and $200 in another.

In Philadelphia the same year, Chase sentenced the writer Thomas Cooper to six months in prison. The same history gives Cooper's fine as $400 in one place and $500 plus court costs in another. The act stayed in force only until March 3, 1801. After Thomas Jefferson became president in 1801, he pardoned Callender, which means he officially forgave him. Jefferson also paid $50 of his own money toward giving back Callender's fine.

#### Newspapers by mail, and who could carry it

Newspapers went to readers through the mail. Under the postal law that members of Congress passed in 1792, readers got newspapers by mail at very low rates. Editors mailed their papers to each other for free. A small-town editor could then reprint news from papers all over the country. Indiana had one newspaper in 1810 and 73 by 1840. In 1840 the United States had about 17 million people, and Europe had about 230 million. Even so, more copies of American newspapers went out each week than of all the newspapers in Europe.

By 1831, 76 out of every 100 people who worked for the federal government outside the army and navy worked for the post office. Postmasters outnumbered soldiers, 8,764 to 6,332.

Letters cost much more to mail than newspapers. From 1799 to 1815, one sheet of paper cost 8 cents to send 40 miles or less, and up to 25 cents to send more than 500 miles. A second sheet doubled the price. In 1845 postal officials began charging by weight instead, and in 1847 they began selling postage stamps.

Some enslaved men carried the mail in the South until 1802. That March, Postmaster General Gideon Granger warned a senator that enslaved post riders, "hourly mixing with people," would "acquire information." "They will learn that a man's rights do not depend on his color," he wrote. "They will, in time, become teachers to their brethren." Brethren means brothers. Granger began by pointing to "the scenes which St. Domingo has exhibited to the world." On Saint-Domingue, a French island colony in the Caribbean, the enslaved people had risen in a revolution. Members of Congress then passed a law, and from 1802 to 1865 the postal laws said that mail carriers had to be "free white persons." A mail contractor, a person paid to carry the mail, who broke the rule had to pay a fine. The Postal Service's own history of Black postal workers names no one who was fined. For 63 years, no Black American, free or enslaved, could legally carry the mail.

#### Freedom's Journal, the first Black-owned newspaper, 1827

In March 1827 a group of free Black New Yorkers met to start a newspaper of their own. It was the first newspaper in the United States owned and run by Black Americans. Samuel Cornish and John Brown Russwurm edited it. Cornish was a Presbyterian minister, a preacher in one of the Protestant churches. Russwurm was one of the first Black Americans to graduate from a college in the United States.

*Freedom's Journal* came out on March 16, 1827, from 5 Varick Street in Manhattan. In the first issue the editors wrote: "We wish to plead our own cause. Too long have others spoken for us." Editors of other New York papers printed attacks on Black people, and Cornish and Russwurm answered them. They also wrote against slavery. A year of the paper cost $3. More than 800 copies went out to readers in 11 states and Washington, D.C., and copies also went to Canada, Europe and Haiti. A man named David Walker was one of the agents who sold subscriptions to it, which were orders to receive the paper for a year.

Russwurm came to support a plan called colonization, which meant sending free Black Americans to live in Africa. Cornish opposed the plan and quit in September 1827. The last issue of *Freedom's Journal* came out on March 28, 1829. Russwurm moved to Liberia, in Africa, and started a newspaper there.

#### The Cherokee Phoenix, 1828 to 1835

The *Cherokee Phoenix* was the first newspaper printed by a Native American nation. In 1825 the members of the Cherokee Nation's council set aside $1,500 for a printing press and type. Samuel Worcester was a missionary, a Christian preacher sent to win people to his faith. He helped the Cherokee set up a print shop at New Echota, their capital. New Echota was in land that the state of Georgia claimed. An iron press came by ship from Boston. Workers cast type for the Cherokee syllabary, the writing system that Sequoyah made. In a syllabary, each symbol stands for a syllable. Sequoyah's has 85 symbols.

The first issue came out on February 21, 1828. Columns in Cherokee ran beside columns in English. The Cherokee leaders who ran the paper opposed every plan to move the Cherokee west, and they used it to argue their side.

Georgia and federal officials made the paper hard to keep going. Colonel Charles Nelson commanded the Georgia Guard, a unit that Georgia officials set up to police the Cherokee land their state claimed. He threatened to shut the paper down and to beat its editor. President Andrew Jackson ordered the federal government's yearly payment to the Cherokee Nation paid to separate people instead of to the Nation. That cut off the paper's money. Georgia officials ordered the paper's white printer to leave. A local sheriff sued the editor, Elijah Hicks, for libel, which means printing false words that harm someone. The last issue came out in May 1834.

In 1835 John Ross, the Principal Chief, which means the Cherokee Nation's top leader, planned to start the paper again. Men of the Georgia Guard went to New Echota, took the press and threw out the type. Two accounts say they also burned the building, and that Stand Watie, a Cherokee who supported moving the Cherokee west, helped them. The records do not name the officer who led them.

In September 1844 a new Cherokee Nation newspaper, the *Cherokee Advocate*, began in Tahlequah, with William Potter Ross as its editor.

<a id="story-elias-boudinot"></a>

#### Elias Boudinot

> **Who:** A Cherokee writer who edited the *Cherokee Phoenix*, the first Native American newspaper, and later, with a small group of Cherokee, signed a treaty that gave up the Cherokee homeland.
>
> **When and where:** New Echota, Cherokee Nation, in present-day Georgia, 1826 to 1835, and Park Hill, Indian Territory, 1837 to 1839.

Elias Boudinot helped raise the money for the Cherokee press and edited its paper. Later he signed away the Cherokee homeland. He was born in the Cherokee Nation, in what is now northwest Georgia. Records give his birth year as 1802, 1803 or about 1804. His Cherokee name was Gallegina, which means "the Buck."

As a young man he studied at a school run by missionaries in Cornwall, Connecticut. There he took the name of Elias Boudinot, the president of the American Bible Society. In Cornwall he became engaged to Harriet Gold, a white woman. Opponents of the marriage burned the couple in effigy. That means they set fire to dummies made to look like them. The two married in 1826.

That year Boudinot went on a speaking tour that included Philadelphia. In a speech called "An Address to the Whites" he asked for money for a Cherokee press, and he collected it. When the *Cherokee Phoenix* began in 1828, its editor was Boudinot. The paper printed reports of the Georgia Guard's campaign against the missionaries in the Cherokee Nation. The Guard's commander, Charles Nelson, threatened to beat Boudinot.

In 1830 members of Congress passed the Indian Removal Act. Under it, the president could make treaties with Native nations to move them west. A treaty is a written agreement between nations. In 1832 Boudinot's cousin John Ridge began to speak openly for moving west, and Boudinot began writing in the paper in favor of it. Principal Chief John Ross opposed moving west on any terms. Ross pressured Boudinot to resign, and he did on August 1, 1832. In December 1835 Boudinot and a small group of Cherokee signed the Treaty of New Echota. In it they gave all Cherokee land east of the Mississippi River to the United States for five million dollars. They also agreed that the Cherokee would move west to Indian Territory, in what is now Oklahoma.

Boudinot moved west to Park Hill, in Indian Territory, in 1837. On June 22, 1839, a group of Cherokee who supported John Ross stabbed him to death. On the same day, other men killed his uncle, Major Ridge, and his cousin John Ridge, who had also signed the treaty. The killers were never identified or tried. In 1890 a man named Allen Ross described a secret meeting before the killings. The men at the meeting decided that the three should die under a Cherokee law. That law said anyone who agreed to sell the Nation's land "should forfeit their lives," which means they should be put to death.

#### Newspapers against slavery, and the men who attacked them, 1831 to 1835

Abolitionists were people who worked to end slavery. On January 1, 1831, William Lloyd Garrison, a white abolitionist, began *The Liberator* in Boston. Garrison demanded an immediate end to slavery, with no payment to the enslavers. About 3,000 people paid for his paper. The drawing across the top of its front page showed whippings and the sale of children, set in Washington, D.C. Garrison believed that "slavery and freedom of the press cannot exist together." By 1835 members of the American Anti-Slavery Society were printing more than a million papers and pamphlets a year.

In the summer of 1835 members of the society mailed their papers to people in the South. On the night of July 29, 1835, a small group of men broke into the post office in Charleston, South Carolina. They took the bags of antislavery papers, and a mob burned them. Opening or holding back the mail was against federal law. Postmaster General Amos Kendall was a close ally of President Andrew Jackson. He gave Southern postmasters permission to refuse to deliver antislavery papers.

On October 21, 1835, a crowd gathered outside *The Liberator*'s office in Boston, where the Boston Female Anti-Slavery Society was meeting. A newspaper of the time put the crowd at 5,000. A member of the society later described the men as "gentlemen of wealth and standing." The men forced the women out, seized Garrison, tied a rope around his waist and dragged him through the streets. They nearly tarred and feathered him. Tarring and feathering means pouring warm pine tar over a person's body and then covering it with feathers, and the tar often blistered or burned the skin. The mayor stopped them and had Garrison held in the city jail overnight for his own safety. Garrison later wrote that "every mail" brought letters telling him he had "only so many days to live."

#### The penny press, 1833

In 1833 Benjamin Day, a New York printer, started *The Sun* partly to bring more work to his print shop. Most daily papers cost six cents. Day sold *The Sun* for one cent a copy, a penny, so people with little money could buy it every day. Boys sold it on the street. Day printed crime stories, and he hired George Wisner to write short reports from the police office. Wisner was the first police reporter in the United States.

In 1835 Day printed in *The Sun* a made-up report that living creatures had been found on the Moon. Sales rose, and critics attacked Day when readers learned it was false. By 1839 *The Sun* sold 50,000 copies a day. Day paid for the paper mostly by selling advertisements. By 1842 New York City had nine daily papers that cost one or two cents.

<a id="story-elijah-lovejoy"></a>

#### Elijah Lovejoy

> **Who:** A white Presbyterian minister and newspaper editor who wrote against slavery and was shot dead by a mob while defending his press.
>
> **When and where:** St. Louis, Missouri, 1833 to 1836, and Alton, Illinois, 1836 to 1837.

On November 7, 1837, a mob in Alton, Illinois, shot and killed Elijah Lovejoy while he defended his printing press. He was born in Albion, Maine, on November 9, 1802. In 1833 he became the editor of the *St. Louis Observer*, a Presbyterian weekly paper in St. Louis, Missouri. Slavery was legal in Missouri. Lovejoy wrote against it. In 1835 a group of leading men in St. Louis signed a letter asking him to tone down what he wrote. He refused.

On April 28, 1836, a white mob in St. Louis chained Francis McIntosh, a free Black steamboat worker, to a tree and burned him alive. Judge Luke Lawless refused to convict anyone and blamed abolitionists. Lovejoy attacked the judge in the *Observer*. In May 1836 men in St. Louis threatened him with mob violence and ran him out of town.

He moved his paper across the Mississippi River to Alton, in the free state of Illinois. Men in Alton who supported slavery destroyed his press three times. They threw one press from a second-floor window. On November 6, 1837, a fourth press arrived by steamboat. Lovejoy and his supporters stored it in a stone warehouse owned by Benjamin Godfrey and Winthrop Gilman.

On the night of November 7, a mob surrounded the warehouse. Its members said they would burn the building and kill every man inside. About twenty men inside had guns. One of them shot and killed a man in the mob named Bishop. A man from the mob climbed a ladder to set fire to the roof. When Lovejoy stepped outside, men in the mob shot him five times. He was 34. The mob went into the warehouse, broke the press and threw it into the river.

In January 1838 Alton's prosecutors, the lawyers who bring charges for the government, put twelve of the press's defenders on trial for riot. Illinois Attorney General Usher F. Linder, the state's top lawyer, joined them. A jury found Gilman not guilty in ten minutes, and the city attorney dropped the charges against the other eleven. On January 19, 1838, prosecutors tried men from the mob for breaking into the warehouse and destroying the press. Among them were Frederick Drucher, William Carr, James M. Hock, David Butler, Horace Beall, Levi Palmer, and two men named Nutter and Jennings. Linder was now their lawyer. The jury found them not guilty. No one was ever charged with killing Lovejoy.

#### The telegraph, 1844, and who owned it

In 1843 members of Congress voted Samuel Morse $30,000 to build a test telegraph line from Washington to Baltimore. A telegraph sends messages along a wire as pulses of electricity. On May 24, 1844, Morse sent the first message over the line from the US Capitol: "What hath God wrought." Alfred Vail received it in Baltimore and sent it back.

Morse and his partners tried to sell the right to use his invention to the federal government and to groups of businessmen. No one bought it. Morse hired Amos Kendall, the former Postmaster General, to run the business. Kendall sold the right to use Morse's patent to separate companies, one region at a time. A patent is the legal right to be the only one to make or use an invention. In 1851 officials of the Census Bureau, the government office that counts the people, reported 75 telegraph companies with 21,147 miles of wire. Private companies owned the lines. From 1844 on, many newspapers printed a section headed "News by Telegraph."

In 1846 the war between the United States and Mexico began. Getting fast news of the war now cost much more than news had cost before. Moses Yale Beach owned *The Sun*. He got the owners of the leading New York papers, six counting his own, to share the cost. That group grew into the New York Associated Press.

<a id="story-frederick-douglass-publisher"></a>

#### Frederick Douglass

> **Who:** A man who escaped slavery in Maryland and started his own newspaper, the *North Star*.
>
> **When and where:** Rochester, New York, from 1847.
>
