> **Movie:** *Becoming Frederick Douglass* (2022), a PBS documentary about his life, directed by Stanley Nelson.

Frederick Douglass started his own newspaper because he believed that Black Americans had to lead the fight for their own freedom. He was born enslaved in Talbot County, Maryland, in February 1818. He escaped on September 3, 1838. In 1841 he spoke about his life in slavery at a meeting of the Massachusetts Anti-Slavery Society on Nantucket island. The society's leaders then asked him to travel and give speeches for pay. In 1845 he published the story of his life. He then gave speeches in Britain and Ireland, and the money from that tour paid to start his paper.

In the late 1840s Douglass broke with Garrison over whether politics could help end slavery. Douglass came to believe that political action could. On December 3, 1847, he published the first issue of the *North Star* in Rochester, New York. Its motto was "Right is of no sex, Truth is of no color, God is the Father of us all, and we are brethren." Brethren means brothers.

The *North Star* was four pages long and came out every week. It had more than 4,000 subscribers in the United States, Europe and the West Indies. On the front page Douglass wrote that the paper would "attack SLAVERY in all its forms and aspects." He also wrote that it would "promote the moral and intellectual improvement of the COLORED PEOPLE." "Colored" was a word Americans of that time used for Black people. Its first printer and publisher was William Cooper Nell, a Black man from Boston.

### 1850 to 1900

A telegraph wire crossed the continent in 1861, and by 1866 one company, Western Union, had more than 90 percent of the country's telegraph business. During the Civil War, Northern editors sent dozens of reporters to the battlefields. Union generals and members of Lincoln's cabinet closed newspapers and had editors arrested without trials.

In 1863 Boston's postmaster hired the first Black American known to work for the federal government. In New York, Joseph Pulitzer and William Randolph Hearst competed for readers, and some of the stories they printed were false. In 1896 postal workers began carrying mail to farm families at their homes. White men drove Black editors out of Memphis in 1892 and out of Wilmington, North Carolina, in 1898. In Wilmington a white mob burned a Black-owned newspaper and murdered Black men in the streets.

#### The Pony Express and the wire across the continent, 1860 to 1861

On April 3, 1860, William H. Russell and his partners, Alexander Majors and William B. Waddell, started the Pony Express. Riders carried mail on horseback nearly 2,000 miles, from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California. The route crossed land where mostly Native Americans lived. The riders changed horses every 10 to 15 miles and covered 75 to 100 miles a day. The first run took ten days.

In March 1861 the riders carried President Abraham Lincoln's inaugural address across in 7 days and 17 hours. An inaugural address is the speech a new president gives on taking office. The company charged as much as $5 for half an ounce of mail, when ordinary postage was ten cents or less. On October 24, 1861, workers finished the first telegraph line across the continent. Two days later the Pony Express shut down.

#### News of the Civil War, 1861 to 1865

The North had far more newspapers than the South when the Civil War began. In 1860 fewer than 10 of every 100 print shops in the country were in the South. The South had 70 of the country's 387 daily papers, and those 70 sold only about 10 of every 100 daily copies. In April 1861 soldiers of the Confederacy, the Southern states that had broken away from the United States, fired on Fort Sumter. The next day the *New York Herald* printed 135,000 copies, about as many as all the South's daily papers together. Only about 20 Southern daily papers were still printing when the war ended.

The editors of the *New York Herald* alone kept more than 40 reporters with the armies. At Gettysburg the telegraph lines had been cut. A. Homer Byington of the *New York Tribune* repaired the wires near Hanover, and in return he got the first use of them. After the Battle of Antietam in September 1862, George W. Smalley of the *New York Tribune* wrote his story on a train to New York. The *Tribune* had thousands of copies on the streets the second morning after the battle. The Associated Press was a group of New York papers that shared news, and Southern papers could no longer get its news. So Southern publishers started their own Press Association in 1862.

Photographs of the time could not show action or reach many readers quickly. The editors of weekly papers such as *Frank Leslie's Illustrated Newspaper* and *Harper's Weekly* sent artists to draw the battles. Engravers carved the drawings into blocks of wood for printing. Readers saw the pictures within about a week.

#### Editors arrested and papers closed, 1861 to 1864

During the Civil War, Union officers and members of Lincoln's cabinet shut down newspapers and arrested editors, most of the time without any court case. The First Amendment states that Congress shall make no law "abridging the freedom ... of the press," which means cutting it back. From April 1861, Lincoln's officials censored reporters' telegraph messages to and from Washington. To censor means to control what people are allowed to send or print. Soldiers arrested editors and closed their presses. Army officers sitting as military courts banished some editors to the Confederacy, which means they forced them to leave the North and not come back.

William Seward, Lincoln's Secretary of State, the cabinet member in charge of dealings with other countries, ordered the arrest of an editor of the *Freeman's Journal*. Officials held the editor for 11 weeks and then let him go without a trial. Edwin Stanton, the Secretary of War, who ran the army for Lincoln, allowed a military governor to destroy the office of the *Sunday Chronicle* in Washington. A military governor was an army officer put in charge of a place. In Canton, Ohio, Archibald McGregor edited the *Stark County Democrat*. He printed words that his opponents called treason, the crime of betraying one's own country, and a mob then destroyed his paper's office. The record does not name the men in the mob. A year later soldiers arrested him without saying what the charge was.

In 1863 General Ambrose Burnside closed the *Chicago Times*, a paper that backed the Democratic Party. Lincoln canceled Burnside's order. He said he was "embarrassed" that his general had failed to weigh the needs of the Union against "the Liberty of the Press."

In May 1864 two New York reporters printed a fake announcement signed with Lincoln's name. It called for a day of fasting and a much larger draft, the government's order for men to join the army. The two men did it to change the price of gold. The *New York World* had printed it. Lincoln ordered General John A. Dix to arrest the *World*'s editors and take over its offices. He canceled the order once it was clear the two reporters had faked the announcement.

#### The first Black postal workers, 1863 to 1869

From 1802 to 1865, federal law had barred anyone but "free white persons" from carrying the mail. In early 1863 John Palfrey, the postmaster of Boston, hired William Cooper Nell as a clerk. On March 3, 1865, members of Congress ended the rule. Their new law said that "no person, by reason of color, shall be disqualified from employment in carrying the mails." That meant no one could be kept from the job because of the color of his skin.

In June 1869 James Christian began delivering mail in Richmond, Virginia. He was the first Black letter carrier known in the United States. Richmond's postmaster, Elizabeth Van Lew, hired him along with other Black clerks and letter carriers.

<a id="story-william-cooper-nell"></a>

#### William Cooper Nell

> **Who:** A Black writer and printer from Boston who printed Frederick Douglass's first newspaper and became the first Black American known to work for the federal government.
>
> **When and where:** Boston, and Rochester, New York, 1840s to 1874.

William Cooper Nell was born in Boston. In the 1840s he went to Rochester, New York, and worked for nearly two years with Frederick Douglass. He was the first printer and publisher of Douglass's newspaper, the *North Star*.

The members of the Boston School Committee, who ran the city's public schools, kept Black children apart from white children. In 1844 Nell and other Black Bostonians sent the committee a petition, a written request signed by many people, asking it to open the schools to their children. Eleven years later, in 1855, the governor of Massachusetts signed a law that banned schools from turning children away because of their race. The same year, Nell published a 396-page book, *The Colored Patriots of the American Revolution*, about Black Americans who fought in the Revolution.

In early 1863, during the Civil War, Boston's postmaster, John Palfrey, hired Nell as a clerk at the Boston Post Office. It was the first job in the federal government known to go to a Black American. At that time federal law still said that only white people could carry the mail. Nell worked at the post office until he died in 1874.

#### One company owns the telegraph, 1866 to 1900

In 1866 Western Union bought its last two big rivals and ended up with more than 90 percent of the country's telegraph business. Percent means out of every 100. Tomas Nonnenmacher of Allegheny College calls it the country's first nationwide industrial monopoly. A monopoly is a company that has no real competition, so it can set its own prices. In almost every session of Congress, members brought bills to control the company or to put the government into the telegraph business itself. Western Union's lobbyists, people paid to persuade lawmakers, blocked nearly all of them.

Between 1867 and 1900, the number of telegrams the company carried rose from 5.8 million a year to 63.2 million. The average price of a telegram fell from $1.09 to 30 cents. Of every dollar customers paid, about 30 to 40 cents was profit for the company.

By the late 1800s the New York Associated Press, run by the owners of a few New York papers, held what the American Antiquarian Society calls a news monopoly. Chicago newspaper owners formed a rival group, the Western Associated Press, and they broke the New York group's hold. In 1892 a new, national Associated Press began.

#### The telephone, 1876 to 1900

Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone in 1876. He offered the patent to Western Union for $100,000, and the company's leaders turned it down. In 1900 the United States had about 1.36 million telephones, about 18 for every 1,000 people, or fewer than 2 telephones for every 100 people. Of every 100 telephone calls, 97 were local calls within one town.

#### Newspapers in Chinese, 1854 and 1855

Before the Civil War there were already American newspapers in German, French, Spanish, Polish, Swedish, Norwegian, Hawaiian and other languages. Chinese was harder to print because it uses thousands of characters instead of an alphabet. The first Chinese-language paper in the country, *Golden Hill's News*, came out in San Francisco in 1854 and lasted a few months.

The second, *The Oriental*, began there on January 4, 1855. Its editor was William Speer, a Presbyterian minister. Its printers drew the characters on stone with a grease pencil and printed from the stone. The paper closed in 1857. No one tried another Chinese paper until the 1870s.

<a id="story-nellie-bly"></a>

#### Nellie Bly

> **Who:** A newspaper reporter who pretended to be mentally ill so that she could report from inside New York City's asylum for women.
>
> **When and where:** Pittsburgh, 1885 to 1887, and New York City, 1887 to 1895.
>
> **Movie:** *Escaping the Madhouse: The Nellie Bly Story* (2019), a Lifetime television film that its makers call a fictionalized account.

In 1887 the reporter Nellie Bly got herself locked in New York City's asylum for women so she could report what happened to the patients there. An asylum was a hospital where people with mental illness were kept. Nellie Bly was the pen name of Elizabeth Cochran. She was born in Cochran's Mills, Pennsylvania, on May 5, 1864.

In 1885 the *Pittsburgh Dispatch* printed an article called "What Girls Are Good For." Cochran wrote an angry letter to the paper answering it, and its editor hired her. At the *Dispatch* her subjects were working girls and poor neighborhoods in Pittsburgh.

In 1887 Bly went to work for Joseph Pulitzer's *New York World*. For her first big story she pretended to be insane until she was locked in the asylum on Blackwell's Island. She stayed ten days. When she arrived, a nurse, Miss Grupe, took her to a cold, wet bathroom. The nurses pulled off her clothes while a group of patients watched from the door. A patient scrubbed her with soft soap. Then three buckets of ice-cold water came down over her head, and Bly did not say who poured them.

Bly saw 52 women tied together by wide leather belts locked around their waists and fastened to one long rope. A nurse, Miss Grady, told a patient named Urena Little-Page that "the doctors say that you are thirty-three instead of eighteen," and the other nurses laughed. Then Grady and the other nurses slapped Little-Page, knocked her head and choked her, and dragged her into a closet. The marks of their fingers stayed on her throat all day. A patient told Bly that "the nurse would beat them if they told."

Bly's reports ran in the *World* and then as a book, *Ten Days in a Mad-House*. A grand jury, a group of citizens who decide whether someone should be charged with a crime, looked into the asylum. Bly wrote that New York City officials had set aside $1,000,000 a year more than ever before for the care of people with mental illness.

Bly then asked her editor to let her travel around the world faster than Phileas Fogg, the hero of Jules Verne's novel *Around the World in Eighty Days*. Bly set out in November 1889. In France she met Verne himself, who asked about her route. The whole trip took 72 days, 6 hours, 11 minutes and 14 seconds. The *World*'s contest to guess her time drew nearly a million entries. She died in New York on January 27, 1922.

<a id="story-ida-b-wells-news-communication"></a>

#### Ida B. Wells

> **Who:** A Black newspaper editor in Memphis who counted lynchings, printed what she found and was driven from her city for it.
>
> **When and where:** Memphis, Tennessee, 1892, and New York City, 1892 to 1895.

Ida B. Wells counted the lynchings in the South and printed the count, and white men in Memphis drove her out of the city for it. A lynching is a killing by a crowd of people, outside the law, with no trial. Wells was born into slavery in Holly Springs, Mississippi, on July 16, 1862. By 1892 she was an editor and part owner of the *Free Speech*, a Black newspaper in Memphis, Tennessee.

In the early morning of March 9, 1892, a white mob took three Black men out of their cells in the Memphis jail and shot them to death. They were Thomas Moss, Calvin McDowell, and a third man whom the records name as Will Stewart or Henry Steward. Moss was part owner of the People's Grocery, a store run by Black people. It was taking business from a white-owned store nearby. Wells wrote that the white store's owner, a man named Barrett, led twelve officers to the grocery at night. The grocery's defenders fired on them and wounded three. Officers then arrested 31 men, and the mob took the three from among them. Wells wrote that Black people in Memphis asked the authorities to bring the killers to justice, and "No attempt was made to do so."

Wells and the other editors of the *Free Speech* advised Black people to leave Memphis. Wells wrote that Black men "left the city by thousands." Those who stayed stopped riding the streetcars. The streetcar company lost so much money that its managers came to the *Free Speech* and asked the editors to tell people to ride again.

Wells began to study lynchings. She used the lists of lynchings that the *Chicago Tribune* printed each year. In 1892 she wrote that mobs had killed 728 Black people in the past eight years. Wells found that only one-third of the 728 had even been charged with rape. Rape means forcing someone into sex. Her list included "the boy Will Lewis," hanged in Tullahoma, Tennessee, "for being drunk and 'sassy' to white folks." It also included a fifteen-year-old girl hanged in Louisiana.

On May 21, 1892, Wells printed an editorial in the *Free Speech*. An editorial is an article that gives the paper's opinion. It listed eight Black men lynched since the last issue, and it described the claim that Black men raped white women as "the old thread-bare lie." Wells was in New York at the time. On May 24 white men in Memphis held a meeting at the Cotton Exchange Building. They sent a group to find the paper's editors. Wells wrote that these men made "open threats of lynching" and did not carry them out only because they could not find the editors. The business manager and half owner, J. L. Fleming, fled the city. Wells wrote that he was later "ordered not to return," and she did not say who gave the order. Letters and telegrams warned Wells that she would be hurt if she came home.

People the paper owed money to then took over the office and sold "the outfit," meaning the printing equipment. Later accounts by the National Park Service and the National Women's History Museum say a mob destroyed or burned the office. Wells, writing in 1892, described no fire.

Wells did not go back. On June 25, 1892, T. Thomas Fortune's *New York Age*, a Black weekly newspaper, printed most of her account under the name "Exiled." It ran on the front page, and 10,000 copies went out across the country. On October 5, 1892, Black women in New York and Brooklyn held a meeting at Lyric Hall and raised the money to print it as a pamphlet, a short printed booklet. It was called *Southern Horrors: Lynch Law in All Its Phases*. In 1895 she published *A Red Record*, 100 pages of tables of lynchings.

#### Rural Free Delivery, 1896

From 1863 people in cities had their mail brought to their homes for free. Farm families still had to travel to a post office to get their letters and newspapers. In 1890 about 41 million Americans, 65 of every 100, lived in the country. One farmer asked, "Why should the cities have fancy mail service and the old colonial system still prevail in the country districts?"

Postmaster General John Wanamaker argued that rural people, the people who lived in the country, needed the information in newspapers. In 1893 Congressman Tom Watson of Georgia won $10,000 to test home delivery in the country. The next Postmaster General, Wilson S. Bissell, did not use it. Members of Congress added $20,000 in 1895 and $10,000 in 1896.

On October 1, 1896, postal officials began Rural Free Delivery at Charles Town, Halltown and Uvilla, in West Virginia. Within a year 44 routes ran in 29 states. Rural families sent more than 10,000 petitions asking for routes. A petition is a written request signed by many people. Rural delivery became permanent on July 1, 1902, with about 8,500 rural carriers.

#### Yellow journalism and the war with Spain, 1895 to 1898

In New York, Joseph Pulitzer owned the *World* and William Randolph Hearst owned the *Journal*. In 1896 Hearst hired away Pulitzer's cartoonist, Richard F. Outcault, whose comic strip had a character called the Yellow Kid. Pulitzer hired another cartoonist to keep drawing the Kid. People began to call the two men's kind of reporting "yellow journalism." The State Department's historians define it as reporting that put exciting stories ahead of facts. Pulitzer and Hearst printed stories about Cuba's fight for independence from Spain, and some of those stories turned out to be false.

On the night of February 15, 1898, the US battleship *Maine* blew up and sank in the harbor of Havana, Cuba. Officials of Spain's government in Cuba wrote an early report that said the explosion started inside the ship. Hearst and Pulitzer printed rumors that someone had planned to sink it. US Navy officers who investigated later said a mine outside the ship caused the explosion. A mine is a bomb placed in the water. By early May the war between the United States and Spain had begun. The State Department's historians say the two papers helped make Americans ready for a war, but that the papers alone did not cause it.

#### A Black newspaper burned in Wilmington, 1898

In 1898 a mob of white men in Wilmington, North Carolina, burned the city's Black newspaper, murdered Black men in the streets and forced the elected city government out. Alex Manly edited the paper, the *Daily Record*. That year he printed an editorial about relationships between Black people and white people. It challenged what white Southerners claimed about those relationships. Democratic Party leaders, with Furnifold Simmons at the head of their campaign, used the editorial to stir up white voters before the November election.

The day after the Democrats won, a meeting of white men in Wilmington passed a set of demands. They ordered Manly to close his paper and leave the city. They also demanded that the mayor and the chief of police resign. On November 10, 1898, Alfred Moore Waddell, a former Confederate officer and congressman, led a crowd of white men to the *Daily Record* office. About 500 men gathered at the start, and the crowd grew to as many as 2,000. They broke in and burned the building.

Later that morning, members of the white mob shot and killed Black men in the streets of Wilmington. Every person reported killed was Black. The shooting started where groups of Black and white men were arguing, and each side there said the other fired first. A white militia company, the Wilmington Light Infantry, had a machine gun mounted on a wagon, which white businessmen had bought before the election. A militia is a group of armed citizens who serve as part-time soldiers. The coroner, the official who looks into deaths, counted 14 men dead. In 2006 a state commission, a group of people chosen to study the killings, found that at least 14 and perhaps as many as 60 men were murdered. North Carolina's state history office notes unconfirmed reports of scores or even hundreds of deaths. The records do not name the men who set the fire or the men who killed.

By late afternoon Waddell and his allies had forced the elected mayor and city council to resign, and the new board of aldermen, the city council, made Waddell mayor. They then banished people from the city, which means they forced them to leave and not come back. Manly came first, and he escaped. Black leaders, successful Black business owners and white Republicans came next. A federal investigation ended in 1900, and no one was charged.

### 1900 to 1950

From 1902, magazine reporters investigated companies and city governments and printed long reports about what they found. During World War I, federal officials ran the government's first large propaganda office. They also barred dozens of newspapers from the mail and filed more than 2,000 criminal cases against people for what they said or printed.

From 1920, radio brought news into homes as it happened. The Westinghouse company owned one of the first stations, KDKA, and then networks paid for by advertisers took over. In World War II, government officials asked newspapers and radio stations to keep military secrets. Japanese Americans forced into camps printed their own newspapers, and camp officials checked what they printed.

#### The muckrakers, 1902 to 1912

Some reporters in the early 1900s dug into one subject and then wrote long reports about it. Editors at magazines such as *McClure's*, *Cosmopolitan* and *Collier's* printed them. The January 1903 issue of *McClure's* contained three such reports. One was part of Ida Tarbell's history of the Standard Oil Company. By 1880 that company controlled the refining of 90 to 95 percent of the oil produced in the United States. Refining is the work of turning crude oil from the ground into products people can use. Another was Lincoln Steffens's report on corruption in the city government of Minneapolis. Corruption means officials using their jobs to get money or favors illegally. The third was Ray Stannard Baker's report on coal miners.

Upton Sinclair spent about seven weeks undercover in the meatpacking plants of Chicago, hiding who he was. Meatpacking plants were the factories where animals were killed and the meat was cut up and packed. His novel *The Jungle* came out as a book in February 1906. He wanted readers to care about the workers, but readers were most upset about what went into their meat. "I aimed at the public's heart, and by accident I hit it in the stomach," Sinclair wrote. In a series that ran in *Collier's* in 1905 and 1906, Samuel Hopkins Adams reported on patent medicines, bottled cures sold with false claims. He wrote that Americans would "swallow huge quantities of alcohol, an appalling amount of opiates and narcotics" in them. On June 30, 1906, President Theodore Roosevelt signed two new laws. Under the Meat Inspection Act, federal inspectors worked in the packing plants. The Pure Food and Drug Act banned food and medicine with false labels or harmful added ingredients from being sold across state lines.

David Graham Phillips attacked members of the US Senate in a series called "The Treason of the Senate." On April 14, 1906, Roosevelt answered with a speech. He compared these writers to the Man with the Muck Rake, a man in John Bunyan's religious book *The Pilgrim's Progress* "who could look no way but downward." Muck is mud and filth. Roosevelt meant it as an insult. The writers took his word "muckraker" as a name to be proud of. By 1912 this kind of reporting had mostly disappeared from the magazines. One reason was that large companies stopped buying advertisements in them.

<a id="story-robert-s-abbott"></a>

#### Robert S. Abbott

> **Who:** The son of formerly enslaved parents who founded the *Chicago Defender* and sent it into the South, where it urged Black families to move north.
>
> **When and where:** Chicago, 1905 to 1940.

Robert S. Abbott started the *Chicago Defender* with 300 copies in 1905 and by 1920 it outsold every other Black newspaper in the country. He was born on St. Simons Island, Georgia, on November 28, 1868. His parents, Thomas and Flora Abbott, had been enslaved. He learned printing at Hampton Institute in Virginia. After he graduated in 1896 he moved to Chicago, where he was shut out of the printing business because he was Black. The record does not name the shops that turned him away. He earned a law degree in 1899. Because he was Black, he could not get work as a lawyer in Indiana and Kansas.

On May 5, 1905, Abbott printed the first issue of the *Chicago Defender* and sold the 300 copies himself. In his paper's headlines and articles he attacked lynching and white supremacy. Lynching is the killing of a person by a mob, with no trial. White supremacy is the belief that white people should rule over everyone else. One read, "When the Mob Comes and You Must Die Take at Least One with You." White papers such as the *Chicago Tribune* printed "colored" after the names of Black people. Abbott printed "(white)" after the names of white people.

At that time 90 of every 100 Black Americans lived in the South, and Abbott sent the paper there. He urged readers to leave the South. In the *Defender* he printed job listings, train schedules, and photos of what he presented as the best schools, parks and housing in Chicago. For four years starting in 1916, more than 10,000 Black Southerners left the South each month. Between 1916 and 1919 about 500,000 left.

Local police in Southern towns tried to stop the paper. They seized copies, and they arrested people who sold it under vagrancy laws, which made it a crime to have no job. Some police departments banned the sale of Black newspapers altogether. The accounts do not name the towns. Abbott arranged for Pullman porters, the Black workers who served passengers on railroad sleeping cars, to carry bundles of the paper south and sell them in secret.

By 1929 the *Defender* sold more than 250,000 copies a week, and Abbott was one of the first Black millionaires. He died in Chicago on February 29, 1940.

#### World War I: the government's propaganda office, 1917 to 1919

The United States entered World War I on April 6, 1917. That month President Woodrow Wilson set up the Committee on Public Information and put George Creel, a former newspaper reporter, in charge. It was the federal government's first large propaganda office. Propaganda is information made and spread to push people toward one opinion.

Creel's staff sent articles to newspapers. Creel later estimated that their material filled 20,000 newspaper columns a week. The committee's staff printed their own paper, the *Official Bulletin*, and about 115,000 copies went out. Its artists made posters, and one showed a German soldier as a gorilla carrying a club. Staff in one division of the committee watched the hundreds of newspapers printed in other languages in the United States. After the war, many Americans concluded that Creel and his staff had pushed the war too hard, and that they had made it harder for people to speak against it.

#### World War I: papers banned from the mail and people jailed for words, 1917 to 1921

Members of Congress passed the Espionage Act on June 15, 1917. Espionage means spying. The act made it a crime to get in the way of the draft, the government's call-up of men into the army, or to stir up disloyalty in the armed forces. Under the act, papers that urged treason, which means betraying one's own country, could not go through the mail. Postmaster General Albert S. Burleson, the head of the post office, told local postmasters to report anything suspicious. By 1918 his officials had barred 74 newspapers from the mail. The New York City postmaster, Thomas G. Patten, stopped *The Masses* magazine from going through the mail, and its November-December 1917 issue was its last. Newspapers printed in German and other languages faced one more rule. Under the Trading with the Enemy Act of October 6, 1917, they had to file English translations of their war news with the local postmaster.

The next year, on May 16, 1918, members of Congress added the Sedition Act to the Espionage Act. Sedition means stirring people up against their government. The new act made it a crime to speak or write anything "disloyal" about the government, the Constitution, the armed forces or the flag. The punishment was up to 20 years in prison and a $10,000 fine. Federal prosecutors filed more than 2,000 cases under the two laws, and more than 1,000 ended in convictions. Federal prosecutors used the Sedition Act mainly against pacifists, people who oppose all war, and against anarchists and socialists. Anarchists want to do away with government. Socialists want the public, rather than private owners, to own big businesses.

On June 16, 1918, the Socialist leader Eugene V. Debs gave a speech against the war to about 1,200 people in Canton, Ohio. A judge sentenced him to 10 years in prison, and the justices of the Supreme Court upheld his conviction in 1919. President Warren G. Harding shortened his sentence, and Debs walked out of prison on Christmas Day 1921.

<a id="story-victor-berger"></a>

#### Victor Berger

> **Who:** An immigrant newspaper owner in Milwaukee whose paper was barred from the mail for opposing World War I, and who was sentenced to 20 years in prison.
>
> **When and where:** Milwaukee, Wisconsin, 1892 to 1929.

Victor Berger's newspaper lost its mailing permit in 1917 because he opposed World War I, and a federal judge sentenced him to 20 years in prison. Berger was born in 1860 to a Jewish family in Austria-Hungary. He came to the United States in 1878 and moved to Milwaukee three years later. There he taught German in the public schools.

In 1892 Berger bought a German-language newspaper. In 1898 he and Eugene V. Debs founded the Social Democratic Party. Twelve years later, Milwaukee voters made him the first Socialist elected to the US House of Representatives. In 1911 he started a daily paper in English, the *Milwaukee Leader*.

Berger opposed the war and said so in his paper. In 1917 an official in Postmaster General Albert S. Burleson's department, the third assistant postmaster general, took away the *Leader*'s "second-class mailing privilege," the permit that let it go by mail as a newspaper. In 1918 federal prosecutors charged Berger under the Espionage Act. He and four other Socialist leaders were convicted in Chicago. In early 1919 Judge Kenesaw Mountain Landis sentenced each of them to 20 years in prison.

In 1918, while his case went on, Milwaukee voters elected Berger to Congress again. In November 1919 the other members of the House refused to let him take his seat. Voters elected him again in a special election, a vote held to fill the empty seat, with 55 percent of the vote, and the members of the House refused him again. In 1921 the justices of the Supreme Court overturned his conviction. Voters elected him to Congress three more times, in 1922, 1924 and 1926. He died in 1929 after a streetcar accident.

#### Radio, and who owned it, 1920 to 1934

Radio station KDKA in Pittsburgh broadcast the results of the presidential election between Warren G. Harding and James M. Cox on the evening of November 2, 1920. KDKA belonged to the Westinghouse company. Its studio was a shed on the roof of a building at the Westinghouse works in East Pittsburgh.

By the end of 1921 eight stations were on the air, and by November 1, 1922, federal officials had licensed 564. At first, money for radio came from two places: selling radio sets and selling advertising. On August 28, 1922, the Queensboro Corporation paid station WEAF in New York $50 for about ten minutes of advertising for its apartments. Over the following years, advertising became the main way American radio was paid for.

In 1926 the National Broadcasting Company, NBC, bought WEAF and set up a permanent network. A network is a group of stations in different cities that carry the same programs. Other networks followed, among them the Columbia Broadcasting System, CBS. The biggest makers of radio equipment and the biggest broadcasters made business deals with each other that could have given them a monopoly, control of radio with no real competition. Members of Congress passed the Radio Act of 1927. Under it, a federal commission decided which station could use which wavelength, the spot on the radio dial where a station is heard. In 1934 they passed the Communications Act, which set up the Federal Communications Commission, the FCC, to oversee radio and messages sent by wire.

#### The president on the radio, 1933 to 1944

President Franklin D. Roosevelt gave his first fireside chat, a talk to the country by radio, on Sunday night, March 12, 1933. On March 6, two days after he took office, he had closed every bank in the country. In the talk Roosevelt explained in simple terms how banks worked to some 60 million listeners, and he told them it was safer to keep money in a reopened bank than under the mattress. When the banks opened again, people put in more money than they took out. Harry Butcher of CBS gave these talks the name "fireside chats." According to Encyclopaedia Britannica, scholars count between 27 and 31 of them, from 1933 to 1944.

#### The War of the Worlds broadcast, 1938

The actor Orson Welles and his Mercury Theatre on the Air performed H. G. Wells's novel *The War of the Worlds* on CBS on the evening of October 30, 1938. Welles was 23. The writer Howard Koch, the producer John Houseman and Paul Stewart had rewritten the story as fake news bulletins about Martians landing in New Jersey. The program did not stop to say it was a play until almost 40 minutes in.

Some listeners believed it and called the police, newspapers and radio stations. The next morning, editors across the country printed stories about a nationwide panic. That night the C. E. Hooper company had asked 5,000 households what they were listening to. Two of every 100 named the Welles program. A. Brad Schwartz, who wrote a book about the broadcast, *Broadcast Hysteria*, found that only some listeners were fooled. He found that their worried phone calls convinced many journalists that the show had caused a panic across the country, and the journalists reported one.

#### Pictures by wire, 1935

Before 1935, newspapers mostly got photographs by mail, train or airplane, and a picture could take up to 85 hours to arrive. The AT&T telephone company had run a service that sent photographs by wire from 1926, but it closed in 1933. On January 1, 1935, Associated Press staff sent their first photograph over wires. It was a picture taken from the air of a plane crash near Morehouseville, New York. Forty-seven newspapers in 25 states received it.

<a id="story-edward-r-murrow"></a>

#### Edward R. Murrow

> **Who:** A CBS radio reporter whose eyewitness reports from Europe before and during World War II made him famous across the United States.
>
> **When and where:** London, 1937 to 1945.
>
> **Movie:** *Good Night, and Good Luck* (2005), directed by George Clooney, about Murrow's television reports on Senator Joseph McCarthy in 1953 and 1954.

Edward R. Murrow's radio reports from Europe for CBS, from 1938 to 1940, made him famous across the United States. He was born in Greensboro, North Carolina, on April 25, 1908. He graduated from Washington State College. He helped bring German scholars who had been driven out by the Nazis to the United States. The Nazis were Adolf Hitler's party, which ruled Germany.

Murrow joined CBS in 1935. In 1937 CBS executives sent him to London to run the network's European office. On the radio he described Germany's moves across Europe as an eyewitness. In 1938 he reported Germany's takeover of Austria and the Munich Conference, a meeting of European leaders. In 1939 he reported the takeover of Czechoslovakia. In 1940 he reported the Battle of Britain, when German planes attacked Britain.

After the war Murrow ran the news department at CBS. In 1954 he made a television program about Senator Joseph McCarthy, who had charged that Communists were working in the government. Communists wanted one party to run the government and the government to own the farms and factories. Murrow died on April 27, 1965.

#### World War II: secrets, propaganda and the Black press, 1941 to 1945

Japanese planes attacked the US Navy base at Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, on December 7, 1941. Twelve days later, on December 19, President Roosevelt set up the Office of Censorship. Censorship means controlling what people may send or print. Its director, Byron Price, had been an editor at the Associated Press. The office had about 13,500 workers, and most of them read letters and cables going into and out of the country. A cable was a message sent by wire under the ocean.

Under Price, the office gave newspapers and radio stations a code of rules, and editors agreed to follow it of their own free will. The code listed topics to keep out of the news: troop and ship movements, how war factories were doing, the president's travels, and even the weather. Price persuaded the reporters Drew Pearson and William L. Laurence not to write about the building of the atomic bomb. On June 13, 1942, Roosevelt set up the Office of War Information. Its staff ran programs, at home and in other countries, that told people how the government said the war was going and what its war plans were.

Federal prosecutors charged far fewer people for their words than in World War I. Philip A. Dynia, writing in the First Amendment Encyclopedia, counts dozens charged, against thousands in 1917 to 1919. Roosevelt kept pressing his attorney general, Francis Biddle, to "indict the seditionists," meaning to charge with crimes the people he saw as turning others against the government.

Writers for Black newspapers such as the *Chicago Defender* reported on the armed forces' separate units for Black troops, white officers placed over Black soldiers, blood supplies kept apart by race, and violence against Black servicemen. They ran a "Double V" campaign: victory over the enemy abroad and victory over prejudice at home. Federal officials threatened to charge Black publishers with sedition. The *Defender*'s publisher, John H. Sengstacke, insisted on meeting Biddle. Biddle agreed to block the charges as long as Black editors did not make their criticism of the war any stronger.

#### Newspapers behind barbed wire, 1942 to 1945

On February 19, 1942, President Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, a written command from the president. Under it, Lieutenant General John L. DeWitt ordered Japanese Americans on the West Coast out of their homes, some with only 48 hours' notice. Soldiers and federal officials forced them into camps because of their Japanese ancestry. The National Archives counts about 122,000 people, and nearly 70,000 of them were American citizens. Another count gives 110,000 to 120,000. The First Amendment Encyclopedia describes them as concentration camps, places where people are held by force without a trial.

Inside the camps, Japanese Americans wrote, printed and handed out their own newspapers. The papers in the first camps, run by the army, were copied on mimeograph machines, which print copies from a cut paper stencil. Army officials required those papers to be written in English only. All ten camps run by the War Relocation Authority had papers in both English and Japanese. Two of them were the *Manzanar Free Press* in California and the *Heart Mountain Sentinel* in Wyoming.

Officials checked what the papers printed. Army officials censored the papers in the first camps. In the later camps, officials of the War Relocation Authority interfered with what the papers printed, and in some cases they censored the papers outright.

#### Television begins, 1927 to 1941

Philo Farnsworth, who was 21, sent the first picture by all-electronic television, a straight line, in his laboratory in San Francisco on September 7, 1927. On July 1, 1941, station WNBT in New York showed the first television advertisement allowed by law, before a baseball game. It showed a Bulova watch face over a map of the United States. It lasted about ten seconds and cost $9.

### 1950 to 2000

In 1950 about 9 of every 100 American homes had a television set, and by 1960, 87 of every 100 did. After the DuMont network closed in 1955, three national television networks were left: NBC, CBS and ABC.

Managers of one Mississippi station, WLBT, cut civil rights news off the air. A church leader and two Mississippi leaders fought the station before the government and in court, and its owners lost their license. In 1971 and 1972 reporters printed a secret history of the Vietnam War and tied a burglary to the White House, and officials in Washington tried to stop them. By 1996 cable channels such as CNN and Fox News showed news all day and night, and the World Wide Web had been open to the public since 1991.

#### Television and the blacklist, 1950 to 1954

In February 1950 Senator Joseph McCarthy of Wisconsin gave a speech in Wheeling, West Virginia. He said that 205 communists worked in the State Department. Communism is a system in which one party runs the government and the government owns the farms and factories. When senators asked him, he could not name a single one.

In June 1950 three former FBI agents published a book called *Red Channels*. They ran a company called American Business Consultants. The book named 151 people who worked in radio and television and claimed they had ties to communism. The company's owners then visited networks, advertisers and sponsors. For a fee, they offered to "clear" the people they had named. To be cleared, a person usually had to give the FBI or the House Un-American Activities Committee, a committee of Congress, the names of other people. Network executives and advertisers fired people on the list. A list of people whom employers refuse to hire or keep is called a blacklist.

In 1954 a Senate hearing on McCarthy's charges against Army officers and officials was shown on television across the country. It lasted 36 days. On camera, Joseph Welch, the Army's lawyer, asked McCarthy, "Have you no sense of decency, sir, at long last?"

That same year Edward R. Murrow showed McCarthy's methods on his weekly CBS program *See It Now*. On December 2, 1954, members of the Senate voted 67 to 22 to condemn McCarthy.

#### Radio and television in Spanish, 1946 to 1961

Raoul A. Cortez was born in Xalapa, Mexico, in 1905. He worked as a reporter for *La Prensa*, a Spanish-language newspaper in San Antonio, Texas. In 1946 he opened KCOR in San Antonio. It was the first all-Spanish radio station owned and run by a Hispanic American. During World War II, federal officials limited broadcasts in languages other than English. To get his license, Cortez told officials that part of the station's purpose was to rally Mexican Americans behind the war effort.

In 1955 Cortez started KCOR-TV, the first television station aimed only at Hispanic viewers. It broadcast on a kind of channel called UHF, and few television sets could pick it up, so advertisers were hard to find. In 1961 he sold the station. The new owners renamed it KWEX.

#### The station that cut the news: WLBT, 1955 to 1971

The managers of WLBT, a television station in Jackson, Mississippi, that carried NBC's programs, cut civil rights news off the air, and a group of citizens fought for years to take away the station's license. The Lamar Life Insurance Company started WLBT in 1953. In the fall of 1955 the lawyer Thurgood Marshall appeared on an NBC program to talk about the Supreme Court's decisions against segregated schools. Segregation means keeping Black and white people apart by law or by force. WLBT staff cut him off and showed a sign that read "Sorry, Cable Trouble from New York." The general manager, Fred Beard, said he did it "because the TV networks were overloading the circuits with Negro propaganda." "Negro" was a word used at that time for Black people.

Station staff also cut away from NBC's evening news when it turned to civil rights. WLBT reporters used racial slurs on the air. The White Citizens' Council, a group that fought to keep segregation, ran a bookstore in the station's lobby. About half the people in WLBT's viewing area were Black, and the station's managers refused them time to answer.

In May 1963 Medgar Evers spoke on WLBT to answer the mayor of Jackson. Evers was the Mississippi field secretary of the NAACP, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, a civil rights group. Three weeks later Byron De La Beckwith shot Evers in the back in the driveway of his home and killed him. That year WLBT again ran the "Cable Trouble" sign, this time over NBC's report on white people attacking protesters at a lunch counter in Jackson. WLBT's own crew had filmed the attack.

In 1963 the Reverend Everett Parker of the United Church of Christ joined Aaron Henry, head of the Mississippi NAACP, and A. D. Beittel, the president of Tougaloo College. They gathered complaints from viewers, knowing that they could be attacked for it. In 1964 they asked the Federal Communications Commission not to renew WLBT's license, the government permit a station needs to broadcast. The commissioners gave the station a one-year renewal without a hearing.

In 1966 judges on a federal appeals court, in an opinion by Warren Burger, ruled that viewers had the right to take part in these cases. In 1969 the judges ordered the commission to take away the owners' license. The owners appealed and lost in 1971. A board of Black and white citizens then ran the station, and it hired some of the first Black television managers in the South.

#### Civil rights news on the page and on the screen, 1955 to 1965

In August 1955 Roy Bryant, his half-brother J. W. Milam and at least one other person took 14-year-old Emmett Till by force from his relatives' home in Mississippi. Bryant and Milam later described beating him and shooting him in the head. Three days later Till's body was found in the Tallahatchie River, weighed down with a 75-pound metal fan from a cotton gin, a machine that cleans cotton. The men had fastened the fan to his neck with barbed wire. An all-white jury found Bryant and Milam not guilty of murder. Afterward, both men told the writer William Bradford Huie, for *Look* magazine, that they had kidnapped and murdered Till.

*Jet*, a weekly news magazine for Black readers published in Chicago by John H. Johnson's company, printed photographs of Till's body on September 15, 1955. *Jet* sold about 425,000 copies a week at the time. The Till issue sold out, and its publishers printed more.

On the night of September 30, 1962, a crowd rioted at the University of Mississippi to stop James Meredith from enrolling as its first Black student. People in the crowd threw a pipe, rocks, bricks and bottles at US marshals. Hundreds of people were hurt, and two men died. One of them was Paul Guihard, a 30-year-old reporter for the French news agency Agence France-Presse, who was covering the story. Someone shot him in the back at close range, and the bullet hit his heart. No one has ever been charged with killing him. Justice Department lawyers closed the case in 2011 without naming anyone.

Alabama state troopers and other officers led by Major John Cloud attacked civil rights marchers with clubs and tear gas on the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma on March 7, 1965. At least 50 marchers went to the hospital. Television cameras filmed the attack, and the film was flown to New York. At about 9:30 that night, the ABC newscaster Frank Reynolds interrupted the network's showing of *Judgment at Nuremberg*, a film about Nazi war crimes, to show it. Nearly 50 million people had tuned in to the film.

<a id="story-walter-cronkite"></a>

#### Walter Cronkite

> **Who:** The CBS anchor who read the evening news to much of the country for 19 years, and who told viewers in 1968 that the Vietnam War was stuck.
>
> **When and where:** New York, 1962 to 1981.
>
> **Movie:** *Walter Cronkite: Witness to History* (2006), a PBS *American Masters* documentary about him.

In 1972 a poll named Walter Cronkite, the anchor of the *CBS Evening News*, "the most trusted man in America." An anchor is the person who reads the news and introduces the reports on a news program. Cronkite was born in St. Joseph, Missouri, on November 4, 1916. He grew up in Houston, Texas, where he wrote for his school newspapers.

In World War II Cronkite reported for the United Press news service. He flew on bombing raids over Germany and covered the D-Day landings in 1944. In 1950 Edward R. Murrow hired him for CBS. In 1962 Cronkite became the anchor of the *CBS Evening News*. Soon after, the program grew from 15 minutes to 30 minutes. It was the first half-hour nightly news program on network television. In 1963 Cronkite told viewers that President John F. Kennedy had been killed. He covered the Moon landing in 1969 and nearly every American spaceflight with a crew from 1961 to 1981.

In 1968 Cronkite went to Vietnam after the Tet Offensive, a large attack by North Vietnamese and Viet Cong forces. On February 27, 1968, he told viewers that the war was "mired in stalemate." A stalemate is a fight that neither side can win. President Lyndon Johnson told his staff, "If I've lost Cronkite, I've lost Middle America." By Middle America he meant ordinary American families. Encyclopaedia Britannica records that some people held this to be the reason Johnson decided not to run for president again that year.

Cronkite ended each program with "And that's the way it is." He left the anchor desk in 1981. He died in New York on July 17, 2009.

#### Vietnam and the reporters, 1965 to 1971

As late as 1964 fewer than two dozen American reporters were in Indochina, the region that includes Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia. By 1968 about 600 journalists from many countries were in Vietnam. More than 60 journalists were killed during the war, and the record of their deaths does not say who killed them. US military officers did not censor the reports from Vietnam. The military's daily news briefings in Saigon were nicknamed "the five o'clock follies." Follies are silly shows.

Some Americans later blamed the press for turning people against the war, and Encyclopaedia Britannica records that the argument goes on. Britannica states that experts who studied the news coverage found that most of the reporting supported the war until 1968. They found that support at home fell most as more American soldiers were killed.

On March 16, 1968, American soldiers of Charlie Company killed unarmed villagers at My Lai in South Vietnam. The counts run from at least 175, found by the Army's own inquiry, to 504, the number of names on a memorial in the village. The soldiers also raped women and girls. Rape means forcing someone into sex by violence or threat. In 1969 Seymour Hersh, a freelance reporter, one who worked for himself rather than for one newspaper, followed a tip and found Lieutenant William Calley. Hersh wrote the first public account of the killings. He won a Pulitzer Prize, a top award for reporting, in 1970. In March 1971 Calley was found guilty of murdering 22 civilians. He was the only soldier convicted, and no one was convicted of rape.

#### The Pentagon Papers, 1971

In 1967 Secretary of Defense Robert McNamara ordered a secret history of what American leaders had done in Vietnam since World War II. It filled 47 volumes. Daniel Ellsberg, who had worked on it, gave copies to *The New York Times* without permission. The *Times* began printing stories about it on June 13, 1971. The papers recorded that President Johnson had planned open war in 1964, a year before the public knew. They also recorded that he ordered the bombing of North Vietnam in 1965, even though intelligence officials had judged that it would not work.

After three days, Justice Department lawyers got a court order that stopped the *Times* from printing more. An order that stops something from being printed before it comes out is called prior restraint. *The Washington Post* also had the papers. On June 30, 1971, the justices of the Supreme Court voted 6 to 3 that the newspapers could keep printing.

Prosecutors charged Ellsberg under the Espionage Act, and he faced up to 115 years in prison. Men working for President Richard Nixon, led in this case by the former CIA officer E. Howard Hunt, broke into the office of Ellsberg's psychiatrist, a doctor who treats mental illness. They were looking for information to damage Ellsberg. In 1973 the judge dismissed all the charges because of this break-in and other wrongdoing by government officials.

In 1972, in a case called *Branzburg v. Hayes*, the justices of the Supreme Court ruled that the Constitution gives reporters no right to refuse to tell a grand jury who their sources are. A grand jury is a group of citizens who decide whether there is enough proof to put someone on trial. A reporter's sources are the people who give the reporter information.

<a id="story-woodward-and-bernstein"></a>

#### Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein

> **Who:** Two young *Washington Post* reporters who showed that a burglary in 1972 was tied to President Nixon's White House.
>
> **When and where:** Washington, D.C., 1972 to 1974.
>
> **Movie:** *All the President's Men* (1976), about their reporting, with Robert Redford as Woodward.

Bob Woodward and Carl Bernstein, two young reporters at *The Washington Post*, tied a 1972 burglary to President Richard Nixon's White House. Early on June 17, 1972, police arrested five men inside the office of the Democratic National Committee, the national leaders of the Democratic Party, in the Watergate building in Washington. One of them, James W. McCord Jr., was the security chief of Nixon's re-election committee. Woodward, born in Illinois in 1943, had covered minor crimes for the *Post* for nine months. Bernstein covered politics in Virginia. With a third reporter, Alfred E. Lewis, they wrote about the arrests for the next morning's paper.

Nixon's press secretary, Ron Ziegler, called it a "third-rate burglary attempt." Most early news stories said the White House had nothing to do with it. Woodward and Bernstein kept reporting. A secret source they called "Deep Throat" gave them information. On October 10, 1972, they reported that the bugging of the Democrats' office, which means hiding microphones there to listen in, came from "a massive campaign of political spying and sabotage" run by White House officials for Nixon's re-election. Sabotage means secretly wrecking someone else's work.

CBS News aired the first part of a two-part report on the story on October 27, 1972. Nixon's aide Charles Colson then threatened William Paley, the head of CBS, and the second part was cut short. The records do not say who at CBS made the cut. That November Nixon won re-election, carrying every state except Massachusetts. In 1973 the *Post* won the Pulitzer Prize for public service for Woodward and Bernstein's reporting.

The reporting was one step among several that led to Nixon's resignation. For two weeks in May 1973, television stations showed a Senate committee's Watergate hearings live. More than 150 public television stations showed them again in the evening. A month after the hearings began, 97 of every 100 Americans had heard of Watergate. A White House aide, Alexander Butterfield, told the committee that Nixon kept a voice-activated tape recorder in rooms of the White House.

On July 24, 1974, the justices of the Supreme Court ordered Nixon to hand over the tapes. One tape showed that on June 23, 1972, he had ordered the FBI to hold back its investigation. Members of the House Judiciary Committee approved three articles of impeachment, formal charges that could lead to his removal from office. On August 9, 1974, Nixon resigned.

In 2005 W. Mark Felt, who had been an associate director of the FBI, one of its top officials, said that he was Deep Throat.

#### Reporters killed in the United States, 1976 to 1990

On June 2, 1976, Don Bolles, a 47-year-old reporter for the *Arizona Republic*, went to a Phoenix hotel to meet a man who had promised him information about land fraud, cheating people in land deals, and organized crime, crime run by gangs. The man never came. When Bolles started his car, a bomb under it exploded. Doctors had to cut off both his legs and one arm, and he died on June 13. In 1977 John Harvey Adamson pleaded guilty to building and planting the bomb. A jury later convicted Max Dunlap of murder and of conspiracy to murder, which means planning a murder with others. He died in prison in 2009. Reporters from many other papers came to Arizona and spent five months finishing Bolles's reporting.

Between 1981 and 1990, killers murdered five Vietnamese American journalists who worked at small papers for refugees from the Vietnam War. Reporters at ProPublica who looked into the killings in 2015 tied them to what the papers printed about Vietnam and its government. Duong Trong Lam, 27, was shot outside his home in San Francisco in 1981. In Houston in 1982 a gunman chased Nguyen Dam Phong from his house and shot him seven times. Pham Van Tap was killed by the smoke from a fire that someone set in his office in Garden Grove, California, while he slept. A message sent to the Vietnamese press after his death said he was killed for printing advertisements for companies that did business with Vietnam. Le Triet was shot at his home in Virginia on September 22, 1990. FBI agents suspected a group led by former South Vietnamese military officers, but they never found enough evidence to charge anyone. No one was ever arrested or charged.

#### Public broadcasting, the fairness rule, cable news and talk radio, 1967 to 1996

In the Public Broadcasting Act of 1967, members of Congress set up the Corporation for Public Broadcasting to hand out federal money to public television and radio stations. People at the corporation started PBS in 1969 and NPR, National Public Radio, in 1970.

On June 1, 1980, Ted Turner's company started CNN, the first television channel to show news 24 hours a day. It reached viewers through cable, wires that carried many channels into homes.

From 1949 the members of the Federal Communications Commission required stations to follow a rule called the fairness doctrine. Stations had to cover important public questions fairly and air more than one side. People attacked on the air had to get a chance to answer. The justices of the Supreme Court upheld the rule in 1969. In June 1987 members of Congress passed a bill to make it a law. President Ronald Reagan vetoed the bill, which means he refused to sign it. He wrote that the rule "requires Federal officials to supervise the editorial practices of broadcasters." That year the commissioners, led by their chairman, Dennis Patrick, voted 4 to 0 to end the rule.

In 1988 Rush Limbaugh began a national radio talk show on which he gave his conservative political opinions, views that favor keeping old ways and limiting government. Within five years an estimated 20 million people listened each week. His show began the year after the fairness doctrine ended. Whether the end of the rule helped talk shows like his grow is argued and not settled.

On October 7, 1996, Rupert Murdoch's company started the Fox News Channel. Roger Ailes, a television producer and former Republican political adviser, ran it.

#### The internet, 1969 to 1996

In late 1969, researchers at the University of California, Los Angeles, sent the first message over ARPANET to the Stanford Research Institute. ARPANET was a computer network paid for by the Defense Department. In 1991 Tim Berners-Lee, a British scientist working in Switzerland, opened the World Wide Web to the public. The web is the system of linked pages that people open over the internet, the worldwide network of connected computers. In 1993 a team at the University of Illinois released Mosaic, the first widely used program for viewing web pages with pictures.

In February 1996 President Bill Clinton signed the Telecommunications Act. Under it, one company could own more television stations, and many media companies merged after it passed. One part made it a crime to send "indecent" material to children online. In 1997 the justices of the Supreme Court struck down that part. They ruled that the internet has the same protection for free speech as printed words.

### 2000 to Today

In a 2025 survey by the Pew Research Center, 86 of every 100 American adults said they got news at least sometimes from a phone, computer or tablet, and 64 of every 100 from television. Newspapers lost most of their advertising money. Researchers at Northwestern University counted close to 3,500 newspapers that closed between 2005 and 2025.

People angry at what reporters wrote killed journalists in their newsrooms and outside their homes. Police arrested reporters at protests and hit them. In 2025 members of Congress took back the federal money for public radio and television.

#### The news on phones and feeds, 2004 to 2025

Mark Zuckerberg and three other Harvard students started Facebook in February 2004. Three former workers at the PayPal company started YouTube in 2005, and Google bought it in November 2006 for $1.65 billion. Twitter began in 2006. A feed is the list of posts a site shows each user. In January 2018 Mark Zuckerberg announced changes to Facebook's feed. Users would see fewer posts from news outlets and businesses and more posts from their friends and family.

Under a law of 1996, known as Section 230, a website cannot be treated as the publisher of what its users post. That means the company that runs the site is not legally responsible, as a newspaper publisher would be, for what users write there.

In 2011, 35 of every 100 American adults owned a smartphone, according to the Pew Research Center. By 2025, 91 of every 100 did. In a Pew survey in August 2025, 53 of every 100 adults said they got news at least sometimes from social media. Thirty-eight of every 100 said they regularly got news on Facebook, and 35 on YouTube. Twenty regularly got news on Instagram, 20 on TikTok and 12 on X, the site called Twitter until 2023. In the same survey, 7 of every 100 said they often read news in a printed newspaper or magazine.

#### False news, measured, 2018

In 2018 three researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Soroush Vosoughi, Deb Roy and Sinan Aral, published a study of news on Twitter. They followed about 126,000 chains of retweets from 2006 to 2017. A retweet is a post shared again on Twitter, and each chain began with one news story that people passed along. About 3 million people shared the stories more than 4.5 million times. Six fact-checking groups had judged which stories were true and which were false. The researchers found that false stories were 70 percent more likely to be shared again than true ones. A true story took about six times as long as a false one to reach 1,500 people. False stories about politics spread fastest.

Some accounts on Twitter were run by computer programs, called bots. When the researchers left out the bots, the result stayed the same. So people, the researchers concluded, spread the false stories.

#### Who owns the feed, 2022 to 2026

In October 2022 Elon Musk bought Twitter for $44 billion. He laid off about half its workers and cut back content moderation, the work of checking posts and removing those that break a site's rules. He began selling blue check marks for $8 a month. Musk renamed the site X in 2023. In March 2025 he sold X to his artificial intelligence company, xAI, in a deal that valued X at $33 billion. In 2026 his rocket company, SpaceX, bought xAI.

On Facebook, Mark Zuckerberg made his own change. In January 2025 he announced that Facebook would end the fact-checking programs it had used for about ten years.

TikTok belonged to ByteDance, a company in China. In April 2024 President Joe Biden signed a law that ordered ByteDance to sell TikTok within a year or see the app banned. The justices of the Supreme Court upheld the law in January 2025. President Donald Trump then delayed the ban several times. In January 2026 a new company took over TikTok in the United States. The software company Oracle, the investment firm Silver Lake and a fund owned by the government of the United Arab Emirates each own 15 percent of it, and ByteDance kept 19.9 percent.

In 2025 David Ellison bought Paramount, the company that owns CBS, and he hired Bari Weiss to run CBS News. In December 2025 a *60 Minutes* report about a prison in El Salvador was pulled from the air three hours before it was to run. The correspondent, Sharyn Alfonsi, wrote that Weiss "spiked our story," which means stopped it, after CBS lawyers had cleared it.

Ellison's company also agreed to buy Warner Bros. Discovery, which owns CNN, for $111 billion. According to NPR, both deals depend on money from his father, Larry Ellison, a founder of Oracle. The top lawyers of 12 states, all of them Democrats, sued over the deal. In September 2026 Paramount's owners settled the lawsuit by agreeing to set up a board meant to keep the owners out of news decisions at CBS and CNN. The purchase was not yet complete at the end of September 2026.

#### Newspapers close: the news deserts, 2005 to 2025

American newspapers took in about $49.4 billion from advertising in 2005 and an estimated $9.8 billion in 2022, according to the Pew Research Center.

Researchers at the Medill school of journalism at Northwestern University count newspapers every year. Their 2025 report found that close to 3,500 newspapers had closed since 2005, almost 40 of every 100. More than 130 closed in the year before the report. Since 2005 the newspaper business had lost more than three of every four of its jobs.

A county with no local newspaper, news website or station is called a news desert. In 2005 just over 150 counties had no local news source, according to the Medill report. In 2025 there were 212, and about 80 of every 100 of them were mostly rural. Another 1,525 counties had only one local source. About 50 million people lived in counties with one source or none. In 2005 there were 3,995 different owners of American newspapers, and in 2025 there were just under 1,900.

The *Chicago Defender*, the paper that urged Black Southerners to move north in the 1910s, ended its print edition in 2019 and publishes only online.

<a id="story-jeff-german"></a>

#### Jeff German

> **Who:** A Las Vegas newspaper reporter who was stabbed to death by an elected official he had written about.
>
> **When and where:** Las Vegas, Nevada, 1980s to 2022.

In 2022 Robert Telles, an elected official in Las Vegas, stabbed the reporter Jeff German to death after German reported on Telles's office. German's work as a reporter in Las Vegas spanned four decades, and at the time of his death he worked for the *Las Vegas Review-Journal*. He wrote about organized crime and dishonest officials, and he hosted a *Review-Journal* podcast about the mob called *Mobbed Up*.

That year German wrote about the office of Robert Telles, who had been elected Clark County Public Administrator. When a person in Clark County dies and no family member can step in at once, workers in that office guard the dead person's property and money until they can hand it to the people who should get it. German's stories described bullying in the office and the punishing of workers who complained. They also described an "inappropriate relationship" between Telles and a staff member. Telles denied it. In June 2022 he lost his election.

On September 2, 2022, Telles stabbed German to death outside German's home. Police found Telles's DNA on German's hands and fingernails. DNA is the chemical code inside every person's cells, and it can show who was at a place. In Telles's home, police found a straw hat and sneakers, cut into pieces, like the ones the killer wore on a security camera video.

A jury found Telles guilty of murder on August 28, 2024. In October 2024 Judge Michelle Leavitt added more time because German was over 60 and Telles had used a deadly weapon. Telles was sentenced to 28 years to life in prison.

#### A newsroom attacked: Annapolis, 2018

On June 28, 2018, Jarrod Ramos walked into the newsroom of the *Capital Gazette* in Annapolis, Maryland, with a shotgun, smoke grenades and extra ammunition. He killed five people who worked there: Gerald Fischman, Rob Hiaasen, John McNamara, Rebecca Smith and Wendi Winters. Ramos held a grudge because in 2011 the paper's reporters had written that he was convicted of harassing a woman he had gone to high school with. In 2021 a jury found that he was responsible for his crimes, and a judge sentenced him to five life terms in prison with no chance of release.

<a id="story-darnella-frazier"></a>

#### Darnella Frazier

> **Who:** A 17-year-old who recorded a Minneapolis police officer killing George Floyd, and whose video became evidence at his trial.
>
> **When and where:** Minneapolis, Minnesota, 2020 to 2021.

Darnella Frazier's phone video of a police officer killing George Floyd reached people around the world. On May 25, 2020, Frazier, who was 17, was walking with her nine-year-old cousin in Minneapolis. She saw the police officer Derek Chauvin kneeling on the neck of George Floyd, a Black man, and she recorded it. Her video showed Chauvin kneeling on Floyd's neck for nine minutes and 29 seconds, and it recorded Floyd's murder.

According to NPR, the video played a major part in starting protests against police violence around the world. At Chauvin's trial in 2021, prosecutors played it again and again, and Frazier testified. The jury found Chauvin guilty of second-degree murder, third-degree murder and second-degree manslaughter, three different legal grades of killing a person. Manslaughter is killing a person without meaning to kill. The journalist Ann Marie Lipinski said, "There is no case without her."

On June 11, 2021, the Pulitzer Prize Board gave Frazier a special citation, an honor outside its usual prizes. The citation identifies "the crucial role of citizens in journalists' quests for truth and justice." Frazier called recording the video a "traumatic life-changing experience."

#### A small-town paper raided: Marion, Kansas, 2023

On August 11, 2023, Police Chief Gideon Cody of Marion, Kansas, led officers in a raid on the weekly *Marion County Record* and on the home of its publisher, Eric Meyer. The officers took computers and reporters' phones. Cody claimed that Meyer and the reporter Phyllis Zorn had committed identity theft or computer crimes by checking a local business owner's driving record. Identity theft means using another person's private information as if you were that person. Meyer's mother, Joan Meyer, was 98 and owned part of the paper. A police camera recorded her telling officers, "Get out of my house!" She died of a heart attack the next afternoon.

Special prosecutors, lawyers brought in from outside to handle the case, later found that no one at the paper had committed a crime. They said Cody had reached a wrong conclusion through "a poor investigation." They said they could not charge anyone over Joan Meyer's death. In August 2024 Cody was charged with felony obstruction of justice, a serious crime of getting in the way of an investigation, for asking the business owner to delete text messages.

#### Reporters arrested, hit and deported, 2017 to 2026

Since 2017 the US Press Freedom Tracker, run by the Freedom of the Press Foundation, has counted attacks on journalists in the United States. By September 2026 it had counted 1,487 assaults and 445 arrests or criminal charges. In 2020 and 2021 together it counted nearly 800 assaults.

In 2025 the tracker counted at least 32 journalists arrested or held and at least 170 assaulted. Most were covering protests against deportation, the sending of immigrants out of the country. On June 9, 2025, police in Los Angeles surrounded and held at least 10 journalists at one protest. In January 2026 the tracker counted at least nine assaults on journalists in the Minneapolis area. Most of those journalists were hit by pepper balls or by pieces of stun grenades, both of them crowd-control weapons. The tracker's January report does not say who fired each one. Pepper balls are small balls fired from a gun that burst into a stinging powder. On January 15, 2026, federal agents held the photographer John Abernathy on the ground.

Mario Guevara was a Spanish-language reporter who covered immigration near Atlanta. He was arrested on June 14, 2025, while he livestreamed a protest near Atlanta, which means he was showing it live on the internet. The Committee to Protect Journalists' account of the case does not name the police who arrested him. Federal officials held him and argued that his filming of police was a danger to public safety. On October 3, 2025, they deported him, sending him out of the country to El Salvador. The Committee to Protect Journalists said it was the first time it had recorded this kind of punishment for reporting.

Starting in 2010, Julian Assange published secret documents about the US wars in Afghanistan and Iraq on his WikiLeaks website. In June 2024 he pleaded guilty under the Espionage Act of 1917.

On February 11, 2025, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt told the Associated Press, the AP, that its reporters could no longer come into the Oval Office with the press pool, the small group of reporters that covers the president up close. The ban was to last until the AP agreed to call the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America. In April a federal judge, Trevor McFadden, ordered the AP's access restored. In October 2025 officials at the Pentagon made reporters agree to have their material checked in order to keep their passes.

#### Public broadcasting loses its federal money, 2025 to 2026

In July 2025 Republican majorities in both houses of Congress passed the Rescissions Act, and President Trump signed it. With the act, members of Congress took back about $1.07 billion already promised to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting for 2026 and 2027, according to the research group USAFacts. That money had gone to NPR, PBS and local public radio and television stations. In May 2025 Trump had signed an order calling for an end to government money for news outlets that did not meet standards of "fairness, accuracy, and nonpartisanship." Nonpartisanship means not taking the side of any political party.

In January 2026 the corporation's board voted to close it after 58 years. Between July 2025 and May 2026, public radio and television stations cut about 550 jobs, according to a count reported by Nieman Lab. Rural stations and stations run by Native nations had gotten a large share of their money from the federal government, and they were hit hardest. By mid-2026 at least one public television station had shut down, and more had announced plans to close. No full count had been published. Stations of every kind saw the number of people giving them money rise between 2024 and 2025.

Officials also pressed commercial broadcasters, the stations paid for by advertising. In 2025 Brendan Carr, the chair of the Federal Communications Commission, pressed ABC to take the talk show *Jimmy Kimmel Live!* off the air. Carr acted after Kimmel made comments about which political side was held by the man accused of killing the activist Charlie Kirk. In 2026 Carr opened an investigation of the talk show *The View* under the rule that stations must give political candidates equal time.

<a id="part-9"></a>

# Part 9: Culture and Play

<a id="ch-art"></a>

## Chapter 32: Art

### Before 1500

All the art made in this land before 1500 was made by the people of Native nations. Potters in the Southwest painted bowls and jars, and carvers in the Ohio valley shaped stone pipes into birds and animals. In the towns of the Mississippi valley and the Southeast, metalworkers hammered copper into sheets and pressed pictures into it. On the Northwest Coast, people carved bone, horn and stone.

No surviving record names the people who made these things. Many of the objects that do survive were buried with the dead in graves and mounds. In the 1800s and 1900s, diggers took them out of the ground, and many of those diggers sold what they found.

#### Painted pottery in the Southwest

The Ancestral Pueblo people were the ancestors of today's Pueblo nations. Their potters made a kind of pottery now called black-on-white. The white is the color of the clay. The potter rolled clay into a long snake and coiled it around in a spiral to build up the pot. Then the potter scraped the coils together until the sides were smooth.

The black paint came from boiled plants, such as beeweed or tansy mustard. It also came from crushed rock with iron in it, such as hematite. Potters made their brushes from the fibers of the yucca plant. At Mesa Verde, people made this pottery from about the year 600 to about 1300.
