In the Mimbres valley of southwestern New Mexico, potters painted bowls from about 1000 to 1130 or 1150. Most of these painted bowls have been found in graves. Archaeologists are scientists who dig up and study the things people left behind long ago. They think people set a bowl over the dead person's face or head. Before they did, someone punched a hole through the bottom of the bowl on purpose. Archaeologists call this a kill hole.

#### Pictures on the rock

A petroglyph is a picture cut or pecked into rock. A pictograph is a picture painted on rock. On the volcanic cliffs west of Albuquerque, New Mexico, there are about 24,000 to 25,000 petroglyphs. They show animals, people, crosses, the brand marks that ranchers burn into cattle, and other images.

Ancestral Pueblo people chipped most of them into the rock with chisels and other stones between 1300 and the 1680s. The oldest are much older and date from about 2000 BC. For some Native nations the petroglyphs still have religious meaning today, and a place in their ceremonies. A ceremony is a set of religious acts that people do together.

#### Pipes, copper and stone in the Ohio and Mississippi valleys

People of the Hopewell culture lived in the Ohio valley from about 100 BC to about AD 400 or 500. Their carvers made smoking pipes of stone in the shapes of animals. The pipes show birds of prey, which are birds that hunt. They also show ducks and other water birds, songbirds, frogs, toads, meat-eating animals and river otters.

One Ohio mound, Tremper Mound in Scioto County, held a store of more than 500 objects. Among them were 136 pipes. Archaeologists thought most of the pipes were carved from Ohio pipestone. When scientists tested some of them, they found that 16 out of every 100 were made of a stone called catlinite. That stone came from quarries in southwestern Minnesota. A quarry is a place where people dig stone out of the ground.

At Etowah, near Cartersville, Georgia, metalworkers hammered copper into thin sheets between about 1250 and 1325. They pushed the design up from the back of the sheet so it stood out on the front. The best-known plates show a dancing figure that archaeologists call the Birdman, or the falcon dancer.

Near Cahokia, in what is now Illinois, a carver made a figure between 1050 and 1200. The carver used a stone called flint clay, which came from near St. Louis, Missouri. It shows a kneeling woman with a pack on her back. She is using a hoe on the back of a snake that has the head of a cat. It was dug up in 1979 and is called the Birger figurine.

At Spiro, in eastern Oklahoma, people built twelve mounds between 850 and 1450, along with grounds for ceremonies and a town. One of the mounds, Craig Mound, held objects of stone, copper, shell, basketry and cloth.

#### Carving on the Northwest Coast

On the Northwest Coast, people carved bone, stone and horn at least 5,000 years ago. The oldest Coast Salish basketry comes from an old fishing camp on the Hoko River, on the Olympic Peninsula. It is about 2,500 years old.

Most carving on the coast was done in cedar wood. Wood rots, so very little of it survives from before 1500. One piece that may be that old is a hat woven from twisted strands of cedar bark. It dates from between 1450 and 1620, and it was found at the mouth of Wapato Creek. Carvers on the coast still work in this tradition today.

#### Who dug the objects up, and where they went

Ephraim Squier and Edwin Davis dug into the Mound City mounds, near Chillicothe, Ohio, in 1846. They took more than 200 stone pipes. Long before the two men came, the pipes had been broken and laid together under the floor of a building used for ceremonies. Davis sold his collection in 1864 for $10,000 to William Blackmore, who ran a museum in Salisbury, England. The collection was sold again in 1931, to the British Museum in London. Fewer than two dozen of the carved animal pipes have been on public display there.

At Etowah, John Rogan dug for the Smithsonian, the national museum in Washington, in 1885. He took the two best-known Birdman plates from a grave lined with stone. The Smithsonian's National Museum of Natural History still holds them.

Craig Mound at Spiro was a burial mound. In 1933 six men who called themselves the Pocola Mining Company paid $50 each. Together they paid $300 to George Evans for the right to dig into the mound for two years. Evans was the grandfather of the children who owned the land. He needed the money to pay off a loan on the land and to treat his grandson's tuberculosis, a disease of the lungs. A local man, R. W. Wall, handled the company's business. A company that sells copies of Spiro objects shows photographs of the dig from 1935 on its website, with notes drawn from a 1952 report on the mound. Those photographs and notes name some of the men who dug: the brothers Bill and Hayden Vandagriff, W. Guinn Cooper, John Hobbs and K. A. McKenzie. The company also hired coal miners, who dug tunnels into the mound.

From 1933 to 1935 the diggers took things out of the graves to sell. They destroyed about a third of the mound. They sold thousands of objects of stone, copper, shell, basketry and cloth to collectors around the world. One pile of objects, found in April 1935, went to a secondhand furniture dealer from Indianapolis, Indiana, for $100.

People who saw the dig described what the diggers did. Beads, pearls and arrowheads lay spilled across the ground. The diggers trampled feather capes and woven cloth. They hauled out decorated shells by the wheelbarrow and dumped them near the entrance, and the shells were crushed under the diggers' feet. They burned ancient cedar poles as firewood. They piled human bones at the edge of their camp, where the bones crumbled to dust.

Forrest Clements, an archaeologist at the University of Oklahoma, tried to stop the dig. In 1935 Oklahoma lawmakers passed a law that required a license to dig at such sites. Clements filed a complaint with the sheriff of LeFlore County. When he left for California, the diggers came back.

The historian David La Vere calls Craig Mound by its other name, the Great Temple Mound. In La Vere's words, "In a fit of spite, just to jab their finger in Clements' eye, they packed the central chamber of the Great Temple Mound with kegs of black powder and touched off a mighty explosion." The blast caved in part of the mound and left a large crack in it. The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History says the Pocola Mining Company was shut down for good in November 1935. It does not say who shut it down.

From 1936 to 1941, University of Oklahoma archaeologists led workers paid by a government jobs program, the Works Progress Administration. The workers took the remains of more than 600 people out of Craig Mound, some whole skeletons and some only parts.

In the Mimbres valley, looters dug up graves to reach the painted bowls. In the 1960s they began using bulldozers and earth movers to get to the bowls faster, and they wiped out many village sites completely. Every Mimbres site has been looted. The records do not name the people who ran the bulldozers.

<a id="story-nathan-jackson-art"></a>

#### Nathan Jackson

> **Who:** A Tlingit carver of totem poles, masks, canoes, carved doors and clan crest panels, of the Sockeye Clan on the Raven side of the Chilkoot Tlingit.
>
> **When and where:** Born August 29, 1938, in southeastern Alaska. He lives in Ketchikan, Alaska.

Nathan Jackson carves in the Northwest Coast tradition that began thousands of years ago. He is Tlingit, of the Sockeye Clan on the Raven side of the Chilkoot Tlingit. A clan is a large group of related families. He carves totem poles, masks, canoes, carved doors and panels that show clan crests, the animal symbols that belong to a clan. He also works metal and dances.

He learned his people's traditions from Jack David, his clan uncle and grandfather. He served in the Army in Germany until 1959. Later he spent 54 days in a hospital with pneumonia, a serious sickness of the lungs. While he was there he whittled small totem poles. "I told the nurses, 'Those totem poles there, they have a price on them,'" he said later. Published accounts of his life disagree about when this happened. One puts it soon after his Army service. Another puts it in his mid-30s.

In the early 1960s he joined the Chilkat Dancers of Haines, Alaska. Then he studied for about three years at the Institute of American Indian Arts in Santa Fe, New Mexico. After that the carver Duane Pasco taught him to work with an adze, a carving tool with a curved blade set across the end of its handle. Through a program of the Alaska State Council on the Arts, he taught apprentices, younger carvers who learn by working beside a master.

In 1995 officials of the National Endowment for the Arts, a US government agency, gave him an honor called a National Heritage Fellowship. He has said that "the traditional way of life is something I identify with."

In 2024, at the age of 86, he carved an eight-foot pole that tells the Tlingit story of Raven and Fog Woman. He began it at the Edwin DeWill Carving Center in Saxman, Alaska. He finished it that autumn at the Arts Council of Princeton, in New Jersey, where it stands in the lobby.

### The 1500s

In the 1500s two European artists drew this land and its people. Each came with a colony that did not last. Jacques Le Moyne drew the French colony in Florida in 1564. John White painted the coast of what is now North Carolina in 1585. In Europe, Theodor de Bry cut copies of both men's pictures into metal plates so that he could print them in books, and he changed them.

#### Jacques Le Moyne in Florida, 1564 and 1565

In 1564 French colonists set up a colony called Fort Caroline, in a part of Florida that Spanish leaders claimed. They brought along an official artist, Jacques Le Moyne, to record it. Le Moyne made many drawings of the fort, the settlers and the land. He also drew the people who already lived there. They were Timucua people.

On September 20, 1565, Pedro Menéndez de Avilés and 500 Spanish soldiers took the fort in an attack at dawn. They killed most of the French settlers they found. Menéndez spared about 50 women and children and shipped them to Havana. Le Moyne escaped, but he lost all of his drawings. Back in France, he drew them again from memory. He died in 1588, and his widow sold the pictures to de Bry, who printed them in 1591. De Bry changed the people and the landscapes to make his books sell better. He also made different versions of the pictures for different buyers.

One painting by Le Moyne, titled *Laudonnière and Athore, 1564*, shows the French commander René de Laudonnière with Athore, a Timucua leader. The year in the title is the year of the meeting the picture shows. Le Moyne lost all his Florida drawings in 1565, so he made this picture after he got back to Europe. The New York Public Library holds it.

<a id="story-john-white-roanoke-art"></a>

#### John White

> **Who:** The English artist on the 1585 voyage to Roanoke Island, and later governor of the 1587 colony there.
>
> **When and where:** Roanoke Island and the coast of what is now North Carolina, 1585 and 1586, and again in 1587. His years of birth and death are not known. He was working from 1577 to 1593.

John White made the first pictures of this land by an English artist. Of all the pictures that Europeans made here on the spot, his are the oldest that survive. Le Moyne drew Florida twenty-one years before White, but Le Moyne's drawings from Florida were lost.

White was probably born in Cornwall, in England. In 1585 he sailed on Sir Richard Grenville's voyage to Roanoke Island as its artist. Walter Raleigh and other men who put money into the voyage paid for it. White worked beside the mathematician Thomas Harriot. The coast they recorded was the land of nations that spoke Algonquian languages, a family of related languages. Among them were the Roanoke, the Secotan and the Croatoan. In July 1585 White visited the town of Secotan and painted it.

In about thirteen months he made more than seventy watercolor pictures of Algonquian towns, people, dances, clothing and fishing, and of plants, birds and fish. He drew each outline in black lead, a kind of pencil. Then he filled it in with watercolor and added touches of gold and silver paint.

In 1590 de Bry printed engravings of White's pictures of people in a book with Harriot's report on the colony. An engraving is a picture cut into a metal plate, so that many copies can be printed from it. De Bry changed some of the pictures. In one of White's watercolors, a Secotan girl holds a small doll dressed in English clothes. De Bry's copy also puts a model of the globe and the sky in her hands.

The British Museum in London owns White's original watercolors, and its staff keep them stored away from light. In the middle of the 1800s, water badly damaged them during a fire at the Sotheby's auction house. Over time, chemical changes have turned the silver paint black.

In 1587 White returned to Roanoke as the governor of a new colony. After the colonists landed, one of them, George Howe, was found dead. He had been shot with sixteen arrows and beaten. The Encyclopedia Virginia account of the colony does not name the men who killed him.

In August 1587 White led an attack on the town of Dasamonquepeuc to pay back Howe's killing. He believed the town's people were Roanoke people, enemies of the English. They turned out to be Croatoan, who were friends of the English. White's men killed a number of them. One account says the dead included a leader named Menatonon, and other accounts name the leader differently. That same year the colonists talked White into sailing back to England, because they did not have enough supplies to last long. When he got back in August 1590, the colonists were gone. The word "Croatoan" was carved on a tree.

### The 1600s

In the English colonies of the 1600s, painters made portraits for rich families, carvers cut pictures into gravestones, and girls stitched needlework. The painter of the best-known portraits of the 1670s is not known by name. One gravestone carver whose name is known is Joseph Lamson. In 1640 a printer in Massachusetts produced the first full book printed in the English colonies. In 1650 a book of poems by a woman living in Massachusetts was printed in London.

In New Mexico, a Spanish friar had Acoma people build a church on top of the steep hill where their town stands, and they had to carry every load up to the top. A friar is a member of a Catholic religious order. Other friars, and Spanish soldiers, burned the masks that Pueblo people used in their ceremonies.

#### Portraits, gravestones and needlework in New England

English colonists built Boston on land of the Massachusett nation, on a peninsula the Massachusett called Mushauwomuk. Experts credit about ten portraits of people in Boston, all painted from 1670 to 1674, to one painter. No record gives the painter's name. Today the painter is called the Freake Painter, after the best-known portrait. An article in *The Magazine Antiques* calls the painter "probably Samuel Clement," but nobody has proved it.

That portrait shows Elizabeth Freake holding her baby daughter, Mary. The Freakes were one of the richest families in Boston. The painter first painted Elizabeth alone, in about 1671. Mary was born on May 6, 1674. X-rays of the painting show that the baby was painted in later. The Worcester Art Museum, in Massachusetts, owns the painting.

Many settlers of New England were Puritans. They were English Protestants, Christians outside the Catholic Church, who wanted a plainer and stricter church. Puritans did not want religious symbols such as crosses and cherubs, carvings of baby angels, on their graves. Carvers cut other pictures into Puritan gravestones: skulls with wings, crossed bones and hourglasses. Many stones carry the Latin words "Memento Mori," which mean "remember you will die."

Joseph Lamson of Charlestown, Massachusetts, who lived from 1658 to 1722, is one carver whose name is known. He carved winged skulls with eyebrows that hook at the ends, inside borders of fruit, vines and flowers. His sons Nathaniel and Caleb and his grandson Joseph carried on the work.

Girls learned needlework from their mothers. Many stitched samplers, strips of cloth that kept a record of stitches and patterns to copy later.

<a id="story-loara-standish-sampler"></a>

#### Loara Standish

> **Who:** A daughter of Myles and Barbara Standish of Plymouth Colony, thought to be the maker of the oldest known sampler made in America.
>
> **When and where:** Duxbury, in Plymouth Colony, in the 1640s or about 1653. She was born after 1627 and died before 1655.

Loara Standish is thought to have stitched the oldest known sampler made in America. It is also the oldest known sampler with a verse. She made it in Duxbury, in Plymouth Colony. English settlers built Plymouth on the site of Patuxet, a Wampanoag town.

Loara was one of the seven children of Myles and Barbara Standish. She was born after 1627 and died before 1655. According to the Pilgrim Hall Museum, she probably made the sampler in her teens. She stitched it in silk thread on linen cloth, with roses, carnations and oak leaves, and a letter S twisted around itself.

She stitched this verse into it: "Loara Standish is my name Lorde guide my hart that I may doe thy will also My hands with such Convenient skill as may Conduce to virtue void of Shame and I will give The glory to thy name." The verse asks God to guide her heart and to give her hands enough skill to do good. She promises to give God the glory.

In 1844 Lucius Alden gave it to the Pilgrim Hall Museum in Plymouth. It has faded from being hung up for so many years. Experts at the museum date it to about 1653. Experts at the Textile Research Centre in Leiden, in the Netherlands, date it to the 1640s.

#### The first books printed and written here

In 1638 the Reverend Jose Glover sailed for Massachusetts with a printing press. He died on the ship. His widow, Elizabeth Glover, set up the press in Cambridge, Massachusetts. She put it in the charge of Stephen Daye, a locksmith.

In 1640 Daye printed *The Whole Booke of Psalmes*, now called the *Bay Psalm Book*. The psalms are 150 poems in the Hebrew Bible. A group of thirty elders, men respected in the colony for their learning, had put them into English verse that could be sung. Among them were John Cotton, Richard Mather and John Eliot. Daye is thought to have printed about 1,700 copies. They sold for twenty pence each. A penny was a small English coin, and pence means pennies. Only eleven copies survive today.

<a id="story-anne-bradstreet"></a>

#### Anne Bradstreet

> **Who:** A poet in the Massachusetts Bay colony, whose book was the first book of poems by someone living in the English colonies.
>
> **When and where:** Born in England in 1612. Came to Massachusetts in 1630. Died in 1672.

Anne Bradstreet wrote the first book of poems by someone living in the English colonies. It was printed in London in 1650 as *The Tenth Muse Lately Sprung Up in America*. In old Greek stories, nine goddesses called the Muses watched over poetry and the other arts, so the title describes her as a tenth one. The title page identifies the writer only as "a Gentlewoman of those parts." Her full name appears inside the book.

She was born in England in 1612 to Thomas and Dorothy Dudley. In about 1628 she married Simon Bradstreet. In 1630 she and her husband sailed to Massachusetts with her parents. The Bradstreets had eight children.

Her brother-in-law, the Reverend John Woodbridge, took her poems to London. In the book's opening pages, Woodbridge wrote that she had not known he was doing it. Later, in a poem called "The Author to Her Book," Bradstreet called Woodbridge a "friend more loving than true" for taking them.

The biographer Charlotte Gordon studied the poems and the letters between Bradstreet and Woodbridge. She found that Bradstreet knew about the plan and helped with it from the start. One poem in the book is about events of 1649. Woodbridge had sailed in 1648, so someone had to send that poem after him.

#### Mission churches and burned masks in New Mexico

Acoma Pueblo is a town built on top of a mesa, a hill with steep sides and a flat top. In December 1598 Acoma people killed the Spanish captain Juan de Zaldívar and eleven to fourteen of his men. Accounts differ on the number. In the Acoma people's own account, Zaldívar's soldiers had raped an Acoma woman. Rape means forcing a person into sex.

Juan de Oñate was the leader of the Spanish colony in New Mexico. In January 1599 Spanish soldiers sent by Oñate attacked Acoma, took the town and burned much of it. They killed hundreds of Acoma men, women and children. Estimates of the dead run from about 300 to about 1,500.

Oñate sentenced the Acoma men over twenty-five to have one foot cut off and to do forced labor for the Spanish for twenty years. Forced labor means being made to work for others, without pay and without the right to leave. Whether the feet were really cut off is disputed.

In 1629 a friar named Juan Ramírez arrived at Acoma. He probably began soon after to have Acoma people build a church on the mesa, called San Esteban del Rey. The exact years of the building are not known. The Acoma workers had to carry every load up the mesa. The loads included roof beams 40 feet long, cut in mountains 30 to 40 miles away.

One account says the builders were enslaved. Another says only that they had to do the work. The surviving records do not say whether they were paid. San Esteban del Rey is the oldest European church in New Mexico that still stands.

Pueblo people made masks for their ceremonies. Katsina masks show spirit beings. They were kept in kivas, rooms used for religious ceremonies. From 1656 to 1665, Alonso de Posada, the head of the Franciscan friars in New Mexico, banned Pueblo ceremonies. He ordered friars to go into the kivas and burn the masks. They also burned prayer sticks, which are sticks made for prayers, and carved figures, or took them away. In 1661 Spanish soldiers raided kivas and burned masks as well. No surviving record counts the masks that friars and soldiers burned.

In 1675 Governor Juan Francisco Treviño had 47 Pueblo religious leaders arrested. Three of them were hanged, and one killed himself. The rest were whipped in public and jailed, until Pueblo men came to Santa Fe and forced their release. Treviño ordered the arrests. Dennis Zotigh's account of these events for the Smithsonian does not name the men who hanged and whipped the prisoners.

One of the freed men was Po'pay, of Ohkay Owingeh. On August 10, 1680, Po'pay led the Pueblo Revolt. Pueblo people killed 21 friars and burned the mission churches across the province.

### 1700 to 1750

A few painters trained in Europe settled in the colonies between 1700 and 1750. They earned their living painting portraits of merchants, planters and officials, because only families with money could pay for a portrait. Two portraits from these years show slavery. One shows an enslaved boy beside the son of a rich Maryland family. The other shows the Royall family, whose money came from slavery. One painter made portraits of two Lenape leaders two years before William Penn's sons took a large part of Lenape land. A colonial governor also took Native art across the ocean. In 1725 he took Cherokee baskets to London, where they are still kept.

#### Portrait painters in the colonies

Henrietta Johnston drew portraits in Charleston, South Carolina, from 1708. John Smibert came from Scotland and painted in Boston from 1729 or 1730.

Justus Engelhardt Kühn came from Germany. In 1708 he applied at Annapolis, Maryland, to become an English subject, with the rights of a person born English. He painted the children of rich Maryland families until he died in 1717. He was the earliest artist known to work for pay in the Middle Atlantic colonies, the group of colonies that included Maryland.

Gustavus Hesselius was born in Sweden in about 1682 and studied art there. He painted portraits in Philadelphia. He also built church organs, among them one for the church of the Moravians, a Protestant group, in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, in 1746. He died in Philadelphia on May 23, 1755. Robert Feke painted portraits in Newport, Rhode Island.

<a id="story-henrietta-johnston"></a>

#### Henrietta Johnston

> **Who:** A portrait artist who worked in pastels. She was the first woman recorded as working for pay as an artist in the English colonies.
>
> **When and where:** Born in northern France in about 1674. Worked in Charleston, South Carolina, from 1708 until she died there on March 9, 1729.

Henrietta Johnston was the first woman recorded as working for pay as an artist in the English colonies. She was also the first artist in the colonies to use pastels. A pastel is a crayon made from a paste of colored powder and resin, a sticky stuff that comes from trees.

She was born in northern France in about 1674. Her family were Protestants. In 1687 they fled to London. Two years earlier, King Louis XIV of France had taken away Protestants' right to practice their religion. He sent soldiers to live in Protestant homes. The king's officers let the soldiers loot the homes and ruin the families. The soldiers tortured some people who would not become Catholic, which means they hurt them on purpose to make them give in. The soldiers stayed until the families became Catholic or left France. In 1694 she married and moved to Ireland, where she learned to draw portraits in pastel. Her first husband died in 1704 and left her with two small children.

Her second husband, Gideon Johnston, was a minister of the Church of England. In 1708 he moved the family to Charleston, where he served as the representative of the bishop of London. The Stono, Kiawah and Etiwan peoples had lived along the rivers at Charleston when English colonists settled there in 1670. The Johnstons were short of money in Charleston, so Henrietta drew portraits of the town's richest families for pay.

Pastels could be bought only in England. In 1711 she sailed to London for supplies. On the voyage home, pirates attacked her ship, and she survived. After Gideon died in 1716, she earned the family's living alone. She died in Charleston on March 9, 1729. About three dozen of her portraits survive.

<a id="story-john-smibert"></a>

#### John Smibert

> **Who:** A Scottish portrait painter in Boston, whose shop and studio showed younger painters copies of European art. He also drew the plans for Faneuil Hall.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Edinburgh, Scotland, in 1688. Newport, Rhode Island, in 1729, then Boston until he died there in 1751.

John Smibert was the first painter with formal art training to work in the thirteen colonies. His father was a wool dyer. In 1728 a church leader named George Berkeley asked Smibert to come to America. Berkeley planned to start a college in Bermuda, where Smibert would teach art. The college was never started.

Smibert reached Newport, Rhode Island, with Berkeley's group in 1729. He painted Berkeley and his party in a picture now at Yale University. By 1729 or 1730 he had moved to Boston. There he painted merchants, such as Peter Faneuil, and Judge Samuel Sewall. He married Mary Williams in 1730.

Portraits alone did not earn Smibert enough, so he also kept a shop. In 1734 he began selling paint, other art supplies and prints. Upstairs, in his studio, he hung copies of famous European paintings that he had made in Europe. He also showed casts there, copies made by pouring material into molds. The historian Richard Saunders calls it "America's first art gallery." Saunders writes that the collection gave Charles Willson Peale, Gilbert Stuart and John Trumbull much of their early training. A biography of Smibert on Encyclopedia.com names John Singleton Copley and Washington Allston as painters who learned from it. Stuart was born in 1755, four years after Smibert died, so he studied the copies after Smibert's death.

In 1742 Smibert drew the plans for Faneuil Hall in Boston.

#### Two portraits that show slavery

In about 1710, Kühn painted Henry Darnall III, the son of a rich Maryland family, when the boy was about eight. He wears fine clothes and holds a bow. Beside him stands a Black boy with a metal collar around his neck. The Black boy was enslaved. His name was not recorded, and neither was the name of whoever put the collar on him. The Maryland Center for History and Culture owns the painting and calls him "Unnamed attendant." One art history website calls the picture the earliest known formal painting of an enslaved African in America.

In 1741 Robert Feke painted Isaac Royall Jr., who was 22, with his wife Elizabeth, their baby daughter Elizabeth, his sister Penelope and his wife's sister-in-law Mary Palmer. Isaac's father, Isaac Royall Sr., had set up a sugar plantation on the island of Antigua. The father got rich by trading in sugar, in rum and in enslaved people. In 1737 the family moved to Medford, Massachusetts, and brought at least 27 enslaved Africans with them. When his father died in 1739, the son got his father's very large fortune, at the age of 20. Harvard Law School owns the painting.

#### Two Lenape leaders painted, 1735

English colonists led by William Penn built Philadelphia on Lenape land. In 1735 Gustavus Hesselius painted two Lenape leaders, Lapowinsa and Tishcohan, for John Penn, a son of William Penn. Lapowinsa is shown as a strong man of about 40. They are the only two Lenape chiefs whose portraits have survived. The Historical Society of Pennsylvania owns them.

In 1737 Lapowinsa and Tishcohan signed a land deal called the Walking Purchase with John Penn and his brother Thomas Penn. The Lenape leaders Nutimus and Menakihikon also signed it. James Logan, who worked for the Penns, showed the Lenape an unsigned copy of a deed from 1686, a paper selling land. He claimed it gave the Penns as much land as a man could walk in a day and a half. The Penns' men cleared a path ahead of time. On September 19, 1737, three walkers set off at a fast pace, and in a day and a half one of them covered more than 60 miles. The Penns' surveyors, the men who measured and marked out the land, then bent the boundary line to take in even more land. In all, the Penns took more than a thousand square miles of Lenape land, and they forced Nutimus and his people to leave their homes.

#### Cherokee baskets taken to London, 1725

Cherokee weavers made baskets from river cane, a tall plant with hollow stems that grows along rivers. They split the cane into thin strips and dyed some of the strips with walnut and pokeberry. Some baskets were double woven. A double-woven basket is two baskets woven one inside the other from the same strips, so both the inside and the outside show a finished pattern.

In 1725 Francis Nicholson, the first governor of South Carolina chosen by the British king, left Charleston for London. He took a set of Cherokee double-woven baskets with him and passed them to Sir Hans Sloane, a collector in London. A note tied to them says, "They will keep anything in them from being wetted by rain." The British Museum in London holds them today.

### 1750 to 1800

From 1750 to 1800, American painters made the portraits of the men who led the Revolution. Several of these painters trained in London. In 1773 Phillis Wheatley's *Poems* was printed in London. It was the first book of poems by an African American, and she was still enslaved in Boston when it came out. Enslaved Black artists worked in these same years, and a few records name them. One of them, Prince Demah, painted portraits in Boston. Later he served during the Revolution in the Massachusetts militia, a part-time army of local men. The painter Charles Willson Peale was paid for portraits with two enslaved people.

#### Painters who went to London

John Singleton Copley was born in Boston on July 3, 1738. In 1766 he sent a painting called *A Boy with a Flying Squirrel* to be shown in London. The London painters Joshua Reynolds and Benjamin West praised it. In 1769 Copley painted Isaac Royall Jr., the rich man from Medford, and his wife. In 1774 Copley left America for England. He painted *Watson and the Shark* there in 1778, and he died in London on September 9, 1815.

The Pennsylvania painter Benjamin West settled in England in 1763 and became the king's official painter of history scenes. West was known for helping young American painters who came to London to learn.

Patience Wright, born Patience Lovell in 1725, made portraits by shaping wax. Britannica gives her birthplace as Bordentown, New Jersey. The American Battlefield Trust says she was born at Oyster Bay, on Long Island in New York, and that her family moved to Bordentown when she was four. She took her wax figures around on tour to show them. In February 1772 she sailed to England. In London she showed wax figures of actors, politicians and nobles. She died in London on March 23, 1786.

<a id="story-charles-willson-peale"></a>

#### Charles Willson Peale

> **Who:** A painter of the leaders of the Revolution, who opened a museum in Philadelphia. He was paid for portraits with two enslaved people.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Chester, Maryland, in April 1741. Worked in Annapolis, then Philadelphia. Died in 1827.

George Washington sat for Charles Willson Peale seven times during his life, so that Peale could paint him. He first trained to make saddles. Then he became interested in art and studied painting in England for three years. Back in Annapolis, Maryland, he joined the Sons of Liberty. The Sons of Liberty were groups of colonists who formed in 1765 to resist a British tax on printed paper, called the Stamp Act.

On May 18, 1772, Peale came to Washington's home at Mount Vernon and stayed two weeks. He painted small portraits of Martha Washington and her children. He also painted George Washington in oil, in the uniform of the Virginia militia.

In 1784 Peale announced a show of 44 portraits of leaders of the Revolution in his home in Philadelphia. Visitors paid to get in. Peale called it the Philadelphia Museum. One account dates the opening of his museum to 1786 instead. Washington paid a yearly fee to support it and gave it two golden pheasants from China. In 1795 Peale's museum was the site of the Columbianum, the first show in America put on by a society of artists.

After Peale died, his family sold the museum's collection of things from nature in 1849. They sold its portraits at auction in 1854.

By 1776 a Maryland plantation owner had given Peale two enslaved people as payment for portraits. Their names were Scarborough and Lucy. The account of this payment does not give the planter's name. Peale freed Scarborough and Lucy in 1786.

Their son, Moses Williams, was born in about 1777. In 1780 Pennsylvania lawmakers passed a law to end slavery slowly, over many years. Under that law Moses Williams was not free. Peale kept him enslaved in his household until about 1802, when Moses was about 25 or 27. Peale trained him for work in the museum: cutting silhouettes, which are outline portraits cut from paper, preserving dead animals for display and building exhibits.

<a id="story-prince-demah"></a>

#### Prince Demah

> **Who:** An enslaved portrait painter in Boston, who later lived free and served as a soldier in the Massachusetts militia.
>
> **When and where:** Baptized in Boston in May 1745. Worked in Boston and London from 1769 to 1778. Died in Boston in March 1778.

Prince Demah painted portraits in Boston while he was enslaved. One of his signed paintings belongs today to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. He and his mother, Daphney, were baptized at Trinity Church in Boston in May 1745.

Henry Barnes was a merchant in Marlborough, Massachusetts. His family already held Daphney in slavery. In 1769 Barnes bought her son, Prince, who was then in his late twenties. Barnes's wife, Christian, wrote to a friend that they planned on "improving his genius in painting." Genius here meant talent. She also wrote that the Boston painter John Singleton Copley would not be willing to teach him.

In October 1770 Barnes took Prince to London. A painter named Pine gave him lessons there. He was probably Robert Edge Pine. Barnes was afraid that Prince would "attempt his freedom," which meant try to escape. He wrote, "I do not let [Prince] converse with any of his own colour here." He meant that he kept Prince from talking with other Black people in London.

In 1773, back in Boston, an advertisement ran at least nine times in the *Boston News-Letter*. It offered the work of a "Negro Artist" who "takes Faces at the lowest Rates." Negro was a word people of that time used for Black people. Taking faces meant painting portraits. That February, Prince painted William Duguid, a Scottish cloth merchant living in Boston. He signed it "Prince Demah Barnes." He also painted, or copied from Copley, portraits of Henry and Christian Barnes.

The Barnes family sided with the king. In late 1775 they left for England, and they left Daphney behind at their Marlborough home. In April 1777 Prince joined a unit of cannon soldiers in the Massachusetts militia under the name Prince Demah. The records do not say how he became free. On March 11, 1778, he wrote his will as "Prince Demah, limner," a painter of portraits, and as a "free Negro." He left everything he had to his mother. He died one week later. The record does not give the cause.

<a id="story-phillis-wheatley"></a>

#### Phillis Wheatley

> **Who:** A poet, the first African American to publish a book of poems. She was enslaved in Boston when the book was printed.
>
> **When and where:** Kidnapped in West Africa as a child and landed in Boston in 1761, at seven or eight years old. Her book was printed in London in 1773. She died in Boston in 1784, at about 31.

Phillis Wheatley wrote the first book of poems by an African American. It came out in London in September 1773, while she was enslaved in Boston. The title page describes her as "Negro Servant to Mr. John Wheatley, of Boston." Servant there stood for enslaved.

She was kidnapped in West Africa as a child. In 1761, when she was seven or eight, she landed in Boston on a slave ship named the *Phillis*. Her first name came from the ship. John Wheatley's letter in her book says only that she "was brought from Africa to America," and it does not name the men who kidnapped her. In Boston, John Wheatley bought her. He wrote that she learned English in sixteen months, taught at home and not in any school. In 1770, when she was about seventeen, a Boston printer named Ezekiel Russell printed her poem on the death of George Whitefield, a preacher who had toured the colonies.

The publisher of her book expected readers to doubt that an enslaved African girl could write poems. So he printed a statement at the front of the book, signed by 18 men of Boston. Among them were Governor Thomas Hutchinson, John Hancock, the Reverend John Moorhead and John Wheatley, listed as "her Master." The men wrote that the poems were "written by PHILLIS, a young Negro Girl, who was but a few Years since, brought an uncultivated Barbarian from Africa, and has ever since been, and now is, under the Disadvantage of serving as a Slave." Uncultivated meant untaught. Barbarian was an insult for a person thought to be wild and without learning. They wrote that she "has been examined by some of the best Judges, and is thought qualified to write them."

One poem in the book is called "To S. M. a young African Painter, on seeing his Works." The Wheatleys freed her by November 1773, soon after the book appeared. In 1778 she married John Peters. She died poor in 1784, at about 31.

#### Two more Black painters, Scipio Moorhead and Joshua Johnson

Scipio Moorhead was an enslaved Black painter in Boston. The scholars Kwame Anthony Appiah and Henry Louis Gates Jr. write that Wheatley's poem to "S. M." may describe two of his paintings. He was held in slavery by the Reverend John Moorhead of Boston, one of the 18 men who signed the statement in Wheatley's book. Sarah Moorhead probably gave Scipio lessons. Appiah and Gates also write that the engraved portrait of Wheatley at the front of her book was based on his painting of her. No signed painting by Scipio Moorhead survives.

Joshua Johnson was born enslaved in Maryland in 1763. His father was a white man named George Johnson. His mother was a woman held in slavery by William Wheeler Sr. Her name was not written down. In 1782 George Johnson bought his 19-year-old son for £25. He sent him to learn the trade of a blacksmith and signed a manumission, a legal paper that freed him. By 1796 Joshua Johnson was listed in Baltimore as a portrait painter. In a 1798 newspaper advertisement, he called himself a "self-taught genius." He wrote that he had faced "many insuperable obstacles," which means problems he could not get past. Amelia Peck of the Metropolitan Museum of Art and Paula M. Bagger write that before Prince Demah's work was found, Johnson was thought to be the earliest African American painter of portraits in oil paint.

#### Mercy Otis Warren's plays

Mercy Otis Warren wrote plays that made fun of the British governor of Massachusetts and attacked his policies. She was born in Barnstable, Massachusetts, on September 14, 1728. The first, *The Adulateur*, came out in a newspaper, the *Massachusetts Spy*, in 1772. Others followed, among them *Defeat* in 1773, *The Group* in 1775, *The Blockheads* in 1776 and *The Motley Assembly* in 1779. All of them came out without her name. The National Women's History Museum says she likely did this to avoid punishment, and so that readers would take the work of a woman seriously. She died in 1814.

<a id="story-gilbert-stuart"></a>

#### Gilbert Stuart

> **Who:** A portrait painter whose unfinished picture of George Washington is the model for the face on the one-dollar bill.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Kingstown, Rhode Island, on December 3, 1755. Worked in London and Dublin, then in the United States from 1793. Died in 1828.

The picture of George Washington on the one-dollar bill is an engraving based on a portrait by Gilbert Stuart. Stuart was born in Kingstown, Rhode Island, on December 3, 1755. In 1775 he sailed to London. There Benjamin West hired him and gave him a studio and a place to live.

In 1787 Stuart left London for Dublin to get away from the people he owed money. He arrived in New York in May 1793.

In 1796 Martha Washington ordered portraits of her husband and herself from Stuart. He painted only Washington's head and neck on a brown background, left the rest of the canvas unfinished and kept it. He never gave it to her, although she asked for it again and again after her husband died in 1799. Stuart used the unfinished head as a model and painted more than a hundred copies of it, 130 by one count. He sold them for $100 each. An engraving of the head, flipped left to right, is on the one-dollar bill.

In 1831 the trustees of the Boston Athenaeum, a library in Boston, bought the original for $1,500. The painting has been called the Athenaeum portrait ever since. Since 1980 the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston and the National Portrait Gallery in Washington have owned it together.

### 1800 to 1850

From about 1825, a group of American painters known as the Hudson River School made landscapes, pictures of the land and sky. Buyers in the cities paid for pictures of the Hudson River valley and the Catskill Mountains. In the same years, federal officials, the officials of the national government, forced Native nations off their land. The painter George Catlin travelled west and painted the people of about fifty nations. Enslaved artists worked too. In South Carolina an enslaved potter named Dave cut his own verses into his jars, starting in 1834, and later signed them "Dave." That was the year the state's lawmakers made it a crime for enslaved people to learn to read and write. News of photography reached the United States in 1839. By the early 1850s, a small photograph in New York cost as little as 25 cents.

#### Black artists in Philadelphia and Baltimore

Moses Williams was born in about 1777, enslaved in the household of the painter Charles Willson Peale. A Maryland planter had given his parents, Scarborough and Lucy, to Peale as payment for portraits. Peale held Moses until about 1802. Then Williams cut silhouettes at Peale's museum in Philadelphia. A silhouette is a portrait that shows only the outline of a face from the side. Williams used a machine called a physiognotrace. It traced the outline of the face of the person being pictured onto paper, through a set of connected rods. Peale's own children learned painting from their father. Karl Cole's account of Williams's life for Davis Art says Williams was not given the chance to paint. The Philadelphia Museum of Art holds silhouettes he cut of the Peale family between 1803 and 1805.

Joshua Johnson was born into slavery in Maryland in 1763. In 1782 his white father, George Johnson, bought him and freed him. From 1796 to 1824 the Baltimore city directories, books that listed the town's people and their trades, listed him as a portrait painter.

In 1805 Peale, the sculptor William Rush and other artists and business leaders founded the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts in Philadelphia. The academy's leaders very seldom let Black students in. Robert Douglass Jr., a Black painter of Philadelphia who lived from 1809 to 1887, was one of the few. He trained at the academy and studied under the painter Thomas Sully. In 1834 he painted the portraits of William Lloyd Garrison and James Forten, two men who worked to end slavery. An article by the Library Company of Philadelphia describes him as Philadelphia's first African American photographer.

In 1844 the academy's leaders gave women artists the room of statues to draw in, on three mornings a week. In 1860 they let women take classes on the body's bones and muscles and draw from copies of ancient statues. In life classes, students draw from a model without clothes. The leaders opened life classes to women in 1868, with women as the models. Men became the models for these classes in 1874.

#### Painters on the road

Many portrait painters of these years had taught themselves. They travelled from town to town and charged somewhat less than painters with training. A story told later says these painters painted bodies ahead of time and added the customer's face when they arrived. The unfinished portraits that survive show the opposite. They have the face done and the body not yet painted, so the painters began with the head.

Ammi Phillips travelled and painted portraits in Connecticut, Massachusetts and New York from the middle of the 1810s until the early 1860s. He was born in Colebrook, Connecticut, on April 24, 1788. For years nobody knew who had painted many of his pictures, and collectors called the unknown painter the "Border Limner." Limner is an old word for a painter of portraits. The collectors Barbara and Larry Holdridge matched those paintings to Phillips. In the mid-1830s, in Dutchess County, New York, he painted *Girl in Red Dress with Cat and Dog*. In 1985 it was bought for the American Folk Art Museum for one million dollars. Phillips died on July 11, 1865.

Edward Hicks, born in Pennsylvania on April 4, 1780, became an apprentice to coach makers at 13. An apprentice is a young worker who learns a trade by working for masters of it. From 1812 he was a minister of the Quakers, a Christian group. He painted 62 versions of *The Peaceable Kingdom*, based on a passage in the book of Isaiah in the Bible. Many versions show William Penn meeting Native people. They stand for the Lenape, on whose land Penn founded his colony. In his own lifetime, Hicks was better known as a minister than as a painter. He died on August 23, 1849.

<a id="story-joseph-whiting-stock"></a>

#### Joseph Whiting Stock

> **Who:** A travelling portrait painter who could not walk. He kept a journal of the paintings he made and what he was paid for them.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Springfield, Massachusetts, on January 30, 1815. Painted in Massachusetts, Rhode Island and New York from 1832. Died in 1855, at the age of forty.

Joseph Whiting Stock painted more than 900 pictures, although he could not walk. He was the third of twelve children in a Springfield, Massachusetts, family. When he was eleven, an oxcart turned over and fell on him. He was paralyzed from the waist down, which means he could not move or feel his legs. He could not leave his bed until he was nineteen.

A doctor suggested that he take up art. He began lessons at seventeen, and his teacher was a painter named Franklin White. He tried a portrait of his sister Eliza. "I attempted my sister Eliza's portrait and made so good a likeness as to induce my friends to encourage me by their patronage," he wrote in his journal. Patronage meant paying him for pictures.

In 1834 a doctor named James Swan hired Stock to make drawings of the human body. Swan also built him a wheelchair. With it, Stock could paint large pictures and be lifted onto trains to travel for work. His first painting trip was a month in Wilbraham, Massachusetts, in 1836. He later spent two years in Warren, Rhode Island, and New Bedford, Massachusetts, and several years in Orange County, New York. He lived with local families while he worked, and sometimes he paid for his room and meals with paintings.

His journal lists more than 900 paintings and what he was paid for them. About a hundred of those paintings are known today. He died of tuberculosis, a disease of the lungs, in 1855, at forty. The Springfield Museums hold his journal.

#### Writers

Mercy Otis Warren, who had written plays against the British governor of Massachusetts in the 1770s, published her history of the American Revolution in three volumes in 1805. Washington Irving set his 1819 story "Rip Van Winkle" in the Catskill Mountains of New York, the same mountains the Hudson River School painted a few years later.

James Fenimore Cooper's novel *The Last of the Mohicans* came out in Philadelphia on February 4, 1826. The Mohican people named in its title were living in New York and Wisconsin that year. Agents from New York and officials of the War Department were making treaties, written agreements between governments, under which the Mohican, by then called the Stockbridge, and the Munsee had to move from New York to Wisconsin.

Ralph Waldo Emerson's long essay *Nature* appeared in 1836. Edgar Allan Poe's poem "The Raven" was first printed in a New York newspaper, the *Evening Mirror*, on January 29, 1845. Other papers printed it at least ten more times in the next few weeks.

#### The Hudson River School, and whose land it painted

The Hudson River School was a group of American landscape painters. They worked from about 1825 to 1870. The name comes from their shared aims more than from one place, but many of them painted the Catskill Mountains west of the Hudson River. Thomas Cole, Thomas Doughty and Asher B. Durand were the first leaders.

In 1826 Cole made his home in the village of Catskill, New York. That land is the homeland of the Muh-he-conneok, the People of the Waters That Are Never Still. Today they are called the Stockbridge-Munsee Band of Mohican Indians. A marker at Cole's house states that they were forced from there.

The Mohican had lost the Hudson valley long before Cole came. Through the 1600s and 1700s, settlers pushed them out. Most moved to Stockbridge, Massachusetts, a mission town, which means a town built around a church where ministers taught Christianity. From 1764 white settlers poured into Stockbridge and took thousands of acres of Mohican land. They squatted on it, which means they settled on it without any right, and they bought it in ways the law did not allow. They also took land to pay off Mohican debts. By 1783 the Mohican had lost all their land in the town. In 1785 a group of them founded New Stockbridge in upstate New York, on land of the Oneida nation.

After an 1822 treaty, Stockbridge people in New York began moving to Wisconsin. By 1831, 225 Stockbridge people and 100 Munsee people had moved there. Agents from New York and commissioners from the War Department arranged the treaties for these moves. From 1832 to 1834, federal officials made them move again, to the east shore of Lake Winnebago. Their reservation, land set aside for them by treaty, is in northeastern Wisconsin today.

While Cole was selling paintings of the Catskills, federal officials were moving Native nations west. On May 28, 1830, President Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act. Under it, the president could make treaties in which Native nations gave up their lands east of the Mississippi River for lands in the west. In 1838 and 1839, federal officials and soldiers forced more than 16,000 Cherokee people from their homeland to Indian Territory, in what is now Oklahoma. At least 4,000 of them died of cold, hunger and disease along the way, by the usual count, and other counts are higher.

<a id="story-thomas-cole"></a>

#### Thomas Cole

> **Who:** A painter of landscapes and one of the first leaders of the Hudson River School.
>
> **When and where:** Born February 1, 1801, in Bolton-le-Moors, Lancashire, England. Came to America in 1818. Lived in Catskill, New York, from 1826. Died there on February 11, 1848.

Thomas Cole was one of the first leaders of the Hudson River School. He was born in England in 1801 and came to America with his family in 1818. They lived first in Philadelphia and then in Steubenville, Ohio. A travelling portrait painter named Stein gave him lessons. Then he studied for two years at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts.

In 1825 Cole put some landscapes in the window of a shop in New York City. The painters John Trumbull and Asher B. Durand saw them and bought them. The next year Cole moved to Catskill. He made pencil sketches outdoors. In winter he painted in his studio. He also spent years painting in Europe, mostly in Italy, from 1829 to 1832 and again from 1841 to 1842.

In 1836 he painted *The Oxbow*, a view from Mount Holyoke, near Northampton, Massachusetts. It shows the valley of the Connecticut River, not the Hudson, and Cole joined two views from the mountain into one picture. On the far hill, the bare strips where trees were cut seem to spell the Hebrew letters for "Noah." The art historian Matthew Baigell was the first to notice them. Cole made the painting for a show in New York in April 1836. His patron, Luman Reed, had suggested it. A patron is a person who pays an artist to make work. In March 1836 Cole wrote to Reed, "Fancy pictures seldom sell & they generally take more time than views so I have determined to paint one of the latter." By "fancy pictures" he meant pictures from his imagination, and by "views" he meant real places. That same year, 1836, he finished *The Course of Empire*, a set of five paintings. The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York has owned *The Oxbow* since 1908.

Cole died in Catskill on February 11, 1848. Durand painted a picture called *Kindred Spirits* in his memory. Cole's house and studio in Catskill are now the Thomas Cole National Historic Site.

#### George Catlin and the people he painted

George Catlin was a lawyer who became a painter. He lived from 1796 to 1872. In 1830 he went to St. Louis to meet William Clark, the federal official in charge of Indian affairs there. From St. Louis, Catlin made five trips west between 1830 and 1836. In 1832 he travelled more than 2,000 miles up the Missouri River. He wrote, "If my life be spared, nothing shall stop me from visiting every nation of Indians on the Continent of North America." By one count he visited 48 nations, and by another, fifty.

In 1832, at a Mandan village in what is now North Dakota, Catlin painted Four Bears, a Mandan leader. His Mandan name was Máh-to-tóh-pa. Catlin called him "the first and most popular man in the nation." Four Bears was a painter too. He painted his own battles on buffalo robes. Catlin got one of those robes in 1832, and it is now at the Smithsonian. A German prince, Maximilian of Wied, travelled up the Missouri with the painter Karl Bodmer in 1833 and 1834. He took another Four Bears robe to Germany. It is in the Linden Museum in Stuttgart.

Catlin sometimes got objects from the people he painted, as proof that his pictures were accurate. One was a Sioux cradle. In 1836 he went to the place in southwestern Minnesota where people dug red stone for pipes. Sioux elders protested strongly, and he went anyway.

Smallpox was a disease caused by a virus. It spread when people were close together, face to face. It caused a fever and a rash that turned into scabs, and about 3 of every 10 people who caught it died. On May 5, 1832, President Jackson signed the Indian Vaccination Act, a law to give Native people vaccinations, shots that protect a person from smallpox. Secretary of War Lewis Cass ran the program through federal Indian agents. The Mandan, the Hidatsa and the Arikara of the upper Missouri were kept out of it. The records do not name the officials who left them out.

On June 18, 1837, the American Fur Company's steamboat *St. Peters* reached Fort Clark, next to the Mandan villages. The fort's trader, Francis Chardon, learned from the captain, Bernard Pratte Jr., that people on board had smallpox. The crew unloaded goods and loaded furs in less than a day, and the boat went on up the river. The boat had brought smallpox to the Mandan villages. About 2,000 Mandan lived there that spring. Smallpox killed most of them, and by October 138 were alive.

Four Bears caught smallpox and died on July 30, 1837. Chardon wrote down Four Bears's last speech: "I have loved the Whites ... and how have they repaid it! With ingratitude!" Ingratitude means not being thankful.

The Seminole leader Osceola sat for Catlin in January 1838 as a dying prisoner. On October 21, 1837, near St. Augustine, Florida, General Thomas Jesup had ordered soldiers to seize Osceola while he was under a white flag of truce. A white flag of truce is a sign that the two sides have stopped fighting to talk. Osceola was held at Fort Marion in St. Augustine and then at Fort Moultrie in South Carolina. There he was very sick with malaria, a disease spread by mosquitoes that brings fever and chills, and with other illnesses. Three painters, Catlin, W. M. Laning and Robert John Curtis, talked him into letting them paint him anyway. Osceola died a prisoner on January 30, 1838. The army doctor, Frederick Weedon, cut off his head and then buried the body. Weedon kept the head and showed it in his drugstore.

On September 23, 1837, Catlin opened his paintings to the public at Clinton Hall in New York, at 50 cents a visit. He called the show his Indian Gallery. He tried to sell it to the United States government, and members of Congress did not buy it. In November 1839 he sailed for England with the gallery, a tepee of buffalo hide and two live bears. He showed the gallery in London, Brussels and Paris. Groups of Native people who were touring Europe with promoters joined him there, 21 Ojibwe and 14 Iowa. Catlin talked them into acting out hunts, dances and even scalpings for the crowds. Scalping means cutting the skin and hair from the top of an enemy's head. In Paris in 1845, the Ojibwe group caught smallpox. Two of them died. The account that records their deaths does not name them.

In 1852 Catlin ran out of money and was put in a London prison for debt. Members of Congress still would not buy the gallery, even after he lowered his price from $65,000 to $25,000. Joseph Harrison, a Pennsylvania railroad owner, paid Catlin's debts and got the gallery for $20,000. He stored it in his boiler factory in Philadelphia. In 1879 Harrison's widow gave the paintings to the Smithsonian.

#### Audubon's birds, and the people he sold

John James Audubon's *The Birds of America* was printed in England from 1827 to 1838. It has 435 pictures of birds, each bird shown at its real size. The historian Gregory Nobles records that the Audubons held nine enslaved people in their household in Henderson, Kentucky, in the 1810s. By the end of that decade, short of money, they sold them. In early 1819 Audubon took two enslaved men down the Mississippi River to New Orleans on a small boat, and there he offered the boat and the two men for sale. The family bought more enslaved people in the 1820s and sold them in 1830, when Audubon moved to England to oversee the printing of the birds. In 1834 Audubon wrote to his wife about the freeing of the enslaved people in Britain's colonies in the West Indies, the islands of the Caribbean. He wrote that the British government had "acted imprudently and too precipitously," which means without enough care and too fast. The surviving record counts the people Audubon held and sold. It does not give their names.

<a id="story-dave-drake"></a>

#### Dave (David Drake)

> **Who:** An enslaved potter and poet who cut his name and his own verses into large jars of hard-fired clay.
>
> **When and where:** Born about 1800 in South Carolina. Worked in the potteries of the Edgefield District from about 1818 to 1864. Listed in the 1870 census as "David Drake, Turner." Believed to have died in the 1870s.

Dave was an enslaved potter who wrote his own verses on the jars he made. He is the only Black potter in Edgefield before the Civil War known to have signed his own work. He was born into slavery around 1800. In the Edgefield District of South Carolina, white factory owners made their potteries grow by using the unpaid work of enslaved men, women and children. At least 76 enslaved people worked at the district's 12 potteries.

The first record of Dave is dated June 13, 1818. It describes "a boy about 17 years old country born," which meant born in America and not brought from Africa. His enslaver, Harvey Drake, mortgaged him to a man named Eldrid Simkins. That meant Drake used Dave to guarantee a loan: if Drake did not pay the money back, Simkins could take Dave. At least four men held Dave in slavery during his life. After Harvey Drake died in 1832, his brother Reuben Drake held him until 1835. Then the Reverend John Landrum held him. When Landrum died in 1846, all 18 of the people he enslaved were put up for sale. The records do not name who sold them. Franklin Landrum held Dave for a time. In 1849 Lewis Miles, who owned the Stony Bluff pottery, bought him.

In 1834 South Carolina's lawmakers made it a crime for enslaved people to learn to read and write. That same year, Dave cut words into a jar: "put every bit all between / surely this jar will hold 14." How he learned to read is not known for sure. He may have learned while he worked at a newspaper, the *Edgefield Hive*, printed by Harvey Drake's business partner Abner Landrum. On July 31, 1840, he wrote on a jar: "Dave belongs to Mr. Miles / wher the oven bakes and the pot biles." So by his own words, Lewis Miles held him in 1840, nine years before the 1849 sale. Accounts of his life do not agree on when Miles first held him or how.

Dave shaped the bottom of each jar on a potter's wheel. Then he built up the top by hand with thick coils of clay. Two of his jars at the Charleston Museum each hold more than 40 gallons.

His family was sold away from him. The records do not say who sold them or where they were taken. One of his legs was amputated, which means it was cut off. How he lost it is not known. One account says an enslaver beat him for writing. Another says he was hurt in a train accident. Neither account has been proved.

He wrote three verses on his pots in 1857, eight in 1858 and seven in 1859. On August 16, 1857, he wrote: "I wonder where is all my relation / Friendship to all, and every nation." In 1862 he wrote: "I made this Jar all of cross, If you dont repent, you will be, lost."

A 2006 survey by Arthur F. Goldberg and James Witkowski counted 169 pots made by Dave or credited to him. More than a hundred, dated from 1849 to 1864, are signed "Dave." His verses and marks appear on 50 of them. Sometimes he added the names of other enslaved potters beside his own: Mark, Abram and Baddler. His last dated pot is from 1864. Dave was free by the end of the Civil War in 1865. The Smithsonian American Art Museum credits his freedom to the Emancipation Proclamation, President Abraham Lincoln's order freeing enslaved people in the states at war with the United States. He took the last name Drake, probably from Harvey Drake, the first man who had held him. The census of 1870, the government's count of everyone in the country, lists him as "David Drake," and his work as "turner," a person who shapes pots on a wheel. His name is not in the census of 1880. He is believed to have died in the 1870s.

#### Photography arrives, 1839

In France, the artist Louis Daguerre worked out a way of making pictures with light. News of his process reached the United States in late August and September 1839. In October or November 1839, Robert Cornelius of Philadelphia took a picture of himself. It is the oldest American portrait photograph that survives.

These first photographs are called daguerreotypes. Each one was made directly on a copper plate coated with silver. It was a single picture, and it could not be copied.

A history of New York's photographers, published by the Bard Graduate Center, says the first American studio that sold portrait photographs opened in New York in 1840. By 1850 New York had 71 daguerreotype studios. By 1853 it had more of them than all of England. Mathew Brady opened his first studio at 205 Broadway in 1844. Cheaper studios on Broadway and on the Bowery made portraits for working people. In the early 1850s, a very small daguerreotype, about 1 5/8 inches by 1 3/8 inches, cost 25 cents. A cheap portrait from a "picture factory," a shop that turned out many portraits fast, cost 50 cents. A medium-sized portrait at Brady's studio cost $2.

<a id="story-frederick-douglass-art"></a>

#### Frederick Douglass

> **Who:** A writer and speaker who escaped slavery. He wrote the story of his own life and sat for 160 known photographs.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Talbot County, Maryland, in February 1818. Escaped slavery on September 3, 1838. Lived in Massachusetts, then Rochester, New York, then Washington. Died in 1895.
>
> **Movie:** *Becoming Frederick Douglass* (2022), a documentary by Stanley Nelson, shown on PBS. It is about his life.

By the count of the historians John Stauffer, Zoe Trodd and Celeste-Marie Bernier, Frederick Douglass sat for more photographs than any other American of the 1800s. He was born into slavery in Talbot County, Maryland, in February 1818. On September 3, 1838, he escaped by train through Baltimore, dressed in a sailor's clothes. Anna Murray, a free Black woman, helped him, and he married her.

On May 1, 1845, his book came out from the Anti-Slavery Office in Boston. It was called *Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave. Written by Himself*. By one count it sold 4,500 copies in four months. By another count it sold 5,000. By 1860 almost 30,000 copies had sold.

In 1849 Douglass wrote about pictures of Black people drawn by white artists. He wrote that "negroes can never have impartial portraits at the hands of white artists." Negroes was a word of that time for Black people, and impartial means fair. "It seems to us next to impossible for white men to take likenesses of black men, without most grossly exaggerating their distinctive features," he wrote.

Douglass sat for photographs again and again. The historians John Stauffer, Zoe Trodd and Celeste-Marie Bernier counted 160 photographs of him. They counted 126 of Abraham Lincoln. Douglass said that "the great cheapness and universality of pictures must exert a powerful, though silent, influence upon the ideas and sentiment of present and future generations." Universality means that pictures were everywhere.

### 1850 to 1900

Photographers of the second half of the 1800s showed Americans the bodies of soldiers killed in the Civil War, and the valleys and mountains of the far West. Books got cheap: the first ten-cent novel of 1860 sold more than 65,000 copies in a few months. *Uncle Tom's Cabin* sold 300,000 copies in the United States in its first year. Several Black artists of these years did their work far from home. The sculptor Edmonia Lewis said she was "practically driven to Rome" by prejudice against her color, and the painter Henry Ossawa Tanner made his career in Paris. At an army fort in Florida, Plains men held as prisoners without trial drew their lives in account books. In New York, the Metropolitan Museum of Art opened in 1872.

#### Writers and cheap books

Nathaniel Hawthorne's novel *The Scarlet Letter* came out on March 16, 1850. Harriet Beecher Stowe's novel *Uncle Tom's Cabin* ran in parts in *The National Era*, a newspaper against slavery, from 1851. In 1852 it came out as a book in two volumes. It sold 10,000 copies in the United States in its first week and 300,000 in its first year. In Britain it sold 1.5 million copies in one year.

Herman Melville's *Moby-Dick* came out in London on October 18, 1851, in 500 copies. It came out in New York on November 14, 1851, in a first printing of 2,915 copies. On July 4, 1855, Walt Whitman paid to print his own book of poems, *Leaves of Grass*. The first edition held twelve poems. Whitman kept adding to it and changing it until he died in 1892.

In 1860 the brothers Erastus and Irwin Beadle began selling novels of about 100 pages for ten cents each. People called them dime novels, because a dime is ten cents. The first was Ann S. Stephens's *Malaeska, the Indian Wife of the White Hunter*, dated June 9, 1860. It sold more than 65,000 copies in its first few months. The Beadles printed 321 of these books in the series.

#### Robert S. Duncanson in Cincinnati

Robert S. Duncanson was a free Black painter who had taught himself to paint. He was born in about 1821 in Fayette, New York, the son of a free Black tradesman. In 1840 he moved to Cincinnati, Ohio, where about 3,000 Black people lived. In about 1850 or 1851, Nicholas Longworth hired him to paint eight landscapes on the walls of the entrance hall of his house, Belmont. Each is about nine feet high. The house is now the Taft Museum of Art. In 1853 Duncanson painted *Uncle Tom and Little Eva*, from Stowe's novel. It is at the Detroit Institute of Arts. During the Civil War he left the United States. He showed his work in Montreal, Canada, in 1864 and in Dublin, Ireland, in 1865. He died in Detroit on December 21, 1872.

#### Photographs of the Civil War dead

Alexander Gardner, born in Paisley, Scotland, in 1821, worked for the New York photographer Mathew Brady from 1856. In 1858 Brady put him in charge of his studio in Washington. In September 1862 Gardner and his team photographed the dead soldiers on the battlefield at Antietam, in Maryland. The American Battlefield Trust estimates that 22,717 soldiers were killed, wounded or missing in that battle.

In October 1862 Brady showed the photographs at his gallery in New York, under a sign that read "The Dead of Antietam." On October 20, 1862, a writer for *The New York Times* reported that crowds of people kept climbing the stairs to see them. "If he has not brought bodies and laid them in our door-yards and along the streets, he has done something very like it," the writer said. Door-yards are the yards in front of houses. The article gave Brady the credit.

Brady put the words "Photographed by Brady" on pictures his employees took. In about November 1862 Gardner stopped working for Brady, probably in part because of this. In May 1863 Gardner and his brother James opened their own studio in Washington and hired many of Brady's former workers. In 1866 Gardner published a book of 100 of the war's photographs in two volumes. Under each picture he printed the name of the man who took it, among them Timothy H. O'Sullivan and James F. Gibson. The book did not sell well.

On July 6, 1863, after the Battle of Gettysburg, Gardner's team photographed a dead soldier among the rocks at a place called Devil's Den. Gardner later called him a Confederate, a soldier of the Southern states that fought the United States to keep slavery. He titled the picture *Home of a Rebel Sharpshooter*. A sharpshooter is a soldier who shoots at a distance with a rifle. In 1975 the historian William A. Frassanito showed that the same body appears in six photographs. The photographers had carried the body from the south edge of Devil's Den to a stone wall, and the rifle beside it was probably put there for the picture. In 1998 the artist James Groves argued that the body was carried the other way, out of the wall and to the first spot. Both men agree that the photographers moved the body. The soldier's name is not known.

<a id="story-winslow-homer"></a>

#### Winslow Homer

> **Who:** A painter who drew the Civil War for a magazine and later painted the sea.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Boston on February 24, 1836. Drew the Civil War for *Harper's Weekly*. Lived in England from 1881 and in Prouts Neck, Maine, from 1883. Died there on September 29, 1910.

Winslow Homer drew the Civil War at the front for *Harper's Weekly*, a magazine. He drew everyday life in the soldiers' camps. He was born in Boston on February 24, 1836. He began as an apprentice at a lithography company. Lithography is a way of printing pictures from drawings made on stone. Then he drew pictures for magazines, among them *Ballou's Pictorial* and *Harper's Weekly*.

He began painting in watercolor in 1873. In 1881 he went to live in Cullercoats, a town in England. In 1883 he moved to Prouts Neck, on the coast of Maine, and the sea became his main subject. He painted people at sea, in pictures such as *The Life Line* and *Fog Warning*. He died at Prouts Neck on September 29, 1910.

<a id="story-edmonia-lewis"></a>

#### Edmonia Lewis

> **Who:** A sculptor of Mississauga Ojibwe and African American descent, who carved in marble in Rome.
>
> **When and where:** Born about July 4, 1844, in Greenbush, New York. Oberlin, Ohio, from 1859. Boston. Rome from 1865 or 1866. Died in London on September 17, 1907.

Edmonia Lewis carved statues in marble in Rome. Before that, at college in Ohio, a group of white men beat her, officials charged her with poisoning two classmates, and college officials kept her from graduating. She was born in Greenbush, New York, in about 1844. On official papers she gave her birth year as 1842, 1844 and 1854 at different times. Her mother, Catherine Mike Lewis, was of Mississauga Ojibwe and African American descent. Edmonia's name at birth was Wildfire. By the age of nine she had lost both parents. As a girl she and her aunts sold Ojibwe baskets, moccasins and embroidered blouses to tourists at Niagara Falls. Her brother Samuel paid for her schooling with money he made in the gold rush.

From 1859 she studied at Oberlin, in Ohio. In the winter of 1862, she gave spiced wine to two white students she lived with, Maria Miles and Christina Ennes, before a sleigh ride. They fell sick. Doctors said they had been poisoned with cantharides, a poison made from blister beetles. Both young women got well.

One night soon after, Lewis was walking home alone. A group of white men dragged her into an open field, beat her badly and left her for dead. The men who did it were never identified. A few days later, officials arrested her for poisoning the two students. She was hurt so badly she could not walk, so her trial was put off. John Mercer Langston, the first Black lawyer in Ohio, defended her. The court dropped the charges, because no one had tested what was in the young women's stomachs, so there was no proof of poison.

About a year later she was accused of stealing art supplies. The record does not name who accused her. That case was dropped too. But Oberlin officials did not let her sign up for her last term, so she could not graduate. In 2022, more than a hundred years after her death, the leaders of Oberlin College gave her a degree.

She went to Boston and made a bust of Colonel Robert Gould Shaw. A bust is a sculpture of a person's head and shoulders. Shaw had led the 54th Massachusetts, a regiment of Black soldiers, in the Civil War. Lewis sold 100 plaster copies of the bust for $15 each, and the money paid her way to Rome. Her passport of 1865 says she was "sent by subscription to Italy having displayed great talents as a sculptor." Sent by subscription means that a group of people paid for the trip. In Rome she carved her work in marble.

In 1878 she told *The New York Times*: "I was practically driven to Rome in order to obtain the opportunities for art culture, and to find a social atmosphere where I was not constantly reminded of my color. The land of liberty had no room for a colored sculptor." Colored was a word of that time for Black people.

Her marble statue *The Death of Cleopatra* was shown at the Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia in 1876. In 1878 the critic William J. Clark called the way it showed death "ghastly" and "absolutely repellant," which means disgusting. Later a gambler named "Blind John" Condon bought it from a saloon in Chicago. He used it to mark the grave of a racehorse named Cleopatra. The Smithsonian American Art Museum's record of the statue states that it was thought lost for almost a century. It was later moved to a construction yard in Cicero, Illinois. The scholars Marilyn Richardson and Dorothy Porter Wesley told a Smithsonian curator, George Gurney, about it. In 1994 the Historical Society of Forest Park, Illinois, gave it to the Smithsonian American Art Museum. Lewis died in London on September 17, 1907.

#### Pictures of the West, and whose land they showed

In July 1861 Carleton Watkins carried a very large camera into Yosemite Valley, in California. It took pictures on glass plates 18 inches by 22 inches. He came back with 30 of these large plates and 100 smaller negatives. His photographs were shown at a gallery in New York in 1862. They helped persuade members of Congress to protect the valley. On June 30, 1864, President Abraham Lincoln signed the Yosemite Grant.

Yosemite Valley was the home of the Ahwahneechee people. In 1851 California's governor, John McDougal, raised a force of about 200 armed volunteers on horseback, called the Mariposa Battalion. Under Major James D. Savage, they invaded the valley in March 1851. According to the National Park Service, the battalion's men burned villages and food supplies, one after another, and forced men, women and children away from their homes. They marched Tenaya, the leader of the Ahwahneechee, and his people to a reservation on the Fresno River. The National Park Service counts that by 1910, more than 90 out of every 100 of the Ahwahneechee who first lived there were dead or missing.

In 1871 the photographer William Henry Jackson and the painter Thomas Moran went to Yellowstone with the Hayden survey, a government expedition. Jackson took the first known photographs of the Yellowstone falls. When President Ulysses S. Grant signed a law on March 1, 1872, Yellowstone became a national park. That year members of Congress paid Moran $10,000 for his painting *The Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone* and hung it in the Capitol.
