On December 6, 2023, officials of the Interior Department announced new rules for NAGPRA, the 1990 law on returning Native remains and sacred objects. The rules took effect on January 12, 2024. A museum must now get the consent of the Native nation, or of the dead person's descendants, before it shows Native human remains or sacred objects. The same consent is needed before staff study them or let others get at them. These remains and objects had been taken from Native graves and lands in earlier years, by men such as the diggers at Mound City in 1846 and at Spiro in the 1930s.

In January 2024 museum leaders closed or covered Native displays. Sean Decatur, president of the American Museum of Natural History in New York, closed its Eastern Woodlands and Great Plains halls on January 27, 2024, and covered seven more cases. He wrote to his staff that the halls came from "an era when museums such as ours did not respect the values, perspectives, and indeed shared humanity of Indigenous peoples." About 500,000 children visit that museum each year on school or camp trips. In October 2023 museum officials had said that about 26 out of every 100 of the 12,000 human remains the museum held were Native American. Staff at the Field Museum in Chicago, the Cleveland Museum of Art and the Metropolitan Museum of Art covered cases or took objects down. Harvard's Peabody Museum closed most of its floors on January 16, 2024, while its staff asked Native leaders which objects to remove. They took down nearly 40. No one has published a count of every museum that did the same.

According to *The Art Newspaper*, from 1990 to early 2024 museums paid less than $60,000 in all in fines for breaking NAGPRA, and those fines came from 20 museums. Kelly Applegate, of the Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe, wrote to the Interior Department that museums had used the law's wording "to not give complete information about the entirety of their collections."

The latest federal count comes from the National Park Service, in a report published on May 29, 2026. Since 1990, museums and federal agencies have reported holding the remains of 222,824 Native people. For 142,389 of them, officials have published a notice naming the nation or the family with the right to them. That notice is a legal step, and it does not mean the person's body has gone home. As of September 30, 2025, the remains of 80,435 people had not yet gone through those legal steps. They were held by 381 museums and 104 federal offices. The report states that each year museums find and report remains they had never listed before. As of September 2026, the 2024 rule was still in force.

Some returns fall outside NAGPRA. On October 29, 2025, the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston gave the descendants of David Drake, the enslaved potter and poet, ownership of two jars he made in 1857. The museum's officials said Drake "was not permitted to possess the jars and did not receive remuneration for them," which means he was not paid. The jars had been sold for the profit of his enslaver, Lewis J. Miles. The family kept one jar and lent it back to the museum. Museum officials bought the other one back from them. On that second jar, called the Poem Jar, Drake wrote: "I made this Jar = for cash / Though its called Lucre trash." Lucre is an old word for money.

<a id="story-jeffrey-gibson"></a>

#### Jeffrey Gibson

> **Who:** A painter and sculptor, a member of the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians and of Cherokee descent.
>
> **When and where:** Born March 31, 1972, in Colorado Springs, Colorado. Grew up in North Carolina, New Jersey, West Germany and South Korea. Lives near Hudson, New York.

In 2024 Jeffrey Gibson was the only artist shown in the United States Pavilion at the Venice Biennale. The Biennale is an international art show held in Venice, Italy, and each country shows its artists in its own building, called a pavilion. According to SITE Santa Fe, one of the show's sponsors, he was the first Native artist to represent the United States there alone. He is a member of the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians and of Cherokee descent. He was born in Colorado Springs, Colorado, on March 31, 1972. His father was a civil engineer for the Defense Department, and the family lived in North Carolina, New Jersey, West Germany and South Korea. Both of his parents had attended boarding schools as children. At the federal boarding schools for Native children, staff had for many years cut the children's hair, taken away their clothes and forbidden them to speak their own languages.

He studied painting at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago and at the Royal College of Art in London. The Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians paid for his study in London. "My chief felt that me going there, being a strong artist, made him stronger," he said, speaking of the chief of the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians. His paintings and sculptures use bright color, detailed patterns and written words. According to the Portland Art Museum, he mixes American, Native and queer history with music and popular culture. Queer is a word many gay and lesbian people use for themselves. He won a MacArthur Fellowship in 2019.

His Venice show ran from April 20 to November 24, 2024. He named it *the space in which to place me*, after a poem by the Oglala Lakota poet Layli Long Soldier. The same sponsor says it was also the first United States pavilion organized by a Native curator, Kathleen Ash-Milby of the Portland Art Museum. A curator is the museum worker who chooses the art for a show and plans it. From September 12, 2025, to June 9, 2026, four large sculptures by Gibson, of a deer, a coyote, a squirrel and a hawk, stood on the front of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. On April 9, 2026, the Obama Foundation said it had asked him to make a wall of 17 round prints for the Obama Presidential Center.

#### Prices, and a picture that is only a file

On May 9, 2022, a buyer paid $195 million at Christie's auction house in New York for Andy Warhol's 1964 portrait of Marilyn Monroe, *Shot Sage Blue Marilyn*. The Associated Press reported that no work by an American artist had ever sold for more at auction. It beat the $110.5 million paid in 2017 for a 1982 painting of a skull by Jean-Michel Basquiat. The money went to a charity for children in Zurich. As of September 2026, no American artist's work had sold for more. In May 2026 a painting by Jackson Pollock, *Number 7A, 1948*, sold for $181.2 million, according to the *Robb Report*.

Georgia O'Keeffe's *Jimson Weed/White Flower No. 1* sold for $44.4 million in 2014. According to the Associated Press, that was the most ever paid at auction for a work by a woman until November 20, 2025, when a painting by the Mexican painter Frida Kahlo sold for $54.7 million.

On March 11, 2021, a digital picture by Mike Winkelmann, who calls himself Beeple, sold at Christie's for more than $69.3 million, according to Al Jazeera. It is a collage of 5,000 pictures he made, one each day, starting on May 1, 2007. The buyer, Vignesh Sundaresan, a programmer based in Singapore, paid in Ether, a kind of digital money. He got a record on a computer network that names him as the owner of the file, and the right to show it. He did not get the copyright, the legal right to copy the work and sell copies. The buyer and the seller both owned shares in digital tokens tied to other Beeple works, and some people called the sale a publicity stunt.

#### Pictures made by computer programs

By the summer of 2022, anyone could type a few words into a website and get a picture back, as NPR reported. In January 2023 Kelly McKernan, Sarah Andersen, Karla Ortiz and other artists sued Stability AI, the company behind the program Stable Diffusion, along with Midjourney and the art website DeviantArt. Accounts give the date as January 12 or January 13. In their lawsuit, the artists say the companies built these programs by feeding them huge collections of pictures gathered from the internet. They say the collection behind Stable Diffusion held more than five billion pictures, copied without asking the people who made them. These are the artists' claims, and no court has yet ruled on whether they are true.

On August 12, 2024, Judge William Orrick in San Francisco let the artists' copyright claims go forward. As of September 2026, the case was still before him, and no trial had been held, according to the court's record of the case.

On November 3, 2018, the computer scientist Stephen Thaler asked the US Copyright Office to register a picture made by his computer program, with the program named as the only author. On August 12, 2019, officials refused, because the picture had no human author. They relied in part on an 1884 Supreme Court case. In that case the justices had called a photograph of the writer Oscar Wilde "an original work of art, the product of plaintiff's intellectual invention." Judges on a federal appeals court agreed with the refusal in 2025. On March 2, 2026, the justices of the Supreme Court declined to hear Thaler's appeal. As the law stood in 2026, according to the National Constitution Center, no one could hold the copyright to a picture made by a program with no human author.

<a id="story-kelly-mckernan"></a>

#### Kelly McKernan

> **Who:** An illustrator and painter, one of three artists who sued the makers of picture-making programs in January 2023.
>
> **When and where:** Born 1986. Nashville, Tennessee.

Kelly McKernan was one of three artists who sued the companies behind picture-making programs in January 2023. McKernan uses the words they and them. They were born in 1986 and live in Nashville, Tennessee, where they teach at the Nossi College of Art and Design. McKernan is a single parent.

In 2002, as a high school student, McKernan joined DeviantArt, a website where artists share their work. For about 20 years they posted paintings there, "not for money," and built a following. In January 2023 McKernan told NPR: "I almost barely make rent most months. I will spend, you know, 30 hours on a painting, and I won't see any money from that until it sells."

People using picture programs had typed the words "in the style of Kelly McKernan" more than 12,000 times. Some people sold the results on websites such as Redbubble, with McKernan's name attached. "There's more and more images with my name attached to it that I can see my hand in, but it's not my work," McKernan said.

On October 30, 2023, Judge William Orrick dismissed most of the claims in the artists' case and allowed them to rewrite them. Cleary Gottlieb, a law firm that represents Midjourney, wrote a report on the ruling. According to that report, he dismissed McKernan's copyright claims because McKernan had not registered those paintings with the Copyright Office. In 2023 *Time* magazine named McKernan to its list of the 100 most influential people in artificial intelligence. By September 2026 McKernan's name was no longer on the list of artists suing.

#### Books

Books for sale carry an identifying number called an ISBN, and in the United States a company called Bowker issues them. By Bowker's figures, reported by the publishing writer Jane Friedman, writers who published their own books got these numbers for 53 percent more new books in 2021 than in 2018. People in the United States spent $2.43 billion on audiobooks in 2025, 9 percent more than in 2024, according to a survey for the Audio Publishers Association.

In the mid-2020s, school and library officials removed or restricted thousands of books. Two groups count this, and their numbers differ because they count different things. PEN America, a group of writers that defends free expression, counts each time school officials remove or restrict a book. It counted 10,046 in the 2023-24 school year and 6,870 in 2024-25. The American Library Association counts attempts it hears about to remove books from school, public and college libraries, listed by title. It counted 4,235 different titles in 2025, and it found that 92 out of every 100 of those attempts were started by "pressure groups, government officials and decision makers."

On June 23, 2018, the board of the Association for Library Service to Children took Laura Ingalls Wilder's name off its award for children's books. The award had carried her name since 1954. The board members wrote that her books include "expressions of stereotypical attitudes inconsistent with ALSC's core values." A stereotype is an unfair, fixed idea about a whole group of people. They acted after critics pointed to how her books show Native and Black people, and after a group that included the American Indian Library Association reviewed the award. In the 1935 book *Little House on the Prairie*, Wilder described one place as somewhere "there were no people. Only Indians lived there." Later printings changed that line. Several characters in the Little House books say that "the only good Indian is a dead Indian." The prize is now called the Children's Literature Legacy Award.

In March 2023 the members of the board of the National Audubon Society voted to keep the name of John James Audubon, who painted *The Birds of America* and who had enslaved people. "The name has come to represent not one person, but a broader love of birds and nature," said the board chair, Susan Bell. Three board members resigned. The leaders of the local Audubon groups in Chicago, Seattle, Portland and Washington, D.C., had already decided to drop the name.

#### Public money and national museums, 2025 and 2026

On May 2, 2025, White House officials sent Congress a budget for 2026 that would have shut down the National Endowment for the Arts. The same day, NEA staff emailed arts groups across the country that their grants were withdrawn or ended because the projects fell outside the President's priorities. On May 5 about a dozen senior NEA staff members resigned. Members of Congress did not close the agency. They gave it $207 million for 2026, the same amount as in 2024 and 2025, according to the Congressional Research Service. On April 3, 2026, White House officials proposed shutting the NEA down again, for 2027. As of September 2026, members of Congress had not decided.

On March 27, 2025, President Donald Trump signed an order titled "Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History." It said the Smithsonian Institution had "come under the influence of a divisive, race-centered ideology." On May 30, Trump announced he had fired Kim Sajet, who had directed the National Portrait Gallery for 12 years. He called her a "highly partisan person." Sajet resigned on June 13, 2025. On August 12, 2025, three White House officials, Lindsey Halligan, Vince Haley and Russell Vought, wrote to the head of the Smithsonian, Lonnie Bunch. They asked for a review of eight Smithsonian museums, among them the American Art Museum and the Portrait Gallery. They told the museums' leaders to begin changing their exhibits within 120 days. On July 24, 2026, Trump signed another order about the Smithsonian, aimed at the National Museum of American History.

<a id="ch-music"></a>

## Chapter 33: Music

### Before 1500

Long before 1500, Native nations in this land made their own music. The music scholar J. Bryan Burton lists what the songs were for in traditional Native life: ceremonies, healing, work, games, courting a sweetheart, storytelling, hunting, farming, war, and social dances. None of the nations north of Mexico had a way of writing tunes down. Singers passed songs on by teaching them, so no singer's name and no song's name from these centuries survives in writing. Some of the instruments survive. Archaeologists, scientists who dig up and study things people left behind, have found wooden flutes and metal-covered panpipes more than a thousand years old. A panpipe is a row of tubes that a player blows across, each tube making a different note. Onondaga and Tlingit singers today still follow rules about where a song may be sung and who owns it.

#### Flutes and panpipes that survive

The oldest known wooden flutes in North America were found in a cave in northeastern Arizona. In 1931 the archaeologist Earl H. Morris explored 15 caves in the Prayer Rock district, which is now part of the Navajo Nation. In the largest cave he found four wooden flutes. That cave is now called Broken Flute Cave.

The flutes were made between the years 620 and 670. The Arizona State Museum in Tucson holds them today. The museum's exhibit identifies them as Ancestral Pueblo flutes, which means the ancestors of today's Pueblo peoples made them. Each flute is a tube of box elder wood between about 68 and 74 centimeters long, a little over two feet. The finger holes are almost the same on each flute, so the maker planned which notes the flute would play. Red, blue and black feathers were tied to one end. Two of the flutes lay broken in trash above a grave. The other two lay whole under a dirt floor, tied together.

Farther east, people of the Hopewell culture lived in the woodlands of eastern North America between the years 1 and 400. "Hopewell" is a name archaeologists gave them, not the name of a nation. In southern Ohio they built earthworks, which are mounds and long banks of piled earth. Archaeologists have found 105 of their panpipes at 55 sites, from Wisconsin and Ontario down to the Gulf Coast. A Hopewell panpipe is three or four tubes of cane, reed or bone, held together by a metal jacket. The metal of 102 jackets is known. Of those, 81 are copper. The others are silver, copper covered with silver, iron, or iron and copper together. Almost all of the panpipes were found buried with the dead. Very few came from places where people lived.

Nobody knows what tunes anyone played on these flutes and panpipes.

#### Drums, rattles, and songs that belong to someone

The Onondaga Nation of what is now central New York is one of the Haudenosaunee nations. Onondaga singers today play a water drum and a horn rattle. The drum is usually made of cedar, with deer hide stretched over the top. The horn rattle is a dried, hollowed animal horn with seeds inside. A rattle made of turtle shell is used only in a few ceremonies.

The Onondaga keep two kinds of songs. Social songs can be sung anywhere. Songs for ceremonies are sung only in the longhouse, the building where ceremonies are held, and the public may not watch them.

Among the Tlingit of what is now southeast Alaska, a song can belong to a clan. A clan is a large family group that traces itself back to shared ancestors. A clan owns its songs, its stories, its crests and the clothing its members wear in ceremonies. The Tlingit word for these owned things is *at.óow*, which means "something owned or purchased." Some songs and stories tell of a clan's losses in a certain place. In the Tlingit view, those songs are the clan's deed to that place, the proof that the place is theirs.

These rules come from the nations' own accounts today. No written record from before 1500 describes them.

<a id="story-r-carlos-nakai-music"></a>

#### R. Carlos Nakai

> **Who:** A flute player from a Navajo (Diné) and Ute family who plays a traditional cedar flute.
>
> **When and where:** Born April 16, 1946, in Flagstaff, Arizona. Still performing in 2026.

R. Carlos Nakai plays a traditional Native cedar flute. Flutes survive from before 1500, but no flute player's name does. Nakai has recorded more than forty albums with Canyon Records in Phoenix, Arizona. The first was *Changes*, in 1983. His concert calendar for 2026 lists shows in Utah and Colorado in September and more in October and November.

Nakai was born in Flagstaff, Arizona, on April 16, 1946. His family is Navajo and Ute. His father, Raymond Nakai, was chairman of the Navajo Nation from 1963 to 1970.

He first studied the trumpet. A car accident ruined the way he shaped his lips against the trumpet's mouthpiece. Someone gave him a cedar flute as a gift and challenged him to master it.

His albums *Canyon Trilogy* and *Earth Spirit* each sold 500,000 copies. They were the first recordings of the traditional Native flute to sell that many. In 2014 the RIAA, the music business group that gives sales awards, named *Canyon Trilogy* a platinum album, its award for one million copies. Between 1994 and 2013 he was nominated for ten Grammy awards. Nakai calls himself "an iconoclastic traditionalist." An iconoclast is a person who breaks with old ways. A traditionalist is a person who keeps them.

### The 1500s

The European music on record from the 1500s in what is now the United States comes from a few places: the coast of Florida, the coast of California, and New Mexico from 1598. It is church singing and soldiers' trumpets. When they came ashore and when they held services, Spanish priests sang Latin hymns, which are songs that praise God, and French and English Protestants sang psalms, which are songs from the Bible. Protestants were Christians who had broken away from the Catholic Church. Native people watched and listened, and Europeans wrote down a few of their reactions. No record from the 1500s names a mission choir or a Native singer trained in church music. The first ones on record come after 1598.

#### Hymns sung at the landings, Florida, 1564 and 1565

In 1564 French Protestants, called Huguenots, built Fort Caroline near the mouth of the St. Johns River, near today's Jacksonville, Florida. They built it on the land of the Timucua people. The Huguenots' leader, René de Laudonnière, wrote that on June 30 he ordered his men to sing aloud on the beach to thank God for their safe arrival. In 1865 the historian Francis Parkman wrote that on the morning they began the fort, the men sang a psalm before they started work.

On September 8, 1565, the Spanish commander Pedro Menéndez de Avilés landed at Seloy, a Timucua town, and founded St. Augustine. His chaplain, Francisco López de Mendoza Grajales, wrote an account of that day. A chaplain is a priest who serves a group of soldiers or travelers. Mendoza wrote that Menéndez came ashore "to the sound of trumpets and salutes of artillery," which means cannons fired as a greeting. Mendoza walked to meet him carrying a cross and singing the *Te Deum*, a Latin hymn of praise to God. "A large number of Indians watched these proceedings and imitated all they saw done," he wrote.

On September 20, 1565, Menéndez's soldiers captured Fort Caroline and killed most of the Frenchmen there. In a letter of October 15, Menéndez wrote that 132 of them had "their throats cut." He gave his reason in the same letter: "they spread the Lutheran sect," meaning the Protestant faith. When Menéndez came back to St. Augustine, Mendoza and his companions walked ahead of him in a line, "singing the Te Deum laudamus." In the weeks after, shipwrecked Frenchmen surrendered to Menéndez at a place called Matanzas. His soldiers killed 111 of them. On October 12 they killed 134 more who had surrendered with their leader, Jean Ribault.

#### Psalms at Drake's landing, California, 1579

In June 1579 the English captain Francis Drake stopped on the California coast to repair his ship, probably at the place now called Drake's Bay. Coast Miwok people lived along that shore. Drake's men stayed for about five weeks. While they were there, they held prayers, sang psalms and read from the Bible, and Miwok people came to watch.

A book about the voyage, *The World Encompassed by Sir Francis Drake*, came out in London in 1628. Drake's nephew, also named Francis Drake, put it together. Its title page states that it was collected "out of the Notes of Master Francis Fletcher." Fletcher was the preacher on the voyage. The title page adds that his notes were checked against other notes made on the same voyage. The scholar Robert Heizer wrote that who wrote it is uncertain. The 1628 book states that the Miwok "tooke such pleasure in our singing of Psalmes" that each time they came, "their first request was Gnaah." That word meant they wanted the Englishmen to sing. In 1947 Heizer, an anthropologist, wrote that *gnaah* seems to be a Coast Miwok word. An anthropologist is a scientist who studies people and the ways they live.

#### New Mexico, 1598

In 1598 Juan de Oñate led Spanish colonists north into New Mexico to start a colony on the lands of the Pueblo peoples. The music historian John Koegel writes that Pueblo people began to hear Spanish military music, and to sing Catholic church songs, some of them in parts, "during the Oñate expedition and its aftermath," meaning the journey and the years after it. The earliest music teachers there that Koegel names are two friars, Catholic men who lived by the rules of a religious order. Fray is the title in front of a friar's name. Fray Bernardo de Marta came in about 1605. Fray Cristóbal de Quiñones died in 1609.

### The 1600s

The colonists' music on record from the 1600s is church music. In New England, congregations, the people who worship together at a church, sang psalms from a book printed in Massachusetts in 1640. For most of the century, each printing of that book contained only the words, with no musical notes. In New Mexico, the friar Cristóbal de Quiñones put an organ in the church at San Felipe Pueblo and trained Pueblo singers to sing church music. Later friars banned Pueblo religious ceremonies. In 1675 a Spanish governor had 47 Pueblo religious leaders arrested, and three were later hanged. In 1619 the crew of an English ship landed about twenty captured Africans in Virginia. Enslaved Africans made music there through the 1600s, but nobody who wrote in those years left a description of it that survives.

#### The Bay Psalm Book, 1640, and lining out

In 1640 Stephen Daye printed *The Whole Booke of Psalmes Faithfully Translated into English Metre* at Cambridge, Massachusetts. People today call it the *Bay Psalm Book*. It was the first book printed in British North America. Richard Mather and other New England ministers turned the Psalms of the Bible into English verse with a steady beat, so that a congregation could sing them. Eleven copies of that first printing survive.

The 1640 book had no printed music. It lists tunes by name, tunes already printed in English psalm books. The ninth edition, printed in 1698, was the first to include music. It contains 13 tunes taken from a music book by John Playford, an Englishman.

In 1644 an assembly of ministers at Westminster, in London, wrote a guide for church services. The guide states that where many people in a congregation could not read, the minister or a person he chose should "read the psalm, line by line, before the singing thereof." This way of singing is called lining out. A leader read or sang one line, and the congregation sang it back. Colonists from England and Scotland brought lining out to America. Members of Old Regular Baptist churches in the United States still sing this way today.

<a id="story-fray-cristobal-de-quinones-music"></a>

#### Fray Cristóbal de Quiñones

> **Who:** A Franciscan friar who built the church at San Felipe Pueblo, put an organ in it, and trained Pueblo singers.
>
> **When and where:** San Felipe Pueblo, a Keres-speaking town in New Mexico. Died in 1609.

Fray Cristóbal de Quiñones put an organ in the church at San Felipe Pueblo and trained singers there to sing church music. Fray is the title of a friar, a man who has joined a Catholic religious order and lives by its rules. Quiñones belonged to the Franciscan order.

San Felipe is a Pueblo town in New Mexico whose people speak the Keres language. Quiñones learned Keres and baptized many Native people in the New Mexico missions. To baptize someone is to make that person a member of the Christian church in a ceremony with water. He was the leader of the Franciscan friars in New Mexico. At San Felipe he built the church, a house for the friars, a pharmacy and a place to care for the sick.

Agustín de Vetancurt, a Franciscan writer in Mexico, later described his work in a book of the lives of Franciscan friars, printed in the 1690s. Vetancurt wrote that Quiñones "installed an organ to enrich the Divine Service and encouraged music-making by the skilled singers" he had trained. By the Divine Service he meant the church service. Quiñones died in 1609. The music historian John Koegel calls him "perhaps the first trained teacher of European music" to live in what is now the US Southwest. Koegel does not give his birthplace or the year he came to New Mexico. Vetancurt's account tells the friar's side only. It does not record what the singers of San Felipe thought of the music they were taught.

#### Church music and banned ceremonies in New Mexico

Other friars taught music in more Pueblo towns. Fray Bernardo de Marta came to New Mexico in about 1605. He taught Pueblo people in many towns to sing and to play European instruments, and he died in 1635. By 1634 Fray Roque de Figueredo was teaching Zuni boys to sing in parts.

A Spanish church leader and a Spanish governor also punished Pueblo people for keeping their own religion. From 1656 to 1665 the Franciscan leader Alonso de Posada forbade Pueblo ceremonies. He ordered friars to invade the sacred kivas, the rooms where Pueblo people held their ceremonies. There the friars burned the masks and took or destroyed sacred objects.

In 1675 the governor, Juan Francisco Treviño, had 47 Pueblo religious leaders arrested and charged with sorcery, which means using magic to do harm. Four were sentenced to be hanged. Three were hanged, and one killed himself. The rest were shamed and whipped in public, then put in prison. The records do not name the men who passed the sentences or carried out the hangings and the whippings. Pueblo people went to Santa Fe and demanded that the prisoners be freed, and the Spanish let them go.

One of the whipped men was Po'pay, a leader from Ohkay Owingeh. On August 10, 1680, Po'pay led the Pueblo nations as they rose up together against the Spanish. The Pueblo fighters killed about 400 Spanish settlers, 21 of them Franciscan friars, and drove the Spanish out of New Mexico for 12 years.

#### What arrived with enslaved Africans

In late August 1619 the crew of an English ship called the *White Lion* landed "20. and odd Negroes," in the words of the colonist John Rolfe, at Point Comfort, Virginia. "Negroes" was a word of that time for Black people. The crew had taken these Africans from a Portuguese slave ship. They came from the Ndongo and Kongo region of West Central Africa.

Enslaved Africans made music in the English colonies through the 1600s, but no one who wrote in those years left a description of it that survives. The first clear description of an early banjo comes from the island of Jamaica. There, in 1687, an English doctor named Hans Sloane wrote about an instrument he called a "strum strump."

### 1700 to 1750

New England ministers began teaching their congregations to sing from written notes around 1720. They started singing schools and printed the first books of music lessons in the colonies. The earliest concert advertised in a Boston newspaper that the music historian Oscar Sonneck found took place in 1731, and a ticket cost five shillings. In Virginia, enslaved Black musicians played the fiddle. Three of them appear in notices that their enslavers put in a newspaper when the men ran away in 1745 and 1746. In 1739 enslaved men rose up near the Stono River in South Carolina, with drums beating. The next year, the men who made South Carolina's laws passed a law to stop enslaved people from using drums and horns, and fined any master who let them.

#### Singing by note and the first singing schools

"By the end of the seventeenth century singing had sunk to a low level in all the colonies," the historian Henry Wilder Foote wrote. New England churches still sang by lining out. In the first 25 years of the 1700s, ministers in New England turned against lining out and called for "regular singing" instead. In 1720 the Reverend Thomas Symmes of Bradford, Massachusetts, published a booklet called *The Reasonableness of Regular Singing, or Singing by Note*. Regular singing meant singing from written notes. Symmes wrote that church singing had got worse because "Singing schools and singing books being laid aside, there was no way to learn."

The Reverend John Tufts of Newbury, Massachusetts, published *An Introduction to the Singing of Psalm Tunes*. It was the first book of music lessons printed in the English colonies. Foote wrote that neither the exact title nor the date of the first edition is known, so its date is disputed. Foote dated it to about 1712. The Sacred Harp Publishing Company, which still prints a book of church songs, dates it to 1721. Tufts traveled to give talks about singing and to set up singing schools, where a teacher taught a class to read and sing music.

In 1721 Thomas Walter, a 25-year-old nephew of the Boston minister Cotton Mather, published *The Grounds and Rules of Musick Explained*, with 24 psalm tunes. James Franklin printed it in Boston. It was the first music in the colonies printed with bar lines, the lines that divide music into equal parts of time. It stayed a favorite for more than forty years and was printed in six editions. Symmes wrote that New England had had singing schools in the colony's early days, but people had stopped holding them. New singing schools spread in the 1720s. The records that survive do not say where the first one met or what a pupil paid.

Young people took up the new singing first. On March 20, 1721, the Boston judge Samuel Sewall wrote in his diary that "Dr. Mather" had preached that night "in the school house to the young musicians." Sewall wrote that the house was full, "and the singing extraordinarily excellent, such as hardly been heard before in Boston."

Other church members fought the change. Symmes reported that in his town, "a great part of the town has for near half a year, been in a mere flame about it." He meant that people had been angry and arguing about it for almost six months. In 1728 the Reverend Nathaniel Chauncey of Connecticut wrote answers to the objections people raised. One objection was that singing by note "leads to the Church of England and will bring in organs quickly." The Church of England was the official church back in England. Another was that the new way must be wrong "because the young people fall in with it."

#### Concerts for a ticket, and a fiddle for a prize

An advertisement in the *Boston News-Letter* of December 1731 listed a "Concert of Music" on several instruments. It was held on December 30, 1731, in Mr. Pelham's great room in Boston, and a ticket cost five shillings. A shilling was a British coin, and 20 shillings made one pound. It is the earliest advertised concert in Boston that Sonneck found. After a concert at Faneuil Hall in 1744, the town's selectmen received 205 pounds for the poor of Boston. The selectmen were the men elected to run the town.

In Virginia, a notice in the *Virginia Gazette* of November 26, 1736, listed prizes for a holiday gathering at Page's Warehouse in Hanover County on November 30. One prize was "A fine Cremona Fiddle to be plaid for, by any number of Country Fiddlers." A Cremona fiddle was a violin made in the town of Cremona, in Italy. In November 1737 the races at John Pinkerton's Old Field in Virginia included a fiddling contest.

#### Fiddles, banjos, and the enslaved musicians who played them

The banjo has West African roots. A 2014 article on the Oxford University Press blog counts more than 60 plucked instruments in West Africa that are likely forerunners of it. The first known mention of a banjo in the mainland colonies is in John Peter Zenger's newspaper, the *New-York Weekly Journal*, in 1736.

In Virginia, enslavers put notices in the *Virginia Gazette* when an enslaved person ran away. Each notice described the person's body, clothes and skills, so that strangers could recognize and catch the person. Playing the fiddle was one of the skills these notices listed. In the issue of November 28 to December 5, 1745, Robert Whitfield of Isle of Wight County offered four pistoles for a young man named Tom, who "plays very well on the Violin." A pistole was a Spanish gold coin used in the colonies. In April 1746 John Thornton of Fredericksburg advertised for another man named Tom, about 46 years old, who "plays on the Violin, and is a Sawyer." A sawyer is a man who saws logs into boards. The University of Virginia's collection of Virginia runaway notices holds three from before 1751 that name a musician: these two men named Tom, and a fiddler named Harry.

<a id="story-harry-fiddler-music"></a>

#### Harry, a fiddler who ran away, perhaps to his wife, 1746

> **Who:** An enslaved man who played the fiddle. The man who held him put a notice in the newspaper for his capture.
>
> **When and where:** Near Jamestown, Virginia, March 1746.

Harry was an enslaved fiddler who ran away in early March 1746 from the man who held him, near Jamestown, Virginia. Everything known about him comes from one notice in the *Virginia Gazette*, printed between March 20 and 27, 1746. The notice gives him no last name.

Harry was about 35 years old and about 5 feet 7 inches tall, with small eyes and "a very large Beard," and he "plays upon the Fiddle." He left in a double-breasted dark cloth coat, two dark cotton jackets, buckskin breeches and a blue greatcoat. Breeches are pants that end at the knee. He had once belonged to Colonel Grymes of Richmond County, Virginia.

William Newgent signed the notice. A later reprint of the notice spells his first name James. Newgent guessed that Harry had gone to Richmond County, "where he has a Wife." He offered one pistole for Harry's return. At the end he added: "As he ran away without any Cause, I desire he may be punish'd by Whipping, as the Law directs." Newgent was asking whoever caught Harry to have him beaten with a whip. The record does not say whether Harry was caught.

#### Drums at Stono, and the 1740 law against drums and horns

On September 9, 1739, about 20 enslaved men seized weapons near the Stono River, south of Charleston, South Carolina. A report written that year called them "Angola Negroes" and named their leader as a man called Jemmy. They marched south toward Spanish Florida. The report says more men joined them, "calling out Liberty," and they "marched on with Colours displayed, and two Drums beating." Colours here means flags. When there were sixty to a hundred of them, they stopped in a field and "set to dancing, Singing and beating Drums, to draw more Negroes to them."

The same report says the rebels killed white men, women and children as they marched. Lieutenant Governor William Bull raised the militia, a force of armed planters, and the militiamen attacked them in the field the same day. The report says the men captured in the field were questioned and then "shot on the Spot," and men who had run back to their plantations were caught there and shot. It does not name who fired. The report counts about 40 Black people and 20 white people killed. Later counts give about 25 white colonists and 35 to 50 rebels killed. Colonists cut off the heads of rebels and set them on stakes along the main roads as a warning. They put most of the captured rebels to death and sold the survivors to the West Indies.

On May 10, 1740, the men of the South Carolina assembly passed the Negro Act. In section 36 they wrote that it was "absolutely necessary to the safety of this Province" to stop enslaved people from "using or keeping of drums, horns, or other loud instruments." The Province was the colony. They gave the reason in the same sentence: such instruments "may call together or give sign or notice to one another of their wicked designs and purposes." They meant that drums and horns could be used to call enslaved people together to rise up.

An overseer was the man who ran the work on a plantation and gave orders to the enslaved people there. Under the law, a master or overseer who let enslaved people beat drums, blow horns or gather in public paid a fine of ten pounds each time. Any master, overseer or other person could seize an enslaved person found off the plantation without a written pass and without a white person. The law named Saturday nights, Sundays and holidays in particular. If an enslaved man found off the plantation carried a weapon, any master, overseer or other person could take the weapon away, seize him and whip him, even if he carried a pass.

### 1750 to 1800

In 1770 a Boston tanner named William Billings published a book of church songs that he had written himself. By 1800 Americans had published about forty books of church music. During the Revolution, officers used drum beats to tell soldiers when to wake, march and fight, and American writers put new words to old tunes. Black musicians played fiddles, horns, drums and banjos in Virginia, in Charleston and in New England. Their names survive mainly in notices that enslavers put in newspapers when enslaved musicians ran away. Slave traders took one of them, Newport Gardner, from Africa as a boy. He became a music teacher in Newport, Rhode Island, and bought his freedom in 1791. That same year, on the Pacific coast, Tadeo Haenke, a man sailing with a Spanish expedition, wrote down Tlingit songs in musical notes.

#### William Billings and the New England singing masters

In 1770 William Billings, a Boston tanner born in 1746, published *The New-England Psalm-Singer*. A tanner turns animal skins into leather. A Library of Congress research guide describes the book as "the first publication consisting of sacred music composed entirely by a native-born American." Sacred music is music for worship. Paul Revere is credited with engraving the picture at the front of the book, which means cutting the picture into a metal plate so it could be printed.

Billings also taught singing schools. He opened one in Boston with John Barry in 1769, and he taught another in Stoughton, Massachusetts, in 1774. The historian Henry Wilder Foote counted about forty American books of church music published before 1800. Most of them were printed in Boston.

<a id="story-william-billings"></a>

#### William Billings

> **Who:** A tanner and singing teacher who wrote about 340 songs for choirs. His 1770 book was the first book of church music written entirely by an American-born composer.
>
> **When and where:** Boston. Born October 7, 1746. Died September 26, 1800.

William Billings wrote about 340 songs for choirs and published them in six books. He did it while working as a tanner and a singing teacher, and he died poor.

He was born in Boston on October 7, 1746. His father died when Billings was 14, and he went to work learning to tan leather. He was mostly self-taught in music, though he may have had some lessons from John Barry of Boston's New South Church. In 1853 a writer named Nathaniel Gould described him as having "one eye blind, one leg shorter than the other, one arm somewhat withered."

His first book, *The New-England Psalm-Singer* of 1770, included his song "Chester." It opens with the words "Let tyrants shake their iron rod." The singers say that they do not fear tyrants or the chains of slavery, because they trust in God. In 1778 Billings printed a new version of "Chester," with five verses, in *The Singing Master's Assistant*. According to the writer David Stowe, soldiers "learned the words by heart" and carried Billings's songs wherever the army sent them.

Other printers copied Billings's tunes without paying him. Copyright is the legal right to decide who may copy and sell a piece of writing or music. Before the Revolution, the men who made Massachusetts's laws voted for a bill, a proposed law, to give Billings that right over his first book. The governor, a Tory loyal to the British king, refused to sign it. Stowe writes that the governor may have refused because Billings had ties to patriots such as Samuel Adams.

In 1794 his friends paid to print his book *The Continental Harmony*. His wife, Lucy, died on March 26, 1795, and left him with six children under 18. In the 1790s he worked as a street cleaner. Billings died poor in Boston on September 26, 1800. He was buried in an unmarked grave on Boston Common.

#### Songs and signals of the Revolution

British officers first sang "Yankee Doodle" to make fun of the colonists. The man most often named as the writer of the words is Richard Shuckburgh, a British army surgeon, in about 1755 or 1758, during the French and Indian War. The date is disputed. In 1768 British soldiers arrived to occupy Boston, and their musicians played the song in the streets to mock the colonists. Early in the war, British and Loyalist troops played it to make fun of the Continental soldiers. Loyalists were colonists who stayed on the British side. The Americans then made up their own verses, and by 1781 "Yankee Doodle" was a favorite American song.

In July 1768 the *Boston Gazette* printed "The Liberty Song." John Dickinson of Pennsylvania wrote its words to the tune of "Heart of Oak," the anthem, or official song, of the British Royal Navy. He sent it to his Massachusetts friend James Otis with a note that "indifferent songs are very powerful on certain occasions." By indifferent he meant songs that were not very good.

In the Continental Army, officers gave orders by drum beat. Under the army rules of Baron von Steuben, each beat had its own name and meaning: "The Reveille" woke the soldiers in the morning, "The General" meant take down the tents and get ready to march, "The Assembly" meant line up at the flags, and "To Arms" meant pick up weapons and get ready to fight. Drummers beat "The Tattoo" at 9 or 10 at night, and at that signal tavern keepers stopped serving the soldiers drinks. According to the American Battlefield Trust, boys under 14 were recommended as drummers, and some fifers were 9 or 10 years old. A fifer plays the fife, a small, high-pitched flute.

#### Black musicians, enslaved and free

Virginia enslavers kept putting notices in the newspapers that named enslaved musicians. On May 4, 1769, William Gregory advertised for Peter, about 44, who had taken with him "a fiddle, which he is much delighted in when he gets any strong drink." On September 8, 1775, David Walker of Dinwiddie County advertised for Jemmy. He wrote that Jemmy "is very fond of singing hymns and preaching," and that he was living near Williamsburg under the name James Williams.

In August 1780 William Allason offered forty pounds for four men who had run away together from near Fauquier Court House, Virginia. One of them was Mark, about 25. He was born on the island of St. Jago, in the Cape Verde Islands off West Africa, and he spoke Portuguese. The notice says Mark "blows the French horn, can play on the fiddle, whistles many tunes well." It says he loved marches and Catholic church music. Allason guessed that the four men planned to get aboard a ship.

In 1774 Philip Vickers Fithian was a tutor, a live-in teacher, to the children of Robert Carter III at Nomini Hall, a plantation in Virginia. His journal records that on a January evening, enslaved people gathered in the schoolroom "& began to play the Fiddle, & dance." Two of Carter's sons, Ben and Harry, joined them, and Fithian sent everyone away. A few days later, he wrote, "several Negroes & Ben, & Harry are playing on a Banjo & dancing."

In Charleston, South Carolina, a notice in the *South Carolina Gazette and General Advertiser* of December 12, 1766, reported a stolen pocketbook. A gentleman lost it on the evening of December 2, as he passed "a croud of negroes assembled at the lower end of Elliott-street, with a banjer playing." A Charleston town rule of 1750 banned beating drums in town without an officer's permission.

A painting on paper called *The Old Plantation*, made between about 1785 and 1795, shows enslaved Black men and women dancing. One man plays an early banjo made from a gourd, a large fruit with a hard shell that can be dried and hollowed out. Another man plays a drum, and two women hold rattles. It is the earliest known painting of a banjo. In 2010 the librarian Susan Shames identified the painter as John Rose, a South Carolina planter who held people in slavery. The Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Folk Art Museum in Williamsburg, Virginia, owns it.

Thomas Jefferson held people in slavery at Monticello, his plantation in Virginia. In his book *Notes on the State of Virginia*, in the 1787 edition, he wrote about Black musicians. He wrote that "In music they are more generally gifted than the whites." Then he doubted that they could write longer, more complicated music: that, he wrote, "is yet to be proved." In a note he called the "Banjar" the instrument "which they brought hither from Africa." In the same passage he wrote that Black people had "no poetry," and he dismissed the published poems of Phillis Wheatley, a Black woman.

In New England, from about 1750, Black communities held their own election days. In New Hampshire and Massachusetts they elected a "king," and in Rhode Island and Connecticut a "governor." The enslavers granted the day off and paid for the feast. The parades had "tambourines, banjos, fiddles and drums," and the feast had rum, gingerbread and "thick, fruit-studded election cakes."

<a id="story-newport-gardner"></a>

#### Newport Gardner

> **Who:** Born Occramer Marycoo in West Africa, enslaved in Newport, Rhode Island, where he became a music teacher and composer.
>
> **When and where:** Born about 1746. Newport, from about 1760. Died in Liberia in 1826.

Newport Gardner was taken from West Africa as a boy, enslaved in Newport, Rhode Island, and became a music teacher there. His name at birth was Occramer Marycoo. He was about 14 when slave traders brought him to Newport.

Caleb Gardner, a merchant and ship captain, bought him and renamed him Newport Gardner. The music writer Sophie Lowe writes that Caleb Gardner "helped enslave some 3,912 human beings" through the slave trade. The enslaved boy learned English and music in Newport. Lowe writes that the best-known account names Andrew Law as his teacher. But Law is first known to have been in Rhode Island in 1783, when Gardner was already in his late thirties. Lowe concludes that he "probably had a variety of musical teachers."

In late December 1791 Gardner and some friends won a lottery. He used his share to buy freedom for himself and his family. He opened a school in Newport where he taught music. He was a deacon, a church member who helps lead it, at Newport's First Congregational Church. In the 1820s he helped found a Black church, according to the historian Edward Andrews. The historian John Millar writes that Gardner joined the new Colored Union Church in 1824.

The writer Eileen Southern credited to him a tune called "Crooked Shanks," printed in 1803. Lowe reports newer research that found the same tune in print in London in 1768, so the credit is uncertain. The words of his anthem, a church song, survive. They begin "Hear the words of the LORD, O ye African race."

He led a group of Black New Englanders to Liberia, in West Africa. Millar counts about 30 of them, and the historian Edward Andrews counts about three dozen. Accounts also differ on when they sailed: late December 1825, or January 4, 1826. Gardner died of disease in Liberia within months, in 1826.

#### Tlingit songs written down, 1791

In 1791 two Spanish ships anchored in Yakutat Bay, in what is now Alaska. Two men named Malaspina and Bustamante led the expedition. The bay was Tlingit land. Several times, Tlingit people sang "to and with" the Spanish sailors.

Tadeo Haenke, a botanist on the ships who had trained in music, wrote the songs down in musical notes on four sheets of paper. A botanist is a scientist who studies plants. The sheets stayed in the Museo de América, a museum in Madrid, Spain, for more than 200 years. The scholar Steve Langdon got pictures of the sheets and sent them to Maria Shaa Tláa Williams, a Tlingit ethnomusicologist. An ethnomusicologist studies the music of a people and its place in their lives. Williams found that the singers used harmony, two or more notes sung together, in part of their singing. She found one song, "Canta de la Paz," that was used to settle a quarrel over a stolen piece of clothing. She then programmed a synthesizer, a machine that makes musical sounds electronically, to play the notes, so people could hear how the songs sounded. Judy Daxootsu Ramos, a Tlingit from Yakutat, said of the old songs, "we're still practicing that today."

### 1800 to 1850

Enslaved Black people in the South between 1800 and 1850 made songs at work and at worship. They also made them on the days off their enslavers allowed, such as Christmas. Frederick Douglass later wrote down what the songs meant, and Harriet Tubman told a writer, Sarah Bradford, how she used hers. In the same years, white performers darkened their faces with burnt cork and sang and danced as Black characters who were lazy, stupid, grinning fools. This blackface minstrel show became one of the most popular kinds of entertainment in the country. The money went to white performers and publishers. Stephen Foster, a white songwriter from Pittsburgh, wrote many of its best-known songs. In Philadelphia a free Black bandleader, Francis Johnson, published more than 200 pieces of music. In the South, singers learned church music from books printed in shape notes, where the shape of each note shows the singer which sound to sing.

#### What the singers said the songs meant

Frederick Douglass was enslaved in Maryland, on Colonel Edward Lloyd's plantation in Talbot County and later on William Freeland's farm. He escaped from slavery in 1838. In 1845 he published the story of his life. In it he wrote that enslaved people sang as they walked to the main farm to collect their monthly food, making up the words as they went. Some people in the North took such singing as a sign that enslaved people were happy. Douglass wrote that this was a mistake: "Slaves sing most when they are most unhappy." He added, "I have often sung to drown my sorrow, but seldom to express my happiness."

In a second book, in 1855, Douglass wrote that enslavers wanted to hear singing. "A silent slave is not liked by masters or overseers," he wrote. When the workers went quiet, the words they heard were "Make a noise." An overseer was the man who drove enslaved people at their work. Teamsters, the men who drove the wagons, sang so that the overseer would know where they were and that the work was going on.

Some songs had a second meaning. In 1836 Douglass and five men planned to escape together. He named them in his book: Henry Harris, John Harris, Sandy Jenkins, Charles Roberts and Henry Bailey. As they planned, they kept singing a hymn, a church song, about being "bound for the land of Canaan." In the Bible, Canaan is the land God promised to the people of Israel after they escaped from slavery in Egypt. Douglass wrote, "the north was our Canaan." Someone betrayed the plan, and it failed. Douglass never found out who.

At Christmas, enslaved people on the Maryland farms played fiddles and beat out rhythms on their own bodies with their hands. This was called "juba" beating. The singers made up the words of the juba songs as they went. Douglass wrote down one verse that begins "We raise de wheat, Dey gib us de corn." It goes on to list the work the enslaved people did and the scraps they were given for it.

Harriet Tubman escaped from slavery in Maryland in September 1849. Later she went back to lead others north. She told the writer Sarah Bradford how she used hymns as signals. People hiding in the woods came out only after she walked past singing a certain hymn twice. If she sang "Moses go down in Egypt" instead, they stayed hidden, "for dere's danger in de way." Bradford printed Tubman's account in 1869.

Douglass and Tubman describe songs with hidden meanings and songs used as signals. A different claim is that the song "Follow the Drinking Gourd" was a map that led people from Alabama north to the Ohio River. That claim comes from a single article printed in 1928 by H. B. Parks, a Texas scientist who studied insects and collected songs. The best-known words of the song were written in 1947 by a folk singer, Lee Hays. The researcher Joel Bresler found that no one ever collected the song in Alabama. He also found no older use of "drinking gourd" to mean the Big Dipper, the group of stars that points to the North Star. Bresler and the scholar James Kelley doubt that the song was ever a map.

#### Congo Square, New Orleans

In 1817 the mayor of New Orleans issued a city law. It limited the gatherings of enslaved people to one place, across Rampart Street at the back of town, on Sunday afternoons. The space was later called Congo Square. There enslaved people sold goods, sang, danced and played music. In 1819 the architect Benjamin Latrobe wrote in his journal of 500 to 600 enslaved people gathered there for dancing. He called the dancing "savage."

City officials stopped the Sunday music and dancing in 1835. It started again, and officials stopped it again in 1851. The records that survive do not give the names of the mayor who limited the gatherings or of the officials who stopped them.

#### Blackface minstrelsy, from about 1830

Blackface minstrelsy was a stage show in which white men darkened their faces with burnt cork and acted as Black people. David Pilgrim of the Jim Crow Museum at Ferris State University writes that white audiences liked seeing Black people shown as "singing, dancing, grinning fools." He writes that these shows helped spread the belief that Black people were lazy, stupid and "inherently less human," which means less human by birth.

Thomas Dartmouth Rice was a white actor, born in New York in 1808. He sang and danced a song called "Jump Jim Crow" in blackface. Pilgrim dates his first performance as Jim Crow to 1828. Other accounts say only that it had become his main act by 1832, when a Philadelphia newspaper notice announced that "Mr. Rice will appear and sing Jim Crow." Rice said he copied a disabled Black man who cared for horses and sang as he worked. He also said he bought the man's clothes to wear on stage. People still argue about when and where this happened, and whether it happened at all. No record names that man, and no record shows that he or any other Black musician was paid for what the minstrels copied.

Rice played to sold-out theaters from about 1832 to 1844, and he took the act to London in 1836. By 1838 people were using "Jim Crow" as an insult for Black people. By the end of the 1800s, "Jim Crow" was the name for the laws and customs that officials and lawmakers used against Black people. Under them, Black people were kept out of white schools, railroad cars and waiting rooms.

On what was probably January 31, 1843, four white men in New York performed for a paying audience as the Virginia Minstrels. They were Dan Emmett, Billy Whitlock, Dick Pelham and Frank Brower. Earlier blackface acts had one singer or dancer. The Virginia Minstrels performed as a group, with fiddles, banjos, tambourines and the bones, a rhythm instrument. From 1845 a group led by Edwin P. Christy, the Christy Minstrels, started many of the features of the minstrel show. The players sat in a half circle. Two comic players called Mr. Tambo and Mr. Bones sat at the ends, and a leader called Mr. Interlocutor sat in the middle.

The money went to the white performers and to the music publishers who printed their songs. Rice became rich. He died poor in 1860.

#### The banjo goes on stage

The banjo came from West African instruments. Enslaved Black people played it in America from at least 1736, about a hundred years before any white man played it on a stage. Joel Walker Sweeney was a white man born in 1810 in Appomattox County, Virginia. He learned to play the banjo from enslaved people there. In April 1839 he played the banjo on a stage in New York. He is the earliest known person to have done so. Four years later, two of the Virginia Minstrels played banjos in their show.

One story says that Sweeney added the banjo's short fifth string. No proof of that exists. Older banjos, and pictures made before his time, already show the short fifth string.

<a id="story-stephen-foster"></a>

#### Stephen Foster

> **Who:** A white songwriter who wrote songs for blackface minstrel shows and for singing at home, and one of the first Americans to earn a living only by writing songs.
>
> **When and where:** Born July 4, 1826, in Lawrenceville, Pennsylvania, now part of Pittsburgh. Worked in Pittsburgh, Cincinnati and New York. Died January 13, 1864, in New York.

Stephen Foster wrote many of the best-known songs of the minstrel shows. He was one of the first Americans to earn a living only by writing songs. He was born on July 4, 1826, in Lawrenceville, which is now part of Pittsburgh.

Foster's family held a Black girl named Kitty as a bound servant. A bound servant had to work for a family, without pay, until a set number of years ran out. The writers of the University of Pittsburgh library's biography of Foster call this arrangement "enslavement in all but name." In 1834 Foster's father wrote that a woman named Mrs. Collins had given the family the girl as "a present." The girl had more than three years left to serve. He wrote that it saved them the cost of hiring a girl.

At nine, Foster sang blackface songs such as "Jim Crow" in a boys' theater set up in a carriage house, and he was paid a small sum each week. He learned the style mostly from songs that white performers wrote to mock Black people. In 1846 and 1847 he kept the money records for his brother's shipping company in Cincinnati. The company made money from cotton picked by enslaved people in the South.

His song "Oh! Susanna" was first advertised in Pittsburgh in September 1847. Within a year the publisher William C. Peters printed it as one of the songs of the Sable Harmonists, a blackface group. At the time, no American song had sold more than 5,000 copies of its sheet music, the printed music people bought to play at home. "Oh! Susanna" sold more than 100,000. Its original second verse used a racist word for Black people and told, as comedy, of an explosion that killed 500 of them.

From 1850 the minstrel leader Edwin P. Christy paid Foster $10 a song for the right to sing each new song first. For "Old Folks at Home" in 1851, Christy paid $15, and the sheet music named Christy as the writer. In 1852 Foster asked to have his own name put back. Christy refused.

That year Foster wrote to Christy about the words of his songs. He said he had made them suitable for "refined people," instead of the "trashy and really offensive words" of other minstrel songs. The University of Pittsburgh writers say he most likely did this to sell more sheet music. His only openly political songs before the Civil War supported the Democrats who opposed ending slavery. One of them, "The Abolition Show" of 1856, attacked the people working to end slavery. Frederick Douglass, however, said in 1855 that songs such as "Old Kentucky Home" and "Uncle Ned" could make listeners feel for enslaved people.

In about 1857 Foster sold his rights to future payments on his songs, in return for money right away. He moved to New York in 1860 and kept writing, including more minstrel songs. In January 1864, while he was ill, he fell in his hotel room and was badly cut on his neck and face. His writing partner, George Cooper, found him lying in a pool of blood. He died at Bellevue Hospital three days later, at 37. His wallet held 37 cents in paper money and three pennies.

Other people later changed the words that are sung today. In 1986 two Kentucky lawmakers, Representative Carl Hines and Senator Georgia Davis Powers, won votes to sing "people" in place of a racist word in "My Old Kentucky Home," the state song since 1928.

#### Church songs: Richard Allen's hymn book and shape notes

Richard Allen, a Philadelphia minister who had been born enslaved, put together two hymn books in 1801, one of 54 hymns and one of 64. The books contain the words and no music. In 1816 Allen formally organized the African Methodist Episcopal Church, a church run by Black Methodists.

Also in 1801, William Little and William Smith printed a music book in Philadelphia called *The Easy Instructor*. Its music is written in shape notes. In shape notes, each note has one of four shapes, and each shape stands for one sound to sing. The book was made for singing schools, classes where a teacher taught people to sing from the page.

In 1844 two Georgia men, Benjamin Franklin White and Elisha J. King, published *The Sacred Harp*, a shape-note book of more than 250 songs. Some of its oldest songs are by William Billings, a Boston singing teacher who wrote church songs in the late 1700s. By 1800 his tunes had mostly dropped out of use in Boston, but singers in the rural South kept them. Sacred Harp singers sit in a square, facing inward, with an empty space in the middle, and they sing in four parts with no instruments. People still sing from the book, and a new edition was printed in 2025.

<a id="story-francis-johnson"></a>

#### Francis Johnson

> **Who:** A free Black bandleader, bugle player and composer in Philadelphia who published more than 200 pieces of music.
>
> **When and where:** Born June 16, 1792, in Philadelphia. Died there April 6, 1844.

Francis Johnson led the band at Philadelphia's dances and balls, and he published more than 200 pieces of music. He was a free Black man. A church record in Philadelphia gives his birth date as June 16, 1792. Some books say he was born on the island of Martinique, but they give no evidence.

He grew up in a free Black neighborhood of Philadelphia. By 15 he could play the flute, the violin, the bugle and the piano. He played in taverns, then as the fiddler at the Exchange Coffee House.

A Philadelphia publisher, George Willig, printed his dance music. The writer Richard Grant, in *Smithsonian* magazine, dates the first piece to 1810 and calls it the first music published by a Black American. Other accounts date his first wide notice to a collection Willig printed in 1818. That year Robert Waln, a former congressman, wrote a book about Philadelphia that called Johnson the "leader of the band at all balls." He played the keyed bugle, a brass horn with keys. He wrote dances, marches and songs.

In November 1837 Johnson took his four-man band to England. Grant writes that no Black American musician had taken a band to Europe before. Some accounts say Johnson played for Queen Victoria. Others say that has not been proven.

In 1842 and 1843, Johnson and nine Black musicians toured eight states. In St. Louis in December 1842, the band members were served with warrants, papers from a court that order an arrest. The charge was being "Free Negros within the State of Missouri without a license." Missouri law required free Black people to hold a license to be in the state. The records do not name the officials who served the warrants. A firemen's club that had hired the band paid a lawyer. The judge closed the case without a ruling, and the band left.

In Allegheny City, Pennsylvania, a mob gathered outside the hall where the band played. The mob attacked the musicians in the street, threw stones, bricks and rotten eggs, and shouted racist insults. Several musicians were badly hurt. The band played the next night anyway. No record names anyone in the mob.

Johnson died on April 6, 1844, when a blood vessel near his heart burst. At his funeral his band played a funeral march he had written. One of the largest funeral crowds in Philadelphia's history came to it.

#### The Hutchinson Family sing against slavery

The Hutchinson Family Singers were brothers from Milford, New Hampshire: John, Asa, Jesse and Judson Hutchinson. They gave their first concert in Milford on November 6, 1840. Their sister Abby joined them when she was about 12. In 1842 they earned up to $130 a concert.

From 1843 they sang songs against slavery. In 1844 they sang "Get Off the Track!" to the tune of a minstrel song, "Old Dan Tucker." In 1845 the Hutchinsons toured Britain with Frederick Douglass.

In the spring of 1847 the Hutchinsons sang in Philadelphia to audiences of Black and white people together. The city's mayor, John Swift, said more concerts would cause a riot. He ruled that no antislavery speech could be given at the hall and that no Black person could sit in the audience. The Hutchinsons refused to sing for a white audience only.

### 1850 to 1900

In 1867 three white Northerners printed the first book of spirituals, the religious songs that enslaved Black people had made. After the Civil War, students at Fisk University, a school for freed Black people, sang those songs on tour to keep their school open. In the war itself, army bands played for soldiers on both sides, and bandsmen carried the wounded. At a government boarding school for Native children in Pennsylvania, the officer in charge gave the boys brass instruments to stop their drumming. The school's own paper said that as the band grew, the boys stopped singing their own songs. From 1890 singers recorded songs on wax cylinders that machines could play back. In 1899 Scott Joplin, a Black pianist in Missouri, published the "Maple Leaf Rag," a piece of ragtime, piano music with a bouncing rhythm. In the South, Black farm workers were making the music later called the blues.

#### Jenny Lind's tour, 1850 to 1852

In January 1850 the showman P. T. Barnum agreed to pay the Swedish singer Jenny Lind $1,000 a concert to tour the United States. She arrived in New York in September 1850, and Barnum sold tickets by auction. She sang 93 concerts for Barnum and earned about $350,000. Barnum made at least $500,000. Lind gave her share to charities, most of it to free schools in Sweden.

#### War songs and army bands, 1859 to 1865

"Dixie" was first sung on April 4, 1859, in New York by Bryant's Minstrels, a white blackface group of performers. It is credited to Dan Emmett, one of the Virginia Minstrels. Since the 1910s or 1920s, people in Mount Vernon, Ohio, have said that Emmett took the song from the Snowdens, a Black family of musicians in Knox County, Ohio. The writers Howard and Judith Sacks suggest it came from the parents of the family, Thomas and Ellen Snowden. Other scholars, such as E. Lawrence Abel, reject the Snowden story outright. In December 1860, in Charleston, South Carolina, a band played "Dixie" after each vote to leave the Union, as people then called the United States. In February 1861 a band played it when Jefferson Davis became president of the Confederacy, the group of Southern states that broke away from the United States.

In 1861 Union soldiers from Massachusetts made up the song "John Brown's Body," about John Brown, who led an 1859 raid on Harpers Ferry, Virginia. They sang it to the tune of a hymn from camp meetings, big outdoor church gatherings. Julia Ward Howe heard soldiers singing it near Washington, D.C. In November 1861 she wrote new words to the same tune. She sold them for $4 to *The Atlantic Monthly*, a magazine. Its editors printed her "Battle Hymn of the Republic" on the front page in February 1862.

In January 1862 the Hutchinson Family sang a song against slavery to Union soldiers in Virginia. Its words included "Let Slavery die!" Some of the soldiers booed. General George McClellan, who opposed using the war to end slavery, then banned the Hutchinsons from singing in the army camps.

Under an army order of August 3, 1861, each Union regiment, one unit of soldiers, could have a band of 24 musicians. In July 1862 members of Congress voted to send the regimental bands home. They kept one band for each brigade, a larger group of soldiers made up of several regiments. Bandsmen also carried the wounded. Albert Mann, a bandsman from Massachusetts, wrote that the army surgeon taught the band to use "stretchers, bandages and tourniquets." A tourniquet is a band tied tight around an arm or leg to stop heavy bleeding. The bandsmen were to go into battle with the regiment, "rescue the wounded, if possible, and carry them to the field hospital."

At the Battle of Gettysburg, fought from July 1 to 3, 1863, the bands of the 26th and 11th North Carolina regiments played while "heavy firing" went on, the 26th's band leader recalled. A British visitor heard a Confederate band play polkas and waltzes while cannon fired.

#### Spirituals written down

Thomas Wentworth Higginson, a white abolitionist, commanded the 1st South Carolina Volunteers in 1862. An abolitionist was a person who worked to end slavery. The regiment was a Union unit of men who had been enslaved. A drummer boy in the regiment told Higginson about a hymn with the words "We'll soon be free." He said that enslaved people in Georgetown, South Carolina, had been whipped for singing it when Abraham Lincoln was elected in 1860. The boy said the enslavers thought "de Lord" in the song meant the Yankees, the Northern soldiers. In a later version of the story, Higginson wrote that the singers had been put in jail. Neither account names the drummer boy, the singers, or the people who punished them.

In 1867 three white Northerners, William Francis Allen, Lucy McKim Garrison and Charles Pickard Ware, published *Slave Songs of the United States*. It contains 136 songs and was the first book of spirituals ever printed. A spiritual is a religious song made by enslaved Black people. Most of the songs in the book came from Gullah Geechee people, Black people of the South Carolina islands. They lived on St. Helena Island and had been freed during the war.

#### The Fisk Jubilee Singers, from 1871

Fisk University opened in Nashville, Tennessee, after the Civil War to teach freed Black people. By 1871 it was running out of money, and its classes met in old buildings of a Union army hospital. George White, a white church worker from the North, kept the school's money and led its music. On October 6, 1871, he set out with nine students on a singing tour to raise money. They were Isaac Dickerson, Maggie Porter, Minnie Tate, Jennie Jackson, Benjamin Holmes, Thomas Rutling, Eliza Walker, Green Evans and Ella Sheppard.

At first they sang spirituals only as extra songs at the end of a concert. Audiences asked for more. White named the group the Jubilee Singers, after the "year of jubilee" in the Bible, when slaves were set free.

After one early concert in Ohio, the singers gave their profit to the victims of the Chicago fire of October 1871. "We had thirty dollars and sent every penny to Chicago and didn't have anything for ourselves," Maggie Porter said. She also said, "There were many times, when we didn't have place to sleep or anything to eat." Ella Sheppard wrote of "the ill treatment at hotels, on railroads, poorly attended concerts, and ridicule." George White and another man walked through sleet, snow and rain from hotel to hotel, looking for one that would take the singers in. The records do not name the hotels that turned them away.

By the spring of 1872 they had raised the $20,000 that White had promised. In March 1872 the singers sang for President Ulysses S. Grant at the White House. One count gives about $40,000 from their first American tours, which lasted about 18 months. In April 1873 they sang for Queen Victoria in England. By May 1874 they had raised nearly $50,000, and that money paid for Jubilee Hall, Fisk's first permanent building, which opened on January 1, 1876. It became a National Historic Landmark in 1975. Over seven years of touring, the singers raised about $150,000.

<a id="story-ella-sheppard"></a>

#### Ella Sheppard

> **Who:** Born into slavery, she became the pianist, arranger and assistant director of the Fisk Jubilee Singers.
>
> **When and where:** Born February 4, 1851, at the Hermitage, Andrew Jackson's plantation near Nashville, Tennessee. Toured the United States and Europe. Died in Nashville in 1914 or 1915 (the records differ).
>
> **Movie:** *Jubilee Singers: Sacrifice and Glory* (2000), a documentary about the group in the PBS series *American Experience*.

Ella Sheppard arranged most of the spirituals that the Fisk Jubilee Singers sang. To arrange a song is to write out the parts for each voice. She was born into slavery on February 4, 1851, at the Hermitage, Andrew Jackson's plantation near Nashville.

Her father, Simon Sheppard, paid $1,800 to buy his own freedom, and then he bought Ella's. The woman who held Ella's mother, Sarah, refused to sell her. She said, "She is mine and she shall die mine. Let Simon get another wife." When Ella was three, her mother was sold to a plantation in Mississippi. Ella did not see her again until she was 15. The records do not name the woman who held Sarah or the person who bought her.

In 1856, after a riot in Nashville, white officials there made stricter rules for free Black people. Simon fell into debt and was afraid that his family would be seized and sold. He took Ella to Cincinnati, Ohio. There a German woman taught her piano. A white teacher taught her in secret, at night, letting her in through the back door.

Her father died of cholera in 1866. Cholera is an infection of the gut that people catch from dirty food or water, and it drains so much water from the body that a person can die. Ella taught music in Gallatin, Tennessee, and saved about $6 in five months. In 1868 she entered Fisk. The money lasted three weeks, and she stayed by giving music lessons and washing dishes.

She played piano, organ and guitar, arranged the spirituals for the group to sing in four parts, and collected more than a hundred songs. On stage she led the singers from her place among them. In the summer of 1875 she wrote down the music of eight spirituals for a printed book of the group's songs. The book did not name her. She later wrote that the old songs "were sacred to our parents, who used them in their religious worship," and that at first the students did not want to sing them for strangers.

Her mother said, "My back was never struck, but my heart is like a checkerboard with its stripes of sorrow." In 1890 Sheppard trained a new group of Jubilee Singers at Fisk.

#### Native songs, drums and the first recordings

The army officer Richard Henry Pratt opened the Carlisle Indian School in Pennsylvania, a boarding school for Native children, in 1879. Students came from 54 or more nations. Early in the school's history, a rule was made that students could not speak their own languages or practice "Indian customs." The school's paper does not say who made the rule. In 1896 an article in that paper, *The Red Man*, stated that the school's aim was "the complete transformation of the Indians." It called any "display of savagery and barbarism, even in song and language," out of place in the school. Those were the paper's words for the students' own songs and languages. The article states that in the first year, the only music heard from the boys' rooms was the drum.

Pratt told a Boston donor, Mrs. Walter Baker, that he wanted to stop the drumming. As the paper quotes him, he said, "If you will give me a set of brass band instruments I will give them to the 'tom tom' boys ... and this will stop the 'tom tom.'" The school band began in 1881. The article states that no one ever ordered the students to stop singing their own songs. It also states that as the band grew, the singers of those songs fell silent.
