Dennison Wheelock, an Oneida student who entered Carlisle in 1885, later led the school band.

On March 30, 1883, Hiram Price, the federal Commissioner of Indian Affairs, issued rules that made the Sun Dance and other religious dances "Indian offenses." The rules named dances and feasts. They did not name songs. The punishment was the loss of rations, the food the government handed out to Native people on reservations. For a first offense, officials could hold back a person's rations for up to ten days. For a later offense, they could hold back rations for 15 to 30 days. They could instead put the person for up to 30 days in the agency prison, the jail at the government office on the reservation. Officials could enforce these rules until 1978.

On December 29, 1890, at Wounded Knee, soldiers of the 7th Cavalry, an army unit on horseback, killed between 250 and 300 Lakota people, most of them women and children. The soldiers had been taking the guns of a Lakota band led by Spotted Elk. His people had taken up a religious movement called the Ghost Dance, whose followers danced in a circle. The Ghost Dance had its own songs. In 1894 James Mooney, a scientist who studied Native peoples, recorded Ghost Dance songs. Library of Congress notes say the singer on those recordings is probably Mooney himself, not a Native singer.

From March 15 to 18, 1890, in Calais, Maine, the scientist Jesse Walter Fewkes recorded Passamaquoddy songs and stories on 36 wax cylinders. The Passamaquoddy are a Native nation whose homeland is along the border between Maine and New Brunswick, in Canada. The singers were Peter Selmore, Newell Josephs and Peter Lacoute. In a Library of Congress essay, Kelly Revak writes that these are "largely credited" as the first recordings of Native American music. Since the 1980s Passamaquoddy speakers have used the recordings to bring old songs back. In 2009 Wayne Newell said people were working on them at home "so we can sort of resurrect older songs."

<a id="story-john-philip-sousa"></a>

#### John Philip Sousa

> **Who:** Leader of the United States Marine Band and writer of more than 100 marches.
>
> **When and where:** Born November 6, 1854, in Washington, D.C. Led the Marine Band from 1880 to 1892, then his own band. Died March 6, 1932, in Reading, Pennsylvania.
>
> **Movie:** *Stars and Stripes Forever* (1952), a Hollywood film loosely based on his memoir.

John Philip Sousa wrote more than 100 marches, including "The Stars and Stripes Forever," the national march of the United States. He was born in Washington, D.C., on November 6, 1854.

His father played in the Marine Band. When Sousa was 13, his father signed him into the Marine Corps as an apprentice musician, a boy learning the work. He did it to keep his son from joining a circus band. Sousa served seven years.

On October 1, 1880, Sousa became the 17th leader of the Marine Band. He led it for 12 years under five presidents, from Rutherford B. Hayes to Benjamin Harrison. In 1892 he formed a band of his own.

On Christmas Day 1896 Sousa was on a ship crossing the Atlantic. He had just learned that his band's manager, David Blakely, had died. On that voyage he began "The Stars and Stripes Forever," and he finished it in April 1897. In 1987 members of Congress voted to make it the national march. Sousa also wrote 15 operettas, short comic operas, and he helped develop the sousaphone, a large brass horn made for marching bands.

#### Recording begins

In December 1877 Thomas Edison's workers built his first phonograph, a machine that recorded sound and played it back. Machines good enough to sell came on the market in 1888.

In 1890 two phonograph companies paid George W. Johnson 20 cents for each two-minute song he recorded on a wax cylinder. Johnson was a Black street whistler, born in Virginia in 1846. The cylinders played in coin-operated machines. No way yet existed to copy a cylinder in large numbers, so Johnson sang the same songs over and over, one cylinder at a time. Between 1890 and 1895 he made an estimated 25,000 to 50,000 cylinders.

His two best sellers were "The Laughing Song," which he wrote, and a whistling song by a white writer that mocked Black people. The title of that song used a racist insult for a Black person. In 1891 "The Laughing Song" was the best-selling record in the country for ten weeks, and Johnson is counted as the first Black recording star. In 1899 Johnson was put on trial for the murder of Roskin Stuart, the woman he lived with as his wife, who had been found beaten in their apartment. He was found not guilty. By 1905 record makers could press many copies from one recording, so they no longer needed him to sing each copy. His friend Len Spencer hired him as a doorman for his office. Johnson died in 1914 and was buried in a grave without a marker.

#### Ragtime, and songs that mocked Black people

Ragtime is music with a "ragged" rhythm. The tune lands between the beats while a steady beat keeps time underneath. On the piano, the left hand keeps the steady beat and the right hand plays the tune. Ragtime began among African Americans in the late 1800s. Accounts differ about the first printed ragtime piece, and they date it to 1895 or 1897.

In 1895 and 1896 Ernest Hogan, a Black performer from Bowling Green, Kentucky, who had started out in minstrel shows, wrote a hit song whose title used a racist insult for Black people. The title said that all Black people look alike. Many other writers copied it. People at the time named these copies after the insult. They were songs that used racist words and pictures to mock Black people.

<a id="story-scott-joplin"></a>

#### Scott Joplin

> **Who:** A Black composer and pianist who wrote the "Maple Leaf Rag" and an opera, *Treemonisha*.
>
> **When and where:** Born in northeastern Texas between mid-1867 and early 1868 (the date is not known for certain). Lived in Texarkana, Sedalia and St. Louis, Missouri, and New York. Died April 1, 1917, in New York.

Scott Joplin wrote the "Maple Leaf Rag," and in his last years he paid to print his own opera. He was born in northeastern Texas. The exact date is not known. The historian Edward A. Berlin places it between June 1867 and the middle of January 1868.

His father, Giles, had been enslaved in North Carolina. His mother, Florence, was born free in Kentucky. She cleaned houses, and Scott learned to play on her employer's piano. A teacher, Julius Weiss, gave him lessons.

Churches and brothels were among the few places where a Black pianist could find steady work. A brothel is a house where men paid women for sex. In 1891 he was a member of the Texarkana Minstrels, a group raising money for a monument to Jefferson Davis, the former president of the Confederacy. In 1894 he moved to Sedalia, Missouri. There he played cornet in a town band and studied music at George R. Smith College.

On August 10, 1899, Joplin signed a contract with John Stark, a Sedalia music store owner and publisher, to publish the "Maple Leaf Rag." Joplin was to get one cent for each copy sold. His first biographer said it sold 75,000 copies in six months. Berlin later found that the first 400 copies took a year to sell, which paid Joplin about $1. Later sales gave him a small, steady income. By 1909 they would have paid him about $600 a year, Berlin found.

He moved to St. Louis in 1901 and to New York in 1907. He wrote an opera, *Treemonisha*. It is set on a Texas plantation after the Civil War, and it tells of a young, educated Black woman who helps free her people from ignorance and superstition. No one would pay to stage it. In 1911 he printed it with his own money. In 1915 he played it in a hall in Harlem, with only a piano.

By 1916 Joplin had syphilis in its late stage. Syphilis is a disease passed from person to person during sex. Without treatment it can spread to the brain, where it causes confusion, changes in personality and dementia, the loss of memory and of the ability to think. On February 2, 1917, he was admitted to Manhattan State Hospital, a hospital for mental illness. He died there of the disease on April 1, 1917. No record describes how he was treated there. He was buried in a grave with no marker.

*Treemonisha* was first fully staged in January 1972, in Atlanta. In 1974, 57 years after his burial, his grave was given a marker. In 1976, 59 years after he died, Joplin won a Pulitzer Prize, a top American award.

#### The blues begins, and nobody wrote it down

The blues is a kind of Black music from the South. It grew out of the songs and calls that enslaved people sang as they worked in the fields. It also grew out of the songs of Black workers on farms, docks and river boats after slavery ended. No one knows who first played the blues, or when. Its beginning is usually placed between 1870 and 1900. In those years, freed Black families in the South who had no land of their own farmed a landowner's fields in return for a share of the crop. This was called sharecropping. The families bought tools, seed and food on credit at the landowner's store prices, and the debt rolled over from year to year and kept them on the land. No written description of the blues from before 1900 is known. The first written accounts come from just after 1900.

### 1900 to 1950

In the first half of the 1900s, record company managers began to record the blues, jazz and the music later called country. Black musicians in the South made the blues and jazz. Country music came from Southern singers and players, white ones like the Carter Family and Black ones like DeFord Bailey and Lesley Riddle. Bessie Smith's first record sold 780,000 copies, and Columbia paid her a set fee for each side and nothing more. The company kept the rest of the money. In 1921 Americans spent $106 million on records. From the 1920s, anyone with a radio could hear music at home for free. Owners and managers of clubs, hotels and concert halls kept Black people out, even Black stars. In 1939 Billie Holiday recorded "Strange Fruit," a song about Black people murdered by white mobs. That same year Marian Anderson sang outdoors in Washington to more than 75,000 people. The leaders of two indoor halls in the city had refused her.

#### The first written accounts of the blues, 1901 to 1903

The first written account of the kind of songs later called the blues comes from 1901 and 1902, in Mississippi. In May and June of both years, Charles Peabody dug into a Native mound in Coahoma County for Harvard University's Peabody Museum. He was an archaeologist, a scientist who digs up and studies things people left behind. He hired nine to fifteen Black men from the town of Clarksdale to do the digging. The men sang while they dug. Peabody wrote in 1903 that bosses sometimes hired a strong singer just to keep workers going. The men's songs were about hard luck, love and pay day. In one line the singer said he had been arrested for murder though he had never harmed anyone. Peabody did not use the word blues.

In about 1903 the bandleader W. C. Handy was waiting for a train at Tutwiler, Mississippi. A man beside him played a guitar by sliding a knife along the strings, and sang. No record names the man. Handy later published the song as "Yellow Dog Blues."

In 1912 Handy sold "The Memphis Blues" for $100. In 1914 he published "Saint Louis Blues." With Harry Pace, a Black banker, he ran a company called Pace and Handy that published music. Handy called himself the "Father of the Blues." Jelly Roll Morton disagreed. In a letter to the magazine *Down Beat*, he wrote that Handy had not started the music.

The singer Gertrude "Ma" Rainey said that in 1902 a girl in Missouri sang her a song about a man who had left a woman. Rainey began singing it in her shows. Paramount Records later advertised her as the "Mother of the Blues." Between 1923 and 1928 she made more than 100 records.

#### Records for Black buyers, and who was paid, 1920 to 1938

On August 10, 1920, Mamie Smith, a Black singer, recorded "Crazy Blues" for the Okeh record company. The songwriter Perry Bradford wrote it. Managers at Victor had turned Smith down after a try-out, so Bradford went to Fred Hager, who ran recording at Okeh. He told Hager that Smith could "do more with those songs than a monkey can do with a peanut." Some white people had already warned Hager not to record Black musicians, and he recorded her anyway. Within two months, buyers had paid a dollar each for 75,000 copies. It was the first blues record to become a big hit.

Record company managers then went looking for Black singers to sell records to Black buyers. By 1922 managers at Okeh were calling these records "race records." In 1921 the Black businessman Harry Pace started Black Swan Records. Black Swan paid its singers fair wages and let them record under their own names. Paramount took over Black Swan in 1924.

Columbia paid Bessie Smith a set fee for each side of a record, and no royalty, while it paid white singers royalties. A royalty is a small payment for every copy sold, paid for as long as the record sells. With a set fee, a singer earned the same whether the record sold a hundred copies or a million.

Robert Johnson, a Black guitarist from Mississippi, recorded 29 songs in 1936 and 1937, in a hotel room in San Antonio and in Dallas, both in Texas. His best seller, "Terraplane Blues," sold about 10,000 copies. His pay for the sessions is not on record. He died near Greenwood, Mississippi, on August 16, 1938, at 27. The cause of his death is not known. One story says he was poisoned, but no one has proved it. In 1998 Mississippi judges ruled that his son, Claud Johnson, was his only heir, the one person with the right to what Johnson left. That right was worth more than $1 million in royalties.

In June 1949 the editors of *Billboard*, a music magazine, renamed its "race records" sales chart "rhythm and blues." A writer named Jerry Wexler suggested the new name.

<a id="story-bessie-smith"></a>

#### Bessie Smith

> **Who:** A Black blues singer whose first record sold 780,000 copies in six months.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Chattanooga, Tennessee, on April 15, 1894 (the 1900 government count of the people gives July 1892). Recorded for Columbia Records from 1923. Died near Clarksdale, Mississippi, on September 26, 1937.
>
> **Movie:** *Bessie* (2015), an HBO drama film, with Queen Latifah as Smith.

Bessie Smith's first record sold 780,000 copies in six months, and she was paid $125 for each side, with no royalty. She was born in Chattanooga, Tennessee. Her family kept April 15, 1894, as her birthday. The 1900 census, the government's count of everyone in the country, gives July 1892.

Both her parents died when she was a child. She and her brother Andrew sang and danced for coins on the streets of Chattanooga. In 1912 she joined a traveling show as a dancer. Ma Rainey sang in the same show.

In 1923 Frank Walker of Columbia Records signed her. Her first record, "Down Hearted Blues," was the one that sold 780,000 copies in six months. Her contract paid her $125 for each side that could be used. Later contracts paid $150 and then $200 a side, and none of them paid a royalty. Record companies paid white singers more, and they gave white singers royalties.

She recorded between 150 and 200 songs. Cary O'Dell's essay for the Library of Congress states 150 in one place and close to 200 in another. On tour she earned up to $2,000 a week, and she traveled in her own railroad car.

On September 26, 1937, the car she rode in hit the back of a slow truck on Route 61 near Clarksdale, Mississippi. Her partner, Richard Morgan, was driving. Her right arm was almost torn off at the elbow. A white doctor from Memphis, Hugh Smith, stopped to help. An ambulance took her to the G. T. Thomas Afro-American Hospital in Clarksdale. Doctors there amputated her arm, which means they cut it off, and she died that morning.

In 1937 the record producer John Hammond wrote that she died because a white hospital refused to treat her. Dr. Smith said the ambulance would never have taken her to a white hospital. Her biographer, Chris Albertson, showed that Hammond's story was a myth.

More than 10,000 people came to her funeral in Philadelphia. Her grave had no stone for more than 30 years, until the singer Janis Joplin helped pay for one. Later Jack Gee Jr., the son of her husband, sued Columbia. The judges ruled against him because he had waited too long to sue. They did not decide whether she had been cheated.

#### Jazz on record, 1917 to 1931

Jazz began in the Black communities of New Orleans in the late 1800s and early 1900s. The first jazz record, though, was made by white musicians. On February 26, 1917, five white musicians from New Orleans recorded two songs in New York for the Victor company. They called themselves the Original Dixieland Jass Band. Victor's managers put the record on sale in May 1917. By some counts it sold more than a million copies. The band's leader, Nick LaRocca, later claimed that he had invented jazz. A story says that in 1915 Victor had asked a Black New Orleans cornet player, Freddie Keppard, to record first, and that he said no. A cornet is a brass horn like a small trumpet. The historian John Edward Hasse calls that story a legend.

The Cotton Club in Harlem, New York, was run by Owney Madden, a gangster who sold illegal liquor. Madden's managers hired Black musicians and dancers, and they let in only white customers, apart from a few Black stars. The club's dancers had to be light-skinned, at least 5 feet 6 inches tall and under 21. Duke Ellington's band played there from December 4, 1927, to June 30, 1931. When Ellington asked, the people running the club let in a few more Black customers.

<a id="story-louis-armstrong"></a>

#### Louis Armstrong

> **Who:** A Black trumpet player and singer from New Orleans who made jazz records with his Hot Five and Hot Seven.
>
> **When and where:** Born in New Orleans. Most sources give August 4, 1901. He often said July 4, 1900. Lived in Chicago and New York. Died in New York on July 6, 1971.
>
> **Movie:** *Louis Armstrong's Black & Blues* (2022), a documentary about him.

Louis Armstrong learned to play the cornet in a home for Black boys in New Orleans, where a judge sent him after an arrest. On New Year's Eve 1912 he fired his stepfather's gun into the air. It was loaded with a blank, a shell with gunpowder but no bullet. Police arrested him, and the next day a judge sent him to the Colored Waif's Home, a reform home for Black boys. There a teacher, Peter Davis, taught him the cornet in the home's band.

In 1922 the bandleader King Oliver invited him to Chicago to play second cornet in his band. From November 1925 Armstrong made records for Okeh with his own groups, the Hot Five and the Hot Seven.

On September 17, 1957, in Grand Forks, North Dakota, a reporter asked Armstrong about the fight over nine Black students entering Central High School in Little Rock, Arkansas. Armstrong said: "The way they are treating my people in the South, the government can go to hell." He called President Dwight Eisenhower "two faced" and said he had "no guts."

Staff at WBKJ, a radio station in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, threw out his records. Officials at the University of Arkansas cancelled his invitation to play a dance. The congressman Adam Clayton Powell said Armstrong "didn't know what he was talking about." On September 24 Eisenhower sent soldiers to protect the students. Armstrong then sent him a telegram: "If you decide to walk into the schools with the little colored kids, take me along Daddy. God bless you."

#### Country music on record: Bristol, 1927

From July 25 to August 5, 1927, Ralph Peer of the Victor record company recorded 76 songs by 19 singers and groups in Bristol, Tennessee. He set up on the third floor of a hat and glove company's building. Each performer got $50 in cash for each side, plus 2½ cents for each record sold. The Carter Family recorded on August 1 and 2, and a singer named Jimmie Rodgers on August 4.

Peer took no salary from Victor. Instead he took a royalty of one cent on each record side, which he split with the singer. He also kept the copyright of the songs he recorded, including old songs passed down from singer to singer. A copyright is the legal right to be paid when a song is printed, recorded or played. In 1928 Peer started a company, Southern Music Publishing, to collect that money. He offered to publish the songs that A. P. Carter of the Carter Family had gathered, if Carter would claim that he wrote them.

<a id="story-maybelle-carter"></a>

#### Maybelle Carter

> **Who:** Guitarist and singer in the Carter Family, who changed how the guitar is played in country music.
>
> **When and where:** Born May 10, 1909, in Nickelsville, Virginia. Recorded at Bristol, Tennessee, in 1927, at 18. Died October 23, 1978, in Hendersonville, Tennessee.
>
> **Movie:** *The Carter Family: Will the Circle Be Unbroken* (2005), a PBS *American Experience* documentary about the family.

Maybelle Carter found a way to play the guitar that made it a lead instrument in country music. She picked out the tune with her thumb on the three low strings and strummed the three high strings with her index finger to keep the rhythm. It is called the thumb-lead style. She first recorded "Wildwood Flower," played this way, in 1928.

She sang and played with Sara Carter and A. P. Carter as the Carter Family. At Bristol in August 1927 she was 18. The Carter Family was paid Victor's rate of $50 a side and 2½ cents for each record sold.

From December 1928 A. P. Carter went looking for old songs with Lesley Riddle. Riddle was a Black guitarist from Burnsville, North Carolina. In 1927 he had lost his right leg at the knee after an accident at a cement plant. On their trips, Carter wrote down the words while Riddle memorized the tunes. Riddle lived with the Carters for a time and taught Maybelle his finger-picking blues guitar style. Maybelle said she learned guitar runs from him, including the ones she played in "Cannonball Blues."

No record shows that Riddle was paid, or named as a writer, for any of the songs he helped gather.

Later Maybelle led a group with her daughters, called Mother Maybelle and the Carter Sisters. From 1968 she toured with her son-in-law, the singer Johnny Cash.

#### The Grand Ole Opry, from 1925

On November 28, 1925, George D. Hay started a country music show on WSM, a Nashville radio station owned by the National Life and Accident Insurance Company. He called it the *WSM Barn Dance*. The first player was a 77-year-old fiddler, Uncle Jimmy Thompson.

On December 10, 1927, the *Barn Dance* came on the air after a program of opera music. The Black harmonica player DeFord Bailey played his "Pan American Blues." Hay then told listeners, "from now on, we will present 'The Grand Ole Opry.'" From 1939 to 1956 one hour of the show went out across the country on the NBC radio network.

<a id="story-deford-bailey"></a>

#### DeFord Bailey

> **Who:** A Black harmonica player, for fifteen years one of the best-loved stars of the Grand Ole Opry.
>
> **When and where:** Born December 14, 1899, in Smith County, Tennessee. Played on Nashville radio from 1926 to 1941. Died July 2, 1982.
>
> **Movie:** *DeFord Bailey: A Legend Lost* (2002), a Nashville Public Television documentary about him.

DeFord Bailey was a Black harmonica player. In 1927 George D. Hay named the Grand Ole Opry right after Bailey played. Bailey was born in Smith County, Tennessee, on December 14, 1899. His family played what he called "Black hillbilly music."

Polio struck him when he was three. Polio is a disease caused by a virus that can damage the nerves that move the muscles. It stunted Bailey's growth and left his back bent.

He played on the *WSM Barn Dance* from June 1926. In December 1927, after his "Pan American Blues," George D. Hay gave the show the name Grand Ole Opry. Accounts of his pay differ. One says he got a fixed $5 at first, less than the white players he toured with. The Country Music Hall of Fame says he was one of the best-paid stars on the show.

He toured the South with white stars such as Roy Acuff, Bill Monroe and Uncle Dave Macon. Hotels and restaurants would not serve him because he was Black. The other players brought him food, or got him into hotels by the fire escape.

In 1941 the managers of most radio stations stopped playing songs licensed by ASCAP, a group that collected money for songwriters. ASCAP's leaders had raised its fees. Managers at WSM told Bailey not to play his ASCAP songs, which were some of his most popular ones. They fired him at the end of 1941. In 1945 Hay wrote a book about the show. In it he called Bailey "lazy" and wrote that he "refused to learn new tunes." Bailey later said that Hay had treated him kindly and had written those words to please his bosses.

After 1941 Bailey ran a shoeshine stand and rented out rooms. He almost never played in public again until 1974. In 2005 he was named to the Country Music Hall of Fame.

#### Radio, the Depression and two fights over pay, 1906 to 1944

In 1906 John Philip Sousa wrote that records and player pianos were becoming a "substitute for human skill, intelligence and soul." He called records "canned music." In 1909 members of Congress passed a copyright law that let anyone record a song without asking, as long as they paid the song's owner a set fee.

Americans spent $106 million on records in 1921. A history of records from the University of Michigan Press says they did not spend that much again until 1945. IASA, a group of sound archivists, says sales did not reach their old peak until the 1950s. In the early 1930s, during the Great Depression, record sales fell to about one tenth of what they had been in the 1920s.

Radio stations paid fees to play songs. The fees went to ASCAP, a group that collected money for songwriters. In 1939 ASCAP's leaders announced higher fees, and radio station owners started their own group to collect fees for songwriters, called BMI. In 1941 managers at almost every station, and at all three national networks, stopped playing ASCAP songs. ASCAP had not wanted writers of blues, gospel, country, folk and Latin music. BMI became the first licensing group to sign them.

On August 1, 1942, James Petrillo, the head of the musicians' union, told its members to stop making records. He wanted musicians to be paid when radio stations and jukeboxes played records instead of hiring live bands. In September 1943 Decca signed an agreement to pay a fee on every record into a union fund. Victor and Columbia signed on November 11, 1944. Union rules still let singers record with voices alone, so for two years singers made records without bands.

#### Gospel, shape notes and prison recordings

Gospel is a kind of Black church music. Thomas A. Dorsey had played piano for Ma Rainey under the name "Georgia Tom." In August 1932 his wife, Nettie, and their newborn son died, and he wrote "Take My Hand, Precious Lord." That year he started the first Black-owned company to publish gospel music. In 1933 he started a national convention of gospel choirs. He led the music at Pilgrim Baptist Church in Chicago for fifty years. "I'm not ashamed of my blues," he said. "It's all the same talent."

Mahalia Jackson came to Chicago from New Orleans in 1927, and Dorsey trained her. She refused to sing the blues. Managers at Decca offered to keep recording her if she sang blues, and she refused. Her "Move On Up a Little Higher" of 1947 sold about two million copies.

In 1934 Judge Jackson, a shape-note singer from Alabama, printed *The Colored Sacred Harp*. Judge was his first name. "Colored" in the title was a word of that time for Black people. It was a book of 77 church songs printed in shape notes, notes whose shapes tell the singer which sound to sing. Eighteen of the songs were his own. He and Bishop J. D. Walker paid to print 1,000 copies, and Jackson sold them door to door.

From June 1933 John Lomax and his son Alan recorded singers in Southern prisons. John Lomax said he wanted music "not yet influenced by jazz and the radio." From 1934 he ran the Library of Congress's folk song collection, for a salary of one dollar. At Angola, the Louisiana state prison, they recorded Huddie Ledbetter, called Lead Belly. He was serving time for stabbing a man in a fight. Years before, he had been convicted in Texas of killing a relative, Will Stafford. He was in prison there from 1918 until the governor of Texas, Pat Neff, pardoned him in 1925, after Lead Belly sang him a song asking to be freed. He left Angola on August 1, 1934. A prison official later wrote that his singing had nothing to do with his release.

John Lomax then managed Lead Belly and took a share of his pay. The two men split over money in 1935. In 1936 Lomax published a book that printed Lead Belly's song "Goodnight, Irene" with both men named as its writers. Lomax had recorded the song. He had not written it. In 1950, the year after Lead Belly died, a group called the Weavers sold 2 million copies of "Goodnight, Irene."

#### Native songs, Hawaiian guitar and a new songwriter

On March 28, 1900, the band of the Carlisle Indian School, a boarding school for Native children in Pennsylvania, played the "Aboriginal Suite" at Carnegie Hall in New York. Its composer and conductor was Dennison Wheelock, an Oneida graduate of the school. Richard Henry Pratt had made him the Carlisle bandmaster in 1892, the first Native bandmaster there. He later became a lawyer and argued cases for Native nations before the Supreme Court.

Scientists recorded thousands of Native songs on wax cylinders in these years. A cylinder is a wax tube that holds two or three minutes of sound. The Library of Congress holds about 10,000 cylinders, and nearly 8,000 of them hold Native songs and speech. Many held sacred songs meant only for ceremonies. One collector, Francis La Flesche, took singers from Oklahoma to Washington, D.C., so that neighbors who objected could not stop him from recording ceremonial songs. No record shows that the singers were paid. From 1907 Frances Densmore recorded the songs of the Ojibwe, Sioux, Mandan, Hidatsa, Tohono O'odham, Seminole and other nations for the Smithsonian Institution.

In 1889 Joseph Kekuku, a Hawaiian student at the Kamehameha School for Boys, found that he could change a guitar's pitch by sliding a steel bar along the strings. In 1893 a group of mostly American businessmen overthrew Hawaii's queen, Liliʻuokalani. Before they moved, John L. Stevens, the top US official in Hawaii, had 162 American sailors and Marines brought ashore. In 1897 Native Hawaiians put 21,269 signatures on petitions, written requests to the government, against joining the United States. In 1898 members of Congress voted to annex Hawaii anyway, which means they made it part of the United States. From 1904 Kekuku played this steel guitar in theaters across the mainland United States.

Irving Berlin, born Israel Beilin, came to New York from the Russian Empire in 1893, at age five. He could not read music, and he could play the piano in only one key. He wrote "Alexander's Ragtime Band" in 1911. He owned his own songs through his own publishing company. He gave all the money from "God Bless America," which Kate Smith first sang in 1938, to the Boy Scouts and Girl Scouts.

<a id="story-woody-guthrie"></a>

#### Woody Guthrie

> **Who:** A folk singer and songwriter who wrote about poor farm families, workers and migrants in the 1930s and 1940s.
>
> **When and where:** Born July 14, 1912, in Okemah, Oklahoma. Lived in Oklahoma, California and New York. Died October 3, 1967, in New York.
>
> **Movie:** *Bound for Glory* (1976), a Hollywood film based loosely on his own book about his life.

Woody Guthrie wrote "This Land Is Your Land" and many other songs about poor farm families and workers. He was born in Okemah, Oklahoma, on July 14, 1912.

His mother, Nora, had Huntington's disease and was put in a hospital. No account names who sent her there. Huntington's is a disease passed down in families. It destroys parts of the brain. A person with it makes movements they cannot control, has changes in mood, and loses the ability to think.

In the 1930s Guthrie joined the farm families who left the Great Plains for California after years of drought, the time called the Dust Bowl. He sang on a Los Angeles radio station, KFVD. In 1940 he made an album called *Dust Bowl Ballads* for Victor.

On February 23, 1940, in a New York hotel, he wrote "This Land Is Your Land." He wrote it as an answer to Irving Berlin's "God Bless America," which Kate Smith sang on the radio. His first title was "God Blessed America for Me." His handwritten copy had two verses that were often left out later. One is about a sign that says "No Trespassing." The other is about hungry people at a relief office, a place that gave out food or money to the poor.

In May 1941 Paul Raver, the head of a federal agency called the Bonneville Power Administration, hired him for one month for $266. His boss, Stephen Kahn, wanted three pages of songs a day for a film about the agency's dams on the Columbia River. Guthrie wrote 26 songs in that month. One of them was "Roll On, Columbia." Kahn later said the government had never gotten "a better investment on its money."

On his guitar Guthrie wrote "This machine kills fascists." Fascists were the followers of the dictators who ruled Italy and Germany. In the Second World War he served in the Merchant Marine, the ships that carried supplies. In 1952 doctors found that he had Huntington's disease. He spent his last years in hospitals in New Jersey and New York, and he died at Creedmoor hospital in New York in 1967, at 55.

#### Strange Fruit, 1939

"Strange Fruit" is a song about the lynching of Black Americans. Lynching means a mob killing a person without a trial, often by hanging. The song describes the bodies of Black people hanging from trees in the South. It describes their bulging eyes and twisted mouths, and the smell of burning flesh.

Abel Meeropol, an English teacher in the Bronx, New York, wrote the song under the name Lewis Allan. He wrote it after he saw a photograph of the lynching of Thomas Shipp and Abram Smith in Marion, Indiana.

On August 7, 1930, a white mob of between 5,000 and 10,000 people broke into the jail in Marion. The mob wanted three young Black men held there. The three were being held for the murder of a white man, Claude Deeter, and the rape of a woman, Mary Ball. Rape means forcing a person to have sex. Men in the mob beat Shipp and Smith, who were both 19, and hanged them. People in the crowd took parts of their bodies as souvenirs. The third prisoner, James Cameron, who was 16, was beaten but lived, after someone in the crowd said he was innocent. Cameron waited about a year in jail for his trial, and accounts of what Mary Ball said there differ. The historian James H. Madison writes that she said she had been raped but that the night was too dark to tell whether Cameron was one of the men. Fran Kaplan of America's Black Holocaust Museum writes that Ball testified she had not been raped at all. Cameron was convicted on a lesser charge, of helping before the crime, and a judge sentenced him to 2 to 21 years. He served four years in prison. In 1993 the governor of Indiana pardoned him. Leaders of the NAACP, a group that fights for the rights of Black Americans, named 27 people they suspected of the lynching. All-white juries found the mob's leaders not guilty.

Billie Holiday first sang "Strange Fruit" at Café Society, a club in New York, in 1939. She closed her show with it. The waiters stopped serving, the room went dark except for a light on her face, and she sang no more songs after it. Managers at Columbia would not record it. John Hammond of Columbia said record stores and radio stations in the South would object. Milt Gabler of Commodore Records recorded it on April 20, 1939. It became her best-selling record.

<a id="story-billie-holiday"></a>

#### Billie Holiday

> **Who:** A Black jazz singer who recorded "Strange Fruit," a song about lynching, in 1939.
>
> **When and where:** Born Eleanora Fagan on April 7, 1915, in Philadelphia. Grew up in Baltimore. Sang in New York. Died July 17, 1959, in New York.
>
> **Movie:** *Billie* (2019), a documentary about her.

Billie Holiday was a Black jazz singer whom federal drug agents arrested three times, the last time in her hospital bed as she was dying. She was born Eleanora Fagan in Philadelphia on April 7, 1915, and grew up in Baltimore.

At nine she was brought before a juvenile court, a court for children, for missing school. The court's judge sent her to the House of the Good Shepherd, a Catholic reform school for girls, a school where courts sent children who were in trouble. As a young girl she ran errands in a brothel, a house where men paid women for sex. She also scrubbed steps and floors in the homes of her neighborhood.

In 1938 she sang with Artie Shaw's band, whose other members were white. At the Lincoln Hotel in New York, the managers made her use the service elevator because white guests complained. She left the band soon after.

Harry Anslinger ran the Federal Bureau of Narcotics, the government's drug police, from 1930 to 1962. On May 16, 1947, federal agents arrested Holiday for having narcotics, illegal drugs, in her New York apartment. She pleaded guilty, and a judge sent her to the Alderson Federal Prison Camp in West Virginia for a year. She said later: "It was called 'The United States of America versus Billie Holiday'. And that's just the way it felt."

Because of the conviction, she lost her New York City cabaret card, the police license a performer needed to work in any club that sold alcohol. After that she sang in concert halls and theaters. In January 1949 a federal agent, George White, arrested her again, in a San Francisco hotel.

In 2015 the writer Johann Hari wrote that Anslinger's agents went after her from 1939 because she sang "Strange Fruit." The jazz writer Lewis Porter points out that no earlier source says this.

In 1959 she was in Metropolitan Hospital in New York with liver and heart disease. On May 31, federal narcotics agents arrested her in her hospital bed and handcuffed her to it. Writing in *TIME* in 2019, John Halpern and David Blistein said that Anslinger ordered the arrest. Police guarded her room until a judge ordered the handcuffs taken off. She died there on July 17, 1959, at 44, with 70 cents in the bank. Her liver was scarred, a disease called cirrhosis, and her heart failed.

#### Marian Anderson at the Lincoln Memorial, 1939

In January 1939 Howard University in Washington, D.C., asked to rent Constitution Hall for an Easter concert by the Black singer Marian Anderson. The hall belonged to the Daughters of the American Revolution, or DAR, a women's group. Its leaders refused. Since 1932 DAR leaders had let only white performers use the hall. Frank Ballou, the head of Washington's public schools, also refused to let her use the hall of Central High School, a white school. The members of the school board backed him.

First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt quit the DAR on February 26, 1939. She wrote that its leaders had "an opportunity to lead in an enlightened way" and had "failed." Harold Ickes, the Secretary of the Interior, then set up a concert on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial. On Easter Sunday, April 9, 1939, Anderson sang there to more than 75,000 people, and millions more heard her on the radio. She began with "My Country, 'Tis of Thee."

<a id="story-marian-anderson"></a>

#### Marian Anderson

> **Who:** A Black contralto, a singer with a low woman's voice, who sang at the Lincoln Memorial in 1939 and was the first Black American singer at the Metropolitan Opera.
>
> **When and where:** Born February 27, 1897, in Philadelphia. Died April 8, 1993, in Portland, Oregon.
>
> **Movie:** *Marian Anderson: The Lincoln Memorial Concert* (1939), a short film of the concert.

Marian Anderson was a contralto, a singer with a low woman's voice. She was the first Black American singer to perform at the Metropolitan Opera in New York. She was born in Philadelphia on February 27, 1897.

As a young woman she applied to a music school in Philadelphia. The school's officials turned her away because they took only white students. In Salzburg, Austria, in 1935, the conductor Arturo Toscanini told her she had "a voice heard once in a hundred years."

In 1939 the DAR's president, Sarah Corbin Robert, and its other leaders kept her out of Constitution Hall. She sang outdoors at the Lincoln Memorial instead, on April 9, 1939.

On January 7, 1955, at 57, she sang at the Metropolitan Opera. She sang the part of Ulrica, a fortune teller, in Verdi's opera *Un ballo in maschera*. She sang at the March on Washington in August 1963. That year she was given the Presidential Medal of Freedom, an award given by the president.

### 1950 to 2000

In the early 1950s Black musicians made rock and roll out of rhythm and blues and gospel. White singers then sold more copies of some of those songs than the Black singers who recorded them first. Record company owners, managers and publishers kept much of the money from songs such as "Hound Dog" and "That's All Right." Big Mama Thornton said she got one check for $500 for "Hound Dog." In Detroit, Berry Gordy built Motown, which became the largest Black-owned business on one magazine's list. Civil rights marchers sang old church songs with new words at their mass meetings. In 1973 a teenage DJ and his sister held a party in the Bronx, in New York City, that people now name as the start of hip-hop. In 1985 senators held a hearing on the words of songs, and leaders of the RIAA, the record companies' own group, agreed to put warning labels on some albums.

#### Rock and roll, and who got paid for it

Sister Rosetta Tharpe, a Black gospel singer from Arkansas, played electric guitar in church music from the late 1930s. Her "Strange Things Happening Every Day," from 1944, was the first gospel record to reach the rhythm and blues sales chart. Some scholars call it the first rock and roll record. She was an influence on Elvis Presley, Little Richard, Chuck Berry and Johnny Cash.

Fats Domino's "The Fat Man," from 1949, had sold a million copies by 1951. Chuck Berry's "Maybellene," from 1955, sold more than a million. When Berry first saw his record, it listed the disc jockey Alan Freed and another man as its co-writers. A disc jockey is a person who plays records on the radio. Co-writers have a right to part of the money a song earns its writers. Berry later won back full credit.

White singers made cover versions of songs by Black singers. A cover version is a new recording of a song that someone else has already recorded. In 1955 Georgia Gibbs, a white singer, copied LaVern Baker's "Tweedle Dee" note for note. Baker's record reached No. 14 on the national pop chart. Gibbs's copy reached No. 1. Baker tried to sue Gibbs for $250,000. She asked Congress to treat such copies as a breach of copyright. Representative Charles Diggs led an investigation by Congress into what he called "song theft." No law came of it.

Pat Boone, a white singer, covered Fats Domino's "Ain't That a Shame" in 1955. It was Boone's first No. 1 record. Domino and his co-writer, Dave Bartholomew, still earned writers' royalties from it. Boone also covered Little Richard's "Tutti Frutti," and Boone's record ranked higher on the national pop chart than Little Richard's own. Little Richard later said that the people running his record company, Specialty Records, had cut his royalty rate without telling him. In 1984 he sued the company and its owner, Art Rupe, for $112 million in royalties he said he was owed. They settled out of court in 1986, which means they reached an agreement and the case never went to trial.

Payola is paying a disc jockey or a radio station in secret to play a record. In 1959 and 1960 members of a House committee, led by Representative Oren Harris, held hearings on payola. Alan Freed refused to sign a statement that he had taken no bribes, and the managers of the radio station WABC fired him in November 1959. In 1962 he told a court he was guilty of taking bribes and paid a $300 fine. In 1960 members of Congress made payola a crime, punished by up to a year in jail. The older song publishers in ASCAP pushed for the hearings, partly because they opposed rock and roll.

#### Hound Dog: Big Mama Thornton and Elvis Presley

The songwriters Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller wrote "Hound Dog." Willie Mae "Big Mama" Thornton, a blues singer from Alabama, recorded it on August 13, 1952. Don Robey's Peacock Records put it out in 1953, and it was No. 1 on the rhythm and blues chart for seven weeks. Robey guessed that it sold 500,000 to 750,000 copies.

Thornton said: "That song sold over two million records. I got one check for $500 and never saw another." Robey put his own name on the copyright form as one of the song's writers.

Elvis Presley recorded "Hound Dog" for RCA on July 2, 1956. His record was No. 1 on the pop chart for 11 weeks and sold about 10 million copies. He followed a reworked version by Freddie Bell and the Bellboys, a band he had heard in Las Vegas that year. Leiber and Stoller earned large royalties only after Presley's record. Thornton died poor in a Los Angeles boarding house in 1984, of heart and liver disease. She was buried in a grave shared with two other people.

<a id="story-elvis-presley"></a>

#### Elvis Presley

> **Who:** A white rock and roll singer from Mississippi and Tennessee whose records sold an estimated 500 million copies.
>
> **When and where:** Born January 8, 1935, in Tupelo, Mississippi. Moved to Memphis, Tennessee, in 1948. Died August 16, 1977, at his Memphis home, Graceland, at 42.
>
> **Movie:** *Elvis* (2022), a Hollywood drama film about him and his manager.

In 1954 Elvis Presley recorded a blues song by a Black singer, and his record of "Hound Dog" followed a song that had been a hit for a Black singer first. His manager took up to half of some of his income. He was born in Tupelo, Mississippi, on January 8, 1935, and his family moved to Memphis in 1948.

He first heard music at his family's church, an Assembly of God church. In Memphis he listened to Black blues and rhythm and blues singers on the radio.

Sam Phillips owned Sun Records in Memphis. He recorded Black blues musicians such as Howlin' Wolf and B. B. King. His office manager, Marion Keisker, said he often told her: "If I could find a white man who had the Negro sound and the Negro feel, I could make a billion dollars." "Negro" was a word of that time for Black people. On the night of July 5, 1954, at Sun, Presley sang "That's All Right," a blues song by the Black singer Arthur Crudup. Phillips recorded it.

Crudup had recorded the song for RCA in 1946. He said later: "I realised I was making everybody rich, and here I was poor." In 1968 a publisher backed out of a $60,000 settlement with him at the last moment. In 1971 a songwriters' group got him more than $10,000 in royalties he had not been paid. He died in 1974.

In November 1955 Phillips and Presley's manager, Colonel Tom Parker, sold Presley's contract to RCA for $40,000. Parker took 25 percent of Presley's pay. In 1967 Presley agreed to raise Parker's share to 50 percent of some of his income. In 1973 Parker sold RCA the rights to all of Presley's old records for $5.4 million. Because of that sale, Presley's family got no royalties on those records after he died. In 1981 Blanchard Tual, a lawyer whom a judge had appointed, called the 50 percent share "extortionate," which means unfairly high. He called the 1973 sale "unethical and poorly handled."

Presley served in the Army from 1958 to 1960. His record sales are estimated at about 500 million copies around the world. He died at Graceland on August 16, 1977, at 42.

#### Motown, soul and gospel

On January 12, 1959, Berry Gordy Jr. of Detroit started a record company with an $800 loan from his family's savings fund. It was later called Motown. From 1960 to 1969, 79 Motown songs reached the top ten of the national pop chart. In 1973 the editors of *Black Enterprise* magazine began ranking the largest Black-owned businesses. Motown was first on that list, with $40 million in sales, and it stayed first until 1983. Gordy sold Motown in 1988 for $61 million.

A group of Detroit studio musicians, later called the Funk Brothers, played on most Motown hits from 1959 to 1972. No Motown record listed their names until Marvin Gaye's album *What's Going On* in 1971. Gordy fined any of them he caught recording for other companies.

Ray Charles had been blind since he was about seven. In "I Got a Woman," from 1954, he mixed gospel with the blues, and some church people objected. In 1961 he refused to play a dance in Augusta, Georgia, when he learned that the audience would be split by race. The promoter sued him, and in 1962 a judge fined him $757. His 1959 contract with ABC-Paramount promised that he would own his master recordings, the original tapes that every copy is made from, in time.

Sam Cooke, a singer from Mississippi who had led the gospel group the Soul Stirrers, started his own record company and his own company to publish his songs. From 1963 his own company owned his master recordings. He was among the first Black artists to control his own business. On December 11, 1964, a Los Angeles motel manager, Bertha Franklin, shot and killed him. A coroner's jury called it justifiable homicide, a killing the law excuses. His family has disputed that account.

James Brown paid for the recording of his 1963 album *Live at the Apollo* himself. On April 4, 1968, Martin Luther King Jr. was shot and killed. James Earl Ray later pleaded guilty to his murder. The next day, Brown gave a free concert in Boston that was shown on television. His song "Say It Loud, I'm Black and I'm Proud" came out that August.

<a id="story-aretha-franklin"></a>

#### Aretha Franklin

> **Who:** A Black singer who recorded "Respect" in 1967.
>
> **When and where:** Born March 25, 1942, in Memphis, Tennessee. Grew up in Detroit, Michigan. Died there August 16, 2018.
>
> **Movie:** *Amazing Grace* (2018), a documentary film of her 1972 gospel concert in a Los Angeles church.

Aretha Franklin took Otis Redding's song "Respect" and turned it into a woman's demand, and it went to No. 1 on the pop chart in 1967. She was born in Memphis, Tennessee, on March 25, 1942. Her father, the Reverend C. L. Franklin, led New Bethel Baptist Church in Detroit, and she sang there as a child. At 14 she recorded a gospel album, *Songs of Faith*. She had her first child at 12 and her second at 15.

She recorded for Columbia from 1960 to 1966 and had few hits. Jerry Wexler then brought her to Atlantic Records. In January 1967 she recorded for one day at FAME Studios in Muscle Shoals, Alabama, before a fight broke out in the studio.

Redding had written and recorded "Respect" in 1965. In his song a man asks for respect when he comes home. Franklin recorded it on February 14, 1967, in New York. She and her sister Carolyn made it a woman's demand. They spelled out the word "R-E-S-P-E-C-T" and added new lines. It was No. 1 on the pop chart for two weeks and on the rhythm and blues chart for eight. It became a song of the women's movement and of the civil rights movement. Redding called it the song "that a girl took away from me."

In October 1970 FBI agents arrested the Black activist Angela Davis. She was charged with kidnapping and with the murder of Judge Harold Haley, who was killed in an attack on a California courthouse. Franklin said, "Angela Davis must go free." In June 1972 an all-white jury found Davis not guilty.

In January 1972 Franklin recorded the gospel album *Amazing Grace* at New Temple Missionary Baptist Church in Los Angeles. It sold more than two million copies. The film made at the same time was not shown until 2018, because the sound and the pictures could not be matched. In 1987 she became the first woman named to the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. She died in Detroit on August 16, 2018.

#### Songs of the civil rights movement

"We Shall Overcome" started as a church hymn, "I'll Overcome Some Day," that Charles Albert Tindley wrote in 1901. In 1945 and 1946 tobacco workers went on strike at a cigar factory in Charleston, South Carolina. One of them, Lucille Simmons, led the strikers in singing "We Will Overcome." Zilphia Horton of the Highlander Folk School learned it from her and printed it in 1947. The folk singer Pete Seeger changed "will" to "shall," because, he said, "'We shall' opens the mouth wider." From 1959 Guy Carawan taught the song to young civil rights workers.

On August 28, 1963, at the March on Washington, Mahalia Jackson sang "I've Been 'Buked and I've Been Scorned." Marian Anderson sang "He's Got the Whole World in His Hands," and Joan Baez led "We Shall Overcome." Odetta sang "I'm On My Way," Peter, Paul and Mary sang "Blowin' in the Wind," and Bob Dylan joined Baez for "When the Ship Comes In." During Martin Luther King Jr.'s speech, Jackson called out to him, "Tell them about the dream, Martin!"

On March 7, 1965, about 600 marchers set out from Selma, Alabama. At the Edmund Pettus Bridge, Alabama state troopers and other officers, led by Major John Cloud, attacked them with nightsticks and tear gas. At least 50 marchers went to the hospital. On March 15 President Lyndon Johnson spoke to Congress and used the song's words: "And we shall overcome." In January 2018, after a court case, the company that held the song's copyright gave it up. Since then anyone may use it freely.

<a id="story-bernice-johnson-reagon"></a>

#### Bernice Johnson Reagon

> **Who:** A Black student in Albany, Georgia, who led singing at civil rights meetings and sang with the SNCC Freedom Singers.
>
> **When and where:** Born October 4, 1942, in Albany, Georgia. Died July 16, 2024.

Bernice Johnson Reagon led the singing at civil rights meetings in Albany, Georgia, and changed the words of old spirituals to fit the protests. Spirituals are religious songs first made by enslaved Black people. She was born in Albany on October 4, 1942.

She joined the NAACP Youth Council in Albany. Officials at Albany State College suspended her for her part in the protests. At mass meetings she took old spirituals and put new words in them. Of one song she said: "So instead I put in freedom and by the second line everyone was singing."

She joined the Freedom Singers of SNCC, the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, with Cordell Reagon, Rutha Mae Harris and Chuck Neblett. She married Cordell Reagon, who had started the group. The group traveled 50,000 miles in nine months to sing about the movement, without taking a single flight, and its first tour raised nearly $50,000 for SNCC. She said of the group, "There weren't soloists, there were song leaders." She called it "a singing newspaper."

In 1973 she started Sweet Honey in the Rock, a group of African American women who sing without instruments. She later worked for the Smithsonian Institution as a curator, a person in charge of a museum's collections. Through radio, film and concerts, she helped people study the songs and stories that Black Americans passed down by word of mouth. She died on July 16, 2024.

<a id="story-bob-dylan"></a>

#### Bob Dylan

> **Who:** A songwriter of the folk music revival of the early 1960s and after, and winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature.
>
> **When and where:** Born Robert Allen Zimmerman on May 24, 1941, in Duluth, Minnesota. Grew up in Hibbing, Minnesota. Moved to New York in 1961.
>
> **Movie:** *No Direction Home: Bob Dylan* (2005), a documentary by Martin Scorsese.

In 2016 Bob Dylan won the Nobel Prize in Literature, a world prize for writers, for his songs. He won it "for having created new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition." He was born Robert Allen Zimmerman in Duluth, Minnesota, on May 24, 1941.

He moved to New York in January 1961 and visited Woody Guthrie, who was then in a mental hospital in New Jersey with Huntington's disease. In 1963 he released the album *The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan*. At the March on Washington that August he sang "Only a Pawn in Their Game."

At the Newport Folk Festival in 1965 he played an electric guitar. The leaders of the folk music world met him with hostility.

#### Country music from Nashville and Bakersfield

Hank Williams learned guitar as a boy in Alabama from a Black street musician, Rufus "Tee-Tot" Payne, who taught him in return for money or meals. Williams had 12 No. 1 country records. He was born with a defect of the spine that caused him pain all his life, and he drank and took painkillers. Grand Ole Opry managers dropped him in August 1952 for drunkenness and missed shows. He died in the back seat of a car near Oak Hill, West Virginia, on January 1, 1953. He was 29.

Patsy Cline recorded "Crazy," a song by Willie Nelson, in 1961. She died in a plane crash near Camden, Tennessee, on March 5, 1963, at 30. In 1973 she became the first woman in the Country Music Hall of Fame.

In the late 1950s Buck Owens, Merle Haggard and other musicians in Bakersfield, California, played country music on electric guitars, often two Fender Telecasters. Nashville records of those years added orchestras and a polished sound, and the Bakersfield musicians broke from it. Many of their listeners were the families of people who had come to California in the Dust Bowl years.

Johnny Cash recorded two concerts for prisoners at Folsom State Prison in California on January 13, 1968. The album ends with "Greystone Chapel," a song by a prisoner, Glen Sherley. It sold 500,000 copies by October 1968. Cash himself never served a prison sentence.

Loretta Lynn's "The Pill," from 1975, is about a wife who is tired of being pregnant and starts taking birth-control pills. The people running a number of country radio stations refused to play it. It still reached No. 5 on the country chart.

In 1967 Charley Pride became the first Black performer on the Grand Ole Opry since DeFord Bailey last played there in 1941. Pride was one of eleven children of sharecroppers from Sledge, Mississippi. Sharecroppers farmed another man's land in return for a share of the crop. His first records went to radio stations without his photograph. He had 30 No. 1 country records, and in 1971 he won the Country Music Association's award for Entertainer of the Year.

#### Hip-hop from the Bronx, 1973 onward

On August 11, 1973, Clive Campbell, a teenage DJ called Kool Herc, played records at a party at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue in the Bronx, New York. A DJ is a person who plays records for dancers or listeners. His sister Cindy Campbell planned the party to earn money for back-to-school clothes. In 2007 city officials named the building the birthplace of hip-hop.

In the same years, fires burned much of the South Bronx. Most were arson, fires set on purpose. Landlords paid people who lived nearby to set fires in the landlords' own buildings, so the landlords could collect insurance money. One landlord collected $125,000 from 21 fires. After a study of the fire service by the RAND Corporation, a research company, city officials closed 12 fire companies in the South Bronx between 1974 and 1976, when the city was nearly out of money. Seven census tracts, small areas the census counts separately, lost more than 97 percent of their buildings to fire and abandonment. About 250,000 people lost their homes.

"Rapper's Delight," by the Sugarhill Gang, came out on September 16, 1979, on Sugar Hill Records. Sylvia Robinson produced it and ran the company's work. It reached No. 36 on the national pop chart. Many writers call it the first rap record that sold widely. It used the music of Chic's song "Good Times." Chic's writers, Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards, got credit only after they threatened to sue. One of its rappers, Big Bank Hank, used rhymes written by Grandmaster Caz and did not credit him.

"The Message," from 1982, by Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five, described poverty in the inner city. Ed "Duke Bootee" Fletcher, Melle Mel, Clifton "Jiggs" Chase and Sylvia Robinson wrote it. In 2002 it became the first hip-hop record added to the National Recording Registry, the Library of Congress's list of recordings chosen to be kept for the future.

<a id="story-dj-kool-herc"></a>

#### DJ Kool Herc

> **Who:** Born Clive Campbell in Jamaica, the DJ at the 1973 Bronx party that people name as the start of hip-hop.
>
> **When and where:** Born April 16, 1955, in Kingston, Jamaica. Moved to the Bronx, New York, in November 1967, at 13.

DJ Kool Herc played records at the 1973 party that people name as the start of hip-hop. He found a way to make the drum part of a record last longer, by playing two copies of the same record. He was born Clive Campbell in Kingston, Jamaica, on April 16, 1955. In November 1967, at 13, he moved to the Bronx.

At parties he played funk records. The "break" of a funk record is its drum part. Herc used two copies of the same record. When the break ended on one, he started it again on the other. He called this the "Merry-Go-Round." He called the dancers who danced to the breaks "b-boys" and "b-girls."

His sister Cindy planned the party of August 11, 1973, at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue. Later someone stabbed Herc at a club called the Executive Playhouse while he was trying to stop a fight. No record names who stabbed him. After that he pulled back from playing. By 1980 he had stopped working as a DJ. No surviving document shows what he earned from hip-hop.

#### Woodstock, music television, compact discs and the lyrics hearing

The Woodstock music festival took place on Max Yasgur's dairy farm in Bethel, New York, from August 15 to 18, 1969. The organizers expected about 50,000 people. Estimates of the crowd run from 400,000 to more than 460,000, and no record names who counted. The fences were not finished, so the festival became free. Three people died. Two died from taking too much of a drug, and a tractor ran over a 17-year-old as he slept. No record names the driver.

The MTV television channel began on August 1, 1981, and played music videos. Its managers said they kept to a "rock format," and they played few Black artists. Walter Yetnikoff, president of CBS Records, threatened to pull CBS's videos unless MTV played Black artists. MTV's managers then put Michael Jackson's "Billie Jean" into heavy rotation, which means they played it often, from March 1983. Compact disc players went on sale in Japan on October 1, 1982, and in the United States in March 1983.

In 1985 Tipper Gore, Susan Baker and two other women in Washington started a group called the Parents Music Resource Center. They made a list of 15 songs they objected to and called it the "Filthy Fifteen." It included Prince's "Darling Nikki." On September 19, 1985, members of the Senate Commerce Committee held a hearing. The musicians Frank Zappa, Dee Snider and John Denver spoke against labels. Zappa called the plan "an ill-conceived piece of nonsense," a badly thought-out idea. On November 1, 1985, leaders of the RIAA, the record companies' own group, agreed to put warning labels on some albums. In 1990 the companies began using a standard "Parental Advisory" sticker. Managers at Walmart and some other stores would not sell albums with the sticker.

In 1978 members of Congress passed the American Indian Religious Freedom Act. In it they wrote that Native "ceremonies have been intruded upon, interfered with, and in a few instances banned." The act does not name the people who did these things. Until that year, federal officials could still enforce the rules against Native religious dances that Hiram Price, the head of the government's Indian office, had issued in 1883.

<a id="story-selena-quintanilla"></a>

#### Selena Quintanilla

> **Who:** A Mexican American singer of Tejano music, the Spanish-language music of Texas.
>
> **When and where:** Born April 16, 1971, in Lake Jackson, Texas. Killed March 31, 1995, in Corpus Christi, Texas, at 23.
>
> **Movie:** *Selena* (1997), a Hollywood drama film about her, with Jennifer Lopez.

Selena Quintanilla was a Mexican American singer of Tejano music, the Spanish-language music of Texas. She was killed at 23 by the woman who ran her fan club. She was born in Lake Jackson, Texas, on April 16, 1971.

She sang with her brother and sister in their father Abraham Quintanilla Jr.'s band, Selena y Los Dinos. She learned the Spanish words of her songs by their sound, with her father's help. She won the Tejano Music Award for Female Vocalist of the Year in 1987 and in each of the next nine years. In 1994 she won a Grammy Award for her album *Live!*

Yolanda Saldívar ran Selena's fan club and managed her clothing stores. Saldívar had secretly taken money from the business, more than $30,000 or more than $60,000 by different counts. Selena meant to fire her.

On March 31, 1995, at a Days Inn motel in Corpus Christi, Texas, Saldívar shot Selena with a gun as Selena tried to leave the room. The bullet hit her lower right shoulder. Selena reached the lobby and named Saldívar. She died at the hospital that afternoon from loss of blood. Saldívar gave herself up to the police more than nine hours later. On October 23, 1995, after a trial in Houston, a jury found her guilty of murder with a deadly weapon, and Judge Mike Westergren sentenced her to life in prison. On March 27, 2025, members of the Texas parole board, who decide whether a prisoner may leave prison early, refused to let her out, and they set her next review for March 2030.

Between 30,000 and 40,000 people came to see Selena's coffin. Her album *Dreaming of You* came out after her death. It made her the first Latin artist whose album entered the national album chart at No. 1.

### 2000 to Today

By 2025, 82 cents of every dollar that American record companies took in came from streaming. Sales of recorded music in the United States had peaked in 1999, when most people bought CDs. Then a free program called Napster let people copy songs from each other's computers. By the record companies' own count, sales fell in 15 of the 16 years from 2000 to 2015. Sales rose again as more people paid for streaming. A streaming service pays a fraction of a cent each time a song is played. It pays the owner of the recording, usually a record company, and not the singer. In a 2018 survey, most working musicians said they earned money from playing live. Dolly Parton, a songwriter from the mountains of Tennessee, died on August 25, 2026, at 80. In September 2026 record companies and musicians were in court against companies whose computer programs make songs.

#### Napster, the iPod and streaming, 1999 to 2025

Shawn Fanning and Sean Parker started Napster in June 1999. It let people copy music files from each other's computers for free. In December 1999 record companies sued. A federal judge ordered Napster to block copyrighted songs. Napster's owners could not do it, so they shut the service down in July 2001. At its peak, in February 2001, it had 26.4 million users by a checked count, though some estimates say 80 million.

On October 23, 2001, Apple's boss, Steve Jobs, showed the iPod, a pocket music player. He said it held "1,000 songs in your pocket." Apple's iTunes Store opened on April 28, 2003, and sold most songs for 99 cents each. By 2014 it had sold 35 billion songs.

Spotify, a company from Sweden, began streaming music in the United States in July 2011. Streaming means playing a song over the internet without buying a copy of it. By March 2026, the company said, Spotify had 300 million paying subscribers around the world.

The Recording Industry Association of America, or RIAA, is the record companies' own group. Its staff count what the companies take in. In 2017 Mark J. Perry of the American Enterprise Institute, a research group, used those figures. He found that sales peaked in 1999 at $20.9 billion, counted in 2016 dollars so that the rise in prices is taken out. Sales then fell in 15 of the 16 years from 2000 to 2015. In 2016 they were $7.57 billion. That year, for the first time, Americans paid more for streaming than for CDs, downloads and ringtones. The RIAA reported in March 2026 that in 2025 the companies took in a record $11.5 billion at wholesale. Wholesale is the price the companies themselves are paid. Of that money, $9.5 billion came from streaming, and $1.04 billion came from vinyl records.

#### What a stream pays

Spotify pays about 70 percent of the money it takes in to the owners of the music, by its own account. About 58.5 percent goes to whoever owns the recording, which is usually a record company. About 12 percent goes to whoever owns the song itself: the songwriter and the publisher, a company that manages the rights to the song. A singer who does not own the recording gets a share from the record company, under the singer's contract.

Spotify does not pay a set price for each play. It pays each owner by that owner's share of all the plays. In February 2025 a company that sends music to streaming services, iMusician, put the average at $0.003 to $0.005 a play, and about $0.004 for a listener in the United States. That is less than half a cent.

From April 1, 2024, Spotify stopped paying anything for a recording played fewer than 1,000 times in a year. Spotify wrote in November 2023 that recordings under that line had earned an average of about 3 cents a month. It wrote that 99.5 percent of all plays were of recordings above the line. In March 2026 Spotify reported that it paid the music business more than $11 billion in 2025. By its count, more than 1,500 artists earned over $1 million from it that year. The artist ranked 100,000th earned about $7,300.

In March 2021 a musicians' group, the United Musicians and Allied Workers, held protests in 31 cities and asked Spotify to pay one cent a play. In 2018 a group called the Music Industry Research Association asked 1,227 American musicians about their work. Most earned money from playing live, and most could not live on music alone. Of the women who answered, 72 percent said they had been treated unfairly because they were women, and 67 percent said they had been sexually harassed, which means they faced unwanted sexual remarks or touching. Of the musicians who were not white, 63 percent said they had been treated unfairly because of their race. The musicians who answered did not name the people who did it.

<a id="story-zoe-keating"></a>

#### Zoë Keating

> **Who:** A cellist and composer who sells her own recordings and publishes what streaming pays her.
>
> **When and where:** Born February 2, 1972, in Guelph, Ontario, Canada, to an English mother and an American father. Worked in San Francisco, California, and later Vermont.

Zoë Keating is a cellist who has published what streaming services paid her, so that other musicians could see real numbers. In September 2019 she posted: "206,011 Spotify streams. $753." That came to a little more than a third of a cent for each play. The company that sent her music to Spotify took no cut.

She was born in Guelph, Ontario, in Canada, on February 2, 1972. She played cello in the band Rasputina from 2002 to 2006. She records alone. She uses a computer to record and repeat her own cello parts as she plays, so that one player sounds like many.

She released her album *One Cello x 16: Natoma* herself, without a record company. It reached No. 1 on the iTunes classical chart four times. In August 2012 she began publishing her income from sales and streaming.

In May 2014 doctors found that her husband, Jeff Rusch, had stage 4 cancer, cancer that has spread through the body. Staff at their insurance company, Anthem, first refused to pay for his hospital stay. The records do not name them. Anthem's staff reversed the refusal after local news stories about it. He died on February 19, 2015.

#### Who owns a recording: masters and songs

Every recorded song has two copyrights. One covers the song itself, its words and tune. The other covers the master, the first recording, which every copy is made from. Whoever owns the master is paid for every copy and every stream of that recording. Sam Cooke's own company owned his master recordings from 1963. Ray Charles's 1959 contract promised that he would own his in time.

In December 2020 Bob Dylan sold the rights to all of his songs to Universal Music Publishing Group. Reporters at *The New York Times* estimated the price at more than $300 million, and other reports said about $400 million.

<a id="story-taylor-swift"></a>

#### Taylor Swift

> **Who:** A songwriter and singer who recorded four of her first six albums again after a music manager bought the master recordings.
>
> **When and where:** Born December 13, 1989, in West Reading, Pennsylvania. Moved to Hendersonville, Tennessee, at 14.
>
> **Movie:** *Miss Americana* (2020), a documentary about her.

Taylor Swift recorded four of her albums a second time. Under her 2018 contract with Universal, she owns the masters of her new recordings. She made the new versions after a music manager bought the masters of her first six albums. She was born in West Reading, Pennsylvania, on December 13, 1989.

At 14 her family moved to Hendersonville, Tennessee. That year a Nashville music publisher signed her as a songwriter, the youngest it had ever signed. After a show at Nashville's Bluebird Cafe on November 3, 2004, she signed with Scott Borchetta's new company, Big Machine Records. Big Machine owned the masters of her first six albums.

On June 30, 2019, the music manager Scooter Braun bought Big Machine for about $330 million, and with it her masters. Swift said she had tried for years to buy them. She said she was offered them only if she signed up to make six more albums for the company. In October 2020 Braun sold the masters to Shamrock Holdings for a reported $405 million. Shamrock is owned by the family of Roy E. Disney.

Swift recorded four of the albums again, and each came out as "Taylor's Version." *Fearless* came out on April 9, 2021, and *Red* on November 12, 2021. *Speak Now* followed on July 7, 2023, and *1989* on October 27, 2023.

Her Eras Tour ran from March 17, 2023, to December 8, 2024, with 149 shows. It took in $2.07 billion, more than any concert tour before it. On May 30, 2025, she said she had bought all six of the original masters from Shamrock. The price was not made public.

#### The Music Modernization Act, 2018

In 2018 members of Congress passed the Music Modernization Act. House members voted for it on April 25, and senators passed it on September 19 with no votes against. President Donald Trump signed it on October 11. The law provides for a nonprofit group, the Mechanical Licensing Collective, to keep a list of who owns each song and to pay songwriters for streams. In 2021 the group began paying out money for songs whose owners nobody had identified.

Recordings made before February 15, 1972, had no federal copyright, so internet radio services did not have to pay for playing them. Many rhythm and blues records of the 1950s and 1960s were made before that date. Under the 2018 law, the singers and musicians on those older records are paid when digital radio plays them.

#### Hip-hop, Latin music and country radio

In 2017 hip-hop and R&B made up 24.5 percent of all the music Americans bought or streamed, more than any other kind. Rock came second, with just under 21 percent. Analysts at Nielsen Music, a company that tracks sales and streams, made the count, and CNBC's reporters wrote about it in January 2018.

In 2025 Latin music brought in $1 billion, 8.8 percent of what the record companies took in across the United States. The RIAA reported in 2026 that it was Latin music's tenth record year in a row.

Jada Watson, a researcher, counts the songs played on country radio. She found that songs by women got 11 percent of the plays by 2022. She reported in 2023 that no song by a Black, Indigenous or other woman of color was in regular daytime rotation. Rotation is the list of songs a station plays over and over each day.

Beyoncé, a Black singer, sang her country song "Daddy Lessons" at the Country Music Association Awards on November 2, 2016. Some country fans said she did not belong there, and the association's staff deleted its online posts about her performance. Her country album *Cowboy Carter*, from 2024, made her the first Black woman with a No. 1 album on the country album chart. The album got no nominations at the Country Music Association Awards that year. On February 2, 2025, it won the Grammy Awards for Album of the Year and Best Country Album.

<a id="story-kendrick-lamar"></a>

#### Kendrick Lamar

> **Who:** A Black rapper and songwriter, the first musician outside classical music and jazz to win the Pulitzer Prize for Music.
>
> **When and where:** Born June 17, 1987, in Compton, California.

In 2018 Kendrick Lamar became the first musician outside classical music and jazz to win the Pulitzer Prize for Music. He was born in Compton, California, on June 17, 1987. His parents had moved there from the South Side of Chicago in 1984. When he was five, he saw a teenage drug dealer killed in a drive-by shooting outside his apartment. No record names the shooter. In seventh grade an English teacher, Regis Inge, introduced him to poetry.

He signed with the record label Top Dawg Entertainment in 2005. His albums include *Good Kid, M.A.A.D City* in 2012 and *To Pimp a Butterfly* in 2015. Protesters in the Black Lives Matter movement used his songs as anthems.

On April 16, 2018, his album *DAMN.* won the Pulitzer Prize for Music. The Pulitzer board called it "a virtuosic song collection unified by its vernacular authenticity and rhythmic dynamism." The board was praising the skill of the songs, their everyday speech and their strong rhythm. The prize was $15,000.

On February 9, 2025, he performed at the Super Bowl halftime show. About 133.5 million people watched, more than had watched any halftime show before. By 2026 he had won 27 Grammy Awards, more than any other rapper.

#### Deaths at music festivals, 2017 and 2021

On October 1, 2017, more than 22,000 people were at the last night of the Route 91 Harvest country music festival in Las Vegas, Nevada. At 10:05 p.m., while the country singer Jason Aldean was playing, Stephen Paddock, who was 64, began shooting into the crowd. He fired from his rooms on the 32nd floor of the Mandalay Bay hotel. In ten minutes he fired more than 1,000 bullets. He killed 58 people that night and wounded at least 413 with gunfire, and about 867 people were hurt in all. Two wounded women died later, in 2019 and 2020, so the official count is 60 dead. Paddock shot himself. Investigators never found out why he did it.

On November 5, 2021, about 50,000 people came to the Astroworld Festival in Houston, Texas. When the rapper Travis Scott, who had started the festival, came on stage, the crowd pushed toward him. Ten people died of compressive asphyxiation, which means they were squeezed so hard they could not breathe. Thousands were hurt. The youngest to die was a boy of 9 or 10. The reports differ. In June 2023 a Harris County grand jury decided not to charge Scott or five others, among them Brent Silberstein, a festival manager for the concert company Live Nation.
