A grand jury is a group of citizens who decide whether someone should be charged with a crime. Families of people who died sued Scott and Live Nation.

#### Machines that make music

Auto-Tune is a computer program that moves a singer's off-key notes onto the right pitch. The engineer Andy Hildebrand invented it, and the company Antares put it on sale on September 19, 1997. In 1998 the singer Cher used it as a sound effect on her song "Believe," the first record sold in stores to use it that way. The rapper and singer T-Pain used it that way on his 2005 album *Rappa Ternt Sanga* and after. Kanye West used it on his 2008 album *808s & Heartbreak*.

On June 1, 2008, a worker at Universal Studios Hollywood used a blowtorch to heat roof shingles and left before they cooled. The fire that followed spread across the studio's backlot, the outdoor area of sets and storage buildings. In 2019 Jody Rosen, a writer for the New York Times Magazine, reported that the same fire had destroyed 118,000 to 175,000 of Universal Music Group's master tapes. He wrote that they might include records by Chuck Berry, Muddy Waters and John Coltrane. A statement from Universal Music Group stated that the report held "numerous inaccuracies," which means many mistakes. The company's leaders confirmed that the masters of one Soundgarden album had burned.

Companies such as Suno and Udio sell computer programs that make whole songs. In June 2024 record companies, led by the RIAA, sued both of them. They said the companies had trained their programs on the record companies' recordings without permission. To train such a program, its makers feed recordings into it, and the program uses them to work out how to make new songs.

Some of the cases were settled, which means the two sides ended them by agreement. Universal settled with Udio in October 2025, and Udio's owners agreed to use only music they had permission to use. Warner settled with Suno in November 2025 and gave it permission to use Warner's music, and BMG settled in August 2026. On September 9, 2026, Suno put out a new version of its program trained on music it had permission to use. In September 2026 Universal and Sony were still suing Suno. In court papers, Suno's lawyers admitted that it had downloaded audio from YouTube. They argued that this was fair use, a use of someone else's work that the law allows in some cases. On September 1, 2026, the songwriter Jason Isbell and three other musicians sued Suno and asked the court to let them speak for other artists too.

In March 2025 a federal judge, Eumi Lee, turned down a request from music publishers. They had asked her to stop the company Anthropic from using song lyrics to train its computer program while their case went on. As of late September 2026, no American court had given a final ruling on whether a company may train a song-making program on recordings without permission.

#### The Kennedy Center, 2025 and 2026

The Kennedy Center is a building for music, theater and dance in Washington, D.C., named for President John F. Kennedy. The National Symphony Orchestra plays there. In February 2025 members of its board chose President Donald Trump as its chairman. Trump then removed board members who had been appointed by Democrats and appointed his allies. On December 18, 2025, board members voted to add his name to the building, CBS News reporters wrote. Representative Joyce Beatty, a member of the board, said she had been muted on the call and that the vote had not been on the list of business for the meeting.

Beatty went to court against the name change. On May 29, 2026, a federal judge, Christopher Cooper, ruled that the board could not rename the building. "Congress gave the Kennedy Center its name, and only Congress can change it," he wrote. He ordered the signs with Trump's name taken down within 14 days. Many performers canceled their shows at the center, saying it had become political, and ticket sales fell. On September 15, 2026, minutes after Judge Cooper again blocked the name change, board members voted to close the building, Anastasia Tsioulcas of NPR reported. Trump wrote that repairs would not begin unless a higher court allowed his name. In a court filing, the center's executive director, Matt Floca, pointed to falling plaster and decay under the roof. He extended the closure to September 30, 2026, and said he would review it each week, reporters at WTOP, a Washington radio station, wrote.

The building did not reopen on September 30. Engineers had found rust and water damage on most of the panels under the building's overhanging roof, which could fall on people below. On October 1, 2026, NBC News and ABC News reported an email in which Floca told the staff that the main building would "remain temporarily closed" while engineers checked whether people could safely use it and get out of it in an emergency. He expected that check to take one to two weeks, and he called that "an assessment timeline, not a reopening date." Judge Cooper asked for weekly reports on the repairs. On October 2 the center's leaders moved the 2026 Kennedy Center Honors, a yearly award show, to Capital One Arena in Washington for December 7, Newsweek reported. It was the first time in nearly 50 years that the show would be held outside the Kennedy Center. As of October 3, 2026, the main building was still closed, with no date set for it to reopen.

<a id="story-dolly-parton"></a>

#### Dolly Parton

> **Who:** A singer and songwriter from Sevier County, in the mountains of Tennessee, who wrote more than 3,000 songs and mailed free books to children.
>
> **When and where:** Born January 19, 1946, in a one-room cabin in Pittman Center, Sevier County, Tennessee. Moved to Nashville in 1964. Died August 25, 2026, in Nashville, at 80.
>
> **Movie:** *Dolly Parton: Here I Am* (2019), a documentary about her.

Dolly Parton wrote more than 3,000 songs, and in 1974 she refused to give Elvis Presley's manager half the rights to one of them. She started a program that mails free books to children, one a month from birth to age five. She died of cancer in Nashville on August 25, 2026, at 80.

She was born on January 19, 1946, in a one-room cabin in Pittman Center, in Sevier County, Tennessee. She was the fourth of 12 children. Her father, Robert Lee Parton, farmed tobacco and could not read or write. He paid the doctor who delivered her with a sack of cornmeal. Her mother was Avie Lee Parton. From age six Dolly sang in her grandfather's church.

By ten she sang on a radio and television show in Knoxville. At 13 she made her first record and sang at the Grand Ole Opry. The day after she finished high school in 1964, she moved to Nashville.

In 1967 the country singer Porter Wagoner hired her for his weekly television show. Their duets made the country Top 10 for six years in a row. From 1969 Wagoner owned nearly half of Owe-Par, the company that she and her uncle Bill Owens had started to publish her songs. Her first No. 1 single as a solo singer was "Joshua," which she wrote by herself. It reached the top of the country chart in February 1971. That same year she recorded "Coat of Many Colors," about her family's poverty. In 1973 she wrote "Jolene" and "I Will Always Love You" within a few days of each other. She wrote "I Will Always Love You" as a goodbye to Wagoner, and she left his show in 1974.

That year Elvis Presley wanted to record "I Will Always Love You." His manager, Colonel Tom Parker, told her that the songwriter always signed over half the publishing rights to any song Presley recorded. Publishing rights are the rights to the song itself. She said no. In 1992 Whitney Houston recorded the song, and her record sold more than 24 million copies around the world. Parton said later, "I made enough money to buy Graceland," Presley's home.

She wrote "9 to 5" for a 1980 film of the same name, in which she also acted. It reached No. 1 on the country and pop charts in February 1981. She sold more than 100 million records, had at least 25 No. 1 country songs, and won 11 Grammy Awards. She turned down the Presidential Medal of Freedom three times.

She became a partner in a theme park in Pigeon Forge, Tennessee, which reopened as Dollywood on May 3, 1986. It has about 4,000 to 4,500 workers, more than any other employer in Sevier County. From 2022 Dollywood paid college costs for workers who chose to go.

In 1995 she started the Imagination Library in Sevier County. The program's website states that she started it because her father could not read or write. The Imagination Library mails one free book a month to each child who signs up, from birth to age five. Her foundation pays the program's running costs and bargains down the price of the books. Local partners raise the money for the books and the mailing, and families pay nothing. By 2026 it had mailed more than 300 million books in five countries.

In the spring of 2020 she gave $1 million to Vanderbilt University Medical Center in Nashville for research on the coronavirus. Her longtime friend Dr. Naji Abumrad had told her that researchers there were making progress. A research paper on Moderna's COVID-19 vaccine listed her fund among its supporters. The US government put about $2.5 billion into that vaccine. After wildfires burned homes near Gatlinburg, Tennessee, in November 2016, her My People Fund paid $1,000 a month for six months to more than 900 families whose homes had burned, and $5,000 in the last month. After Hurricane Helene in 2024, she and her businesses gave $2 million.

Ed Christman wrote in the magazine *Billboard* in August 2026 that Parton owned her own songs for her whole career. From 1969, though, Porter Wagoner owned nearly half of Owe-Par, her song-publishing company. The two later settled a lawsuit between them, and their 1980 album came out as part of that settlement. Sony Music owns her recordings from her years with RCA, and probably from her Columbia years, about 23 albums in all. From 1995 she owned most of her new recordings, through her own record label.

Her husband, Carl Thomas Dean, whom she married in 1966, died on March 3, 2025. On August 21, 2026, she went into the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Center in Nashville. She died four days later. Her family did not say what kind of cancer she had. Her nephew Bryan Seaver, her head of security for more than 20 years, announced her death, as she had asked him to. That day Representative Tim Burchett of Tennessee said, "Tennessee lost one of our greatest ambassadors in Dolly Parton." President Trump ordered flags at federal buildings flown at half-staff for a week. Her family asked people who wanted to honor her to support the Imagination Library. They held a private funeral on August 28, and she was buried beside her husband in Nashville.

<a id="ch-storytelling-evolution"></a>

## Chapter 34: Storytelling Evolution

### Before 1500

Before 1500, people in Native nations here acted out stories. A dancer in a mask took on the part of a spirit or an animal. Dancers did this in religious ceremonies and to ask the animals to give themselves to hunters. Among the Pueblo peoples, men carved dolls of these spirits so that girls would learn who each one was.

Some of what is known about these traditions comes from the nations themselves. Haudenosaunee leaders published a policy on their masks in 1995, and an Ojibwe teacher explained his people's storytelling rules in 2024. Older evidence survives in the ground. People built wide open squares called plazas and large round rooms for ceremonies, and they painted masked figures on walls and pots.

#### Playing someone who is not you

The Pueblo peoples, among them the Hopi, are Native nations of the Southwest. In their religion, katsinam are spirit beings. There are more than 500 of them. Pueblo men wear katsina masks and special clothing in dances. People believe that the spirit shown on the mask is present with or inside the dancer while the dance goes on. Men also carve katsina dolls and give them to girls, so the girls learn who each spirit is.

Homol'ovi is a group of ancestral Hopi settlements near Winslow, in what is now Arizona. Ancestral means belonging to the people who lived there long ago, whose descendants live there now. Archaeologists are scientists who dig up and study what people left behind long ago. A review published by the Archaeological Conservancy states that the katsina religion reached Homol'ovi around 1350.

In what is now Alaska, the Yup'ik people held a winter ceremony in which dancers wore masks and took on the spirits of the animals the masks showed. Ann Fienup-Riordan, quoted in *Archaeology* magazine in 2015, said that the dancers asked the animals to give themselves to hunters in the coming year. After a dance, people usually burned the masks, broke them or left them out on the tundra, the flat treeless land of the far north. People lived at Nunalleq, a village near Quinhagak, from 1300 to the 1650s. Archaeologists dug up masks there that are the oldest complete Yup'ik masks anywhere. The masks were made before 1650, while people lived in the village.

Medicine societies among the Haudenosaunee use masks of wood and of cornhusk. The Haudenosaunee are six nations whose lands stretch across what is now New York State and into Canada. In 1995 the Grand Council of the Haudenosaunee published a policy on these masks. The policy defines a medicine society only as Haudenosaunee who have taken part in the medicine. It states that all the masks are sacred, whatever their size or age, and that only members of a medicine society should make masks. It also states that the masks must not be shown in public, and that photographs and drawings of them should not be used in public displays. The Haudenosaunee have not published a date for when the societies began.

#### Rules about who tells what, and when

Some nations set rules about which stories may be told, by whom, and at what time of year. An Ojibwe teacher described his people's rules in 2024. A Tlingit heritage group describes the Tlingit rules.

Ojibwe people tell their sacred stories, called aadizookaanag, only in winter. James Vukelich Kaagegaabaw is of Turtle Mountain Ojibwe descent. In 2024 he said that tellers wait until the lakes freeze over and snow covers the ground. By then the amphibians and reptiles, animals such as frogs and snakes, are asleep for the winter, and so are the bears. He said the spirits in the stories are thought to be asleep too, and "you wouldn't want to be thought of as gossiping about them." If someone tells the stories out of season, he said, "a frog or a toad may jump into your bed."

The Tlingit live in Southeast Alaska. They belong to clans, large family groups that trace back to the same ancestors. Each clan owns its crests, the animal and spirit figures that stand for the clan. It also owns the stories, songs and names that go with each crest. The Tlingit word for this sacred clan property is at.óow. The Sealaska Heritage Institute, led by Rosita Worl, published the first list of Tlingit clan crests in 2023. Its writers say that a clan got the right to a crest when an ancestor met a spirit being or what they call an "animal person." They add that a clan "often acquired" the right "as payment for the life of an ancestor," and the article does not say more about that payment. Clan members hold the crest and its stories through the generations.

#### Places built to hold a crowd

At Cahokia, in what is now Illinois across the Mississippi River from St. Louis, people built a Grand Plaza of about 47 acres. It was the largest of the city's five plazas. The builders cut down a ridge of sand and moved the sand to fill low places and make a level surface. R. Thunen of the University of North Florida writes that archaeologists see the plazas as the places where people from all around gathered for their most important ceremonies, meetings and social events.

At Chaco Canyon, in what is now northwestern New Mexico, the people of Chaco built a great kiva called Casa Rinconada. A kiva is a round room, partly underground, used for ceremonies. Casa Rinconada is about 63 feet across inside, with a bench around the wall and 34 small openings, called niches, set into the wall. A tunnel 39 feet long ran under the floor. Through it, a person, perhaps a leader of the ceremonies, could enter the kiva unseen and then come up suddenly in front of the people there. The Chaco Research Archive states that building probably began in about the middle of the 1000s and that people stopped using the kiva in the early 1100s.

#### What the record does not have

No person from before 1500 in this land who acted, danced or told stories is named in any surviving record.

### The 1500s

The first European play on record in what is now the United States was acted on April 30, 1598, on the bank of the Rio Grande. Spanish soldiers and priests acted it, and they made Manso people, who lived near their camp, take part. The Spanish belonged to an expedition, a large group of soldiers, priests and settlers, led by Juan de Oñate. They had come north from Mexico to take New Mexico for the king of Spain. Later that year Oñate's soldiers acted a second play at a pueblo, a Native town, farther north. No other European play acted in this land in the 1500s is on record.

#### April 30, 1598: the play at the river

Oñate's expedition reached the Rio Grande near present-day San Elizario, Texas, on April 20, 1598. On April 30 the colonists held a Mass of thanksgiving, a Catholic church service, in a chapel that Oñate had ordered set up in a grove of cottonwood trees. That day Oñate also read out a statement called "La Toma," which means "the taking." In it he claimed for King Philip II of Spain all the land that the river drained. Accounts differ on whether he read it before or after the play. Manso people lived near the camp.

After the Mass the expedition put on a play nearby. Captain Marcos Farfán de los Godos, one of Oñate's officers, wrote it. The stage was bare ground, and a canvas curtain hung between two tree trunks behind it. Soldiers and friars played the main parts. Friars are Catholic priests who belong to a religious order.

Members of the expedition made Manso people found near the camp take part in the play, the historian Marc Simmons writes. Simmons does not say who gave the order. In the play the Manso acted the parts of the Pueblo people who lived farther north. An officer who watched described the story. Friars arrive in New Mexico, and the Native people there kneel and ask to be baptized. Baptism is the Catholic ceremony with water that makes a person a member of the church. At the end, the people watching cheered and fired their guns into the air. No copy of the script survives, and its title is not known.

<a id="story-marcos-farfan-de-los-godos"></a>

#### Marcos Farfán de los Godos

> **Who:** A captain in Juan de Oñate's expedition who wrote the first European play on record in what is now the United States.
>
> **When and where:** The Rio Grande near present-day San Elizario, Texas, April 30, 1598.

Marcos Farfán de los Godos wrote the play that Oñate's expedition acted on April 30, 1598. He came from the city of Seville, in Spain. He passed muster with two servants, 16 horses, a tent, weapons and armor. Passing muster means he was checked, and what he brought was written on the expedition's list of men, called a muster roll.

Farfán opened the play himself with a speech, in which he said he was unworthy to have written such a poor play and offered it for the fun of his fellow soldiers and of Oñate.

In November 1598 Farfán led a party west from the Hopi villages to look for mines. They reached the Verde Valley, in what is now Arizona. Near present-day Jerome they marked out 14 or 15 mining claims, pieces of ground where they said they had the right to dig for ore, rock that holds metal. What happened to Farfán after 1599, and when he died, is not known.

#### The same expedition at Acoma

About eight months after the play, men of the same expedition attacked Acoma Pueblo. Acoma is a town built on top of a mesa, a steep hill with a flat top.

In early December 1598, Oñate's nephew Juan de Zaldívar and his soldiers climbed the mesa and demanded food. The All Pueblo Council of Governors is a council of the leaders of the Pueblo nations. In 2023 its leaders said that the soldiers had demanded food and supplies. They said the soldiers had also forced the Acoma to promise loyalty to the king of Spain. In the Acoma people's own account, as the Rio Grande Sun newspaper reported it in 2019, the soldiers also raped an Acoma woman. Rape means forcing a person into sex. Acoma people killed Zaldívar and between 11 and 14 of his men. Accounts differ on the number.

In January 1599 Oñate sent Zaldívar's brother, Vicente de Zaldívar, with about 70 soldiers. Oñate declared a war "by fire and blood." The soldiers fought their way up the mesa. Over two or three days of fighting, they killed Acoma men, women and children and burned much of the pueblo. No one counted the Acoma dead. Published estimates run from about 300 to about 1,500. The figure given most often is about 800 men, women and children, and it is the figure the Pueblos themselves use. The soldiers took about 500 people prisoner.

In February 1599 Oñate put the prisoners on trial and sentenced them. Every Acoma man over 25 was to have one foot cut off and to be forced to work for Spanish masters for twenty years, as their slaves. Males from 12 to 25, and females over 12, got the same twenty years of forced work. Oñate ordered the old people handed over as slaves to the Plains Apache, and children under 12 taken from their families and given to the friars. Under that order, Acoma girls were taken south to Mexico and placed in convents, houses where nuns live. The National Park Service's account gives about 70 girls, and the All Pueblo Council of Governors gives 60 children. The records do not name the men who took them. None is known to have come home. Oñate also sentenced two Hopi men captured in the fighting to have their right hands cut off.

Oñate's sentence is in the written record. Acoma people have passed down their own account since 1599: Oñate had the right feet of 24 captive men cut off. The Associated Press, NPR and the New York Times have reported that number. No one has traced it to a written record from the time. The historians Marc Simmons and John Kessell doubt that the cutting was carried out.

In 1612 or 1613 Spanish officials charged Oñate with 30 crimes. In 1614 judges in Mexico found him guilty of 12 of them, including using too much force at Acoma. The judges ordered him out of New Mexico for life and barred him from Mexico City for four years. One account says five years. They also fined him 6,000 ducats, which were Spanish gold coins.

#### Los Moros y Cristianos

Oñate's soldiers acted a second play in 1598, after the expedition reached a Tewa pueblo. The Spanish renamed it San Juan and made it their first capital. Today that pueblo is called Ohkay Owingeh. The play was *Los Moros y Cristianos*, which means *The Moors and the Christians*. The Moors were Muslims. The play shows the battles between Muslims and Christians in Spain from the 700s to the 1400s. The leaders of each side make long speeches, and the battle scenes are full of clashing weapons.

New Mexicans have acted the play now and then in recent times, most of all a group of actors from Chimayó. Actors performed it at the University of New Mexico in 1998, for the 400th anniversary of Oñate's colony.

### The 1600s

The first play in English on record in what is now the United States is known only from the orders of a Virginia county court in 1665. A man named Edward Martin had reported the actors to the court, and the court tried them. In New Mexico, Spanish priests went into Pueblo ceremonial rooms and burned the masks used in the dances. In 1680 the Pueblos drove the Spanish out and brought back their own ceremonies.

#### Plays stopped in England, and a play at Harvard

England's lawmakers meet in Parliament, which has two parts, the House of Lords and the House of Commons. On September 2, 1642, members of both houses ordered that "Public Stage Plays shall cease" for as long as "these sad causes and set Times of Humiliation do continue." The order calls those times "Public Calamities" and "Seasons of Humiliation," set aside for "sad and pious Solemnity." It means times of public trouble, kept for sad and serious worship. The order describes plays as "Spectacles of Pleasure, too commonly expressing lascivious Mirth and Levity." Spectacles are shows, and mirth means fun. Lascivious means rude about sex, and levity means joking about serious things.

In 1690 students at Harvard College, in Cambridge, Massachusetts, acted *Gustavus Vasa*, a tragedy by Benjamin Colman. A tragedy is a serious play with a sad ending. Local officials disapproved of the play. Arthur Hornblow, who wrote a history of the American theatre in 1919, called it the first play written by an American to be acted in America.

#### August 27, 1665: a play, a complaint and a court

On August 27, 1665, three men named Cornelius Watkinson, Philip Howard and William Darby acted a play called *Ye Bare and Ye Cubb* in Accomack County, Virginia. The court record does not say where. A local history site, Secrets of the Eastern Shore, says they acted it at Fowkes Tavern near Pungoteague. A man named Edward Martin reported the play to the court. John Fawsett, the king's attorney for the county, brought the case. The king's attorney was the lawyer who brought cases to court in the king's name.

On November 16, 1665, Fawsett accused the three men in the county court. The judges of the court ordered the men to come to the next court "in those habilemts that they then acted in." Habilemts is the court clerk's short spelling of habiliments, an old word for clothes, so the men had to come in their costumes. They also had to bring a written copy of the verses and speeches. The judges ordered the sheriff to hold Watkinson and Howard until they gave security, a promise backed by money or property that they would come back. They ordered him to arrest Darby.

At a court in January 1666, the judges found the three men "not guilty of fault." They ordered Edward Martin, who had reported the men, to pay all the costs of the case. The record does not say whether the men acted the play in front of the judges. The court orders are the only record of the play from its own time.

<a id="story-william-darby-1665"></a>

#### William Darby

> **Who:** One of the three men who acted *Ye Bare and Ye Cubb* in Virginia in 1665, and the one the sheriff was ordered to arrest.
>
> **When and where:** Accomack County, Virginia, August 27, 1665, and the county court, November 1665 to January 1666.

William Darby is one of the first people on record to act a play in English in what is now the United States. The Accomack County court record calls him an "actour" of *Ye Bare and Ye Cubb*. Later writers say he wrote the play or helped write it. The reference book *American Eras* lists it as "*Ye Bare and Ye Cubb*, by William Darby." Writers at the Oscar G. Brockett Center for Theatre History call him "one of the piece's authors."

In November 1665 the judges ordered the sheriff to arrest Darby "to answere at his ma'ties suit." That meant he had to answer a case brought in the name of His Majesty, the king. For the other two actors, the judges ordered only that they be held until they gave security that they would come back. In January 1666 the judges found all three men not guilty.

The court record is the only account of Darby from his own time. It does not say what work he did, when he was born or when he died.

#### Pueblo ceremonies attacked, and brought back

In New Mexico, Spanish officials and priests tried to end the Pueblo ceremonies that the masked dancers performed. Franciscan friars had set up Catholic churches in several Pueblo towns. The Franciscans are one group of Catholic friars. From 1656 to 1665, the Franciscan leader Alonso de Posada forbade the Pueblo people to hold their ceremonies. He ordered the missionaries, priests sent to win people over to Christianity, to go into the kivas, burn the masks there, and take or destroy the sacred objects. Armed Spanish soldiers protected the missionaries while they did it.

In 1675 Governor Juan Francisco Treviño ordered the arrest of 47 Pueblo religious leaders for sorcery. Sorcery means using magic to do harm. Spanish officials sentenced four of the men to death by hanging. They hanged three of them, and the fourth killed himself. They shamed the others, whipped them in public and put them in prison. Pueblo men then came to Santa Fe and demanded that the prisoners be freed, and the Spanish let them go. One of the men freed was Po'pay of Ohkay Owingeh.

Po'pay planned a revolt of all the Pueblo towns at once. He sent runners carrying knotted ropes to the towns, and the people in each town untied one knot a day. When the last knot was gone, the revolt would begin. On August 9, 1680, the Spanish caught two of the runners, Pedro Omtua and Nicolas Catua of Tesuque Pueblo, and tortured them. Dennis Zotigh's account for the Smithsonian does not say how. When Po'pay learned the two had been caught, he started the revolt a day early, on August 10. Pueblo fighters killed about 400 people, including 21 of the 33 Spanish priests in New Mexico. About 2,000 settlers who survived fled south to El Paso. After the Spanish left, the Pueblo people destroyed the churches and went back to their own religious ceremonies. The Spanish stayed away for 12 years.

#### What the record does not show

In the 1600s English colonists enslaved Africans. They owned them as property and forced them to work without pay. Writers for the American Battlefield Trust state that religion, storytelling, music and dancing were important parts of enslaved people's lives, and helped them keep African ways alive from parents to children. No record from the 1600s describes a performance by an enslaved person in the English colonies. The earliest known picture of a stick dance, a dance of enslaved people, is a watercolor called *The Old Plantation*, painted in the late 1700s.

### 1700 to 1750

Two of the first actors in the first playhouse in the English colonies were servants, bound by contract to the man who built it. That playhouse went up in Williamsburg, Virginia, between 1716 and 1718. Builders in Charleston, South Carolina, put up a theatre made for plays in 1735 and 1736. A British actor, Anthony Aston, worked in the colonies in the early 1700s. In Boston, a judge of the colony's high court wrote against acting a play. The preacher George Whitefield, who had prepared to act plays as a schoolboy, preached in the colonies. According to newspaper reports that Benjamin Franklin read, Whitefield once preached to 25,000 people in the fields.

#### The first actors and the first playhouses

The British actor Anthony Aston reached Charleston, South Carolina, in about 1702 and wrote a play about the colony there. Accounts give his arrival as 1701, 1702 or 1703. No copy of his play survives.

In 1716 a merchant named William Levingston signed a contract with Charles Stagg and his wife, Mary Stagg. The Staggs were his indentured servants. An indentured servant was a person bound by a contract to work for a master for a set number of years. Under the contract, Levingston agreed to build a playhouse in Williamsburg, and the Staggs agreed to act and dance in it. The first play on record there was acted in 1718. Lieutenant Governor Alexander Spotswood, the colony's leader at the time, sponsored it. No list of the plays acted in Levingston's playhouse survives.

Williamsburg stands on land that the Paspahegh and Chiskiack peoples used before the English came. Both belonged to Tsenacomoco, a group of nations that spoke related Algonquian languages and that Powhatan led until 1618.

In Charleston, a company of actors put on Thomas Otway's tragedy *The Orphan* on January 24, 1735. They acted it in the "Court-room" of Charles Shepheard's tavern on Broad Street, a room that colony officials rented for trials. The company gave six shows through March. A ticket cost forty shillings in South Carolina money. A shilling was a unit of money, and South Carolina money was worth less than English money, so the ticket was worth a little less than six English shillings.

Most of the actors' names are not recorded. A dancer named Henry Holt probably led them. Builders then put up a theatre on Dock Street, made for plays. It opened on February 12, 1736, with George Farquhar's comedy *The Recruiting Officer*.

The Etiwan people lived on the Charleston peninsula until 1672. That year the colony's Grand Council, the group of men who governed it, decided to build the town there. Colonists paid the Etiwan in trade goods to move away. Maurice Mathews, one of the colonists who probably arranged it, wrote in 1680 that the settlers paid the Etiwan "to remove them from their old habitations," meaning their old homes.

In Philadelphia, a company led by Walter Murray and Thomas Kean gave its first show on August 22, 1749, and acted Joseph Addison's tragedy *Cato* that month.

<a id="story-anthony-aston"></a>

#### Anthony Aston

> **Who:** A British lawyer who became an actor and wrote a play about South Carolina while he was there.
>
> **When and where:** Charleston, the Albemarle region of North Carolina, New York and Virginia, about 1701 to 1703.

Anthony Aston told his own story in the preface to his play *The Fool's Opera*, printed in 1730 or 1731. A preface is a short piece at the front of a book in which the writer speaks to the reader. Aston listed himself as "a gentleman, lawyer, poet, actor, soldier, sailer, exciseman, publican." An exciseman collected taxes on goods, and a publican ran a tavern.

He wrote that he reached Charleston "full of lice, shame, poverty, nakedness and hunger." There he "turned player and poet and wrote one play on the subject of the country." A player was an actor. That play does not survive.

He then spent about a month in the Albemarle region of North Carolina, where two settlers, Allen and Abraham Waights, supported him. On the way to New York, a storm blew his ship off course to the coast of Virginia. In New York he spent a winter "acting, writing, courting, fighting." Then he sailed to Virginia, and later he went back to England.

<a id="story-william-levingston"></a>

#### William Levingston

> **Who:** A merchant and dancing teacher who built the first playhouse in the English colonies, with two indentured servants as his actors.
>
> **When and where:** New Kent County and Williamsburg, Virginia, 1716 to 1723.

William Levingston built the first theatre in the English colonies, in Williamsburg, Virginia. Before that, he ran a dancing school that traveled around New Kent County. Charles and Mary Stagg were its star dancers, and they were his indentured servants.

Their contract, dated July 11, 1716, and recorded at Yorktown, set out how the theatre would work. Charles Stagg was an actor, a violin player and a dancer. Mary Stagg was an actor. The three agreed to share the costs of costumes, music and everything else needed to put on plays.

On November 21, 1716, Levingston bought land in Williamsburg. On it he built a house, a kitchen, a stable, a bowling alley and the theatre. He borrowed money from Dr. Archibald Blair with the property as security. In 1723 Blair foreclosed, which means he took the property because the debt was not paid.

Charles Stagg died in Williamsburg in 1735 or early 1736. After his death, Mary Stagg earned her living by holding dancing parties. College of William and Mary students acted plays in the theatre in 1735 and 1736. In 1745 a group of Virginia men bought the building and gave it to Williamsburg to use as a town hall.

#### Boston against plays

On March 2, 1714, Samuel Sewall, a judge of the Massachusetts high court who later became its chief justice, wrote a letter against a plan to act a play in the Council Chamber in Boston. The Council Chamber was the room where the colony's council met. Sewall wrote that even the Romans had not been so set on plays as to "turn their Senate House into a Play-House." He went on: "Let not Christian Boston goe beyond Heathen Rome in the practice of Shamefull vanities." No record shows that the play was ever acted.

#### Preaching as performance

George Whitefield was an English preacher who first came to the colonies in 1738. He made a preaching tour of the colonies from 1739 to 1741. According to newspaper reports that Benjamin Franklin read, Whitefield once preached outdoors to 25,000 people. As a schoolboy of about twelve in Gloucester, England, he wrote later, he "was very fond of reading plays." He stayed away from school "for days together to prepare myself for acting them."

Franklin heard Whitefield preach from the courthouse steps on Market Street in Philadelphia. Franklin wanted to know how far the preacher's voice carried. He walked backward down the street until he could no longer hear clearly. Then he worked out how many people could stand in a half circle that size, giving each person two square feet. He "computed that he might well be heard by more than thirty thousand."

Franklin also noticed that Whitefield spoke each sermon better every time he repeated it on tour. By then "every accent, every emphasis, every modulation of voice, was so perfectly well turn'd and well plac'd." Modulation means raising and lowering the voice. Franklin wrote that a preacher who traveled could improve a sermon "by so many rehearsals." A rehearsal is a practice run of a performance.

#### Pinkster and Black election days

In New York, enslaved Black people gathered for a holiday called Pinkster, with music and dancing. In Connecticut, Black communities chose their own governor.

Dutch settlers brought Pinkster to New Netherland, later New York, in the 1620s. The oldest written account of Pinkster appeared in the *New-York Weekly Journal* in March 1737. It describes a gathering in fields outside New York City, with African-style musical instruments. Enslavers gave the people they held time off for the holiday. For many enslaved Africans it was a chance to see loved ones and family members who lived some distance away. Africans and Europeans alike drank, played games, made music and danced at these gatherings, with dances called the jig, the breakdown and the double shuffle.

In Connecticut, Black communities held their own elections for a governor, possibly as early as 1749. A man named Hercules served as governor at New London in 1749. The voting took place the day after the white colonists' elections, and the celebration went on for a full week. Some of the clothes people wore were borrowed from the men and women who enslaved them. By custom, the enslaver of the man elected was expected to help pay for food, decorations and liquor.

### 1750 to 1800

A family company of actors from London landed in Virginia in 1752 and toured the colonies. One reference work describes their *Merchant of Venice* in Williamsburg that year as the beginning of truly professional theatre in America. Between 1750 and 1761, lawmakers in Massachusetts, Pennsylvania and Rhode Island passed laws against plays. In 1774, as the fight with Britain grew, the delegates to the First Continental Congress promised to discourage plays. Shortly before the war, the leading company of actors left for the West Indies. During the war, British soldiers acted a play in Boston, and American officers acted a play at Valley Forge. After the war the actors came back. The first plays by American writers that professional actors performed reached the stage in these years, and one of them brought a new character to it, the plain-spoken Yankee.

#### Laws against plays

In 1750 members of the Massachusetts General Court, the colony's lawmakers, passed "An Act for preventing Stage-Plays, and other Theatrical Entertainments." The act stated that plays "tend to increase immorality, impiety, and a contempt of religion." Impiety means a lack of respect for God. The act set fines for anyone who put on a play or took part in one.

On May 31, 1759, members of the Pennsylvania House of Representatives voted through a law against acting plays, with a fine of five hundred pounds. Two years later the lawmakers of Rhode Island passed "an act to Prevent Stage Plays and other Theatrical Entertainments." In 1762 members of the New Hampshire House of Representatives refused to let a company of actors into the town of Portsmouth. They said that plays had a "peculiar influence on the minds of young people and greatly endanger their morals." Peculiar here means special, and morals are a person's ideas of right and wrong.

On May 5, 1766, New Yorkers learned that members of the British Parliament had voted to end the Stamp Act. The Stamp Act was a British tax that many colonists had protested. A crowd tore down the theatre in Chapel Street, where a comedy called *The Twin Rivals* was advertised for that night. David Malinsky, writing in the *Journal of the American Revolution* in 2013, says that the New York Sons of Liberty did it. The Sons of Liberty were secret groups of colonists, sometimes violent, who fought the Stamp Act. Malinsky writes that the crowd severely beat an actor who was dressed as a woman and killed a small child. The older accounts record only that the theatre was destroyed. No record names the child, the actor, or who led the crowd.

#### 1752: the first touring company

In 1752 the London actor Lewis Hallam led a company of actors to Virginia. It included members of his family, among them his son Lewis, about twelve years old. It opened in Williamsburg with Shakespeare's *The Merchant of Venice* on September 15, 1752. William Dunlap, an early historian of the American stage, gave the date as September 5. The company acted tragedies by Shakespeare and Joseph Addison, and comedies by William Congreve and Richard Steele. *Hamlet*, *Othello* and *Richard III* were among its plays.

The company played Williamsburg, Annapolis, Philadelphia and New York. Hallam had trouble getting permission to act in New York and Philadelphia, and he did not even try in Boston. In New York, Hallam built a theatre on Nassau Street in 1754.

Lewis Hallam then died in Jamaica, where the company had gone to perform. His widow, Sarah Hallam, married the actor and manager David Douglass. In 1758 they formed the American Company. Douglass built a theatre in Philadelphia in 1759. In Annapolis he opened a brick theatre on March 3, 1760, that held five to six hundred people.

Charles Daly, writing in 1896, says Douglass also built a theatre in Chapel Street, New York, in 1761. Gabriel Furman's notes name another man, Phil Miller, as its builder.

<a id="story-lewis-hallam-younger"></a>

#### Lewis Hallam the Younger

> **Who:** A boy in the first touring company of actors in the colonies, who grew up to be the leading actor and manager of the American Company.
>
> **When and where:** Born about 1740 in England. Came to Virginia in 1752. Died in Philadelphia on November 1, 1808.

Lewis Hallam the Younger spent about fifty years on the stage in America. He was about twelve years old when his father's company landed in Virginia in 1752. The historian William Dunlap got that story from Hallam himself.

In 1758, at eighteen, Hallam became the leading man of the American Company, which his mother and stepfather ran. He acted in *The Prince of Parthia* in 1767, the first play by an American writer that professional actors staged. He also acted in *The Contrast* in 1787.

His mother died in 1774, and his stepfather retired to Jamaica. Hallam then took over the family company. Shortly before the Revolution, he moved to the West Indies. He brought the company back in 1784 or 1785, depending on the account, and managed it until 1796. He kept acting until shortly before he died. *Encyclopaedia Britannica* describes him as "known as a quarrelsome and financially inept manager," which means he argued with people and handled money badly.

<a id="story-nancy-hallam"></a>

#### Nancy Hallam

> **Who:** An actress and singer in the American Company, and the subject of an early painting of an actress in a role in America.
>
> **When and where:** Annapolis, Maryland, 1770 and 1771.

Nancy Hallam was an actress whom the painter Charles Willson Peale painted in the costume of one of her roles. She was the niece of Sarah Hallam Douglass. She trained as a singer in England from 1760 to 1765, and she was acting with the American Company by 1766. In 1769 she moved from the parts of young women to leading roles.

In 1770 in Annapolis, she played Imogen in Shakespeare's *Cymbeline*. Imogen is a princess who disguises herself as a young man named Fidele. On September 6, 1770, the *Maryland Gazette* printed a letter signed only with the initials "Y.Z." It praised her "Delicacy of Manner" and "the Musick of her Tongue."

Peale painted her dressed as Fidele, and the painting was on view by September 1771. Colonial Williamsburg owns it today. Nancy Hallam went back to Britain in 1773. What happened to her after that, and when she died, is not known.

#### The first American plays

Thomas Godfrey wrote a tragedy called *The Prince of Parthia*. The American Company acted it at the Southwark Theatre in Philadelphia on April 24, 1767. It was the first play by an American writer that professional actors performed. Godfrey had died of a disease called yellow fever in 1763, so he never saw it on the stage.

Mercy Otis Warren of Massachusetts wrote plays in which she attacked the policies of the colony's British governor. They were printed without her name. The first appeared in a newspaper, the *Massachusetts Spy*. At the time, Massachusetts law banned acting plays.

Royall Tyler wrote a comedy called *The Contrast*. It opened at the John Street Theatre in New York in 1787. It was the first comedy by an American that professional actors performed. Tyler wrote it after he met Thomas Wignell, the American Company's leading comic actor. Its leading character, Jonathan, has rough, plain-spoken manners. He is a Yankee, a word that can mean a person from New England. Playwrights after Tyler kept writing Yankee characters like him. *Encyclopaedia Britannica* describes Jonathan as "the predecessor of many such in years to follow," meaning the first of many characters like him.

<a id="story-mercy-otis-warren"></a>

#### Mercy Otis Warren

> **Who:** A Massachusetts writer who used plays to attack the royal government at a time when Massachusetts law banned acting them.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Barnstable, Massachusetts, on September 14, 1728. Wrote plays from 1772 to 1779. Died in 1814.

Mercy Otis Warren wrote five plays against the royal government in Massachusetts and signed none of them. Her first, *The Adulateur*, came out in 1772 in the *Massachusetts Spy* newspaper. In it she attacked the policies of the British governor of Massachusetts. *The Defeat* followed in 1773, *The Group* in 1775, *The Blockheads* in 1776 and *The Motley Assembly* in 1779.

The National Women's History Museum's biography of her states that she likely left her name off the plays to avoid being punished, and also so that readers would take her work seriously even though a woman wrote it. In 1805 she published a history of the American Revolution in three volumes.

#### Congress against plays, and armies acting them

The First Continental Congress was a meeting of delegates, men chosen by each colony to speak for it. On October 20, 1774, they signed an agreement called the Continental Association. In its eighth article they promised to "discourage every species of extravagance and dissipation." Extravagance means spending too much, and dissipation means wasting time and money on pleasure. The list that followed named horse racing, cockfighting, "shews, plays, and other expensive diversions and entertainments." Shortly before the war, the American Company left for the West Indies.

British soldiers acted a play in Boston while American troops surrounded the city. On December 2, 1775, they staged *Zara*, a tragedy by the British writer Aaron Hill, in Faneuil Hall. The poster states that it was put on "by a Society of Ladies and Gentlemen." General John Burgoyne wrote a prologue for it, a speech given before the play begins. Francis Rawdon-Hastings, a British officer, is said to have read it. The money from tickets went to the widows and children of soldiers.

American officers at Valley Forge acted Joseph Addison's *Cato* in the spring of 1778. Lieutenant Colonel William Bradford Jr. wrote in a letter that "Cato was performed before a very numerous & splendid audience." He wrote that "His Excellency and Lady" were there, and that the performance was "admirable." His letter uses only that title and gives no names. Accounts date the performance May 4 or May 11, 1778. The audience was officers and their guests. Shawn David McGhee, writing in the *Journal of the American Revolution* in 2024, argues that it may have been a reading of the play rather than a full staging.

In October 1778 the delegates to Congress asked the states to stop "theatrical entertainments." On October 16 the delegates voted that any official who would "act, promote, encourage or attend such plays, shall be deemed unworthy to hold such office."

#### After the war

Lewis Hallam the Younger brought the American Company back from the West Indies in 1784 or 1785 and started it up again.

The Massachusetts law of 1750 still banned plays. In 1791 a group of men who wanted a theatre in Boston tried and failed to get it repealed, which means ended by a vote. In 1792 they opened the "New Exhibition Room" on Board Alley anyway. They sometimes advertised its plays as "moral lectures," talks meant to teach right from wrong. Governor John Hancock forced it to close in June 1793.

### 1800 to 1850

In 1828 a white actor named Thomas Dartmouth Rice blacked his face with burnt cork and played a Black man as a fool. White audiences paid to laugh at the act, and by 1843 four white men in the same makeup were performing together as a group. The first known Black theatre company in the United States had opened in New York in 1821. Police arrested its actors in the middle of a play. In 1824 a young actor from the company, Ira Aldridge, left for England. In the United States he faced discrimination, which means he was treated worse because he was Black.

In the same years, actors played Shakespeare in city theatres and on boats on the rivers. In 1849 the fans of two rival actors fought outside a New York theatre. City officials gave soldiers the order to fire into the crowd, and the soldiers killed at least 22 people.

#### The African Theatre, New York, 1821 to 1823

The first known Black theatre company in the United States opened in New York in 1821. Its founder, William Brown, was a free Black man from the West Indies who had worked as a steward, a servant on a ship. He ran a tea garden behind his house at 38 Thomas Street, an outdoor place for refreshments and shows, with music on Sunday afternoons. In 1821 he opened a theatre with about 300 seats on the second floor of a building at Mercer and Bleecker Streets. Its actors were Black. It opened with Shakespeare's *Richard III*. Accounts give the first night as September 17, 21 or 24, 1821. A ticket cost 25 cents, or 50 cents for a better seat.

On the first night, an enslaved man played the king in a robe made from a window curtain. After that, an actor named James Hewlett took over the part. The company also played Shakespeare's *Othello* and other plays such as *The Poor Soldier*. White New Yorkers came too, and some of them made trouble.

A group of people that included a man named George Bellmont broke into the theatre. They attacked the actors and wrecked the costumes and scenery. Police arrested Bellmont and several of the others.

Brown then moved his company next door to the Park Theatre, run by a white manager named Stephen Price. Brown's company played *Richard III* on the same nights as Price's company. White members of the audience shouted at Brown's actors and broke up the show. According to the Shakespeare Theatre Company, which has published Hewlett's history, Price started a riot because he hoped to destroy Brown's company. During one performance, police arrested the actors and put them in jail. The police let them go only after they promised to stop acting Shakespeare. The surviving records do not give the date or name the officers.

Mordecai Noah, the editor of a newspaper called the *National Advocate*, mocked the company in print. He warned that free Black New Yorkers might one day "outvote the whites." In October 1822 Noah's newspaper included a notice that the theatre was closing because of an outbreak of a disease called yellow fever. A playbill is a printed poster for a show. The last known playbill of the company is from June 1823.

In London, the English comedian Charles Mathews mocked the company in his show *A Trip to America*, although he had never been to its theatre. In May 1824 James Hewlett answered him in a letter in the *National Advocate*: "Was this well for a brother actor?"

<a id="story-william-alexander-brown"></a>

#### William Alexander Brown

> **Who:** A Black ship's steward from the West Indies who started the first known Black theatre company in the United States, and wrote the first known play by a Black writer to be acted there.
>
> **When and where:** New York City, 1816 to 1823.

William Brown wrote *The Drama of King Shotaway*, the first known play by a Black writer to be staged in the United States. Accounts give his full name two ways, as William Alexander Brown and as William Henry Brown.

In 1816 Brown bought a house on Thomas Street in New York. On Sunday afternoons he offered music and other shows in the tea garden behind it. In September 1821 he opened his theatre with *Richard III*.

Neighbors and police complained about the tea garden again and again until it closed. Brown moved his company several times. A group of people broke in and attacked his actors. Police arrested his actors in the middle of a play and freed them only when they promised to stop acting Shakespeare.

In 1823 Brown staged *King Shotaway*. It told the story of the war that the Black Caribs of the Caribbean island of St. Vincent fought against English and French settlers in 1796. The Black Caribs, now called the Garifuna, were a people whose ancestors were both free Africans and Native people of the Caribbean. No copy of the play survives. The last known playbill of Brown's company dates from June 1823. What happened to Brown after that is not known.

<a id="story-ira-aldridge"></a>

#### Ira Aldridge

> **Who:** A Black actor from New York who left the United States in 1824 and spent more than forty years acting Shakespeare in Britain and Europe.
>
> **When and where:** Born in New York about July 24, 1807. Went to England in 1824. Died on tour in Łódź, Poland, on August 7, 1867.

Ira Aldridge became a successful Shakespearean actor in Britain and across Europe. He is not known to have acted on a stage in the United States after he left. He went to the African Free School in New York. As a teenager he acted with William Brown's company.

In the United States, Aldridge faced discrimination, which means he was treated worse because he was Black. In 1824 he sailed to England. In October 1825 he played Oroonoko in a play called *The Revolt of Surinam, or A Slave's Revenge*, at a London theatre. A writer in *The Times* of London made fun of the shape of his lips. The same writer said his skin was not dark enough for him to play Othello.

Aldridge played Othello anyway, and King Lear and Macbeth. In 1828 he became the manager of the theatre in Coventry, England. In 1833 he took over the part of Othello at the Theatre Royal, Covent Garden, in London. *Encyclopaedia Britannica* describes that first appearance there as "highly successful."

He also played white characters, such as Shylock and Richard III, wearing greasepaint, a thick stage makeup, and a wig. On the last night of a run, he spoke to the audience against slavery. Rulers in Prussia, Austria and Russia gave him honors, and in 1863 he became a British citizen.

After the Civil War, Aldridge planned a tour of the United States and agreed to act in New York in September 1867. He died in Poland that August, before he could make the trip.

#### Blackface minstrelsy: the act and the makeup

In blackface minstrelsy, white actors darkened their faces with burnt cork and acted Black people as fools. A caricature is a picture or an act that makes fun of people by blowing up some of their features. Minstrel actors built caricatures of Black people and acted them as singing, dancing, grinning fools. White audiences paid to watch. Writers at the Jim Crow Museum at Ferris State University state that Rice and the actors who copied him helped to spread the belief that Black people were lazy, stupid and less than human. They write that the shows also helped white people argue for keeping Black people apart from them.

Thomas Dartmouth Rice was a white actor who did short comic acts between the scenes of plays. In 1828 he first went on stage as "Jim Crow," a Black character acted as a fool, with his skin blacked with burnt cork. Rice said he copied a Black man he had seen. Some accounts say the man was old, enslaved and walked with difficulty. Others say he was a ragged stable boy. No record names him.

Rice took the act from Louisville to Cincinnati, Pittsburgh and Philadelphia, and he reached New York in 1832. The act made him rich and famous. He died poor in New York on September 19, 1860. By 1838 people were using "Jim Crow" as an insult for Black people. By the end of the 1800s, "Jim Crow" was the name for the segregation laws and customs, under which Black Americans had to live apart from white Americans. Segregation means keeping people apart by race. Those laws came after 1877 and lasted until the mid-1960s.

On January 31, 1843, four white men in New York performed together in blackface as the Virginia Minstrels, the first group act of its kind. Years later, Black performers took up minstrelsy too, and they also blacked their faces with burnt cork. They acted the same caricatures that white actors had invented. In the 1840s one young Black dancer was already working in blackface.

<a id="story-william-henry-lane"></a>

#### William Henry Lane (Master Juba)

> **Who:** A young Black dancer, known on stage as Master Juba, who danced in blackface and who toured with a white minstrel company.
>
> **When and where:** New York and London, 1840s. Born about 1825, died about 1854.

William Henry Lane was a Black dancer, known on stage as Master Juba. The reference book *Notable Black American Men* states that he was the only Black dancer of his time to get top billing, which means his name came first on the posters, in a minstrel company whose other members were all white. He toured with that company in the United States and in Britain. He learned to dance in the Five Points, a neighborhood in New York. By the early 1840s he was dancing for food and for coins people tossed him. Charles Dickens described a young Black dancer in the Five Points in a book in 1842, and later writers decided the dancer was Lane.

A letter printed in a newspaper called the *Sunday Flash*, in 1841 or 1842, made a charge against the showman P. T. Barnum. The letter said that Barnum had made the Black boy up in blackface and advertised him as John Diamond, an Irish-American dancer who performed in blackface. It also said that Barnum staged fake dance contests with him: "Not one dollar is ever bet or staked." The historian Eric Lott called the act "a black man imitating a white man imitating a black man." Lane later danced against the real John Diamond in public dance contests.

In 1848 Lane went to London with the Ethiopian Serenaders, a white minstrel company. A writer for *The Times* of London said that Lane "was compelled to repeat his efforts three times," which means the crowd made him dance again and again. He died in about 1854, when he was about 29. Overwork and too little food probably killed him, but no record states the cause of his death.

#### Shakespeare on the rivers

Actors carried plays to river towns by boat. In 1816 the actor Noah Ludlow bought a flatboat, a wide boat with a flat bottom, 25 feet long, at Olean, New York. He named it Ludlow's Noah's Ark. He and eleven others floated down the Allegheny, Ohio and Mississippi rivers and stopped to perform wherever they could.

In 1831 the British-born actor William Chapman built a boat called the Floating Theatre at Pittsburgh. It was 14 feet wide and 100 feet long, the first boat built to be a theatre. Chapman and his family acted plays such as Shakespeare's *The Taming of the Shrew* at each landing, with songs and dances added. When they reached New Orleans, they broke up the boat and went back to Pittsburgh on a steamboat to build another. From 1836 Chapman used a small steamboat to tow the theatre back up the river.

A night on the Floating Theatre began with a play. Then came a speech and a set of short scenes and songs. A ticket cost fifty cents, and people who had no cash could pay with fruit, potatoes or bacon. Minstrel shows in the same years acted comic versions of Shakespeare, with titles such as "Julius Sneezer."

#### May 10, 1849: the Astor Place riot

On May 10, 1849, soldiers in New York fired into a crowd outside the Astor Opera House, on Astor Place. City officials and their own general had given the order. The crowd had come to stop the English actor William Charles Macready from playing Shakespeare's *Macbeth*. The historian Nigel Cliff counts between 22 and 31 dead.

The quarrel began between two actors. Edwin Forrest, the American star, was jealous of Macready. In 1846, in a theatre in Edinburgh, Scotland, Forrest hissed at Macready from a private box.

On May 7, Forrest's supporters stopped Macready's *Macbeth* inside the opera house by throwing rotten eggs, potatoes, shoes and pieces of ripped-up seats. Forty-seven New Yorkers, including the writers Herman Melville and Washington Irving, signed a letter asking Macready to play again. Captain Isaiah Rynders and the writer Ned Buntline put up posters that spoke to working men. Rynders belonged to Tammany Hall, a political group in New York. The posters read "WORKINGMEN! SHALL AMERICANS OR ENGLISH RULE IN THIS CITY?" The two men also handed out free tickets.

On May 10 a crowd of about 10,000 gathered outside the opera house. Mayor Caleb Woodhull had called out the militia. A militia is an army of part-time soldiers who have other jobs. General Charles Sandford brought about 350 soldiers of the Seventh Regiment, one unit of that army. People in the crowd threw stones at the building and at the soldiers. Frederick Talmadge was the city's recorder, an elected city officer who also served as a judge. He told General William Hall, "You must order your men to fire." Sandford said his men would not "stand and be pounded to death with stones." Then the sheriff, whose name no record gives, said, "you have permission to fire." Sandford gave the order. The soldiers fired first over the crowd's heads. Then they lowered their guns and fired into the crowd.

Betsy Golden Kellem, writing in *Smithsonian* magazine in 2017, counts 18 dead that night. Five more died of their wounds in the next few days, 23 in all. Miguel Hernandez, writing in the *New York Almanack*, counts 25. Cliff counts between 22 and 31. Kellem writes that many of those shot were bystanders, people who were only watching. Seven of the dead were Irish immigrants. The dead included carpenters, clerks, printers and laborers, both men and women. About 48 people in the crowd were hurt, along with 50 to 70 police officers and 141 soldiers. The next night, in more fighting near Astor Place, a young boy was killed.

A jury later found that the events "justified the authorities in giving the order to fire." In September 1849 Buntline and nine others were found guilty of starting the riot, fined and jailed. Kellem does not name the judge. Kellem calls the shooting "the most significant loss of civilian life in New York since the Revolution."

<a id="story-edwin-forrest"></a>

#### Edwin Forrest

> **Who:** An American-born star actor whose fans rioted against his English rival, William Charles Macready, at Astor Place in 1849.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Philadelphia on March 9, 1806. Acted from about 1817 to 1872. Died December 12, 1872.

Edwin Forrest was an American star actor. In 2006 the Theatre Alliance of Greater Philadelphia, a group of the city's theaters, called him "America's first superstar of the stage and the highest paid actor in the world in the mid-nineteenth century." He first acted at eleven, at the South Street Theatre in Philadelphia. He became a star playing Othello at New York's Bowery Theatre in 1826.

From 1828 Forrest paid prizes for new American plays that had a leading part written for him. The first winner was *Metamora*, by John Augustus Stone. Its hero is Metacom, a leader of the Wampanoag nation, whom the English called King Philip. Forrest, a white actor, played him from December 15, 1829. At the end of the play, Metamora kills his wife to save her from the settlers, and then he dies. The theatres made record profits from the play, and Stone got very little of the money.

An English visitor, Thomas Hamilton, called Forrest "a coarse and vulgar actor." Hamilton also wrote that his audience "were enraptured," meaning they loved him. In 1846 Forrest hissed Macready in Edinburgh, and in May 1849 Forrest's fans in New York rioted against Macready. No record shows that Forrest led the crowd or was at Astor Place that night.

In 1850 Forrest beat the writer Nathaniel Parker Willis with a whip in Washington Square, in New York. Willis took him to court and won $2,500. Forrest's wife, Catherine, won their divorce case on January 24, 1852, after a six-week trial in New York. She got the divorce, and Forrest had to pay her money every year. He kept acting almost until he died, partly to pay it.

### 1850 to 1900

From 1852 until well after 1900, white actors in blackface toured the country playing the enslaved people in stage versions of *Uncle Tom's Cabin*, a novel written against slavery. In 1865 a working actor, John Wilkes Booth, shot President Abraham Lincoln in a theatre where he often performed. From 1881 theatre managers in New York and Boston built a new kind of show called vaudeville. Buffalo Bill's Wild West opened in 1883. Native performers in the show acted out attacks on settlers. Black minstrels such as Billy Kersands worked in the same burnt-cork makeup that white minstrels wore. In 1894 the first paying customers in New York watched films, and most of those films showed stage performers doing their acts.

#### The Tom shows

Harriet Beecher Stowe published *Uncle Tom's Cabin*, a novel against slavery, in 1852. That year she refused to let it be made into a play, writing that "it would not be advisable." She never earned a cent from any stage version of it.

Theatre managers staged it anyway. The version that lasted opened in Troy, New York, on September 27, 1852. The manager, G. C. Howard, paid his 22-year-old cousin, George L. Aiken, $40 and a gold watch to write it in a week. When Aiken's play reached New York in July 1853, it ran for about 300 performances.

White actors in blackface played the enslaved characters. In Troy, the company's leading man, Green Germon, did not want to play a blacked-up character. He feared audiences would then expect minstrel dances and "Jim Crow" songs from him. The manager's wife, Mrs. Howard, played the enslaved girl Topsy and danced a minstrel dance called a breakdown. In January 1854 Thomas Dartmouth Rice, the actor who had created "Jim Crow," played Uncle Tom at New York's Bowery Theatre.

P. T. Barnum put on a version by Henry J. Conway at his American Museum in New York. His advertisement stated that this version "does not foolishly and unjustly elevate the Negro above the white man in intellect or morals." Negro was a word of that time for a Black person. The advertisement promised white audiences that the play would not show Black people as being as smart or as good as white people.

People called these stage versions Tom shows. In the 1890s between 400 and 500 touring companies were playing the story. An agent's price list from 1893 offered actors to play Uncle Tom by the week, with "prime" ones at $60, "fair" ones at $50 and "culls" at $40. Culls were the leftovers, the worst of the lot. By 1902, one report counted a quarter of a million performances. A dozen companies were still touring the story in 1927.

<a id="story-charlotte-cushman"></a>

#### Charlotte Cushman

> **Who:** A Boston-born actress who played men's parts, including Romeo and Hamlet, as well as women's parts.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Boston on July 23, 1816. Acted in the United States and Britain from 1835 to 1875. Lived in Rome from 1852. Died in Boston on February 18, 1876.

*Encyclopaedia Britannica* describes Charlotte Cushman as "the first native-born star on the American stage." A Philadelphia theater group has called Edwin Forrest, who was born in Philadelphia ten years before her, "America's first superstar of the stage," so the two descriptions do not agree on who came first. Cushman first trained to sing opera. Her voice failed after she sang parts that were too high for it, and she turned to acting. In 1836 she played Lady Macbeth.

Cushman played men's parts as well as women's. In London in 1845, and again in 1854 and 1855, she played Romeo while her sister Susan played Juliet. She also played Hamlet.

From 1848 Cushman lived with the writer Matilda Hays, and people in Europe knew the two women as a couple. In 1852 Cushman settled in Rome, among a group of American women who were artists. She later lived with the sculptor Emma Stebbins. Cushman helped the career of the sculptor Edmonia Lewis, whose mother was of Ojibwe and African American descent.

During the Civil War, Cushman acted to raise money for the care of Union soldiers. In 1869 doctors began treating her for breast cancer. She kept acting and reading on stage. She announced her farewell at least seven times before her last performance in Boston on May 15, 1875.

#### April 14, 1865: an actor at Ford's Theatre

The man who killed President Abraham Lincoln was an actor. John Wilkes Booth came from a family of actors, and he often performed at Ford's Theatre in Washington. On April 14, 1865, he learned that Lincoln would come that night to see a comedy called *Our American Cousin*.

That night Booth found the president's box almost unguarded. He went in, barred its outer door from the inside, and waited for a line that he knew would bring a big laugh. Then he burst into the box and shot Lincoln once in the back of the head with a small pistol called a derringer. Booth also slashed Major Henry Rathbone, one of Lincoln's guests, in the shoulder with a knife. The play stopped at the line "you sockdologizing old man-trap," a joking insult made of slang of the time.

Booth jumped from the box to the stage below. He broke his left leg in the fall, though some people believe the leg broke later. Accounts differ on what he shouted: "Sic semper tyrannis," Latin for "Thus always to tyrants," or "The South is avenged!", or both. Lincoln died the next morning.

The federal government bought the theatre in 1866. Edwin Stanton, the Secretary of War, ordered it turned into offices. On June 9, 1893, workers were digging in the basement to put in an electric light plant, and a brick pillar that held up the floors gave way. Part of the inside of the building fell in. Twenty-two clerks who worked there were killed, and at least 68 were hurt. An inquest jury, a jury that looks into a death, met to find out why. It found three men guilty of criminal negligence, which means carelessness so serious it is a crime. The three were Colonel Fred C. Ainsworth, the head of the office whose clerks worked there, the engineer, and George Dant, the contractor in charge of the building. The jury blamed Dant most, because he had not propped up the brick pillars before the digging began. The charges against all of them were later dropped. In 1968 the restored theatre held its first public performance since Lincoln's death.

<a id="story-edwin-booth"></a>

#### Edwin Booth

> **Who:** An American actor of Shakespeare who played Hamlet a record hundred nights in a row, and the older brother of John Wilkes Booth.
>
> **When and where:** Born in Bel Air, Maryland, on November 13, 1833. Acted mostly in New York and on tour. Died in New York on June 7, 1893.
>
> **Movie:** *Prince of Players* (1955), a feature film about his life.

Edwin Booth played Hamlet about a hundred nights in a row in New York in 1864 and 1865. That was a record, and no actor broke it until 1922. He was the son of the actor Junius Brutus Booth. Edwin supported the Union in the Civil War. His brother John Wilkes supported the Confederacy, the group of Southern states whose leaders broke away from the United States to keep slavery.

Edwin Booth once saved the life of Robert Lincoln, the president's son. Late in 1863 or early in 1864, on a train platform in Jersey City, New Jersey, Robert slipped into the gap between the platform and a moving train. Booth grabbed his coat collar and pulled him out. Robert Lincoln described the rescue in a letter in 1909.

After his brother killed President Lincoln, Edwin Booth stayed off the stage for about nine months. He came back as Hamlet in January 1866. He opened his own theatre in New York in 1869. It never made a profit, and in 1874 it went bankrupt, which means Booth could not pay its debts. In 1879 a salesman named Mark Gray fired two shots at him on a stage in Chicago and missed. In 1888 Booth bought a house in New York and founded The Players, a private club, in it. He kept an upper floor as his home, and he died there.

#### Vaudeville begins

Vaudeville was a show made of many short, separate acts, one after another. In 1881 Tony Pastor, a theatre manager, took over a theatre on 14th Street in New York. He sold no alcohol and kept the acts clean, so that women and families would come. *Encyclopaedia Britannica* credits Pastor with the first show of the kind later called vaudeville.

In 1883 Benjamin Franklin Keith opened a museum of oddities on Washington Street in Boston. Its first exhibit was a very small baby, three months old, shown to paying customers as "Baby Alice." Keith added a theatre with 123 seats. He ran a "continuous" show there from 10 in the morning to 11 at night, so customers could walk in at any time. From 1885 Keith and Edward F. Albee ran the Bijou Theatre in Boston together. The two men went on to build a chain of vaudeville theatres.

<a id="story-billy-kersands"></a>

#### Billy Kersands

> **Who:** A Black minstrel comedian, the most popular Black comedian of his day, who performed in burnt-cork blackface.
>
> **When and where:** Born about 1842 in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. Toured the United States and Europe. Died on June 30, 1915, in Artesia, New Mexico.

Billy Kersands was a Black comedian who blacked his face with burnt cork and played the character that white minstrels had invented. He worked in Black minstrel companies such as Sam Hague's Georgia Minstrels. On stage he played a slow, foolish Black man. He filled his wide mouth with billiard balls, or with a cup and saucer, to get laughs. Tom Fletcher, a Black performer who knew him, wrote that Kersands once told Queen Victoria that if his mouth were any bigger, his ears would have to be moved.

In 1872 Charles Callender, a tavern owner, bought the Black minstrel company that Kersands worked in. When Kersands and other stars asked for more pay and better treatment, Callender fired them. Most of them later came back to him.

Kersands earned about $15 a week in 1879, and by 1882 he was reportedly earning $80 a week, only a little less than a white minstrel star. On tours of Europe he earned up to $250 a week. White and Black audiences in the South came to see him. Because he drew such crowds, some theatre owners relaxed their rules limiting Black customers to separate sections of the theatre.

People asked Kersands why he never moved to vaudeville. Fletcher recorded his answer: "All of my money came from the people of the South, the white and the colored, while playing down there." Colored was a word of that time for Black people. Kersands died shortly after a show, at about 73.

#### The Wild West: Lakota performers

In 1883 William F. Cody, called Buffalo Bill, started a show called Buffalo Bill's Wild West, near North Platte, Nebraska. In its arena, Native performers acted out attacks on stagecoaches, wagon trains and a settler's cabin. Then cowboys and soldiers drove them off, and in the last scene Cody rode to the rescue.

A reservation is land that United States officials set aside for a Native nation, and an Indian agent was the federal official who ran it from an office called an agency. On June 6, 1885, at the Standing Rock Agency, the Hunkpapa Lakota leader Sitting Bull signed a contract to tour with the show for four months. It paid him $50 a week and let him sell his own photographs and autographs. James McLaughlin, the Indian agent at Standing Rock, signed as a witness.

Most Lakota men in the show earned less. In July 1890 the Lakota performer No Neck said that the men had been paid $25 a month. In early 1891 Cody and Nate Salsbury, who had started the show with him, wrote to the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, the federal official over all the agents, that the men would be paid $25 a month, that men they called "chiefs" would get $30 to $60 and that women would get $10. To hire Lakota people from their reservations, Cody needed permits, written permission from federal officials.

Several performers died on the show's tours of Europe. Surrounded by the Enemy, an Oglala Lakota man, died of a lung infection in London in 1887 and was buried there. Four months before him, a one-year-old boy named Red Penny, the son of Little Chief and Good Robe, died and was buried in the same London cemetery. Chief Hawick died of typhoid fever on January 1, 1890, and Featherman died of smallpox. Typhoid fever and smallpox are serious diseases that often killed people then. Both men had been left in a hospital in Marseilles, France. Wounds One Another died after he fell from a train in Germany, with $108 in wages still owed to him. No full count of the deaths survives.

More and more Lakota performers died on the tours, and others came home in poor condition. John Noble, the Secretary of the Interior, ordered an investigation because of those deaths and the state of the men coming home. He also stopped giving new permits for Native performers. In July 1890 No Neck told reporters that no more Lakota would go for less than $50 a month. He also said that Cody had given him "a suit of clothes, paid my wages, and gave me $100 besides," and had told him to give "a good report of the treatment of the Indians."
