The magazine *Archaeology* gives the count as 20,000 beads, and another published count gives about 10,000. Melvin Fowler dug up this burial in a mound called Mound 72 between 1967 and 1971. He described both bodies at the center as men. In 2016 a team led by Thomas Emerson of the Illinois State Archaeological Survey studied the bones again. They found that the two were a man and a woman, with other pairs of a man and a woman buried around them.

Mound 72 holds about 272 people, buried at different times over about a century. Archaeologists judge that almost 62 percent of them were sacrifices, people whom others at Cahokia killed on purpose as part of the burial ceremonies. No written record names them or the people who killed them.

#### Colors from plants and earth

Red ochre is iron oxide, a mineral made of iron and oxygen. It can be brown, red or yellow. Accounts written after Europeans arrived say that the Karankawa people of the Texas coast painted symbols on their faces with ochre, using their fingers or the stalks of plants. The Karankawa got their ochre by trade from inland. At a burial site called Mitchell Ridge, red ochre stains the bones of 18 people.

Porcupine quillwork is an art that Native people of North America practiced before Europeans arrived. A quill is one of the stiff, hollow spines that cover a porcupine. The Huron, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Cree and Gwich'in were among the nations that did quillwork. Men hunted the porcupines, and women did the work. They flattened the quills with an awl, a pointed tool, or with a piece of bone, then dyed them and sewed them onto moccasins, pouches, baby carriers and clothing.

Red came from the bark of the tamarack tree, from spruce cones and from berries, and black from walnuts and wild grapes. For yellow, quillworkers used wild sunflower, pine bark or willow root. Blueberries and larkspur, a flower, made blue. Writers at the Penn Museum in Philadelphia list these dye plants. The art is much older than the quilled pieces in the Penn Museum. Among the oldest there are pieces that George Catlin collected between 1832 and 1839.

### The 1500s

Spanish, French and English explorers and soldiers came to this land in the 1500s. A French group led by René de Laudonnière built Fort Caroline in Florida in 1564. Spanish and English newcomers wrote down what the Native people they met were wearing: deerskin, cloth of bark fiber and feathers, with ornaments of pearls. In 1540 the soldiers of Hernando de Soto dug up Native graves at the town of Cofitachequi to take the pearls buried there.

De Soto's men also found Spanish beads and a dagger at Cofitachequi. They had come from a Spanish colony started on the coast in 1526. In 1598 Spanish colonists drove churro sheep into New Mexico, onto the land of the Pueblo peoples. Wool from those sheep went into Native, Spanish and Mexican weaving for about 300 years.

#### Cloth and pearls at Cofitachequi, 1540

In May 1540 Hernando de Soto's army reached Cofitachequi, a Native town beside a river in the Southeast. A Portuguese man who marched with the army wrote an account of the march, printed in Portugal in 1557. His name is not known. He is called the Gentleman of Elvas, after the Portuguese town of Elvas. He described what the people of the town wore and what they kept.

A woman ruled the town. No record gives her own name, and the Spanish called her the Lady of Cofitachequi. She crossed the river by canoe to meet de Soto and gave him mantles, which are cloaks, and deerskins. Then she took a long string of pearls from her own neck and put it around his. He gave her a gold ring set with a ruby.

Elvas wrote that the town's storehouses held mantles woven from yarn made of tree bark. Other mantles were made of feathers colored white, green, red and yellow, and people wore them in winter. The storehouses also held deerskins with many panels drawn on them, and some of the deerskins had been made into leggings, stockings and shoes. Elvas wrote that everyone in the town wore shoes and clothes.

De Soto was looking for treasure. According to Elvas, the ruler told him to search the town's graves for pearls. She had seen how much the Spaniards valued them. De Soto's men dug up the graves. They took the pearls, and small figures of babies and birds made from pearls. The writers who tell this story give different amounts. Richard Hakluyt's English translation of Elvas says the men found "fourteen rows of pearls." An editor's note in a later printing gives 392 pounds. Other translations give 14 arrobas. An arroba is a Spanish weight of about 25 pounds, so 14 arrobas is about 350 pounds. Other accounts give about 200 pounds.

In the same town, de Soto's men found a dagger and beads. They came from a colony that Lucas Vázquez de Ayllón had started in 1526 on the coast of today's South Carolina or Georgia. Ayllón died there, and the surviving colonists left within about two months.

De Soto then took the ruler with him as a prisoner, guarded by enslaved women. On the march she told her guards she needed to relieve herself. She walked into the woods and escaped. She carried off a cane box full of pearls that had not yet been drilled.

#### What an Algonquian leader wore, 1585

In 1585 the English painter John White painted Native people who spoke Algonquian languages, a large family of related languages. Thomas Hariot wrote the words that went with the pictures. One painting shows a leader of one of these peoples, dressed for a great hunt or a feast. He wears an apron of animal skin with a fringe, and a tail hangs down behind it. His quiver, the case that holds his arrows, is tied to the tail.

Feathers decorate his hair. One side of his head is shaved. Hariot wrote that the shaving kept the hair from tangling in the bowstring.

#### Spanish clothes in St. Augustine, 1565 to 1600

Spanish soldiers and settlers founded St. Augustine, in Florida, in 1565, on land where the Timucua people lived. Archaeologists from the Florida Museum have dug up many of the things the colonists wore. Rich residents wore costly cloth trimmed with metal lace, buttons, beads and metal ornaments. Buttons were worn mostly by soldiers and the rich.

Most people tied their plain clothes shut with laces. Each lace was tipped with a small metal end, called an aglet, so it could pass through a hole. Many soldiers in the town married Native women.

Juan de Cevadilla was the official in Mexico who collected the pay for the soldiers of St. Augustine. He died suddenly in 1590. His widow was Doña Petronilla. Doña is a Spanish title of respect for a woman. He left her a carved bed covered with a thin layer of gold. Over the bed hung a cloth roof, called a canopy, made of taffeta from China with designs stitched into it. Taffeta is a smooth silk cloth. He also left her a large amount of costly cloth and clothing.

#### Churro sheep and red from Mexico

Juan de Oñate led Spanish colonists north from Mexico onto the land of the Pueblo peoples in New Mexico in 1598. They came on the road called El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the Royal Road of the Inland Country. They brought churro sheep, a Spanish breed. By the 1700s the churros in New Mexico numbered in the hundreds of thousands. For the next 300 years their wool was the base of Native, Spanish and Mexican weaving there.

Before the sheep came, Pueblo weavers worked in cotton on upright looms. The Spanish brought a loom that lay flat on the floor. Weavers in New Mexico later used it to make Rio Grande blankets and serapes, a kind of blanket that can be worn as a cloak. After the Spanish brought churro wool and new dyes, wool became the main thread for weaving there, and the old Pueblo cotton weaving declined.

Far to the south, in Oaxaca, Puebla and Tlaxcala in Mexico, Native people had long bred a small insect called cochineal to make red dye. As early as the 100s BC they used it to dye cloth and feathers and to color books painted by hand. After Spanish soldiers conquered Mexico, traders carried cochineal around the world. Native Mexicans still did all the skilled work and all the labor of making it. Writers at Harvard's science museums note that they were never given credit for it.

### The 1600s

In the English colonies of the 1600s, lawmakers in Virginia and Massachusetts wrote laws about who could wear what. In Massachusetts, a person whose property was worth less than 200 pounds was not allowed to wear silk hoods, gold or silver lace, or boots called "great boots." Judges in the county courts fined people who did.

Lists of belongings made after New England colonists died record clothes in red, blue, violet, grey and green, as well as black.

In New Mexico, Spanish soldiers and colonists demanded a woven cotton blanket from each Pueblo household every year. This was tribute, a payment that conquerors force a conquered people to make.

#### Virginia taxes clothing, 1619

The General Assembly of Virginia, the colony's lawmaking body, met for the first time on July 30, 1619. At that meeting its members passed a law "against excesse in apparel," meaning too much spending on clothes. They voted that each man's share of all public costs, collected through the church, would be set by his clothes. An unmarried man paid according to his own clothes. A married man paid according to his own clothes and his wife's.

A Virginia resolution of 1621 states the aim to "supress excess in cloaths." Under it, men who held no office in the colony could not wear gold in their clothes.

<a id="story-mary-ring-styles"></a>

#### Mary Ring

> **Who:** A widow of Plymouth Colony. The list of her belongings made after her death records her clothing, with the color of many pieces.
>
> **When and where:** Leiden in Holland, then Plymouth Colony, 1629 to 1631.

Mary Ring owned a red petticoat, a violet petticoat, two violet waistcoats and three blue aprons. A petticoat was a skirt, and a waistcoat was a vest or short jacket. A list of her belongings, made after she died, records these clothes and many more. Caleb Johnson wrote notes on her list for the Plymouth Colony Archive Project. He points out that the list shows the English colonists of Plymouth wore violet, red, blue and grey as well as black and white.

Mary Ring was the widow of William Ring, who died in Leiden, in Holland, in the 1620s. She came to Plymouth in 1629 or 1630 with her children Elizabeth, Susanna and Andrew. The English had built Plymouth in 1620 on the site of Patuxet, a town of the Wampanoag people. About 2,000 Wampanoag had lived in the area. Before 1620 a wave of sickness, now called the Great Dying, killed most of the people of Patuxet. The few who lived left to join other Wampanoag towns.

Mary Ring died on July 15 or 19, 1631. When a colonist died, everything the person owned was listed and given a value. This list is called a probate inventory. Mary Ring's inventory gives values in pounds, shillings and pence, the English money of the time. Her red petticoat was worth 16 shillings, the highest value of any piece of her clothing except a hooded cloak called a huke.

The inventory also lists a black kirtle, which is a kind of gown, and a waistcoat of "mingled coloured" cloth. It lists an apron in murrey, a dark purplish red, and pieces of blue cloth and red cloth. She owned blue stockings, white Irish stockings and a piece of grey kersey, which is a rough wool. She also owned six ruffs, which were stiff, pleated collars, and seven smocks, which were long linen shirts worn under the other clothes. She had three linen caps, two hats and two pairs of shoes. Her will left green cloth "to make a coat."

She signed her own will, and she owned books. Governor William Bradford and Edward Winslow owed her money when she died.

#### Colors in a Puritan closet

The Puritan colonists of Massachusetts wore colors they called "sad" colors. Puritans were English Protestants who wanted their leaders to strip the Church of England of the customs it still shared with the Catholic Church. Sad then meant serious, not unhappy. A list from 1638 names some of them: liver color, tawny, russet, purple, French green, orange and "deer colour."

The historian David Hackett Fischer writes that black cloth was kept for the ruling elders, the men who led the church, and for the families who governed the colony. A portrait of Governor John Winthrop, painted in about 1629, shows him in black velvet with slashed sleeves. The slashes were cuts in the sleeve that showed the cloth underneath.

Lists of belongings and bills from the colony record "pinck hose," "green sleeves," and "a Scarlet petticoat with Silver Lace." Hose were stockings. Fischer writes that Winthrop's own niece, Mary Downing, was scolded for wearing a little lace. His sentence about her does not say who scolded her.

#### Massachusetts dress laws, 1634 to 1682

A law that limits what people may wear, or spend on clothes, according to their rank is called a sumptuary law. The General Court of Massachusetts Bay was the colony's body of lawmakers and magistrates, the colony's chief officials and judges. Its members passed their first sumptuary law in 1634. It banned "new fashions, or long hair," silver and gold hatbands and belts, cloth woven with gold thread, and lace. It also limited slashes, cuts in a sleeve that showed the cloth underneath. The magazine *Atlas Obscura* gives the limit as two slashes in a sleeve, and the historian David Hackett Fischer gives it as one. A person caught wearing these things had to give them up. A law of 1639 banned more kinds of lace and banned short sleeves.

In 1651 the members of the General Court wrote that they felt "utter detestation," which means hatred, when "men or weomen of meane condition" dressed like gentlemen. Mean condition meant low rank. The lawmakers named gold or silver lace, gold or silver buttons, laces tied at the knees and "great boots." For women of that rank they named silk hoods and silk scarves. Anyone whose property was worth less than 200 pounds owed a fine of 10 shillings each time he or she wore them.

Magistrates, officers, soldiers and their families did not have to obey this law. Neither did people who had once been rich and had lost their money. The lawmakers gave the selectmen, the elected men who ran each town, the power to tax people who dressed above their rank.

Judges in the county courts enforced the law. In 1653 judges in Essex County heard 18 cases. They let 12 of the people go, because they were worth more than 200 pounds. Ten years later, in 1663, the lawmakers made the law cover children and servants too. They also barred tailors from making the forbidden clothes. A first offense brought a warning, a second a fine of 20 shillings, and later offenses up to 40 shillings.

Seven married women of Northampton faced charges of wearing silk at the Hampshire County court in 1673. The judges found all but one of them not guilty. At the same court, 9 married women of Springfield faced the same charge, along with 9 of Hadley, 7 of Hatfield and 3 of Westfield.

Between about 1680 and 1682, the five towns of Northampton, Hadley, Hatfield, Westfield and Springfield were charged at the county court. Their selectmen had failed to tax residents who wore silk "beyond their ranks." James Russell Trumbull, who wrote the history of Northampton, reports that nothing more was heard of these charges.

<a id="story-hannah-lyman-1676"></a>

#### Hannah Lyman

> **Who:** A Northampton girl of about 16 who was fined for wearing silk, and who wore it even while she stood charged before the court.
>
> **When and where:** Northampton, Massachusetts, 1676.

In 1676 the judges of the Hampshire County court in Massachusetts fined Hannah Lyman of Northampton 10 shillings for wearing silk. She was about 16 years old. She was charged with wearing silk "in a flaunting manner, in an offensive way and garbe, not only before, but when she stood presented." Flaunting means showing off, and garbe meant clothing. To stand presented meant to stand charged before the court. The words say she wore silk even then. Her father, Richard Lyman, had died.

Northampton stood on the land of the Nonotuck people. On September 24, 1653, John Pynchon got a deed to that land from seven Nonotuck men, including Chickwalloppe. A deed is a paper that hands over land. He paid 100 fathoms of wampum, which are strings of shell beads, and 10 wool coats. A fathom is 6 feet. The historian Margaret Bruchac writes that the Nonotuck signers probably understood the deed as an agreement to share the land. She writes that they probably expected to keep their own right to hunt, fish and plant there.

King Philip's War was fought in 1675 and 1676. Metacom, a leader of the Wampanoag whom the English called King Philip, led several Native nations against the New England colonies. About 9,000 people died in the war, and by some counts about half of all the Native people of New England died. On August 12, 1676, a Native man fighting for the colonists shot Metacom dead. The colonists sold hundreds of Native captives into slavery. During the war the Northampton minister Solomon Stoddard asked the colony's leaders to act against "that intolerable pride in clothes and hair." In November 1675 the members of the General Court passed a law listing the sins they said were common in the colony.

On March 27, 1676, at the Hampshire County court in Northampton, 23 people were charged "for wearing silk in a flaunting manner and for long hair and other extravagances." Extravagances meant spending too much on show. Six were married women. Six were unmarried, and the town's historian thought they were probably young girls. The rest were young men. The judges warned them and made each one pay court fees of 2 shillings 6 pence. The wife of Samuel Holton had been charged before, so the judges fined her 10 shillings. Hannah Lyman was charged at a later session of the same court.

That March the county judges also fined 45 people from Springfield, Westfield, Hadley and Hatfield for silk and long hair. They were 11 married women, 15 unmarried women and 19 young men. Counts of the Northampton cases differ. The town's historian, James Russell Trumbull, gives the numbers above. The magazine *American Heritage* and the historian David Hackett Fischer write that Hannah Lyman was one of 36 young women of Northampton charged that year.

#### Blankets taken as tribute in New Mexico

After 1598 some Spanish colonists in New Mexico, called encomenderos, held the right to collect tribute from Pueblo households. The Beyond Origins of New Mexico Families project studied these encomenderos. It reports that by the 1660s each household owed one fanega of corn in the spring. A fanega was a Spanish measure of grain. In the fall each household owed one woven cotton blanket, called a manta, or one hide. The Spanish king allowed no more than 35 encomenderos at a time.

Ginés de Herrera Horta was a Spanish legal officer in Oñate's colony. In 1601 he testified that soldiers demanded a blanket each year from each household. When people said they had no blankets to give, the soldiers took the blankets off the women who were wearing them and left the women naked. The Spanish records of these seizures give no names for the women whose blankets were taken.

In 1680 most of the Pueblo peoples rose up against the Spanish colonists in the Pueblo Revolt, led by Po'pay of San Juan Pueblo. They killed about 400 Spaniards and forced about 2,000 settlers to flee New Mexico for about 12 years. Among the Pueblo people's complaints was the tribute of labor, ground corn and cloth that the colonists had forced them to hand over.

### 1700 to 1750

What a man wore on his head showed his rank in the English colonies between 1700 and 1750. The historian Thomas Ford calls the wig a badge of rank. A traveler in Maryland in the 1740s wrote that only a few men of the highest rank wore wigs, and that other men wore caps.

Enslavers dressed the people they enslaved in coarse, cheap cloth. In 1740 the lawmakers of South Carolina made that a law. They named cheap fabrics and barred enslaved people from wearing anything finer. They ordered constables, local officers who kept order, and anyone else who found finer clothes on an enslaved person to take them away and keep them. In the 1740s, South Carolina planters began growing indigo, a plant that gives a blue dye, in large amounts and shipping the dye to England. Enslaved people did the work of turning the leaves into dye.

#### Wigs and caps

A wig of this time was called a peruke. A wigmaker built it from rows of hair sewn onto a cap of net and ribbon. Wigmakers used human hair and also hair from horses, cows and goats. The historian Thomas Ford writes that a wigmaker preferred to measure a customer whose head was shaved, so the wig would fit. He calls the wig "an important badge of social rank."

A traveler in Maryland in the 1740s wrote that only a few men of "the very elevated Sort" wore wigs. Ordinary men wore caps of wool or yarn. Better-off men wore caps of white linen or cotton, even on journeys of 50 miles.

Some rich men, including Councillor Robert Carter, a member of the governor's council, and Dr. John Sequeira, had enslaved men trained to shave them and to dress their hair. Ford writes that rich planters may sometimes have dressed their enslaved coachmen and house servants in white wigs.

#### The 1740 clothing law in South Carolina

In September 1739, enslaved people in South Carolina rose up against their enslavers in the Stono Rebellion. On May 10, 1740, the lawmakers of the South Carolina assembly passed the Negro Act. Its full name was An Act for the Better Ordering and Governing Negroes and Other Slaves in this Province. Negro was the word the lawmakers of that time used for a Black person. Section 40 of the act was about clothes.

Section 40 began: "whereas, many of the slaves in this Province wear clothes much above the condition of slaves, for the procuring whereof they use sinister and evil methods." It barred any owner from letting an enslaved person "have or wear any sort of apparel whatsoever, finer, other, or greater value than Negro cloth, duffels, kerseys, osnabrigs, blue linen, check linen or coarse garlix, or calicoes, checked cottons, or Scotch plaids." The lawmakers claimed that enslaved people were getting clothes finer than the lawmakers thought slaves should wear, by wrong and wicked means. Servants in livery, a uniform the master chose, did not fall under this rule.

Many of the cloths on that list were coarse, which means rough and thick. Calicoes and checked cottons were cotton cloths. Garlix was a linen, and the law calls it "coarse." Negro cloth was a coarse cloth made for enslaved people's clothes. Osnaburg was a coarse, plain cloth first woven from flax in the German city of Osnabrück. Kersey was a thick, coarse wool, and duffel was a heavy wool used for blankets and coats. An earlier South Carolina act, passed in 1735, had already named cheap cloth for enslaved people's clothing.

The law required "all and every constable and other persons" to seize finer clothes from any enslaved person wearing them. A constable was a local officer who kept order. The person who seized the clothes could keep them "to his or their own use." An owner who thought the clothes had been taken wrongly could take the matter to a justice of the peace, a local judge. The surviving records do not show how often anyone seized clothes under this law.

<a id="story-jack-gambia-1745"></a>

#### Jack

> **Who:** A man taken from Gambia and enslaved in Virginia, who ran away within five weeks of his sale.
>
> **When and where:** Hanover County, Virginia, 1745.

Jack and another man ran away wearing new clothes: jackets and breeches, which were short pants that ended at the knee, of napped cotton with no buttons and no buttonholes, shirts of osnaburg, and felt hats. Napped cloth has been brushed so that its surface is soft and fuzzy. Almost everything known about him comes from an advertisement that his owner, Margaret Arbuthnott of Hanover County, placed in the *Virginia Gazette* in October 1745 to get him back.

Slave traders had brought Jack and another man from Gambia, in West Africa, on the ship *Ranger*. On September 5, 1745, the traders sold them at Newcastle, Virginia. The advertisement does not name the traders. Neither man spoke English. Both were nearly 6 feet tall. Arbuthnott described Jack as having a scar over his right eyebrow. The other man, whose name the advertisement does not give, had what Arbuthnott described as "3 small Strokes on each Side of his Face."

Arbuthnott accused the two men of taking a damask tablecloth, fine Scottish linen, checked cloth, a white linen shirt and a silk handkerchief. Damask is cloth woven with a pattern that shows in the weave. She offered a reward to anyone who caught them and brought them back.

The record does not say whether Jack was caught.

#### Indigo blue, 1739 to 1750

Indigo seeds came to South Carolina with the first English settlers in 1670. In the late 1730s and early 1740s, hundreds of South Carolina planters tried out new crops, and indigo was one of them. From 1739, Eliza Lucas tried growing indigo at Wappoo Plantation, on Wappoo Creek west of the Ashley River, near Charleston. She was 17 and managed the plantation and the 20 people enslaved on it. She worked first with an indigo maker from the island of Montserrat. She had the most success with an indigo maker of African descent whom her father hired from the French West Indies. In 1744 she used her crop to make seed and shared it with other planters.

The historian Nic Butler of the Charleston County Public Library writes that her part has been greatly exaggerated in recent times. Many of her neighbors were following the same steps. Her husband, Charles Pinckney, whom she married in 1744, published her methods in articles in 1744 and 1745 under the name "Agricola."

South Carolina's lawmakers voted to pay planters a bounty, a reward from the government, of 1 shilling for each pound of indigo in 1744. They canceled it in 1746. In 1748 members of the British Parliament, the lawmakers in London, voted a bounty of 6 pence a pound, starting in 1749. Planters began shipping large amounts of indigo to England in 1747. Exports rose from about 5,000 pounds in 1745 and 1746 to about 130,000 pounds in 1748.

Enslaved people of African descent did almost all of the work. They planted and tended the indigo. They built the vats, which were big tubs for making dye, and filled them with water and cut leaves. After the leaves soaked, the workers beat the liquid with paddles or with buckets that had no bottoms. They added lime, made from burnt oyster shells, so that the blue settled out. Then workers scooped the blue mud into bags, dried it and cut it into cubes.

Charles Woodmason wrote in 1755 that 15 enslaved workers could plant and tend 50 acres of indigo. He wrote that it took 25 skilled workers to turn that crop into dye. The accounts of indigo making from these years do not name the enslaved workers who made the dye. One enslaved man who built the vats is named. He was Quash, a carpenter whom the Lucas family held in slavery at Wappoo. In 1744 George Lucas, Eliza's father, wrote that "Quashe" should build a wooden indigo works at the family's Garden Hill plantation. Eliza told her father that Quash had spent 33 days building indigo vats at other Lucas plantations. On April 16, 1746, the minister Alexander Garden baptized him. The historian Tiffany Momon, who wrote about his life, calls him John "Quash" Williams.

South Carolina's indigo was shipped to England for British cloth makers. South Carolinians bought most of their own cloth from England, already dyed.

### 1750 to 1800

From the Stamp Act tax of 1765 until the Revolution, colonists who opposed British taxes agreed again and again to stop buying British goods, including cloth. A refusal like this is called a boycott. In 1774 delegates at the First Continental Congress, a meeting of leaders from the colonies, voted to ban British goods in every colony from December 1. Women held public spinning meetings. During the boycott of 1768 and 1769, a colonist who wore homespun, cloth spun and woven in America, often at home, showed that he or she backed the boycott. Harvard's graduating class of 1768 voted not to wear imported British clothes at their graduation.

In 1789 George Washington took the oath as the first president in a suit of brown wool woven in Connecticut. Furniture makers in the new country copied a style of sharp edges, legs that grew thinner toward the floor, and inlaid eagles. It is now called the Federal style. In Spanish New Orleans in 1786, the governor ordered Black women and women of mixed race to stop wearing feathers and jewels in their hair and to wear it plain or covered with a cloth.

#### Homespun as a protest, 1765 to 1776

During the boycotts of British goods in the 1760s, Boston merchants opened spinning schools again. In Hartford, members of a society offered a prize of 12 pounds to whoever made the most yards of wool cloth in a year. Newspaper printers ran reports of spinning meetings in Massachusetts, Connecticut and Rhode Island. In Newport one spinner was a woman of 70 who had never spun a thread before. Only six of the newspaper stories called the spinners "Daughters of Liberty."

In August 1769 women met at their minister's house in Brookfield, Massachusetts, starting at 5 in the morning. A report of the meeting said the best young spinner at the linen wheel, a spinning wheel for linen thread, spun 70 knots of yarn. A knot was a measured length of yarn. One married woman did her morning housework and made cheese first. Then she rode more than 2 miles carrying her own spinning wheel, spun 53 knots between 9 and 7, and went home to milk the cows.

In the autumn of 1767, the seniors at Harvard College voted not to drink tea or wear imported British clothes at their commencement, the ceremony at which students graduate. They did it to protest the Townshend taxes on goods from Britain. The printed sheets for the 1768 commencement, which listed the statements the graduates would argue for, were on paper made in New England. The next year's seniors did the same.

<a id="story-charity-clarke"></a>

#### Charity Clarke

> **Who:** A young New Yorker who wrote to her cousin in London that American women would spin, weave and dress in their own cloth rather than buy British clothes.
>
> **When and where:** Her father's estate called Chelsea, on Manhattan, 1768 to 1774.

In 1769 Charity Clarke, who was 21 or 22, wrote to her cousin in London. She told him what she would do if the English did not give Americans the liberty they asked for. The historian Alan Singer dates the letter June 1769, and other accounts date it December 8, 1769. She would lead "a fighting army of Amazons" and gather "a number of ladies armed with spinning wheels." In old Greek stories the Amazons were a nation of women warriors. Her ladies would have helpers "who shall all learn to weave and keep sheep," and they would all be "clothed with the work of our hands." They would be "no more slave to fashion and ceremony."

Charity Clarke was born in New York on June 28, 1747. She grew up on her father's estate, called Chelsea, on the island of Manhattan. Between 1768 and 1774 she wrote letters to her cousin Joseph Jekyll, a lawyer in London. Columbia University holds the letters today.

In 1774 she wrote to him again: "Though this body is not clad with silken garments, these limbs are armed with strength."

In 1778 she married the Rev. Benjamin Moore of Trinity Church. Their son, Clement Clarke Moore, wrote the poem "A Visit from St. Nicholas."

#### Wigs in Williamsburg, 1769 to 1775

Edward Charlton came to Williamsburg, Virginia, from London and became the town's leading barber and wigmaker. His account book for 1769 to about 1775 shows that in one year he sold sixty brown wigs of a style called the "dress bob." They cost 43 shillings each. For shaving a man and dressing his wig for a year, Charlton usually charged 2 pounds 3 shillings. Peter Pelham paid 1 pound 5 shillings, and Speaker Randolph, the leader of the colony's lawmakers, paid 4 pounds. In 1769 eight barbers and wigmakers worked in Williamsburg.

Wigmakers needed hair. George Long of Petersburg, another Virginia town, advertised that he would pay one shilling an ounce for human hair.

Wigs were going out of fashion in England, and Charlton retired shortly before the Revolution.

#### Indigo's peak and end

In 1775 South Carolina planters shipped more than one million pounds of indigo to England. Enslaved workers did almost all of the work of making it. The British bounty on indigo ran out in 1777, during the war with Britain. Some planters grew indigo again after the war ended in 1783. In the 1790s most of them gave up indigo, and many turned to cotton.

#### The tignon order in New Orleans, 1786

New Orleans was a Spanish colony in 1786. On June 2 of that year, Governor Esteban Rodríguez Miró issued a set of rules called the *bando de buen gobierno*, the order of good government. One rule was about the hair of Black women and women of mixed race. It said they could "no longer have feathers nor jewelry in their hair." They had to wear their hair plain or cover it with a *pañuelo*, a head cloth. People later called such a cloth a tignon.

The historian Virginia Meacham Gould writes that Miró aimed the rule at women who dressed "too elegantly" or "competed too freely with white women for status." She found little written evidence that officials enforced the rule, and no record that anyone was punished under it.

Portraits painted in New Orleans in the early 1800s show free Black women and women of mixed race wearing head wraps tied in many different styles. Gould reads the head wraps in these portraits as a mark of distinction.

<a id="story-george-washington-styles"></a>

#### George Washington

> **Who:** The first president, who took the oath of office in a suit made from American wool.
>
> **When and where:** Mount Vernon, Virginia, and New York City, January to April 1789.

George Washington took the oath as the first president of the United States on April 30, 1789, in New York, wearing a suit of brown wool cloth made in Connecticut. Three weeks before, on April 8, 1789, he wrote: "I shall allways take a peculiar pleasure in giving every proper encouragement in my power to the manufactures of my Country." Manufactures meant goods made by hand or by machine.

In January 1789 a writer in *The Federal Gazette* had urged American leaders to wear clothing made in America. He signed himself "a Philadelphia mechanic." A mechanic then meant a skilled worker who made things. The Hartford Woolen Manufactory in Connecticut had just begun making cloth. A merchant in Philadelphia could not get the cloth for Washington. Henry Knox, then the secretary of war, dealt with the Hartford factory himself. The cloth reached Alexandria, Virginia, in early April. Washington left Mount Vernon for New York on April 16.

The staff at Mount Vernon believe that Cavan Boa made the coat, waistcoat and breeches. Boa was Washington's indentured tailor, a servant bound to work for him for a set number of years. Kathrin Breitt Brown makes copies of old clothes for Mount Vernon. She calls the coat "well-made but hastily finished," and she thinks Boa probably had help. Washington asked for six large engraved buttons.

In England the color of the cloth was called London brown. Americans called it Congress brown. The coat came to the collection at Mount Vernon in 1933.

Washington did not wear a wig. He powdered his own hair.

#### The Federal style, 1780 to 1820

From about 1780 to 1820, American cabinetmakers made furniture in a style now called Federal. A cabinetmaker is a skilled maker of fine furniture. Federal pieces had legs that grew thinner toward the floor, and sharp edges. Makers covered them with veneers, thin sheets of fine wood laid over the surface. They inlaid pictures of eagles, urns and bellflowers, setting small pieces of different wood into the surface.

The main wood was mahogany, and makers also used satinwood, maple and birch. American makers copied designs from English pattern books by George Hepplewhite and Thomas Sheraton. Makers included John and Thomas Seymour in Boston and Duncan Phyfe in New York.

### 1800 to 1850

The cotton spun in American mills between 1800 and 1850 came from Southern plantations, where enslaved people grew and picked it. Workers in New England mills spun and wove that cotton into cloth. Workers in some mills in Rhode Island and in Lowell, Massachusetts, also wove a rough, cheap cloth that planters bought to dress the people they enslaved.

Fashionable women wore high-waisted white cotton dresses in the early 1800s. Later they wore tight corsets, stiff garments laced around the body. They also wore wide skirts held out by layers of petticoats, which are skirts worn under the outer skirt. Men stopped powdering their hair and cut it short. Some still wore knee breeches, pants that ended at the knee, and by the 1840s men wore narrow trousers. A government report in 1811 stated that two-thirds of all the clothes Americans wore were made at home. People who could pay for it had a tailor or a seamstress, a woman who sewed for pay, make their clothes. The first shops that sold clothes already made stood near the docks, and their customers were sailors and other working men.

#### What fashionable people wore, 1800 to 1850

In the first ten years of the 1800s, the fashionable dress for a woman had its waistline just under the breasts. It was made of muslin, a thin cotton cloth, and white was the most fashionable color. White dresses were hard to keep clean, and cleaning them cost money. For every day, women wore printed cottons and patterned silks, and wool in cold weather.

Men in the same years stopped powdering their hair and cut it short. They gave up embroidered silk and lace for plain wool coats in dark colors. Some still wore knee breeches. Others wore pantaloons, tight pants that reached the calf or the ankle. By the 1840s the frock coat was the standard coat for men. It was a fitted coat with a skirt that reached to just above the knee. Men wore it with narrow trousers and vests of brightly patterned silk.

In the early 1830s women's sleeves puffed out wide from the shoulder. This shape was called the gigot, or leg-of-mutton, sleeve. Mutton is sheep meat. Skirts became very wide, and women wore more and more petticoats under them. A petticoat is a skirt worn under another skirt. Under the dress, a woman wore a corset, a stiff garment laced tight around the body from the chest to the hips.

By the 1840s a fashionable corset ran from a woman's breasts down over her hips. Heavy cords and strips of whalebone stiffened it. Whalebone is a stiff, bendable material from the mouths of some whales. A long, flat piece of steel, wood or whalebone, called a busk, ran down the front. Sleeves were cut so tight that a woman often could not lift her arms higher than her shoulders. By the end of the decade some women wore six or seven petticoats.

*Godey's Lady's Book* was a magazine for women, published in Philadelphia from 1830. Each issue opened with a fashion plate, a picture of the latest dresses colored by hand. Louis Godey, the publisher, said that coloring the plates cost $8,000 in 1859. Sarah Josepha Hale edited the magazine from 1837 to 1877. About 10,000 copies of each issue went out in 1837, about 40,000 two years later and about 150,000 by 1860.

#### Cotton picked in the South, woven in the North

The owners and workers of the cotton mills in Lowell, Massachusetts, depended on cotton grown in the South by enslaved people. US Senator Charles Sumner called the tie between Southern planters and New England mill owners an "unholy union." On one side, he said, stood "the cotton planters and fleshmongers of Louisiana and Mississippi." On the other stood "the cotton spinners and traffickers of New England." A fleshmonger was a person who traded in human beings, and a trafficker was a trader.

In Lowell, workers at the Merrimack Company printed calico, cotton cloth printed with colored patterns. The company's owners hired skilled printers from England. The head printer they hired in 1825 was paid more than the company's treasurer, the officer in charge of its money.

Solomon Northup described how the cotton was picked. Northup was a free Black man, born in Minerva, New York. In 1841 two white men who called themselves Merrill Brown and Abram Hamilton offered him work with a circus. They took him to Washington and gave him a drink that drugged him. He woke up alone in the dark, in chains, in a slave pen near the US Capitol. A slave pen was a building where traders locked up enslaved people until they were sold. The slave trader James H. Burch beat him for saying he was free. In New Orleans, Burch's partner Theophilus Freeman sold him, and enslavers in Louisiana held him until January 1853. For almost ten years he picked cotton on the plantation of Edwin Epps, on Bayou Boeuf.

Northup wrote that the pickers had to be in the field as soon as it was light. They stayed until it was too dark to see, with 10 or 15 minutes at noon to eat cold bacon. At night each picker's basket was weighed. An ordinary day's work was 200 pounds of cotton. Epps and his drivers, the men who ran the work in the field, whipped anyone who brought in less. The more a picker came up short, the more lashes he or she got. A lash is one blow of the whip.

Epps set each picker's daily amount by what that person had shown he or she could pick. Northup called a woman named Patsey "the most remarkable cotton picker on Bayou Boeuf." He wrote that 500 pounds a day was not unusual for her. In his words, she "would surely have been beaten if she failed to produce twice as much" as the 200 pounds of an ordinary day's work.

#### Cloth made for enslaved people's clothes

Planters called the rough fabric they bought for enslaved people's clothes "negro cloth" or "slave cloth." The names covered several coarse fabrics. Two of them were osnaburg, a coarse plain cloth, and kersey, a thick, coarse wool. Both were on the list in South Carolina's 1740 law, which barred enslaved people from wearing anything finer. Another was linsey-woolsey, a cheap cloth of wool mixed with cotton or linen. Jeans was a cotton and wool cloth woven in a twill, a weave that makes thin diagonal lines.

The Hazard family owned a woolen mill in Peace Dale, Rhode Island, where workers made this rough cloth for Southern planters to clothe the people they enslaved. In the 1820s Isaac Peace Hazard traveled through the South taking orders from plantation owners. By 1845 the owners of 17 of Rhode Island's 40 textile mills had made this cloth their main product. Workers in the Lowell mills made it too.

Southern buyers told the Hazards what they wanted. One wrote in 1824 that the cloth "would not suit servants unless it was blue." By "servants" he meant enslaved people. A complaint of the time described clothes "as thin as baize, threads not beat close together, others split all to pieces." Baize is a thin wool cloth.

Enslavers handed out clothing on set days. On Colonel Edward Lloyd's plantation in Maryland it came once a year. In Charleston, the people Mary Pringle enslaved as house servants got a summer share and a winter share. In the 1850s Stephen Duncan owned the Carlisle plantation in Mississippi. There each man got enough cloth for three shirts, two pairs of summer pants and one pair of winter pants. He also got a coat and two pairs of shoes. Each child got four slips, short loose dresses. John Potter's rice plantation in South Carolina used 1,800 yards of cloth a year for the 400 people he enslaved. That came to about 4.5 yards for each person.

Harriet Jacobs was enslaved in Edenton, North Carolina, in the household of Dr. James Norcom. In her book she calls him Dr. Flint. She wrote: "I have a vivid recollection of the linsey-woolsey dress given me every winter by Mrs. Flint. How I hated it! It was one of the badges of slavery." Her grandmother's work, she wrote, "supplied my scanty wardrobe." Scanty means too little.

In 1841 the slave trader Theophilus Freeman held Solomon Northup and other captives in his slave pen in New Orleans. Northup wrote that the traders made the captives wash and made the men shave. Then they gave each person "a new suit each, cheap, but clean." The men got a hat, a coat, a shirt, pants and shoes, and the women a calico dress and a handkerchief to tie around the head.

<a id="story-frederick-douglass-styles"></a>

#### Frederick Douglass

> **Who:** A man enslaved in Maryland who described the clothes he was given as a child, and who escaped to freedom dressed as a sailor.
>
> **When and where:** Talbot County and Baltimore, Maryland, the 1820s to 1838.

As a child, Frederick Douglass had nothing to wear but one coarse linen shirt that reached to his knees. It came from the clothing that Colonel Edward Lloyd and his overseers, the men who ran the work for him, handed out each year. He had no shoes, stockings, jacket or trousers, "in hottest summer and coldest winter." He had no bed. On the coldest nights he took a bag used for carrying corn to the mill, crawled into it and slept on the cold, damp clay floor. He wrote: "My feet have been so cracked with the frost, that the pen with which I am writing might be laid in the gashes."

Douglass was born enslaved in Talbot County, Maryland. As a child he lived on the home plantation of Colonel Edward Lloyd. Lloyd enslaved people on several farms, and they came to the home plantation for their food and their yearly clothing.

Each enslaved adult got two coarse linen shirts, one pair of linen trousers, one jacket, one pair of winter trousers "made of coarse negro cloth," one pair of stockings and one pair of shoes a year. Douglass wrote that all of it "could not have cost more than seven dollars." Children too young to work in the fields got only two coarse linen shirts a year. "When these failed them," he wrote, "they went naked until the next allowance-day."

When he was about seven or eight, his owners sent him to Baltimore. Before he left, Lucretia Auld told him he could have a pair of trousers if he scrubbed the dirt off his skin first. She was the daughter of his old master. He wrote: "The thought of owning a pair of trousers was great indeed!"

On September 3, 1838, Douglass escaped from Baltimore by train. He wrote: "I had on a red shirt and a tarpaulin hat, and a black cravat tied in sailor fashion carelessly and loosely about my neck." A tarpaulin hat was a sailor's waterproof hat, and a cravat was a cloth tied around the neck. He carried a paper called a sailor's protection, borrowed from a friend who was a sailor. It described a free American sailor, and Douglass used it in place of papers showing he was free.

Anna Murray, a free Black woman who washed other people's clothes for pay, helped him. She married him in New York that same month. According to *The Frederick Douglass Encyclopedia*, her laundry work gave her access to sailors' clothing, and she got some of it for him. Other accounts say she sewed the sailor's outfit herself. She also gave him part of her savings, and she sold one of her feather beds to add to it.

#### The first ready-made clothes

The first clothes sold ready to wear in America were sold in the early 1800s at shops called slop shops. They stood on the streets next to the docks of Boston, New York, Philadelphia and Baltimore, and of smaller whaling and fishing towns. The people who bought these clothes were sailors and other working men. The clothes came in one size, and a sailor heading out to sea made them fit as best he could.

Between 1840 and 1860, more and more clothing makers sewed cheap clothes for planters to give to enslaved people. Many New York firms made what they called "Negro clothing." A planter who bought these clothes did not have to use the time of enslaved workers to sew them.

### 1850 to 1900

In the second half of the 1800s, makers began selling sewing machines to families, and chemists began making dyes from coal tar. Isaac Singer began making sewing machines in 1851. From 1856 his partner, Edward Clark, let families pay for one a few dollars a month. In 1856 a chemistry student in London made the first man-made dye to be sold, a purple, from chemicals in coal tar. In 1873 a tailor in Reno and a merchant in San Francisco got a patent for work pants with metal rivets, small metal pins that hold cloth together. A patent is a government paper that gives an inventor the right to be the only one to make an invention for a set number of years. The riveted pants were later called blue jeans.

In 1851 a few leaders of the fight for women's rights wore short skirts over trousers, and men mocked them for it. In 1876 members of San Francisco's Board of Supervisors, the men who made the city's laws, ordered that every man in the county jail have his hair cut to one inch. Sheriff Matthew Nunan used the order to cut off Chinese prisoners' long braids. A federal judge later found that the order was meant only for the Chinese. From 1879, the staff at the Carlisle Indian School in Pennsylvania cut Native children's hair and took away their clothes.

#### The Bloomer costume, 1851 to 1854

In February 1851, Elizabeth Smith Miller visited Amelia Bloomer in Seneca Falls, New York, wearing a dress that reached the knee, over trousers. It was sometimes called the Turkish dress. Bloomer began wearing it too. She printed articles and pictures of it in her newspaper, *The Lily*. Elizabeth Cady Stanton, a leader of the fight for women's rights, also wore it. People named the outfit bloomers, after Amelia Bloomer, the woman best known for wearing it and speaking up for it.

Bloomer wrote that "letters came pouring in upon me by the hundreds from women all over the country" asking about the dress. The number of copies of *The Lily* sent out each month rose from 500 to 4,000, by the count of the National Park Service. Another count gives 3,000.

Men mocked the women who wore it and called them "Amazons," after the women warriors of old Greek stories. Some young women who wore it were turned away when they asked to join a church. By about 1854, Stanton and other leaders had gone back to long skirts and corsets. They feared that wearing the dress took attention away from their fight for the right to vote.

#### Hoops, sewing machines and paper patterns

In 1856 women began to wear the cage crinoline, a frame of steel hoops that held a skirt out wide. With it, women no longer needed the heavy stacks of petticoats, sometimes as many as seven, that they had worn to get the same shape.

Isaac Singer began making sewing machines in 1851. He used the lockstitch, a stitch that locks two threads together, which Elias Howe had invented. Sewing a man's frock coat, a fitted coat with a skirt to the knee, by hand took almost 17 hours. By machine it took two and a half.

In 1856 a Singer machine cost about $100. That September, Edward Clark, Singer's partner, began to sell machines on installments, which means a buyer paid a little each month. The magazine *American Heritage* gives the terms as $5 a month. Earlier in 1856 Clark had offered $50 off a new Singer for any old sewing machine, even a worthless one.

In 1863 Ebenezer Butterick and his wife, Ellen Augusta Pollard Butterick, of Sterling, Massachusetts, began selling sewing patterns cut from tissue paper. A pattern is a set of paper shapes that a person who sews pins to cloth and cuts around. By one report, the idea came from Ellen Butterick, who was tired of patterns that came in only one size. The Buttericks' patterns came in a range of standard sizes. Members of the family cut and folded the first ones at home. They sold patterns for men's and boys' clothes first, and added women's dresses in 1866.

<a id="story-elizabeth-keckley"></a>

#### Elizabeth Keckley

> **Who:** A dressmaker, born enslaved, who bought her freedom with money from her sewing and made Mary Todd Lincoln's dresses.
>
> **When and where:** Virginia, St. Louis and Washington, D.C., 1818 to 1868.

Elizabeth Keckley paid for her own freedom with money she earned by sewing, after her customers lent her the price. Later she made the dresses of Mary Todd Lincoln, the wife of President Abraham Lincoln.

Keckley was born enslaved in February 1818 at Dinwiddie Court House, Virginia. The Burwell family enslaved her and her mother, Agnes. Her father was Armistead Burwell, of the family that enslaved her. Agnes made clothes for 82 people: the 12 members of the Burwell family and the 70 people they enslaved. As Keckley grew up, she helped her mother make the clothes.

Her old master sent her to work for his eldest son, Robert Burwell, a minister, and his wife. When she was nearly 18, she moved with them to Hillsboro, North Carolina, where Robert Burwell led a church. A schoolmaster named Bingham had promised Mrs. Burwell that he would "subdue," or crush, what he called Keckley's "stubborn pride." He whipped her. When she asked him why, he hit her with a chair and knocked her to the floor.

While she lived in Hillsboro, a white man raped her again and again for four years. Rape means forcing a person to have sex. Keckley wrote that the man "had base designs upon me" and "persecuted me for four years." She refused to name him. "I spare the world his name," she wrote. She gave birth to his son, George, the only child she ever had.

In St. Louis, the Garland family who owned her lived on the money her sewing brought in. She wrote: "With my needle I kept bread in the mouths of seventeen persons for two years and five months." She wrote that "the best ladies in St. Louis" were her customers.

Her owner agreed to free her and George for $1,200. One of her customers, Mrs. Le Bourgeois, raised the money among Keckley's other customers. Keckley and her son were freed on November 15, 1855. She took the money only as a loan, and she paid back every cent from her sewing.

She moved to Washington in 1860 and later employed 20 seamstresses. Abraham Lincoln took office on March 4, 1861. At eight o'clock the next morning, Tuesday, she went to the White House. Three other dressmakers were already waiting, and Mary Todd Lincoln chose Keckley. She wrote that she made "fifteen or sixteen dresses" for Mrs. Lincoln that spring and summer. Her customers also included Varina Davis, the wife of Jefferson Davis.

In the summer of 1862, people freed from slavery were coming to Washington from Maryland and Virginia. In August 1862 Keckley and other Black residents of Washington started the Contraband Relief Association to help them. During the Civil War, Union soldiers used the word "contraband" for people who had escaped slavery. Its members gave out food, shelter, clothing and medical care, and in the first year they handed out 5,150 pieces of clothing. In 1868 she published a book about her life, *Behind the Scenes, or, Thirty Years a Slave, and Four Years in the White House*. The Smithsonian holds a purple velvet gown she made for Mrs. Lincoln. She died in Washington in May 1907.

#### New colors from coal tar, 1856 on

Every dye before 1856 came from plants, insects, shellfish or minerals. Indigo blue came from a plant, cochineal red from an insect and red ochre from a mineral. In 1856 William Henry Perkin, an 18-year-old student at the Royal College of Chemistry in London, was on his Easter break. He was trying to make quinine, a drug for the disease malaria. He worked with chemicals that come from coal tar, a thick black liquid made from coal. Instead of quinine he made a purple dye, now called mauve or mauveine. It was the first man-made dye sold for use. In 1857 he opened a factory near London.

By 1859 chemists were making other new colors from coal tar, such as fuchsine, a deep crimson red. These are called aniline dyes, after aniline, one of the coal-tar chemicals used to make them.

<a id="story-levi-strauss-jacob-davis"></a>

#### Levi Strauss and Jacob Davis

> **Who:** A tailor in Reno who put metal rivets on work pants, and the San Francisco merchant who shared the patent with him.
>
> **When and where:** Reno, Nevada, and San Francisco, California, 1870 to 1875.

Jacob Davis put copper rivets, small metal pins that hold cloth together, on work pants so that the seams would not tear. On May 20, 1873, he and Levi Strauss's company got a patent for the idea. A patent is a government paper that gives an inventor the right to be the only one to make an invention for a set number of years. The riveted pants were later called blue jeans.

Davis was born Jacob Youphes in the city of Riga on May 14, 1831. He came to New York in 1854 and changed his name. By 1869 he ran a tailor shop in Reno, Nevada.

A woman asked Davis to make strong work pants for her husband, a woodcutter. Davis had been using copper rivets on horse blankets. He put rivets at the weak points in the seams and pockets. In a court statement, Davis dated this to January 1871. Other accounts date it to December 1870.

Levi Strauss was born in Buttenheim, Bavaria, on February 26, 1829. He came to the United States in 1847 and reached San Francisco in 1854. There he sold cloth and clothing to stores as Levi Strauss & Co.

The patent, number 139,121, covered "a metal rivet or eyelet at each edge of the pocket opening to prevent the ripping of the seam." Davis and Levi Strauss & Co. shared it. In January 1874 they took A. B. Elfelt and others to court over the patent. On February 10, 1875, the judge decided for them. They had asked for $20,000 and were awarded $2,000.

Davis ran the San Francisco factory that made the riveted pants. Strauss died on September 26, 1902, and Davis died in 1908.

#### Cutting Chinese men's braids in San Francisco, 1876 to 1879

Chinese men in the 1800s shaved the front of the head and wore the rest of their hair in one long braid called a queue. Stephen Field, a federal judge, later wrote that Chinese men saw the loss of the queue as a disgrace that brought "misfortune and suffering after death."

In 1873 members of San Francisco's Board of Supervisors, the men who made the city's laws, voted for an order to cut prisoners' hair. Mayor William Alvord vetoed, or rejected, the hair-cutting part.

In April 1876 California's lawmakers passed a law about lodging houses, buildings that rent out rooms. It made it a crime to sleep in a room with less than 500 cubic feet of air for each person. That is about the space of a room 8 feet long, 8 feet wide and 8 feet high. A history of the case by the Federal Judicial Center, the research office of the federal courts, states that the law was aimed at Chinese residents. On June 14, 1876, members of the Board of Supervisors voted that every man jailed in the county have his hair cut to one inch from the scalp. Field later wrote: "The ordinance was intended only for the Chinese in San Francisco." An ordinance is a city law.

In April 1878 Ho Ah Kow was found guilty under the lodging law and fined $10. Field's opinion in his case does not name the judge who sentenced him. His sentence was five days in the county jail if he did not pay. He did not pay, and he went to jail. Sheriff Matthew Nunan cut off his queue. Nunan and his deputies, the officers who worked under him, cut off other men's queues too. The records do not say how many.

Ho Ah Kow sued Nunan. On July 7, 1879, Justice Field ruled that the hair order went against the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution. That amendment states that no state may deny any person the equal protection of the laws, which means the same treatment under the law. Field wrote that the order was not meant to stop prisoners from escaping. Its purpose, he wrote, was "merely to aggravate the severity of his confinement." That means its purpose was to make the prisoner's time in jail harder to bear.

#### Uniforms and short hair at Carlisle, 1879 on

Richard Henry Pratt, an Army officer, opened the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania in 1879 for Native children. In 1892 Pratt said his aim was to "Kill the Indian in him and save the man." In a proclamation of December 2024, President Joe Biden stated that federal officials had tried to make Native children give up their own ways of life "by stripping them of their languages, religions, and cultures." At Carlisle the staff cut the children's hair and took away their clothes. They dressed the boys in military uniforms and the girls in Victorian dresses, the long dresses of the time.

Carlisle's photographer, John N. Choate, took pictures of students when they arrived. He photographed the same students again after they had been at the school for a while. His "before and after" pictures show a student in the Native clothes he or she arrived in, then the same student in a school uniform. One pair has the caption "Tom Torlino, Navajo. As he entered the school in 1882. As he appeared three years later."

#### Shirtwaists and the Gibson Girl, 1890s

In the 1890s women wore a separate skirt and a shirtwaist, a blouse cut like a man's shirt. Women who worked for pay wore it every day. Sleeves puffed out wide again and were biggest around 1895. Most working men wore the sack suit, a loose jacket with pants.

About 50,000 people rode bicycles in 1885, and about 10 million in 1896, by one estimate. Some women rode in bloomers, but most wore shorter skirts.

Charles Dana Gibson lived from 1867 to 1944. He drew for *Life*, *Collier's Weekly*, *Harper's Weekly* and other magazines. In the 1890s he drew a young woman whom people called the Gibson Girl. The Library of Congress showed his drawings in an exhibition. Its writers say she "pursued higher education, romance, marriage, physical well-being, and individuality" with more freedom than young women had had before. Pursued means went after. They also write that from the 1890s until World War I she "set the standard for beauty, fashion, and manners."

### 1900 to 1950

New man-made materials went into the things Americans wore and handled every day in the first half of the 1900s. Leo Baekeland made Bakelite, a hard plastic, in 1907. Chemists at the DuPont company made nylon in 1935, and it went on sale as women's stockings in 1939. In the 1920s many women cut their hair short and wore shorter, looser dresses. Black women built companies that sold hair products to Black customers, and Madam C. J. Walker and Annie Malone each grew rich from that work.

Government officials also used clothes and hair to control people. In 1902 the U.S. commissioner of Indian affairs, the head of the federal office for Native affairs, told reservation officials to make Native men cut their hair. Reservations were lands the government had set aside for Native nations. In 1942 officials in Washington limited how much cloth a dress or a suit could use. In June 1943, servicemen in Los Angeles beat Mexican American young men and tore off their zoot suits, outfits with very wide pants and long coats. Police officers then arrested many of the bloodied young men.

#### The order to cut Native men's hair, 1902

William A. Jones was the U.S. commissioner of Indian affairs, the head of the federal office for Native affairs. On January 11, 1902, he sent a letter to the superintendents, the officials who ran the federal reservations and the offices on them. In it he told them to make Native men cut their hair and wrote: "The wearing of long hair by the male population of your agency is not in keeping with the advancement they are making, or will soon be expected to make, in civilization." He called short hair "a great step in advance."

Jones wrote that "Indian costume and blanket" should be discouraged, and that "Indian dances and so-called Indian feasts should be prohibited." He claimed that the paint Native people wore caused "the majority of blindness among the Indians of the United States." He told the superintendents they could force men to obey by holding back their rations and their jobs. Rations were the food and supplies that officials handed out on reservations. Each superintendent had to report his progress by June 30, 1902.

Charles Burton was the superintendent for the Hopi and the Navajo. The historian Tisa Wenger writes that he reportedly used "whips, guns, and sheep shears" to enforce the order. The surviving accounts do not say how many men were forced to cut their hair.

The letter drew an outcry, and writers at *Harper's Weekly* criticized it in February 1902. Jones backed down. Officials then received new instructions to use "persuasion and example, rather than force."

#### Shirtwaists, short hair and short skirts

The shirtwaist, the blouse cut like a man's shirt, stayed the everyday top for working women in the early 1900s. Young immigrant women sewed shirtwaists in New York factories. The Triangle Waist Company made them on the top floors of a building in New York. On March 25, 1911, a fire there killed 146 workers. Most of them were young immigrant women, and some were only 14. A stairwell door on the ninth floor was locked, and dozens of workers jumped from the windows. The owners, Max Blanck and Isaac Harris, were tried for manslaughter, a killing the law treats as less serious than murder. The jury found them not guilty on December 27, 1911, because the prosecutors could not prove that the owners knew the doors were locked.

In the 1920s many women cut their hair into a short style called a bob. Dresses hung straight from the shoulders, with the waistline low on the hips. This slim, straight shape is often called the flapper look. Hemlines, the bottom edges of skirts, rose until 1926 and then began to fall.

Many women gave up stiff, formal layers for lighter, looser clothes. With new fabrics such as jersey, a soft knitted cloth, and "artificial silk," a man-made cloth that looked like silk, more women could dress in the new styles. Fashion historians at the Fashion Institute of Technology call this change a "democratization of fashion," which means that fashion spread to ordinary people.

#### Hair care built by Black women

Annie Turnbo was born on August 9, 1877, in Metropolis, Illinois. Her parents had been enslaved in Kentucky. She made a hair product she called Wonderful Hair Grower and sold it door to door. In 1902 she moved to St. Louis and opened a shop. She later named her company Poro.

In 1918 she opened Poro College in St. Louis. It was a building that held a factory, a store, rooms where students slept, a gym, a chapel and an auditorium. Nearly 200 people worked there. About 75,000 women, in several parts of the world, trained in her Poro system. She later became known as Annie Malone. In 1924 she paid nearly $40,000 in taxes.

<a id="story-madam-cj-walker"></a>

#### Madam C. J. Walker

> **Who:** A Black businesswoman, born to parents who had been enslaved, who built a hair-care company and trained thousands of women to sell her products.
>
> **When and where:** St. Louis, Denver and Indianapolis, 1889 to 1919.
>
> **Movie:** *Two Dollars and a Dream* (1987), a documentary about her life by Stanley Nelson.

Madam C. J. Walker built a company that made hair products for Black women. She trained thousands of women to sell them. She was born Sarah Breedlove on December 23, 1867, in Delta, Louisiana. Her parents had been enslaved.

Her parents died when she was 7, and she married at 14. In 1889 she moved to St. Louis, where she washed clothes for pay and worked as a cook. Her hair began to fall out. A skin disease, harsh hair products, poor food and a home without running water all played a part. In 1904 she began using Annie Turnbo's hair product, and she became one of Turnbo's sales agents in St. Louis.

In July 1905 she moved to Denver and began selling her own product, "Madam Walker's Wonderful Hair Grower." She married Charles Joseph Walker in 1906 and took his name. In 1910 she moved her company to Indianapolis and built a factory there.

By 1917, according to her company, nearly 20,000 women had trained with it. According to the National Women's History Museum, she employed 40,000 people. She gave money to the YWCA, the Young Women's Christian Association. She also gave $5,000 to the NAACP, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, for its work against lynching, the killing of a person by a mob without a trial.

She died on May 25, 1919. Accounts of her wealth differ. One account puts it between half a million and a million dollars. According to the National Women's History Museum, it was more than $1 million.

#### Plastics and nylon

In 1907 the chemist Leo Baekeland made Bakelite. He heated two chemicals, phenol and formaldehyde, under pressure. Bakelite was the first plastic made entirely from chemicals, rather than from plants or animals. He got a patent for his method on December 7, 1909. A patent is a government paper that gives an inventor the right to be the only one to make an invention for a set number of years. Makers used Bakelite for jewelry, telephones, radios and billiard balls, and in cars.

Nylon went on sale as women's stockings. On October 24, 1939, the DuPont company sold its first 4,000 pairs to the wives of its employees in Wilmington, Delaware. They sold out in three hours. On May 16, 1940, called Nylon Day, four million pairs went on sale in stores across the country at about $1.15 a pair. They sold out in two days. Some sources give the date as May 15.

Japanese forces attacked Pearl Harbor, in Hawaii, on December 7, 1941. For the rest of World War II, DuPont's nylon went into parachutes, tire cords, ropes and other war goods instead of stockings. Stockings came back in 1945. In Pittsburgh, 40,000 people stood in a line more than a mile long for 13,000 pairs.

<a id="story-wallace-carothers"></a>

#### Wallace Carothers

> **Who:** The chemist who led the DuPont laboratory where nylon was made.
>
> **When and where:** DuPont's research station, called the Experimental Station, 1928 to 1937.

Wallace Carothers led the team at DuPont that made two of the most widely used man-made materials of the 1900s, neoprene and nylon. In April 1930 his team made neoprene, a man-made rubber. On February 28, 1935, Gerard Berchet, a chemist working under Carothers, made half an ounce of the nylon later used in stockings.

Carothers was born on April 27, 1896, in Burlington, Iowa. He started work at DuPont's Experimental Station on February 6, 1928.

Carothers had depression. Depression is an illness that brings long periods of deep sadness and makes it hard to think and to work. He wrote: "I suffer from neurotic spells of diminished capacity." He meant that at times his mind could not work as well as usual. In the summer of 1936 he was treated in a psychiatric hospital, a hospital for illnesses of the mind. His sister Isobel died in January 1937.

On April 29, 1937, at age 41, Carothers killed himself in Philadelphia by taking cyanide, a poison. His daughter, Jane, was born in November 1937, seven months after his death. DuPont officials announced nylon to the public on October 27, 1938.

<a id="story-ann-lowe"></a>

#### Ann Lowe

> **Who:** A Black dressmaker from Alabama who made gowns for rich families in Tampa and New York, while the wider public hardly knew her name.
>
> **When and where:** Alabama, New York and Tampa, 1898 to 1950.

Ann Lowe made gowns for Jacqueline Kennedy, the actress Olivia de Havilland and the heiress Marjorie Merriweather Post, but she stayed almost unknown to the wider public. She was born about 1898 in Clayton, Alabama, into a family of Black dressmakers. Her great-grandmother was an enslaved woman, and her great-grandfather was a plantation owner.

Her mother, Jane, and her grandmother, Georgia, made dresses for well-known families in Montgomery, and Ann learned the trade from them. Her mother died in 1914, when Ann was 16, and Ann took over the business.

In 1917 she went to the S. T. Taylor Design School in New York. She was taught in a classroom by herself, apart from the white students. The accounts of her life do not name who ordered it. She was ready to graduate after six months. She then made gowns in Tampa, Florida, and opened her own dress shop there in 1920.

In 1928 she moved to New York with $20,000. For years she made gowns to order for stores such as Henri Bendel, Neiman Marcus and Saks Fifth Avenue. The actress Olivia de Havilland wore a gown Lowe made when she accepted her Academy Award in 1946. The credit for that dress went to the name "Sonia Rosenberg," not to Lowe. The record does not say who gave that credit.

In 2023 the Winterthur Museum showed 40 of her gowns. The museum's description of the show describes her work as part of "a legacy of Black women's knowledge and skills that began as enslaved labor."

#### Cloth rules in World War II, 1942 to 1946

On April 8, 1942, officials of the War Production Board issued General Limitation Order L-85. The War Production Board was the federal agency whose officials controlled materials during the war. Its chairman was Donald M. Nelson. The order set how long and how wide women's coats, dresses, suits and skirts could be.

The order banned hoods, capes and scarves attached to coats, and belts and hems more than 2 inches wide. A hem is the folded-up bottom edge of a piece of clothing. It also banned cuffs, turned-back bands of cloth, on long jacket sleeves and on slacks, which are loose pants. It banned pleats, tucks or gathers, which are folds or bunches of extra cloth, all over a garment. Wedding gowns, dresses for pregnant women, children's clothes, burial gowns and religious robes did not fall under the rules. The rules lasted until 1946.

On December 27, 1941, Stanley Marcus, a co-owner of the Neiman-Marcus department stores, was asked to head the board's section for women's and children's clothing. Makers and stores that broke the rules could be fined or jailed. In April 1942 the board's officials also limited the elastic used in bras and in girdles, tight underwear that shaped the waist and hips. Nylon and rubber went to the military.

#### The zoot suit attacks in Los Angeles, June 1943

A zoot suit had high-waisted, very wide pants that narrowed at the ankle and a long coat with wide lapels, the folded-back flaps at the front of a coat below the collar. It began among Black men in Harlem, in New York. In Los Angeles in the early 1940s young Mexican American men wore it. So did some Filipino American and Japanese American young men, and some Mexican American young women. The War Production Board's officials had stopped the making of zoot suits because they used so much cloth.

From June 3 to June 8, 1943, sailors, soldiers and Marines, joined by civilians, went through the Mexican American neighborhoods of Los Angeles. They hunted young men in zoot suits, beat them, tore off their clothes and burned the suits in street fires. The National WWII Museum says the attacks began on June 3 with about 50 sailors. Another account says about 11 sailors started them, and about 200 joined the next day. By the later days, thousands of servicemen had joined.

More than 150 people were injured. Los Angeles police officers stood by while the attackers claimed they were defending themselves. The officers arrested bloodied and bruised Mexican American men for "disturbing the peace." They arrested nearly 600 Mexican Americans, by the National WWII Museum's count, or more than 500 by another count. The police arrested far fewer servicemen, and no soldiers were arrested for the beatings.

On June 8, 1943, Navy and Marine Corps commanders ordered their men to stay out of Los Angeles, and the attacks stopped. Members of the Los Angeles City Council voted for a resolution, a statement of what they wanted, to make wearing a zoot suit in the city a crime. No such law was ever passed.

Governor Earl Warren of California chose a committee to study the attacks. Its members reported that most of the people attacked were Mexican Americans or Black people. On the cause of the attacks, they wrote that "the existence of race prejudice cannot be ignored." Race prejudice means hating or looking down on people because of their race.

### 1950 to 2000

After the mid-1950s, the people who designed American clothes began to take their ideas from teenagers, and plastics went into everyday clothes and furniture. In the 1950s young men copied the jeans, white T-shirts and leather jackets that film stars wore. The first suits made partly of polyester, a plastic made into thread, went on sale in 1951. From 1950 the furniture company Herman Miller sold chairs that the designers Charles and Ray Eames had shaped from plastic and glass fiber.

People also went to court over clothes and hair. In 1969 seven of the nine justices, the judges of the Supreme Court, the highest court in the country, ruled that students could wear black armbands to school to protest a war. Judges disagreed about boys' long hair, and in 1981 a federal judge allowed an airline to ban a Black woman's braids. In 1995 state and federal officers found 72 Thai workers held behind razor wire in El Monte, California, sewing clothes that were sold in American chain stores.

#### Jeans, T-shirts and teenagers in the 1950s

In the early 1950s the leading women's style was still the "New Look" that Christian Dior showed in 1947. It had a tight waist and a full skirt. By the middle of the decade, dressmakers cut dresses straighter and slimmer, and designers began to take ideas from teenagers.

Young men took up a working-class look: jeans, a white T-shirt and a leather jacket, with the hair greased back. Marlon Brando wore it in the film *The Wild One* in 1953, and James Dean wore it in *Rebel Without a Cause* in 1955. Fashion historians at the Fashion Institute of Technology describe the look as young people turning away from their parents' generation. Young men who wore it got a reputation as rebels and troublemakers. By the end of the decade, boys wore jeans to most places.

#### Polyester and wash-and-wear

Two British chemists, John Rex Whinfield and James Tennant Dickson, patented polyester in 1941. In 1946 the DuPont company bought the right to make it in the United States, and DuPont named its polyester fiber Dacron.

On May 8, 1951, Hart, Schaffner & Marx of New York began selling men's suits made of cloth that was 55 percent Dacron and 45 percent wool. According to the Hagley Museum and Library, it was the first polyester fiber sold to the public anywhere in the world. The makers of the cloth liked it because it did not crease or wear through easily and was easy to clean. In 1953 DuPont opened a Dacron plant in Kinston, North Carolina.

Clothes made with Dacron could be washed and worn without ironing, so they were sold as "wash and wear." Most of the ironing time they saved was women's time.

In the 1970s, with man-made cloth, people could buy fashionable styles at any price. Polyester and other man-made fabrics were so common that people called the decade the "Polyester Decade." Men wore leisure suits, a casual kind of suit often made of man-made cloth, as a cheap stand-in for a regular suit. People dancing at disco clubs wore satin, sequins (tiny shiny disks sewn onto cloth) and Lycra, a stretchy man-made cloth. By the late 1970s people wore sweatshirt cloth and leggings, once clothes for the gym, every day.

<a id="story-charles-ray-eames"></a>

#### Charles and Ray Eames
