A judge sentenced James "Yankee" Sullivan, who arranged the fight, to two years in prison. Sullivan served two months. He then paid a $200 bond, money a court keeps if a person breaks a promise, and promised not to fight for two years, and he was let out. The records do not say what happened to Lilly.

In 1849 Tom Hyer beat Sullivan in 17 minutes and 18 seconds in Maryland and won a purse, the prize money, of $10,000.

#### Written rules for ball games

Players in many towns played bat-and-ball games that went by local names, such as town ball. On 4 July 1833 two groups of town ball players from Philadelphia met in Camden, New Jersey, and joined to form one club, the Olympic. In 1838 the club printed its rules and its list of members.

On 23 September 1845 the members of the Knickerbocker Base Ball Club of New York adopted twenty written rules. Two members, William Wheaton and William Tucker, wrote them down. A game ended when one side scored 21 runs. Three outs ended a side's turn at bat. A fielder put a runner out by throwing the ball to a baseman, not by hitting the runner with it. The members were merchants, lawyers and doctors. They played at the Elysian Fields in Hoboken, New Jersey.

On 19 June 1846 the Knickerbockers played the New York club under the new rules in one of the first recorded games between two clubs. One account says the New York club won 23 to 1. Another says the Knickerbockers won.

Albert Spalding and the members of a committee he asked for later spread a story about how baseball began that was not true. In 1905 Spalding, a maker of sporting goods, asked for a study of how baseball began. Abner Graves, a 71-year-old mining engineer, wrote to an Ohio newspaper that Abner Doubleday had invented baseball in Cooperstown, New York, in 1839. Graves had been 5 years old in 1839. Doubleday was then a cadet, a student training to be an army officer, at West Point. The historian Victor Salvatore found that baseball does not appear in any of Doubleday's 67 surviving diaries. Other writers say he mentioned it once in his letters or diaries. No member of Spalding's committee met Graves or wrote to him. In a report of 30 December 1907 the committee's chairman, Abraham Mills, wrote that Doubleday had invented the game. Spalding wanted to show that baseball owed nothing to any English game. Salvatore titled his article about Doubleday "The Man Who Didn't Invent Baseball."

#### Children, toys and the circus

In 1838 Francis, Field and Francis opened on North Second Street in Philadelphia. It was Philadelphia's first toy maker and one of the first in the country. The owners sold toys brought from France and Germany and made toys of their own. According to the Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia, their toy fire engine pulled by horses is believed to be the first toy made in a factory in the United States.

In 1825 the city leaders of Wilmington, Delaware, banned public shows. Joshua Purdy Brown put up a canvas tent for his circus just outside the city line. With his own tent, Brown could set up his circus in any town, and the circus became a traveling show.

<a id="story-lucy-larcom"></a>

#### Lucy Larcom

> **Who:** A girl who went to work in a mill at 11 and later wrote about it.
>
> **When and where:** Beverly and Lowell, Massachusetts, 1824 to the 1840s.

Lucy Larcom was born in Beverly, Massachusetts, on 5 March 1824. She later wrote about her childhood there. She and her friends shaped burrs from burdock plants into chairs, cradles and sofas for their dolls. They played school on the doorsteps and climbed over the wall onto the hill. She wrote that the neighborhood children, from large families, enjoyed "a little wholesome neglect." She meant that the grown-ups mostly left them alone, and that this was good for them.

Her father, a retired sea captain, died in 1832. In 1835 her mother, Lois Larcom, moved the family to Lowell, a mill town. There she ran a boarding house for women who worked in the mills, cooking and keeping house for up to forty of them. Each boarder paid her $1.25 a week. In her book about her childhood, Lucy wrote down the words that sent her to work: "The children will have to leave school and go into the mill." She was 11.

She went to work at the Lawrence Manufacturing Company as a doffer. A doffer's job was to take full bobbins off the spinning machines and put on empty ones, about every 45 minutes. A bobbin is a spool that holds thread. At first she told her family, "It is just like play." Between changes, she and the other little girls played games in a corner.

In winter the working day ran from first daylight to 7:30 at night. She earned one dollar a week plus her board, and her family needed the money, so she could not go on to high school. She wrote that mill work "was not, and could not be, the right sort of life for a child." The mill rules banned books, so she pasted poems cut from newspapers all over the side of her window seat in the mill. She and her sister Emeline published poems in two magazines, the *Operatives' Magazine* and the *Offering*. Larcom taught school in Illinois from 1846 to 1853 and at a school called Wheaton Seminary from 1854 to 1862. Her first book of poems came out in 1854. Her book about her childhood, *A New England Girlhood*, came out in 1889. She died in Boston on 17 April 1893.

### 1850 to 1900

In 1869 Harry Wright put together the Cincinnati Red Stockings, the first known baseball team whose players were all openly paid. That same year, students from Rutgers and Princeton played the first college football game. In 1891 a teacher named James Naismith invented basketball. Black jockeys won most of the early Kentucky Derbies. Isaac Murphy, who was born enslaved, won it three times. In baseball, the men who ran the leagues shut Black players out, first in 1867 and again in 1887.

Adults also began to organize children's play. In 1885 or 1886 members of a Boston health group put piles of sand in chapel yards for small children, and people in other cities opened playgrounds in the 1890s. Many children had no time to play. The census of 1900, the government's count of everyone in the country, counted more than 1.75 million children under 15 at work.

#### The first paid team and new games

Harry Wright found ten men to pay for the Cincinnati Red Stockings in 1869, including himself and his brother George. They won all 57 of their games against clubs in the national association of that time. That September they traveled to San Francisco, and they became the first club to play on both coasts. In 1870 the Brooklyn Atlantics beat them in 11 innings while 20,000 people watched.

On 6 November 1869 Rutgers beat Princeton 6 to 4 at New Brunswick, New Jersey, in the first college football game. Each side had 25 players. They could kick the ball or hit it with their fists or hands, but they could not hold it or trip anyone. About 100 people watched. The game looked more like soccer than like football today.

In the winter of 1891 James Naismith was a young teacher from Canada at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts. Luther Gulick told him to take a class that needed a game to play indoors in winter: "Naismith, I want you to take that class and see what you can do with it." Naismith wrote 13 rules. He asked the janitor for two boxes to use as goals, and the janitor brought two peach baskets instead. Nine players played on each side. Accounts date the first game to 21 or 29 December 1891.

On 6 April 1896 James Connolly, a 27-year-old Harvard student from Boston, won the hop, skip and jump at Athens, Greece. That event is now called the triple jump. It was the first final of the first modern Olympic Games, so Connolly was the first modern Olympic champion. A dean at Harvard had warned him that he might not be let back into the college if he left to compete, and he went anyway.

Families bought new games to play at home. In 1860 Milton Bradley sold a board game called *The Checkered Game of Life*. Buyers took more than 45,000 copies by 1861. In 1866 Bradley printed rules for croquet, a lawn game played by hitting wooden balls with mallets.

#### The color line in baseball

A color line was a rule, written or unwritten, that kept Black people out. In 1867 the members of the National Association of Base Ball Players, the group that ran club baseball, put in place a formal ban on Black players and Black clubs.

Some Black men still played baseball for pay after that. Bud Fowler did in 1878. The Society for American Baseball Research calls him the first acknowledged Black professional baseball player. William Edward White, who had been born enslaved, played one game for Providence in 1879. He lived as a white man and gave his race as white in the census. In 1884 Moses Fleetwood Walker and his brother Weldy played for Toledo in the American Association, which was then a major league. They were the first Black major-league players known to the public as Black men.

In 1887 Cap Anson, the captain of the Chicago club, said his team would not play Newark if Newark's two Black players took the field. They were Walker and the pitcher George Stovey. On 14 July 1887 Newark played Chicago without them.

That same day, at a meeting in Buffalo, New York, the owners of the International League, whom the surviving accounts do not name, voted 6 to 4 to tell the league's secretary, C. D. White, to approve no more contracts with Black players. The owners of teams with only white players voted for the ban, and those with a Black player voted against it.

Two Black players stayed in the league because their contracts had been signed before the vote: Frank Grant of Buffalo and Walker, who moved to Syracuse. Walker played in the league until 1889. After him, no Black player played in the International League until Jackie Robinson joined the Montreal Royals in 1946. The owners in the major leagues never wrote down a rule against Black players. They kept Black players out by an unwritten agreement among themselves.

<a id="story-moses-fleetwood-walker"></a>

#### Moses Fleetwood Walker

> **Who:** A catcher, the first major-league player known to the public as a Black man.
>
> **When and where:** Ohio, Toledo, Newark and Syracuse, 1856 to 1924.

Moses Fleetwood Walker was born in Mount Pleasant, Ohio, on 7 October 1856. He studied at Oberlin College and then studied law at the University of Michigan.

He caught for Toledo in 1883. In a game that year that did not count in the standings, Cap Anson of Chicago used a racist slur about Walker and said his team would never again play a team with Walker on it.

On 1 May 1884 Walker played his first major-league game for Toledo, at Louisville. He played 42 games and batted .263, which means he got a hit in about 26 of every 100 times at bat. He often caught the ball barehanded, with little padding. Toledo's pitcher Tony Mullane later said Walker "was the best catcher I ever worked with, but I disliked a Negro." "Negro" was a word of the time for a Black person. Mullane said he threw his pitches without looking at the signals Walker gave him.

In September 1884 Toledo's manager got a letter warning that a mob would attack if Walker played in Richmond, Virginia. David Zang's account of Walker's life does not name the men who wrote it. The men who ran the Toledo team released Walker before the trip.

Walker played for Newark in 1887 and for Syracuse in 1888 and 1889. His contracts had been signed before the International League owners' vote, so he could keep playing.

On 9 April 1891 a group of white men attacked Walker outside a saloon in Syracuse. One of them, Patrick Murray, threw a stone that hit Walker in the head. Walker stabbed Murray with a pocketknife and killed him. On 3 June 1891 an all-white jury found Walker not guilty of second-degree murder, which means killing someone on purpose but without planning it ahead.

In September 1898 Walker was found guilty of robbing the mail, and he spent a year in jail. He later ran an opera house, a theater, in Cadiz, Ohio. In 1908 he and his brother Weldy published *Our Home Colony*, a book arguing that Black Americans should move to Africa. He died of pneumonia, an infection of the lungs, in Cleveland on 11 May 1924, at 67.

#### Black jockeys

Oliver Lewis rode the horse Aristides to win the first Kentucky Derby on 17 May 1875. The horse's trainer, Ansel Williamson, had been born enslaved in 1806. Black jockeys won 15 of the first 28 Kentucky Derbies.

<a id="story-isaac-murphy"></a>

#### Isaac Murphy

> **Who:** A jockey born into slavery who won the Kentucky Derby three times.
>
> **When and where:** Kentucky and the Eastern racetracks, 1861 to 1896.

Isaac Burns Murphy was born into slavery in Clark County, Kentucky, on 6 January 1861. His father, Jerry Burns, joined the Union Army in 1864 and died that fall in the hospital at Camp Nelson.

Murphy won the Kentucky Derby in 1884, 1890 and 1891. He was the first jockey to win it three times and the first to win it two years in a row. By his own count he won 628 of his 1,412 races.

The racing writer Terry Conway writes that Murphy was said to earn $15,000 to $20,000 a year. The average family of four then earned about $1,200 a year. In 1887 he and his wife, Lucy, bought a 10-room house in Lexington for $10,000.

In 1890 he rode the favorite, Firenze, in a race called the Monmouth Handicap. He swayed in the saddle and fell off after the finish. The race officials, called stewards, said he was drunk and barred him from riding for a time. Murphy said he had been drugged. One account says he blamed a sudden loss of weight. Someone had bet heavily against his horse, and that betting made some people suspect a crime. The accounts of the race do not say who placed those bets.

Murphy died in Lexington in February 1896, at 35. Accounts give the cause as pneumonia or heart failure. How much money he left is not known. After he died, Lucy Murphy could not pay back a $5,500 loan from Gus Luigart, and she lost the house in a lawsuit. It was sold at auction in 1900.

He was buried in African Cemetery No. 2 in Lexington. In later years the grave had no marker. In 1955 he became the first jockey named to the Racing Hall of Fame. In 1967 his body was moved to a site near the grave of the racehorse Man o' War, and later to the Kentucky Horse Park.

#### Football deaths

Football players in the 1890s wore no helmets, no mouthpieces and no padding. Reporters at a New York newspaper, the *World*, counted at least eight deaths and more than 200 serious injuries in the 1897 season. Its list included broken bones, fractured skulls, twisted necks and crushed chests.

On 30 October 1897 Richard Von Gammon, a 17-year-old University of Georgia player, dove into a pile of players to make a tackle against the University of Virginia in Atlanta. He lay still on the field and died early the next morning of a concussion, which is an injury to the brain from a hard blow to the head.

Georgia's lawmakers voted to ban football at the state's colleges. Von Gammon's mother, Rosalind Burns Gammon, wrote to her representative. She asked that her son's death not be used as an argument against the sport. Governor William Atkinson vetoed the ban on 7 December 1897, which means he refused to sign it and it did not become law.

On 30 October 1898 a Tennessee newspaper, the *Knoxville Tribune*, printed a full-page editorial, an article giving the paper's own opinion, calling for a ban. The editorial listed three deaths and gave no names. Two players' heads struck together and one of them died. A player at the bottom of a pile had his neck broken. A player kicked in the head by a heavy shoe died three days later.

#### Women on bicycles

Frances Willard learned to ride a bicycle at 53. In 1895 she published a book about it. As a girl in the country she had almost no toys except the ones she made herself, such as a wooden plow. She practiced on the bicycle for three months. She wrote that women who rode "must, when riding, dress more rationally," which meant in clothes that made sense for the job.

In an article printed on 2 February 1896, Susan B. Anthony told the reporter Nellie Bly that the bicycle "has done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world." To emancipate means to set free. Anthony said that bloomers, which were loose pants gathered at the ankle, or very short skirts were the right clothes for riding.

#### The first playgrounds

Dr. Marie Zakrzewska wrote to a Boston health group, the Massachusetts Emergency and Hygiene Association. She told its leaders that in Berlin's public parks, children rich and poor dug and played in heaps of sand.

Accounts give two different years for the first sand in Boston. Joseph Lee, who wrote a book about helping the poor in 1902, gives 1886. That year, he wrote, members of the association put three piles of yellow sand in the yards of a children's mission, a church charity for children, and of two chapels, which are small churches. A 1925 history by the Playground and Recreation Association of America says that in 1885 a large sand pile was put in the yard of the Children's Mission on Parmenter Street.

By 1887 there were ten sand piles, and about 400 children came each day. The children's favorite games in the sand were "house" and "funeral." By 1900 members of the association ran 21 playgrounds, 20 of them in school yards.

In the 1890s people in other cities opened playgrounds too. Donors in Philadelphia started two summer playgrounds in 1893. In 1894 a playground opened at Hull-House in Chicago, with swings, a may-pole, a tall pole that children danced around holding ribbons, a sand pile and benches. A kindergarten teacher and a policeman ran it, and the policeman usually captained one of the baseball teams. In 1897 the members of a New York City committee wrote in a report that New York "has as yet not a single municipal playground," meaning none run by the city. Jacob Riis was the committee's secretary.

People began to build amusement rides in these years too. In 1884 LaMarcus Thompson opened a roller coaster, the Switchback Railway, at Coney Island in Brooklyn. A ride cost 5 cents, and the car went just over 6 miles an hour.

#### The children who had no time to play

In 1870 census takers counted working children for the first time. They found more than 750,000 workers under 15. That count left out children who worked on their own family's farm or in its shop. By 1900 more than 1.75 million children under 15 had jobs. After 1880 most working children aged 10 to 14 worked somewhere other than a farm.

In 1870 one child in eight had a job. By 1900 more than one in five did. The census counts do not name the employers. In 1900 about 25,000 of the nearly 100,000 workers in the cloth mills of the South were children under 16. Children in the mills worked 12-hour days, six days a week.

#### Cherokee ball play, 1890

In 1890 the researcher James Mooney described the Eastern Cherokee ball game in North Carolina. In the fall a game took place somewhere on the reservation, the land where the Eastern Cherokee lived, at least every other week. Each player carried two sticks just under 3 feet long, each with a net of twisted squirrel skin or hemp. For 7 to 28 days before a game, a player did not eat rabbit or frog or hot or salted food, and did not touch a woman.

Before a game an old man named Standing Water scratched each player with a comb made of seven sharp splinters of turkey leg bone. He pressed the teeth into the skin from shoulder to elbow and from elbow to wrist, and down each leg. He also cut an X on each player's chest and back. The scratches added up to nearly three hundred cuts. Mooney wrote that the cuts were shallow but painful, and that the players took them willingly as part of the ritual they believed would help them win.

No order banning the Cherokee or the Choctaw ball game in these years is on record. The games drew large crowds, including local white people.

### 1900 to 1950

From 1900 to 1950, adults set up clubs, troops and leagues for children's free time: 4-H clubs in 1902, the Boy Scouts in 1910, the Girl Scouts in 1912 and Little League baseball in 1939. Children also spent many free hours watching and listening. They went to Saturday movies, followed radio shows and read comic books. In Muncie, Indiana, in the 1930s, at least half of the children at Saturday movies stayed five or six hours.

In 1905 at least 18 people died playing football, and President Theodore Roosevelt called coaches to the White House. The major leagues were the top professional baseball teams. Their white owners kept Black players out until Jackie Robinson played for Brooklyn in 1947. Black players had their own leagues from 1920. In the 1920s and 1930s, white officials and white swimmers in many Northern cities separated the public pools by race and kept Black children out of the pools where other children learned to swim.

#### Clubs and troops for children

In 1902 A. B. Graham started a youth program in Clark County, Ohio. Its first clubs were a Tomato Club and a Corn Growing Club, and they are counted among the beginnings of 4-H. On 8 February 1910 William D. Boyce, a Chicago publisher, filed the legal papers that made the Boy Scouts of America an official organization.

On 12 March 1912 Juliette Gordon Low signed up 18 girls in Savannah, Georgia, as the first troop of what she called Girl Guides. The name changed to Girl Scouts in 1913. The Savannah girls started a basketball league and went camping.

#### Choctaw and Chickasaw ball play, 1903

Choctaw and Chickasaw people met near Allen, in Indian Territory, each spring and fall to race horses and play the stick-and-ball game. Allen is now in Oklahoma. In the spring of 1903 about 300 people came and bet on a game. A player hit a Choctaw player with a ball stick, and a fight spread through the crowd. The Choctaw Nation's mounted police, called Lighthorsemen, and US marshals, who were federal police officers, stopped it. After that fight the twice-yearly games between the two nations ended.

#### Football deaths and the rules of 1906

At least 18 people died from playing football in the 1905 season. The counts differ. The NCAA's published history of its own beginnings states 18 deaths and 149 serious injuries. Reporters at the *Chicago Tribune* counted 19 deaths, and reporters at another newspaper, the *Cincinnati Commercial Tribune*, counted 25. The writer Aaron Gordon later checked the newspaper reports. He found about 20 deaths tied to football that year, 11 of them directly from football injuries. The cause of the others was not clear.

Some of the dead were high-school boys. Harold Moore, 19, a Union College player, was knocked out in a game against New York University. He died six hours later of bleeding inside his brain. In Rockville, Indiana, a broken rib pierced the heart of Carl Osborne, a high-school player, and killed him at once. Robert Brown, 16, of Sedalia, Missouri, was paralyzed by a neck injury and died without waking.

On 9 October 1905 President Theodore Roosevelt met coaches and graduates from Harvard, Yale and Princeton at the White House. They signed a statement against rough play. In December 1905 Henry MacCracken, the head of New York University, called a meeting of college leaders on 9 December. At a second meeting, on 28 December, the men from 62 colleges formed a group. In 1910 its members renamed it the National Collegiate Athletic Association, the NCAA. The rules of the game were changed for 1906. A team now had to gain 10 yards, not 5, to keep the ball. Jumping over the line was banned, and the forward pass was allowed.

<a id="story-jack-johnson"></a>

#### Jack Johnson

> **Who:** A Black heavyweight boxing champion. After he beat a white former champion in 1910, white crowds attacked Black people across the country.
>
> **When and where:** Galveston, Texas, Sydney, Reno, Chicago and Leavenworth, 1878 to 1946.

Jack Johnson was born in Galveston, Texas, on 31 March 1878. On 26 December 1908 he beat Tommy Burns in Sydney, Australia, and became the heavyweight boxing champion of the world. Heavyweights are the boxers in the heaviest weight class.

On 4 July 1910 in Reno, Nevada, he fought James Jeffries, a white former champion. Before the fight Jeffries said he was fighting "for the sole purpose of proving that a white man is better than a Negro." "Negro" was a word of the time for a Black person. Jeffries's own helpers stopped the fight in the 15th round, and Johnson won.

That night white crowds attacked Black people in more than 25 states. Between 11 and 26 people were killed, and hundreds were hurt. In Uvalda, Georgia, white gunmen fired into a work camp and killed three Black workers. In New York City a crowd clubbed a Black man to death. In Norfolk, Virginia, more than 300 white Navy sailors hunted Black people in the streets. The records do not name the people who were killed or the people who killed them.

Officials in many states and cities banned showing the film of the fight. In 1912 the members of Congress banned carrying boxing films from one state to another. The ban lasted until 1940.

In July 1912 Johnson opened a nightclub in Chicago, the Café de Champion, where Black and white customers mixed. On 18 October 1912 he was arrested under the Mann Act, a federal law of 1910. It made it a crime to take "any woman or girl" across state lines "for the purpose of prostitution or debauchery, or for any other immoral purpose." Prostitution means selling sex, and debauchery meant wild, immoral living. Federal prosecutors, the lawyers who bring charges for the government, used the law against Johnson because he traveled with white women. In June 1913 an all-white jury, a group of citizens who decide whether a person is guilty, found him guilty. Judge Kenesaw Mountain Landis ordered him to spend a year and a day in prison. Johnson fled to Canada and Europe and stayed away for seven years. He gave himself up on 20 July 1920 and served his sentence at Leavenworth prison in Kansas.

On 10 June 1946 he died in a car crash near Franklinton, North Carolina, after the staff of a diner that served only white people refused to serve him. On 24 May 2018 President Donald Trump pardoned him. A pardon is an official act by a president or governor that forgives a crime and ends its punishment.

#### Black jockeys forced out

Jimmy Winkfield of Kentucky was a jockey, a rider in horse races. He won the Kentucky Derby, a horse race held each spring in Louisville, in 1901 and 1902. No Black jockey has won it since. In 1904 he left to ride in Russia, and later he rode in France. On 21 January 1912 a Louisville newspaper, the *Courier-Journal*, printed the headline "Negro Jockeys Now Extinct."

Two economists, scholars who study money and business, Michael Leeds and Hugh Rockoff, studied why Black jockeys were driven out of American racing. They found that white jockeys attacked Black jockeys during races. The white riders boxed them in, ran them into the rail and hit them with their whips. Owners then stopped hiring Black jockeys, so that their horses would not be hurt. Henry King rode in the 1921 Kentucky Derby. No Black jockey rode in it again until 2000.

#### Jim Thorpe and his medals

Jim Thorpe was a Sac and Fox athlete, born in 1887 near Prague, in what is now Oklahoma. He played football at the Carlisle Indian Industrial School for the coach Glenn "Pop" Warner. At the 1912 Olympic Games in Stockholm, Sweden, he won the pentathlon, a contest of five track and field events, and the decathlon, a contest of ten. In the decathlon he beat the second-place man by 688 points.

In January 1913 Roy Johnson, a reporter for the *Worcester Telegram* in Massachusetts, reported that Thorpe had been paid to play minor-league baseball, in the lower leagues below the major leagues, in North Carolina in 1909 and 1910. Accounts of his pay run from $2 a game to $35 a week. Olympic athletes then had to be amateurs, people who were never paid to play a sport. Thorpe wrote to James E. Sullivan of the Amateur Athletic Union that he "was simply an Indian schoolboy and did not know all about such things." James Ring Adams wrote in the magazine of the National Museum of the American Indian that Warner and Moses Friedman, the head of the Carlisle school, may have written the letter for him.

Sullivan and the other officials of the Amateur Athletic Union took away Thorpe's amateur standing. The members of the International Olympic Committee struck out his wins. Their own rules allowed a complaint only within 30 days of the Games, and the newspaper report came about six months later. Warner took the medals from Thorpe's house and sent them back to Stockholm. Hugo Wieslander, who had come second in the decathlon, refused the gold medal.

Thorpe played major-league baseball for the New York Giants and other teams from 1913 to 1915 and from 1917 to 1919. He played pro football for the Canton Bulldogs for $250 a game. In 1920 he became the first president of the league that later took the name National Football League. In his last years he worked as a film extra, a laborer and a doorman. He died of heart failure in 1953, at 65.

In 1982 a researcher, Florence Ridlon, found the 30-day rule in the 1912 rule book. On 13 October 1982 the leaders of the International Olympic Committee named Thorpe a co-champion, sharing each title with the second-place man: Hugo Wieslander in the decathlon and Ferdinand Bie in the pentathlon. On 15 July 2022 they named him the only champion of both events.

#### Baseball and the Negro Leagues

The first modern World Series was played in October 1903. The Boston Americans beat the Pittsburgh Pirates 5 games to 3. The owners of the two teams, Henry Killilea of Boston and Barney Dreyfuss of Pittsburgh, arranged it. About 100,000 people watched the eight games. There was no series in 1904, because the owners of the New York Giants refused to play.

On 13 February 1920 Rube Foster, the owner and manager of the Chicago American Giants, met other owners of Black teams at a YMCA in Kansas City. Together they started the Negro National League. It had eight teams in its first year. The league closed in 1931, during the Great Depression, when millions of people lost their jobs. Teams in other Negro Leagues kept playing until 1948.

In December 2020 the leaders of Major League Baseball began counting seven Negro Leagues of 1920 to 1948 as major leagues. That added about 3,400 players to the major-league record. On 28 May 2024 they added the Negro League players' numbers to the official record books.

<a id="story-babe-ruth"></a>

#### Babe Ruth

> **Who:** A pitcher and home-run hitter for Boston and New York.
>
> **When and where:** Baltimore, Boston and New York, 1895 to 1948.

George Herman Ruth was born in Baltimore on 6 February 1895. On 13 June 1902, when he was seven, he entered St. Mary's Industrial School for Boys. It was a reform school, a school meant to correct boys' behavior, and an orphanage, a home for children without parents. The school's records called him "incorrigible," which means a child no one can control. He spent most of the next 12 years there. Jacques Kelly, a writer for the *Baltimore Sun*, wrote in 1995 that Ruth's parents decided to place him at the school. Writers have argued about their reasons for many years. A teacher there, Brother Matthias, taught him baseball.

He pitched for the Boston Red Sox from 1914 to 1919. The owner of the Boston team, Harry Frazee, sold him to the New York Yankees for $100,000. The sale was made in December 1919 and announced in January 1920.

Ruth hit 54 home runs in 1920 and 60 in 1927, and he finished his career with 714. In 1936 he was one of the first five players chosen for the Baseball Hall of Fame. Cancer in the back of his nose and throat killed him on 16 August 1948, at 53.

#### Movies, radio and comic books

Children in the 1920s and 1930s spent many of their free hours at the movies. In 1929 Walt Disney started Mickey Mouse Clubs that met at Saturday matinees, the afternoon showings. In a study printed in 2001, Richard Butsch gathered studies of movie audiences from the 1930s. In Muncie, Indiana, at least half of the children at Saturday matinees stayed five or six hours. In a working-class part of New Haven, Connecticut, more than half the children went twice a week or more. Researchers of the time found that children were choosing movies over outdoor games. A child in the Bronx, in New York City, said that when the film broke, the children booed, stamped their feet and often got into fist fights.

Adults worried about how watching movies affected children. In 1930 the mayor of Chelsea, Massachusetts, closed a theater because of how children in the audience behaved. From 1929 to 1933 researchers paid by the Payne Fund, a private group that gave money to good causes, carried out 13 studies of how watching movies changed children's behavior.

*Little Orphan Annie*, a radio show, began in Chicago in 1930 and was broadcast across the country from 6 April 1931. It had about 6 million listeners of all ages before it went off the air in 1942.

Superman first appeared in a comic book, *Action Comics* number 1, on 18 April 1938. A comic book cost 10 cents. In 1944 a survey for the publishers found that 95 of every 100 boys and 91 of every 100 girls aged 6 to 11 read comic books, about 12 a month. In 1940 Sterling North, a newspaper book editor in Chicago, called comic books "badly drawn, badly written and badly printed." He wrote that they strained children's eyes and nerves. Comic books were burned in the 1940s. The Comic Book Legal Defense Fund's history of these burnings does not name who burned them.

Lizzie Magie patented a board game called *The Landlord's Game* in 1904. Monopoly grew out of it, and Parker Brothers began selling Monopoly on 5 November 1935.

<a id="story-babe-didrikson-zaharias"></a>

#### Babe Didrikson Zaharias

> **Who:** A track star, basketball player and golfer who won Olympic gold and helped start women's professional golf.
>
> **When and where:** Texas, Los Angeles and golf courses in the United States and Britain, 1911 to 1956.

Mildred Didrikson was born in Port Arthur, Texas, on 26 June 1911, the sixth of seven children of Norwegian immigrants. She became known as Babe.

In 1930 managers at the Employers Casualty Insurance Company in Dallas hired her to do office work and to play on the company's women's basketball team, the Golden Cyclones. At the national track championships of 1932 she was the company's whole team. In three hours she won five events and tied for first in a sixth. She scored more points than any other team.

At the 1932 Olympic Games in Los Angeles she won the javelin and the 80-meter hurdles. In the high jump she won second place, because the officials ruled that going over the bar head first was a foul.

Later that year the Amateur Athletic Union's officials banned her from amateur sport, the contests for unpaid athletes, because her name appeared in an advertisement for a car. Her family needed money, so she played for pay. She toured with a men's traveling baseball team, the House of David.

She took up golf. In 1935 officials of the US Golf Association barred her from amateur golf after complaints from members of the Texas Women's Golf Association. She married the wrestler George Zaharias in 1938. She helped found the Ladies Professional Golf Association, in 1948 or 1950 by different accounts. She won the US Women's Open in 1948, 1950 and 1954. From 1950 she lived with the golfer Betty Dodd, and the two hid that they were a couple.

In April 1953 she had cancer of the bowel. Surgeons removed the cancer and gave her a colostomy. In that operation, surgeons bring the end of the large bowel out through an opening cut in the belly, so that body waste collects in a bag outside the body. Fourteen weeks later she was playing golf again, and in 1954 she won the US Women's Open. The cancer came back in 1955, and she died of it on 27 September 1956, at 45.

<a id="story-jesse-owens"></a>

#### Jesse Owens

> **Who:** A runner and jumper who won four gold medals at the Olympic Games in Nazi Germany.
>
> **When and where:** Alabama, Cleveland and Berlin, 1913 to 1980.
>
> **Movie:** *Race* (2016), a drama film about Owens.

James Cleveland Owens was born in Oakville, Alabama, on 12 September 1913, the son of a sharecropper, a farmer who paid his rent with part of his crop. His family moved to Cleveland, Ohio, when he was nine. A teacher heard his initials, "J.C.," as "Jesse."

On 25 May 1935, at a college track meet in Ann Arbor, Michigan, he set five world records and tied a sixth in about 45 minutes.

In August 1936 he won the 100 meters, the long jump, the 200 meters and the relay at the Olympic Games in Berlin. Adolf Hitler's Nazi government ruled Germany then. The Nazis taught that white people they called "Aryans" were a superior race.

Back home, Owens had to ride the freight elevator, the one used for goods, to reach a party in his honor at the Waldorf Astoria hotel in New York. Accounts do not name who sent him there. President Franklin Roosevelt never invited him to the White House. Owens said later, "Hitler didn't snub me. It was our president who snubbed me. The president didn't even send me a telegram."

When Owens refused to finish a tour of Europe, Avery Brundage and other officials of the Amateur Athletic Union barred him from amateur sport. He earned money by racing against horses. Later he went bankrupt, which means he could not pay his debts. He said, "I had four gold medals, but you can't eat four gold medals." In 1976 he received the Presidential Medal of Freedom. Lung cancer killed him in Tucson, Arizona, on 31 March 1980.

#### Who was kept out of the pools

From 1935 to 1943, jobless workers paid by a federal program, the Works Progress Administration, built about 6,000 athletic fields and playgrounds and 770 new swimming pools. Each year tens of millions of Americans swam in city pools.

Jeff Wiltse, who wrote a book about public pools called *Contested Waters*, studied who was allowed in. In the 1920s and 1930s, many cities in the North began letting men and women swim in the same public pools. Wiltse found that white officials and white swimmers in those cities then separated the pools by race. He wrote that "most northern whites did not want black men to have the opportunity to interact with white women" at the pools. Black children in those cities could not use the pools where other children learned to swim.

John O'Toole, the head of public welfare in St. Louis, opened the Fairground Park pool to Black swimmers on 21 June 1949. He said, "They are taxpayers and citizens, too." About 30 to 40 Black people came. Crowds of white young men gathered with baseball bats and bricks and beat Black people as they left the pool. The crowd grew to thousands. Twelve people were hurt, and police arrested seven, three white and four Black. The published accounts of the attack do not name the attackers. Afterward, so few people came to the pool that it lost money, and it was closed.

<a id="story-carl-stotz"></a>

#### Carl Stotz and the first Little League boys

> **Who:** A Williamsport man who organized baseball for his nephews and the neighborhood boys, and two of the boys who played.
>
> **When and where:** Williamsport, Pennsylvania, 1938 to 1955.

In the summer of 1938 Carl Stotz, 28, tried out rules and field sizes with his nephews, Jimmy and Major Gehron, and other boys from his neighborhood in Williamsport, Pennsylvania. He had no children of his own.

In 1939 Stotz, George Bebble and Bert Bebble each managed a team. Three local businesses paid $30 each for uniforms, and the teams took their names: Lycoming Dairy, Lundy Lumber and Jumbo Pretzel. Thirty boys played. The bases were 60 feet apart, and the pitcher threw from 40 feet. On 6 June 1939 Lundy Lumber beat Lycoming Dairy 23 to 8 on a vacant lot. It was the first Little League game.

Two boys on the Lycoming Dairy team were Bill Bair and Al "Sonny" Yearick. Yearick later became the first Little Leaguer to play baseball for pay, in the minor leagues. Both men died in January 2020. A volunteer remembered that they talked about Stotz and about how Little League had helped them stay out of trouble.

Only boys could play. Stotz said in 1973, "When we started the Little League, the idea of a girl playing baseball, even with other girls, was simply unthinkable." He left Little League's national company in November 1955 over "commercialization and central control," which meant that he objected to the league being run as a business from one head office.

#### Women's professional baseball, 1943 to 1954

From 1943 to 1954 more than 600 women played in the All-American Girls Professional Baseball League. Philip Wrigley, the owner of the Chicago Cubs, started it. The league's rules required players to wear skirts and lipstick and banned pants. During spring training they went to evening classes at a charm school, a school that taught manners and how to look and dress. No Black women were recruited or hired. The accounts of the league do not name who made that choice.

<a id="story-josh-gibson"></a>

#### Josh Gibson

> **Who:** A catcher and home-run hitter whom the white major-league owners never signed.
>
> **When and where:** Georgia and Pittsburgh, 1911 to 1947.
>
> **Movie:** *Soul of the Game* (1996), a television drama about several Negro Leagues players, with Mykelti Williamson as Gibson.

Josh Gibson was born in Buena Vista, Georgia, on 21 December 1911. In 1926 his family moved to Pittsburgh. There he worked in an air-brake factory and at a steel company.

On 25 July 1930 the catcher for the Homestead Grays, a Black team near Pittsburgh, was hurt in a game. The Grays' owner, Cum Posey, called Gibson, 18, out of the stands to catch. Gibson played for the Grays and for the Pittsburgh Crawfords. In 1937 the Crawfords' owner, Gus Greenlee, sold him back to the Grays for $2,500 and two players. People called him "the Black Babe Ruth."

The white owners of the major-league teams kept Black players out, so Gibson never played in their leagues. His plaque in the Baseball Hall of Fame states that he hit "almost 800" home runs. In 1943 doctors told him he had a brain tumor. He died in Pittsburgh on 20 January 1947, at 35, less than three months before Jackie Robinson played his first game for Brooklyn.

Since 2024 the major-league record books have included the Negro Leagues. A batting average shows how often a player got a hit: .466 means about 47 hits in every 100 times at bat. Gibson's .466 for 1943 is the highest for a single season in those records, and his career average of .372 is also the highest.

<a id="story-jackie-robinson"></a>

#### Jackie Robinson

> **Who:** The first Black player in the white major leagues since the 1880s.
>
> **When and where:** Georgia, California, Kansas City and Brooklyn, 1919 to 1972.
>
> **Movie:** *42* (2013), a drama film with Chadwick Boseman as Robinson. An earlier film, *The Jackie Robinson Story* (1950), starred Robinson as himself.

Jackie Robinson was born in Cairo, Georgia, on 31 January 1919, the youngest of five children of sharecroppers, farmers who paid their rent with part of their crop. His father left, and in 1920 the family moved to Pasadena, California. At the University of California, Los Angeles, he was the first athlete to earn varsity letters, awards for playing on the college's top teams, in four sports.

On 6 July 1944, as a soldier at Fort Hood, Texas, he refused to move to the back of an Army bus. Officers charged him with disobeying orders. A panel of nine white officers found him not guilty.

In 1945 he played for the Kansas City Monarchs of the Negro Leagues. On 28 August 1945 Branch Rickey, the head of the Brooklyn Dodgers, met him. Robinson asked, "Are you looking for a Negro who is afraid to fight back?" Rickey answered, "I need a Negro player with guts enough not to fight back." Rickey signed him for $600 a month. Robinson played the 1946 season for the Montreal Royals, a minor-league team.

He played his first game for Brooklyn on 15 April 1947, before 26,623 people. More than 14,000 of them were Black. During that first season, Ben Chapman, the manager of the Philadelphia team, told his players to "call Robinson everything and anything they wanted to." Chapman and his players shouted racial slurs, insulting names for Black people, at him. Chapman told him to "go back to the cotton fields." They kept it up until officials in the office of Happy Chandler, the commissioner who ran baseball, ordered them to stop.

Robinson got letters, signed by no one, telling him to leave baseball. Arthur Mann, who worked for Rickey, gave two of them to the police. A sportswriter, Stanley Woodward, reported that St. Louis players had threatened to strike rather than play against him. The St. Louis owners and managers denied it. The National League's president, Ford Frick, said he would suspend any player who went on strike. A St. Louis player, Enos Slaughter, cut Robinson's leg with the metal spikes on his shoe and left a seven-inch gash.

Robinson was named the first Rookie of the Year, the best first-year player, in 1947 and Most Valuable Player in 1949. He died on 24 October 1972, at 53. In 1997 officials of Major League Baseball retired his number, 42, for every team, so that new players could no longer be given it.

### 1950 to 2000

Between 1950 and 2000, the way children got to school and spent their afternoons changed. In 1969, 47.7 of every 100 American children in kindergarten through eighth grade usually walked or biked to school, and 12.2 were driven. A 1995 survey counted only how children got to school on one day, and on that day 44.9 of every 100 went by car. Diaries of how children spent their days in 1981 and 1997 showed more time in organized sports and lessons, and less time in free play and watching television. From 1972 children could also play video games for a quarter in arcades, and from 1977 on game machines at home.

Little League officials kept girls out from 1951 until 1974. After Title IX became law in 1972, the number of girls playing high-school sports rose from about 294,000 to about 2.7 million by 1999. Boxing officials took Muhammad Ali's title after he refused to be drafted in 1967. US Olympic officials suspended Tommie Smith and John Carlos and sent them out of the Olympic Village, where the athletes lived, after they protested on the medal stand in 1968. Two television networks, CBS and NBC, showed the first Super Bowl in 1967 to about 51 million viewers.

<a id="story-kathryn-johnston"></a>

#### Kathryn "Tubby" Johnston

> **Who:** A girl who played Little League baseball under a boy's name. Little League officials then banned girls.
>
> **When and where:** Corning, New York, 1950.

In the spring of 1950 Kathryn Johnston played baseball with boys on a sandlot near her home in Corning, New York. She wanted to play on a Little League team, and only boys could play on Little League teams.

She described what she did next: "I ran into my brother's room, got a pair of his slacks, put on a baseball cap and signed up as Tubby Johnston." She took the name Tubby from a comic strip, *Little Lulu*. She tucked her hair under her cap and went to the tryouts with her brother.

She made the King's Dairy team and played first base. Then she told the coach she was a girl. He said she was good enough to make the team, so she could stay. More people came to the games once word got out.

In 1951 Little League officials made a rule that no girls could play. Johnston said later, "It's known as the Tubby Rule because I was the reason why they put that rule in." In 1974, after the ban ended, she wrote to Little League's headquarters. The officials there checked her story and wrote back that she was the first girl to play in Little League.

#### Who could play Little League

Little League officials also stopped a team of Black boys from playing on for a title. In 1955 the Cannon Street YMCA in Charleston, South Carolina, entered its all-star team of 14 Black boys in the city Little League tournament. The adults who ran the 61 other teams, all of them white, pulled every team out rather than play them. Accounts do not name those adults. Cannon Street won the city and state titles because no one would play them.

At the regional tournament in Rome, Georgia, officials ruled that a team that had not won its games on the field could not go on. Little League's president agreed with the ruling. The managers of the white leagues left Little League and started their own league for white teams only. Little League officials invited the Cannon Street boys to watch the Little League World Series in Williamsport. The crowd there chanted "Let them play." One of the players, John Rivers, said in 2023, "So we didn't talk about it. So it tells me how painful it was."

In 1972 Maria Pepe, 12, pitched three games for a Little League team in Hoboken, New Jersey. Little League officials told the Hoboken league to drop her or lose its right to be part of Little League, and the Hoboken league's officials dropped her. Robert Stirrat, a Little League vice president, said, "as far as we're concerned, the incident is closed."

Members of the National Organization for Women, a women's rights group, took Pepe's case to New Jersey's civil rights office. In 1973 Sylvia Pressler, the officer hearing the case, ruled that keeping girls out broke the state's law. She wrote, "The institution of Little League is as American as the hot dog and apple pie. There is no reason why that part of Americana should be withheld from girls." Little League's officials asked a higher court to overturn the ruling, and they lost in 1974. Little League held a charter from Congress, a paper that gave it official standing. In December 1974 President Gerald Ford signed a law that changed the charter to let girls play. That year nearly 30,000 girls signed up for Little League's new softball program.

#### Who could swim

When Black Americans won the right to use city pools, some city officials closed the pools instead. In 1963 officials in Jackson, Mississippi, closed four public pools rather than let Black residents swim in them. They gave up a fifth pool, and the YMCA then ran it for white people only. On 14 June 1971, in *Palmer v. Thompson*, five Supreme Court justices, the judges of the nation's highest court, ruled that closing the pools to everyone was lawful. Four justices disagreed.

On 18 June 1964 Black and white protesters jumped into the pool of the Monson Motor Lodge in St. Augustine, Florida. The motel's manager, James Brock, poured muriatic acid, a strong acid used to clean pools, into the water. A photograph of him doing it ran in newspapers across the country.

Jeff Wiltse, who wrote a book about the history of public pools, found that when Black swimmers won equal use of city pools, white swimmers "generally abandoned them for private pools," which means most of them left. He wrote that city officials then treated public pools as less important.

#### Television and the Super Bowl

The Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10 in Los Angeles on 15 January 1967. It was the first championship game between the two professional football leagues of the time. Tickets cost $6 to $12. Two television networks, CBS and NBC, both showed the game, to about 51 million viewers. A 30-second advertisement cost $42,000.

From the third game, in 1969, the official name was the Super Bowl. Lamar Hunt, who founded one of the two leagues, took the name from his children's toy, a Super Ball.

In November 1990 Arizona's voters refused to make Martin Luther King Jr.'s birthday a state holiday. NFL officials then moved the 1993 Super Bowl from Tempe, Arizona, to Pasadena, California. Arizona hosted the Super Bowl in 1996.

<a id="story-muhammad-ali"></a>

#### Muhammad Ali

> **Who:** The heavyweight boxing champion whose title was taken from him when he refused to be drafted into the Army.
>
> **When and where:** Louisville, Rome, Houston, Atlanta and Zaire, 1942 to 2016.

Cassius Clay was born in Louisville, Kentucky, on 17 January 1942. When he was 12, someone stole his bicycle. A police officer, Joe Martin, taught boxing, and he got Clay started in the sport.

Clay won an Olympic gold medal in Rome in 1960. On 25 February 1964, at 22, he beat Sonny Liston for the heavyweight title. He then joined the Nation of Islam, a Black Muslim religious group, and took the name Muhammad Ali.

On 28 April 1967, during the Vietnam War, Ali went to Houston to be drafted, which means ordered by law to join the Army. He had already said, "I ain't got no quarrel with them Viet Cong," the fighters the US Army was fighting in Vietnam. He refused three times to step forward when his name was called. That same day the members of the New York State Athletic Commission suspended his boxing license, and officials of the World Boxing Association took away his title. Officials of other boxing commissions did the same. On 20 June 1967, in a federal court in Houston, a jury of six white men and six white women found him guilty of draft evasion, which means refusing to serve when drafted. The judge sentenced him to five years in prison and a $10,000 fine.

He could not box for more than three years. He fought again on 26 October 1970, in Atlanta. On 28 June 1971 all eight Supreme Court justices who heard his appeal overturned his conviction. On 30 October 1974 he beat George Foreman in Zaire, in Africa, and won the title back.

Ali retired in 1981. In 1984 he said he had Parkinson's syndrome, a disease of the brain that makes the body shake and move slowly. He died on 3 June 2016.

#### The 1968 Olympic protest

Tommie Smith won the 200 meters at the Olympic Games in Mexico City on 16 October 1968, in a world-record 19.83 seconds. John Carlos came third. Peter Norman of Australia came second. During the US national anthem, Smith and Carlos each raised a fist in a black glove. They stood in black socks without shoes to stand for poor people. All three men wore the badge of a protest group, the Olympic Project for Human Rights.

Smith said they were protesting "the lack of black assistant coaches," the taking of Muhammad Ali's title, and the "lack of access to good housing."

Avery Brundage, the head of the International Olympic Committee, called the protest "a domestic political statement unfit for the apolitical, international forum." He meant that the protest was about politics inside the United States, and that the Olympic Games were a world meeting place that should be kept free of politics. The US Olympic Committee's officials refused at first to suspend the two men. Brundage then threatened to ban the whole US track team. The US officials suspended Smith and Carlos and sent them out of the Olympic Village. The sports commentator Brent Musburger called them "black-skinned storm troopers." Storm troopers were the street fighters of Hitler's Nazi party. Smith, Carlos and their families got death threats.

Both men later played pro football. Smith coached track at Oberlin College and taught at Santa Monica College. Norman was left off Australia's 1972 Olympic team, although his times qualified him. Accounts differ on why. Lawmakers in Australia's parliament apologized to him in 2012, six years after he died. Smith and Carlos carried his coffin at his funeral.

#### Players and owners

In December 1969 Curt Flood, a St. Louis Cardinals outfielder, refused to be traded to another team. A television reporter, Howard Cosell, said to him, "You're a man who makes $90,000 a year, which isn't exactly slave wages." Flood answered, "A well-paid slave is nonetheless a slave." He sued baseball's commissioner. On 19 June 1972 five Supreme Court justices ruled against him and three sided with him.

About three years later, in 1975, an arbitrator named Peter Seitz ruled in a case brought by two pitchers, Andy Messersmith and Dave McNally. An arbitrator is a person both sides agree will settle a dispute. Seitz ruled that a team could renew a player's contract without his permission for only one season. After that the player was a free agent, free to sign with any team.

#### Girls' sports after Title IX

President Richard Nixon signed Title IX into law on 23 June 1972. Under it, no school or college program that gets money from the federal government may shut a person out because of sex. In the 1971-72 school year 294,015 girls and 3,666,917 boys played high-school sports. Girls were about 7 of every 100 players. By 1977-78 about 2.1 million girls played. In 1999-2000, 2,675,874 girls and 3,861,749 boys played, and girls were about 41 of every 100, according to counts by the National Federation of State High School Associations.

In 1979 Yale University had 13 women's varsity teams, the college's top teams. Writers for Yale's library later stated in an online exhibit that those teams got "only a grudging fraction of the resources" given to the men's teams.

<a id="story-chris-ernst"></a>

#### Chris Ernst

> **Who:** The captain of Yale's women's rowing team, who led a protest that won the team a locker room.
>
> **When and where:** Yale University, New Haven, Connecticut, 1972 to 1977.
>
> **Movie:** *A Hero for Daisy* (1999), a documentary about Ernst by Mary Mazzio.

Chris Ernst grew up in Scituate, Massachusetts. In high school she beat boys at arm wrestling to win time on the gymnastics equipment.

She began rowing at Yale in her second year and was captain of the women's team by her last year. The showers at the boathouse were for the men's team only. After practice, the women waited on a bus in wet clothes while the men showered. Then they rode back to campus to wash.

In early 1976 the 19 women on the team wrote "Title IX" on their bodies and went into the office of Joni Barnett, Yale's director of women's sports. They took off their clothes, and Ernst read a statement that began, "These are the bodies Yale is exploiting." To exploit someone means to use them for your own gain.

A *New York Times* reporter called the university that day. Yale officials set up a trailer with running water and planned a $250,000 addition to the boathouse. By 1977 the women had a locker room.

Ernst was a backup rower for the 1976 Olympic team, the first Olympic Games with women's rowing. In 1980 she became the first woman in the plumbers' union in New Haven. In 1986 she won a world rowing title.

<a id="story-billie-jean-king"></a>

#### Billie Jean King

> **Who:** A tennis champion who started the Women's Tennis Association and beat Bobby Riggs in a match called the "Battle of the Sexes."
>
> **When and where:** Long Beach, California, and Houston, Texas, 1943 to 1973 and after.

Billie Jean King was born in Long Beach, California, on 22 November 1943. At 11 she switched from softball to tennis after her parents suggested a more "ladylike" sport. She saved $8 to buy her first racket and took free lessons on the city's public courts. As a young player she was kept out of a group photograph because she wore shorts her mother had sewn instead of a tennis dress. The account does not name who left her out.

In June 1973 she founded the Women's Tennis Association, a group that represents women players. On 20 September 1973 she beat Bobby Riggs, who was 55, 6-4, 6-3, 6-3, at the Houston Astrodome, in a match people called the "Battle of the Sexes." About 30,000 people watched in the stadium and about 50 million on television in the United States. She won $100,000.

King won 39 Grand Slam titles, the four biggest tennis championships. In 2009 she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

#### Arcades and game machines at home

Some computer games were made for school. In 1971 three student teachers from Carleton College, Don Rawitsch, Bill Heinemann and Paul Dillenberger, made *The Oregon Trail* for a junior high class in Minneapolis. It was first played on 3 December 1971. A Minnesota computer group for schools put out new versions in 1975 and 1985, and Oregon Trail games have sold more than 65 million copies.

In August 1972 Nolan Bushnell and Allan Alcorn of the company Atari put a test machine of their game *Pong* in a bar called Andy Capp's Tavern in Sunnyvale, California. *Pong* was a simple tennis game played on a screen. The bar's owner soon called them because the machine had stopped working. Its coin box was jammed full of quarters. Atari sold *Pong* from 29 November 1972, at 25 cents a game, and sold more than 8,000 machines by the end of 1974. Bushnell said players sat "shoulder to shoulder" and could talk, laugh and challenge each other.

Sears sold a home version of *Pong* for $98.95 at Christmas 1975. Atari's home game machine came out in 1977 for $199, and that one machine sold about 30 million by 1992. In October 1980 the company Midway began selling the arcade game *Pac-Man* in North America. Its designer, Toru Iwatani, wanted "a nonviolent, cheerful game" that women would play. By 1981 *Pac-Man* machines had taken in more than $1 billion in quarters.

By 1982 there were about 30 million game machines of all makes in American homes, and about 35 million households had children aged 6 to 16. Then sales fell, from about $3.2 billion in 1983 to about $100 million in 1985. In September 1983 workers for Atari buried about 728,000 unsold game cartridges in a landfill at Alamogordo, New Mexico. Sales rose again after Nintendo began selling its home machine in the United States in 1985. Nintendo's Game Boy, a game machine small enough to hold in the hands, came out in 1989 for $89.95.

In December 1993 and March 1994 Senators Joe Lieberman and Herb Kohl led public hearings, meetings where senators question witnesses, on violent video games such as *Mortal Kombat*. Leaders of the game companies then set up the Entertainment Software Rating Board. From 13 September 1994 its staff put age ratings on games.

#### The Miracle on Ice

The US Olympic hockey team beat the Soviet Union 4 to 3 at Lake Placid, New York, on 22 February 1980. The American players were college players with an average age of 21, coached by Herb Brooks. Two days later they beat Finland and won the gold medal.

#### The Iroquois Nationals

In 1983 Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) people formed their own national lacrosse team, and the Grand Council of the Haudenosaunee approved it. Officials of the International Lacrosse Federation turned the team down for 1986 and accepted it as a member nation in 1988. In 1990 the team played in the world championship in Perth, Australia, and finished fifth of five.

#### What a child's afternoon looked like

In 1969, 47.7 of every 100 children in kindergarten through eighth grade usually walked or biked to school, 12.2 were driven and 38.3 rode the school bus. A national survey in 1995 used a different measure: how children got to school on the survey day. On that day 44.9 of every 100 went by car, and about 14 walked or biked. Noreen McDonald and other researchers took these figures from national surveys of how Americans travel, in a study of 2011.

The researchers Sandra Hofferth and John Sandberg compared diaries of how children spent their time in 1981 and in 1997. Children spent more time in school, day care, sports and art lessons. They spent less time in free play, housework and watching television. The drop in free play showed up among children whose mothers stayed home as well as those whose mothers had jobs.

More mothers did work for pay. In 1975, 47 of every 100 mothers with children under 18 were working or looking for work. By 2000 it was 73 of every 100, according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics.

In the fall of 1995 about 6.9 million children aged 5 to 14, or 18 of every 100, regularly looked after themselves for part of the week. On average they did so for about six hours a week. About 15 million children that age took part in sports, lessons or clubs, according to the US Census Bureau.

Organized sport also became more private. In a survey of adults published in 2025, about 4 of every 100 who were born in the 1950s said they had played on a private club or travel team as children. For those born in the 1990s it was 13 of every 100. The researchers, Chris Knoester and Chris Bjork, found that children whose parents had more schooling were more likely to play on these teams.

### 2000 to Today

Since 2000, much of children's free time has moved onto phones and into games played online, often with strangers. Researchers at the Pew Research Center, which surveys American teenagers, found that 73 of every 100 teenagers aged 13 to 17 had or could use a smartphone in 2014-15. By 2022 it was 95 of every 100. Fewer children walked to school or played outdoors. In 2022 the average sports family spent $883 a year on one child's main sport. Researchers disagree about whether screens harm children's attention and mood.

In sport, doctors found a brain disease in dead football players. A team doctor who had sexually abused more than 500 girls and women pleaded guilty, and judges gave him prison sentences so long that he will die in prison. College athletes won the right to be paid, betting on games became legal in most states, and the men's soccer World Cup was played in the United States, Canada and Mexico in 2026.

#### Phones and social media

Researchers at the Pew Research Center ask American teenagers aged 13 to 17 how they use phones and the internet. In 2014-15, 24 of every 100 said they were online "almost constantly." In 2022 it was 46 of every 100, and in 2025 it was 40. In Pew's 2025 survey, about 90 of every 100 teenagers used YouTube, and about 60 used TikTok. That year 64 of every 100 teenagers had used an AI chatbot, a computer program that writes answers in plain language.

Common Sense Media, a group that studies children and media, surveyed children in 2021. Children aged 8 to 12 spent an average of 5 hours 33 minutes a day on screens for fun, not counting schoolwork. Teenagers aged 13 to 18 spent 8 hours 39 minutes. In 2019 the figures had been 4 hours 44 minutes and 7 hours 22 minutes. When a child used two screens at once, the researchers counted the time on both, so two hours of screen time can fit into one hour of the day. Its authors wrote that they could not tell how much of the rise came from the COVID-19 pandemic.

On 23 May 2023 the US Surgeon General, Vivek Murthy, the country's top public health doctor, issued an advisory, a public warning, about social media. The advisory states that "we do not yet have enough evidence to determine if social media is sufficiently safe for children and adolescents." It cites a study of 6,595 American children aged 12 to 15. Those who spent more than 3 hours a day on social media had double the risk of symptoms of depression and anxiety. In the advisory, Murthy asked lawmakers to set safety rules and limits for children's use.

State lawmakers began to keep phones out of classrooms. In 2023 Florida's lawmakers passed a law banning students' phone use during class time. By January 2026, lawmakers in 26 states had banned phones for the whole school day, from the first bell to the last, according to a count by the group Ballotpedia. By July 2026, lawmakers in at least 39 states and Washington, DC, had passed rules requiring schools to ban or limit phones, according to a tally by *Education Week*. The two counts differ because they count different kinds of laws.

#### Games played online, and with strangers

*Minecraft* is a game of building and digging in a world of blocks, played alone or with others. It came out in 2011. By 2023 it had sold more than 300 million copies, more than any other video game. *Roblox* opened in 2006. Its players build games and play each other's games. According to the company, half of all American children under 16 play it each month. *Fortnite* came out in 2017. In its best-known version, up to 100 players land on an island and fight until one player or team is left.

*Fortnite* is free to play. The companies behind *Fortnite* and *Roblox* sell game money, called V-Bucks in *Fortnite* and Robux in *Roblox*, which players buy with real money and spend on costumes and other items inside the game.

On 19 December 2022 officials of the Federal Trade Commission, the government agency that enforces laws protecting buyers, accused Epic Games, the maker of *Fortnite*, of breaking the law. They said the company had collected information on children under 13 without their parents' permission. They said the game's settings turned on live voice and text chat for children, and that the company matched "children and teens with strangers to play Fortnite together." Children had been "bullied, threatened, harassed," some of them sexually, and "exposed to dangerous and psychologically traumatizing issues such as suicide." Epic employees had urged the company to change those settings as early as 2017. In a settlement, an agreement that ended the case, Epic Games agreed to pay $520 million.

In June 2025 four lawsuits were filed against the company that runs *Roblox*. The people who brought them accused the company of letting adults use the game for the sexual exploitation of children, which means using children for sex acts or sexual pictures. From January 2026 every *Roblox* player had to prove their age, with an ID or a video scan of the face, before chatting. Chat was also limited to players of similar ages.

Esports are video game contests played for prize money. The first *Fortnite* World Cup, held from 26 to 28 July 2019 in New York City, paid $30 million in prizes. About 40 million players tried to qualify.

<a id="story-kyle-giersdorf"></a>

#### Kyle "Bugha" Giersdorf

> **Who:** A 16-year-old who won the first Fortnite World Cup and $3 million.
>
> **When and where:** Arthur Ashe Stadium, New York City, 28 July 2019.

Kyle Giersdorf was born on 30 December 2002. His father, who also played video games, got him started on *Fortnite*. Kyle played under the name "Bugha."

On 25 March 2019 he joined an esports team called Sentinels. That summer he qualified for the first *Fortnite* World Cup, out of about 40 million players who tried.

On 28 July 2019, at 16, he played six games against 99 other finalists in Arthur Ashe Stadium in New York City. He scored 59 points, and the second-place player scored 33. He won $3 million, more than any other *Fortnite* player has won in total. Hours after he won, someone broke into his Twitter account and his account on Twitch, a website where players show their games live to viewers.

Later he became a streamer on Twitch, playing his games live for viewers there.

#### What is measured

Fewer children walk or bike to school. In 1969, 47.7 of every 100 children in kindergarten through eighth grade usually did. In 2009 it was 12.7 of every 100, according to national travel surveys studied by Noreen McDonald and other researchers. In 2017, among students aged 5 to 17, 9.6 of every 100 usually walked and 1.1 biked, according to a later government travel survey.

Children also had less free time. Sandra Hofferth, a researcher, compared diaries of how children aged 6 to 12 spent their days. Their free time fell from about 57 hours a week in 1981 to about 48 hours in 2003. From 1997 to 2003 the share who played a sport on the diary days fell from 76 to 60 of every 100. The share who spent time in outdoor activities fell from 16 to 10 of every 100. Hofferth's diaries end in 2003.

The National Survey of Children's Health is a government survey of parents. In 2023 it found that 55 of every 100 children aged 6 to 17 played on a sports team or took sports lessons. Children from richer homes played more. In 2012, 35.5 of every 100 children in homes earning under $25,000 a year played a sport regularly, against 49.1 of every 100 in homes earning $100,000 or more. By 2024 the gap between those two groups had grown to 20.2 points, according to the Sports and Fitness Industry Association.

Organized sport costs money. In a 2022 survey by the Aspen Institute and Utah State University, the average parent spent $883 in a year on one child's main sport. Soccer averaged $1,188 and basketball $1,002. Travel to games and tournaments cost more than any other part. The richest families spent about four times as much as the poorest.

In 2012, 15 of the 50 states had rules that recommended or required a daily recess, according to a 2013 report by the research group Bridging the Gap.

Doctors measure obesity by comparing a child's weight with the child's height. From 1971 to 1974, 5.2 of every 100 children aged 2 to 19 had obesity. From 2017 to March 2020 it was 19.7 of every 100, about 14.7 million children, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In the poorest homes it was 25.8 of every 100, and in the richest homes 11.5.

#### What researchers disagree about

ADHD stands for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder. Doctors diagnose it when a child has trouble paying attention, or is overactive and acts without thinking, badly enough to cause problems in more than one place, such as at home and at school. In national surveys of parents, 9.5 of every 100 children aged 4 to 17 had been diagnosed with ADHD in 2007, and 11 of every 100 in 2011, a rise of 42 percent since 2003. In 2022, 11.4 of every 100 children aged 3 to 17 had been diagnosed, about 7.1 million children, according to a 2024 study by M. L. Danielson and other researchers.

In 2013 the American Psychiatric Association changed its rules for diagnosing ADHD. Its manual of mental disorders now allowed a diagnosis when symptoms began by age 12 instead of age 7. The researchers who counted the diagnoses wrote that the rise "could also reflect better detection" and more awareness, not only more children with ADHD. They also wrote that the survey changed its methods in 2022, which makes it harder to compare 2022 with earlier years.

Researchers have studied whether screens are linked to attention problems. In 2018 a team at the University of Southern California, led by Chaelin Ra and Adam Leventhal, followed 2,587 high-school students in Los Angeles County for two years. None had serious ADHD symptoms at the start. Students who used more kinds of digital media many times a day later reported more ADHD symptoms. Among students who used no kind of media that often, 4.6 of every 100 reported the symptoms. Among students who used seven kinds, 9.5 of every 100 did. The researchers called the link "modest." They wrote that more research was needed "to determine whether this association is causal," which means whether the media use caused the symptoms. The students rated their own symptoms, and doctors did not diagnose them.

Other researchers studied something different: how well teenagers felt. In 2019 the Oxford researchers Orben and Przybylski studied surveys of 355,358 teenagers in the United States and Britain. They found that technology use explained "at most 0.4%" of the differences in how well teenagers felt. That is less than half of one percent. They called the link "too small to warrant policy change," meaning too small to be a reason for new laws or rules.

In 2024 the psychologist Jonathan Haidt of New York University published a book called *The Anxious Generation*. He wrote that phone and social media companies had "rewired childhood" by taking the place of play and time with friends. The psychologist Candice Odgers of the University of California, Irvine, answered in the science journal *Nature* on 29 March 2024. She wrote that the book's "repeated suggestion that digital technologies are rewiring our children's brains and causing an epidemic of mental illness is not supported by science." She wrote that studies had found "a mix of no, small and mixed associations." She agreed that the social media companies needed to make large changes.

#### Football and the brain

Mike Webster was a center for the Pittsburgh Steelers who played 17 seasons in the NFL, from 1974 to 1990, and won four Super Bowls. After he retired he lost his memory, suffered from depression and pain, and at times lived in his pickup truck or in train stations. He died of a heart attack on 24 September 2002, at 50.

Bennet Omalu, a doctor in Pittsburgh who examines bodies to find out why people died, studied Webster's brain. He found clumps of protein unlike those of Alzheimer's disease. In July 2005 Omalu and other doctors described the disease in a medical journal. It is called chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE. Doctors link it to repeated blows to the head. Its signs can include problems with behavior, mood and thinking. It often gets worse over time, and it can lead to dementia, the loss of the ability to think and remember. Doctors can find it only by examining the brain after death.

The NFL's own brain injury committee had been set up in 1994 by the league's commissioner, Paul Tagliabue. He named Elliot Pellman to lead it, a doctor who treated joints and muscles, not the brain. From 2003 the committee's papers stated that concussions, brain injuries from a hard blow to the head, caused no lasting harm in NFL players. In May 2006 committee members wrote to the journal asking it to take back Omalu's paper. Years later Jeff Miller, a league official, told members of Congress that "there is a link between football-related head trauma and chronic traumatic encephalopathy."

More than 4,500 former players sued the NFL, saying the league had hidden the dangers. In April 2015 Judge Anita Brody approved a settlement to pay retired players with brain illness for 65 years, expected to cost more than $1 billion. Families of players who died before 2006 were not covered, so Webster's family got nothing from it. The NFL's own Retirement Board had already paid his family $1.8 million in 2005, after finding that football caused his brain injuries. Until 2021 the dementia tests used to judge claims were scored as if Black players started with lower thinking skills than other players. That made it harder for Black players to prove dementia and be paid. The news accounts of the lawsuit do not name who set that scoring rule. After a lawsuit, NFL officials said in June 2021 that they would stop.

Children were hurt in football too. About 23,000 football brain injuries a year that did not kill the player sent people to emergency rooms, and 90 of every 100 of those hurt were aged 5 to 18. Pop Warner, a youth football program, had 9.5 percent fewer players in 2012 than in 2010, according to Robert Boland of New York University.

By 2023 researchers at Boston University had found CTE in the brains of 345 of the 376 former NFL players they studied. They warned that families who suspected the disease were the ones who gave the brains. So the figure does not mean that 92 of every 100 NFL players have CTE.

#### The team doctor who abused gymnasts

Larry Nassar worked with the USA Gymnastics national team from 1986. From 1996 to 2014 he was its national medical coordinator, the doctor in charge of the gymnasts' care. From 1997 to 2016 he was also a doctor for athletes at Michigan State University. During appointments he said were treatment for pain, he put his ungloved finger into girls' vaginas. Sometimes a parent was in the room and could not see what he was doing. More than 500 girls and women were abused. Some were as young as 6.

Many adults were told and did not stop him. Athletes said they told Michigan State employees about him as early as 1997.
